citations.quote:
Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$. A point multiset is a finite ordered list $P=(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})$ with $N\ge1$ and $x_i=(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{id})\in[0,1)^d$; repeated points are counted with their multiplicities. For $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_d)\in[0,1]^d$, its anchored half-open box and its volume are
$$B(u):=\prod_{j=1}^d[0,u_j),\qquad \operatorname{vol}(B(u)):=\prod_{j=1}^d u_j.$$
The **star discrepancy** of $P$ is
$$D_N^*(P):=\sup_{u\in[0,1]^d}\left|\frac1N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\mathbf 1_{B(u)}(x_i)-\prod_{j=1}^d u_j\right|.$$
An infinite sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ in $[0,1)^d$ is **uniformly distributed** if $D_N^*(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})\to0$ as $N\to\infty$.
For a bounded Riemann-integrable $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$, the **cube integral** and the point-set **cube quadrature** are
$$I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f(x)\,dx,\qquad Q_P(f):=\frac1N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}f(x_i),$$
where $I_d$ is the Riemann integral of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]. No randomness is part of $Q_P$.

Let $b\ge2$ be an integer. A **base-$b$ elementary interval** in dimension $d$ is
$$E=\prod_{j=1}^d[a_jb^{-k_j},(a_j+1)b^{-k_j}),$$
where each $k_j\ge0$ and each $a_j$ is an integer with $0\le a_j<b^{k_j}$. For integers $m\ge0$ and $0\le t\le m$, a point multiset $P$ is a **$(t,m,d)$-net in base $b$** if it has $b^m$ entries and every base-$b$ elementary interval with $\sum_{j=1}^d k_j=m-t$ contains exactly $b^t$ entries, counted with multiplicity. A sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ in $[0,1)^d$ is a **$(t,d)$-sequence in base $b$** if for every $m\ge t$ and $k\ge0$, the aligned block $(x_{kb^m},\ldots,x_{(k+1)b^m-1})$ is a $(t,m,d)$-net.

For a prime integer $p$, we have $p\ge2$ ([[def-prime]]). Write $\mathbb F_p:=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$, which is a field by [[thm-z-mod-p-is-a-field]]. By [[thm-division-algorithm-in-z]], each residue class has exactly one representative in $\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$, and every $n\in\{0,\ldots,p^m-1\}$ has a unique base-$p$ expansion $n=\sum_{r=1}^m n_{r-1}p^{r-1}$ with digits $n_{r-1}\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$. The integer powers use [[def-integer-power]]. A **digital point set** in base $p$ is generated from matrices $C_1,\ldots,C_d\in\mathbb F_p^{m\times m}$ as follows. For each such $n$, let $v(n)=(n_0,\ldots,n_{m-1})^T\in\mathbb F_p^m$, interpreting each digit as its residue class, and compute $y^{(j)}=C_jv(n)$ in $\mathbb F_p^m$. Taking the unique representatives $y^{(j)}_r\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$, set
$$x_{n,j}:=\sum_{r=1}^m y^{(j)}_r p^{-r}.$$
Since $0\le y^{(j)}_r\le p-1$, the finite geometric sum gives $0\le x_{n,j}\le\sum_{r=1}^m(p-1)p^{-r}=1-p^{-m}<1$; the identity follows by telescoping with the integer-power laws [[lem-power-laws]], and $p^{-m}>0$ by [[lem-power-monotone]] and [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]. It is a **digital $(t,m,d)$-net** only if this generated point multiset also satisfies the stated $(t,m,d)$-net counting condition; arbitrary generator matrices need not do so.

A **digital sequence** is generated by infinite matrices $C_j=(c^{(j)}_{r,k})_{r,k\ge1}$ over $\mathbb F_p$. For each $n\ge0$, pad its finite base-$p$ expansion with zero digits and, for every $r,j$, compute the finite field sum $y_{r,j}(n)=\sum_{k\ge1}c^{(j)}_{r,k}n_{k-1}$; only finitely many summands are nonzero. Let $\widetilde y_{r,j}(n)\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$ be its unique integer representative. The output coordinate is the real series
$$x_{n,j}:=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\widetilde y_{r,j}(n)p^{-r}.$$
This series is defined by [[def-series]] and converges: its terms satisfy $0\le\widetilde y_{r,j}(n)p^{-r}\le(p-1)p^{-r}$; since $p\ge2$, [[lem-of-inverse-positive]] gives $p^{-1}\in(0,1)$, and the bounding geometric series $\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(p-1)p^{-r}$ converges to $1$ by [[thm-geometric-series]]. The comparison theorem [[thm-direct-comparison-test]] therefore gives convergence of the output series. Its sum lies in $[0,1]$; the resulting points are required to lie in $[0,1)^d$. It is a digital $(t,d)$-sequence when it also satisfies the aligned-block net condition above. No discrepancy rate follows from these definitions alone.

derivations.claim: For $u\in[0,1]^d$, the point $x$ lies in $\prod_{j=1}^d[0,u_j)$ exactly when $u_j>1/2$ for every $j$, because the box is half-open. The point count is therefore one if all these inequalities hold and zero otherwise.
If some $u_j\le1/2$, the count is zero, so the discrepancy is $\prod_j u_j\le u_j\le1/2$. Since $d\ge2$, $1-2^{-d}\ge3/4>1/2$, so this case contributes less than $1-2^{-d}$.
If every $u_j>1/2$, the count is one and the discrepancy is $1-\prod_j u_j$. The product exceeds $2^{-d}$, so this value is less than $1-2^{-d}$.

For each integer $k\ge3$, the box endpoint $u^{(k)}=(1/2+1/k,\ldots,1/2+1/k)$ lies in $[0,1]^d$ and has discrepancy $1-(1/2+1/k)^d\to1-2^{-d}$. Thus the supremum is at least $1-2^{-d}$, while steps 2.1–2.2 bound every box error above by this value; hence $D_1^*(P)=1-2^{-d}$. Substitution gives $D_1^*(P)=3/4$ for $d=2$ and $7/8$ for $d=3$.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An admitted domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain (its boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function, with $\Omega$ on one side) with fixed $r_0>0$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$ such that for every $x\in\overline\Omega$ there is an orthogonal map $Q_x$ for which
$$x+Q_x\{z\in\mathbb R^d:0<|z|<r_0,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}\subset\Omega.$$
An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. For a finite ordered list of distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, its Gram matrix is $K_X=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$. The kernel is **strictly positive definite** if $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every such $X$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$; the nonstrict positive-semidefinite condition replaces $>$ by $\ge$. Only strict positivity is used for the ordinary interpolation solve below.

For an integer $m\ge1$, let $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$ be the real polynomials of total degree at most $m-1$, with an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$, where $J=\dim\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. The evaluation matrix on $X$ is $P_X=(p_j(x_i))_{i,j}$. The sites are **$m$-unisolvent** for this polynomial space when $P_X$ has linearly independent columns. A kernel is **strictly conditionally positive definite of order $m$** when, for every finite distinct $X$ and this evaluation matrix, $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$ satisfying $P_X^{\mathsf T}c=0$. Thus strict conditional positivity is a strict inequality on the moment-null subspace; it is stronger than the corresponding nonstrict inequality.

For data $y\in\mathbb R^N$, the strictly positive definite interpolation system is $K_Xa=y$. For an order-$m$ strictly conditionally positive definite kernel and $m$-unisolvent sites, the polynomially augmented interpolation system is
$$\begin{bmatrix}K_X&P_X\\P_X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$
Whenever the relevant system has a unique solution, its kernel-plus-polynomial function $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iK(x,x_i)+\sum_j b_jp_j(x)$ is called the interpolant. Invertibility for the stated strict hypotheses is supplied by [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]].

For a finite nonempty site set $X\subset\Omega$, the **fill distance** is $h_X=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{x_i\in X}|x-x_i|$. If $N\ge2$, the **separation radius** and **mesh ratio** are $q_X=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}|x_i-x_j|$ and $\rho_X=h_X/q_X$, respectively. These are exact geometric quantities, independent of any floating-point solver.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An admitted domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain (its boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function, with $\Omega$ on one side) with fixed $r_0>0$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$ such that for every $x\in\overline\Omega$ there is an orthogonal map $Q_x$ for which
$$x+Q_x\{z\in\mathbb R^d:0<|z|<r_0,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}\subset\Omega.$$
An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. For a finite ordered list of distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, its Gram matrix is $K_X=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$. The kernel is **strictly positive definite** if $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every such $X$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$; the nonstrict positive-semidefinite condition replaces $>$ by $\ge$. Only strict positivity is used for the ordinary interpolation solve below.

For an integer $m\ge1$, let $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$ be the real polynomials of total degree at most $m-1$, with an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$, where $J=\dim\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. The evaluation matrix on $X$ is $P_X=(p_j(x_i))_{i,j}$. The sites are **$m$-unisolvent** for this polynomial space when $P_X$ has linearly independent columns. A kernel is **strictly conditionally positive definite of order $m$** when, for every finite distinct $X$ and this evaluation matrix, $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$ satisfying $P_X^{\mathsf T}c=0$. Thus strict conditional positivity is a strict inequality on the moment-null subspace; it is stronger than the corresponding nonstrict inequality.

For data $y\in\mathbb R^N$, the strictly positive definite interpolation system is $K_Xa=y$. For an order-$m$ strictly conditionally positive definite kernel and $m$-unisolvent sites, the polynomially augmented interpolation system is
$$\begin{bmatrix}K_X&P_X\\P_X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$
Whenever the relevant system has a unique solution, its kernel-plus-polynomial function $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iK(x,x_i)+\sum_j b_jp_j(x)$ is called the interpolant. Invertibility for the stated strict hypotheses is supplied by [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]].

For a finite nonempty site set $X\subset\Omega$, the **fill distance** is $h_X=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{x_i\in X}|x-x_i|$. If $N\ge2$, the **separation radius** and **mesh ratio** are $q_X=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}|x_i-x_j|$ and $\rho_X=h_X/q_X$, respectively. These are exact geometric quantities, independent of any floating-point solver.

definition_support.quote:
Let $p\ge0$ be an integer, let $Y=(y_1,\ldots,y_N)$ be distinct and $(p+1)$-unisolvent for $\Pi_p(\mathbb R^d)$, and let $K$ be a real strictly conditionally positive-definite kernel of order $p+1$. Fix a center $x$, an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$ of $\Pi_p$, and a homogeneous constant-coefficient differential functional $L$ of order $t\le p$ for which all section derivatives in [[alg-augmented-rbf-finite-difference-weights]] exist. Let $(w,v)$ be the exact output of that procedure and put $r_Y=\max_i|y_i-x|$. Then the procedure returns success, and for every $q\in\Pi_p$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^Nw_iq(y_i)=Lq(x).$$
If $f\in C^{p+1}(U)$ on an open convex set $U$ containing the compact convex hull $H=\operatorname{conv}\{x,y_1,\ldots,y_N\}$, then
$$\left|\sum_iw_if(y_i)-Lf(x)\right|\le C_{d,p}\left(\sum_i|w_i|\right)r_Y^{p+1}\max_{|\alpha|=p+1}\sup_{z\in H}|D^\alpha f(z)|.$$
Consequently, when $r_Y>0$, a separately proved bound $\sum_i|w_i|\le C_wr_Y^{-t}$ yields the order $C_{d,p}C_wr_Y^{p+1-t}$ truncation bound. Unisolvence alone is not asserted to provide this weight-norm bound.

Assume the Axiom of Choice when using the well-definedness results below; it is inherited conservatively from the published $L^2$ completeness supplier. Let $d\ge1$ and $s>d/2$. Write $L^2_s(\mathbb R^d)$ for the equivalence classes modulo Lebesgue-almost-everywhere equality of measurable complex functions $g$ satisfying
$$\|g\|_{L^2_s}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+|\xi|^2)^s|g(\xi)|^2\,d\xi<\infty.$$
For such $g$, the **inverse Fourier representative** is the function
$$U_g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}g(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The whole-space Bessel-potential space $H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ consists of these representatives, with norm $\|U_g\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}=\|g\|_{L^2_s}$. For the admitted domain $\Omega$ of [[def-rbf-kernels-sites-and-augmented-interpolation]], define $H^s(\Omega)$ to be the restrictions $U|_\Omega$ of whole-space members, with the quotient norm
$$\|u\|_{H^s(\Omega)}=\inf\{\|U\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}:U|_\Omega=u\}.$$
The whole-space inner product is $\langle U_g,U_h\rangle_{H^s}=\int (1+|\xi|^2)^s g(\xi)\overline{h(\xi)}\,d\xi$, linear in the first variable as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].
The inverse Fourier map is injective, whole-space representatives are continuous, the whole-space model is Hilbert, and Schwartz functions are dense in that norm; these facts are supplied by [[lem-matern-weighted-fourier-space-is-hilbert-and-injective]] and [[lem-schwartz-dense-in-fourier-bessel-potential-space]]. The restriction quotient is a norm by bounded point evaluation; its Hilbert realization as the restricted native space is proved in [[lem-restricted-matern-native-space-is-sobolev]]. No extension operator or identification with an intrinsic fractional Sobolev norm on $\Omega$ is part of this definition.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

derivations.claim: Write $W_s(\xi)=(1+|\xi|^2)^{s/2}$. By [F2] and [F3], $$\int|g(\xi)|d\xi\le\left(\int W_s(\xi)^2|g(\xi)|^2d\xi\right)^{1/2}\left(\int W_s(\xi)^{-2}d\xi\right)^{1/2}<\infty.$$ Hence $U_g$ is bounded by $\|g\|_1$ and continuous by [F7] applied to the pointwise-continuous exponential integrand dominated by $|g|$. The same estimate gives the displayed evaluation bound with $C_{d,s}=\|W_s^{-1}\|_2$.

The kernels $G_\epsilon$ are nonnegative and have integral one by [F4]. For each fixed $\delta>0$, scaling $y=\sqrt\epsilon z$ and [F7] show $$\int_{|y|\ge\delta}G_\epsilon(y)dy=\int_{|z|\ge\delta/\sqrt\epsilon}e^{-\pi|z|^2}dz\longrightarrow0\qquad(\epsilon\downarrow0).$$

Suppose $U_g(x)=0$ for every $x$. For $\epsilon>0$ and $\eta\in\mathbb R^d$, the double integral of $|g(\xi)|e^{-\pi\epsilon|x|^2}$ is finite by step 1.1 and [F4]. Thus [F5] and [F4] give $$0=\int U_g(x)e^{-\pi\epsilon|x|^2}e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\eta}dx=\int g(\xi)\epsilon^{-d/2}e^{-\pi|\xi-\eta|^2/\epsilon}d\xi=(g*G_\epsilon)(\eta).$$

Given $\tau>0$, translation continuity [F6] supplies $\delta>0$ such that $\|g(\cdot-y)-g\|_1<\tau$ when $|y|<\delta$. Tonelli and the triangle inequality then give $$\|g*G_\epsilon-g\|_1\le\int G_\epsilon(y)\|g(\cdot-y)-g\|_1dy\le\tau+2\|g\|_1\int_{|y|\ge\delta}G_\epsilon(y)dy.$$ Step 1.2 makes the last term tend to zero; as $\tau$ was arbitrary, $g*G_\epsilon\to g$ in $L^1$.

Step 2.1 says $g*G_\epsilon=0$ for every $\epsilon$, whereas step 2.2 says these convolutions converge to $g$ in $L^1$. Hence $\|g\|_1=0$, so $\int |g|=0$ and [F9] gives $g=0$ almost everywhere. This proves injectivity.

Multiplication $g\mapsto W_sg$ is a linear isometry of the weighted $L^2_s$ space onto ordinary complex $L^2(\lambda_d)$, with inverse $h\mapsto W_s^{-1}h$. By [F8] the latter is Hilbert under the declared choice assumption. Step 3.1 makes the inverse Fourier image isometric and one-to-one, so the whole-space $H^s$ is Hilbert; step 1.1 makes its restriction quotient norm positive on nonzero functions.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

If $T$ is self-adjoint on a nonzero finite-dimensional real inner product space and its
eigenvalues are ordered as

$$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n,$$

then

$$\lambda_1=\max_{v\ne0} R_T(v)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda_n=\min_{v\ne0} R_T(v).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric, where $p\ge1$. Then
$$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_{\|v\|_2=1}|v^{\mathsf T}Av|=\max_j|\lambda_j|,$$
where $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p$ are the eigenvalues of $A$.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

For every real $p$,
$$\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{k^p}\text{ converges}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p>1.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: By [F5] choose a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^d\to[0,1]$ equal to one on $\overline B(0,1/2)$ and supported in $B(0,1)$. Set $\eta(\xi)=(\rho(\xi)+\rho(-\xi))/2$. Then $\eta$ is smooth, even, nonnegative, at most one, still equals one on the half-radius ball, and is supported in the unit ball. Define $\psi(z)=\int\eta(\xi)e^{2\pi iz\cdot\xi}d\xi$. Reflection invariance of Lebesgue measure [F3] and Euler's formula [F9] make $\psi$ real and even, and monotonicity [F7] gives $\psi(0)=\int\eta\ge\lambda(B(0,1/2))>0$.

Since $\eta$ is smooth and compactly supported, it is Schwartz by [F8], so $\widehat\eta$ is Schwartz and $\psi(z)=\widehat\eta(-z)$ is Schwartz as well. For $|z|\ge1$, choose a coordinate $j$ with $|z_j|\ge|z|/\sqrt d$; the Schwartz seminorm $\sup_\xi|\xi_j^M\widehat\eta(\xi)|<\infty$ gives $|\psi(z)|\le C_M|z|^{-M}$. For $|z|\le1$, [F7] and $|e^{2\pi iz\cdot\xi}|=1$ from [F9] give $|\psi(z)|\le\int\eta$. Combining the two bounds yields $|\psi(z)|\le C'_M(1+|z|)^{-M}$.

Fix $i$. The open balls $B(x_j,q)$ are pairwise disjoint because center distances are at least $2q$. If $n\le|x_i-x_j|/q<n+1$, then $B(x_j,q)\subset B(x_i,(n+2)q)$. Translation invariance and dilation change of variables in [F3] give $\lambda(B(x,r))=r^d\lambda(B(0,1))$; this unit-ball measure is finite and positive. Finite additivity on the disjoint balls therefore bounds the number of such $j$ by $(n+2)^d$. Hence, for any integer $M>d+1$ and $T\ge1$, [step 2.1] yields the uniform row-sum estimate $$\sum_{j\ne i}\left|\psi\!\left(T(x_i-x_j)/q\right)\right|\le C_MT^{-M}\sum_{n\ge1}(n+2)^dn^{-M}.$$ For $n\ge1$, $(n+2)^d\le3^dn^d$, so this series is bounded by $3^d\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-(M-d)}$, which converges by [F11] because $M-d>1$. Choose one fixed $T$ large enough that this upper bound is at most $\psi(0)/2$.

For any $c\in\mathbb C^N$, the quadratic form of $H_{ij}=\psi(T(x_i-x_j)/q)$ satisfies $$c^*Hc\ge\left(\psi(0)-\max_i\sum_{j\ne i}|H_{ij}|\right)\|c\|_2^2\ge\frac{\psi(0)}2\|c\|_2^2,$$ because each off-diagonal pair is bounded using $2|c_i||c_j|\le|c_i|^2+|c_j|^2$. By the change of variables $\zeta=(q/T)\xi$, $$\int_{|\xi|\le T/q}\left|\sum_jc_je^{-2\pi ix_j\cdot\xi}\right|^2d\xi\ge\int\eta(q\xi/T)\left|\sum_jc_je^{-2\pi ix_j\cdot\xi}\right|^2d\xi=(T/q)^d c^*Hc.$$ The first inequality uses $0\le\eta\le1$ and support in the unit ball.

On $|\xi|\le T/q$ and $q\le1$, set $B=(a^2+4\pi^2T^2)q^{-2}$. Then $a^2+4\pi^2|\xi|^2\le a^2+4\pi^2T^2/q^2\le B$. Monotonicity and the power laws [F10] give $$w(\xi)\ge A B^{-s}=A\left(a^2+4\pi^2T^2\right)^{-s}q^{2s}.$$ Using the Fourier quadratic-form identity from [F1] and step 4.1 gives $c^*K_Xc\ge c_0q^{2s-d}\|c\|_2^2=c_0q^{2\nu}\|c\|_2^2$ for a constant $c_0>0$ independent of $X,q,N$. Thus [F4] yields $\lambda_{\min}(K_X)\ge c_0q^{2\nu}$.

By [F4], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis and write $K_X=Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf T}$. If $Q=(q_{ij})$, then $$\operatorname{tr}(K_X)=\sum_i(K_X)_{ii}=\sum_{i,j}q_{ij}^2\lambda_j=\sum_j\lambda_j=N,$$ since each column of $Q$ has unit norm and [F2] gives diagonal entries $k(0)=1$. By step 5.1 all eigenvalues are positive, so $\lambda_{\max}(K_X)\le N$. In this eigenbasis the induced 2-norms of $K_X$ and $K_X^{-1}$ are $\lambda_{\max}$ and $1/\lambda_{\min}$, respectively, by [F6]. The definition $\kappa_2(K_X)=\|K_X\|_2\|K_X^{-1}\|_2$ therefore gives $\kappa_2(K_X)\le c^{-1}Nq^{-2\nu}$. The $N=1$ case follows directly from $k(0)=1$ and the same definition.

citations.quote:
The **exact augmented RBF finite-difference weight procedure** has the following inputs: a dimension $d\ge1$; an integer polynomial degree $r\ge0$; a finite ordered stencil $Y=(y_1,\ldots,y_N)\subset\mathbb R^d$ of distinct sites that is $(r+1)$-unisolvent for $\Pi_r(\mathbb R^d)$; a real kernel $K$ strictly conditionally positive definite of order $r+1$; an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$ of $\Pi_r(\mathbb R^d)$; a center $x\in\mathbb R^d$; a homogeneous constant-coefficient differential functional $L=\sum_{|\alpha|=t}c_\alpha D^\alpha$ with $0\le t\le r$; and a neighborhood of $x$ on which every section $z\mapsto K(z,y_i)$ has continuous derivatives through order $t$. Here $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d$, $|\alpha|=\sum_j\alpha_j$, and $D^\alpha$ is the corresponding partial derivative. All arithmetic in this procedure is exact real arithmetic.

The input is supplied with total, correct oracles for admissibility and exact evaluation. The admissibility oracle returns whether all the stated input conditions hold, including the polynomial-basis condition, global strict conditional positive definiteness, and continuous section differentiability on the supplied neighborhood. On an affirmative answer, the evaluation oracles return the exact real values $K(y_i,y_j)$, $p_j(y_i)$, $(L_zK(z,y_i))|_{z=x}$, and $(Lp_j)(x)$ for the finitely many requested indices. Oracle calls are primitive operations in this model; neither global kernel admissibility nor differentiation is claimed to be decidable by real arithmetic alone.

Query the admissibility oracle. If it returns false, return `inadmissible-input`. Otherwise use the evaluation oracles to form $P_{ij}=p_j(y_i)$, $b_i=(L_zK(z,y_i))|_{z=x}$, $\ell_j=(Lp_j)(x)$, and
$$M=\begin{bmatrix}K_Y&P\\P^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad g=\begin{bmatrix}b\\ell\end{bmatrix}.$$
Solve $Mz=g$ by exact Gaussian elimination with deterministic nonzero-pivot row selection: set $A=M$, $c=g$, and $n=N+J$. For $k=1,\ldots,n$, choose the least $i\ge k$ with $A_{ik}\ne0$; if none exists, return `singular-system`. Swap rows $i$ and $k$ in both $A$ and $c$. For each $j=k+1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order, set $\mu=A_{jk}/A_{kk}$, replace row $j$ by row $j-\mu\,\mathrm{row}_k$ in $A$ and $c$, and set $A_{jk}=0$. After all pivots, set $z_n=c_n/A_{nn}$; then, for $k=n-1,n-2,\ldots,1$ in decreasing order, set $z_k=(c_k-\sum_{j=k+1}^n A_{kj}z_j)/A_{kk}$. Return `success` with the first $N$ coordinates $w$ of $z$ and the remaining $J$ polynomial multipliers. The stated strict hypotheses imply that `singular-system` is unreachable, as proved by [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]].

The returned $w$ is an exact mathematical weight vector. The nonsingularity lemma [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]] makes `singular-system` unreachable for every input that passes the stated strict hypotheses. This definition makes no floating-point stability or solver-error claim.

Let $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ be a finite ordered list of distinct sites in $\mathbb R^d$. If $K$ is strictly positive definite, then $K_X$ is invertible and $K_Xa=y$ has a unique solution for every $y\in\mathbb R^N$. If $K$ is strictly conditionally positive definite of order $m$ and $X$ is $m$-unisolvent for $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$, then the augmented matrix in [[def-rbf-kernels-sites-and-augmented-interpolation]] is invertible and its system has a unique solution for every right-hand side.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An admitted domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain (its boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function, with $\Omega$ on one side) with fixed $r_0>0$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$ such that for every $x\in\overline\Omega$ there is an orthogonal map $Q_x$ for which
$$x+Q_x\{z\in\mathbb R^d:0<|z|<r_0,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}\subset\Omega.$$
An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. For a finite ordered list of distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, its Gram matrix is $K_X=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$. The kernel is **strictly positive definite** if $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every such $X$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$; the nonstrict positive-semidefinite condition replaces $>$ by $\ge$. Only strict positivity is used for the ordinary interpolation solve below.

For an integer $m\ge1$, let $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$ be the real polynomials of total degree at most $m-1$, with an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$, where $J=\dim\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. The evaluation matrix on $X$ is $P_X=(p_j(x_i))_{i,j}$. The sites are **$m$-unisolvent** for this polynomial space when $P_X$ has linearly independent columns. A kernel is **strictly conditionally positive definite of order $m$** when, for every finite distinct $X$ and this evaluation matrix, $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$ satisfying $P_X^{\mathsf T}c=0$. Thus strict conditional positivity is a strict inequality on the moment-null subspace; it is stronger than the corresponding nonstrict inequality.

For data $y\in\mathbb R^N$, the strictly positive definite interpolation system is $K_Xa=y$. For an order-$m$ strictly conditionally positive definite kernel and $m$-unisolvent sites, the polynomially augmented interpolation system is
$$\begin{bmatrix}K_X&P_X\\P_X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$
Whenever the relevant system has a unique solution, its kernel-plus-polynomial function $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iK(x,x_i)+\sum_j b_jp_j(x)$ is called the interpolant. Invertibility for the stated strict hypotheses is supplied by [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]].

For a finite nonempty site set $X\subset\Omega$, the **fill distance** is $h_X=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{x_i\in X}|x-x_i|$. If $N\ge2$, the **separation radius** and **mesh ratio** are $q_X=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}|x_i-x_j|$ and $\rho_X=h_X/q_X$, respectively. These are exact geometric quantities, independent of any floating-point solver.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

derivations.claim: Let $M$ be the augmented matrix and $g$ its right side in [F1]. It is square and invertible by [F2]. Initially the leading $0\times0$ pivot block is invertible. Inductively suppose the first $k-1$ pivots have been nonzero. After their row swaps and elimination, the row-equivalent matrix has block form $\begin{bmatrix}U&B\\0&S\end{bmatrix}$ with $U$ invertible and $S$ the remaining Schur complement. The block matrix is invertible, so $S$ is invertible: if $Sz=0$, then $(-U^{-1}Bz,z)$ would be a nonzero vector in its kernel. If the first column of $S$ were zero, its first coordinate vector would be a nonzero kernel vector. Thus the finite set of remaining entries in column $k$ contains a nonzero entry, and the algorithm's least-index rule finds a nonzero pivot. Row swaps and adding multiples of pivot rows are invertible elementary row operations, so they preserve the solution set. After $N+J$ pivots the matrix is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, and descending substitution returns the unique solution. Therefore the singular-system status is unreachable under the hypotheses.

Writing the returned vector as $(w,v)$, its lower block equation is $P^{\mathsf T}w=\ell$. For each basis polynomial $p_j$, this says $\sum_iw_ip_j(y_i)=Lp_j(x)$. Every $q\in\Pi_p$ is a linear combination $q=\sum_ja_jp_j$, so multiplying these identities by $a_j$ and summing, using linearity of $L$, gives $\sum_iw_iq(y_i)=Lq(x)$.

Let $T_pf$ be the Taylor polynomial of $f$ at $x$ of total degree at most $p$. Since $t\le p$, its derivatives at $x$ through order $t$ agree with those of $f$, so $LT_pf(x)=Lf(x)$. Applying step 2.1 to $T_pf$ gives $\sum_iw_iT_pf(y_i)=Lf(x)$.

Subtract the identity in step 3.1 from the sampled sum for $f$. For every $i$, [F3] bounds $|f(y_i)-T_pf(y_i)|$ by $C_{d,p}|y_i-x|^{p+1}$ times the derivative supremum on $H$, since each segment lies in the convex hull $H$. The triangle inequality and $|y_i-x|\le r_Y$ now give the stated truncation estimate. When $r_Y>0$, the additional weight bound yields the final conditional rate.

$$\|g\|_{L^2_s}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+|\xi|^2)^s|g(\xi)|^2\,d\xi<\infty.$$
For such $g$, the **inverse Fourier representative** is the function
$$U_g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}g(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The whole-space Bessel-potential space $H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ consists of these representatives, with norm $\|U_g\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}=\|g\|_{L^2_s}$. For the admitted domain $\Omega$ of [[def-rbf-kernels-sites-and-augmented-interpolation]], define $H^s(\Omega)$ to be the restrictions $U|_\Omega$ of whole-space members, with the quotient norm
$$\|u\|_{H^s(\Omega)}=\inf\{\|U\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}:U|_\Omega=u\}.$$
The whole-space inner product is $\langle U_g,U_h\rangle_{H^s}=\int (1+|\xi|^2)^s g(\xi)\overline{h(\xi)}\,d\xi$, linear in the first variable as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].
The inverse Fourier map is injective, whole-space representatives are continuous, the whole-space model is Hilbert, and Schwartz functions are dense in that norm; these facts are supplied by [[lem-matern-weighted-fourier-space-is-hilbert-and-injective]] and [[lem-schwartz-dense-in-fourier-bessel-potential-space]]. The restriction quotient is a norm by bounded point evaluation; its Hilbert realization as the restricted native space is proved in [[lem-restricted-matern-native-space-is-sobolev]]. No extension operator or identification with an intrinsic fractional Sobolev norm on $\Omega$ is part of this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Put $g_R=g\mathbf1_{B(0,R)}$. By [F3], $$\|g-g_R\|_{L^2_s}^2=\int_{|\xi|>R}(1+|\xi|^2)^s|g(\xi)|^2d\xi\longrightarrow0\qquad(R\to\infty).$$ Choose $R$ so this norm is less than a prescribed $\varepsilon/2$.

Let $f$ be any Schwartz function and define $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$. Polynomial multiples of derivatives of $f$ have arbitrarily rapid decay by [F5], so they and their derivatives are integrable, including on each coordinate line with the other coordinates fixed. Differentiation in $\xi$ is justified by dominated convergence [F6] using these integrable moments. Apply [F7] on each coordinate line to such a function and its Fourier exponential: the derivative products are integrable and the boundary product tends to zero. Absolute Fubini [F6] then combines the coordinate identities and shows that every $\xi^\gamma D_\xi^\alpha\widehat f(\xi)$ is a finite linear combination of Fourier transforms of derivatives of polynomial multiples of $f$. Each such function is in $L^1$ by [F5], so its Fourier transform is bounded; hence $\widehat f$ is Schwartz and in $L^1$. In particular $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^s|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi<\infty$, by polar integration [F6].

On the bounded ball $O=B(0,R+1)$, the weight $(1+|\xi|^2)^s$ is bounded above by a finite constant $C_R$. The restriction of $g_R$ to $O$ lies in $L^2(O)$, so [F2] gives $\phi\in C_c^\infty(O)$ with $\|g_R-\phi\|_{L^2(O)}<\varepsilon/(2\sqrt{C_R})$. Extending $\phi$ by zero is still smooth and compactly supported on $\mathbb R^d$ because its support is compactly contained in $O$, and $$\|g_R-\phi\|_{L^2_s}^2\le C_R\|g_R-\phi\|_{L^2(O)}^2<\varepsilon^2/4.$$

For $\epsilon>0$, absolute Fubini [F6] and the Gaussian transform [F6] give $$\int\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}e^{-\pi\epsilon|\xi|^2}d\xi=\int f(y)\epsilon^{-d/2}e^{-\pi|x-y|^2/\epsilon}dy=(f*G_\epsilon)(x),$$ where $G_\epsilon(z)=\epsilon^{-d/2}e^{-\pi|z|^2/\epsilon}$. Since $\widehat f\in L^1$, dominated convergence sends the left side to $\int\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}d\xi$. The right side tends to $f(x)$: given $\varepsilon>0$, continuity at $x$ gives $\delta>0$ such that $|f(x-z)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ for $|z|<\delta$. Since $G_\epsilon$ has total mass one, the contribution from this ball is at most $\varepsilon$; boundedness of $f$ and the Gaussian tail estimate from scaling make the contribution on $|z|\ge\delta$ tend to zero. Thus Fourier inversion holds and $f=U_{\widehat f}\in H^s$.

For any multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$, differentiation under the integral is justified by the compactly supported integrable moments. For each coordinate, apply [F7] with the smooth compactly supported factor $(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\phi(\xi)$ (or a derivative of it) and the inverse Fourier exponential; both derivative products are integrable and the boundary product is zero outside a bounded interval. Repetition and absolute Fubini [F6] give $$x^\beta D_x^\alpha U_\phi(x)=(-1)^{|\beta|}(2\pi i)^{-|\beta|}\int \partial_\xi^\beta\big((2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\phi(\xi)\big)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}d\xi.$$ The right side is uniformly bounded by the $L^1$ norm of a smooth compactly supported function. Hence every Schwartz seminorm of $U_\phi$ is finite, so $U_\phi$ is Schwartz.

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 show that $C_c^\infty$ frequency functions are dense in the weighted Fourier norm. Step 3.1 shows their inverse transforms are Schwartz. Steps 1.2 and 2.2 show every Schwartz function belongs to $H^s$, and [F4] identifies the normed Fourier images injectively with the functions in $H^s$. Thus Schwartz functions are dense in $H^s(\mathbb R^d)$.

u},\qquad \lambda_{\max}(K_X)\le N,\qquad \kappa_2(K_X)\le c^{-1}Nq^{-2
u}.$$
The eigenvalues and condition number are those of the exact real symmetric positive-definite matrix. For $N=1$, $K_X=[1]$ and $\kappa_2(K_X)=1$.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An admitted domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain (its boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function, with $\Omega$ on one side) with fixed $r_0>0$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$ such that for every $x\in\overline\Omega$ there is an orthogonal map $Q_x$ for which
$$x+Q_x\{z\in\mathbb R^d:0<|z|<r_0,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}\subset\Omega.$$
An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. For a finite ordered list of distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, its Gram matrix is $K_X=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$. The kernel is **strictly positive definite** if $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every such $X$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$; the nonstrict positive-semidefinite condition replaces $>$ by $\ge$. Only strict positivity is used for the ordinary interpolation solve below.

For an integer $m\ge1$, let $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$ be the real polynomials of total degree at most $m-1$, with an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$, where $J=\dim\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. The evaluation matrix on $X$ is $P_X=(p_j(x_i))_{i,j}$. The sites are **$m$-unisolvent** for this polynomial space when $P_X$ has linearly independent columns. A kernel is **strictly conditionally positive definite of order $m$** when, for every finite distinct $X$ and this evaluation matrix, $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$ satisfying $P_X^{\mathsf T}c=0$. Thus strict conditional positivity is a strict inequality on the moment-null subspace; it is stronger than the corresponding nonstrict inequality.

For data $y\in\mathbb R^N$, the strictly positive definite interpolation system is $K_Xa=y$. For an order-$m$ strictly conditionally positive definite kernel and $m$-unisolvent sites, the polynomially augmented interpolation system is
$$\begin{bmatrix}K_X&P_X\\P_X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$
Whenever the relevant system has a unique solution, its kernel-plus-polynomial function $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iK(x,x_i)+\sum_j b_jp_j(x)$ is called the interpolant. Invertibility for the stated strict hypotheses is supplied by [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]].

For a finite nonempty site set $X\subset\Omega$, the **fill distance** is $h_X=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{x_i\in X}|x-x_i|$. If $N\ge2$, the **separation radius** and **mesh ratio** are $q_X=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}|x_i-x_j|$ and $\rho_X=h_X/q_X$, respectively. all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is

   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear

leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $n\ge 1$, let either $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with
$p\ge 1$ or $p=\infty$, and let
$A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ be an invertible real matrix
([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]), so that the linear system
$Ax=b$ has the unique solution $x=A^{-1}b$ for every right-hand side
$b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The **condition number of the linear system** (equivalently,
of the matrix $A$) with respect to the induced $p$-norm of
[[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]], using its separately defined infinity case when
$p=\infty$, is

$$\kappa_p(A)\;:=\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_p\;\in\;[1,+\infty).$$

**The value is at least one and is never infinite.** The inverse $A^{-1}$ is the
unique two-sided inverse of $A$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]),
so $AA^{-1}=I_n$ and $A^{-1}A=I_n$. For rational finite $p$,
submultiplicativity and normalisation are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]].
For $p=\infty$, the same properties follow directly from the defining
supremum: $\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\lVert A\rVert_\infty\lVert x\rVert_\infty$
and applying this estimate twice gives submultiplicativity, while
$I_nx=x$ gives $\lVert I_n\rVert_\infty=1$. Hence in either case

$$1=\lVert I_n\rVert_p=\lVert AA^{-1}\rVert_p\le\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_p=\kappa_p(A).$$

Equivalently, $\kappa_p(A)$ is the product of the largest factor by which $A$
stretches a nonzero vector and the largest factor by which $A^{-1}$ stretches
one. Applying the same estimate to $A^{-1}$ in place of $A$ gives
$\kappa_p(A^{-1})=\kappa_p(A)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Suppose $N\ge2$ and write $q=q_X\le1$. Choose $z_0$ and $R>0$ with $\Omega\subset B(z_0,R)$. The site balls $B(x_i,q)$ are pairwise disjoint and lie in $B(z_0,R+1)$. Their measures are $q^d\lambda(B(0,1))$ by [F2], so finite additivity and the positive finite unit-ball measure give $$Nq^d\lambda(B(0,1))\le(R+1)^d\lambda(B(0,1)),$$ and therefore $N\le C_\Omega q^{-d}$.
Since $q\le1$, combine [F1] with step 1.1 to get $\kappa_2(K_X)\le C_1q^{-(d+2\nu)}=C_1q^{-2s}$.
The mesh-ratio bound implies $q=h_X/\rho_X\ge h_X/\rho_0$, so $q^{-2s}\le\rho_0^{2s}h_X^{-2s}$. Step 2.1 gives the desired estimate.

at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Since $w=A(a^2+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{-s}$, the two positive functions $(a^2+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^s$ and $(1+|\xi|^2)^s$ have ratio bounded above and below by positive constants: compare $a^2+4\pi^2r^2$ with $1+r^2$ separately using the minimum and maximum of $a^2$ and $4\pi^2$, and use monotonicity of the positive power [F7]. Multiplying by $A^{-1}$ and taking square roots gives the displayed norm equivalence. Thus the weighted $L^2$ norms defining $\mathcal H_k$ and $H^s$ are equivalent and have the same representatives by injectivity [F1,F2]; completeness of $H^s$ implies completeness of $\mathcal H_k$.

For a complex coefficient vector $c=(c_j)$, the Hermitian quadratic form of the Gram matrix is $$c^*K_Xc=\int_{\mathbb R^d}w(\xi)\left|\sum_{j=1}^Nc_je^{-2\pi ix_j\cdot\xi}\right|^2d\xi.$$ If it is zero, [F6] says $w$ times the squared modulus of the continuous exponential sum vanishes almost everywhere. Since $w>0$, the sum is zero almost everywhere. A continuous function zero almost everywhere is zero everywhere, because any point of nonzero value would have a neighborhood on which its modulus is bounded below, and such a neighborhood contains a positive-measure box [F5].

The spectral representative of $k(\cdot-y)$ is $w(\xi)e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\xi}$. Its $\mathcal H_k$ norm squared is $\int w=1$, and for $U_g\in\mathcal H_k$, $$\langle U_g,k(\cdot-y)\rangle_k=\int g(\xi)e^{2\pi i y\cdot\xi}d\xi=U_g(y).$$ The integral exists because Cauchy--Schwarz bounds $\int|g|$ by $\|g\|_k(\int w)^{1/2}$. Hence point evaluation is continuous and the stated kernel sections reproduce it.

If $U$ is orthogonal to every section centered at $y\in\mathbb R^d$, step 2.1 gives $U(y)=0$ for every $y$. Fourier injectivity [F1] then makes $U=0$ in $\mathcal H_k$. By [F3] the span of all sections is dense.

Choose $v=(1,t,\ldots,t^{d-1})$ so that the numbers $v\cdot x_j$ are pairwise distinct. For each pair $i
e j$, the polynomial $(x_i-x_j)\cdot(1,t,\ldots,t^{d-1})$ is nonzero because $x_i-x_j
e0$; [F4] says its zero set is finite. The ordered field $\mathbb R$ has $0<1$, so the natural multiples $0,1,1+1,\ldots$ are strictly increasing and $\mathbb R$ is infinite. Thus a real $t$ exists outside the finite union of root sets. Restrict the vanishing exponential sum to $\xi=uv$ and differentiate at $u=0$ for orders $r=0,\ldots,N-1$. This gives $\sum_jc_j(v\cdot x_j)^r=0$. For each $j$, the Lagrange polynomial $$L_j(t)=\prod_{i
e j} rac{t-v\cdot x_i}{v\cdot x_j-v\cdot x_i}$$ has degree at most $N-1$ and satisfies $L_j(v\cdot x_i)=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. derivations.claim: The set $\mathcal N_\Omega$ is a linear subspace. If $U_n\in\mathcal N_\Omega$ converges to $U$ in native norm, then for each $x\in\Omega$, [F2] gives $|U_n(x)-U(x)|\le C_x\|U_n-U\|_k\to0$; hence $U(x)=0$ and $U\in\mathcal N_\Omega$. Thus $\mathcal N_\Omega$ is closed.

For $y\in\Omega$, the section $k_y=k(\cdot-y)$ lies in $\mathcal N_\Omega^\perp$: for every $N\in\mathcal N_\Omega$, $\langle N,k_y\rangle_k=N(y)=0$ by reproduction [F2]. If $U\in\mathcal N_\Omega^\perp$ is orthogonal to every $k_y$ with $y\in\Omega$, then [F2] gives $U(y)=0$ for all $y\in\Omega$, so $U\in\mathcal N_\Omega$. For each site $x_i$, the residual is orthogonal to $k(\cdot-x_i)$; by reproduction [F1], $(f-\Pi_Xf)(x_i)=0$. Thus $\Pi_Xf$ interpolates the data. Its coefficients solve $K_Xc=(f(x_i))_i$, which has a unique solution by [F2], so it is the unique kernel interpolant.

Put $e=f-s_Xf=(I-\Pi_X)f$. Self-adjointness of $I-\Pi_X$ and reproduction give $$e(x)=\langle e,k(\cdot-x)\rangle=\langle e,(I-\Pi_X)k(\cdot-x)\rangle.$$ Cauchy--Schwarz [F4] yields $|e(x)|\le\|e\|P_X(x)\le\|f\|P_X(x)$ by contractivity of the orthogonal projection.

The projection of $k(\cdot-x)$ has the form $\sum_jv_jk(\cdot-x_j)$. Reproduction and orthogonality at all sites give $K_Xv=k_X(x)$, so $v=K_X^{-1}k_X(x)$ by [F2]. Expanding the squared residual norm and using this equation gives $$P_X(x)^2=\|k(\cdot-x)\|^2-\|\Pi_Xk(\cdot-x)\|^2=k(0)-k_X(x)^*K_X^{-1}k_X(x).$$ It is nonnegative because it is a squared norm.

Its norm is equivalent to the restriction-quotient norm of $H^s(\Omega)$: for constants $c,C>0$ depending only on $d,\nu,a$,

No extension theorem or intrinsic fractional-domain norm is asserted.

u>0$, $s=
u+d/2$, and choose an integer $m>

The estimate has no separation or mesh-ratio hypothesis.

Let $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\subset\Omega$ be distinct and nonempty, and let $\mathcal H_k(\Omega)$ be the restricted Matérn native RKHS. For every $f\in\mathcal H_k(\Omega)$, the unique kernel interpolant $s_Xf=\sum_jc_jk(\cdot-x_j)$ is the orthogonal projection of $f$ onto $V_X=\operatorname{span}\{k(\cdot-x_j):1\le j\le N\}$. Define
$$P_X(x)=\|(I-\Pi_X)k(\cdot-x)\|_{\mathcal H_k(\Omega)},$$
where $\Pi_X$ is that projection. Then for every $x\in\Omega$,
$$|f(x)-s_Xf(x)|\le P_X(x)\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k(\Omega)},\qquad P_X(x)^2=k(0)-k_X(x)^*K_X^{-1}k_X(x)\ge0.$$
where $K_X=(k(x_i-x_j))$ and $k_X(x)=(k(x_i-x))_{i=1}^N$.

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]],
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An admitted domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain (its boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function, with $\Omega$ on one side) with fixed $r_0>0$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$ such that for every $x\in\overline\Omega$ there is an orthogonal map $Q_x$ for which
$$x+Q_x\{z\in\mathbb R^d:0<|z|<r_0,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}\subset\Omega.$$
An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. For a finite ordered list of distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, its Gram matrix is $K_X=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$. The kernel is **strictly positive definite** if $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every such $X$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$; the nonstrict positive-semidefinite condition replaces $>$ by $\ge$. Only strict positivity is used for the ordinary interpolation solve below.

For an integer $m\ge1$, let $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$ be the real polynomials of total degree at most $m-1$, with an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$, where $J=\dim\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. The evaluation matrix on $X$ is $P_X=(p_j(x_i))_{i,j}$. The sites are **$m$-unisolvent** for this polynomial space when $P_X$ has linearly independent columns. A kernel is **strictly conditionally positive definite of order $m$** when, for every finite distinct $X$ and this evaluation matrix, $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$ satisfying $P_X^{\mathsf T}c=0$. Thus strict conditional positivity is a strict inequality on the moment-null subspace; it is stronger than the corresponding nonstrict inequality.

For data $y\in\mathbb R^N$, the strictly positive definite interpolation system is $K_Xa=y$. For an order-$m$ strictly conditionally positive definite kernel and $m$-unisolvent sites, the polynomially augmented interpolation system is
$$\begin{bmatrix}K_X&P_X\\P_X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$
Whenever the relevant system has a unique solution, its kernel-plus-polynomial function $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iK(x,x_i)+\sum_j b_jp_j(x)$ is called the interpolant. Invertibility for the stated strict hypotheses is supplied by [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]].

For a finite nonempty site set $X\subset\Omega$, the **fill distance** is $h_X=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{x_i\in X}|x-x_i|$. If $N\ge2$, the **separation radius** and **mesh ratio** are $q_X=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}|x_i-x_j|$ and $\rho_X=h_X/q_X$, respectively. These are exact geometric quantities, independent of any floating-point solver.

derivations.claim: For every row index $i$, the equal sites give $K_{i1}=\phi(|x_i-x_1|)=\phi(|x_i-x_2|)=K_{i2}$. Thus the first two columns, and by symmetry the first two rows, coincide.

The nonzero vector $e_1-e_2$ is therefore in the nullspace of the Gram matrix, so the matrix is singular. This example violates the distinct-site hypothesis in [F1] and is not a counterexample to the interpolation theorem.

If $T$ is self-adjoint on a nonzero finite-dimensional real inner product space and its
eigenvalues are ordered as

$$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n,$$

then

$$\lambda_1=\max_{v\ne0} R_T(v)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda_n=\min_{v\ne0} R_T(v).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $n\ge 1$, let either $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with
$p\ge 1$ or $p=\infty$, and let
$A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ be an invertible real matrix
([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]), so that the linear system
$Ax=b$ has the unique solution $x=A^{-1}b$ for every right-hand side
$b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The **condition number of the linear system** (equivalently,
of the matrix $A$) with respect to the induced $p$-norm of
[[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]], using its separately defined infinity case when
$p=\infty$, is

$$\kappa_p(A)\;:=\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_p\;\in\;[1,+\infty).$$

**The value is at least one and is never infinite.** The inverse $A^{-1}$ is the
unique two-sided inverse of $A$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]),
so $AA^{-1}=I_n$ and $A^{-1}A=I_n$. For rational finite $p$,
submultiplicativity and normalisation are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]].
For $p=\infty$, the same properties follow directly from the defining
supremum: $\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\lVert A\rVert_\infty\lVert x\rVert_\infty$
and applying this estimate twice gives submultiplicativity, while
$I_nx=x$ gives $\lVert I_n\rVert_\infty=1$. Hence in either case

$$1=\lVert I_n\rVert_p=\lVert AA^{-1}\rVert_p\le\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_p=\kappa_p(A).$$

Equivalently, $\kappa_p(A)$ is the product of the largest factor by which $A$
stretches a nonzero vector and the largest factor by which $A^{-1}$ stretches
one. Applying the same estimate to $A^{-1}$ in place of $A$ gives
$\kappa_p(A^{-1})=\kappa_p(A)$.

([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

derivations.claim: The cube is bounded and Lipschitz. At a boundary point $p$, let $I$ be the nonempty set of active coordinates ($p_j=0$ or $1$), with inward signs $\sigma_j=1$ at $0$ and $-1$ at $1$. Put $u_j=\sigma_j/\sqrt{|I|}$ for $j\in I$ and $u_j=0$ otherwise. In the orthogonal coordinates $x=p+y+tu$ with $y\perp u$, a sufficiently small neighborhood has no constraints from inactive coordinates, and the active inequalities reduce to $$t>\max_{j\in I}(-\sqrt{|I|}\,\sigma_j y_j).$$ This is the epigraph of a finite maximum of linear functions, hence a local Lipschitz graph with the cube on one side. The cube also satisfies the uniform cone condition. For $x\in[0,1]^d$, choose signs $\sigma_j=1$ if $x_j\le1/2$ and $-1$ otherwise, and put $u=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_d)/\sqrt d$. If $u=e_1$ take $Q_x=I$; otherwise put $v=(e_1-u)/|e_1-u|$ and $Q_x=I-2vv^{\mathsf T}$, which is orthogonal and sends $e_1$ to $u$. Choose $0<\theta<\pi/2$ with $\cos\theta/\sqrt d-\sin\theta>0$, and set $r_0=1/2$. For any cone vector $z$, $z_1>|z|\cos\theta$ and $|z-z_1e_1|<|z|\sin\theta$. Hence $\sigma_j(Q_xz)_j\ge z_1/\sqrt d-|z-z_1e_1|>|z|(\cos\theta/\sqrt d-\sin\theta)>0$ for each coordinate. Each coordinate moves toward the cube's interior by less than $r_0$, so $x+Q_xz\in(0,1)^d$.

Distinct midpoint sites have fill distance at most $\sqrt d/(2m)$. Since $m$ is odd, $x_0\in X_m$. By continuity in [F2], choose $\epsilon_m>0$ so that $|1-k(\delta e_1)|<1/m$ whenever $0<\delta<\epsilon_m$, then choose $0<\delta_m<\min\{\epsilon_m,1/(4m^2)\}$. Strict positive definiteness for $x_0$ and $x_0+\delta_me_1$ makes $1-k(\delta_me_1)>0$, so $0<1-k(\delta_me_1)<1/m$. Put $Z_m=X_m\cup\{x_0+\delta_me_1\}$. The new site is inside the cube because $\delta_m<1/(4m^2)<1/2$. Every other grid site is at distance at least $1/m$ from $x_0$, while $\delta_m<1/(4m^2)<1/(2m)$, so the new site is distinct from all grid sites. At the boundary corner $0$, the nearest grid point is $\left(1/(2m),\ldots,1/(2m)\right)$, at distance $\sqrt d/(2m)$; the new site has squared distance $d/4+\delta_m+\delta_m^2>d/(4m^2)$, so $\min_{z\in Z_m}|z|=\sqrt d/(2m)$. For $D_m(x)=\min_{z\in Z_m}|x-z|$, the triangle inequality gives $|D_m(x)-D_m(y)|\le|x-y|$. Since $x_n=(1/n,\ldots,1/n)\in\Omega$ for $n\ge2$ and $x_n\to0$, $D_m(x_n)\to D_m(0)$; the fill-distance supremum therefore satisfies $h_{Z_m}\ge\sqrt d/(2m)\ge1/(2m)$. Adding a site cannot increase fill distance, so also $h_{Z_m}\le\sqrt d/(2m)\to0$. The separation radius satisfies $0<q_{Z_m}\le\delta_m/2<1/(8m^2)$; consequently $\rho_{Z_m}=h_{Z_m}/q_{Z_m}>4m\to\infty$.

Let $u$ be the unit vector with entries $1/\sqrt2$ and $-1/\sqrt2$ at the new site and $x_0$, and zero elsewhere. The corresponding Rayleigh quotient is $$u^{\mathsf T}K_{Z_m}u=\tfrac12(1+1-2k(\delta_me_1))=1-k(\delta_me_1).$$ Hence [F3] gives $0<\lambda_{\min}(K_{Z_m})\le1-k(\delta_me_1)<1/m$. By [F3] choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $Q$ and write $K_{Z_m}=Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf T}$. Since every diagonal entry is $1$, $$\operatorname{tr}K_{Z_m}=|Z_m|=\sum_{i,j}q_{ij}^2\lambda_j=\sum_j\lambda_j,$$ so $\lambda_{\max}(K_{Z_m})$ is at least the average eigenvalue, namely $1$. For a unit vector $v=Qc$, orthogonality gives $\|K_{Z_m}v\|_2^2=\sum_j\lambda_j^2c_j^2\le\lambda_{\max}(K_{Z_m})^2$, with equality at a top eigenvector; the same calculation for $K_{Z_m}^{-1}$ gives induced 2-norm $1/\lambda_{\min}(K_{Z_m})$. Thus [F4] gives $\kappa_2(K_{Z_m})=\lambda_{\max}(K_{Z_m})/\lambda_{\min}(K_{Z_m})>m$. Together with step 1.2, this gives $h_{Z_m}\to0$, $\rho_{Z_m}\to\infty$, and condition number tending to infinity.
