Let $s\ge1$ be an integer and let $a=x_0<\cdots<x_s=b$ be a finite partition, and on each cell $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ choose an integer degree $n_i\ge0$ and real controls $c_{i,0},\ldots,c_{i,n_i}$. For $t=(x-x_i)/(x_{i+1}-x_i)\in[0,1]$, define the Bernstein basis polynomial
$$B_{k,n_i}(t)=\iota\binom{n_i}{k}t^k(1-t)^{n_i-k},\qquad 0\le k\le n_i,$$
where $\binom{n_i}{k}$ is the natural binomial coefficient from [[def-binomial-coefficient]], $\iota$ is the canonical embedding of [[def-canonical-natural]] into $\mathbb R$, and finite sums use [[def-finite-sum]]. The cell polynomial is $p_i(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n_i}c_{i,k}B_{k,n_i}(t)$. These cell polynomials form a piecewise Bernstein representation. To require continuity at a shared node, impose the additional endpoint-control condition $c_{i,n_i}=c_{i+1,0}$; continuity is not part of the representation unless that condition is imposed.

For degree two this formula reads $p_i(x)=c_{i,0}(1-t)^2+\iota\binom21\,c_{i,1}t(1-t)+c_{i,2}t^2$.

For all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$(x+y)^{n} \;=\; \sum_{k<n+1} \iota\binom{n}{k}\, x^{k}\, y^{\,n-k},$$

where the powers are the integer powers of [[def-integer-power]], the sum is the
real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] over $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$, the difference
$n-k$ is a genuine one because $k \le n$ throughout the range, and $\iota$ is the
canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]].

**The coefficient is $\iota\binom{n}{k}$ and not $\binom{n}{k}$.** A binomial
coefficient is a natural number, that is a von Neumann natural, that is a set; it
is not an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and it enters the field through $\iota$.

**The identity is stated in $\mathbb{R}$ and only in $\mathbb{R}$.** The same
proof uses nothing but commutativity, associativity, distributivity and
natural-number multiples of a ring element, so a commutative-ring version is
available wherever rings are; rings are not available at this point in the
reading order, and the ring statement is a separate statement, to be made where
they are. See the Remarks below.

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put

$$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$

the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite
([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes
sense for every subset.

**$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by
[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies.

**$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be
a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries
$[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$
onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport
clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its
two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a
bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same
cardinality.

**Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set

$$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$,

$$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$

**$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is
*not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence
lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a
theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a
count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove.

**Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.**

- $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of
  cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$
  ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a
  one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved.
- $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$
  then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$.
- $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has
  $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$
  ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]).
- $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one
  $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so
  $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$.
- $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, both instances of the
  above.
For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ exactly one of $m < n$, $m = n$, $m > n$ holds. In particular the order ([[def-nat-order]]) is total.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[thm-recursion]]):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

- $m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$
  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-field]]).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of [[lem-power-laws]]: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors ([[lem-of-no-zero-divisors]]).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
([[lem-of-inverse-unique]]).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ ([[def-integers]]) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]],
[[def-int-operations]]). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:
5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function** $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.
In any field $F$ ([[def-field]]), for every $a \in F$ we have $0 \cdot a = 0$.

derivations.claim: Fix a cell and $t\in[0,1]$. Both $t$ and $1-t$ are nonnegative, so their natural powers are nonnegative by induction using the recursive definition [F10] and closure of nonnegative reals under multiplication. By [F3]–[F4], $\binom nk$ is a natural that is either zero or positive; [F5] sends its zero case to zero, and [F6] sends its positive case to a positive real. Thus every $B_{k,n}(t)\ge0$.
Apply [F2] with $x=t$ and $y=1-t$. Since $t+(1-t)=1$, [F10] and induction give $1^n=1$, so the displayed Bernstein basis terms sum to one.

By [F8]–[F9], let $c_{\min}$ and $c_{\max}$ be the minimum and maximum of the finite control list. For each $k$, [F1], step 1.1, and [F7] give $c_{\min}B_{k,n}(t)\le c_{i,k}B_{k,n}(t)\le c_{\max}B_{k,n}(t)$: the control differences and basis weights are nonnegative, so their products are nonnegative. Summing with [F7] and using step 1.2 gives $c_{\min}\le p_i(x)\le c_{\max}$. Therefore nonnegative controls imply $p_i(x)\ge0$. Each $p_i$ is a polynomial in $x$ after substituting the affine local coordinate, so it is continuous on its cell by [F11]. For $n_i\ge1$, [F3], [F5], [F10], step 1.2, and [F12] give $B_{0,n_i}(0)=B_{n_i,n_i}(1)=1$ and all other endpoint basis values zero; for $n_i=0$ the sole basis term is constantly one. Given $\varepsilon>0$, the minimum of the two positive continuity radii for the adjacent cell restrictions then gives continuity of the piecewise function at that node; at cell interiors continuity follows from [F11], and at the outer endpoints it follows from the single adjacent cell restriction. **Inputs:** An integer $n\ge2$, strictly increasing real nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{n-1}$, and real values $y_0,\ldots,y_{n-1}$. All operations here are over the real numbers.

**Output:** Slopes $m_0,\ldots,m_{n-1}$ and the piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant determined by these nodes, values, and slopes under [[def-piecewise-cubic-hermite-interpolant]].

Put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$ and $d_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/h_i$ for $0\le i<n-1$. Write $\operatorname{sgn}(r)\in\{-1,0,1\}$ for the sign of a real number.

- If $n=2$, set $m_0=m_1=d_0$.
- If $n\ge3$, for each interior node $1\le k\le n-2$, set $m_k=0$ when $d_{k-1}d_k\le0$. When $d_{k-1}d_k>0$, put $w_1=2h_k+h_{k-1}$, $w_2=h_k+2h_{k-1}$, and
  $$m_k=\frac{w_1+w_2}{w_1/d_{k-1}+w_2/d_k}.$$
- For $n\ge3$, at the left endpoint compute
  $$\widehat m_0=\frac{(2h_0+h_1)d_0-h_0d_1}{h_0+h_1}.$$
  Set $m_0=0$ if $\operatorname{sgn}(\widehat m_0)\ne\operatorname{sgn}(d_0)$. Otherwise set $m_0=3d_0$ if $d_0d_1<0$ and $|\widehat m_0|>3|d_0|$; in all remaining cases set $m_0=\widehat m_0$.
- For $n\ge3$, at the right endpoint compute
  $$\widehat m_{n-1}=\frac{(2h_{n-2}+h_{n-3})d_{n-2}-h_{n-2}d_{n-3}}{h_{n-2}+h_{n-3}}.$$
  Apply the preceding clip and cap rule with $d_0,d_1$ replaced by $d_{n-2},d_{n-3}$ and $m_0,\widehat m_0$ replaced by $m_{n-1},\widehat m_{n-1}$.

For $n\ge3$, the algorithm returns the Hermite pieces from the stated values and selected slopes. The two-node branch is the line through the two input points.

derivations.claim: Each $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i$ is positive, so every secant $d_i$ is defined and finite. In the two-node branch both slopes equal the already defined secant, and neither endpoint formula is evaluated. When $n\ge3$, the endpoint denominators $h_0+h_1$ and $h_{n-2}+h_{n-3}$ exist and are positive.

The interior harmonic-mean branch is entered only when $d_{k-1}d_k>0$. Thus both secants are nonzero and have the same sign; the weights $w_1=2h_k+h_{k-1}$ and $w_2=h_k+2h_{k-1}$ are positive. The two terms $w_1/d_{k-1}$ and $w_2/d_k$ therefore have that same nonzero sign, so their sum is nonzero and finite. The endpoint clip and cap branches only compare finite real quantities and introduce no division. Hence every output slope is defined and finite.

derivations.claim: At an interior node $k$ whose adjacent secants have nonpositive product, [F1] sets $m_k=0$. If their product is positive, write $r=d_k/d_{k-1}>0$ and $W=w_1+w_2=3(h_{k-1}+h_k)$. Dividing instead by $d_{k-1}$ gives $m_k/d_{k-1}=W/(w_1+w_2/r)\le W/w_1\le3$, since $w_1=2h_k+h_{k-1}\ge h_k+h_{k-1}$.

For a nonzero first secant, put $q=d_1/d_0$. The raw endpoint ratio is $\widehat m_0/d_0=1+\frac{h_0}{h_0+h_1}(1-q)$. If $q\ge0$, this ratio is at most $1+h_0/(h_0+h_1)<2$; clipping makes it zero if it is nonpositive. If $q<0$, the ratio is greater than $1$, and the cap branch reduces it to $3$ exactly when it exceeds $3$. Thus the final ratio is in $[0,3]$. If $d_0=0$, the raw endpoint value is either zero or has sign different from $d_0$, so the clip sets it to zero. The reflected argument proves the same bound at the right endpoint.

For two nodes both selected slopes equal $d_0$, so they are zero when $d_0=0$ and their ratios to $d_0$ are $1$ otherwise. For $n\ge3$, if $d_i=0$, its interior endpoint slopes are set to zero by the nonpositive-product branch, and a first or last endpoint slope is zero by the clip rule. If $d_i\ne0$, each of its endpoint slopes is either an interior slope covered by step 1.1 or an endpoint slope covered by step 1.2. These cases prove both alternatives in the statement.

For $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, continuity at $x\in[a,b]$ means that for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that
$|f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $t\in[a,b]$ and $|t-x|<\delta$.
Differentiability at an interior point $c$ means that the two-sided limit
$$
f'(c)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}
$$
exists in the real field; differentiability on $(a,b)$ means this holds at
every interior point. For higher derivatives, define recursively
$f^{(j+1)}=(f^{(j)})'$ on the points where the derivative exists. The class
$C^{n+1}$ on an open interval means that these derivatives through order
$n+1$ exist and are continuous there.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the segment between $c$ and $x$, and put
$$
P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(x-c)^j.
$$
Then
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac1{n!}\int_c^x f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\,dt.
$$
If $M\ge0$ and $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $c$ and $x$, then
$$
|f(x)-P_n(x)|\le\frac{M|x-c|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.
$$
The formula and bound include $x=c$ and oriented endpoints.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $f$ is **bounded on $K$**: there is a real
$M \ge 0$ with

$$|f(x)| \le M \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, $f[K]$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-bounded-set]]).

**The hypothesis is compactness of $K$, not of $A$**, and it cannot be relaxed
to boundedness of $K$ or to closedness of $K$ alone: the identity is unbounded
on the closed set $[0,\infty)$, and $x \mapsto 1/x$ is unbounded on the bounded
set $(0,1)$. The general statement of that is
[[thm-compactness-is-necessary-for-evt-and-uniform-continuity]], later on this
page.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.

set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

derivations.claim: By [F3], $f'$ is continuous. It cannot take both a positive and a negative value on $[a,b]$, since [F5] would then give a zero of $f'$, contradicting $|f'|\ge c$. Thus $f'$ has one sign throughout. On each grid cell [F4] gives $d_j=f'(\xi_j)$ for some interior $\xi_j$, so all secants have that sign and $|d_j|\ge c$. Since $a<b$ and $h=(b-a)/N>0$, the grid is admissible for [F1], and [F8] makes $[a,b]$ compact. Since $f'$, $f''$, and $f'''$ are continuous by [F3], [F7] supplies $M_1,M_2,M_3\ge0$ with $|f'|\le M_1$, $|f''|\le M_2$, and $|f'''|\le M_3$ on $[a,b]$.

Fix an interior node $x_k$ and set $s=f'(x_k)$ and $q=f''(x_k)$. Applying [F6] with degree two at $x_k$ to $x_k-h$ and $x_k+h$ and dividing the remainders by $h$ gives $d_{k-1}=s-hq/2+e_-$ and $d_k=s+hq/2+e_+$, where $|e_-|,|e_+|\le M_3h^2/6$. Since $|s|\ge c$, for sufficiently small $h$ both secants stay bounded away from zero. The identity $1/(s+u)=1/s-u/s^2+u^2/(s^2(s+u))$ then gives, with a uniform constant, $1/d_{k-1}=1/s+hq/(2s^2)+O(h^2)$ and $1/d_k=1/s-hq/(2s^2)+O(h^2)$.

On a uniform grid the two weights in [F1] are both $3h$, so the interior slope equals $2/(1/d_{k-1}+1/d_k)$. The first-order terms in step 1.2 cancel, giving $1/d_{k-1}+1/d_k=2/s+O(h^2)$. Since $|s|\le M_1$, the leading term has magnitude at least $2/M_1$; thus the denominator stays bounded away from zero for sufficiently small $h$, and its reciprocal yields $m_k=s+O(h^2)$ with a constant uniform in $k$.

At the left endpoint, [F6] at $a$ gives $d_0=f'(a)+hf''(a)/2+O(M_3h^2)$ and $d_1=f'(a)+3hf''(a)/2+O(M_3h^2)$, by expanding $f(a+h)$ and $f(a+2h)$. Therefore the raw endpoint estimate in [F1] is $\widehat m_0=(3d_0-d_1)/2=f'(a)+O(M_3h^2)$. For small $h$ it has the sign of $f'(a)$; step 1.1 gives that same sign for $d_0,d_1$, so neither the sign clip nor the opposite-sign cap changes it. Reflecting the expansions at $b$ gives the identical $O(h^2)$ error for $m_N$.

The interior and endpoint estimates above use the bounds $M_1,M_2,M_3$ and $c^{-1}$ on the fixed interval; their constants and smallness thresholds are therefore uniform in the node index. Taking a common maximum for the error constants and a common positive minimum for the thresholds gives $C,h_0$ valid at every interior node and both endpoints. The finite list $|m_j-f'(x_j)|$, $0\le j\le N$, has a maximum by [F9], and the uniform pointwise estimate bounds it by $Ch^2$.

**Inputs:** An integer $n\ge2$, strictly increasing real nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{n-1}$, and real values $y_0,\ldots,y_{n-1}$. All operations here are over the real numbers.

**Output:** Slopes $m_0,\ldots,m_{n-1}$ and the piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant determined by these nodes, values, and slopes under [[def-piecewise-cubic-hermite-interpolant]].

Put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$ and $d_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/h_i$ for $0\le i<n-1$. Write $\operatorname{sgn}(r)\in\{-1,0,1\}$ for the sign of a real number.

- If $n=2$, set $m_0=m_1=d_0$.
- If $n\ge3$, for each interior node $1\le k\le n-2$, set $m_k=0$ when $d_{k-1}d_k\le0$. When $d_{k-1}d_k>0$, put $w_1=2h_k+h_{k-1}$, $w_2=h_k+2h_{k-1}$, and
  $$m_k=\frac{w_1+w_2}{w_1/d_{k-1}+w_2/d_k}.$$
- For $n\ge3$, at the left endpoint compute
  $$\widehat m_0=\frac{(2h_0+h_1)d_0-h_0d_1}{h_0+h_1}.$$
  Set $m_0=0$ if $\operatorname{sgn}(\widehat m_0)\ne\operatorname{sgn}(d_0)$. Otherwise set $m_0=3d_0$ if $d_0d_1<0$ and $|\widehat m_0|>3|d_0|$; in all remaining cases set $m_0=\widehat m_0$.
- For $n\ge3$, at the right endpoint compute
  $$\widehat m_{n-1}=\frac{(2h_{n-2}+h_{n-3})d_{n-2}-h_{n-2}d_{n-3}}{h_{n-2}+h_{n-3}}.$$
  Apply the preceding clip and cap rule with $d_0,d_1$ replaced by $d_{n-2},d_{n-3}$ and $m_0,\widehat m_0$ replaced by $m_{n-1},\widehat m_{n-1}$.

For $n\ge3$, the algorithm returns the Hermite pieces from the stated values and selected slopes. The two-node branch is the line through the two input points.
For every admissible input to [[alg-pchip-slope-selection]], each branch is defined over $\mathbb R$ and every selected slope is finite; in particular, the algorithm never divides by zero.

For the data in [[def-piecewise-cubic-hermite-interpolant]], each piece has the prescribed endpoint values and slopes: $P_i(x_i)=y_i$, $P_i(x_{i+1})=y_{i+1}$, $P_i'(x_i)=m_i$, and $P_i'(x_{i+1})=m_{i+1}$. The resulting interpolant is $C^1$ on $[x_0,x_N]$ (with the corresponding one-sided derivatives at the endpoints). On a single interval, if the four prescribed endpoint data are the values and derivatives of a polynomial $q$ of degree at most three, then $P_i=q$ on that interval.

Let $p$ be the single Hermite piece from [[def-piecewise-cubic-hermite-interpolant]] on $[x_0,x_1]$, with $h=x_1-x_0>0$, endpoint values $y_0,y_1$, slopes $m_0,m_1$, and secant $d=(y_1-y_0)/h$. If $d\ne0$ and $\alpha=m_0/d$, $\beta=m_1/d$ both lie in $[0,3]$, then $p$ is monotone from $y_0$ to $y_1$ and stays between those values. If $d=0$ and $m_0=m_1=0$, then $p$ is constant.

For any input to [[alg-pchip-slope-selection]], consider an interval with secant $d_i$. If $d_i=0$, the selected slopes at both endpoints of that interval are zero. If $d_i\ne0$, then $m_i/d_i$ and $m_{i+1}/d_i$ both belong to $[0,3]$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], the algorithm defines one finite slope at each input node. Its output consists of Hermite pieces sharing the same value and selected slope at each common node, so [F3] gives interpolation and $C^1$ matching.
Fix a cell with $d_i\ne0$. By [F5], both slopes normalized by $d_i$ lie in $[0,3]$; [F4] therefore makes this piece monotone from $y_i$ to $y_{i+1}$ and keeps it between those values.

If $d_i=0$, [F5] gives zero slopes at both endpoints, and [F4] makes that Hermite piece constant at its common endpoint value. For nondecreasing input, every $d_i\ge0$, so each nonflat cell is nondecreasing by step 1.2, the flat cells are constant by the calculation above, and the pieces agree at nodes by step 1.1; concatenating the cells gives a nondecreasing function. The nonincreasing case is identical with all inequalities reversed.

**Inputs:** An integer $n\ge2$, strictly increasing real nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{n-1}$, and real values $y_0,\ldots,y_{n-1}$. All operations here are over the real numbers.

**Output:** Slopes $m_0,\ldots,m_{n-1}$ and the piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant determined by these nodes, values, and slopes under [[def-piecewise-cubic-hermite-interpolant]].

Put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$ and $d_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/h_i$ for $0\le i<n-1$. Write $\operatorname{sgn}(r)\in\{-1,0,1\}$ for the sign of a real number.

- If $n=2$, set $m_0=m_1=d_0$.
- If $n\ge3$, for each interior node $1\le k\le n-2$, set $m_k=0$ when $d_{k-1}d_k\le0$. When $d_{k-1}d_k>0$, put $w_1=2h_k+h_{k-1}$, $w_2=h_k+2h_{k-1}$, and
  $$m_k=\frac{w_1+w_2}{w_1/d_{k-1}+w_2/d_k}.$$
- For $n\ge3$, at the left endpoint compute
  $$\widehat m_0=\frac{(2h_0+h_1)d_0-h_0d_1}{h_0+h_1}.$$
  Set $m_0=0$ if $\operatorname{sgn}(\widehat m_0)\ne\operatorname{sgn}(d_0)$. Otherwise set $m_0=3d_0$ if $d_0d_1<0$ and $|\widehat m_0|>3|d_0|$; in all remaining cases set $m_0=\widehat m_0$.
- For $n\ge3$, at the right endpoint compute
  $$\widehat m_{n-1}=\frac{(2h_{n-2}+h_{n-3})d_{n-2}-h_{n-2}d_{n-3}}{h_{n-2}+h_{n-3}}.$$
  Apply the preceding clip and cap rule with $d_0,d_1$ replaced by $d_{n-2},d_{n-3}$ and $m_0,\widehat m_0$ replaced by $m_{n-1},\widehat m_{n-1}$.

For $n\ge3$, the algorithm returns the Hermite pieces from the stated values and selected slopes. The two-node branch is the line through the two input points.
For every admissible input to [[alg-pchip-slope-selection]], each branch is defined over $\mathbb R$ and every selected slope is finite; in particular, the algorithm never divides by zero.

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, let $x_0<\cdots<x_N$ be real nodes, let $y_0,\ldots,y_N\in\mathbb R$ be values, and let $m_0,\ldots,m_N\in\mathbb R$ be prescribed slopes. For $0\le i<N$ put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$ and $t=(x-x_i)/h_i$ on $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$. Define
$$H_{00}(t)=2t^3-3t^2+1,\quad H_{01}(t)=-2t^3+3t^2,\quad H_{10}(t)=t^3-2t^2+t,\quad H_{11}(t)=t^3-t^2.$$
The cubic Hermite piece on $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ is
$$P_i(x)=y_iH_{00}(t)+y_{i+1}H_{01}(t)+h_im_iH_{10}(t)+h_im_{i+1}H_{11}(t).$$
The piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant is the function whose restriction to each such interval is $P_i$; adjacent pieces use their common prescribed value $y_i$ at a shared node. The slopes $m_i$ are input data, not values inferred from neighboring pieces.

For the data in [[def-piecewise-cubic-hermite-interpolant]], each piece has the prescribed endpoint values and slopes: $P_i(x_i)=y_i$, $P_i(x_{i+1})=y_{i+1}$, $P_i'(x_i)=m_i$, and $P_i'(x_{i+1})=m_{i+1}$. The resulting interpolant is $C^1$ on $[x_0,x_N]$ (with the corresponding one-sided derivatives at the endpoints). On a single interval, if the four prescribed endpoint data are the values and derivatives of a polynomial $q$ of degree at most three, then $P_i=q$ on that interval.

Let $a<b$, let $f$ be $C^3$ on an open interval containing $[a,b]$, and suppose $|f'(x)|\ge c>0$ for every $x\in[a,b]$. For an integer $N\ge2$, put $h=(b-a)/N>0$ and $x_j=a+jh$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. Let $m_j$ be the slopes selected by [[alg-pchip-slope-selection]] from the values $f(x_j)$. There are constants $C,h_0>0$, depending on $f$, $c$, and $[a,b]$, such that for every such grid with $h<h_0$,
$$\max_{0\le j\le N}|m_j-f'(x_j)|\le Ch^2.$$

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the segment between $c$ and $x$, and put
$$
P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(x-c)^j.
$$
Then
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac1{n!}\int_c^x f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\,dt.
$$
If $M\ge0$ and $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $c$ and $x$, then
$$
|f(x)-P_n(x)|\le\frac{M|x-c|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.
$$
The formula and bound include $x=c$ and oriented endpoints.

For $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, continuity at $x\in[a,b]$ means that for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that
$|f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $t\in[a,b]$ and $|t-x|<\delta$.
Differentiability at an interior point $c$ means that the two-sided limit
$$
f'(c)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}
$$
exists in the real field; differentiability on $(a,b)$ means this holds at
every interior point. For higher derivatives, define recursively
$f^{(j+1)}=(f^{(j)})'$ on the points where the derivative exists. The class
$C^{n+1}$ on an open interval means that these derivatives through order
$n+1$ exist and are continuous there.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $f$ is **bounded on $K$**: there is a real
$M \ge 0$ with

$$|f(x)| \le M \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, $f[K]$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-bounded-set]]).

**The hypothesis is compactness of $K$, not of $A$**, and it cannot be relaxed
to boundedness of $K$ or to closedness of $K$ alone: the identity is unbounded
on the closed set $[0,\infty)$, and $x \mapsto 1/x$ is unbounded on the bounded
set $(0,1)$. The general statement of that is
[[thm-compactness-is-necessary-for-evt-and-uniform-continuity]], later on this
page.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

For real $x,y$, $|xy|=|x||y|$ and $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$. For complex
$z,w$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$, and if $w\ne0$ then
$|z/w|=|z|/|w|$.

derivations.claim: Since $a<b$ and $h=(b-a)/N>0$, the grid is admissible and $[a,b]$ is compact by [F9]. By [F7] and [F8], choose $M\ge0$ with $|f'''|\le M$ on $[a,b]$. Fix a cell $[x_i,x_i+h]$ and let $T_2$ be the degree-two Taylor polynomial of $f$ at $x_i$. By [F6], the residual $r=f-T_2$ satisfies $r(x_i)=r'(x_i)=0$ and, for every $x\in[x_i,x_i+h]$, $|r(x)|\le Mh^3/6$; at the right endpoint it also satisfies $|r(x_i+h)|\le Mh^3/6$ and $|r'(x_i+h)|\le Mh^2/2$. The derivative bound is [F6] applied to $f'$ with degree one.

Let $H$ be the exact-derivative Hermite piece for $f$ on this cell. The PCHIP piece $P_h$ and $H$ have identical endpoint values. By [F3], their difference is $h(m_i-f'(x_i))H_{10}(t)+h(m_{i+1}-f'(x_i+h))H_{11}(t)$. Since [F2] guarantees these PCHIP slopes are defined and $|H_{10}(t)|=t(1-t)^2\le1$, $|H_{11}(t)|\le1$, [F5] gives $|P_h(x)-H(x)|\le2C_sh^3$ for every $x$ in the cell.

For this exact-derivative Hermite piece $H$, linearity of the formula [F3] and reproduction [F4] give $H=T_2+H_r$, where $H_r(t)=r(x_i+h)H_{01}(t)+hr'(x_i+h)H_{11}(t)$. On $0\le t\le1$, $|H_{01}(t)|=t^2(3-2t)\le1$ and $|H_{11}(t)|=t^2(1-t)\le1$, so $|H_r(t)|\le(1/6+1/2)Mh^3=2Mh^3/3$. Together with $|r(x)|\le Mh^3/6$ from step 1.1, this yields $|H(x)-f(x)|\le5Mh^3/6$ for every $x$ in the cell.

Combining steps 2.1 and 1.2 gives $|P_h(x)-f(x)|\le(5M/6+2C_s)h^3$ for every $x\in[a,b]$, since the cells cover the interval. The constants do not depend on $i$ or $N$; put $C=5M/6+2C_s$. To justify the maximum in the statement, admissibility of the grid for [F1] gives $x_0<\cdots<x_N$, so $a<b$. By [F4], $P_h$ is $C^1$ and hence continuous on $[a,b]$; by [F7], $f$ is continuous there. Set $E(x)=|P_h(x)-f(x)|$. For $x,z\in[a,b]$, applying the triangle inequality twice gives $\bigl||P_h(x)-f(x)|-|P_h(z)-f(z)|\bigr|\le |(P_h(x)-f(x))-(P_h(z)-f(z))|\le |P_h(x)-P_h(z)|+|f(x)-f(z)|$, so $E$ is continuous on $[a,b]$. By [F9], $[a,b]$ is compact, and it is nonempty; [F10] therefore gives a point where $E$ attains its maximum. The pointwise bound just proved bounds that maximum by $Ch^3$.

Let $s\ge1$ be an integer and let $a=x_0<\cdots<x_s=b$ be a finite partition, and on each cell $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ choose an integer degree $n_i\ge0$ and real controls $c_{i,0},\ldots,c_{i,n_i}$. For $t=(x-x_i)/(x_{i+1}-x_i)\in[0,1]$, define the Bernstein basis polynomial
$$B_{k,n_i}(t)=\iota\binom{n_i}{k}t^k(1-t)^{n_i-k},\qquad 0\le k\le n_i,$$
where $\binom{n_i}{k}$ is the natural binomial coefficient from [[def-binomial-coefficient]], $\iota$ is the canonical embedding of [[def-canonical-natural]] into $\mathbb R$, and finite sums use [[def-finite-sum]]. The cell polynomial is $p_i(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n_i}c_{i,k}B_{k,n_i}(t)$. These cell polynomials form a piecewise Bernstein representation. To require continuity at a shared node, impose the additional endpoint-control condition $c_{i,n_i}=c_{i+1,0}$; continuity is not part of the representation unless that condition is imposed.

For degree two this formula reads $p_i(x)=c_{i,0}(1-t)^2+\iota\binom21\,c_{i,1}t(1-t)+c_{i,2}t^2$.

On each cell of a representation from [[def-piecewise-bernstein-representation]], the polynomial value lies between the minimum and maximum of that cell's controls. In particular, nonnegative controls imply a nonnegative polynomial throughout the cell. If every cell has nonnegative controls and adjacent endpoint controls agree, the piecewise function is continuous and nonnegative on the entire partition. This is a control-value guarantee; positivity at a finite set of sample nodes alone is not among the hypotheses.

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put

$$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$

the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite
([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes
sense for every subset.

**$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by
[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies.

**$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be
a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries
$[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$
onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport
clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its
two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a
bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same
cardinality.

**Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set

$$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$,

$$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$

**$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is
*not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence
lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a
theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a
count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove.

**Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.**

- $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of
  cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$
  ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a
  one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved.
- $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$
  then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$.
- $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has
  $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$
  ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]).
- $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one
  $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so
  $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$.
- $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, both instances of the
  above.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[thm-recursion]]):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

citations.quote: Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval and let $a\le t_1<\cdots<t_r\le b$ with $r\ge2$. A natural cubic spline with knots $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ is a $C^2$ function on $[a,b]$ that is a polynomial of degree at most three on every $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, has second derivative zero at $t_1$ and $t_r$, and is extended linearly on $[a,t_1]$ and $[t_r,b]$ when those intervals are nonempty. The knots $t_j$ are the distinct breakpoints; repeated observations at the same input do not create additional knots.

**Inputs:** An integer $n\ge2$, strictly increasing real nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{n-1}$, and real values $y_0,\ldots,y_{n-1}$. All operations here are over the real numbers.

**Output:** Slopes $m_0,\ldots,m_{n-1}$ and the piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant determined by these nodes, values, and slopes under [[def-piecewise-cubic-hermite-interpolant]].

Put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$ and $d_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/h_i$ for $0\le i<n-1$. Write $\operatorname{sgn}(r)\in\{-1,0,1\}$ for the sign of a real number.

- If $n=2$, set $m_0=m_1=d_0$.
- If $n\ge3$, for each interior node $1\le k\le n-2$, set $m_k=0$ when $d_{k-1}d_k\le0$. When $d_{k-1}d_k>0$, put $w_1=2h_k+h_{k-1}$, $w_2=h_k+2h_{k-1}$, and
  $$m_k=\frac{w_1+w_2}{w_1/d_{k-1}+w_2/d_k}.$$
- For $n\ge3$, at the left endpoint compute
  $$\widehat m_0=\frac{(2h_0+h_1)d_0-h_0d_1}{h_0+h_1}.$$
  Set $m_0=0$ if $\operatorname{sgn}(\widehat m_0)\ne\operatorname{sgn}(d_0)$. Otherwise set $m_0=3d_0$ if $d_0d_1<0$ and $|\widehat m_0|>3|d_0|$; in all remaining cases set $m_0=\widehat m_0$.
- For $n\ge3$, at the right endpoint compute
  $$\widehat m_{n-1}=\frac{(2h_{n-2}+h_{n-3})d_{n-2}-h_{n-2}d_{n-3}}{h_{n-2}+h_{n-3}}.$$
  Apply the preceding clip and cap rule with $d_0,d_1$ replaced by $d_{n-2},d_{n-3}$ and $m_0,\widehat m_0$ replaced by $m_{n-1},\widehat m_{n-1}$.

For $n\ge3$, the algorithm returns the Hermite pieces from the stated values and selected slopes. The two-node branch is the line through the two input points.

For every input to [[alg-pchip-slope-selection]], the resulting interpolant is $C^1$ and interpolates all input values. On each cell with nonzero secant $d_i$, the interpolant is monotone from $y_i$ to $y_{i+1}$ and stays between those endpoint values; on a cell with $d_i=0$ it is constant. In particular, if the input values are nondecreasing (respectively nonincreasing), the complete interpolant is nondecreasing (respectively nonincreasing). No $C^2$ matching is asserted.

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

derivations.claim: Each displayed piece has endpoint values $S_0(0)=1$, $S_0(1)=0$, $S_1(0)=S_1(1)=0$, $S_2(0)=0$, and $S_2(1)=1$, so the pieces interpolate the given table. By [F4], their first derivatives are $S_0'=-6/5+3t^2/5$, $S_1'=-3/5+6t/5$, and $S_2'=3/5+6t/5-3t^2/5$; the derivative values match at both shared knots. Their second derivatives are $S_0''=6t/5$, $S_1''=6/5$, and $S_2''=6/5-6t/5$; these match at shared knots, and $S_0''(0)=S_2''(1)=0$. By [F1], this is a natural cubic spline.
For $0<t<1$, $S_1(t)=-3t(1-t)/5<0$, although every tabulated value is nonnegative. Thus the natural cubic spline undershoots the data range on the middle cell.

The secants are $d_0=-1$, $d_1=0$, and $d_2=1$. By [F2], the interior slopes at nodes $1$ and $2$ are both zero because each neighboring pair includes a zero secant; the Hermite piece joining the two zero values with zero slopes is constant zero. By [F3], the first and last PCHIP pieces remain between $1$ and $0$, and between $0$ and $1$, respectively. Hence PCHIP is nonnegative throughout the interval and does not reproduce the natural spline's undershoot.

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, let $x_0<\cdots<x_N$ be real nodes, let $y_0,\ldots,y_N\in\mathbb R$ be values, and let $m_0,\ldots,m_N\in\mathbb R$ be prescribed slopes. For $0\le i<N$ put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$ and $t=(x-x_i)/h_i$ on $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$. Define
$$H_{00}(t)=2t^3-3t^2+1,\quad H_{01}(t)=-2t^3+3t^2,\quad H_{10}(t)=t^3-2t^2+t,\quad H_{11}(t)=t^3-t^2.$$
The cubic Hermite piece on $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ is
$$P_i(x)=y_iH_{00}(t)+y_{i+1}H_{01}(t)+h_im_iH_{10}(t)+h_im_{i+1}H_{11}(t).$$
The piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant is the function whose restriction to each such interval is $P_i$; adjacent pieces use their common prescribed value $y_i$ at a shared node. The slopes $m_i$ are input data, not values inferred from neighboring pieces.

There are constants $C,h_0>0$, depending only on $f$, $c$, and $[a,b]$, such that for every such grid with $h<h_0$,
$$\max_{x\in[a,b]}|P_h(x)-f(x)|\le Ch^3.$$
The assertion is limited to uniform grids and intervals on which the derivative stays bounded away from zero; it makes no third-order claim at an extremum.

$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

derivations.claim: The secants on $[-2h,-h]$, $[-h,0]$, $[0,h]$, and $[h,2h]$ are $-3h$, $-h$, $h$, and $3h$. At $x=-h$, the equal-width weights are $3h,3h$, so [F1] gives $m(-h)=6h/(3h/(-3h)+3h/(-h))=-3h/2$. At $x=0$ the adjacent secants have opposite signs, so [F1] gives $m(0)=0$.
With $t=(x+h)/h$ on $[-h,0]$, [F2] gives $P_h(x)/h^2=H_{00}(t)-\frac32H_{10}(t)=1-\frac32t+\frac12t^3$, whereas $f(x)/h^2=(1-t)^2$. Therefore $(P_h(x)-f(x))/h^2=\frac12t(1-t)^2$.

On this cell, step 2.1 gives the error $E(x)=|P_h(x)-f(x)|=\frac{h^2}{2}t(1-t)^2$, since $0\le t\le1$. This expression is a polynomial in $x$ through $t=(x+h)/h$, so [F4] makes it differentiable, hence continuous, on the cell. As $h>0$, the interval $[-h,0]$ is nonempty and compact by [F5]; [F6] therefore gives an attained maximum of $E$ there. Since $t=1/3$ corresponds to a point of the cell and step 2.1 gives $E=2h^2/27$ at that point, the maximum is at least $2h^2/27$. Any uniform bound $|P_h-f|\le Ch^3$ on these grids with $C$ independent of $n$ would imply $2/27\le Ch=C/n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, which is impossible as $n\to\infty$. The hypothesis $|f'|\ge c>0$ in [F3] also fails because [F4] gives $f'(0)=0$.

Continuity and nonempty compactness justify the local maximum; a uniform Ch^3 bound implies 2/27<=C/n, impossible. f'(0)=0, so the earlier nonstationary theorem is not misapplied. The reader replaces the shrinking five-node interval by grids on one fixed domain, closing the nonfatal witness-quantifier gap in the original comparison with a theorem whose constants depend on [a,b]; the original local computation was already correct. No outside item consumes this example, no substantial prerequisite is missing, and no AC is used.

citations.quote:
Let $J\ge1$, $N=2^J$, and $x\in\mathbb R^N$, with the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Put $a^{(0)}=x$. For $r=1,\ldots,J$ and $0\le k<2^{J-r}$ define
$$a^{(r)}_k=\frac{a^{(r-1)}_{2k}+a^{(r-1)}_{2k+1}}{\sqrt2},\qquad d^{(r)}_k=\frac{a^{(r-1)}_{2k}-a^{(r-1)}_{2k+1}}{\sqrt2}.$$
The finite periodic Haar transform $T_Hx$ is the length-$N$ vector obtained by listing $a^{(J)}_0$, then $d^{(J)}_0$, then the entries of $d^{(J-1)}$, and continuing through $d^{(1)}$. The input is already of even dyadic length; this convention uses no padding and no endpoint extension.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: For any real $u,v$, the two outputs of one Haar pair satisfy $((u+v)/\sqrt2)^2+((u-v)/\sqrt2)^2=u^2+v^2$ by expansion and cancellation of the cross terms. Thus the pair map has matrix $2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ whose transpose times itself is the identity; applying it to disjoint coordinate pairs preserves the squared Euclidean norm.

At stage $r$, the approximation coordinates are replaced by their pair-map outputs, with the second outputs recorded as $d^{(r)}$ and the first outputs passed to stage $r+1$. Therefore the map from the original vector to all stored stage outputs is a composition of the orthogonal pair maps and a coordinate permutation. It is orthogonal; hence its transpose is its inverse and it preserves squared norm.

Let $L\ge1$, let $N$ be even with $N\ge2L$, and let $h=(h_0,\ldots,h_{L-1})\in\mathbb R^L$. Set $g_j=(-1)^j h_{L-1-j}$ for $0\le j<L$, and set $h_j=g_j=0$ for all other integers $j$. The pair $(h,g)$ is an admissible orthogonal filter pair when
$$\sum_jh_j=\sqrt2,\quad \sum_jg_j=0,\quad \sum_jh_jh_{j-2r}=\delta_{r0},\quad \sum_jg_jg_{j-2r}=\delta_{r0},\quad \sum_jh_jg_{j-2r}=0\quad(r\in\mathbb Z).$$
Here $\delta_{r0}=1$ for $r=0$ and $0$ for $r\ne0$.
For $x\in\mathbb R^N$, define
$$a_k=\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}h_jx_{(2k+j)\bmod N},\qquad d_k=\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}g_jx_{(2k+j)\bmod N}\qquad(0\le k<N/2).$$
This is the one-level periodic analysis map. It has no padding: the indices are reduced modulo $N$. Its matrix $W$ has the $N/2$ rows for $a_k$ followed by the $N/2$ rows for $d_k$. Synthesis is, by definition, multiplication by $W^T$. A multilevel transform repeats this one-level rule on the approximation vector while its current length $M$ is even and $M\ge2L$, then stops; the boundary convention at every level is periodic modulo that level's current length.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Fix row types $a,b\in\{h,g\}$ and row indices $k,\ell\in\{0,\ldots,N/2-1\}$. A coordinate can contribute to both rows only when $2k+j\equiv2\ell+r\pmod N$ for taps $j,r\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}$. Hence the row inner product is the sum of $a_jb_r$ over such pairs. The difference $j-r$ lies in $[-L+1,L-1]$, whose width is $2L-2<N$; so at most one representative of the congruence class modulo $N$ occurs. Since $N$ and $2(\ell-k)$ are even, that representative, when present, is $2s$ for an integer $s$. The inner product is therefore the filter correlation $\sum_j a_jb_{j-2s}$, which equals $1$ exactly for the same filter and $s=0$, and equals $0$ otherwise by [F1]. In the same-filter case $s=0$ forces $k=\ell$, because $k,\ell$ lie in a complete residue system modulo $N/2$. Thus the $N$ rows are orthonormal.

A square real matrix with orthonormal rows satisfies $WW^T=I_N$; hence it is invertible with inverse $W^T$, so also $W^TW=I_N$. It follows that $\|Wx\|_2^2=x^TW^TWx=\|x\|_2^2$. A multilevel transform is a composition of these one-level orthogonal maps and coordinate permutations; composing their transposes in reverse order gives its inverse and preserves norm.

derivations.claim: Write $r=\sqrt3$. Direct addition gives $\sum h_j=8/(4\sqrt2)=\sqrt2$. The numerator of $\sum g_j$ is $(1-r)-(3-r)+(3+r)-(1+r)=0$, and the numerator of $\sum jg_j$ is $-(3-r)+2(3+r)-3(1+r)=0$. Thus $g$ has the required zero sum and two vanishing moments.

With denominator $32$, the numerator of $\sum h_j^2$ is $(4+2r)+(12+6r)+(12-6r)+(4-2r)=32$, so the zero-shift autocorrelation is $1$. The only possible nonzero even-shift autocorrelation of a four-tap filter is at shift $2$ or $-2$; at shift $2$ its numerator is $(3-r)(1+r)+(1-r)(3+r)=2r-2r=0$, and the shift $-2$ sum is the same by reindexing. Reversal with alternating signs gives $\sum g_j^2=1$ and $\sum g_jg_{j-2}=h_3h_1+h_2h_0=0$.

For the cross-correlation $\sum_jh_jg_{j-2s}$, only $s=-1,0,1$ can have overlapping taps. These sums are respectively $h_0g_2+h_1g_3=h_0h_1-h_1h_0=0$, $h_0g_0+h_1g_1+h_2g_2+h_3g_3=0$ by pairwise cancellation, and $h_2g_0+h_3g_1=h_2h_3-h_3h_2=0$. For all other integers $s$ the supports do not overlap, so the sum is zero. Together with steps 1.1 and 1.2 this verifies every condition in [F2].

For an integer $J\ge0$, put $h=2^{-J}$ and $I_{J,k}=[kh,(k+1)h]$ for $0\le k<2^J$. For an integrable real function $f$ on $[0,1]$, its Haar cell-average projection is the piecewise constant function
$$P_Jf(x)=\frac1h\int_{I_{J,k}}f(t)\,dt\quad\text{when }x\in[kh,(k+1)h).$$
The value at $x=1$ is defined by the average on the last cell. The half-open intervals give an unambiguous partition for point values; changing endpoint values does not change the integrals or the $L^2$ error.

Let $q\ge1$ be an integer and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,1]$. A real function $f:U\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the smooth derivative-bound class $\mathcal S^q$ when it is $C^q$ on $U$ in the sense of [[def-continuity-and-derivative-on-real-interval]]. For $0\le r\le q$ define $M_r(f)=\sup_{0\le t\le1}|f^{(r)}(t)|$, with $f^{(0)}=f$. These derivative bounds are finite because the derivatives are continuous on the compact interval. They are bounds on the restriction to $[0,1]$, not a norm on arbitrary extensions to $U$; no claim that this class exhausts $W^{q,\infty}(0,1)$ is part of the definition.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the closed interval between $c$ and $x$, and define
$P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(c)(t-c)^j/j!$. If $x\ne c$, there is a point
$\xi$ strictly between $c$ and $x$ such that
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}(x-c)^{n+1}.
$$
For $x=c$, the remainder is zero.

derivations.claim: Fix one cell $I$ of length $h$ and put $\bar f_I=h^{-1}\int_If$. Expanding both sides gives $\int_I|f(x)-\bar f_I|^2\,dx=\frac1{2h}\int_I\int_I|f(x)-f(y)|^2\,dy\,dx,$ because each side equals $\int_If^2-h^{-1}(\int_If)^2$.
For $x,y\in I$, [F3] and [F2] give $|f(x)-f(y)|\le M_1|x-y|\le M_1h$. Hence the double integral in step 1.1 is at most $h^2M_1^2\cdot h^2$, so $\int_I|f-\bar f_I|^2\le h^3M_1^2/2$.
There are $1/h$ cells with disjoint interiors. Summing their squared errors gives $\|f-P_Jf\|_2^2\le h^2M_1^2/2$. Taking nonnegative square roots proves the stated bound.

Let $c\in\mathbb R^N$. For $m\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$, choose any set $S_m$ of $m$ indices whose absolute coefficients are among the $m$ largest, resolving ties arbitrarily. The hard m-term retention $H_m(c)$ has coordinate $c_i$ for $i\in S_m$ and $0$ otherwise. For a threshold $\lambda\ge0$, the soft-threshold vector $S_\lambda(c)$ has coordinates
$$S_\lambda(c)_i=\operatorname{sign}(c_i)(|c_i|-\lambda)_+,\qquad (t)_+=\max(t,0),$$
with $\operatorname{sign}(0)=0$. Soft thresholding shrinks retained coefficients; it is not defined by a prescribed number of retained terms.

derivations.claim: Since $U^TU=I_N$, $x=U^Tc$. Orthogonality gives $\|x-U^TP_Sc\|_2^2=\|U^T(c-P_Sc)\|_2^2=\|c-P_Sc\|_2^2=\sum_{i\notin S}|c_i|^2.$ This proves the exact discarded-tail identity.

Minimizing the tail is equivalent to maximizing $\sum_{i\in S}|c_i|^2$ among sets with at most $m$ indices. A maximizing set can include no zero coefficient while omitting a nonzero one; and if it includes $j$ while omitting $i$ with $|c_i|>|c_j|$, replacing $j$ by $i$ strictly increases that sum. Since the index set is finite, a maximizing set exists, and every set of $m$ largest absolute coefficients is maximizing; when fewer than $m$ coefficients are nonzero, adding zero coordinates changes no error. Let $V\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ be invertible and suppose there are constants $0<A\le B<\infty$ such that
$$A\|z\|_2^2\le\|Vz\|_2^2\le B\|z\|_2^2\quad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb R^N.$$
Call $V$ a finite Riesz synthesis matrix and call $A,B$ Riesz bounds. For a signal $x\in\mathbb R^N$, the analysis coefficients are $c=V^{-1}x$ and synthesis is $x=Vc$. The inverse analysis matrix and synthesis matrix form a biorthogonal coordinate pair; unless $A=B=1$, coefficient truncation errors need not equal Euclidean tail energy.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For an integer $J\ge3$, a coarse block $a=(a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3)$, a real $s>0$, and $p>0$, define the finite wavelet-coefficient Besov quasi-norm
$$\|(a,d)\|_{b^s_{p,p}(J)}^p=\sum_{\nu=0}^3|a_\nu|^p+\sum_{j=2}^{J-1}2^{jp(s+1/2-1/p)}\sum_{k=0}^{2^j-1}|d_{j,k}|^p.$$
This is the wavelet coefficient convention, with one coarse block and detail blocks indexed by their number $2^j$ of coefficients. At the critical relation $p=(s+1/2)^{-1}$, every scale weight equals $1$, so the quasi-norm is exactly the $\ell^p$ quasi-norm of the full coefficient vector. This finite coefficient definition does not assert equivalence with an intrinsic function-space Besov norm.

Let $U\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ satisfy $U^TU=UU^T=I_N$, let $x\in\mathbb R^N$, and set $c=Ux$. For any $S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ let $P_Sc$ retain exactly the coordinates in $S$. Then
$$\|x-U^TP_Sc\|_2^2=\sum_{i\notin S}|c_i|^2.$$
Consequently, for every $0\le m\le N$, $H_m(c)$ from [[def-na-hard-soft-coefficient-thresholding]] minimizes reconstruction error over all choices retaining at most $m$ coefficients. Its squared error is exactly the sum of the discarded squared coefficients.

derivations.claim: Since $s>0$, $p<2$, and [F1] gives $\sum_{n=1}^N|c_n|^p=\|c\|_{b^s_{p,p}(J)}^p$. Arrange the absolute coefficients in nonincreasing order $b_1\ge\cdots\ge b_N\ge0$. For each $n$, $n b_n^p\le\sum_{r=1}^n b_r^p\le\|c\|_{b^s_{p,p}(J)}^p$, so $b_n^2\le\|c\|_{b^s_{p,p}(J)}^2 n^{-2/p}$.

By [F2], the squared best m-term error is $\sum_{n=m+1}^N b_n^2$. Because $2/p>1$, the decreasing function $t^{-2/p}$ satisfies $\sum_{n=m+1}^N n^{-2/p}\le\int_m^\infty t^{-2/p}\,dt=\frac{p}{2-p}m^{1-2/p}.$ Combining this with step 1.1 and taking square roots gives a factor $m^{1/2-1/p}=m^{-s}$, since $1/p=s+1/2$. When $m=N$, the actual error is zero by retaining every coefficient, so the bound still holds.

citations.quote: Let $J\ge3$ and $N=2^J$. Starting with $a^{(0)}=x\in\mathbb R^N$, for $\ell=1,\ldots,J-2$ apply one-level periodic analysis with the D4 pair of [[def-na-daubechies-d4-filter]] to the current approximation vector $a^{(\ell-1)}$, whose length is $N/2^{\ell-1}\ge8$. Store the detail vector $d^{(\ell)}$ and set the next approximation to $a^{(\ell)}$. Stop with the length-four vector $a^{(J-2)}$. The output consists of that coarse vector and all detail vectors, ordered from coarsest details to finest. At every stage indices are reduced modulo that stage's current length; there is no padding or symmetric extension.

The pair $(h,g)$ in [[def-na-daubechies-d4-filter]] is admissible in [[def-na-periodic-orthogonal-compact-filter-dwt]]. In addition, $\sum_{j=0}^3j^rg_j=0$ for $r=0,1$, so the high-pass filter annihilates constant and affine data.

For every admissible pair $(h,g)$, every even $N\ge2L$, and every $x\in\mathbb R^N$, the analysis matrix $W$ in [[def-na-periodic-orthogonal-compact-filter-dwt]] is orthogonal. Thus synthesis $W^T$ is its inverse and $\|Wx\|_2^2=\|x\|_2^2$. Every multilevel transform defined there is also orthogonal, with inverse given by reversing the stages and applying each stage's transpose.

derivations.claim: Expanding the recursion shows that the detail row at stage $\ell$, translated to its first input index, has taps at indices $t=2^{\ell-1}r+\sum_{v=1}^{\ell-1}2^{v-1}s_v$, where each of $r,s_1,\ldots,s_{\ell-1}$ ranges over $\{0,1,2,3\}$; each tuple contributes $g_r\prod_{v=1}^{\ell-1}h_{s_v}$ at that index, and the effective coefficient at $t$ is the sum of these products over all tuples with that index. This follows by substituting the low-pass sum at each earlier stage into the current high-pass sum. The largest such index is $3(2^\ell-1)$, so the row is supported in at most $3(2^\ell-1)+1$ consecutive locations. Because $\ell\le J-2$, this number is $3\cdot2^\ell-2\le3\cdot2^{J-2}-2<N$, so the locations are distinct modulo $N$.

Regard the effective taps in step 1.1 before reducing their input positions modulo $N$. A low-pass stage maps an affine input sequence $p(n)=\alpha+\beta n$ to an affine sequence: $\sum_{s=0}^3h_sp(2k+s)=2\beta k\sum h_s+\alpha\sum h_s+\beta\sum s h_s$, which is affine in $k$. Repeating this argument keeps the coarse sequence affine. The next high-pass stage applied to an affine sequence $A+Bk$ gives $A\sum g_s+B(2k\sum g_s+\sum s g_s)=0$ by [F2]. Therefore the effective detail tap row has zero sum and zero first moment. After summing all tuple contributions at each lifted location, periodic reduction assigns the resulting effective coefficients to residues. Step 1.1 confines these locations to one interval of fewer than $N$ consecutive integers, so reduction modulo $N$ is injective on that interval and the row lifts back to the same interval.

By [F3], each row of the full multilevel analysis matrix has squared Euclidean norm $1$. If its support has $S$ locations with coefficients $z_1,\ldots,z_S$, then $(\sum_{i=1}^S|z_i|)^2\le S\sum_{i=1}^S|z_i|^2=S$, since $S\sum_i|z_i|^2-(\sum_i|z_i|)^2=\sum_{i<j}(|z_i|-|z_j|)^2\ge0$. Hence its $\ell^1$ norm is at most $\sqrt S$. The detail block at stage $\ell$ has the length of the current approximation after downsampling, namely $N/2^\ell=2^{J-\ell}$ rows. This and the affine cancellation from step 2.1 establish every clause of the Statement.

Let $q\ge1$ be an integer and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,1]$. A real function $f:U\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the smooth derivative-bound class $\mathcal S^q$ when it is $C^q$ on $U$ in the sense of [[def-continuity-and-derivative-on-real-interval]]. For $0\le r\le q$ define $M_r(f)=\sup_{0\le t\le1}|f^{(r)}(t)|$, with $f^{(0)}=f$. These derivative bounds are finite because the derivatives are continuous on the compact interval. They are bounds on the restriction to $[0,1]$, not a norm on arbitrary extensions to $U$; no claim that this class exhausts $W^{q,\infty}(0,1)$ is part of the definition.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the closed interval between $c$ and $x$, and define
$P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(c)(t-c)^j/j!$. If $x\ne c$, there is a point
$\xi$ strictly between $c$ and $x$ such that
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}(x-c)^{n+1}.
$$
For $x=c$, the remainder is zero.

The row's affine cancellation from [F1] removes the degree-one Taylor polynomial of $f$ at $c$ from the coefficient sum.
