Let $n\ge1$ and let $T_n=(t_{i-j})_{0\le i,j<n}$ be Hermitian positive definite, so $t_{-r}=\overline{t_r}$. For $0\le k\le n$, set $T_k=(t_{i-j})_{0\le i,j<k}$, with $T_0$ empty, and for $0\le k<n$ set $g_k=(t_1,\ldots,t_k)^T$, with $g_0$ empty. Define $\phi_0$ empty and $
u_0=t_0$. For each $0\le k\le n-2$, let $J_k$ reverse $k$ coordinates, put $c_k=J_k\overline{g_k}$, and set
$$\alpha_{k+1}:= rac{t_{k+1}-c_k^*\phi_k}{
u_k},\qquad \phi_{k+1}:= egin{pmatrix}\phi_k-J_k\overline{\phi_k}\,\alpha_{k+1}\ \alpha_{k+1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad 
u_{k+1}:=
u_k(1-|\alpha_{k+1}|^2).$$
Every denominator used is strictly positive; $T_k\phi_k=g_k$ and $
u_k=t_0-g_k^*\phi_k>0$ for $0\le k<n$. Computing through order $n-1$ takes $O(n^2)$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(n)$ working storage. This is the complex matrix-bordering extension; the real ACVF forecast procedure remains [[alg-durbin-levinson-forecast-recursion]].

**Input:** An integer $n\ge1$, a Hermitian Toeplitz lag list $(t_{-(n-1)},\ldots,t_{n-1})$ satisfying $t_{-r}=\overline{t_r}$, and a right-hand side $b\in\mathbb C^n$. The real covariance forecast procedure remains [[alg-durbin-levinson-forecast-recursion]]; this procedure solves a general Hermitian matrix equation with arbitrary $b$.

**Output:** Either a vector $x\in\mathbb C^n$ or one of the statuses invalid-input, nonpositive-pivot(k), or zero-gohberg-semencul-denominator.

1. Reject invalid-input if the lag list or right-hand side has the wrong length, or if the Hermitian lag equalities fail. Set $T_{ij}=t_{i-j}$.

   $$\alpha_{k+1}=(t_{k+1}-c_k^*\phi_k)/\nu_k,\qquad \phi_{k+1}=(\phi_k-J_k\overline{\phi_k}\,\alpha_{k+1},\,\alpha_{k+1})^T,\qquad \nu_{k+1}=\nu_k(1-|\alpha_{k+1}|^2).$$

3. With $\phi=\phi_{n-1}$ and $\nu=\nu_{n-1}$, form
   $$v=(-J_{n-1}\overline{\phi}/\nu,\ 1/\nu)^T,\qquad u=J_n\overline v.$$

4. Do not form dense triangular matrices. For any $a,y\in\mathbb C^n$, compute

For a Hermitian positive-definite input, [[lem-complex-hermitian-toeplitz-reflection-recursion]] gives positive reflection pivots, so $u_0=1/\nu_{n-1}>0$. The formula is the complex Hermitian extension; it makes no finite-precision stability claim.

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and

2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Put $g=(t_1,\ldots,t_{n-1})^T$, $c=J_{n-1}\overline g$, and $\phi=\phi_{n-1}$. Then $T_n= egin{pmatrix}T_{n-1}&c\c^*&t_0\end{pmatrix}$ and $T_{n-1}\phi=g$ by [F1]–[F2]. The reversal identity gives $T_{n-1}^{-1}c=J_{n-1}\overline\phi$. Moreover, $c^*T_{n-1}^{-1}c=g^T\overline\phi=\overline{g^*\phi}=g^*\phi$, because $T_{n-1}^*=T_{n-1}$ implies $(T_{n-1}^{-1})^*=(T_{n-1}^*)^{-1}=T_{n-1}^{-1}$. Thus the Schur complement is $t_0-c^*T_{n-1}^{-1}c=
u_{n-1}>0$. In $T_nv=e_{n-1}$, the top block equation gives $v_{0:n-2}=-T_{n-1}^{-1}c\,v_{n-1}=-J_{n-1}\overline\phi\,v_{n-1}$; substituting this in the last equation gives $
u_{n-1}v_{n-1}=1$. Hence $v= inom{-J_{n-1}\overline\phi/
u_{n-1}}{1/
u_{n-1}}$. Thus $v=T_n^{-1}e_{n-1}$.

Entrywise, $J_n\overline{T_n}J_n=T_n$ because $\overline{t_{j-i}}=t_{i-j}$. Also $X^*=(T_n^{-1})^*=(T_n^*)^{-1}=T_n^{-1}=X$. The first-column block equation $g u_0+T_{n-1}u_{1:n-1}=0$ gives $u_{1:n-1}=-u_0\phi$, and step 2.1 gives $v_{0:n-2}=-u_0J_{n-1}\overline\phi$.

Since the first row and column of $Z_n$ and $Z_n^*$ vanish, $D_{0j}=X_{0j}=\overline{u_j}$ and $D_{i0}=X_{i0}=u_i$; these are the corresponding first row and column of $(u u^*-(Z_nv)(Z_nv)^*)/u_0$. For $1\le i,j<n$, subtract $(T_nX)_{i-1,j-1}=I_{i-1,j-1}$ from $(T_nX)_{ij}=I_{ij}$. The identity entries agree because $i=j$ exactly when $i-1=j-1$. The right side in step 4.1 is $-g\,\overline{u_j}+(J_{n-1}\overline g)\,\overline{v_{j-1}}$. The shift is nilpotent, $Z_n^n=0$. Summing $Z_n^qD(Z_n^*)^q$ for $q=0,\ldots,n-1$ telescopes to $X-Z_n^nX(Z_n^*)^n=X$. Each triangular Toeplitz product in step 6.1 evaluates at most $n(n+1)/2$ products and a comparable number of additions; the four products therefore cost $O(n^2)$. For $N\ge1$, a vector $c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{N-1})^T\in\mathbb C^N$ generates the circulant matrix
$$C(c)_{ij}:=c_{(i-j)\bmod N}\qquad(0\le i,j<N).$$
For $n\ge1$ and $0\le j<n$, let $e_j\in\mathbb C^n$ be the coordinate vector with $(e_j)_i=1$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. For $a\in\mathbb C^n$, $J_na$ is the reversed vector, $(J_na)_i=a_{n-1-i}$; $J_0$ is the unique map on the empty vector. The canonical unitary DFT is the map $\mathcal F_N$ of [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]; the unnormalised DFT used for operation counts is $D_N:=\sqrt N\,\mathcal F_N$.

These conventions specify matrix orientation, conjugation, normalization, and boundary indexing; in particular, circulant eigenvalues below use the negative-sign canonical DFT.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ be the complex vector space of all functions $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-function-space]], [[def-vector-space]]). For $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ define the **unitary discrete Fourier transform** $\mathcal F_Nf:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ by

$$(\mathcal F_Nf)(k):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,e^{-2\pi ikx/N},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $[x]_N$ is the class of the integer $x$ in $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]], [[lem-congruence-is-an-equivalence-relation]]), $e^z=\exp z$ is the complex exponential ([[def-complex-exponential]]), and $N^{-1/2}$ is the rational power of the positive real $N$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]), read in $\mathbb C$ through the embedded copy of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).

**The summands depend only on classes, and the transform is periodic in $k$.** Each summand $f([x]_N)e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ is a complex number determined by the class $[x]_N$ and the integer $k$, and the classes $[0]_N,\dots,[N-1]_N$ are pairwise distinct and exhaust $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-standard-representatives-modulo-n]]); so the display is the finite sum, over the finite group, of the family $x\mapsto f(x)N^{-1/2}e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$, and reindexing by any other representative list leaves it unchanged ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], part 1). Reindexing by the transition $x\mapsto x+N$ uses $e^{-2\pi ik(x+N)/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ik}$ and $e^{-2\pi ik}=1$ for every integer $k$, because $-2\pi k\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). For periodicity in $k$, the same two facts give $e^{-2\pi i(k+N)x/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ix}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ for every integer $x$, so $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k+N)=(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Consequently $\mathcal F_Nf$ factors through the quotient $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and is a well-defined function on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, and $\mathcal F_N$ is a map $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$.

**Form in terms of characters.** Define $\chi_k([m]):=\exp(2\pi ikm/N)$ for $k,m\in\mathbb Z$. The assignment is well defined on classes because replacing $m$ by $m+N$ multiplies the exponential by $e^{2\pi ik}=1$ ([[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]); it is multiplicative, $\chi_k(x+y)=\chi_k(x)\chi_k(y)$, by the addition law ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]); and it takes values of modulus $1$, since $|\exp(i\theta)|=1$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). Thus the $\chi_k$ are characters of the finite group $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ (homomorphisms into the unit circle; no continuity is required on a discrete group), and the definition reads

$$(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z/N}f(x)\,\chi_{-k}(x),$$

with the positive-sign transform obtained by replacing $k$ with $-k$. This fixes the negative-sign, $N^{-1/2}$-normalised convention of the whole page: the forward transform carries the minus sign in the exponent and the factor $N^{-1/2}$, and the inverse transform of the inversion theorem carries the plus sign with the same factor. A different, unnormalised convention is introduced later on this page for the algorithmic part; the two are related by a single explicit rescaling recorded there.

**Linearity, recorded for later use.** For $a,b\in\mathbb C$ and $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ one has $\mathcal F_N(af+bg)=a\,\mathcal F_Nf+b\,\mathcal F_Ng$: the identity holds at each $k$ by distributivity in $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) and the elementary laws of finite sums over a fixed finite index set, which follow from the recursion clauses of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] by induction on an enumeration. Nothing else about $\mathcal F_N$ — unitarity, invertibility, the convolution law — is asserted here; those are proved in the items that follow.

Let $N\ge1$, $c\in\mathbb C^N$, and let $C(c)$ be the circulant of [[def-toeplitz-circulant-and-displacement-notation]]. Put
$$\lambda_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j e^{-2\pi i k j/N}=\sqrt N\,(\mathcal F_Nc)(k),\qquad 0\le k<N.$$
Then
$$C(c)=\mathcal F_N^{-1}\,\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_{N-1})\,\mathcal F_N.$$
Consequently, $C(c)$ is invertible exactly when every $\lambda_k\ne0$. For $b\in\mathbb C^N$, $C(c)x=b$ is solvable exactly when $(\mathcal F_Nb)(k)=0$ for every zero mode $\lambda_k=0$; on nonzero modes every solution has $(\mathcal F_Nx)(k)=(\mathcal F_Nb)(k)/\lambda_k$, while its zero-mode coordinates are free.

The square records the identity $\mathcal F_NC(c)=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)\mathcal F_N$; the two paths send each input vector to the same Fourier-coordinate vector. The proof below establishes this identity from the finite convolution sums.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}
\mathbb C^N \arrow[r,"C(c)"] \arrow[d,"\mathcal F_N"'] & \mathbb C^N \arrow[d,"\mathcal F_N"] \\
\mathbb C^N \arrow[r,"\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)"] & \mathbb C^N
\end{tikzcd}
```

The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

All vector and matrix indices below start at $0$. A rectangular Toeplitz matrix $T\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$, where $m,n\ge1$, is specified by lags $t_r\in\mathbb C$ for $-(n-1)\le r\le m-1$ and has entries
$$T_{ij}:=t_{i-j}\qquad(0\le i<m,\ 0\le j<n).$$
For a square matrix $T\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, Hermitian Toeplitz means $t_{-r}=\overline{t_r}$ for $0\le r<n$. It is positive definite when $x^*Tx>0$ for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb C^n$, where $x^*:=\overline{x}^{\,T}$ and the product is the matrix product of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]].

For $N\ge1$, a vector $c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{N-1})^T\in\mathbb C^N$ generates the circulant matrix
$$C(c)_{ij}:=c_{(i-j)\bmod N}\qquad(0\le i,j<N).$$
For $n\ge1$ and $0\le j<n$, let $e_j\in\mathbb C^n$ be the coordinate vector with $(e_j)_i=1$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. For $a\in\mathbb C^n$, $J_na$ is the reversed vector, $(J_na)_i=a_{n-1-i}$; $J_0$ is the unique map on the empty vector. The lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix of $a$ is $L(a)\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with $L(a)_{ij}=a_{i-j}$ when $i\ge j$, and $0$ otherwise. The canonical unitary DFT is the map $\mathcal F_N$ of [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]; the unnormalised DFT used for operation counts is $D_N:=\sqrt N\,\mathcal F_N$.

These conventions specify matrix orientation, conjugation, normalization, and boundary indexing; in particular, circulant eigenvalues below use the negative-sign canonical DFT.

**Input:** An integer $n\ge1$, a Hermitian Toeplitz lag list $(t_{-(n-1)},\ldots,t_{n-1})$ satisfying $t_{-r}=\overline{t_r}$, and a right-hand side $b\in\mathbb C^n$. All arithmetic in this definition is exact. The real covariance forecast procedure remains [[alg-durbin-levinson-forecast-recursion]]; this procedure solves a general Hermitian matrix equation with arbitrary $b$.

**Output:** Either a vector $x\in\mathbb C^n$ or one of the statuses invalid-input, nonpositive-pivot(k), or zero-gohberg-semencul-denominator.

1. Reject invalid-input if the lag list or right-hand side has the wrong length, or if the Hermitian lag equalities fail. Set $T_{ij}=t_{i-j}$.
2. If $t_0\le0$, return nonpositive-pivot(0). Initialize $\phi_0$ empty and $\nu_0=t_0$. For $k=0,\ldots,n-2$, form $g_k=(t_1,\ldots,t_k)^T$, $c_k=J_k\overline{g_k}$, and
   $$\alpha_{k+1}=(t_{k+1}-c_k^*\phi_k)/\nu_k,\qquad \phi_{k+1}=(\phi_k-J_k\overline{\phi_k}\,\alpha_{k+1},\,\alpha_{k+1})^T,\qquad \nu_{k+1}=\nu_k(1-|\alpha_{k+1}|^2).$$
   If a required $\nu_k$ is not positive, return nonpositive-pivot(k) before dividing; if a newly computed $\nu_{k+1}\le0$, return nonpositive-pivot(k+1).
3. With $\phi=\phi_{n-1}$ and $\nu=\nu_{n-1}$, form
   $$v=(-J_{n-1}\overline{\phi}/\nu,\ 1/\nu)^T,\qquad u=J_n\overline v.$$
   If $u_0=0$, return zero-gohberg-semencul-denominator.
4. Do not form dense triangular matrices. For any $a,y\in\mathbb C^n$, compute
   $$(L(a)y)_i=\sum_{j=0}^{i}a_{i-j}y_j,\qquad (L(a)^*y)_i=\sum_{j=i}^{n-1}\overline{a_{j-i}}y_j.$$
   Return

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real-valued stochastic process on one
probability space, so each $X_t$ is a real random variable and each finite
tuple has its pushforward law
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]).
We call $X$ a **time series** here because its index set is $\mathbb Z$.

The process is **strictly stationary** when for every integer $r\ge1$, every
$t_1,\ldots,t_r\in\mathbb Z$, and every shift $m\in\mathbb Z$,
$$\mathcal L(X_{t_1+m},\ldots,X_{t_r+m})=\mathcal L(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_r}).$$
This condition concerns the full finite-dimensional laws and imposes no moment
condition by itself.

The process is **weakly stationary** when $E[|X_t|^2]<\infty$ for every
$t\in\mathbb Z$, its mean $\mu:=E[X_t]$ is independent of $t$, and for every
$h\in\mathbb Z$ the covariance
$$\gamma(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t)$$
is independent of $t$. Expectation, variance, and covariance have the meanings
in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] and
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Strict stationarity alone therefore
does not supply the moment hypotheses needed for covariance or sample-mean
claims.

For a weakly stationary real process $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$, its
**autocovariance function** (ACVF) is
$$\gamma(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t),\qquad h\in\mathbb Z,$$
which is independent of $t$ by [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]].

For a finite data vector $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R$, where $n\ge1$, let
$$\bar x_n:=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n x_t.$$
Its **biased sample ACVF** is the zero-extended sequence on $\mathbb Z$ given by
$$\widehat\gamma_n(h):=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^{n-|h|}(x_{t+|h|}-\bar x_n)(x_t-\bar x_n),\qquad |h|<n,$$
and $\widehat\gamma_n(h):=0$ for $|h|\ge n$. The absolute lag makes
$\widehat\gamma_n(-h)=\widehat\gamma_n(h)$.

For comparison, define the **pair-count-normalized rescaling**
$$\widetilde\gamma_n(h):=\frac1{n-|h|}\sum_{t=1}^{n-|h|}(x_{t+|h|}-\bar x_n)(x_t-\bar x_n),\qquad |h|<n,$$
and set it to zero for $|h|\ge n$. Its denominator is positive on the stated
domain. The names specify the denominator convention; they assert no
unbiasedness formula.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

the autocovariance function of a weakly stationary real process. Set
$\gamma(-r)=\gamma(r)$. Require every leading covariance matrix
$\Gamma_k=(\gamma(i-j))_{i,j=1}^k$ to be positive definite for $1\le k\le m$.

**Output:** Coefficient vectors $\phi_k=(\phi_{k,1},\ldots,\phi_{k,k})^T$
and error-variance values $\nu_k$ for $1\le k\le m$.

**Instructions:** Set $\nu_0=\gamma(0)$,
$\kappa_1=\gamma(1)/\nu_0$, $\phi_{1,1}=\kappa_1$, and
$\nu_1=\nu_0(1-\kappa_1^2)$. For each $k=2,\ldots,m$, set
$\kappa_k=[\gamma(k)-\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\phi_{k-1,j}\gamma(k-j)]/\nu_{k-1}$,
$\phi_{k,j}=\phi_{k-1,j}-\kappa_k\phi_{k-1,k-j}$ for $1\le j<k$,
$\phi_{k,k}=\kappa_k$, and $\nu_k=\nu_{k-1}(1-\kappa_k^2)$.

assumption makes each division well-defined; this is proved in
[[thm-durbin-levinson-solves-the-prediction-equations]]. The procedure operates
on covariance input and makes no Gaussian or conditional-expectation claim.

   If $u_0=0$, return zero-gohberg-semencul-denominator.
4. Do not form dense triangular matrices. For any $a,y\in\mathbb C^n$, compute

derivations.claim: Centering and weak stationarity give $E[X_t]=0$ and $\gamma(0)=\operatorname{Var}(X_t)$ for every $t$. From the autoregression and innovation orthogonality, $$\gamma(0)=\operatorname{Var}(\tfrac12X_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t)=\tfrac14\gamma(0)+\tfrac34,$$ so $\gamma(0)=1$.

For the separate general-RHS solve, set $T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1\end{pmatrix}$ as in the Statement. For each nonzero $z\in\mathbb C^2$, $z^*Tz=|z_1+z_2/2|^2+3|z_2|^2/4>0$, so $T$ is Hermitian positive definite. Its first lag data are $t_0=1,t_1=1/2$, hence $\alpha_1=t_1/t_0=1/2$, $\phi_1=\alpha_1=1/2$, and $\nu_1=t_0(1-|\alpha_1|^2)=3/4$. The endpoint columns from [F5] are $$v=(-2/3,4/3)^T,\qquad u=J_2v=(4/3,-2/3)^T,\qquad u_0=4/3>0.$$ The lower triangular Toeplitz products are $$L(u)L(u)^*=\begin{pmatrix}16/9&-8/9\\-8/9&20/9\end{pmatrix},\qquad L(Z_2v)L(Z_2v)^*=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&4/9\end{pmatrix}.$$ Therefore the formula in [F5] gives $$T^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}4/3&-2/3\\-2/3&4/3\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^{-1}b=(2/3,2/3)^T.$$ Direct multiplication also verifies $T(2/3,2/3)^T=(1,1)^T$.

u_1=1(1-1/4)=3/4$. At order two, $$\kappa_2= rac{\gamma(2)-\phi_{1,1}\gamma(1)}{
u_1}= rac{1/4-(1/2)(1/2)}{3/4}=0,$$ so $\phi_2=(\phi_{1,1}-\kappa_2\phi_{1,1},\kappa_2)^T=(1/2,0)^T$ and $
u_2=
u_1(1-\kappa_2^2)=3/4$. By steps 1.1 and 2.1, $\Gamma_1=[1]$ and $\Gamma_2=T$. Step 1.2 proves $T$ Hermitian positive definite, so the real leading covariance blocks are positive definite; [F3] applies and [F4] identifies this vector as the unique prediction solution.

For $1\le k\le d$, the mode-$k$ unfolding $A_{(k)}$ has $n_k$ rows and $\prod_{j\ne k}n_j$ columns. derivations.claim: For a mode-$k$ unfolding, the map from a multi-index $(i_1,\ldots,i_d)$ to the matrix position consisting of row $i_k$ and the ordered tuple of all other indices is a bijection: the row and column tuple recover every original index exactly once. For a cut-$k$ unfolding, splitting the tuple into $(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and $(i_{k+1},\ldots,i_d)$ is also a bijection with the original multi-index set. $$ \operatorname{mlrank}(A)=\bigl(\operatorname{rank}A_{(1)},\ldots,\operatorname{rank}A_{(d)}\bigr). $$
If $U\in\mathbb F^{m\times n_k}$, the mode-$k$ product $A\times_k U$ is the tensor with mode-$k$ size $m$ and entries
$$ (A\times_k U)_{i_1,\ldots,i_{k-1},j,i_{k+1},\ldots,i_d} =\sum_{i_k=1}^{n_k}A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}U_{j,i_k}. $$
The product is bilinear in the entries; no conjugation is used in this tensor contraction.

A Tucker representation with mode ranks bounded by $r=(r_1,\ldots,r_d)$ is a factorization
$$ A=G\times_1 U_1\times_2\cdots\times_d U_d, $$
where $U_k\in\mathbb F^{n_k\times r_k}$ and $G\in\mathbb F^{r_1\times\cdots\times r_d}$. Separately, write
$$ \mathcal T_r=\{B\in\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}:\operatorname{rank}B_{(k)}\le r_k\text{ for each }k\} $$
for the multilinear-rank-bounded set used in approximation statements.
For tensors $A,B$ of the same finite shape, every mode unfolding and every cut unfolding preserves the Frobenius inner product and norm.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, where $m,n\ge1$, have a singular value decomposition
$$ A=\sum_{j=1}^{q}\sigma_j u_jv_j^*,\qquad \sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_q>0, $$
where $q=\operatorname{rank}(A)$. For an integer $k\ge0$, put
$$ A_k=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(k,q)}\sigma_j u_jv_j^*, \qquad \delta_k^2=\sum_{j=k+1}^{q}\sigma_j^2 $$
with an empty sum equal to zero. Then $\operatorname{rank}(A_k)\le k$, $\|A-A_k\|_F=\delta_k$, and every matrix $B$ with $\operatorname{rank}(B)\le k$ satisfies $\|A-B\|_F\ge\delta_k$.

derivations.claim: Let $P_k=U_kU_k^*$ be the orthogonal projection used in mode $k$, and let $\mathcal P_k$ denote its action on that mode. The projections $\mathcal P_k$ commute for distinct modes, since they act on different tensor indices. By [F4], $\widehat A=\mathcal P_1\cdots\mathcal P_dA$. The telescoping identity gives $A-\widehat A=\sum_{k=1}^d\mathcal P_1\cdots\mathcal P_{k-1}(I-\mathcal P_k)A$. For $k<\ell$, the $k$th summand lies in the kernel of $\mathcal P_k$, while the $\ell$th lies in its range. These summands are orthogonal, so their squared norms add.

Each $\mathcal P_j$ is an orthogonal projection and hence a contraction: its range and kernel are orthogonal, so applying it cannot increase the squared norm. Consequently, $\|A-\widehat A\|_F^2=\sum_{k=1}^d\|\mathcal P_1\cdots\mathcal P_{k-1}(I-\mathcal P_k)A\|_F^2\le\sum_{k=1}^d\|(I-\mathcal P_k)A\|_F^2$. By [F2], $\|(I-\mathcal P_k)A\|_F$ is the Frobenius error of truncating $A_{(k)}$ to rank $r_k$.

Fix any $B\in\mathcal T_r$. Its mode-$k$ unfolding has rank at most $r_k$ by [F1], so [F3] implies $\|(I-\mathcal P_k)A\|_F\le\|A_{(k)}-B_{(k)}\|_F=\|A-B\|_F$. Substitute this bound for each $k$ in step 2.1 to obtain $\|A-\widehat A\|_F^2\le d\|A-B\|_F^2$. Since it holds for every $B\in\mathcal T_r$, taking the infimum and square roots proves the claim.

Work in exact arithmetic over $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Inputs are a tensor $A\in\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}$, a proposed CP component count $R\in\mathbb N_0$, initial factor matrices $F_k\in\mathbb F^{n_k\times R}$, and a finite sweep budget $N_{\max}\in\mathbb N_0$. The objective is
$$ \Phi(F_1,\ldots,F_d)=\left\|A-\sum_{j=1}^{R}F_1(:,j)\otimes\cdots\otimes F_d(:,j)\right\|_F^2. $$
On every exit, return the tuple $(F_1,\ldots,F_d,\widehat A,\text{status})$, where
$$ \widehat A=\sum_{j=1}^{R}F_1(:,j)\otimes\cdots\otimes F_d(:,j) $$
is evaluated from the factor matrices as they stand at that exit. If $R=0$, return the empty factor matrices, the zero model, and status “rank-zero-model” immediately. If $N_{\max}=0$, return the current factors and model with status “budget-exhausted”. Otherwise, for each of at most $N_{\max}$ sweeps, visit modes $k=1,\ldots,d$ in that order. With the other factors fixed, form $Z_k$ whose rows are indexed by all tuples $(i_\ell)_{\ell\ne k}$ and whose column $j$ is
$$ (Z_k)_{(i_\ell)_{\ell\ne k},j}=\prod_{\ell\ne k}(F_\ell)_{i_\ell,j}. $$
The mode-$k$ unfolding model is $A_{(k)}\approx XZ_k^{\mathsf T}$. If $Z_k$ is not full column rank, halt and return the current factors and model with status “rank-deficient-design”; no factor has changed at this block. If it has full column rank, solve the equivalent adjoint problem
$$ \min_{Y\in\mathbb F^{R\times n_k}}\|A_{(k)}^*-\overline{Z_k}Y\|_F $$
and replace $F_k$ by $Y^*$. The matrix $\overline{Z_k}$ has full column rank, so the minimizer is unique by [[lem-full-column-rank-matrix-least-squares-solution]]. After each completed sweep, increment the sweep counter. Return the current factors and model with status “budget-exhausted” after the $N_{\max}$th completed sweep. This finite-budget procedure guarantees neither convergence nor a global best CP approximation.

Let $p,r,s\ge1$, let $M\in\mathbb F^{p\times r}$ have full column rank, and let $Y\in\mathbb F^{p\times s}$. Among all $W\in\mathbb F^{r\times s}$, the function $W\mapsto\|Y-MW\|_F$ has the unique minimizer
$$ W_*=(M^*M)^{-1}M^*Y. $$

Taking adjoints preserves the Frobenius norm and rewrites it as $\|A_{(k)}^*-\overline{Z_k}X^*\|_F^2$. Since $Z_k$ has full column rank, so does $\overline{Z_k}$; [F2] therefore makes the algorithm's update the unique minimizer of this block objective. The old factor is an admissible candidate, so the updated objective is at most the old one.

A rank-deficient-design branch stops before changing a factor, so the objective is identical before and after that branch. Every other executed update satisfies step 1.1; chaining these finitely many inequalities across any completed part of a sweep proves the objective is nonincreasing through all successful exact block updates. This asserts no convergence or global optimality.

For $A\in\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}$, its canonical polyadic rank (CP rank) is the least integer $R\ge0$ for which
$$ A=\sum_{q=1}^{R}a_q^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes a_q^{(d)},\qquad a_q^{(k)}\in\mathbb F^{n_k}. $$
The empty sum is zero, so the zero tensor has CP rank $0$. The coordinate expansion
$$ A=\sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{n_d} A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}\,e_{i_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_d}^{(d)} $$
shows that the set of admissible finite integers $R$ is nonempty. The well-ordering of $\mathbb N_0$ therefore makes the least such $R$ well-defined.

derivations.claim: Set $W=e_2\otimes e_1\otimes e_1+e_1\otimes e_2\otimes e_1+e_1\otimes e_1\otimes e_2$. It has an explicit three-term CP expression, so its CP rank is at most three. Its first-mode slices are $W_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $W_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. They are linearly independent, and $\det(xW_1+yW_2)=-x^2$.

Suppose $W$ had a two-term expression $a\otimes b\otimes c+a'\otimes b'\otimes c'$. The first-mode slices being independent forces $a,a'$ to be independent. If $b,b'$ or $c,c'$ were dependent, every linear combination of the two slices would have matrix rank at most one, so its determinant would vanish identically, contrary to $\det(xW_1+yW_2)=-x^2$. Thus both pairs are independent. For any $x,y$, the pencil slice is $(xa_1+ya_2)bc^{\mathsf T}+(xa'_1+ya'_2)b'c'^{\mathsf T}$. Its determinant is a nonzero constant times $(xa_1+ya_2)(xa'_1+ya'_2)$. Independence of $a,a'$ makes the two linear factors nonproportional, so this determinant has two distinct zero lines; it cannot equal $-x^2$, which vanishes on the repeated line $x=0$. This contradiction proves $\operatorname{rank}_{CP}(W)>2$, hence it is exactly three.

For every $\varepsilon>0$, define $W_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{-1}\bigl((e_1+\varepsilon e_2)^{\otimes3}-e_1^{\otimes3}\bigr)$. This is a difference of two elementary tensors, with the scalar absorbed into one factor, so its CP rank is at most two. Expanding gives $W_\varepsilon=W+\varepsilon(e_2\otimes e_2\otimes e_1+e_2\otimes e_1\otimes e_2+e_1\otimes e_2\otimes e_2)+\varepsilon^2e_2^{\otimes3}$, so $\|W_\varepsilon-W\|_F\to0$. Thus the infimal rank-two approximation error is zero. Since step 2.1 shows $W$ itself has rank three, no rank-at-most-two tensor attains that infimum.

Fix a field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, an integer $d\ge2$, and positive integers $n_1,\ldots,n_d$. A finite order-$d$ tensor of shape $(n_1,\ldots,n_d)$ is an array $A=(A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d})$ indexed by $1\le i_k\le n_k$. Its Frobenius inner product and norm are
$$ \langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{n_d}\overline{A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}B_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}, \qquad \|A\|_F=\sqrt{\langle A,A\rangle_F}. $$
For a matrix, rank means the dimension of its column image and the Frobenius inner product is the same entrywise formula. The adjoint $M^*$ is conjugate transpose (transpose over $\mathbb R$).

For $1\le k\le d$, the mode-$k$ unfolding $A_{(k)}$ has $n_k$ rows and $\prod_{j\ne k}n_j$ columns. Its row index is $i_k$ and its column index is the remaining tuple in increasing mode order, lexicographically ordered. Its entry at that row and column is the corresponding entry of $A$. For $1\le k<d$, the cut-$k$ unfolding $A^{\langle k\rangle}$ has row tuple $(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and column tuple $(i_{k+1},\ldots,i_d)$, each lexicographically ordered. These conventions fix all reshapes used below.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}$ with $d\ge2$. A tensor-train (TT) representation consists of integers $r_0=r_d=1$, internal bond sizes $r_1,\ldots,r_{d-1}\in\mathbb N_0$, and cores
$$ G_k\in\mathbb F^{r_{k-1}\times n_k\times r_k}\quad(1\le k\le d) $$
such that
$$ A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d} =\sum_{\alpha_1=1}^{r_1}\cdots\sum_{\alpha_{d-1}=1}^{r_{d-1}} G_1(1,i_1,\alpha_1)G_2(\alpha_1,i_2,\alpha_2)\cdots G_d(\alpha_{d-1},i_d,1). $$
An empty bond index set gives an empty sum, hence the zero tensor; in particular, all internal bond sizes zero represent zero. A bond size $r_k$ is the storage dimension contracted between cores $k$ and $k+1$. The cut-$k$ unfolding groups modes $1,\ldots,k$ against $k+1,\ldots,d$ as fixed in [[def-finite-tensor-arrays-and-frobenius-inner-product]].

For an internal bond $k$, an invertible matrix $S\in\mathbb F^{r_k\times r_k}$ gives a gauge transformation by replacing the two adjacent cores with
$$ \widetilde G_k(\alpha,i,\beta)=\sum_{\gamma=1}^{r_k}G_k(\alpha,i,\gamma)S_{\gamma\beta}, \qquad \widetilde G_{k+1}(\beta,j,\eta)=\sum_{\gamma=1}^{r_k}(S^{-1})_{\beta\gamma}G_{k+1}(\gamma,j,\eta). $$
Their contraction is unchanged because $\sum_\beta S_{\gamma\beta}(S^{-1})_{\beta\gamma'}=\delta_{\gamma,\gamma'}$.

The left matricization of core $G_k$ has row index $(\alpha_{k-1},i_k)$ and column index $\alpha_k$. The core is left-isometric if this matrix $L_k$ satisfies $L_k^*L_k=I_{r_k}$. The right matricization has row index $\alpha_{k-1}$ and column index $(i_k,\alpha_k)$; the core is right-isometric if its matrix $R_k$ satisfies $R_kR_k^*=I_{r_{k-1}}$. A TT is in mixed canonical gauge about core $\ell$ when cores $k<\ell$ are left-isometric and cores $k>\ell$ are right-isometric.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}$, $d\ge2$, and let $A^{\langle k\rangle}$ denote its cut-$k$ unfolding. For sequential TT-SVD, let $r_k$ be its retained bond size and $\delta_k$ its discarded singular-value tail at cut $k$. For rounding, let the input TT represent $A$ and use the same notation for the output bond sizes and recorded tails. Then both procedures satisfy
$$ \|A-\widehat A\|_F^2\le\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}\delta_k^2. $$
If no positive singular value is discarded, the output is exactly $A$. In full-rank TT-SVD, $r_k=\operatorname{rank}(A^{\langle k\rangle})$ for every cut, and these are the minimal possible TT bond sizes among exact representations.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: Choose an SVD $A=U\Sigma V^*$ and put $D=\Sigma\Sigma^*$ and $R=U^*(I-P)U$. Then $D$ is diagonal positive semidefinite and $R$ is an orthogonal projector. By [F1]–[F3], $\|(I-P)A\|_2^2=\|RDR\|_2$ and $\|(I-P)(AA^*)^qA\|_2^2=\|RD^{2q+1}R\|_2$.

If $\lambda=\|RDR\|_2=0$, [step 1.1] gives $\|(I-P)A\|_2=0$, so the asserted inequality follows. If $\lambda>0$, choose a unit eigenvector $x$ for the top eigenvalue of $RDR$; then $Rx=x$ and $\lambda=x^*Dx=\sum_i d_i|x_i|^2$, with $d_i\ge0$. The weights $|x_i|^2$ sum to $1$, so [F4] for $t\mapsto t^{2q+1}$ gives $\lambda^{2q+1}\le\sum_i d_i^{2q+1}|x_i|^2=x^*D^{2q+1}x\le\|RD^{2q+1}R\|_2$.
Substitute $\lambda=\|(I-P)A\|_2^2$ from step 1.1 into step 2.1 and take the nonnegative $(2q+1)$st root. This yields the asserted inequality, also for $q=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice so that the repository's Lebesgue measure
on each positive-dimensional real coordinate space is a measure. A **standard
real Gaussian scalar** has Lebesgue density
$$\varphi_R(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}.$$
A **normalized complex Gaussian scalar** is $z=(x+iy)/\sqrt2$ for independent
standard real Gaussian scalars $x,y$; its density on $\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb
R^2$ is $\varphi_C(z)=\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $\mathbb E|z|^2=1$.

For $F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, an **iid standard Gaussian matrix** in
$F^{a\times b}$ has independent entries with the corresponding scalar law.
For $ab>0$, its expectations are finite-dimensional Lebesgue integrals
against the product density. If $a=0$ or $b=0$, the matrix space has one
element, the empty matrix; its law assigns that element probability one,
and the expectation of any function is its value there. Independence means
the product-density factorization, with this one-point convention for an
empty product.
The normalized complex convention is fixed throughout; it is not the
unnormalized law $x+iy$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $T$ be an orthogonal operator on
$\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean inner product
([[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for every
Lebesgue measurable $E$ and

$$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; \lambda_n(E).$$

Both the orientation-preserving operators, of determinant $1$, and those of
determinant $-1$ are covered, since only the absolute value of the determinant
enters; nothing is asserted here about which matrices occur in either class.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If there are no entry coordinates, the matrix is deterministic and its law is unchanged. Otherwise regard the matrix as its finite list of real coordinates. Multiplying the independent scalar densities in [F1] gives joint density $C e^{-\|G\|_F^2/2}$ over $\mathbb R$ or $C'e^{-\|G\|_F^2}$ over $\mathbb C$. The maps $G\mapsto U^*GV$ are real-linear isometries for the Frobenius norm; their real Jacobian matrix $O$ satisfies $O^TO=I$, hence $|\det O|=1$. By [F2], this real orthogonal map preserves measure, also in the complex case viewed in $\mathbb R^{2ab}$. Its inverse preserves the Frobenius norm, so integrating over the preimage of any Borel set gives the same density integral over that set. Hence the transformed matrix has the same law.

In the nonempty-coordinate case, the density in [F1] factors over all transformed entries because its exponent is the sum of the entrywise squared moduli and its normalizing constant is the product of the scalar normalizers. Thus the entries remain independent and each retains its original scalar law. For an empty matrix the assertion about entries is vacuous.

Apply the invariance with $U=W$ and $V=I$. For two nonempty disjoint row blocks, integrating out the other entries leaves the product of their block densities, which proves independence and the declared standard block laws. An empty block has the prescribed deterministic law and is independent of every other block, since each event for it has probability zero or one.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice so that the repository's Lebesgue measure
on each positive-dimensional real coordinate space is a measure. A **standard
real Gaussian scalar** has Lebesgue density
$$\varphi_R(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}.$$
A **normalized complex Gaussian scalar** is $z=(x+iy)/\sqrt2$ for independent
standard real Gaussian scalars $x,y$; its density on $\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb
R^2$ is $\varphi_C(z)=\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $\mathbb E|z|^2=1$.

For $F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, an **iid standard Gaussian matrix** in
$F^{a\times b}$ has independent entries with the corresponding scalar law.
For $ab>0$, its expectations are finite-dimensional Lebesgue integrals
against the product density. If $a=0$ or $b=0$, the matrix space has one
element, the empty matrix; its law assigns that element probability one,
and the expectation of any function is its value there. Independence means
the product-density factorization, with this one-point convention for an
empty product.
The normalized complex convention is fixed throughout; it is not the
unnormalized law $x+iy$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval. Suppose $f$ and $\partial_tf$ are continuous on $D\times I$, one slice $f_{t_*}$ is absolutely improperly integrable, and for every compact interval $C\subseteq I$ there is a nonnegative improperly integrable $g_C$ with $|\partial_tf(x,t)|\le g_C(x)$ for $x\in D$ and $t\in C$. Then every slice is absolutely improperly integrable, the function $F(t)=\int_Df(x,t)\,dx$ is continuously differentiable, and

$$F'(t)=\int_D\partial_tf(x,t)\,dx.$$

The parameter derivative may be passed through the improper multiple integral under an integrable uniform derivative bound.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Take independent copies of $X,Y$, with covariance entries $(C_X)_{ij}=\mathbb E(X_iX_j)$ and $(C_Y)_{ij}=\mathbb E(Y_iY_j)$, and represent them as independent linear images of standard Gaussian coordinates using [A1]. For $0<t<1$ put $Z(t)=\sqrt tY+\sqrt{1-t}X$ and $F_\beta(z)=\beta^{-1}\log\sum_{i=1}^Ne^{\beta z_i}$ with $w_i=e^{\beta z_i}/\sum_je^{\beta z_j}$. The soft maximum has at most linear growth, so its Gaussian slice is integrable. On each compact subinterval of $(0,1)$, $|\partial_tF_\beta(Z(t))|\le\|\nabla F_\beta\|_2(\|Y\|_2/(2\sqrt t)+\|X\|_2/(2\sqrt{1-t}))$ has an integrable uniform bound, so [F3] passes the derivative under the finite Gaussian integral. For the coordinate integration by parts, fix all coordinates but $r=g_j$, and let $\varphi(r)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-r^2/2}$. The functions to which it is applied are first derivatives of $F_\beta$ composed with linear maps; they and their $r$ derivatives are smooth and bounded for fixed $\beta$. On $[-R,R]$, [F5] with $u=f$ and $v=\varphi$ gives $\int_{-R}^R r f(r)\varphi(r)\,dr=\int_{-R}^R f'(r)\varphi(r)\,dr-[f(r)\varphi(r)]_{-R}^R$. The boundary term tends to zero since $f$ is bounded and $\varphi(\pm R)\to0$. The integrands are dominated by constant multiples of $|r|\varphi(r)$ and $\varphi(r)$, respectively, so [F4] takes $R\to\infty$. Both majorants are integrable. Their bounds are uniform in the other coordinates, and [F6] integrates the resulting identity over those coordinates. Applying this coordinatewise to a linear image $W=L g$ gives $\mathbb E[W_i f(W)]=\sum_j\operatorname{Cov}(W_i,W_j)\mathbb E[\partial_jf(W)]$, including singular covariance matrices. Apply it separately to $X,Y$ in the derivative to obtain $\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb EF_\beta(Z(t))=\frac12\sum_{i,j}(C_Y-C_X)_{ij}\mathbb E[\partial_{ij}F_\beta(Z(t))]$. Since $\partial_{ij}F_\beta=\beta(w_i\mathbf1_{i=j}-w_iw_j)$, symmetry rewrites this as $\frac\beta4\mathbb E\sum_{i,j}w_iw_j(\mathbb E(Y_i-Y_j)^2-\mathbb E(X_i-X_j)^2)\ge0$ by the assumed increment order.

Integrate the nonnegative derivative on $(0,1)$. As $t\downarrow0$ or $t\uparrow1$, $Z(t)$ converges pointwise to $X$ or $Y$ and $|F_\beta(Z(t))|$ is bounded by a constant plus $\|X\|_2+\|Y\|_2$, so [F4] gives endpoint continuity and $\mathbb EF_\beta(Y)\ge\mathbb EF_\beta(X)$. For every $z\in\mathbb R^N$, $\max_i z_i\le F_\beta(z)\le\max_i z_i+\log N/\beta$. Letting $\beta\to\infty$ proves the asserted expected-maximum comparison.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $G\in F^{a\times b}$ have the iid Gaussian law of
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. If $U,V$
are compatible orthogonal matrices for $F=\mathbb R$ or unitary matrices for
$F=\mathbb C$, then $U^*GV$ has the same iid law as $G$. In particular, if
$W\in F^{n\times n}$ is orthogonal/unitary and $\Omega\in F^{n\times\ell}$
is iid Gaussian, then any two disjoint row blocks of $W^*\Omega$ are

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

derivations.claim: A fixed proper real or complex linear subspace $L\subsetneq F^\ell$ has probability zero for one Gaussian row: choose an orthogonal/unitary coordinate change sending $L$ into $\{z_1=0\}$, use [F2], and integrate the density over this coordinate subspace. It is Lebesgue-null: inside each bounded box $[-M,M]^d$ it lies in a coordinate hyperplane coverable by a box of width $2\varepsilon$ and bounded remaining sides, whose volume tends to zero with $\varepsilon$; [F4] makes that hyperplane null, and countable subadditivity covers the whole hyperplane.

Induct on the number $j\le k$ of revealed rows. The first row is nonzero almost surely by step 1.1 applied to the zero subspace. The dependence event for $j$ rows is measurable because it is the common zero set of the finitely many $j\times j$ minors. If the first $j-1$ rows are independent, their span is proper since $j-1<k<\ell$; for each fixed such tuple, step 1.1 makes the section of the event that row $j$ lies in their span null. The exceptional dependent tuples are null by induction. Applying [F3] to the nonnegative indicator of dependence gives probability zero for the first $j$ rows to be dependent. The induction is finite and concludes at $j=k$.
Outside this null event, the $k$ rows are linearly independent, hence the row rank equals $k$.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, and let $(X_i)_{i=1}^N$ and $(Y_i)_{i=1}^N$ be
finite centered real Gaussian families. If $\mathbb E(X_i-X_j)^2\le\mathbb E(Y_i-Y_j)^2$ for every
$i,j$, then $\mathbb E\max_iX_i\le\mathbb E\max_iY_i$.
Here a finite centered real Gaussian family means a finite real vector that
is a real-linear image of finitely many independent standard real Gaussian
scalars.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: Write $(SGT)_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{i=1}^r\sum_{j=1}^sS_{\alpha i}G_{ij}T_{j\beta}$. Expanding gives $\mathbb E\|SGT\|_F^2=\sum_{\alpha=1}^a\sum_{\beta=1}^b\sum_{i,u=1}^r\sum_{j,v=1}^sS_{\alpha i}T_{j\beta}S_{\alpha u}T_{v\beta}\mathbb E(G_{ij}G_{uv})$. Independence, zero means, and unit variances give $\mathbb E(G_{ij}G_{uv})=\mathbf1_{i=u}\mathbf1_{j=v}$, so this reduces to $\sum_{\alpha,\beta,i,j}S_{\alpha i}^2T_{j\beta}^2=(\sum_{\alpha,i}S_{\alpha i}^2)(\sum_{j,\beta}T_{j\beta}^2)=\|S\|_F^2\|T\|_F^2$.

For unit vectors $x\in\mathbb R^a,y\in\mathbb R^b$, set $u=S^Tx$, $v=Ty$, $U=\|u\|$, $V=\|v\|$, and define centered Gaussian processes $X_{xy}=u^TGv+zUV$ and $Y_{xy}=Vg^Tu+Uh^Tv$, where $z\in\mathbb R$, $g\in\mathbb R^r$, and $h\in\mathbb R^s$ are independent standard real Gaussian variables/vectors, independent of $G$. For a second pair $(x',y')$, write $u'=S^Tx'$, $v'=Ty'$, $U'=\|u'\|$, $V'=\|v'\|$, $c=u^Tu'$, and $d=v^Tv'$. At each index both processes have variance $2U^2V^2$, and their cross-covariances are $\operatorname{Cov}(X_{xy},X_{x'y'})=cd+UU'VV'$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{xy},Y_{x'y'})=cVV'+UU'd$. The difference is $(UU'-c)(VV'-d)\ge0$ by Cauchy–Schwarz; subtracting twice the covariance from the sum of the two variances gives $\mathbb E(X_{xy}-X_{x'y'})^2\le\mathbb E(Y_{xy}-Y_{x'y'})^2$.

Apply [F2] to increasing finite subsets of normalized rational vectors in the product of unit spheres. They are dense; both sample paths are continuous, and their absolute suprema are bounded by $\|S\|_2\|T\|_2(\|G\|_F+|z|)$ for $X$ and $\|T\|_2\|Sg\|_2+\|S\|_2\|T^Th\|_2$ for $Y$. These bounds are integrable because independence and unit coordinate variances give $\mathbb E\|G\|_F^2=rs$, $\mathbb E z^2=1$, $\mathbb E\|Sg\|_2^2=\|S\|_F^2$, and $\mathbb E\|T^Th\|_2^2=\|T\|_F^2$. Dominated convergence [F4] passes the finite comparisons to the full spheres. For fixed $G$, $z\mapsto\sup_{x,y}(u^TGv+zUV)$ is convex with integrable growth, so Jensen [F3] gives $\mathbb E_z\sup_{x,y}X_{xy}\ge\sup_{x,y}\mathbb E_zX_{xy}=\sup_{x,y}u^TGv=\|SGT\|_2$.

For every unit $x,y$, $Y_{xy}\le\|T\|_2\|Sg\|_2+\|S\|_2\|T^Th\|_2$. Taking suprema and expectations, [F3] applied to the convex square gives $\mathbb E\|Sg\|_2\le(\mathbb E\|Sg\|_2^2)^{1/2}=\|S\|_F$ and $\mathbb E\|T^Th\|_2\le\|T\|_F$. Combining with step 2.1 proves the spectral estimate.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Input a fixed matrix $A\in F^{m\times n}$, a positive integer sketch width $\ell$,
and a Gaussian draw primitive as in
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. Draw
$\Omega\in F^{n\times\ell}$ with iid entries in the chosen field and form
$Y=A\Omega$. Select $Q$ deterministically by scanning columns of $Y$ in
order, subtracting projections onto already retained columns, skipping zero
residuals, and normalizing each nonzero residual. In the complex case fix each
phase by making its first nonzero coordinate positive real. Return this
orthonormal basis $Q$ and the approximation $\widehat A=QQ^*A$.

Empty ranges return the empty basis. All operations use exact arithmetic.
No truncated rank-$k$ factorization, finite-precision stability result, or
deterministic error certificate is part of the procedure.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

derivations.claim: Choose the SVD from [F1] and set $\widetilde\Omega=V^*\Omega=[\Omega_1^T\ \Omega_2^T]^T$. Left multiplication by $U^*$ carries the sample range to $\operatorname{Ran}(\Sigma\widetilde\Omega)$, preserves the operator norm because it maps unit vectors bijectively to unit vectors by [F3], and carries $QQ^*$ to the orthogonal projector $P$ onto that range. It suffices to prove the estimate for $\Sigma$.

Since $\Omega_1$ has full row rank, put $\Omega_1^\dagger=\Omega_1^*(\Omega_1\Omega_1^*)^{-1}$, so $\Omega_1\Omega_1^\dagger=I_k$. Let $Y=\Sigma[\Omega_1^T\ \Omega_2^T]^T$ and $C=Y\Omega_1^\dagger[I_k\ 0]$. The range of $C$ lies in $\operatorname{Ran}(Y)$, hence $(I-P)C=0$.

select $\widetilde Q_j$ from its range by the same scan, then form
$A\widetilde Q_j$ and select $Q_j$ from its range by that scan. Return $Q_q$.
Thus exact QR/range orthogonalization follows each application of $A^*$ and
$A$; empty or rank-deficient ranges return bases of their actual ranges. The procedure is defined in exact arithmetic and makes no
finite-precision error guarantee.

let $q\ge0$ be an integer. Then
$$\|(I-P)A\|_2\le\|(I-P)(AA^*)^qA\|_2^{1/(2q+1)}.$$

integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$

Induction gives $S_q=\operatorname{Ran}((AA^*)^qA\Omega)$, including empty ranges and $q=0$. Thus the range specified directly in the statement agrees with the algorithm's output range for Gaussian draws. For a general measurable sketch, the statement specifies $P$ directly and requires no Gaussian sampling step.

Set $Z=\|(I-P)(AA^*)^qA\|_2$. By [F2], $\|(I-P)A\|_2\le Z^{1/(2q+1)}$ pointwise. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice so that the repository's Lebesgue measure
on each positive-dimensional real coordinate space is a measure. A **standard
real Gaussian scalar** has Lebesgue density
$$\varphi_R(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}.$$
A **normalized complex Gaussian scalar** is $z=(x+iy)/\sqrt2$ for independent
standard real Gaussian scalars $x,y$; its density on $\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb
R^2$ is $\varphi_C(z)=\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $\mathbb E|z|^2=1$.

For $F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, an **iid standard Gaussian matrix** in
$F^{a\times b}$ has independent entries with the corresponding scalar law.
For $ab>0$, its expectations are finite-dimensional Lebesgue integrals
against the product density. If $a=0$ or $b=0$, the matrix space has one
element, the empty matrix; its law assigns that element probability one,
and the expectation of any function is its value there. Independence means
the product-density factorization, with this one-point convention for an
empty product.
The normalized complex convention is fixed throughout; it is not the
unnormalized law $x+iy$.

For $p,q>0$, $B(p,q)=\Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)/\Gamma(p+q)$.

For $s>0$, define $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$.

The integral is improper at both $0$ and $+\infty$. $$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$

$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$

property.
For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, and $\Gamma(1)=1$.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

derivations.claim: Write $G=\begin{bmatrix}g\\H\end{bmatrix}$ with first row $g$ and remaining $k-1$ rows $H$. If $k=1$, set $P=I_{k+p}$; then $GG^*=gg^*=gPg^*$ and the inverse-diagonal identity is immediate. If $k>1$, [F2] gives full row rank of $H$, so $P=I-H^*(HH^*)^{-1}H$ is the orthogonal projector onto $\ker H$, of dimension $(k+p)-(k-1)=p+1$. To obtain the inverse entry without an assumed block-inverse formula, solve $GG^*\binom{x}{y}=\binom{1}{0}$. The lower equation gives $y=-(HH^*)^{-1}Hg^*x$, and substitution into the upper equation gives $(gPg^*)x=1$. Full row rank of $G$ from [F2] makes $GG^*$ invertible and $gPg^*>0$, hence $((GG^*)^{-1})_{11}=x=(gPg^*)^{-1}$.

For each fixed $H$, choose orthonormal coordinates in which $P$ is diagonal with $p+1$ ones. Independence of $g$ from $H$ and invariance [F7] show that $gPg^*$ is a sum of $p+1$ independent squared real Gaussians, or squared moduli of normalized complex Gaussians. Apply [F10] separately on the open half-lines via $x=\sqrt u$ and $x=-\sqrt u$ (absolute derivative $1/(2\sqrt u)$); the omitted point has zero measure. Adding the two densities gives the real square density $u^{-1/2}e^{-u/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}=u^{-1/2}e^{-u/2}/(\sqrt2\Gamma(1/2))$ by [F6]. For the complex square law, [F11] applied to the normalized density gives $1=\pi^{-1}\sigma(S^1)\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr=\sigma(S^1)/(2\pi)$, so $\sigma(S^1)=2\pi$. Applying the same formula with any nonnegative Borel function of $r^2$, and then [F10] with $u=r^2$, shows that the squared modulus has density $e^{-u}$ on $(0,\infty)$. The first real square is thus Gamma$(1/2,2)$ and the complex square Gamma$(1,1)$, the latter normalized by [F12]. If independent Gamma variables have common scale $\theta$ and shapes $a,b$, [F5] and the diffeomorphism $(u,v)\mapsto(u,s=u+v)$ of the positive quadrant onto $0<u<s$, of determinant one in [F10], show that their sum has convolution density with normalization $1/(\theta^{a+b}\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b))$ and numerator $e^{-s/\theta}\int_0^s u^{a-1}(s-u)^{b-1}du$. For each $s>0$, substituting $u=st$ by [F10] and using [F3] makes this $e^{-s/\theta}s^{a+b-1}B(a,b)$, which is the Gamma density of shape $a+b$ and scale $\theta$. Iterating this finite convolution gives $gPg^*\sim\Gamma((p+1)/2,2)$ over $\mathbb R$ and $gPg^*\sim\Gamma(p+1,1)$ over $\mathbb C$. Tonelli [F5] integrates first over $g$ and then over $H$, so the reciprocal law holds unconditionally for the first diagonal entry; row permutation invariance gives the same law for every index.

Integrating the Gamma density with the scaling $u=\theta t$ from [F10] yields $\mathbb E U^{-1}=\theta^{-1}\Gamma(a-1)/\Gamma(a)$ for $U\sim\Gamma(a,\theta)$ and $a>1$. Using the Gamma recurrence [F12] gives $\Gamma(a)=(a-1)\Gamma(a-1)$. Thus step 2.1 gives $\mathbb E((GG^*)^{-1})_{11}=1/(p-1)$ over $\mathbb R$ and $1/p$ over $\mathbb C$.

By step 2.1 all inverse diagonal entries have the same reciprocal-Gamma law and finite mean in the stated ranges, so $\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}(GG^*)^{-1}$ is $k$ times the value in step 3.1. Put $B=G^*(GG^*)^{-1}$. Then $GB=I_k$, $BG$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, so $GBG=G$, $BGB=B$, $(GB)^*=GB$, and $(BG)^*=BG$; these are the four Penrose equations [F8], hence uniqueness [F9] gives $B=G^\dagger$. Also $B^*B=(GG^*)^{-1}$, and therefore $\|G^\dagger\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}(GG^*)^{-1}$ almost surely.

Apply [F13] on the open positive quadrant using the inverse diffeomorphism $(s,t)\mapsto(x,y)=(st,s(1-t))$, with $s>0$, $0<t<1$ and absolute Jacobian $s$. In these coordinates the density factors into a Gamma$(a+b,\theta)$ factor in $s$ and a Beta$(a,b)$ factor in $t$ after scaling by the common scale $\theta$. Thus $\mathbb E t^q=B(a+q,b)/B(a,b)$; [F3] gives $c_R(q)=\Gamma(k/2)\Gamma(q+1/2)/(\sqrt\pi\Gamma(k/2+q))$ over $\mathbb R$ and $c_C(q)=\Gamma(k)\Gamma(q+1)/\Gamma(k+q)$ over $\mathbb C$. Invariance makes the same moment hold for $|\langle v,u\rangle|$ for every fixed unit $u$.

For $a,s>0$, $\Gamma(a+s)/\Gamma(a)\le(a+s)^s$. If $U\sim\Gamma(x,1)$, direct integration and [F10] give $\mathbb EU=\Gamma(x+1)/\Gamma(x)=x$. The density makes $\log U$ integrable, since $u^{x-1}|\log u|$ is integrable near zero and the exponential factor controls infinity. Thus [F4] gives $\psi(x):=\Gamma'(x)/\Gamma(x)=\mathbb E\log U$. Jensen [F5] for the convex function $-\log$ yields $\mathbb E\log U\le\log\mathbb EU=\log x$. Integrating $\psi$ from $a$ to $a+s$ yields $\log\Gamma(a+s)-\log\Gamma(a)\le s\log(a+s)$ and hence the ratio bound.

For an integer $p\ge1$, $\Gamma((p+1)/2)\ge\sqrt\pi(p/(2e))^{p/2}$. If $p=2r$, use [F10] and [F6] to write $\Gamma(r+1/2)=\sqrt\pi\prod_{j=1}^r(j-1/2)$; [F7] gives $(\log x)''=-1/x^2<0$. For $j\ge2$, midpoint concavity yields $\log(j-1/2)\ge\int_{j-1}^j\log x\,dx$; for $j=1$, $\log(1/2)\ge\int_0^1\log x\,dx=-1$. The product is at least $\sqrt\pi(r/e)^r$. If $p=2r+1$, [F10] gives $\Gamma((p+1)/2)=r!$ and midpoint concavity gives $\log(r!)\ge\int_{1/2}^{r+1/2}\log x\,dx$; hence $r!\ge\sqrt{2e}((r+1/2)/e)^{r+1/2}\ge\sqrt\pi((r+1/2)/e)^{r+1/2}$, since $e>2$ from its series and $\pi<4$ from the unit disk lying in a square of area $4$. Also $p!\ge(p/e)^p$ follows from $\sum_{j=1}^p\log j\ge\int_1^p\log x\,dx$.

Put $M=(GG^*)^{-1}$. By the pseudoinverse identity in [F1], $X^2=\lambda_{\max}(M)$ by [F11]. For each fixed positive $M$, choose a unit eigenvector $u$ for its largest eigenvalue. Then $v^*Mv\ge\lambda_{\max}(M)|\langle v,u\rangle|^2$, so integrating over $v$ and using the sphere moment $c_F(q)$ from step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E_v(v^*Mv)^q\ge\lambda_{\max}(M)^q c_F(q)$. Tonelli [F8] interchanges the nonnegative integrals over $G$ and $v$. For each fixed $v$, invariance [F2] makes $v^*Mv$ distributed as $M_{11}$. Using the reciprocal Gamma law [F1] and dividing by $c_F(q)$ gives exactly $C_R(q)$ or $C_C(q)$ in the statement.

Use the real moment bound from step 2.1 with $q=p/2$, the Gamma-ratio estimate in step 1.2, and the lower bound in step 1.3 to obtain $\mathbb E X^p\le(e\sqrt{k+p}/p)^p$. For the complex case, use the $C_C$ moment bound from step 2.1 with $q=p$, the ratio estimate from step 1.2, and the factorial bound in step 1.3 twice to obtain $\mathbb E X^{2p}\le(e\sqrt{k+p}/p)^{2p}$. Jensen for the convex powers gives $\mathbb E X\le(\mathbb E X^p)^{1/p}$ in the real case and $\mathbb E X\le(\mathbb E X^{2p})^{1/(2p)}$ in the complex case. For either exponent $r=p$ or $r=2p$, the pointwise inequality $t^r\mathbf1_{\{X>t\}}\le X^r$ implies $\mathbb P\{X>t\}\le\mathbb EX^r/t^r$; using the moment bounds and also $\mathbb P\{X>t\}\le1$ gives the displayed tails. Since $r>1$ for $p\ge2$, $t\mapsto(a/t)^r$ is integrable on $[1,\infty)$, so these tails are integrable at infinity.
