citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice so that the repository's Lebesgue measure
on each positive-dimensional real coordinate space is a measure. A **standard
real Gaussian scalar** has Lebesgue density
$$\varphi_R(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}.$$
A **normalized complex Gaussian scalar** is $z=(x+iy)/\sqrt2$ for independent
standard real Gaussian scalars $x,y$; its density on $\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb
R^2$ is $\varphi_C(z)=\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $\mathbb E|z|^2=1$.

For $F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, an **iid standard Gaussian matrix** in
$F^{a\times b}$ has independent entries with the corresponding scalar law.
For $ab>0$, its expectations are finite-dimensional Lebesgue integrals
against the product density. If $a=0$ or $b=0$, the matrix space has one
element, the empty matrix; its law assigns that element probability one,
and the expectation of any function is its value there. Independence means
the product-density factorization, with this one-point convention for an
empty product.
The normalized complex convention is fixed throughout; it is not the
unnormalized law $x+iy$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $G\in F^{a\times b}$ have the iid Gaussian law of
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. If $U,V$
are compatible orthogonal matrices for $F=\mathbb R$ or unitary matrices for
$F=\mathbb C$, then $U^*GV$ has the same iid law as $G$. In particular, if
$W\in F^{n\times n}$ is orthogonal/unitary and $\Omega\in F^{n\times\ell}$
is iid Gaussian, then any two disjoint row blocks of $W^*\Omega$ are
independent standard Gaussian matrices.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $k\ge1$, $\ell>k$, and let $G\in F^{k\times\ell}$ have iid standard
real Gaussian or normalized complex Gaussian entries. Then
$\operatorname{rank}(G)=k$ almost surely.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $k\ge1$ and let $p$ be a positive integer, with $p\ge2$ over $\mathbb R$
and $p\ge1$ over normalized $\mathbb C$. Let $G\in F^{k\times(k+p)}$ have iid entries as in
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. Then $G$
has full row rank almost surely and
$$\mathbb E\|G^\dagger\|_F^2= \begin{cases}k/(p-1),&F=\mathbb R,\\k/p,&F=\mathbb C.\end{cases}$$
The complex entry convention is variance one, $\mathbb E|G_{ij}|^2=1$. Write
$G^\dagger=G^+$ for the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]. On the full-row-rank event,
$$G^\dagger=G^*(GG^*)^{-1},\qquad (G^\dagger)^*G^\dagger=(GG^*)^{-1}.$$
Here $U\sim\Gamma(a,\theta)$ means that $U$ has density
$u^{a-1}e^{-u/\theta}/(\theta^a\Gamma(a))$ for $u>0$. For every diagonal
index $i$, $((GG^*)^{-1})_{ii}$ has distribution $1/U$ with
$U\sim\Gamma((p+1)/2,2)$ over $\mathbb R$ and $U\sim\Gamma(p+1,1)$ over
$\mathbb C$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] and
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]].

For every matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or
$\mathbb C$, there exists a unique matrix $A^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$
satisfying the four Penrose equations of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]].

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $k\ge1$ and let $p$ be a positive integer, with $p\ge2$ over $\mathbb R$
and $p\ge1$ over normalized $\mathbb C$. Let $G\in F^{k\times(k+p)}$ have iid entries as in
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. Then $G$
has full row rank almost surely and
$$\mathbb E\|G^\dagger\|_F^2= \begin{cases}k/(p-1),&F=\mathbb R,\\k/p,&F=\mathbb C.\end{cases}$$
The complex entry convention is variance one, $\mathbb E|G_{ij}|^2=1$. Write
$G^\dagger=G^+$ for the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]. On the full-row-rank event,
$$G^\dagger=G^*(GG^*)^{-1},\qquad (G^\dagger)^*G^\dagger=(GG^*)^{-1}.$$
Here $U\sim\Gamma(a,\theta)$ means that $U$ has density
$u^{a-1}e^{-u/\theta}/(\theta^a\Gamma(a))$ for $u>0$. For every diagonal
index $i$, $((GG^*)^{-1})_{ii}$ has distribution $1/U$ with
$U\sim\Gamma((p+1)/2,2)$ over $\mathbb R$ and $U\sim\Gamma(p+1,1)$ over
$\mathbb C$.

For $p,q>0$, define $B(p,q)=\int_0^1t^{p-1}(1-t)^{q-1}\,dt$.

The integral is improper at both endpoints. The exact convergence theorem [[thm-real-beta-integral-convergence]] proves that it exists precisely for the displayed positive parameters and therefore discharges the definition's existence obligation.
For $p,q>0$, $B(p,q)=\Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)/\Gamma(p+q)$.

For $s>0$, define $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$.

The integral is improper at both $0$ and $+\infty$. Its convergence for every $s>0$, and its failure for $s\le0$, are proved in [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]], which justifies the definition on exactly the displayed domain. The integrand is positive, so $\Gamma(s)>0$ throughout $(0,\infty)$.
For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, and $\Gamma(1)=1$.
For each real $p\ge1$, the function $\phi_p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ defined by $\phi_p(t)=|t|^p$ is finite, continuous, Borel measurable and convex. Here $0^p=0$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex. For a positive finite family of points in $C$ and nonnegative weights summing to one, $f$ of their weighted Euclidean sum is at most the weighted sum of their $f$-values. Explicitly, if $N\ge1$, $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in C$, $\lambda_j\ge0$, and $\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_j=1$, then

$$f\left(\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_jx_j\right)\le\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_jf(x_j).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in \mathbb{R}$
with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k < n$. Write

$$A := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad G := \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)^{1/n},$$

the **arithmetic mean** and the **geometric mean**, where the $n$-th root exists
because $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]],
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]) and $n$ denotes the canonical field image
$n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural number n, which is invertible since $n \ge 1$
([[lem-of-naturals-positive]], [[lem-of-q-embeds]]). Then

$$\prod_{k<n} a_k \le A^{n}, \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad G \le A,$$

and equality holds in either form if and only if $a_0 = a_1 = \dots = a_{n-1}$.

The proof is **Cauchy's forward-backward induction**: the statement is proved
first along a doubling sequence, by doubling, and then pulled back from a member
of that sequence to every smaller $n$ by a descent that replaces the missing
entry with the arithmetic mean of the others. That is why the induction below
runs over the doubling scheme and not over $n$ directly.

One point of hygiene decides how the doubling scheme is written. The doubling
index has to be a **natural number**, because it is used as the length of a list,
as a bound on an index, and as the starting point of a descent. The symbol $2^{j}$
would not do: [[def-integer-power]] defines powers of a *real* base, so $2^{j}$
denotes a power of the real field element $2\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ under that definition, rather than a natural-number-valued operation, and so cannot
index anything. The doubling sequence is therefore defined inside $\mathbb{N}$,
by recursion ([[thm-recursion]]):

$$N_0 = 1, \qquad N_{j+1} = N_j + N_j \quad (j \in \mathbb{N}),$$

and the induction below runs over $j$, with $N_j$ as the list length. No
identity relating $N_j$ to any real power is needed anywhere, and none is claimed.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[thm-recursion]]):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

**Why this item is first.** The published definition of the integral does not
cover this page. [[def-darboux-integral]] is stated for reals $a < b$, because
the partitions it quantifies over are those of [[def-partition-and-refinement]],
whose standing hypothesis is $a < b$: with $a = b$ the chain
$a = t_0 < \dots < t_n = b$ is unsatisfiable. So $\int_a^b f$ is an undefined
symbol whenever $a \ge b$, and every additivity statement below would be
ill-formed as it is usually written. This item extends the notation, and nothing
else: the object it names is still the Darboux integral of
[[def-darboux-integral]].

Let $u, v \in \mathbb{R}$ and write

$$[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v] \;:=\; \text{the closed interval with endpoints } u \text{ and } v$$

([[def-interval]]). Let $f$ be a real-valued function whose domain contains that
interval. Say that **$f$ is integrable between $u$ and $v$** when either $u = v$,
or $u \ne v$ and the restriction of $f$ to $[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v]$ is bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux integrable there ([[def-darboux-integral]],
[[def-darboux-sums]]). For such $f$ define

$$\int_u^v f \;:=\; \begin{cases} \text{the Darboux integral of } f \text{ over } [u,v] & \text{if } u < v, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } u = v, \\[2pt] -\displaystyle\int_v^u f & \text{if } u > v. \end{cases}$$

**There is nothing to check for consistency.** The three clauses are indexed by
the three cases of trichotomy, $u < v$, $u = v$ and $u > v$, which are mutually
exclusive and exhaustive; no pair of them ever applies to the same $(u,v)$. In
particular the first clause is untouched, so on $u < v$ this is the published
integral verbatim and every published theorem about it applies unchanged.

**The middle clause is a stipulation, not a computation.** It is *not* claimed
that $0$ is a value forced by the $u < v$ definition in any limiting sense; that
definition simply says nothing at $u = v$, and $\int_u^u f := 0$ is what is
written there. It is also unconditional: no hypothesis on $f$ beyond being
defined at $u$ is asked for, since the case $u = v$ never refers to a partition.

### The two consequences used throughout the page

**Antisymmetry, for every pair.** For all reals $u, v$ with $f$ integrable
between them,

$$\int_u^v f \;=\; -\int_v^u f .$$

Indeed if $u < v$ then $v > u$ and the third clause reads
$\int_v^u f = -\int_u^v f$, which rearranges to the display; if $u = v$ both
sides are $0$; and if $u > v$ the third clause is the display itself.

**Absolute values agree.** Consequently
$\bigl|\int_u^v f\bigr| = \bigl|\int_v^u f\bigr|$ for every such pair.

**An obligation recorded here and discharged elsewhere.** With this convention
the additivity identity

$$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f$$

holds for **every** arrangement of $u, v, w$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable, not only for $u < v < w$. That is a theorem and not part of this
definition; it is proved as the last clause of
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], and nothing on this page uses it before it
is proved there.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order ([[def-nat-order]]); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
([[lem-nat-add-commutative]]) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume Countable Choice. For shape $a>0$ and rate $b>0$, the **shape-rate Gamma distribution**
$\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b)$ is the probability measure on $(0,\infty)$ with
density
$$f_{a,b}(\lambda)=\frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}$$
relative to Lebesgue measure. Its normalization is proved in
[[lem-gamma-density-normalization]]. The second argument is a rate, not a scale.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $k\ge1$ and let $p$ be a positive integer, with $p\ge2$ over $\mathbb R$
and $p\ge1$ over normalized $\mathbb C$. Let $G\in F^{k\times(k+p)}$ have iid entries as in
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. Then $G$
has full row rank almost surely and
$$\mathbb E\|G^\dagger\|_F^2= \begin{cases}k/(p-1),&F=\mathbb R,\\k/p,&F=\mathbb C.\end{cases}$$
The complex entry convention is variance one, $\mathbb E|G_{ij}|^2=1$. Write
$G^\dagger=G^+$ for the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]. On the full-row-rank event,
$$G^\dagger=G^*(GG^*)^{-1},\qquad (G^\dagger)^*G^\dagger=(GG^*)^{-1}.$$
Here $U\sim\Gamma(a,\theta)$ means that $U$ has density
$u^{a-1}e^{-u/\theta}/(\theta^a\Gamma(a))$ for $u>0$. For every diagonal
index $i$, $((GG^*)^{-1})_{ii}$ has distribution $1/U$ with
$U\sim\Gamma((p+1)/2,2)$ over $\mathbb R$ and $U\sim\Gamma(p+1,1)$ over
$\mathbb C$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: On the full-row-rank event of [F3], set $M=(G_1G_1^*)^{-1}$. For a fixed unit $v\in\mathbb C^k$, choose a unitary $U_0$ with $U_0e_1=v$. By [F2], $U_0^*G_1$ has the same law as $G_1$, and its inverse Gram matrix is $U_0^*MU_0$; hence $v^*Mv$ has the same law as $M_{11}$. The Moore--Penrose formula in [F4] gives $\|G_1^\dagger v\|_2^2=v^*Mv$, so [F4] makes this variance $1/U$ for $U\sim\Gamma(p+1,1)$. The formula in [F4] also gives $G_1G_1^\dagger=I_k$, hence $G_1^\dagger v\ne0$. Conditional on $G_1$, a row of $G_2G_1^\dagger v$ is a fixed linear functional of one isotropic normalized complex Gaussian row. Completing $G_1^\dagger v/\|G_1^\dagger v\|_2$ to a unitary basis and using [F2] shows that this functional is a normalized complex Gaussian with variance $v^*Mv$; the $d$ rows are conditionally independent. The full-row-rank set is open because it is the union of the nonzero-minor sets. On this set the inverse formula in [F4] is continuous; setting $Z=0$ on its null complement therefore gives a Borel version, equal almost surely to the stated product. This justifies the expectations without changing their values.

Apply [F13] in $\mathbb R^2$ to the radial density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ from [F1]. Since this is a probability density, $1=\pi^{-1}\sigma(S^1)\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr$; substitution $u=r^2$ by [F12] makes the integral $\Gamma(1)/2=1/2$ by [F6], so $\sigma(S^1)=2\pi$. Applying [F13] to the indicator of $\{z:|z|^2\in E\}$ for a Borel set $E\subseteq(0,\infty)$, and again substituting $u=r^2$, gives $\mathbb P(|g|^2\in E)=\int_E e^{-u}\,du$. Thus the squared modulus is $\Gamma(1,1)$. For independent $X\sim\Gamma(r,1)$ and $Y\sim\Gamma(s,1)$, the map $(x,y)\mapsto(t=x+y,w=x/(x+y))$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism from $(0,\infty)^2$ to $(0,\infty)\times(0,1)$, with inverse $(t,w)\mapsto(tw,t(1-w))$ and inverse Jacobian determinant $t$. By [F12], their joint density in these coordinates is $t^{r+s-1}e^{-t}w^{r-1}(1-w)^{s-1}/(\Gamma(r)\Gamma(s))$. Integrating in $w$ by Tonelli [F8] and applying the Beta--Gamma identity [F6] gives the $\Gamma(r+s,1)$ density in $t$. Finite induction therefore makes the squared norm of $j$ independent normalized complex Gaussian coordinates $\Gamma(j,1)$. Euler integration [F6] gives its $q$th moment $\Gamma(j+q)/\Gamma(j)$ and gives $\mathbb E U^{-q}=\Gamma(p+1-q)/\Gamma(p+1)$ for $U\sim\Gamma(p+1,1)$ when $0<q<p+1$. Integrating first over $G_2$ and then $G_1$ by [F8], for each fixed unit $v\in\mathbb C^k$ and $1\le j\le d$ this yields $\mathbb E\|P_jZv\|_2^{2q}=\frac{\Gamma(j+q)\Gamma(p+1-q)}{\Gamma(j)\Gamma(p+1)},$ where $P_j$ keeps the first $j$ rows.

Define $P_0Z=0$. On an auxiliary finite product probability space, let $h\in\mathbb C^k$ have iid normalized complex Gaussian coordinates, independent of $(G_1,G_2)$, and put $v=h/\|h\|_2$ when $h\ne0$ and $v=e_1$ when $h=0$; the latter event has probability zero by [F1]. The law of $v$ is unitary invariant by [F2]. For $k=1$, $\mathbb E|v_1|^{2q}=1$. For $k\ge2$, $X=|h_1|^2$ and $Y=\sum_{i=2}^k|h_i|^2$ are independent with laws $\Gamma(1,1)$ and $\Gamma(k-1,1)$ by step 2.1. The change $s=X+Y$, $t=X/(X+Y)$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with Jacobian $s$ and factors the joint density into a $\Gamma(k,1)$ density in $s$ and a Beta$(1,k-1)$ density in $t$ by [F12]. Thus [F6] gives $c_k(q):=\mathbb E|v_1|^{2q}=\frac{\Gamma(k)\Gamma(q+1)}{\Gamma(k+q)},$ which also equals $1$ when $k=1$. For each fixed $Z$, choose a unit right singular vector $u$ of $P_jZ$ for its largest singular value (possible by [F9]). Its SVD gives $\|P_jZv\|_2^2\ge\|P_jZ\|_2^2|u^*v|^2$. Average over the auxiliary $v$; unitary invariance replaces $u$ by $e_1$, so the left side is at least $c_k(q)\|P_jZ\|_2^{2q}$ after raising to power $q$. Integrate over $Z$ by [F8] and use step 2.1, then divide by $c_k(q)>0$, to obtain $\mathbb E\|P_jZ\|_2^{2q}\le \frac{\Gamma(j+q)\Gamma(k+q)\Gamma(p+1-q)} {\Gamma(j)\Gamma(k)\Gamma(q+1)\Gamma(p+1)}.$ The eigenvector is selected only for each fixed finite matrix in this pointwise inequality; no measurable eigenvector is used.

The law of $Z$ is left-unitary invariant by [F2], since left multiplication acts only on $G_2$. Conditional coordinate second moments give $\mathbb E_{G_2}\|G_2G_1^\dagger\|_F^2=d\|G_1^\dagger\|_F^2$; [F4] and [F8] therefore give $\mathbb E\|Z\|_F^2=dk/p<\infty$. For integer $1\le q\le p$, apply Jensen [F7] to the nonnegative variable $\|P_jZ\|_2^2$ and use step 3.1. The Gamma functional equation [F6] then gives $\mathbb E\|P_jZ\|_2^2\le \left[\frac{(k)_q(j)_q}{q!(p)_{\downarrow q}}\right]^{1/q},$ where $(b)_q=b(b+1)\cdots(b+q-1)$ and $(p)_{\downarrow q}=p(p-1)\cdots(p-q+1)$.

By AM--GM [F7], $(k)_q^{1/q}\le k+(q-1)/2$ and $(j)_q^{1/q}\le j+(q-1)/2$. We also have $(q!)^{1/q}\ge q/e$: for $q=1$ this is immediate since the first two terms of the defining series give $e>1$; for $q\ge2$, on each $[r-1,r]$ with $2\le r\le q$, monotonicity of $\log$ in [F10] gives $\int_{r-1}^r\log t\,dt\le\log r$. Additivity and monotonicity of integration [F11] yield $\int_1^q\log t\,dt\le\sum_{r=2}^q\log r=\log(q!)$, the last equality following by induction from the product law in [F10]. The primitive $t\log t-t$ has derivative $\log t$ by [F10], and $\log$ is integrable on $[1,q]$ by [F11], so the fundamental theorem gives $\int_1^q\log t\,dt=q\log q-q+1$. Hence $\log(q!)\ge q\log q-q+1\ge q\log(q/e)$, because $\log e=1$ and the quotient law holds by [F10]. Since $\log$ is strictly increasing and both arguments are positive, $q!\ge(q/e)^q$. Finally, pair the first and last, second and penultimate, and so on among the $q$ factors of $(p)_{\downarrow q}$. Each complete pair has product $(p-i)(p-q+1+i)=p(p-q+1)+i(q-1-i)\ge p(p-q+1).$ If $q$ is odd, the unpaired middle factor is $p-(q-1)/2$, and $\left(p-\frac{q-1}{2}\right)^2=p(p-q+1)+\frac{(q-1)^2}{4} \ge p(p-q+1).$ Thus $(p)_{\downarrow q}^{1/q}\ge\sqrt{p(p-q+1)}$.

Take $q=\lceil p/2\rceil$ in step 4.1. Then $q\ge p/2$, $p-q+1\ge p/2$, and $(q-1)/2\le p/4$. Step 5.1 gives, for $1\le j\le d$, $\mathbb E\|P_jZ\|_2^2\le C\ell p^{-2}(j+p/4),\qquad C=2\sqrt2e.$ Indeed, the denominator in step 5.1 is at least $(q/e)\sqrt{p(p-q+1)}\ge p^2/(2\sqrt2e)$, while $k+(q-1)/2\le k+p/4\le\ell$ and $j+(q-1)/2\le j+p/4$. This proves the displayed half-order bound. For $q=p$, $(p)_{\downarrow p}=p!$, so step 5.1 bounds both denominator roots by $p/e$ and their product from below by $(p/e)^2$. The numerator factors are at most $k+p/2\le\ell$ and $j+p/2$. Substitution into step 4.1 gives $\mathbb E\|P_jZ\|_2^2\le e^2\ell p^{-2}(j+p/2).$ Both bounds also hold at $j=0$ because $P_0Z=0$.

If $S=0$, both claims hold. Otherwise set $\sigma=\|S\|_2>0$ and diagonalize $S^*S$ by [F9] as $W^*\operatorname{diag}(\sigma^2w_1,\ldots,\sigma^2w_d)W$, where $0\le w_i\le1$. The Frobenius singular-value formula in [F9] gives $\|S\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}(S^*S)=\sigma^2\sum_iw_i$, hence $\sum_iw_i=\|S\|_F^2/\sigma^2$. For $w\in[0,1]^d$, define $f(w)=\mathbb E\|\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w_i})Z\|_2^2$. It is finite because $0\le w_i\le1$ and operator norm is bounded by Frobenius norm in [F9], so $f(w)\le\mathbb E\|Z\|_F^2<\infty$ by step 4.1. It is convex because for every fixed unit vector $u$, $\|\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w_i})Zu\|_2^2=\sum_iw_i|(Zu)_i|^2$ is linear in $w$, and taking the unit-vector maximum and then expectation preserves convexity. It is invariant under coordinate permutations by the row-unitary invariance of $Z$ from [F2]. For each subset $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ put $\lambda_J=\prod_{i\in J}w_i\prod_{i\notin J}(1-w_i)$. These are nonnegative, sum to $\prod_i(w_i+1-w_i)=1$, and satisfy $\sum_{J\ni i}\lambda_J=w_i$; hence the convex combination of indicator vectors is $w$ and its mean cardinality is $\sum_iw_i$. Finite Euclidean Jensen [F7] gives $f(w)\le\sum_J\lambda_Jf(\mathbf1_J)$. By permutation invariance and step 6.1, $f(\mathbf1_J)=\mathbb E\|P_{|J|}Z\|_2^2\le h(|J|)$ for each of the two affine bounds $h(j)$ there. Since $h$ is affine, $f(w)\le\sum_J\lambda_Jh(|J|)=h(\sum_iw_i)$; this includes every endpoint $w_i=0$ or $1$ and never uses a row count above $d$. Finally, left-unitary invariance and the diagonalization of $S^*S$ give $\mathbb E\|SZ\|_2^2=\mathbb E\|\operatorname{diag}(\sigma\sqrt{w_i})WZ\|_2^2 =\sigma^2f(w)$. Substitution of each affine $h$ proves both asserted inequalities.

risk_review.notes: Checked conditional variance v*Mv and Borel inverse on the open full-rank set, with zero extension. Gamma convolution and Beta sphere averaging yield the exact moment ratio for 1<=q<=p. Finite Jensen gives first moments; paired descending factors and factorial integrals yield both affine bounds at q=ceil(p/2) and q=p. Convex coordinate-subset interpolation uses 2^d explicit nonnegative weights summing to one, preserves their expected cardinality, and transfers to S*S eigenvalues. S=0, j=0, k=1, weights 0/1 and p=2 are covered. No sharp complex comparison or measurable eigenvector choice is assumed.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Apply the column scan specified in
[[alg-gaussian-randomized-range-finder]] to any $Y\in F^{m\times s}$,
$F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, allowing $s=0$. It terminates and returns an
orthonormal basis $Q$ of $\operatorname{Ran}(Y)$. On each output-rank stratum
$Q$ is Borel measurable, with the variable-size output interpreted in the
finite disjoint union of the matrix spaces $F^{m\times r}$. The projector
$QQ^*$ is a Borel function of $Y$. Consequently the range-finder projector
and $\|(I-QQ^*)A\|_2$ are Borel functions of the sketch for fixed $A$.

Input a fixed matrix $A\in F^{m\times n}$, a positive integer sketch width $\ell$,
and a Gaussian draw primitive as in
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. Draw
$\Omega\in F^{n\times\ell}$ with iid entries in the chosen field and form
$Y=A\Omega$. Select $Q$ deterministically by scanning columns of $Y$ in
order, subtracting projections onto already retained columns, skipping zero
residuals, and normalizing each nonzero residual. In the complex case fix each
phase by making its first nonzero coordinate positive real. Return this
orthonormal basis $Q$ and the approximation $\widehat A=QQ^*A$.

Empty ranges return the empty basis. All operations use exact arithmetic.
No truncated rank-$k$ factorization, finite-precision stability result, or
deterministic error certificate is part of the procedure.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $G\in F^{a\times b}$ have the iid Gaussian law of
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. If $U,V$
are compatible orthogonal matrices for $F=\mathbb R$ or unitary matrices for
$F=\mathbb C$, then $U^*GV$ has the same iid law as $G$. In particular, if
$W\in F^{n\times n}$ is orthogonal/unitary and $\Omega\in F^{n\times\ell}$
is iid Gaussian, then any two disjoint row blocks of $W^*\Omega$ are
independent standard Gaussian matrices.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $k\ge1$, $\ell>k$, and let $G\in F^{k\times\ell}$ have iid standard
real Gaussian or normalized complex Gaussian entries. Then
$\operatorname{rank}(G)=k$ almost surely.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $k\ge1$ and let $p$ be a positive integer, with $p\ge2$ over $\mathbb R$
and $p\ge1$ over normalized $\mathbb C$. Let $G\in F^{k\times(k+p)}$ have iid entries as in
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. Then $G$
has full row rank almost surely and
$$\mathbb E\|G^\dagger\|_F^2= \begin{cases}k/(p-1),&F=\mathbb R,\\k/p,&F=\mathbb C.\end{cases}$$
The complex entry convention is variance one, $\mathbb E|G_{ij}|^2=1$. Write
$G^\dagger=G^+$ for the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]. On the full-row-rank event,
$$G^\dagger=G^*(GG^*)^{-1},\qquad (G^\dagger)^*G^\dagger=(GG^*)^{-1}.$$
Here $U\sim\Gamma(a,\theta)$ means that $U$ has density
$u^{a-1}e^{-u/\theta}/(\theta^a\Gamma(a))$ for $u>0$. For every diagonal
index $i$, $((GG^*)^{-1})_{ii}$ has distribution $1/U$ with
$U\sim\Gamma((p+1)/2,2)$ over $\mathbb R$ and $U\sim\Gamma(p+1,1)$ over
$\mathbb C$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] and
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]].

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $k\ge1$, $p\ge2$, $\ell=k+p$, and $d,a\ge1$ be integers. Let
$G_1\in\mathbb C^{k\times\ell}$ and $G_2\in\mathbb C^{d\times\ell}$ be
independent matrices with iid normalized complex Gaussian entries as in
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]], so
$\mathbb E|g|^2=1$. Put $Z=G_2G_1^\dagger$, where $G_1^\dagger$ is the
Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse of [[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]. For every
fixed $S\in\mathbb C^{a\times d}$, writing $C=2\sqrt2e$ with
$e=\exp(1)$ as in [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], one has
$$\mathbb E\|SZ\|_2^2\le\frac{C\ell}{p^2}\left(\|S\|_F^2+\frac p4\|S\|_2^2\right),$$
$$\mathbb E\|SZ\|_2^2\le\frac{e^2\ell}{p^2}\left(\|S\|_F^2+\frac p2\|S\|_2^2\right).$$
Here $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the induced operator norm of
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] and
$\|\cdot\|_F$ is the Frobenius norm of [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. These
are coarse second-moment bounds; no sharp complex Chevet comparison is assumed.
The values on the null event where $G_1$ loses row rank may be set to zero in
these integrals.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[thm-recursion]]):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Choose an SVD $A=U\Sigma V^*$ and fix any deterministic analysis rank $a$ with $1\le a<\ell$. Write $V^*\Omega=[\Omega_1^T\ \Omega_2^T]^T$ with the first $a$ rows in $\Omega_1$. By [F2] these blocks are independent normalized complex Gaussian matrices, and by [F3] $\Omega_1$ has full row rank almost surely. In SVD coordinates set $Y=\Sigma V^*\Omega$ and $C_0=Y\Omega_1^\dagger[I_a\ 0]$; then $\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)\subseteq\operatorname{Ran}(Y)$. Since $\Omega_1\Omega_1^\dagger=I_a$, the first $a$ rows of $\Sigma-C_0$ vanish and its remaining rows are $[-T\ \ W]$, where $T=\Sigma_{>a}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger$ and $W=\Sigma_{>a}$. For the projector $\widetilde P$ onto $\operatorname{Ran}(Y)$, $(I-\widetilde P)C_0=0$. For any vector $z$, the two terms in $z=\widetilde Pz+(I-\widetilde P)z$ are orthogonal, so $\|(I-\widetilde P)z\|_2\le\|z\|_2$; taking the unit-vector supremum shows that this projector is contractive. Thus $\|(I-\widetilde P)\Sigma\|_2^2\le\|[-T\ \ W]\|_2^2$. The block identity $[-T\ \ W][-T\ \ W]^*=TT^*+WW^*$ and [F5] give $\|[-T\ \ W]\|_2^2=\|TT^*+WW^*\|_2$. The operator-norm triangle inequality follows by applying the vector triangle inequality to each unit vector and taking the supremum; the SVD gives $\|TT^*\|_2=\|T\|_2^2$ and $\|WW^*\|_2=\|W\|_2^2$. Hence $\|[-T\ \ W]\|_2^2\le\|T\|_2^2+\|W\|_2^2 =\|\Sigma_{>a}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2^2+\sigma_{a+1}^2$. Unitary invariance transfers this to $E^2\le\sigma_{a+1}^2+ \|\Sigma_{>a}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2^2$, where $E=\|(I-P)A\|_2$. This uses no inverse of $\Sigma_{1:a}$ and includes $\operatorname{rank}(A)<a$. For every draw $E\le\|A\|_2$; by [F1] it is measurable, so exceptional rank-loss sets do not change its expectation.

Put $\sigma=\sigma_{k+1}$ and $R=\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j^2$. If $\sigma=0$, then $R=0$ and all tail singular values vanish, so step 1.1 with $a=k$ gives $E=0$ almost surely. Otherwise $R\ge\sigma^2>0$; set $x=R/(p\sigma^2)>0$ and $b=\sigma\sqrt{\ell/p}$. By [F6], it suffices to prove $\mathbb E E^2/b^2\le(1+e\sqrt x)^2$.

Suppose $x\ge1$. Apply the second bound in [F4] to step 1.1 at $a=k$, with oversampling $p$. Since $\|\Sigma_{>k}\|_2=\sigma$ and $\|\Sigma_{>k}\|_F^2=R$ by [F5], $\mathbb E E^2/b^2\le p/\ell+e^2(x+1/2) \le1+e^2x+e^2/2\le(1+e\sqrt x)^2.$ The last inequality uses $e<3<4$ from [F7] and $\sqrt x\ge1$.

Suppose $1/7\le x\le1$. The first bound in [F4] at $a=k$ gives $\mathbb E E^2/b^2\le1+C(x+1/4)$. Set $y=\sqrt x$ and $a_0=2\sqrt2-e$. The difference $[(1+e\sqrt x)^2-(1+C(x+1/4))]/e$ is $f(y)=2y-a_0y^2-1/\sqrt2$. The series in [F7] gives $27/10<e<11/4$: the partial sum through $1/5!$ is $163/60>27/10$, and the tail after $1/4!$ is at most $(1/5!)\sum_{j\ge0}(1/6)^j=1/100$, so $e\le65/24+1/100=1631/600<11/4$. For the tail estimate, every ratio between successive terms after $1/5!$ is at most $1/6$ by the factorial recurrence, and [F7] sums the resulting geometric majorant. The square comparisons $49/25<2<289/144$ and $7<64/9$ give $7/5<\sqrt2<17/12$ and $\sqrt7<8/3$. Hence $0<a_0<2/15$, $1/\sqrt2<5/7$, and $2/\sqrt7>3/4$. The identity $f((1-t)u+tv)-(1-t)f(u)-tf(v)=a_0t(1-t)(u-v)^2\ge0$ shows $f$ is concave on $[1/\sqrt7,1]$. Therefore it lies above the chord joining its endpoint values, and $f(1/\sqrt7)>3/4-2/105-5/7=1/60>0$, $f(1)>2-2/15-5/7=121/105>0$. This proves $\mathbb E E^2/b^2\le(1+e\sqrt x)^2$ throughout the region.

Suppose $0<x\le1/7$. Let $s=\lfloor p/4\rfloor$, $p'=p-s$, and $a=k+s$. Then $p'\ge\lceil3p/4\rceil\ge2$, $s+1>p/4$, and $a+p'=\ell$, so $1\le a<\ell$. Put $\sigma'=\sigma_{k+s+1}$ and $R'=\sum_{j>k+s}\sigma_j^2$. The first $s+1$ terms in $R$ are at least $(\sigma')^2$, hence $(\sigma')^2\le R/(s+1)$; also $R'\le R$. Apply step 1.1 at this $a$ and the first bound in [F4] with oversampling $p'$. The same sketch and projector are used; only the deterministic SVD partition rank changes. This gives $\mathbb E E^2\le(\sigma')^2+ C\ell(p')^{-2}\bigl(R'+(p'/4)(\sigma')^2\bigr).$ Since $b^2=\sigma^2\ell/p$, $\ell\ge p$, and $p'\ge3p/4$, division yields $\mathbb E E^2/b^2\le x\left[\frac{p^2}{\ell(s+1)}+\frac{Cp^2}{(p')^2} +\frac{Cp^2}{4p'(s+1)}\right] \le x\left[4+\frac{16}{9}C+\frac43C\right]=xK^2,$ where $K^2=4+(28/9)C$. These estimates include $p=2,3$, when $s=0$.

Since $2<9801/4900$, squaring gives $\sqrt2<99/70$. From this and the bound $e<11/4$ proved in step 3.2, $C<1089/140$ and therefore $K^2<4+(28/9)(1089/140)=141/5$. Since $441/64<7$ and $e>27/10$, we have $\sqrt7+e>213/40$ and $(213/40)^2=45369/1600>141/5$. Thus $K<\sqrt7+e$, and $x\le1/7$ implies $K\sqrt x\le(\sqrt7+e)\sqrt x\le1+e\sqrt x$. Step 3.3 now yields $\mathbb E E^2/b^2\le(1+e\sqrt x)^2$ in the last region.

The cases $x\ge1$, $1/7\le x\le1$, and $0<x\le1/7$ exhaust $x>0$; the zero-tail case was handled in step 2.1. Taking square roots in steps 3.1, 3.2 and 4.1 gives $\mathbb E E\le b(1+e\sqrt x) =\sqrt{\ell/p}\,\sigma+(e\sqrt\ell/p)\sqrt R$. Finally $\sqrt{\ell/p}=\sqrt{1+k/p}\le1+\sqrt{k/p} \le1+\sqrt{k/(p-1)}$, so the original expected-error bound follows without changing its field, dimensions, constants, or sketch width.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $G\in F^{a\times b}$ have the iid Gaussian law of
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. If $U,V$
are compatible orthogonal matrices for $F=\mathbb R$ or unitary matrices for
$F=\mathbb C$, then $U^*GV$ has the same iid law as $G$. In particular, if
$W\in F^{n\times n}$ is orthogonal/unitary and $\Omega\in F^{n\times\ell}$
is iid Gaussian, then any two disjoint row blocks of $W^*\Omega$ are
independent standard Gaussian matrices.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $k\ge1$, $\ell>k$, and let $G\in F^{k\times\ell}$ have iid standard
real Gaussian or normalized complex Gaussian entries. Then
$\operatorname{rank}(G)=k$ almost surely.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $k\ge1$ and let $p$ be a positive integer, with $p\ge2$ over $\mathbb R$
and $p\ge1$ over normalized $\mathbb C$. Let $G\in F^{k\times(k+p)}$ have iid entries as in
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. Then $G$
has full row rank almost surely and
$$\mathbb E\|G^\dagger\|_F^2= \begin{cases}k/(p-1),&F=\mathbb R,\\k/p,&F=\mathbb C.\end{cases}$$
The complex entry convention is variance one, $\mathbb E|G_{ij}|^2=1$. Write
$G^\dagger=G^+$ for the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]. On the full-row-rank event,
$$G^\dagger=G^*(GG^*)^{-1},\qquad (G^\dagger)^*G^\dagger=(GG^*)^{-1}.$$
Here $U\sim\Gamma(a,\theta)$ means that $U$ has density
$u^{a-1}e^{-u/\theta}/(\theta^a\Gamma(a))$ for $u>0$. For every diagonal
index $i$, $((GG^*)^{-1})_{ii}$ has distribution $1/U$ with
$U\sim\Gamma((p+1)/2,2)$ over $\mathbb R$ and $U\sim\Gamma(p+1,1)$ over
$\mathbb C$.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
For $G\in F^{k\times(k+p)}$ as in
[[lem-wide-gaussian-pseudoinverse-frobenius-moments]], put $X=\|G^\dagger\|_2$.
For $0<q<(p+1)/2$ over $\mathbb R$ and $0<q<p+1$ over normalized $\mathbb C$,
$$\mathbb E X^{2q}\le C_R(q):=\frac{2^{-q}\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma((p+1)/2-q)\Gamma(k/2+q)}{\Gamma((p+1)/2)\Gamma(k/2)\Gamma(q+1/2)},$$
$$\mathbb E X^{2q}\le C_C(q):=\frac{\Gamma(p+1-q)\Gamma(k+q)}{\Gamma(p+1)\Gamma(k)\Gamma(q+1)}.$$
For integers $p\ge2$, writing $\ell=k+p$ and $a=e\sqrt\ell/p$,
$$\mathbb E X^p\le a^p\quad(F=\mathbb R),\qquad \mathbb E X^{2p}\le a^{2p}\quad(F=\mathbb C).$$
Consequently $\mathbb E X\le a$ and
$$\mathbb P\{X>t\}\le\min(1,(a/t)^p)\quad(F=\mathbb R),\qquad \mathbb P\{X>t\}\le\min(1,(a/t)^{2p})\quad(F=\mathbb C),$$
for $t>0$. In the randomized range-finder application $p\ge2$, so these tails
are integrable at infinity.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $a,r,s,b$ be positive integers, let $S\in\mathbb R^{a\times r}$ and $T\in\mathbb R^{s\times b}$ be fixed,
and let $G\in\mathbb R^{r\times s}$ have independent standard real Gaussian
entries. Then
$$\mathbb E\|SGT\|_F^2=\|S\|_F^2\|T\|_F^2,\qquad \mathbb E\|SGT\|_2\le\|S\|_2\|T\|_F+\|S\|_F\|T\|_2.$$
The spectral estimate in this lemma is real-field only.

Let $A\in F^{m\times n}$, $k\ge1$, and $k<\ell\le\min(m,n)$. Partition an
$n\times\ell$ matrix $\Omega$ in right-singular-vector coordinates as
$V^*\Omega=[\Omega_1^T\ \Omega_2^T]^T$, where $\Omega_1\in F^{k\times\ell}$
has full row rank. If $Q$ is any orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{Ran}(A\Omega)$,
then
$$\|(I-QQ^*)A\|_2\le\sigma_{k+1}+\|\Sigma_2\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2,$$
where $A=U\Sigma V^*$ is an SVD, $\Sigma_2$ is the trailing block, and
$\sigma_{k+1}=0$ when fewer than $k+1$ singular values are positive. No
inverse of the leading singular-value block is used, so this includes
$\operatorname{rank}(A)<k$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, let

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

be a singular value decomposition with $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0$, and fix an
integer $k$ with $0\le k<\dim V$. Define

$$T_kv:=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(k,r)} s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j.$$

Then $\operatorname{rank}T_k\le k$, one has

$$\lVert T-T_k\rVert=s_{k+1}$$

with the convention $s_{k+1}=0$ when $k\ge r$, and every linear map
$A:V\to W$ with $\operatorname{rank}A\le k$ satisfies

$$\lVert T-A\rVert\ge s_{k+1}.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Apply the column scan specified in
[[alg-gaussian-randomized-range-finder]] to any $Y\in F^{m\times s}$,
$F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, allowing $s=0$. It terminates and returns an
orthonormal basis $Q$ of $\operatorname{Ran}(Y)$. On each output-rank stratum
$Q$ is Borel measurable, with the variable-size output interpreted in the
finite disjoint union of the matrix spaces $F^{m\times r}$. The projector
$QQ^*$ is a Borel function of $Y$. Consequently the range-finder projector
and $\|(I-QQ^*)A\|_2$ are Borel functions of the sketch for fixed $A$.

derivations.claim: By [F9], $\sigma_{k+1}$ is the optimal rank-$k$ comparator. Choose an SVD $A=U\Sigma V^*$ and write $V^*\Omega=[\Omega_1^T\ \Omega_2^T]^T$ with $k$ top rows. By [F1] the blocks are independent standard Gaussian matrices; by [F2] and the wide-row-rank result $\Omega_1$ has full row rank almost surely. Thus [F6] gives $\|A-QQ^*A\|_2\le\sigma_{k+1}+\|\Sigma_2\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2$ off a null set. By [F10], every basis choice gives the same Borel projector as the finite scan. The error is therefore measurable and bounded by $\|A\|_2$ for every draw, so the exceptional null set does not change its expectation.

Fix $\Omega_1$ and integrate first over the independent block $\Omega_2$. By [F5], $\mathbb E_{\Omega_2}\|\Sigma_2\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2\le\|\Sigma_2\|_2\|\Omega_1^\dagger\|_F+\|\Sigma_2\|_F\|\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2$. Tonelli [F8] and the finite moments [F3]–[F4] justify this iterated expectation.

Take expectation over $\Omega_1$. By [F7] and [F3], $\mathbb E\|\Omega_1^\dagger\|_F\le\sqrt{k/(p-1)}$; [F4] supplies $\mathbb E\|\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2\le e\sqrt{k+p}/p$. Since $\|\Sigma_2\|_2=\sigma_{k+1}$ and $\|\Sigma_2\|_F=(\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j^2)^{1/2}$, substituting into steps 1.1–2.1 gives the claimed bound.

The comparator $\sigma_{k+1}$ is the minimum spectral error among all

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $A\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ be fixed, let $k\ge2$, $p\ge2$ be integers
with $\ell=k+p\le\min(m,n)$, and draw $\Omega\in\mathbb C^{n\times\ell}$
with iid normalized complex Gaussian entries satisfying $\mathbb E|g|^2=1$.
Let $Q$ be the exact finite-scan range-finder basis of
$\operatorname{Ran}(A\Omega)$ returned by
[[alg-gaussian-randomized-range-finder]], and put $P=QQ^*$. Then
$$\mathbb E\|(I-P)A\|_2\le\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{p}}\,\sigma_{k+1} +\frac{e\sqrt\ell}{p}\left(\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
In particular, the original approved bound with leading coefficient

unchanged; only the analysis may use a larger SVD partition rank.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice so that the repository's Lebesgue measure
on each positive-dimensional real coordinate space is a measure. A **standard
real Gaussian scalar** has Lebesgue density
$$\varphi_R(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}.$$
A **normalized complex Gaussian scalar** is $z=(x+iy)/\sqrt2$ for independent
standard real Gaussian scalars $x,y$; its density on $\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb
R^2$ is $\varphi_C(z)=\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $\mathbb E|z|^2=1$.

For $F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, an **iid standard Gaussian matrix** in
$F^{a\times b}$ has independent entries with the corresponding scalar law.
For $ab>0$, its expectations are finite-dimensional Lebesgue integrals
against the product density. If $a=0$ or $b=0$, the matrix space has one
element, the empty matrix; its law assigns that element probability one,
and the expectation of any function is its value there. Independence means
the product-density factorization, with this one-point convention for an
empty product.
The normalized complex convention is fixed throughout; it is not the
unnormalized law $x+iy$.

Assume Countable Choice. Apply the column scan specified in

finite disjoint union of the matrix spaces $F^{m\times r}$. The projector
$QQ^*$ is a Borel function of $Y$. Consequently the range-finder projector
and $\|(I-QQ^*)A\|_2$ are Borel functions of the sketch for fixed $A$.

Input a fixed matrix $A\in F^{m\times n}$, a positive integer sketch width $\ell$,
and a Gaussian draw primitive as in

measure. Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ be fixed, $k\ge2$, $p\ge2$,
$\ell=k+p\le\min(m,n)$, and draw $\Omega\in\mathbb R^{n\times\ell}$ with

$\operatorname{Ran}(A\Omega)$, then
$$\mathbb E\|A-QQ^*A\|_2\le \left(1+\sqrt{\frac{k}{p-1}}\right)\sigma_{k+1} +\frac{e\sqrt{k+p}}{p}\left(\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j^2\right)^{1/2}.$$

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $(\Xi,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a
probability space, let $A\in F^{m\times n}$ be fixed, let $\ell\ge1$ be an
integer, and let $q\ge0$ be an integer. Let $\Omega:\Xi\to F^{n\times\ell}$
be measurable and let $P:\Xi\to F^{m\times m}$ be a measurable orthogonal
projector-valued map whose value $P(\xi)$ projects onto
$\operatorname{Ran}((AA^*)^qA\Omega(\xi))$. For Gaussian sketches this is
the output range of [[alg-randomized-power-subspace-iteration-with-qr]].
Assume
$$\mathbb E\|(I-P)(AA^*)^qA\|_2<\infty,$$
where expectation is with respect to $\mathbb P$. Then
$$\mathbb E\|(I-P)A\|_2\le \left(\mathbb E\|(I-P)(AA^*)^qA\|_2\right)^{1/(2q+1)}.$$
This is a transfer inequality; it assumes the powered error expectation has
already been bounded.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Assume Countable Choice. For fixed $A\in F^{m\times n}$, sketch width
$\ell\ge1$, and integer $q\ge0$, the basis returned by
[[alg-randomized-power-subspace-iteration-with-qr]] is Borel measurable on
each output-rank stratum. Its projector and spectral error on $A$ are Borel
functions of $\Omega$, including rank-deficient and zero samples.

By [F4], the output projector is measurable, so the transfer hypothesis is satisfied. By [F2], its range is the sample range for $B$. Substitute the resulting bound for $\mathbb E\|(I-QQ^*)B\|_2$ into the transfer inequality [F2]. Taking the nonnegative $1/(2q+1)$ power gives exactly the displayed expression.

product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice so that the repository's Lebesgue measure
on each positive-dimensional real coordinate space is a measure. A **standard
real Gaussian scalar** has Lebesgue density
$$\varphi_R(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}.$$
A **normalized complex Gaussian scalar** is $z=(x+iy)/\sqrt2$ for independent
standard real Gaussian scalars $x,y$; its density on $\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb
R^2$ is $\varphi_C(z)=\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $\mathbb E|z|^2=1$.

For $F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, an **iid standard Gaussian matrix** in
$F^{a\times b}$ has independent entries with the corresponding scalar law.
For $ab>0$, its expectations are finite-dimensional Lebesgue integrals
against the product density. If $a=0$ or $b=0$, the matrix space has one
element, the empty matrix; its law assigns that element probability one,
and the expectation of any function is its value there. Independence means
the product-density factorization, with this one-point convention for an
empty product.
The normalized complex convention is fixed throughout; it is not the
unnormalized law $x+iy$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Since $x\mapsto1/x$ is decreasing, $\sum_{j=k+1}^n1/j\ge\int_{k+1}^{n+1}dx/x=\log((n+1)/(k+1))$, which diverges with $n$. The coefficient $e\sqrt{k+p}/p$ is positive and fixed, while the first-term coefficient and $\sigma_{k+1}$ are fixed.
