The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Use the periodic cardinal-assignment model of
[[def-ewald-pme-cardinal-assignment-model]], with integers $M_r\ge1$, order
$P\ge2$, grid size $N_g=\prod_rM_r$, a retained signed mode $k$ satisfying
$|k_r|<M_r/2$, and $D(k)\ne0$. Put $u_r=k_r/M_r$,
$a_k(t)=e^{-2\pi i k\cdot t}$, and
$$r_{k,n}=\prod_{r=1}^3 \frac{\overline{D_r(k_r+n_rM_r)}}{\overline{D_r(k_r)}},\qquad D_r(m)=e^{-\pi iPm/M_r}\operatorname{sinc}(\pi m/M_r)^P.$$
Then the single-particle assignment factor and the spread-grid coefficient obey
the absolutely convergent identities
$$b_k(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}r_{k,n}a_{k+n\odot M}(t),\qquad z_k=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}r_{k,n}\rho_{k+n\odot M},$$
where $(n\odot M)_r=n_rM_r$ and
$\rho_j=\sum_iq_i e^{-2\pi i j\cdot t_i}$. In particular
$$z_k-\rho_k=\sum_{n\ne0}r_{k,n}\rho_{k+n\odot M}.$$
The mesh coefficient also has the exact finite representation
$z_k=\sum_iq_i b_k(t_i)$, so no cell-volume or grid-size factor remains after
the displayed $\sqrt{N_g}$ conversion. The alias bound below uses only the Fourier series of
the compact spline; the lattice Poisson theorem is not applied to that spline.

For $u_r\ne0$ define
$$a_r(P,u_r)=\sum_{m\ne0}\left|\frac{u_r}{u_r+m}\right|^P, \qquad a_r(P,0)=0,\qquad A_k=\prod_{r=1}^3(1+a_r(P,u_r))-1.$$
Then $|b_k(t)-a_k(t)|\le A_k$, $|b_k(t)|\le1+A_k$, and
$|z_k-\rho_k|\le Q A_k$ for $Q=\sum_i|q_i|$. For $J\ge1$ and
$0<|u_r|<1/2$,
$$a_r(P,u_r)\le 2\frac{|u_r|^P}{(1-|u_r|)^P}\sum_{m=1}^\infty m^{-P},\qquad \sum_{|m|>J}\left|\frac{u_r}{u_r+m}\right|^P\le 2\frac{|u_r|^P}{(1-|u_r|)^P}\frac{\lfloor J\rfloor^{1-P}}{P-1}.$$
Thus every alias controller has a finite p-series remainder bound.
The periodic assignment also satisfies $\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal G}w_\ell(t)=1$,
so the spread-grid zero mode is $\sum_{\ell}g_\ell=\sum_iq_i=0$ for neutral data.

Fix neutral point-source data $(A,V,\Lambda,\kappa_k,(x_i,q_i)_{i=1}^n)$ from
[[def-ewald-three-dimensional-periodic-source-data]], an Ewald parameter
$\alpha>0$, integers $M_1,M_2,M_3\ge1$, an assignment order $P\ge2$, and write
$N_g=M_1M_2M_3$. Let $\mathcal G=\prod_{r=1}^3\{0,\ldots,M_r-1\}$ and take
$W_P$ from [[def-ewald-causal-cardinal-spline-window]]. Define the periodic
causal assignment weights, for $t\in[0,1)^3$ and $\ell\in\mathcal G$, by
$$w_\ell(t)=\prod_{r=1}^3\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z} W_P(M_rt_r-\ell_r-jM_r).$$
The sums are finite because $W_P$ is supported on $[0,P]$. They collect every
support index into its grid residue; if $P>M_r$, distinct support indices that
wrap to the same residue are added. The spread grid is
$$g_\ell=\sum_{i=1}^n q_iw_\ell(t_i),\qquad t_i=A^{-1}x_i\pmod{\mathbb Z^3}.$$

Use the negative-sign unitary tensor DFT convention
$$\widehat g_M(k)=N_g^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal G}g_\ell e^{-2\pi i\sum_{r=1}^3k_r\ell_r/M_r},$$
which is the product transform of
[[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]. Signed frequency
representatives are chosen before evaluating windows. A retained set
$\mathcal K\subset\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}$ is finite, symmetric under
$k\mapsto-k$, injective modulo $(M_1,M_2,M_3)$, and satisfies
$|k_r|<M_r/2$ for each coordinate. In particular, even-grid Nyquist modes are
not silently retained.

For $u\in\mathbb R$, put $\operatorname{sinc}(u)=\sin(u)/u$ when $u\ne0$ and
$\operatorname{sinc}(0)=1$. Define
$$D(k)=\prod_{r=1}^3e^{-\pi iPk_r/M_r} \operatorname{sinc}(\pi k_r/M_r)^P.$$
Only modes with $D(k)\ne0$ are admissible for division. A computed
implementation must first certify a strictly positive lower bound for
$|D(k)|$; otherwise it returns `denominator-inconclusive` without dividing.
For $k\in\mathcal K$, define
$$a_k(t)=e^{-2\pi i k\cdot t},\quad b_k(t)=\frac{\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal G}w_\ell(t) e^{-2\pi i\sum_rk_r\ell_r/M_r}}{\overline{D(k)}},\quad \rho_k=\sum_iq_i a_k(t_i),\quad z_k=\frac{\sqrt{N_g}\,\widehat g_M(k)}{\overline{D(k)}}.$$
The denominator is the complex conjugate of the printed window multiplier; this
sign is part of the definition. Set
$$c_k=\frac{4\pi}{V|\kappa_k|^2} e^{-|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)}.$$
The exact retained reciprocal energy is
$$E_{\mathcal K}=\frac12\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k|\rho_k|^2,$$
and the mesh reciprocal energy is
$$E_M=\frac12\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k|z_k|^2.$$

Let $\mathfrak d_k(t)$ be the declared physical mesh derivative: it is
$\nabla_xb_k(t)=A^{-T}\nabla_tb_k(t)$ wherever the classical derivative
exists. A grid knot is a point with $M_rt_r\in\mathbb Z$ for some coordinate
$r$. At a $P=2$ knot, take the one-sided vector limits from all adjacent open
mesh boxes. Define $\mathfrak d_k(t)$ to be any selected one-sided limit or the
arithmetic average of all those limits. This is a procedure value and does not
assert that the classical derivative exists there. The
energy-gradient mesh force is
$$F_{M,i}=-q_i\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\overline{z_k}\mathfrak d_k(t_i)\right).$$
Define the diagonal mesh-self correction and corrected reciprocal energy by
$$C_M=\frac12\sum_iq_i^2\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k (|b_k(t_i)|^2-1),\qquad E_M^{\mathrm{corr}}=E_M-C_M.$$
Whether the declared force is the derivative of this corrected energy, and the
error bound it satisfies, are proved separately.

Assume Countable Choice and neutral finite source data on the cell $A\mathbb Z^3$
from [[def-ewald-three-dimensional-periodic-source-data]]. Fix $\alpha>0$,
integers $M_r\ge1$, an order $P\ge2$, and a finite symmetric set
$\mathcal K\subset\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}$ whose signed representatives are
injective modulo $(M_1,M_2,M_3)$ and satisfy $|k_r|<M_r/2$. Require $D(k)\ne0$
for every $k\in\mathcal K$, and let $c_k=4\pi e^{-|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)}/(V|\kappa_k|^2)$ be the positive Ewald coefficient. Use the assignment factors $a_k,b_k,\rho_k,z_k$ of [[def-ewald-pme-cardinal-assignment-model]], and put $Q=\sum_j|q_j|$.

For a query point $x$ write $t=A^{-1}x$ modulo $\mathbb Z^3$ and define the retained exact and mesh reciprocal potentials by
$$U_{\mathcal K}(x)=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k\operatorname{Re}(\rho_k\overline{a_k(t)}),\qquad U_{M,\mathcal K}(x)=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k\operatorname{Re}(z_k\overline{b_k(t)}).$$
Define $E_{\mathcal K}=\frac12\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k|\rho_k|^2$ and $E_{M,\mathcal K}=\frac12\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k|z_k|^2$. For each mode let $A_k$ be the source-alias controller in [[lem-ewald-pme-spline-alias-and-dft-normalization]], and let $B_k$ be the derivative-alias controller in [[lem-ewald-pme-derivative-window-alias-bound]].

Let a complex-vector derivative/gather value $d_k(t)$ satisfy $\|d_k(t)-\mathfrak d_k(t)\|_2\le H_k$ for a stated $H_k\ge0$, where $\mathfrak d_k$ is the declared derivative branch of [[def-ewald-pme-cardinal-assignment-model]] and $\nabla_x=A^{-T}\nabla_t$. The uncorrected mesh and exact reciprocal forces are
$$F^d_{M,i}=-q_i\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k\operatorname{Re}(\overline{z_k}d_k(t_i)),\qquad F_{\mathcal K,i}=-q_i\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k\operatorname{Re}(\overline{\rho_k}\nabla_xa_k(t_i)).$$
Then for every query point $x$,
$$|U_{M,\mathcal K}(x)-U_{\mathcal K}(x)|\le Q\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_kA_k(2+A_k),\qquad |E_{M,\mathcal K}-E_{\mathcal K}|\le\frac{Q^2}{2}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_kA_k(2+A_k),$$
and for every particle $i$,
$$\|F^d_{M,i}-F_{\mathcal K,i}\|_2\le |q_i|Q\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k\bigl[|\kappa_k|A_k+(1+A_k)B_k+(1+A_k)H_k\bigr].$$

For the declared energy-gradient gather $d_k=\mathfrak d_k$ (so $H_k=0$), the mesh force is $-\nabla_{x_i}E_{M,\mathcal K}$ wherever the classical derivative exists. This holds everywhere for $P\ge3$ and off the assignment knots for $P=2$; at a $P=2$ knot the selected one-sided derivative or its average is a procedure value, with the same bound but without a differentiability claim.

The optional diagonal self correction is
$$C_M=\frac12\sum_iq_i^2\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k(|b_k(t_i)|^2-1),\qquad E^{\rm corr}_{M,\mathcal K}=E_{M,\mathcal K}-C_M.$$
For its finite cyclic implementation, set $h_k=c_k/|D(k)|^2$ on $\mathcal K$,
$$\gamma_d=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}h_ke^{-2\pi i\sum_rk_rd_r/M_r},\qquad S_i=\sum_{\ell,m\in\mathcal G}w_\ell(t_i)w_m(t_i)\gamma_{\ell-m}.$$
Then $\gamma$ is real and even, $S_i=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k|b_k(t_i)|^2$, and, on every differentiable branch (or as the same declared one-sided branch at a $P=2$ knot),
$$\nabla_{x_i}(S_i/2)=\sum_{\ell,m\in\mathcal G}w_\ell(t_i)\nabla_xw_m(t_i)\gamma_{\ell-m}.$$
Consequently this local cyclic-kernel expression computes $C_M$ and its derivative exactly in real arithmetic.
The finite tensor-transform gathers also have the exact real-arithmetic forms
$$U_{M,\mathcal K}(x)=\operatorname{Re}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal G}w_\ell(t_x)u_\ell,\qquad u_\ell=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\frac{c_kz_k}{D(k)}e^{2\pi i\sum_rk_r\ell_r/M_r},$$
$$F_{M,i}=-q_i\operatorname{Re}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal G}\lambda_\ell\nabla_xw_\ell(t_i),\qquad \lambda_\ell=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\frac{c_k\overline{z_k}}{\overline{D(k)}}e^{-2\pi i\sum_rk_r\ell_r/M_r}.$$

citations.quote:
Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]) and let
$f : K \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $K$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$
is uniformly continuous on $K$ ([[def-uniform-continuity-real]]).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], proved there from the cover machinery of
metric spaces; the proof below uses the open-cover definition of compactness
in $\mathbb{R}$ directly. That the two
statements are the same statement in two vocabularies is
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], clauses 1, 2 and 5, immediately above.

**Choice-free proof.** The argument below uses the open-cover definition of compactness directly. It considers every continuity neighbourhood at once and extracts only a finite subcover, so no countable or global choice function is selected.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

derivations.claim: Set $\theta(x)=\omega g(x)$. By [F1], $e^{i\theta(x)}=\cos(\theta(x))+i\sin(\theta(x))$.

The scalar difference quotient gives $\theta'(x)=\omega g'(x)$. Apply [F3] with $A=[a,b]$, $B=\mathbb R$, $v=\theta$, and $u=\sin$ or $\cos$: every $x\in[a,b]$ is a limit point of $[a,b]$ since $a<b$, and $\theta(x)$ is a limit point of $\mathbb R$, where both outer functions are differentiable by [F2]. Thus [F2] and step 1.1 give the componentwise derivative $-\omega g'(x)\sin(\theta(x))+i\omega g'(x)\cos(\theta(x))=i\omega g'(x)e^{i\theta(x)}$, including the one-sided endpoint derivatives. Continuity follows from continuity of $g'$, $g$, and the trigonometric functions.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, and suppose $Dg(x)$ is invertible for every $x\in U$. Let $K\subseteq U$ be compact and Jordan measurable. For a bounded function $f:g(K)\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is Riemann integrable on $g(K)$;
2. $x\mapsto f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|$ is Riemann integrable on $K$.

When either condition holds,
$$\int_{g(K)}f(y)\,dy=\int_K f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|\,dx.$$

For all real $u,v$,
$$\sin(u-v)=\sin u\cos v-\cos u\sin v,\qquad \cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v.$$ The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.
$\sin\pi=0$, and $\sin x>0$ for every $x$ with $0<x<\pi$. Thus $\pi$ is the first positive zero of sine.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.
Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be a closed nondegenerate rectangle, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Its graph has content zero in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$.

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its boundary $\partial E$ is null, equivalently has content zero.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded and Jordan measurable, let $f,g:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded, and suppose $\{x\in E:f(x)\ne g(x)\}$ has content zero. Then $f$ is Riemann integrable over $E$ if and only if $g$ is, and when they are integrable their integrals are equal.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

If $a<b$, $g\in C^1[a,b]$ is real-valued and $\omega\in\mathbb R$, then $x\mapsto e^{i\omega g(x)}$ is continuously differentiable and
$$\frac{d}{dx}e^{i\omega g(x)}=i\omega g'(x)e^{i\omega g(x)}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Every $z\ne0$ has a unique representation $z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$ with $r=|z|>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

The following descriptions give the same function $\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$: the power series $\sum x^n/\iota(n!)$; the product limit $\lim_n(1+x/\iota(n))^n$; the normalized solution of $y'=y,\ y(0)=1$; the normalized continuous multiplicative function; and the compact-uniform limit of the Picard iterates.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

Let $f$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval $[a,R]$ with $R>a$. The improper integral over the right-unbounded interval is
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_a^R f(x)\,dx,$$
provided this limit exists as a finite real number. In that case the improper integral **converges**; otherwise it diverges. In particular, a limit of $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ is divergence, not convergence to an extended-real value.

If $f$ is Riemann integrable on every $[R,b]$ with $R<b$, define
$$\int_{-\infty}^b f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to-\infty}\int_R^b f(x)\,dx$$
under the same finite-limit convention. All finite integrals use the oriented convention.

If $f$ has a possible singularity at $c\in(a,b)$, define
$$\int_a^b f:=\int_a^c f+\int_c^b f$$
only when the two one-sided improper integrals converge separately. Cancellation between divergent sides is not allowed.

Likewise, for any finite split point $s$, define
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f:=\int_{-\infty}^{s}f+\int_s^\infty f$$
only when both tails converge. More generally, an interval with several singular ends is split into finitely many one-ended pieces, each of which must converge separately. Independence of the permitted split point is a theorem, not part of this definition.

An improper integral of $f$ is **absolutely convergent** when the corresponding improper integral of $|f|$ converges. It is **conditionally convergent** when the integral of $f$ converges but the integral of $|f|$ does not.

For an integral with several singular ends, absolute convergence means absolute convergence on every separately defined one-ended piece. Conditional convergence means convergence of every piece and failure of absolute convergence on at least one piece. Thus the terminology never permits cancellation between distinct singular ends.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

Let $a<b$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be continuous, and $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Define
$$I_\omega(f,g;[a,b]) := \int_a^b f(x)e^{i\omega g(x)}\,dx.$$
The complex Riemann integral here means the real Riemann integral of the real part plus $i$ times the real Riemann integral of the imaginary part. Euler's formula [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and continuity of sine and cosine, which follows from [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and differentiability implying continuity [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], make $e^{i\omega g}$ continuous. The product is continuous, so both component integrals exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. A function is in $C^r[a,b]$ when it and its derivatives through order $r$ are continuous on $[a,b]$, with one-sided endpoint derivatives. A phase is nonstationary on $[a,b]$ when $g\in C^1[a,b]$ and $|g'(x)|\ge c$ everywhere for some fixed $c>0$. For such a phase and differentiable $h$, put $T_g^0h=h$ and $T_g^{j+1}h=(T_g^jh/g')'$ whenever that derivative exists.

This is an exact-real definition. A later numerical implementation must separately state its moment errors and any floating-point solve error.

The integral $\int_a^\infty f$ converges if and only if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there is $A>a$ such that
$$A\le u<v\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\left|\int_u^v f\right|<\varepsilon.$$
At a finite right singular endpoint $b$, replace the condition by $b-\delta<u<v<b$; at a finite left endpoint use $a<u<v<a+\delta$; at $-\infty$ use $u<v\le-A$. In each case all displayed proper integrals must exist.

Suppose $0\le f\le g$ eventually toward a singular end. If the improper integral of $g$ converges there, then the integral of $f$ converges. If instead $|f|\le g$ eventually and $\int g$ converges, then $\int f$ converges absolutely and hence converges.

The same assertions hold separately at $+\infty$, at $-\infty$, and at either finite singular endpoint.

derivations.claim: Write $u_0=\operatorname{Re}\alpha>0$. For finite $R$, the substitution $y=\sqrt{u_0}x$ in [F1] gives $\int_{-R}^Re^{-u_0x^2}dx=u_0^{-1/2}\int_{-\sqrt{u_0}R}^{\sqrt{u_0}R}e^{-y^2}dy$; letting $R\to\infty$ and using [F17] shows that the real Gaussian majorant has finite one-sided integrals. Since $|e^{-\alpha x^2}|=e^{-u_0x^2}$ by [F20], [F42] gives absolute convergence of each real and imaginary tail; [F37] and [F39] specify these one-sided limits and [F38] defines their two-sided sum $F(\alpha)$. By [F18], every finite-interval complex integral exists; the cut-additivity clause of [F15], applied componentwise at $0$, shows $F_R(\alpha)=\int_{-R}^Re^{-\alpha x^2}dx\to F(\alpha)$. On $S_R=[-R,R]^2$, the integrand is continuous by Euler's formula [F20], differentiability and continuity of sine, cosine and the real exponential [F21], [F22], [F25], and polynomial continuity [F32]; also $e^{-\alpha(x^2+y^2)}=e^{-\alpha x^2}e^{-\alpha y^2}$ by [F19]. Its real and imaginary parts are integrable by [F14]. Expanding the complex product into four real products, applying [F16] to each, using the complex-coordinate formulas [F35], and using linearity [F15] yields $F_R(\alpha)^2=\int_{S_R}e^{-\alpha(x^2+y^2)}d(x,y)$.

Put $D_s=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le s^2\}$ and $A_{\varepsilon,R}=D_R\setminus\operatorname{int}D_\varepsilon$. On $K_+=[\varepsilon,R]\times[0,\pi]$ and $K_-=[\varepsilon,R]\times[-\pi,0]$, the polar map $P(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ has determinant $r$ by [F21] and [F5]. Each rectangle has an open rectangular neighborhood with positive radial coordinate and angular width strictly below $2\pi$. If two points there have the same image, equal Euclidean norms give equal radii; after division by that radius, their trigonometric pairs agree. [F2] then gives sine of the angle difference zero and cosine equal to one. By [F3], the difference is $m\pi$; repeated use of [F4], with evenness from [F5] when $m<0$, gives cosine $(-1)^m$, so $m$ is even. The neighborhood's angular width below $2\pi$ forces the difference to be zero. Thus each map is injective on a neighborhood and its derivative is invertible there because the determinant is positive. By [F30], every point in the upper half-annulus has a canonical polar angle in $[0,2\pi)$; if the second coordinate is positive, [F6], [F5], and [F3] rule out an angle in $(\pi,2\pi)$, while if it is zero [F3] leaves only $0$ or $\pi$. For a lower-half point with negative second coordinate, its canonical angle is in $(\pi,2\pi)$ by the same sign facts, and subtracting $2\pi$ places it in $(-\pi,0)$ without changing its trigonometric pair; points with zero second coordinate use angle $0$ or $-\pi$. These arguments prove that the images are exactly the upper and lower closed half-annuli. For $s>0$, their curved boundary arcs are graphs of $\pm\sqrt{s^2-x^2}$; the radicand is continuous by [F32], and for nonnegative $u,v$ one has $|\sqrt u-\sqrt v|^2\le|u-v|$ by [F26] and algebra, proving continuity of those graphs. Each radial segment is a constant-function graph after exchanging coordinates if needed. Each graph has content zero by [F8]; their finite unions do as well by combining finite covers from [F9]. Thus the half-annuli are bounded with content-zero boundary and hence Jordan by [F11]; they are compact by [F10]. Now apply [F1] separately to the real and imaginary parts on each. By componentwise Fubini [F16], each transformed integral is $\pi\int_\varepsilon^R e^{-\alpha r^2}r\,dr$. Writing $\alpha=A+iB$ and differentiating the Euler representation with [F20]--[F24] gives $(e^{-\alpha r^2})'=-2\alpha r e^{-\alpha r^2}$; componentwise [F29] therefore evaluates this radial integral as $(e^{-\alpha\varepsilon^2}-e^{-\alpha R^2})/(2\alpha)$. Their intersection is two radial segments, content-zero by the same graph argument. On a bounding rectangle, the zero extensions of the two half-annulus integrands sum to the annulus integrand off those segments and to twice it on them; [F12] removes this content-zero difference, while linearity [F15] adds the componentwise integrals. Thus $\int_{A_{\varepsilon,R}}e^{-\alpha(x^2+y^2)}d(x,y)=\pi(e^{-\alpha\varepsilon^2}-e^{-\alpha R^2})/\alpha$. The same circle-graph argument makes $D_\varepsilon$ compact Jordan; [F14] integrates the continuous real and imaginary parts there. For $h=e^{-\alpha(x^2+y^2)}$, [F20] and [F33] give $|h|=e^{-u_0(x^2+y^2)}\le1$; the containing square has area $4\varepsilon^2$ by [F34], and [F13], [F15], [F40] give $|\int_{D_\varepsilon}h|\le\int_{D_\varepsilon}|h|\le4\varepsilon^2$. On the containing square, the zero extensions over $D_\varepsilon$ and $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ sum to $h$ off the boundary circle and to $2h$ on it; [F12] removes this content-zero difference and linearity [F15] gives $\int_{D_R}h=\int_{D_\varepsilon}h+\int_{A_{\varepsilon,R}}h$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ therefore gives $\int_{D_R}h=\pi(1-e^{-\alpha R^2})/\alpha$.

Set $E_R=S_R\setminus\operatorname{int}D_R$. It is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F10]; its boundary is contained in $\partial S_R\cup\partial D_R$. The square boundary is a finite union of line graphs and the circle boundary is the pair of continuous semicircle graphs proved in step 1.2, so [F8] and [F9] make this union content zero and [F11] makes $E_R$ Jordan. Both $E_R$ and $D_R$ are compact Jordan subsets of $S_R$, so their zero extensions are integrable by [F13] and [F14]. On $S_R$ these extensions sum to $h$ off $\partial D_R$ and to $2h$ on the content-zero circle; [F12] and linearity [F15] therefore give $\int_{E_R}h+\int_{D_R}h=\int_{S_R}h$. Every point of $E_R$ has $x^2+y^2\ge R^2$, so $|x|\ge R/\sqrt2$ or $|y|\ge R/\sqrt2$. Put $G=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-u_0x^2}dx<\infty$ and $H(t)=\int_{|x|\ge t}e^{-u_0x^2}dx$; $H(t)\to0$ by [F37] and the convergent nonnegative improper Gaussian integral [F17]. By [F19], the majorant factors as $e^{-u_0x^2}e^{-u_0y^2}$. On finite bounding rectangles, [F13], [F15], and [F16] bound its integral over the vertical and horizontal tail strips by $2H(R/\sqrt2)G$. For $h(x,y)=e^{-\alpha(x^2+y^2)}$, [F40] bounds the complex integral's modulus by the integral of $|h|$, so it is at most $2H(R/\sqrt2)G$. The integrand is continuous on the compact Jordan set $E_R$, so its components are integrable by [F14]. Passing to the one-dimensional Gaussian tail limits preserves this bound. It tends to zero, so the square and disc integrals have the same limit. Also $|e^{-\alpha R^2}|=e^{-u_0R^2}\to0$: [F33] makes this nonnegative function decreasing in $R$, and a positive limiting lower bound would contradict the finite Gaussian integral [F1], [F17]. Steps 1.1 and 1.2, with $e^{-\alpha R^2}\to0$, now give $F(\alpha)^2=\pi/\alpha$.

The function $F$ is continuous on the right half-plane. Fix a compact neighborhood with $\operatorname{Re}\alpha,\operatorname{Re}\beta\ge c_0>0$. On $[-R,R]$, differentiating $e^{-(\beta+t(\alpha-\beta))x^2}$ in $t$ by [F20]--[F24] and applying [F29] gives $|e^{-\alpha x^2}-e^{-\beta x^2}|\le R^2|\alpha-\beta|$. By [F40], the finite-interval contribution to $|F(\alpha)-F(\beta)|$ is therefore at most $2R^3|\alpha-\beta|$. Each omitted tail is bounded by $\int_{|x|>R}e^{-c_0x^2}dx$, which tends to zero as $R\to\infty$ by [F37], [F39], and the scaled Gaussian integral [F1], [F17]; choosing $R$ and then $|\alpha-\beta|$ proves continuity. To justify the branch continuously, write $\alpha=x+iy$, $q=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, $u=\sqrt{(q+x)/2}>0$, and $v=y/(2u)$. For nonnegative $s,t$, $|\sqrt{s}-\sqrt{t}|^2\le|s-t|$, so [F26] and [F32] make $q,u,v$ continuous. Also $2uv=y$ and $u^2-v^2=((q+x)^2-y^2)/(2(q+x))=x$ since $q^2=x^2+y^2$, hence $(u+iv)^2=\alpha$. Let $\theta=\arg\alpha\in(-\pi,\pi]$ from [F31]. Since $x=|\alpha|\cos\theta>0$, $\cos\theta>0$. On $[-\pi,-\pi/2]$, [F4] writes $\cos\theta=\sin(\theta+\pi/2)\le0$ by [F5], [F6]; on $[\pi/2,\pi]$, put $t=\theta-\pi/2\in[0,\pi/2]$ and use period $2\pi$, oddness, and [F6] to get $\cos\theta=\sin(\pi+t)=\sin(t-\pi)=-\sin(\pi-t)\le0$. Hence $-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2$. Then the specified square root has positive real part because its argument is $\theta/2\in(-\pi/4,\pi/4)$ and cosine is positive there by [F4], [F6]. Both it and $u+iv$ square to $\alpha$; since complex numbers form a field [F35], any two roots differ only by sign, and their positive real parts force equality. Thus $H(\alpha)=F(\alpha)(u+iv)/\sqrt\pi$ is continuous; steps 2.1 and $(u+iv)^2=\alpha$ give $H(\alpha)^2=(F(\alpha)^2/\pi)\alpha=1$. On any line segment, if the endpoint values of $H$ were $1$ and $-1$, [F7] applied to its continuous real part would force that part to vanish somewhere, impossible for a value in $\{-1,1\}$. Therefore $H$ is constant along every segment. At $\alpha=1$, [F17] gives $H(1)=1$, so $F(\alpha)=\sqrt\pi\,\alpha^{-1/2}$.

Fix $\lambda>0$ and $\sigma=\pm1$, and for $\varepsilon>0$ set $\alpha=\varepsilon-i\sigma\lambda/2$. For any $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $T>R>0$, [F27] gives the phase derivative and [F28] justifies integration by parts on $[R,T]$. The amplitude derivative is $(e^{-\varepsilon u^2}/u)'=-2\varepsilon e^{-\varepsilon u^2}-e^{-\varepsilon u^2}/u^2$ by [F22]--[F24]; the boundary terms are at most $2/(\lambda R)$. For $\varepsilon>0$, using $u\ge R$ and then [F22], [F23], [F29], and [F36] gives $\int_R^\infty2\varepsilon e^{-\varepsilon u^2}du\le R^{-1}\int_R^\infty2\varepsilon u e^{-\varepsilon u^2}du=e^{-\varepsilon R^2}/R\le1/R$; when $\varepsilon=0$ this derivative term is zero. then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Input real endpoints $a<b$, a real frequency $\omega\ne0$, and an integer $m\ge0$. Set
$$\mu_0=(e^{i\omega b}-e^{i\omega a})/(i\omega).$$
For $k=1,\ldots,m$ in increasing order, set
$$\mu_k=(b^ke^{i\omega b}-a^ke^{i\omega a})/(i\omega)-k\mu_{k-1}/(i\omega).$$
Return the complex list $(\mu_0,\ldots,\mu_m)$. The divisions are defined by $\omega\ne0$. The procedure works in exact real and complex arithmetic; its exact moment identities are stated and proved separately on this page.

If $a<b$, $g\in C^1[a,b]$ is real-valued and $\omega\in\mathbb R$, then $x\mapsto e^{i\omega g(x)}$ is continuously differentiable and
$$\frac{d}{dx}e^{i\omega g(x)}=i\omega g'(x)e^{i\omega g(x)}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $a<b$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be continuous, and $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Define
$$I_\omega(f,g;[a,b]) := \int_a^b f(x)e^{i\omega g(x)}\,dx.$$
The complex Riemann integral here means the real Riemann integral of the real part plus $i$ times the real Riemann integral of the imaginary part. The product is continuous, so both component integrals exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. A function is in $C^r[a,b]$ when it and its derivatives through order $r$ are continuous on $[a,b]$, with one-sided endpoint derivatives. A phase is nonstationary on $[a,b]$ when $g\in C^1[a,b]$ and $|g'(x)|\ge c$ everywhere for some fixed $c>0$. For such a phase and differentiable $h$, put $T_g^0h=h$ and $T_g^{j+1}h=(T_g^jh/g')'$ whenever that derivative exists.

$$F(\alpha)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-\alpha u^2}\,du$$
equals $\sqrt{\pi}\,\alpha^{-1/2}$, where $\alpha^{-1/2}$ uses the continuous square-root branch with $\arg\alpha\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$. Consequently, for every $\lambda>0$ and $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$, the ordinary two-sided improper Fresnel integral exists and
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{i\sigma\lambda u^2/2}\,du=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}}e^{i\sigma\pi/4}.$$

Let $R>0$, $\lambda>0$, $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$, and $H\in C_c^1((-R,R);\mathbb C)$. Then
$$\left|\int_{-R}^RH(u)e^{i\sigma\lambda u^2/2}\,du\right|\le\frac{6\|H\|_\infty+R\|H'\|_\infty}{\sqrt\lambda}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion

Let $f$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval $[a,R]$ with $R>a$. The improper integral over the right-unbounded interval is
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_a^R f(x)\,dx,$$
provided this limit exists as a finite real number. In that case the improper integral **converges**; otherwise it diverges. In particular, a limit of $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ is divergence, not convergence to an extended-real value.

If $f$ is Riemann integrable on every $[R,b]$ with $R<b$, define
$$\int_{-\infty}^b f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to-\infty}\int_R^b f(x)\,dx$$
under the same finite-limit convention. All finite integrals use the oriented convention.

If $f$ has a possible singularity at $c\in(a,b)$, define
$$\int_a^b f:=\int_a^c f+\int_c^b f$$
only when the two one-sided improper integrals converge separately. Cancellation between divergent sides is not allowed.

Likewise, for any finite split point $s$, define
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f:=\int_{-\infty}^{s}f+\int_s^\infty f$$
only when both tails converge. More generally, an interval with several singular ends is split into finitely many one-ended pieces, each of which must converge separately. Independence of the permitted split point is a theorem, not part of this definition.

An improper integral of $f$ is **absolutely convergent** when the corresponding improper integral of $|f|$ converges. It is **conditionally convergent** when the integral of $f$ converges but the integral of $|f|$ does not.

For an integral with several singular ends, absolute convergence means absolute convergence on every separately defined one-ended piece. Conditional convergence means convergence of every piece and failure of absolute convergence on at least one piece. Thus the terminology never permits cancellation between distinct singular ends.

Suppose $0\le f\le g$ eventually toward a singular end. If the improper integral of $g$ converges there, then the integral of $f$ converges. If instead $|f|\le g$ eventually and $\int g$ converges, then $\int f$ converges absolutely and hence converges.

The same assertions hold separately at $+\infty$, at $-\infty$, and at either finite singular endpoint.

derivations.claim: Put $D(u)=A(u)-A(0)\chi(u)-A'(0)u\chi(u)$. Then $D(0)=D'(0)=0$. Near zero, twice applying [F3] gives $D(u)=u^2B(u)$ with $B(u)=\int_0^1(1-t)D''(tu)\,dt$; differentiating this finite parameter integral twice is justified by [F9] and gives $B\in C^2$. Away from zero set $B=D/u^2$. These definitions agree near zero, $B$ is compactly supported, and $\|B\|_{C^2}\le C_{R,\chi}\|A\|_{C^4}$. Thus $A=A(0)\chi+A'(0)u\chi+u^2B$.

By [F10], the integral of $u\chi(u)e^{i\sigma\lambda u^2/2}$ is zero: the integrand is odd and vanishes outside $[-R,R]$. Let $S=1-\chi$. Since $S=0$ near $0$, apply [F4] and [F5] twice on finite truncations of each half-line. All boundary terms vanish at the inner endpoints because $S=0$ there, and at infinity because $S/u\to0$ and $((S/u)'/u)\to0$. The final amplitude $K(u)=\left(\frac{(S/u)'}{u}\right)'$ is continuous, vanishes near $0$, and is $O(|u|^{-4})$ on both tails; [F7] makes its phase-weighted improper integral absolutely convergent. Taking one-sided limits in the finite integration-by-parts identities and using [F6] gives $\int_{\mathbb R}S(u)e^{i\sigma\lambda u^2/2}\,du=\frac{1}{(i\sigma\lambda)^2}\int_{\mathbb R}K(u)e^{i\sigma\lambda u^2/2}\,du$. Apply [F8] on finite truncations and pass to the limits from [F7] to bound the latter modulus by $\lambda^{-2}\int_{\mathbb R}|K(u)|du=C_\chi\lambda^{-2}$.

Since $\chi=1$ near zero, [F1] and step 2.1 give $A(0)\int\chi(u)e^{i\sigma\lambda u^2/2}\,du=A(0)\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}}e^{i\sigma\pi/4}+O(C_\chi\|A\|_{C^4}\lambda^{-2}).$ For the last term in step 1.1, one integration by parts gives $\int u^2B e^{i\sigma\lambda u^2/2}=-(i\sigma\lambda)^{-1}\int(B+uB')e^{i\sigma\lambda u^2/2}$; the boundary term vanishes by compact support. Apply [F2] to $H=B+uB'\in C_c^1$ and the bound on $\|B\|_{C^2}$ to obtain $O(C_{R,\chi}\|A\|_{C^4}\lambda^{-3/2})$. Since $\lambda^{-2}\le\lambda^{-3/2}$ for $\lambda\ge1$, adding the three contributions and applying the complex scalar triangle inequality in [F8] proves the stated estimate.

$$Q_L=p(b)e^{i\omega g(b)}-p(a)e^{i\omega g(a)}$$

every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

$$I_\omega(h,g;[a,b])=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\frac{(-1)^j}{(i\omega)^{j+1}}\left[\frac{T_g^jh(x)}{g'(x)}e^{i\omega g(x)}\right]_a^b+\frac{(-1)^r}{(i\omega)^r}I_\omega(T_g^rh,g;[a,b]).$$
Consequently,
$$\left|I_\omega(h,g;[a,b])-\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\frac{(-1)^j}{(i\omega)^{j+1}}\left[\frac{T_g^jh(x)}{g'(x)}e^{i\omega g(x)}\right]_a^b\right|\le\frac{b-a}{|\omega|^r}\|T_g^rh\|_\infty.$$
For fixed $h,g,r$, the remainder is $O(|\omega|^{-r})$; the constant is the displayed derivative norm, not a frequency-uniform assertion about varying $h$ or $g$.

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

derivations.claim: For any $p\in C^1[a,b]$, [F2] gives $(pe^{i\omega g})'=(L_\omega p)e^{i\omega g}$. Apply [F3] to the real and imaginary components of $p$ and $e^{i\omega g}$; the product rule and cancellation of the two $i\omega g'p$ terms yield $I_\omega(L_\omega p,g)=[pe^{i\omega g}]_a^b$. With $p$ from [F1] and $r=f-L_\omega p$, componentwise linearity [F6] gives $I_\omega(f,g)-Q=I_\omega(r,g)$.
The coefficient equations imply $A(\widehat c-c)=\rho$, so $\widehat c-c=A^{-1}\rho$. The endpoint formula is linear in the coefficient vector, hence $Q(\widehat c)-Q=d^\top A^{-1}\rho$.
The hypotheses on $f,g,\psi_k$ make $r\in C^s[a,b]$. Apply [F4] to $r$ to obtain the displayed exact expansion and bound its integral remainder by $(b-a)|\omega|^{-s}\|T_g^sr\|_\infty$.

With $x=A^{-1}\rho$, [F8] gives $d^\top x=\langle x,\overline d\rangle$ and $\|\overline d\|_2=\|d\|_2$; Cauchy--Schwarz [F5] therefore gives $|d^\top A^{-1}\rho|\le\|d\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2\|\rho\|_2$. The definition $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2$ and nonsingularity give the displayed condition-number form.

Since $c=A^{-1}y$, $\|c\|_2\le\|A^{-1}\|_2\|y\|_2$. Linearity of $T_g$ gives $T_g^jr=T_g^jf-\sum_kc_kT_g^j(L_\omega\psi_k)$. At each endpoint, [F5] bounds the corresponding divided sum by $\|c\|_2\|v_j(a)\|_2$ or $\|c\|_2\|v_j(b)\|_2$; [F7] combines it with the amplitude term. On the interval [F5] bounds $\|\sum_kc_kT_g^s(L_\omega\psi_k)\|_\infty$ by $\|c\|_2K_s$, and [F7] gives $\|T_g^sr\|_\infty\le\|T_g^sf\|_\infty+\|c\|_2K_s$. Substitution in the expansion from step 2.1 gives the stated $E_j,V_j,K_s$ bound.
The complex triangle inequality [F7] combines the exact-collocation bound in step 3.1 with step 2.2, giving the stated integral bound for $Q(\widehat c)$.

1. $f$ is Riemann integrable on $g(K)$;
2. $x\mapsto f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|$ is Riemann integrable on $K$.

When either condition holds,
$$\int_{g(K)}f(y)\,dy=\int_K f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|\,dx.$$

If $K\subseteq U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $K$ compact and $U$ open, then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $K$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq U$.

A phase is nonstationary on $[a,b]$ when $g\in C^1[a,b]$ and $|g'(x)|\ge c$ everywhere for some fixed $c>0$. Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,

derivations.claim: Let $Q_n^\ast=\sum_jf(c_j)\mu_j$. By [F1] and [F5], linearity of the integral gives $Q_n^\ast=I_\omega(p_n,g)$; by [F2] and the finite-sum triangle inequality [F4], $|Q_n^\ast-Q_n|\le\eta_n$. The same linearity gives $I_\omega(f,g)-Q_n=I_\omega(r,g)+(Q_n^\ast-Q_n)$.

The endpoint nodes and [F1] give $r(a)=r(b)=0$, so the first boundary term in [F3] vanishes. Applying [F3] to $r$ leaves $I_\omega(r,g)=-\frac{[(T_gr/g')e^{i\omega g}]_a^b}{(i\omega)^2}+\frac{I_\omega(T_g^2r,g)}{(i\omega)^2}.$

Input $a<b$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, real $g\in C^1[a,b]$ with $|g'|\ge c>0$, complex $f\in C[a,b]$, an integer $n\ge2$, and complex-valued $C^1$ functions $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_n:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ linearly independent over $\mathbb C$. Also input distinct collocation nodes $a=x_1<\cdots<x_n=b$. Define $L_\omega\psi=\psi'+i\omega g'\psi$, form $A_{jk}=L_\omega\psi_k(x_j)$ and $y_j=f(x_j)$. If $A$ is singular, return failure status and no quadrature value. Otherwise solve $Ac=y$ in exact arithmetic, put $p=\sum_{k=1}^nc_k\psi_k$, and return
$$Q_L=p(b)e^{i\omega g(b)}-p(a)e^{i\omega g(a)}$$
with $A,c$, and $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2$, where vector norms are Euclidean and $\|A\|_2=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$ is the induced matrix norm. This is a finite collocation procedure; residual and conditioning claims for the nonsingular branch are stated separately on this page. Rounded factorization error is outside this exact-arithmetic definition.

Let $a<b$, $s\ge1$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, complex-valued $f\in C^s[a,b]$, and real-valued $g\in C^{s+1}[a,b]$ with $|g'|\ge c>0$. Use a nonsingular collocation system from [[alg-na-levin-collocation-quadrature]], with complex-valued basis functions $\psi_k:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ in $C^{s+1}[a,b]$. Write $A_{jk}=L_\omega\psi_k(x_j)$, $y_j=f(x_j)$, $c=A^{-1}y$, $p=\sum_kc_k\psi_k$, $Q=p(b)e^{i\omega g(b)}-p(a)e^{i\omega g(a)}$, and $r=f-L_\omega p$. Then
$$I_\omega(f,g;[a,b])-Q=I_\omega(r,g;[a,b])=\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\frac{(-1)^j}{(i\omega)^{j+1}}\left[\frac{T_g^jr(x)}{g'(x)}e^{i\omega g(x)}\right]_a^b+\frac{(-1)^s}{(i\omega)^s}I_\omega(T_g^sr,g;[a,b]).$$
Put $E_j=|T_g^jf(a)/g'(a)|+|T_g^jf(b)/g'(b)|$, $V_j=\|v_j(a)\|_2+\|v_j(b)\|_2$ for $v_{j,k}(x)=T_g^j(L_\omega\psi_k)(x)/g'(x)$, and $K_s=(\sum_k\|T_g^s(L_\omega\psi_k)\|_\infty^2)^{1/2}$. Then
$$|I_\omega(f,g)-Q|\le\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\frac{E_j+\|A^{-1}\|_2\|y\|_2V_j}{|\omega|^{j+1}}+\frac{b-a}{|\omega|^s}\left(\|T_g^sf\|_\infty+\|A^{-1}\|_2\|y\|_2K_s\right).$$
If an approximate coefficient vector $\widehat c$ has exact residual $\rho=A\widehat c-y$ and endpoint vector $d_k=\psi_k(b)e^{i\omega g(b)}-\psi_k(a)e^{i\omega g(a)}$, its output satisfies
$$|Q(\widehat c)-Q|\le\|d\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2\|\rho\|_2=\|d\|_2\frac{\kappa_2(A)}{\|A\|_2}\|\rho\|_2.$$
If $B_s$ denotes the right-hand side of the preceding collocation bound, then
$$|I_\omega(f,g)-Q(\widehat c)|\le B_s+\|d\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2\|\rho\|_2.$$
All vector norms are Euclidean, $\|A\|_2=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$ is the induced matrix norm, and $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2$.
Thus a small nodal residual alone does not provide an integral-error bound; the smooth residual terms and inverse solve amplification are also required.

derivations.claim: Direct differentiation gives $p_\varepsilon(0)=1$, $p_\varepsilon(1)=0$, $p_\varepsilon'(0)=-i\omega$, and $p_\varepsilon'(1)=\varepsilon$. Therefore $L_\omega p_\varepsilon(0)=0$ and $L_\omega p_\varepsilon(1)=\varepsilon$. The basis functions are linearly independent because $p_\varepsilon$ is nonconstant, and [F1] gives $A_\varepsilon=\begin{bmatrix}i\omega&i\omega\\i\omega&i\omega+\varepsilon\end{bmatrix},\qquad \det A_\varepsilon=i\omega\varepsilon\ne0.$

For $f=0$, the exact right-hand side and solution are zero. Multiplying $A_\varepsilon$ by $\widehat c=(-1,1)$ gives $\rho=(0,\varepsilon)$, while the associated polynomial is $\widehat p=-\psi_1+\psi_2=p_\varepsilon$. Its endpoint values give $Q(\widehat c)=0\cdot e^{i\omega}-1=-1$. Hence the exact integral is $0$ and the endpoint error has magnitude $1$ although $\|\rho\|_2=\varepsilon$.

Solving $A_\varepsilon z=(0,1)$ gives $z=(-1/\varepsilon,1/\varepsilon)$, so $\|A_\varepsilon^{-1}\|_2\ge\sqrt2/\varepsilon$. Also $\|A_\varepsilon\|_2\ge\|A_\varepsilon(1,0)^T\|_2=\sqrt2\,\omega$. Thus $\kappa_2(A_\varepsilon)\ge2\omega/\varepsilon\to\infty$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The factor in [F2] records this amplification; the residual norm alone cannot certify a small quadrature error.

$$I_\omega(f,g;[a,b])=\frac{1}{i\omega}\left[\frac{f(x)e^{i\omega g(x)}}{g'(x)}\right]_a^b+f(x_0)e^{i\omega g(x_0)}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{|\omega g''(x_0)|}}e^{i\sigma\pi/4}+\mathcal R_\omega,$$
where
$$|\mathcal R_\omega|\le\left(C_{R,\eta}\|A\|_{C^4}+|T_gh(a)/g'(a)|+|T_gh(b)/g'(b)|+(b-a)\|T_g^2h\|_\infty\right)|\omega|^{-3/2}.$$
On the neighborhood where $h=0$, define $T_gh$ and $T_g^2h$ to be $0$; elsewhere use the recurrence from [[def-na-finite-interval-oscillatory-integral]]. The nonstationary norm is taken over the two closed intervals away from that neighborhood.

Let $a<b$, $r\ge1$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, $g\in C^{r+1}[a,b]$ be real-valued with $|g'|\ge c>0$, and $h\in C^r[a,b]$ be complex-valued. With $T_g h=(h/g')'$ and $T_g^0h=h$ as in [[def-na-finite-interval-oscillatory-integral]], one has
$$I_\omega(h,g;[a,b])=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\frac{(-1)^j}{(i\omega)^{j+1}}\left[\frac{T_g^jh(x)}{g'(x)}e^{i\omega g(x)}\right]_a^b+\frac{(-1)^r}{(i\omega)^r}I_\omega(T_g^rh,g;[a,b]).$$
Consequently,
$$\left|I_\omega(h,g;[a,b])-\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\frac{(-1)^j}{(i\omega)^{j+1}}\left[\frac{T_g^jh(x)}{g'(x)}e^{i\omega g(x)}\right]_a^b\right|\le\frac{b-a}{|\omega|^r}\|T_g^rh\|_\infty.$$
For fixed $h,g,r$, the remainder is $O(|\omega|^{-r})$; the constant is the displayed derivative norm, not a frequency-uniform assertion about varying $h$ or $g$.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Input $a<b$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, continuous $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$, continuous real $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, an integer $n\ge1$, distinct nodes $a=c_0<\cdots<c_n=b$, and for each Lagrange basis polynomial $\ell_j$ a complex moment estimate $\widehat\mu_j\in\mathbb C$ with real error bound $\epsilon_j\ge0$ satisfying $|\widehat\mu_j-\int_a^b\ell_j(x)e^{i\omega g(x)}dx|\le\epsilon_j$. Put $f_j=f(c_j)$. Form $p_n=\sum_{j=0}^nf_j\ell_j$ using [[lem-na-lagrange-interpolation-on-distinct-nodes]], then return
$$Q_n=\sum_{j=0}^nf_j\widehat\mu_j,\qquad \eta_n=\sum_{j=0}^n|f_j|\epsilon_j.$$
For $g(x)=x$, expand each real-node Lagrange polynomial as $\ell_j(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n a_{jk}x^k$, run [[alg-na-fourier-polynomial-moments]] through $k=n$, and set $\widehat\mu_j=\sum_{k=0}^na_{jk}\mu_k$ and $\epsilon_j=0$. For general nonstationary $g$, a user may obtain bounded moments by applying [[alg-na-nonstationary-moment-expansion]] to each $\ell_j$ with a certified derivative bound. The exact-moment branch for a general phase is conditional on supplied exact moments; no general exact moment solver for arbitrary nonlinear $g$ is asserted here.

Input real endpoints $a<b$, a real frequency $\omega\ne0$, and an integer $m\ge0$. Set
$$\mu_0=(e^{i\omega b}-e^{i\omega a})/(i\omega).$$
For $k=1,\ldots,m$ in increasing order, set
$$\mu_k=(b^ke^{i\omega b}-a^ke^{i\omega a})/(i\omega)-k\mu_{k-1}/(i\omega).$$
Return the complex list $(\mu_0,\ldots,\mu_m)$. The divisions are defined by $\omega\ne0$. The procedure works in exact real and complex arithmetic; its exact moment identities are stated and proved separately on this page.

For real endpoints $a<b$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and an integer $m\ge0$, the output of [[alg-na-fourier-polynomial-moments]] satisfies $\mu_k=\int_a^b x^k e^{i\omega x}\,dx$ for every $0\le k\le m$, with
$$\mu_0=\frac{e^{i\omega b}-e^{i\omega a}}{i\omega},\qquad \mu_k=\frac{b^ke^{i\omega b}-a^ke^{i\omega a}}{i\omega}-\frac{k}{i\omega}\mu_{k-1}\quad(k\ge1).$$
Thus all polynomial moments for the Fourier phase $g(x)=x$ are obtained by a finite exact recurrence.

Let $a<b$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, $f\in C^2[a,b]$ be complex-valued, and $g\in C^3[a,b]$ be real-valued with $|g'|\ge c>0$. Use the endpoint Lagrange rule from [[alg-na-filon-nodal-moment-quadrature]] and put $r=f-p_n$. If $\mu_j=\int_a^b\ell_j e^{i\omega g}$ and the rule uses $\widehat\mu_j$ with $|\widehat\mu_j-\mu_j|\le\epsilon_j$, then
$$|I_\omega(f,g;[a,b])-Q_n|\le\frac{|T_gr(a)/g'(a)|+|T_gr(b)/g'(b)|+(b-a)\|T_g^2r\|_\infty}{|\omega|^2}+\eta_n.$$
With exact moments $\eta_n=0$, this is an $O(|\omega|^{-2})$ endpoint-interpolation error bound. The constant depends on the fixed amplitude, phase, nodes, and derivative norms.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].
