Throughout this page, $\mathbb R$ is a commutative field with $1>0$, a total order compatible with addition and multiplication, and the least-upper-bound property. Let $\mathbb D=\{m2^e:m,e\in\mathbb Z\}$ be its dyadic subring. For $d\in\{2,3\}$, a nonempty finite indexed site list is a finite list
$$S=((\iota_1,p_1,w_1),\ldots,(\iota_N,p_N,w_N)),$$
where every $\iota_i\in\mathbb Z$ is a distinct stable identifier, every $p_i\in\mathbb D^d$, and each optional weight $w_i$ is either absent (meaning $0$) or belongs to $\mathbb D$. In unweighted mode, a duplicate means equal coordinates; collapse each such class to its least identifier. In weighted mode, a duplicate means an equal coordinate-weight pair; collapse only equal pairs to the least identifier. Equal coordinates with unequal weights remain distinct weighted sites.

The unweighted deduplicated set keeps, for each coordinate value $p$, the entry with least identifier among entries at $p$, and records each discarded identifier in a duplicate map. The weighted deduplicated set keeps the least identifier for each exact pair $(p,w)$ and records only repeated pairs in its duplicate map. A weighted computation retains different weights at the same coordinate; their power values are compared by the ordinary power-distance rule, so a dominated weight may be hidden.

For a finite point set $P\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, its convex hull is the set of all finite convex combinations of points of $P$. Its affine dimension is the dimension of its affine hull. A tuple $p_0,\ldots,p_d$ is affinely independent when the vectors $p_1-p_0,\ldots,p_d-p_0$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^d$; here a basis means every vector has a unique linear expansion in those vectors. This convention makes nondegenerate simplex coordinates unique.

Take a fixed finite universe $U$ of indexed sites as in [[def-indexed-geometric-site-set]], dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$, and an ordered tuple of $d+2$ sites from $U$ with distinct identifiers. Rank all identifiers of $U$ in increasing order, starting at rank $0$, and define
$$P(\varepsilon)=\det\bigl((p_i,h_i+\varepsilon^{2^{r_i}},1)\bigr)_{i=0}^{d+1}.$$
Regard $\varepsilon$ as a positive formal infinitesimal in the rational-function field $\mathbb R(\varepsilon)$, ordered so a nonzero polynomial has the sign of its coefficient at its least nonzero exponent. Expand this finite polynomial exactly and return the sign of its coefficient at the least exponent with nonzero coefficient. If the base is degenerate, return status degenerate-base. The same universe $U$ and ranks are used for every predicate tuple. The procedure never chooses or evaluates a numerical $\varepsilon$. Its returned sign is the declared stable-id convention for the displayed weighted lifted determinant. When all weights are zero, its constant term is the raw lifted determinant in [[def-certified-geometric-predicate-determinants]]; for nonzero weights, replace that determinant's squared-norm column by $\|p_i\|^2-w_i$ before applying this convention.

derivations.claim: Fix $x\in\operatorname{conv}(P)$. A feasible representation is a vector $(\lambda_i)_{i\in P}$ with $\lambda_i\ge0$, $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$, and $\sum_i\lambda_i p_i=x$. Its formal height is $H(\lambda)=\sum_i\lambda_i h_i$. If its support has more than $d+1$ sites, the vectors $(p_i,1)\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ are linearly dependent, so there is a nonzero vector $(\alpha_i)$ on that support with $\sum_i\alpha_i=0$ and $\sum_i\alpha_i p_i=0$. Such a vector has both positive and negative entries. Choose one of the two directions $\lambda+t\alpha$ that does not increase $H$ and increase $|t|$ until a coefficient first becomes zero. This preserves feasibility and reduces support. Repeating finitely gives a feasible representation of support at most $d+1$ with no greater height.

There are finitely many supports of size at most $d+1$. For any affinely independent support, its coefficients representing $x$ are unique; any dependent support reduces by step 1.1. Therefore the minimum formal height among feasible representations is attained among a finite nonempty set of basic supports.

Exclude temporarily the finite union of convex hulls of subsets of at most $d$ sites. For an $x$ outside this union, choose a minimizing support of smallest cardinality; it has exactly $d+1$ sites, is affinely independent, and has strictly positive coefficients $\lambda_i$. Indeed, a dependent support reduces by step 1.1 without increasing its minimal height, contradicting minimal cardinality. For any other site $q$, write its unique affine coordinates $q=\sum_i\alpha_i p_i$, $\sum_i\alpha_i=1$. For sufficiently small positive $t$, replacing $\lambda_i$ by $\lambda_i-t\alpha_i$ and adding coefficient $t$ at $q$ remains feasible. Minimality gives $h_q-\sum_i\alpha_i h_i\ge0$. Hence the hyperplane through the lifted support sites lies below every lifted site and its projected simplex contains $x$.

The set excluded in step 3.1 lies in a finite union of proper affine subspaces. A line segment in any open ball of $\operatorname{int}\operatorname{conv}(P)$ can be chosen in a direction not parallel to any of these subspaces; each subspace then removes at most one point of the segment. Thus the complement is dense in the interior. The interior is dense in the whole convex hull: join any hull point to a fixed interior point, and every point of the joining segment other than the hull endpoint is interior by convexity. There are finitely many $d$-tuples of sites, hence finitely many lower simplices; their projected simplices are closed. Step 3.1 puts a dense subset of $\operatorname{conv}(P)$ in their union, so that finite union covers the entire convex hull.

If a lower hyperplane contained at least $d+2$ lifted sites, its projected face would contain a nondegenerate $d$-tuple and an additional site, contradicting the nonzero determinant from [F3]. Thus every full-dimensional lower cell is a simplex. If two projected lower simplices have support planes $L_1,L_2$, all their vertices lie on or above both supporting planes. For a point $x$ in the intersection of their projections, the two lifted convex combinations at $x$ therefore force $L_1(x)\ge L_2(x)$ and $L_2(x)\ge L_1(x)$; hence $L_1(x)=L_2(x)$. On each simplex the corresponding plane difference has one sign at every vertex, so its zero set is a face. If $L_1=L_2$, the nonzero determinant [F3] forces the same $d+1$ vertices. Thus intersections are common faces.

The supporting inequality for a formal lift has nonnegative constant-term difference at each site; otherwise its negative constant coefficient would force a negative formal sign by [F3]. The constant terms therefore give the unperturbed weak support inequalities, and [F4] identifies them with empty power spheres.

derivations.claim:
Fix a vertex $v$ of $Q$ and let $C$ be the convex hull of its other vertices. Since $v$ is extreme, $v
otin C$. Writing $C$ as the continuous image of the compact coefficient simplex shows that $C$ is compact, so choose $q\in C$ minimizing $\|v-q\|$. For every $y\in C$ and $0<t\le1$, $q+t(y-q)\in C$, hence $\|v-q-t(y-q)\|^2\ge\|v-q\|^2$. Expanding, dividing by $t$, and letting $t\downarrow0$ gives $(v-q)\cdot(y-q)\le0$. Therefore $\ell(x)=(v-q)\cdot x$ satisfies $\ell(v)-\ell(y)\ge\|v-q\|^2>0$ for every $y\in C$. Choose $\delta>0$ smaller than every gap $g_u=\ell(v)-\ell(u)>0$ over the other vertices. The section $Q_v=Q\cap\{\ell=\ell(v)-\delta\}$ is a cross-section of the cone generated by the directions $u-v$. Indeed, the segment $[v,u]$ meets it at $x_u=v+ rac{\delta}{g_u}(u-v)$, and if $x=\lambda_vv+\sum_{u
e v}\lambda_uu\in Q_v$, then $\mu_u=\lambda_ug_u/\delta$ are nonnegative, sum to $1$, and give $x=\sum_{u
e v}\mu_ux_u$. Thus $Q_v=\operatorname{conv}\{x_u:u
e v\}$. The cone is four-dimensional because the vertex differences span $\mathbb R^4$, so its transverse section is three-dimensional. A face of this cone is generated by the directions of the corresponding face of $Q$ through $v$: a supporting linear inequality of the cone restricts to a supporting inequality of $Q$ tight at $v$, and conversely the facets active at $v$ define the cone. Therefore its extreme rays correspond to edges at $v$, and its three-dimensional faces correspond to facets of $Q$ containing $v$. A facet of $Q$ not containing $v$ misses the section because all its vertices lie below the section level. Intersecting cone faces with the transverse section lowers dimension by one, so the vertices of $Q_v$ correspond to edges of $Q$ at $v$ and its facets correspond to facets of $Q$ containing $v$. Write $d_v,t_v$ for the numbers of vertices and facets of $Q_v$.

Choose a facet $F_0$ of $Q_v$. A viewpoint just outside a relative-interior point of $F_0$ gives a Schlegel projection onto its plane: each ray through an interior point of $F_0$ enters $Q_v$ there and, by convexity and boundedness, has a unique exit point on the opposite boundary. The set of such viewpoints contains an open region. The exit points cover $F_0$; uniqueness makes projected facet interiors disjoint, and shared edges project to shared boundaries. Choose the viewpoint generically within this region so projected vertices are distinct and no three projected vertices are collinear. A pair coincidence forces the viewpoint onto the line through that pair; collinearity of three projected vertices forces it into the plane through those three noncollinear vertices. These finitely many proper algebraic sets cannot exhaust an open region: each lies in the zero set of a nonzero polynomial, and a nonzero polynomial cannot vanish on an open set (in one variable it has finitely many roots; induction on the variables applied to its coefficient polynomials proves the claim). Triangulate each projected convex polygonal facet by joining one vertex to its nonadjacent vertices. This yields a triangulation of $F_0$ with $d_v$ sites and $k_v$ hull sites, where $k_v$ is the number of vertices of $F_0$ and $k_v\ge3$.
There are $t_v-1$ bounded facets in the Schlegel triangulation, and each contributes at least one triangle, so $t_v-1\le T_v$. By [F1], $T_v=2d_v-2-k_v$. Therefore $t_v\le2d_v-1-k_v\le2d_v-4$.

Let $T$ be a nondegenerate triangle with ordered vertices $p_0,p_1,p_2\in\mathbb D^2$. For $x\in\mathbb R^2$, its **barycentric coordinates** are the unique scalars $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ satisfying $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$ and $x=\sum_i\lambda_i p_i$. They are exact for dyadic $x$: they are obtained by solving the invertible $2\times2$ system with columns $p_1-p_0,p_2-p_0$. The point is in $T$ exactly when all $\lambda_i\ge0$.

Given vertex data $f_0,f_1,f_2\in\mathbb R$, the **barycentric affine interpolant** on $T$ is $I_Tf(x)=\sum_i\lambda_i f_i$. A point-location result is a containing triangle of the triangulation, with a shared-edge or shared-vertex result allowed when the point lies on a face; outside the convex hull its status is `outside-hull` and no containing triangle is returned.

For a nonempty finite unweighted indexed site set $P$, the **nearest-site query** returns a site minimizing $\|x-p\|^2$, breaking ties by the least stable identifier. Its hull status is `inside-hull` for $x\in\operatorname{conv}P$ and `outside-hull` otherwise. The minimizer is returned in either case.

Use the unweighted deduplicated coordinate set of [[def-indexed-geometric-site-set]]. If its affine dimension is zero, its output is its single site. If its affine dimension is one, sort by the first varying coordinate (use $x$ if it varies, otherwise $y$) and take the chain joining consecutive sites; this is the lower-dimensional output and contains no triangles.

For affine dimension two, a **triangulation of the sites** is a finite family of nondegenerate closed triangles whose vertices are sites, whose union is the convex hull, and whose pairwise intersections are common faces. Its 1-skeleton is the graph with these sites as vertices and all triangle sides as edges; it is connected. The bounded faces of this plane graph are exactly the chosen triangles, and its one unbounded face is the exterior of the convex hull. The boundary edges of the convex hull are subdivided at every site on that boundary. A triangle is **weakly empty-circle** when no site lies strictly inside its circumdisk; other sites may lie on its boundary.

For each site $p$, its closed **Voronoi cell** is
$$V(p)=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\|x-p\|^2\le\|x-q\|^2\text{ for every site }q\}.$$
A tie belongs to every minimizing cell. The **Delaunay graph** has one vertex for each site and an edge $pq$ exactly when $V(p)\cap V(q)$ contains a nontrivial line segment. A **Voronoi vertex** is a point belonging to at least three distinct cells. It is dual to the convex polygon of the nearest sites; [[lem-voronoi-vertex-empty-circle]] proves that those sites are vertices on one empty circle centered at that point. A **Delaunay triangulation** is a triangulation refining these polygonal Delaunay faces and having weakly empty circumdisks. In a cocircular face the triangulation need not be unique; the chosen algorithmic refinement is the fixed-universe convention of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]].

The convex-hull boundary is the boundary of the union of the triangles. An unbounded Voronoi cell corresponds to a site on that boundary. No minimum-angle or other mesh-quality condition is part of these definitions.

$$P(X)=y_0+(y_1-y_0)\frac{X-a}{b-a}.$$

For a finite triangulation of the convex hull of $n$ distinct planar sites of affine dimension two, let $k$ be the number of sites on the hull boundary, $E$ the number of edges, and $T$ the number of bounded triangular faces. Then

derivations.claim: Consider any triangulation of a convex polygon whose interior edges all have the legal lifted incircle sign. The determinant identity [F2] is polynomial in the height entries, so it remains true coefficientwise for the formal heights [F3]; exact signs are supplied by [F5]. Across a shared edge the affine triangle planes agree on the edge. The legal sign says the opposite vertex of either triangle lies on or above the continuation of the other plane; the two tests are equivalent because the difference of the planes vanishes on the shared edge and changes sign across it. Thus the piecewise-affine height has nondecreasing slope when crossing the edge. For any triangle $\tau$ and any vertex $q$, choose $x$ in the interior of $\tau$ so $xq$ crosses edges transversely and avoids every other vertex; finitely many lines are forbidden. Along $xq$ the slope is nondecreasing, so the height at $q$ is at least the value of the plane through $\tau$ there. Every triangle plane therefore supports all lifted vertices from below; taking constant terms gives weakly empty original circumdisks.

In ordinary mode, `CHOOSE-SUPERTRIANGLE(P,0)` enumerates finitely many dyadic triples at each height and performs finitely many exact tests on each. [F1] guarantees an admissible candidate, so some finite height contains one and this search terminates; [F5] supplies terminating exact tests. The initial supertriangle is a triangulation and has no interior edge, so its edges are vacuously legal. Each input site lies strictly inside it by [F1]. The batch algorithm calls `INSERT(p,none)`, whose exact locator scans the finite current triangle list and tests each triangle with finitely many orientation predicates; [F5] makes every test terminate. Because the current triangles cover the supertriangle, the scan finds a containing face or an interior edge. Duplicate collapse excludes an existing vertex, and strict containment excludes a hull edge, so these are the only cases. An edge incidence lookup supplies the two faces of an interior edge. A supplied face or edge certificate is checked with the same exact predicates by the update procedure, without a scan; an invalid certificate returns its stated status. Splitting a face replaces it by three nondegenerate triangles covering it. Splitting an interior edge at its strict interior point replaces its two incident faces by four nondegenerate triangles covering their union. Both operations preserve a nonoverlapping triangulation.

Each flip strictly lowers the common potential [F4]. There are finitely many triangulations of the fixed augmented vertex set, so no state can recur and every recursive legalization terminates. The final triangulation has all edges legal; step 1.1 then proves it is the lower triangulation for that prefix. This re-establishes the induction invariant after every insertion, including the initial prefix.

After the last insertion, step 4.1 leaves every triangle plane supporting all augmented lifted vertices from below. The coherent perturbation has no four coplanar lifted sites over a nondegenerate projected triangle by [F3], so these current triangles are full lower simplices.

By [F6], the lower simplices form a triangulation of the supertriangle. The three synthetic identifiers lie below all input identifiers; hence every input rank in the augmented universe is its input-only rank plus three. All input perturbation exponents are multiplied by $8$, the common substitution $\varepsilon\mapsto\varepsilon^8$, which preserves every first-nonzero-coefficient sign on input-only tuples. Its lower triangles remain lower after adding the supervertices: [F1] places them strictly outside each input circumcircle, so the added support differences have positive constant term and remain positive formally. For a weighted site $(p,w)$, define its power distance from $x\in\mathbb R^3$ by
$$\pi_{(p,w)}(x)=\|x-p\|^2-w.$$
Its lifted point is $\widehat p=(p,\|p\|^2-w)\in\mathbb R^4$. A lower face of the lifted convex hull is a face supported by a nonvertical hyperplane $z=\ell(x)$ with every lifted site on or above that hyperplane. The projection of the union of lower faces is the **regular subdivision** of the projected sites; a simplex in that subdivision has an empty power sphere, meaning its common power distance is no larger than that of any input site.

The lex-refined lift is interpreted over the ordered rational-function field of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]], using one fixed finite universe of all input sites. When every weight is zero, the regular subdivision is the ordinary 3D Delaunay subdivision and power spheres are circumspheres. A weighted site is **original-hidden** if its unperturbed lift is not a vertex of any lower face of the original lifted convex hull, and **formal-hidden** if its lex-refined lift is not a vertex of any lower face of the fixed formal lifted convex hull. These notions can differ; the algorithm's `hidden` report means formal-hidden. A nonsimplicial lower face is refined with the same fixed-universe lexicographic lift convention. For projected affine dimension below three, the algorithm reports `lower-dimensional` with that dimension and the exact deduplicated site list, and makes no tetrahedralization claim. A tetrahedral output is claimed only on the full-dimensional branch with nondegenerate projected bases.

Input is a finite indexed list of dyadic sites in $\mathbb R^3$, each with an optional dyadic weight. Collapse only exact duplicate coordinate-weight pairs, retaining the least identifier. If the projected set has affine dimension less than three, return `lower-dimensional`, that dimension, and the exact deduplicated list; do not assert tetrahedra.

For affine dimension three, fix the finite lexicographic universe before insertion. Process sites in stable-id order (any stated permutation is allowed if it is fixed before processing). At each prefix, enumerate every four-site subset. If its projected base is affinely dependent, record that tuple with status `degenerate-base` and omit it from tetrahedral candidates. Otherwise solve the unique affine height plane through its four lifted sites. Retain the tetrahedron exactly when every other lifted site in that prefix lies on or above this plane in the ordered formal field of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]].

After adding a site, delete old tetrahedra whose plane the new lift violates, retain old tetrahedra still supporting, and add every newly supporting tetrahedron containing the inserted site. This finite set difference is the **cavity repair**; no geometric connectivity or running-time bound is asserted. After the final prefix, report the retained lower tetrahedra, the finite `degenerate-base` tuple list, and every weighted site absent from the lower tetrahedra as `hidden`, meaning formal-hidden in the fixed formal lift, without asserting original-hidden status.

For ordinary orientation use [[alg-certified-dyadic-geometric-predicate]]. For weighted lower tests, form the exact dyadic matrix with lifted column $\|p\|^2-w$ and evaluate the finite formal perturbation coefficients using exact integer determinant signs from [[alg-exact-dyadic-determinant-sign]]. The raw exact predicate keeps zero; the formal lift is applied only by this algorithm's declared tie convention.

Let $d\in\{2,3\}$, let $p_0,\ldots,p_d,q\in\mathbb D^d$, and let their dyadic weights be $w_0,\ldots,w_d,w_q$ (zero when absent). Assume $p_0,\ldots,p_d$ are affinely independent. If $c\in\mathbb R^d$ and $R\in\mathbb R$ satisfy
$$\|p_i-c\|^2-w_i=R\qquad(0\le i\le d),$$
define the power difference
$$\Delta(q)=\|q-c\|^2-w_q-R.$$
Let $O_d$ be the determinant of the rows $(p_i,1)$ for $i=0,\ldots,d$, and let $P_d$ be the determinant of the $d+2$ rows $(p_i,\|p_i\|^2-w_i,1)$, including the query row $(q,\|q\|^2-w_q,1)$. Then
$$P_d=-O_d\Delta(q),\qquad O_dP_d=-O_d^2\Delta(q).$$
Thus the sign of $O_dP_d$ is positive, zero or negative exactly when $q$ is respectively inside, on or outside the power sphere. When all weights are zero, this is the ordinary circumsphere convention.

Fix one finite universe $U$ of uniquely indexed dyadic sites and weights and a dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$. For an ordered tuple of $d+2$ distinct sites whose first $d+1$ sites are affinely independent, the lexicographic lift procedure in [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]] is the determinant sign of one common formal lifted configuration. Every exact nonzero power determinant retains its original sign, every exact zero has a nonzero polynomial tie determinant, and all tuples therefore receive mutually coherent signs. No numeric perturbation parameter is selected or assumed.

For every finite encoded dyadic point tuple and every orientation or lifted
determinant request in
[[alg-certified-dyadic-geometric-predicate]], the returned raw sign equals the
exact determinant sign, including zero, and the procedure terminates. A
nondegenerate incircle/insphere side result agrees with the orientation-
normalized convention in
[[lem-lifted-determinant-sign-matches-sphere-side]].

Input: a finite $s\times s$ matrix $M$ of exact dyadic rationals with $s\ge1$. Output: the
sign of its exact determinant, including zero.

1. In row $i$, write each nonzero entry in reduced form
   $M_{ij}=a_{ij}/2^{b_{ij}}$ in reduced form with $b_{ij}\ge0$ and
   $a_{ij}$ odd when $b_{ij}>0$; write a zero entry with $b_{ij}=0$. Set
   $k_i=\max_j b_{ij}$ and form
   $N_{ij}=2^{k_i}M_{ij}$, an integer matrix.
2. Compute $\sum_{\pi\in S_s}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_iN_{i,\pi(i)}$
   using arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic.
3. Return the sign of this integer sum.

Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $P$ be a finite indexed weighted site set of affine dimension $d$ in $\mathbb R^d$. Lift each site to height $h_i=\|p_i\|^2-w_i+\varepsilon^{2^{r_i}}$ in the fixed ordered formal field of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]]. A **lower simplex** is the projection of $d+1$ affinely independent lifted sites whose graph hyperplane has every lifted site on or above it. Then the lower simplices cover $\operatorname{conv}(P)$ and intersect in common faces. Each lower simplex has a weakly empty power sphere for the original unperturbed weighted sites.

derivations.claim: There are finitely many insertion prefixes, finitely many four-site subsets at each prefix, and finitely many sites to test against each subset. Projected base ranks are decided by [F5]; each weighted determinant coefficient is a finite dyadic sum of products and its sign is computed exactly by [F6]. Hence every enumeration terminates.

If a previously supporting tetrahedron remains supporting after insertion, its old four vertices still define the same plane and all old sites remain above it; it is retained exactly when the new site is also above it. Any newly supporting four-site subset not present in the preceding prefix contains the inserted site. Thus the set difference described in [F2] is precisely the new finite lower-facet list, and there is no unprocessed repair loop.

At the final prefix, every retained tetrahedron has an affinely independent projected base and satisfies all formal supporting inequalities by the exhaustive test [F2]. Conversely, every full-dimensional lower simplex in [F7] is one of the enumerated four-site subsets and passes every test, so it is retained. The two lists are therefore identical; [F7] gives coverage, common-face intersections, and weak empty-power-sphere correctness. In zero-weight mode the power distance is ordinary squared distance, so these are Delaunay tetrahedra.

A site that is a vertex of a lower face lies on the lower boundary over its projected point. By [F7], that point lies in a full lower tetrahedron; if the site were not one of its four vertices, its lift would lie on the tetrahedron's support plane, giving a zero formal determinant on an independent projected base, contrary to [F4]. Hence every lower-hull vertex appears in a retained tetrahedron. Conversely every retained tetrahedron is a lower face by step 3.1, so each of its four sites is a lower-hull vertex. Thus absence from all retained tetrahedra is equivalent to being formal-hidden by [F1]. Every degenerate projected four-tuple is separately recorded by [F2], while affine dimension below three takes the explicit status branch in [F1].
The finite enumerations and finite prefix list in step 1.1 terminate in every case and use no arbitrary choice; ties use the fixed formal order [F4]. This proves the theorem.

Draw one permutation uniformly from all $n!$ permutations of the distinct input sites. Initialize the fixed-universe supertriangle and current triangulation as in [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]], and maintain a directed acyclic graph (DAG) whose leaves correspond one-to-one with current triangulation triangles. Initially the DAG has one leaf for the supertriangle.

For each next site $p$, start at the root. At each node, order its child triangles lexicographically by their sorted vertex identifiers and test each child by the same three signed-orientation containment tests used by `INSERT` in [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]]. Descend to the unique child containing $p$ until reaching a current leaf $T$. Under the augmented general-position condition, $p$ lies in the interior of a unique triangle at every stage; the located leaf therefore supplies the face certificate `face(T)`. Call `INSERT(p,face(T))` from [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]]. The update verifies that certificate, uses it without a triangle scan, and returns the ordered replacement events. Process those events in order: for a face split, replace the old leaf by pointers to its three new triangle leaves; for an interior-edge split, replace each of the two old leaves by pointers to the two new triangles whose interiors meet that old triangle; for a flip, point each of the two old leaves to both new triangle leaves. Each event names the triangles and overlap map as specified by the insertion procedure. A leaf replaced later is treated in the same way, so the graph remains acyclic and its current leaves correspond exactly to the current triangulation. The insertion procedure also accepts an interior-edge certificate from callers whose admissible inputs permit edge hits; this randomized variant's general-position condition excludes that case. Each internal node has at most three children. After construction, remove synthetic-vertex triangles for the returned Delaunay triangulation; the history DAG is the insertion-time point-location structure.

For every nonempty finite indexed dyadic planar site set, after duplicate collapse the algorithm of [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]] terminates. In the affine-dimension-two branch, after each insertion the augmented triangles are exactly the $d=2$ lower simplices of the inserted sites together with the three synthetic vertices, as defined in [[lem-lower-lifted-facets-cover-the-convex-hull]], using the restriction of the common fixed-universe formal heights to that prefix. Uninserted sites are excluded from the prefix support tests; the universe and ranks remain fixed throughout. After removing synthetic vertices, the output triangulates the input convex hull with weakly empty original circumdisks and coherent lexicographic ties. In dimensions zero and one, the algorithm returns the defined single site or consecutive chain.

$$T=2n-2-k,\qquad E=3n-3-k.$$
In particular $T<2n$ and $E<3n$.

derivations.claim: Let $S_r$ be the unordered set of the first $r$ input sites, and let $p_r$ be the last site among them. Conditional on $S_r$, $p_r$ is uniform on $S_r$. The augmented triangulation has $m=r+3$ vertices and its fixed hull has $k=3$ sites, so [F3] gives $T_r=2r+1$ and $E_r=3r+3$. The conditional expected degree of uniform $p_r$ equals the average input-site degree, hence is at most $(2E_r)/r=6+6/r\le12$. The number of final triangles incident to $p_r$ is its degree. During local legalization, the initial face split creates three triangles and each flip adds two triangles while increasing that degree by one; if the final degree is $d_r$, at most $2d_r-3$ triangle nodes are created in that stage. Thus expected DAG nodes per stage are at most $21$, and the DAG has expected $O(n)$ nodes.

Fix a stage $r$ and condition on $S_r$. Let $k_r(q)$ count the triangles of its Delaunay triangulation whose circumdisks contain a future site $q$, and let $k_r(q,p_r)$ count those also incident to $p_r$. Since the triangulation $T_r$ is determined by the unordered set $S_r$, it is fixed under this conditioning. Each triangle has at most three input vertices, so uniformity of $p_r$ gives $\mathbb E[k_r(q,p_r)\mid S_r]\le3k_r(q)/r$. The new final triangles are exactly those of $T_r$ incident to $p_r$, and therefore $\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{\Delta\in T_r\setminus T_{r-1}}|K(\Delta)|\,\middle|\,S_r\right]=\sum_{q\notin S_r}\mathbb E[k_r(q,p_r)\mid S_r]\le\frac3r\sum_{q\notin S_r}k_r(q)$.

Count first the triangles in the final Delaunay triangulations $T_r$ that are created at a stage; for such a triangle $\Gamma$, let $K(\Gamma)$ be the set of later input sites strictly inside its circumdisk. A DAG walk visits only triangle nodes containing its query: a split's children partition the replaced triangle, and a flip's two linked children together cover each of the two replaced triangles. If a visited node is destroyed by a face split, it is the old Delaunay triangle $\Gamma$ being split; the query lies inside it and hence in $K(\Gamma)$. If it is destroyed by a flip, the flip removes an old Delaunay triangle $\Gamma$ whose circumdisk contains the inserted site, together with one triangle incident to that site. The latter triangle lies in the same disk because its vertices are in the disk and the disk is convex. Charge either visited node to $\Gamma$. Each old $\Gamma$ is deleted once and is paired with at most one inserted-site triangle, so it receives at most two charges per query. Consequently the total number of visits is $O(n+\sum_{\Gamma}|K(\Gamma)|)$.

Conditional on $S_r$, the next site $q=p_{r+1}$ is uniform among the $n-r$ remaining sites, so $\sum_{q\notin S_r}k_r(q)=(n-r)\mathbb E[k_r(p_{r+1})\mid S_r]$. Every old triangle's plane supports all sites in $S_r$ by [F2]. By [F4], a future site is strictly inside its circumcircle exactly when its lifted point is formally below this plane; augmented general position excludes equality. Thus precisely the triangles counted by $k_r(p_{r+1})$ cease to support after the insertion, and [F2] returns the new lower triangulation, so this count is exactly the number of old triangles destroyed. The hull remains the same supertriangle, so [F3] gives $T_{r+1}-T_r=2$; the number destroyed is the number of final triangles created minus $2$, hence at most that number. After averaging over $S_r$, the set $S_{r+1}$ is a uniform $(r+1)$-subset and $p_{r+1}$ is uniform within it; step 1.1 bounds the expected number of final triangles created by $12$. Thus $\mathbb E[k_r(p_{r+1})]\le12$, and averaging step 1.2 gives a stage-$r$ expected conflict sum at most $36(n-r)/r$.

Summing the bound of step 2.2 over $r=1,\ldots,n-1$ gives at most $36n\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}1/r=O(n\log n)$. Step 2.1 then bounds expected DAG traversal work by $O(n\log n)$. The located face is passed to `INSERT` and verified with at most four exact orientation calls per insertion; the update does not run the triangle scan, so this adds only $O(n)$ predicate calls. Triangle updates and storage are expected $O(n)$.

At stage $r$ the augmented triangulation has $r+3$ vertices, so the inserted site's degree is at most $r+2$. By step 1.1, which counts at most $2d_r-3$ new triangle nodes when the final degree is $d_r$, each stage creates $O(r)$ nodes and the whole DAG has $O(n^2)$ nodes. Each of $n$ queries visits at most all those nodes, with at most three child tests per node by [F1]. Thus worst-case total location work is $O(n^3)$. The count is in exact predicate calls; arbitrary-precision bit cost is not included.

Let $I$ be a nonempty finite totally ordered set, let $d\ge1$, and assign a point $\xi_i\in\mathbb R^d$ to each $i\in I$. A **cluster** is a nonempty subset of $I$. For a cluster $\tau$, write $X_\tau=\{\xi_i:i\in\tau\}$, $\operatorname{diam}(\tau)=\max_{i,j\in\tau}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$, and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)=\min_{i\in\tau,j\in\sigma}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$. These extrema exist because the index sets are finite and nonempty; repeated geometric points are allowed.

A **balanced cluster tree with leaf threshold $b$**, where $1\le b\le |I|$, is the rooted binary tree whose root is $I$, whose children of an internal cluster $\tau$ are its first $\lfloor|\tau|/2\rfloor$ and last $\lceil|\tau|/2\rceil$ indices in the fixed order, and which stops splitting at clusters of size at most $b$. Its two children are disjoint and their union is $\tau$.

For the column side, let $J$ be a nonempty finite totally ordered set, assign points $\zeta_j\in\mathbb R^d$ for $j\in J$, and build its balanced cluster tree by the same rule with its own threshold $1\le b_J\le|J|$. Column clusters are nonempty subsets $\sigma\subseteq J$, with $X_\sigma=\{\zeta_j:j\in\sigma\}$ and $\operatorname{diam}(\sigma)=\max_{j,j'\in\sigma}\|\zeta_j-\zeta_{j'}\|_2$. For a row cluster $\tau\subseteq I$ and a column cluster $\sigma\subseteq J$, set $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)=\min_{i\in\tau,j\in\sigma}\|\xi_i-\zeta_j\|_2$. Row and column roles distinguish the assignments even when the index sets overlap. In the square case with a common point assignment, take $J=I$ and $\zeta_i=\xi_i$.

Fix an admissibility parameter $\eta>0$. A pair of clusters $(\tau,\sigma)$ is **admissible** when $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)>0$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)\ge\eta\max(\operatorname{diam}(\tau),\operatorname{diam}(\sigma))$. The strict positive-distance condition keeps coincident or intersecting clusters in the near field, including diagonal singleton blocks.

The **block-cluster tree** starts at $(I,J)$. It stops at a pair if that pair is admissible or if both clusters are leaves. Otherwise, if only one cluster is nonleaf, it splits that cluster. If both are nonleaf, it splits the cluster of larger cardinality; ties are resolved by splitting the row cluster. The children of a split are the corresponding child-cluster pairs. Its terminal pairs are called **block-cluster leaves**. Admissible leaves are **far blocks**; nonadmissible leaves, which have two leaf clusters, are **near blocks**.

derivations.claim: At depth zero the root has size $n=\lceil n/2^0\rceil$. If a cluster at depth $h$ has size at most $\lceil n/2^h\rceil$, each child has size at most $\lceil\lceil n/2^h\rceil/2\rceil=\lceil n/2^{h+1}\rceil$, since the split sizes differ by at most one. Induction proves the size bound at every depth.
Put $H=\lceil\log_2(n/b)\rceil$. Then $2^H\ge n/b$, so $\lceil n/2^H\rceil\le b$. By step 1.1 every cluster at depth $H$ has size at most $b$ and is a leaf; hence the tree depth is at most $H$.

If a leaf is not the root, its parent has an integer size $m>b$, so the smaller child has size $\lfloor m/2\rfloor\ge\lfloor(b+1)/2\rfloor\ge b/2$. The same lower bound on leaf size holds when the root is a leaf because then there is one leaf and $n\ge b/2$. Since the leaves partition $I$, their number $L$ satisfies $Lb/2\le n$, hence $L\le2n/b$. A full binary tree with $L$ leaves has $L-1$ internal nodes, so it has $2L-1\le4n/b-1$ nodes.

derivations.claim: If a block node $(\tau,\sigma)$ is split on the row side, its child rectangles $(\tau_i,\sigma)$ are disjoint and cover $\tau\times\sigma$ because the $\tau_i$ partition $\tau$. If it is split on the column side, the rectangles $(\tau,\sigma_j)$ are disjoint and cover $\tau\times\sigma$ because the $\sigma_j$ partition $\sigma$. Thus every split replaces a block by a disjoint cover of that block.

Each split increases the depth of one cluster in a finite tree, so along every branch the sum of the remaining row and column depths decreases and the recursion terminates. Induct on this finite sum: a terminal node is its own terminal cover; a nonterminal node has children whose terminal covers partition their respective rectangles by the induction hypothesis, and step 1.1 shows that their union is a disjoint cover of the parent rectangle. Applying this to the root $(I,J)$ proves that the terminal rectangles partition $I\times J$.

Two distinct terminal rectangles lie in different children of their first common split, whose rectangles are disjoint by step 1.1. Hence all terminal rectangles are pairwise disjoint, completing the partition claim.

**Input:** A field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, positive integers $m,n$, a finite factor list $U_s\in\mathbb F^{m\times r_s}$ and $V_s\in\mathbb F^{n\times r_s}$ representing $M=\sum_s U_sV_s^*$, a rank cap $0\le k\le\min(m,n)$, and a Frobenius tolerance $\delta\ge0$. The conjugate transpose $M^*$ and Frobenius norm are those of [[def-finite-tensor-arrays-and-frobenius-inner-product]].

**Procedure:** Concatenate the factors as $U=[U_1\ \cdots\ U_p]$ and $V=[V_1\ \cdots\ V_p]$, so $M=UV^*$. Take compact singular value decompositions $U=Q_UR_U$ and $V=Q_VR_V$, where the columns of $Q_U,Q_V$ are orthonormal and span the respective column spaces. Form the core $C=R_UR_V^*$ and compute an SVD $C=P\Sigma Q^*$. Let its positive singular values be $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_t>0$. Find the smallest $q\in\{0,\ldots,\min(k,t)\}$ for which $e_q:=(\sum_{j>q}s_j^2)^{1/2}\le\delta$. If no such $q$ exists, return **tolerance-not-met**. Otherwise return **success** with factors $\widehat U=Q_UP_{[:,1:q]}\Sigma_q$ and $\widehat V=Q_VQ_{[:,1:q]}$, where $\Sigma_q=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_q)$, and the exact discarded-tail certificate $e_q$; when $q=0$, use empty $m\times0$ and $n\times0$ factors.

The compact decompositions retain only positive singular directions. If the factor list is empty or its represented matrix is zero, then $t=0$ and the procedure returns the rank-zero representation because $\delta\ge0$. Any SVD choices in repeated singular subspaces are permitted. No result is returned when the requested cap cannot certify the tolerance.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Fix a field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, an integer $d\ge2$, and positive integers $n_1,\ldots,n_d$. A finite order-$d$ tensor of shape $(n_1,\ldots,n_d)$ is an array $A=(A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d})$ indexed by $1\le i_k\le n_k$. Its Frobenius inner product and norm are
$$ \langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{n_d}\overline{A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}B_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}, \qquad \|A\|_F=\sqrt{\langle A,A\rangle_F}. $$
For a matrix, rank means the dimension of its column image and the Frobenius inner product is the same entrywise formula. The adjoint $M^*$ is conjugate transpose (transpose over $\mathbb R$).

For $1\le k\le d$, the mode-$k$ unfolding $A_{(k)}$ has $n_k$ rows and $\prod_{j\ne k}n_j$ columns. Its row index is $i_k$ and its column index is the remaining tuple in increasing mode order, lexicographically ordered. Its entry at that row and column is the corresponding entry of $A$. For $1\le k<d$, the cut-$k$ unfolding $A^{\langle k\rangle}$ has row tuple $(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and column tuple $(i_{k+1},\ldots,i_d)$, each lexicographically ordered. These conventions fix all reshapes used below.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, where $m,n\ge1$, have a singular value decomposition
$$ A=\sum_{j=1}^{q}\sigma_j u_jv_j^*,\qquad \sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_q>0, $$
where $q=\operatorname{rank}(A)$. For an integer $k\ge0$, put
$$ A_k=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(k,q)}\sigma_j u_jv_j^*, \qquad \delta_k^2=\sum_{j=k+1}^{q}\sigma_j^2 $$
with an empty sum equal to zero. Then $\operatorname{rank}(A_k)\le k$, $\|A-A_k\|_F=\delta_k$, and every matrix $B$ with $\operatorname{rank}(B)\le k$ satisfies $\|A-B\|_F\ge\delta_k$.

derivations.claim: The compact SVDs in [F1] give $U=Q_UR_U$ and $V=Q_VR_V$ with orthonormal columns in $Q_U,Q_V$. Hence $M=Q_U(R_UR_V^*)Q_V^*=Q_UCQ_V^*$. If $C=P\Sigma Q^*$ is its SVD, then $M=(Q_UP)\Sigma(Q_VQ)^*$; both outer factors have orthonormal columns, so completing them by orthonormal bases gives an SVD of $M$. Thus the core and $M$ have the same positive singular values.

On success, the output factors in [F1] form the rank-$q$ truncation of the lifted SVD in step 1.1. Its retained singular values are positive and their singular vectors are orthonormal, so its rank is exactly $q$. Applying [F4] gives $\|M-\widehat M\|_F=(\sum_{j>q}s_j(M)^2)^{1/2}\le\delta$. By the minimal choice in [F1], every smaller $r<q$ has discarded tail greater than $\delta$; [F4] then rules out every rank-at-most-$r$ approximation meeting the tolerance. If the algorithm fails, then $k<t$ and the tail at $k$ is greater than $\delta$ (otherwise $q=k$ would pass); [F4] rules out every rank-at-most-$k$ approximation. This includes $q=0$, $k=0$, zero factors, and repeated singular values.

Let $I$ be a nonempty finite totally ordered set, let $d\ge1$, and assign a point $\xi_i\in\mathbb R^d$ to each $i\in I$. A **cluster** is a nonempty subset of $I$. For a cluster $\tau$, write $X_\tau=\{\xi_i:i\in\tau\}$, $\operatorname{diam}(\tau)=\max_{i,j\in\tau}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$, and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)=\min_{i\in\tau,j\in\sigma}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$. These extrema exist because the index sets are finite and nonempty; repeated geometric points are allowed.

A **balanced cluster tree with leaf threshold $b$**, where $1\le b\le |I|$, is the rooted binary tree whose root is $I$, whose children of an internal cluster $\tau$ are its first $\lfloor|\tau|/2\rfloor$ and last $\lceil|\tau|/2\rceil$ indices in the fixed order, and which stops splitting at clusters of size at most $b$. Its two children are disjoint and their union is $\tau$.

For the column side, let $J$ be a nonempty finite totally ordered set, assign points $\zeta_j\in\mathbb R^d$ for $j\in J$, and build its balanced cluster tree by the same rule with its own threshold $1\le b_J\le|J|$. Column clusters are nonempty subsets $\sigma\subseteq J$, with $X_\sigma=\{\zeta_j:j\in\sigma\}$ and $\operatorname{diam}(\sigma)=\max_{j,j'\in\sigma}\|\zeta_j-\zeta_{j'}\|_2$. For a row cluster $\tau\subseteq I$ and a column cluster $\sigma\subseteq J$, set $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)=\min_{i\in\tau,j\in\sigma}\|\xi_i-\zeta_j\|_2$. Row and column roles distinguish the assignments even when the index sets overlap. In the square case with a common point assignment, take $J=I$ and $\zeta_i=\xi_i$.

Fix an admissibility parameter $\eta>0$. A pair of clusters $(\tau,\sigma)$ is **admissible** when $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)>0$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)\ge\eta\max(\operatorname{diam}(\tau),\operatorname{diam}(\sigma))$. The strict positive-distance condition keeps coincident or intersecting clusters in the near field, including diagonal singleton blocks.

The **block-cluster tree** starts at $(I,J)$. It stops at a pair if that pair is admissible or if both clusters are leaves. Otherwise, if only one cluster is nonleaf, it splits that cluster. If both are nonleaf, it splits the cluster of larger cardinality; ties are resolved by splitting the row cluster. The children of a split are the corresponding child-cluster pairs. Its terminal pairs are called **block-cluster leaves**. Admissible leaves are **far blocks**; nonadmissible leaves, which have two leaf clusters, are **near blocks**.

Fix a field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, an integer $d\ge2$, and positive integers $n_1,\ldots,n_d$. A finite order-$d$ tensor of shape $(n_1,\ldots,n_d)$ is an array $A=(A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d})$ indexed by $1\le i_k\le n_k$. Its Frobenius inner product and norm are
$$ \langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{n_d}\overline{A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}B_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}, \qquad \|A\|_F=\sqrt{\langle A,A\rangle_F}. $$
For a matrix, rank means the dimension of its column image and the Frobenius inner product is the same entrywise formula. The adjoint $M^*$ is conjugate transpose (transpose over $\mathbb R$).

For $1\le k\le d$, the mode-$k$ unfolding $A_{(k)}$ has $n_k$ rows and $\prod_{j\ne k}n_j$ columns. Its row index is $i_k$ and its column index is the remaining tuple in increasing mode order, lexicographically ordered. Its entry at that row and column is the corresponding entry of $A$. For $1\le k<d$, the cut-$k$ unfolding $A^{\langle k\rangle}$ has row tuple $(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and column tuple $(i_{k+1},\ldots,i_d)$, each lexicographically ordered. These conventions fix all reshapes used below.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $I,J$ be nonempty finite index sets with point assignments as in [[def-hlr-cluster-trees-and-geometric-admissibility]], and let $\mathcal P$ be the block-cluster leaves of [[lem-hlr-block-cluster-leaves-partition-index-pairs]]. Fix an integer rank cap $k\ge1$. An **H-matrix representation with cap $k$** assigns to each far block $b=(\tau,\sigma)\in\mathcal P$ factors $U_b\in\mathbb F^{\tau\times r_b}$ and $V_b\in\mathbb F^{\sigma\times r_b}$ with $0\le r_b\le k$, representing that block by $U_bV_b^*$. Each near block is stored as its full dense matrix $D_b\in\mathbb F^{\tau\times\sigma}$. Since $\mathcal P$ partitions $I\times J$, these blocks determine a unique represented matrix $\widetilde A\in\mathbb F^{I\times J}$.

The rank cap on far blocks is an assumption about the representation or the target's approximability; geometric admissibility alone does not imply that a given matrix block has low rank. Near blocks remain dense and receive no low-rank guarantee.

derivations.claim: For $z=x/y$ one has $(1-z)\sum_{\ell=0}^{r-1}z^\ell=1-z^r$. Since $y-x>0$, division by $y(1-x/y)$ gives the exact identity $\frac1{y-x}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{r-1}\frac{x^\ell}{y^{\ell+1}}+\frac{x^r}{y^r(y-x)}$.

Because $0\le x_i/y_j\le a/b=q$ and $y_j-x_i\ge b-a$, step 1.1 gives $|K_{ij}-\widetilde K_{ij}|=x_i^r/(y_j^r(y_j-x_i))\le q^r/(b-a)$. Each summand of $\widetilde K$ is the outer product of $(x_i^\ell)_{i=1}^m$ and $(y_j^{-(\ell+1)})_{j=1}^n$, so its column image lies in the span of at most $r$ vectors and its rank is at most $r$.

Summing the squared entrywise bound from step 2.1 over the $mn$ entries and using [F2] gives $\|K-\widetilde K\|_F\le\sqrt{mn}\,q^r/(b-a)$. The sample clusters have distance at least $b-a$ and diameters at most $a$ and $c$; since $b-a>0$, the additional inequality in the Statement implies admissibility by [F1]. The rank bound in step 2.1 and $k\ge r$ then meet the far-block representation in [F3].

**Input:** A field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, positive integers $m,n$, a finite factor list $U_s\in\mathbb F^{m\times r_s}$ and $V_s\in\mathbb F^{n\times r_s}$ representing $M=\sum_s U_sV_s^*$, a rank cap $0\le k\le\min(m,n)$, and a Frobenius tolerance $\delta\ge0$. The conjugate transpose $M^*$ and Frobenius norm are those of [[def-finite-tensor-arrays-and-frobenius-inner-product]].

**Procedure:** Concatenate the factors as $U=[U_1\ \cdots\ U_p]$ and $V=[V_1\ \cdots\ V_p]$, so $M=UV^*$. Take compact singular value decompositions $U=Q_UR_U$ and $V=Q_VR_V$, where the columns of $Q_U,Q_V$ are orthonormal and span the respective column spaces. Form the core $C=R_UR_V^*$ and compute an SVD $C=P\Sigma Q^*$. Let its positive singular values be $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_t>0$. Find the smallest $q\in\{0,\ldots,\min(k,t)\}$ for which $e_q:=(\sum_{j>q}s_j^2)^{1/2}\le\delta$. If no such $q$ exists, return **tolerance-not-met**. Otherwise return **success** with factors $\widehat U=Q_UP_{[:,1:q]}\Sigma_q$ and $\widehat V=Q_VQ_{[:,1:q]}$, where $\Sigma_q=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_q)$, and the exact discarded-tail certificate $e_q$; when $q=0$, use empty $m\times0$ and $n\times0$ factors.

The compact decompositions retain only positive singular directions. If the factor list is empty or its represented matrix is zero, then $t=0$ and the procedure returns the rank-zero representation because $\delta\ge0$. Any SVD choices in repeated singular subspaces are permitted. No result is returned when the requested cap cannot certify the tolerance.

Let $M=\sum_s U_sV_s^*$ be the finite matrix input to [[alg-hlr-core-svd-recompression-with-tolerance]], and let $k$ and $\delta\ge0$ be its rank cap and Frobenius tolerance. If the algorithm returns **success** with rank $q$, its returned matrix $\widehat M$ has rank $q$ and satisfies $\|M-\widehat M\|_F=(\sum_{j>q}s_j(M)^2)^{1/2}\le\delta$. No lower-rank matrix meets the same tolerance. If the algorithm returns **tolerance-not-met**, no matrix of rank at most $k$ meets the tolerance.

Fix a field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, an integer $d\ge2$, and positive integers $n_1,\ldots,n_d$. A finite order-$d$ tensor of shape $(n_1,\ldots,n_d)$ is an array $A=(A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d})$ indexed by $1\le i_k\le n_k$. Its Frobenius inner product and norm are
$$ \langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{n_d}\overline{A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}B_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}, \qquad \|A\|_F=\sqrt{\langle A,A\rangle_F}. $$
For a matrix, rank means the dimension of its column image and the Frobenius inner product is the same entrywise formula. The adjoint $M^*$ is conjugate transpose (transpose over $\mathbb R$).

For $1\le k\le d$, the mode-$k$ unfolding $A_{(k)}$ has $n_k$ rows and $\prod_{j\ne k}n_j$ columns. Its row index is $i_k$ and its column index is the remaining tuple in increasing mode order, lexicographically ordered. Its entry at that row and column is the corresponding entry of $A$. For $1\le k<d$, the cut-$k$ unfolding $A^{\langle k\rangle}$ has row tuple $(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and column tuple $(i_{k+1},\ldots,i_d)$, each lexicographically ordered. These conventions fix all reshapes used below.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: At a leaf $v$, the routine compresses its exact contribution $M_v$; by [F1] and [F2], $\|M_v-\widehat M_v\|_F=\rho_v=e_v\le\theta_v$.

Suppose $v$ is internal with children $v_1,v_2$. Their exact targets add to $M_v$, and their returned approximations add to the matrix $Z_v$ supplied to the core-SVD call. The Frobenius triangle inequality from [F3,F4] gives $\|M_v-Z_v\|_F\le e_{v_1}+e_{v_2}$. By [F1,F2], $\|Z_v-\widehat M_v\|_F=\rho_v$, hence $\|M_v-\widehat M_v\|_F\le e_{v_1}+e_{v_2}+\rho_v=e_v$. Step 1.1 is the leaf base case; induction over the finite tree proves the root error bound. The recurrence for $e_v$ gives $e_{\rm root}=\sum_{v\in T}\rho_v\le\sum_{v\in T}\theta_v\le\delta_b$.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $I,J$ be nonempty finite index sets with point assignments as in [[def-hlr-cluster-trees-and-geometric-admissibility]], and let $\mathcal P$ be the block-cluster leaves of [[lem-hlr-block-cluster-leaves-partition-index-pairs]]. Fix an integer rank cap $k\ge1$. An **H-matrix representation with cap $k$** assigns to each far block $b=(\tau,\sigma)\in\mathcal P$ factors $U_b\in\mathbb F^{\tau\times r_b}$ and $V_b\in\mathbb F^{\sigma\times r_b}$ with $0\le r_b\le k$, representing that block by $U_bV_b^*$. Each near block is stored as its full dense matrix $D_b\in\mathbb F^{\tau\times\sigma}$. Since $\mathcal P$ partitions $I\times J$, these blocks determine a unique represented matrix $\widetilde A\in\mathbb F^{I\times J}$.

The rank cap on far blocks is an assumption about the representation or the target's approximability; geometric admissibility alone does not imply that a given matrix block has low rank. Near blocks remain dense and receive no low-rank guarantee.

Let $I,J$ be nonempty finite index sets with finite cluster trees, and construct the block-cluster tree as in [[def-hlr-cluster-trees-and-geometric-admissibility]]. Its terminal rectangles $\tau\times\sigma$ are pairwise disjoint and their union is $I\times J$.

**Input:** An H-matrix representation $\widetilde A$ on a finite block-cluster partition $\mathcal P$ as in [[def-hlr-and-h2-block-matrix-representations]], and a vector $x\in\mathbb F^J$.

**Procedure:** Initialize $y\in\mathbb F^I$ to zero. For every far block $b=(\tau,\sigma)$ with factors $U_b,V_b$, compute $z_b=V_b^*x|_\sigma$ and add $U_bz_b$ to $y|_\tau$. For every near block with dense entries $D_b$, compute $D_bx|_\sigma$ and add it to $y|_\tau$. Return $y$. All arithmetic is exact; contributions to a row cluster are summed over its block leaves.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $\widetilde A$ is the matrix obtained by placing its stored block matrices on their index rectangles and putting no entries outside those rectangles.

By [F2], each pair $(i,j)\in I\times J$ lies in exactly one leaf rectangle. By [F3], the algorithm adds the contribution $\widetilde A_{ij}x_j$ to output coordinate $i$ from that leaf, and no other leaf includes that entry. Summing over the finite partition gives $y_i=\sum_{j\in J}\widetilde A_{ij}x_j$ for every $i\in I$, which is exactly $y=\widetilde A x$.

**Procedure:** For each near block, store the exact dense sum $A_b+B_b$ and report local error $e_b=0$. For each far block, run [[alg-hlr-bottom-up-recompression]] on its factor-sum tree with cap $k$. If any block returns **tolerance-not-met**, return that status and the block identity; otherwise store the root factors, report the certified error bound $e_b$ returned by that routine, and retain the block partition. The input's node budgets sum to at most $\delta_b$, so $e_b\le\delta_b$ by the bottom-up error guarantee.

**Input:** H-matrix representations $A\in\mathbb F^{I\times K}$ and $B\in\mathbb F^{K\times J}$, a recursively generated output block-cluster partition as in [[def-hlr-cluster-trees-and-geometric-admissibility]], a rank cap $k\ge1$, local tolerances $\delta_b\ge0$ for far output blocks, and for each output block $b=(\tau,\sigma)$ a finite intermediate-cluster family $\mathcal K_b$ partitioning $K$ such that the restrictions $A_{\tau\kappa}$ and $B_{\kappa\sigma}$ are available in dense or factorized form for each $\kappa\in\mathcal K_b$. For a far output block, its factor-sum tree has one exact product term for each $\kappa\in\mathcal K_b$ and node tolerances totaling at most $\delta_b$. This compatibility condition is part of the input.

**Procedure:** For each output block, use the exact identity $C_b=\sum_{\kappa\in\mathcal K_b}A_{\tau\kappa}B_{\kappa\sigma}$. If the output block is near, form and store this dense sum exactly and report $e_b=0$. For a far output block, convert each product term to factor form: $UV^*\cdot PQ^*=U(V^*P)Q^*$ when both factors are low rank; $UV^*\cdot D=U(D^*V)^*$ and $D\cdot PQ^*=(DP)Q^*$ when one factor is dense; and $D_1D_2=D_1(D_2^*)^*$ when both are dense. These formulas produce factors with matching inner dimensions. Run [[alg-hlr-bottom-up-recompression]] on the resulting finite factor-sum tree with cap $k$. If any block returns **tolerance-not-met**, return that status and block identity; otherwise store the root factors and its certified bound $e_b\le\delta_b$.

Use [[alg-hlr-bottom-up-recompression]] on a finite factor-sum tree for one admissible block over $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, with exact arithmetic, rank cap $k\ge1$, node tolerances $\theta_v\ge0$, and $\sum_v\theta_v\le\delta_b$. Let $T_v$ be the subtree rooted at $v$, and let $M_v$ be the sum of its exact leaf contributions. Whenever all calls in $T_v$ succeed, the returned factors represent a matrix $\widehat M_v$ of rank at most $k$, and the reported bound satisfies
$$\|M_v-\widehat M_v\|_F\le e_v=\sum_{w\in T_v}\rho_w\le\sum_{w\in T_v}\theta_w.$$

$$\operatorname{rank}(\widehat M_{\rm root})\le k,\qquad \|M_{\rm root}-\widehat M_{\rm root}\|_F\le e_{\rm root}=\sum_w\rho_w\le\sum_w\theta_w\le\delta_b.$$

Let $I,J$ be nonempty finite index sets with finite cluster trees, and construct the block-cluster tree as in [[def-hlr-cluster-trees-and-geometric-admissibility]]. Its terminal rectangles $\tau\times\sigma$ are pairwise disjoint and their union is $I\times J$.

Fix a field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, an integer $d\ge2$, and positive integers $n_1,\ldots,n_d$. A finite order-$d$ tensor of shape $(n_1,\ldots,n_d)$ is an array $A=(A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d})$ indexed by $1\le i_k\le n_k$. Its Frobenius inner product and norm are
$$ \langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{n_d}\overline{A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}B_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}, \qquad \|A\|_F=\sqrt{\langle A,A\rangle_F}. $$
For a matrix, rank means the dimension of its column image and the Frobenius inner product is the same entrywise formula. The adjoint $M^*$ is conjugate transpose (transpose over $\mathbb R$).

For $1\le k\le d$, the mode-$k$ unfolding $A_{(k)}$ has $n_k$ rows and $\prod_{j\ne k}n_j$ columns. Its row index is $i_k$ and its column index is the remaining tuple in increasing mode order, lexicographically ordered. Its entry at that row and column is the corresponding entry of $A$. For $1\le k<d$, the cut-$k$ unfolding $A^{\langle k\rangle}$ has row tuple $(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and column tuple $(i_{k+1},\ldots,i_d)$, each lexicographically ordered. These conventions fix all reshapes used below.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

For addition, write $\widehat S=\widetilde A+\widetilde B+\Delta$. Expanding the squared Frobenius norm as the finite entry inner product and applying [F5] gives the triangle inequality. Therefore $\|A+B-\widehat S\|_F\le\|A-\widetilde A\|_F+\|B-\widetilde B\|_F+\|\Delta\|_F\le\epsilon_A+\epsilon_B+\delta$.

For multiplication, put $E_A=\widetilde A-A$ and $E_B=\widetilde B-B$. Since $\widehat C=\widetilde A\widetilde B+\Delta$, expansion gives $AB-\widehat C=-(E_AB+AE_B+E_AE_B+\Delta)$. Let $I$ be a nonempty finite totally ordered set, let $d\ge1$, and assign a point $\xi_i\in\mathbb R^d$ to each $i\in I$. A **cluster** is a nonempty subset of $I$. For a cluster $\tau$, write $X_\tau=\{\xi_i:i\in\tau\}$, $\operatorname{diam}(\tau)=\max_{i,j\in\tau}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$, and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)=\min_{i\in\tau,j\in\sigma}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$. These extrema exist because the index sets are finite and nonempty; repeated geometric points are allowed.

A **balanced cluster tree with leaf threshold $b$**, where $1\le b\le |I|$, is the rooted binary tree whose root is $I$, whose children of an internal cluster $\tau$ are its first $\lfloor|\tau|/2\rfloor$ and last $\lceil|\tau|/2\rceil$ indices in the fixed order, and which stops splitting at clusters of size at most $b$. Its two children are disjoint and their union is $\tau$.

For the column side, let $J$ be a nonempty finite totally ordered set, assign points $\zeta_j\in\mathbb R^d$ for $j\in J$, and build its balanced cluster tree by the same rule with its own threshold $1\le b_J\le|J|$. Column clusters are nonempty subsets $\sigma\subseteq J$, with $X_\sigma=\{\zeta_j:j\in\sigma\}$ and $\operatorname{diam}(\sigma)=\max_{j,j'\in\sigma}\|\zeta_j-\zeta_{j'}\|_2$. For a row cluster $\tau\subseteq I$ and a column cluster $\sigma\subseteq J$, set $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)=\min_{i\in\tau,j\in\sigma}\|\xi_i-\zeta_j\|_2$. Row and column roles distinguish the assignments even when the index sets overlap. In the square case with a common point assignment, take $J=I$ and $\zeta_i=\xi_i$.

Fix an admissibility parameter $\eta>0$. A pair of clusters $(\tau,\sigma)$ is **admissible** when $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)>0$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)\ge\eta\max(\operatorname{diam}(\tau),\operatorname{diam}(\sigma))$. The strict positive-distance condition keeps coincident or intersecting clusters in the near field, including diagonal singleton blocks.

The **block-cluster tree** starts at $(I,J)$. It stops at a pair if that pair is admissible or if both clusters are leaves. Otherwise, if only one cluster is nonleaf, it splits that cluster. If both are nonleaf, it splits the cluster of larger cardinality; ties are resolved by splitting the row cluster. The children of a split are the corresponding child-cluster pairs. Its terminal pairs are called **block-cluster leaves**. Admissible leaves are **far blocks**; nonadmissible leaves, which have two leaf clusters, are **near blocks**.

Let $I$ be a finite ordered set of size $n\ge1$, and let $b$ be an integer with $1\le b\le n$. In the balanced cluster tree of [[def-hlr-cluster-trees-and-geometric-admissibility]], every cluster at depth $h$ has size at most $\lceil n/2^h\rceil$. The tree has depth at most $\lceil\log_2(n/b)\rceil$, at most $2n/b$ leaves, and at most $4n/b-1$ nodes.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $I,J$ be nonempty finite index sets with point assignments as in [[def-hlr-cluster-trees-and-geometric-admissibility]], and let $\mathcal P$ be the block-cluster leaves of [[lem-hlr-block-cluster-leaves-partition-index-pairs]]. Fix an integer rank cap $k\ge1$. An **H-matrix representation with cap $k$** assigns to each far block $b=(\tau,\sigma)\in\mathcal P$ factors $U_b\in\mathbb F^{\tau\times r_b}$ and $V_b\in\mathbb F^{\sigma\times r_b}$ with $0\le r_b\le k$, representing that block by $U_bV_b^*$. Each near block is stored as its full dense matrix $D_b\in\mathbb F^{\tau\times\sigma}$. Since $\mathcal P$ partitions $I\times J$, these blocks determine a unique represented matrix $\widetilde A\in\mathbb F^{I\times J}$.

The rank cap on far blocks is an assumption about the representation or the target's approximability; geometric admissibility alone does not imply that a given matrix block has low rank. Near blocks remain dense and receive no low-rank guarantee.

In the H-matrix setting of [[def-hlr-and-h2-block-matrix-representations]], an **H² representation** assigns a row basis $U_\tau\in\mathbb F^{\tau\times r_\tau}$ to every row cluster $\tau$ and a column basis $V_\sigma\in\mathbb F^{\sigma\times s_\sigma}$ to every column cluster $\sigma$, with $0\le r_\tau,s_\sigma\le k$. For every internal row cluster $\tau$ with children $\tau_1,\tau_2$, it stores transfer matrices $E^U_{\tau_i}\in\mathbb F^{r_{\tau_i}\times r_\tau}$ satisfying

$$U_\tau|_{\tau_i}=U_{\tau_i}E^U_{\tau_i}\qquad(i=1,2).$$

For every internal column cluster $\sigma$ with children $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$, it stores transfer matrices $E^V_{\sigma_j}\in\mathbb F^{s_{\sigma_j}\times s_\sigma}$ satisfying $V_\sigma|_{\sigma_j}=V_{\sigma_j}E^V_{\sigma_j}$. These identities are the **nested-basis conditions**. An admissible block leaf $(\tau,\sigma)$ is represented by $U_\tau S_{\tau\sigma}V_\sigma^*$ with coupling matrix $S_{\tau\sigma}\in\mathbb F^{r_\tau\times s_\sigma}$; near block leaves remain dense.

Let $\mathcal P_{\rm far}$ denote the admissible leaves of the block-cluster partition. The row interaction list of $\tau$ is $\mathcal L_U(\tau)=\{\sigma:(\tau,\sigma)\in\mathcal P_{\rm far}\}$, and the column interaction list of $\sigma$ is $\mathcal L_V(\sigma)=\{\tau:(\tau,\sigma)\in\mathcal P_{\rm far}\}$. An H² representation may impose a bound on these list lengths or on their total count; any complexity theorem must state which bound it uses.

**Storage convention:** Store the basis arrays explicitly only at leaf clusters. Store each internal cluster's child-to-parent transfer matrices; the basis of an internal cluster is reconstructed recursively from its children and these transfers.

**Input:** An H-matrix representation $\widetilde A$ on a finite block-cluster partition $\mathcal P$ as in [[def-hlr-and-h2-block-matrix-representations]], and a vector $x\in\mathbb F^J$.

**Procedure:** Initialize $y\in\mathbb F^I$ to zero. For every far block $b=(\tau,\sigma)$ with factors $U_b,V_b$, compute $z_b=V_b^*x|_\sigma$ and add $U_bz_b$ to $y|_\tau$. For every near block with dense entries $D_b$, compute $D_bx|_\sigma$ and add it to $y|_\tau$. Return $y$. All arithmetic is exact; contributions to a row cluster are summed over its block leaves.

**Input:** An H² representation $\widetilde A$ with row bases $U_\tau$, column bases $V_\sigma$, transfer matrices from [[def-h2-nested-cluster-bases-and-interaction-lists]], and a vector $x\in\mathbb F^J$.

**Procedure:**

1. Initialize an upward coefficient vector $z_\sigma$ for each column cluster. At each leaf $\sigma$, set $z_\sigma=V_\sigma^*x|_\sigma$. At each internal cluster $\sigma$ with children $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$, set $z_\sigma=\sum_{j=1}^2(E^V_{\sigma_j})^*z_{\sigma_j}$.
2. Initialize a downward coefficient vector $w_\tau=0$ for each row cluster and an output vector $y=0$. For each admissible leaf $(\tau,\sigma)$, add $S_{\tau\sigma}z_\sigma$ to $w_\tau$. For each near leaf $(\tau,\sigma)$, add $D_{\tau\sigma}x|_\sigma$ to $y|_\tau$.
3. Traverse the row tree from root to leaves. For each parent $\tau$ and child $\tau_i$, add $E^U_{\tau_i}w_\tau$ to $w_{\tau_i}$. At each row leaf $\tau$, add $U_\tau w_\tau$ to $y|_\tau$. Return $y$.

The upward and downward traversals follow the finite cluster trees; block and cluster contributions are accumulated in exact arithmetic.

derivations.claim: Let $h=\lceil\log_2(n/k)\rceil$. By [F1], each split descends one level in either the row tree or the column tree, whose depths are each at most $h$ by [F2]. Hence the block tree has depth at most $2h$. At each level, the first counting hypothesis bounds the total participating far-block side sizes by $2sn$.

Each far H block stores at most $k(|\tau|+|\sigma|)$ scalar factor entries. Summing over at most $2h+1$ levels gives $O(sk n(h+1))$ far storage. Every near block has both cluster sizes at most $k$ by [F1], so it stores at most $k^2$ entries; the second counting hypothesis bounds total near storage by $s\lceil n/k\rceil k^2=O(sk n)$ because $k\le n$. This proves the H storage bound.

In [F5], a far-block product first multiplies an $r_b\times|\sigma|$ factor by $x|_\sigma$ and then a $|\tau|\times r_b$ factor by the result, so it costs $O(k(|\tau|+|\sigma|))$. A near-block product costs $O(|\tau||\sigma|)\le O(k^2)$. The same level and near-block counts used in step 2.1 therefore give H matvec work $O(sk n(h+1))=O(sk n\log_2(2n/k))$.

By the storage convention in [F4], the leaf row and column bases require at most $2kn$ entries because the leaves partition $I$ and each basis rank is at most $k$. By [F2], each tree has $O(n/k)$ nodes, so all $k\times k$ transfer matrices require $O(kn)$ entries. The third counting hypothesis gives $O(kn)$ entries for all coupling matrices, and step 2.1 bounds dense near blocks by $O(sk n)$. Thus H² storage is $O(sk n)$.

The leaf basis products in [F5] cost $O(kn)$ because their index sets partition $I$ and $J$. Each transfer product costs at most $O(k^2)$ and there are $O(n/k)$ internal clusters by [F2]; each coupling product costs at most $O(k^2)$ and the third hypothesis bounds their number by $s\lceil n/k\rceil$. Dense near products cost $O(sk n)$ by step 2.1. Summing gives H² matvec work $O(sk n)$.

**Input:** An exact factorization $A=LU$ of a square matrix $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, where $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $n\ge1$, with $L$ block lower triangular and $U$ block upper triangular on a common ordered cluster partition; an integer rank cap $k\ge1$; and a nonnegative local Frobenius tolerance for each admissible off-diagonal block of $L$ and $U$. The factorization $A=LU$ is supplied as a hypothesis, not computed by this procedure.

**Procedure:** Copy every dense nearfield block and every diagonal block exactly. For each strictly lower admissible block $D_b\in\mathbb F^{m_b\times n_b}$ of $L$ and each strictly upper admissible block $D_b$ of $U$, form the one-pair factor list $(D_b,I_{n_b})$, representing $D_b=D_bI_{n_b}^*$, and pass it to [[alg-hlr-core-svd-recompression-with-tolerance]] with effective cap $\min(k,m_b,n_b)$ and its given local tolerance. Keep structural zero blocks zero. If any compression reports **tolerance-not-met**, return that status and the factor/block identity. Otherwise return $\widehat L,\widehat U$ and the local discarded-tail bounds $\epsilon_b^L,\epsilon_c^U$ reported by the recompressions. The exact diagonal blocks preserve block triangularity; no claim is made that the compressed factors are exact factors of $A$.

Let $M=\sum_s U_sV_s^*$ be the finite matrix input to [[alg-hlr-core-svd-recompression-with-tolerance]], and let $k$ and $\delta\ge0$ be its rank cap and Frobenius tolerance. If the algorithm returns **success** with rank $q$, its returned matrix $\widehat M$ has rank $q$ and satisfies $\|M-\widehat M\|_F=(\sum_{j>q}s_j(M)^2)^{1/2}\le\delta$. No lower-rank matrix meets the same tolerance. If the algorithm returns **tolerance-not-met**, no matrix of rank at most $k$ meets the tolerance.

For any finite matrix partition into disjoint blocks, if each local residual satisfies $\|E_b\|_F\le\delta_b$, then the assembled residual satisfies $\|E\|_F\le(\sum_b\delta_b^2)^{1/2}$. In particular, let $A,B$ be conformable finite real or complex matrices, and let $\widetilde A,\widetilde B$ be approximations with $\|A-\widetilde A\|_F\le\epsilon_A$ and $\|B-\widetilde B\|_F\le\epsilon_B$. If a successful block addition or block product from [[alg-hlr-block-addition]] or [[alg-hlr-block-product]] returns $\widehat S$ or $\widehat C$, with disjoint output blocks $b$ and local Frobenius errors $e_b\le\delta_b$, put $\delta=(\sum_b\delta_b^2)^{1/2}$. Then

$$\|A+B-\widehat S\|_F\le\epsilon_A+\epsilon_B+\delta,$$

and

$$\|AB-\widehat C\|_F\le\epsilon_A\|B\|_F+\|A\|_F\epsilon_B+\epsilon_A\epsilon_B+\delta.$$

Fix a field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, an integer $d\ge2$, and positive integers $n_1,\ldots,n_d$. A finite order-$d$ tensor of shape $(n_1,\ldots,n_d)$ is an array $A=(A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d})$ indexed by $1\le i_k\le n_k$. Its Frobenius inner product and norm are
$$ \langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{n_d}\overline{A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}B_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}, \qquad \|A\|_F=\sqrt{\langle A,A\rangle_F}. $$
For a matrix, rank means the dimension of its column image and the Frobenius inner product is the same entrywise formula. The adjoint $M^*$ is conjugate transpose (transpose over $\mathbb R$).

For $1\le k\le d$, the mode-$k$ unfolding $A_{(k)}$ has $n_k$ rows and $\prod_{j\ne k}n_j$ columns. Its row index is $i_k$ and its column index is the remaining tuple in increasing mode order, lexicographically ordered. Its entry at that row and column is the corresponding entry of $A$. For $1\le k<d$, the cut-$k$ unfolding $A^{\langle k\rangle}$ has row tuple $(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and column tuple $(i_{k+1},\ldots,i_d)$, each lexicographically ordered. These conventions fix all reshapes used below.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, where $m,n\ge1$, have a singular value decomposition
$$ A=\sum_{j=1}^{q}\sigma_j u_jv_j^*,\qquad \sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_q>0, $$
where $q=\operatorname{rank}(A)$. For an integer $k\ge0$, put
$$ A_k=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(k,q)}\sigma_j u_jv_j^*, \qquad \delta_k^2=\sum_{j=k+1}^{q}\sigma_j^2 $$
with an empty sum equal to zero. Then $\operatorname{rank}(A_k)\le k$, $\|A-A_k\|_F=\delta_k$, and every matrix $B$ with $\operatorname{rank}(B)\le k$ satisfies $\|A-B\|_F\ge\delta_k$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) that is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F V = n$ ([[def-dimension]]), and let $U$ be a
linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then

1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;
2. $\dim_F U = n$ **if and only if** $U = V$;
3. **Extension, with no choice principle.** Every linearly independent
   $A_0 \subseteq U$ is contained in a basis of $U$: there is a basis $B$ of $U$
   with $A_0 \subseteq B \subseteq U$. Claim 1 is the case $A_0 = \varnothing$.
   Since $V$ is itself a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), claim 3
   applies with $V$ in place of $U$, and hence to **any** finite-dimensional
   vector space over $F$ in place of the pair $(V, U)$.

**Nothing above uses a choice principle**, and claim 3 in particular is the
finite-dimensional substitute for the Zorn-based extension theorem stated earlier
on this page. In finite dimension the extension terminates on its own, because
[[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] bounds the size
of an independent set and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]] then supplies a largest
one; no selection is made anywhere.

**Finiteness is essential in claim 2.** Without it the equality case fails: the
companion page exhibits a
proper linear subspace of an infinite-dimensional space whose basis is
equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.

For $A\in M_n(F)$, let $L_A:M_{n\times1}(F)\to M_{n\times1}(F)$ be
$L_A(x)=Ax$. Then $A$ is invertible if and only if $L_A$ is a linear
isomorphism.

More generally, if $T:V\to W$ is a linear isomorphism between finite-dimensional
spaces and $\mathcal B,\mathcal C$ are ordered bases, then
$[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}$ is invertible and

$$[T^{-1}]_{\mathcal C}^{\mathcal B}=([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C})^{-1}.$$

derivations.claim: The factor compression in [F1] copies every near and diagonal block and gives local discarded-tail errors on the disjoint admissible blocks. By [F2] these are the actual local Frobenius residuals, so [F3] gives $\|L-\widehat L\|_F\le\epsilon_L$ and $\|U-\widehat U\|_F\le\epsilon_U$.

Write $A-\widehat A=LU-\widehat L\widehat U=(L-\widehat L)U+\widehat L(U-\widehat U)$. For conformable $X,Y$, entrywise Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] gives $|(XY)_{ij}|^2\le(\sum_\ell|X_{i\ell}|^2)(\sum_\ell|Y_{\ell j}|^2)$; summing over $i,j$ gives $\|XY\|_F^2\le\|X\|_F^2\|Y\|_F^2$. Also $\|X+Y\|_F^2=\|X\|_F^2+\|Y\|_F^2+2\operatorname{Re}\langle X,Y\rangle_F\le(\|X\|_F+\|Y\|_F)^2$ by [F4,F5], so the Frobenius triangle inequality follows. Together with step 1.1 this yields $\|A-\widehat A\|_F\le\epsilon_L\|U\|_F+\|\widehat L\|_F\epsilon_U=\eta$.

For any matrix $R$, [F7] gives $\|R\|_2=\sigma_1(R)$, while [F8] at rank cap zero gives $\|R\|_F=(\sum_j\sigma_j(R)^2)^{1/2}$. Hence $\|R\|_2\le\|R\|_F$. Applying this to $R=A-\widehat A$ and using step 2.1 proves $\|A-\widehat A\|_2\le\eta$.

Let $E=\widehat A-A$ and $q=\|A^{-1}\|_2\eta<1$. For every $x$, the operator-norm definition [F6] gives $\|A^{-1}Ex\|_2\le\|A^{-1}\|_2\|E\|_2\|x\|_2\le q\|x\|_2$ by step 3.1. If $\widehat A x=0$, then $x=-A^{-1}Ex$, so $\|x\|_2\le q\|x\|_2$ and therefore $x=0$. Thus $\widehat A$ is injective. By [F9], its image has dimension $n$; [F10] makes that image all of $\mathbb F^n$, so its multiplication map is an isomorphism and [F11] gives invertibility.

Set $F=A^{-1}E$. The definition [F6] gives $\|F\|_2\le q$ by the same estimate as in step 4.1. Since $\widehat A=A(I+F)$ is invertible, so is $I+F$. For $z=(I+F)^{-1}y$, the vector triangle inequality from [F5] gives $\|z\|_2\le\|y\|_2+\|Fz\|_2\le\|y\|_2+q\|z\|_2$, hence $\|(I+F)^{-1}\|_2\le(1-q)^{-1}$. Since $\widehat A^{-1}=(I+F)^{-1}A^{-1}$ and $(I+F)^{-1}-I=-(I+F)^{-1}F$, operator-norm submultiplicativity follows from [F6] and gives $\|\widehat A^{-1}-A^{-1}\|_2\le q\|A^{-1}\|_2/(1-q)=\|A^{-1}\|_2^2\eta/(1-q)$.
