Let $I$ be a nonempty finite totally ordered set, let $d\ge1$, and assign a point $\xi_i\in\mathbb R^d$ to each $i\in I$. A **cluster** is a nonempty subset of $I$. For a cluster $\tau$, write $X_\tau=\{\xi_i:i\in\tau\}$, $\operatorname{diam}(\tau)=\max_{i,j\in\tau}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$, and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)=\min_{i\in\tau,j\in\sigma}\|\xi_i-\xi_j\|_2$. These extrema exist because the index sets are finite and nonempty; repeated geometric points are allowed.

A **balanced cluster tree with leaf threshold $b$**, where $1\le b\le |I|$, is the rooted binary tree whose root is $I$, whose children of an internal cluster $\tau$ are its first $\lfloor|\tau|/2\rfloor$ and last $\lceil|\tau|/2\rceil$ indices in the fixed order, and which stops splitting at clusters of size at most $b$. Its two children are disjoint and their union is $\tau$.

For the column side, let $J$ be a nonempty finite totally ordered set, assign points $\zeta_j\in\mathbb R^d$ for $j\in J$, and build its balanced cluster tree by the same rule with its own threshold $1\le b_J\le|J|$. Column clusters are nonempty subsets $\sigma\subseteq J$, with $X_\sigma=\{\zeta_j:j\in\sigma\}$ and $\operatorname{diam}(\sigma)=\max_{j,j'\in\sigma}\|\zeta_j-\zeta_{j'}\|_2$. For a row cluster $\tau\subseteq I$ and a column cluster $\sigma\subseteq J$, set $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)=\min_{i\in\tau,j\in\sigma}\|\xi_i-\zeta_j\|_2$. Row and column roles distinguish the assignments even when the index sets overlap. In the square case with a common point assignment, take $J=I$ and $\zeta_i=\xi_i$.

Fix an admissibility parameter $\eta>0$. A pair of clusters $(\tau,\sigma)$ is **admissible** when $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)>0$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\sigma)\ge\eta\max(\operatorname{diam}(\tau),\operatorname{diam}(\sigma))$. The strict positive-distance condition keeps coincident or intersecting clusters in the near field, including diagonal singleton blocks.

The **block-cluster tree** starts at $(I,J)$. It stops at a pair if that pair is admissible or if both clusters are leaves. Otherwise, if only one cluster is nonleaf, it splits that cluster. If both are nonleaf, it splits the cluster of larger cardinality; ties are resolved by splitting the row cluster. The children of a split are the corresponding child-cluster pairs. Its terminal pairs are called **block-cluster leaves**. Admissible leaves are **far blocks**; nonadmissible leaves, which have two leaf clusters, are **near blocks**.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $I,J$ be nonempty finite index sets with point assignments as in [[def-hlr-cluster-trees-and-geometric-admissibility]], and let $\mathcal P$ be the block-cluster leaves of [[lem-hlr-block-cluster-leaves-partition-index-pairs]]. Fix an integer rank cap $k\ge1$. An **H-matrix representation with cap $k$** assigns to each far block $b=(\tau,\sigma)\in\mathcal P$ factors $U_b\in\mathbb F^{\tau\times r_b}$ and $V_b\in\mathbb F^{\sigma\times r_b}$ with $0\le r_b\le k$, representing that block by $U_bV_b^*$. Each near block is stored as its full dense matrix $D_b\in\mathbb F^{\tau\times\sigma}$. Since $\mathcal P$ partitions $I\times J$, these blocks determine a unique represented matrix $\widetilde A\in\mathbb F^{I\times J}$.

The rank cap on far blocks is an assumption about the representation or the target's approximability; geometric admissibility alone does not imply that a given matrix block has low rank. Near blocks remain dense and receive no low-rank guarantee.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, let

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

be a singular value decomposition with $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0$, and fix an
integer $k$ with $0\le k<\dim V$. Define

$$T_kv:=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(k,r)} s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j.$$

Then $\operatorname{rank}T_k\le k$, one has

$$\lVert T-T_k\rVert=s_{k+1}$$

with the convention $s_{k+1}=0$ when $k\ge r$, and every linear map
$A:V\to W$ with $\operatorname{rank}A\le k$ satisfies

$$\lVert T-A\rVert\ge s_{k+1}.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

**Input:** A field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, positive integers $m,n$, a finite factor list $U_s\in\mathbb F^{m\times r_s}$ and $V_s\in\mathbb F^{n\times r_s}$ representing $M=\sum_s U_sV_s^*$, a rank cap $0\le k\le\min(m,n)$, and a Frobenius tolerance $\delta\ge0$. The conjugate transpose $M^*$ and Frobenius norm are those of [[def-finite-tensor-arrays-and-frobenius-inner-product]].

**Procedure:** Concatenate the factors as $U=[U_1\ \cdots\ U_p]$ and $V=[V_1\ \cdots\ V_p]$, so $M=UV^*$. Take compact singular value decompositions $U=Q_UR_U$ and $V=Q_VR_V$, where the columns of $Q_U,Q_V$ are orthonormal and span the respective column spaces. Form the core $C=R_UR_V^*$ and compute an SVD $C=P\Sigma Q^*$. Let its positive singular values be $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_t>0$. Find the smallest $q\in\{0,\ldots,\min(k,t)\}$ for which $e_q:=(\sum_{j>q}s_j^2)^{1/2}\le\delta$. If no such $q$ exists, return **tolerance-not-met**. Otherwise return **success** with factors $\widehat U=Q_UP_{[:,1:q]}\Sigma_q$ and $\widehat V=Q_VQ_{[:,1:q]}$, where $\Sigma_q=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_q)$, and the exact discarded-tail certificate $e_q$; when $q=0$, use empty $m\times0$ and $n\times0$ factors.

The compact decompositions retain only positive singular directions. If the factor list is empty or its represented matrix is zero, then $t=0$ and the procedure returns the rank-zero representation because $\delta\ge0$. Any SVD choices in repeated singular subspaces are permitted. No result is returned when the requested cap cannot certify the tolerance.

Let $M=\sum_s U_sV_s^*$ be the finite matrix input to [[alg-hlr-core-svd-recompression-with-tolerance]], and let $k$ and $\delta\ge0$ be its rank cap and Frobenius tolerance. If the algorithm returns **success** with rank $q$, its returned matrix $\widehat M$ has rank $q$ and satisfies $\|M-\widehat M\|_F=(\sum_{j>q}s_j(M)^2)^{1/2}\le\delta$. No lower-rank matrix meets the same tolerance. If the algorithm returns **tolerance-not-met**, no matrix of rank at most $k$ meets the tolerance.

Fix a field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, an integer $d\ge2$, and positive integers $n_1,\ldots,n_d$. A finite order-$d$ tensor of shape $(n_1,\ldots,n_d)$ is an array $A=(A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d})$ indexed by $1\le i_k\le n_k$. Its Frobenius inner product and norm are

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and $0<\epsilon<1$. There is a finite set $\mathcal N\subseteq S^{d-1}$ such that every $u\in S^{d-1}$ has some $v\in\mathcal N$ with $\|u-v\|_2\le\epsilon$, and
$$|\mathcal N|\le(1+2/\epsilon)^d.$$
Here $S^{d-1}=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u\|_2=1\}$ by [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. Such a set is called an $\epsilon$-net of the sphere.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: egard $H$ as a complex Hermitian matrix when $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$. By [F1], it has an orthonormal eigenbasis over $\mathbb C$; every eigenvalue is real because $Hv=\lambda v$ and $H=H^*$ give $\lambda\|v\|_2^2=v^*Hv=\overline{v^*Hv}=\overline\lambda\|v\|_2^2$. Choose a unit eigenvector $z$ for an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of largest absolute value. The diagonalization shows $\|H\|_2=|\lambda|$ over $\mathbb C$. If $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$, set $u=z$. If $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$, write $z=a+ib$; since $H$ and $\lambda$ are real, $Ha=\lambda a$ and $Hb=\lambda b$, and at least one of $a,b$ is nonzero. Normalize a nonzero part as $u$. The same diagonalization bounds the real operator norm by $|\lambda|$, while $u$ attains that bound, so $|u^*Hu|=|\lambda|=\|H\|_2$ over either field. [F1, choose, algebra]
Apply [F2] in real dimension $q=d$ when $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$, and $q=2d$ when $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$, to obtain the stated net-size bound and a $v\in\mathcal N$ with $\|u-v\|_2\le1/4$.

Since $H=H^*$ and $u,v$ are unit vectors, $|u^*Hu-v^*Hv|\le|(u-v)^*Hu|+|v^*H(u-v)|\le2\|u-v\|_2\|H\|_2\le\|H\|_2/2$, using [F3] and the definition of operator norm. Therefore $|v^*Hv|\ge|u^*Hu|-\|H\|_2/2=\|H\|_2/2$, proving the claimed bound.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice so that the repository's Lebesgue measure
on each positive-dimensional real coordinate space is a measure. A **standard
real Gaussian scalar** has Lebesgue density
$$\varphi_R(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}.$$
A **normalized complex Gaussian scalar** is $z=(x+iy)/\sqrt2$ for independent
standard real Gaussian scalars $x,y$; its density on $\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb
R^2$ is $\varphi_C(z)=\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $\mathbb E|z|^2=1$.

For $F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, an **iid standard Gaussian matrix** in
$F^{a\times b}$ has independent entries with the corresponding scalar law.
For $ab>0$, its expectations are finite-dimensional Lebesgue integrals
against the product density. If $a=0$ or $b=0$, the matrix space has one
element, the empty matrix; its law assigns that element probability one,
and the expectation of any function is its value there. Independence means
the product-density factorization, with this one-point convention for an
empty product.
The normalized complex convention is fixed throughout; it is not the
unnormalized law $x+iy$.

Assume Countable Choice. The scalar and finite product densities in
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]] have total
mass one. A real entry has mean zero and second moment one; a normalized
complex entry has mean zero and $\mathbb E|z|^2=1$. The image of two independent
real entries under $(x,y)\mapsto(x+iy)/\sqrt2$ has density
$\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$. These facts justify the probability laws in that definition.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb K^n$
have dimension $d\ge1$. Choose a matrix $Q\in\mathbb K^{n\times d}$
whose columns are an orthonormal basis of $U$, so $Q^*Q=I_d$. For
$0\le i<n$, define the **$i$-th row leverage score of $U$** by
$$
\ell_i(U):=\|e_i^*Q\|_2^2,
$$
where $e_i$ is the $i$-th standard coordinate vector. The following item
proves that this value is independent of the chosen orthonormal basis, so the
definition is well-defined.

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb K^n$
have dimension $d\ge1$. Choose a matrix $Q\in\mathbb K^{n\times d}$
whose columns are an orthonormal basis of $U$, so $Q^*Q=I_d$. For
$0\le i<n$, define the **$i$-th row leverage score of $U$** by
$$
\ell_i(U):=\|e_i^*Q\|_2^2,
$$
where $e_i$ is the $i$-th standard coordinate vector. The following item
proves that this value is independent of the chosen orthonormal basis, so the
definition is well-defined.

derivations.claim: Let $Q'$ be another orthonormal basis matrix of $U$, and set $W=Q^*Q'$. Since each column of $Q'$ lies in $U=\operatorname{Ran}(Q)$, the orthogonal projection $QQ^*$ fixes it, so $Q'=QQ^*Q'=QW$. Thus $W^*W=Q'^*QQ^*Q'=Q'^*Q'=I_d$. The square matrix $W$ is unitary, and right multiplication by $W$ preserves the Euclidean norm of every row; hence $\|e_i^*Q'\|_2^2=\|e_i^*Q\|_2^2$ for every $i$.
Writing $q_j$ for column $j$ of $Q$, finite-sum reordering gives $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\ell_i=\sum_i\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}|Q_{ij}|^2=\sum_j\|q_j\|_2^2=d$, because every column is a unit vector.

Put $P=QQ^*$. Then $P=P^*$ and $P^2=P$ by [F2], so $e_i=Pe_i+(I-P)e_i$ is an orthogonal decomposition. Also $\ell_i=\|Q^*e_i\|_2^2=\|QQ^*e_i\|_2^2=\|Pe_i\|_2^2$, using $Q^*Q=I_d$. Therefore $0\le\ell_i\le\|e_i\|_2^2=1$, and $\ell_i=0$ exactly when $Q^*e_i=0$, which is exactly when row $i$ of $Q$ is zero.

Input $A\in\mathbb K^{n\times p}$, $b\in\mathbb K^n$, a supplied sketch
$S\in\mathbb K^{m\times n}$, and a finite nonnegative integer SVD sweep
budget $N$, where $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Form
$C=SA$ and $c=Sb$, and call
[[alg-rank-thresholded-least-squares-by-svd]] on $(C,c)$ with threshold
$\tau=0$ and budget $N$.

If the call returns exact-arithmetic convergence with an exact SVD record,
return `success`, the exact rank $r=\operatorname{rank}(C)$, the canonical
minimum-norm vector $\widehat x=C^+c$, and the separately computed sketched
and physical residuals $\|C\widehat x-c\|_2$ and
$\|A\widehat x-b\|_2$. The exact-arithmetic solve-error certificate is
zero. If the SVD call returns `inconclusive`, return its status and supplied
partial diagnostics without claiming a minimizer. In finite precision, return
the computed candidate and the two residual reports separately; mark the rank
`unverified` unless a certified interval separates every singular-value
comparison from zero, and report a solve-error certificate only when the
solver supplies one. No finite-precision accuracy guarantee is part of this
procedure.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and $\tau\ge0$, where $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. Let $A=U\Sigma V^*$ be an exact SVD. Define $\Sigma_\tau$ by retaining $\sigma_i$ when $\sigma_i>\tau$ and replacing each $\sigma_i\le\tau$ by zero, and set $A_\tau=U\Sigma_\tau V^*$. Put $q=\#\{i:\sigma_i>\tau\}$, the spectral numerical rank of $A$ at threshold $\tau$. The vector $x_\tau=A_\tau^+b$ is the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm least-squares solution for the truncated model $A_\tau x\approx b$. An exact-arithmetic run of [[alg-rank-thresholded-least-squares-by-svd]] that converges within its supplied finite sweep budget and supplies this SVD record returns $x_\tau$; a failure or exhausted budget returns `inconclusive`. No convergence within an arbitrary budget is asserted. Moreover,
$$\|A-A_\tau\|_2=\sigma_{q+1}\le\tau,\qquad \|Ax_\tau-b\|_2\le\|A_\tau x_\tau-b\|_2+\tau\|x_\tau\|_2,$$
with $\sigma_{p+1}=0$ when $q=p=\min(m,n)$. If every discarded singular value is zero, then $A_\tau=A$ and $x_\tau$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares solution for the original matrix. If a positive singular value is discarded, no original-matrix least-squares optimality is asserted.

derivations.claim: Set $C=SA$ and $c=Sb$. By [F1], the converged call uses threshold zero and returns $\widehat x=C_0^+c$, where $C_0$ retains exactly the singular values of $C$ that are strictly positive.
In an exact SVD $C=U\Sigma V^*$, zero singular values contribute zero terms and every positive singular value is retained at threshold zero. Thus $C_0=U\Sigma V^*=C$, including the rank-zero case.

Apply [F2] to the truncated matrix $C_0$. It says that $C_0^+c$ is its unique minimum-norm least-squares solution. By step 2.1, $C_0=C$, so $\widehat x$ is the unique minimum-norm minimizer of $\|Cx-c\|_2=\|SAx-Sb\|_2$; the zero-threshold rank count is precisely the number of positive singular values of $C$, hence $\operatorname{rank}(C)$.

citations.quote:
Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $n,m\ge1$, and use
$\|x\|_2^2=\sum_i|x_i|^2$ on $\mathbb K^n$. For a fixed subspace
$U\subseteq\mathbb K^n$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$, a matrix
$S\in\mathbb K^{m\times n}$ is an **$\varepsilon$-subspace embedding
for $U$** when
$$
(1-\varepsilon)\|x\|_2^2\le\|Sx\|_2^2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|x\|_2^2\quad\text{for every }x\in U.
$$

For an integer $d$ with $0\le d\le n$ and $0<\delta<1$,
a distribution $\mathcal D$ on $m\times n$
matrices is an **$(\varepsilon,\delta)$ oblivious $\ell_2$ subspace
embedding for dimension $d$** if, for every fixed $d$-dimensional
subspace $U\subseteq\mathbb K^n$ chosen independently of the draw,
$$
\Pr_{S\sim\mathcal D}\{S\text{ is an }\varepsilon\text{-subspace embedding for }U\}\ge1-\delta.
$$
The subspace is fixed before sampling, but the guarantee is stated separately
for each such $U$; it does not assert that one draw preserves all
$d$-dimensional subspaces simultaneously. For a matrix $A$, an embedding
of $\operatorname{Ran}(A)$ means the property on its column space. For
least-squares residuals $Ax-b$, the relevant subspace is
$\operatorname{span}(\operatorname{Ran}(A),b)$.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ with $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
and $m\ge n$.

A **full QR factorisation** of $A$ is a factorisation

$$A=QR,$$where $Q\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ is orthogonal or unitary and $R\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ is upper trapezoidal. A **reduced QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A=\widehat Q\widehat R,$$where $\widehat Q\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ has orthonormal columns ($\widehat Q^*\widehat Q=I_n$) and $\widehat R\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ is upper triangular. A **column-pivoted QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A\Pi=\widehat Q R,$$

where $\Pi$ is a permutation matrix acting on columns, $\widehat Q$ has
orthonormal columns, and $R$ is upper trapezoidal or upper triangular according
to whether the full or reduced form is used. Computationally, one obtains these
factorisations by successive Householder reflectors or Givens transformations
that zero entries below the diagonal, with the pivoted version choosing the next
column after a permutation.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ with $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
and $m\ge n$.

1. Successive Householder reflectors or Givens transformations can zero the
   subdiagonal entries column by column and produce a full QR factorisation
   $A=QR$ and hence a reduced QR factorisation $A=\widehat Q\widehat R$.
2. In dense real arithmetic, Householder QR uses
   $$2mn^2-\frac{2}{3}n^3+O(mn)$$
   scalar operations, while dense Givens QR uses
   $$3mn^2-n^3+O(mn)$$
   scalar operations.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

derivations.claim: If $y\in\mathbb K^d$ is nonzero, full column rank gives $Ay\ne0$; then [F1] gives $\|SAy\|_2^2\ge(1-\varepsilon)\|Ay\|_2^2>0$. Thus $SA$ has full column rank. The reduced QR factorization in [F2] exists. If $Rv=0$, then $SAv=QRv=0$; injectivity of $SA$ forces $v=0$, so $R$ is nonsingular and $P_S=R^{-1}$ is defined.

For any $y\in\mathbb K^d$, $SAP_Sy=QRR^{-1}y=Qy$, so $\|SAP_Sy\|_2^2=\|Qy\|_2^2=\|y\|_2^2$ by [F2]. Since $AP_Sy\in\operatorname{Ran}(A)$, [F1] yields $(1-\varepsilon)\|AP_Sy\|_2^2\le\|y\|_2^2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|AP_Sy\|_2^2$.

For every unit $y$, step 2.1 implies $1/\sqrt{1+\varepsilon}\le\|AP_Sy\|_2\le1/\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}$. By [F3], the minimum and maximum of these values over the unit sphere are $\sigma_{\min}(AP_S)$ and $\sigma_{\max}(AP_S)$, respectively. This proves both singular-value bounds.

The lower bound in step 3.1 is positive, so the ratio defining $\kappa_2$ is valid. Dividing the upper singular-value bound by the lower one gives $\kappa_2(AP_S)\le\sqrt{(1+\varepsilon)/(1-\varepsilon)}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice so that the repository's Lebesgue measure
on each positive-dimensional real coordinate space is a measure. A **standard
real Gaussian scalar** has Lebesgue density
$$\varphi_R(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}.$$
A **normalized complex Gaussian scalar** is $z=(x+iy)/\sqrt2$ for independent
standard real Gaussian scalars $x,y$; its density on $\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb
R^2$ is $\varphi_C(z)=\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $\mathbb E|z|^2=1$.

For $F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, an **iid standard Gaussian matrix** in
$F^{a\times b}$ has independent entries with the corresponding scalar law.
For $ab>0$, its expectations are finite-dimensional Lebesgue integrals
against the product density. If $a=0$ or $b=0$, the matrix space has one
element, the empty matrix; its law assigns that element probability one,
and the expectation of any function is its value there. Independence means
the product-density factorization, with this one-point convention for an
empty product.
The normalized complex convention is fixed throughout; it is not the
unnormalized law $x+iy$.

Assume Countable Choice. The scalar and finite product densities in
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]] have total
mass one. A real entry has mean zero and second moment one; a normalized
complex entry has mean zero and $\mathbb E|z|^2=1$. The image of two independent
real entries under $(x,y)\mapsto(x+iy)/\sqrt2$ has density
$\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$. These facts justify the probability laws in that definition.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $G\in F^{a\times b}$ have the iid Gaussian law of
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. If $U,V$
are compatible orthogonal matrices for $F=\mathbb R$ or unitary matrices for
$F=\mathbb C$, then $U^*GV$ has the same iid law as $G$. In particular, if
$W\in F^{n\times n}$ is orthogonal/unitary and $\Omega\in F^{n\times\ell}$
is iid Gaussian, then any two disjoint row blocks of $W^*\Omega$ are
independent standard Gaussian matrices.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $m\ge1$, and let $g_1,\ldots,g_m$ be independent standard real
Gaussian scalars or independent normalized complex Gaussian scalars, with
$\mathbb E|g_j|^2=1$. For $0<t<1$,
$$
\Pr\left\{\left|\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m|g_j|^2-1\right|\ge t\right\}\le2e^{-mt^2/8}.
$$

Let $d\ge1$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$H\in\mathbb K^{d\times d}$ be Hermitian. Regard $\mathbb C^d$ as
$\mathbb R^{2d}$ for distances. A $1/4$-net $\mathcal N$ of the unit
sphere exists with $|\mathcal N|\le9^d$ over $\mathbb R$, and
$|\mathcal N|\le9^{2d}$ over $\mathbb C$. For every such net,
$$
\|H\|_2\le2\max_{v\in\mathcal N}|v^*Hv|.
$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Choose an orthonormal basis matrix $Q\in\mathbb K^{n\times d}$ for $U$, and let $\mathcal N$ be a $1/4$-net of its unit sphere with $|\mathcal N|\le9^{2d}$, which covers the real case too. For each fixed $v\in\mathcal N$, $Qv$ is a unit vector. Extend $Qv$ to an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb K^n$ by applying [F4] to its orthogonal complement; [F3] then shows that $GQv$ has $m$ independent standard Gaussian coordinates.

For each fixed $v\in\mathcal N$, apply [F5] with $t=\varepsilon/2$ to obtain $\Pr\{|\|SQv\|_2^2-1|\ge\varepsilon/2\}\le2e^{-m\varepsilon^2/32}$. The finite union bound [F9] for the fixed finite net gives $\Pr\{\exists v\in\mathcal N:|\|SQv\|_2^2-1|\ge\varepsilon/2\}\le2\,9^{2d}e^{-m\varepsilon^2/32}\le2e^{2d\log9-6d-6\log(1/\delta)}\le\delta$. Here the sample-size hypothesis gives $m\varepsilon^2/32\ge6(d+\log(1/\delta))$, and $\log2+2d\log9<6d$ for $d\ge1$.

On the complementary event, put $H=Q^*S^*SQ-I_d$. This is Hermitian and $|v^*Hv|=|\|SQv\|_2^2-1|<\varepsilon/2$ for every $v\in\mathcal N$. By [F6], $\|H\|_2\le\varepsilon$. For nonzero $y$, [F7] and [F8] give $|y^*Hy|\le\|y\|_2\|Hy\|_2\le\|H\|_2\|y\|_2^2$; the zero vector satisfies the same inequality. Therefore $(1-\varepsilon)\|y\|_2^2\le\|SQy\|_2^2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|y\|_2^2$. Since $Q$ is an isometry onto $U$, [F1] identifies this as the required embedding inequality for every $x=Qy\in U$.

Let $B_1,\ldots,B_m$ be independent centered random Hermitian $q\times q$ matrices, $q,m\ge1$. Suppose $R>0$, $v\ge0$, and
$$\|B_i\|_{\rm op}\le R\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad\|\mathbb E B_i^2\|_{\rm op}\le v\quad(1\le i\le m).$$
Writing $Y=\sum_{i=1}^m B_i$, for $0<s<3/R$ one has
$$\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}\exp(sY)\le q\exp\left(\frac{ms^2v}{2(1-sR/3)}\right).$$
Consequently, for $u>0$ when $v>0$,
$$\mathbb P\{\lambda_{\max}(Y)\ge u\}\le q\exp\left(-\frac{u^2}{2(mv+Ru/3)}\right).$$
For every $b>0$, the following convenient forms also hold:
$$\mathbb P\left\{\lambda_{\max}(Y)>\sqrt{2mvb}+\frac{2Rb}{3}\right\}\le qe^{-b},\qquad\mathbb P\left\{\|Y\|_{\rm op}>\sqrt{2mvb}+\frac{2Rb}{3}\right\}\le2qe^{-b}.$$

derivations.claim: Write $z_i=Q^*e_i\in\mathbb K^d$, so $\|z_i\|_2^2=\ell_i$. For draw $j$, let $J_j$ be its sampled index and define $Y_j=z_{J_j}z_{J_j}^*/\pi_{J_j}$. By [F2], the $Y_j$ are independent and $\mathbb E Y_j=\sum_{i:\pi_i>0}z_i z_i^*=Q^*Q=I_d$; terms with $\pi_i=0$ have $z_i=0$ by [F1] and contribute zero.

Put $R=d/\beta\ge1$ and $B_j=Y_j-I_d$. The rank-one identity $(z_i z_i^*)^2=\ell_i z_i z_i^*$ and $\pi_i\ge\beta\ell_i/d$ give $\|Y_j\|_2=\ell_{J_j}/\pi_{J_j}\le R$ and $Y_j^2\preceq RY_j$. Thus $\|B_j\|_2\le\max(1,R-1)\le R$, $\mathbb E B_j=0$, and $0\preceq\mathbb E B_j^2=\mathbb E Y_j^2-I_d\preceq(R-1)I_d\preceq RI_d$. Hence [F3] applies with both bounds equal to $R$.

Set $a=\log(2d/\delta)$. By [F3], $\Pr\{\|\sum_{j=1}^mB_j\|_2>\sqrt{2mRa}+2Ra/3\}\le2d e^{-a}=\delta$. Under the first sample-size condition, $m\varepsilon^2\ge8Ra$, so $\sqrt{2mRa}\le m\varepsilon/2$. Also $m\varepsilon/2\ge4Ra/\varepsilon\ge2Ra/3$, since $0<\varepsilon<1$. Thus the Bernstein threshold is at most $m\varepsilon$.

From the sampled-row definition in [F2], $Q^*S^*SQ=m^{-1}\sum_jY_j$, so $Q^*S^*SQ-I_d=m^{-1}\sum_jB_j$. Step 2.1 therefore proves $\|Q^*S^*SQ-I_d\|_2\le\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. For nonzero $y$, [F5] and [F6] imply $|y^*(Q^*S^*SQ-I_d)y|\le\|y\|_2\|(Q^*S^*SQ-I_d)y\|_2\le\varepsilon\|y\|_2^2$; the same holds for zero $y$. Thus $(1-\varepsilon)\|y\|_2^2\le\|SQy\|_2^2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|y\|_2^2$, and because $Q$ is an isometry onto its range, this is the embedding property in [F4].

If $0<\delta\le1/2$ and $d\ge1$, then $d/\delta\ge2$, hence $\log(2d/\delta)=\log(d/\delta)+\log2\le2\log(d/\delta)$. Therefore the second stated sample-size condition implies the first. Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] and
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]].

For every matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or
$\mathbb C$, there exists a unique matrix $A^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$
satisfying the four Penrose equations of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]].

derivations.claim: By [F1], $P^*=P$ and $Q^*=Q$. Also $P^2=MM^\dagger MM^\dagger=M(M^\dagger M M^\dagger)=MM^\dagger=P$, and $Q^2=M^\dagger M M^\dagger M=(M^\dagger M M^\dagger)M=M^\dagger M=Q$. Hence both products are self-adjoint idempotents.

The range of $P$ is contained in $\operatorname{Ran}(M)$ because $P=MM^\dagger$, while $PM=M$ by [F1], so $\operatorname{Ran}(M)\subseteq\operatorname{Ran}(P)$. Thus $\operatorname{Ran}(P)=\operatorname{Ran}(M)$. The range of $Q$ is contained in $\operatorname{Ran}(M^\dagger)$, and $QM^\dagger=M^\dagger$ by [F1], so these ranges are equal.

A self-adjoint idempotent is the orthogonal projection onto its range: each vector $x$ decomposes as $Px+(I-P)x$, the first term lies in the range, the second lies in the kernel, and self-adjointness makes the range orthogonal to the kernel. The same argument applies to $Q$. If $M$ has full row rank, $\operatorname{Ran}(M)=\mathbb F^p$, so step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{Ran}(P)=\mathbb F^p$ and therefore $P=I_p$.

Input a real or complex matrix $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ with $m\ge n$, a target $k$ with $0\le k<n$, a factor $f\ge1$, and a finite swap cap $S\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$. The exact-arithmetic version is specified below. In finite precision, $A$ denotes the represented matrix: each real and imaginary component, and $f$, is a finite binary floating-point number, interpreted as its exact dyadic rational value. The arithmetic format and rounding rule are fixed for a run. A nonfinite input or required rounded intermediate returns `range-failure`. This mode makes no rank claim about an unspecified matrix before input rounding.

For the finite-precision rank test, copy the represented $A$ into exact rational complex arithmetic. Scan columns from left to right with a current pivot row, select the first nonzero entry at or below that row, interchange rows, and eliminate entries below it by exact rational row operations. If no such entry exists, skip that column. Increment the pivot row only after a nonzero pivot. The number $r$ of pivots is the reported exact represented-input rank. Return `rank-deficient-input` if $r<n$; otherwise continue with rank status `full-column-rank`. This test uses unbounded-size rational integers, not the rounded QR diagonal or a numerical-rank threshold. In exact mode, use the same finite row-elimination instructions over the exact input field to decide the rank condition in step 1.

The finite-precision mode additionally takes a finite real binary format $\mathcal F$ containing $0,1,-1$ and closed under sign changes, a fixed rounding rule, and a certificate-pass budget $C\in\mathbb N_0$ (default $1$; $C=0$ disables certification). Real and imaginary parts are stored separately. For a real rational result within the format's finite range, $\operatorname{fl}$ returns its specified nearest representable value, with a fixed tie rule, or its specified directed rounding; a result outside that range returns `range-failure`. Exact zeros are copied as zero. Real addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division mean their exact rational result followed by this rounding; check each divisor before dividing. A real square root of a nonnegative represented number is rounded by comparing that number with squares of the finitely many nonnegative format values: bracket its root, then use the selected directed endpoint or compare with the squared midpoint for nearest rounding. A negative argument or a root beyond the finite range returns `range-failure`. Thus no exact irrational arithmetic oracle or unbounded precision search is part of this mode. A nonfinite input or any failed required scalar operation immediately returns `range-failure` with any completed partial data.

Use the following fixed scalar conventions throughout the rounded core. For $z=a+ib$ and $w=c+id$, complex addition/subtraction round their two real components; multiplication returns $\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(ac)-\operatorname{fl}(bd))+i\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(ad)+\operatorname{fl}(bc))$. For division compute $d_0=\operatorname{fl}(c^2)+\operatorname{fl}(d^2)$ with the addition rounded, require $d_0>0$, compute the rounded product $z\overline w$, and divide its two real components by $d_0$, rounding each. Conjugation and sign changes are exact copies. For a vector, compute its squared norm by rounding each real-component square and summing them with rounding in increasing coordinate order, real part before imaginary part; apply the rounded nonnegative square root. Dot products use the above rounded complex products and a left-to-right rounded sum. These rules specify every norm and score calculation below; a nonzero vector whose required computed norm is zero returns `range-failure`.

The initial permutation is $\Pi=I_n$, with original labels $1,\ldots,n$. A rounded full QR sweep of a fixed current column order starts from $B=A\Pi$, $\widehat Q=I_m$ and an empty transformation record. During the initial pivoted sweep, at column $j=1,\ldots,n$ compute the rounded norms of $B(j:m,\ell)$ for $\ell=j,\ldots,n$, choose the largest, breaking ties by smallest original column label, and swap the full columns of $B$ and their labels. A fixed-order sweep skips these pivot searches. In either sweep, if $B(j+1:m,j)=0$ entrywise, record no transformation and continue. Otherwise copy $z=B(j:m,j)$, compute its rounded norm $r>0$, and set $\phi=1$ if $z_1=0$; if $z_1\ne0$, compute its rounded modulus $a>0$ and divide its two components by $a$ to form $\phi$. Set $\alpha=-\operatorname{fl}(r\phi)$, $v_1=\operatorname{fl}(z_1-\alpha)$ and $v_i=z_i$ for $i>1$. Compute the rounded squared norm $\widehat d$ of $v$, require $\widehat d>0$, and put $\widehat\tau=\operatorname{fl}(2/\widehat d)$. Record the active index $j$ and the exact dyadic components of this nonzero stored $v$ before updating anything.

For each column $\ell=j,\ldots,n$, compute the rounded dot product $a_\ell=v^*B(j:m,\ell)$ from the old column, set $h_\ell=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau a_\ell)$, then replace each active entry by $\operatorname{fl}(B_{i\ell}-\operatorname{fl}(v_{i-j+1}h_\ell))$. For each row $a=1,\ldots,m$ of $\widehat Q$, compute $b_a=\widehat Q(a,j:m)v$ from its old row, set $g_a=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau b_a)$, and replace each active entry by $\operatorname{fl}(\widehat Q_{ai}-\operatorname{fl}(g_a\overline v_{i-j+1}))$. Finally set $B(j+1:m,j)$ to exact zeros by assignment. At the end return $\widehat R=B$, the full $m\times m$ candidate $\widehat Q$, the final permutation and the ordered record. The imposed zeros are part of this rounded procedure, not a claim of exact annihilation; the certificate measures their effect as well as all rounding. There are at most $n\le mn$ reflector updates per sweep. Empty active tails are skipped, and no norm or quotient is required for them.

In finite precision step 1 uses this pivoted sweep, and step 2 uses a fresh fixed-order sweep on the represented input $A$ in its current order. Each fresh sweep resets $\widehat Q$ and its transformation record. Before the triangular solves, decide singularity of its represented $\widehat R_{11}$ by the same exact rational elimination as the input rank test; if singular, return `singular-selected-block`. Otherwise solve $\widehat R_{11}X=\widehat R_{12}$ and $\widehat R_{11}Y=I_k$ by rounded back-substitution: for each right-hand-side column, process rows $i=k,\ldots,1$, sum $\widehat R_{ih}x_h$ in increasing $h=i+1,\ldots,k$, subtract from the supplied right-hand side, check the diagonal divisor and use the complex division above. Compute $\omega_i$ as the rounded norm of row $i$ of $Y$, $\gamma_j$ as the rounded norm of column $j$ of $\widehat R_{22}$, and $c_{ij}$ as the rounded modulus of $X_{ij}$. Compute $t_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(\omega_i\gamma_j)$ and $s_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt{\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(c_{ij}^2)+\operatorname{fl}(t_{ij}^2))})$. Scan these finite candidate lists for the step-4 maxima and its stated tie rules. The diagnostics $(X,Y,(\omega_i),(\gamma_j),(c_{ij}),(s_{ij}))$ are rounded candidates, not exact inverse or score identities. For $k=0$ there are no such solves or score lists.

The numbered instructions below specify exact arithmetic; the preceding rounded instructions replace the corresponding factorization, solve and score operations in finite precision.

1. If $A$ is not full column rank, return `rank-deficient-input`. Otherwise initialize a column permutation $\Pi$ and the full column-pivoted QR factorization $A\Pi=QR$, where $Q\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}$ is unitary and $R\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ is upper trapezoidal. At each pivot choose a remaining column of maximal residual $2$-norm, resolving ties by the smallest original column index. Partition $R=\begin{bmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&R_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ after the first $k$ rows and columns. Do not return the reduced QR form. The selected first $k$ columns then have a nonsingular leading block. For $k=0$, return this full factorization with `success`.
2. For $k>0$, refactor the current fixed column order in the full QR form, without further pivoting whenever needed, using unitary Householder or Givens transformations. If the selected leading block is singular, return `singular-selected-block`.
3. Form $X=R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}$. For $1\le i\le k$ let $\omega_i=\|e_i^*R_{11}^{-1}\|_2$; for $1\le j\le n-k$ let $\gamma_j=\|R_{22}(:,j)\|_2$. Define the swap score $s_{ij}=\bigl(|X_{ij}|^2+(\omega_i\gamma_j)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$.
4. If $\max_{i,j}|X_{ij}|>f$, choose the lexicographically first pair attaining the largest $|X_{ij}|$. Otherwise, if $\max_{i,j}s_{ij}>f$, choose the lexicographically first pair attaining the largest score. If neither inequality holds, return `success` and the factors, permutation, $X$, and maximum score. The first branch retains the usual coefficient-triggered swap; the second controls the trailing residual needed for the strong spectral comparison.
5. When a violating pair was chosen, if the swap count is already $S$, return `swap-budget-exhausted` with the current partial factors. Otherwise interchange the chosen selected and trailing columns in the current permutation. In exact arithmetic restore triangular form with Givens rotations; in finite precision discard the old factors and record, since step 2 recomputes them from $A$ in the new fixed order. Increment the swap count and return to step 2.

The statuses are `success`, `rank-deficient-input`, `singular-selected-block`, `swap-budget-exhausted`, and `range-failure`. In particular, ordinary column-pivoted QR is only the initialization: the procedure does not assert that its output alone satisfies the strong bounds. Both modes return the full factor shape and available diagnostics. A finite-precision `success` is a candidate until the following separate certificate is verified. The rounded dense $\widehat Q$ is never asserted to be unitary.

For each recorded active dyadic vector $v$, define the embedded exact rational matrix
$$H=I-\frac{2vv^*}{v^*v}$$
on its active coordinates, with identity on the preceding coordinates. Its denominator is a strictly positive exact rational. It is exactly unitary: writing $P=vv^*/(v^*v)$ gives $P^*=P$, $P^2=P$ and $(I-2P)^*(I-2P)=I$. Thus the ordered sweep record represents the exact unitary product $W=H_1\cdots H_t$; an empty record represents $I_m$. This product corresponds to the final fresh sweep only, and is distinct from the rounded $\widehat Q$ and the nonunitary rounded update coefficients $\widehat\tau$. Its rational representation requires no normalization by an irrational vector norm.

Certification is finite optional postprocessing, independent of the core status. For a nonsuccess status assign `not-applicable`. On success with $C=0$, assign `uncertified`. With $C\ge1$ perform the following one exact rational pass, using unbounded-size integer numerators and denominators; no retry until success is allowed.

- Check factor dimensions, that $\Pi$ is a permutation of $1,\ldots,n$, that $\widehat R$ is exactly upper trapezoidal, and that each recorded vector has the declared active dimension and is nonzero. Reconstruct each $H$ by the displayed rational formula, multiply them in the recorded order, and verify entrywise $W^*W=I_m$. Any failed check sets `uncertified`.
- For $k>0$, apply exact rational elimination to $\widehat R_{11}$. If singular, the certificate is `uncertified`. Otherwise compute its exact inverse $Y_0$ by elimination on $[\widehat R_{11}\;I_k]$, normalizing each nonzero pivot and eliminating above and below it. Form $Z=Y_0\widehat R_{12}$ and the exact nonnegative rational score squares
$$q_{ij}=|Z_{ij}|^2+\left(\sum_{a=1}^k|(Y_0)_{ia}|^2\right)\left(\sum_{b=1}^{m-k}|(\widehat R_{22})_{bj}|^2\right).$$
  Set $b_{ij}=\sqrt{q_{ij}}$, stored as a symbolic nonnegative square root, and check the rational inequalities $q_{ij}\le f^2$ for every $i,j$. These are equivalent to all $b_{ij}\le f$. They certify the exact scores of the represented blocks, independently of rounded $X,Y,\omega,\gamma,s$. For $k=0$ this list and every inverse condition are absent.
- Compute exactly $E=A\Pi-W\widehat R$ and $e^2=\sum_{a,b}|E_{ab}|^2$. Set $\varepsilon=\sqrt{e^2}$, again a symbolic nonnegative square root; then $\|A\Pi-W\widehat R\|_2\le\|E\|_F=\varepsilon$. If all structural and score checks passed, return `certified` with the rational record, reconstructed $W$, $(q_{ij})$, $(b_{ij})$, $E,e^2,\varepsilon$ and their check outcomes; otherwise return `uncertified` with any completed data. There is no extra residual tolerance implicit in the certificate: its actual residual bound $\varepsilon$ is reported, however large, and any application requiring a small bound must check that separately.

This single finite pass uses at most the prescribed positive pass budget; a supplied certificate is accepted only by recomputing these exact checks. Certification does not change the core status or rounded candidates. It gives precisely a nonsingular $\widehat R_{11}$ when $k>0$, rigorous combined-score bounds $b_{ij}\le f$, and an exact unitary representation $W$ with the reported reconstruction bound. The bounds concern the represented input $A$; a claim about different intended data also needs its separately supplied input-error bound. Ordinary rounded score or residual evaluations do not establish this certificate.

Row swaps and subtracting a multiple of one row from another are invertible operations; they preserve all linear dependence relations among columns. At completion the echelon matrix has $r$ nonzero rows with distinct pivot columns, and all remaining rows vanish. Its pivot columns are independent by triangular back-substitution, and its image is contained in the $r$-dimensional space of vectors supported on the nonzero rows. Its rank is therefore exactly $r$, which equals the original rank. The same finite argument applies to the represented selected-block singularity test. Thus no rounded pivot threshold or undecidable limiting test is involved in either finite-precision rank decision. In exact mode the same rank-preserving operations and finite pivot scans apply over the exact input field, using the assumed exact arithmetic and comparisons.

Each QR initialization or refactorization has finitely many pivot scans and at most $mn$ local updates by [F1]. Their scalar operations terminate individually in the specified model. A zero target is skipped, and division is performed only after its denominator check. An inadmissible rounded operation exits with `range-failure`; a singular selected block exits with `singular-selected-block`. Otherwise triangular solves and inverse-row calculations use finitely many nonzero diagonal divisions, and finitely many norms and comparisons produce a score-test pass. In exact arithmetic the corresponding finite QR eliminations, norms, and comparisons are defined by the exact model; the same singular-block branch prevents an undefined solve.

Starting with zero swaps, every score-test pass either returns success, returns another nonsuccess status, or finds a violation. At a violation the procedure returns when the count is already $S$; otherwise it increments the count and repeats. Hence there are at most $S$ swaps and $S+1$ score-test passes. Each has finite work by step 2.1. The rank-deficient and $k=0$ QR branches return earlier. The optional QR certificate check uses only its fixed finite budget, so failure to certify cannot cause another unbounded loop or change a core status. The ordered exit branches assign exactly one core status.

The ID endpoint branches [F2] return after constructing finite empty or identity matrices. Every interior call terminates by step 3.1. Nonsuccess is propagated with both certificate statuses not applicable. On success the permutation determines distinct valid selected indices, and insertion and permutation of finitely many entries constructs $T$ in finite work. Every finite candidate entry is rational in the represented mode. Thus all entries of $D$, all squared moduli and their finite sum and maximum are exactly computable rationals, regardless of their magnitude; the symbolic square root $\sqrt{r^2}$ requires no rounded conversion. Identity and rational inequality checks terminate, assigning either `certified` or `uncertified`; endpoint certificate statuses are not required. This proves termination and well-definedness of all outputs and statuses.

On an ID-certified branch the explicit checks [F2] give $T(:,J)=I_k$ and $c^2\le f^2$. Since $f\ge1$ and all moduli are nonnegative, $|T_{ab}|^2\le c^2\le f^2$ gives $|T_{ab}|\le f$. For every unit vector $x\in\mathbb F^n$, apply [F3] to each row of $D$ to obtain $|(Dx)_a|^2\le\sum_b|D_{ab}|^2$. Summing over rows gives $\|Dx\|_2^2\le\sum_{a,b}|D_{ab}|^2=r^2$. Taking the supremum over unit $x$ proves $\|D\|_2\le\sqrt{r^2}$ for the actual reconstruction residual. This uses only the direct exact data and no RRQR score certificate, as claimed.

Input a finite real or complex matrix $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ with $m\ge n\ge1$, an integer $k$ with $0\le k\le n$, a factor $f\ge1$, a finite swap cap $S\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$, and an arithmetic mode: exact arithmetic or finite precision. Finite-precision inputs and the arithmetic format have the represented-dyadic meaning specified by the called QR algorithm; all exact certificate calculations below use unbounded-size rational arithmetic on those represented values. In that mode supply the called QR procedure's finite real format, rounding rule and optional certificate-pass budget $C\in\mathbb N_0$ (default $1$); forward them unchanged on the interior call. Its exact unitary $W$ is reconstructed from the final sweep's dyadic reflector record, and its score and residual bounds may be symbolic nonnegative square roots of exact rationals. The direct ID check below uses only rational candidate entries and does not require evaluating those square roots. The procedure returns an algorithm status in `success`, `rank-deficient-input`, `singular-selected-block`, `swap-budget-exhausted`, or `range-failure`. On a successful branch it returns the selected index list $J$ and coefficient matrix $T$; finite-precision outputs are candidates until their certification status is checked. For $1\le k<n$, it also returns the RRQR diagnostics specified in step 4, including the rank status, selected-block conditioning data, and score data. In finite precision it returns separately the underlying RRQR certificate status and certificate data, and an ID-certificate status for the returned $J,T$.

1. If $k=0$, return `success`, $J=\varnothing$, and the unique $0\times n$ matrix $T$. Then $A(:,J)T=0$. Set the block, rank, and conditioning diagnostics to not applicable and both certificate statuses to `not-required`. This branch includes $A=0$.
2. If $k=n$, return `success`, $J=(1,\ldots,n)$, and $T=I_n$. Then $A(:,J)T=A$. Set the block, rank, and conditioning diagnostics to not applicable and both certificate statuses to `not-required`.
3. If $1\le k<n$, call [[alg-strong-rank-revealing-qr-with-finite-swaps]] on $(A,k,f,S)$ in the requested arithmetic mode. In exact arithmetic, propagate each nonsuccess status without returning $J,T$. In finite precision, propagate each nonsuccess status, including `range-failure`, without returning $J,T$; retain any partial diagnostics supplied by the called procedure. On either mode's nonsuccess branch set both certificate statuses to `not-applicable` and return no ID-certificate data.
4. On success, let $\Pi$ be the returned column permutation. In exact arithmetic retain the full factorization $A\Pi=QR$ with unitary $Q$ and partition its upper-trapezoidal factor after its first $k$ rows and columns as
   $$R=\begin{bmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&R_{22}\end{bmatrix}.$$
   In finite precision use the returned candidate factors $\widehat Q,\widehat R$ and the corresponding blocks; the exact unitary transformation representation $W$ remains part of the certificate data in step 5. Let $J$ be the ordered list of original column indices in the first $k$ positions of $\Pi$. Set $X=R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}$ in exact arithmetic, or use the returned candidate $X$ in finite precision, and define $T$ by $T\Pi=[I_k\ \ X]$. Retain for the final output $J,T$, the full factor ($Q$ or $\widehat Q$), and the diagnostics $(\Pi,R_{11},R_{12},R_{22},X,(\omega_i)_i,(\gamma_j)_j,(s_{ij})_{ij},\max_{i,j}|X_{ij}|,\max_{i,j}s_{ij})$, where $\omega_i=\|e_i^*R_{11}^{-1}\|_2$, $\gamma_j=\|R_{22}(:,j)\|_2$, and $s_{ij}=(|X_{ij}|^2+(\omega_i\gamma_j)^2)^{1/2}$. In finite precision these are candidate values; retain validated enclosures only when supplied by the certificate. Continue to step 5 before returning.
5. In exact arithmetic, the returned decomposition and diagnostics refer to the exact successful factorization; set both certificate statuses to `not-required`. In finite precision, retain the called procedure's RRQR certificate status and any completed data $(W,(b_{ij}),\varepsilon)$, including its dyadic reflector record and exact squared quantities, unchanged and independently of the following direct ID check; fields not computed on an `uncertified` branch remain absent. If a candidate $X$ or other required output is nonfinite, return `range-failure` without $J,T$, with both certificate statuses `not-applicable`. Otherwise form $T$ by copying the candidate entries and inserting exact zeros and ones, so no new rounding changes $X$. For the actual returned $J,T$, compute in exact rational complex arithmetic
   $$D=A-A(:,J)T,\qquad r^2=\sum_{a=1}^m\sum_{b=1}^n|D_{ab}|^2,\qquad c^2=\max_{a,b}|T_{ab}|^2.$$
   Check the dimensions, distinct valid indices in $J$, the entrywise identity $T(:,J)=I_k$, and $c^2\le f^2$. Set the ID-certificate status to `certified` exactly when these checks pass, and otherwise to `uncertified`. Return the exact rational data $(D,r^2,c^2)$ and the check outcomes in either case. The residual bound is the symbolic nonnegative square root $\sqrt{r^2}$, so its reporting requires no floating-point square root or range conversion. A `certified` ID therefore obeys
   $$T(:,J)=I_k,\qquad \max_{a,b}|T_{ab}|\le f,\qquad \|A-A(:,J)T\|_2\le\sqrt{r^2}.$$
   This direct certificate is independent of the RRQR certificate: it can certify the actual interpolation and this explicit residual bound even when RRQR score certification is unavailable. It does not certify the RRQR singular-value comparison or replace its score and unitary-reconstruction conditions. No iterative certificate search or rounding-based equality test is used. Return `success` with these outputs and the two separately assigned certificate statuses.

The error theorem below concerns exact-arithmetic success. It gives no finite-precision error bound for a returned candidate; a strong singular-value-relative bound additionally requires verified RRQR score and factorization information. Step 5 supplies its separate direct bound for the actual represented output, without asserting that it equals the exact-arithmetic trailing-block bound.

Input a real or complex matrix $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ with $m\ge n$, a target $k$ with $0\le k<n$, a factor $f\ge1$, and a finite swap cap $S\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$. The exact-arithmetic version is specified below. In finite precision, $A$ denotes the represented matrix: each real and imaginary component, and $f$, is a finite binary floating-point number, interpreted as its exact dyadic rational value. The arithmetic format and rounding rule are fixed for a run. A nonfinite input or required rounded intermediate returns `range-failure`. This mode makes no rank claim about an unspecified matrix before input rounding.

For the finite-precision rank test, copy the represented $A$ into exact rational complex arithmetic. Scan columns from left to right with a current pivot row, select the first nonzero entry at or below that row, interchange rows, and eliminate entries below it by exact rational row operations. If no such entry exists, skip that column. Increment the pivot row only after a nonzero pivot. The number $r$ of pivots is the reported exact represented-input rank. Return `rank-deficient-input` if $r<n$; otherwise continue with rank status `full-column-rank`. This test uses unbounded-size rational integers, not the rounded QR diagonal or a numerical-rank threshold. In exact mode, use the same finite row-elimination instructions over the exact input field to decide the rank condition in step 1.

The finite-precision mode additionally takes a finite real binary format $\mathcal F$ containing $0,1,-1$ and closed under sign changes, a fixed rounding rule, and a certificate-pass budget $C\in\mathbb N_0$ (default $1$; $C=0$ disables certification). Real and imaginary parts are stored separately. For a real rational result within the format's finite range, $\operatorname{fl}$ returns its specified nearest representable value, with a fixed tie rule, or its specified directed rounding; a result outside that range returns `range-failure`. Exact zeros are copied as zero. Real addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division mean their exact rational result followed by this rounding; check each divisor before dividing. A real square root of a nonnegative represented number is rounded by comparing that number with squares of the finitely many nonnegative format values: bracket its root, then use the selected directed endpoint or compare with the squared midpoint for nearest rounding. A negative argument or a root beyond the finite range returns `range-failure`. Thus no exact irrational arithmetic oracle or unbounded precision search is part of this mode. A nonfinite input or any failed required scalar operation immediately returns `range-failure` with any completed partial data.

Use the following fixed scalar conventions throughout the rounded core. For $z=a+ib$ and $w=c+id$, complex addition/subtraction round their two real components; multiplication returns $\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(ac)-\operatorname{fl}(bd))+i\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(ad)+\operatorname{fl}(bc))$. For division compute $d_0=\operatorname{fl}(c^2)+\operatorname{fl}(d^2)$ with the addition rounded, require $d_0>0$, compute the rounded product $z\overline w$, and divide its two real components by $d_0$, rounding each. Conjugation and sign changes are exact copies. For a vector, compute its squared norm by rounding each real-component square and summing them with rounding in increasing coordinate order, real part before imaginary part; apply the rounded nonnegative square root. Dot products use the above rounded complex products and a left-to-right rounded sum. These rules specify every norm and score calculation below; a nonzero vector whose required computed norm is zero returns `range-failure`.

The initial permutation is $\Pi=I_n$, with original labels $1,\ldots,n$. A rounded full QR sweep of a fixed current column order starts from $B=A\Pi$, $\widehat Q=I_m$ and an empty transformation record. During the initial pivoted sweep, at column $j=1,\ldots,n$ compute the rounded norms of $B(j:m,\ell)$ for $\ell=j,\ldots,n$, choose the largest, breaking ties by smallest original column label, and swap the full columns of $B$ and their labels. A fixed-order sweep skips these pivot searches. In either sweep, if $B(j+1:m,j)=0$ entrywise, record no transformation and continue. Otherwise copy $z=B(j:m,j)$, compute its rounded norm $r>0$, and set $\phi=1$ if $z_1=0$; if $z_1\ne0$, compute its rounded modulus $a>0$ and divide its two components by $a$ to form $\phi$. Set $\alpha=-\operatorname{fl}(r\phi)$, $v_1=\operatorname{fl}(z_1-\alpha)$ and $v_i=z_i$ for $i>1$. Compute the rounded squared norm $\widehat d$ of $v$, require $\widehat d>0$, and put $\widehat\tau=\operatorname{fl}(2/\widehat d)$. Record the active index $j$ and the exact dyadic components of this nonzero stored $v$ before updating anything.

For each column $\ell=j,\ldots,n$, compute the rounded dot product $a_\ell=v^*B(j:m,\ell)$ from the old column, set $h_\ell=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau a_\ell)$, then replace each active entry by $\operatorname{fl}(B_{i\ell}-\operatorname{fl}(v_{i-j+1}h_\ell))$. For each row $a=1,\ldots,m$ of $\widehat Q$, compute $b_a=\widehat Q(a,j:m)v$ from its old row, set $g_a=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau b_a)$, and replace each active entry by $\operatorname{fl}(\widehat Q_{ai}-\operatorname{fl}(g_a\overline v_{i-j+1}))$. Finally set $B(j+1:m,j)$ to exact zeros by assignment. At the end return $\widehat R=B$, the full $m\times m$ candidate $\widehat Q$, the final permutation and the ordered record. The imposed zeros are part of this rounded procedure, not a claim of exact annihilation; the certificate measures their effect as well as all rounding. There are at most $n\le mn$ reflector updates per sweep. Empty active tails are skipped, and no norm or quotient is required for them.

In finite precision step 1 uses this pivoted sweep, and step 2 uses a fresh fixed-order sweep on the represented input $A$ in its current order. Each fresh sweep resets $\widehat Q$ and its transformation record. Before the triangular solves, decide singularity of its represented $\widehat R_{11}$ by the same exact rational elimination as the input rank test; if singular, return `singular-selected-block`. Otherwise solve $\widehat R_{11}X=\widehat R_{12}$ and $\widehat R_{11}Y=I_k$ by rounded back-substitution: for each right-hand-side column, process rows $i=k,\ldots,1$, sum $\widehat R_{ih}x_h$ in increasing $h=i+1,\ldots,k$, subtract from the supplied right-hand side, check the diagonal divisor and use the complex division above. Compute $\omega_i$ as the rounded norm of row $i$ of $Y$, $\gamma_j$ as the rounded norm of column $j$ of $\widehat R_{22}$, and $c_{ij}$ as the rounded modulus of $X_{ij}$. Compute $t_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(\omega_i\gamma_j)$ and $s_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt{\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(c_{ij}^2)+\operatorname{fl}(t_{ij}^2))})$. Scan these finite candidate lists for the step-4 maxima and its stated tie rules. The diagnostics $(X,Y,(\omega_i),(\gamma_j),(c_{ij}),(s_{ij}))$ are rounded candidates, not exact inverse or score identities. For $k=0$ there are no such solves or score lists.

The numbered instructions below specify exact arithmetic; the preceding rounded instructions replace the corresponding factorization, solve and score operations in finite precision.

1. If $A$ is not full column rank, return `rank-deficient-input`. Otherwise initialize a column permutation $\Pi$ and the full column-pivoted QR factorization $A\Pi=QR$, where $Q\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}$ is unitary and $R\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ is upper trapezoidal. At each pivot choose a remaining column of maximal residual $2$-norm, resolving ties by the smallest original column index. Partition $R=\begin{bmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&R_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ after the first $k$ rows and columns. Do not return the reduced QR form. The selected first $k$ columns then have a nonsingular leading block. For $k=0$, return this full factorization with `success`.
2. For $k>0$, refactor the current fixed column order in the full QR form, without further pivoting whenever needed, using unitary Householder or Givens transformations. If the selected leading block is singular, return `singular-selected-block`.
3. Form $X=R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}$. For $1\le i\le k$ let $\omega_i=\|e_i^*R_{11}^{-1}\|_2$; for $1\le j\le n-k$ let $\gamma_j=\|R_{22}(:,j)\|_2$. Define the swap score $s_{ij}=\bigl(|X_{ij}|^2+(\omega_i\gamma_j)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$.
4. If $\max_{i,j}|X_{ij}|>f$, choose the lexicographically first pair attaining the largest $|X_{ij}|$. Otherwise, if $\max_{i,j}s_{ij}>f$, choose the lexicographically first pair attaining the largest score. If neither inequality holds, return `success` and the factors, permutation, $X$, and maximum score. The first branch retains the usual coefficient-triggered swap; the second controls the trailing residual needed for the strong spectral comparison.
5. When a violating pair was chosen, if the swap count is already $S$, return `swap-budget-exhausted` with the current partial factors. Otherwise interchange the chosen selected and trailing columns in the current permutation. In exact arithmetic restore triangular form with Givens rotations; in finite precision discard the old factors and record, since step 2 recomputes them from $A$ in the new fixed order. Increment the swap count and return to step 2.

The statuses are `success`, `rank-deficient-input`, `singular-selected-block`, `swap-budget-exhausted`, and `range-failure`. In particular, ordinary column-pivoted QR is only the initialization: the procedure does not assert that its output alone satisfies the strong bounds. Both modes return the full factor shape and available diagnostics. A finite-precision `success` is a candidate until the following separate certificate is verified. The rounded dense $\widehat Q$ is never asserted to be unitary.

For each recorded active dyadic vector $v$, define the embedded exact rational matrix
$$H=I-\frac{2vv^*}{v^*v}$$
on its active coordinates, with identity on the preceding coordinates. Its denominator is a strictly positive exact rational. It is exactly unitary: writing $P=vv^*/(v^*v)$ gives $P^*=P$, $P^2=P$ and $(I-2P)^*(I-2P)=I$. Thus the ordered sweep record represents the exact unitary product $W=H_1\cdots H_t$; an empty record represents $I_m$. This product corresponds to the final fresh sweep only, and is distinct from the rounded $\widehat Q$ and the nonunitary rounded update coefficients $\widehat\tau$. Its rational representation requires no normalization by an irrational vector norm.

Certification is finite optional postprocessing, independent of the core status. For a nonsuccess status assign `not-applicable`. On success with $C=0$, assign `uncertified`. With $C\ge1$ perform the following one exact rational pass, using unbounded-size integer numerators and denominators; no retry until success is allowed.

- Check factor dimensions, that $\Pi$ is a permutation of $1,\ldots,n$, that $\widehat R$ is exactly upper trapezoidal, and that each recorded vector has the declared active dimension and is nonzero. Reconstruct each $H$ by the displayed rational formula, multiply them in the recorded order, and verify entrywise $W^*W=I_m$. Any failed check sets `uncertified`.
- For $k>0$, apply exact rational elimination to $\widehat R_{11}$. If singular, the certificate is `uncertified`. Otherwise compute its exact inverse $Y_0$ by elimination on $[\widehat R_{11}\;I_k]$, normalizing each nonzero pivot and eliminating above and below it. Form $Z=Y_0\widehat R_{12}$ and the exact nonnegative rational score squares
$$q_{ij}=|Z_{ij}|^2+\left(\sum_{a=1}^k|(Y_0)_{ia}|^2\right)\left(\sum_{b=1}^{m-k}|(\widehat R_{22})_{bj}|^2\right).$$
  Set $b_{ij}=\sqrt{q_{ij}}$, stored as a symbolic nonnegative square root, and check the rational inequalities $q_{ij}\le f^2$ for every $i,j$. These are equivalent to all $b_{ij}\le f$. They certify the exact scores of the represented blocks, independently of rounded $X,Y,\omega,\gamma,s$. For $k=0$ this list and every inverse condition are absent.
- Compute exactly $E=A\Pi-W\widehat R$ and $e^2=\sum_{a,b}|E_{ab}|^2$. Set $\varepsilon=\sqrt{e^2}$, again a symbolic nonnegative square root; then $\|A\Pi-W\widehat R\|_2\le\|E\|_F=\varepsilon$. If all structural and score checks passed, return `certified` with the rational record, reconstructed $W$, $(q_{ij})$, $(b_{ij})$, $E,e^2,\varepsilon$ and their check outcomes; otherwise return `uncertified` with any completed data. There is no extra residual tolerance implicit in the certificate: its actual residual bound $\varepsilon$ is reported, however large, and any application requiring a small bound must check that separately.

This single finite pass uses at most the prescribed positive pass budget; a supplied certificate is accepted only by recomputing these exact checks. Certification does not change the core status or rounded candidates. It gives precisely a nonsingular $\widehat R_{11}$ when $k>0$, rigorous combined-score bounds $b_{ij}\le f$, and an exact unitary representation $W$ with the reported reconstruction bound. The bounds concern the represented input $A$; a claim about different intended data also needs its separately supplied input-error bound. Ordinary rounded score or residual evaluations do not establish this certificate.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ have full column rank, $m\ge n$, and let the exact-arithmetic version of [[alg-strong-rank-revealing-qr-with-finite-swaps]] return `success` with full QR factorization
$$A\Pi=Q\begin{bmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&R_{22}\end{bmatrix},$$
where $Q\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}$ is unitary and the displayed $R$ is upper trapezoidal with $m$ rows. Let the target satisfy $0\le k<n$ and the factor satisfy $f\ge1$. For $1\le k<n$, assume $R_{11}\in\mathbb F^{k\times k}$ is nonsingular and put $X=R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}$. Put $g=(1+f^2k(n-k))^{1/2}$. Then
$$\sigma_i(R_{11})\ge\frac{\sigma_i(A)}{g}\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad \sigma_j(R_{22})\le g\,\sigma_{k+j}(A)\quad(1\le j\le n-k).$$
For $k=0$, the second comparison is the equality $R_{22}=Q^*A\Pi$ with $g=1$. These conclusions use the combined score in the algorithm; the bound on $X$ alone is not used as a substitute for control of $R_{22}$. For a computed candidate $\widehat R$ with the algorithm's verified certificate $(W,(b_{ij}),\varepsilon)$, put $\widetilde A=W\widehat R\Pi^*$. No full-column-rank assumption on $\widetilde A$ is required beyond nonsingularity of $\widehat R_{11}$ when $k>0$. Then the corresponding residual-adjusted bounds are
$$\sigma_i(\widehat R_{11})\ge\frac{\sigma_i(A)-\varepsilon}{g}\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad \sigma_j(\widehat R_{22})\le g\bigl(\sigma_{k+j}(A)+\varepsilon\bigr)\quad(1\le j\le n-k).$$
For $k=0$, these reduce to $\sigma_j(\widehat R)\le\sigma_j(A)+\varepsilon$. Computed scores alone do not certify either conclusion.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n\ge1$, $s\ge0$, $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$ be Hermitian positive semidefinite, $S\in\mathbb F^{n\times s}$, and $B=A^{1/2}S$. If $P_{\operatorname{Ran}(B)}$ denotes the orthogonal projection onto the range of $B$, then

$$\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}=A^{1/2}P_{\operatorname{Ran}(B)}A^{1/2}=A^{1/2}B(B^*B)^\dagger B^*A^{1/2}=A^{1/2}BB^\dagger A^{1/2}.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $M\in\mathbb F^{p\times q}$ be any finite real or complex matrix, and let $M^\dagger$ be its unique Moore-Penrose inverse. Then $P=MM^\dagger$ and $Q=M^\dagger M$ are self-adjoint idempotents. The range of $P$ is $\operatorname{Ran}(M)$, and the range of $Q$ is $\operatorname{Ran}(M^\dagger)$. Thus both are orthogonal projections. If $M$ has full row rank, then $MM^\dagger=I_p$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

derivations.claim: Put $M=A^{1/2}$, $Y=MS$, and let $P=P_{\operatorname{Ran}(Y)}$. By [F1], $A-\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}=M(I-P)M=X^*X$ for $X=(I-P)M$, since $P$ is self-adjoint and idempotent. A singular value decomposition from [F4] writes $X=U_X\Sigma_XV_X^*$ and $X^*X=V_X\Sigma_X^2V_X^*$; [F5] therefore gives $\|A-\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}\|_2=\|X\|_2^2$.

By [F2], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $U$ of $A$. The diagonal matrix whose entries are the nonnegative square roots of its eigenvalues is a positive-semidefinite square root, hence it is $A^{1/2}$ by uniqueness [F6]. Thus in this basis, $M=U\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda_1^{1/2},\Lambda_2^{1/2})U^*$ and $U^*Y=\begin{bmatrix}\Lambda_1^{1/2}\Omega_1\\\Lambda_2^{1/2}\Omega_2\end{bmatrix}$. For any unit vector $x=U(x_1,x_2)$, set $c=\Omega_1^\dagger x_1$. Then [F3] gives $\Omega_1c=x_1$, and $Yc=U\begin{bmatrix}\Lambda_1^{1/2}x_1\\\Lambda_2^{1/2}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger x_1\end{bmatrix}\in\operatorname{Ran}(Y)$.

Orthogonal projection gives the shortest distance to its range, so $\|(I-P)Mx\|_2\le\|Mx-Yc\|_2 =\|\Lambda_2^{1/2}(x_2-\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger x_1)\|_2$. Write $G=\Lambda_2^{1/2}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger$ and $H=\Lambda_2^{1/2}$. For unit $(x_1,x_2)$, the last norm is at most $\|G\|_2\|x_1\|_2+\|H\|_2\|x_2\|_2 \le(\|G\|_2^2+\|H\|_2^2)^{1/2}$ by the scalar Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Taking the supremum over unit $x$ yields $\|X\|_2^2\le\|G\|_2^2+\|H\|_2^2$.

Since $H$ is diagonal with nonnegative entries, [F2] and [F5] give $\|H\|_2^2=\lambda_{k+1}$, including the declared empty-tail convention. Combine this with step 1.1 and step 2.1 to obtain $\|A-\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}\|_2\le\lambda_{k+1}+\|\Lambda_2^{1/2}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2^2$.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ over $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with $m,n\ge1$, and let $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and $J=(j_1,\ldots,j_k)$ be ordered lists of distinct row and column indices. For $k=0$, both lists and all selected matrices have zero size, with ordinary empty-matrix multiplication. Define $C=A(:,J)\in\mathbb F^{m\times k}$, $R=A(I,:)\in\mathbb F^{k\times n}$, and the cross matrix $W=A(I,J)\in\mathbb F^{k\times k}$, using the same orders in $I,J,W$.

The **skeleton CUR core** is $U_{\mathrm{skel}}=W^\dagger$ and its reconstruction is $\widehat A_{\mathrm{skel}}=C W^\dagger R$. The **projected least-squares CUR core** is $U_{\mathrm{proj}}=C^\dagger A R^\dagger$ and its reconstruction is
$\widehat A_{\mathrm{proj}}=C(C^\dagger A R^\dagger)R=(CC^\dagger)A(R^\dagger R)$.

For $k=0$, both reconstructions are the zero $m\times n$ matrix.

The Moore-Penrose theorem in the dependencies guarantees that these formulas are single-valued for singular as well as nonsingular $C,R,W$. The two core constructions may yield the same matrix: for $A=[1]$ and $I=J=(1)$, both cores equal $[1]$. The projection residual bound on the A page applies only to $\widehat A_{\mathrm{proj}}$; it is not asserted for the skeleton core $W^\dagger$.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $m,n\ge1$, and let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$. Choose an integer $0\le k\le\min(m,n)$ and ordered lists $I$ and $J$ of $k$ distinct valid row and column indices, respectively. Let $C=A(:,J)$, $R=A(I,:)$, and $W=A(I,J)\in\mathbb F^{k\times k}$ as in [[def-cur-reconstruction-cores]]. If $\operatorname{rank}(A)=\operatorname{rank}(W)=k$, then the skeleton CUR reconstruction satisfies
$C W^\dagger R=A$.
For $k=0$, use the empty-matrix convention: a rank-zero $A$ is zero and the empty product reconstructs the zero $m\times n$ matrix.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] and
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]].

For every matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or
$\mathbb C$, there exists a unique matrix $A^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$
satisfying the four Penrose equations of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]].

derivations.claim: Direct extraction gives $C=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$, $R=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}$, and $W=I_2$. Since $I_2$ satisfies the four Penrose equations [F3], uniqueness [F4] gives $W^\dagger=I_2$; [F1] therefore gives the reconstruction $CR$.

Multiplication yields $CR=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\1&1&2\end{bmatrix}=A$. The identity $I_2$ satisfies the Penrose equations [F3], hence equals $W^\dagger$ by uniqueness [F4]. The third row of $A$ is the sum of the first two, and the first two are independent, so $\operatorname{rank}(A)=2=\operatorname{rank}(W)$. Hence [F2] also applies and confirms the exact skeleton CUR identity.
