Let $N\ge0$, $I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, source positions $z_j\in\mathbb C$ and charges $q_j\in\mathbb C$ for $j\in I$, and target positions equal to the same labelled positions. A root square is a closed square of side $s_0>0$ containing every source position. Its cells are the dyadic subsquares obtained by repeatedly bisecting each side. At each split use half-open child squares, with the outer top and right edges included in the last child, so every point belongs to exactly one child. A **finite quadtree** is a finite rooted tree of such cells in which each internal cell has its four geometric children and each leaf contains at most $s$ labels for a fixed integer $s\ge1$. Empty children are retained as geometric cells but are skipped in source and target lists. For a cell $C$, write $c_C$ for its center, $s_C$ for its side length, $I_C=\{j:z_j\in C\}$, and $a_C=s_C/\sqrt2$ for the radius of its circumscribed disk.

A cell pair $(C,D)$ is **source-separated from target-separated** when $R_{CD}:=|c_D-c_C|>a_C+a_D$; $C$ is the source cell and $D$ the target cell. For every such pair fix an analytic logarithm $L_{CD}$ on the open disk $\{w:|w-(c_D-c_C)|<R_{CD}\}$. This disk excludes zero and contains all differences $z_i-z_j$ with $i\in I_D$, $j\in I_C$. For each direct near particle pair $(j,i)$ fix one value $L_{ji}$ of the logarithm of $z_i-z_j$, when this difference is nonzero. Once the recursive rule below terminates, for a collision-free configuration define the exact target potential and its complex derivative using the resulting lists as follows:
Here $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal N$ denote the far and direct near lists produced by that rule.
$$u_i:=\sum_{(j,i)\in\mathcal N}q_jL_{ji}+\sum_{\substack{(C,D)\in\mathcal F\\ i\in I_D}}\ \sum_{j\in I_C}q_jL_{CD}(z_i-z_j),\qquad g_i:=\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{q_j}{z_i-z_j}.$$
Thus each ordered source-target pair contributes its source charge times the fixed direct-near branch value or the fixed far-cell branch value prescribed by its list entry. The complex derivative is independent of the chosen logarithm values.

The **recursive interaction decomposition** of an ordered pair of nonempty cells $(C,D)$ is defined as follows. If $C=D$ is a leaf, record as direct near pairs all $(j,i)\in I_C\times I_D$ with $j\ne i$. If $C=D$ is internal, replace $(C,D)$ by all ordered pairs $(E,F)$ of its nonempty children. If $C\ne D$ and $R_{CD}>a_C+a_D$, record the far cell pair $(C,D)$. If both cells are leaves and the pair is not separated, record all direct near particle pairs $(j,i)\in I_C\times I_D$ with $j\ne i$. Let $\mathbb S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ with its usual surface-area measure $dS$, normalized so $\int_{\mathbb S^2}dS=4\pi$. For an integer $\ell\ge0$, let $\mathcal H_\ell$ be the complex vector space of restrictions to $\mathbb S^2$ of homogeneous degree-$\ell$ polynomials $P(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ satisfying $\Delta P=0$. Give $\mathcal H_\ell$ the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb S^2}f\overline g\,dS$, linear in the first argument. An orthonormal basis is not fixed by this definition; the addition-theorem item proves that $\dim\mathcal H_\ell=2\ell+1$ and that such a finite basis exists.

If $Y_{\ell m}\in\mathcal H_\ell$ is later chosen from an orthonormal basis and $v\ne0$, its associated homogeneous harmonic polynomial is $H_{\ell m}(v)=|v|^\ell Y_{\ell m}(v/|v|)$. At $v=0$ use the polynomial value: $H_{00}(0)=Y_{00}$ and $H_{\ell m}(0)=0$ for $\ell>0$. This is the regular-solid-harmonic convention used in the 3D evaluator.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal P_\ell$ be the homogeneous degree-$\ell$ polynomials in three variables; it has $\binom{\ell+2}{2}$ monomials. For a homogeneous polynomial $g$ of degree $d$, direct differentiation and Euler's identity give $\Delta(|x|^{2s}g)=2s(2d+2s+1)|x|^{2s-2}g+|x|^{2s}\Delta g$. If $\ell\ge2$, put $n=\ell-2$, $J=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, $A_j=2(j+1)(2n-2j+3)$, $c_0=1/A_0$, and $c_j=-c_{j-1}/A_j$ for $1\le j\le J$. For $f\in\mathcal P_n$, the degree-$\ell$ polynomial $q=\sum_{j=0}^Jc_j|x|^{2(j+1)}\Delta^jf$ satisfies $\Delta q=f$: the coefficients of $|x|^{2j}\Delta^jf$ telescope by $c_0A_0=1$ and $c_jA_j+c_{j-1}=0$, and $\Delta^{J+1}f=0$. Hence $\Delta:\mathcal P_\ell\to\mathcal P_{\ell-2}$ is onto; for $\ell=0,1$ the target is zero.

Restriction of a homogeneous polynomial to $\mathbb S^2$ is injective, because homogeneity recovers its value at every nonzero $x$ from its value at $x/|x|$. Rank-nullity therefore gives $\dim\mathcal H_\ell=\binom{\ell+2}{2}-\binom{\ell}{2}=2\ell+1$ for $\ell\ge2$, and direct counting gives $1$ and $3$ for $\ell=0,1$. Gram-Schmidt on any finite spanning list gives an orthonormal basis; no choice axiom is used.

For an orthonormal basis define $K_\ell(\omega,\omega')=\sum_mY_{\ell m}(\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\omega')}$. A unitary basis change leaves this sum unchanged, and rotations carry one orthonormal basis of $\mathcal H_\ell$ to another, so $K_\ell$ is rotation-invariant. Thus $K_\ell(\omega,\omega)$ is constant in $\omega$; integrating it over the sphere gives $2\ell+1$, so this constant is $(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$.

Fix $\omega'$. After rotating it to the third coordinate axis, use $w=x_1+ix_2$ and $\bar w=x_1-ix_2$. A rotation sends these to $e^{i\theta}w$ and $e^{-i\theta}\bar w$, so an invariant monomial $w^a\bar w^b x_3^c$ must have $a=b$. The invariant homogeneous polynomials are therefore sums of $(x_1^2+x_2^2)^j x_3^{\ell-2j}$, whose restrictions to the sphere are polynomials $f(t)$ of degree at most $\ell$, with $t=x_3$. The polar-coordinate Laplacian is $\partial_{rr}+2r^{-1}\partial_r+r^{-2}\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$; applying it to $r^\ell f(\cos\theta)$ gives $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}f=-\ell(\ell+1)f$. For a zonal $f$, the angular term is $(\sin\theta)^{-1}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\partial_\theta f)=(1-t^2)f''-2tf'$ by $t=\cos\theta$, so $(1-t^2)f''-2tf'+\ell(\ell+1)f=0$. Writing $f(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\ell}a_kt^k$ yields $(k+2)(k+1)a_{k+2}+\bigl(\ell(\ell+1)-k(k+1)\bigr)a_k=0$. For $\ell\ge1$, the equation at $k=\ell-1$, using $a_{\ell+1}=0$, gives $2\ell a_{\ell-1}=0$; descending through $k=\ell-3,\ell-5,\ldots$ forces every coefficient of parity opposite to $\ell$ to vanish. For $k=\ell-2,\ell-4,\ldots$, the coefficient $\ell(\ell+1)-k(k+1)$ is positive, so each lower coefficient of parity $\ell$ is determined by the next one. Thus the zonal solution space has dimension at most one (for $\ell=0$ it is the constants). The function $K_\ell(\cdot,\omega')$ is a zonal harmonic, and $K_\ell(\omega',\omega')=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)>0$, so a nonzero such solution exists. Define $P_\ell(t)=K_\ell(\omega,\omega')/K_\ell(\omega',\omega')$ when $t=\omega\cdot\omega'$. Rotation invariance makes this depend only on $t$, and $P_\ell(1)=1$. The diagonal value in step 3.1 now gives the displayed addition theorem.

Cauchy-Schwarz applied to the finite basis sum gives $|K_\ell(\omega,\omega')|\le\sqrt{K_\ell(\omega,\omega)K_\ell(\omega',\omega')}=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$. Dividing by the diagonal constant proves $|P_\ell(t)|\le1$.

Fix $\omega'\in\mathbb S^2$ and let $u(x)=|\omega'-x|^{-1}$ for $|x|<1$. The radial formula $\Delta |x-\omega'|^{-1}=f''(r)+2f'(r)/r=0$ away from $\omega'$ shows $u$ is harmonic in the unit ball. Its homogeneous Taylor term of degree $\ell$ is therefore harmonic, since the homogeneous terms in $\Delta u=0$ of each degree vanish separately; it is also invariant under rotations fixing $\omega'$. By step 4.1 it has the form $b_\ell r^\ell P_\ell(\omega\cdot\omega')$. On the ray $x=r\omega'$, $u(r\omega')=(1-r)^{-1}=\sum_{\ell\ge0}r^\ell$, so coefficient comparison gives $b_\ell=1$. Finally $u(r\omega)=(1-2r(\omega\cdot\omega')+r^2)^{-1/2}$, whose Taylor series in $r$ has radius at least $1$: its possible denominator zeros are $t\pm i\sqrt{1-t^2}$, both of modulus one. This proves the generating identity for $0\le r<1$.

Let $N\ge0$, $I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, source positions $z_j\in\mathbb C$ and charges $q_j\in\mathbb C$ for $j\in I$, and target positions equal to the same labelled positions. A root square is a closed square of side $s_0>0$ containing every source position. Its cells are the dyadic subsquares obtained by repeatedly bisecting each side. At each split use half-open child squares, with the outer top and right edges included in the last child, so every point belongs to exactly one child. A **finite quadtree** is a finite rooted tree of such cells in which each internal cell has its four geometric children and each leaf contains at most $s$ labels for a fixed integer $s\ge1$. Empty children are retained as geometric cells but are skipped in source and target lists. For a cell $C$, write $c_C$ for its center, $s_C$ for its side length, $I_C=\{j:z_j\in C\}$, and $a_C=s_C/\sqrt2$ for the radius of its circumscribed disk.

A cell pair $(C,D)$ is **source-separated from target-separated** when $R_{CD}:=|c_D-c_C|>a_C+a_D$; $C$ is the source cell and $D$ the target cell. For every such pair fix an analytic logarithm $L_{CD}$ on the open disk $\{w:|w-(c_D-c_C)|<R_{CD}\}$. This disk excludes zero and contains all differences $z_i-z_j$ with $i\in I_D$, $j\in I_C$. For each direct near particle pair $(j,i)$ fix one value $L_{ji}$ of the logarithm of $z_i-z_j$, when this difference is nonzero. Once the recursive rule below terminates, for a collision-free configuration define the exact target potential and its complex derivative using the resulting lists as follows:
Here $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal N$ denote the far and direct near lists produced by that rule.
$$u_i:=\sum_{(j,i)\in\mathcal N}q_jL_{ji}+\sum_{\substack{(C,D)\in\mathcal F\\ i\in I_D}}\ \sum_{j\in I_C}q_jL_{CD}(z_i-z_j),\qquad g_i:=\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{q_j}{z_i-z_j}.$$
Thus each ordered source-target pair contributes its source charge times the fixed direct-near branch value or the fixed far-cell branch value prescribed by its list entry. The complex derivative is independent of the chosen logarithm values.

The **recursive interaction decomposition** of an ordered pair of nonempty cells $(C,D)$ is defined as follows. If $C=D$ is a leaf, record as direct near pairs all $(j,i)\in I_C\times I_D$ with $j\ne i$. If $C=D$ is internal, replace $(C,D)$ by all ordered pairs $(E,F)$ of its nonempty children. If $C\ne D$ and $R_{CD}>a_C+a_D$, record the far cell pair $(C,D)$. If both cells are leaves and the pair is not separated, record all direct near particle pairs $(j,i)\in I_C\times I_D$ with $j\ne i$. In every other case, if exactly one cell is nonleaf, split that cell; if both are nonleaf, split the one of larger side length, breaking a tie by splitting the source cell. Replace the pair by the child pairs having nonempty source and target sets. For $N\ge1$, start at the root pair; for $N=0$, make no recursive calls and set both lists to empty. The resulting lists are the **far interaction list** $\mathcal F$ and the **direct near-pair list** $\mathcal N$. Their termination and exact pair-partition property are mathematical assertions, proved separately.

For a far pair $(C,D)$ put $\rho_{CD}=(a_C+a_D)/R_{CD}<1$ and $Q_C=\sum_{j\in I_C}|q_j|$. Two leaves are adjacent when their closed squares meet. A tree is **2:1 level-restricted** when any adjacent leaves have depths differing by at most one. It is **linear-size level-restricted for this decomposition** when it is 2:1 level-restricted and there are fixed constants $C_T,C_V$ such that its number $T$ of nonempty cells and the number $V$ of recursive cell-pair inspections satisfy $T\le C_T\max(1,N)$ and $V\le C_V\max(1,N)$. A list is **bounded** when there are fixed constants $C_F,C_N$ with $|\mathcal F|\le C_F T$ and $|\mathcal N|\le C_N\max(1,N)$. The work theorem uses these explicit counts; 2:1 balance alone is not asserted to supply them.

Use the data, quadtree and interaction decomposition of [[def-finite-planar-quadtree-fmm-pair-lists]]. Fix an expansion order $p\ge1$. If two different labels have the same position, return status `collision` before evaluating any singular interaction: the requested potential is undefined. Otherwise take as input a finite quadtree from the definition, together with its point-to-cell membership arrays and leaf threshold $s$. For $N=0$ return empty outputs. For $N\ge1$, construct $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal N$ by the recursive decomposition in the definition. The tree and point-to-cell membership are preprocessing inputs; their construction is not part of the arithmetic passes below.

Using the supplied membership data, make a root-first list of nonempty cells: at each nonempty internal cell inspect its four children and recurse only into children $E$ with $I_E\ne\varnothing$; never descend into an empty subtree. Use the reverse list order for the bottom-up pass and the root-first order for the top-down pass. Use exact complex arithmetic throughout. For each nonempty leaf $C$ form the particle-to-multipole (P2M) moments
$$M_n(C)=\sum_{j\in I_C}q_j(z_j-c_C)^n,\qquad 0\le n\le p.$$
For the upward multipole-to-multipole (M2M) pass, process nonempty internal cells bottom-up. For each such parent $C$ and each $0\le n\le p$, form its moments from its nonempty children by
$$M_n(C)=\sum_{\substack{E\text{ child of }C\\ I_E\ne\varnothing}}\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr(c_E-c_C)^{n-r}M_r(E).$$
An empty child has zero moments and is skipped. Thus the upward pass visits only parent-child edges whose two cells are nonempty.

Initialize the local coefficient vector of every nonempty cell to zero before processing any far pair. For each far pair $(C,D)$ set $\delta=c_D-c_C$, $R=|\delta|$, choose the fixed logarithm $L_{CD}$, and add to the target cell $D$'s local coefficients the multipole-to-local (M2L) coefficients
$$L_0(D)\mathrel{+}=M_0(C)L_{CD}(\delta)-\sum_{n=1}^p\frac{M_n(C)}{n\delta^n},$$
$$L_k(D)\mathrel{+}=(-1)^{k+1}\left(\frac{M_0(C)}{k\delta^k}+\sum_{n=1}^p\binom{n+k-1}{k}\frac{M_n(C)}{n\delta^{n+k}}\right),\quad 1\le k\le p.$$
After all M2L additions, perform a top-down downward local-to-local (L2L) pass over parent-child edges whose two cells are nonempty. For each parent $D$ and each nonempty child $E$, add
$$L_j(E)\mathrel{+}=\sum_{k=j}^p\binom kj L_k(D)(c_E-c_D)^{k-j},\qquad 0\le j\le p.$$
For a target $i$ in leaf $D$, return the far potential $\sum_{k=0}^pL_k(D)(z_i-c_D)^k$ and far derivative $\sum_{k=1}^p kL_k(D)(z_i-c_D)^{k-1}$. Add the exact direct near contributions $q_jL_{ji}$ and $q_j/(z_i-z_j)$, respectively, for $(j,i)\in\mathcal N$. Denote the resulting potential and derivative approximations by $\widetilde u_i$ and $\widetilde g_i$, respectively. The derivative output differentiates the truncated local polynomial and adds the exact near derivatives; its value is independent of logarithm branches.

derivations.claim: For $|w|<1$, the geometric series $1/(1+t)=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}(-t)^r$ converges uniformly on each closed disk $|t|\le r_0<1$. Integrating it from $0$ to $w$ gives the analytic branch identity $\log(1+w)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{m+1}w^m/m$.

For a nonempty child cell $E$ of $C$, write $z_j-c_C=(z_j-c_E)+(c_E-c_C)$ and apply the finite binomial theorem to its $n$th power. Summing over the sources in each nonempty child and then over the nonempty children gives $M_n(C)=\sum_E\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr(c_E-c_C)^{n-r}M_r(E)$ for every $n\le p$; empty children contribute zero. This is exactly the M2M pass.

If a parent local polynomial is $\sum_{k=0}^pL_k(z-c_D)^k$, put $z-c_D=(z-c_E)+(c_E-c_D)$ and expand each power. The coefficient of $(z-c_E)^j$ is $\sum_{k=j}^p\binom kjL_k(c_E-c_D)^{k-j}$; hence L2L exactly re-centers the polynomial without adding truncation error.

For a far pair $(C,D)$, put $z-c_C=D_0+x$ with $D_0=c_D-c_C$ and $|x|\le a_D$. Then $|D_0+x|\ge R-a_D>a_C$. Substituting $w=-(z_j-c_C)/(z-c_C)$ into the branch-normalized series from step 1.1 and summing the finite source set gives $M_0(C)L_{CD}(z-c_C)-\sum_{n\ge1}M_n(C)/[n(z-c_C)^n]$. The branch is $L_{CD}$ because both $z-c_C$ and $z-z_j$ lie in its disk and the difference of their logarithms is the series that vanishes at $z_j=c_C$. The convergence is absolute because $|z_j-c_C|/|z-c_C|<1$.

For a far pair put $D=c_D-c_C$, $x=z-c_D$ and $y=z_j-c_C$. By [F1], $|x-y|\le|x|+|y|<R=|D|$. The branch-normalized logarithm therefore has expansion $L_{CD}(D+x-y)=L_{CD}(D)+\sum_{m\ge1}(-1)^{m+1}(x-y)^m/(mD^m)$.

Expand $(x-y)^m$ by the binomial theorem and set $m=n+k$. For $n\ge1,k\ge0$, the coefficient of $x^ky^n$ is $(-1)^{k+1}\binom{n+k-1}{k}/(nD^{n+k})$, since $\binom{n+k}{k}/(n+k)=\binom{n+k-1}{k}/n$. The terms with $n=0$ are $M_0L_{CD}(D)$ for $k=0$ and $(-1)^{k+1}M_0/(kD^k)$ for $k\ge1$; the terms with $k=0,n\ge1$ are $-M_n/(nD^n)$. Summing $y^n$ over sources replaces it by $M_n$, and retaining $0\le n,k\le p$ yields precisely the M2L formulas in [F2].

Substitution of a target point into the re-centered degree-$p$ polynomial is exactly L2P, and termwise differentiation gives its derivative formula. These are finite polynomial identities and require no additional convergence assumption.

Let $N\ge0$, $I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, source positions $z_j\in\mathbb C$ and charges $q_j\in\mathbb C$ for $j\in I$, and target positions equal to the same labelled positions. A root square is a closed square of side $s_0>0$ containing every source position. Its cells are the dyadic subsquares obtained by repeatedly bisecting each side. At each split use half-open child squares, with the outer top and right edges included in the last child, so every point belongs to exactly one child. A **finite quadtree** is a finite rooted tree of such cells in which each internal cell has its four geometric children and each leaf contains at most $s$ labels for a fixed integer $s\ge1$. Empty children are retained as geometric cells but are skipped in source and target lists. For a cell $C$, write $c_C$ for its center, $s_C$ for its side length, $I_C=\{j:z_j\in C\}$, and $a_C=s_C/\sqrt2$ for the radius of its circumscribed disk.

A cell pair $(C,D)$ is **source-separated from target-separated** when $R_{CD}:=|c_D-c_C|>a_C+a_D$; $C$ is the source cell and $D$ the target cell. For every such pair fix an analytic logarithm $L_{CD}$ on the open disk $\{w:|w-(c_D-c_C)|<R_{CD}\}$. This disk excludes zero and contains all differences $z_i-z_j$ with $i\in I_D$, $j\in I_C$. For each direct near particle pair $(j,i)$ fix one value $L_{ji}$ of the logarithm of $z_i-z_j$, when this difference is nonzero. Once the recursive rule below terminates, for a collision-free configuration define the exact target potential and its complex derivative using the resulting lists as follows:
Here $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal N$ denote the far and direct near lists produced by that rule.
$$u_i:=\sum_{(j,i)\in\mathcal N}q_jL_{ji}+\sum_{\substack{(C,D)\in\mathcal F\\ i\in I_D}}\ \sum_{j\in I_C}q_jL_{CD}(z_i-z_j),\qquad g_i:=\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{q_j}{z_i-z_j}.$$
Thus each ordered source-target pair contributes its source charge times the fixed direct-near branch value or the fixed far-cell branch value prescribed by its list entry. The complex derivative is independent of the chosen logarithm values.

The **recursive interaction decomposition** of an ordered pair of nonempty cells $(C,D)$ is defined as follows. If $C=D$ is a leaf, record as direct near pairs all $(j,i)\in I_C\times I_D$ with $j\ne i$. If $C=D$ is internal, replace $(C,D)$ by all ordered pairs $(E,F)$ of its nonempty children. If $C\ne D$ and $R_{CD}>a_C+a_D$, record the far cell pair $(C,D)$. If both cells are leaves and the pair is not separated, record all direct near particle pairs $(j,i)\in I_C\times I_D$ with $j\ne i$. In every other case, if exactly one cell is nonleaf, split that cell; if both are nonleaf, split the one of larger side length, breaking a tie by splitting the source cell. Replace the pair by the child pairs having nonempty source and target sets. For $N\ge1$, start at the root pair; for $N=0$, make no recursive calls and set both lists to empty. The resulting lists are the **far interaction list** $\mathcal F$ and the **direct near-pair list** $\mathcal N$. Their termination and exact pair-partition property are mathematical assertions, proved separately.

For a far pair $(C,D)$ put $\rho_{CD}=(a_C+a_D)/R_{CD}<1$ and $Q_C=\sum_{j\in I_C}|q_j|$. Two leaves are adjacent when their closed squares meet. A tree is **2:1 level-restricted** when any adjacent leaves have depths differing by at most one. It is **linear-size level-restricted for this decomposition** when it is 2:1 level-restricted and there are fixed constants $C_T,C_V$ such that its number $T$ of nonempty cells and the number $V$ of recursive cell-pair inspections satisfy $T\le C_T\max(1,N)$ and $V\le C_V\max(1,N)$. A list is **bounded** when there are fixed constants $C_F,C_N$ with $|\mathcal F|\le C_F T$ and $|\mathcal N|\le C_N\max(1,N)$. The work theorem uses these explicit counts; 2:1 balance alone is not asserted to supply them.

Use the data, quadtree and interaction decomposition of [[def-finite-planar-quadtree-fmm-pair-lists]]. Fix an expansion order $p\ge1$. If two different labels have the same position, return status `collision` before evaluating any singular interaction: the requested potential is undefined. Otherwise take as input a finite quadtree from the definition, together with its point-to-cell membership arrays and leaf threshold $s$. For $N=0$ return empty outputs. For $N\ge1$, construct $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal N$ by the recursive decomposition in the definition. The tree and point-to-cell membership are preprocessing inputs; their construction is not part of the arithmetic passes below.

Using the supplied membership data, make a root-first list of nonempty cells: at each nonempty internal cell inspect its four children and recurse only into children $E$ with $I_E\ne\varnothing$; never descend into an empty subtree. Use the reverse list order for the bottom-up pass and the root-first order for the top-down pass. Use exact complex arithmetic throughout. For each nonempty leaf $C$ form the particle-to-multipole (P2M) moments
$$M_n(C)=\sum_{j\in I_C}q_j(z_j-c_C)^n,\qquad 0\le n\le p.$$
For the upward multipole-to-multipole (M2M) pass, process nonempty internal cells bottom-up. For each such parent $C$ and each $0\le n\le p$, form its moments from its nonempty children by
$$M_n(C)=\sum_{\substack{E\text{ child of }C\\ I_E\ne\varnothing}}\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr(c_E-c_C)^{n-r}M_r(E).$$
An empty child has zero moments and is skipped. Thus the upward pass visits only parent-child edges whose two cells are nonempty.

Initialize the local coefficient vector of every nonempty cell to zero before processing any far pair. For each far pair $(C,D)$ set $\delta=c_D-c_C$, $R=|\delta|$, choose the fixed logarithm $L_{CD}$, and add to the target cell $D$'s local coefficients the multipole-to-local (M2L) coefficients
$$L_0(D)\mathrel{+}=M_0(C)L_{CD}(\delta)-\sum_{n=1}^p\frac{M_n(C)}{n\delta^n},$$
$$L_k(D)\mathrel{+}=(-1)^{k+1}\left(\frac{M_0(C)}{k\delta^k}+\sum_{n=1}^p\binom{n+k-1}{k}\frac{M_n(C)}{n\delta^{n+k}}\right),\quad 1\le k\le p.$$
After all M2L additions, perform a top-down downward local-to-local (L2L) pass over parent-child edges whose two cells are nonempty. For each parent $D$ and each nonempty child $E$, add
$$L_j(E)\mathrel{+}=\sum_{k=j}^p\binom kj L_k(D)(c_E-c_D)^{k-j},\qquad 0\le j\le p.$$
For a target $i$ in leaf $D$, return the far potential $\sum_{k=0}^pL_k(D)(z_i-c_D)^k$ and far derivative $\sum_{k=1}^p kL_k(D)(z_i-c_D)^{k-1}$. Add the exact direct near contributions $q_jL_{ji}$ and $q_j/(z_i-z_j)$, respectively, for $(j,i)\in\mathcal N$. Denote the resulting potential and derivative approximations by $\widetilde u_i$ and $\widetilde g_i$, respectively. The derivative output differentiates the truncated local polynomial and adds the exact near derivatives; its value is independent of logarithm branches.

Let $N\ge1$ and $p\ge1$. Suppose the finite quadtree and recursive interaction decomposition supplied to [[alg-planar-laplace-fmm-fixed-order]] are linear-size level-restricted and have bounded lists in the exact sense of [[def-finite-planar-quadtree-fmm-pair-lists]]: $T,V\le C\,N$, $K:=|\mathcal F|\le C\,T$, and $J:=|\mathcal N|\le C\,N$ for a constant $C$ independent of $N,p$. Counting each complex addition, multiplication, division by a nonzero number, coefficient copy, cell-pair inspection, and evaluation of a fixed logarithm branch at one argument as one operation, the FMM passes and direct near evaluation use at most
$$C_0\bigl(N(p+1)+(T+K)(p+1)^2+V+J\bigr)$$
operations for an absolute implementation constant $C_0$. Hence the total counted work is $O(N(p+1)^2)$, and therefore $O(Np^2)$ for $p\ge1$. The input quadtree construction and point-to-cell preprocessing are not included; a highly clustered input must report its actual tree depth, node count, and list/traversal counts before a linear-in-$N$ conclusion is made.

derivations.claim: At depth $h$ the cell along the corner path containing $0$ has side length $2^{-h}$. For every $h<M$, $2^{-M}<2^{-h}$, so both $0$ and $2^{-M}$ lie in that same cell; at the next split the second point is on the midpoint boundary and is assigned to the upper child, while $0$ is assigned to the lower child. Therefore the tree has a nonempty path through depth $M$ and at least $M+1$ nonempty cells, although $N=2$.

With fixed $p=1$, $Np^2=2$ is constant as $M$ varies, whereas [F2] makes the passes visit at least the $M$ nonempty parent-child edges on the path from step 1.1. This family violates the uniform node bound $T\le C_TN$ required in [F3], so the theorem's hypotheses do not give a uniform $O(Np^2)$ bound over arbitrarily clustered inputs.

Let $N\ge0$, $I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, source positions $z_j\in\mathbb C$ and charges $q_j\in\mathbb C$ for $j\in I$, and target positions equal to the same labelled positions. A root square is a closed square of side $s_0>0$ containing every source position. Its cells are the dyadic subsquares obtained by repeatedly bisecting each side. At each split use half-open child squares, with the outer top and right edges included in the last child, so every point belongs to exactly one child. A **finite quadtree** is a finite rooted tree of such cells in which each internal cell has its four geometric children and each leaf contains at most $s$ labels for a fixed integer $s\ge1$. Empty children are retained as geometric cells but are skipped in source and target lists. For a cell $C$, write $c_C$ for its center, $s_C$ for its side length, $I_C=\{j:z_j\in C\}$, and $a_C=s_C/\sqrt2$ for the radius of its circumscribed disk.

A cell pair $(C,D)$ is **source-separated from target-separated** when $R_{CD}:=|c_D-c_C|>a_C+a_D$; $C$ is the source cell and $D$ the target cell. For every such pair fix an analytic logarithm $L_{CD}$ on the open disk $\{w:|w-(c_D-c_C)|<R_{CD}\}$. This disk excludes zero and contains all differences $z_i-z_j$ with $i\in I_D$, $j\in I_C$. For each direct near particle pair $(j,i)$ fix one value $L_{ji}$ of the logarithm of $z_i-z_j$, when this difference is nonzero. Once the recursive rule below terminates, for a collision-free configuration define the exact target potential and its complex derivative using the resulting lists as follows:
Here $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal N$ denote the far and direct near lists produced by that rule.
$$u_i:=\sum_{(j,i)\in\mathcal N}q_jL_{ji}+\sum_{\substack{(C,D)\in\mathcal F\\ i\in I_D}}\ \sum_{j\in I_C}q_jL_{CD}(z_i-z_j),\qquad g_i:=\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{q_j}{z_i-z_j}.$$
Thus each ordered source-target pair contributes its source charge times the fixed direct-near branch value or the fixed far-cell branch value prescribed by its list entry. The complex derivative is independent of the chosen logarithm values.

The **recursive interaction decomposition** of an ordered pair of nonempty cells $(C,D)$ is defined as follows. If $C=D$ is a leaf, record as direct near pairs all $(j,i)\in I_C\times I_D$ with $j\ne i$. If $C=D$ is internal, replace $(C,D)$ by all ordered pairs $(E,F)$ of its nonempty children. If $C\ne D$ and $R_{CD}>a_C+a_D$, record the far cell pair $(C,D)$. If both cells are leaves and the pair is not separated, record all direct near particle pairs $(j,i)\in I_C\times I_D$ with $j\ne i$. In every other case, if exactly one cell is nonleaf, split that cell; if both are nonleaf, split the one of larger side length, breaking a tie by splitting the source cell. Replace the pair by the child pairs having nonempty source and target sets. For $N\ge1$, start at the root pair; for $N=0$, make no recursive calls and set both lists to empty. The resulting lists are the **far interaction list** $\mathcal F$ and the **direct near-pair list** $\mathcal N$. Their termination and exact pair-partition property are mathematical assertions, proved separately.

For a far pair $(C,D)$ put $\rho_{CD}=(a_C+a_D)/R_{CD}<1$ and $Q_C=\sum_{j\in I_C}|q_j|$. Two leaves are adjacent when their closed squares meet. A tree is **2:1 level-restricted** when any adjacent leaves have depths differing by at most one. It is **linear-size level-restricted for this decomposition** when it is 2:1 level-restricted and there are fixed constants $C_T,C_V$ such that its number $T$ of nonempty cells and the number $V$ of recursive cell-pair inspections satisfy $T\le C_T\max(1,N)$ and $V\le C_V\max(1,N)$. A list is **bounded** when there are fixed constants $C_F,C_N$ with $|\mathcal F|\le C_F T$ and $|\mathcal N|\le C_N\max(1,N)$. The work theorem uses these explicit counts; 2:1 balance alone is not asserted to supply them.

Use the data, quadtree and interaction decomposition of [[def-finite-planar-quadtree-fmm-pair-lists]]. Fix an expansion order $p\ge1$. If two different labels have the same position, return status `collision` before evaluating any singular interaction: the requested potential is undefined. Otherwise take as input a finite quadtree from the definition, together with its point-to-cell membership arrays and leaf threshold $s$. For $N=0$ return empty outputs. For $N\ge1$, construct $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal N$ by the recursive decomposition in the definition. The tree and point-to-cell membership are preprocessing inputs; their construction is not part of the arithmetic passes below.

Using the supplied membership data, make a root-first list of nonempty cells: at each nonempty internal cell inspect its four children and recurse only into children $E$ with $I_E\ne\varnothing$; never descend into an empty subtree. Use the reverse list order for the bottom-up pass and the root-first order for the top-down pass. Use exact complex arithmetic throughout. For each nonempty leaf $C$ form the particle-to-multipole (P2M) moments
$$M_n(C)=\sum_{j\in I_C}q_j(z_j-c_C)^n,\qquad 0\le n\le p.$$
For the upward multipole-to-multipole (M2M) pass, process nonempty internal cells bottom-up. For each such parent $C$ and each $0\le n\le p$, form its moments from its nonempty children by
$$M_n(C)=\sum_{\substack{E\text{ child of }C\\ I_E\ne\varnothing}}\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr(c_E-c_C)^{n-r}M_r(E).$$
An empty child has zero moments and is skipped. Thus the upward pass visits only parent-child edges whose two cells are nonempty.

Initialize the local coefficient vector of every nonempty cell to zero before processing any far pair. For each far pair $(C,D)$ set $\delta=c_D-c_C$, $R=|\delta|$, choose the fixed logarithm $L_{CD}$, and add to the target cell $D$'s local coefficients the multipole-to-local (M2L) coefficients
$$L_0(D)\mathrel{+}=M_0(C)L_{CD}(\delta)-\sum_{n=1}^p\frac{M_n(C)}{n\delta^n},$$
$$L_k(D)\mathrel{+}=(-1)^{k+1}\left(\frac{M_0(C)}{k\delta^k}+\sum_{n=1}^p\binom{n+k-1}{k}\frac{M_n(C)}{n\delta^{n+k}}\right),\quad 1\le k\le p.$$
After all M2L additions, perform a top-down downward local-to-local (L2L) pass over parent-child edges whose two cells are nonempty. For each parent $D$ and each nonempty child $E$, add
$$L_j(E)\mathrel{+}=\sum_{k=j}^p\binom kj L_k(D)(c_E-c_D)^{k-j},\qquad 0\le j\le p.$$
For a target $i$ in leaf $D$, return the far potential $\sum_{k=0}^pL_k(D)(z_i-c_D)^k$ and far derivative $\sum_{k=1}^p kL_k(D)(z_i-c_D)^{k-1}$. Add the exact direct near contributions $q_jL_{ji}$ and $q_j/(z_i-z_j)$, respectively, for $(j,i)\in\mathcal N$. Denote the resulting potential and derivative approximations by $\widetilde u_i$ and $\widetilde g_i$, respectively. The derivative output differentiates the truncated local polynomial and adds the exact near derivatives; its value is independent of logarithm branches.

Assume the collision-free exact-arithmetic branch of [[alg-planar-laplace-fmm-fixed-order]] with order $p\ge1$. For each target $i$ in leaf $D_i$, let $\mathcal F_i=\{(C,D)\in\mathcal F:i\in I_D\}$ be its far cell interactions. For $(C,D)\in\mathcal F_i$ put $R_{CD}=|c_D-c_C|$, $\rho_{CD}=(a_C+a_D)/R_{CD}<1$, and $Q_C=\sum_{j\in I_C}|q_j|$. If $u_i$ is the exact fixed-branch logarithmic potential and $\widetilde u_i$ the algorithm output, then
$$|u_i-\widetilde u_i|\le\sum_{(C,D)\in\mathcal F_i}\frac{Q_C\rho_{CD}^{p+1}}{(p+1)(1-\rho_{CD})}.$$
If $g_i=\sum_{j\ne i}q_j/(z_i-z_j)$ and $\widetilde g_i$ is the algorithm's complex derivative output, then
$$|g_i-\widetilde g_i|\le\sum_{(C,D)\in\mathcal F_i}\frac{Q_C}{R_{CD}}\frac{\rho_{CD}^{p}}{1-\rho_{CD}}.$$
Near interactions are exact. The second estimate is branch-independent; no floating-point rounding error is included.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice for the weak-derivative uniqueness interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$1\le p\le\infty$. For either real or complex scalars, the displayed
$W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ formula from
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] is independent of the representatives
of its Sobolev and derivative classes and defines a norm: it is finite,
absolutely homogeneous, subadditive, and zero exactly on the zero $L^p$ class.
This holds at $p=1$ and $p=\infty$, and when $k=0$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the only class is zero and the formula is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Suppose
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact
set $K_0\subset\Omega$. Let $E_0u$ denote the extension of a representative of
$u$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$, and for $|\alpha|\le k$ let
$E_0(D^\alpha u)$ denote the extension by zero of the corresponding
derivative representative. Then
$$E_0u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad D^\alpha(E_0u)=E_0(D^\alpha u)\quad\text{almost everywhere, }|\alpha|\le k,$$
and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0(D^\alpha u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$. The case
$k=0$ is included, and complex scalars are handled by the same bilinear
pairing.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Let $g$ equal the slope of $v$ on the interior of each partition interval, with arbitrary values at the finitely many breakpoints. Both $v$ and $g$ are bounded, hence square integrable on $(0,1)$. Integration by parts on each partition interval gives $\int_0^1 v\varphi'=-\int_0^1g\varphi$ for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$: the interior endpoint terms cancel because $v$ is continuous, and the outer endpoint terms vanish because $\varphi$ is compactly supported. Thus [F2] identifies $g$ as the weak derivative, and [F1] gives $v\in W^{1,2}(0,1)$.

Put $L=\max_i |(v|_{[x_{i-1},x_i]})'|$. For $0<\delta<1/4$, let $\chi_\delta$ be zero on $[0,\delta]\cup[1-\delta,1]$, linear from zero to one on $[\delta,2\delta]$, equal to one on $[2\delta,1-2\delta]$, and linear from one to zero on $[1-2\delta,1-\delta]$. Then $v_\delta=\chi_\delta v$ is continuous and piecewise quadratic, with compact support in $[\delta,1-\delta]$. Its piecewise derivative is bounded; integration by parts on its finitely many pieces cancels interior boundary terms by continuity, as in step 1.1, so $v_\delta\in W^{1,2}(0,1)$. Since $|v(x)|\le L\min(x,1-x)$, its difference from $v$ is supported on strips of total length at most $4\delta$; there $|v|\le2L\delta$, $|v'|\le L$, and $|\chi_\delta'|\le1/\delta$. The product rule therefore gives $\|v-v_\delta\|_{L^2}^2\le16L^2\delta^3$ and $\|(v-v_\delta)'\|_{L^2}^2\le36L^2\delta$. The $W^{1,2}$ formula in [F1] then gives $v_\delta\to v$ in $W^{1,2}(0,1)$ as $\delta\to0^+$.

Extend $v_\delta$ by zero to $V_\delta\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R)$ using [F5]. Choose the [F6] bump with $r=1/2$ and $R=1$. Its integral $c$ is finite because it is bounded and supported in $(-1,1)$, and $c\ge1$ because it equals $1$ on an interval of length $1$. Normalize it by $c$ and take its mollifier family from [F7]. The convolution $V_\delta*\rho_\varepsilon$ is smooth by [F10]. Differentiating under the integral and integrating by parts on the finitely many polynomial pieces of $V_\delta$ gives $(V_\delta*\rho_\varepsilon)'=V_\delta'*\rho_\varepsilon$: interior boundary terms cancel by continuity and outer terms vanish by compact support. By [F8]–[F9], the function and its derivative converge in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ to $V_\delta$ and $V_\delta'$ as $\varepsilon\to0^+$. The normalized bump has support in $[-1,1]$, so $0<\varepsilon<\delta$ places the convolution support inside $(0,1)$ and it belongs to $C_c^\infty(0,1)$.

Given $\eta>0$, choose $\delta$ so that step 2.1 gives $\|v-v_\delta\|_{W^{1,2}}<\eta/2$, and then choose sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ in step 3.1 so that $\|v_\delta-(V_\delta*\rho_\varepsilon)|_{(0,1)}\|_{W^{1,2}}<\eta/2$. The triangle inequality [F4] gives a $C_c^\infty(0,1)$ approximation to $v$ within $\eta$. Since $\eta$ was arbitrary, [F3] yields $v\in H^1_0(0,1)$.

Work over the real field with standard coordinate inner products. Let
$A_h\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive definite (equivalently,
positive definite in the Cholesky convention of
[[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]) and let
$P\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}$ have full column rank, where $1\le m\le n$.
The map $P$ sends coarse-grid coordinate vectors to fine-grid coordinate
vectors; its Euclidean adjoint is the transpose $P^{\mathsf T}$ by
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]]. Define the **Galerkin
coarse matrix**

$$A_H:=P^{\mathsf T}A_hP.$$

Whenever $A_H$ is invertible, define the **exact Galerkin coarse-correction
error map**

$$C:=I_n-PA_H^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}A_h.$$

This definition is conditional on invertibility of $A_H$. The next theorem
proves that condition from positive definiteness of $A_h$ and full column rank
of $P$. The formula is in exact real arithmetic; a rediscretized operator is
not identified with $A_H$ unless equality is separately shown.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be Hermitian positive definite, let $b\in\mathbb C^n$,
and let $\phi$ be the quadratic energy from
[[def-quadratic-energy-of-a-hermitian-positive-definite-linear-system]]. Then
the system $Ax=b$ has a unique solution $x_*$, and for every $x\in\mathbb C^n$
one has

$$\phi(x)-\phi(x_*)=\tfrac12\|x-x_*\|_A^2.$$

In particular, $x_*$ is the unique minimizer of $\phi$.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be Hermitian positive definite in the sense of
[[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]. For vectors
$u,v\in\mathbb C^n$, define the **energy inner product**

$$\langle u,v\rangle_A:=\langle Au,v\rangle,$$

where $\langle \cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the standard coordinate inner product of
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Because $A$ is Hermitian positive
definite, this is an inner product on $\mathbb C^n$, and its induced norm

$$\|u\|_A:=\sqrt{\langle u,u\rangle_A}$$

is the **energy norm** of $u$.

Equivalently, if $A=LL^*$ is the Cholesky factorization from
[[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]], then
$\langle u,v\rangle_A=\langle L^*u,L^*v\rangle$ and
$\|u\|_A=\|L^*u\|_2$.

For matrices of the appropriate shapes and a scalar $\lambda$,

$$(A+B)^{\mathsf T}=A^{\mathsf T}+B^{\mathsf T},\qquad (\lambda A)^{\mathsf T}=\lambda A^{\mathsf T},\qquad (A^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}=A,$$

and

$$(AB)^{\mathsf T}=B^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}.$$

Thus transpose is linear and involutive and reverses products.

derivations.claim: For every nonzero $q\in\mathbb R^m$, full column rank gives $Pq\ne0$, so $q^{\mathsf T}A_Hq=(Pq)^{\mathsf T}A_h(Pq)>0$. Also $A_H^{\mathsf T}=P^{\mathsf T}A_h^{\mathsf T}P=A_H$ by [F4]. Thus $A_H$ is symmetric positive definite and [F2] makes it invertible; [F1] therefore defines $C$.

From $P^{\mathsf T}A_hP=A_H$, direct multiplication gives $CP=P-PA_H^{-1}A_H=0$ and $P^{\mathsf T}A_hC=P^{\mathsf T}A_h-A_HA_H^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}A_h=0$. Moreover, $$C^2=I_n-2PA_H^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}A_h+PA_H^{-1}(P^{\mathsf T}A_hP)A_H^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}A_h=C.$$

Transposing $A_HA_H^{-1}=I=A_H^{-1}A_H$ and using [F4] shows that $(A_H^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$ is an inverse of $A_H^{\mathsf T}=A_H$. If $B$ and $D$ are two-sided inverses of $A_H$, then $B=B(A_HD)=(BA_H)D=D$, so the inverse is unique and $(A_H^{-1})^{\mathsf T}=A_H^{-1}$. Thus [F4] yields $C^{\mathsf T}A_h=A_h-A_hPA_H^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}A_h=A_hC$, so $C$ is self-adjoint in [F3]. Also $P^{\mathsf T}A_hC=0$ says $\operatorname{Ran}(C)\subseteq\operatorname{Ran}(P)^{\perp_{A_h}}$. If $w$ is in that complement, then $P^{\mathsf T}A_hw=0$, so [F1] gives $Cw=w$; therefore every such $w$ is in $\operatorname{Ran}(C)$ and the ranges are equal.
The identities in step 2.1 and the range equality in step 3.1 prove all stated projection properties.

This is a finite aggregation-based algebraic multigrid **setup** procedure; it
constructs a hierarchy and does not claim that any cycle converges. All
arithmetic and comparisons below are exact. An admissible input consists of an
integer $n_0\ge1$, a real symmetric positive-definite matrix
$A_0=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n_0\times n_0}$ whose off-diagonal
entries satisfy $a_{ij}\le0$, a real threshold $0<\theta<1$, a coarse-size
threshold $n_{\min}\ge1$, and a real level cap $L\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}$. A
matrix with these sign and definiteness conditions is the matrix class used
here. The terms
**strength graph**, **aggregate**, **prolongation**, and **Galerkin hierarchy**
are defined by the steps below.

Initialize $\ell=0$ once and retain $A_0$ in the output. Then execute the
following level steps.

1. Set $n_\ell=\dim A_\ell$. If
   $n_\ell\le n_{\min}$, return status `coarse-reached`.
2. If $\ell+1>L$ before the next aggregation attempt, return status
   `level-cap`.
3. On vertices $1,\ldots,n_\ell$, place an undirected edge $\{i,j\}$ for
   $i\ne j$ exactly when $a_{ij}^{(\ell)}<0$ and at least one of
   $$-a_{ij}^{(\ell)}\ge\theta\max_{k\ne i}(-a_{ik}^{(\ell)}),\qquad -a_{ij}^{(\ell)}\ge\theta\max_{k\ne j}(-a_{jk}^{(\ell)})$$
   holds. This finite graph is the strength graph at level $\ell$.
4. Let $U=\{1,\ldots,n_\ell\}$ and start with no aggregates. While $U\ne\varnothing$, let $i$ be the smallest element of $U$, create one aggregate
   $$C_r=\{i\}\cup\bigl(N(i)\cap U\bigr),$$
   where $N(i)$ is its strength-graph neighbour set, then remove every element of $C_r$ from $U$. This produces an ordered family of aggregates.
5. Let $n_{\ell+1}$ be the number of aggregates. If $n_{\ell+1}\ge n_\ell$, return status `coarsening-stalled` with the hierarchy through level $\ell$. Otherwise form the indicator prolongation
   $$(P_\ell)_{ir}=1\text{ if }i\in C_r,\qquad (P_\ell)_{ir}=0\text{ otherwise},$$
   form the Galerkin coarse matrix $A_{\ell+1}=P_\ell^{\mathsf T}A_\ell P_\ell$, append $P_\ell,A_{\ell+1}$, replace $\ell$ by $\ell+1$, and return to step 1.

The result contains all completed matrices and prolongations and exactly one
status: `coarse-reached`, `level-cap`, or `coarsening-stalled`. Reaching any
status is not a convergence or quality certificate.

$$C^2=C,\qquad CP=0,\qquad P^{\mathsf T}A_hC=0,\qquad C^{\mathsf T}A_h=A_hC.$$

Consequently $\operatorname{Ran}(C)=\operatorname{Ran}(P)^{\perp_{A_h}}$;
$C$ is the orthogonal projector onto that complement in the energy inner
product $\langle x,y\rangle_{A_h}:=x^{\mathsf T}A_hy$.

Let $n\ge 1$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$; over $\mathbb R$ the same definition uses transpose
instead of conjugate transpose.

The matrix $A$ is **Hermitian positive definite** if $A=A^*$ and

where $L$ is lower triangular and every diagonal entry of $L$ is a positive real

The Hermitian terminology matches

derivations.claim: At any aggregation pass the unassigned set $U$ is finite and nonempty. The selected smallest vertex $i$ belongs to the new aggregate, so at least one vertex is removed. No previously removed vertex can reappear because every neighbour is intersected with $U$. Thus the aggregates are pairwise disjoint and, when the finite loop ends at $U=\varnothing$, cover all current indices. Each aggregate is nonempty. If $Pz=0$, choose any row index in aggregate $r$; its row has a single $1$ in column $r$, so that component of $Pz$ is $z_r=0$. This holds for every $r$, hence $P$ has full column rank.

By [F2] and step 1.1, $A_{\ell+1}=P_\ell^{\mathsf T}A_\ell P_\ell$ is SPD. For distinct aggregate columns $r\ne s$, disjointness gives $$(A_{\ell+1})_{rs}=\sum_{i\in C_r}\sum_{j\in C_s}a_{ij}^{(\ell)}\le0,$$ since $i\ne j$ in every summand and the fine matrix has nonpositive off-diagonal entries. Symmetry follows from symmetry of $A_\ell$. Induction over successful levels proves the same matrix class at each returned level.

Each aggregation pass is finite by step 1.1. A pass is attempted only when $\ell+1\le L$, so the number of attempts is an integer at most $\lfloor L\rfloor$. At each outer iteration, step 1 returns `coarse-reached` when $n_\ell\le n_{\min}$; otherwise the cap test in [F1] returns `level-cap` when $\ell+1>L$. If neither branch applies, a pass is performed and either $n_{\ell+1}\ge n_\ell$ returns `coarsening-stalled`, or the procedure advances to the next level. These ordered branches exhaust the procedure, so it terminates with exactly one listed status.
The preceding steps establish the partition, rank, matrix-class and status claims. No step asserts a contraction factor.

Fix a finite Galerkin hierarchy of real SPD matrices
$A_j\in\mathbb R^{n_j\times n_j}$, $0\le j\le J$, with $n_j\ge1$, and
full-column-rank prolongations $P_j\in\mathbb R^{n_j\times n_{j-1}}$
satisfying $A_{j-1}=P_j^{\mathsf T}A_jP_j$ for $1\le j\le J$. Choose
nonnegative integer sweep counts $\nu_1,\nu_2$, a positive integer cycle
count $\gamma$, and matrices $K_j^{\mathrm{pre}},K_j^{\mathrm{post}}\in
\mathbb R^{n_j\times n_j}$ for $1\le j\le J$; $^{\mathsf T}$ denotes the
transpose of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]. An invocation
$\operatorname{Cycle}(j,x,b)$ takes $x,b\in\mathbb R^{n_j}$ and returns the
vector specified by these instructions for the system $A_jz=b$:

1. If $j=0$, return the exact solution $A_0^{-1}b$.
2. Starting from $x$, perform $\nu_1$ pre-sweeps
   $x\leftarrow x+K_j^{\mathrm{pre}}(b-A_jx)$ and set $r=b-A_jx$.
3. Set $e=0$. For $t=1,\ldots,\gamma$, replace $e$ by the recursive iterate
   $$e\leftarrow\operatorname{Cycle}(j-1,e,P_j^{\mathsf T}r).$$
4. Correct $x\leftarrow x+P_je$, then perform $\nu_2$ post-sweeps
   $x\leftarrow x+K_j^{\mathrm{post}}(b-A_jx)$; return $x$.

The V-cycle is $\gamma=1$ and the W-cycle is $\gamma=2$. The definition fixes
exact arithmetic and specifies an iterate; it makes no accuracy or convergence
claim. Setup cost, floating-point error, and termination are separate claims.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be Hermitian positive definite, let $b\in\mathbb C^n$,
and let $\phi$ be the quadratic energy from
[[def-quadratic-energy-of-a-hermitian-positive-definite-linear-system]]. Then
the system $Ax=b$ has a unique solution $x_*$, and for every $x\in\mathbb C^n$
one has

$$\phi(x)-\phi(x_*)=\tfrac12\|x-x_*\|_A^2.$$

In particular, $x_*$ is the unique minimizer of $\phi$.

citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $L$ and its form $a$ be as in [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. **Homogeneous problem.** Given $F\in H^{-1}(\Omega)$ ([[def-h-minus-one-as-the-dual-of-h-one-zero]]), a **weak solution** of $Lu=F$ with zero boundary values is a class $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1_0(\Omega).$$ **Inhomogeneous problem.** Additionally assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for the trace supplier, and let $n\ge2$ and $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]), let $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega):=W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$ in the boundary scale of [[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]] and let $T$ be the trace operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. A weak solution with boundary data $g$ is a class $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $Tu=g$ and $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. The defining identities are identities between functionals on the $H^1_0$ classes, so they are independent of the chosen almost-everywhere representatives of $u$, of the coefficients and of the data ([[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); the boundary condition is imposed through the trace of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], never by pointwise evaluation. The Dirichlet condition is imposed by $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ in the homogeneous problem and by $Tu=g$ in the inhomogeneous problem; testing against $v\in H^1_0$ expresses the weak equation and does not by itself impose boundary data; the integrals are the ones proved absolutely convergent in [[lem-elliptic-form-is-well-defined-and-bounded]].

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Let $a^{ij},b^i,c:\Omega\to\mathbb K$, $i,j=1,\dots,n$, be measurable ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]) and essentially bounded ([[def-l-infinity-on-a-measure-space]], [[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]), with bounds $$|a^{ij}|\le M_a,\quad |b^i|\le M_b,\quad |c|\le M_c\quad\text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$ and suppose the **uniform ellipticity** condition holds: there is $\theta>0$ with $$\operatorname{Re}\Big(\sum_{i,j=1}^n a^{ij}(x)\xi_j\overline{\xi_i}\Big)\ge\theta|\xi|^2\qquad\text{for a.e. }x\in\Omega\text{ and all }\xi\in\mathbb C^n .$$ The associated **divergence-form expression** is $$Lu:=-D_i(a^{ij}D_ju)+b^iD_iu+cu$$ (Einstein summation over $i,j$), and the associated sesquilinear form on $H^1(\Omega)$ is $$a(u,v):=\int_\Omega\Big(a^{ij}D_ju\overline{D_iv}+b^iD_iu\overline{v}+cu\overline{v}\Big)dx .$$ The form is linear in $u$ and conjugate-linear in $v$, in the convention of [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]; the classical Dirichlet problem consists of $Lu=f$ in $\Omega$ with prescribed boundary values. The operator is determined by the coefficient functions only a.e., and all later statements about $a$ are statements about those classes. Where the domain and boundary data demand it ([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]], [[cor-inhomogeneous-weak-dirichlet-problem-by-a-trace-lifting]]) the domain is additionally a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]). The convention is the complex sesquilinear one with conjugation in the second slot, as the plan's convention audit directs; the real case is the same with conjugation read as the identity.

positive definite in the Cholesky convention of

$P\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}$ have full column rank, where $1\le m\le n$.
The map $P$ sends coarse-grid coordinate vectors to fine-grid coordinate
vectors; its Euclidean adjoint is the transpose $P^{\mathsf T}$ by
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]]. Define the **Galerkin
coarse matrix**

$$A_H:=P^{\mathsf T}A_hP.$$

Whenever $A_H$ is invertible, define the **exact Galerkin coarse-correction
error map**

$$C:=I_n-PA_H^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}A_h.$$

This definition is conditional on invertibility of $A_H$. The next theorem
proves that condition from positive definiteness of $A_h$ and full column rank

not identified with $A_H$ unless equality is separately shown.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $v:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and affine
on each interval of a finite partition $0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N=1$, with
$v(0)=v(1)=0$. Then the Sobolev class of $v$ belongs to
$H^1_0(0,1)=W^{1,2}_0((0,1);\mathbb R)$, where $W^{1,2}_0$ is the norm
closure of $C_c^\infty(0,1)$ in $W^{1,2}(0,1)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

For any finite Galerkin hierarchy and parameters admitted by
[[alg-finite-galerkin-v-cycle]], every invocation of the recursive procedure
terminates. For the work estimate, fix an integer $d\ge1$ and let $L\ge0$
range over integers. Set $q=2^d$, and let the hierarchy have sizes $N_j=q^j$
for $0\le j\le L$, so its finest size is $N=N_L=q^L$ and each coarsening step
divides the size by the fixed factor $q$.
Suppose each level with $N_j$ unknowns has $cN_j$ arithmetic work outside
recursion for a fixed $c>0$, the base solve at $N_0=1$ has fixed bounded
positive cost, and each cycle makes a fixed positive integer $\gamma$
recursive calls. With $d,c,\gamma$ fixed, the work recurrence

$$T(N)=cN+\gamma T(N/q)$$

has order $\Theta(N)$ when $\gamma<q$, $\Theta(N\log N)$ when $\gamma=q$,
and $\Theta(N^{\log_q\gamma})$ when $\gamma>q$, as $L\to\infty$. These are
arithmetic-work bounds conditional on the stated uniform per-level cost and
coarsening assumptions. They do not imply convergence or include setup cost.

derivations.claim: For the V-cycle, $T_V(N)=cN+T_V(N/4)$. Repeated substitution gives $$T_V(N)=cN\sum_{r=0}^{L-1}4^{-r}+T_V(1).$$ The sum lies between $1$ and $4/3$, and $T_V(1)=\Theta(1)$, so $T_V(N)=\Theta(N)$. This is also the $\gamma=1<4$ case of [F1].

For the W-cycle, $T_W(N)=cN+2T_W(N/4)$, so $$T_W(N)=cN\sum_{r=0}^{L-1}2^{-r}+2^LT_W(1).$$ The sum lies between $1$ and $2$, while $2^L=\sqrt N$; consequently both terms are $O(N)$ and the first is a positive $cN$ lower bound. Hence $T_W(N)=\Theta(N)$, agreeing with [F1] because $\gamma=2<4$.

citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $L$ and its form $a$ be as in [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. **Homogeneous problem.** Given $F\in H^{-1}(\Omega)$ ([[def-h-minus-one-as-the-dual-of-h-one-zero]]), a **weak solution** of $Lu=F$ with zero boundary values is a class $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1_0(\Omega).$$ **Inhomogeneous problem.** Additionally assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for the trace supplier, and let $n\ge2$ and $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]), let $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega):=W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$ in the boundary scale of [[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]] and let $T$ be the trace operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. A weak solution with boundary data $g$ is a class $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $Tu=g$ and $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. The defining identities are identities between functionals on the $H^1_0$ classes, so they are independent of the chosen almost-everywhere representatives of $u$, of the coefficients and of the data ([[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); the boundary condition is imposed through the trace of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], never by pointwise evaluation. The Dirichlet condition is imposed by $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ in the homogeneous problem and by $Tu=g$ in the inhomogeneous problem; testing against $v\in H^1_0$ expresses the weak equation and does not by itself impose boundary data; the integrals are the ones proved absolutely convergent in [[lem-elliptic-form-is-well-defined-and-bounded]].

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Let $a^{ij},b^i,c:\Omega\to\mathbb K$, $i,j=1,\dots,n$, be measurable ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]) and essentially bounded ([[def-l-infinity-on-a-measure-space]], [[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]), with bounds $$|a^{ij}|\le M_a,\quad |b^i|\le M_b,\quad |c|\le M_c\quad\text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$ and suppose the **uniform ellipticity** condition holds: there is $\theta>0$ with $$\operatorname{Re}\Big(\sum_{i,j=1}^n a^{ij}(x)\xi_j\overline{\xi_i}\Big)\ge\theta|\xi|^2\qquad\text{for a.e. }x\in\Omega\text{ and all }\xi\in\mathbb C^n .$$ The associated **divergence-form expression** is $$Lu:=-D_i(a^{ij}D_ju)+b^iD_iu+cu$$ (Einstein summation over $i,j$), and the associated sesquilinear form on $H^1(\Omega)$ is $$a(u,v):=\int_\Omega\Big(a^{ij}D_ju\overline{D_iv}+b^iD_iu\overline{v}+cu\overline{v}\Big)dx .$$ The form is linear in $u$ and conjugate-linear in $v$, in the convention of [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]; the classical Dirichlet problem consists of $Lu=f$ in $\Omega$ with prescribed boundary values. The operator is determined by the coefficient functions only a.e., and all later statements about $a$ are statements about those classes. Where the domain and boundary data demand it ([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]], [[cor-inhomogeneous-weak-dirichlet-problem-by-a-trace-lifting]]) the domain is additionally a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]). The convention is the complex sesquilinear one with conjugation in the second slot, as the plan's convention audit directs; the real case is the same with conjugation read as the identity.

Work over the real field with standard coordinate inner products. Let
$A_h\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive definite (equivalently,
positive definite in the Cholesky convention of
[[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]) and let
$P\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}$ have full column rank, where $1\le m\le n$.
The map $P$ sends coarse-grid coordinate vectors to fine-grid coordinate
vectors; its Euclidean adjoint is the transpose $P^{\mathsf T}$ by
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]]. Define the **Galerkin
coarse matrix**

$$A_H:=P^{\mathsf T}A_hP.$$

Whenever $A_H$ is invertible, define the **exact Galerkin coarse-correction
error map**

$$C:=I_n-PA_H^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}A_h.$$

This definition is conditional on invertibility of $A_H$. The next theorem
proves that condition from positive definiteness of $A_h$ and full column rank
of $P$. The formula is in exact real arithmetic; a rediscretized operator is
not identified with $A_H$ unless equality is separately shown.

Let $A_h$ be symmetric positive definite, let $C$ be the Galerkin projector
of [[thm-galerkin-coarse-correction-is-energy-orthogonal-projector]], and let
$S\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be a linear pre-smoothing error map. For the
energy inner product of [[def-energy-inner-product-and-norm-for-a-hermitian-positive-definite-matrix]],
define the **$A_h$-adjoint** of $S$ by

$$S^{*_{A_h}}:=A_h^{-1}S^{\mathsf T}A_h.$$

This is well-defined because $A_h$ is invertible. For all $x,y$,
$\langle Sx,y\rangle_{A_h}=x^{\mathsf T}S^{\mathsf T}A_hy
=\langle x,S^{*_{A_h}}y\rangle_{A_h}$, so it is the adjoint with respect to
that energy inner product. The **symmetric two-grid error map** is

$$E:=S^{*_{A_h}}CS.$$

It maps an input error through pre-smoothing $S$, exact coarse correction $C$,
and the $A_h$-adjoint post-smoother.

For the nested one-dimensional Poisson grids and prolongation of
[[lem-one-dimensional-poisson-smoothing-and-approximation]], take the
pre-smoothing error map to be $S^\nu$, with $S=I-A_h/\lambda_{\max}(A_h)$,
and take the post-smoother to be its $A_h$-adjoint. The resulting symmetric
two-grid error map satisfies

$$\|E\|_{A_h}\le\frac{2}{2\nu+1}\le\frac23<1\qquad(\nu\ge1),$$

uniformly for all even $N=2M\ge4$. This proves one concrete level-uniform
two-grid rate; it does not assert convergence of an arbitrary AMG hierarchy.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $v:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and affine
on each interval of a finite partition $0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N=1$, with
$v(0)=v(1)=0$. Then the Sobolev class of $v$ belongs to
$H^1_0(0,1)=W^{1,2}_0((0,1);\mathbb R)$, where $W^{1,2}_0$ is the norm
closure of $C_c^\infty(0,1)$ in $W^{1,2}(0,1)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space, let
$T:V\to V$ be linear, and let $\mathcal E$ be an orthonormal basis of $V$. Write

$$A=[T]_{\mathcal E}^{\mathcal E}.$$

Then:

1. $T$ is self-adjoint if and only if $A=A^*$.
2. $T$ is normal if and only if $AA^*=A^*A$.

Over $\mathbb R$, $A^*$ is just $A^{\mathsf T}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint, and let $v\in V$ be nonzero. The **Rayleigh quotient** of $v$ for
$T$ is

$$R_T(v):=\frac{\langle Tv,v\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Because $\langle v,v\rangle>0$ for nonzero $v$ in an inner product space, this
quotient is a well-defined real number.

Let $T:V\to V$ be self-adjoint on an $n$-dimensional real inner product space,
and list its eigenvalues in weakly decreasing order:

$$\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n.$$

Then for every $1\le k\le n$,

$$\lambda_k=\min_{\dim W=n-k+1}\ \max_{0\ne v\in W} R_T(v)=\max_{\dim U=k}\ \min_{0\ne v\in U} R_T(v).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

derivations.claim: Suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. By [F2], $A$ represents a self-adjoint endomorphism in the standard orthonormal basis, and [F3] identifies its Rayleigh quotient with $q_A$. Taking $k=m$ in [F4] gives $\lambda_{\min}=\min_{\dim W=1}\max_{x\in W\setminus\{0\}}q_A(x)$. On each one-dimensional $W$, homogeneity gives the same quotient for every nonzero vector, and every nonzero $x$ spans such a $W$; hence this minimum is exactly $\min_{x\ne0}q_A(x)$. By [F5], write $x=\sum_j c_ju_j$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues $\lambda_j$; then $q_A(x)=\sum_j\lambda_jc_j^2/\sum_jc_j^2$, which equals $\lambda_{\min}$ exactly when every nonzero coefficient belongs to the least-eigenvalue eigenspace.

Suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$. By [F2], $A$ represents a self-adjoint endomorphism in the standard orthonormal basis; by [F1] this endomorphism is normal, so [F6] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $u_1,\ldots,u_m$. Every eigenvalue is real because if $Au_j=\lambda_j u_j$, then $\overline{u_j^*Au_j}=u_j^*A^*u_j=u_j^*Au_j$, so $\lambda_j\|u_j\|^2$ is real and $\|u_j\|^2>0$. For $x=\sum_j c_ju_j\ne0$, the quotient is the weighted average $\sum_j\lambda_j|c_j|^2/\sum_j|c_j|^2$, so it is at least the least eigenvalue and equals it exactly when all nonzero coefficients lie in its eigenspace.

In either field, the least eigenspace is nonzero, so [F7] gives a unique orthogonal decomposition of each vector into its $E_{\min}$ and $E_{\min}^{\perp}$ parts; define $P_{\min}$ to be the first component. Uniqueness makes $P_{\min}$ linear, since sums and scalar multiples of decompositions are the corresponding decompositions. At least one $P_{\min}e_j$ is nonzero, since otherwise linearity and the fact that the standard vectors span $\mathbb F^m$ would imply $P_{\min}=0$, contradicting $E_{\min}\ne\{0\}$. The first such $j$ is uniquely determined by the fixed basis order. Normalize this projection. Over $\mathbb C$, its first nonzero coordinate $z$ is changed to $|z|>0$ by multiplication by $\overline z/|z|$; over $\mathbb R$, multiplication by $z/|z|$ makes that coordinate positive. These unit-modulus rescalings preserve the eigenvector and its Rayleigh quotient. The minimizer characterization in steps 1.1 and 1.2 proves the result.

Fix a field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, an integer $d\ge2$, and positive integers $n_1,\ldots,n_d$. A finite order-$d$ tensor of shape $(n_1,\ldots,n_d)$ is an array $A=(A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d})$ indexed by $1\le i_k\le n_k$. Its Frobenius inner product and norm are
$$ \langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{i_1=1}^{n_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{n_d}\overline{A_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}B_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}, \qquad \|A\|_F=\sqrt{\langle A,A\rangle_F}. $$
For a matrix, rank means the dimension of its column image and the Frobenius inner product is the same entrywise formula. The adjoint $M^*$ is conjugate transpose (transpose over $\mathbb R$).

For $1\le k\le d$, the mode-$k$ unfolding $A_{(k)}$ has $n_k$ rows and $\prod_{j\ne k}n_j$ columns. Its row index is $i_k$ and its column index is the remaining tuple in increasing mode order, lexicographically ordered. Its entry at that row and column is the corresponding entry of $A$. For $1\le k<d$, the cut-$k$ unfolding $A^{\langle k\rangle}$ has row tuple $(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and column tuple $(i_{k+1},\ldots,i_d)$, each lexicographically ordered. These conventions fix all reshapes used below.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from

Fix a field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, an order $d\ge2$, and positive physical dimensions $n_1,\ldots,n_d$. The finite coefficient space is the tensor-array space $\mathcal H=\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}$ with the Frobenius pairing and lexicographic index conventions of [[def-finite-tensor-arrays-and-frobenius-inner-product]]. A **normalized finite state** is an array $\psi\in\mathcal H$ with $\|\psi\|_F=1$.

An **open-boundary matrix-product state (MPS), or tensor train (TT), presentation** is a TT core list from [[def-tensor-train-cores-bond-ranks-and-canonical-gauges]] with $r_0=r_d=1$ whose contraction is $\psi$. In particular, each core has shape $r_{k-1}\times n_k\times r_k$ and the shared internal indices are summed.

$$\psi_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(A_1^{(i_1)}A_2^{(i_2)}\cdots A_d^{(i_d)}\right).$$

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

derivations.claim: Let $M\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ be any core matricization. Scan its columns in order, starting with an empty list and retaining a column exactly when it is not in the span of those already retained. At termination the retained columns are independent, and every skipped column lies in their final span; hence they span the column image of $M$ and their count is $q=\operatorname{rank}(M)$ by [F2]. If $q>0$, apply [F4] to obtain a matrix $Q$ with orthonormal columns spanning those retained columns; their Gram–Schmidt coordinates form an upper triangular $R_{11}$ with nonzero diagonal. If $q=0$, then $M=0$ and use the empty factorization.

Move the retained column indices to the front by a permutation $\Pi$. Every remaining column lies in the span of $Q$, so it equals $Q$ times its coordinate vector $Q^*$ applied to that column. Thus $M\Pi=Q[R_{11}\ R_{12}]$ for some $R_{12}$, with $Q^*Q=I_q$; equivalently $M=QB$ where $B=[R_{11}\ R_{12}]\Pi^*$. This is an exact rank-revealing thin QR factorization for every rectangular shape.

Starting at the left boundary, apply step 2.1 to each left matricization of cores $1,\ldots,s-1$. Replace the current core matricization $M$ by $Q$ and absorb $B$ into the next core. Since $M=QB$, the shared-index contraction in [F1] is unchanged; $Q^*Q=I_q$ makes the replaced core left-isometric by [F3]. Induction over the swept cores gives the required left-isometric prefix.

Starting at the right boundary, apply step 2.1 to the adjoint $M^*$ of each right matricization of cores $d,\ldots,t+1$. If $M^*\Pi=QB$, then $M=\Pi B^*Q^*$. Replace the current right matricization by $Q^*$ and absorb $\Pi B^*$ into the preceding core. The shared-index contraction in [F1] is unchanged, and $Q^*Q=I_q$ makes the replaced matricization right-isometric by [F3]. Induction gives the right-isometric suffix and preserves the represented array, while leaving cores $k<s$ untouched. If $t<d$, the final absorption into core $t$ can change the contracted center coefficients; if $t=d$, there is no right sweep.

The scan drops only columns already in the span of retained columns, so each bond dimension changes only from its former size to the exact matrix rank. If any swept matricization had rank zero, that core would be zero and the full TT contraction would be zero, contrary to the nonzero-state hypothesis; hence every reduced swept bond has positive dimension. Steps 3.1 and 3.2 establish the exact mixed canonical gauge.
