Let a finite open-boundary TT have order $d\ge2$ and be in the following mixed gauge about a one-site or two-site center window $J=[k,k+w-1]$, where $w\in\{1,2\}$: every core strictly left of $J$ is left-isometric and every core strictly right of $J$ is right-isometric. The center coefficient array has shape $r_{k-1}\times n_k\times\cdots\times n_{k+w-1}\times r_{k+w-1}$, with boundary ranks interpreted as one, and $x$ is its vectorization in the fixed lexicographic order. Hold every core outside $J$ fixed. Contracting the fixed prefix and suffix defines a linear embedding $E$ from center coefficients to the full tensor space. Then $E^*E=I$, so $\|Ex\|_F=\|x\|_2$. For every finite Hermitian Hamiltonian input $H$, the effective matrix
$$H_{\mathrm{eff}}:=E^*HE$$
is Hermitian and satisfies
$$\langle Ex,HEx\rangle_F=x^*H_{\mathrm{eff}}x.$$

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $m\ge1$, and let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}$ satisfy $A^*=A$. Define
$$q_A(x):=\frac{x^*Ax}{x^*x}\qquad(x\in\mathbb F^m\setminus\{0\}).$$
Then $q_A$ has a minimum $\lambda_{\min}$, equal to the least eigenvalue of $A$, and its minimizers are precisely the nonzero vectors in the lowest eigenspace $E_{\min}=\ker(A-\lambda_{\min}I)$. There is a deterministic choice of a unit minimizer: let $P_{\min}$ be the orthogonal projection onto $E_{\min}$, scan the standard basis $e_1,\ldots,e_m$, and take the first $j$ with $P_{\min}e_j\ne0$. Normalize $P_{\min}e_j$; over $\mathbb C$, if $z$ is its first nonzero coordinate, multiply by $\overline z/|z|$, and over $\mathbb R$ multiply by $z/|z|$.

Fix a field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, an order $d\ge2$, and positive physical dimensions $n_1,\ldots,n_d$. The finite coefficient space is the tensor-array space $\mathcal H=\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}$ with the Frobenius pairing and lexicographic index conventions of [[def-finite-tensor-arrays-and-frobenius-inner-product]]. A **normalized finite state** is an array $\psi\in\mathcal H$ with $\|\psi\|_F=1$.

An **open-boundary matrix-product state (MPS), or tensor train (TT), presentation** is a TT core list from [[def-tensor-train-cores-bond-ranks-and-canonical-gauges]] with $r_0=r_d=1$ whose contraction is $\psi$. In particular, each core has shape $r_{k-1}\times n_k\times r_k$ and the shared internal indices are summed.

A **periodic MPS presentation** consists of positive integers $r_0,\ldots,r_d$ with $r_d=r_0$ and matrices $A_k^{(i_k)}\in\mathbb F^{r_{k-1}\times r_k}$ for each $1\le i_k\le n_k$. It represents the array
$$\psi_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(A_1^{(i_1)}A_2^{(i_2)}\cdots A_d^{(i_d)}\right).$$
A finite MPS/TT state is a normalized array admitting at least one of these exact presentations; a presentation need not be unique or canonical.

A **finite Hermitian Hamiltonian input** is a linear endomorphism $H:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ whose matrix in the standard lexicographic basis satisfies $H^*=H$, where $*$ is conjugate transpose as in [[def-finite-tensor-arrays-and-frobenius-inner-product]]. This page uses only that finite-dimensional Hermitian input and makes no claim about how a physical model assembles it. For nonzero $\psi$, its Rayleigh energy is
$$\mathcal E_H(\psi)=\frac{\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle_F}{\|\psi\|_F^2};$$
for a normalized state this equals $\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle_F$.

derivations.claim: Since $E^*E=I$ by [F1], the current center state $\psi_0=Ex_0$ has norm $\|x_0\|_2=1$, and the updated state $\psi_*=Ex_*$ has norm $\|x_*\|_2=1$. Thus both are admissible normalized states under [F3].
By [F2], $x_*^*H_{\mathrm{eff}}x_*\le x_0^*H_{\mathrm{eff}}x_0$. Use the pullback identity in [F1] on both sides and then [F3] to obtain $\mathcal E_H(\psi_*)\le\mathcal E_H(\psi_0)$.

Work in exact arithmetic over a fixed field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and order $d\ge2$. The inputs are:

- a normalized finite MPS/TT state $\psi\in\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}$ together with one concrete presentation of $\psi$, either an open-boundary TT core list or periodic trace matrices; the supplied presentation must contract to $\psi$;
- a finite Hermitian Hamiltonian $H$ on that same tensor-array coefficient space;
- a positive integer sweep budget $M$;
- a window width $w\in\{1,2\}$; and
- optionally, positive integer rank caps $c_1,\ldots,c_{d-1}$.

The procedure is the following.

1. If the supplied presentation is in periodic trace form, convert it exactly to the open-boundary TT form using [[lem-na-periodic-mps-to-open-tt]]. Otherwise take the supplied open-boundary core list. Keep the resulting open-boundary core list.

2. For each of $M$ full sweeps, perform one forward pass and one backward pass. For width $w$, the windows are the $d$ single sites when $w=1$, or the $d-1$ adjacent site pairs when $w=2$. Visit them in increasing order in the forward pass and decreasing order in the backward pass.

3. Before each window update, place the TT in mixed canonical gauge about that window using the deterministic rank-revealing QR sweeps of [[lem-na-mixed-canonical-qr-gauge-preserves-state]]. Contract the fixed left and right cores to form the isometric center embedding $E$ and compute the finite effective matrix $H_{\mathrm{eff}}=E^*HE$.

4. Apply the exact ground-vector rule of [[lem-na-finite-hermitian-ground-vector-with-deterministic-tie]] to $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$. Let $x$ be the resulting unit eigenvector and replace the center coefficient vector by $x$. Record its local Rayleigh energy $x^*H_{\mathrm{eff}}x=\lambda_{\min}$ and residual $\|H_{\mathrm{eff}}x-\lambda_{\min}x\|_2$.

5. For a two-site window, reshape the updated center as a matrix with row index (left bond, first physical index) and column index (second physical index, right bond). Compute an exact compact SVD $X=U\Sigma V^*$. In a forward pass replace the first core by the reshape of $U$ and absorb $\Sigma V^*$ into the second core. In a backward pass absorb $U\Sigma$ into the first core and replace the second core by the reshape of $V^*$. Retain every positive singular direction, so this split changes no tensor entries. For a one-site window, keep that site as the center.

6. After each complete forward/backward sweep, if rank caps were supplied, apply [[alg-tensor-train-rounding]] to the current TT and record its cut tails $\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_{d-1}$ and $\tau=(\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}\delta_k^2)^{1/2}$. If $\tau<1$, normalize the rounded tensor and continue from it. If $\tau\ge1$, discard that rounded candidate, retain the last normalized unrounded tensor, and record status **rounding-skipped**. If no rank caps were supplied, do not round.

Return the final normalized TT state, the energy and local-residual records, all accepted discarded-tail records, and status **budget-complete** or **rounding-skipped** according to whether any requested rounding was skipped.

Let $\psi_0=Ex_0$ be a normalized finite MPS in mixed canonical gauge about a one-site or two-site center, with $\|x_0\|_2=1$. Let $H_{\mathrm{eff}}=E^*HE$ be its effective Hermitian matrix, and replace the center by the deterministic unit ground vector $x_* $ of $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$, giving $\psi_*=Ex_*$. Then $\psi_*$ is normalized and
$$\mathcal E_H(\psi_*)\le\mathcal E_H(\psi_0).$$
This claim is before any bond truncation.

Work in exact arithmetic over $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. The input is a valid TT core list for a tensor of order $d\ge2$ and exactly one of rank caps $c_1,\ldots,c_{d-1}\in\mathbb N_0$ or absolute tail tolerances $\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_{d-1}\in[0,\infty)$.

1. **Left orthogonalize without truncation.** For $k=1,\ldots,d-1$, reshape core $G_k$ into a matrix with rows $(\alpha_{k-1},i_k)$ and columns $\alpha_k$. Compute an exact compact SVD $M=U\Sigma V^*$, replace $G_k$ by the reshape of $U$, and absorb $\Sigma V^*$ into the next core along their common bond. Omitting zero singular directions is exact. The resulting cores $G_1,\ldots,G_{d-1}$ are left-isometric.

2. **Truncate from right to left.** For $k=d,d-1,\ldots,2$, reshape the current $G_k$ into a matrix $M_k$ with rows $\alpha_{k-1}$ and columns $(i_k,\alpha_k)$, and compute an exact compact SVD $M_k=U_k\Sigma_kV_k^*$. If its positive singular values are $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_s>0$, choose $q_{k-1}=\min(c_{k-1},s)$ for rank caps, or the least $q_{k-1}\in\{0,\ldots,s\}$ with $\sum_{j>q_{k-1}}\sigma_j^2\le\tau_{k-1}^2$ for tolerances. Record $\delta_{k-1}=(\sum_{j>q_{k-1}}\sigma_j^2)^{1/2}$. Replace $G_k$ by the reshape of the first $q_{k-1}$ rows of $V_k^*$ and absorb $U_{k,1:q}\Sigma_{k,1:q}$ into the previous core.

If $q_{k-1}=0$, the represented tensor becomes zero; set all remaining internal ranks to zero and their unperformed tails to zero. If the input represents zero, return the all-zero-rank representation and zero tails immediately. The output is the rounded core list and all recorded cut tails. No finite-precision error guarantee is part of this exact-arithmetic procedure.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}$, $d\ge2$, and let $A^{\langle k\rangle}$ denote its cut-$k$ unfolding. For sequential TT-SVD, let $r_k$ be its retained bond size and $\delta_k$ its discarded singular-value tail at cut $k$. For rounding, let the input TT represent $A$ and use the same notation for the output bond sizes and recorded tails. Then both procedures satisfy
$$ \|A-\widehat A\|_F^2\le\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}\delta_k^2. $$
If no positive singular value is discarded, the output is exactly $A$. In full-rank TT-SVD, $r_k=\operatorname{rank}(A^{\langle k\rangle})$ for every cut, and these are the minimal possible TT bond sizes among exact representations.

Let $\mathcal H=\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}$ be a finite tensor-array space over $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $H:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ be self-adjoint, and let $\psi,\phi\in\mathcal H$ satisfy $\|\psi\|_F=\|\phi\|_F=1$. Then
$$\left|\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle_F-\langle\phi,H\phi\rangle_F\right|\le 2\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\psi-\phi\|_F.$$

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $V$ be a normed space. For all $x,y\in V$,
$$\bigl|\|x\|-\|y\|\bigr|\le \|x-y\|.$$
In particular, the norm map is $1$-Lipschitz for the norm metric.

derivations.claim: There are finitely many local updates in the sweep. Each exact local solve preserves normalization and weakly decreases energy by [F2]; each intervening exact SVD split preserves the represented tensor and therefore its norm and energy by [F1]. Induction over this finite sequence shows that every intermediate state stays normalized and its energy does not exceed the preceding one. Hence $\mathcal E_H(\psi_*)\le\mathcal E_H(\psi_0)$.

The tails $\delta_k$ are those recorded by [F3]. By [F4], $e:=\|\psi_*-\widetilde\psi\|_F\le\tau$. The triangle inequality [F6] gives $1=\|\psi_*\|_F\le e+\|\widetilde\psi\|_F$, so $\|\widetilde\psi\|_F\ge1-e\ge1-\tau>0$ and $\phi$ is defined.

By [F7], $|1-\|\widetilde\psi\|_F|\le e$. Also, homogeneity [F6] and $\phi=\widetilde\psi/\|\widetilde\psi\|_F$ give $\|\phi-\widetilde\psi\|_F=|1-\|\widetilde\psi\|_F|$. Therefore $\|\phi-\psi_*\|_F\le\|\phi-\widetilde\psi\|_F+\|\widetilde\psi-\psi_*\|_F\le2e\le2\tau.$

Apply [F5] to the unit states $\phi$ and $\psi_*$ to get $\mathcal E_H(\phi)\le\mathcal E_H(\psi_*)+4\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\tau$. Combine this with step 1.1 to obtain the claimed bound relative to $\psi_0$. The same inequality gives the asserted upper bound on any post-rounding increase.

boundaries.evidence: The normalized input ψ0 and finite tensor shape are fixed in the Statement.
At τ=0, step 1.2 gives zero rounding error and the normalized state remains defined; for all τ<1 it proves a positive lower norm bound.
The unit case is explicit: step 1.2 proves ||tildeψ||≥1−τ>0, including any accepted τ arbitrarily close to 1.

boundaries.reason: The energy perturbation and local exact solve require no spectral gap or simple eigenvalue.

boundaries.evidence: The strict endpoint τ<1 is used in step 1.2; the Statement makes no normalized-output claim for τ≥1.
Step 1.1 uses finitely many updates and exact finite SVDs; local tie choices are deterministic by the algorithm.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is an upper-bound implication, not a biconditional.
The theorem is an upper-bound implication, not a biconditional.

derivations.claim: Fix one update window. Each entry of its prefix and suffix interface and of its effective Hamiltonian is a finite sum of products of core entries and fixed entries of $H$. Therefore these entries depend continuously on the canonical core arrays. By the assumed componentwise convergence at every stage, the center vectors and effective Hamiltonians at this window converge to limits $x_*$ and $H_{\mathrm{eff},*}$.

For every sweep index $m$ and every unit vector $y$ in this fixed center coefficient space, the exact update at the chosen window gives $x_m^*H_{\mathrm{eff},m}x_m\le y^*H_{\mathrm{eff},m}y$ by [F1] and [F3]. Taking the limit as $m\to\infty$ preserves the inequality because matrix multiplication is continuous, giving $x_*^*H_{\mathrm{eff},*}x_*\le y^*H_{\mathrm{eff},*}y$ for every unit $y$. Thus the limiting center minimizes its local Rayleigh quotient and, by [F3], is a lowest eigenvector.

The update-window list is finite. Apply steps 1.1 and 2.1 to each window in that list. Every limiting center is therefore a local Rayleigh minimizer with all other limiting cores fixed, which is exactly coordinatewise stationarity as defined in the Statement. The argument makes no comparison with states outside those local coordinate spaces.

An **open-boundary matrix-product state (MPS), or tensor train (TT), presentation** is a TT core list from [[def-tensor-train-cores-bond-ranks-and-canonical-gauges]] with $r_0=r_d=1$ whose contraction is $\psi$. In particular, each core has shape $r_{k-1}\times n_k\times r_k$ and the shared internal indices are summed.

A **periodic MPS presentation** consists of positive integers $r_0,\ldots,r_d$ with $r_d=r_0$ and matrices $A_k^{(i_k)}\in\mathbb F^{r_{k-1}\times r_k}$ for each $1\le i_k\le n_k$. It represents the array
$$\psi_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(A_1^{(i_1)}A_2^{(i_2)}\cdots A_d^{(i_d)}\right).$$
A finite MPS/TT state is a normalized array admitting at least one of these exact presentations; a presentation need not be unique or canonical.

A **finite Hermitian Hamiltonian input** is a linear endomorphism $H:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ whose matrix in the standard lexicographic basis satisfies $H^*=H$, where $*$ is conjugate transpose as in [[def-finite-tensor-arrays-and-frobenius-inner-product]]. This page uses only that finite-dimensional Hermitian input and makes no claim about how a physical model assembles it. For nonzero $\psi$, its Rayleigh energy is
$$\mathcal E_H(\psi)=\frac{\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle_F}{\|\psi\|_F^2};$$
for a normalized state this equals $\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle_F$.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $m\ge1$, and let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}$ satisfy $A^*=A$. Define
$$q_A(x):=\frac{x^*Ax}{x^*x}\qquad(x\in\mathbb F^m\setminus\{0\}).$$
Then $q_A$ has a minimum $\lambda_{\min}$, equal to the least eigenvalue of $A$, and its minimizers are precisely the nonzero vectors in the lowest eigenspace $E_{\min}=\ker(A-\lambda_{\min}I)$. There is a deterministic choice of a unit minimizer: let $P_{\min}$ be the orthogonal projection onto $E_{\min}$, scan the standard basis $e_1,\ldots,e_m$, and take the first $j$ with $P_{\min}e_j\ne0$. Normalize $P_{\min}e_j$; over $\mathbb C$, if $z$ is its first nonzero coordinate, multiply by $\overline z/|z|$, and over $\mathbb R$ multiply by $z/|z|$.

- a normalized finite MPS/TT state $\psi\in\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}$ together with one concrete presentation of $\psi$, either an open-boundary TT core list or periodic trace matrices; the supplied presentation must contract to $\psi$;

derivations.claim: The squared norm of $\psi$ is $8/9+1/9=1$. Since $\psi\psi^*$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{span}\{\psi\}$, $H\psi=-\psi$ and $Hx=x$ for every $x\perp\psi$. The width-two center spans all four coordinates, so $H_{\mathrm{eff}}=H$. Its ground eigenspace is $\operatorname{span}\{\psi\}$, and its ground projection sends $|00\rangle$ to $(2\sqrt2/3)\psi$; [F3]'s rule therefore returns exactly $\psi$. The backward pass leaves it unchanged. Reshaping $\psi$ into a $2\times2$ matrix gives $\operatorname{diag}(2\sqrt2/3,1/3)$; its singular values are distinct and ordered as written, so rank-one rounding in [F4] retains $(2\sqrt2/3)|00\rangle$, records discarded tail $\tau=1/3$, and after normalization gives $|00\rangle$.

The rounded energy is the value from step 1.1, so its increase from the exact-sweep energy is $-7/9-(-1)=2/9>0$. The bound in [F5] permits at most $4\cdot1\cdot(1/3)=4/3$, which indeed exceeds $2/9$. This exhibits a possible post-truncation increase while satisfying the discarded-weight estimate.

thm-first-companion-pencil-is-strong-lin.claim: For every regular grade-m square matrix polynomial, the fixed first Frobenius companion pencil and its reversal are unimodularly equivalent to P and its reversal with identity blocks; determinant, eigenvector recovery, and infinity multiplicity follow.

citations.quote:
Fix integers $n,m\ge1$ and coefficient matrices $A_0,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. The **grade-$m$ matrix polynomial** is
$$P(\lambda):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^j.$$
When $P$ is not identically zero, its actual degree is the degree of its largest nonzero scalar entry and can be smaller than the declared grade $m$; the zero polynomial has no actual degree. It is **regular** when the scalar polynomial $\det P(\lambda)$ is not identically zero. Write $x^*$ for conjugate transpose, $\langle u,v\rangle:=v^*u$ for the Euclidean inner product, $\|x\|_2:=(x^*x)^{1/2}$ for the Euclidean vector norm, and $\|M\|_F:=(\sum_{r,s}|M_{rs}|^2)^{1/2}$ for the Frobenius matrix norm.

The **grade-$m$ homogeneous polynomial** is
$$P_h(\alpha,\beta):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\alpha^j\beta^{m-j}.$$
A projective parameter $[\alpha:\beta]$ is a nonzero pair $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb C^2$ modulo common multiplication by a nonzero scalar. A **homogeneous eigenpair** is $([\alpha:\beta],x)$ with $x\in\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$ and $P_h(\alpha,\beta)x=0$. This condition is independent of the representative because $P_h(c\alpha,c\beta)=c^mP_h(\alpha,\beta)$. If $\beta\ne0$, the associated finite parameter is $\lambda=\alpha/\beta$ and $P_h(\alpha,\beta)=\beta^mP(\lambda)$. The point $[1:0]$ is the parameter at infinity; there $P_h(1,0)=A_m$, so it is an eigenvalue exactly when $A_m$ is singular. For regular $P$, the algebraic multiplicity at a finite $\lambda_0$ is the order of the zero of $\det P$ at $\lambda_0$. The **reversal** is $P^{\rm rev}_m(\mu):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_{m-j}\mu^j=\mu^mP(1/\mu)$; the algebraic multiplicity at infinity is the order of the zero of $\det P^{\rm rev}_m$ at $\mu=0$. The order of a zero at $0$ is the largest integer $r$ for which $\mu^r$ divides the scalar polynomial.

Let $P(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^j$ be as in [[def-matrix-polynomial-and-homogeneous-eigenpairs]]. For $m\ge1$, define $mn\times mn$ block matrices $A_c,B_c$ by
$$A_c:=\begin{bmatrix}A_{m-1}&A_{m-2}&\cdots&A_0\\-I_n&0&\cdots&0\\0&-I_n&\ddots&\vdots\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&0\\0&\cdots&-I_n&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad B_c:=\begin{bmatrix}-A_m&0&\cdots&0\\0&-I_n&\cdots&0\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\0&\cdots&0&-I_n\end{bmatrix}.$$
The **first Frobenius companion pencil** with the sign convention used here is
$$L(\lambda):=A_c-\lambda B_c=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda A_m+A_{m-1}&A_{m-2}&\cdots&A_0\\-I_n&\lambda I_n&\cdots&0\\0&-I_n&\ddots&\vdots\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\lambda I_n\end{bmatrix}.$$
For a vector $x\in\mathbb C^n$ and finite $\lambda$, its **companion lift** is $z(\lambda,x):=(\lambda^{m-1}x,\lambda^{m-2}x,\ldots,\lambda x,x)^T\in\mathbb C^{mn}$; when $m=1$, this is simply $x$.

derivations.claim: For $m\ge2$, partition the columns of $L$ as $u=(z_1,\ldots,z_{m-1})$ and $x=z_m$, and the rows as the top block row and the lower $m-1$ block rows; write the resulting blocks as $L=\begin{bmatrix}C&E\\D&G\end{bmatrix}$. The lower-left block $D(\lambda)$ is upper block-bidiagonal with $-I_n$ on its diagonal and $\lambda I_n$ on its superdiagonal. Thus $D=-(I-\lambda S)$ for the nilpotent upper block shift $S$, so $D^{-1}=-(I+\lambda S+\cdots+\lambda^{m-2}S^{m-2})$ is polynomial and $\det D=(-1)^{n(m-1)}$. The lower equations with zero right-hand side are $Du+Gx=0$; solving them gives $z_j=\lambda^{m-j}x$. Substitution into the top row shows that the Schur complement is $E-CD^{-1}G=P(\lambda)$. To compute the determinant, swap the top and lower row groups, with sign $(-1)^{n^2(m-1)}$, obtaining $\begin{bmatrix}D&G\\C&E\end{bmatrix}$. Left multiplication by $\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\-CD^{-1}&I\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant one and gives $\begin{bmatrix}D&G\\0&P\end{bmatrix}$, whose determinant is $\det D\det P$. Since $\det D=(-1)^{n(m-1)}$, the total sign is $(-1)^{n^2(m-1)+n(m-1)}=(-1)^{n(n+1)(m-1)}=1$, so $\det L=\det P$. For $m=1$, $L=P$ directly.

For the partition in step 1.1, left multiplication by $\begin{bmatrix}I&-CD^{-1}\\0&I\end{bmatrix}$ clears the top-left block and leaves $P$ in the top-right block, since $E-CD^{-1}G=P$. Left multiplication of the lower rows by $D^{-1}$ makes the lower-left block $I$ and the lower-right block $H:=D^{-1}G$. Right multiplication by $\begin{bmatrix}I&-H\\0&I\end{bmatrix}$ clears that lower-right block; a block-column permutation then gives $\operatorname{diag}(P,I_{(m-1)n})$. Each operation and its inverse has polynomial entries and determinant a nonzero constant, so their products are unimodular.

Put $L_h(\alpha, eta):= eta A_c-\alpha B_c$. If $ eta
e0$, then $L_h= eta L(\alpha/ eta)$, so step 1.1 gives $\det L_h= eta^{mn}\det P(\alpha/ eta)=\det P_h(\alpha, eta)$. Both sides are polynomials in $(\alpha, eta)$. Fix any $ eta
e0$; the identity holds for every $\alpha$, so their coefficients in powers of $\alpha$ agree. Each such coefficient is a polynomial in $ eta$ and agrees for every $ eta
e0$; as univariate polynomials with infinitely many common values they are identical, so the identity holds also at $ eta=0$. For finite $\lambda$, the lower rows of $L(\lambda)z=0$ force $z_j=\lambda^{m-j}z_m$; if $z
e0$ then $z_m
e0$, and the top row is $P(\lambda)z_m=0$. Conversely, for each nonzero $x$ with $P(\lambda)x=0$, the lift in [F2] is nonzero and the lower rows vanish while the top row is $P(\lambda)x$. At infinity, $L_h(1,0)=-B_c=\operatorname{diag}(A_m,I_n,\ldots,I_n)$, so its kernel consists exactly of $(x,0,\ldots,0)^T$ with $A_mx=0$.

For the reversal pencil $\mu A_c-B_c$, reorder the block columns as $(z_2,\ldots,z_m,z_1)$. Its lower equations are $z_i-\mu z_{i-1}=0$; on the first $m-1$ reordered block columns their coefficient matrix is lower block-bidiagonal with $I_n$ on its diagonal and $-\mu I_n$ on its subdiagonal, so its determinant is $1$ and its inverse is polynomial by the finite nilpotent-shift expansion. Solving these equations gives $z_i=\mu^{i-1}z_1$; substitution into the top row gives $\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_{m-j}\mu^j=P^{\rm rev}_m(\mu)$. The same row elimination, normalization by this polynomial inverse, column clearing, and block permutation used in step 2.1 therefore give $\operatorname{diag}(P^{\rm rev}_m,I_{(m-1)n})$ by unimodular polynomial matrices. For $m=1$ the reversal pencil equals $P^{\rm rev}_1$ directly.

The reversal determinant identity is $\det P^{\rm rev}_m(\mu)=\mu^{mn}\det P(1/\mu)$. If $d=\deg\det P$, write $\det P(\lambda)=c_d\lambda^d+\cdots+c_0$ with $c_d\ne0$; then $\det P^{\rm rev}_m(\mu)=c_d\mu^{mn-d}+\cdots+c_0\mu^{mn}$, whose zero order at $0$ is exactly $mn-d$. Step 3.1 shows the reversal pencil has the same zero order, and step 2.2 identifies the homogeneous companion spectrum and eigenspaces. In the permutation expansion of $\det P(\lambda)$, every product has $n$ factors of degree at most $m$; degree $mn$ can occur only by taking the $\lambda^m$ coefficient from each factor, so its coefficient is $\det A_m$. Thus invertibility of $A_m$ is equivalent to $d=mn$ and no infinity eigenvalue; singularity gives $d<mn$ and positive multiplicity at infinity. The geometric multiplicity is $\dim\ker A_m$ by step 2.2 and is not used to infer the zero order.

derivations.claim: From the lower residual equations in [F2], $z_{k-1}=\lambda z_k-e_k$. Back-substitution from $x=z_m$ gives $z_j=\lambda^{m-j}x-\sum_{k=j+1}^{m}\lambda^{k-j-1}e_k$ for $1\le j<m$; when $j=m$ the same formula has an empty sum.

Substitute these expressions into the top row from [F2]. The terms containing $x$ sum to $\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^jx=P(\lambda)x$. For fixed $e_k$, its coefficient is the negative of $\sum_{j=m-k+1}^{m}A_j\lambda^{j-m+k-1}$: the $z_1$ term contributes $-(\lambda A_m+A_{m-1})\lambda^{k-2}e_k$, and each $z_j$ term for $2\le j<k$ contributes $-A_{m-j}\lambda^{k-j-1}e_k$. Thus $e_1=P(\lambda)x-\sum_{k=2}^{m}Q_k(\lambda)e_k$, which is the claimed identity.

We first derive the finite-dimensional Euclidean estimates used here. For $u,v\in\mathbb C^d$ with $v\ne0$, set $c:=\langle u,v\rangle/\|v\|_2^2$. Direct expansion gives $\|u-cv\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2-|\langle u,v\rangle|^2/\|v\|_2^2\ge0$, hence $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$; if $v=0$ the inequality is immediate. Since $\|u+v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|v\|_2^2+2\operatorname{Re}\langle u,v\rangle\le(\|u\|_2+\|v\|_2)^2$, taking nonnegative square roots gives $\|u+v\|_2\le\|u\|_2+\|v\|_2$. For any matrix $M$ and vector $v$, apply the derived inner-product bound to each row of $M$ and $\bar v$ to obtain $|(Mv)_r|^2\le(\sum_s|M_{rs}|^2)\|v\|_2^2$; summing over rows gives $\|Mv\|_2\le\|M\|_F\|v\|_2$. Now put $y=e_1+\sum_{k=2}^mQ_ke_k=P(\lambda)x$. Repeated use of the derived triangle inequality gives $\|y\|_2\le\|e_1\|_2+\sum_{k=2}^m\|Q_ke_k\|_2$. Applying the rowwise matrix estimate to each $Q_k$ gives the claimed bound. For the companion lift, each lower row vanishes by construction and the top row is $P(\lambda)x$.

To see why no uniform unscaled transfer factor follows, take the fixed scalar polynomial $P(\lambda)=\lambda^2+1$. For any $t>0$, set $x=t/(t^2+1)$, $z_2=x$, and $z_1=tx-1$. Hence the block-pencil residual norm is $1$ and the polynomial residual is $t$, which is unbounded as $t\to\infty$. thm-exact-coefficientwise-weighted-backw.claim: For any nonzero homogeneous projective parameter and nonzero vector, the weighted Frobenius backward-error infimum is attained and equals the residual divided by the vector norm and weighted homogeneous coefficient norm.

citations.quote:
Let $P(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^j$ be regular of grade $m$, let $[\alpha:\beta]$ be a projective parameter, let $x\in\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$, and choose positive weights $\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_m$. Write $r:=P_h(\alpha,\beta)x$. The **coefficientwise weighted Frobenius backward error** is the infimum
$$\eta_F(P,[\alpha:\beta],x;\omega):=\inf\left\{\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}\frac{\|\Delta A_j\|_F^2}{\omega_j^2}\right)^{1/2}:\ \sum_{j=0}^{m}(A_j+\Delta A_j)\alpha^j\beta^{m-j}x=0,\quad \Delta A_j\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\right\}.$$
The perturbations of distinct coefficients are unrestricted and measured in the displayed weighted product norm; no symmetry or other coefficient structure is imposed. Replacing $(\alpha,\beta)$ by $(c\alpha,c\beta)$ for $c\ne0$ multiplies the constraint by $c^m$ and leaves its zero set unchanged, so the infimum depends only on $[\alpha:\beta]$. The infimum is defined for finite and infinite projective parameters. The next theorem proves that it is attained and gives its exact value.

citations.quote: Let $\mathbb C(\lambda)$ denote the field of quotients of complex scalar polynomials. Let $R(\lambda)\in\mathbb C(\lambda)^{n\times n}$ with $n\ge1$ be a square matrix whose entries are rational functions of $\lambda$. Write each entry as a reduced scalar fraction (common polynomial factors have been cancelled), and let $q(\lambda)$ be the monic least common multiple of their denominators. Thus the zero set $\mathcal P:=\{\lambda:q(\lambda)=0\}$ is exactly the set of poles of at least one entry. Define the pole-free domain $\Omega:=\mathbb C\setminus\mathcal P$ and the polynomial matrix $N(\lambda):=q(\lambda)R(\lambda)$, whose entries are polynomials as in [[def-matrix-polynomial-and-homogeneous-eigenpairs]]. Fix integers $n,m\ge1$ and coefficient matrices $A_0,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. The **grade-$m$ matrix polynomial** is
$$P(\lambda):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^j.$$
When $P$ is not identically zero, its actual degree is the degree of its largest nonzero scalar entry and can be smaller than the declared grade $m$; the zero polynomial has no actual degree. It is **regular** when the scalar polynomial $\det P(\lambda)$ is not identically zero. Write $x^*$ for conjugate transpose, $\langle u,v\rangle:=v^*u$ for the Euclidean inner product, $\|x\|_2:=(x^*x)^{1/2}$ for the Euclidean vector norm, and $\|M\|_F:=(\sum_{r,s}|M_{rs}|^2)^{1/2}$ for the Frobenius matrix norm.

The **grade-$m$ homogeneous polynomial** is
$$P_h(\alpha,\beta):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\alpha^j\beta^{m-j}.$$
A projective parameter $[\alpha:\beta]$ is a nonzero pair $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb C^2$ modulo common multiplication by a nonzero scalar. A **homogeneous eigenpair** is $([\alpha:\beta],x)$ with $x\in\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$ and $P_h(\alpha,\beta)x=0$. This condition is independent of the representative because $P_h(c\alpha,c\beta)=c^mP_h(\alpha,\beta)$. If $\beta\ne0$, the associated finite parameter is $\lambda=\alpha/\beta$ and $P_h(\alpha,\beta)=\beta^mP(\lambda)$. The point $[1:0]$ is the parameter at infinity; there $P_h(1,0)=A_m$, so it is an eigenvalue exactly when $A_m$ is singular. For regular $P$, the algebraic multiplicity at a finite $\lambda_0$ is the order of the zero of $\det P$ at $\lambda_0$. The **reversal** is $P^{\rm rev}_m(\mu):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_{m-j}\mu^j=\mu^mP(1/\mu)$; the algebraic multiplicity at infinity is the order of the zero of $\det P^{\rm rev}_m$ at $\mu=0$. The order of a zero at $0$ is the largest integer $r$ for which $\mu^r$ divides the scalar polynomial.

Let $P(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^j$ be as in [[def-matrix-polynomial-and-homogeneous-eigenpairs]]. For $m\ge1$, define $mn\times mn$ block matrices $A_c,B_c$ by
$$A_c:=\begin{bmatrix}A_{m-1}&A_{m-2}&\cdots&A_0\\-I_n&0&\cdots&0\\0&-I_n&\ddots&\vdots\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&0\\0&\cdots&-I_n&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad B_c:=\begin{bmatrix}-A_m&0&\cdots&0\\0&-I_n&\cdots&0\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\0&\cdots&0&-I_n\end{bmatrix}.$$
The **first Frobenius companion pencil** with the sign convention used here is
$$L(\lambda):=A_c-\lambda B_c=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda A_m+A_{m-1}&A_{m-2}&\cdots&A_0\\-I_n&\lambda I_n&\cdots&0\\0&-I_n&\ddots&\vdots\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\lambda I_n\end{bmatrix}.$$
For a vector $x\in\mathbb C^n$ and finite $\lambda$, its **companion lift** is $z(\lambda,x):=(\lambda^{m-1}x,\lambda^{m-2}x,\ldots,\lambda x,x)^T\in\mathbb C^{mn}$; when $m=1$, this is simply $x$.

Let $P$ be a regular $n\times n$ grade-$m$ matrix polynomial with $m\ge1$, and let $L(\lambda)=A_c-\lambda B_c$ be the pencil of [[def-first-frobenius-companion-pencil]]. A square matrix polynomial is **unimodular** when its determinant is a nonzero constant. The pencil $L$ is a **strong linearization** of $P$ if there are unimodular polynomial matrices $U,V$ with $ULV=\operatorname{diag}(P,I_{(m-1)n})$ and unimodular polynomial matrices $\widetilde U,\widetilde V$ with $\widetilde U(\mu)(\mu A_c-B_c)\widetilde V(\mu)=\operatorname{diag}(P^{\rm rev}_m,I_{(m-1)n})$. Such matrices exist. In particular, $\det(A_c-\lambda B_c)=\det P(\lambda)$; finite eigenvectors correspond by $x\mapsto z(\lambda,x)$; and the infinite eigenspaces correspond by $x\mapsto(x,0,\ldots,0)^T$ from $\ker A_m$ to $\ker(-B_c)$. The algebraic multiplicity of infinity in both problems is $mn-\deg\det P$. Thus if $A_m$ is invertible there are no infinite eigenvalues; if $A_m$ is singular there is at least one, with geometric multiplicity $\dim\ker A_m$, which need not equal its algebraic multiplicity.

derivations.claim: The discriminant is $(1/2)^2-4(1)(2)=1/4-8=-31/4$. The quadratic formula therefore gives the two roots $\lambda_\pm=-1/4\pm i\sqrt{31}/4$. Neither is infinite because the leading coefficient $A_2=1$ is invertible.
Direct expansion gives $\det L(\lambda)=\lambda(\lambda+1/2)+2=\lambda^2+(1/2)\lambda+2=P(\lambda)$, so these two values are precisely the finite companion-pencil eigenvalues.

For either root, $P(\lambda_\pm)\cdot1=0$, and its companion lift is $z=(\lambda_\pm,1)^T$. Multiplication gives $L(\lambda_\pm)z=((\lambda_\pm+1/2)\lambda_\pm+2,-\lambda_\pm+\lambda_\pm)^T=(P(\lambda_\pm),0)^T=(0,0)^T$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

### Finite sums of vectors

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

### Linear combinations

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector
$w \in V$ is a **linear combination of elements of $S$** when there are
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with
$w = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$.

**The empty case is a real case.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), and at $n = 0$ the sum is the empty sum, which is
$0_V$. So $0_V$ is a linear combination of elements of every subset of $V$,
including $S = \varnothing$. The lists are indexed from $0$, so a linear
combination of length $n$ is $\lambda_0 v_0 + \dots + \lambda_{n-1}v_{n-1}$; no
statement here is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

### The span

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq V$. Write

$$L(S) \;:=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i \;:\; n \in \mathbb{N},\ \lambda : n \to F,\ v : n \to S \,\Bigr\}$$

for the set of linear combinations of elements of $S$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]). Then

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;=\; L(S).$$

In particular $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$, and for every
$S \subseteq V$ the span of $S$ contains $0_V$ as the empty linear combination.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

For every finite matrix over a field,
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A)=\operatorname{crank}(A).$$
Both dimensions equal the number of pivots in any echelon form of $A$.

Let $A\in M_r(F)$ and $D\in M_s(F)$. For either block-triangular matrix

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&D\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{or}\quad M=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\C&D\end{pmatrix},$$

one has $\chi_M(x)=\chi_A(x)\chi_D(x)$, including $r=0$ or $s=0$.

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space,

$$\sigma_F(T)=\{\lambda\in F:\chi_T(\lambda)=0\}.$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

derivations.claim: For each integer $k\ge0$, put $\mathcal R_k=\operatorname{span}\{A^jBe_\ell:0\le j<k,\ 1\le\ell\le m\}$. Then $\mathcal R_{k+1}=\mathcal R_k+A\mathcal R_k+\operatorname{im}B$. If $\mathcal R_{k+1}=\mathcal R_k$, then $\operatorname{im}B\subseteq\mathcal R_k$ and $A\mathcal R_k\subseteq\mathcal R_k$, so every later space equals $\mathcal R_k$. Otherwise each inclusion is strict; if no equality occurs before $\mathcal R_n$, its dimension has increased at least $n$ times from zero, hence $\mathcal R_n=F^n$. Therefore $\mathcal R=\mathcal R_n$ is the smallest $A$-invariant subspace containing $\operatorname{im}B$.

Let $(E,H)$ be reachable on $F^d$. If $[\lambda I-E\ \ H]$ had rank less than $d$ over $\mathbb C$, row-rank equality and rank-nullity applied to its adjoint would give a nonzero $y\in\mathbb C^d$ with $y^*(\lambda I-E)=0$ and $y^*H=0$. Induction then gives $y^*E^jH=\lambda^j y^*H=0$ for every $j<d$, contradicting reachability; for real data the real reachable columns complexify to span $\mathbb C^d$. Thus the horizontal rank is $d$ for every complex $\lambda$.

This gives a basis matrix $P$ whose first $r$ columns span $\mathcal R$. Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $n\ge0$ and $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, and let $Q^*$ denote transpose over $\mathbb R$ and conjugate transpose over $\mathbb C$. A **complex Schur pair** for $A$ is a pair $(Q,T)$ with $Q^*Q=I$ and $A=QTQ^*$, where $T$ is upper triangular.

For real $A$, a **real Schur pair** is a pair $(Q,T)$ with $Q^TQ=I$ and $A=QTQ^T$, where $T$ is block upper triangular and every diagonal block is either a real $1\times1$ block or a real $2\times2$ block with negative characteristic-polynomial discriminant. Such a $2\times2$ block has one nonreal conjugate eigenvalue pair. The definition does not assert that a finite shift strategy reaches such a pair.

For $B=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{2\times2}$, its characteristic-polynomial discriminant means the exact real number $\Delta(B)=(a+d)^2-4(ad-bc)$. “Negative discriminant” means the exact comparison $\Delta(B)<0$.

Let $(A,B)$ be a regular pencil of order $n$. A **complex generalized Schur
form** is a factorisation
$$Q^*AZ=S,\qquad Q^*BZ=T,$$
where $Q,Z\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ are unitary in the sense of
[[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]], and $S,T$ are
upper triangular as in
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. For its
$i$th one-by-one diagonal block, $[s_{ii}:t_{ii}]$ is the
**diagonal homogeneous pair**.

For real $A,B$, a **real generalized Schur form** has
$$Q^TAZ=S,\qquad Q^TBZ=T,$$
where $Q,Z$ are orthogonal, $S$ is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks
of size one or two, and $T$ is upper triangular. Each one-by-one diagonal
block has a nonzero real homogeneous pair. For a two-by-two diagonal block
$(S_{kk},T_{kk})$, the **diagonal homogeneous roots** are the zeros of
$\det(\beta S_{kk}-\alpha T_{kk})$ in $[\alpha:\beta]$; such a block has a
nonreal conjugate pair of finite roots. A singular pencil is outside this
definition.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal A$ be a nonempty set of matrices in $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, and let $\mathcal b$ be a nonempty subset of $\mathbb C^n$. A **uniform residual certificate** consists of a point matrix $R\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, a point vector $\widehat x\in\mathbb C^n$, and numbers $q,r\ge0$ such that
$$
\|I-RA\|_2\le q,\qquad \|R(b-A\widehat x)\|_2\le r
$$
for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and $b\in\mathcal b$. Here $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the operator norm induced by the Euclidean vector norm, as in [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. The certificate is **usable** when $q<1$; in that case its reported error radius is $r/(1-q)$. The point-data case is $\mathcal A=\{A\}$ and $\mathcal b=\{b\}$.

This definition specifies mathematical upper bounds; it does not specify how a computation establishes them.

If $(R,\widehat x,q,r)$ is usable uniform residual certificate data for nonempty $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and $\mathcal b\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, then for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and $b\in\mathcal b$, the equation $Ax=b$ has a unique solution $x_A(b)$ and
$$
\|x_A(b)-\widehat x\|_2\le\frac{r}{1-q}.
$$

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n,m,p\ge1$, $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, and $C\in F^{p\times n}$. A matrix is **Hurwitz** when every complex eigenvalue has strictly negative real part, as in [[def-hurwitz-matrix-and-continuous-lyapunov-equation]]. It is **Schur stable** when every complex eigenvalue has modulus strictly less than one.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **continuously stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Hurwitz. The pair $(A,C)$ is **continuously detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Hurwitz.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **discretely stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Schur stable. The pair $(A,C)$ is **discretely detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Schur stable. These are exact existential properties of the given finite matrices. A residual size or an approximate spectral estimate does not itself establish any of them.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space over $F$,
and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. If the characteristic polynomial of $T$ splits
over $F$, then $V$ has an orthonormal basis in which the matrix of $T$ is upper
triangular.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.
Every nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb C[x]$ splits over $\mathbb C$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $F$ be a field and let $A\in M_n(F)$. If $n\geq1$, regard $xI_n-A$ as a matrix over the commutative polynomial ring $F[x]$. The **characteristic polynomial of $A$** is

$$\chi_A(x):=\det(xI_n-A)\in F[x].$$

For $n=0$, define the characteristic polynomial of the unique $0\times0$ matrix to be the constant polynomial $1$. This agrees with the empty-product convention and makes the characteristic polynomial monic of degree $0$ in the zero-sized case.

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space,

$$\sigma_F(T)=\{\lambda\in F:\chi_T(\lambda)=0\}.$$

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, the unique endomorphism and every power of it is the zero map on the zero domain; its operator norm is zero, so the assertion holds with $C_r=0$. Assume now $n\ge1$ and regard a real matrix, if present, as a complex matrix. Its characteristic polynomial is a nonconstant complex polynomial, so [F5] and [F2] give $M=UTU^*$ with $U$ unitary and $T=D+N$, where $D$ is diagonal and $N$ is strictly upper triangular. Similar matrices have the same eigenvalues: $Mv=\lambda v$ is equivalent to $T(U^*v)=\lambda(U^*v)$. By [F7] and [F8], the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries of $T$; hence $\rho(M)=\max_i|T_{ii}|=\|D\|_2$, where the last equality follows directly from the Euclidean induced norm. Set $\rho=\rho(M)<r$. Each occurrence of $N$ in a product raises the row-to-column index, while $D$ preserves it, so every word containing at least $n$ copies of $N$ is zero.

Expand $(D+N)^k$ as the sum of noncommuting words. The terms with exactly $j$ copies of $N$ number $\binom{k}{j}$, vanish for $j\ge n$, and for $j<n$ have norm at most $\rho^{k-j}\|N\|_2^j$ by [F3] and $\|D\|_2=\rho$. Thus $\|T^k\|_2\le\sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,n-1)}\binom{k}{j}\rho^{k-j}\|N\|_2^j.$ Because $U$ and $U^*$ preserve vector norms by [F6] and $U^*$ maps the unit sphere onto itself, the induced norm [F4] gives $\|M^k\|_2=\|UT^kU^*\|_2=\|T^k\|_2$.

If $\rho=0$, then $D=0$ and $T=N$, so $T^k=0$ for $k\ge n$; taking $C_r=\max_{0\le k<n}\|T^k\|_2r^{-k}$ proves the claim. If $0<\rho<r$, each fixed $j<n$ satisfies $\binom{k}{j}\rho^{k-j}\|N\|_2^j/r^k\le c_j k^j(\rho/r)^k$ for a finite $c_j$. The ratio of consecutive terms $k^j(\rho/r)^k$ tends to $\rho/r<1$, so this sequence is bounded. Summing its finitely many bounds over $0\le j<n$ gives a finite $C_r$ in step 2.1.

If for some $\lambda$ with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$ the horizontal matrix $H_\lambda=[\lambda I-A\;B]$ has rank less than $n$, [F2] and [F3] applied over $\mathbb C$ to $H_\lambda^*$ give a nonzero $y\in\mathbb C^n$ with $y^*(\lambda I-A)=0$ and $y^*B=0$. By [A1], the same real or complex $K$ acts on this vector, so $y^*(A-BK)=\lambda y^*$. Thus $\det(\lambda I-(A-BK))=0$, contradicting that $A-BK$ is Hurwitz.

Suppose $(A,C)$ is continuously detectable and fix its same-field injection $L$ from [F1]. If $V_\lambda=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda I-A\\C\end{bmatrix}$ has rank less than $n$, rank-nullity over $\mathbb C$ gives a nonzero $x\in\mathbb C^n$ with $(\lambda I-A)x=0$ and $Cx=0$. Hence $(A-LC)x=\lambda x$, which contradicts that $A-LC$ is Hurwitz because $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$.

Suppose $(A,B)$ is discretely stabilizable and fix its same-field Schur feedback $K$ from [F1]. If $[\lambda I-A\;B]$ has rank less than $n$ for some $|\lambda|\ge1$, the same complex left-kernel argument as in step 1.1 gives a nonzero $y$ with $y^*(A-BK)=\lambda y^*$. Thus $\det(\lambda I-(A-BK))=0$, contradicting Schur stability.

Suppose $(A,C)$ is discretely detectable and fix its same-field Schur injection $L$ from [F1]. If the vertical matrix has rank less than $n$ for some $|\lambda|\ge1$, its complex kernel contains a nonzero $x$ and $Cx=0$, so $(A-LC)x=\lambda x$. This contradicts Schur stability.

citations.quote:
Inputs are an order $d\ge0$ real or complex Schur matrix $T$, or a regular real or complex generalized Schur pair $(S,T)$, with the declared diagonal block partition. Complex Schur and QZ forms have scalar blocks; real Schur forms have scalar blocks or real $2\times2$ blocks; real generalized Schur forms have real $1\times1$ or $2\times2$ blocks. Each generalized diagonal block pair must be regular. Optional accumulated factors are exact unitary/orthogonal products; if omitted they are identity. Other inputs are a CARE selector (strict left half-plane) or DARE selector (strict unit disk), a required integer selected dimension $0\le r\le d$, nonnegative integer budgets $K$ and $W$, a positive local separation threshold $\eta$, and either an exact arithmetic controller or a bounded outward evaluator.

Use the CARE selector with an ordinary Schur form and the DARE selector with a generalized Schur form; an unmatched form-selector combination returns invalid-form.

Before any charged operation, initialize attempts, accepted swaps and primitive/evaluator counts to zero, diagnostic lists to empty, and every uncomputed diagnostic to unavailable. In particular, the actual selected dimension, block labels, boundary and separation predicates, and initial inversion count remain unavailable until their respective scans or tests finish; the requested dimension $r$ is always retained separately. Report only completed tests and certificates, together with the last committed arrays and factors, on an early exit. Unavailable predicates assert neither truth nor falsity.

The entries of the input arrays are treated as their exact represented real or complex values. All local transformed arrays and accumulated factors are retained exactly as finite products; a rounded dense copy is only a separately evaluated diagnostic. Before each scalar primitive or outward evaluation, return work-budget-exhausted if no units of $W$ remain; otherwise consume one unit before requesting the operation. Charge validation, label and inversion-count scans, local construction, and the final ordering scan to this same budget. For rational or dyadic arrays, the exact core uses rational arithmetic and positive square roots, with exact real-algebraic sign comparisons where needed. Exact decisions on arbitrary real inputs are an exact-real arithmetic model, not a bit-computability claim. The bounded-evaluator branch returns arithmetic-inconclusive whenever a needed zero, sign, division, or normalization remains unresolved.

1. Validate dimensions, the declared block pattern, and regularity of each generalized diagonal pair in one finite scan. For ordinary scalar blocks over either field classify $t_{ii}$ by $\operatorname{Re}t_{ii}<0$ or $>0$ for CARE; for real $2\times2$ blocks first verify negative discriminant and then classify by trace less than or greater than zero. For generalized scalar blocks over either field $[s_{ii}:t_{ii}]$, verify the pair is nonzero and classify by $|s_{ii}|<|t_{ii}|$ or $|s_{ii}|>|t_{ii}|$ for DARE; thus $t_{ii}=0$, $s_{ii}\ne0$ is complementary and represents infinity without division. For a real generalized $2\times2$ block, verify $\det(T_b)\ne0$ and that $\det(S_b-\lambda T_b)$ has negative discriminant; its conjugate roots have common squared modulus $\det(S_b)/\det(T_b)$, so classify by strict comparison of this ratio with one, cross-multiplying with the certified sign of $\det(T_b)$. Exact equality with the selected boundary returns boundary-spectrum. A bounded enclosure touching the boundary returns separation-inconclusive. Require that the selected block sizes sum to $r$, or return dimension-mismatch. Invalid patterns or singular local homogeneous pairs return invalid-form. Compute the initial inversion count once by scanning all ordered block pairs after classification.

2. Give every whole block its selected or complementary label. Locate the leftmost adjacent complementary-selected inversion. If none exists, return ordered with the current exact arrays and accumulated factors. If an inversion exists but $K$ swap attempts have already been made, return swap-budget-exhausted. Otherwise consume one attempt before starting its local construction. Never split a real conjugate pair.

3. Let $p,q\in\{1,2\}$ be the two adjacent block sizes (over $\mathbb C$, $p=q=1$), with local blocks
$$T_{JJ}=\begin{bmatrix}A&C\\0&B\end{bmatrix}$$
for ordinary Schur form, or
$$S_{JJ}=\begin{bmatrix}A&C\\0&B\end{bmatrix},\qquad T_{JJ}=\begin{bmatrix}D&F\\0&E\end{bmatrix}$$
for QZ form. With column-vectorization, form the local coefficient system
$$H=I_q\otimes A-B^T\otimes I_p,\qquad h=-\operatorname{vec}(C)$$
for ordinary Schur, with unknown $\operatorname{vec}(R)$, and
$$H=\begin{bmatrix}I_q\otimes A&-B^T\otimes I_p\\I_q\otimes D&-E^T\otimes I_p\end{bmatrix},\qquad h=-\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{vec}(C)\\\operatorname{vec}(F)\end{bmatrix}$$
for QZ, with unknown $[\operatorname{vec}(R);\operatorname{vec}(L)]$. The transpose in $B^T$ and $E^T$ is intentional, also over $\mathbb C$. Solve $Hx=h$ and $HY=I$ by finite Gaussian elimination with complete pivoting: at each stage scan the finite remaining submatrix, choose an entry of largest certified modulus with lexicographic ties, swap rows and columns, eliminate, and back-substitute while undoing column permutations. An exact all-zero remaining submatrix returns swap-singular. An unresolved pivot or range failure returns separation-inconclusive or range-failure. Verify $Hx=h$ and $HY=I$ exactly, or verify a usable approximate-inverse certificate $\|I-YH\|_2\le\theta<1$ and still solve $Hx=h$ exactly. In the latter case it gives $\|H^{-1}\|_2\le\|Y\|_2/(1-\theta)$. In the exact-inverse branch take $\beta=\|Y\|_F$ in exact arithmetic, or an outward upper bound for that norm; in the approximate-inverse branch take an outward bound for $\|Y\|_2/(1-\theta)$. Require $\eta\beta\le1$; otherwise return swap-separation-inconclusive. Record the threshold, solves, pivot decisions and certificate.

4. For ordinary Schur form set $V=[R;I_q]$. For QZ set $V=[R;I_q]$ and $W_L=[L;I_q]$. Complete the columns of $V$, and separately $W_L$, to exact orthonormal bases by Gram–Schmidt: process the graph columns first, then $e_1,\ldots,e_{p+q}$, skipping exactly zero residuals and normalizing each nonzero residual by the positive square root of its squared norm. The graph columns are independent because their last $q$ rows form $I_q$; the coordinate scan completes a basis. An unresolved zero or normalization decision in bounded mode returns arithmetic-inconclusive.

5. Let $Z_{\rm loc}$ be the ordinary orthogonal/unitary completion; for QZ let $Z_{\rm loc}$ be the right completion and $Q_{\rm loc}$ the left completion. Propose the local transform $Z_{\rm loc}^*T Z_{\rm loc}$ in the ordinary case, or $Q_{\rm loc}^*SZ_{\rm loc}$ and $Q_{\rm loc}^*TZ_{\rm loc}$ in the QZ case. Apply it to the entire affected row and column panels, including upper off-diagonal blocks. The lower-left block is set to exact zero only by the local equations solved in step 3. For a real QZ form, factor each newly formed real $2\times2$ diagonal block as $T_b=L_bR_b$ by Gram–Schmidt on its two columns, apply the embedded $L_b^*$ to the corresponding rows of both arrays, and update $Q_{\rm loc}\leftarrow Q_{\rm loc}L_b$ with the same embedded factor; such a block is nonsingular because its roots are finite and nonreal. A size-one infinite pair requires no division by its zero second coordinate. Commit the provisional panels and factor updates only after every required local operation succeeds, incrementing accepted swaps by one as part of that same commit; otherwise return the previous committed arrays with a failed-attempt diagnostic and leave accepted swaps unchanged.

6. After a committed exchange, swap the two labels and sizes and return to step 2. Ordinary accumulated factors are updated by right multiplication with $Z_{\rm loc}$; generalized accumulated factors are updated as $Q\leftarrow QQ_{\rm loc}$ and $Z\leftarrow ZZ_{\rm loc}$. The first $r$ columns of the updated factor are reported as the selected basis candidate; in QZ the right factor $Z$, not the left factor $Q$, supplies the right deflating basis.

On every exit return the current partial form, exact product factors, status, selected dimension, boundary and separation predicates, initial inversion count, attempts, accepted swaps, primitive/evaluator counts, original residual certificates, local inverse-norm certificates, and any residual transport data. Other statuses are work-budget-exhausted, arithmetic-inconclusive, range-failure, invalid-form, dimension-mismatch, boundary-spectrum, separation-inconclusive, swap-singular, swap-separation-inconclusive, and swap-budget-exhausted. ordered is distinct from any Riccati acceptance status. Reordering a computed form does not assert a structured Hamiltonian or symplectic backward-error theorem.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $m,n\ge1$, $A\in F^{m\times m}$ and $B\in F^{n\times n}$. Spectra of real matrices are taken over $\mathbb C$. The map $\mathcal S_{A,B}$ of [[def-sylvester-operator-and-separation-number]] is invertible if and only if

$$
\sigma(A)\cap(-\sigma(B))=\varnothing.
$$

Equivalently, for every $C\in F^{m\times n}$, the equation $AX+XB=C$ has a unique solution if and only if this spectral condition holds. The same condition is equivalent to $\operatorname{sep}(A,-B)>0$.
Let $D$ be an integral domain. A nonzero polynomial $f\in D[x]$ of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct roots in $D$.

Let $T:V\to V$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over
a field $F$. Then $T$ is invertible if and only if $\det(T)\neq0$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

Let $n_1,n_2\ge1$, $n=n_1+n_2$, and let $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be
block upper triangular with the same two-block partition of sizes $n_1,n_2$,
with diagonal blocks $A_{11},A_{22}$ and
$B_{11},B_{22}$. For every $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$,
$$\det(\beta A-\alpha B) =\det(\beta A_{11}-\alpha B_{11})\det(\beta A_{22}-\alpha B_{22}).$$

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $E\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, and let $0\le q<1$ satisfy $\|E\|_2\le q$. Then $I-E$ is invertible and
$$
\|(I-E)^{-1}\|_2\le \frac1{1-q}.
$$

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

derivations.claim: For an ordinary complex scalar block the diagonal entry itself classifies the root, while a real $2\times2$ block with negative discriminant has conjugate roots with real part $\operatorname{tr}(T_b)/2$. For a generalized scalar pair $[s:t]$, a finite root is $s/t$, so $|s|<|t|$ is exactly the disk predicate and $t=0$, $s\ne0$ is infinity and complementary. For a real generalized $2\times2$ pair with finite nonreal roots, the root product is $\det(S_b)/\det(T_b)=|\lambda|^2$. Thus the procedure labels whole blocks exactly and detects equality at the selector boundary.

For ordinary adjacent diagonal blocks $A,B$, column-wise expansion gives $\operatorname{vec}(AR-RB)=(I_q\otimes A-B^T\otimes I_p)\operatorname{vec}R$. The selected and complementary spectra are disjoint, so [F2] applied to $X\mapsto AX+X(-B)$ makes this square coefficient operator invertible, giving a unique local solve.

For generalized adjacent pairs $(A,D)$ and $(B,E)$, their homogeneous root sets are disjoint and both pairs are regular. The polynomials $\det(A-\zeta D)$ and $\det(B-\zeta E)$ are nonzero of degrees at most $p,q$; among $p+q+1$ distinct real integers, [F3] gives a $\zeta$ for which $A_0=A-\zeta D$ and $B_0=B-\zeta E$ have nonzero determinants, hence are invertible by [F4]. Each homogeneous root $[\alpha:\beta]$ maps injectively to $\mu=\beta/(\alpha-\zeta\beta)$, an eigenvalue of $DA_0^{-1}$ because $D-\mu A_0=-(\beta A-\alpha D)/(\alpha-\zeta\beta)$; this also maps infinity to zero, and maps the second pair to $EB_0^{-1}$, so the ordinary spectra remain disjoint. If $AR-LB=0$ and $DR-LE=0$, then $A_0R=LB_0$, hence $R=A_0^{-1}LB_0$ and $DA_0^{-1}L=LEB_0^{-1}$; [F2] forces $L=0$, then $R=0$. The square generalized Sylvester system has zero kernel, so [F5] makes it invertible; for real blocks its real coefficient matrix has the same nonzero determinant as its complexification.

For ordinary input, $Q_0^*AQ_0=T_0+R_0$ and $Q_{\rm new}=Q_0V$ imply $Q_{\rm new}^*AQ_{\rm new}=V^*T_0V+V^*R_0V$. For QZ, substituting $Q_{\rm new}=Q_0U$ and $Z_{\rm new}=Z_0V$ into the two input relations gives residuals $U^*R_AV$ and $U^*R_BV$; [F9] preserves their Frobenius norms. These unstructured residual relations assert no structured pencil perturbation.

Each exact Gaussian-elimination pivot is nonzero; row and column permutations and row eliminations preserve the solution set. A zero remaining block before all pivots would contradict the invertibility in steps 1.2–1.3. Back-substitution gives the unique exact solution and applying the same operations to the coordinate vectors gives the inverse. In the approximate branch, $\|I-YH\|_2\le\theta<1$ and [F10] make $YH$ invertible; finite-dimensional square rank and [F11] give $\|H^{-1}\|_2=\|(YH)^{-1}Y\|_2\le\|Y\|_2/(1-\theta)$. Thus each committed swap has an exact solve and valid recorded inverse bound.

Every complementary-selected inversion can be removed by swapping an adjacent complementary-selected pair, which decreases the inversion count by one and leaves all other relative block orders unchanged. Thus $I\le b(b-1)/2$ and, after $I$ successful swaps, no inversion remains. The finite scans, local systems, and exact return branches in [F1] give a finite declared status; exhausted $K$ or $W$ returns its budget status.

The columns of $[R;I_q]$ and $[L;I_q]$ are independent because their last $q$ rows form $I_q$. Applying [F6] gives orthonormal graph columns; if their span is proper, some standard coordinate vector lies outside it, so the finite scan completes each required local basis.

In the ordinary case $AR-RB=-C$ gives $\begin{bmatrix}A&C\\0&B\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}R\\I_q\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}R\\I_q\end{bmatrix}B$. Writing $[R;I_q]=Z_1R_v$ with $R_v$ invertible shows the leading transformed block is similar to $B$. The quotient map $\pi(x,y)=x-Ry$ has kernel this graph and satisfies $\pi T_{JJ}=A\pi$, so its restriction to the orthogonal complement is an isomorphism onto the quotient and the trailing block is similar to $A$. Embedded local unitary updates preserve the surrounding block triangular zeros because rows below the pair vanish in its columns and columns before the pair vanish in its rows; the solved equations make the new lower-left block zero. Similarity preserves the characteristic polynomial and negative discriminant of a real $2\times2$ block, so whole conjugate pairs remain intact.

In the generalized case the two local equations give $S_{JJ}[R;I_q]=[L;I_q]B$ and $T_{JJ}[R;I_q]=[L;I_q]E$. Writing the graph matrices as $Z_1R_v$ and $Q_1R_w$ gives a zero lower-left block and a leading pair strictly equivalent to $(B,E)$. The full homogeneous determinant changes only by nonzero factors under exact left/right transforms [F7] and factors across diagonal pairs [F8]; cancelling the nonzero leading polynomial shows that the trailing pair has exactly the old first pair's homogeneous roots with multiplicity, including infinity and regularity. A real $2\times2$ pair with a finite nonreal conjugate root pair has nonsingular $T$ block, since otherwise its determinant polynomial has degree at most one. The prescribed QR restores triangularity of this block; applying the same left factor to both QZ arrays and to $Q$ changes the homogeneous determinant only by a nonzero factor and preserves the lower-left zero. An infinite scalar pair keeps its zero second coordinate and is never divided by it. The left update changes $Q$, while the right update changes $Z$, so the selected right deflating basis comes from $Z$.

The initial structure scan costs $O(d^2)$ scalar/evaluator units. Each local solve has order at most eight, each basis completion has bounded local dimension, and each panel update touches $O(d)$ entries; therefore $k$ attempts cost $O(d^2+kd)$. On success $k=I\le b(b-1)/2\le d(d-1)/2$, giving $O(d^3)$ worst-case swap work. Evaluating $L_0$ bounded-support input factors on $r$ columns costs $O(L_0dr+Idr)$; dense residual multiplication costs its separate $O(d^3)$. These counts do not bound algebraic bit cost or evaluator implementation cost.

Under the stated sufficient conditions, including enough $W$ for every scan through the final ordered return, steps 2.2 and 4.1–4.3 show that all selected blocks move before every complementary block without splitting real pairs; the first $r$ factor columns therefore span the selected invariant subspace or right deflating subspace of the represented computed form. Step 1.4 transports only the original unstructured residual certificate. Algorithm [F1] returns explicitly on boundary, separation, arithmetic, range, form, and budget failures; none of those statuses proves nonexistence of a stabilizing Riccati solution or supplies structured backward error.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n,m,p\ge1$, $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, and $C\in F^{p\times n}$. A matrix is **Hurwitz** when every complex eigenvalue has strictly negative real part, as in [[def-hurwitz-matrix-and-continuous-lyapunov-equation]]. It is **Schur stable** when every complex eigenvalue has modulus strictly less than one.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **continuously stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Hurwitz. The pair $(A,C)$ is **continuously detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Hurwitz.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **discretely stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Schur stable. The pair $(A,C)$ is **discretely detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Schur stable. These are exact existential properties of the given finite matrices. A residual size or an approximate spectral estimate does not itself establish any of them.

For $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n,m,p\ge1$, $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, and $C\in F^{p\times n}$, the following necessary conditions hold.

If $(A,B)$ is continuously stabilizable, then $\operatorname{rank}[\lambda I-A\;B]=n$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$. If it is discretely stabilizable, the same rank is $n$ for every $|\lambda|\ge1$.

If $(A,C)$ is continuously detectable, then $\operatorname{rank}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda I-A\\C\end{bmatrix}=n$ for every $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$. If it is discretely detectable, the same rank is $n$ for every $|\lambda|\ge1$.

This proves the necessary half of the PBH tests. The converse pole-placement implication is not asserted here.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $n,m\ge0$, and let $A\in F^{n\times n}$ and $B\in F^{n\times m}$. The real case is viewed over $\mathbb C$ when a complex spectral parameter or rank is used. Define
$$\mathcal R=\operatorname{span}_F\{A^jBe_\ell:0\le j<n,\ 1\le\ell\le m\},\qquad r=\dim_F\mathcal R,$$
where a span of an empty family is $\{0\}$. Then there is an invertible $P\in F^{n\times n}$ such that
$$P^{-1}AP=\begin{bmatrix}A_r&D\\0&A_u\end{bmatrix},\qquad P^{-1}B=\begin{bmatrix}B_r\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$
The pair $(A_r,B_r)$ is reachable on $F^r$ in the displayed algebraic sense, and empty blocks are permitted. For every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$,
$$\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}[\lambda I-A\ \ B]=n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lambda\notin\sigma_{\mathbb C}(A_u^{\mathbb C}),$$
where $A_u^{\mathbb C}$ is the complexification of $A_u$ when $F=\mathbb R$ and is $A_u$ itself when $F=\mathbb C$.

If $r=n$, then for every prescribed list $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n\in F$ there is a gain $K\in F^{m\times n}$ satisfying
$$\det(zI-A+BK)=\prod_{j=1}^n(z-\mu_j).$$
Thus a real reachable pair can be assigned any real pole list, including repetitions, and a complex reachable pair any complex list. The pole-placement claim does not assert arbitrary nonreal conjugate-pair placement for a real pair.

Let $A\in M_r(F)$ and $D\in M_s(F)$. For either block-triangular matrix

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&D\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{or}\quad M=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\C&D\end{pmatrix},$$

one has $\chi_M(x)=\chi_A(x)\chi_D(x)$, including $r=0$ or $s=0$.

For every finite matrix over a field,
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A)=\operatorname{crank}(A).$$
Both dimensions equal the number of pivots in any echelon form of $A$.

derivations.claim: Necessity in all four assertions is exactly [F2]. This proves the forward implications from stabilizability or detectability to the stated rank tests, including every point on each closed boundary.

Fix either forbidden closed region $\Omega=\{\lambda:\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0\}$ or $\Omega=\{\lambda:|\lambda|\ge1\}$. Suppose the horizontal rank test holds for all $\lambda\in\Omega$, and apply [F3] to $(A,B)$ over the original field $F$. The uncontrollable block $A_u$ has no eigenvalue in $\Omega$, so its eigenvalues lie in the open left half-plane or open unit disk, respectively. Assign the reachable block repeated pole $-1$ or $0$ by [F3], obtaining $K_r$. With its decomposition matrix $P$, set $K=[K_r\ 0]P^{-1}$; if $r=0$ take $K=0$, and if $r=n$ omit the empty trailing block. Then $P^{-1}(A-BK)P=\begin{bmatrix}A_r-B_rK_r&D\\0&A_u\end{bmatrix}$. By [F4] its eigenvalues are the assigned stable poles and those of $A_u$, with multiplicity; hence $A-BK$ is Hurwitz or Schur stable, and $K\in F^{m\times n}$.

For every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$, $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}[\bar\lambda I-A^*\ \ C^*]=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda I-A\\C\end{bmatrix}$ because these matrices are adjoints and [F5] applies. Each forbidden region is invariant under conjugation, so its vertical test for $(A,C)$ is the horizontal test for $(A^*,C^*)$. Step 1.2 supplies $J\in F^{p\times n}$ with $A^*-C^*J$ Hurwitz or Schur stable. Its adjoint $A-J^*C$ has conjugate eigenvalues with the same real parts and moduli, so $L=J^*\in F^{n\times p}$ is the required injection. This proves both detectability converses, including their boundary cases.
