The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ with $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
and $m\ge n$.

1. Successive Householder reflectors or Givens transformations can zero the
   subdiagonal entries column by column and produce a full QR factorisation
   $A=QR$ and hence a reduced QR factorisation $A=\widehat Q\widehat R$.
2. In dense real arithmetic, Householder QR uses
   $$2mn^2-\frac{2}{3}n^3+O(mn)$$
   scalar operations, while dense Givens QR uses
   $$3mn^2-n^3+O(mn)$$
   scalar operations.

Assume AC, and let $d,n,p$ be positive integers. Let $U\in\mathbb R^d$,
$q\in\mathbb R^n$, and $r\in\mathbb R^p$ be mutually independent Gaussian vectors with
$$U\sim N_d(m,P),\qquad q\sim N_n(0,Q),\qquad r\sim N_p(0,R),$$
where $P,Q,R$ are symmetric positive semidefinite. Let
$F\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ and $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$, and set
$$X=FU+q,\qquad Y=HX+r,\qquad P^-:=FPF^T+Q,\qquad S:=HP^-H^T+R.$$
If $S$ is positive definite, put $K:=P^-H^TS^{-1}$. Then $(X,Y)$ is jointly
Gaussian with mean $(Fm,HFm)$ and covariance
$$\begin{pmatrix}P^-&P^-H^T\\HP^-&S\end{pmatrix},$$
and for every $y\in\mathbb R^p$ an everywhere-defined conditional law is
$$\mathcal L(X\mid Y=y)=N_n\!\left(Fm+K(y-HFm),\,P^--KSK^T\right).$$
The conditional covariance is positive semidefinite even if $P$, $Q$, or
$R$ is singular. It also equals the Joseph expression
$$(I-KH)P^-(I-KH)^T+KRK^T.$$
No inverse of a state, process-noise, or measurement-noise covariance is
used.

derivations.claim: Write $\bar r_R$ and $\bar r_-$ for the padded column counts. They satisfy $\bar r_R\ge p$ and $\bar r_-\ge n$, so $Z^T$ has $\bar r_R+\bar r_-\ge p+n$ rows, as required for the reduced QR. Padding either factor with zero columns leaves its Gram matrix unchanged. Multiplication of the prearray by its transpose therefore gives $$ZZ^T=\begin{bmatrix} L_R^{\mathrm{pad}}(L_R^{\mathrm{pad}})^T+HL^-_{\mathrm{pad}}(L^-_{\mathrm{pad}})^TH^T&HL^-_{\mathrm{pad}}(L^-_{\mathrm{pad}})^T\\ L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}(L^-_{\mathrm{pad}})^TH^T&L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}(L^-_{\mathrm{pad}})^T \end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}S&HP^-\\P^-H^T&P^- \end{bmatrix}.$$

Initially set $L^0=R^T$ and partition it at dimensions $p,n$. Since $Z^T=UR$ and $U^TU=I$, $L^0(L^0)^T=R^TR=ZZ^T$. Block multiplication gives $L^0_{11}(L^0_{11})^T=S$, $L^0_{21}(L^0_{11})^T=P^-H^T$, and $L^0_{21}(L^0_{21})^T+L^0_{22}(L^0_{22})^T=P^-$. The positive-definite matrix $S=L^0_{11}(L^0_{11})^T$ makes $L^0_{11}$ invertible, so its diagonal entries are nonzero. Let $D$ be the diagonal matrix whose entries are the signs of those entries, and set $L=L^0\operatorname{diag}(D,I_n)$. This flips the first $p$ columns of $L^0$, making the diagonal of $L_{11}=L^0_{11}D$ positive. Because $\operatorname{diag}(D,I_n)$ is orthogonal, $LL^T=L^0(L^0)^T$; moreover $L_{21}=L^0_{21}D$ and $L_{22}=L^0_{22}$. Hence all three displayed block identities remain true.

Because $S\succ0$ and $S=L_{11}L_{11}^T$, the square matrix $L_{11}$ is invertible. From the cross-block identity, $L_{21}=P^-H^T L_{11}^{-T}$; hence $$L_{21}L_{21}^T=P^-H^TL_{11}^{-T}L_{11}^{-1}HP^- =P^-H^TS^{-1}HP^-.$$ Subtracting this equality from the lower-right identity in step 2.1 gives the stated posterior covariance. Since it is also $L_{22}L_{22}^T$, it is positive semidefinite even when $L_{22}$ is singular.

The solve $L_{11}z=v$ gives $$L_{21}z=L_{21}L_{11}^{-1}v =P^-H^TL_{11}^{-T}L_{11}^{-1}v =P^-H^TS^{-1}v.$$ When $n,p\ge1$ and these blocks arise in a model satisfying [F2], these are its one-step Gaussian conditional update formulas; for zero-dimensional blocks this lemma asserts only the matrix identities. The matrix calculations themselves are deterministic and use no choice beyond [A1].

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $x=(x_j),y=(y_j)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the dot product
$x\cdot y=\sum_{j<n}x_jy_j$ computed from left to right in an arithmetic model
with unit roundoff $u$ satisfying $nu<1$
([[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]), where every
product $x_jy_j$, every rounded product
$p_j:=\operatorname{fl}(x_jy_j)$, and every intermediate sum lies in the normal
range. Let $s_1:=p_0$ and, for $1\le k<n$, let
$s_{k+1}:=\operatorname{fl}(s_k+p_k)$. Then:

1. **Componentwise form.** There are reals $\delta_0,\dots,\delta_{n-1}$ with
   $|\delta_j|\le\gamma_n:=nu/(1-nu)$ such that
   $$s_n=\sum_{j<n}x_jy_j(1+\delta_j).$$
2. **Normwise form.**
   $$|s_n-x\cdot y|\;\le\;\gamma_n\sum_{j<n}|x_jy_j|\;\le\;\gamma_n\,\lVert x\rVert_1\lVert y\rVert_1,$$
   where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$ is the published $1$-norm
   ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]])
   and $|\cdot|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]).

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $m\ge n\ge1$, undergo successful QR steps of [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]], with $mu<1$. Use $\kappa_m$ from [[lem-scaled-householder-step-meets-local-backward-error-premise]] and set $\beta_Q=(1+\kappa_m)^n-1$. The exact orthogonal product represented by the stored reflectors has reduced first $n$ columns $\widehat Q$, and the computed triangular block is $\widehat R$. Then
$$A+\Delta A=\widehat Q\widehat R,\qquad \|\Delta A\|_F\le\beta_Q\|A\|_F.$$
If applying the stored reflectors in the same order to a separate vector $b$, by their rounded rank-one updates without column overwrites, succeeds at every update, the resulting full vector $\widehat c$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat c-Q_{\rm full}^Tb\|_2\le\beta_Q\|b\|_2.$$
The bounds are $O(u)$ for fixed dimensions. An explicitly rounded dense product for $Q_{\rm full}$ is not asserted exactly orthogonal.

Let $G,E\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and set $\widehat G=G+E$. Then
$$\|\widehat G\widehat G^T-GG^T\|_F \le 2\|G\|_F\|E\|_F+\|E\|_F^2.$$
The estimate is valid for all ranks, including $G=0$ and rank-deficient
factors.

Let $q\ge n\ge1$, $u>0$, and let $\kappa_q$ be the local scaled-Householder
coefficient of [[lem-scaled-householder-step-meets-local-backward-error-premise]]
at active row dimension $q$. Set
$$\beta_{q,n}=(1+\kappa_q)^n-1,\qquad C_{q,n}=200qn.$$
If $C_{q,n}u<1$, then
$$\beta_{q,n}\le\eta_{q,n}:=\frac{C_{q,n}u}{1-C_{q,n}u}.$$
Thus the QR backward-error factor can be bounded by the stated rational
dimension-dependent expression in this precision range.

derivations.claim: Exact-zero operations satisfy the relative model with error factor zero, so the rounded-factor expansion underlying [F1] also covers zero products and partial sums in the present model. An empty inner product is exact zero. For each entry of a nonempty product $UV$, [F1] therefore gives an error at most $\gamma_r\sum_j|U_{ij}V_{jk}|$. Apply [F5] to the vectors $(|U_{ij}|)_j$ and $(|V_{jk}|)_j$, then square and sum over entries: $$\sum_{i,k}\left(\sum_j|U_{ij}||V_{jk}|\right)^2 \le\sum_{i,k}\left(\sum_j|U_{ij}|^2\right) \left(\sum_j|V_{jk}|^2\right) =\|U\|_F^2\|V\|_F^2.$$ Therefore $\|\widehat{UV}-UV\|_F\le\gamma_r\|U\|_F\|V\|_F$. Disjoint product blocks add by the Frobenius norm definition, and separately bounded input-factor errors add by the triangle inequality.

Apply [F2] to $\widehat G^T$, which has $q\ge n$ rows and $n$ columns. Transposing its factorization gives $$\widehat G+\Delta^T=R^T\widehat Q^T=L\widehat Q^T, \qquad \|\Delta^T\|_F\le\beta_{q,n}\|\widehat G\|_F.$$ Set $E=(\widehat G-G)+\Delta^T$. Then $\|E\|_F\le\epsilon$. Since $\widehat Q^T\widehat Q=I$, the transposed factorization also gives $$LL^T=L\widehat Q^T\widehat QL^T =(G+E)(G+E)^T.$$

Apply [F3] to the factor identity and perturbation $E$ from step 1.2. It gives $\|LL^T-GG^T\|_F\le2\|G\|_F\epsilon+\epsilon^2$ for the stated $\beta_{q,n}$ choice. Under $200qnu<1$, [F4] makes this epsilon no larger than the version using $\eta_{q,n}$. Since $t\mapsto2\|G\|_Ft+t^2$ is increasing for $t\ge0$, the same covariance bound follows with the rational-envelope epsilon. The argument permits zero singular values and places no structural restriction on the perturbation of $GG^T$.

citations.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_k$ for
$0\le k\le T$, and positive observation dimensions $p_k$ for
$1\le k\le T$. Inputs are real finite matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times
d_{k-1}}$, $H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, observation vectors
$y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$, and an initial mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$.
For each covariance supply a rectangular real factor
$$L_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times r_0},\qquad L_{Q,k}\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times r_{Q,k}},\qquad L_{R,k}\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times r_{R,k}},$$
where each column count is any finite nonnegative integer. The represented
covariances are $P_0=L_0L_0^T$, $Q_k=L_{Q,k}L_{Q,k}^T$, and
$R_k=L_{R,k}L_{R,k}^T$. Thus zero columns and rank-deficient factors are
allowed. The admissible statistical inputs are those of
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] for which
the canonical innovation $S_k=H_kP_k^-H_k^T+R_k$ is positive definite at each
step. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited only for the
interpretation as a posterior; the finite matrix procedure itself uses no
probability-space choice.

Choose a unit roundoff $u$ in the no-underflow operationwise model of
[[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]].
During an update, whenever an entry $a$ of a supplied matrix, factor, or
vector is read as an arithmetic operand or copied into a QR prearray, first
convert it to $\operatorname{fl}(a)$ in that format. Return `range-failure`
at that read if conversion fails under the same no-underflow rule. Read
operands from left to right; for products and block copies, visit output
entries column by column, with increasing row index within each column.
Repeat the conversion on each such read; the supplied arrays themselves
remain unchanged. The formulas below use these converted entries during
execution, while $P_0,Q_k,R_k,F_k,H_k,y_k,m_0$ denote the original exact
target data in comparisons with the canonical recursion. In particular,
conversion errors must be included in any certified local error bounds.
For $T=0$, return the input pair immediately without reading or converting
its entries.
Every matrix or vector product below is evaluated as left-to-right dot
products. A nonzero nonnormal intermediate, nonfinite result, zero innovation
diagonal, or failed factorization returns a status and the first failing step;
it is not coerced into a covariance
estimate. Each arithmetic and factorization failure has a declared return;
there is no iterative convergence loop or unbounded refinement search.

The QR operation used below is the following unpivoted reduced procedure on
$A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with floating-point entries and $m\ge n\ge1$. Initialize a working array
$R^{(0)}=A$ and an empty ordered reflector list. For $j=1,\ldots,n$, take
$x=R^{(j-1)}_{j:m,j}$ and $B=R^{(j-1)}_{j:m,j+1:n}$, call
[[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] on $(x,B)$,
and, on success, replace the active block by its returned $C_+$. If the call
fails, return its first status and step. Store the exact orthogonal reflector
represented by the returned record, or the identity for its identity branch.
After $n$ successful steps, return the computed upper-triangular block
$R=R^{(n)}_{1:n,1:n}$ and the ordered reflector list representing the exact
product $Q_{\rm full}$ whose first $n$ columns are the reduced $Q$ factor.
Do not materialize a rounded dense $Q$. The conventions are those of
[[def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations]].

Initialize $m_{0|0}=m_0$ and $L_{0|0}=L_0$. At step $k$, perform the
following operations in order.

1. Compute the rounded mean prediction $\widehat m_{k|k-1}
=\operatorname{fl}(F_k\widehat m_{k-1|k-1})$. Form the rounded factor product
$\widehat X_k=\operatorname{fl}(F_kL_{k-1|k-1})$. Concatenate
$\widehat G_k=[\widehat X_k\;L_{Q,k}]$ and append zero columns until its
column count is $q_k=\max(d_k,r_{k-1|k-1}+r_{Q,k})$. Apply the above
reduced Householder QR procedure to
$\widehat G_k^T\in\mathbb R^{q_k\times d_k}$. On success let $R_k^{p}$ be
its reduced upper factor and set $L_{k|k-1}= (R_k^{p})^T$. No diagonal
positivity or full-rank condition is imposed on this prediction factor.

2. Compute $\widehat v_k=\operatorname{fl}
(y_k-\operatorname{fl}(H_k\widehat m_{k|k-1}))$. Pad $L_{R,k}$ with zero
columns to $\bar r_k=\max(p_k,r_{R,k})$ columns. Compute
$\widehat Y_k=\operatorname{fl}(H_kL_{k|k-1})$ and form the block prearray
$$\widehat Z_k= \begin{bmatrix} L_{R,k}^{\mathrm{pad}} & \widehat Y_k\\ 0 & L_{k|k-1} \end{bmatrix}.$$
Apply the above reduced Householder QR procedure to
$\widehat Z_k^T\in\mathbb R^{(\bar r_k+d_k)\times(p_k+d_k)}$. Its row
count is at least its column count: the prediction step gives
$L_{k|k-1}\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_k}$, and $\bar r_k\ge p_k$. On success
transpose its reduced upper factor and partition the resulting lower factor as
$$\widehat L_k=\begin{bmatrix}\widehat L_{11,k}&0\\ \widehat L_{21,k}&\widehat L_{22,k}\end{bmatrix},$$
with block sizes $p_k$ and $d_k$. If any diagonal entry of $\widehat
L_{11,k}$ is zero, return `innovation-factorization-failure`. Otherwise,
for each $i=1,\ldots,p_k$, multiply column $i$ of the whole factor
$\widehat L_k$ by the sign of its diagonal entry. These exact sign changes
make $\widehat L_{11,k}$ have positive diagonal and preserve
$\widehat L_k\widehat L_k^T$ and its lower block structure. Use the resulting
factor blocks below. No invertibility or positive diagonal is required of
$\widehat L_{22,k}$.

3. Solve $\widehat L_{11,k}\widehat z_k=\widehat v_k$ by forward
substitution in the order of
[[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]]. Set
$$\widehat m_{k|k}=\operatorname{fl} (\widehat m_{k|k-1}+\widehat L_{21,k}\widehat z_k),\qquad L_{k|k}=\widehat L_{22,k}.$$
Do not form a covariance downdate or an explicit matrix inverse. The
factor-defined covariance $L_{k|k}L_{k|k}^T$ is positive semidefinite as an
exact product of the returned entries; no claim is made that a separately
rounded materialization of that product remains positive semidefinite.

4. If any arithmetic operation or QR call returns a failure status, return the
first such failure and its step; if the leading innovation block has a zero
diagonal, return innovation-factorization-failure. Otherwise the finite loop
returns the predicted and updated mean/factor arrays with success. The success
status records arithmetic and factorization completion only.

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the output is $(m_0,L_0)$ with no update
status. In exact arithmetic, the result implements the covariance and mean map of
[[alg-kalman-filter]]. The prediction factor identity is supplied by
[[lem-square-root-kalman-prediction-factor-identity]], and the measurement
block identity by
[[lem-square-root-kalman-measurement-block-factor-identity]]. Under the
inherited AC assumption
its statistical interpretation is the one in
[[thm-kalman-filter-is-exact-posterior]]. The nearby covariance supplied by
an unstructured QR backward error may introduce cross-correlations between
model blocks. Therefore no backward-stability claim within the original
independent-noise state-space model, and no uniform-in-time accuracy or
stability claim, is part of this procedure.

On every admitted finite input of [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]], the formation and application procedure terminates with its specified identity, reflector or first-failure return. Each specified separate-block application also terminates with its output or first failure. The zero-column branch returns the identity action and the copied block without evaluating a reflector denominator. In a successful nonzero-column branch the stored vector is nonzero, so its associated exact real reflector is orthogonal and also acts unitarily on complex blocks. This statement asserts neither unconditional arithmetic success nor a backward-error bound for a successful call.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge 1$, and let $b\in F^n$.

If $L=(\ell_{ij})\in M_n(F)$ is lower triangular with every diagonal entry
$\ell_{ii}\ne 0$, the **forward substitution solve** of $Lx=b$ is the recursive
construction

$$x_i:=\frac{1}{\ell_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j<i}\ell_{ij}x_j\right)\qquad(0\le i<n).$$If $U=(u_{ij})\in M_n(F)$ is upper triangular with every diagonal entry $u_{ii}\ne 0$, the **backward substitution solve** of $Ux=b$ is the recursive construction$$x_i:=\frac{1}{u_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j>i}u_{ij}x_j\right)\qquad(n-1\ge i\ge 0).$$

The triangular vocabulary is from
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. The matrix
product convention from [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] is the one
used when later items rewrite these recursions as matrix equations.

derivations.claim: Every matrix or vector product in [F1] is evaluated by finitely many left-to-right dot products because all dimensions are finite. Each scalar operation, including conversion of a supplied entry at its read, either returns a finite value in the declared arithmetic model or the first range-failure status. Concatenation, zero padding, and block partitioning use finitely many entries.

Each QR call processes a finite number of columns and, within a column, a finite number of active entries. By [F2], each reflector step terminates with an identity, reflector, or range-failure result; hence a QR call either returns its reduced factor or a finite failure status. The lower-triangular innovation solve has finitely many forward-substitution row updates by [F3]; its diagonal is nonzero because [F1] returns failure before the solve otherwise.

A reduced Householder QR call on an $M\times N$ array ($M\ge N\ge1$) has $N$ passes. Pass $j$ forms a reflector using $O(M-j+1)$ scalar operations and applies it to at most $N-j$ trailing columns using $O((M-j+1)(N-j))$ operations; scans and status checks have no larger order. Summing over $j$ gives $O(MN^2)$. Hence the prediction and measurement QR calls at step $k$ cost $O(q_kd_k^2)$ and $O((\bar r_k+d_k)(p_k+d_k)^2)$, respectively. A failure can only shorten these loops.

The outer loop has at most $T$ steps, and for $T=0$ the algorithm returns its initial pair immediately. By steps 1.1 and 1.2, every entered step terminates; therefore the whole procedure returns after finitely many operations with a declared status. No success or accuracy guarantee is asserted by this termination result.

The products $F_k\widehat m_{k-1|k-1}$ and $F_kL_{k-1|k-1}$ cost $O(d_kd_{k-1})$ and $O(d_kd_{k-1}\rho_{k-1})$. The product $H_kL_{k|k-1}$ costs $O(p_kd_k^2)$; the innovation product, triangular solve, factor sign changes, and all block copying/padding cost at most $O((\bar r_k+d_k)(p_k+d_k)^2+q_kd_k^2)$ because $p_k,d_k\ge1$, $q_k\ge r_{Q,k}$, and $\bar r_k\ge r_{R,k}$. Input conversions add at most one scalar rounding per supplied operand read or copied entry, so they do not change these orders. Together with step 1.3, summing over $k$ gives the stated count. For $T=0$ there is only the constant-time return, with no entry conversions.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_T$,
and positive observation dimensions $p_1,\ldots,p_T$. The input is a
linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with
matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_{k-1}}$ and
$H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, initial mean $m_0$, and symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariances $P_0,Q_k,R_k$. Its state and observation
equations are
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k,$$
where $q_k\sim N(0,Q_k)$ and $r_k\sim N(0,R_k)$ are centered and mutually
independent across all times and of $X_0$.

The admissible data are vectors $y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$ for which every
innovation covariance encountered below is positive definite. Positive
definite means $u^TS_ku>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$. The
algorithm returns predicted and updated means and covariances and the
innovation and gain at each time. Initialize
$$m_{0|0}=m_0,\qquad P_{0|0}=P_0.$$
For $k=1,\ldots,T$, perform:

1. Predict:
$$m_{k|k-1}=F_km_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k.$$
2. Form the innovation and its covariance:
$$v_k=y_k-H_km_{k|k-1},\qquad S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k.$$
3. Factor $S_k=L_kL_k^T$ with lower-triangular $L_k$ having positive
diagonal, using
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Solve $L_kU_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. This
defines $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, hence
$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}$, without explicitly forming $S_k^{-1}$.
4. Update:
$$m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the returned pair is $(m_0,P_0)$. No
inverse of $P_0$, $Q_k$, or $R_k$ is used. This item defines the procedure
and makes no complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim.

Let $P^-=L^- (L^-)^T$ and $R=L_RL_R^T$, with real factors of arbitrary
rank. Let $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ and suppose
$$S=H P^-H^T+R\succ0.$$
Pad $L_R$ with zero columns to at least $p$ columns and $L^-$ with zero
columns to at least $n$ columns. Denote the resulting factors by
$L_R^{\mathrm{pad}}$ and $L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}$, and form
$$Z=\begin{bmatrix}L_R^{\mathrm{pad}}&HL^-_{\mathrm{pad}}\\0&L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}\end{bmatrix}.$$
Then $Z^T$ has at least $p+n$ rows. Take an exact reduced QR factorization
$Z^T=UR$ with $U^TU=I$ and set $L=R^T$. For each $i=1,\ldots,p$,
multiply column $i$ of $L$ by the sign of its diagonal entry. This makes the
first $p$ diagonal entries positive; the signs are well defined because
$S\succ0$. Partition the resulting $L$ as
$$L=\begin{bmatrix}L_{11}&0\\L_{21}&L_{22}\end{bmatrix}$$
at the observation and state dimensions. Then
$$L_{11}L_{11}^T=S,\qquad L_{21}L_{11}^T=P^-H^T,$$
and
$$L_{22}L_{22}^T=P^- -P^-H^TS^{-1}HP^-.$$
For innovation $v=y-Hm^-$, the exact solve $L_{11}z=v$ gives
$m^-+L_{21}z=m^-+P^-H^TS^{-1}v$. Thus the factor update has exactly the
canonical one-step mean and covariance; $L_{22}$ may be singular.

Let $G\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}$, with $q\ge n\ge1$, be an exact prediction or
measurement prearray. Work in the operationwise no-underflow model with
$0<u<1$ and $qu<1$. Let $\widehat G$ be its computed version and assume
$$\|\widehat G-G\|_F\le e_{\mathrm{form}}+e_{\mathrm{in}},$$
where $e_{\mathrm{form}},e_{\mathrm{in}}\ge0$, $e_{\mathrm{form}}$ bounds
rounded products used to form the array, and $e_{\mathrm{in}}$ bounds
separately specified input-factor uncertainty. If
the successful scaled-Householder QR of $\widehat G^T\in\mathbb R^{q\times
n}$ has reduced upper factor $R$ and $L=R^T$, set
$$\kappa_q=\kappa_q(u),\qquad \beta_{q,n}=(1+\kappa_q)^n-1,\qquad \epsilon=e_{\mathrm{form}}+e_{\mathrm{in}}+ \beta_{q,n}\|\widehat G\|_F,$$
where $\kappa_q$ is the explicit local coefficient in
[[lem-scaled-householder-step-meets-local-backward-error-premise]]. Then
$$\|LL^T-GG^T\|_F\le2\|G\|_F\epsilon+\epsilon^2.$$
If $200qnu<1$, the rational envelope lemma
[[lem-square-root-kalman-householder-error-rational-envelope]] gives
$\beta_{q,n}\le\eta_{q,n}:=200qnu/(1-200qnu)$. In that regime the same
conclusion holds with
$\epsilon=e_{\mathrm{form}}+e_{\mathrm{in}}+\eta_{q,n}\|\widehat G\|_F$.
For one left-to-right rounded product $\widehat{UV}$ with positive inner
dimension $r\ge1$ and $ru<1$, a valid choice is
$e_{\mathrm{form}}=\gamma_r\|U\|_F\|V\|_F$. A product with zero inner
dimension is exactly zero and contributes zero to $e_{\mathrm{form}}$; for

conclusion allows rank loss and does not imply
that the nearby joint covariance has the original independent-noise block
structure.

Let $S=S^T\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ satisfy
$x^TSx\ge\mu\|x\|_2^2$ for all $x\in\mathbb R^p$, with $\mu>0$.
Let $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, $D=D^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, and
let symmetric $E_S$ and matrices $E_B,E_D$ satisfy
$$\|E_S\|_F\le e_S<\mu,\qquad \|E_B\|_F\le e_B,\qquad \|E_D\|_F\le e_D.$$
Put $\widehat S=S+E_S$, $\widehat B=B+E_B$,
$\widehat D=D+E_D$, $\Phi=D-BS^{-1}B^T$, and
$\widehat\Phi=\widehat D-\widehat B\widehat S^{-1}\widehat B^T$.
If $b\ge\|B\|_2$, define $\beta=(\mu-e_S)^{-1}$. Then
$\widehat S\succeq(\mu-e_S)I\succ0$ and
$$\|\widehat S^{-1}\|_2\le\beta,\qquad \|\widehat S^{-1}-S^{-1}\|_2\le\mu^{-1}\beta e_S,$$
$$\|\widehat B\widehat S^{-1}-BS^{-1}\|_2 \le e_B\beta+b\mu^{-1}\beta e_S,$$
and
$$\|\widehat\Phi-\Phi\|_2 \le e_D+2b e_B\beta+b^2\mu^{-1}\beta e_S+e_B^2\beta.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $p\ge1$ and $T\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be nonsingular, define
$$
\sigma_{\min}(T):=\min_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Tx\|_2,
$$
and let $z_*=T^{-1}y$. For any computed vector $\widehat z$ with residual
$r=T\widehat z-y$,
$$
\|\widehat z-z_*\|_2\le\frac{\|r\|_2}{\sigma_{\min}(T)}.
$$
If $S=TT^T$ also satisfies $x^TSx\ge\nu\|x\|_2^2$ for all $x$, with
$\nu>0$, then $\sigma_{\min}(T)\ge\sqrt\nu$ and therefore
$$
\|\widehat z-z_*\|_2\le\frac{\|r\|_2}{\sqrt\nu}.
$$

derivations.claim: Put $\delta_{k-1}^P=\|\widehat P_{k-1|k-1}-P_{k-1|k-1}\|_2$ and $\delta_{k-1}^m=\|\widehat m_{k-1|k-1}-m_{k-1|k-1}\|_2$. By [F1], [F5] and the prediction defect, $$\|\widehat P_k^--P_k^-\|_2 \le f_k^2\delta_{k-1}^P+e_k^P,\qquad \|\widehat m_k^--m_k^-\|_2 \le f_k\delta_{k-1}^m+e_k^m.$$

Let $C_H=\begin{bmatrix}H_k\\I\end{bmatrix}$. Direct block multiplication gives $J_k(\widehat P_k^-)-J_k(P_k^-)=C_H(\widehat P_k^--P_k^-)C_H^T$. For every $x$, $\|C_Hx\|_2^2=\|H_kx\|_2^2+\|x\|_2^2\le (1+h_k^2)\|x\|_2^2$, so [F5] and the joint defect imply $$\|\widehat J_k-J_k(P_k^-)\|_2 \le(1+h_k^2)(f_k^2\delta_{k-1}^P+e_k^P)+e_k^J.$$ If $\delta_{k-1}^P\le\Delta_{k-1}$, the right side is at most $\varepsilon_k$. Each of its observation, cross, and state blocks therefore has operator error at most $\varepsilon_k$: every block is obtained by left- and right-multiplying by coordinate projections of operator norm at most one, so [F5] and submultiplicativity give the bound.

Assume $\delta_{k-1}^P\le\Delta_{k-1}$ and suppress $k$. Write $E_S=\widehat S-S$, $E_B=\widehat B-B$, and $E_D=\widehat D-P^-$. Step 2.1 bounds their operator norms by $\varepsilon\le\mu/2$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|x^TE_Sx|\le\varepsilon\|x\|_2^2$, hence $\widehat S\succeq(\mu-\varepsilon)I\succ0$. The same inequality applied to $y=Sx$ and $y=\widehat Sx$ gives $\|S^{-1}\|_2\le\mu^{-1}$ and $\|\widehat S^{-1}\|_2\le\beta:=(\mu-\varepsilon)^{-1}\le2/\mu$. The resolvent identity $\widehat S^{-1}-S^{-1}=-S^{-1}E_S\widehat S^{-1}$ then bounds the inverse difference by $\mu^{-1}\beta\varepsilon$. Expanding the gain and Schur differences as in [F4], now applying operator-norm triangle and product inequalities throughout, yields $$\|\widehat B\widehat S^{-1}-BS^{-1}\|_2\le\beta\varepsilon+b\mu^{-1}\beta\varepsilon\le C^K\varepsilon,$$ $$\|\widehat P_{k|k}-P_{k|k}\|_2\le\varepsilon+2b\beta\varepsilon+b^2\mu^{-1}\beta\varepsilon+\beta\varepsilon^2\le C^P\varepsilon.$$ Here [F2] identifies the represented posterior as the Schur complement, and $\beta\varepsilon^2\le\varepsilon$. Finally, $\|\widehat B\widehat S^{-1}\|_2\le(b+\varepsilon)\beta\le1+2b/\mu=K^\#$. These estimates use operator block bounds directly, without a Frobenius conversion.

The innovation residual and computed-innovation defect give $$\|\widehat v_k-v_k\|_2\le h_k\|\widehat m_k^--m_k^-\|_2+e_k^v.$$ Let $z_k^*=\widehat L_{11,k}^{-1}\widehat v_k$. By [F6] and the $\widehat S_k\succeq(\mu_k/2)I$ bound from step 3.1, $\|\widehat z_k-z_k^*\|_2\le\sqrt{2/\mu_k}\,\rho_k$, as included in the Statement. Because $\widehat L_{11,k}\widehat z_k=\widehat v_k+\xi_k$ with $\|\xi_k\|_2\le\rho_k$, [F2] gives $\widehat L_{21,k}\widehat z_k= \widehat B_k\widehat S_k^{-1}(\widehat v_k+\xi_k)$. Subtract the exact mean equation in [F1], insert and subtract $\widehat B_k\widehat S_k^{-1}v_k$, and use step 3.1. The result is $$\|\widehat m_{k|k}-m_{k|k}\|_2\le (1+h_kK_k^\#)(f_k\delta_{k-1}^m+e_k^m) +C_k^K\varepsilon_k r_k+ K_k^\#(e_k^v+\rho_k)+e_k^u.$$

Add the covariance bound in step 3.1 to the mean bound in step 4.1. Using $\delta_{k-1}^P,\delta_{k-1}^m\le\Delta_{k-1}$ and the definition of $\varepsilon_k$ yields $$\|\widehat m_{k|k}-m_{k|k}\|_2+ \|\widehat P_{k|k}-P_{k|k}\|_2 \le A_k\Delta_{k-1}+\eta_k=\Delta_k.$$ Induction from the stated $\Delta_0$ proves the bound for each $k$. Repeated substitution of the scalar recurrence gives the displayed product-and-sum formula at $T$. Since each assumption and step concerns only the finite indices $1,\ldots,T$, no uniform-in-time conclusion follows.

Let $P^-=L^- (L^-)^T$ and $R=L_RL_R^T$, with real factors of arbitrary
rank. Let $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ and suppose
$$S=H P^-H^T+R\succ0.$$
Pad $L_R$ with zero columns to at least $p$ columns and $L^-$ with zero
columns to at least $n$ columns. Denote the resulting factors by
$L_R^{\mathrm{pad}}$ and $L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}$, and form
$$Z=\begin{bmatrix}L_R^{\mathrm{pad}}&HL^-_{\mathrm{pad}}\\0&L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}\end{bmatrix}.$$
Then $Z^T$ has at least $p+n$ rows. Take an exact reduced QR factorization
$Z^T=UR$ with $U^TU=I$ and set $L=R^T$. For each $i=1,\ldots,p$,
multiply column $i$ of $L$ by the sign of its diagonal entry. This makes the
first $p$ diagonal entries positive; the signs are well defined because
$S\succ0$. Partition the resulting $L$ as
$$L=\begin{bmatrix}L_{11}&0\\L_{21}&L_{22}\end{bmatrix}$$
at the observation and state dimensions. Then
$$L_{11}L_{11}^T=S,\qquad L_{21}L_{11}^T=P^-H^T,$$
and
$$L_{22}L_{22}^T=P^- -P^-H^TS^{-1}HP^-.$$
For innovation $v=y-Hm^-$, the exact solve $L_{11}z=v$ gives
$m^-+L_{21}z=m^-+P^-H^TS^{-1}v$. Thus the factor update has exactly the
canonical one-step mean and covariance; $L_{22}$ may be singular.

derivations.claim: The exact Gram matrix is $$ZZ^T=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}.$$ Its innovation variance is $2$, its cross covariance is $1$, and its exact posterior covariance is $1-1/2=1/2$.

The perturbed array and its Gram matrix are $$\widehat Z=\begin{bmatrix}1&11/10\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad \widehat Z\widehat Z^T= \begin{bmatrix}221/100&11/10\\11/10&1\end{bmatrix}.$$ Here $\|E\|_F=1/10$, $\|Z\|_F=\sqrt3$, and the Gram difference is $\begin{bmatrix}21/100&1/10\\1/10&0\end{bmatrix}$, whose Frobenius norm is $\sqrt{641}/100$; it is bounded by [F1]. The perturbed innovation remains positive, and its Schur complement is $$1-\frac{(11/10)^2}{221/100} =1-\frac{121}{221}=\frac{100}{221}>0.$$ This differs from $1/2$ by $-21/442$.

By [F2], the perturbed Schur complement is exactly the represented factor product $L_{22}L_{22}^T$, so it is positive semidefinite; here it is the positive scalar $100/221$. The nonzero prearray perturbation changes the posterior covariance, while the factor representation retains positive semidefiniteness.

At each precision, let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be an instance of [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]] specialized to a finite binary format of integer precision $p\ge2$ and integer normal-exponent bounds $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$. Its normal values are $\pm m2^{j-p+1}$ for integers $2^{p-1}\le m<2^p$ and $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$, with $N_{\min}=2^{j_{\min}}$ and $N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{j_{\max}-p+1}$. The rounding rule is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even by the parity of the normalized significand. Each precision in a mixed-precision procedure has its own format, range, and valid unit-roundoff bound. On every real exact result that is zero or normal, $\operatorname{fl}$ uses this rule; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range $x$, $\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt{x})$ is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression $ab+c$; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_T$,
and positive observation dimensions $p_1,\ldots,p_T$. The input is a
linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with
matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_{k-1}}$ and
$H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, initial mean $m_0$, and symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariances $P_0,Q_k,R_k$. Its state and observation
equations are
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k,$$
where $q_k\sim N(0,Q_k)$ and $r_k\sim N(0,R_k)$ are centered and mutually
independent across all times and of $X_0$.

The admissible data are vectors $y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$ for which every
innovation covariance encountered below is positive definite. Positive
definite means $u^TS_ku>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$. The
algorithm returns predicted and updated means and covariances and the
innovation and gain at each time. Initialize
$$m_{0|0}=m_0,\qquad P_{0|0}=P_0.$$
For $k=1,\ldots,T$, perform:

1. Predict:
$$m_{k|k-1}=F_km_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k.$$
2. Form the innovation and its covariance:
$$v_k=y_k-H_km_{k|k-1},\qquad S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k.$$
3. Factor $S_k=L_kL_k^T$ with lower-triangular $L_k$ having positive
diagonal, using
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Solve $L_kU_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. This
defines $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, hence
$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}$, without explicitly forming $S_k^{-1}$.
4. Update:
$$m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the returned pair is $(m_0,P_0)$. No
inverse of $P_0$, $Q_k$, or $R_k$ is used. This item defines the procedure
and makes no complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim.

Let $P^-=L^- (L^-)^T$ and $R=L_RL_R^T$, with real factors of arbitrary

$$L_{11}L_{11}^T=S,\qquad L_{21}L_{11}^T=P^-H^T,$$

For innovation $v=y-Hm^-$, the exact solve $L_{11}z=v$ gives

derivations.claim: In precision $p=24$, the exact sum $1+c=2-2^{-24}$ is halfway between the representable predecessor $2-2^{-23}$ and $2$; ties-to-even rounds it to $2$. Hence the computed $B$ is $(2,2)^T$. The next exact addition is $4+2^{-22}$, halfway between $4$ and its next representable successor $4+2^{-21}$; ties-to-even rounds it to $S_{\rm fl}=4$. All these operands and results are normal.

The computed gain is $K=(1/2,1/2)^T$. Multiplication gives $(KS)K^T=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$ exactly, so the rounded subtractive update is $$P_{\rm sub}= \begin{bmatrix}0&-2^{-24}\\-2^{-24}&0\end{bmatrix}.$$ Its eigenvalues are $2^{-24}$ and $-2^{-24}$, so it is indefinite. This shows cancellation can lose positive semidefiniteness even with an exact positive-definite prior and positive measurement variance. By contrast, when the factor procedure succeeds, [F3] gives a represented covariance that is an exact factor product; this example makes no claim that rounding a later materialization of that product preserves the property.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_k$ for
$0\le k\le T$, and positive observation dimensions $p_k$ for
$1\le k\le T$. Inputs are real finite matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times
d_{k-1}}$, $H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, observation vectors
$y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$, and an initial mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$.
For each covariance supply a rectangular real factor
$$L_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times r_0},\qquad L_{Q,k}\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times r_{Q,k}},\qquad L_{R,k}\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times r_{R,k}},$$
where each column count is any finite nonnegative integer. The represented
covariances are $P_0=L_0L_0^T$, $Q_k=L_{Q,k}L_{Q,k}^T$, and
$R_k=L_{R,k}L_{R,k}^T$. Thus zero columns and rank-deficient factors are
allowed. The admissible statistical inputs are those of
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] for which
the canonical innovation $S_k=H_kP_k^-H_k^T+R_k$ is positive definite at each
step. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited only for the
interpretation as a posterior; the finite matrix procedure itself uses no
probability-space choice.

Choose a unit roundoff $u$ in the no-underflow operationwise model of
[[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]].
During an update, whenever an entry $a$ of a supplied matrix, factor, or
vector is read as an arithmetic operand or copied into a QR prearray, first
convert it to $\operatorname{fl}(a)$ in that format. Return `range-failure`
at that read if conversion fails under the same no-underflow rule. Read
operands from left to right; for products and block copies, visit output
entries column by column, with increasing row index within each column.
Repeat the conversion on each such read; the supplied arrays themselves
remain unchanged. The formulas below use these converted entries during
execution, while $P_0,Q_k,R_k,F_k,H_k,y_k,m_0$ denote the original exact
target data in comparisons with the canonical recursion. In particular,
conversion errors must be included in any certified local error bounds.
For $T=0$, return the input pair immediately without reading or converting

Let $P^-=L^- (L^-)^T$ and $R=L_RL_R^T$, with real factors of arbitrary
rank. Let $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ and suppose

columns to at least $n$ columns. Denote the resulting factors by
$L_R^{\mathrm{pad}}$ and $L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}$, and form
$$Z=\begin{bmatrix}L_R^{\mathrm{pad}}&HL^-_{\mathrm{pad}}\\0&L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}\end{bmatrix}.$$

$Z^T=UR$ with $U^TU=I$ and set $L=R^T$. For each $i=1,\ldots,p$,
multiply column $i$ of $L$ by the sign of its diagonal entry. This makes the
first $p$ diagonal entries positive; the signs are well defined because
$S\succ0$. Partition the resulting $L$ as
$$L=\begin{bmatrix}L_{11}&0\\L_{21}&L_{22}\end{bmatrix}$$
at the observation and state dimensions. Then
$$L_{11}L_{11}^T=S,\qquad L_{21}L_{11}^T=P^-H^T,$$
and
$$L_{22}L_{22}^T=P^- -P^-H^TS^{-1}HP^-.$$

$m^-+L_{21}z=m^-+P^-H^TS^{-1}v$. Thus the factor update has exactly the

The canonical covariance update is $P^+=0-0\cdot1^{-1}\cdot0=0$ and the canonical mean update is $2+0\cdot1^{-1}\cdot5=2$. They agree with the factor output in step 2.1. The zero posterior factor is admissible by [F3]; no Cholesky factor of a positive-definite state covariance is required.

rank. Let $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ and suppose
$$S=H P^-H^T+R\succ0.$$

columns to at least $n$ columns. Denote the resulting factors by
$L_R^{\mathrm{pad}}$ and $L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}$, and form

$m^-+L_{21}z=m^-+P^-H^TS^{-1}v$. Thus the factor update has exactly the
canonical one-step mean and covariance; $L_{22}$ may be singular.

Fix a finite horizon $T$ and let $(m_{k|k},P_{k|k})$ and
$(m_k^-,P_k^-)$ be the exact real-arithmetic prediction and update recursions
of [[alg-kalman-filter]]. Let
$$S_k=H_kP_k^-H_k^T+R_k,\qquad B_k=P_k^-H_k^T,\qquad v_k=y_k-H_km_k^-.$$
Suppose each innovation has a certified lower bound
$$x^TS_kx\ge\mu_k\|x\|_2^2\quad(x\in\mathbb R^{p_k}),\qquad \mu_k>0.$$
Let the procedure [[alg-finite-budget-square-root-kalman-filter]] output represented covariances
$\widehat P_{k|k}=\widehat L_{k|k}\widehat L_{k|k}^T$ and means
$\widehat m_{k|k}$. At step $k$, assume certified local bounds
$$\begin{aligned} &\|\widehat P_k^--(F_k\widehat P_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k)\|_2\le e_k^P,\\ &\|\widehat J_k-J_k(\widehat P_k^-)\|_2\le e_k^J,\\ &\|\widehat m_k^--F_k\widehat m_{k-1|k-1}\|_2\le e_k^m,\\ &\|\widehat v_k-(y_k-H_k\widehat m_k^-)\|_2\le e_k^v,\\ &\|\widehat L_{11,k}\widehat z_k-\widehat v_k\|_2\le\rho_k,\\ &\|\widehat m_{k|k}-(\widehat m_k^-+\widehat L_{21,k}\widehat z_k)\|_2\le e_k^u, \end{aligned}$$
where
$$J_k(P)=\begin{bmatrix}H_kPH_k^T+R_k&H_kP\\PH_k^T&P\end{bmatrix}$$
and $\widehat J_k=\widehat L_k\widehat L_k^T$ is the joint covariance
represented by the measurement QR blocks. Let $f_k\ge\|F_k\|_2$,
$h_k\ge\|H_k\|_2$, $b_k\ge\|B_k\|_2$, and
$r_k\ge\|v_k\|_2$ be certified finite upper bounds. Choose
$\Delta_0\ge\|\widehat m_{0|0}-m_0\|_2+
\|\widehat P_{0|0}-P_0\|_2$.

Define recursively
$$c_k^H=1+h_k^2,\qquad \varepsilon_k=c_k^H(f_k^2\Delta_{k-1}+e_k^P)+e_k^J.$$
If $\varepsilon_k\le\mu_k/2$, put
$$K_k^\#=1+2b_k/\mu_k,\qquad C_k^K=\frac2{\mu_k}\left(1+\frac{b_k}{\mu_k}\right),\qquad C_k^P=2+\frac{4b_k}{\mu_k}+2\left(\frac{b_k}{\mu_k}\right)^2,$$
$$A_k=(1+h_kK_k^\#)f_k+ (C_k^Kr_k+C_k^P)c_k^Hf_k^2,$$
$$\eta_k=(1+h_kK_k^\#)e_k^m+ (C_k^Kr_k+C_k^P)(c_k^He_k^P+e_k^J)+ K_k^\#(e_k^v+\rho_k)+e_k^u, \qquad \Delta_k=A_k\Delta_{k-1}+\eta_k.$$
Then each $\widehat S_k$ is positive definite, the factor update is
defined, and, with $z_k^*=\widehat L_{11,k}^{-1}\widehat v_k$,
$$\|\widehat z_k-z_k^*\|_2\le \frac{\rho_k}{\sigma_{\min}(\widehat L_{11,k})} \le\sqrt{\frac2{\mu_k}}\,\rho_k,$$
where $\sigma_{\min}(T)=\min_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Tx\|_2$. Also
$$\|\widehat m_{T|T}-m_{T|T}\|_2+ \|\widehat P_{T|T}-P_{T|T}\|_2\le\Delta_T.$$
Equivalently,
$$\Delta_T=\left(\prod_{k=1}^T A_k\right)\Delta_0+ \sum_{j=1}^T\left(\prod_{k=j+1}^T A_k\right)\eta_j,$$
where an empty product is $1$. The bound is finite-horizon and explicitly
conditioned on the innovation margins and data scales. It implies no
uniform-in-time stability or accuracy claim.

derivations.claim: The signal part of the observation variance is $HP^-H^T=10^{-6}$, so $R/(HP^-H^T)=10^{-6}$ and the observation noise is small relative to the predicted signal variance. The innovation variance and cross covariance are $$S=10^{-6}+10^{-12}=\frac{1000001}{10^{12}},\qquad B=10^{-3}.$$ Thus the exact gain is $$K=\frac{B}{S}=\frac{10^9}{1000001}.$$

In the scalar block QR, $L_{11}^2=S$ and $L_{21}L_{11}=B$, so $L_{21}/L_{11}=K$. If $L_{11}\widehat z-v=\rho=10^{-9}$, then $\widehat z=(v+\rho)/L_{11}$. The induced mean-update error is therefore $$L_{21}\widehat z-Kv=K\rho=\frac{1}{1000001} \approx9.99999000001\times10^{-7}.$$ An absolute solve residual of $10^{-9}$ has produced an update error about $10^{-6}$ because the gain is about $10^3$. The $K^\#\rho$ term in [F2] provides a certified upper-bound counterpart when only a gain norm bound is available.

For $n\ge1$, let

$$H_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac1k,\qquad \gamma_n=H_n-\log n.$$

The sequence $(\gamma_n)$ is strictly decreasing and is bounded below by
$1-\log2$. It therefore converges to a constant $\gamma$ satisfying
$0<\gamma<1$, and

$$H_n=\log n+\gamma+o(1).$$

Consequently, $H_n/\log n\to1$ as $n\to\infty$, with the quotient considered
for $n\ge2$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: For each $n\ge M$, [F1] and [F2] give $$\gamma_n-\gamma_{n+1} =\int_n^{n+1}\frac{dt}{t}-\frac1{n+1} =\int_n^{n+1}\left(\frac1t-\frac1{n+1}\right)dt.$$ The integrand is nonnegative and at most $1/n-1/(n+1)$ on this interval. Therefore $$0\le\gamma_n-\gamma_{n+1}\le\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}.$$

Summing step 1.1 for $n=M,\ldots,K$ telescopes to $$0\le\gamma_M-\gamma_{K+1}\le\frac1M-\frac1{K+1}.$$ Let $K\to\infty$ and use $\gamma_{K+1}\to\gamma$ from [F1]. Since $\gamma_M=H_M-\log M$, the claimed two-sided bound follows.

The next lemma proves that the improper integral converges locally uniformly on
the open right half-plane, so this definition is well posed exactly on the

The improper integral

$$\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt$$

converges locally uniformly on $\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}z>0\}$.

Euler's Gamma function is holomorphic on the half-plane

In a Dedekind-complete ordered field, the natural numbers are unbounded above.

derivations.claim: For each integer $m\ge0$, let $V_m=\{w\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}w>-m-1\}$ and define $G_m(w)=\Gamma(w+m+1)/(w(w+1)\cdots(w+m))$ as a meromorphic function on $V_m$. Its numerator is holomorphic on this half-plane by [F1] and [F2], and its denominator is a polynomial.

For every $w\in V_m$, $\operatorname{Re}(w+m+1)>0$. Applying [F3] at $w+m+1$ and cancelling the common meromorphic factor $w+m+1$ gives $G_{m+1}(w)=G_m(w)$ on the overlap $V_m\subset V_{m+1}$. By [F4], the union of the $V_m$ is $\mathbb C$, so these compatible meromorphic formulas define a meromorphic continuation of Euler's Gamma function on the whole plane.

Choose $m\ge1$ large enough that $z\in V_m$; then $z+1\in V_{m-1}$. Because $z$ is not a nonpositive integer, the denominator factors below are nonzero. The glued formulas give $\Gamma(z)=\Gamma(z+m+1)/(z(z+1)\cdots(z+m))$ and $\Gamma(z+1)=\Gamma(z+m+1)/((z+1)\cdots(z+m))$. Multiplying the first identity by $z$ yields the second.

equal the standard entire integral functions with their usual normalizations.

$$(a)_0=1,\qquad (a)_k=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(a+j),\qquad {}_2F_1(a,b;c;z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_k(b)_k}{(c)_k k!}z^k.$$

$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we

same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence

The series in [F1] has infinite radius by step 1.1, so [F3] gives $$\operatorname{erf}'(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^kz^{2k}}{k!}=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\exp(-z^2),$$ using [F2] and the definition of the exponential series. Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb C$ be any piecewise-$C^1$ path with $\gamma(0)=0$ and $\gamma(1)=z$. On a smooth piece, put $\eta_h=\gamma(s+h)-\gamma(s)$. Complex differentiability gives $\operatorname{erf}(\gamma(s)+\eta_h)-\operatorname{erf}(\gamma(s))=\operatorname{erf}'(\gamma(s))\eta_h+\eta_h\epsilon(\eta_h)$ with $\epsilon(\eta)\to0$ as $\eta\to0$; set $\epsilon(0)=0$. equal the standard entire integral functions with their usual normalizations.

For $a,b,c,z\in\mathbb C$ with $c\notin\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}$ and $|z|<1$,

For an integer $n\ge0$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define

$$J_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}, \qquad I_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}.$$

These are the integer-order Bessel and modified Bessel functions used on this
page. For real $x\ge0$, the scaled modified Bessel value means
$I_n^{\mathrm{sc}}(x)=e^{-x}I_n(x)$. This notation does not assert a finite

derivations.claim: For $z\ne0$, every term is nonzero, and cancellation of the factorials gives $|a_{k+1}|/|a_k|=|z|^2/[4(k+1)(k+n+1)]$. This ratio decreases to $0$. At $z=0$, the series have only the possible order-zero constant term, so every tail after $k=0$ is zero without using a quotient.

For $z\ne0$ and $k\ge K+1$ the ratios are at most $q$, so $\sum_{k=K+1}^{\infty}|a_k|\le |a_{K+1}|\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q^j =|a_{K+1}|/(1-q)$. At $z=0$ the same tail bound holds because the tail is zero. On each disk $|z|\le R$, put $q_R=R^2/[4(K+2)(K+n+2)]$. For sufficiently large $K$, $q_R<1$ and the nonzero-argument tail is bounded uniformly by $\sup_{|z|\le R}|a_{K+1}(z)|/(1-q_R)$; at $z=0$ it is zero. Thus the series converge uniformly on every disk.

For derivative order $d\in\{1,2\}$, put $m=2k+n$. When $m\ge d$, the absolute value of the formal derivative term on $|z|\le R$ is at most $b_k=m(m-1)\cdots(m-d+1)R^{m-d}/(2^m k!(k+n)!)$. For $R>0$ the ratio $b_{k+1}/b_k$ equals $R^2/[4(k+1)(k+n+1)]$ times a factor tending to $1$, so it tends to $0$. The ratio test makes $\sum b_k$ finite; the Weierstrass test then gives uniform convergence of each formal derivative series on the disk. The finitely many terms with $m<d$ have zero derivative, and a disk of radius $R=0$ is immediate.

For complex parameters $p,q$ with $\operatorname{Re}p>0$ and
$\operatorname{Re}q>0$, define Euler's Beta function by

$$B(p,q):=\int_0^1 t^{p-1}(1-t)^{q-1}\,dt,$$

again using the real logarithm on $(0,1)$ to define the complex powers.

The Beta-Gamma theorem below justifies convergence on exactly this pair of right
half-planes.

Let $S=\mathbb C\setminus\{x\in\mathbb R:x\le0\}$ be the slit plane. Then $S$ is
a complex domain, star-shaped with respect to $1$, and homologically simply
connected. The principal logarithm $\operatorname{Log}$
([[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]]) is the
unique holomorphic $F:S\to\mathbb C$ with

$$\exp(F(z))=z\ \ (z\in S)\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(1)=0,$$

and it satisfies $\operatorname{Log}'(z)=1/z$ on $S$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and write $f=u+iv:U\to\mathbb C$. The following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$.
2. Under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$, the map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $Df(a)$ is multiplication by a complex number.
3. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f(a)=0$.
4. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations

$$ u_x(a)=v_y(a),\qquad u_y(a)=-v_x(a). $$

When these conditions hold,

$$ f'(a)=u_x(a)+iv_x(a)=v_y(a)-iu_y(a)=\partial_zf(a). $$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, define

$$\Gamma(z):=\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt,$$

where for $t>0$ one uses the real logarithm convention
$t^{z-1}:=\exp((z-1)\log t)$.

The next lemma proves that the improper integral converges locally uniformly on
the open right half-plane, so this definition is well posed exactly on the

The improper integral

$$\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt$$

converges locally uniformly on $\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}z>0\}$.

The **Euler-Mascheroni constant** is

$$ \gamma:=\lim_{N\to\infty}\left(\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac1n-\log N\right), $$

provided the limit exists.

For $n\ge1$, let

$$H_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac1k,\qquad \gamma_n=H_n-\log n.$$

The sequence $(\gamma_n)$ is strictly decreasing and is bounded below by
$1-\log2$. It therefore converges to a constant $\gamma$ satisfying
$0<\gamma<1$, and

$$H_n=\log n+\gamma+o(1).$$

Consequently, $H_n/\log n\to1$ as $n\to\infty$, with the quotient considered
for $n\ge2$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let each $f_n:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose $f_n\to f$ locally uniformly on $\Omega$. Then $f$ is holomorphic and

$$f_n^{(k)}\longrightarrow f^{(k)}$$

locally uniformly on $\Omega$ for every natural $k$, with $f^{(0)}=f$.

A locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$ the $k$th derivatives converge locally uniformly to the $k$th derivative of the limit.

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

derivations.claim: For $w=z/n$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, the path $1+tw$ lies in the principal-logarithm domain. Its derivative integrand is continuous on $[0,1]$ and is integrable by [F3]. By [F2], [F3], and the real-parameter chain rule, $$\operatorname{Log}(1+w)=\int_0^1\frac{w}{1+tw}\,dt,\qquad w-\operatorname{Log}(1+w)=\int_0^1\frac{tw^2}{1+tw}\,dt.$$ Since $|1+tw|^2=1+2t\operatorname{Re}w+t^2|w|^2\ge1$, the summand has absolute value at most $|z|^2/(2n^2)$. Summing this bound is uniform on every compact subset of the right half-plane. Each summand is holomorphic there, so the series converges locally uniformly and defines a holomorphic function by [F11].

For $N\ge1$, the Beta integrals satisfy $$B(z,1)=\frac1z,\qquad B(z,N+1)=\frac{N}{z+N}B(z,N).$$ For the base formula, apply [F3] componentwise on $[\varepsilon,1]$ to the primitive $t^z/z$ and let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$; the lower boundary tends to $0$ since $|\varepsilon^z|=\varepsilon^{\operatorname{Re}z}$. For $N\ge1$, differentiate $g(t)=t^z(1-t)^N$ on $[\varepsilon,1]$. By [F6], $$g'(t)=zt^{z-1}(1-t)^N-Nt^z(1-t)^{N-1}.$$ The derivative is continuous and integrable on this compact interval by [F3]. Applying the componentwise fundamental theorem and then letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives $zB(z,N+1)=NB(z+1,N)$; both boundary terms vanish. The integrand identity $t^{z-1}(1-t)^{N-1}=t^{z-1}(1-t)^N+t^z(1-t)^{N-1}$ and [F4] give $B(z,N)=B(z,N+1)+B(z+1,N)$. Combining these two equalities yields $(z+N)B(z,N+1)=NB(z,N)$, proving the recurrence. Iterating it from $B(z,1)=1/z$ gives $$B(z,N+1)=\frac{N!}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+N)}.$$ All denominators are nonzero because $\operatorname{Re}(z+j)>0$ for $j\ge0$.

Fix $z$ with $a:=\operatorname{Re}z>0$, and define $K_N(u)=(1-u/N)^N$ for $0\le u\le N$ and $K_N(u)=0$ for $u>N$. For $0\le u<N$, [F5] and [F12] give $$\log(1-u/N)=-\int_0^{u/N}\frac{ds}{1-s}\le-\frac{u}{N},$$ so $0\le K_N(u)\le e^{-u}$ by exponential monotonicity and the addition law; the same bound holds at $u=N$. On a fixed interval $[0,R]$, for $N>2R$, $$N\log(1-u/N)=-u-\delta_N(u),\qquad 0\le\delta_N(u)=N\int_0^{u/N}\frac{s}{1-s}\,ds\le\frac{R^2}{N}.$$ The mean value theorem in [F10] and $e^t\le1$ for $t\le0$ give $|K_N(u)-e^{-u}|\le R^2/N$ uniformly on $[0,R]$.

Define $$A_N(z):=\frac{N!\,N^z}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+N)},\qquad N^z:=\exp(z\log N).$$ By step 1.2 and the substitution $u=Nt$ in [F12], $$A_N(z)=N^zB(z,N+1) =\int_0^N u^{z-1}\left(1-\frac{u}{N}\right)^Ndu.$$ The real logarithm laws in [F5] preserve the stated power convention under this substitution.

By [F7], $|u^{z-1}|=u^{a-1}$. For each real or imaginary component, the integral difference on $[0,R]$ is bounded, using [F4], by $$\frac{R^2}{N}\int_0^R u^{a-1}\,du=\frac{R^{a+2}}{aN}.$$ On $[R,\infty)$, $K_N(u)\le e^{-u}$ bounds the difference in each component by $2\int_R^\infty u^{a-1}e^{-u}\,du$, which tends to $0$ as $R\to\infty$ by [F8]. First choosing $R$ large and then $N$ large proves $A_N(z)\to\Gamma(z)$.

Let $\ell_N(z)$ be the defining partial sum through $N$ and put $$P_N(z):=z\exp(\gamma_E z)\prod_{n=1}^N\left(1+\frac zn\right)e^{-z/n}.$$ The principal-log identity $\exp(\operatorname{Log}w)=w$, the exponential addition law in [F6], and the formula from step 1.2 give $$\exp(\ell_N(z))=P_N(z)^{-1},\qquad P_N(z)A_N(z)=\exp\!\left(z(\gamma_E+\log N-H_N)\right).$$ By [F9] the second expression tends to $1$. By step 1.1, $\ell_N(z)\to\ell_+(z)$; continuity of the complex exponential gives $P_N(z)\to\exp(-\ell_+(z))$. Step 2.2 gives $A_N(z)\to\Gamma(z)$, so $$\exp(-\ell_+(z))\Gamma(z)=1.$$ Multiplying by $\exp(\ell_+(z))$ and using the addition law proves $e^{\ell_+(z)}=\Gamma(z)$.
