Let $p>0$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$. If any component of $\alpha$ is odd, then
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=0.$$
If $\alpha_j=2k_j$ for $j=1,2,3$, then
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=\pi^{3/2}\prod_{j=1}^3\frac{(2k_j)!}{4^{k_j}k_j!\,p^{k_j+1/2}}.$$
For every $q\in\mathbb N_0$, differentiation with respect to $p$ is valid and
$$\frac{d^q}{dp^q}\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=(-1)^q\int_{\mathbb R^3}\|x\|_2^{2q}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx.$$

For $g_{\alpha,a,A}$ from [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]], let $e_j$ be the $j$th coordinate vector. With terms having negative indices interpreted as zero,
$$\partial_{x_j}g_{\alpha,a,A}=\alpha_jg_{\alpha-e_j,a,A}-2ag_{\alpha+e_j,a,A},\qquad \partial_{A_j}g_{\alpha,a,A}=-\alpha_jg_{\alpha-e_j,a,A}+2ag_{\alpha+e_j,a,A}.$$
The second spatial derivative and kinetic operator are
$$\partial_{x_j}^2g_{\alpha,a,A}=\alpha_j(\alpha_j-1)g_{\alpha-2e_j,a,A}-2a(2\alpha_j+1)g_{\alpha,a,A}+4a^2g_{\alpha+2e_j,a,A},$$
$$-\frac12\Delta g_{\alpha,a,A}=\sum_{j=1}^3\left(-\frac{\alpha_j(\alpha_j-1)}2g_{\alpha-2e_j,a,A}+a(2\alpha_j+1)g_{\alpha,a,A}-2a^2g_{\alpha+2e_j,a,A}\right).$$
Consequently every kinetic integral of finite contractions is a finite linear combination of overlap integrals with these shifted multi-indices.

For every $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and real $T$, the extension in [[def-boys-function-and-coulomb-auxiliary-recurrence]] satisfies
$$0<F_m(T)\le\frac1{2m+1},\qquad F_m(0)=\frac1{2m+1},$$
$$F_m(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-T)^k}{k!(2m+2k+1)},\qquad \frac{d}{dT}F_m(T)=-F_{m+1}(T).$$
The upper bound in the first display is asserted for $T\ge0$. For $T>0$ the function also satisfies
$$2T F_{m+1}(T)=(2m+1)F_m(T)-e^{-T},\qquad F_m(T)=\frac{\gamma(m+\tfrac12,T)}{2T^{m+1/2}}.$$
The complete Gamma factor at a half-integer is
$$\Gamma(m+\tfrac12)=\frac{(2m)!}{4^m m!}\sqrt\pi.$$

For $p>0$, $P,C\in\mathbb R^3$, and $\eta=pq/(p+q)$ with $p,q>0$, the Hermite Coulomb auxiliaries of [[def-hermite-gaussian-coulomb-auxiliary-functions]] satisfy
$$R^n_{000}(p,P-C)=(-2p)^nF_n(p\|P-C\|^2),$$
$$R^n_{t+1,u,v}=(P_1-C_1)R^{n+1}_{tuv}+tR^{n+1}_{t-1,u,v},$$
with the corresponding coordinate formulas for increasing $u$ or $v$ and with negative-index terms zero. The one-center and two-center base Coulomb integrals are
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{e^{-p\|x-P\|^2}}{\|x-C\|}\,dx=\frac{2\pi}{p}F_0(p\|P-C\|^2),$$
$$\int\!\!\int\frac{e^{-p\|x-P\|^2}e^{-q\|y-Q\|^2}}{\|x-y\|}\,dy\,dx=\frac{2\pi^{5/2}}{pq\sqrt{p+q}}F_0(\eta\|P-Q\|^2).$$
For a primitive pair expansion $g_ag_b=\sum_{tuv}E_{ab}^{tuv}\Lambda_{tuv}$, the nuclear attraction integral is
$$V_C(g_a,g_b)=\frac{2\pi}{p}\sum_{tuv}E_{ab}^{tuv}R^0_{tuv}(p,P-C).$$
For two primitive pairs, with coefficients $E_{ab}$ and $E_{cd}$ and centers $P,Q$, the Coulomb integral is
$$G(g_a,g_b;g_c,g_d)=\frac{2\pi^{5/2}}{pq\sqrt{p+q}}\sum_{tuv}\sum_{\tau\nu\phi}\overline{E_{ab}^{tuv}}E_{cd}^{\tau\nu\phi}(-1)^{\tau+\nu+\phi}R^0_{t+\tau,u+\nu,v+\phi}(\eta,P-Q).$$
All sums are finite; the largest Boys order is bounded by the total polynomial degree in the participating primitives.

Let $a,b>0$, $A,B\in\mathbb R^3$, $p=a+b$, $\mu=ab/p$, and $P=(aA+bB)/p$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\exp(-a\|x-A\|_2^2)\exp(-b\|x-B\|_2^2)=\exp(-\mu\|A-B\|_2^2)\exp(-p\|x-P\|_2^2).$$
For any multi-indices $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N_0^3$, the polynomial factor $(x-A)^\alpha(x-B)^\beta$ is a finite polynomial in $x-P$ of total degree at most $|\alpha|+|\beta|$. Moreover, $P=(a/p)A+(b/p)B$ lies on the closed segment from $A$ to $B$.

derivations.claim: For $A=B=0$, [F5] gives $g_ag_b=e^{-p\|x\|^2}$, so [F1] evaluates the overlap as $(\pi/p)^{3/2}$. For kinetic energy, substitute [F2] and use both moments in [F1]: $$3b(\pi/p)^{3/2}-2b^2\frac{3}{2p}(\pi/p)^{3/2}=\frac{3ab\pi^{3/2}}{p^{5/2}}.$$

In [F4], set $C=P=0$; then the Boys argument is zero and [F3] gives $V_0=2\pi/p$. For the two-electron integral, both pair centers are zero and their only Hermite coefficient is $1$, so [F4] with $F_0(0)=1$ gives $2\pi^{5/2}/(pq\sqrt{p+q})$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and real $T$, the extension in [[def-boys-function-and-coulomb-auxiliary-recurrence]] satisfies
$$0<F_m(T)\le\frac1{2m+1},\qquad F_m(0)=\frac1{2m+1},$$
$$F_m(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-T)^k}{k!(2m+2k+1)},\qquad \frac{d}{dT}F_m(T)=-F_{m+1}(T).$$
The upper bound in the first display is asserted for $T\ge0$. For $T>0$ the function also satisfies
$$2T F_{m+1}(T)=(2m+1)F_m(T)-e^{-T},\qquad F_m(T)=\frac{\gamma(m+\tfrac12,T)}{2T^{m+1/2}}.$$
The complete Gamma factor at a half-integer is
$$\Gamma(m+\tfrac12)=\frac{(2m)!}{4^m m!}\sqrt\pi.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $m,N\in\mathbb N_0$, $T\ge0$, and $N+2\ge T$. Then
$$\left|F_m(T)-\sum_{k=0}^N\frac{(-T)^k}{k!(2m+2k+1)}\right|\le\frac{T^{N+1}}{(N+1)!(2m+2N+3)}.$$
In particular, this is a valid finite Taylor certificate whenever $0\le T\le1$.

Let $m\ge0$, $T>0$, and let $I_m=[c_m-r_m,c_m+r_m]$ enclose $F_m(T)$ while $J=[c_e-r_e,c_e+r_e]$ encloses $e^{-T}$. The exact upward recurrence image for $F_{m+1}$ has radius at most
$$\frac{(2m+1)r_m+r_e}{2T},$$
and the exact downward recurrence image for $F_m$, from an interval of radius $r_{m+1}$ for $F_{m+1}$, has radius at most
$$\frac{2Tr_{m+1}+r_e}{2m+1}.$$
If each full affine image is formed exactly before its two endpoints are converted outward once, and both conversions are finite, the stored interval radius exceeds the exact-image radius by the mean of the two endpoint-rounding errors. Iterating the displayed bounds with these rounding contributions gives valid finite error-amplification estimates over any requested order range for which every conversion is finite. An implementation rounding at intermediate primitive nodes must also propagate those nodes' rounding contributions; the final two conversion errors alone do not bound its total widening. If any required conversion overflows, no finite recurrence interval or finite propagated estimate is asserted for that step. Upward recurrence is undefined at $T=0$; direct values $F_m(0)=1/(2m+1)$ are exact.

Every call to [[alg-certified-boys-finite-budget-branch-evaluation]] terminates after finitely many operations bounded by its declared caps. Whenever it returns `success` on $\mathcal T\subset[0,\infty)$, each returned interval $I_m$ contains the exact range $\{F_m(T):T\in\mathcal T\}$ for $0\le m\le M$ and has the absolute and any reported relative accuracy required by [[def-certified-evaluation-result-contract]]. It may instead return `inconclusive`, `domain`, or `range`; no success for every finite input or cap is asserted.

Input a nonnegative integer $M$, a finite dyadic interval $\mathcal T=[T_-,T_+]\subset[0,\infty)$, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, a finite integer work cap $W$, a finite integer precision cap $P\ge2$, and a dyadic format with precision $2\le p\le P$, exponent bounds and elementary truncation index $K\ge1$. These are the backend parameters of [[def-certified-evaluation-result-contract]]. The output is a table of real dyadic intervals $I_m$ for $0\le m\le M$, with status `success`, `inconclusive`, `domain`, or `range`.

All arithmetic uses [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]. Every real elementary call means a typed DAG call to [[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] at the supplied format and fixed $K$. Embed an exact rational argument by outward rounding; check the domain of the entire rounded argument before calling. Square roots use the outward square-root operation. No machine elementary value is an endpoint certificate. Maintain a shared work counter: charge each arithmetic operation, conversion, comparison, loop update, summand and primitive child operation before executing it. Interrupt a child when the remaining counter reaches zero. A cap exhaustion, unresolved enclosure test, intermediate overflow, or child non-success on otherwise valid data makes the affected seed or directional candidate unavailable; if no candidate succeeds, return `inconclusive`. Return `range` only when a certified bound proves that an exact requested table value lies outside the largest finite magnitude of the supplied format. Invalid original inputs give `domain`; a domain test obscured only by intermediate rounding gives `inconclusive`.

1. Validate the stated input conditions and supported format. Process the distinct endpoints in increasing order; process the distinct seed orders $m\in\{0,M\}$ in increasing order. At an endpoint $\tau=0$, form the exact rationals $1/(2m+1)$ for every $0\le m\le M$. If any exact value exceeds the largest finite magnitude of the format, return `range`; otherwise round the rationals outward to the output format. Use this table without a recurrence. A rational is retained exactly internally, but a non-dyadic rational is not returned as a singleton dyadic interval.

2. For each positive endpoint $\tau$, perform refinements $k=0,1,\ldots,W-1$, subject to the shared work counter. At refinement $k$, try the two seed orders separately using their own $m$ and $s=m+\tfrac12$:

   - If $0<\tau\le1$, evaluate the Taylor polynomial through $N=k$ from [[thm-boys-integral-identities-series-and-incomplete-gamma]], then enlarge by the outward upper bound for $\tau^{N+1}/((N+1)!(2m+2N+3))$ from [[lem-boys-small-taylor-remainder]]. The condition $N+2\ge\tau$ holds throughout this branch.
   - If $1<\tau\le2m+1$, use $N=2^k$ panels of [[lem-boys-positive-midpoint-enclosure]], in increasing node order $j=1,\ldots,N$, and enlarge the positive midpoint sum by $(m+\tau)/(2N)$. Its dyadic nodes are formed exactly before storage; evaluate their exponentials by the finite real elementary call.
   - If $\tau>2m+1$, request the Gamma target from [[alg-certified-gamma-loggamma-evaluation]] on the exact rectangle $[s,s]+i[0,0]$, with positive exact rational child absolute tolerance $q/2^{k+2}$, where $q$ is constructed by starting at $q=1$ and repeatedly replacing $q$ by $q/2$ until $q\le\varepsilon_a$. Charge every comparison and halving to the shared counter; exhaustion returns `inconclusive`. Thus $0<q\le\varepsilon_a$ without restricting the parent tolerance to rational values. Supply no relative request, base format precision $p_0=p$, the same exponent bounds and fixed elementary truncation $K$, child precision cap $P$, and child work cap $w=\lfloor R/4\rfloor$, where $R$ is the remaining parent work at call entry. If $w<1$, stop `inconclusive`. Debit its actual work, including unsuccessful work, to the parent counter. A successful child rectangle has real projection containing the real number $\Gamma(s)$: its reality follows from the positive-real Euler integral, also evaluated by the half-integer identity in [[thm-boys-integral-identities-series-and-incomplete-gamma]]. Use this projection as the real Gamma enclosure. Evaluate $e^{-\tau}$ by the real elementary call, and use [[lem-boys-incomplete-gamma-large-t-tail-bound]] to form the enclosing interval for $F_m(\tau)$. Compute $\tau^s=\tau^m\sqrt\tau$ and $\tau^{s-1}=\tau^s/\tau$ by outward operations; the exact denominator $1-\max(s-1,0)/\tau$ is positive. Replace a negative lower endpoint by zero, retaining the upper endpoint. A child `range`, a child `domain` on this valid positive argument, or a child `inconclusive` invalidates that seed attempt and permits the next bounded refinement; no child status is propagated as a range claim for the Boys output.

   A finite seed interval is available to its direction only when its radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. A failed attempt does not invalidate a successfully enclosed seed for the other direction. Every panel and child loop is subject to the counter, even when its formal index bound is very large.

3. At each refinement obtain one finite real interval $J$ for $e^{-\tau}$. From an available order-zero seed form the upward candidate for orders $0,\ldots,M$; from an available order-$M$ seed form the downward candidate for orders $M,\ldots,0$. Use the exact affine recurrence maps in [[lem-boys-upward-downward-recurrence-error-amplification]]: compute each affine image's endpoints by exact rational endpoint arithmetic, then convert those two endpoints outward once. If either conversion overflows, discard that directional candidate at this refinement. Otherwise record the two conversion errors and propagate the lemma's radius bounds, including half their sum at each step. This prescription avoids omitting rounding at intermediate nodes. A table is admissible only if every entry satisfies the propagated bound and the requested absolute and, if requested, zero-excluding relative-radius test. Keep the admissible candidate with smaller maximum radius, ties upward. If neither direction is admissible, continue to the next refinement. Once an endpoint table is chosen, proceed to the next endpoint. No upward division is attempted at zero.

4. With both endpoint tables, form $I_m=\operatorname{hull}(I_m(T_+),I_m(T_-))$ for every requested order, using endpoint minima and maxima. By $F'_m(T)=-F_{m+1}(T)<0$ from [[thm-boys-integral-identities-series-and-incomplete-gamma]], this encloses the full range over $\mathcal T$. Return `success` only after every output radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$ and, when relative tolerance is requested, the interval excludes zero and satisfies the relative-radius test in [[def-certified-evaluation-result-contract]]. Otherwise return `inconclusive`. Exhausting the finite refinement list or shared work counter also returns `inconclusive`. At a positive endpoint, return `range` only if a certified lower bound for some requested exact Boys value exceeds the largest finite magnitude of the format; a merely overflowing enclosure endpoint gives `inconclusive`. No branch promises success for every valid box or finite cap.

derivations.claim: The exact identity in [F1] divides a difference of two terms. By [F1] and [F3], $F_0(T)=1-T/3+R_F$ with $|R_F|\le T^2/10$. By [F2], $e^{-T}=1-T+R_e$ with $|R_e|\le T^2$ for $T\le1$: for $k\ge2$, $k!\ge2^{k-1}$, so $\sum_{k\ge2}1/k!\le\sum_{k\ge2}2^{1-k}=1$. Therefore $$\left|(F_0(T)-e^{-T})-\frac{2T}{3}\right|\le\frac{11}{10}T^2,$$ so for $T\le1/4$ the positive difference is at least $T/4$. The two terms being subtracted each tend to one as $T\downarrow0$.

Applying [F4] with $m=0$ gives a factor $1/(2T)$ on both seed radii, which diverges as $T\downarrow0$ for fixed nonzero radii. The stated stored-radius formula follows only for a full affine image with one finite conversion per endpoint; a primitive subtraction error must also be divided by $2T$ before adding the final division error. In contrast, [F3] gives a direct Taylor enclosure with error $T^2/10$. The algorithm [F5] can therefore select the direct small-argument branch and return only a certified interval; the example makes no claim that every requested tolerance succeeds under every finite cap.

For pair densities $f,g$ arising as finite products of Gaussian contractions in [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]], let
$$\mathcal C(f,g)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\overline{f(x)}g(y)}{\|x-y\|_2}\,dy\,dx.$$
Then $\mathcal C$ is a well-defined Hermitian positive-semidefinite sesquilinear form on their finite linear span, and
$$|\mathcal C(f,g)|^2\le\mathcal C(f,f)\mathcal C(g,g).$$
For orbitals $\phi_a,\phi_b,\phi_c,\phi_d$ and pair densities $f_{ab}=\overline{\phi_a}\phi_b$, the integral convention in [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]] gives
$$|G(\phi_a,\phi_b;\phi_c,\phi_d)|\le\sqrt{G(\phi_a,\phi_b;\phi_a,\phi_b)G(\phi_c,\phi_d;\phi_c,\phi_d)},$$
where each diagonal quantity is nonnegative. For the real finite energy functional in [[def-finite-gaussian-basis-variational-energy-and-gradient]], let $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}$, $D\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$, and define the input-basis density coefficients $W_{ab}=\sum_{p,q=1}^r C_{ap}D_{pq}C_{bq}$. Here the input basis functions $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n$ are Gaussian contractions, and the tensor supplied to that functional is required to satisfy $G_{abcd}=G_{ab,cd}=G(\phi_a,\phi_b;\phi_c,\phi_d)\in\mathbb R$. Real-valued contractions in particular give real entries; a primitive basis is the singleton-contraction special case. Reindexing the finite two-body energy gives $E_2=\tfrac12\sum_{a,b,c,d}W_{ab}W_{cd}G_{ab,cd}$. Thus for any finite set $S$ of input-basis quartets omitted from that contraction,
$$B_S=\frac12\sum_{(a,b,c,d)\in S}|W_{ab}W_{cd}|\sqrt{G_{ab,ab}G_{cd,cd}}$$
is an accumulated upper bound for the absolute omitted energy contribution. This does not assert that a screened integral is zero.

Every invocation of [[alg-finite-gaussian-basis-integral-recurrence-evaluation]] terminates after finitely many operations bounded by its work and child-evaluator caps. If it returns `success`, each integral interval contains the exact integral range over the supplied parameter boxes. For the real energy/gradient branch, the returned energy interval and gradient-error bound contain the corresponding values of the finite functional in [[def-finite-gaussian-basis-variational-energy-and-gradient]]. The reported discarded-energy bound is at least the sum of the absolute Cauchy–Schwarz bounds for all skipped terms. The evaluator may return `inconclusive`, `domain`, or `range`; no universal success or exact-sparsity claim is made.

**Inputs.** A finite list of input basis contractions $\phi_a=\sum_{i=1}^{q_a}d_{ai}g_{ai}$, $1\le a\le n$, from [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]], represented by finite dyadic intervals for real centers and positive exponents and finite dyadic intervals or complex rectangles for coefficients; a finite nuclear list $((C_\ell,w_\ell))_{\ell=1}^J$ whose centers and signed real weights are represented by finite dyadic intervals; a requested subset $\mathcal I\subseteq\{S,T,V,G\}$ of integral outputs (overlap, kinetic, nuclear attraction, and Coulomb); and Boolean energy and gradient requests, with a gradient request requiring an energy request. Require at least one requested output. Supply a positive integral tolerance $\varepsilon_I$ for every requested integral and for integrals used internally by an energy request; supply a positive energy tolerance $\varepsilon_E$ when energy is requested and, for a gradient request, an optional positive gradient tolerance defaulting to $\varepsilon_E$. An optional positive screening tolerance is allowed only for an energy request. Also supply finite positive integer work and precision caps $W,P$ and a dyadic format of precision $2\le p\le P$ with exponent bounds and fixed elementary truncation index $K\ge1$. A primitive request is the singleton-contraction case. An energy/gradient request additionally requires $n,r\ge1$, real primitive-contraction coefficients $d_{ai}$ and real nuclear data, real matrices $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times r},D\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$ given by dyadic boxes (exact matrices are singleton boxes), and uniform finite bounds $B\ge\sup\|C\|_F$, $M_D\ge\sup\|D\|_F$ from [[def-finite-gaussian-basis-variational-energy-and-gradient]]. Internal primitive labels $(a,i)$ are distinct from the input basis labels $a$; $C$ is a subsequent transform of the input basis.

**Outputs.** A status `success`, `inconclusive`, `domain`, or `range`; outward real intervals or complex rectangles for the integrals in $\mathcal I$; an energy interval when energy is requested; a gradient center and Frobenius gradient-error bound when gradient is requested; and a separately accumulated discarded-energy bound when screening is enabled. Success encloses every parameter value in the input boxes. No status declares an omitted integral zero.

**Finite calls and accounting.** Use [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] for arithmetic. Every real elementary call means a typed DAG call to [[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] at the supplied format and $K$. Enclose $\pi$ by the Machin identity in [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]] and the $K$-term arctangent series with geometric tails from [[lem-range-reduced-exp-log-and-arctan-series-enclosures]], using exact rational tail endpoints before final outward conversion. A shared counter charges each conversion, comparison, loop update, arithmetic operation, recurrence update and summand, including every primitive operation executed by a child. Check the counter before executing an operation and interrupt any child at exhaustion. A required Boys call receives remaining work $R$ as its finite work cap, precision cap $P$, the same format and $K$, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_I/2$ and no relative request; its actual work is charged to the parent. A required child non-success on otherwise valid data or an intermediate overflow makes the current integral evaluation `inconclusive`; a rounded intermediate failing a domain certification on valid original data is also `inconclusive`. Return `range` only when a certified lower bound for a requested exact output component exceeds the largest finite magnitude of the format or a certified upper bound is below its negative. A mere overflow of a conservative intermediate or enclosure endpoint is not enough to claim `range`. Invalid original inputs return `domain`; cap exhaustion returns `inconclusive`. These choices are conservative and need not permit success under every cap or tolerance.

1. Validate the request specification, positive exponent lower endpoints, finite input boxes, indices in $\mathbb N_0^3$, supported format and positive tolerances/caps. Invalid original data return `domain`. If energy/gradient is requested, verify realness and dimensions and certify the norm bounds by outward Frobenius upper bounds on the complete boxes. If this sufficient norm test cannot certify the supplied bounds, return `inconclusive`; do not claim that an unknown represented matrix violates its bound. Form finite primitive-pair and quartet lists for the requested integrals and any energy/gradient dependencies, lexicographically. Include all shifted overlap pairs required by the kinetic raising/lowering formula; a negative index contributes zero.

2. For each ordered primitive pair with exponents $a,b$, indices $\alpha,\beta$ and centers $A,B$, compute $p=a+b$, $P=(aA+bB)/p$, and $K_{ab}=\exp(-ab\|A-B\|^2/p)$ by outward arithmetic and the real elementary call. Compute the Hermite coefficients by [[thm-cartesian-pair-hermite-expansion-and-coefficient-recurrence]], raising the first primitive in x,y,z order and then the second, storing each intermediate degree table until its successors have been formed. The final table has $\prod_{j=1}^3(\alpha_j+\beta_j+1)$ entries; every intermediate table update is also charged. Compute overlap by the finite shifted polynomial expansion and the moments in [[lem-cartesian-gaussian-moments-and-parameter-derivatives]], and kinetic by [[thm-cartesian-gaussian-raising-lowering-and-kinetic-recurrences]]. Certified square roots and integer powers evaluate all half-integer factors in those moment formulas.

3. To evaluate an attraction primitive pair, put $L=|\alpha|+|\beta|$ and use exponent $\eta=p$ and center difference $P-C_{\rm nuc}$. To evaluate a primitive Coulomb quartet, including any diagonal self quartet, put $L=|\alpha|+|\beta|+|\gamma|+|\delta|$, $\eta=pq/(p+q)$ and center difference $P-Q$, where the second pair has exponent $q$. Form the nonnegative Boys argument interval $\mathcal T=\eta\|P-Q\|^2$, with the evident attraction substitution, using interval squaring and the positive exponent bounds. Request Boys orders $0,\ldots,L$ from [[alg-certified-boys-finite-budget-branch-evaluation]]. If rounding prevents certification of a required positive denominator, return `inconclusive`.

4. Initialize $R^j_{000}=(-2\eta)^jF_j(\mathcal T)$ for $0\le j\le L$. For total derivative degree $d=1,\ldots,L$, enumerate $(t,u,v)$ lexicographically with $t+u+v=d$, choose its first nonzero coordinate in x,y,z order, and apply that coordinate's recurrence in [[thm-gaussian-coulomb-hermite-recurrences-and-integral-formulas]] for $0\le j\le L-d$. Negative-index terms are zero. For example, when $t>0$, use $R^j_{tuv}=(P_1-Q_1)R^{j+1}_{t-1,u,v}+(t-1)R^{j+1}_{t-2,u,v}$. Each predecessor is at a smaller derivative degree and within its stored Boys-order range. Contract the finite Hermite sums in that theorem to get each primitive integral.

5. Contract primitive integrals to input-basis integrals by the finite coefficient sums. For overlap, kinetic and attraction the coefficient is $\overline{d_{ai}}d_{bj}$. For the defined pair-density Coulomb convention, the primitive quartet coefficient is $d_{ai}\overline{d_{bj}}\overline{d_{ck}}d_{dl}$: expand $\overline{f_{ab}(x)}f_{cd}(y)$ in [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]]. In the real energy branch these are the four real contraction coefficients. Cache only identical ordered parameter boxes, angular indices, format and truncation context; an $R$ cache record also stores its cutoff $L$. Reuse a table only if its stored cutoff is at least the needed cutoff; otherwise compute the larger table under the counter.

6. Optional Coulomb-energy screening applies to whole input-basis quartets, before their off-diagonal primitive quartets are evaluated. First compute every required contracted diagonal $G_{ab,ab}$ without screening by steps 2–5, including all coefficients $d$. Obtain finite nonnegative upper endpoints $U_{ab}$ from their real projections, justified by [[thm-positive-coulomb-bilinear-cauchy-schwarz-screening]]. Form the outward real interval $W_{ab}=\sum_{p,q}C_{ap}D_{pq}C_{bq}$ and its upper absolute bound $A_{ab}=\max(|\inf W_{ab}|,|\sup W_{ab}|)$. Compute nonnegative outward upper bounds $Q_{abcd}\ge\sqrt{U_{ab}U_{cd}}$ and $w_{abcd}\ge\tfrac12A_{ab}A_{cd}Q_{abcd}$. Enumerate all ordered candidate basis quartets lexicographically, with no unrecorded symmetry compression. Skip a quartet only if the outward accumulated sum after adding $w_{abcd}$ is at most the screening tolerance; otherwise compute its primitive sums. Store a skipped real entry as $[-Q_{abcd},Q_{abcd}]$ and report the actual accumulated weighted sum. Thus entrywise radius uses $Q$, while the discarded-energy bound uses $w$. Even a skipped integral must pass its requested integral-tolerance test. No screening is required or performed when this optional real-energy branch is absent.

7. If energy or gradient is requested, form the one-body matrix on the input basis by $H_{ab}=T_{ab}+\sum_{\ell=1}^Jw_\ell V_{C_\ell}(\phi_a,\phi_b)$, using the supplied signed nuclear weights, and form the Coulomb tensor $G$ on that basis. Use the midpoint tensors $\widetilde H,\widetilde G$ and largest entrywise radii $\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_4$, including every screened interval. Evaluate the finite polynomial $E(C;D,\widetilde H,\widetilde G)$ by outward arithmetic over the full $C,D$ boxes, and enlarge its interval by $\delta_E=M_DrnB^2\varepsilon_2+\tfrac12M_D^2r^2n^2B^4\varepsilon_4$ from [[thm-gaussian-contraction-error-energy-gradient-bounds]]. If gradient is requested, evaluate every formal partial derivative of this same finite polynomial by differentiating its two and four factors of $C$ and using outward finite sums. If their intervals have midpoints $c_{a\mu}$ and radii $\rho_{a\mu}$, return gradient center $c$ with outward upper Frobenius error bound $\sqrt{\sum_{a,\mu}\rho_{a\mu}^2}+\delta_\nabla$, where $\delta_\nabla=2nrBM_D\varepsilon_2+2n^2r^2B^3M_D^2\varepsilon_4$. This includes uncertainty in $C,D$ as well as integral error; nuclear and contraction-coefficient uncertainty was already included in the integral boxes. Count all these operations. If a final certified bound proves that a requested output range lies wholly outside the finite format, return `range`; a final endpoint overflow without this proof returns `inconclusive`. Return `success` only when every requested integral radius, energy radius and gradient-error bound meets its own declared tolerance; all remaining failures return `inconclusive`.

An $R$ table with cutoff $L$ stores $\sum_{d=0}^L(L-d+1)\binom{d+2}{2}$ entries. All input, pair, primitive-quartet and auxiliary tables are finite. Every update and child evaluation is also subject to the shared finite work counter, so valid inputs may return `inconclusive` when their tolerance or work requirement cannot be certified.

For Burgers' flux $f_B(s)=s^2/2$, define $G\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ as follows. If $a\le b$, set
$$ G(a,b)=\begin{cases} a^2/2,&a\ge0,\\ b^2/2,&a<0\text{ and }b\le0,\\ 0,&a<0<b. \end{cases} $$ If $b<a$, set $$ G(a,b)=\frac12\max\{a^2,b^2\}. $$
This is the Godunov flux for the convex Burgers flux: for increasing states it
uses the minimum of $f_B$ on $[a,b]$, and for decreasing states it uses the
maximum of $f_B$ on $[b,a]$. It is proposed as a particular numerical flux in
the scheme of [[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. Its continuity and
consistency are verified in the pair.

derivations.claim: On each open region cut out by $a=b$, $a=0$, and $b=0$, the displayed formula in [F1] is either a polynomial, zero, or $(a^2+b^2+|a^2-b^2|)/4$, so it is continuous there.

At a boundary with $a=b>0$ both adjacent formulas tend to $a^2/2$; at $a=b<0$ both tend to $a^2/2$; at $a=0\le b$ the left and right limits are zero; at $a\le0=b$ the limits are zero. On the remaining axis portions $a=0>b$ and $b=0<a$, a neighborhood lies in the single shock branch $b<a$, whose formula is continuous there. At $(a,b)=(0,0)$ every branch has absolute value at most $\max\{a^2,b^2\}/2$, which tends to zero. These checks cover every branch boundary and prove continuity on all of $\mathbb R^2$.
On the diagonal, if $a\ge0$ the first branch gives $G(a,a)=a^2/2$; if $a<0$ the second branch gives $G(a,a)=a^2/2$. Thus $G(a,a)=f_B(a)$ for all $a$, and [F2] makes $G$ a consistent numerical flux.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Use the cells, time levels, states and interface fluxes from
[[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. For $J_n^m=[t_n^m,t_{n+1}^m)$,
the **piecewise-constant state reconstruction** and **face-flux reconstruction**
are the measurable functions
$$ \mathcal U_m(x,t)=U_j^{m,n},\qquad \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n} $$ whenever $(x,t)\in I_j^m\times J_n^m$. Values on cell or time-grid boundaries may be assigned arbitrarily, since those boundaries have two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. In particular, for almost every $(x,t)$, $$ \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=F\!\left(\mathcal U_m(x,t),\mathcal U_m(x+h_m,t)\right). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then

$$\|\tau_h f-f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(h \to 0).$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

derivations.claim: Fix a closed bounded interval $I$ and $T'<T$, with common state bound $M$ on $I\times[0,T']$. For $0<\epsilon<T'$, let $K=I\times[\epsilon,T']$. If $E=\{(x,t)\in K:|u(x,t)|>M\}$ had positive measure, then $E=\bigcup_{r\ge1}E_r$, where $E_r=\{(x,t)\in K:|u(x,t)|\ge M+1/r\}$. By countable subadditivity in [F3], some $E_r$ has positive measure. Since $|\mathcal U_m|\le M$ almost everywhere on $K$, it follows that $\|\mathcal U_m-u\|_{L^1(K)}\ge r^{-1}|E_r|>0$ for every $m$, contradicting strong $L^1$ convergence on $K$. Thus $|u|\le M$ almost everywhere on $K$. Taking $\epsilon=1/r$ for sufficiently large integers $r$ covers $I\times(0,T')$; any bounded interval is contained in a closed bounded one, so $u$ is locally essentially bounded up to $t=0$.

On each compact K away from t=0, cut off u to a bounded rectangle. Fact F3 gives an L1 cutoff, F2 gives translation continuity, and F7 preserves the translated L1 norm; hence U_m(·+h_m,·) converges to u in L1(K).

On a compact K, all state values lie in a common compact interval. Heine-Borel and the extreme-value theorem bound F on the compact square, and Heine-Cantor makes F uniformly continuous there. The inputs converge in measure, and K has finite measure by F3, so splitting into small-error and exceptional sets proves L1 convergence of F(a_m,b_m) to F(u,u)=f(u).

For all sufficiently large m, h_m<1, so the local state bound on the interval enlarged by 1 bounds both flux inputs on I×(0,ε); step 1.1 bounds u. Compactness and continuity bound F and f on their state ranges. The strip error is at most a fixed constant times λ₂(I×(0,ε))=|I|ε by F8; convergence away from zero follows from step 3.1, and then ε↓0 gives the full local L1 limit.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Use the cells, time levels, states and interface fluxes from
[[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. For $J_n^m=[t_n^m,t_{n+1}^m)$,
the **piecewise-constant state reconstruction** and **face-flux reconstruction**
are the measurable functions
$$ \mathcal U_m(x,t)=U_j^{m,n},\qquad \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n} $$ whenever $(x,t)\in I_j^m\times J_n^m$. Values on cell or time-grid boundaries may be assigned arbitrarily, since those boundaries have two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. In particular, for almost every $(x,t)$, $$ \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=F\!\left(\mathcal U_m(x,t),\mathcal U_m(x+h_m,t)\right). $$

Let $(U_j^{m,n})$ be a scheme from
[[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]], with reconstruction
$(\mathcal U_m,\mathcal Q_m)$ as in
[[def-finite-volume-space-time-reconstruction]]. For a test function
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$, define its space-time
cell average
$$ \Phi_j^{m,n}=\frac1{h_m\tau_m}\int_{t_n^m}^{t_{n+1}^m}\int_{I_j^m}\varphi(x,t)\,dx\,dt. $$ If $N\ge1$ is such that $\varphi$ vanishes for $t\ge t_{N-1}^m$, then $$ \sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}h_m U_j^{m,0}\Phi_j^{m,0} +\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}h_m U_j^{m,n} (\Phi_j^{m,n}-\Phi_j^{m,n-1}) +\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\tau_m Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n} (\Phi_{j+1}^{m,n}-\Phi_j^{m,n})=0. $$
All sums are finite because $\varphi$ is compactly supported in space and time.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(\mathcal U_m,
\mathcal Q_m)$ be reconstructions from
[[def-finite-volume-space-time-reconstruction]] for schemes using a continuous
consistent flux $F$ for a continuous physical flux $f$ as in
[[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. Suppose $h_m\to0$,
$\mathcal U_m\to u$ strongly in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R\times(0,T))$, and
for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and $T'<T$ there is
$M_{I,T'}<\infty$ such that $|\mathcal U_m|\le M_{I,T'}$ almost everywhere on
$I\times[0,T']$ for every $m$. Then $u$ is locally essentially bounded up to
the initial face and, for every bounded interval $I$ and $T'<T$,
$$ \|\mathcal Q_m-f(u)\|_{L^1(I\times(0,T'))}\longrightarrow0. $$

Let $T>0$, let $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let
$u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$. A measurable
function $u\colon\mathbb R\times(0,T)\to\mathbb R$ is a **locally bounded
distributional weak solution** of $u_t+f(u)_x=0$ with initial datum $u_0$ if
for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and every $T'<T$ it is
essentially bounded on $I\times(0,T')$, and, for every
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$,
$$ \int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dx\,dt +\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0. $$
The integrals are local: if a test is supported in $I\times[-S,T']$ with $I$
bounded and $T'<T$, the local essential bound makes $u$ bounded on
$I\times(0,T']$, and continuity of $f$ makes $f(u)$ bounded on that bounded
range. The initial integral is finite because $u_0$ is locally integrable and
$\varphi(\cdot,0)$ is compactly supported. This is the local
integrability version of the weak identity in
[[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]], whose
published formulation assumes a global $L^\infty$ bound. This definition adds
no entropy inequality or strong local $L^1$ trace requirement.

Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $\Pi_T=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$, let
$f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and let
$u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$. A bounded
measurable $u\colon\Pi_T\to\mathbb R$ is a **distributional weak solution** of
the Cauchy problem $u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$, $u(\cdot,0)=u_0$, if for
every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n\times(-\infty,T))$ --- test functions
whose support may meet the initial plane $t=0$ --- one has
$$\int_{\Pi_T}\Bigl(u\,\varphi_t+f(u)\cdot\nabla_x\varphi\Bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0.$$
Equivalently $u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\Pi_T)$, together
with the displayed initial boundary term
([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]],
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]). The integrals are absolutely
convergent: $u$ is bounded, $f(u)$ is bounded on the bounded range of $u$, and
$\varphi$ has compact support, so the pairings are $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ pairings
and are representative-independent ([[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]; the product-space identities
are those of [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] and
[[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]). The condition is an
equality in the $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ classes of $u$ and $f(u)$; it involves no
pointwise assignment of $u$ on $\{t=0\}$, and the initial datum enters only
through the boundary term ([[def-scalar-conservation-law-and-flux]]). For the
entropy formulation of this page the initial condition is instead imposed as a
strong local $L^1$ trace ([[def-kruzhkov-entropy-solution]]).

derivations.claim: Fix $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$. Its time support on $[0,T)$ is contained in $[0,T_\varphi]$ for some $T_\varphi<T$. For all sufficiently large $m$, choose $N_m\ge3$ with $T_\varphi<t_{N_m-2}^m<t_{N_m-1}^m<t_{N_m}^m<T$. By [F1] and [F2] these are precisely the scheme states and face fluxes of the reconstruction, so [F3] gives the exact summed update identity for this test.

The initial term in [F3] converges to the desired boundary term. Indeed, $h_mU_j^{m,0}=\int_{I_j^m}u_0$, while $\Phi_j^{m,0}$ is the average of $\varphi$ on $I_j^m\times[0,\tau_m)$. Smoothness gives $|\Phi_j^{m,0}-\varphi(x,0)|\le C_\varphi(h_m+\tau_m)$ for $x\in I_j^m$; summing the resulting errors over the finitely many cells meeting the support bounds the total by $C_\varphi(h_m+\tau_m)\int_K|u_0|\to0$ on a fixed compact $K$.

For $n\ge1$, the difference $\Phi_j^{m,n}-\Phi_j^{m,n-1}$ differs from $h_m^{-1}\int_{I_j^m}\int_{J_n^m}\varphi_t$ by at most $C_\varphi\tau_m^2$, by Taylor's formula in time for the smooth function $t\mapsto h_m^{-1}\int_{I_j^m}\varphi(x,t)\,dx$. After multiplication by $h_mU_j^{m,n}$ and summation over $O(h_m^{-1})$ cells and $O(\tau_m^{-1})$ time slabs in the fixed support, the total error is $O(\tau_m)$. The missing first-slab integral is also $O(\tau_m)$ because $|\mathcal U_m|$ is uniformly bounded on the compact support and $\varphi_t$ is bounded. Hence the time sum in [F3] differs from $\int_0^T\int\mathcal U_m\varphi_t$ by a quantity tending to zero.

For each $j,n$, translation of a cell interval and the fundamental theorem of calculus give $\tau_m(\Phi_{j+1}^{m,n}-\Phi_j^{m,n}) =\int_{J_n^m}\int_{I_j^m}\frac1{h_m}\int_0^{h_m}\varphi_x(x+s,t)\,ds\,dx\,dt$. Its difference from $\int_{J_n^m}\int_{I_j^m}\varphi_x$ is at most $C_\varphi h_m^2\tau_m$, by the bound on $\varphi_{xx}$. The numerical face fluxes are uniformly bounded on cells meeting the test support because $F$ is continuous on the compact state square supplied by local boundedness. Summing over the finitely many cells and time slabs meeting the test support gives total error $O(h_m)$. Thus the flux sum in [F3] differs from $\int_0^T\int\mathcal Q_m\varphi_x$ by a quantity tending to zero.

Strong local $L^1$ convergence gives $\int\mathcal U_m\varphi_t\to\int u\varphi_t$ on times bounded away from zero. On $I\times(0,\epsilon)$, the local uniform bound for both $\mathcal U_m$ and $u$ makes the integral difference at most a constant times $|I|\epsilon$; letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves convergence on the full test support. By [F4], $\int\mathcal Q_m\varphi_x\to\int f(u)\varphi_x$ on that support. Step 2.1 gives the initial term limit, and steps 2.2–2.3 identify the limits of the discrete sums. Taking the limit in [F3] proves the weak identity. By [F4], $u$ is locally essentially bounded, and [F5] identifies it as the stated local weak solution.

Let $T>0$, let $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let
$u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$. A measurable
function $u\colon\mathbb R\times(0,T)\to\mathbb R$ is a **locally bounded
distributional weak solution** of $u_t+f(u)_x=0$ with initial datum $u_0$ if
for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and every $T'<T$ it is
essentially bounded on $I\times(0,T')$, and, for every
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$,
$$ \int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dx\,dt +\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0. $$
The integrals are local: if a test is supported in $I\times[-S,T']$ with $I$
bounded and $T'<T$, the local essential bound makes $u$ bounded on
$I\times(0,T']$, and continuity of $f$ makes $f(u)$ bounded on that bounded
range. The initial integral is finite because $u_0$ is locally integrable and
$\varphi(\cdot,0)$ is compactly supported. This is the local
integrability version of the weak identity in
[[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]], whose
published formulation assumes a global $L^\infty$ bound. This definition adds
no entropy inequality or strong local $L^1$ trace requirement.

Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $f\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^n)$
([[def-scalar-conservation-law-and-flux]]), and let $u$ be a piecewise $C^1$
distributional weak solution
([[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]]) with
two-sided $C^1$ interface $\Gamma$ and traces as in
[[def-piecewise-smooth-shock-and-one-sided-traces]]. Orient the unit
space--time normal $\nu=(\nu_t,\nu_x)$ from the minus side to the plus side.
Then at every $\zeta\in\Gamma\subset U$,
$$[u](\zeta)\nu_t(\zeta)+[f](\zeta)\cdot\nu_x(\zeta)=0,$$
where $[u]=u^+-u^-$ and $[f]=f(u^+)-f(u^-)$.

In one space dimension, for a graph $x=s(t)$ with minus side $x<s(t)$ and plus
side $x>s(t)$, $\nu=(-s'(t),1)/\sqrt{1+s'(t)^2}$, so the condition is
$s'(t)[u](t)=[f](t)$ at every graph point. If $[u]\ne0$ in one dimension, then
$s'=[f]/[u]$; if $[u]=0$, then $[f]=0$ and the relation is $0=0$, with no speed
constraint.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Use the cells, time levels, states and interface fluxes from
[[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. For $J_n^m=[t_n^m,t_{n+1}^m)$,
the **piecewise-constant state reconstruction** and **face-flux reconstruction**
are the measurable functions
$$ \mathcal U_m(x,t)=U_j^{m,n},\qquad \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n} $$ whenever $(x,t)\in I_j^m\times J_n^m$. Values on cell or time-grid boundaries may be assigned arbitrarily, since those boundaries have two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. In particular, for almost every $(x,t)$, $$ \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=F\!\left(\mathcal U_m(x,t),\mathcal U_m(x+h_m,t)\right). $$

For Burgers' flux $f_B(s)=s^2/2$, define $G\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ as follows. If $a\le b$, set
$$ G(a,b)=\begin{cases} a^2/2,&a\ge0,\\ b^2/2,&a<0\text{ and }b\le0,\\ 0,&a<0<b. \end{cases} $$ If $b<a$, set $$ G(a,b)=\frac12\max\{a^2,b^2\}. $$
This is the Godunov flux for the convex Burgers flux: for increasing states it
uses the minimum of $f_B$ on $[a,b]$, and for decreasing states it uses the
maximum of $f_B$ on $[b,a]$. It is proposed as a particular numerical flux in
the scheme of [[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. Its continuity and

The map $G$ defined in [[def-godunov-flux-for-burgers]] is continuous on

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $T>0$, $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, $u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$, and $F\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with $F(a,a)=f(a)$ for every $a\in\mathbb R$. For each $m$, form the conservative finite-volume scheme and space-time reconstruction of [[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]] and [[def-finite-volume-space-time-reconstruction]] using $h_m,\tau_m\to0$ and initial cell averages of $u_0$. Suppose reconstructions converge strongly in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R\times(0,T))$ to $u$, and for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and $T'<T$ there is $M_{I,T'}<\infty$ such that $|\mathcal U_m|\le M_{I,T'}$ almost everywhere on $I\times[0,T']$ for every $m$. Then $u$ is a locally bounded distributional weak solution in the sense of [[def-locally-bounded-distributional-weak-solution]]; explicitly, for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$,
$$
\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dx\,dt +\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0.
$$
The strong convergence and local uniform bounds are hypotheses, not conclusions. No CFL condition or entropy inequality is assumed, so the theorem proves a weak limit only; it does not claim Kruzhkov entropy admissibility. If the limit is also globally essentially bounded, this identity is the published bounded weak formulation in [[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]].

Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $f\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^n)$, and
$\Pi_T=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$. The unknown and initial datum are equivalence
classes $[u]\in L^\infty(\Pi_T)$ and
$[u_0]\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$, where
equality is Lebesgue-a.e. ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]).

For $k\in\mathbb R$ define the **Kruzhkov entropy pair**
$$\eta_k(s)=|s-k|,\qquad q_k(s)=\operatorname{sgn}(s-k)\bigl(f(s)-f(k)\bigr),$$
with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then $\eta_k$ is convex
and $q_k'=\eta_k'f'$ almost everywhere, so $(\eta_k,q_k)$ is a locally Lipschitz convex
entropy--entropy flux pair ([[def-convex-entropy-entropy-flux-pair]]).

The class $[u]$ is a **Kruzhkov entropy solution** of
$u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$ with initial trace $[u_0]$ if:

(i) for every $k\in\mathbb R$ and every nonnegative
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Pi_T)$,
$$\int_{\Pi_T}\bigl(\eta_k(u)\,\varphi_t+q_k(u)\cdot\nabla_x\varphi\bigr)\,dx\,dt\ge0,$$
that is, $\partial_t\eta_k(u)+\operatorname{div}_x q_k(u)\le0$ in
$\mathcal D'(\Pi_T)$; and

(ii) for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{0<t<\min\{\delta,T\}}\int_K|u(t,x)-u_0(x)|\,dx=0.$$

The integral in (i) is independent of the representative because its integrand
is unchanged almost everywhere. For (ii), Fubini's theorem gives locally
integrable spatial sections for almost every $t$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); the
displayed slice integral is defined for those times and its essential supremum
ignores the exceptional null set. If $u$ or $u_0$ is changed on a null set in
its respective space, Fubini's theorem shows that the slice-integral function
changes only for a null set of times, so the trace condition is well defined on
the equivalence classes: this is the **strong local $L^1$ initial trace**.

Taking $k$ above and below the essential range of $u$ makes $\eta_k$ equal
$k-u$ and $u-k$, whose $t$- and $x$-derivatives cancel the constant terms
against compactly supported test functions, so the entropy inequalities imply
the weak conservation law of
[[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]] tested
against nonnegative test functions, hence by linearity against all test
functions.

To recover the Cauchy boundary term, apply the interior weak identity to
$\varphi(t,x)\zeta(t/\delta)$, where $\zeta$ is smooth and nondecreasing,
$\zeta=0$ on $(-\infty,1/2]$ and $\zeta=1$ on $[1,\infty)$.
For $\delta>0$ this product is supported away from $t=0$, so it is
an admissible interior test. The term containing $\zeta'/\delta$
converges to $\int u_0(x)\varphi(0,x)\,dx$ by (ii), while the other terms
converge on the compact support. This proves the full weak formulation with
initial datum $u_0$, rather than only its interior equation.

derivations.claim: With the now-defined value u0(0)=0, the cell averages are Uj^{m,0}=0 for j<0 and 1 for j≥0; the point value at x=0 does not affect a cell integral. The only face pairs along the resulting step are (0,0), (0,1) and (1,1), whose fluxes are 0,0,1/2. The ratio τm/hm=2 and max[0,1]|fB′|=1, so the usual noninteraction bound fails.

Assume inductively $U_j^{m,n}=0$ for $j<n$ and $1$ for $j\ge n$. If $j<n$, both face fluxes are $0$, so the state remains $0$. At $j=n$, the left flux is $0$ and the right flux is $1/2$, hence $U_n^{m,n+1}=1-2(1/2-0)=0$. For $j>n$ both fluxes are $1/2$, so those states remain $1$. Therefore the step shifts to $U_j^{m,n+1}=0$ for $j<n+1$ and $1$ for $j\ge n+1$.

On $[2nh_m,2(n+1)h_m)$, the numerical jump is at $nh_m$, while the limit jump is at $t/2\in[nh_m,(n+1)h_m)$. The profiles differ only on a strip of width at most $h_m$ and height $1$, so the $L^1$ error on every bounded space-time rectangle is at most $h_mT'\to0$. All states are bounded by $1$. By [F4], the limit $u(x,t)=0$ for $x<t/2$ and $1$ for $x>t/2$ is a locally bounded distributional weak solution with those initial data.

Take $k=1/2$. Then $\eta_k(0)=\eta_k(1)=1/2$, while $q_k(0)=1/8$ and $q_k(1)=3/8$. Choose nonnegative $\alpha\in C_c^\infty((0,T))$ with $\int\alpha>0$ and nonnegative $\beta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\beta(0)>0$, and set $\psi(x,t)=\alpha(t)\beta(x-t/2)$. This is an admissible nonnegative test. To evaluate its time term, put $B=\int_{\mathbb R}\beta(y)\,dy$. Differentiating the smooth compactly supported test and changing variables gives $\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_t(x,t)\,dx=B\alpha'(t)-\frac12\alpha(t)\int_{\mathbb R}\beta'(y)\,dy=B\alpha'(t)$; the last integral is zero because $\beta$ is compactly supported. Therefore $\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\eta_k(u)\psi_t\,dx\,dt=\frac12B(\alpha(T)-\alpha(0))=0$. Splitting the flux integral at $x=t/2$ and applying the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $\int_{\mathbb R}q_k(u)\psi_x\,dx=(1/8-3/8)\psi(t/2,t)=-\frac14\alpha(t)\beta(0)$. Thus the integral in [F5] equals $-\frac14\beta(0)\int\alpha<0$, contradicting the required entropy inequality. The weak limit is not Kruzhkov entropic.

$\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ consists of those classes for which

seminorm on bounded locally integrable classes. It is unchanged by modifying

Every initial cell average lies in $I$, since $a_-\le u_0\le a_+$ almost everywhere on its cell.

If $a$ or $c$ increases, monotonicity of $F$ in its first or second coordinate makes $H$ nondecreasing in that variable. If $b_2\ge b_1$, coordinate Lipschitz bounds give $H(a,b_2,c)-H(a,b_1,c)\ge(b_2-b_1)\bigl(1-\lambda(L_1+L_2)\bigr)\ge0.$ Thus $H$ is nondecreasing in all coordinates. Consistency gives $H(s,s,s)=s$.

Suppose $U^n$ takes values in $I$. Coordinatewise comparison with the constant triples $(a_-,a_-,a_-)$ and $(a_+,a_+,a_+)$, followed by step 1.2, yields $a_-=H(a_-,a_-,a_-)\le U_j^{n+1}\le H(a_+,a_+,a_+)=a_+$. Induction from step 1.1 proves the range bound at every time.

Let $S$ denote the sequence update. If $x,y\in I^{\mathbb Z}$ and $\sum_j|x_j-y_j|<\infty$, monotonicity gives $|Sx-Sy|\le S(x\vee y)-S(x\wedge y)$ coordinatewise. The difference on the right is summable: the update formula and the coordinate Lipschitz bounds make its flux differences summable. For any $z,w$ with $\sum_j|z_j-w_j|<\infty$, summing the update over $-N\le j\le N$ yields $\sum_{j=-N}^N(Sz_j-Sw_j)=\sum_{j=-N}^N(z_j-w_j)-\lambda(d_N-d_{-N-1}),\quad d_j:=F(z_j,z_{j+1})-F(w_j,w_{j+1}).$ The coordinate Lipschitz bounds make $\sum_j|d_j|<\infty$, so both boundary terms tend to zero. The update difference is absolutely summable, and hence $\sum_j(Sz_j-Sw_j)=\sum_j(z_j-w_j)$. Applying this to $z=x\vee y$ and $w=x\wedge y$ proves $\|Sx-Sy\|_1\le\|x-y\|_1$.

The initial neighbor difference is summable by step 1.1. The update commutes with integer shifts because the same $H$ is applied at every index. Apply step 2.2 to $x=U^n$ and its shift $y_j=U_{j+1}^n$ to obtain $\sum_j|U_{j+1}^{n+1}-U_j^{n+1}|\le\sum_j|U_{j+1}^{n}-U_j^{n}|.$ Induction proves the stated TVD bound.

Adding and subtracting $F(U_j^n,U_j^n)$ in the update and using the two coordinate Lipschitz bounds gives $|U_j^{n+1}-U_j^n|\le\lambda\bigl(L_2|U_{j+1}^n-U_j^n|+L_1|U_j^n-U_{j-1}^n|\bigr).$ Multiply by $h/\tau=1/\lambda$, sum over $j$, and use step 3.1 to obtain the time-increment estimate.

Let $u_0\in\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ and put $V:=\operatorname{TV}(u_0)$.
Let $U^n=(U_j^n)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ be generated by
[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]] under its full invariant-interval
CFL bound. Define the update map
$$H(a,b,c):=b-\lambda\bigl(F(b,c)-F(a,b)\bigr).$$
Then $H$ is nondecreasing in each coordinate on $I^3$ and $H(s,s,s)=s$ for
$s\in I$. Consequently,
$$a_-\le U_j^n\le a_+\quad(j\in\mathbb Z,\ n\ge0),\qquad \sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|U_{j+1}^n-U_j^n|\le V\quad(n\ge0).$$
Moreover, for every $n\ge0$,
$$\frac h\tau\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|U_j^{n+1}-U_j^n|\le (L_1+L_2)V.$$
For a sequence $x=(x_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$, the notation
$\|x\|_1:=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|x_j|$ is used only when this sum is finite;
$x\vee y$ and $x\wedge y$ mean the coordinatewise maximum and minimum.

Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $f\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^n)$, and
$\Pi_T=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$. The unknown and initial datum are equivalence
classes $[u]\in L^\infty(\Pi_T)$ and
$[u_0]\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$, where
equality is Lebesgue-a.e. ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]).

For $k\in\mathbb R$ define the **Kruzhkov entropy pair**
$$\eta_k(s)=|s-k|,\qquad q_k(s)=\operatorname{sgn}(s-k)\bigl(f(s)-f(k)\bigr),$$
with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then $\eta_k$ is convex
and $q_k'=\eta_k'f'$ almost everywhere, so $(\eta_k,q_k)$ is a locally Lipschitz convex
entropy--entropy flux pair ([[def-convex-entropy-entropy-flux-pair]]).

The class $[u]$ is a **Kruzhkov entropy solution** of
$u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$ with initial trace $[u_0]$ if:

(i) for every $k\in\mathbb R$ and every nonnegative
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Pi_T)$,
$$\int_{\Pi_T}\bigl(\eta_k(u)\,\varphi_t+q_k(u)\cdot\nabla_x\varphi\bigr)\,dx\,dt\ge0,$$
that is, $\partial_t\eta_k(u)+\operatorname{div}_x q_k(u)\le0$ in
$\mathcal D'(\Pi_T)$; and

(ii) for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{0<t<\min\{\delta,T\}}\int_K|u(t,x)-u_0(x)|\,dx=0.$$

The integral in (i) is independent of the representative because its integrand
is unchanged almost everywhere. For (ii), Fubini's theorem gives locally
integrable spatial sections for almost every $t$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); the
displayed slice integral is defined for those times and its essential supremum
ignores the exceptional null set. If $u$ or $u_0$ is changed on a null set in
its respective space, Fubini's theorem shows that the slice-integral function
changes only for a null set of times, so the trace condition is well defined on
the equivalence classes: this is the **strong local $L^1$ initial trace**.

Taking $k$ above and below the essential range of $u$ makes $\eta_k$ equal
$k-u$ and $u-k$, whose $t$- and $x$-derivatives cancel the constant terms
against compactly supported test functions, so the entropy inequalities imply
the weak conservation law of
[[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]] tested
against nonnegative test functions, hence by linearity against all test
functions.

To recover the Cauchy boundary term, apply the interior weak identity to
$\varphi(t,x)\zeta(t/\delta)$, where $\zeta$ is smooth and nondecreasing,
$\zeta=0$ on $(-\infty,1/2]$ and $\zeta=1$ on $[1,\infty)$.
For $\delta>0$ this product is supported away from $t=0$, so it is
an admissible interior test. The term containing $\zeta'/\delta$
converges to $\int u_0(x)\varphi(0,x)\,dx$ by (ii), while the other terms
converge on the compact support. This proves the full weak formulation with
initial datum $u_0$, rather than only its interior equation.

derivations.claim: If $s\ge k$, then $s\vee k=s$ and $s\wedge k=k$, so $G_k(s,s)=f(s)-f(k)=q_k(s)$. If $s<k$, then $s\vee k=k$ and $s\wedge k=s$, so $G_k(s,s)=f(k)-f(s)=q_k(s)$.

First suppose $k\in I$. Put $X=(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)$ and let $X^+$ and $X^-$ be its coordinatewise maximum and minimum with $(k,k,k)$. Both triples lie in $I^3$. By [F1], the two numbers $H(X)$ and $H(k,k,k)=k$ lie between $H(X^-)$ and $H(X^+)$; therefore $|H(X)-k|\le H(X^+)-H(X^-).$ Expanding the definition of $H$, the right side is $|U_j^n-k|-\lambda\bigl(G_k(U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)-G_k(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n)\bigr),$ which gives the claimed inequality after rearrangement.

If $k<a_-$, every state is above $k$ by the range assertion in [F1]. Then $|U_j^n-k|=U_j^n-k$ and $G_k(a,b)=F(a,b)-F(k,k)$ for state pairs; substituting the scheme recurrence makes the displayed left side zero. If $k>a_+$, every state is below $k$, so $|U_j^n-k|=k-U_j^n$ and $G_k(a,b)=F(k,k)-F(a,b)$; substitution again gives zero. The cases $k=a_-$ and $k=a_+$ are already covered by step 2.1.

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable and $\int f\,d\mu<+\infty$, then
$f(x)<+\infty$ for almost every $x$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: For every $t$, $W_m(\cdot,t)$ is piecewise constant with values in $I$ and spatial variation at most $V$: on each time slab it is a convex combination of two states whose variations are at most $V$ by [F2]. Here the variation of a piecewise-constant section on an interval is the sum of the absolute jump sizes inside that interval. Fix an integer $R\ge1$ and consider any sequence $v_m$ of such sections on $[-R,R]$. At each rational point in $[-R,R]$, the values lie in the compact interval $I$. The bounded-value subsequence at one rational point exists by [F6]; explicitly, partition $I$ into finitely many closed intervals of length at most $2^{-1}$, take the first interval containing infinitely many values, and repeat inside it with successive meshes $2^{-2},2^{-3},\ldots$, always selecting the first subinterval with infinitely many retained indices. The nested intervals have diameters tending to zero, so the least increasing indices in the nested sets give a convergent subsequence. Use the enumeration fixed by [F5], and repeat this deterministic extraction successively on the current subsequence at each enumerated rational that lies in $[-R,R]$, skipping the others. The nested subsequences yield a diagonal subsequence converging at every rational point; each interval and index is selected by a least-index rule, so this uses no choice axiom. Given $\delta>0$, choose a finite rational partition of $[-R,R]$ with mesh at most $\delta$, possible by [F4]. For each subinterval $J=[r_i,r_{i+1}]$ and any two selected functions $v_p,v_q$, variation gives $|v_p(x)-v_q(x)|\le|v_p(r_i)-v_q(r_i)|+\operatorname{Var}_J(v_p)+\operatorname{Var}_J(v_q)$ for almost every $x\in J$. Integrating and summing yields $\|v_p-v_q\|_{L^1([-R,R])}\le 2\delta V+2R\max_i|v_p(r_i)-v_q(r_i)|.$ For the fixed partition the maximum tends to zero as $p,q\to\infty$; then taking $\delta\downarrow0$ proves the selected sections are Cauchy in local $L^1$.

On each slab, $\partial_tW_m=(U_j^{n+1}-U_j^n)/\tau_m$ on cell $I_j$. By [F2], its $L^1(\mathbb R)$ norm is at most $C:=(L_1+L_2)V$. Integrating over any time interval gives $\|W_m(\cdot,t)-W_m(\cdot,s)\|_{L^1(\mathbb R)}\le C|t-s|.$ Use the enumeration fixed by [F5] and process its indices together with integers $R\ge1$ in order of increasing sum. For each pair $(\ell,R)$, if $q_\ell\in[0,T]$, apply step 1.1 at time $q_\ell$ on $[-R,R]$; otherwise skip that pair. The resulting diagonal extraction covers every rational time in $[0,T]$ and every integer interval. The subsequence converges in $L^1([-R,R])$ at every rational time for every integer $R$; this recursive construction uses no choice axiom.

Fix $R$ and $\varepsilon>0$, and put $\delta:=\varepsilon/(4(C+1))$. Choose a finite set of rational times in $[0,T]$ that is a $\delta$-net: include $0$, choose $q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,T]$ with $T-q<\delta$ (using $q=0$ if $T<\delta$), and subdivide $[0,q]$ by rational points with gaps below $\delta$, possible by [F4]. At those finitely many times the subsequence in step 2.1 is Cauchy in $L^1([-R,R])$. For any $t\in[0,T]$, choose a net time $s$ within the gap bound; the triangle inequality and the uniform time estimate in step 2.1 give $\|W_p(\cdot,t)-W_q(\cdot,t)\|_{L^1([-R,R])}\le 2C|t-s|+\|W_p(\cdot,s)-W_q(\cdot,s)\|_{L^1([-R,R])}.$ Thus the subsequence is uniformly Cauchy in time in local $L^1$. For fixed $t,R$, its bounded measurable sections have an $L^1([-R,R])$ limit: for each $j$, let $N_j$ be the least integer such that all $p,q\ge N_j$ have $L^1([-R,R])$ difference below $2^{-j}$, which exists by Cauchyness. Put $\widehat N_j:=\max_{1\le r\le j}N_r$ and recursively choose the least increasing indices $n_j\ge\widehat N_j$. Then both $n_j,n_{j+1}\ge N_j$, so successive differences have norms below $2^{-j}$. By [F8] their pointwise absolute sum is finite almost everywhere, and dominated convergence [F7] gives the $L^1$ limit. Uniqueness makes these limits consistent as $R$ increases, and the uniform Cauchy estimate makes $t\mapsto u(t)$ continuous in each local $L^1$ norm. The subsequence is also Cauchy in $L^1([-R,R]\times(0,T))$ for every integer $R$, by integrating its uniform-in-time Cauchy bound. For each $j$, let $M_j$ be the least integer such that all $p,q\ge M_j$ have difference below $2^{-j}$ on every cylinder with integer $R\le j$; this exists because there are finitely many such cylinders and the sequence is Cauchy on each. Put $\widehat M_j:=\max_{1\le r\le j}M_r$ and recursively choose the least increasing indices $m_j\ge\widehat M_j$. For every fixed integer $R$ and every $j\ge R$, both $m_j,m_{j+1}\ge M_j$, so their successive differences have norm below $2^{-j}$ on that cylinder. [F8] then gives a finite pointwise sum of differences almost everywhere on each cylinder, and [F7] yields a measurable space-time limit $v$ with strong local $L^1$ convergence. For each integer $R$, the sum of the $L^1([-R,R]\times(0,T))$ norms of these successive differences is finite. By [F9], for almost every $t$ their spatial absolute sum is integrable on $[-R,R]$; hence $W_{m_j}(\cdot,t)$ converges almost everywhere in $x$ there to $v(\cdot,t)$. Since all these sections and their limit take values in the bounded interval $I$, dominated convergence [F7] gives convergence to $v(\cdot,t)$ in $L^1([-R,R])$. But this is a subsequence of the sequence that converges in $L^1([-R,R])$ to $u(t)$ for every $t$, so uniqueness of the $L^1$ limit gives $v(\cdot,t)=u(t)$ for almost every $t$. Intersecting these full-measure time sets over integer $R$ shows that the space-time limit and the continuous local-$L^1$ map are the same limit on all bounded intervals.

Every $W_m$ takes values in $I$, so its local $L^1$ limit also takes values in $I$ almost everywhere: if, for example, $u(t)>a_+$ on a set of positive measure, then some set where $u(t)\ge a_++1/r$ has positive measure, contradicting $L^1$ convergence from functions bounded by $a_+$. The same argument applies to the lower bound.

For $r<0$, translation invariance of Lebesgue measure gives the same bound as for $-r$, so $\|u_0(\cdot+r)-u_0\|_{L^1(\mathbb R)}\le |r|V$ for every $r\in\mathbb R$. On each cell, the initial cell-average error is controlled by translations: $\sum_j\int_{I_j}|u_0(x)-U_j^0|\,dx\le\frac1h\int_{-h}^{h}\int_{\mathbb R}|u_0(x+r)-u_0(x)|\,dx\,dr\le hV.$ The first inequality follows by writing each cell average as an integral over that same cell, applying the triangle inequality, and changing variables to $r=y-x$; the restriction that $x$ and $x+r$ lie in the same cell can only decrease the integral. Since $W_m(\cdot,0)=U^0$, step 3.1 gives $u(0)=u_0$ in local $L^1$.

On each slab, $|W_m-U_j^n|=\theta|U_j^{n+1}-U_j^n|$. Integrating in time contributes the factor $\tau_m/2$; the time-increment bound in [F2] gives, on $[0,T]$, $\|W_m-\mathcal U_m\|_{L^1(\mathbb R\times(0,T))}\le\frac{(T+\tau_m)\tau_m}{2}(L_1+L_2)V\longrightarrow0.$ Consequently $\mathcal U_m$ converges strongly in local space-time $L^1$ to the same limit as $W_m$.

Right-continuous cell representatives make the rational-partition variation estimate valid almost everywhere; summing the interval variations costs at most 2δV. The global L1 time-difference bound C|t-s| controls differences, not individually nonintegrable sections. Finite rational time nets include 0 and approach T, so the Cauchy estimate is uniform on [0,T].
