if, for every $u\in N$, $A(u)$ has $m$ distinct real eigenvalues, written in
increasing order $\lambda_1(u)<\cdots<\lambda_m(u)$. An **$i$th characteristic
family** on $N$ is a $C^2$ right-eigenvector field $r_i:N\to\mathbb R^m\setminus\{0\}$
with $A(u)r_i(u)=\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$. It is **genuinely nonlinear** on $N$ if
$D\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$ is nowhere zero there; after shrinking $N$ its sign is
constant. It is **linearly degenerate** on $N$ if $D\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)=0$
throughout $N$. Rescaling $r_i$ by a nonzero constant changes the wave-strength
parameter but not the family.

For $Q=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, a locally bounded map $u:Q\to G$ is a
**distributional weak solution with initial data $u_0$** if
$$\int_Q\bigl(u\cdot\varphi_t+f(u)\cdot\varphi_x\bigr)\,dt\,dx=0$$
for every vector test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)$ and
$u(t,\cdot)\to u_0$ in $L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^m)$ as
$t\downarrow0$. A **Riemann initial datum** is the step
$u_0(x)=u_L$ for $x<0$ and $u_0(x)=u_R$ for $x>0$.

In this weak-solution clause, $u$ is required to be Lebesgue measurable and
$f\circ u\in L^1_{\rm loc}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$, so the test-function integral is
defined. Local boundedness gives $u\in L^1_{\rm loc}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$.

On a neighborhood where an eigenvector field $r_i$ is $C^2$, the local
$i$-rarefaction curve through $u_0$ is the unique local solution
$$\frac{dR_i}{d\sigma}(\sigma;u_0)=r_i(R_i(\sigma;u_0)),\qquad R_i(0;u_0)=u_0.$$
The parameter $\sigma$ is the signed integral-curve parameter for the chosen
normalization of $r_i$. Existence on a common small interval for nearby $u_0$
follows from [[cor-uniform-picard-lindelof-for-nearby-initial-values]]; the
$C^2$ flow on a compact local tube follows from
[[thm-c2-ode-flow-on-common-tube]]. No global integral curve is asserted.

For a system as in [[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]], a
discontinuity with constant states $u_L,u_R\in G$ and speed $s\in\mathbb R$ is
a **Rankine–Hugoniot jump** if
$$f(u_R)-f(u_L)=s(u_R-u_L).$$
For a system strictly hyperbolic on $N\subseteq G$, states $u_L,u_R\in N$,
and $1\le i\le m$, it is a **strict Lax $i$-shock** if it is a Rankine–Hugoniot jump and
$$\lambda_j(u_L)<s\ (j<i),\qquad \lambda_i(u_R)<s<\lambda_i(u_L),\qquad s<\lambda_j(u_R)\ (j>i).$$
An empty family of inequalities is omitted. A linearly-degenerate contact has
equal $i$-speeds on both sides, so it is not a strict Lax shock.

For a conservation system as in
[[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]], constant states
$u_L,u_R\in G$, and a constant speed $s$, define
$u(t,x)=u_L$ for $x<st$ and $u(t,x)=u_R$ for $x>st$, and let
$u_0(x)=u_L$ for $x<0$ and $u_0(x)=u_R$ for $x>0$ (values on the jump lines
are immaterial). Then $u$ is a distributional weak solution with initial datum
$u_0$ in the sense of [[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]]
if and only if
$$f(u_R)-f(u_L)=s(u_R-u_L).$$

Fix $\gamma>1$ and admissible left/right primitive states
$(\rho_K,u_K,p_K)$, $K\in\{L,R\}$, with $\rho_K,p_K>0$ and
$c_K=\sqrt{\gamma p_K/\rho_K}$. Set
$$A_K=\frac{2}{(\gamma+1)\rho_K},\qquad B_K=\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma+1}p_K.$$
For a trial star pressure $p>0$, the wave pressure response from side $K$ is
$$f_K(p)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{2c_K}{\gamma-1}\left[\left(\dfrac p{p_K}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/(2\gamma)}-1\right],&0<p\le p_K,\\(p-p_K)\sqrt{\dfrac{A_K}{p+B_K}},&p\ge p_K.\end{cases}$$
The two formulas agree at $p=p_K$. The **star-pressure residual** is
$$\Phi(p)=f_L(p)+f_R(p)+u_R-u_L,\qquad p>0.$$
This is a scalar root equation; it does not itself define a Riemann solution.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

For a side state $K=(\rho_K,u_K,p_K)$ and any trial pressure $p>0$, the
rarefaction/shock branches defined in
[[def-euler-star-pressure-response]] give the scalar velocity response
$f_K(p)$ along the corresponding acoustic wave. For a left 1-wave the star velocity is
$u_*=u_L-f_L(p)$; for a right 3-wave it is $u_*=u_R+f_R(p)$. The star density
on a rarefaction branch is
$$\rho_*(p)=\rho_K(p/p_K)^{1/\gamma},$$
and on a compressive shock branch, with $q=p/p_K>1$ and
$\beta=(\gamma-1)/(\gamma+1)$, it is
$$\rho_*(p)=\rho_K\frac{q+\beta}{\beta q+1}.$$
The shock branches satisfy the strict acoustic Lax inequalities. When the two
pressure responses match at a positive $p$, their star states are joined by a
linearly-degenerate contact at speed $u_*$.

derivations.claim: On $0<p\le p_K$, differentiation gives $f'_K(p)=\frac{c_K}{\gamma p_K}\left(\frac p{p_K}\right)^{-(\gamma+1)/(2\gamma)}>0$; on $p\ge p_K$, it gives $f'_K(p)=\frac{\sqrt{A_K}(p+p_K+2B_K)}{2(p+B_K)^{3/2}}>0$. At $p=p_K$ both derivatives equal $1/\sqrt{\gamma\rho_Kp_K}$, so $f_K$ is $C^1$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$. Thus $\Phi$ is also $C^1$ and strictly increasing.

For $p\ge2p_K$, we have $p-p_K\ge p/2$ and $p+B_K\le3p/2$, because $0<B_K<p_K\le p/2$. The shock formula therefore gives $f_K(p)\ge\sqrt{A_Kp/6}$. The stated $P$ exceeds both $2p_K$ and $6D^2/K^2$, so $f_L(P)+f_R(P)\ge K\sqrt{P/6}>D$, and consequently $\Phi(P)>0$.

The rarefaction formula in [F1] tends to $-2c_K/(\gamma-1)$ as $p\downarrow0$, hence $\lim_{p\downarrow0}\Phi(p)=\Phi(0+)$. If this limit is nonnegative, strict increase makes $\Phi(p)>0$ for every $p>0$, so there is no positive zero.

If $\Phi(0+)<0$, continuity at the extended endpoint $0$ gives some $\epsilon\in(0,P)$ with $\Phi(\epsilon)<0$. Applying [F2] to $\Phi$ on $[\epsilon,P]$ gives a zero in $(\epsilon,P)$; strict increase from step 1.1 makes it unique on $(0,\infty)$. Thus $0<p_*<P$.

Taking the limits in [F3] using step 2.1 gives the left tail velocity $v_L=u_L+2c_L/(\gamma-1)$ and the right tail velocity $v_R=u_R-2c_R/(\gamma-1)$, so $v_R-v_L=\Phi(0+)$. If this right-minus-left gap is positive, the tails leave a vacuum interval; at equality they meet. If it is negative, step 3.1 gives the unique positive pressure at which the two wave responses match and the contact joins their star states. This proves the stated threshold and matching interpretation.

On a neighborhood where an eigenvector field $r_i$ is $C^2$, the local
$i$-rarefaction curve through $u_0$ is the unique local solution
$$\frac{dR_i}{d\sigma}(\sigma;u_0)=r_i(R_i(\sigma;u_0)),\qquad R_i(0;u_0)=u_0.$$
The parameter $\sigma$ is the signed integral-curve parameter for the chosen
normalization of $r_i$. Existence on a common small interval for nearby $u_0$
follows from [[cor-uniform-picard-lindelof-for-nearby-initial-values]]; the
$C^2$ flow on a compact local tube follows from
[[thm-c2-ode-flow-on-common-tube]]. No global integral curve is asserted.

Let $G\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $f:G\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^3$, and
let $\bar u\in G$ be a state where $A(\bar u)=Df(\bar u)$ has $m$ distinct
real eigenvalues $\lambda_1(\bar u)<\cdots<\lambda_m(\bar u)$.
Fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and its $i$th eigenpair
$(\lambda_i(\bar u),r_i(\bar u))$. There are a neighborhood $N_0$ of $\bar u$,
$\eta>0$, and $C^1$ functions $v_i(\sigma,u_0),s_i(\sigma,u_0)$ for
$u_0\in N_0$, $|\sigma|<\eta$, such that, with $\ell_i(u_0)$ the dual left
eigenvector normalized by $\ell_i(u_0)\cdot r_i(u_0)=1$,
$$\ell_i(u_0)\cdot v_i(\sigma,u_0)=1,\qquad S_i(\sigma;u_0)=u_0+\sigma v_i(\sigma,u_0),$$
and for $\sigma\ne0$ the pair $(u_0,S_i(\sigma;u_0))$ satisfies
Rankine–Hugoniot with speed $s_i(\sigma,u_0)$. Also
$S_i(0;u_0)=u_0$ and $\partial_\sigma S_i(0;u_0)=r_i(u_0)$. If the $i$th
field is genuinely nonlinear on $N_0$ and
$d_i(u):=D\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$ has constant nonzero sign, then all sufficiently
small nonzero strengths with $\sigma d_i(u_0)<0$ give strict Lax $i$-shocks.

Fix a local characteristic family on a neighborhood where it is either
genuinely nonlinear with constant sign $d_i=D\lambda_i\,r_i\ne0$, or linearly
degenerate. For a genuinely nonlinear family define
$$\Psi_i(\sigma;u)=\begin{cases}R_i(\sigma;u),&\sigma d_i>0,\\S_i(\sigma;u),&\sigma d_i<0,\\u,&\sigma=0.\end{cases}$$
where $R_i$ is the local rarefaction curve and $S_i$ the local shock curve of
[[lem-local-characteristic-shock-curve]]. For a linearly degenerate family set
$\Psi_i(\sigma;u)=R_i(\sigma;u)$ for either sign; its nonzero-strength wave is
the contact of [[lem-linearly-degenerate-characteristic-contact]]. The
parameter $\sigma$ is local and is restricted so the entire curve stays in the
chosen neighborhood.

derivations.claim: For a linearly-degenerate family, [F1] directly gives the claim. For a genuinely nonlinear family, each branch in [F3] is $C^1$ on its closed half-neighborhood by [F1] and [F2]. At $\sigma=0$ both values equal $u$, both state derivatives equal the identity, and both strength derivatives equal $r_i(u)$.

At a boundary point $(u,0)$, the first-order expansions of either branch are $u+h+r_i(u)\sigma+o(\|h\|+|\sigma|)$ for state increment $h$; the remainder is uniform over the two branches because there are only two and each is $C^1$. Thus the joined function is differentiable there with derivative $(h,\sigma)\mapsto h+r_i(u)\sigma$. The branch derivatives tend to this common derivative as $\sigma\to0$, so the joined derivative is continuous.
The derivatives and values just obtained prove $C^1$ regularity and the asserted value and strength derivative at zero.

For the data of [[def-euler-star-pressure-response]], let
$$\Phi(0+):=u_R-u_L-\frac{2(c_L+c_R)}{\gamma-1}.$$
The residual $\Phi$ is $C^1$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.
If $\Phi(0+)<0$, then $\Phi$ has exactly one zero $p_*>0$. By the acoustic
wave-response lemma this is the unique positive pressure at which the left and
right wave curves can be joined by a contact. It lies in the
explicit bracket $0<p_*<P$, where, writing
$D=\max\{0,u_L-u_R\}$ and $K=\sqrt{A_L}+\sqrt{A_R}$,
$$P=2\max\{p_L,p_R\}+\frac{6D^2}{K^2}+p_L.$$
If $\Phi(0+)\ge0$, then there is no positive matching pressure. The limiting
left and right rarefaction-tail velocities are ordered with a vacuum gap, or
coincide at the zero-pressure equality threshold. No other vacuum condition is
asserted.

Assume exact-real arithmetic in which each arithmetic operation, comparison,
square root, real power on a positive argument, scalar residual evaluation,
and call to the one-step Newton procedure terminates. **Inputs:**
admissible primitive states $(\rho_L,u_L,p_L)$ and $(\rho_R,u_R,p_R)$, gas
constant $\gamma>1$, pressure-width tolerance $\tau>0$, and iteration budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$. **Outputs:** `inadmissible-input`, `vacuum`,
`pressure-bracket` with an interval, or `budget-exhausted` with an interval.
The procedure never treats a nonzero residual tolerance as an exact root.

1. If $\rho_L,\rho_R,p_L,p_R$ are not all positive or $\gamma\le1$, return
   `inadmissible-input` before evaluating a wave response.
2. Compute $\Phi(0+)$ from
   [[thm-euler-star-pressure-root-and-vacuum-criterion]]. If $\Phi(0+)\ge0$,
   return `vacuum`.
3. Otherwise set the bracket $[a,b]=[0,P]$ with $P$ from that theorem. Its
   endpoint convention is $\Phi(a):=\Phi(0+)<0<\Phi(b)$.
4. For at most $N$ iterations, in this order:
   1. If $b-a\le\tau$, return `pressure-bracket` with $[a,b]$.
   2. Let $m=(a+b)/2$. Call
      [[alg-finite-budget-newton-for-vector-residuals]] on the scalar residual
      $F(p)=\Phi(p)$ over the open domain $(0,\infty)$, starting at $m$, with
      residual tolerance $0$ and update budget $1$.
   3. If Newton returns $(r,\texttt{root})$, return `pressure-bracket` with
      $[r,r]$. If it
      returns `iteration-budget-exhausted` with last iterate $q$ and
      $a+(b-a)/4\le q\le b-(b-a)/4$, use $q$ as the query. In every other
      status or when this central-quarter test fails, use $m$ as the query.
   4. Evaluate $\Phi$ at the query. If it is zero, return `pressure-bracket`
      with the singleton interval. If negative, replace $a$ by the query; if
      positive, replace $b$ by the query.
5. After the budget, return `pressure-bracket` if the width is at most $\tau$;
   otherwise return `budget-exhausted` with the current bracket.

The returned interval uses the zero lower endpoint as a limiting endpoint, not
an admissible pressure. This algorithm gives a finite status and bracket; the
separate theorem below proves its invariant and width reduction. It makes no
claim that an exhausted budget found a root.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$ ([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]) with Jacobian $J_F$ as in
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. The matrix of $DF(x)$ in the standard
basis is $J_F(x)$ by
[[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].
**Inputs:** $x_0\in U$, residual
tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$, and update budget $N\in\mathbb N_0$.
**Output:** the last valid iterate and one of `root`, `singular-jacobian`,
`invalid-trial`, or `iteration-budget-exhausted`.

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N$, in this order:

1. Compute $F(x_k)$. If $\|F(x_k)\|_2\le\varepsilon$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{root})$. Here `root` means the residual tolerance was met; it
   does not certify an exact zero when $\varepsilon>0$.
2. If $k=N$, return $(x_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted})$.
3. Call [[alg-newton-correction-for-vector-residuals]] with
   $A=J_F(x_k)$ and $r=F(x_k)$. If it returns `singular-jacobian`, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{singular-jacobian})$.
4. Let $s_k$ be its correction. If $x_k+s_k\notin U$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{invalid-trial})$. Otherwise set $x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k$.

It makes no arbitrary-start, global-convergence, or discretization-error claim.

Let $n\ge1$, let $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be a linear map, and let
$r\in\mathbb R^n$ be a residual vector. If $A$ is not invertible in the sense
of [[def-invertible-euclidean-linear-map]], return
$(\texttt{singular-jacobian},\varnothing)$. If $A$ is invertible, return
$(\texttt{correction},s)$, where $s$ is the unique vector solving
$$As=-r.$$

Use the following exact-arithmetic procedure, with exact real zero tests.
Represent $A$ by its matrix in the standard basis, with indices $0\le i,j<n$.

1. To compute the determinant of any matrix $M=(m_{ij})$ below, initialize
   $d=0$. Enumerate the permutations $\sigma$ of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ in
   lexicographic order. For each, count its inversions
   $\nu(\sigma)=\#\{(i,j):i<j,\ \sigma(i)>\sigma(j)\}$, multiply
   $p=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}m_{\sigma(i),i}$ in increasing index order, and add
   $(-1)^{\nu(\sigma)}p$ to $d$. The resulting $d$ is the determinant in
   [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]].
2. Compute $d=\det(A)$ by step 1. If $d=0$, return
   $(\texttt{singular-jacobian},\varnothing)$, using
   [[thm-real-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]] for the
   invertibility test.
3. Otherwise, for $j=0,\ldots,n-1$, copy $A$ to $A_j$, replace column $j$
   by $-r$, compute $d_j=\det(A_j)$ by step 1, and set $s_j=d_j/d$.
   Return $(\texttt{correction},s)$, the solution specified by
   [[thm-cramers-rule-over-a-commutative-ring]] over $\mathbb R$.

The output is a linear correction, not a claim that $r$ came from a nonlinear
function or that applying the correction decreases a residual.

A midpoint query lies in its central half; any accepted Newton query is in the central quarter, and all other Newton outcomes use the midpoint. Let $m\ge1$, let $G\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let
$f:G\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^3$ ([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]];
the $C^3$ convention is that of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
The one-dimensional conservation system with state domain $G$ is
$$u_t+\partial_x f(u)=0,\qquad u(t,x)\in G,$$
where $u$ is the conserved state and $f$ its flux. Its flux Jacobian is
$A(u)=Df(u)$. The system is **strictly hyperbolic on an open set $N\subseteq G$**
if, for every $u\in N$, $A(u)$ has $m$ distinct real eigenvalues, written in
increasing order $\lambda_1(u)<\cdots<\lambda_m(u)$. An **$i$th characteristic
family** on $N$ is a $C^2$ right-eigenvector field $r_i:N\to\mathbb R^m\setminus\{0\}$
with $A(u)r_i(u)=\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$. It is **genuinely nonlinear** on $N$ if
$D\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$ is nowhere zero there; after shrinking $N$ its sign is
constant. It is **linearly degenerate** on $N$ if $D\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)=0$
throughout $N$. Rescaling $r_i$ by a nonzero constant changes the wave-strength
parameter but not the family.

For $Q=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, a locally bounded map $u:Q\to G$ is a
**distributional weak solution with initial data $u_0$** if
$$\int_Q\bigl(u\cdot\varphi_t+f(u)\cdot\varphi_x\bigr)\,dt\,dx=0$$
for every vector test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)$ and
$u(t,\cdot)\to u_0$ in $L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^m)$ as
$t\downarrow0$. A **Riemann initial datum** is the step
$u_0(x)=u_L$ for $x<0$ and $u_0(x)=u_R$ for $x>0$.

In this weak-solution clause, $u$ is required to be Lebesgue measurable and
$f\circ u\in L^1_{\rm loc}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$, so the test-function integral is
defined. Local boundedness gives $u\in L^1_{\rm loc}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$.

Fix a local characteristic family on a neighborhood where it is either
genuinely nonlinear with constant sign $d_i=D\lambda_i\,r_i\ne0$, or linearly
degenerate. For a genuinely nonlinear family define
$$\Psi_i(\sigma;u)=\begin{cases}R_i(\sigma;u),&\sigma d_i>0,\\S_i(\sigma;u),&\sigma d_i<0,\\u,&\sigma=0.\end{cases}$$
where $R_i$ is the local rarefaction curve and $S_i$ the local shock curve of
[[lem-local-characteristic-shock-curve]]. For a linearly degenerate family set
$\Psi_i(\sigma;u)=R_i(\sigma;u)$ for either sign; its nonzero-strength wave is
the contact of [[lem-linearly-degenerate-characteristic-contact]]. The
parameter $\sigma$ is local and is restricted so the entire curve stays in the
chosen neighborhood.

Under the hypotheses of [[def-mixed-characteristic-wave-curve]], the map
$(\sigma,u)\mapsto\Psi_i(\sigma;u)$ is $C^1$ near $(0,\bar u)$, with
$\Psi_i(0;u)=u$ and $\partial_\sigma\Psi_i(0;u)=r_i(u)$.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

For a conservation system as in
[[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]], constant states
$u_L,u_R\in G$, and a constant speed $s$, define
$u(t,x)=u_L$ for $x<st$ and $u(t,x)=u_R$ for $x>st$, and let
$u_0(x)=u_L$ for $x<0$ and $u_0(x)=u_R$ for $x>0$ (values on the jump lines
are immaterial). Then $u$ is a distributional weak solution with initial datum
$u_0$ in the sense of [[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]]
if and only if
$$f(u_R)-f(u_L)=s(u_R-u_L).$$

Let $G\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $f:G\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^3$, and
let $\bar u\in G$ be a state where $A(\bar u)=Df(\bar u)$ has $m$ distinct
real eigenvalues $\lambda_1(\bar u)<\cdots<\lambda_m(\bar u)$.
Fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and its $i$th eigenpair
$(\lambda_i(\bar u),r_i(\bar u))$. There are a neighborhood $N_0$ of $\bar u$,
$\eta>0$, and $C^1$ functions $v_i(\sigma,u_0),s_i(\sigma,u_0)$ for
$u_0\in N_0$, $|\sigma|<\eta$, such that, with $\ell_i(u_0)$ the dual left
eigenvector normalized by $\ell_i(u_0)\cdot r_i(u_0)=1$,
$$\ell_i(u_0)\cdot v_i(\sigma,u_0)=1,\qquad S_i(\sigma;u_0)=u_0+\sigma v_i(\sigma,u_0),$$
and for $\sigma\ne0$ the pair $(u_0,S_i(\sigma;u_0))$ satisfies
Rankine–Hugoniot with speed $s_i(\sigma,u_0)$. Also
$S_i(0;u_0)=u_0$ and $\partial_\sigma S_i(0;u_0)=r_i(u_0)$. If the $i$th
field is genuinely nonlinear on $N_0$ and
$d_i(u):=D\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$ has constant nonzero sign, then all sufficiently
small nonzero strengths with $\sigma d_i(u_0)<0$ give strict Lax $i$-shocks.

Let $r_i$ be linearly degenerate on a neighborhood and let $R_i(\sigma;u_0)$
be its local rarefaction curve. Then the states $u_0$ and
$u_1=R_i(\sigma;u_0)$ are joined by a Rankine–Hugoniot jump of speed
$\lambda_i(u_0)$, and the corresponding moving discontinuity is a weak
solution. The characteristic speed is equal on the two sides; this is a
contact wave, not a strict Lax shock.

Let $r_i$ be a $C^1$ genuinely nonlinear field on a neighborhood, with
$D\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$ of constant nonzero sign. If $\sigma\ne0$ satisfies
$\sigma D\lambda_i(u_0)r_i(u_0)>0$ and is sufficiently small, then the
left/right data $u_0,R_i(\sigma;u_0)$ are connected by a centered rarefaction
fan. It is a self-similar weak solution with those Riemann data.

derivations.claim: Define $\mathcal W(u_L,\sigma)=\Psi_m(\sigma_m;\Psi_{m-1}(\sigma_{m-1};\cdots\Psi_1(\sigma_1;u_L)\cdots))$ and $F(u_L,u_R,\sigma)=\mathcal W(u_L,\sigma)-u_R$. By [F2] and [F3], $F$ is $C^1$, $F(\bar u,\bar u,0)=0$, and the columns of $D_\sigma F(\bar u,\bar u,0)$ are $r_1(\bar u),\ldots,r_m(\bar u)$.

2.1 These eigenvectors are linearly independent by strict hyperbolicity, so $D_\sigma F$ is invertible. Applying [F4] with parameter $(u_L,u_R)$ gives neighborhoods $P$ of $(\bar u,\bar u)$ and $Q$ of $0$, and a unique $C^1$ vector $\sigma(u_L,u_R)\in Q$ for every pair in $P$. If $u_L=u_R$, then $\sigma=0$ solves the composition equation by [F2], so this is the unique strength vector. Choose $\eta>0$ with $(-\eta,\eta)^m\subseteq Q$. Since the IFT solution $\sigma(u_L,u_R)$ is continuous and vanishes at $(\bar u,\bar u)$, shrink $\delta>0$ so both radius-$\delta$ state balls lie in $P$ and every corresponding IFT solution lies in $(-\eta,\eta)^m$.

Shrink these neighborhoods so all intermediate states stay in $N$. Since $N$ is a neighborhood of $\bar u$ and there are finitely many continuous wave curves, this is possible. The characteristic-speed gaps at $\bar u$ are positive; continuity of eigenvalues, shock speeds and rarefaction speeds lets us further shrink the neighborhoods until the speed range of each family lies in a disjoint interval ordered by $i$.

For each strength, use the rarefaction fan from [F8] when $\sigma_iD\lambda_i r_i>0$, the Lax shock from [F6] when it is negative, and the contact from [F7] for a linearly-degenerate family. Each shock/contact satisfies Rankine–Hugoniot, hence is a weak jump by [F5].

The family speed intervals from step 3.1 are disjoint and ordered, so the elementary waves paste into a single-valued self-similar profile from $u_L$ to $u_R$. Each fan satisfies the equation classically by [F8]; integration by parts across each shock/contact gives boundary coefficient $[f]-s[u]=0$ by [F5], [F6], and [F7], and the continuous fan edges contribute no jump term. Thus the pasted profile is a distributional weak solution. Its wave speeds are bounded, so its nonconstant region has length at most a constant times $t$ and its $L^1_{\rm loc}$ trace is the Riemann step as $t\downarrow0$. The endpoint states match by the composition equation in step 1.1. Uniqueness of $\sigma$ from step 2.1 gives uniqueness of this ordered local elementary-wave construction, not of arbitrary weak solutions.

For states $u_L,u_R$ in the open state domain $G$ of
[[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]], a **Roe matrix** is a map
$\widetilde A:G\times G\to\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ such that, for all
$u,u_L,u_R\in G$,
$$\widetilde A(u,u)=Df(u),\qquad \widetilde A(u_L,u_R)(u_R-u_L)=f(u_R)-f(u_L),$$
and $\widetilde A(u_L,u_R)$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb R$ with real
eigenvalues. The map $\widetilde A$ is also continuous at each diagonal pair
$(u,u)$. If $\widetilde A=R\Lambda R^{-1}$, define
$|\widetilde A|=R|\Lambda|R^{-1}$ by replacing each diagonal eigenvalue with
its absolute value. The **Roe flux associated with this matrix** is
$$\widehat f_{\rm Roe}(u_L,u_R)=\tfrac12(f(u_L)+f(u_R))-\tfrac12|\widetilde A(u_L,u_R)|(u_R-u_L).$$
The jump identity is an algebraic conservation property. This definition does
not assert entropy admissibility of the approximate wave pattern.

For the scalar case of [[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]],
use its definition of a weak solution on $Q=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. An
**entropy pair** on $G$ is a function $\eta\in C^2(G)$ that is convex on each
interval component of $G$, together with $q\in C^1(G)$ satisfying
$q'(u)=\eta'(u)f'(u)$. A weak solution $u$ is **entropy-admissible for this

Fix $\gamma>1$. In one space dimension the conserved state is
$U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathbb R^3$, where $\rho$ is density, $m$ momentum, and
$E$ total energy per unit volume. The **admissible-state set** is the open set
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\ E>m^2/(2\rho)\}.$$
The ideal-gas pressure on this set is
$$p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}\right)>0,$$
the velocity is $u=m/\rho$, and the flux is
$$F(U)=\left(m,\frac{m^2}{\rho}+p,\frac{m}{\rho}(E+p)\right).$$
The sound speed is $c=\sqrt{\gamma p/\rho}$. These definitions apply only
on $\mathcal G_\gamma$; a state with nonpositive density or nonpositive
internal energy is inadmissible. The set is open because $\rho$ and
$E-m^2/(2\rho)$ are continuous on $\rho>0$ and the inequalities are strict;
all displayed flux functions are smooth on this domain.

For $U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathcal G_\gamma$, put $u=m/\rho$,
$H=(E+p)/\rho$, and $c=\sqrt{\gamma p/\rho}$. The flux Jacobian has the
three simple real eigenvalues and right eigenvectors
$$\lambda_-=u-c,\qquad r_-=(1,u-c,H-uc)^T,$$
$$\lambda_0=u,\qquad r_0=(1,u,u^2/2)^T,$$
$$\lambda_+=u+c,\qquad r_+=(1,u+c,H+uc)^T.$$
The middle field is linearly degenerate; the acoustic fields are genuinely
nonlinear, with $D\lambda_-r_-=-(\gamma+1)c/(2\rho)$ and
$D\lambda_+r_+=(\gamma+1)c/(2\rho)$.

For a system as in [[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]], a
discontinuity with constant states $u_L,u_R\in G$ and speed $s\in\mathbb R$ is
a **Rankine–Hugoniot jump** if
$$f(u_R)-f(u_L)=s(u_R-u_L).$$
For a system strictly hyperbolic on $N\subseteq G$, states $u_L,u_R\in N$,
and $1\le i\le m$, it is a **strict Lax $i$-shock** if it is a Rankine–Hugoniot jump and
$$\lambda_j(u_L)<s\ (j<i),\qquad \lambda_i(u_R)<s<\lambda_i(u_L),\qquad s<\lambda_j(u_R)\ (j>i).$$
An empty family of inequalities is omitted. A linearly-degenerate contact has
equal $i$-speeds on both sides, so it is not a strict Lax shock.

$U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathbb R^3$, where $\rho$ is density, $m$ momentum, and
$E$ total energy per unit volume. The **admissible-state set** is the open set
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\ E>m^2/(2\rho)\}.$$
The ideal-gas pressure on this set is
$$p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}\right)>0,$$
the velocity is $u=m/\rho$, and the flux is
$$F(U)=\left(m,\frac{m^2}{\rho}+p,\frac{m}{\rho}(E+p)\right).$$
The sound speed is $c=\sqrt{\gamma p/\rho}$. These definitions apply only
on $\mathcal G_\gamma$; a state with nonpositive density or nonpositive
internal energy is inadmissible. The set is open because $\rho$ and
$E-m^2/(2\rho)$ are continuous on $\rho>0$ and the inequalities are strict;
all displayed flux functions are smooth on this domain.

Fix $\gamma>1$ and admissible left/right primitive states
$(\rho_K,u_K,p_K)$, $K\in\{L,R\}$, with $\rho_K,p_K>0$ and
$c_K=\sqrt{\gamma p_K/\rho_K}$. Set
$$A_K=\frac{2}{(\gamma+1)\rho_K},\qquad B_K=\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma+1}p_K.$$
For a trial star pressure $p>0$, the wave pressure response from side $K$ is
$$f_K(p)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{2c_K}{\gamma-1}\left[\left(\dfrac p{p_K}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/(2\gamma)}-1\right],&0<p\le p_K,\\(p-p_K)\sqrt{\dfrac{A_K}{p+B_K}},&p\ge p_K.\end{cases}$$
The two formulas agree at $p=p_K$. The **star-pressure residual** is
$$\Phi(p)=f_L(p)+f_R(p)+u_R-u_L,\qquad p>0.$$
This is a scalar root equation; it does not itself define a Riemann solution.

For the data of [[def-euler-star-pressure-response]], let
$$\Phi(0+):=u_R-u_L-\frac{2(c_L+c_R)}{\gamma-1}.$$
The residual $\Phi$ is $C^1$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.
If $\Phi(0+)<0$, then $\Phi$ has exactly one zero $p_*>0$. By the acoustic
wave-response lemma this is the unique positive pressure at which the left and
right wave curves can be joined by a contact. It lies in the
explicit bracket $0<p_*<P$, where, writing
$D=\max\{0,u_L-u_R\}$ and $K=\sqrt{A_L}+\sqrt{A_R}$,
$$P=2\max\{p_L,p_R\}+\frac{6D^2}{K^2}+p_L.$$
If $\Phi(0+)\ge0$, then there is no positive matching pressure. The limiting
left and right rarefaction-tail velocities are ordered with a vacuum gap, or
coincide at the zero-pressure equality threshold. No other vacuum condition is
asserted.

Assume exact-real arithmetic in which each arithmetic operation, comparison,
square root, real power on a positive argument, scalar residual evaluation,
and call to the one-step Newton procedure terminates. **Inputs:**
admissible primitive states $(\rho_L,u_L,p_L)$ and $(\rho_R,u_R,p_R)$, gas
constant $\gamma>1$, pressure-width tolerance $\tau>0$, and iteration budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$. **Outputs:** `inadmissible-input`, `vacuum`,
`pressure-bracket` with an interval, or `budget-exhausted` with an interval.
The procedure never treats a nonzero residual tolerance as an exact root.

1. If $\rho_L,\rho_R,p_L,p_R$ are not all positive or $\gamma\le1$, return
   `inadmissible-input` before evaluating a wave response.
2. Compute $\Phi(0+)$ from
   [[thm-euler-star-pressure-root-and-vacuum-criterion]]. If $\Phi(0+)\ge0$,
   return `vacuum`.
3. Otherwise set the bracket $[a,b]=[0,P]$ with $P$ from that theorem. Its
   endpoint convention is $\Phi(a):=\Phi(0+)<0<\Phi(b)$.
4. For at most $N$ iterations, in this order:
   1. If $b-a\le\tau$, return `pressure-bracket` with $[a,b]$.
   2. Let $m=(a+b)/2$. Call
      [[alg-finite-budget-newton-for-vector-residuals]] on the scalar residual
      $F(p)=\Phi(p)$ over the open domain $(0,\infty)$, starting at $m$, with
      residual tolerance $0$ and update budget $1$.
   3. If Newton returns $(r,\texttt{root})$, return `pressure-bracket` with
      $[r,r]$. If it
      returns `iteration-budget-exhausted` with last iterate $q$ and
      $a+(b-a)/4\le q\le b-(b-a)/4$, use $q$ as the query. In every other
      status or when this central-quarter test fails, use $m$ as the query.
   4. Evaluate $\Phi$ at the query. If it is zero, return `pressure-bracket`
      with the singleton interval. If negative, replace $a$ by the query; if
      positive, replace $b$ by the query.
5. After the budget, return `pressure-bracket` if the width is at most $\tau$;
   otherwise return `budget-exhausted` with the current bracket.

The returned interval uses the zero lower endpoint as a limiting endpoint, not
an admissible pressure. This algorithm gives a finite status and bracket; the
separate theorem below proves its invariant and width reduction. It makes no
claim that an exhausted budget found a root.

Let $m\ge1$, let $G\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let
$f:G\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^3$ ([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]];
the $C^3$ convention is that of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
The one-dimensional conservation system with state domain $G$ is
$$u_t+\partial_x f(u)=0,\qquad u(t,x)\in G,$$
where $u$ is the conserved state and $f$ its flux. Its flux Jacobian is
$A(u)=Df(u)$. The system is **strictly hyperbolic on an open set $N\subseteq G$**
if, for every $u\in N$, $A(u)$ has $m$ distinct real eigenvalues, written in
increasing order $\lambda_1(u)<\cdots<\lambda_m(u)$. An **$i$th characteristic
family** on $N$ is a $C^2$ right-eigenvector field $r_i:N\to\mathbb R^m\setminus\{0\}$
with $A(u)r_i(u)=\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$. It is **genuinely nonlinear** on $N$ if
$D\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$ is nowhere zero there; after shrinking $N$ its sign is
constant. It is **linearly degenerate** on $N$ if $D\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)=0$
throughout $N$. Rescaling $r_i$ by a nonzero constant changes the wave-strength
parameter but not the family.

For $Q=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, a locally bounded map $u:Q\to G$ is a
**distributional weak solution with initial data $u_0$** if
$$\int_Q\bigl(u\cdot\varphi_t+f(u)\cdot\varphi_x\bigr)\,dt\,dx=0$$
for every vector test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)$ and
$u(t,\cdot)\to u_0$ in $L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^m)$ as
$t\downarrow0$. A **Riemann initial datum** is the step
$u_0(x)=u_L$ for $x<0$ and $u_0(x)=u_R$ for $x>0$.

In this weak-solution clause, $u$ is required to be Lebesgue measurable and
$f\circ u\in L^1_{\rm loc}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$, so the test-function integral is
defined. Local boundedness gives $u\in L^1_{\rm loc}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$.

Let $f:G\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^3$, let $\bar u\in G$, and suppose on an open
neighborhood $N$ of $\bar u$ the system is strictly hyperbolic and each
characteristic field is either genuinely nonlinear or linearly degenerate. Then
there are $\delta,\eta>0$ such that, whenever
$\|u_L-\bar u\|_2<\delta$ and $\|u_R-\bar u\|_2<\delta$, there is a unique
strength vector $\sigma\in(-\eta,\eta)^m$ satisfying
$$u_R=\Psi_m(\sigma_m;\Psi_{m-1}(\sigma_{m-1};\cdots\Psi_1(\sigma_1;u_L)\cdots)).$$
For the Riemann initial datum $u_0(x)=u_L$ for $x<0$ and $u_R$ for $x>0$,
the corresponding ordered superposition, with waves in increasing family
order, is a self-similar weak solution, meaning it has the form
$u(t,x)=q(x/t)$ for $t>0$. Its nonzero
genuinely nonlinear waves are rarefactions when $\sigma_iD\lambda_i r_i>0$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: By [F2], each weak derivative $\partial_iv_i$ is in $L^2$, so their finite sum $\operatorname{div}v$ is in $L^2(D)$.
For $v\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^d)$, each component derivative has integral zero by one-dimensional integration along its coordinate, hence $\int_D\operatorname{div}v=0$.

By [A1, F1], choose $v_n\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^d)$ converging to $v$ in $H^1$. Then $\operatorname{div}v_n\to\operatorname{div}v$ in $L^2$ by [F2]. Applying [F3] to the difference shows their integrals converge; the zero integrals in step 1.2 therefore give $\int_D\operatorname{div}v=0$.

$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: For $v\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^d)$, expanding the symmetric gradient gives $2|\varepsilon(v)|^2=|\nabla v|^2+\sum_{i,j}\partial_jv_i\partial_iv_j$ pointwise.

For each $i,j$, apply [F3] to $h=v_i\partial_i v_j$, which is compactly supported and smooth. The product rule gives $\int_D\partial_jv_i\partial_iv_j=-\int_Dv_i\partial_j\partial_iv_j$. Summing in $j$ and using equality of mixed derivatives gives $-\sum_i\int_Dv_i\partial_i(\operatorname{div}v)$. Apply [F3] again to $h=v_i\operatorname{div}v$ and sum in $i$ to obtain $\sum_i\int_D(\partial_iv_i)\operatorname{div}v=\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2$.

By [A1, F1], approximate any $v\in H^1_0$ by such smooth fields in $H^1$. All three squared norms in the identity converge by [F2] and continuity of the finite sums, so the identity passes to the limit. Its nonnegative divergence term gives the displayed inequality.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

derivations.claim: Fix one graph chart, with Lipschitz constant $L$, and a smaller horizontal ball $C$ whose closure lies in its base. Shrink its radius $r$ until the chart's upper height $H_{\rm chart}$ satisfies $H_{\rm chart}-\sup_C\varphi>4(L+1)r$. Choose $c$ with $\sup_C\varphi+3(L+1)r<c<H_{\rm chart}-(L+1)r$ and $0<\rho<r$. Then the closed ball $\overline B((x'_0,c),\rho)$ stays in the cylinder. Set $U=\{(x',x_d):x'\in C,\ \varphi(x')<x_d<H\}$ with $c+\rho<H<H_{\rm chart}$.

If $x\in U$, $z\in\overline B((x'_0,c),\rho)$, and $w=(1-t)x+tz$ with $0<t<1$, then $z'\in C$ and convexity keeps $w'\in C$. Since $|z'-x'|\le2r$, Lipschitz continuity gives $\varphi(w')\le\varphi(x')+2Lrt$. Also $c-\rho>\sup_C\varphi+2Lr$, so $w_d>(1-t)\varphi(x')+t(c-\rho)>\varphi(x')+2Lrt\ge\varphi(w')$, and $w_d<H$ by convexity of the vertical interval. Thus $w\in U$; the endpoints belong to $U$ as well, proving star-shapedness with respect to the closed ball.

The boundary $\partial D$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F1]. At any $p\in\partial D$, a chart containing $p$ writes the boundary locally as $x_d=\varphi(x')$, with $p_d=\varphi(p')$ strictly below the chart's upper height. Shrinking a horizontal ball $C$ about $p'$ makes its closure lie in the chart base and makes the height-gap inequality of step 1.1 hold; the choices there then produce a patch $U=\{(x',x_d):x'\in C,\ \varphi(x')<x_d<H\}$ star-shaped with respect to its selected closed ball by step 2.1. Since $p$ lies inside the chart and inside the open set with $x'\in C$ and $x_d<H$, there is an ambient open ball $N$ about $p$ whose closure lies in that chart and open set. For every $x\in N\cap D$, the chart description gives $x_d>\varphi(x')$, so $x\in U$ and $N\cap D\subset U$. Let $\mathscr N$ be the family of all pairs $(N,U)$ obtained this way from the finite chart atlas and admissible local choices; the preceding existence argument shows that its first components cover $\partial D$, without choosing a patch simultaneously for every boundary point. Compactness supplies a finite subfamily $(N_i,U_i)$, $1\le i\le m$, whose neighborhoods cover $\partial D$. Their union is an open neighborhood of the compact boundary, so some relative collar $\{x\in D:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial D)<\delta\}$ lies in that union and hence in $\bigcup_{i=1}^mU_i$. The remainder $K_\delta=\{x\in\overline D:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial D)\ge\delta\}$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F1], and is contained in $D$ because every point of $\overline D\setminus D$ lies on $\partial D$. Finitely many balls with closures in $D$ cover $K_\delta$; each ball is convex and star-shaped with respect to a smaller concentric ball. Together these sets form a finite star-shaped cover of $D$.

The intersection graph is connected: if it split into two nonempty graph components, the unions of the corresponding open sets would be disjoint nonempty relatively open subsets whose union is $D$, contradicting connectedness. Order the cover and set $E_i=U_i\setminus\bigcup_{j<i}U_j$. Then the $E_i$ are disjoint measurable sets with $E_i\subset U_i$ and union $D$. A finite connected graph has a spanning tree.

Each tree-edge intersection is nonempty and open, so it contains a ball. Choose a nonnegative smooth bump supported in that ball. Its integral is strictly positive; dividing by that integral gives $\psi_{ij}\in C_c^\infty(U_i\cap U_j)$ with integral one.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

derivations.claim: If $Q=\{0\}$, the unique map $R:Q\to V$ is a bounded right inverse and the claim is complete. Otherwise, since the scalar field is real, replacing $v$ by $-v$ changes the sign of $b(v,q)$; hence the displayed supremum equals the supremum of $|b(v,q)|/(\|v\|\|q\|)$. By [F3], $\|B^*q\|_V\ge\beta\|q\|_Q$.

On $Q$, define $c(q,r):=(B^*q,B^*r)_V$. It is bounded by $\|B\|^2\|q\|\|r\|$ and coercive with constant $\beta^2$ by step 1.1. For arbitrary $g\in Q$, the functional $r\mapsto(g,r)_Q$ is bounded, so [F2] gives a unique $q\in Q$ with $(B^*q,B^*r)_V=(g,r)_Q$ for all $r$. The adjoint identity implies $BB^*q=g$.

Set $Rg:=B^*q$, with $q$ from step 2.1. Uniqueness in Lax–Milgram makes this assignment linear, and the adjoint identity in [F3] gives $BRg=g$. Also $\|Rg\|^2=(g,q)\le\|g\|\|q\|$ while step 2.1 gives $\beta\|q\|\le\|Rg\|$. If $Rg=0$ the desired bound is immediate; otherwise combine and divide to obtain $\|Rg\|\le\beta^{-1}\|g\|$. Thus $R$ is the claimed bounded right inverse.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a matching affine simplicial mesh of $\Omega$ as defined
in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Fix $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and an integer $q\ge1$. On each
cell let $\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q)$ denote the
restrictions to $K$ of $\mathbb K^q$-valued polynomials of total degree at
most $k$. The **broken polynomial space** is the finite product
$$V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:=\prod_{K\in\mathcal T}\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q),$$
viewed as functions defined almost everywhere cell by cell. For an interior
facet $F=K\cap K'$, the **jump** is the difference of the two polynomial
traces, with either fixed ordering of $K,K'$; its vanishing is independent of
that ordering. The **conforming polynomial space** is
$$V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}:=\{v\in V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:v|_{F,K}=v|_{F,K'}\text{ on every interior facet }F\}.$$
The **zero-boundary subspace** consists of those $v\in V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}$
whose polynomial trace is zero on every boundary facet. These are algebraic
definitions. The Sobolev inclusions and the zero-boundary closure conclusion
are proved separately in the corresponding local theorems on matching
piecewise polynomials and zero-boundary values. If $\mathcal T=\varnothing$,
then $\Omega=\varnothing$ by the mesh definition; the empty product is the
zero vector space consisting of the unique empty function, and the trace
conditions are vacuous.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded polyhedral open set with a finite matching
affine simplicial mesh, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $v$ be a real-valued
conforming piecewise polynomial whose polynomial trace vanishes on every boundary
facet. Then
$$v\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega),\qquad \|v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}.$$
Here $W^{1,p}_0$ is the norm closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$; no C1
trace characterization is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1<p<\infty$ and $p'=p/(p-1)$. For each facet $F$ of
$\widehat S_d$, restriction of smooth functions extends uniquely to a
bounded linear trace map
$$\gamma_F:W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)\to L^p(F;\mathbb R).$$
For real-valued $u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)$ and
$G\in W^{1,p'}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R^d)$, the facet traces satisfy
$$\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,\operatorname{div}G+\nabla u\cdot G\,dx =\sum_{F\subset\partial\widehat S_d}\int_F\gamma_Fu\,\gamma_FG\cdot\widehat n_F\,dS.$$
Here $\gamma_FG$ is the componentwise trace and $\widehat n_F$ is the
outward unit normal. The bounded C1-domain trace and Green theorems are not
used for the simplex.

Assume Countable Choice. For every $1\le p<\infty$ there is
$C_{d,p}<\infty$ such that for all
$u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)$,
$$\|u-u_{\widehat S_d}\|_{L^p(\widehat S_d)} \le C_{d,p}|u|_{W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)},\qquad u_{\widehat S_d}:=|\widehat S_d|^{-1}\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,dx.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1\le p<\infty$, integer $r\ge1$,
integer $s\ge0$, and real-valued $v\in W^{\max(r,s),p}(\widehat S_d)$.
There is a polynomial $q\in\mathbb P_{r-1}(\widehat S_d)$, chosen by
matching all means $\int_{\widehat S_d}D^\alpha q=
\int_{\widehat S_d}D^\alpha v$ for $|\alpha|\le r-1$, such that:

- if $0\le s\le r$, then
  $\|v-q\|_{W^{s,p}(\widehat S_d)}\le C|v|_{W^{r,p}(\widehat S_d)}$;
- if $s>r$, then
  $\|v-q\|_{W^{s,p}(\widehat S_d)}\le
  C\sum_{j=r}^{s}|v|_{W^{j,p}(\widehat S_d)}$.

The second clause assumes $v\in W^{s,p}$; constants depend only on
$d,p,r,s$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1<p<\infty$ and $p'=p/(p-1)$. For each facet $F$ of
$\widehat S_d$, restriction of smooth functions extends uniquely to a
bounded linear trace map
$$\gamma_F:W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)\to L^p(F;\mathbb R).$$
For real-valued $u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)$ and
$G\in W^{1,p'}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R^d)$, the facet traces satisfy
$$\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,\operatorname{div}G+\nabla u\cdot G\,dx =\sum_{F\subset\partial\widehat S_d}\int_F\gamma_Fu\,\gamma_FG\cdot\widehat n_F\,dS.$$
Here $\gamma_FG$ is the componentwise trace and $\widehat n_F$ is the
outward unit normal. The bounded C1-domain trace and Green theorems are not
used for the simplex.

Let F be complete for a multiplicative absolute value and V a finite-dimensional normed F-vector space. For any basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$, its coordinate sup norm $\|\sum a_iv_i\|_\infty=\max_i|a_i|$ is bounded above and below by positive multiples of the given norm. For $n=0$ both norms are zero. Consequently V is complete and every linear subspace is closed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1<p<\infty$ and $p'=p/(p-1)$. For each facet $F$ of
$\widehat S_d$, restriction of smooth functions extends uniquely to a
bounded linear trace map
$$\gamma_F:W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)\to L^p(F;\mathbb R).$$
For real-valued $u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)$ and
$G\in W^{1,p'}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R^d)$, the facet traces satisfy
$$\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,\operatorname{div}G+\nabla u\cdot G\,dx =\sum_{F\subset\partial\widehat S_d}\int_F\gamma_Fu\,\gamma_FG\cdot\widehat n_F\,dS.$$
Here $\gamma_FG$ is the componentwise trace and $\widehat n_F$ is the
outward unit normal. The bounded C1-domain trace and Green theorems are not
used for the simplex.

derivations.claim: On each reference facet, the P1 facet mass matrix is positive definite because $\int_Fp^2>0$ for every nonzero affine polynomial. Its inverse defines the dual functions $\widehat\psi_z$; affine scaling in [F2] gives $\|\psi_{z,F}\|_{L^2(F)}\le C h_F^{-(d-1)/2}$. The trace map in [F3] therefore makes every coefficient of $I_hv$ a bounded linear functional on the H1 trace of an adjacent cell. Shared coefficients define a continuous P1 function. If $v\in H^1_0$, [F4] makes all selected boundary-facet averages zero, so $I_hv$ has zero boundary nodal values and belongs to $H^1_0$ by [F1].

The coefficients reproduce every global affine polynomial: on the selected facet its trace is P1 and the dual moment equals its value at $z$. Shape regularity bounds the number of cells at each vertex: each simplex's vertex solid angle has a positive lower bound, while the total angle is at most $2\pi$ in dimension two or $4\pi$ in dimension three. The vertex-star graph is connected as follows. Choose a small chart cylinder meeting only cells incident to the vertex. At an interior vertex, a small ball lies in $D$. At a boundary vertex, the Lipschitz chart represents this local part of $D$ as the region above a Lipschitz graph; within a smaller base ball, vertical paths to a common height above the graph and a horizontal segment at that height connect any two points. Hence this local part is path connected. Join interior points of any two incident cells by a polygonal path there and perturb its finitely many segments to avoid the finite mesh skeleton of codimension at least two. The path then crosses only facet interiors and gives a facet-adjacency chain among cells incident to the vertex. Adjacent cell diameters are comparable by [F2]. Thus vertex-patch diameters and overlap are uniformly bounded.

Let $\omega_K$ be the union of cells meeting a vertex of $K$. Shape regularity bounds the number of cells at each vertex: each has a solid angle bounded below by the reference-cell shape bound, whereas the total angle is at most $2\pi$ in dimension two and $4\pi$ in dimension three. Each vertex-star graph is connected by step 1.2, and all stars of vertices of $K$ contain $K$, so their union is connected; neighboring cell diameters are comparable by [F2]. For adjacent cells $T,T'$ with common facet $F$, let $m_T,m_{T'}$ be their volume means. Cell Poincare and trace in [F3] give $\|w-m_T\|_{L^2(F)}\le Ch_K^{1/2}\|
abla w\|_{L^2(T)}$ and the analogous bound on $T'$. Since $|F|^{1/2}\asymp h_K^{(d-1)/2}$, it follows that $|m_T-m_{T'}|\le Ch_K^{(2-d)/2}\|
abla w\|_{L^2(T\cup T')}$. A path of bounded length through the patch graph then compares all cell means to one fixed $c_K$ and proves $\|w-c_K\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}\le Ch_K\|
abla w\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Applying the scaled trace estimate of [F3] and $\|\psi_{z,F_z}\|_{L^2(F_z)}\le Ch_K^{-(d-1)/2}$ gives $|\int_{F_z}\psi_{z,F_z}(w-c_K)|\le Ch_K^{1-d/2}\|
abla w\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$ for every vertex of $K$.

Suppose $v\in H^2(D)$. On each cell $T\subset\omega_K$, Bramble--Hilbert and affine scaling in [F2, F3] give $p_T\in P_1(T)$ with $\|v-p_T\|_{L^2(T)}\le Ch_T^2\|D^2v\|_{L^2(T)}$ and $\|
abla(v-p_T)\|_{L^2(T)}\le Ch_T\|D^2v\|_{L^2(T)}$. For adjacent cells $T,T\prime$ sharing a facet $F$, the scaled trace estimate applied to $v-p_T$ and its first derivatives gives $\|p_T-p_{T\prime}\|_{L^2(F)}\le Ch_K^{3/2}\|D^2v\|_{L^2(T\cup T\prime)}$ and $|F|^{1/2}|
abla p_T-
abla p_{T\prime}|\le Ch_K^{1/2}\|D^2v\|_{L^2(T\cup T\prime)}$. The second bound controls the full gradient difference, and the first then controls its constant part. Normalize both cell diameters by $h_K$. Shape regularity and comparability across the shared facet bound the normalized affine maps and their inverses; there are only finitely many vertex-orderings. Their closure is a compact set of nondegenerate reference-pair configurations. Finite-dimensional norm equivalence [F5] varies continuously on this compact set, so its constants are uniform; affine scaling then gives $\|p_T-p_{T\prime}\|_{H^1(T)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(T\cup T\prime)}$. A bounded path through the connected cell-star graph lets one fixed cell polynomial $p\in P_1$ satisfy $\|v-p\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}\le Ch_K^2\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$ and $\|
abla(v-p)\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. This uses only local approximation and does not impose boundary values on $v$.

The reference P1 basis satisfies $\|\varphi_z\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K^{d/2}$ and $\|
abla\varphi_z\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K^{d/2-1}$. Since $I_h$ reproduces constants, step 2.1 bounds $\|I_hw-c_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|
abla w\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$ and $\|
abla I_hw\|_{L^2(K)}\le C\|
abla w\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Together with the patch Poincare bound for $w-c_K$, these prove the $L^2$ approximation and local H1 stability. Summing and using bounded overlap proves global H1-seminorm stability.

Facet duality reproduces every affine polynomial at every vertex, so $I_hp=p$ on $K$. Apply the local H1 stability from step 3.1 to $v-p$ and use step 2.2 to get $\|\nabla(v-I_hv)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Summing over cells and using the bounded patch overlap from step 3.1 proves the global H1 approximation estimate.

citations.quote: Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and Lipschitz. Here Lipschitz means that its compact boundary has a finite atlas of rigidly moved cylinders in which $D$ is the strict epigraph $x_d>\varphi(x')$ of a Lipschitz function. There are finitely many bounded open sets $U_i\subset D$ covering $D$, each star-shaped with respect to a closed ball $\overline B_i\subset U_i$, and the graph joining $i,j$ when $U_i\cap U_j\ne\varnothing$ is connected. There are measurable sets $E_i\subset U_i$ partitioning $D$ and, for every edge of a spanning tree of this graph, a function $\psi_{ij}\in C_c^\infty(U_i\cap U_j)$ with integral one.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: Root the finite spanning tree. Set $g_i=\mathbf1_{E_i}q$, $m_i=\int_Dg_i$, and let $M_i$ be the sum of $m_j$ over the subtree rooted at $i$. For a nonroot vertex $i$ with parent-edge bump $\psi_i$, set $q_i=g_i+\sum_{j\text{ child of }i}M_j\psi_j-M_i\psi_i$; at the root omit the final term. Every summand is supported in $U_i$ by [F1].

Since each bump integrates to one, a nonroot patch has integral $m_i+\sum_jM_j-M_i=0$ by the subtree identity $M_i=m_i+\sum_jM_j$. At the root, the integral is $m_{\rm root}+\sum_jM_j=M_{\rm root}=\sum_i m_i=\int_Dq=0$.

In the sum of all $q_i$, every tree-edge term $-M_i\psi_i$ at a child cancels the $+M_i\psi_i$ term at its parent, leaving $\sum_i g_i=q$ almost everywhere because the $E_i$ partition $D$. All coefficients and operations are linear in $q$.

For every subtree, $|M_i|=|\int_{\cup_{j\text{ in subtree }i}E_j}q|\le\|q\|_1\le|D|^{1/2}\|q\|_2$ by [F2], and $\|g_i\|_2\le\|q\|_2$. The triangle inequality applied to the definition in step 1.1 gives $\|q_i\|_2\le\|q\|_2+|D|^{1/2}\|q\|_2\sum_{e\text{ incident to }i}\|\psi_e\|_2=D_i\|q\|_2$.
