$S_L<S_R$. A signal speed means the propagation speed of one wave in the
particular Riemann solution being approximated. If the HLL model is used as an
enclosing approximation to that fan, its admissibility hypothesis is that
every such speed lies in $[S_L,S_R]$; this definition supplies no general
wave-speed bound.
Set $f_L=f(u_L)$ and $f_R=f(u_R)$. The HLL flux is
$$\widehat f_{\rm HLL}=\begin{cases}f_L,&0\le S_L,\\\dfrac{S_Rf_L-S_Lf_R+S_LS_R(u_R-u_L)}{S_R-S_L},&S_L<0<S_R,\\f_R,&S_R\le0.\end{cases}$$
In the middle case the model has three constant regions separated by the two
waves $S_L,S_R$ and one intermediate state. The wave-speed enclosure is a
separate hypothesis whenever an approximation claim uses it.

When $S_L<0<S_R$, the HLL intermediate state
$$u_* =\frac{S_Ru_R-S_Lu_L-(f_R-f_L)}{S_R-S_L}$$
together with the assigned model flux
$$f_* = f_L+S_L(u_*-u_L)$$
satisfies the two model balances
$$f_*-f_L=S_L(u_*-u_L),\qquad f_R-f_*=S_R(u_R-u_*).$$
This $f_*$ is the middle formula in [[def-hll-two-wave-flux]]. In general
$f_*\ne f(u_*)$, even when $u_*\in G$; the model is not asserted to be a
weak solution of the original conservation law. For equal states
the HLL flux is consistent. A finite-volume update using the same HLL flux at
each periodic interface is conservative: for any finite periodic array with
adjacent pairs in the flux domain, define
$$U_j^{new}=U_j-\nu\bigl(\widehat f_{\rm HLL}(U_j,U_{j+1})-\widehat f_{\rm HLL}(U_{j-1},U_j)\bigr).$$

not prove that they enclose a nonlinear Riemann fan.

Let $m,N\ge1$, let $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be a state domain, and let
$\Phi:\mathcal A^N\to\mathcal A^N$ be a one-step update on $N$ cell states.
A set $K\subseteq\mathcal A$ is **convex** if
$\theta U+(1-\theta)V\in K$ for every $U,V\in K$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$.
It is a **convex invariant domain for $\Phi$** if it is convex and
$\Phi(K^N)\subseteq K^N$. The word invariant refers only to this stated
one-step map and its stated admissible inputs; it asserts no invariance for a
different flux, time integrator, or exact Riemann evolution.

Use the first-order HLL update of
[[def-pe03-first-order-hll-finite-volume-update]]. At a face with left and right
states $U_L,U_R$, supplied speeds $S_L<0<S_R$, and physical flux values
$F_L=F(U_L),F_R=F(U_R)$, define
$$U_*:=\frac{S_RU_R-S_LU_L-(F_R-F_L)}{S_R-S_L}.$$
If the one-sided CFL bounds $2\nu(-S_L)\le1$ and $2\nu S_R\le1$ hold, the
averages of the HLL fan over the adjacent left and right half-cells are,
respectively,
$$A^-=(1-2\nu(-S_L))U_L+2\nu(-S_L)U_*,\qquad A^+=(1-2\nu S_R)U_R+2\nu S_RU_*.$$
For every cell $i$, the updated mean satisfies
$$U_i^+=\frac12\left(A^+_{i-1/2}+A^-_{i+1/2}\right),$$
where each face uses its own supplied speeds and intermediate state.

By [F2], $U_i^+=\tfrac12(A^+_{i-1/2}+A^-_{i+1/2})$. This is a convex combination of two members of $K$, so $U_i^+\in K$ for every cell. The argument is one-step and uses only the supplied HLL speeds and the explicit CFL bounds.

Use the conservation-system convention of
[[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]]: on an open convex state
domain $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, the flux is $F:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R^m$.
A **convex entropy pair** is a pair $(\eta,q)$ with $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal A)$,
$q\in C^1(\mathcal A)$, positive-semidefinite Hessian $D^2\eta$, and
$$Dq(U)=D\eta(U)\,DF(U)\qquad(U\in\mathcal A).$$
The **entropy variable** is the column vector $v(U)=\nabla\eta(U)$; gradients
are represented as columns, so the compatibility equation above means
$\nabla q(U)=DF(U)^T v(U)$. The **entropy potential** is
$\psi(U)=v(U)^T F(U)-q(U)$. This definition does not assert that every convex
$\eta$ admits a flux $q$; the compatibility equation is part of the hypothesis.

Let $(\eta,q)$ be a convex entropy pair on an open domain $\mathcal A$, with
entropy variable $v$ and potential $\psi$ as in
[[def-pe03-system-entropy-pair-and-potential]]. A continuous two-point flux
$F^{ec}:\mathcal A\times\mathcal A\to\mathbb R^m$ is **entropy-conservative
in Tadmor's sense** if it is consistent and symmetric,
$F^{ec}(U,U)=F(U)$, and satisfies the exact jump identity
$$\bigl(v(U_R)-v(U_L)\bigr)^T F^{ec}(U_L,U_R)=\psi(U_R)-\psi(U_L)$$
for every pair $U_L,U_R\in\mathcal A$. This definition asserts no existence
for a prescribed entropy pair.

Let $(\eta,q)$ be an entropy pair with entropy variable $v$ and potential
$\psi$, and let $F^{ec}$ be a consistent entropy-conservative flux as in
[[def-pe03-tadmor-entropy-conservative-flux]]. For each pair
$(U_L,U_R)\in\mathcal A^2$, choose a symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix
$D(U_L,U_R)\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$. The associated **entropy-stable
dissipative flux** is
$$F^{es}(U_L,U_R):=F^{ec}(U_L,U_R)-\frac12D(U_L,U_R)(v(U_R)-v(U_L)).$$
Positive semidefinite means $z^TD(U_L,U_R)z\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^m$.
No fully discrete time-step property is included.

derivations.claim: At a face, [F2]–[F3] give $[v]^TF^{es}=[\psi]-\tfrac12[v]^TD[v]\le[\psi]$, since $[v]^TD[v]\ge0$. This uses only positive semidefiniteness, including the case where the jump or dissipation vanishes.

Write $[v]_{i+1/2}=v_{i+1}-v_i$ and $[\psi]_{i+1/2}=\psi_{i+1}-\psi_i$, and use the arithmetic means in the definition of $\widehat q$. Then $-v_i^TF^{es}_{i+1/2}+\widehat q_{i+1/2}=\tfrac12[v]_{i+1/2}^TF^{es}_{i+1/2}-\tfrac12(\psi_i+\psi_{i+1})$ and $v_i^TF^{es}_{i-1/2}-\widehat q_{i-1/2}=\tfrac12[v]_{i-1/2}^TF^{es}_{i-1/2}+\tfrac12(\psi_{i-1}+\psi_i)$. Fix $\gamma>1$. In one space dimension the conserved state is
$U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathbb R^3$, where $\rho$ is density, $m$ momentum, and
$E$ total energy per unit volume. The **admissible-state set** is the open set
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\ E>m^2/(2\rho)\}.$$
The ideal-gas pressure on this set is
$$p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}\right)>0,$$
the velocity is $u=m/\rho$, and the flux is
$$F(U)=\left(m,\frac{m^2}{\rho}+p,\frac{m}{\rho}(E+p)\right).$$
The sound speed is $c=\sqrt{\gamma p/\rho}$. These definitions apply only
on $\mathcal G_\gamma$; a state with nonpositive density or nonpositive
internal energy is inadmissible. The set is open because $\rho$ and
$E-m^2/(2\rho)$ are continuous on $\rho>0$ and the inequalities are strict;
all displayed flux functions are smooth on this domain.

For a two-state problem for a flux $f$ on the open state domain $G$ of
[[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]], choose explicit speeds
$S_L<S_R$. A signal speed means the propagation speed of one wave in the
particular Riemann solution being approximated. If the HLL model is used as an
enclosing approximation to that fan, its admissibility hypothesis is that
every such speed lies in $[S_L,S_R]$; this definition supplies no general
wave-speed bound.
Set $f_L=f(u_L)$ and $f_R=f(u_R)$. The HLL flux is
$$\widehat f_{\rm HLL}=\begin{cases}f_L,&0\le S_L,\\\dfrac{S_Rf_L-S_Lf_R+S_LS_R(u_R-u_L)}{S_R-S_L},&S_L<0<S_R,\\f_R,&S_R\le0.\end{cases}$$
In the middle case the model has three constant regions separated by the two
waves $S_L,S_R$ and one intermediate state. The wave-speed enclosure is a
separate hypothesis whenever an approximation claim uses it.

Fix $\gamma>1$. For $U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathcal G_\gamma$, let
$e=E-m^2/(2\rho)$, $p=(\gamma-1)e$, $u=m/\rho$, and
$c=\sqrt{\gamma p/\rho}$. If $a\ge |u|+c$, then both split states
$$U_\delta=U+\delta F(U),\qquad \delta\in\{-1/a,1/a\},$$
belong to $\mathcal G_\gamma$, where $F(U)=(m,m^2/\rho+p,u(E+p))$.
More precisely, with $x=1+\delta u$ their density and internal-energy density are
$$\rho_\delta=\rho x,\qquad e_\delta=e x-\frac{\delta^2p^2}{2\rho x}>0.$$

Fix $\gamma>1$ and $\varepsilon>0$. The ideal-gas admissible set
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\ E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}>0\right\}$$
and the positive-margin set $K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$ from
[[def-pe03-euler-positive-margin-domain]] are convex, and
$K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$ is closed in $\mathbb R^3$.

Use the first-order HLL update of
[[def-pe03-first-order-hll-finite-volume-update]]. At a face with left and right
states $U_L,U_R$, supplied speeds $S_L<0<S_R$, and physical flux values
$F_L=F(U_L),F_R=F(U_R)$, define
$$U_*:=\frac{S_RU_R-S_LU_L-(F_R-F_L)}{S_R-S_L}.$$
If the one-sided CFL bounds $2\nu(-S_L)\le1$ and $2\nu S_R\le1$ hold, the
averages of the HLL fan over the adjacent left and right half-cells are,
respectively,
$$A^-=(1-2\nu(-S_L))U_L+2\nu(-S_L)U_*,\qquad A^+=(1-2\nu S_R)U_R+2\nu S_RU_*.$$
For every cell $i$, the updated mean satisfies
$$U_i^+=\frac12\left(A^+_{i-1/2}+A^-_{i+1/2}\right),$$
where each face uses its own supplied speeds and intermediate state.

Let $K$ be a convex set in the state domain, and consider a periodic uniform
mesh and one first-order HLL update as defined in
[[def-pe03-first-order-hll-finite-volume-update]]. Assume every cell mean
$U_i\in K$. At every face impose the **HLL fan-average hypothesis** that the
two adjacent half-cell averages $A^-,A^+$ from
[[lem-pe03-hll-half-cell-riemann-averages]] lie in $K$, with that lemma's local
CFL bounds. Then every updated mean $U_i^+$ belongs to $K$. A sufficient
condition for the fan-average hypothesis is that every HLL intermediate state
$U_*\in K$, because the stated CFL makes each half-cell average a convex
combination of a cell state and $U_*$. The result does not assert a bound on
exact nonlinear wave speeds.

Substituting $S_L=-a$, $S_R=a$ into [F2] and using the intermediate-state formula in [F5] gives $U_* = \tfrac12(U_L+F_L/a)+\tfrac12(U_R-F_R/a)$. The two weights are nonnegative and sum to one, so [F4] implies $U_*\in\mathcal G_\gamma$.

The assumed speed bound gives $a>0$ and the displayed CFL gives $2\nu a\le1$, so both HLL half-cell averages have nonnegative convex-combination coefficients. Thus every HLL intermediate state and cell state lies in $\mathcal G_\gamma$, and [F6] yields $U_i^+\in\mathcal G_\gamma$ for each cell. By [F1], this means positive density and pressure. The proof makes no claim for the other HLL branches or for fully discrete entropy.

Use the conservation-system convention of
[[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]]: on an open convex state
domain $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, the flux is $F:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R^m$.
A **convex entropy pair** is a pair $(\eta,q)$ with $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal A)$,
$q\in C^1(\mathcal A)$, positive-semidefinite Hessian $D^2\eta$, and
$$Dq(U)=D\eta(U)\,DF(U)\qquad(U\in\mathcal A).$$
The **entropy variable** is the column vector $v(U)=\nabla\eta(U)$; gradients
are represented as columns, so the compatibility equation above means
$\nabla q(U)=DF(U)^T v(U)$. The **entropy potential** is
$\psi(U)=v(U)^T F(U)-q(U)$. This definition does not assert that every convex
$\eta$ admits a flux $q$; the compatibility equation is part of the hypothesis.

Let $(\eta,q)$ be a convex entropy pair on an open domain $\mathcal A$, with
entropy variable $v$ and potential $\psi$ as in
[[def-pe03-system-entropy-pair-and-potential]]. A continuous two-point flux
$F^{ec}:\mathcal A\times\mathcal A\to\mathbb R^m$ is **entropy-conservative
in Tadmor's sense** if it is consistent and symmetric,
$F^{ec}(U,U)=F(U)$, and satisfies the exact jump identity
$$\bigl(v(U_R)-v(U_L)\bigr)^T F^{ec}(U_L,U_R)=\psi(U_R)-\psi(U_L)$$
for every pair $U_L,U_R\in\mathcal A$. This definition asserts no existence
for a prescribed entropy pair.

Let $(\eta,q)$ be an entropy pair with entropy variable $v$ and potential
$\psi$, and let $F^{ec}$ be a consistent entropy-conservative flux as in
[[def-pe03-tadmor-entropy-conservative-flux]]. For each pair
$(U_L,U_R)\in\mathcal A^2$, choose a symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix
$D(U_L,U_R)\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$. The associated **entropy-stable
dissipative flux** is
$$F^{es}(U_L,U_R):=F^{ec}(U_L,U_R)-\frac12D(U_L,U_R)(v(U_R)-v(U_L)).$$
Positive semidefinite means $z^TD(U_L,U_R)z\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^m$.
No fully discrete time-step property is included.

derivations.claim: Here $\eta''(u)=1$, $\eta'(u)=u$, and $q'(u)=u^2=\eta'(u)f'(u)$, so this is a convex entropy pair. Thus $v=u$ and $\psi=uf-q=u^3/6$ by [F1].

The displayed $f^{ec}$ is polynomial, hence continuous, is symmetric, and satisfies $f^{ec}(u,u)=u^2/2=f(u)$. Moreover, $(u_R-u_L)f^{ec}(u_L,u_R)=\frac{u_R^3-u_L^3}{6}=\psi(u_R)-\psi(u_L)$, so [F2] applies using $\psi=u^3/6$ from step 1.1.

Taking $D=1$ in [F3], at $(1,0)$ we have $f^{ec}=1/6$, $[v]=-1$, and $[\psi]=-1/6$. Therefore $[v]f^{es}-[\psi]=(-1)(1/6+1/2)-(-1/6)=-1/2$. In general the same substitution gives residual $-\tfrac12(u_R-u_L)^2\le0$, using the formula in step 2.1.

Use the conservation-system convention of
[[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]]: on an open convex state
domain $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, the flux is $F:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R^m$.
A **convex entropy pair** is a pair $(\eta,q)$ with $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal A)$,
$q\in C^1(\mathcal A)$, positive-semidefinite Hessian $D^2\eta$, and
$$Dq(U)=D\eta(U)\,DF(U)\qquad(U\in\mathcal A).$$
The **entropy variable** is the column vector $v(U)=\nabla\eta(U)$; gradients
are represented as columns, so the compatibility equation above means
$\nabla q(U)=DF(U)^T v(U)$. The **entropy potential** is
$\psi(U)=v(U)^T F(U)-q(U)$. This definition does not assert that every convex
$\eta$ admits a flux $q$; the compatibility equation is part of the hypothesis.

Let $(\eta,q)$ be a convex entropy pair on an open domain $\mathcal A$, with
entropy variable $v$ and potential $\psi$ as in
[[def-pe03-system-entropy-pair-and-potential]]. A continuous two-point flux
$F^{ec}:\mathcal A\times\mathcal A\to\mathbb R^m$ is **entropy-conservative
in Tadmor's sense** if it is consistent and symmetric,
$F^{ec}(U,U)=F(U)$, and satisfies the exact jump identity
$$\bigl(v(U_R)-v(U_L)\bigr)^T F^{ec}(U_L,U_R)=\psi(U_R)-\psi(U_L)$$
for every pair $U_L,U_R\in\mathcal A$. This definition asserts no existence
for a prescribed entropy pair.

Let $(\eta,q)$ be an entropy pair with entropy variable $v$ and potential
$\psi$, and let $F^{ec}$ be a consistent entropy-conservative flux as in
[[def-pe03-tadmor-entropy-conservative-flux]]. For each pair
$(U_L,U_R)\in\mathcal A^2$, choose a symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix
$D(U_L,U_R)\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$. The associated **entropy-stable
dissipative flux** is
$$F^{es}(U_L,U_R):=F^{ec}(U_L,U_R)-\frac12D(U_L,U_R)(v(U_R)-v(U_L)).$$
Positive semidefinite means $z^TD(U_L,U_R)z\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^m$.
No fully discrete time-step property is included.

Let $(\eta,q)$ be a convex entropy pair on an open set $\mathcal A$, with
entropy variable $v$ and potential $\psi$ as in
[[def-pe03-system-entropy-pair-and-potential]]. On a periodic mesh of $N\ge2$
cells of width $\Delta x>0$, let differentiable states $U_i(t)\in\mathcal A$
satisfy
$$\dot U_i=-\frac{F^{es}_{i+1/2}-F^{es}_{i-1/2}}{\Delta x},$$
where every face flux is the entropy-stable dissipative flux of
[[def-pe03-entropy-stable-dissipative-flux]]. Define
$$\widehat q_{i+1/2}:=\left(\frac{v_i+v_{i+1}}2\right)^T F^{es}_{i+1/2}-\frac{\psi_i+\psi_{i+1}}2.$$
Then each cell satisfies
$$\frac{d}{dt}\eta(U_i)+\frac{\widehat q_{i+1/2}-\widehat q_{i-1/2}}{\Delta x}\le0.$$
Summing over the periodic mesh gives nonincrease of total discrete entropy.
This is a semidiscrete result; it asserts no entropy inequality for a chosen
fully discrete time integrator.

derivations.claim: The Rankine–Hugoniot speed from states $u_L=1,u_R=0$ is $(f(0)-f(1))/(0-1)=1/2$. Since $f'(0)=0<1/2<1=f'(1)$, it is a compressive shock. Its entropy production is $q(0)-q(1)-\tfrac12(\eta(0)-\eta(1))=-1/3+1/4=-1/12<0$, so it satisfies the quadratic entropy inequality.

The entropy-conservative Burgers flux is $f^{ec}=(u_L^2+u_Lu_R+u_R^2)/6$: it is symmetric and diagonal-consistent, and $(u_R-u_L)f^{ec}=(u_R^3-u_L^3)/6=[\psi]$, so [F2] applies. Hence $f^{ec}(1,0)=1/6$ and [F3] gives $f^{es}(1,0)=2/3$. With $[u]=-1$ and $[\psi]=-1/6$ from step 1.1, the Tadmor residual is $[u]f^{es}-[\psi]=-2/3+1/6=-1/2<0$.

Equal-state faces have flux $f^{es}(1,1)=1/2$ and $f^{es}(0,0)=0$ by [F2]–[F3]. Thus the left state adjacent to the jump updates to $1-\tfrac12(2/3-1/2)=11/12$, and the right state updates to $0-\tfrac12(0-2/3)=1/3$. The jump is spread over two intermediate values. This is a finite computation only; [F4] does not certify the forward-Euler step's entropy inequality. The interface flux value was obtained in step 2.1.

Fix $\gamma>1$. In one space dimension the conserved state is
$U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathbb R^3$, where $\rho$ is density, $m$ momentum, and
$E$ total energy per unit volume. The **admissible-state set** is the open set
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\ E>m^2/(2\rho)\}.$$
The ideal-gas pressure on this set is
$$p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}\right)>0,$$
the velocity is $u=m/\rho$, and the flux is
$$F(U)=\left(m,\frac{m^2}{\rho}+p,\frac{m}{\rho}(E+p)\right).$$
The sound speed is $c=\sqrt{\gamma p/\rho}$. These definitions apply only
on $\mathcal G_\gamma$; a state with nonpositive density or nonpositive
internal energy is inadmissible. The set is open because $\rho$ and
$E-m^2/(2\rho)$ are continuous on $\rho>0$ and the inequalities are strict;
all displayed flux functions are smooth on this domain.

Fix $\gamma>1$. For $U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathcal G_\gamma$, let
$e=E-m^2/(2\rho)$, $p=(\gamma-1)e$, $u=m/\rho$, and
$c=\sqrt{\gamma p/\rho}$. If $a\ge |u|+c$, then both split states
$$U_\delta=U+\delta F(U),\qquad \delta\in\{-1/a,1/a\},$$
belong to $\mathcal G_\gamma$, where $F(U)=(m,m^2/\rho+p,u(E+p))$.
More precisely, with $x=1+\delta u$ their density and internal-energy density are
$$\rho_\delta=\rho x,\qquad e_\delta=e x-\frac{\delta^2p^2}{2\rho x}>0.$$

Fix $\gamma>1$ and $\varepsilon>0$. The ideal-gas admissible set
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\ E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}>0\right\}$$
and the positive-margin set $K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$ from
[[def-pe03-euler-positive-margin-domain]] are convex, and
$K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$ is closed in $\mathbb R^3$.

Use the first-order HLL update of
[[def-pe03-first-order-hll-finite-volume-update]]. At a face with left and right
states $U_L,U_R$, supplied speeds $S_L<0<S_R$, and physical flux values
$F_L=F(U_L),F_R=F(U_R)$, define
$$U_*:=\frac{S_RU_R-S_LU_L-(F_R-F_L)}{S_R-S_L}.$$
If the one-sided CFL bounds $2\nu(-S_L)\le1$ and $2\nu S_R\le1$ hold, the
averages of the HLL fan over the adjacent left and right half-cells are,
respectively,
$$A^-=(1-2\nu(-S_L))U_L+2\nu(-S_L)U_*,\qquad A^+=(1-2\nu S_R)U_R+2\nu S_RU_*.$$
For every cell $i$, the updated mean satisfies
$$U_i^+=\frac12\left(A^+_{i-1/2}+A^-_{i+1/2}\right),$$
where each face uses its own supplied speeds and intermediate state.

Fix $\gamma>1$ and a periodic uniform mesh. Suppose every cell state
$U_i\in\mathcal G_\gamma$. Apply the first-order HLL update of
[[def-pe03-first-order-hll-finite-volume-update]]. At each face $(i+1/2)$ choose a symmetric HLL
branch $S_L=-a_{i+1/2}$, $S_R=a_{i+1/2}$ with
$$a_{i+1/2}\ge\max\bigl(|u_i|+c_i,|u_{i+1}|+c_{i+1}\bigr),\qquad 2\nu a_{i+1/2}\le1.$$
Then one first-order HLL update preserves $\mathcal G_\gamma$; in particular,
every updated density and pressure is strictly positive. This is the symmetric
local Lax–Friedrichs branch with a stated speed bound, not a claim that arbitrary
HLL speed estimates are valid or that the bound is necessary.

Let $F:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R^m$ be the flux of the one-dimensional system in
[[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]]. On a periodic uniform
mesh of $N\ge2$ cells of width $h>0$, let $U_i\in\mathcal A$ be the cell means
and put $\nu=\Delta t/h\ge0$. At each face $(i+1/2)$ choose explicit speeds
$S_{L,i+1/2}<0<S_{R,i+1/2}$ and evaluate the middle branch of the HLL flux
[[def-hll-two-wave-flux]] on $(U_i,U_{i+1})$. The **first-order HLL update** is
$$U_i^+=U_i-\nu\bigl(\widehat F_{i+1/2}-\widehat F_{i-1/2}\bigr),\qquad i\pmod N.$$
The speeds are supplied data. Neither this definition nor later algebraic
results assert that they enclose the wave speeds of an exact nonlinear Riemann
solution.

For a two-state problem for a flux $f$ on the open state domain $G$ of
[[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]], choose explicit speeds
$S_L<S_R$. A signal speed means the propagation speed of one wave in the
particular Riemann solution being approximated. If the HLL model is used as an
enclosing approximation to that fan, its admissibility hypothesis is that
every such speed lies in $[S_L,S_R]$; this definition supplies no general
wave-speed bound.
Set $f_L=f(u_L)$ and $f_R=f(u_R)$. The HLL flux is
$$\widehat f_{\rm HLL}=\begin{cases}f_L,&0\le S_L,\\\dfrac{S_Rf_L-S_Lf_R+S_LS_R(u_R-u_L)}{S_R-S_L},&S_L<0<S_R,\\f_R,&S_R\le0.\end{cases}$$
In the middle case the model has three constant regions separated by the two
waves $S_L,S_R$ and one intermediate state. The wave-speed enclosure is a
separate hypothesis whenever an approximation claim uses it.

derivations.claim: The kinetic energy density is $\rho u^2/2=5\times10^{-13}$ and $p/(\gamma-1)=5/2\times10^{-12}$, so $E=3\times10^{-12}$. Hence [F1] gives the specified pressure and positive internal energy, so both states lie in $\mathcal G_\gamma$.

Their sound speed satisfies $c^2=7/50000<(3/250)^2$, hence $|u|+c<1/100+3/250=11/500=a$. Also $\nu a=1/4$, so $2\nu a=1/2\le1$. The symmetric-speed hypotheses in [F2]–[F5] hold, with the positive admissibility verified in step 1.1.

At the discontinuity, substitution of $S_L=-a,S_R=a$ into [F7] and the HLL intermediate-state formula of [F4] gives $U_*=(U_L+F_L/a+U_R-F_R/a)/2$. Both split states are in $\mathcal G_\gamma$ by [F2], so $U_*\in\mathcal G_\gamma$ by [F3]. At equal-state faces, the same middle-state formula gives $U_*=U_L$ or $U_R$. Substituting the shared face fluxes in [F6], or equivalently using [F4], yields $U_i^+=(3/4)U_L+(1/4)U_*$ and $U_{i+1}^+=(3/4)U_R+(1/4)U_*$. Convexity keeps both states in $\mathcal G_\gamma$, and [F1] gives positive density and pressure, using the CFL verification in step 2.1.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $V$ be a Banach space and let $W\subseteq V$ be a closed linear subspace,
equipped with the restricted norm. Then $W$ is a Banach space.

derivations.claim: Define $\ell(q):=\int_Dq\,dx$. By [F2], $|\ell(q)|\le |D|^{1/2}\|q\|_2$, and linearity of the integral makes $\ell$ a bounded real linear functional. Its kernel is exactly $L^2_0(D)$.

The kernel of a continuous functional is closed: if $q_n\in L^2_0(D)$ and $q_n\to q$ in $L^2$, then $|\ell(q)|=|\ell(q-q_n)|\le |D|^{1/2}\|q-q_n\|_2\to0$, so $\ell(q)=0$. Thus $L^2_0(D)$ is a closed linear subspace of $L^2(D)$.

The inner product on $L^2(D)$ restricts to an inner product on $L^2_0(D)$ and induces the inherited $L^2$ norm. By [F1], $L^2(D)$ is complete; by [F3] and step 2.1, its closed subspace $L^2_0(D)$ is complete. Therefore it is a real Hilbert space with the restricted inner product.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$

   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

$n\ge1$, let $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ be nonnegative with
$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$.

and
$$\Omega_\varepsilon=\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)>\varepsilon\},\qquad\Omega_\varepsilon=\mathbb R^n\ \text{when }\Omega=\mathbb R^n .$$

for every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le k$,
$$D^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*u)=\rho_\varepsilon*(D^\alpha u)\qquad\text{on }\Omega_\varepsilon,$$
as pointwise smooth functions for the constructed representatives and as
almost-everywhere classes. Here $D^\alpha u$ is extended by zero off $\Omega$
in the convolution.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.
a bounded Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure

Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and $\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every** set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable with $$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$
Then $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

derivations.claim: Choose $c\in K$ and $s\in(0,1)$, and put $T_s(x)=c+s(x-c)$ and $U_s=T_s^{-1}(K)$. Since $K$ is convex and $c$ is interior, $T_s(\overline K)$ is a compact subset of $K$; hence $U_s$ is an open simplex containing $\overline K$ with positive distance from $\overline K$ to $U_s^c$. Define $u_s=u\circ T_s$ on $U_s$. For $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U_s)$, change variables $y=T_s(x)$ in the weak derivative identity of $u$; with $\widetilde\psi(y)=\psi(T_s^{-1}y)$ one has $D_{y_i}\widetilde\psi=s^{-1}(D_{x_i}\psi)\circ T_s^{-1}$, so the identity gives $D_i u_s=s(D_i u)\circ T_s$ distributionally.

For any $g\in L^2(K)$, extend it by zero to $\mathbb R^d$. Given $\eta>0$, choose $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ with $\|g-\phi\|_{L^2(K)}<\eta$ by [F2]. Because $T_s(K)\subset K$, change of variables [F3] gives $\|(g-\phi)\circ T_s\|_{L^2(K)}\le s^{-d/2}\eta$, while uniform continuity of $\phi$ on $\overline K$ gives $\|\phi\circ T_s-\phi\|_{L^2(K)}\to0$ as $s\to1^-$. The triangle inequality and arbitrary $\eta$ therefore show $\|g\circ T_s-g\|_{L^2(K)}\to0$.
Apply step 1.2 to $g=u$ and to every $g=D_i u$. By step 1.1, $D_i u_s=s(D_i u)\circ T_s$, and $s\to1$; hence $u_s|_K\to u$ in the full $H^1(K)$ norm as $s\to1^-$.

Choose $s$ close enough to $1$ that $\|u_s-u\|_{H^1(K)}<\varepsilon/2$, and let $r=\operatorname{dist}(\overline K,U_s^c)>0$. Choose the bump from [F4] and then $0<\delta<r$. The zero extension of $u_s$ is locally integrable by [F8], so $w_\delta=(\rho_\delta*E_0u_s)$ is smooth by [F7]. On $K$, [F6] gives $D_iw_\delta=\rho_\delta*E_0(D_i u_s)$. Each zero extension is in $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$; [F5] therefore gives $\|w_\delta-u_s\|_{H^1(K)}\to0$ as $\delta\to0^+$. Choose $\delta<r$ small enough to make this norm less than $\varepsilon/2$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice for the published Sobolev interfaces cited below. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and use real scalars. $L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$ means the $d$-tuple of real $L^2$ equivalence classes, with norm $\|v\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^d\|v_j\|_2^2$. The test space $C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$ consists of real smooth functions compactly supported in $D$.

For $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$, say that $g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)$ is its distributional divergence when
$$
\int_D v\cdot\nabla\phi\,dx=-\int_D g\phi\,dx\qquad\text{for every }\phi\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R).
$$
The $L^2$ class $g$ is unique when it exists. Indeed, if $g_1,g_2$ both satisfy the identity, put $h=g_1-g_2\in L^2(D)$. Every compact $C\subset D$ has finite Lebesgue measure by [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $\int_C|h|\le |C|^{1/2}\|h\|_{L^2(D)}<\infty$. Thus $h\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. Subtracting the two divergence identities gives $\int_Dh\phi=0$ for every real test $\phi$; splitting a complex test into real and imaginary parts gives the same identity for complex tests. Injectivity of the regular-distribution map in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]] therefore yields $h=0$ almost everywhere, hence $g_1=g_2$ as $L^2$ classes. Define
$$
H(\operatorname{div};D):=\{v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d):\text{there is }g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)\text{ with }g=\operatorname{div}v\text{ distributionally}\},
$$
and equip it with the graph norm
$$
\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div};D)}:=\bigl(\|v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}.
$$
The Sobolev notation $H^1(D)=W^{1,2}(D)$ and $H^1_0(D)=W^{1,2}_0(D)$ uses the norm and zero-boundary closure conventions of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. No pointwise boundary value is part of this definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim: For $w\in H^1(D)$ put $L_v(w):=\int_D(v\cdot\nabla w+(\operatorname{div}v)w)$. The two integrals are finite by [F3], and Cauchy–Schwarz in $\mathbb R^2$ gives $|L_v(w)|\le\|v\|_2\|\nabla w\|_2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2\|w\|_2\le\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div};D)}\|w\|_{H^1(D)}.$ Thus $L_v$ is a bounded real linear functional on $H^1(D)$.

For every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$, [F1] gives $L_v(\phi)=0$. If $z\in H^1_0(D)$, then for each $\varepsilon>0$, [F2] gives such a $\phi$ with $\|z-\phi\|_{H^1}<\varepsilon$; step 1.1 yields $|L_v(z)|=|L_v(z-\phi)|\le\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\varepsilon$. Since this holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, $L_v(z)=0$. Therefore $L_v$ is constant on each coset of $H^1_0(D)$ and defines $\gamma_n v$ on $T_D$.

For any $[w]\in T_D$, step 2.1 makes $L_v(w)$ the same for every representative. Applying step 1.1 to every representative $w+z$, $z\in H^1_0(D)$, and taking the infimum of their $H^1$ norms gives $|\langle\gamma_n v,[w]\rangle|\le\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div};D)}\|[w]\|_{T_D}$. Hence $\gamma_n v$ is bounded with the claimed norm.

Let $\widehat K,K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nondegenerate open simplices and let $F_K:\widehat K\to K$ be the orientation-preserving affine bijection $F_K(\widehat x)=A_K\widehat x+b_K$, where $J_K:=\det A_K>0$. For a measurable vector field $\widehat v$ on $\widehat K$, define its contravariant Piola push-forward by
$$
(\mathcal P_K\widehat v)(x):=J_K^{-1}A_K\widehat v(F_K^{-1}(x)),\qquad x\in K.
$$
The inverse pull-back is $\widehat v(\widehat x)=J_KA_K^{-1}v(F_K(\widehat x))$. Facet normals are oriented consistently with the chosen orientation of $F_K$; the associated oriented surface vector transforms by $n\,ds=J_KA_K^{-T}\widehat n\,d\widehat s$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Write $v_i(F_K(\widehat x))=J_K^{-1}\sum_j(A_K)_{ij}\widehat v_j(\widehat x)$. The chain rule [F2] for $F_K^{-1}$ gives $\partial_{x_i}=\sum_k(A_K^{-1})_{ki}\partial_{\widehat x_k}$; since $A_K$ is constant, summing the derivatives gives $(\operatorname{div}_xv)\circ F_K=J_K^{-1}\sum_{i,k,j}(A_K^{-1})_{ki}(A_K)_{ij}\partial_{\widehat x_k}\widehat v_j=J_K^{-1}\sum_j\partial_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v_j.$ The middle equality uses $A_K^{-1}A_K=I$.

Choose oriented tangent vectors $\widehat t_1,\ldots,\widehat t_{d-1}$ on $\widehat F$. Under $F_K$ the tangent vectors are $A_K\widehat t_i$; multilinearity of the determinant gives the oriented area-normal transformation $n_F ds=\operatorname{cof}(A_K)\widehat n_{\widehat F}d\widehat s$. Since $A_K$ is invertible, $\operatorname{cof}(A_K)=J_KA_K^{-T}$. Therefore the Piola flux element satisfies $v\cdot n_F\,ds=(J_K^{-1}A_K\widehat v)\cdot(J_KA_K^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F})\,d\widehat s=\widehat v\cdot\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat s.$ Integrating over the corresponding facets proves the flux identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For an open set $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, let $T_D=H^1(D)/H^1_0(D)$ be the trace quotient of [[lem-na-hdiv-weak-normal-trace]], and let $\gamma_n:H(\operatorname{div};D)\to T_D'$ be its weak normal trace. Define
$$
H_0(\operatorname{div};D):=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};D):\gamma_n v=0\text{ in }T_D'\}.
$$
Thus zero normal trace means that the Green-duality functional vanishes on every H1 trace class; no pointwise normal value is required.

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev-space interfaces below. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and $v\in H(\operatorname{div};D)$. Define the trace quotient
$$T_D:=H^1(D)/H^1_0(D),\qquad \|[w]\|_{T_D}:=\inf_{z\in H^1_0(D)}\|w+z\|_{H^1(D)}.$$
Then the formula
$$
\langle\gamma_n v,[w]\rangle:=\int_D\bigl(v\cdot\nabla w+(\operatorname{div}v)w\bigr)\,dx
$$
is independent of the representative $w$, defines a bounded real linear functional $\gamma_n v\in T_D'$, and satisfies $\|\gamma_n v\|_{T_D'}\le\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div};D)}$. This functional is the weak normal trace; no pointwise boundary value is asserted.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume Countable Choice for the published Sobolev interfaces cited below. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and use real scalars. $L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$ means the $d$-tuple of real $L^2$ equivalence classes, with norm $\|v\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^d\|v_j\|_2^2$. The test space $C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$ consists of real smooth functions compactly supported in $D$.

For $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$, say that $g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)$ is its distributional divergence when
$$
\int_D v\cdot\nabla\phi\,dx=-\int_D g\phi\,dx\qquad\text{for every }\phi\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R).
$$
The $L^2$ class $g$ is unique when it exists. Indeed, if $g_1,g_2$ both satisfy the identity, put $h=g_1-g_2\in L^2(D)$. Every compact $C\subset D$ has finite Lebesgue measure by [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $\int_C|h|\le |C|^{1/2}\|h\|_{L^2(D)}<\infty$. Thus $h\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. Subtracting the two divergence identities gives $\int_Dh\phi=0$ for every real test $\phi$; splitting a complex test into real and imaginary parts gives the same identity for complex tests. Injectivity of the regular-distribution map in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]] therefore yields $h=0$ almost everywhere, hence $g_1=g_2$ as $L^2$ classes. Define
$$
H(\operatorname{div};D):=\{v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d):\text{there is }g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)\text{ with }g=\operatorname{div}v\text{ distributionally}\},
$$
and equip it with the graph norm
$$
\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div};D)}:=\bigl(\|v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}.
$$
The Sobolev notation $H^1(D)=W^{1,2}(D)$ and $H^1_0(D)=W^{1,2}_0(D)$ uses the norm and zero-boundary closure conventions of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. No pointwise boundary value is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: Since $\operatorname{div}v\in L^2(D)$ by [F5], and $|D|<\infty$ by [F3], [F4] shows $\operatorname{div}v\in L^1(D)$. The constant class $1$ is an admissible element of $H^1(D)$ by [F3] and the definition of the weak Sobolev norm, so its trace class $[1]$ lies in $T_D$.
Apply [F2] with $w=1$. Since $\nabla1=0$, Green duality gives $\langle\gamma_n v,[1]\rangle=\int_D\operatorname{div}v\,dx$.
By [F1], $\gamma_n v=0$ as an element of $T_D'$ acting on $T_D$, so its value at $[1]\in T_D$ is zero. The identity in step 2.1 therefore gives $\int_D\operatorname{div}v=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

$$
\langle\gamma_n v,[w]\rangle:=\int_D\bigl(v\cdot\nabla w+(\operatorname{div}v)w\bigr)\,dx
$$

For an open set $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, let $T_D=H^1(D)/H^1_0(D)$ be the trace quotient of [[lem-na-hdiv-weak-normal-trace]], and let $\gamma_n:H(\operatorname{div};D)\to T_D'$ be its weak normal trace. Define
$$
H_0(\operatorname{div};D):=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};D):\gamma_n v=0\text{ in }T_D'\}.
$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume Countable Choice for the published Sobolev interfaces cited below. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and use real scalars. $L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$ means the $d$-tuple of real $L^2$ equivalence classes, with norm $\|v\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^d\|v_j\|_2^2$. The test space $C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$ consists of real smooth functions compactly supported in $D$.

For $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$, say that $g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)$ is its distributional divergence when
$$
\int_D v\cdot\nabla\phi\,dx=-\int_D g\phi\,dx\qquad\text{for every }\phi\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R).
$$
The $L^2$ class $g$ is unique when it exists. Indeed, if $g_1,g_2$ both satisfy the identity, put $h=g_1-g_2\in L^2(D)$. Every compact $C\subset D$ has finite Lebesgue measure by [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $\int_C|h|\le |C|^{1/2}\|h\|_{L^2(D)}<\infty$. Thus $h\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. Subtracting the two divergence identities gives $\int_Dh\phi=0$ for every real test $\phi$; splitting a complex test into real and imaginary parts gives the same identity for complex tests. Injectivity of the regular-distribution map in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]] therefore yields $h=0$ almost everywhere, hence $g_1=g_2$ as $L^2$ classes. Define
$$
H(\operatorname{div};D):=\{v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d):\text{there is }g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)\text{ with }g=\operatorname{div}v\text{ distributionally}\},
$$
and equip it with the graph norm
$$
\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div};D)}:=\bigl(\|v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}.
$$
The Sobolev notation $H^1(D)=W^{1,2}(D)$ and $H^1_0(D)=W^{1,2}_0(D)$ uses the norm and zero-boundary closure conventions of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. No pointwise boundary value is part of this definition.

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev-space interfaces below. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and $v\in H(\operatorname{div};D)$. Define the trace quotient
$$T_D:=H^1(D)/H^1_0(D),\qquad \|[w]\|_{T_D}:=\inf_{z\in H^1_0(D)}\|w+z\|_{H^1(D)}.$$
Then the formula
$$
\langle\gamma_n v,[w]\rangle:=\int_D\bigl(v\cdot\nabla w+(\operatorname{div}v)w\bigr)\,dx
$$
is independent of the representative $w$, defines a bounded real linear functional $\gamma_n v\in T_D'$, and satisfies $\|\gamma_n v\|_{T_D'}\le\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div};D)}$. This functional is the weak normal trace; no pointwise boundary value is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: Let $(v_n)$ be Cauchy in the graph norm. By [F1] applied componentwise, $v_n\to v$ in $L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$ and $\operatorname{div}v_n\to g$ in $L^2(D)$ for some $v,g$. For every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$, the distributional identity gives $\int_D v_n\cdot\nabla\phi=-\int_D(\operatorname{div}v_n)\phi$. Holder's inequality [F4] passes both pairings to their $L^2$ limits, so $\int_Dv\cdot\nabla\phi=-\int_Dg\phi$. Hence $g=\operatorname{div}v$ distributionally, $v\in H(\operatorname{div};D)$, and [F2] gives graph-norm convergence $v_n\to v$.

The displayed graph inner product is the sum of the real $L^2$ inner products of $v$ and its divergence, so it induces exactly the graph norm. By step 1.1 that norm is complete; therefore H(div) is Hilbert.

By [F3], if $v_n\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ and $v_n\to v$ in H(div), then $\gamma_n v_n\to\gamma_n v$ in $T_D'$. Since each $\gamma_n v_n=0$, the limit trace is zero, so $v\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$. This proves closedness; [F5] and step 2.1 show that the restricted inner-product space is complete.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. For every $u \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $u \ne 0$ and every real $c$, the affine
   hyperplane

   ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(H_{u,c}) = 0$, and so is every subset of it.
2. Every proper linear subspace $W \subsetneq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-linear-subspace]]) is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(W) = 0$.

At $n = 1$ a hyperplane is the singleton $\{c/u_0\}$ and the only proper linear
subspace is $\{0\}$.

Let $\widehat K,K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nondegenerate open simplices and let $F_K:\widehat K\to K$ be the orientation-preserving affine bijection $F_K(\widehat x)=A_K\widehat x+b_K$, where $J_K:=\det A_K>0$. For a measurable vector field $\widehat v$ on $\widehat K$, define its contravariant Piola push-forward by
$$
(\mathcal P_K\widehat v)(x):=J_K^{-1}A_K\widehat v(F_K^{-1}(x)),\qquad x\in K.
$$
The inverse pull-back is $\widehat v(\widehat x)=J_KA_K^{-1}v(F_K(\widehat x))$. Facet normals are oriented consistently with the chosen orientation of $F_K$; the associated oriented surface vector transforms by $n\,ds=J_KA_K^{-T}\widehat n\,d\widehat s$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded, connected polyhedral Lipschitz domain. A matching affine simplicial mesh and its shape regularity have the exact meaning of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]; additionally, call the mesh facet-connected when its dual graph (one vertex per cell and one edge per shared $(d-1)$-facet) is connected. Write $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}K$.

For $k\ge0$, $\mathbb P_k(K)$ is the real scalar polynomial space of total degree at most $k$, and $\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k$ is the real homogeneous scalar polynomial space of degree exactly $k$ (for $k=0$, the constants). Define
$$\operatorname{RT}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)+x\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k(K),\qquad \operatorname{BDM}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)\quad(k\ge1).$$
For either local family $X_k$, its global H(div)-conforming space is
$$X_k(\mathcal T_h)=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};D):v|_K\in X_k(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T_h\}.
$$
The zero-normal RT0 flux space and mean-zero P0 pressure space are
$$V_h:=\operatorname{RT}_0(\mathcal T_h)\cap H_0(\operatorname{div};D),\qquad Q_h:=\{q\in L^2(D):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K,\ \int_Dq=0\}.$$
For each mesh facet $F$, fix one unit normal $n_F$; on a cell boundary use the outward unit normal $n_K$, which equals either $n_F$ or $-n_F$. The notation $\mathbb P_0(\mathcal T_h)$ means cellwise constants. No existence of a mesh for every $D$ is asserted by this definition.

derivations.claim: For BDM, if $\widehat v\in\mathbb P_k(\widehat K)^d$, then $\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$ is a vector polynomial of degree at most $k$ in $x$ because $F^{-1}$ is affine. Multiplication by the constant matrix $J^{-1}A$ preserves this degree, so [F1] maps BDM into BDM. Applying the same argument to the inverse affine map proves onto-ness.

Write an RT field as $\widehat v(\widehat x)=\widehat p(\widehat x)+\widehat x\widehat q(\widehat x)$ with $\widehat p\in\mathbb P_k^d$ and homogeneous $\widehat q$ of degree $k$. The push-forward of the first term is in $\mathbb P_k^d$. For the second term, use $\widehat x=A^{-1}(x-b)$: its image is $J^{-1}(x-b)\widehat q(A^{-1}(x-b))$. The degree-$k$ homogeneous part of $\widehat q(A^{-1}(x-b))$ is $q_k(x):=\widehat q(A^{-1}x)$, with remainder of degree at most $k-1$ (zero when $k=0$). Thus $(x-b)\widehat q(A^{-1}(x-b))=xq_k(x)+p_k(x)$ for some vector polynomial $p_k$ of degree at most $k$: all terms from $x$ times the remainder and from $b$ times the full scalar polynomial have degree at most $k$. Therefore the image lies in $\operatorname{RT}_k(K)$.

The inverse Piola map is the contravariant Piola map for the orientation-preserving affine bijection $F^{-1}$, up to the displayed inverse formula in [F1]. The same polynomial decomposition from step 1.2 applied to $F^{-1}$ maps $\operatorname{RT}_k(K)$ into $\operatorname{RT}_k(\widehat K)$. Hence the forward inclusion is onto.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open. If $v\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$, then $\operatorname{div}v\in L^1(D)$ and
$$\int_D\operatorname{div}v\,dx=0.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded, connected polyhedral Lipschitz domain. A matching affine simplicial mesh and its shape regularity have the exact meaning of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]; additionally, call the mesh facet-connected when its dual graph (one vertex per cell and one edge per shared $(d-1)$-facet) is connected. Write $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}K$.

For $k\ge0$, $\mathbb P_k(K)$ is the real scalar polynomial space of total degree at most $k$, and $\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k$ is the real homogeneous scalar polynomial space of degree exactly $k$ (for $k=0$, the constants). Define
$$\operatorname{RT}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)+x\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k(K),\qquad \operatorname{BDM}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)\quad(k\ge1).$$
For either local family $X_k$, its global H(div)-conforming space is
$$X_k(\mathcal T_h)=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};D):v|_K\in X_k(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T_h\}.
$$
The zero-normal RT0 flux space and mean-zero P0 pressure space are
$$V_h:=\operatorname{RT}_0(\mathcal T_h)\cap H_0(\operatorname{div};D),\qquad Q_h:=\{q\in L^2(D):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K,\ \int_Dq=0\}.$$
For each mesh facet $F$, fix one unit normal $n_F$; on a cell boundary use the outward unit normal $n_K$, which equals either $n_F$ or $-n_F$. The notation $\mathbb P_0(\mathcal T_h)$ means cellwise constants. No existence of a mesh for every $D$ is asserted by this definition.

For an open set $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, let $T_D=H^1(D)/H^1_0(D)$ be the trace quotient of [[lem-na-hdiv-weak-normal-trace]], and let $\gamma_n:H(\operatorname{div};D)\to T_D'$ be its weak normal trace. Define
$$
H_0(\operatorname{div};D):=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};D):\gamma_n v=0\text{ in }T_D'\}.
$$
Thus zero normal trace means that the Green-duality functional vanishes on every H1 trace class; no pointwise normal value is required.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $\operatorname{div}v_h$ is cellwise constant; by [F1], its global mean is zero. Thus $\operatorname{div}v_h\in Q_h$.

If $v_h\in Z_h$, test its defining orthogonality with the admissible choice $q_h=\operatorname{div}v_h$ from step 1.1. Then $0=b(v_h,q_h)=-\|\operatorname{div}v_h\|_{L^2(D)}^2$, so its divergence vanishes in $L^2$. Conversely, if $\operatorname{div}v_h=0$, the defining integral $b(v_h,q_h)$ is zero for every $q_h\in Q_h$. This proves the equality, including the case $Q_h=\{0\}$.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nondegenerate open simplex. For every $u\in H^1(K;\mathbb R)$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a function $u_\varepsilon$ smooth on an open neighborhood of $\overline K$ with $\|u_\varepsilon-u\|_{H^1(K)}<\varepsilon$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

On the reference simplex choose a facet $\widehat F$ opposite a vertex $a$, and parameterize inward segments by $x(y,t)=(1-t)y+ta$, $y\in\widehat F$, $0\le t\le\tfrac12$. For fixed $y$ and $t$ in $[\tfrac14,\tfrac12]$, the fundamental theorem of calculus and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|u(y)|^2\le2|u(x(y,t))|^2+2t\int_0^t |(a-y)\cdot\nabla u(x(y,s))|^2,ds.$ Integrate in $y$ and $t$. The segment Jacobian is a fixed positive constant times $(1-t)^{d-1}$, bounded above and below on this interval; $|a-y|$ is bounded on the compact reference simplex. Changing variables in the first integral and using Fubini [F4] in the second bounds $\|u\|_{L^2(\widehat F)}^2$ by $C_d(\|u\|_{L^2(\widehat K)}^2+\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\widehat K)}^2)$.

For a general affine simplex write $x=b+A\widehat x$ and $\widehat u=u\circ F$. The affine change of variables [F5] gives $\|\widehat u\|_{L^2(\widehat K)}^2=|\det A|^{-1}\|u\|_{L^2(K)}^2$ and $\|\nabla_{\widehat x}\widehat u\|_2^2\le |\det A|^{-1}\|A\|^2\|\nabla_xu\|_2^2$. Facet surface measure scales by the corresponding cofactor, with factor comparable to $h_K^{d-1}$; substituting [F2] into step 1.1 yields the asserted $h_K^{-1}$ and $h_K$ factors.

For smooth-neighborhood approximants $u_n\to u$ in $H^1(K)$ from [F1], step 2.1 applied to $u_n-u_m$ makes their facet restrictions Cauchy in $L^2(F)$. Define $\gamma_Fu$ as this limit. If another such sequence is chosen, the same bound applied to the difference of the sequences shows the same limit, so the trace is well-defined. Passing to the limit in step 2.1 gives the displayed bound for $u$.

derivations.claim: Fix a compact $(d-1)$-simplex $G$ contained in the relative interior of $F$. A sufficiently small open tube around $G$ has closure in $D$. Cover its closure by finitely many balls whose larger concentric balls still have closure in $D$; [F2] supplies a smooth cutoff equal to one on each smaller ball and supported in its larger ball. The function $\chi=1-\prod_i(1-\chi_i)$ is compactly supported in $D$ and equals one near $G$. The zero extension $W$ of $\chi w$ belongs to $H^1(\mathbb R^d)$: for a test function $\psi$, the weak product rule follows directly from $\int_D\chi w\,\partial_i\psi=\int_Dw\,\partial_i(\chi\psi)-\int_Dw(\partial_i\chi)\psi=-\int_D(\chi\partial_iw+w\partial_i\chi)\psi,$ and compact support of $\chi$ removes any boundary term on extension.

Let $W_\varepsilon=\rho_\varepsilon*W$ with the mollifier of [F2]. By [F3] applied to $W$ and its weak derivatives, and by derivative commutation on the tube where $\chi=1$, $W_\varepsilon\to w$ in $H^1$ on every smaller tube around $G$. Each $W_\varepsilon$ is smooth by [F4]. Cover $G$ by finitely many smaller simplices on each side whose shared facet portions lie in that tube. The trace bound [F1] on each smaller simplex shows the traces of $W_\varepsilon$ converge in $L^2$ there to the local traces of $w$. By locality and uniqueness of the bounded trace extension, these are the restrictions of the elementwise traces defined on $K_+$ and $K_-$. The smooth $W_\varepsilon$ has identical restrictions from both sides, so the two traces are equal; their limits are equal as well.

Countably many compact facet simplices $G$ exhaust the relative interior of $F$; its boundary has $(d-1)$-dimensional measure zero. Step 2.1 gives equality on each such patch, hence equality almost everywhere on all of $F$.
