derivations.claim: On the reference simplex $\widehat S_d=\{x_i>0,\sum_i x_i<1\}$, each coordinate facet has outward normal $-e_i$ and area $1/(d-1)!$, while the top facet has outward normal $(1,\ldots,1)/\sqrt d$ and area $\sqrt d/(d-1)!$. For $\widehat v=a+cx$, the constant-vector facet fluxes sum to zero by [F3], and the flux sum of $cx$ is $c/(d-1)!=dc|\widehat S_d|$. If all facet fluxes vanish then $c=0$; the coordinate-facet fluxes then force each $a_i=0$. The flux map is injective between spaces of dimension $d+1$, hence bijective.

For any physical simplex, [F2] transports the reference flux degrees of freedom bijectively, so the same unisolvence holds. On each facet, $(a+cx)\cdot n$ is constant because $x\cdot n$ is constant on its supporting hyperplane; equal integrated fluxes therefore give equal normal components.

Let $v$ be a piecewise RT0 field with matching shared-facet fluxes. For $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)$, apply [F3] to $\phi v$ cellwise and sum: interior facet terms cancel by step 2.1 and the common value of $\phi$, and boundary terms vanish because $\phi$ is compactly supported. Thus $\int_Dv\cdot\nabla\phi=-\sum_K\int_K(\operatorname{div}v)\phi$. The cellwise divergence is constant and in $L^2$, so $v\in H(\operatorname{div};D)$ by definition.

Conversely, let $v$ be a piecewise RT0 field in H(div), with global $L^2$ divergence $g$. For every test supported in one cell, the global distributional identity and cellwise Gauss–Green give zero pairing with $g$ minus that cell's polynomial divergence. This difference is in $L^2(K)$ and hence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(K)$ by [F7]; extending from real to complex tests by linearity, injectivity [F7] makes the difference zero almost everywhere on the cell. For arbitrary $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)$, summing cellwise Green formulas and comparing with the global distributional identity yields $\sum_{F=K^+\cap K^-\,\mathrm{interior}}\int_F\phi(v_{K^+}\cdot n_{K^+}+v_{K^-}\cdot n_{K^-})=0$. Each normal sum is constant on its facet. If one were nonzero, choose a nonnegative smooth test supported in a small ball around a relative-interior point of that facet, meeting no other facet, and positive on a subpatch; the sum would be a nonzero constant times a positive surface integral, a contradiction. Hence all interior fluxes match.

Suppose the interior fluxes match. For $w\in H^1(D)$, approximate each restriction $w|_K$ in H1 by smooth-neighborhood functions using [F5]. The trace bound [F4] and volume convergence pass cellwise Gauss–Green to each restriction. Interior traces of $w$ agree by [F4], and the normal components of $v$ agree by step 2.1, so interior terms cancel. If $c_F$ denotes the constant outward normal component on a boundary facet $F$, the resulting identity is $\int_D(v\cdot\nabla w+\operatorname{div}v\,w)=\sum_{F\subset\partial D}c_F\int_F\gamma_Fw$. By [F6] this is the weak normal-trace functional; in particular, if every boundary flux is zero then $v\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$.

Conversely, if $v\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$, its zero trace and the identity in step 4.1 give $\sum_{F\subset\partial D}c_F\int_F\gamma_Fw=0$ for every $w\in H^1(D)$. For any selected boundary facet, choose a smooth function on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in a small ball about a relative-interior point of that facet, positive on a subpatch, and meeting no other boundary facet; its restriction lies in $H^1(D)$. The sum then reduces to the selected $c_F$ times a positive surface integral, so $c_F=0$. Thus every boundary facet flux vanishes.

For $q\in Q$, the right inverse [F3] gives $B_Dq\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, so [F7] places $B_Dq$ in $V$. Its graph norm is finite.

Define $B:V\to Q$ by $(Bv,q)_Q=b(v,q)$. Since $b(v,q)=-\int_Dq\operatorname{div}v$ and [F2] places the divergence in $Q$, $Bv=-\operatorname{div}v$. For $v\in Z$, the graph norm equals $\|v\|_2$, and $a(v,v)\ge\kappa_{\max}^{-1}\|v\|_2^2=\kappa_{\max}^{-1}\|v\|_V^2$.

For nonzero $q\in Q$, choose $v=-B_Dq$. Then $b(v,q)=\|q\|_2^2$ by [F3]. The Poincare bound [F4] gives $\|B_Dq\|_V^2=\|B_Dq\|_2^2+\|q\|_2^2\le(1+L^2C_{\rm div}^2)\|q\|_2^2$. Therefore the inf-sup constant for $b$ on $V\times Q$ is at least $(1+L^2C_{\rm div}^2)^{-1/2}>0$.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral domain, $d\in\{2,3\}$, and set $V:=H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ and $Q:=L^2_0(D)$ with the real graph and integral inner products from [[def-na-hdiv-space]] and [[lem-na-l2-zero-mean-hilbert]]. A permeability tensor $K(x)$ is a measurable real symmetric $d\times d$ matrix field for which there are constants $0<\kappa_{\min}\le\kappa_{\max}<\infty$ satisfying
$$\kappa_{\min}|\xi|^2\le \xi\cdot K(x)\xi\le\kappa_{\max}|\xi|^2$$
for almost every $x\in D$ and every $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$. It is positive definite almost everywhere, so $K^{-1}$ is measurable and has eigenvalues between $\kappa_{\max}^{-1}$ and $\kappa_{\min}^{-1}$. Define
$$a(u,v):=\int_DK^{-1}u\cdot v,\qquad b(v,q):=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v,$$
and the weighted flux norm $\|v\|_{K^{-1}}:=a(v,v)^{1/2}$. For data $F\in V'$ and $f\in Q$, the no-flow mixed Darcy problem is to find $(u,p)\in V\times Q$ such that
$$a(u,v)+b(v,p)=F(v)\quad(v\in V),\qquad b(u,q)=-\int_D f q\quad(q\in Q).$$
The pressure space's zero-mean constraint fixes the additive constant (Neumann) gauge; $u\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ encodes zero weak normal flux on the full boundary. In the standard source-only Darcy problem used for hybridization, $F=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded, connected polyhedral Lipschitz domain. A matching affine simplicial mesh and its shape regularity have the exact meaning of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]; additionally, call the mesh facet-connected when its dual graph (one vertex per cell and one edge per shared $(d-1)$-facet) is connected. Write $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}K$.

For $k\ge0$, $\mathbb P_k(K)$ is the real scalar polynomial space of total degree at most $k$, and $\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k$ is the real homogeneous scalar polynomial space of degree exactly $k$ (for $k=0$, the constants). Define
$$\operatorname{RT}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)+x\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k(K),\qquad \operatorname{BDM}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)\quad(k\ge1).$$

$$X_k(\mathcal T_h)=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};D):v|_K\in X_k(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T_h\}.
$$
The zero-normal RT0 flux space and mean-zero P0 pressure space are
$$V_h:=\operatorname{RT}_0(\mathcal T_h)\cap H_0(\operatorname{div};D),\qquad Q_h:=\{q\in L^2(D):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K,\ \int_Dq=0\}.$$

$$ (P_0g)|_K=|K|^{-1}\int_Kg. $$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice, a conforming affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$ from [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]], and $v\in H^1(D;\mathbb R^d)$. The facet trace inequality of [[lem-na-simplex-h1-facet-trace-bound]] makes each moment $m_F(v):=\int_F\gamma_Fv\cdot n_F$ finite. On each cell $K$, use its outward normals to prescribe the $d+1$ facet moments (with sign reversed when $n_F$ points inward to $K$); by RT0 flux unisolvence in [[lem-na-rt0-unisolvence-and-global-conformity]], there is a unique $I_Kv\in\operatorname{RT}_0(K)$ with those moments. Define $I_hv$ by $(I_hv)|_K=I_Kv$. The elementwise traces of the global H1 field agree almost everywhere across each shared facet by [[lem-na-h1-interior-facet-traces-agree]], so the shared moment is single-valued in the fixed orientation; the same unisolvence result gives $I_hv\in\operatorname{RT}_0(\mathcal T_h)\subset H(\operatorname{div};D)$. No canonical facet-moment definition on rough H(div)-only input is made here.

Assume Countable Choice and the mesh conventions of [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]]. On each $d$-simplex $K$, $\operatorname{RT}_0(K)=\{a+cx:a\in\mathbb R^d,c\in\mathbb R\}$ has dimension $d+1$, and the $d+1$ integrated outward facet-normal fluxes determine its element uniquely. A piecewise RT0 field belongs to $H(\operatorname{div};D)$ exactly when its oriented integrated fluxes match across every shared facet; such a field belongs to $H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ exactly when its normal component (equivalently its integrated outward flux) also vanishes on every boundary facet.

Assume Countable Choice. For a nondegenerate affine simplex $K$ with diameter $h_K$ and shape bound $h_K/r_K\le\gamma$, and any facet $F$, every $u\in H^1(K)$ has a well-defined trace $\gamma_Fu\in L^2(F)$ and
$$
\|\gamma_Fu\|_{L^2(F)}^2\le C(d,\gamma)\bigl(h_K^{-1}\|u\|_{L^2(K)}^2+h_K\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(K)}^2\bigr).
$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nondegenerate open simplex. For every $u\in H^1(K;\mathbb R)$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a function $u_\varepsilon$ smooth on an open neighborhood of $\overline K$ with $\|u_\varepsilon-u\|_{H^1(K)}<\varepsilon$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded, connected polyhedral Lipschitz domain. A matching affine simplicial mesh and its shape regularity have the exact meaning of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]; additionally, call the mesh facet-connected when its dual graph (one vertex per cell and one edge per shared $(d-1)$-facet) is connected. Write $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}K$.

For $k\ge0$, $\mathbb P_k(K)$ is the real scalar polynomial space of total degree at most $k$, and $\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k$ is the real homogeneous scalar polynomial space of degree exactly $k$ (for $k=0$, the constants). Define
$$\operatorname{RT}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)+x\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k(K),\qquad \operatorname{BDM}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)\quad(k\ge1).$$
For either local family $X_k$, its global H(div)-conforming space is
$$X_k(\mathcal T_h)=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};D):v|_K\in X_k(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T_h\}.
$$
The zero-normal RT0 flux space and mean-zero P0 pressure space are
$$V_h:=\operatorname{RT}_0(\mathcal T_h)\cap H_0(\operatorname{div};D),\qquad Q_h:=\{q\in L^2(D):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K,\ \int_Dq=0\}.$$
For each mesh facet $F$, fix one unit normal $n_F$; on a cell boundary use the outward unit normal $n_K$, which equals either $n_F$ or $-n_F$. The notation $\mathbb P_0(\mathcal T_h)$ means cellwise constants. No existence of a mesh for every $D$ is asserted by this definition.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim: Let $a_F$ be the vertex opposite facet $F$ in $K$ and define $\phi_{K,F}(x)=(x-a_F)/(d|K|)$. On $F$, $(x-a_F)\cdot n_K$ is the altitude $H_F$, so $\int_F\phi_{K,F}\cdot n_K=H_F|F|/(d|K|)=1$ by the simplex pyramid identity $d|K|=H_F|F|$. On any other facet, $a_F$ and $x$ lie in its hyperplane, hence $\phi_{K,F}\cdot n_K=0$. Thus $I_Kv=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}m_{K,F}(v)\phi_{K,F}$, where $m_{K,F}$ is the outward moment. By [F2], [F7], and Cauchy–Schwarz, $|m_{K,F}(v)|\le C(h_K^{(d-2)/2}\|v\|_K+h_K^{d/2}\|\nabla v\|_K)$. Also [F3] gives $\|\phi_{K,F}\|_K\le C h_K|K|^{-1/2}\le C h_K^{1-d/2}$. Multiplying and summing the fixed $d+1$ terms proves $\|I_Kv\|_K\le C(\|v\|_K+h_K\|\nabla v\|_K)$. Squaring and summing cells yields the global stability estimate since $h_K\le h$.

The divergence of $I_Kv\in\operatorname{RT}_0(K)$ is constant. For smooth-neighborhood approximants to $v|_K$ from [F5], Gauss–Green [F4] says the sum of their outward facet moments equals the integral of their divergence. The trace bound [F2] and H1 convergence let both sides pass to the limit, so $\int_K\operatorname{div}I_Kv=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}m_{K,F}(v)=\int_K\operatorname{div}v$. Dividing by $|K|$ gives the stated cell average.

If $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, choose compactly supported smooth vector fields converging to it in H1 by [F5]. Their boundary facet moments are zero; the trace bound [F2] passes this zero moment to $v$. Hence $I_hv$ has zero boundary facet flux, and [F1] gives membership in $H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$; [F6] then gives $I_hv\in V_h$.

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and Lipschitz, with $d\in\{2,3\}$. Under Countable Choice there is a bounded linear map $B_D:L^2_0(D)\to H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ such that
$$\operatorname{div}B_Dq=q,\qquad \|\nabla B_Dq\|_2\le C_{\rm div}(D)\|q\|_2.$$
For a chosen finite cover and tree decomposition from [[lem-na-lipschitz-domain-finite-star-shaped-cover]] and [[lem-na-finite-cover-zero-mean-data-decomposition]], one valid bound is $C_{\rm div}(D)=\sum_i C_{U_i}D_i$; it is finite and independent of any finite-element mesh.

Assume Countable Choice, a shape-regular mesh with $h=\max_Kh_K$, and $I_h$ from [[def-na-rt0-h1-interpolation]]. There is $C$ depending only on dimension and the shape bound such that every $v\in H^1(D;\mathbb R^d)$ satisfies
$$\|I_hv\|_{L^2(D)}\le C(\|v\|_{L^2(D)}+h\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}),\qquad (\operatorname{div}I_hv)|_K=|K|^{-1}\int_K\operatorname{div}v.$$
If $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, then $I_hv\in V_h$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and suppose its first coordinate projection is contained in an interval $(a,b)$ of width $L=b-a$. For every real $v\in H^1_0(D)$,
$$\|v\|_{L^2(D)}\le L\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2(D)}\le L\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}.$$

The input $B_Dq_h$ is in H1_0, so [F2] gives $S_hq_h\in V_h$. Linearity follows from the linear divergence lift and interpolation.

The stability estimate [F2] and [F1], [F3] imply $\|S_hq_h\|_2\le C_I C_{\rm div}(L+h)\|q_h\|_2\le C_R\|q_h\|_2,$ because $h\le\operatorname{diam}D$. The right-inverse identity from step 1.1 then yields $\|S_hq_h\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}^2=\|S_hq_h\|_2^2+\|q_h\|_2^2\le(1+C_R^2)\|q_h\|_2^2$.

For nonzero $q_h\in Q_h$, take $v_h=-S_hq_h$. Then $b(v_h,q_h)=\|q_h\|_2^2$ and $\|v_h\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\le\sqrt{1+C_R^2}\|q_h\|_2$ by step 2.1. Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open. If $v\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$, then $\operatorname{div}v\in L^1(D)$ and
$$\int_D\operatorname{div}v\,dx=0.$$

For a finite conforming simplicial mesh of bounded $D$, define $P_0:L^2(D)\to\mathbb P_0(\mathcal T_h)$ cellwise by
$$ (P_0g)|_K=|K|^{-1}\int_Kg. $$
Then $P_0$ is linear, equals the identity on piecewise constants, is the $L^2$-orthogonal projection onto that space, satisfies $\|P_0g\|_2\le\|g\|_2$, and preserves the integral $\int_DP_0g=\int_Dg$.

Assume Countable Choice, a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral $D$ in dimension two or three, and a shape-regular conforming mesh. Let $C_I$ be the mesh-independent constant in the RT0 interpolation estimate and let $L$ be a coordinate-slab width for $D$. If $B_D$ is the actual right inverse of [[thm-na-bounded-lipschitz-domain-divergence-right-inverse]], define
$$S_hq_h:=I_hB_Dq_h,\qquad C_R:=C_I C_{\rm div}(L+\operatorname{diam}D).$$
Then $S_h:Q_h\to V_h$ is a linear right inverse of divergence and $\|S_hq_h\|_{L^2(D)}\le C_R\|q_h\|_{L^2(D)}$. Consequently $\|S_hq_h\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\le\sqrt{1+C_R^2}\|q_h\|_2$. When $Q_h\ne\{0\}$, the RT0/P0 inf-sup constant satisfies $\beta_h\ge(1+C_R^2)^{-1/2}$ uniformly in mesh size.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

$$a(u,v)+b(v,p)=F(v),\qquad b(u,q)=-\int_Dfq$$
for all $v\in V,q\in Q$. The graph norm on the flux and zero-mean pressure norm make these equations well-posed; the mean-zero pressure convention fixes the Neumann gauge.

Let $C_I$ be the mesh-independent constant in the RT0 interpolation estimate and let $L$ be a coordinate-slab width for $D$. If $B_D$ is the actual right inverse of [[thm-na-bounded-lipschitz-domain-divergence-right-inverse]], define
$$S_hq_h:=I_hB_Dq_h,\qquad C_R:=C_I C_{\rm div}(L+\operatorname{diam}D).$$
Then $S_h:Q_h\to V_h$ is a linear right inverse of divergence and $\|S_hq_h\|_{L^2(D)}\le C_R\|q_h\|_{L^2(D)}$. Consequently $\|S_hq_h\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\le\sqrt{1+C_R^2}\|q_h\|_2$. When $Q_h\ne\{0\}$, the RT0/P0 inf-sup constant satisfies $\beta_h\ge(1+C_R^2)^{-1/2}$ uniformly in mesh size.

Assume Countable Choice and the mesh conventions of [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]]. With $V_h=\operatorname{RT}_0(\mathcal T_h)\cap H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$, $Q_h=\mathbb P_0(\mathcal T_h)\cap L^2_0(D)$ and $b(v_h,q_h)=-\int_Dq_h\operatorname{div}v_h$, the discrete kernel
$$Z_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:b(v_h,q_h)=0\text{ for every }q_h\in Q_h\}$$
is exactly $\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{div}v_h=0\}$.

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral domain, $d\in\{2,3\}$, and set $V:=H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ and $Q:=L^2_0(D)$ with the real graph and integral inner products from [[def-na-hdiv-space]] and [[lem-na-l2-zero-mean-hilbert]]. A permeability tensor $K(x)$ is a measurable real symmetric $d\times d$ matrix field for which there are constants $0<\kappa_{\min}\le\kappa_{\max}<\infty$ satisfying
$$\kappa_{\min}|\xi|^2\le \xi\cdot K(x)\xi\le\kappa_{\max}|\xi|^2$$
for almost every $x\in D$ and every $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$. It is positive definite almost everywhere, so $K^{-1}$ is measurable and has eigenvalues between $\kappa_{\max}^{-1}$ and $\kappa_{\min}^{-1}$. Define
$$a(u,v):=\int_DK^{-1}u\cdot v,\qquad b(v,q):=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v,$$
and the weighted flux norm $\|v\|_{K^{-1}}:=a(v,v)^{1/2}$. For data $F\in V'$ and $f\in Q$, the no-flow mixed Darcy problem is to find $(u,p)\in V\times Q$ such that
$$a(u,v)+b(v,p)=F(v)\quad(v\in V),\qquad b(u,q)=-\int_D f q\quad(q\in Q).$$
The pressure space's zero-mean constraint fixes the additive constant (Neumann) gauge; $u\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ encodes zero weak normal flux on the full boundary. In the standard source-only Darcy problem used for hybridization, $F=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V,Q$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $F\in V\prime$, $G\in Q\prime$ be bounded data. Suppose bounded bilinear forms $a,b$ and $(u,p)\in V\times Q$ satisfy
$$a(u,v)+b(v,p)=F(v),\qquad b(u,q)=G(q)$$

$$U_h=\delta_u+\alpha_*^{-1}\{M_a(\delta_u+R_h)+M_b\delta_p\}+R_h,$$
$$P_h=\delta_p+\beta_h^{-1}\{M_a(U_h+\delta_u)+M_b\delta_p\}.$$

derivations.claim: Start with a hybrid solution. Its jump constraints and zero boundary flux, together with [F2], make $u_h$ a member of $V_h$. Summing the cell balances against any cellwise constant mean-zero $q_h$ gives the discrete second mixed equation.

Conversely let $(u_h,p_h)$ be the unique conforming solution. Its cell balances hold by [F4]. Let $W_h$ be the broken flux space and define the jump map $J:W_h\to\mathbb R^{\mathcal F_h^i}$ by $J_F(v)=\int_F(v_{K^+}\cdot n_{K^+}+v_{K^-}\cdot n_{K^-})$. Its kernel consists of fields with matching interior fluxes, hence lies in $V_h$ by [F2]. Define $\ell(v)=\sum_K[a_K(u_h,v_K)-\int_Kp_h\operatorname{div}v_K]$. The conforming first equation gives $\ell=0$ on $\ker J$.

Suppose there are at least two cells. Every cell is incident to an interior facet because the dual graph is connected and has more than one vertex. The local space $W_K$ therefore contains a basis flux with nonzero total outward flux, so $D_K:W_K\to\mathbb R$, $D_Kv=\int_K\operatorname{div}v$, is onto. The homogeneous local saddle block has equations $a_K(u,v)-pD_Kv=0$ for all $v\in W_K$ and $D_Ku=0$. Taking $v=u$ gives $a_K(u,u)=0$, so [F6] gives $u=0$; then surjectivity of $D_K$ forces $p=0$. The square finite-dimensional block is injective and hence invertible.

Let $c=|D|^{-1}\sum_K|K|p_K$ and set $\bar p_K=p_K-c$. Then $\bar p\in Q_h$. Sum the local first equations against a conforming test $v_h\in V_h$. The facet-multiplier terms cancel by normal continuity; the constant pressure term contributes $-c\int_D\operatorname{div}v_h=0$ by [F7]. The remaining equation is $a(u_h,v_h)-\int_D\bar p\operatorname{div}v_h=0$. Thus $(u_h,\bar p)$ is the conforming mixed solution, which is unique by [F3].

The map $J$ is onto: for each interior facet $F$, use [F5] on one adjacent cell with zero flux on its other facets and zero field on all other cells; its image is the coordinate vector for $F$. Since $\ell$ vanishes on $\ker J$, the formula $\mu(Jv):=\ell(v)$ is well-defined and linear on $\mathbb R^{\mathcal F_h^i}$. Write $\mu(y)=\sum_F\mu_Fy_F$ and choose $\lambda_F=-\mu_F$. Then $\ell(v)+\sum_F\lambda_FJ_F(v)=0$ for all broken $v$. Taking tests supported in one cell yields each local hybrid equation; balances were already shown, so $(u_h,p_h,\lambda)$ is hybrid. This proves the correspondence before quotienting the pressure gauge.

Invert the local blocks to express each $(u_K,p_K)$ as an affine function of the multiplier vector $\lambda$, with source-dependent right sides. Substitution into $J_F(u)=0$ gives a linear system solely on the finitely many interior-facet multipliers; this is static condensation. Existence and correspondence follow from steps 1.1–2.2. For its homogeneous nullspace, any multiplier vector yields a homogeneous hybrid solution, hence by step 2.1 a conforming solution with zero source. Uniqueness [F3] forces $u=0$ and $p_K=c$ for one global constant. The local equations then read $\sum_{F\subset\partial K,\ F\mathrm{interior}}(\lambda_F-c)\int_Fv_K\cdot n_K=0$ for all $v_K\in W_K$, since Gauss–Green and the zero physical-boundary flux give $D_Kv_K=\sum_{F\mathrm{interior}}\int_Fv_K\cdot n_K$. Using the independent facet basis [F5] gives $\lambda_F=c$ on every interior facet. Conversely a common constant vector is a null vector by the gauge identity in [F1]. Thus the kernel is exactly the constant gauge.

For one cell there are no interior multipliers. All its facets are physical boundary facets, so zero boundary flux and local unisolvence [F2] force $W_K=\{0\}$; also $Q_h=\{0\}$. The hybrid cell pressure is arbitrary, but every two such values differ by the common gauge, so the quotient contains one solution, corresponding to the zero conforming pair.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for the published Sobolev interfaces cited below. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and use real scalars. $L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$ means the $d$-tuple of real $L^2$ equivalence classes, with norm $\|v\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^d\|v_j\|_2^2$. The test space $C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$ consists of real smooth functions compactly supported in $D$.

For $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$, say that $g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)$ is its distributional divergence when
$$
\int_D v\cdot\nabla\phi\,dx=-\int_D g\phi\,dx\qquad\text{for every }\phi\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R).
$$
The $L^2$ class $g$ is unique when it exists. Indeed, if $g_1,g_2$ both satisfy the identity, put $h=g_1-g_2\in L^2(D)$. Every compact $C\subset D$ has finite Lebesgue measure by [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $\int_C|h|\le |C|^{1/2}\|h\|_{L^2(D)}<\infty$. Thus $h\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. Subtracting the two divergence identities gives $\int_Dh\phi=0$ for every real test $\phi$; splitting a complex test into real and imaginary parts gives the same identity for complex tests. Injectivity of the regular-distribution map in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]] therefore yields $h=0$ almost everywhere, hence $g_1=g_2$ as $L^2$ classes. Define
$$
H(\operatorname{div};D):=\{v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d):\text{there is }g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)\text{ with }g=\operatorname{div}v\text{ distributionally}\},
$$
and equip it with the graph norm
$$
\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div};D)}:=\bigl(\|v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}.
$$
The Sobolev notation $H^1(D)=W^{1,2}(D)$ and $H^1_0(D)=W^{1,2}_0(D)$ uses the norm and zero-boundary closure conventions of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. No pointwise boundary value is part of this definition.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim: Let $K_1=\{0<y<x<1\}$ and $K_2=\{0<x<y<1\}$. The affine formulas $p_1(x,y)=y$ and $p_2(x,y)=x$ agree on $x=y$ and attain the four stated vertex values, so they define a continuous piecewise-P1 function. Their negative gradients are $q_1=(0,-1)$ and $q_2=(-1,0)$, each with classical divergence zero. With fixed diagonal normal $n=(1,-1)/\sqrt2$, $q_1\cdot n=1/\sqrt2$ and $q_2\cdot n=-1/\sqrt2$, so the jump magnitude is $\sqrt2$.

For $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)$, integration by parts on the two triangles shows that the distributional divergence of the piecewise field is the nonzero line measure on the diagonal with density $q_1\cdot n-q_2\cdot n=\sqrt2$ in this orientation (the distributional pairing is the negative of the summed outward boundary flux). To see it cannot be an $L^2$ function, choose a nonnegative smooth $\psi$ supported in the open diagonal with positive line integral and a smooth transverse cutoff $\eta$ with $\eta(0)=1$; set $\phi_\varepsilon(y,t)=\psi(y)\eta(t/\varepsilon)$ in tubular coordinates, extended by zero. The surface pairing is the fixed nonzero number $\sqrt2\int\psi$, whereas $\|\phi_\varepsilon\|_{L^2(D)}=O(\varepsilon^{1/2})$. If the distribution were represented by $g\in L^2(D)$, [F2] would give $|\int g\phi_\varepsilon|\le\|g\|_2\|\phi_\varepsilon\|_2\to0$, a contradiction. By [F1] the field is not in H(div).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded, connected polyhedral Lipschitz domain. A matching affine simplicial mesh and its shape regularity have the exact meaning of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]; additionally, call the mesh facet-connected when its dual graph (one vertex per cell and one edge per shared $(d-1)$-facet) is connected. Write $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}K$.

For $k\ge0$, $\mathbb P_k(K)$ is the real scalar polynomial space of total degree at most $k$, and $\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k$ is the real homogeneous scalar polynomial space of degree exactly $k$ (for $k=0$, the constants). Define
$$\operatorname{RT}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)+x\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k(K),\qquad \operatorname{BDM}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)\quad(k\ge1).$$
For either local family $X_k$, its global H(div)-conforming space is
$$X_k(\mathcal T_h)=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};D):v|_K\in X_k(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T_h\}.
$$
The zero-normal RT0 flux space and mean-zero P0 pressure space are
$$V_h:=\operatorname{RT}_0(\mathcal T_h)\cap H_0(\operatorname{div};D),\qquad Q_h:=\{q\in L^2(D):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K,\ \int_Dq=0\}.$$
For each mesh facet $F$, fix one unit normal $n_F$; on a cell boundary use the outward unit normal $n_K$, which equals either $n_F$ or $-n_F$. The notation $\mathbb P_0(\mathcal T_h)$ means cellwise constants. No existence of a mesh for every $D$ is asserted by this definition.

Assume Countable Choice and the mesh conventions of [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]]. On each $d$-simplex $K$, $\operatorname{RT}_0(K)=\{a+cx:a\in\mathbb R^d,c\in\mathbb R\}$ has dimension $d+1$, and the $d+1$ integrated outward facet-normal fluxes determine its element uniquely. A piecewise RT0 field belongs to $H(\operatorname{div};D)$ exactly when its oriented integrated fluxes match across every shared facet; such a field belongs to $H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ exactly when its normal component (equivalently its integrated outward flux) also vanishes on every boundary facet.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

derivations.claim: The gradient is $\nabla p=(-1,0)$, so $q+\nabla p=0$ pointwise. The three outward unit normals are $(-1,0)$ on $x=0$, $(0,-1)$ on $y=0$, and $(1,1)/\sqrt2$ on the hypotenuse. Their facet lengths are $1,1,\sqrt2$, respectively. Therefore the integrated fluxes are $-1$, $0$, and $(1/\sqrt2)\sqrt2=1$.

Their sum is zero, equal to $\int_K\operatorname{div}q=0$ by [F2]. Since $q$ is in RT0 and the fluxes are its facet degrees of freedom by [F1], the data also uniquely determine this constant flux among RT0 fields.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral domain, $d\in\{2,3\}$, and set $V:=H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ and $Q:=L^2_0(D)$ with the real graph and integral inner products from [[def-na-hdiv-space]] and [[lem-na-l2-zero-mean-hilbert]]. A permeability tensor $K(x)$ is a measurable real symmetric $d\times d$ matrix field for which there are constants $0<\kappa_{\min}\le\kappa_{\max}<\infty$ satisfying
$$\kappa_{\min}|\xi|^2\le \xi\cdot K(x)\xi\le\kappa_{\max}|\xi|^2$$
for almost every $x\in D$ and every $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$. It is positive definite almost everywhere, so $K^{-1}$ is measurable and has eigenvalues between $\kappa_{\max}^{-1}$ and $\kappa_{\min}^{-1}$. Define
$$a(u,v):=\int_DK^{-1}u\cdot v,\qquad b(v,q):=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v,$$
and the weighted flux norm $\|v\|_{K^{-1}}:=a(v,v)^{1/2}$. For data $F\in V'$ and $f\in Q$, the no-flow mixed Darcy problem is to find $(u,p)\in V\times Q$ such that
$$a(u,v)+b(v,p)=F(v)\quad(v\in V),\qquad b(u,q)=-\int_D f q\quad(q\in Q).$$
The pressure space's zero-mean constraint fixes the additive constant (Neumann) gauge; $u\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ encodes zero weak normal flux on the full boundary. In the standard source-only Darcy problem used for hybridization, $F=0$.

Assume Countable Choice, the Darcy data in [[def-na-neumann-darcy-mixed-problem]], and a facet-connected shape-regular mesh. For at least two cells, set $C_R$ as in the stable lift theorem and define
$$\widehat\beta=(1+C_R^2)^{-1/2},\quad M_a=\kappa_{\min}^{-1},\quad M_b=1,\quad\alpha_*=\kappa_{\max}^{-1}.$$
Let $(u,p)$ solve the continuous source-only Darcy problem ($F=0$) and $(u_h,p_h)$ the RT0/P0 Galerkin system. For any $w_h\in V_h,r_h\in Q_h$, put $\delta_u=\|u-w_h\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}$, $\delta_p=\|p-r_h\|_2$, and
$$R_h=\widehat\beta^{-1}M_b\delta_u,$$
$$U_h=\delta_u+\alpha_*^{-1}\{M_a(\delta_u+R_h)+M_b\delta_p\}+R_h,$$
$$P_h=\delta_p+\widehat\beta^{-1}\{M_a(U_h+\delta_u)+M_b\delta_p\}.$$
Then the discrete pair exists uniquely and
$$\|u-u_h\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\le U_h,\qquad \|p-p_h\|_2\le P_h,\qquad \|u-u_h\|_{K^{-1}}\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1/2}U_h.$$
For a one-cell mesh $V_h=Q_h=\{0\}$, so the unique discrete pair is $(0,0)$; the nonzero-$Q_h$ error theorem is not invoked. The constants display permeability contrast and do not assert contrast-independent robustness.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Assume the no-flow Darcy data of [[def-na-neumann-darcy-mixed-problem]] and a facet-connected conforming mesh from [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]]. Let $\mathcal F_h^i$ be its interior facets. On each cell $K$, let
$$W_K:=\{v\in\operatorname{RT}_0(K):v\cdot n_K=0\text{ on every boundary facet of }D\text{ contained in }\partial K\}.$$
The broken flux space is $W_h:=\prod_{K\in\mathcal T_h}W_K$, the cell pressure space is $M_h:=\prod_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\mathbb R$, and the skeleton multiplier space is $\Lambda_h:=\prod_{F\in\mathcal F_h^i}\mathbb R$. The scalar $\lambda_F$ is constant on facet $F$ and uses the fixed orientation only to label that facet; local equations use the outward normal of each cell.

For the source-only problem $F=0$, a hybrid solution $(u_h,p_h,\lambda_h)\in W_h\times M_h\times\Lambda_h$ for $f\in Q$ satisfies, for every cell $K$, every $v_K\in W_K$, and every interior facet $F=K^+\cap K^-$,
$$\int_KK^{-1}u_K\cdot v_K-\int_Kp_K\operatorname{div}v_K+\sum_{F\subset\partial K,\ F\in\mathcal F_h^i}\lambda_F\int_Fv_K\cdot n_K=0,$$
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}u_K=\int_Kf,$$
$$\int_F(u_{K^+}\cdot n_{K^+}+u_{K^-}\cdot n_{K^-})=0.$$
Because each RT0 normal component is constant on a facet, the last equation is pointwise normal-flux matching. With physical-boundary flux zero, the transformation $p_K\mapsto p_K+c$ for all cells and $\lambda_F\mapsto\lambda_F+c$ leaves the hybrid equations unchanged: in the local first equation the change is $-c\int_K\operatorname{div}v_K+c\sum_{F\text{ interior}}\int_Fv_K\cdot n_K=0$ by Gauss–Green and the zero physical-boundary flux; the mass and jump equations do not use pressure or multipliers. This is the common pressure gauge.

Assume Countable Choice and the source-only Darcy system and hybrid equations of [[def-na-hybridized-rt0-darcy-system]] on a facet-connected mesh. The hybrid solutions modulo the common pressure shift $(p,\lambda)\mapsto(p+c,\lambda+c)$ are in one-to-one correspondence with the conforming RT0/P0 Darcy solution. If the mesh has at least two cells, every local flux-pressure saddle block is invertible; eliminating these local variables gives a linear system on the interior-facet multipliers whose nullspace is exactly the one-dimensional constant gauge. For one cell, the conforming flux and mean-zero pressure spaces are zero and the hybrid pressure is entirely gauge.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

Assume Countable Choice and the mesh conventions of [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]]. On each $d$-simplex $K$, $\operatorname{RT}_0(K)=\{a+cx:a\in\mathbb R^d,c\in\mathbb R\}$ has dimension $d+1$, and the $d+1$ integrated outward facet-normal fluxes determine its element uniquely. A piecewise RT0 field belongs to $H(\operatorname{div};D)$ exactly when its oriented integrated fluxes match across every shared facet; such a field belongs to $H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ exactly when its normal component (equivalently its integrated outward flux) also vanishes on every boundary facet.

derivations.claim: Each cell has area $1/2$. The field $\theta_1=(x-1,y)$ has zero normal component on $x=1$ and $y=0$, and unit integrated outward flux on the diagonal from $K_1$; $\theta_2=(x,y-1)$ has zero normal component on $x=0$ and $y=1$, and unit integrated outward flux on the diagonal from $K_2$. Their divergences are both $2$, so $\int_{K_i}\operatorname{div}\theta_i=1$ by [F3]. The two zero-boundary conditions and the single free facet degree of freedom make each $\theta_i$ a basis of its local space by [F4]. Direct integration gives $\int_{K_1}|\theta_1|^2=\int_0^1\int_0^x((x-1)^2+y^2)\,dy\,dx=\tfrac16,$ and reflection symmetry gives $\int_{K_2}|\theta_2|^2=1/6$.

Write $u_i=t_i\theta_i$. The cell balances in [F1] give $t_1=\int_{K_1}f=1/2$ and $t_2=\int_{K_2}f=-1/2$. For a local test $v_i=s\theta_i$, its integrated divergence is $s$ and its interior outward flux is $s$. The first hybrid equation is therefore $t_i s/6-p_i s+\lambda s=0$ for every real $s$, equivalently $t_i/6-p_i+\lambda=0$. The jump equation is $t_1+t_2=0$, which the balance values satisfy.

Solving the local equations gives $p_1=1/12+\lambda$ and $p_2=-1/12+\lambda$. Since the cells have equal area, their global mean is $\lambda$; choose the mean-zero gauge $\lambda=0$ to obtain the stated pressures. After local elimination the single skeleton equation is $t_1+t_2=0$, independent of $\lambda$, so its one-dimensional nullspace consists exactly of common constant shifts. This is the constant gauge described in [F2].

Let $K\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite, let $R\in\mathbb R^{N\times r}$ have full column rank and satisfy $\ker K=\operatorname{range}R$, and let $f\in\mathbb R^N$ be compatible in the sense $R^Tf=0$. Define the gauge solve as the procedure:

1. Form the square augmented matrix and right-hand side
$$
\begin{bmatrix}K&R\\R^T&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad \begin{bmatrix}f\\0\end{bmatrix}.
$$
2. Solve for $(u,\gamma)\in\mathbb R^N\times\mathbb R^r$.
3. Return $u$, which is the representative satisfying $R^Tu=0$.

The input hypotheses must be checked for the particular stiffness matrix. The procedure does not identify an omitted nullspace or assert a load is compatible.

derivations.claim: Suppose $(x,\eta)$ lies in the nullspace of the augmented matrix. Then $Kx+R\eta=0$ and $R^Tx=0$. Multiplying the first equation by $x^T$ gives $x^TKx+x^TR\eta=0$, and the second equation makes the second term zero; hence $x^TKx=0$.

For any $y\in\mathbb R^N$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, positive semidefiniteness gives $(x+ty)^TK(x+ty)=2t y^TKx+t^2y^TKy\ge0$. If $y^TKx\ne0$, choosing $t$ with the opposite sign and sufficiently small magnitude makes the right side negative. Thus $y^TKx=0$ for every $y$, so $Kx=0$.

Since $\ker K=\operatorname{range}R$, write $x=Ra$. Then $0=R^Tx=R^TRa$; full column rank makes $R^TR$ positive definite, so $a=0$ and $x=0$. The first null equation now gives $R\eta=0$, and full column rank yields $\eta=0$. The augmented square matrix is injective and therefore nonsingular by finite-dimensional rank-nullity.

Nonsingularity gives a unique solution for every right-hand side. For the right-hand side $[f;0]$, multiply $Ku+R\gamma=f$ by $R^T$. Symmetry of $K$ and $KR=0$ imply $R^TK=0$, so $R^TR\gamma=R^Tf=0$ and positive definiteness gives $\gamma=0$. Hence $Ku=f$ and $R^Tu=0$. Conversely, any vector satisfying those two equations with multiplier zero solves the augmented system, so its uniqueness follows from step 3.1.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open. If $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, then $\operatorname{div}v\in L^2(D)$ and $\int_D\operatorname{div}v=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $f,g\in L^1(\mu)$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $f=g$ almost everywhere;
2. for every measurable $A$,
   $$\int_A f\,d\mu=\int_A g\,d\mu.$$

For integrable real or complex $h$, the notation in condition 2 means
$\int_A h\,d\mu:=\int h\chi_A\,d\mu$; the product is integrable because
$|h\chi_A|\le|h|$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz open set, where Lipschitz means that $\partial D$ has a finite rigidly moved graph-chart atlas. Here $H^1_0(D)$ is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(D)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Since $D$ has finite measure, Holder makes every $L^2$ class integrable, so the zero-mean condition is well-defined ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]). Define
$$V:=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q:=L^2_0(D):=\{q\in L^2(D;\mathbb R):\int_Dq=0\}.$$
Equip $V$ with $\|v\|_V:=\|
abla v\|_{L^2(D)}$ and $Q$ with $\|q\|_Q:=\|q\|_{L^2(D)}$. The local Poincare inequality [[lem-na-homogeneous-dirichlet-poincare]] makes the first a norm equivalent to the usual $H^1$ norm. For $v\in V$, define $\varepsilon(v):=(
abla v+
abla v^T)/2$ and $b(v,q):=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v$. For viscosity $
u>0$, set $a_
u(u,v):=2
u\int_D\varepsilon(u):\varepsilon(v)$, where $X:Y=\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}Y_{ij}$. The continuous domain class is all bounded connected Lipschitz $D$; the exact mini-element mesh class is the narrower polygonal/polyhedral conforming affine simplicial class.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, open, bounded, connected, and Lipschitz. Use the real spaces $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ and $Q=L^2_0(D)$, norms $\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}$ and $\|q\|_Q=\|q\|_{L^2(D)}$, and $b(v,q)=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v$ as in [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]]. For a real normed space $X$, write $X'$ for its continuous real dual with operator norm $\|F\|_{X'}=\sup_{\|x\|_X\le1}|F(x)|$. Let $\mu\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $0<\mu_0\le\mu(x)\le\mu_1<\infty$ almost everywhere, let $\lambda\ge0$ be a scalar, and let $f\in V'$. For any $w,z\in H^1(D;\mathbb R^d)$ define $\varepsilon(w)=(\nabla w+\nabla w^T)/2$ and
$$a_\mu(w,z)=2\int_D\mu\,\varepsilon(w):\varepsilon(z),\qquad \mathcal E_\lambda(w,z)=a_\mu(w,z)+\lambda\int_D\operatorname{div}w\,\operatorname{div}z,$$
and $\sigma_\lambda(w)=2\mu\varepsilon(w)+\lambda(\operatorname{div}w)I_d$. The homogeneous-Dirichlet model restricts these forms to $V$, with displacement zero on the full boundary; an example may prescribe a different boundary partition but gains no well-posedness claim from this definition. This is a linear small-strain model; no nonlinear, injectivity, or contrast-independent estimate is asserted.

Countable Choice is inherited through the imported Sobolev and Stokes-space conventions; this definition makes no arbitrary-index selection.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and suppose its first coordinate projection is contained in an interval $(a,b)$ of width $L=b-a$. For every real $v\in H^1_0(D)$,
$$\|v\|_{L^2(D)}\le L\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2(D)}\le L\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. For bounded open $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, put $\varepsilon(v)=(
abla v+
abla v^T)/2$. Then
$$2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2^2=\|
abla v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2,$$
so $\|
abla v\|_2\le\sqrt2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear
in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.

derivations.claim: Since $|\varepsilon(v)|_F\le|\nabla v|_F$ and $|\operatorname{div}v|\le\sqrt d|\nabla v|_F$, [F4] gives $|\mathcal E_\lambda(u,v)|\le(2\mu_1+d\lambda)\|u\|_V\|v\|_V$. The form is real, symmetric, and bounded.
By [F3] and $\mu\ge\mu_0$, $\mathcal E_\lambda(v,v)\ge2\mu_0\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2^2\ge\mu_0\|v\|_V^2$; the volumetric term is nonnegative.
By [F1]–[F2], $V$ is complete in $\|\cdot\|_V$. Applying [F5] to the bounded functional $f$ and the form of steps 1.1–1.2 yields a unique $u\in V$.

Testing with $v=u$ gives $\mathcal E_\lambda(u,u)=f(u)\le\|f\|_{V'}\|u\|_V$ and, by step 1.2, $\mu_0\|u\|_V^2\le\|f\|_{V'}\|u\|_V$. If $u\ne0$, divide by $\mu_0\|u\|_V$; if $u=0$, the claimed bound is immediate. Substitution into the energy identity gives the second estimate.

The form bounds in step 1.1 and the coercivity constant $\mu_0$ in step 1.2 satisfy the hypotheses of [F6] on every finite-dimensional conforming $V_h$. Thus its Galerkin solution is unique and the stated $M/\alpha$ estimate is exactly $M=2\mu_1+d\lambda$, $\alpha=\mu_0$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, open, bounded, connected, and Lipschitz. Use the real spaces $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ and $Q=L^2_0(D)$, norms $\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}$ and $\|q\|_Q=\|q\|_{L^2(D)}$, and $b(v,q)=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v$ as in [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]]. For a real normed space $X$, write $X'$ for its continuous real dual with operator norm $\|F\|_{X'}=\sup_{\|x\|_X\le1}|F(x)|$. Let $\mu\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $0<\mu_0\le\mu(x)\le\mu_1<\infty$ almost everywhere, let $\lambda\ge0$ be a scalar, and let $f\in V'$. For any $w,z\in H^1(D;\mathbb R^d)$ define $\varepsilon(w)=(\nabla w+\nabla w^T)/2$ and
$$a_\mu(w,z)=2\int_D\mu\,\varepsilon(w):\varepsilon(z),\qquad \mathcal E_\lambda(w,z)=a_\mu(w,z)+\lambda\int_D\operatorname{div}w\,\operatorname{div}z,$$
and $\sigma_\lambda(w)=2\mu\varepsilon(w)+\lambda(\operatorname{div}w)I_d$. The homogeneous-Dirichlet model restricts these forms to $V$, with displacement zero on the full boundary; an example may prescribe a different boundary partition but gains no well-posedness claim from this definition. This is a linear small-strain model; no nonlinear, injectivity, or contrast-independent estimate is asserted.

Countable Choice is inherited through the imported Sobolev and Stokes-space conventions; this definition makes no arbitrary-index selection.

Assume Countable Choice, as in the imported model and mini-element spaces. Use the model, spaces, and sign convention of [[def-linear-elasticity-displacement-formulation-and-data]]. For finite $\lambda>0$, set $p=-\lambda\operatorname{div}u\in Q$ and write the mixed equations
$$
a_\mu(u,v)+b(v,p)=f(v),\qquad b(u,q)-\lambda^{-1}(p,q)_{L^2(D)}=0
$$
for all $v\in V$ and $q\in Q$. The pressure belongs to $Q$ by [[lem-linear-elasticity-mixed-pressure-gauge-is-well-defined]], which uses the zero-mean-divergence result. At the endpoint $\lambda=\infty$, define $\lambda^{-1}=0$ and impose $b(u,q)=0$; this is the incompressible constraint. At $\lambda=0$ use the primal displacement problem with $p=0$, not a mixed saddle system.

For a connected polygonal or polyhedral $D$ in dimension $d=2$ or $3$ with a conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh, the discrete pair $(V_h,Q_h)$ is exactly the P1-bubble/P1 mini-element pair of [[def-na-mini-element-p1-bubble-p1-spaces]]. The discrete mixed equations use the same $a_\mu,b,\lambda^{-1}$ and replace $V,Q$ by $V_h,Q_h$.
Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open. If $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, then $\operatorname{div}v\in L^2(D)$ and $\int_D\operatorname{div}v=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. For bounded open $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, put $\varepsilon(v)=(
abla v+
abla v^T)/2$. Then
$$2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2^2=\|
abla v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2,$$
so $\|
abla v\|_2\le\sqrt2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2$.

Assume Countable Choice. On the spaces $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ and $Q=L^2_0(D)$ of [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]], equipped with $\|v\|_V=\|
abla v\|_2$, the form $b(v,q)=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v$ is bounded by $\sqrt d$. Its inf-sup constant satisfies
$$\inf_{q
e0}\sup_{v
e0} rac{b(v,q)}{\|v\|_V\|q\|_2}\ge C_{m div}(D)^{-1}.$$

On the mini-element spaces of [[def-na-mini-element-p1-bubble-p1-spaces]], there is a Fortin operator $\Pi_h:V\to V_h$ preserving $b(v,q_h)$ for every $q_h\in Q_h$, with $\|\Pi_hv\|_V\le C_F\|v\|_V$. The constant depends only on $d$ and the mesh shape-regularity bound, not on $h$. Consequently
$$\beta_h\ge (C_FC_{\rm div}(D))^{-1}.$$

e\{0\}$, assume $V
e\{0\}$. Define $B:V	o Q$ by $(Bv,q)_Q=b(v,q)$ and set $ eta:=\inf_{q
e0}\sup_{v
e0}b(v,q)/(\|v\|_V\|q\|_Q)>0$. Suppose $Z:=\ker B$ is closed and $a(z,z)\ge\alpha\|z\|_V^2$ on $Z$, with $\alpha>0$. For every $F\in V'$ and $G\in Q'$, there is a unique $(u,p)\in V	imes Q$ satisfying
$$a(u,v)+b(v,p)=F(v),\qquad b(u,q)=G(q),$$
for all $v\in V,q\in Q$. If $M_a=\|a\|$, then one stability bound is
$$\|u\|_V\le eta^{-1}\|G\|+\alpha^{-1}(\|F\|+M_a eta^{-1}\|G\|),\qquad \|p\|_Q\le eta^{-1}(\|F\|+M_a\|u\|_V).$$

Assume Countable Choice and the data of [[def-linear-elasticity-displacement-formulation-and-data]]. For every finite $\lambda\ge0$ there is a unique $u\in V$ such that $\mathcal E_\lambda(u,v)=f(v)$ for every $v\in V$. It satisfies
$$
\|u\|_V\le\mu_0^{-1}\|f\|_{V'},\qquad \sqrt{\mathcal E_\lambda(u,u)}\le\mu_0^{-1/2}\|f\|_{V'}.
$$
For every finite-dimensional conforming subspace $V_h\subset V$, the Galerkin solution $u_h$ is unique and
$$
\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac{2\mu_1+d\lambda}{\mu_0}\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.
$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and suppose its first coordinate projection is contained in an interval $(a,b)$ of width $L=b-a$. For every real $v\in H^1_0(D)$,
$$\|v\|_{L^2(D)}\le L\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2(D)}\le L\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, let $0<\lambda<\infty$, and let $u\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$. Since $D$ has finite measure, Hölder's inequality makes every $L^2(D)$ representative integrable, and almost-everywhere equal representatives have the same integral. Thus the local mean-zero space
$$Q_D:=\left\{q\in L^2(D;\mathbb R):\int_Dq=0\right\}.$$
Set $p=-\lambda\operatorname{div}u$. Then $p\in Q_D$. If additionally $d\in\{2,3\}$ and $D$ is nonempty, connected, and Lipschitz, this $Q_D$ is exactly the space $Q=L^2_0(D)$ of [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]], so $p$ belongs to the mixed elasticity model's pressure space.

derivations.claim: The pointwise bounds $|\varepsilon(v)|_F\le|\nabla v|_F$ and $|\operatorname{div}v|\le\sqrt d|\nabla v|_F$, together with [F9], give $|a_\mu(u,v)|\le2\mu_1\|u\|_V\|v\|_V$ and $|b(v,q)|\le\sqrt d\|v\|_V\|q\|_Q$. By [F3], $a_\mu(v,v)\ge2\mu_0\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2^2\ge\mu_0\|v\|_V^2$.

The space $V$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(D;\mathbb R^d)$ and its gradient norm is equivalent to the $H^1$ norm by [F8]; $Q$ is the closed kernel of the bounded integral functional on $L^2(D)$. Thus both are real Hilbert spaces under [A1]. Also $Q\ne\{0\}$: two disjoint positive-measure balls inside $D$ give a nonzero difference of indicator functions with zero integral. And $V\ne\{0\}$: choose a ball $B(x_0,r)$ with closure in $D$ and set $\phi(x)=\exp(-1/(r^2-|x-x_0|^2))$ inside it and zero outside. Its derivatives vanish at the sphere, so $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)$ is nonzero and $(\phi,0,\ldots,0)\in V$.

For finite $\lambda>0$, take the primal solution from [F7] and set $p_\lambda=-\lambda\operatorname{div}u_\lambda$. By [F2, F10], $p_\lambda\in Q$. Then $a_\mu(u_\lambda,v)+b(v,p_\lambda)=a_\mu(u_\lambda,v)+\lambda(\operatorname{div}u_\lambda,\operatorname{div}v)=f(v)$, while $b(u_\lambda,q)-\lambda^{-1}(p_\lambda,q)=-(\operatorname{div}u_\lambda,q)+(\operatorname{div}u_\lambda,q)=0$. Conversely, any mixed solution has $s=\operatorname{div}u+\lambda^{-1}p\in Q$ by [F2]; its second equation gives $(s,q)=0$ for every $q\in Q$, hence $s=0$ by choosing $q=s$. It therefore solves the unique primal equation and has the same pressure.

At $\lambda=0$, use the primal solution and set $p_0=0$ by convention. At $\lambda=\infty$, apply [F6] to $V,Q$, $a=a_\mu$, and $b$ with $G=0$: [F1] and step 1.1 give bounded forms, step 1.1 gives coercivity on all of $V$, [F4] gives the inf-sup bound, and step 1.2 gives real Hilbert spaces with both $V,Q$ nonzero. This yields a unique mean-zero pair $(u_\infty,p_\infty)$.

For each discrete pair, [F5] supplies a positive $\beta_h$ bounded below independently of $h$. For finite $\lambda>0$ or $\lambda=\infty$, write $c=\lambda^{-1}\ge0$, with $c=0$ at infinity. A homogeneous discrete mixed solution $(w_h,r_h)$ satisfies $a_\mu(w_h,v_h)+b(v_h,r_h)=0$ and $b(w_h,q_h)-c(r_h,q_h)=0$. Test with $v_h=w_h$ and $q_h=r_h$ and subtract the second equality from the first to get $a_\mu(w_h,w_h)+c\|r_h\|_Q^2=0$. Step 1.1 forces $w_h=0$, and then discrete inf-sup forces $r_h=0$. The square finite-dimensional block matrix is injective, hence bijective, so the discrete system has a unique solution for every right-hand side.

The same stability estimate applies to any solution of $a_\mu(w,v)+b(v,r)=F(v)$, $b(w,q)-c(r,q)=G(q)$ when the inf-sup constant is $\beta>0$. Put $U=\|w\|_V$, $P=\|r\|_Q$, $F_0=\|F\|_{V'}$, and $G_0=\|G\|_{Q'}$. Testing with $v=w$ and $q=r$ and subtracting gives $\mu_0U^2\le F_0U+G_0P$. The first equation and inf-sup give $\beta P\le F_0+2\mu_1U$. With $S=F_0+G_0$ and $A=1+2\mu_1/\beta$, substitution, using $F_0G_0\le S^2/4$, yields $\mu_0U^2\le ASU+S^2/(4\beta)$. Solving this quadratic gives $U\le C_US$, where $C_U=(A+\sqrt{A^2+\mu_0/\beta})/(2\mu_0)$; then $P\le C_PS$ with $C_P=\beta^{-1}(1+2\mu_1C_U)$. Thus $U+P\le C_*S$ for $C_*=C_U+C_P$, and these constants do not depend on $c$.

For $0<\lambda\le\mu_0$, let $P_h:Q\to Q_h$ be the $L^2$-orthogonal projection. It exists uniquely: in a basis of the finite-dimensional $Q_h$, its defining normal equations have the positive-definite Gram matrix $((q_i,q_j))$, and orthogonality gives $\|p-P_hp\|_Q=\inf_{q_h\in Q_h}\|p-q_h\|_Q$. The second mixed equation gives $p_h=-\lambda P_h\operatorname{div}u_h$. Hence the first is the symmetric discrete equation $a_h(u_h,v_h)=f(v_h)$, where $a_h(w,v)=a_\mu(w,v)+\lambda(P_h\operatorname{div}w,P_h\operatorname{div}v)$. It is bounded by $M_0=2\mu_1+d\mu_0$ and coercive by $\mu_0$.

For any $w_h\in V_h$, subtract the equation for $a_h(w_h,\cdot)$ from the continuous primal equation. For every $v_h\in V_h$ this gives $a_h(u_h-w_h,v_h)=a_h(u-w_h,v_h)+\lambda((I-P_h)\operatorname{div}u,(I-P_h)\operatorname{div}v_h)$. Since $p=-\lambda\operatorname{div}u$, $\lambda(I-P_h)\operatorname{div}u=-(I-P_h)p$; orthogonal projection gives $\|I-P_h\|\le1$, while $\|\operatorname{div}v_h\|_2\le\sqrt d\|v_h\|_V$, so Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the remainder by $\sqrt d\|p-P_hp\|_Q\|v_h\|_V$. Testing with $v_h=u_h-w_h$ and using coercivity yields the displacement estimate; if $u_h=w_h$ it is immediate, and otherwise divide by $\mu_0\|u_h-w_h\|_V$ and take the infimum over $w_h$: $\|u-u_h\|_V\le\left(1+\frac{M_0}{\mu_0}\right)\inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|u-w_h\|_V+\frac{\sqrt d}{\mu_0}\inf_{q_h\in Q_h}\|p-q_h\|_Q$. Moreover, $p-p_h=(I-P_h)p-\lambda P_h\operatorname{div}(u-u_h)$, so $\|p-p_h\|_Q\le\inf_{q_h\in Q_h}\|p-q_h\|_Q+\mu_0\sqrt d\|u-u_h\|_V$. Adding these bounds gives the claimed product-space best-approximation estimate with a constant depending only on $d,\mu_0,\mu_1$.

Testing the continuous primal equation with $u$ and the equivalent discrete $a_h$ equation with $u_h$, coercivity gives $\|u\|_V,\|u_h\|_V\le\mu_0^{-1}\|f\|_{V'}$. The pressure identities and $\lambda\le\mu_0$ then give $\|p\|_Q\le\lambda\sqrt d\|u\|_V\le\sqrt d\|f\|_{V'}$ and $\|p_h\|_Q\le\lambda\sqrt d\|u_h\|_V\le\sqrt d\|f\|_{V'}$.

For $\lambda=0$, [F7] gives the solution bounds and the displacement estimate with constant $2\mu_1/\mu_0$; $p_0=p_{h,0}=0$. For $0<\lambda\le\mu_0$, step 4.2 gives uniform solution bounds and step 4.1 the uniform best-approximation estimate. For $\lambda\ge\mu_0$ or $\lambda=\infty$, step 2.3 with the continuous inf-sup bound [F4] and discrete bound [F5] gives uniform solution bounds. For the same upper range, $c=\lambda^{-1}\le\mu_0^{-1}$ and $|\mathcal A_\lambda((u,p),(v,q))|\le2\mu_1\|u\|_V\|v\|_V+\sqrt d\|v\|_V\|p\|_Q+\sqrt d\|u\|_V\|q\|_Q+\mu_0^{-1}\|p\|_Q\|q\|_Q$, so its product-space operator norm is at most $M=2\mu_1+2\sqrt d+\mu_0^{-1}$, independently of $\lambda$.

Write $\|(v,q)\|_{V\times Q}=\|v\|_V+\|q\|_Q$. Let $x=(u,p)$ be the continuous solution, $x_h=(u_h,p_h)$ its Galerkin solution, and fix $y_h=(v_h,q_h)\in V_h\times Q_h$. Galerkin orthogonality gives $\mathcal A_\lambda(x_h-y_h,z_h)=\mathcal A_\lambda(x-y_h,z_h)$ for every $z_h=(w_h,r_h)$. Thus $x_h-y_h$ solves the discrete mixed system with data $F_h(w_h)=\mathcal A_\lambda(x-y_h,(w_h,0))$ and $G_h(r_h)=\mathcal A_\lambda(x-y_h,(0,r_h))$. The bound on $\mathcal A_\lambda$ gives $\|F_h\|+\|G_h\|\le2M\|x-y_h\|_{V\times Q}$. Applying the stability bound of step 2.3 with $\beta\ge\min(C_{\rm div}(D)^{-1},\beta_*)>0$, then the triangle inequality and the infimum over $y_h$, gives the required estimate with a constant at most $1+2MC_*$. Combining this with steps 1.3–2.1, 2.2, 4.1–4.2, and 5.1 covers every $\lambda\in[0,\infty]$.

2. Solve for $(u,\gamma)\in\mathbb R^N\times\mathbb R^r$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, open, bounded, connected, and Lipschitz. Use the real spaces $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ and $Q=L^2_0(D)$, norms $\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}$ and $\|q\|_Q=\|q\|_{L^2(D)}$, and $b(v,q)=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v$ as in [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]]. For a real normed space $X$, write $X'$ for its continuous real dual with operator norm $\|F\|_{X'}=\sup_{\|x\|_X\le1}|F(x)|$. Let $\mu\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $0<\mu_0\le\mu(x)\le\mu_1<\infty$ almost everywhere, let $\lambda\ge0$ be a scalar, and let $f\in V'$. For any $w,z\in H^1(D;\mathbb R^d)$ define $\varepsilon(w)=(\nabla w+\nabla w^T)/2$ and
$$a_\mu(w,z)=2\int_D\mu\,\varepsilon(w):\varepsilon(z),\qquad \mathcal E_\lambda(w,z)=a_\mu(w,z)+\lambda\int_D\operatorname{div}w\,\operatorname{div}z,$$
and $\sigma_\lambda(w)=2\mu\varepsilon(w)+\lambda(\operatorname{div}w)I_d$. The homogeneous-Dirichlet model restricts these forms to $V$, with displacement zero on the full boundary; an example may prescribe a different boundary partition but gains no well-posedness claim from this definition. This is a linear small-strain model; no nonlinear, injectivity, or contrast-independent estimate is asserted.

Countable Choice is inherited through the imported Sobolev and Stokes-space conventions; this definition makes no arbitrary-index selection.

The stress is constant, so its row-wise divergence is zero. The displacement vanishes at $x=0$. Multiplication by the outward unit normals $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, and $(0,-1)$ on the right, top, and bottom edges gives the three displayed tractions.
