The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of [[def-linear-elasticity-displacement-formulation-and-data]]. For every finite $\lambda\ge0$ there is a unique $u\in V$ such that $\mathcal E_\lambda(u,v)=f(v)$ for every $v\in V$. It satisfies
$$
\|u\|_V\le\mu_0^{-1}\|f\|_{V'},\qquad \sqrt{\mathcal E_\lambda(u,u)}\le\mu_0^{-1/2}\|f\|_{V'}.
$$
For every finite-dimensional conforming subspace $V_h\subset V$, the Galerkin solution $u_h$ is unique and
$$
\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac{2\mu_1+d\lambda}{\mu_0}\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.
$$

Assume Countable Choice and the model and mixed conventions of [[def-linear-elasticity-displacement-formulation-and-data]] and [[def-linear-elasticity-near-incompressible-mixed-mini-pair]]. Let $D$ be bounded, connected, and Lipschitz, $d\in\{2,3\}$, $0<\mu_0\le\mu\le\mu_1$, and $f\in V'$. For every $\lambda\in[0,\infty]$ the continuous problem has a unique solution; at $\lambda=0$ use the primal problem and set $p_0=0$, while at $\lambda=\infty$ impose $\operatorname{div}u=0$. If $D$ is polygonal or polyhedral and $\{\mathcal T_h\}$ is any conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh family with a common shape-regularity bound, the mini-element discrete problem has a unique solution for every $h$ and every $\lambda\in[0,\infty]$, with $p_{h,0}=0$. There is a constant $C$ depending only on $d,D,\mu_0,\mu_1$ and the common shape-regularity bound, but independent of $\lambda$ and $h$, such that
$$\|u_\lambda\|_V+\|p_\lambda\|_Q\le C\|f\|_{V'},\qquad \|u_\lambda-u_{h,\lambda}\|_V+\|p_\lambda-p_{h,\lambda}\|_Q\le C\inf_{v_h\in V_h,\,q_h\in Q_h}\bigl(\|u_\lambda-v_h\|_V+\|p_\lambda-q_h\|_Q\bigr).$$
At $\lambda=\infty$ the constraint is $\operatorname{div}u=0$. The estimate makes no heterogeneous-coefficient robustness claim beyond the displayed dependence.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d=2$ or $3$, be a bounded connected Lipschitz polygonal/polyhedral domain with a conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$. On a simplex $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d$, define the scalar interior bubble $b_K=(d+1)^{d+1}\prod_{i=0}^d\lambda_i$. Let
$$S^1_h=\{w\in C^0(\overline D):w|_K\in P_1(K)\},\quad S^1_{h,0}=S^1_h\cap H^1_0(D).$$
The **mini-element spaces** are
$$V_h=[S^1_{h,0}]^d\oplus\bigoplus_{K\in\mathcal T_h}b_K\mathbb R^d\subset H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q_h=S^1_h\cap L^2_0(D).$$
Each bubble is extended by zero off its cell. The zero-boundary conformity of the piecewise affine part is supplied by [[thm-zero-boundary-piecewise-polynomials-in-w10p]]. The local/global dimensions are proved in the next dimension lemma.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. For bounded open $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, put $\varepsilon(v)=(
abla v+
abla v^T)/2$. Then
$$2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2^2=\|
abla v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2,$$
so $\|
abla v\|_2\le\sqrt2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2$.

derivations.claim: Set $\eta(t)=\exp(-1/((t-1/4)(3/4-t)))$ for $1/4<t<3/4$ and $\eta(t)=0$ otherwise. At each endpoint every derivative from the interior is a finite sum of reciprocal-distance powers multiplied by $\exp(-c/\text{distance})$ for some $c>0$, hence tends to zero; so $\eta\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$. Put $\psi(x,y)=\eta(x)\eta(y)$ and $u=(\partial_y\psi,-\partial_x\psi)$. Equality of mixed derivatives gives $\operatorname{div}u=0$. Since $\eta(1/2)>0$ and $\eta(1/4)=0$, the mean value theorem gives $y\in(1/4,1/2)$ with $\eta'(y)>0$; hence $u_1(1/2,y)=\eta(1/2)\eta'(y)>0$. Thus $u\ne0$ and is compactly supported in $D$.

Let $f=-\operatorname{div}(2\varepsilon(u))\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^2)$. For $v\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^2)$, integration by parts and symmetry of $2\varepsilon(u)$ give $2(\varepsilon(u),\varepsilon(v))=(f,v)$. By [A1, F5], choose such tests converging to any given $v\in V$ in $H^1$; [F4] makes both pairings continuous under this convergence, so the identity holds for every $v\in V$.

A P1 vector field in this mesh vanishes at every boundary vertex and is determined by its center value $z=(a,b)$. On the bottom triangle the edge vectors from the center to its corners are $(-1/2,-1/2)$ and $(1/2,-1/2)$; its affine gradient $G$ maps both to $-z$. Subtracting gives the first column of $G$ zero, and adding gives the second column $(2a,2b)$, so divergence is $2b$. On the right triangle the edge vectors are $(1/2,-1/2)$ and $(1/2,1/2)$; subtraction gives the second column zero and addition the first column $(-2a,-2b)$, hence divergence is $-2a$. On the top triangle the edge vectors are $(1/2,1/2)$ and $(-1/2,1/2)$; subtraction gives the first column zero and addition the second column $(-2a,-2b)$, hence divergence is $-2b$. On the left triangle the edge vectors are $(-1/2,1/2)$ and $(-1/2,-1/2)$; subtraction gives the second column zero and addition the first column $(2a,2b)$, hence divergence is $2a$. If all four divergences vanish, then $a=b=0$, so the elementwise divergence-free subspace is exactly $\{0\}$.

Since $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the volumetric term vanishes and step 1.2 gives $\mathcal E_\lambda(u,v)=f(v)$ for every $v\in V$ and every finite $\lambda\ge0$. By [F1], this identifies the same nonzero $u$ as the unique continuous solution for each such $\lambda$.

Let $u_{h,\lambda}$ be the P1 Galerkin solution, which exists uniquely by [F1]. Testing with $u_{h,\lambda}$, using [F6] with $\mu=1$, and applying [F4] gives $\|u_{h,\lambda}\|_V\le\|f\|_{V'}$ and $\lambda\|\operatorname{div}u_{h,\lambda}\|_2^2\le\|f\|_{V'}^2$. Thus along every sequence $\lambda_n\to\infty$ the discrete solutions are bounded in the finite-dimensional P1 space and have a convergent subsequence; the divergence of its limit is zero because the divergence norms tend to zero and convergence in $H^1$ implies convergence of divergence in $L^2$. The limit is zero by step 1.3. If the full family did not converge to zero, a sequence bounded away from zero would have such a zero-convergent subsequence, a contradiction. Hence $u_{h,\lambda}\to0$ and the reverse triangle inequality gives $\|u-u_{h,\lambda}\|_V\to\|u\|_V>0$.

The mini mixed comparison is exactly the scoped result [F2] under the spaces [F3]; its estimate keeps the best-approximation term and its constant is independent of $\lambda$ on this mesh family. No conclusion about a P1 rate as $h\to0$ is used.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Orient every top-dimensional cell of a matching simplicial mesh by the
ambient orientation of $\mathbb R^d$, and orient each facet by the induced
boundary convention of [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. In the sum
of the oriented boundaries of all top-dimensional cells, every interior
facet occurs twice with opposite signs; every boundary facet occurs once.

Let $a<b$ and choose an integer $N\ge1$ and points
$$a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N=b.$$
The **oriented interval mesh** is the ordered family of cells $I_j=(x_{j-1},x_j)$, $1\le j\le N$, each oriented from left to right. Write $h_j=x_j-x_{j-1}>0$. For an integer $p\ge0$, the **broken polynomial space** is
$$V_h^{\mathrm{br}}=\prod_{j=1}^N\mathbb P_p(I_j),$$
with functions interpreted cell by cell. At an interior node $x_j$, write $w^-_j=w|_{I_j}(x_j)$ for the trace from the left cell and $w^+_j=w|_{I_{j+1}}(x_j)$ for the trace from the right cell; the chosen face normal points from left to right, and the jump is $[w]_j=w^+_j-w^-_j$. At $a$ and $b$, the outward normals are $-1$ and $+1$, respectively.

The published matching-affine-simplicial-mesh convention used elsewhere on the A page has dimension $d\ge2$. This definition supplies the distinct one-dimensional interval and trace convention; it makes no assertion about multidimensional cells.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: In the DG equation on each cell take $v=u_h$. The time term is $\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\|u_h\|_{L^2(K)}^2$. When $d\ge2$, since $\beta$ is constant, $-\int_K\beta u_h\cdot\nabla u_h=-\frac12\int_K\operatorname{div}(\beta u_h^2)=-\frac12\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_F(\beta\cdot n_{K,F})u_h^2$ by [F2] and [A1]. When $d=1$ and $K=(x_{j-1},x_j)$, [F3] gives the same endpoint identity $-\int_K\beta u_h\,\partial_xu_h=-\frac12\sum_{e\in\partial K}(\beta n_{K,e})u_h(e)^2$. Sum over cells; [F4] pairs opposite normals on each interior facet for $d\ge2$, and [F5] gives opposite normals at every shared interval endpoint.

Fix an interior facet oriented from $K^-$ to $K^+$ and put $b=\beta\cdot n_F$. The two face terms from step 1.1 and the two upwind numerical-flux terms combine to $-\frac b2((u^-)^2-(u^+)^2)+b\widehat u(u^--u^+)$. If $b>0$, then $\widehat u=u^-$ and this is $\frac b2(u^+-u^-)^2$; if $b<0$, then $\widehat u=u^+$ and this is $\frac{|b|}{2}(u^+-u^-)^2$. For $b=0$ it vanishes. This scalar calculation also applies to the single endpoint quadrature in dimension one.

On an outflow boundary face, $b=\beta\cdot n>0$ and $\widehat u=u_h$, so the volume and flux terms combine to $\frac b2u_h^2$. On an inflow face, $b<0$ and $\widehat u=g$, so they combine to $\frac{|b|}{2}u_h^2-|b|gu_h=\frac{|b|}{2}(u_h-g)^2-\frac{|b|}{2}g^2$. Faces with $b=0$ contribute zero.

If $\int_{\Gamma_-}|\beta\cdot n|g^2\,dS<\infty$, all boundary terms in step 2.2 are integrable, since the polynomial traces are bounded on the finitely many bounded facets. Substituting steps 2.1 and 2.2 into the tested DG sum gives the finite displayed identity. If that inflow integral is infinite, the inequality $g^2\le2(g-u_h)^2+2u_h^2$ and finiteness of the weighted polynomial-trace integral force $\int_{\Gamma_-}|\beta\cdot n|(u_h-g)^2\,dS=+\infty$; the displayed identity then reads $+\infty=+\infty$, without subtracting infinite integrals. For $g=0$ all dissipation terms are nonnegative and the finite identity proves the stability statement.

Let $K$ be a cell in the one-dimensional interval or $d\ge2$ matching affine-simplex branch of [[def-pe04-upwind-dg-transport-discretization]], and fix an integer degree $p\ge0$. Let $(K,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a finite measure space as in [[def-measure-space]], let $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ have the raw measurable-function meaning of [[def-calligraphic-l-p-on-a-measure-space]], and let $W=\mathbb P_p(K)\subseteq\mathcal L^2(\mu)$. For $u\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ define its **cellwise L2 projection relation** to be the set
$$\mathcal P_K(u)=\left\{p\in\mathbb P_p(K):\int_K(u-p)w\,d\mu=0\text{ for every }w\in\mathbb P_p(K)\right\}.$$
For a mesh, the broken relation is the product of these cell relations. The measure $\mu$ is required to give positive measure to every nonempty relatively open subset of $K$ when existence and uniqueness are claimed. This definition does not itself assert that the set is a singleton. Whenever a later result proves that the relation has a unique member, write $\Pi_Ku$ for that member.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim: Choose the finite monomial basis $\{\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_M\}$ of $\mathbb P_p(K)$. Its Gram matrix $G_{ij}=\int_K\phi_i\phi_j\,d\mu$ is positive definite: for every nonzero coefficient vector $c$, the polynomial $q=\sum_i c_i\phi_i$ is continuous and nonzero at some point of $K$, so it is bounded away from zero on a nonempty relatively open subset; full support gives $c^TGc=\int_Kq^2\,d\mu>0$. Each moment $b_i=\int_Ku\phi_i\,d\mu$ is finite by [F2]. The invertible system $Gc=b$ therefore has a unique solution, and $p=\sum_i c_i\phi_i$ satisfies [F1].

For any $w\in\mathbb P_p(K)$, write $u-w=(u-\Pi_Ku)+(\Pi_Ku-w)$. The first term is orthogonal to the second by [F1], hence $\|u-w\|_2^2=\|u-\Pi_Ku\|_2^2+\|\Pi_Ku-w\|_2^2\ge\|u-\Pi_Ku\|_2^2$. Taking square roots proves best approximation.

Input a dimension $d\ge2$, a finite matching affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$ whose boundary faces are paired by translations to form a periodic mesh, a constant velocity $\beta\in\mathbb R^d$, one cell mean $U_K\in\mathbb R$ per cell, and a step $\Delta t>0$. The output is either `CFL-inadmissible` or an updated vector of cell means $U^+=(U_K^+)_{K\in\mathcal T_h}$. Let $V_K=\int_K1\,dx$ be the cell volume and $A_F=\int_F1\,dS$ the face area. Here a cell face is a codimension-one facet, as in [[def-pe04-upwind-dg-transport-discretization]]. For each face $F\subset\partial K$, let $n_{K,F}$ be the outward unit normal, $b_{K,F}=\beta\cdot n_{K,F}$, and $K_F$ the neighboring cell across that periodic face. With $b^+=\max(b,0)$ and $b^- =\min(b,0)$, the upwind flux out of $K$ is
$$\widehat f_{K,F}=b_{K,F}^+U_K+b_{K,F}^-U_{K_F}.$$

Compute
$$\lambda_K=\frac{\Delta t}{V_K}\sum_{F\subset\partial K}A_Fb_{K,F}^+.$$
If $\lambda_K>1$ for any cell, return `CFL-inadmissible` without updating the state. Otherwise, the **degree-zero upwind forward-Euler update** is admissible and its output is
$$U_K^+=U_K-\frac{\Delta t}{V_K}\sum_{F\subset\partial K}A_F\widehat f_{K,F}.$$
This is the degree-zero specialization of [[def-pe04-upwind-dg-transport-discretization]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: By [F2] with the constant vector field $\beta$, $\sum_FA_Fb_{K,F}=0$, hence $\sum_FA_F(-b_{K,F})^+=\sum_FA_Fb_{K,F}^+$. Rewriting [F1] gives $U_K^+=(1-\lambda_K)U_K+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\frac{\Delta tA_F(-b_{K,F})^+}{V_K}U_{K_F}$. All coefficients are nonnegative by $\lambda_K\le1$, and their sum is $(1-\lambda_K)+\lambda_K=1$.

Convexity of $\eta$ and the convex-combination formula in step 1.1 give $V_K\eta(U_K^+)\le V_K(1-\lambda_K)\eta(U_K)+\Delta t\sum_FA_F(-b_{K,F})^+\eta(U_{K_F})$. Sum over cells. Each incoming coefficient for an upwind cell $J$ is paired with the equal outgoing coefficient $\Delta tA_Fb_{J,F}^+$ on that same periodic face, so these terms exactly fill the subtracted $V_J\lambda_J\eta(U_J)$ contributions. Therefore $\sum_KV_K\eta(U_K^+)\le\sum_KV_K\eta(U_K)$.

Multiply the update [F1] by $V_K$ and sum over cells. Every periodic interior face contributes one shared flux with each of its two opposite outward normals, so its two signed contributions cancel. This proves $\sum_KV_KU_K^+=\sum_KV_KU_K$.

On an affine element in dimension $d\ge1$, diagonal-norm SBP data consist of a nodal state vector with $N_K$ entries, a positive diagonal matrix $H_K\in\mathbb R^{N_K\times N_K}$, and derivative matrices $D_{K,\ell}$, $1\le\ell\le d$. Put $Q_{K,\ell}=H_KD_{K,\ell}$. For each face $F$ let $R_{K,F}$ select its face nodes from the volume nodes, let $M_{K,F}$ be a positive diagonal face quadrature matrix, and let $n_{K,F}$ be its constant outward unit normal. The data are **SBP compatible** when
$$D_{K,\ell}\mathbf1=0,\qquad R_{K,F}\mathbf1=\mathbf1_F,\qquad Q_{K,\ell}+Q_{K,\ell}^{T}=\sum_{F\subset\partial K} n_{K,F,\ell}R_{K,F}^{T}M_{K,F}R_{K,F}$$
for each coordinate $\ell$. The rows of $R_{K,F}$ select the nodes used by the face quadrature; on an interior face, the two cells have the same face nodes and weights under the face identification and opposite normals. In dimension one, $R_L$ and $R_R$ select the left and right endpoint nodes with normals $-1$ and $+1$.

This is conditional algebraic data: the definition does not assert that every mesh has such a rule. The identities include exact affine metric factors and no curved-element metric approximation.

Fix constant transport velocity $\beta\in\mathbb R^d$ and SBP data from [[def-pe04-diagonal-norm-sbp-element-data]]. For each cell $K$, let $U_K(t)$ be the vector of nodal values, $Q_{K,\ell}=H_KD_{K,\ell}$, and $U_{K,F}=R_{K,F}U_K$. Set $b_{K,F}=\beta\cdot n_{K,F}$. At each interior face, use the trace from the cell with positive outward speed when $b_{K,F}>0$, and the neighboring trace when $b_{K,F}<0$; at boundary faces use the inflow data on $b_{K,F}<0$ and the interior trace on $b_{K,F}\ge0$. Denote this upwind scalar trace by $\widehat U_{K,F}$.

The **upwind SBP-SAT semidiscretization** is
$$H_K\dot U_K+\sum_{\ell=1}^d\beta_\ell Q_{K,\ell}U_K+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}R_{K,F}^{T}M_{K,F}\,b_{K,F}(\widehat U_{K,F}-U_{K,F})=0.$$
The sign of the SAT correction is fixed by this equation. The definition is spatial only and makes no fully discrete claim.

derivations.claim:
Multiply the cell equation in [F2] on the left by $U_K^T$. The derivative term is $\frac12\frac{d}{dt}(U_K^TH_KU_K)$ because $H_K$ is symmetric. For each direction, the scalar identity $U_K^TQ_{K,\ell}U_K=\frac12U_K^T(Q_{K,\ell}+Q_{K,\ell}^T)U_K$ and [F1] give the face contribution $\frac12\sum_F b_{K,F}U_{K,F}^TM_{K,F}U_{K,F}$ after summing with coefficients $\beta_\ell$. Including the SAT term, the cell energy equation is
$$\frac12\frac{d}{dt}(U_K^TH_KU_K)+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\left(b_{K,F}\widehat U_{K,F}^TM_{K,F}U_{K,F}-\frac{b_{K,F}}2U_{K,F}^TM_{K,F}U_{K,F}\right)=0.$$

Fix an interior face oriented from $K^-$ to $K^+$ and a paired node $q$. Its paired face weights are equal by [F1]. If $b_F>0$, both upwind traces are $U^-_{F,q}$, so the two contributions in step 1.1 sum to $\frac{\omega_{F,q}b_F}{2}(U^-_{F,q}-U^+_{F,q})^2$. If $b_F<0$, the upwind traces are $U^+_{F,q}$ and the sum is $\frac{\omega_{F,q}|b_F|}{2}(U^+_{F,q}-U^-_{F,q})^2$. If $b_F=0$, both contributions vanish.

At a boundary face with $b_{K,F}>0$, $\widehat U_{K,F}=U_{K,F}$, so each node contributes $\omega_{F,q}b_{K,F}U_{F,q}^2/2$. When $b_{K,F}<0$, $\widehat U_{K,F}=g_{F,q}$, so the contribution is $\omega_{F,q}|b_{K,F}|(U_{F,q}-g_{F,q})^2/2-\omega_{F,q}|b_{K,F}|g_{F,q}^2/2$. Zero-speed faces contribute zero.

Sum the contributions from steps 2.1 and 2.2 over all cells. Each paired interior node appears once in the jump sum, and boundary nodes appear once in the corresponding inflow or outflow sum, yielding the displayed identity. Positivity of the face weights makes every dissipation term nonnegative; hence zero inflow data imply $dE_h/dt\le0$.

boundary convention of [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. In the sum
of the oriented boundaries of all top-dimensional cells, every interior

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Let $a<b$ and choose an integer $N\ge1$ and points
$$a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N=b.$$
The **oriented interval mesh** is the ordered family of cells $I_j=(x_{j-1},x_j)$, $1\le j\le N$, each oriented from left to right. Write $h_j=x_j-x_{j-1}>0$. For an integer $p\ge0$, the **broken polynomial space** is
$$V_h^{\mathrm{br}}=\prod_{j=1}^N\mathbb P_p(I_j),$$
with functions interpreted cell by cell. At an interior node $x_j$, write $w^-_j=w|_{I_j}(x_j)$ for the trace from the left cell and $w^+_j=w|_{I_{j+1}}(x_j)$ for the trace from the right cell; the chosen face normal points from left to right, and the jump is $[w]_j=w^+_j-w^-_j$. At $a$ and $b$, the outward normals are $-1$ and $+1$, respectively.

The published matching-affine-simplicial-mesh convention used elsewhere on the A page has dimension $d\ge2$. This definition supplies the distinct one-dimensional interval and trace convention; it makes no assertion about multidimensional cells.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

For every finite measure $\mu$ on a bounded nondegenerate interval or nondegenerate affine simplex $K$ that assigns positive measure to every nonempty relatively open subset, every integer degree $p\ge0$ with $\mathbb P_p(K)\subseteq\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ as in [[def-pe04-cellwise-l2-projection]], and every $u\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, the set $\mathcal P_K(u)$ contains exactly one polynomial $\Pi_Ku$. For each $w\in\mathbb P_p(K)$,
$$\|u-\Pi_Ku\|_{L^2(K)}\le\|u-w\|_{L^2(K)}.$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Multiplying the exact PDE by $w\in\mathbb P_p(K)$ and integrating by parts with [F3] when $d\ge2$ gives its weak equation. When $d=1$, apply [F12] to the product $\beta u w$ on each interval to obtain the same endpoint weak equation. In both branches the exact inflow trace is $g$ and the outflow trace is the exact upwind trace.

For $d\ge2$, each cell is a nondegenerate simplex whose interior is dense in the cell by [F6]. Every nonempty relatively open subset therefore intersects the interior in a nonempty Euclidean-open set, which contains a Euclidean ball. For $d=1$, each cell is an open interval by [F7], so every nonempty relatively open subset contains a Euclidean ball. In either branch [F5] and [A1] give that ball positive Lebesgue measure. Thus Lebesgue measure has full support on every cell.

Each cell is bounded and Borel: this follows from the interval description [F7] when $d=1$ and from the closed affine-simplex description [F6] when $d\ge2$. Choose a finite-radius ball containing the cell. By [F5] the ball is Lebesgue measurable with finite measure, while [F8] makes the cell measurable; [F9] and [F10] then give $\lambda_d(K)\le\lambda_d(B)<\infty$.

The full-support condition in step 1.2 and finite-measure condition in step 1.3 let us invoke the cellwise projection lemma [F11] on every cell. Since $u(t,\cdot)$ is continuous and each cell has finite measure, it belongs to $L^2(K)$; hence $\Pi_hu$ is well defined.

Set $	heta=u_h-\Pi_hu$, so $u_h-u=	heta+\eta$. Subtract the exact weak equation in step 1.1 from [F1] and test with $v_h=	heta$. To justify differentiating projection orthogonality [F2], choose a monomial basis $\{\phi_i\}$ of $\mathbb P_p(K)$ and its fixed Gram matrix. By the construction in [F11], the projection coefficients solve that fixed finite linear system with moments $\int_Ku(t)\phi_i\,dx$. Since $u_t$ is continuous on the compact space-time cell, [F12] and uniform continuity show that the difference quotients of $u$ converge uniformly in $x$ to $u_t$; the bounded test polynomials and finite measure from step 1.3 therefore allow passage through each moment integral. The coefficients, and hence $\Pi_Ku$, are differentiable in time, so differentiating [F2] gives $(\eta_t,	heta)_K=0$. If $p=0$, then $
abla	heta=0$; if $p\ge1$, then $
abla	heta\in\mathbb P_{p-1}(K)^d$. Since $ eta$ is constant, in either case $ eta\cdot
abla	heta\in\mathbb P_p(K)$ and $(\eta, eta\cdot
abla	heta)_K=0$. This leaves only the transport error and the upwind face-flux differences.

Integrate the remaining $-(\beta\theta,\nabla\theta)_K$ by parts using [F3] for $d\ge2$ and [F12] on intervals for $d=1$, then pair cells using [F4] for $d\ge2$ or the endpoint convention in [F7] for $d=1$. At an interior face the homogeneous upwind terms combine to $\frac12\int_F|\beta\cdot n_F|[\theta]^2$; at inflow the volume term is $\frac12\int_{\Gamma_-}|\beta\cdot n|\theta^2$, and at outflow the homogeneous term is $\frac12\int_{\Gamma_+}(\beta\cdot n)\theta^2$. By the face flux differences from step 3.1, inflow contributes no projection residual because both fluxes use $g$; interior and outflow residuals move to the right with signs $+\int_F(\beta\cdot n_F)\eta^{\mathrm{up}}[\theta]$ and $-\int_{\Gamma_+}(\beta\cdot n)\eta\theta$, respectively. Hence
$$\frac12\frac d{dt}\|\theta\|_2^2+\frac12\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^{\mathrm{int}}}\int_F|\beta\cdot n_F|[\theta]^2+\frac12\int_{\Gamma_-}|\beta\cdot n|\theta^2+\frac12\int_{\Gamma_+}(\beta\cdot n)\theta^2=\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^{\mathrm{int}}}\int_F(\beta\cdot n_F)\eta^{\mathrm{up}}[\theta]-\int_{\Gamma_+}(\beta\cdot n)\eta\theta.$$

For each interior face use $|b||\eta^{\mathrm{up}}||[\theta]|\le\frac{|b|}{4}[\theta]^2+|b||\eta^{\mathrm{up}}|^2$, and on outflow use $b|\eta||\theta|\le\frac b4\theta^2+b|\eta|^2$. Absorbing the first terms into the half-dissipation terms of step 4.1 and dropping the remaining nonnegative boundary and jump terms gives $\frac d{dt}\|\theta\|_2^2\le2R_h(t)^2$.
Integrating the differential inequality gives $\|\theta(T)\|_2^2\le\|\theta(0)\|_2^2+2\int_0^TR_h(t)^2dt$. Since $u_h-u=\theta+\eta$, the triangle inequality at $T$ gives the stated estimate.

citations.quote:
Let $d\ge2$, let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh, and consider $U_t+\sum_{\ell=1}^d\partial_{x_\ell}F_\ell(U)=0$ with state domain $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^m$. Assume a common convex entropy $\eta$ and, for each direction $\ell$, an entropy flux $q_\ell$ so that $(\eta,q_\ell)$ satisfies [[def-pe03-system-entropy-pair-and-potential]] for the directional flux $F_\ell$. Write $v=\nabla\eta$ and $\psi_\ell=v^TF_\ell-q_\ell$. For every direction, supply a symmetric consistent two-point flux $F_\ell^{ec}$ satisfying [[def-pe03-tadmor-entropy-conservative-flux]], namely
$$\bigl(v(U_R)-v(U_L)\bigr)^TF_\ell^{ec}(U_L,U_R)=\psi_\ell(U_R)-\psi_\ell(U_L).$$

On each cell use diagonal-norm SBP data from [[def-pe04-diagonal-norm-sbp-element-data]]. Put $Q_{K,\ell}=H_KD_{K,\ell}$; let $U_i^K\in\mathcal A$ be the nodal states; and let the face restrictions select paired face nodes with matching positive weights on the two incident cells. For an oriented interior face node with normal $n$ from the minus trace to the plus trace, set $F_n(U)=\sum_\ell n_\ell F_\ell(U)$ and $\psi_n(U)=\sum_\ell n_\ell\psi_\ell(U)$. Given any fixed coefficient $\alpha_{F,q}\ge0$, define the normal interface flux
$$\widehat F_{n,F,q}^*(U^-,U^+)=\sum_{\ell=1}^d n_\ell F_\ell^{ec}(U^-,U^+)-\frac{\alpha_{F,q}}2\bigl(v(U^+)-v(U^-)\bigr).$$
The coefficient is the same when the face orientation is reversed. Thus the flux is conservative and consistent, and its entropy contraction is
$$[v]^T\widehat F_{n,F,q}^*=[\psi_n]-\frac{\alpha_{F,q}}2\lVert[v]\rVert^2\le[\psi_n],$$
by the directional Tadmor identities in [[def-pe03-tadmor-entropy-conservative-flux]]. On physical boundary faces supply a consistent normal flux and require the boundary entropy contribution below to be nonnegative.

Write $\omega_{F,q}$ for the $q$th diagonal entry of $M_F$. Define the boundary entropy contribution
$$\mathcal B_h(t)=\sum_{F\subset\partial\Omega}\sum_q\omega_{F,q}\bigl(v(U_{F,q})^T\widehat F_{n_F}^*-\psi_{n_F}(U_{F,q})\bigr).$$
The selected boundary flux is entropy admissible when $\mathcal B_h(t)\ge0$. The **flux-differencing SBP semidiscretization** on each element is
$$H_K\dot U^K+2\sum_{\ell=1}^d\bigl(Q_{K,\ell}\circ F_\ell^{ec}(U^K,U^K)\bigr)\mathbf1+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}R_{K,F}^TM_{K,F}\bigl(\widehat F_{n_{K,F}}^*-F_{n_{K,F}}(U_{K,F})\bigr)=0,$$
where $\circ$ is entrywise matrix multiplication and $F_\ell^{ec}(U^K,U^K)$ is the matrix with $(i,j)$ entry $F_\ell^{ec}(U_i^K,U_j^K)$. These are conditional method data: compatible SBP data and directional entropy-conservative fluxes are hypotheses, not asserted to exist for every mesh or entropy pair. The interior numerical flux is explicitly defined once those data and $\alpha_{F,q}$ are supplied. Curved elements are excluded.

On an affine element in dimension $d\ge1$, diagonal-norm SBP data consist of a nodal state vector with $N_K$ entries, a positive diagonal matrix $H_K\in\mathbb R^{N_K\times N_K}$, and derivative matrices $D_{K,\ell}$, $1\le\ell\le d$. Put $Q_{K,\ell}=H_KD_{K,\ell}$. For each face $F$ let $R_{K,F}$ select its face nodes from the volume nodes, let $M_{K,F}$ be a positive diagonal face quadrature matrix, and let $n_{K,F}$ be its constant outward unit normal. The data are **SBP compatible** when
$$D_{K,\ell}\mathbf1=0,\qquad R_{K,F}\mathbf1=\mathbf1_F,\qquad Q_{K,\ell}+Q_{K,\ell}^{T}=\sum_{F\subset\partial K} n_{K,F,\ell}R_{K,F}^{T}M_{K,F}R_{K,F}$$
for each coordinate $\ell$. The rows of $R_{K,F}$ select the nodes used by the face quadrature; on an interior face, the two cells have the same face nodes and weights under the face identification and opposite normals. In dimension one, $R_L$ and $R_R$ select the left and right endpoint nodes with normals $-1$ and $+1$.

This is conditional algebraic data: the definition does not assert that every mesh has such a rule. The identities include exact affine metric factors and no curved-element metric approximation.

Use the conservation-system convention of
[[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]]: on an open convex state
domain $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, the flux is $F:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R^m$.
A **convex entropy pair** is a pair $(\eta,q)$ with $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal A)$,
$q\in C^1(\mathcal A)$, positive-semidefinite Hessian $D^2\eta$, and
$$Dq(U)=D\eta(U)\,DF(U)\qquad(U\in\mathcal A).$$
The **entropy variable** is the column vector $v(U)=\nabla\eta(U)$; gradients
are represented as columns, so the compatibility equation above means
$\nabla q(U)=DF(U)^T v(U)$. The **entropy potential** is
$\psi(U)=v(U)^T F(U)-q(U)$. This definition does not assert that every convex
$\eta$ admits a flux $q$; the compatibility equation is part of the hypothesis.

Let $(\eta,q)$ be a convex entropy pair on an open domain $\mathcal A$, with
entropy variable $v$ and potential $\psi$ as in
[[def-pe03-system-entropy-pair-and-potential]]. A continuous two-point flux
$F^{ec}:\mathcal A\times\mathcal A\to\mathbb R^m$ is **entropy-conservative
in Tadmor's sense** if it is consistent and symmetric,
$F^{ec}(U,U)=F(U)$, and satisfies the exact jump identity
$$\bigl(v(U_R)-v(U_L)\bigr)^T F^{ec}(U_L,U_R)=\psi(U_R)-\psi(U_L)$$
for every pair $U_L,U_R\in\mathcal A$. This definition asserts no existence
for a prescribed entropy pair.

Orient every top-dimensional cell of a matching simplicial mesh by the
ambient orientation of $\mathbb R^d$, and orient each facet by the induced
boundary convention of [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. In the sum
of the oriented boundaries of all top-dimensional cells, every interior
facet occurs twice with opposite signs; every boundary facet occurs once.

derivations.claim: For a fixed cell and direction write $F_{ij}^{ec}=F_\ell^{ec}(U_i,U_j)$ and $\psi_i=\psi_\ell(U_i)$. Symmetry of $F_\ell^{ec}$ from [F4] gives $2\sum_{i,j}Q_{ij}v_i^TF_{ij}^{ec}=\sum_{i,j}Q_{ij}(v_i-v_j)^TF_{ij}^{ec}+\sum_{i,j}(Q_{ij}+Q_{ji})v_j^TF_{ij}^{ec}$. By [F4] the first sum is $\sum_{i,j}Q_{ij}(\psi_i-\psi_j)=-\sum_j\psi_j(Q^T\mathbf1)_j=-\sum_F\sum_q\omega_{F,q}n_{K,F,\ell}\psi_\ell(U_{F,q})$, since $Q\mathbf1=0$ and $Q^T\mathbf1=(Q+Q^T)\mathbf1$ by [F2]. The second sum is $\sum_F\sum_q\omega_{F,q}n_{K,F,\ell}v(U_{F,q})^TF_\ell(U_{F,q})$ by [F2], diagonal face selection, and consistency from [F4]. Summing directions and the potential identity in [F3] proves the volume entropy boundary identity.

The chain rule gives $\frac{d}{dt}\sum_iH_{ii}\eta(U_i)=\sum_iH_{ii}v(U_i)^T\dot U_i$. Since the semidiscrete equation is $H\dot U+V+SAT=0$, the entropy rate is the negative of the volume and SAT contractions. Combining the volume contraction from step 1.1 with $-v^TR^TM(\widehat F_n^*-F_n)$ cancels the physical flux and leaves, on each cell face, $\sum_q\omega_{F,q}(\psi_{n_F}(U_{F,q})-v(U_{F,q})^T\widehat F_{n_F,q}^*)$.

Sum the cell entropy rates from step 2.1. By [F5] the two cell contributions at an ordinary interior face can be written in one orientation as $-[\psi_n]+[v]^T\widehat F_{n,F,q}^*$. For an identified periodic pair, [A2] supplies the same reversed orientation and matching weights, so the same calculation applies. Substitution of the flux definition in [F1] and the directional jump identity [F4] makes each interface contribution $-\alpha_{F,q}\lVert[v]\rVert^2/2$. The remaining physical boundary-cell contributions are $-\mathcal B_h$ by definition. Moving these terms to the left gives the asserted identity, and [A1] gives nonincrease.

For each component, the constant-vector contraction of the volume term is $2\sum_{i,j}Q_{ij}F^{ec}(U_i,U_j)=\sum_{i,j}(Q_{ij}+Q_{ji})F^{ec}(U_i,U_j)$. The SBP identity and diagonal face selection [F2] reduce this to the physical normal-flux quadrature on the cell boundary, since consistency of the directional fluxes in [F4] gives $F^{ec}(U_i,U_i)=F(U_i)$. The constant-vector contraction of the SAT [F1] subtracts that physical flux and leaves only the numerical normal-flux quadrature. Its contributions cancel on interior faces by normal reversal and flux conservation [F1, F5]; for the periodic conclusion, the paired contributions cancel by [A2]. Thus the quadrature-weighted total state is constant on a periodic mesh with the stated pairing.

Input an initial pair $(t,y)$, a step $h>0$, an open time-state domain $D$, and a right-hand-side evaluator for $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$. Before each query, check that its time-state pair is in $D$; return domain-failure with that stage index if it is not. If the evaluator reports failure, return evaluation-failure with that stage index. Execute:

1. Query $f(t,y)$. On success set $Y_1=y+h f(t,y)$.
2. Query $f(t+h,Y_1)$. On success set $Y_2=\frac34y+\frac14\bigl(Y_1+h f(t+h,Y_1)\bigr)$.
3. Query $f(t+h/2,Y_2)$. On success set $y^+=\frac13y+\frac23\bigl(Y_2+h f(t+h/2,Y_2)\bigr)$.
4. If $(t+h,y^+)\notin D$, return output-domain-failure; otherwise return success with $(t+h,y^+)$.

The procedure uses only explicit function evaluations; it has no implicit stage solve. If a numerical evaluator can fail even at a domain point, its failure is returned unchanged with the corresponding stage index. The exact mathematical method assumes all queried values exist.

Let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite periodic matching affine simplicial mesh in $d\ge2$, let $\beta\in\mathbb R^d$ be constant, and apply [[alg-pe04-first-order-upwind-forward-euler]] with $\lambda_K\le1$ for every cell. Assume Countable Choice for the imported affine-simplex Green formula. Then the cell-volume-weighted mean is conserved:
$$\sum_KV_KU_K^+=\sum_KV_KU_K.$$
For every convex function $\eta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, the weighted discrete entropy does not increase:
$$\sum_KV_K\eta(U_K^+)\le\sum_KV_K\eta(U_K).$$

Assume the smoothness and compact-tube hypotheses of [[prop-explicit-rk-order-conditions-through-four]]. The step in [[alg-ssprk33]] has uniform local order at least three.

For an autonomous field, take an initial state $y\in C$, where $C$ is a convex subset of the state domain, and let $E_h(u)=u+h f(u)$ be the forward-Euler map. If $E_h(C)\subseteq C$ and all displayed stages are admitted, then every SSPRK(3,3) stage and the output lie in $C$. If $\Phi:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex, meaning $\Phi(\theta u+(1-\theta)v)\le\theta\Phi(u)+(1-\theta)\Phi(v)$ for $u,v\in C$ and $0\le\theta\le1$, and $\Phi(E_h(u))\le\Phi(u)$ for every $u\in C$, then $\Phi$ does not increase at any of the three stages or at the output.

For a nonautonomous field, assume the initial state $y\in C$ and that the forward-Euler maps at the actual stage start times $t$, $t+h$, and $t+h/2$ preserve $C$ and satisfy the stated $\Phi$ inequality on all admitted stage states. These conditions are premises of the theorem; the method alone does not assert positivity, total-variation diminishing, or any universal invariant-region property.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). The function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$. The parameter interval is the closed interval of [[def-interval]].

It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct $x,y$ and $0<t<1$. No strict inequality is required at $t=0$ or $t=1$, where the two sides coincide. The empty set and a singleton support convex functions, and strict convexity on either is vacuous.

Input a dimension $d\ge2$, a finite matching affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$ whose boundary faces are paired by translations to form a periodic mesh, a constant velocity $\beta\in\mathbb R^d$, one cell mean $U_K\in\mathbb R$ per cell, and a step $\Delta t>0$. The output is either `CFL-inadmissible` or an updated vector of cell means $U^+=(U_K^+)_{K\in\mathcal T_h}$. Let $V_K=\int_K1\,dx$ be the cell volume and $A_F=\int_F1\,dS$ the face area. Here a cell face is a codimension-one facet, as in [[def-pe04-upwind-dg-transport-discretization]]. For each face $F\subset\partial K$, let $n_{K,F}$ be the outward unit normal, $b_{K,F}=\beta\cdot n_{K,F}$, and $K_F$ the neighboring cell across that periodic face. With $b^+=\max(b,0)$ and $b^- =\min(b,0)$, the upwind flux out of $K$ is
$$\widehat f_{K,F}=b_{K,F}^+U_K+b_{K,F}^-U_{K_F}.$$

Compute
$$\lambda_K=\frac{\Delta t}{V_K}\sum_{F\subset\partial K}A_Fb_{K,F}^+.$$
If $\lambda_K>1$ for any cell, return `CFL-inadmissible` without updating the state. Otherwise, the **degree-zero upwind forward-Euler update** is admissible and its output is
$$U_K^+=U_K-\frac{\Delta t}{V_K}\sum_{F\subset\partial K}A_F\widehat f_{K,F}.$$
This is the degree-zero specialization of [[def-pe04-upwind-dg-transport-discretization]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the spatially autonomous SSPRK(3,3) step has exactly the three displayed convex-combination stages. Set $C=\mathbb R^{\mathcal T_h}$ and $\Phi(U)=\sum_KV_K\eta(U_K)$. For $U,V\in C$ and $0\le t\le1$, apply [F5] in each cell and multiply by $V_K>0$ from [F6]; summing proves convexity of $\Phi$.

The state space $C$ is convex and $\Phi$ is convex. By [F2], every forward-Euler image of a cell-state vector lies in $C$ and has no larger $\Phi$ value under the assumed cell CFL. Thus the hypotheses of the convex-transfer clause [F3] hold at the same $\Delta t$.

Applying [F3] to the three stages in [F1] gives $\Phi(U^{n+1})\le\Phi(U^n)$, which is the asserted weighted entropy inequality. The flux-differencing semidiscrete entropy theorem is not used in this transfer.

On an affine element in dimension $d\ge1$, diagonal-norm SBP data consist of a nodal state vector with $N_K$ entries, a positive diagonal matrix $H_K\in\mathbb R^{N_K\times N_K}$, and derivative matrices $D_{K,\ell}$, $1\le\ell\le d$. Put $Q_{K,\ell}=H_KD_{K,\ell}$. For each face $F$ let $R_{K,F}$ select its face nodes from the volume nodes, let $M_{K,F}$ be a positive diagonal face quadrature matrix, and let $n_{K,F}$ be its constant outward unit normal. The data are **SBP compatible** when
$$D_{K,\ell}\mathbf1=0,\qquad R_{K,F}\mathbf1=\mathbf1_F,\qquad Q_{K,\ell}+Q_{K,\ell}^{T}=\sum_{F\subset\partial K} n_{K,F,\ell}R_{K,F}^{T}M_{K,F}R_{K,F}$$
for each coordinate $\ell$. The rows of $R_{K,F}$ select the nodes used by the face quadrature; on an interior face, the two cells have the same face nodes and weights under the face identification and opposite normals. In dimension one, $R_L$ and $R_R$ select the left and right endpoint nodes with normals $-1$ and $+1$.

This is conditional algebraic data: the definition does not assert that every mesh has such a rule. The identities include exact affine metric factors and no curved-element metric approximation.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $D\mathbf1=0$ and $HD+D^TH=\operatorname{diag}(-1,0,1)=B$, so the derivative and norm satisfy the stated SBP identity. The three-point Gauss–Lobatto rule is exact through degree three, while both the quadratic entropy integrand $u_h^2$ and cubic entropy flux $u_h^3$ exceed that degree for a quadratic polynomial; the pointwise collocation therefore underintegrates these nonlinear products.

At the chosen state, $f(U)=(9/2,1/2,2)^T$ and $\widehat f_{\partial}=13/4$. Hence $Df(U)=(-27/4,-5/4,17/4)^T$ and $H^{-1}B(\widehat f_{\partial}-f(U_{\partial}))=(15/4,0,15/4)^T$. The semidiscrete residual is therefore $(-3,-5/4,8)^T$, so $\dot U=(3,5/4,-8)^T$.

The discrete entropy rate is $\dot E=U^TH\dot U=(-3)(1/3)(3)+(-1)(4/3)(5/4)+(-2)(1/3)(-8)=2/3>0$. This exact periodic state contradicts the asserted universal nonincrease, despite the SBP identity; it does not contradict the entropy-stable flux-differencing theorem, which uses a different volume flux.

derivations.claim: For the central flux, both faces of cell 1 see the same pair $(u_1,u_2)$ and hence the same flux; likewise for cell 2. Thus $\dot u_1=\dot u_2=0$ and $E=\frac h2(u_1^2+u_2^2)$ has $\dot E=0$.

Fix constant transport velocity $\beta\in\mathbb R^d$ and SBP data from [[def-pe04-diagonal-norm-sbp-element-data]]. For each cell $K$, let $U_K(t)$ be the vector of nodal values, $Q_{K,\ell}=H_KD_{K,\ell}$, and $U_{K,F}=R_{K,F}U_K$. Set $b_{K,F}=\beta\cdot n_{K,F}$. At each interior face, use the trace from the cell with positive outward speed when $b_{K,F}>0$, and the neighboring trace when $b_{K,F}<0$; at boundary faces use the inflow data on $b_{K,F}<0$ and the interior trace on $b_{K,F}\ge0$. Denote this upwind scalar trace by $\widehat U_{K,F}$.

The **upwind SBP-SAT semidiscretization** is
$$H_K\dot U_K+\sum_{\ell=1}^d\beta_\ell Q_{K,\ell}U_K+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}R_{K,F}^{T}M_{K,F}\,b_{K,F}(\widehat U_{K,F}-U_{K,F})=0.$$
The sign of the SAT correction is fixed by this equation. The definition is spatial only and makes no fully discrete claim.

Let $d\ge1$. If $d=1$, let the cells be a finite oriented interval mesh from [[def-pe04-one-dimensional-interval-mesh-and-broken-polynomials]]; if $d\ge2$, let them form a finite matching affine simplicial mesh. On every cell assume diagonal-norm SBP data of [[def-pe04-diagonal-norm-sbp-element-data]], with paired interior face nodes, equal paired weights, and opposite outward normals. Let $\beta\in\mathbb R^d$ be constant, and let the differentiable nodal state $U_K(t)$ solve the upwind SBP-SAT method of [[def-pe04-upwind-sbp-sat-transport-discretization]] with prescribed inflow values $g_{F,q}$ where $b_{K,F}:=\beta\cdot n_{K,F}<0$. Fix gravity $g>0$ and a stationary bed $b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. A shallow-water state is a pair $U=(h,m)$ with depth $h\ge0$ and momentum $m\in\mathbb R$. Its admissible wet/dry state set is
$$K=\{(h,m):h>0,\ m\in\mathbb R\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.$$
For $U\in K$, define velocity by $u=m/h$ when $h>0$ and $u=0$ when $h=0$. Thus a dry state has both $h=0$ and $m=0$. Define the free surface by $\eta=h+b$ and the physical flux by
$$F(U)=\begin{cases}(m,\ m^2/h+gh^2/2),&h>0,\\(0,0),&U=(0,0).\end{cases}$$
For a continuously differentiable bed, the one-dimensional shallow-water balance law is
$$U_t+\partial_xF(U)=(0,-gh\,b_x).$$
The source is evaluated as zero at a dry state.

A discrete lake-at-rest profile with level $\eta_0$ has $m_i=0$ and $h_i+b_i=\eta_0$ in every wet cell; cells with $h_i=0$ are dry and satisfy $b_i\ge\eta_0$.

On each compact interval $I\subset\mathbb R$, $h_k^0\ge0$ gives $(h_0)_-\le|h_0-h_k^0|$, so $\int_I(h_0)_-\le\|h_0-h_k^0\|_{L^1(I)}\to0$. Let $m,N\ge1$, let $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be a state domain, and let
$\Phi:\mathcal A^N\to\mathcal A^N$ be a one-step update on $N$ cell states.

derivations.claim: Fix a face and set $b^*=\max(b_L,b_R)$. If a side cell is wet, its free surface is $\eta_0$, so its reconstructed depth is $(\eta_0-b^*)_+$. If a side cell is dry, then $b_s\ge\eta_0$ and $b^*\ge b_s$, so its reconstructed depth is $(b_s-b^*)_+=0=(\eta_0-b^*)_+$. Thus both reconstructed depths equal $H=(\eta_0-b^*)_+$, and both reconstructed velocities are zero.

If $H>0$, the states on the face are equal to $(H,0)$ and the middle HLL formula has speeds $-\sqrt{gH}$ and $\sqrt{gH}$, so its flux is $F(H,0)=(0,gH^2/2)$. If $H=0$, both states and speeds are zero and the dry branch returns $(0,0)$. Thus in either case the common flux is $(0,gH^2/2)$.

On the side belonging to a cell of depth $h_s$, the correction in [F2] changes this common flux to $(0,g h_s^2/2)$. Therefore the right corrected flux of cell $i$ and the left corrected flux of that same cell are both $(0,g h_i^2/2)$. Their difference is zero, so the update leaves every $U_i$ unchanged.

Since $s\mapsto s_+$ is $1$-Lipschitz and $a_+-(-a)_+=a$, this yields $|\delta_{i,+}-\delta_{i,-}-b'(x_i)d|\le C_0d^2$. The same local derivative bounds give $0\le\delta_{i,\pm}\le C_1d$, with constants depending only on $I$ and $b$.

For $h\ge0$ and $\delta\ge0$, write $(h-\delta)_+^2=h^2-2h\delta+R(h,\delta)$. If $\delta\le h$, then $R=\delta^2$; if $\delta>h$, then $R=2h\delta-h^2$, which lies between $0$ and $\delta^2$ because $\delta^2-(2h\delta-h^2)=(\delta-h)^2$. For $0<d\le1$, steps 1.1 and [F1] therefore give $$\left|(S_i^n)_2+g h_i^n b'(x_i)\right|\le gH C_0d+\frac{g}{2d}(\delta_{i,+}^2+\delta_{i,-}^2)\le C_2d.$$ For $d\ge1$, both squared positive parts in [F1] lie in $[0,H^2]$, so $|(S_i^n)_2|\le gH^2/(2d)$. Since $|b'(x_i)|\le\sup_I|b'|$, it follows that $$\left|(S_i^n)_2+g h_i^n b'(x_i)\right|\le \frac{gH^2}{2d}+gH\sup_I|b'|\le C_3d.$$ Taking $C=\max(C_2,C_3)$ proves the stated estimate for every $d>0$.

Now let $d\to0$ and fix a compact space-time rectangle. For all sufficiently small $d$, the centers of cells meeting this rectangle lie in a fixed compact interval, so the estimate in step 2.1 and $|b'(x)-b'(x_i)|\le \tfrac12d\sup|b''|$ on a fixed enlargement show that $\mathcal S_d-(0,-g h_d b'(x))\to0$ uniformly there. Since $b'$ is bounded on compact intervals and $h_d\to h$ strongly in local $L^1$, $(0,-g h_d b'(x))\to(0,-ghb'(x))$ strongly in local $L^1$, proving the asserted source convergence.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then

$$\|\tau_h f-f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(h \to 0).$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f_n,f : X \to \mathbb R$ be measurable with $f_n,f \in L^1(\mu)$. If $f_n \to f$
in $L^1(\mu)$, then $f_n \to f$ in measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f_n,f : X \to \mathbb R$ be measurable. If $f_n \to f$ in measure, then there
is a strictly increasing sequence $(n_k)_{k \ge 0}$ of natural numbers such
that $f_{n_k} \to f$ $\mu$-almost everywhere.

The construction below uses the **least** admissible index at each stage, so no
choice principle is spent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Fix a compact space-time rectangle $Q$ and a fixed compact enlargement $Q'$ containing $Q$ and every spatial translate $Q+d_k$ for all sufficiently large $k$. Choose local bounds $H,M$ so that $0\le h_k\le H$ and $|u_k|\le M$ on $Q'$. Strong local $L^1$ convergence implies the same bounds for $h,u$ almost everywhere on $Q'$: the sum $|h_k-h|+|u_k-u|$ tends to zero in $L^1(Q')$, so [F4] gives a subsequence on which both converge almost everywhere and inherit the bounds. By [F3], multiplying $h,u$ by the indicator of $Q'$ therefore gives $L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ functions. The given strong convergence gives $h_k\to h$ and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(Q)$. Applying [F2] to the cutoffs shows $h(\cdot+d_k,\cdot)\to h$ and $u(\cdot+d_k,\cdot)\to u$ in $L^1(Q)$. Strong local convergence on $Q'$ and the triangle inequality then show $h_k(\cdot+d_k,\cdot)\to h$ and $u_k(\cdot+d_k,\cdot)\to u$ in $L^1(Q)$ as well.

Let $L$ be a Lipschitz constant for $b$ on the spatial enlargement, and write $h_k^+(x,t)=h_k(x+d_k,t)$ and $u_k^+(x,t)=u_k(x+d_k,t)$. Hydrostatic clipping changes either adjacent depth by at most $Ld_k$. Take any subsequence of $k$. By step 1.1, the sum of the four errors $|h_k-h|+|u_k-u|+|h_k^+-h|+|u_k^+-u|$ converges to zero in measure on $Q$; [F4] gives a further subsequence on which all four errors tend to zero almost everywhere. At a point where $h>0$, both cell depths are eventually larger than $Ld_k$, so neither reconstructed state is clipped to zero and both reconstructed velocities converge to $u$. At a point where $h=0$, the hypothesis gives $u=0$ and both cell velocities converge to zero; resetting either velocity to zero when its reconstructed depth vanishes therefore still gives convergence to $u$. The reconstructed depths in both states converge to $h$ as well. Thus along this common further subsequence both reconstructed primitive states converge almost everywhere to $(h,u)$. Since the starting subsequence was arbitrary, every subsequence has such a further subsequence.

At a wet limit state $h>0$, the two face inputs tend to the same $(h,hu)$; the left, middle and right HLL branches all tend to $F(h,hu)$, and the formulas agree at the branch boundaries. At a dry limit state, $h=0$ and $u=0$, so both reconstructed fluxes and both speeds tend to zero. In the middle branch write $\alpha=a_R$, $\beta=-a_L$; its equivalent formula is $\widehat F=(\alpha F_L^*+\beta F_R^*)/(\alpha+\beta)-[\alpha\beta/(\alpha+\beta)](U_R^*-U_L^*)$. Here $\alpha\beta/(\alpha+\beta)\le\max(\alpha,\beta)$, which tends to zero at the dry state, while $F_L^*,F_R^*,U_L^*,U_R^*$ tend to zero. The outer branches also tend to zero. Thus along the almost-everywhere convergent further subsequence from step 2.1, the HLL flux tends almost everywhere to $F(h,hu)$. The same equivalent formula and $\alpha,\beta\le M+\sqrt{gH}$ give a uniform bound on the fluxes on $Q$.

Starting from any subsequence, step 2.1 supplies a further subsequence with almost-everywhere convergence of both face inputs; step 3.1 gives almost-everywhere convergence of its fluxes and a uniform bound. Since $Q$ has finite measure by [F3], [F5] yields $L^1(Q)$ convergence along that further subsequence. If the full flux sequence failed to converge in $L^1(Q)$, some subsequence would stay a fixed positive distance from $F(h,hu)$, contradicting this property. Therefore $\mathcal F_k\to F(h,hu)$ in $L^1(Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, the convergence is local.

At a face of the scheme in [[def-pe05-hydrostatic-hll-scheme]], write $\alpha=a_R$ and $\beta=-a_L$. There are coefficients $p,q\ge0$ such that
$$\widehat F^h=p h_L^*-q h_R^*,\qquad p\le\alpha,\qquad q\le\beta.$$
If $\alpha>0$ and $h_L^*>0$, then $p<\alpha$; if $\beta>0$ and $h_R^*>0$, then $q<\beta$. These statements include the branches where one speed is zero and the all-dry branch.

derivations.claim: Suppose $h_R^*=0$. Then $u_R^*=c_R^*=0$. If both speeds are zero, [F1] makes the full flux zero. If $a_L<0=a_R$, the second branch is $F_R^*=(0,0)$. If $a_L=0<a_R$, the speed definition forces $u_L^*\ge c_L^*$. When $h_L^*>0$, this gives $\widehat F^h=h_L^*u_L^*>0$; when $h_L^*=0$, both states and the flux are dry and zero. In the middle branch, [F2] gives $\widehat F^h=p h_L^*\ge0$; it is strictly positive for a wet left state and otherwise both states are dry and the full flux is zero.

Suppose instead $h_L^*=0$. Then $u_L^*=c_L^*=0$. If both speeds vanish, the full flux is zero. If $a_L=0<a_R$, the first branch is $F_L^*=(0,0)$. If $a_L<0=a_R$, the speed definition forces $u_R^*\le-c_R^*$. For $h_R^*>0$ this makes $\widehat F^h=h_R^*u_R^*<0$; if $h_R^*=0$, the full flux is zero. In the middle branch, [F2] gives $\widehat F^h=-q h_R^*\le0$, strictly negative for a wet right state and otherwise zero with both states dry.
The two orientations show that zero mass flux at a dry face occurs only when the selected outer state is dry or both reconstructed states are dry; in each case [F1] gives zero momentum flux as well.

Let $d,\tau>0$, $I_i=[id,(i+1)d)$, $t_n=n\tau$, and $J_n=[t_n,t_{n+1})$. Suppose vector states and shared face fluxes satisfy
$$d(U_i^{n+1}-U_i^n)+\tau(\widehat F_{i+1/2}^n-\widehat F_{i-1/2}^n)=d\tau S_i^n$$
as in [[def-pe05-hydrostatic-hll-scheme]]. For $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T);\mathbb R^2)$ define the space-time cell average
$$\Phi_i^n=\frac1{d\tau}\int_{J_n}\int_{I_i}\varphi(x,t)\,dx\,dt.$$
Choose $N$ such that $\varphi$ vanishes for $t\ge t_{N-1}$. Then
$$\sum_i d\,U_i^0\cdot\Phi_i^0+\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\sum_i d\,U_i^n\cdot(\Phi_i^n-\Phi_i^{n-1})+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\sum_i\tau\,\widehat F_{i+1/2}^n\cdot(\Phi_{i+1}^n-\Phi_i^n)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\sum_i d\tau\,S_i^n\cdot\Phi_i^n=0.$$
Every sum is finite because the test is compactly supported.

Let $b\in C^2(\mathbb R)$, let the uniform cell width be $d>0$, let $x_i$ be the center of cell $i$, and let $0\le h_i^n\le H$ on a fixed compact space-time cylinder. Set $b_i=b(x_i)$, $\delta_{i,+}=(b(x_i+d)-b(x_i))_+$, and $\delta_{i,-}=(b(x_i-d)-b(x_i))_+$. For the source term $S_i^n$ in [[def-pe05-hydrostatic-hll-scheme]],
$$S_i^n=\left(0,\frac{g}{2d}\left((h_i^n-\delta_{i,+})_+^2-(h_i^n-\delta_{i,-})_+^2\right)\right),$$
there is a constant $C$ depending only on the compact interval, $b$, $g$, and $H$ such that
$$\left|S_i^{(2)}+g h_i b'(x_i)\right|\le C d.$$
For time slabs $J_n=[n\tau,(n+1)\tau)$, define the piecewise-constant source reconstruction $\mathcal S_d(x,t)=S_i^n$ on $[x_i-d/2,x_i+d/2)\times J_n$. Consequently, as $d\to0$, if the corresponding piecewise-constant depth reconstructions $h_d$ converge strongly in $L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R\times(0,T))$ to $h$ and are locally uniformly bounded, then $\mathcal S_d\to(0,-ghb')$ strongly in $L^1_{\rm loc}$.

At a face of the scheme in [[def-pe05-hydrostatic-hll-scheme]], write $\alpha=a_R$ and $\beta=-a_L$. There are coefficients $p,q\ge0$ such that
$$\widehat F^h=p h_L^*-q h_R^*,\qquad p\le\alpha,\qquad q\le\beta.$$
If $\alpha>0$ and $h_L^*>0$, then $p<\alpha$; if $\beta>0$ and $h_R^*>0$, then $q<\beta$. These statements include the branches where one speed is zero and the all-dry branch.

At any face in [[def-pe05-hydrostatic-hll-scheme]], if the reconstructed right state is dry, then $\widehat F^h\ge0$, and $\widehat F=(0,0)$ whenever $\widehat F^h=0$. If the reconstructed left state is dry, then $\widehat F^h\le0$, and again $\widehat F^h=0$ implies $\widehat F=(0,0)$.

Fix gravity $g>0$ and a stationary bed $b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. A shallow-water state is a pair $U=(h,m)$ with depth $h\ge0$ and momentum $m\in\mathbb R$. Its admissible wet/dry state set is
$$K=\{(h,m):h>0,\ m\in\mathbb R\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.$$
For $U\in K$, define velocity by $u=m/h$ when $h>0$ and $u=0$ when $h=0$. Thus a dry state has both $h=0$ and $m=0$. Define the free surface by $\eta=h+b$ and the physical flux by
$$F(U)=\begin{cases}(m,\ m^2/h+gh^2/2),&h>0,\\(0,0),&U=(0,0).\end{cases}$$
For a continuously differentiable bed, the one-dimensional shallow-water balance law is
$$U_t+\partial_xF(U)=(0,-gh\,b_x).$$
The source is evaluated as zero at a dry state.

A discrete lake-at-rest profile with level $\eta_0$ has $m_i=0$ and $h_i+b_i=\eta_0$ in every wet cell; cells with $h_i=0$ are dry and satisfy $b_i\ge\eta_0$.

derivations.claim: Write $p_R$ for the left-state coefficient at face $i+1/2$, $q_L$ for the right-state coefficient at face $i-1/2$, and use analogous notation for the two inflow coefficients. Expanding the first component of [F1] with [F2] gives $h_i^{n+1}=h_i^n-\lambda(p_R h_{i,+}^*+q_L h_{i,-}^*)+\lambda(q_R h_{i+1,-}^*+p_L h_{i-1,+}^*)$. The inflow terms are nonnegative and the total outflow is at most $(a_{R,i+1/2}-a_{L,i-1/2})h_i^n$, so the CFL gives $h_i^{n+1}\ge0$.

If $h_i^n>0$ and at least one outgoing speed is positive, the corresponding outflow term is strictly below its speed bound times $h_i^n$: this follows from [F2] if the reconstructed depth is positive, and is immediate if that reconstructed depth is zero. By step 1.1 and the CFL, $h_i^{n+1}>0$. If both outgoing speeds are zero, the outflow is zero and step 1.1 gives $h_i^{n+1}\ge h_i^n>0$. Thus a wet cell remains wet and is in $K$ by [F4].

If $h_i^n=0$, then $m_i^n=0$ and [F1] gives $h_{i,+}^*=h_{i,-}^*=0$, so both corrections on this cell vanish. Its left face has dry right state and its right face has dry left state. By [F3], the left mass flux is nonnegative and the right mass flux nonpositive; if the updated depth is zero, nonnegativity forces both mass fluxes to vanish.

In the zero-depth case of step 2.2, [F3] makes both full HLL face fluxes zero. The cell corrections also vanish, so its updated momentum is zero and its updated state lies in $K$ by [F4]. If instead that initially dry cell has positive updated depth, its updated state lies in $K$ by [F4] as well. Together with step 2.1, this proves that every updated state lies in $K$ under the stated CFL condition.

Multiplying the first component of each update by $\Delta x$ and summing over the finite chain cancels every interior shared mass flux, because the one-sided corrections have zero first component. This gives $\Delta x\sum_{i=1}^N(h_i^{n+1}-h_i^n)=-\Delta t(\widehat F^h_{N+1/2}-\widehat F^h_{1/2})$. Thus only boundary discharge changes finite-domain water; periodic identification makes the right-hand side zero. Combining this identity with steps 2.1 and 3.1 proves the theorem.

If $M$ is a compact topological manifold with boundary $A=\partial M$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $A$ and a homeomorphism
$$c:A\times[0,1)\xrightarrow{\sim}V,\qquad c(x,0)=x.$$
Consequently $A\hookrightarrow M$ is an unbased cofibration, and $M\setminus A\hookrightarrow M$ is a homotopy equivalence. The manifold is Hausdorff and second countable by convention. All three conclusions require no AC.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$
If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then $f^*=g^*:H^n(Y;G)\to H^n(X;G)$ for every integer $n$ and every abelian coefficient group $G$.

For a topological space $X$ and an abelian group $G$, the singular chain groups
and boundary maps of [[def-singular-boundary-operator]] form the
**singular chain complex**
$$C_\bullet(X;G):=\bigl(\cdots\to C_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\partial_n}C_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots\bigr),$$
because [[thm-the-singular-boundary-squares-to-zero]] gives
$\partial_{n-1}\partial_n=0$.

Its degree-$n$ cycles and boundaries are
$$Z_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G):=\ker\partial_n,\qquad B_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G):=\operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1},$$
in the sense of [[def-cycle-and-boundary-subobjects-of-a-complex]].

The **$n$th singular homology group** is the homology object of this chain
complex:
$$H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G):=Z_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\big/B_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G),$$
equivalently $H_n(C_\bullet(X;G))$ in the notation of
[[def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex]]. When the coefficient group is
$\mathbb Z$, write simply $C_n(X)$ and $H_n(X)$ when no confusion can arise.

For a space $X$ and an abelian group $G$, a degree-$n$ **singular cocycle** is a cochain in $Z^n(X;G)=\ker\delta^n$ and a degree-$n$ **singular coboundary** belongs to $B^n(X;G)=\operatorname{im}\delta^{n-1}$, for the positive coboundary convention of [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]]. The square-zero lemma [[lem-the-singular-coboundary-squares-to-zero]] implies $B^n\subseteq Z^n$: if $\varphi=\delta^{n-1}\psi$, then $\delta^n\varphi=0$.

The **singular cohomology group with coefficients in $G$** is
$$H^n(X;G)=Z^n(X;G)/B^n(X;G)\quad(n\ge0),\qquad H^n(X;G)=0\quad(n<0).$$
This is the abelian quotient with addition $[\varphi]+[\psi]=[\varphi+\psi]$: changing either representative by a coboundary changes the sum by a coboundary. Thus two cocycles represent the same class exactly when their difference is $\delta^{n-1}\eta$ for some degree-$(n-1)$ cochain $\eta$. In degree zero, $B^0=0$ because $C^{-1}=0$; hence $H^0=\ker\delta^0$. The zero convention in negative degrees agrees with the same kernel/image construction on the zero cochain groups.

If coefficients are a module over a commutative ring, the same groups and maps are modules and linear maps, and this is their module quotient. Empty $X$ or zero coefficients give zero cohomology in every degree. The notation does not define cohomology as the dual of homology; such identifications require their own theorems. No choice of cocycle representatives and no AC is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: Put $M=\overline\Omega$. It is compact by boundedness and closedness. Near each boundary point a Lipschitz graph chart $x_3=\phi(x')$ straightens $M$ by the explicit homeomorphism $(x',x_3)\mapsto(x',x_3-\phi(x'))$ to a closed halfspace neighborhood. Interior points use Euclidean balls. These charts show that $M$ is a Hausdorff second-countable three-manifold with topological boundary exactly $\partial\Omega$ and interior exactly $\Omega$. Its orientation is the standard Euclidean orientation on its interior; this is precisely the orientation convention for manifolds with boundary in [F2]. By [F1], $\Omega\hookrightarrow M$ is a homotopy equivalence. Contractibility of $\Omega$, [F3], and factorization through a point give $H^2(M;\mathbb R)=0$: the point has one singular simplex in each degree, and its real cochain differentials are successively zero and identity, so its positive cohomology is zero. Also $M$ is path connected: its interior is path connected by contractibility, and a half-chart path joins any boundary point to its interior. The augmentation identifies $H_0(M;\mathbb R)$ with $\mathbb R$, because any difference of points is the boundary of a path and every zero-chain of coefficient sum zero is a finite linear combination of such differences. The boundary is nonempty: a ray from any interior point eventually leaves the bounded set and its first exit point is a boundary point.

By [F2], $H_1(M,\partial M;\mathbb R)=0$. The exact sequence in [F3] then makes $H_0(\partial M;\mathbb R)\to H_0(M;\mathbb R)$ injective. The boundary is a two-manifold by the graph charts, hence locally path connected, so its connected components are path components. If there were two, choose one point in each. Their difference is nonzero in $H_0(\partial M;\mathbb R)$: the sum of coefficients on the first path component defines a linear functional on zero-chains which kills every one-simplex boundary, yet sends this difference to one. Its image in $H_0(M;\mathbb R)$ is zero since the two points are joined by a path in $M$, contradicting injectivity. Therefore the nonempty boundary is connected. No finite-element incidence matrix is used to infer this continuum topological claim.
