citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then

$$\|\tau_h f-f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(h \to 0).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used through the cited Countable-Choice and
Dependent-Choice interfaces (completed-product Fubini, approximate identities,
the fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions), for
the countable selections of cutoffs and mollifier scales below, and through the
earlier ACL reconstruction lemma. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be
open, $n\ge1$, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
For an almost-everywhere class $u$ on $\Omega$ the following are equivalent:

1. $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$;
2. $u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $u$ has one measurable ACL representative
   $u^*$ whose classical coordinate derivatives $\partial_i u^*$ exist almost
   everywhere, are measurable, and belong to $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

In that case $\partial_i u^*$ is a representative of $D_i u$ for every
$i$, that is, $D_i u=\partial_i u^*$ almost everywhere.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, there is only the zero class, its representative
$u^*=0$ is ACL, and every displayed assertion holds vacuously.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ be nonnegative with
$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$.
For $\varepsilon>0$ put $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$
and
$$\Omega_\varepsilon=\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)>\varepsilon\},\qquad\Omega_\varepsilon=\mathbb R^n\ \text{when }\Omega=\mathbb R^n .$$
Then $\rho_\varepsilon*u$ is defined and smooth on $\Omega_\varepsilon$, and
for every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le k$,
$$D^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*u)=\rho_\varepsilon*(D^\alpha u)\qquad\text{on }\Omega_\varepsilon,$$
as pointwise smooth functions for the constructed representatives and as
almost-everywhere classes. Here $D^\alpha u$ is extended by zero off $\Omega$
in the convolution.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, bounded and convex. If $u\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, then $u$ has a representative $u^{*}$ with
$$|u^{*}(x)-u^{*}(y)|\le\|Du\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\,|x-y|\qquad(x,y\in\Omega),$$
and $u^{*}=u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$. Conversely, every Lipschitz function $f:\Omega\to\mathbb K$ with constant $L$ lies in $W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)$ and $\|Df\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le L$ for real scalars, while $\|Df\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le\sqrt2 L$ for complex scalars. In both cases the real-linear derivative has operator norm at most $L$ almost everywhere.

**Gradient convention.** For a weak gradient $Dv=(D_1v,\ldots,D_nv)$ we write $|Dv|=(\sum_{i=1}^n|D_iv|^2)^{1/2}$ for its Euclidean norm and $\|Dv\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}:=\||Dv|\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ for the essential supremum of that norm, as in [[lem-pointwise-potential-bound-for-compactly-supported-smooth-functions]]. For real scalars this norm equals the derivative operator norm. For complex scalars it is the Frobenius norm of the real-linear map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^2$ and can exceed its operator norm: $f(x)=x_1+ix_2$ is $1$-Lipschitz but $|Df|=\sqrt2$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ both assertions hold vacuously.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used for the published ACL characterisation
and the Countable-Choice interfaces cited in the proof. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and let $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be
Lipschitz with constant $L\ge0$. Put
$$D_F:=\{\,t\in\mathbb R : F \text{ is differentiable at } t\,\},\qquad N_F:=\mathbb R\setminus D_F .$$

1. **Membership.** $F\circ u\in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and
   $F\circ u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ if and only if $F(u)\in L^p(\Omega)$.
   This holds automatically if $F(0)=0$, and also if $p<\infty$ and
   $\lambda_n(\Omega)<\infty$.
2. **Level-set clause.** $N_F$ has Lebesgue measure zero, and for every
   Lebesgue-null set $N\subseteq\mathbb R$ (no measurability of $N$ is
   assumed), every measurable representative $\hat u$ of $u$ and every
   measurable representative $\hat v_i$ of $D_iu$ satisfy: the set
   $Z_{i,N}:=\{x\in\Omega : \hat v_i(x)\neq0$ and $\hat u(x)\in N\}$ has
   Lebesgue outer measure zero. In particular $D_iu=0$ almost everywhere
   on the part of $\Omega$ where $u$ takes values in $N_F$.
3. **Chain rule with the level-set convention.** Let $\hat u$ and
   $\hat v_i$ be measurable representatives of $u$ and $D_iu$. Define
   $$\Phi_i(x):=\begin{cases}F'(\hat u(x))\,\hat v_i(x),&\hat u(x)\in D_F,\\ 0,&\hat u(x)\in N_F.\end{cases}$$
   Then $\Phi_i$ agrees almost everywhere with a measurable function,
   determines an element of $L^p(\Omega)$, and is a representative of the
   weak derivative:
   $$D_i(F\circ u)=\Phi_i\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n .$$
   That is, the classical product $F'(u)\,D_iu$ is used where $F$ is
   differentiable at $u$, and on the remaining preimage the product is
   taken as zero. Moreover, for every Borel function
   $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $g=F'$ almost everywhere, the class of
   $g(u)D_iu$ is the same, and $D_i(F\circ u)=g(u)D_iu$ almost
   everywhere.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$ every assertion is vacuous. The constant case
$L=0$, the endpoint exponents $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ and the case $n=1$ are
included. No assertion is made about the pointwise derivative of an
arbitrary representative of $u$, and none about a pointwise derivative of
$F$ at a point where $F$ fails to be differentiable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $1\le p<\infty$, and let $u,v\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\cap L^\infty(\Omega)$. Then $uv\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ and $D_j(uv)=(D_ju)v+u(D_jv)$ a.e. for every $j$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes

otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y

u$ for $x

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ is the completion of the product measure
$\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], is a complete normed space over
$\mathbb K$.

Both endpoints $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, as is $k=0$, where the
assertion reduces to the completeness of $L^p$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the zero space and the assertion is trivial.
The Axiom of Choice is used only to derive Countable Choice for the two
published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative
selection inside the finitely many coordinate classes is finite and
choice-free.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

derivations.claim: Localize $F$ by a finite smooth partition subordinate to an interior set and boundary graph charts. Rotate a chart so that $\Omega$ is $x_3>\phi(x')$. Its localized whole-space $H^1$ function is zero below this graph and has support away from the chart sides. Translate that localized function upward by $t e_3$. Its support now lies at least $t/\sqrt{1+L^2}$ from the graph, because $\phi$ is $L$-Lipschitz. Mollification with radius less than $t/(2(1+L))$ produces a smooth function compactly supported in $\Omega$. Translation and then sufficiently fine mollification converge in whole-space $H^1$ by [F1]. The localized interior term is mollified directly. Summing the finite approximations proves $F|_\Omega\in H_0^1$. Conversely a sequence of compactly supported smooth approximants in the closure definition has zero extensions Cauchy in $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$, with exactly the original norm differences. The limit is the zero extension of its $L^2$ limit and proves the converse. Lipschitz boundaries have three-dimensional measure zero, since every graph has zero vertical section measure, so support in $\overline\Omega$ causes no additional $L^2$ term.

For clause 2 localize $f$ in a graph chart and write its vertical height as $s=x_3-\phi(x')>0$. The continuous boundary value is zero. For almost every $x'$, [F2] and continuity at the boundary give $|f(x',\phi(x')+s)|^2\le s\int_0^s|\partial_3f(x',\phi(x')+r)|^2\,dr.$ To justify the endpoint, first integrate the ACL identity between $\varepsilon$ and $s$, then let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$; the $L^2$ derivative is integrable along almost every finite vertical segment, and continuity gives the endpoint limit. Choose a fixed smooth scalar $\eta$ that is zero on $(-\infty,1]$ and one on $[2,\infty)$, and multiply by $\eta(s/t)$. The construction, Sobolev chain rule and bounded-Sobolev product rule in [F3]–[F4] justify this nonsmooth-in-space factor and bound its weak gradient by $C(1+L)/t$. The norm of its extra gradient term is bounded by $C\|\nabla f\|_{L^2(0<s<2t)}$, using the displayed inequality and integration in $s,x'$, and hence tends to zero. The removed function and gradient terms also tend to zero by absolute continuity of their integrals. These cutoffs lie away from the boundary and can be mollified inside $\Omega$; compact chart supports handle their other sides. Sum the finite local approximations and the interior term. Thus $f$ is in the asserted closure.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The covariant affine Piola map for $N_h^1$ and contravariant affine Piola map for $N_h^2$ use the orientation-preserving cell maps and conventions of [[def-covariant-contravariant-piola-maps-and-hdiv-hcurl]]. Their differential and moment identities are those of [[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]]. The edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom are respectively the oriented edge circulation, oriented face-normal flux, and cell integral.

In the two conformity conditions above, each cellwise polynomial restriction has a unique polynomial representative on its closed cell, and those representatives define the displayed edge and face integrals. Thus the global edge and face moments are part of the assembled-space definition; their correspondence with all cochains is proved by the local unisolvence and commuting-moment items, not inferred from rough-field traces.

On an oriented tetrahedron $K$ with vertices $x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3$, let $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$ for $0\le i<j\le3$. Then the six edge circulations $\ell_{rs}(v)=\int_{[x_r,x_s]}v\cdot t_{rs}\,ds$ satisfy $\ell_{rs}(\phi_{ij})=\delta_{(r,s),(i,j)}$. The six functions form a basis of the local space $\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:i<j\}=\{a+b\times x:a,b\in\mathbb R^3\}$, so these edge circulations are unisolvent degrees of freedom.

For $k\ge1$ and a smooth $(k-1)$-form $\eta$ on a neighbourhood of $\Delta^k$ in its affine span,
$$\int_{\Delta^k}d\eta=\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^i\int_{\Delta^{k-1}}\delta_i^*\eta,$$
where the integrals and ordered face maps use the standard affine-simplex conventions. No Stokes theorem for manifolds with corners is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

Orient every top-dimensional cell of a matching simplicial mesh by the
ambient orientation of $\mathbb R^d$, and orient each facet by the induced
boundary convention of [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. In the sum
of the oriented boundaries of all top-dimensional cells, every interior
facet occurs twice with opposite signs; every boundary facet occurs once.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d=2$ or $3$ and let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ map a reference
simplex to an affine cell with $\det A>0$. The contravariant Piola map
$\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{div}}\widehat v=(\det A)^{-1}A\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$
maps $H(\operatorname{div},\widehat S_d)$ into $H(\operatorname{div},K)$ and
$$\operatorname{div}(\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{div}}\widehat v) =(\det A)^{-1}(\widehat{\operatorname{div}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}.$$
The covariant Piola map
$\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{curl}}\widehat v=A^{-T}\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$
maps $H(\operatorname{curl},\widehat S_d)$ into $H(\operatorname{curl},K)$;
in $d=2$ its scalar curl is
$(\det A)^{-1}(\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}$,
and in $d=3$ its vector curl is
$(\det A)^{-1}A(\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}$.
For every $\widehat u\in W^{1,2}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)$, the scalar
pullback $u=\widehat u\circ F^{-1}$ belongs to $W^{1,2}(K;\mathbb R)$ and
its gradient satisfies
$$\nabla u=\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{curl}}(\widehat\nabla\widehat u).$$
For smooth fields, contravariant normal fluxes satisfy
$v\cdot n\,dS=\widehat v\cdot\widehat n\,d\widehat S$; covariant tangential
pullbacks satisfy $v(F(\widehat x))\cdot A\widehat\tau=
\widehat v(\widehat x)\cdot\widehat\tau$ for every reference tangent
$\widehat\tau$. Thus edge line integrals and normal-flux moments are
preserved, and face tangential moments transform with this pullback and
the induced facet surface Jacobian. These formulas record the chosen
orientation; reversing a facet orientation reverses its signed moment.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

derivations.claim: For each cell $K$, define $I_K^0f$ by its four vertex values, $I_K^1u$ by its six edge circulations, $I_K^2v$ by its four face-normal fluxes, and $I_K^3g$ by its cell integral. The vertex basis $\lambda_i$ is dual to vertex evaluation. By [F1], the local edge-moment map is bijective, so any six prescribed edge values determine one local field; in particular they define $I_K^1u$. For $RT_0(K)$, the face flux map is injective: if all four fluxes of $q(x)=a+cx$ vanish, [F3] gives $3c|K|=\int_K\operatorname{div}q=0$, so $c=0$; then $a\cdot n_F=0$ for all four face normals. Three reference-tetrahedron face area vectors are linearly independent, and the invertible cofactor map in [F5] preserves this independence on $K$, so $a=0$. Since $RT_0(K)$ has dimension four, the four moments are bijective and any four prescribed values determine one field, defining $I_K^2v$. A constant is determined by its cell integral, so $I_K^3g$ is also unique.

On a shared triangular face, the tangential trace of a local Nedelec field is a linear combination of the three Whitney edge traces on that face: a basis function from an edge containing the opposite vertex has zero tangential trace because the gradient of the opposite barycentric coordinate is normal to the face. The three face-edge circulations are unisolvent by the same endpoint calculation as [F1]. A global assignment gives the same oriented circulation from either incident tetrahedron, so the two tangential traces agree. Cellwise curl integration by parts, using [F3] on $u\times\varphi$ for a compactly supported smooth test $\varphi$, then cancels all interior face terms by [F4]; boundary terms vanish because $\varphi$ is compactly supported. Hence the assembled edge field has a distributional curl equal to its piecewise polynomial curl in $L^2$ and lies in the global $H(\operatorname{curl})$ space.

The identity $\sum_{j
e i}\phi_{ij}=-
abla\lambda_i$ (where $\phi_{ji}:=-\phi_{ij}$) follows from $\sum_j\lambda_j=1$ and $\sum_j
abla\lambda_j=0$; hence $
abla I_K^0f\in N_0(K)$. On an oriented edge $e=[x_i,x_j]$, [F6] gives $\int_e
abla I_K^0f\cdot t_e\,ds=I_K^0f(x_j)-I_K^0f(x_i)=f(x_j)-f(x_i)=\int_e
abla f\cdot t_e\,ds$. The two fields lie in the local Nedelec space, and [F1] makes the edge moments unisolvent, so $
abla I_K^0f=I_K^1
abla f$ on every cell.

Each $\operatorname{curl}\phi_{ij}=2\nabla\lambda_i\times\nabla\lambda_j$ is constant, so $\operatorname{curl}I_K^1u\in RT_0(K)$. For every oriented face $F$, Stokes [F2] gives $\int_F\operatorname{curl}(I_K^1u)\cdot n_F\,dS=\sum_{e\subset\partial F}\operatorname{sgn}(e,F)\int_e I_K^1u\cdot t_e\,ds=\int_F\operatorname{curl}u\cdot n_F\,dS$. The first equality uses the affine moment convention [F5]; the second uses the defining edge moments. Both curls are in $RT_0(K)$ and the four face moments are unisolvent by step 1.1, so $\operatorname{curl}I_K^1u=I_K^2\operatorname{curl}u$.

On a tetrahedron $K$, Gauss–Green [F3] gives $\int_K\operatorname{div}(I_K^2v)\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\operatorname{sgn}(F,K)\int_F I_K^2v\cdot n_F\,dS=\int_K\operatorname{div}v\,dx$. Since $\operatorname{div}(a+cx)=3c$ is constant, equality of these cell integrals proves $\operatorname{div}I_K^2v=I_K^3\operatorname{div}v$ on $K$. More generally, every local RT0 normal trace is constant on a planar face because $x\cdot n_F$ is constant there; a shared oriented face moment therefore determines the same physical normal component from both cells. Summing cellwise Gauss–Green against a compact test function cancels interior terms by [F4], while boundary terms vanish, so the assembled face field has distributional divergence equal to its piecewise constant divergence in $L^2$.

For any discrete $q_h\in W_h^0$, $u_h\in N_h^1$, or $v_h\in N_h^2$, its restriction to each cell is a polynomial and extends smoothly to a neighborhood of that cell. Apply the local identities in steps 1.3, 2.1 and 2.2 to these restrictions. The local interpolant is the identity on the corresponding finite-element input by the local moment unisolvence and construction in step 1.1, so the identities show $\nabla q_h|_K$, $\operatorname{curl}u_h|_K$, and $\operatorname{div}v_h|_K$ lie in their next local spaces. The edge moments of $\nabla q_h$ are endpoint differences of shared vertex values by step 1.3. The face fluxes of $\operatorname{curl}u_h$ are signed sums of the shared global edge values by step 2.1, so adjacent cells assign the same oriented flux to every shared face. The divergence target $N_h^3$ has only cellwise constant data and imposes no cross-cell matching. The assemblies in steps 1.2 and 2.2 give the required H(curl) and H(div) membership. Hence all three discrete differentials map between the stated global spaces, proving the subcomplex assertion.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for the graph-space uniqueness and $L^2$ conventions of [[def-na-hcurl-space]]. Let $V_h=N_h^1$ be the lowest-order edge space on a finite tetrahedral mesh, as in [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. It is finite dimensional: restriction to the finitely many cells injects it into the finite product of the local spaces, each spanned by at most six Whitney edge fields. Injectivity holds because the cells cover $\Omega$ up to their measure-zero facets. Use the componentwise real $L^2$ inner product defined in [[def-na-hcurl-space]]. Define its curl kernel and the $L^2$ gauge space by
$$K_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{curl}v_h=0\},\qquad Z_h:=V_h\cap K_h^\perp.$$
The quotient $\dot V_h:=V_h/K_h$ has norm $\|[v_h]\|_{\operatorname{curl}}:=\|\operatorname{curl}v_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$; this is well-defined and positive definite because two representatives differ by an element of $K_h$. The bilinear form induced by curl-curl is $a_h([u_h],[v_h])=(\operatorname{curl}u_h,\operatorname{curl}v_h)_{L^2}$. A representative of a quotient solution is fixed by the gauge condition $u_h\in Z_h$. The mixed gauge system uses a multiplier $p_h\in K_h$:
$$a_h(u_h,v_h)+(p_h,v_h)_{L^2}=f(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h),\qquad (u_h,q_h)_{L^2}=0\quad(q_h\in K_h).$$
The quotient energy norm, rather than the full $H(\operatorname{curl})$ norm, is the norm controlled by this definition.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space, with the inner product linear in its first argument. For every linear functional $f:V\to\mathbb F$, there is a unique $w\in V$ such that

$$f(v)=\langle v,w\rangle\qquad\text{for every }v\in V.$$

The map $w\mapsto(v\mapsto\langle v,w\rangle)$ is a conjugate-linear bijection from $V$ to its algebraic dual. This includes $V=0$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This is the full algebraic dual: no topology, norm, or continuity condition is imposed.

derivations.claim: On $Z_h$, the bilinear form $a_h(u,v)=(\operatorname{curl}u,\operatorname{curl}v)_{L^2}$ is an inner product: if $a_h(u,u)=0$, then $u\in K_h$ and $u\in K_h^\perp$, hence $u=0$. The finite-dimensional Riesz theorem [F3] applied to $f|_{Z_h}$ gives a unique $u_h\in Z_h$ with $a_h(u_h,z_h)=f(z_h)$ for every $z_h\in Z_h$. Applying [F3] to the $L^2$ inner product on the finite-dimensional $K_h$ gives a unique $p_h\in K_h$ with $(p_h,q_h)_{L^2}=f(q_h)$ for all $q_h\in K_h$. The zero subspace cases are included in [F3].

Restrict the $L^2$ inner product to the finite-dimensional space $V_h$. Its orthogonal complement of $K_h$ is $V_h\cap K_h^\perp=Z_h$ by [F1], so [F2] gives $V_h=Z_h\oplus K_h$. Thus each $v_h$ has a unique orthogonal decomposition $v_h=z_h+q_h$. Since $\operatorname{curl}q_h=0$ and $(p_h,z_h)=0$, the two identities of step 1.1 give $a_h(u_h,v_h)+(p_h,v_h)=f(z_h)+f(q_h)=f(v_h)$. Also $u_h\in Z_h$ gives the gauge equation. Any solution must restrict to the unique Riesz problems on $Z_h$ and $K_h$, proving uniqueness.

For any real inner product $c(\cdot,\cdot)$ and any nonzero $w$, positivity of $c(v-tw,v-tw)$ at $t=c(v,w)/c(w,w)$ gives $|c(v,w)|^2\le c(v,v)c(w,w)$; if $w=0$ the inequality is immediate. Thus the norm of the functional $z\mapsto c(u,z)$ is at most $\|u\|_c$, and when $u\ne0$ equality is attained at $z=u$; when $u=0$ both sides vanish. Applying this argument to $a_h$ and the $L^2$ product, together with the Riesz identities of step 1.1, proves both exact dual-norm identities. For the constraint, if $q_h\ne0$ choose $v_h=q_h$; then $\operatorname{curl}q_h=0$, $\|v_h\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}=\|q_h\|_2$, and $b(v_h,q_h)=\|q_h\|_2^2$, so the inf-sup constant is at least one. For the upper bound, the same positive-square argument with the $L^2$ inner product gives $|b(v_h,q_h)|\le\|v_h\|_2\|q_h\|_2\le\|v_h\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}\|q_h\|_2$. On $Z_h$, $a_h(v_h,v_h)=\|[v_h]\|_{\operatorname{curl}}^2$, which gives coercivity constant one in the declared quotient norm.

Assume AC. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary.

1. An $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ class $F$ that vanishes almost everywhere outside $\overline\Omega$ restricts to $H_0^1(\Omega)$, and every $H_0^1(\Omega)$ class has an $H^1$ zero extension.
2. If $f\in H^1(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ and $f=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, then $f\in H_0^1(\Omega)$.
3. The zero extension $U$ of $u\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ belongs to $H(\operatorname{curl};\mathbb R^3)$, with $\operatorname{curl}U$ equal to the zero extension of $\operatorname{curl}u$; both component norms are preserved. Also $\nabla H_0^1(\Omega)\subset H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and its elements have zero curl.

All statements apply componentwise to vector fields where appropriate.

Assume AC. Let $U\in H(\operatorname{curl};\mathbb R^3)$ be real and supported in a fixed bounded measurable set $A$ of finite measure. There are real fields $w\in H^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $p\in H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ depending linearly on $U$ such that $U=w+\nabla p$, $\operatorname{div}w=0$, $\operatorname{curl}w=\operatorname{curl}U$, and
$$\|w\|_2\le\|U\|_2,\qquad \|\nabla w\|_2=\|\operatorname{curl}U\|_2,\qquad \|p\|_{H^1}\le C_A\|U\|_2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set whose boundary is locally a Lipschitz graph, with $D$ on one side in each chart. It need not be connected. There is one linear operator $E:H^1(D)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $Ef=f$ almost everywhere on $D$, which maps $H^2(D)$ boundedly into $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Its support can be confined to a fixed bounded neighborhood of $\overline D$. The bounds depend only on a finite choice of boundary charts and cutoffs. In particular no mesh enters them.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for weak-derivative uniqueness and the real $L^2$ product below, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open. Here $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is the set of triples of real scalar $L^2$ classes from [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Define
$$ (u,v)_{L^2(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=1}^3\int_\Omega u_jv_j\,dx,\qquad \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$
Each scalar pairing is well-defined and induces its quotient norm by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]; the finite sum is therefore a real inner product on the triple space with the displayed norm. A test field $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ means a triple of real-valued members of the test-function space $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. Writing $\varphi=(\varphi_x,\varphi_y,\varphi_z)$, its classical curl is the coordinate expression of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
$$\operatorname{curl}\varphi=(\partial_y\varphi_z-\partial_z\varphi_y,\partial_z\varphi_x-\partial_x\varphi_z,\partial_x\varphi_y-\partial_y\varphi_x).$$
For $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the triple of scalar distributions whose action on a vector test field is the sum of the three component pairings, determined by
$$\langle \operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,dx,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$
The integral is finite because $u$ and the smooth compactly supported field $\operatorname{curl}\varphi$ are componentwise in $L^2$ and scalar Cauchy–Schwarz applies. On tests supported in a fixed compact $K\Subset\Omega$, the same estimate gives $|\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle|\le C_{u,K}\max_{|\alpha|\le1}\sup_K|D^\alpha\varphi|$ with a finite $C_{u,K}$. This proves continuity on each fixed-support test space; the LF universal property of [[lem-test-function-lf-topology-universal-property]], for the test topology of [[def-test-function-topology]], makes the pairing a vector distribution on $\Omega$.
If this vector distribution is represented by an $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ class, that class is unique almost everywhere componentwise by the injection of locally integrable functions into scalar distributions in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], under the stated Countable Choice assumption.
Define
$$H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\text{ is represented by an element of }L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)\}$$
with graph norm $\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. No boundary condition is imposed by this definition. Fields are real-valued; equality is equality of almost-everywhere classes.

Assume Countable Choice for the published Sobolev interfaces cited below. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and use real scalars. $L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$ means the $d$-tuple of real $L^2$ equivalence classes, with norm $\|v\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^d\|v_j\|_2^2$. The test space $C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$ consists of real smooth functions compactly supported in $D$.

For $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$, say that $g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)$ is its distributional divergence when
$$
\int_D v\cdot\nabla\phi\,dx=-\int_D g\phi\,dx\qquad\text{for every }\phi\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R).
$$
The $L^2$ class $g$ is unique when it exists. Indeed, if $g_1,g_2$ both satisfy the identity, put $h=g_1-g_2\in L^2(D)$. Every compact $C\subset D$ has finite Lebesgue measure by [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $\int_C|h|\le |C|^{1/2}\|h\|_{L^2(D)}<\infty$. Thus $h\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. Subtracting the two divergence identities gives $\int_Dh\phi=0$ for every real test $\phi$; splitting a complex test into real and imaginary parts gives the same identity for complex tests. Injectivity of the regular-distribution map in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]] therefore yields $h=0$ almost everywhere, hence $g_1=g_2$ as $L^2$ classes. Define
$$
H(\operatorname{div};D):=\{v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d):\text{there is }g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)\text{ with }g=\operatorname{div}v\text{ distributionally}\},
$$
and equip it with the graph norm
$$
\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div};D)}:=\bigl(\|v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}.
$$
The Sobolev notation $H^1(D)=W^{1,2}(D)$ and $H^1_0(D)=W^{1,2}_0(D)$ uses the norm and zero-boundary closure conventions of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. No pointwise boundary value is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The covariant affine Piola map for $N_h^1$ and contravariant affine Piola map for $N_h^2$ use the orientation-preserving cell maps and conventions of [[def-covariant-contravariant-piola-maps-and-hdiv-hcurl]]. Their differential and moment identities are those of [[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]]. The edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom are respectively the oriented edge circulation, oriented face-normal flux, and cell integral.

In the two conformity conditions above, each cellwise polynomial restriction has a unique polynomial representative on its closed cell, and those representatives define the displayed edge and face integrals. Thus the global edge and face moments are part of the assembled-space definition; their correspondence with all cochains is proved by the local unisolvence and commuting-moment items, not inferred from rough-field traces.

On an oriented tetrahedron $K$ with vertices $x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3$, let $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$ for $0\le i<j\le3$. Then the six edge circulations $\ell_{rs}(v)=\int_{[x_r,x_s]}v\cdot t_{rs}\,ds$ satisfy $\ell_{rs}(\phi_{ij})=\delta_{(r,s),(i,j)}$. The six functions form a basis of the local space $\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:i<j\}=\{a+b\times x:a,b\in\mathbb R^3\}$, so these edge circulations are unisolvent degrees of freedom.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh. The four face-normal fluxes are unisolvent on each $RT_0(K)$, and matching face fluxes assemble a global $H(\operatorname{div})$ field. For smooth scalar $f$, smooth vector fields $u,v$, and the canonical interpolants determined by vertex values, oriented edge circulations, oriented face-normal fluxes, and cell integrals, the interpolation maps satisfy cellwise
$$
abla I_h^0f=I_h^1
abla f,\qquad \operatorname{curl}I_h^1u=I_h^2\operatorname{curl}u,\qquad \operatorname{div}I_h^2v=I_h^3\operatorname{div}v.$$
Any assignment of one real oriented value to each global mesh edge determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^1$; any assignment of one real oriented flux to each global mesh face determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^2$. These assemblies belong to $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$, respectively, with the global spaces and conventions of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Applying the local moment identities to polynomial cell restrictions also proves that the global finite-element spaces form the subcomplex $W_h^0\xrightarrow{
abla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$. The canonical interpolation identities themselves apply to smooth inputs; they do not extend the canonical edge moments to arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ inputs.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a matching simplicial mesh as in
[[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Set $C_{-1}(\mathcal T;\mathbb Z)=0$.
For $0\le k\le d$, let
$C_k(\mathcal T;\mathbb Z)$ be the free abelian group generated by ordered
$k$-faces $[v_0,\ldots,v_k]$, with the orientation relation
$$[v_{\pi(0)},\ldots,v_{\pi(k)}]=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)[v_0,\ldots,v_k]$$
for every permutation $\pi$. Define $\partial_0:C_0\to C_{-1}$ to be the
zero map. For $1\le k\le d$, define the **simplicial boundary**
homomorphism $\partial_k:C_k\to C_{k-1}$ on a generator by
$$\partial_k[v_0,\ldots,v_k]:=\sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^j [v_0,\ldots,\widehat v_j,\ldots,v_k].$$
This is the oriented incidence convention; no geometric
integration is part of the definition. The identity
$\partial_{k-1}\partial_k=0$ is proved directly from this alternating
formula in the following lemma.

For every simplicial complex $K$ and abelian group $G$, there is a canonical
natural isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{simp}}(K;G)\cong H_n(|K|;G)$ for all $n$.
When the vertex set has a supplied total order, it is induced by the
simplicial-to-singular chain map of [[def-simplicial-to-singular-chain-map]],
extended $G$-linearly. Different supplied orders induce the same homology map.
For an arbitrary vertex set, the isomorphism is defined compatibly on its
finite subcomplexes and requires no choice principle.

If $X$ is a nonempty contractible topological space, then for every $n\geq 0$
and every abelian group $G$,
$$H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\cong H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(\ast;G),$$
where $\ast$ denotes a one-point space.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous. The map $f$ is **nullhomotopic** if there is a point $y_0\in Y$ such that $f$ is homotopic to the constant map $c_{y_0}:X\to Y$, $c_{y_0}(x)=y_0$ ([[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]]).

A nonempty topological space $X$ is **contractible** if every continuous map $f:X\to Y$ to every topological space $Y$ is nullhomotopic.

This definition separates the property of the space from the particular map $\operatorname{id}_X$. The next corollary proves that it is equivalent to the familiar condition that the identity map be nullhomotopic.

For every $1\le k\le d$, the boundary maps of
[[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]] satisfy
$$\partial_{k-1}\circ\partial_k=0.$$

Assume Countable Choice for weak-derivative uniqueness and the real $L^2$ product below, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open. Here $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is the set of triples of real scalar $L^2$ classes from [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Define
$$ (u,v)_{L^2(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=1}^3\int_\Omega u_jv_j\,dx,\qquad \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$
Each scalar pairing is well-defined and induces its quotient norm by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]; the finite sum is therefore a real inner product on the triple space with the displayed norm. A test field $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ means a triple of real-valued members of the test-function space $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. Writing $\varphi=(\varphi_x,\varphi_y,\varphi_z)$, its classical curl is the coordinate expression of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
$$\operatorname{curl}\varphi=(\partial_y\varphi_z-\partial_z\varphi_y,\partial_z\varphi_x-\partial_x\varphi_z,\partial_x\varphi_y-\partial_y\varphi_x).$$
For $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the triple of scalar distributions whose action on a vector test field is the sum of the three component pairings, determined by
$$\langle \operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,dx,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$
The integral is finite because $u$ and the smooth compactly supported field $\operatorname{curl}\varphi$ are componentwise in $L^2$ and scalar Cauchy–Schwarz applies. On tests supported in a fixed compact $K\Subset\Omega$, the same estimate gives $|\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle|\le C_{u,K}\max_{|\alpha|\le1}\sup_K|D^\alpha\varphi|$ with a finite $C_{u,K}$. This proves continuity on each fixed-support test space; the LF universal property of [[lem-test-function-lf-topology-universal-property]], for the test topology of [[def-test-function-topology]], makes the pairing a vector distribution on $\Omega$.
If this vector distribution is represented by an $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ class, that class is unique almost everywhere componentwise by the injection of locally integrable functions into scalar distributions in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], under the stated Countable Choice assumption.
Define
$$H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\text{ is represented by an element of }L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)\}$$
with graph norm $\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. No boundary condition is imposed by this definition. Fields are real-valued; equality is equality of almost-everywhere classes.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

Let $X$ be a topological space. For each integer $n\geq 0$, a
**singular $n$-simplex in $X$** is a continuous map
$$\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$$
from the standard topological simplex of
[[def-standard-topological-simplex-and-its-affine-face-maps]]. Write
$S_n(X)$ for the set of all singular $n$-simplices in $X$.

The **singular chain group with integer coefficients** is the free abelian group
on $S_n(X)$:
$$C_n(X;\mathbb Z):=\bigoplus_{\sigma\in S_n(X)}\mathbb Z[\sigma].$$
Thus an element of $C_n(X;\mathbb Z)$ is a finite formal sum
$$\sum_{k=1}^m a_k\sigma_k,\qquad a_k\in\mathbb Z,\ \sigma_k\in S_n(X).$$

If $G$ is an abelian group, the **singular chain group with coefficients in
$G$** is
$$C_n(X;G):=C_n(X;\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z} G,$$
using the tensor product of
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]. The page's
convention is that coefficients are attached through this tensor-product
construction, not by choosing a preferred $G$-basis of singular simplices.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

derivations.claim: If $\mathcal T=\varnothing$, [F12] gives $\Omega=\varnothing$; by [F1] and [F4] all real chain, cochain, and finite-element spaces are zero, and [F11] gives $H_k(\varnothing;\mathbb R)=0$. All cohomology and harmonic statements then reduce to the unique maps and decompositions of zero spaces, and the nonempty contractible branch is inapplicable. Suppose henceforth that $\mathcal T\ne\varnothing$. In degree zero, the vertex basis $\lambda_i$ is dual to vertex evaluation; a value at each vertex determines a unique affine function on each incident tetrahedron, and common-face traces agree because they agree at the face vertices. Thus $J^0:W_h^0\to C^0$ is a bijection. In degree one, [F2] makes the six local edge moments a bijection between each local Nedelec space and its six edge values. The definition of $N_h^1$ imposes one value for each globally oriented edge. Any global assignment therefore determines the unique local fields on each cell, and [F3] makes their assembly a global H(curl) field; conversely, zero global moments force every cell restriction to vanish by [F2]. Thus $J^1:N_h^1\to C^1$ is a bijection.

In degree two, the four oriented face fluxes determine each local $RT_0$ field by [F3]. The definition of $N_h^2$ imposes one value for every global oriented face; these values determine unique local fields and [F3] assembles them into a global H(div) field. Zero global fluxes force every local field to vanish, so $J^2:N_h^2\to C^2$ is a bijection. In degree three, a constant is determined by its cell integral, so $J^3:N_h^3\to C^3$ is a bijection.

The dual differential $\delta^k$ evaluates a cochain on the oriented boundary of each $(k+1)$-simplex. For $k=0$, its value on an oriented edge is the terminal nodal value minus the initial value; for $k=1$, its value on a face is the signed sum of its boundary-edge circulations; and for $k=2$, its value on a tetrahedron is the signed sum of its boundary-face fluxes. By [F3] these are exactly the degrees of freedom of $\nabla$, $\operatorname{curl}$, and $\operatorname{div}$. Thus $J^{k+1}d_h=\delta^kJ^k$ for each differential. By [F8], $\delta^{k+1}\delta^k=0$, so these maps are cochain complexes and the bijections induce isomorphisms on cohomology.

Write $Z_k=\ker\partial_k$ and $B_k=\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}$; [F8] gives $B_k\subseteq Z_k$. Identify each cochain with its coordinate functional on the oriented simplex basis. Then $\ker\delta^k$ consists exactly of functionals vanishing on $B_k$, namely $B_k^\perp$. The image of $\delta^{k-1}=\partial_k^*$ lies in $Z_k^\perp$, since $(\partial_k^*\ell)(z)=\ell(\partial_kz)=0$ for $z\in Z_k$. These two subspaces have the same dimension: $\dim\operatorname{im}\partial_k^*=\operatorname{rank}\partial_k=\dim C_k-\dim Z_k=\dim Z_k^\perp$, so $\operatorname{im}\partial_k^*=Z_k^\perp$. Restricting a functional in $B_k^\perp$ to $Z_k$ therefore descends to $Z_k/B_k$ and has kernel $Z_k^\perp$. Every functional on $Z_k/B_k$ pulls back to a functional on $Z_k$ vanishing on $B_k$; extend a finite basis of $Z_k$ to one of $C_k$ and set the added basis values to zero. This proves surjectivity of restriction and hence $H^k(C^*)=B_k^\perp/Z_k^\perp\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(Z_k/B_k,\mathbb R)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(H_k^{\mathrm{simp}}(\mathcal T;\mathbb R),\mathbb R)$. Since these spaces are finite dimensional, their real duals have the same dimension.

By [F5], $H_k^{\mathrm{simp}}(\mathcal T;\mathbb R)\cong H_k(|\mathcal T|;\mathbb R)$. If $|\mathcal T|=\overline\Omega$ is nonempty, connected, and contractible in the sense of [F7], [F6] makes this group $\mathbb R$ for $k=0$ and zero for $k>0$. Steps 1.1–2.2 therefore show that the discrete cohomology is one-dimensional in degree zero and zero in positive degrees, which is exactness of the displayed finite sequence, including surjectivity of its last map. The globally constant functions lie in $W_h^0$ and have zero gradient, so the one-dimensional degree-zero kernel consists exactly of constants.

For arbitrary topology, let $Z_h^1=\ker\operatorname{curl}$ and $B_h^1=\nabla W_h^0$. By step 3.1, $B_h^1\subseteq Z_h^1$. The space $Z_h^1$ is finite dimensional as a subspace of $N_h^1$, so [F10] applied inside $Z_h^1$ gives $Z_h^1=B_h^1\oplus(Z_h^1\cap(B_h^1)^\perp)$ with orthogonality from [F9]. The second summand has dimension $\dim(Z_h^1/B_h^1)=\dim H^1(C^*)=\dim H_1(|\mathcal T|;\mathbb R)$ by steps 3.1–2.2 and the duality proved in step 4.1. Applying the same [F10] argument to $Z_h^2=\ker\operatorname{div}$ and $B_h^2=\operatorname{curl}N_h^1\subseteq Z_h^2$ gives the asserted second harmonic space and dimension. These are discrete cohomology components, not an assertion that a continuum sequence is exact.

risk_review.notes: Six steps checked including empty mesh: moment bijections assemble global graph fields and identify differential with real incidence coboundary. Finite linear duality is proved by annihilators and basis extension; simplicial-singular comparison then gives natural dual homology. Contractibility is explicitly closure contractibility. Harmonic dimensions use finite orthogonal splitting, without asserting continuum exactness or requiring full AC.

citations.quote:
Assume AC. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz open set. There are bounded real linear maps $R:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and $Q:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to H_0^1(\Omega)$ such that
$$u=Ru+\nabla Qu,\qquad \|Ru\|_{H^1}+\|Qu\|_{H^1}\le C_\Omega\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}.$$
No contractibility, connected boundary, or mesh hypothesis is required. The scalar estimate uses the full H(curl) norm; no estimate by curl alone is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary.

1. An $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ class $F$ that vanishes almost everywhere outside $\overline\Omega$ restricts to $H_0^1(\Omega)$, and every $H_0^1(\Omega)$ class has an $H^1$ zero extension.
2. If $f\in H^1(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ and $f=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, then $f\in H_0^1(\Omega)$.
3. The zero extension $U$ of $u\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ belongs to $H(\operatorname{curl};\mathbb R^3)$, with $\operatorname{curl}U$ equal to the zero extension of $\operatorname{curl}u$; both component norms are preserved. Also $\nabla H_0^1(\Omega)\subset H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and its elements have zero curl.

All statements apply componentwise to vector fields where appropriate.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded connected contractible Lipschitz polyhedron. If $u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ has distributional curl zero, then there is $p\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $u=\nabla p$ almost everywhere; $p$ is unique up to an additive constant.

Assume AC. A nonempty bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ has nonempty connected boundary. In particular the connected-boundary clause of the regular-decomposition theorem follows from the domain assumptions in the discrete-compactness theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set whose boundary is locally a Lipschitz graph, with $D$ on one side in each chart. It need not be connected. There is one linear operator $E:H^1(D)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $Ef=f$ almost everywhere on $D$, which maps $H^2(D)$ boundedly into $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Its support can be confined to a fixed bounded neighborhood of $\overline D$. The bounds depend only on a finite choice of boundary charts and cutoffs. In particular no mesh enters them.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Ω\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. If
$u\in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$$D_i u=0\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega\qquad(1\le i\le n),$$
then for every connected component $C$ of $\Omega$ there is a constant
$c_C\in\mathbb K$ such that $u=c_C$ almost everywhere on $C$. The empty
domain has no components, so its conclusion is vacuous.

The proof assumes full AC as stated, but uses it only through Countable Choice
for the Sobolev representative, Lebesgue, and mollification interfaces cited
below. No full-AC selection is made in the ball propagation argument.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$, $B=B(x_0,r)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $r>0$, $1\le p<\infty$, and $u\in W^{1,p}(B;\mathbb K)$ with ball average $u_B=|B|^{-1}\int_Bu$. Then $\|u-u_B\|_{L^p(B)}\le C(n,p)\,r\,\|Du\|_{L^p(B)}$.

Assume countable choice. On complex $L^2$, $\mathcal F_2^2f=Rf$, $Rf(x)=f(-x)$, and $\mathcal F_2^{-1}=R\mathcal F_2$. For $f\in L^2$, the truncated integrals $\int_{|x|\le R}f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,dx$ converge in $L^2$ to $\mathcal F_2f$ as $R\to\infty$. The corresponding positive-sign integrals converge in $L^2$ to $\mathcal F_2^{-1}f$. No pointwise convergence is asserted.

The map $\mathcal F:L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to BUC(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ is complex-linear and $\sup_\xi|\widehat f(\xi)|\le\|f\|_1$. Here $n\ge1$ and $BUC$ means bounded uniformly continuous functions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], is a complete normed space over
$\mathbb K$.

Both endpoints $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, as is $k=0$, where the
assertion reduces to the completeness of $L^p$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the zero space and the assertion is trivial.
The Axiom of Choice is used only to derive Countable Choice for the two
published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative
selection inside the finitely many coordinate classes is finite and

derivations.claim: Let $u$ lie in the left-hand kernel and take $u=z+\nabla q$ from [F1]. Then $\operatorname{curl}z=0$. By [F2], $z=\nabla r$ for $r\in H^1(\Omega)$. Since each $z_j\in H^1$, its weak derivatives give all second derivatives of $r$, so $r\in H^2(\Omega)$. Extend $r$ by [F3] to $a\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. This has a continuous representative: Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|\widehat a\|_1\le\|(1+|\xi|^2)\widehat a\|_2\|(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1}\|_2<\infty$ in dimension three, and its positive-sign inverse integral $g(x)$ is the reflection of the integral Fourier transform of $\widehat a$, hence continuous by [F4]. Its truncated integrals converge uniformly to $g$, since the error is bounded by the $L^1$ Fourier tail, which tends to zero by dominated convergence. They converge in $L^2$ to $a$ by [F4]. On every finite-measure ball the uniform convergence is also $L^2$ convergence, so uniqueness of the $L^2$ limit there shows $g=a$ almost everywhere. Smooth compactly supported approximants to $a$ converge in $H^2$ by [F4] and uniformly by the same Fourier bound applied to their differences; no unproved $L^1$ inversion assumption on $a$ is made. Consequently $r$ has a continuous representative on $\overline\Omega$.

On any compact patch of the interior of a planar boundary face there is an inward rectangular slab of fixed height $b>0$ inside $\Omega$. For a smooth function on this slab, the one-dimensional fundamental theorem in the normal direction and Cauchy–Schwarz give $\|f|_{s=0}\|_{L^2(\text{patch})}^2\le \frac{2}{b}\|f\|_{L^2(\text{slab})}^2+2b\|\partial_s f\|_{L^2(\text{slab})}^2.$ This defines a bounded $H^1$ face restriction by smooth approximation: the already proved Lipschitz extension [F3] on a bounded rectangular slab, followed by the whole-space density theorem [F4] at $k=1$, gives the required dense smooth restrictions. Since $z\in H_0^1(\Omega)$, approximating by compactly supported smooth vector fields shows that the restriction of $z$ to this patch is zero. Approximate $a$ from step 1.1 in $H^2$ by the smooth functions of [F4]; their gradients converge in $H^1$ on the slab and their values converge uniformly. Thus the restriction of $r$ is its continuous face value and the tangential derivatives of that restriction are the restrictions of the tangential components of $\nabla r=z$: integrate the smooth tangential derivative identity against a compactly supported smooth test on the face and pass to the limit using the slab estimate. These derivatives are zero. By [F3] in dimension two, the continuous boundary value of $r$ is constant on each connected planar face interior. One may split disconnected faces into their finitely many polygonal components. Continuity makes those constants extend to their closures. Since the boundary is connected by [F2] and these finitely many closed faces cover it, its continuous image under $r$ is a connected subset of a finite set of constants, hence one constant $c$.

Now $r-c\in H^1(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ vanishes on the boundary. By [F1] it lies in $H_0^1(\Omega)$. Thus $u=\nabla(q+r-c)$ belongs to the right-hand range. Its reverse inclusion follows directly from [F1], so the claimed relative kernel identity holds. This proves weak relative exactness using the actual boundary closure and continuum topology, rather than inferring it from mesh cohomology.

For the norm estimate, zero-extend $q\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ to $Q\in H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ by [F1], and fix a ball $B\supset\overline\Omega$ with $A=B\setminus\overline\Omega$ of positive measure. Ball Poincare in [F3] gives $\|Q-Q_B\|_{L^2(B)}\le C_B\|\nabla q\|_2$. Since $Q=0$ on $A$, $|Q_B||A|^{1/2}\le\|Q-Q_B\|_{L^2(B)}$. The triangle inequality therefore gives $\|q\|_2\le C_B(1+(|B|/|A|)^{1/2})\|\nabla q\|_2$, proving the asserted $H^1$ bound. If a sequence of gradients is Cauchy in $L^2$, this estimate makes its scalar representatives Cauchy in $H^1$. The space $H_0^1$ is closed by its definition as a closure, and complete as a closed subspace of $H^1$. Its limit's gradient is the given $L^2$ limit, so the gradient range is closed.
