Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron with a matching shape-regular affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T_h$. There are a positive continuous piecewise affine function $g_h$, a smooth bounded vector field $b$ on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, and positive constants $c,C,r,\epsilon_0$, independent of the mesh, with the following properties. On $K$, $c h_K\le g_h\le C h_K$ and $\operatorname{Lip}(g_h)\le C$, where $h_K=\operatorname{diam}K$. Put
$$F_{t,y}^{\pm}(x)=x+t g_h(x)(\pm b(x)+r y),\qquad |y|\le1,\quad 0<t\le\epsilon_0.$$
The maps are uniformly bi-Lipschitz on their domain. For the plus sign, $F_{t,y}^{+}(\overline\Omega)\subset\Omega$. For the minus sign, $F_{t,y}^{-}(\partial\Omega)\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline\Omega$, at distance at least $ctg_h(x)$ from $\partial\Omega$. The same interior distance lower bound holds for the plus sign at boundary points. The images of $K$ and all homotopies $s\mapsto F_{st,y}^{\pm}(x)$, $x\in K$, lie within distance $Ct h_K$ of $K$. Their intersections with $\Omega$ are contained in a vertex patch $\omega_K$ of uniformly bounded overlap, after decreasing $\epsilon_0$ if necessary. All constants may depend on $\Omega$ and the shape-regularity bound. No ratio of global maximum to minimum mesh size occurs.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh. The four face-normal fluxes are unisolvent on each $RT_0(K)$, and matching face fluxes assemble a global $H(\operatorname{div})$ field. For smooth scalar $f$, smooth vector fields $u,v$, and the canonical interpolants determined by vertex values, oriented edge circulations, oriented face-normal fluxes, and cell integrals, the interpolation maps satisfy cellwise
$$
abla I_h^0f=I_h^1
abla f,\qquad \operatorname{curl}I_h^1u=I_h^2\operatorname{curl}u,\qquad \operatorname{div}I_h^2v=I_h^3\operatorname{div}v.$$
Any assignment of one real oriented value to each global mesh edge determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^1$; any assignment of one real oriented flux to each global mesh face determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^2$. These assemblies belong to $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$, respectively, with the global spaces and conventions of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Applying the local moment identities to polynomial cell restrictions also proves that the global finite-element spaces form the subcomplex $W_h^0\xrightarrow{
abla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$. The canonical interpolation identities themselves apply to smooth inputs; they do not extend the canonical edge moments to arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ inputs.

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$
For every smooth map $F:M\to N$ and every form $\omega$ on $N$, $$d(F^*\omega)=F^*(d\omega).$$

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. Independence of other positive affine coordinates is the forward justification [[lem-simplex-integrals-are-independent-of-affine-coordinate-identification]].

For $k\ge1$ and a smooth $(k-1)$-form $\eta$ on a neighbourhood of $\Delta^k$ in its affine span,
$$\int_{\Delta^k}d\eta=\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^i\int_{\Delta^{k-1}}\delta_i^*\eta,$$
where the integrals and ordered face maps use the standard affine-simplex conventions. No Stokes theorem for manifolds with corners is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

For a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^n$ and a test function $\varphi$, every multi-index $\alpha$ satisfies $\partial^\alpha(T*\varphi)=(\partial^\alpha T)*\varphi=T*(\partial^\alpha\varphi)$, as smooth functions on their common safe domain.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Fix a nonnegative
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ of unit mass with
$\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$, put
$\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$, and define the
interior mollification
$$u_\varepsilon(x)=(\rho_\varepsilon*\widetilde u)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widetilde u(y)\,\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy,$$
where $\widetilde u$ is a representative of $u$ extended by zero to
$\mathbb R^n$. Then $u_\varepsilon\to u$ in $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every
open $U\subset\subset\Omega$; equivalently $u_\varepsilon\to u$ in
$W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. The exponent $p=1$ is included, and
no assertion about density or convergence in the $W^{k,\infty}$ norm is made.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

derivations.claim: On a shape-regular cell, change variables to a fixed reference tetrahedron using the affine differential-form pullback. To verify the scaling, let $A_K$ be the linear part of its affine reference map. Its columns are edge vectors, so $\|A_K\|\le\sqrt3h_K$. Shape regularity gives $\rho_K\ge h_K/\sigma$, and the inscribed ball yields $|\det A_K|=6|K|\ge8\pi(h_K/\sigma)^3$. If $s_1\ge s_2\ge s_3$ are its singular values, then $s_1,s_2\le\sqrt3h_K$ and $s_1s_2s_3=|\det A_K|$, so $s_3\ge c_\sigma h_K$. Thus $s_{\min}(A_K)$ and $\|A_K\|$ are both comparable to $h_K$. Reference finite-dimensional norm equivalence now gives $\|v_h\|_{L^2(K)}^2\simeq\sum_{\sigma\subset K,\,\dim\sigma=k}h_K^{3-2k}\left|\int_\sigma v_h\right|^2,\qquad \|v_h\|_{L^\infty(K)}+h_K\|dv_h\|_{L^\infty(K)}\le C h_K^{-3/2}\|v_h\|_{L^2(K)}.$ Norm equivalence follows directly because the moment map is an injective linear map on the finite reference space [F2]; the maximum and minimum of its norm on the Euclidean unit sphere are finite and strictly positive. The inverse estimate follows the same way for polynomial coefficients and their first derivatives. These arguments apply to degrees zero through three, taking $d=0$ in top degree.

We first justify all boundary and weak-differential operations used below. Using the smooth field $b$ from [F1], replace $g_h$ temporarily by the constant one and let $S_t^+$ be the average pullback by $x\mapsto x+t(b(x)+ry)$. Its image on $\overline\Omega$ has interior clearance $ct$. In coordinates the pullback coefficients are the minors displayed above, with $D_xF=I+tDb(x)$. The change of variables $z=x+t(b(x)+ry)$ writes this operator as integration against a smooth kernel in $x,z$, including the smooth pullback coefficients; hence it maps $L^2$ forms to forms smooth on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$. More explicitly, with $\psi_t(x)=x+tb(x)$ it is the pullback $\psi_t^*(\check\rho_{tr}*\widetilde u)$, where $\check\rho(y)=\rho(-y)$ and $\widetilde u$ is zero extension of the coefficient vector: the pullback minors are independent of $y$. Smoothness thus follows directly from the coefficient convolution theorem [F5] and finite smooth composition, rather than from an unstated parameter differentiation theorem. Pullback commutes with weak $d$: locally mollify on the interior image, apply the smooth pullback identity [F3] there, and pass in $L^2$ using [F5] for the finite exterior-derivative sums and the change of variables [F6]. Averaging preserves this identity. The same change of variables bounds $S_t^+$ on $L^2$ uniformly for small $t$. On restrictions of globally smooth forms it tends to the identity, and these restrictions are $L^2$ dense by [F4] (a compactly supported smooth form on the open domain extends smoothly by zero). A three-term approximation then proves $S_t^+u\to u$ in $L^2$ for every $u$; applied to $du$ it proves graph convergence for $u\in H\Lambda^k$. The graph differential is closed in the complete finite-product $L^2$ space [F4]: if $u_j\to u$ and $du_j\to f$ in $L^2$, pass each coefficient weak test identity to the limit by Cauchy–Schwarz to obtain $du=f$. In particular smooth-neighborhood forms are graph dense.

Fix $x\in\sigma\subset K$. The map $y\mapsto F_{\epsilon,y}^{\pm}(x)$ is translation and scalar dilation with Jacobian $(\epsilon r g_h(x))^3$. The coefficients of its pullback on the tangent space of $\sigma$ are bounded by [F1]. Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] in $y$, $g_h\simeq h_K$, and [F1] therefore give $\int_{B_1}\rho(y)|((F_{\epsilon,y}^{\pm})^*u)_x|\,dy\le C\epsilon^{-3/2}h_K^{-3/2}\|u\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}.$ For the minus sign use the zero extension; its sampled $L^2$ norm is bounded by the same patch norm. Integrating over $\sigma$, whose $k$-volume is at most $C h_K^k$, bounds each moment by $C\epsilon^{-3/2}h_K^{k-3/2}\|u\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. This also proves independence of representatives and absolute integrability. Reconstruction and step 1.1 give the first claimed bound after summing the bounded-overlap patches. At boundary simplices the outward images lie strictly outside $\overline\Omega$, so every minus moment there vanishes.

For a piecewise Whitney form with all boundary tangential moments zero, zero extension has distributional $d$ equal to its piecewise $d$, extended by zero. Indeed integrate cellwise against a compact test form: the interior-face terms cancel by matching tangential traces [F2], and boundary terms vanish because zero boundary moments give zero entire tangential polynomial trace. Use $S_t^-$, defined as in step 1.2 with $-b$, on that zero extension. It is smooth and zero on a collar of the boundary, since every outward sample from sufficiently near the boundary lies outside $\overline\Omega$. It converges in the graph norm by the same pullback and density argument. Therefore the relative Whitney form belongs to the graph closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, as asserted. For a general member of that closure, zero extension commutes with $d$ by passage from compactly supported approximants. Conversely, if a Whitney form belongs to this closure, its zero extension has no boundary surface contribution to $d$. Cellwise integration by parts identifies that contribution with its polynomial tangential trace on the relative interior of each boundary face. Such a surface distribution cannot be an $L^2$ function unless its coefficient is zero: testing with a fixed smooth tangential function times a normal cutoff of width $\delta$ leaves a fixed surface pairing while its $L^2$ volume pairing tends to zero. Thus the tangential polynomial trace vanishes on every boundary face. Its boundary subsimplex moments vanish as well. This proves the stated equality of spaces; top degree has no boundary moments or trace condition.

For $k=0,1,2$ and smooth forms, Stokes and pullback commutation [F3] on $\sigma$ give $m_\sigma^{\pm,k+1}(du)=\sum_{\tau\subset\partial\sigma}\operatorname{sgn}(\tau,\sigma)m_\tau^{\pm,k}(u)$. The restriction of $g_h$ to a simplex is affine and common to all incident cells; thus its tangential derivative and the shift on every face agree, even though ambient derivatives jump across mesh faces. Stokes is valid for this smooth restriction. Reconstruction [F2] proves commutation for smooth full inputs and compactly supported relative inputs in degrees zero through two. Use step 1.2 for full graph density and the defining closure for relative graph density. The $L^2$ bounds in step 2.1 and closedness of distributional $d$ pass these identities to precisely those graph domains. In degree three, $d$ vanishes on both the input and reconstructed form, so the terminal identity is zero.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, and let $x\in H$. Then there is exactly one point $p\in C$ with $\|x-p\|=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$, that is, a unique nearest point of $C$ to $x$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be closed and convex with $x\in H$, and let $p\in C$. Then $p$ is the nearest point of $C$ to $x$ if and only if

$$\operatorname{Re}\langle x-p,\ y-p\rangle\le0 \qquad \text{for every } y\in C .$$

In particular, for the nearest point the inequality holds, and conversely any $p\in C$ satisfying the inequality is nearest.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

citations.quote: There is also a boundary-corrected family of projections $\pi_{h,0}^k:L^2\Lambda^k(\Omega)\to E_{h,0}^k$, where $E_{h,0}^k=E_h^k\cap H_0\Lambda^k(\Omega)$ and $H_0\Lambda^k$ is the graph closure of compactly supported smooth forms. These have the same uniform bounds, are the identity on $E_{h,0}^k$, and commute in degrees zero through two on the homogeneous complex; the terminal degree-three differential is zero.

Assume AC. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz open set. There are bounded real linear maps $R:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and $Q:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to H_0^1(\Omega)$ such that
$$u=Ru+\nabla Qu,\qquad \|Ru\|_{H^1}+\|Qu\|_{H^1}\le C_\Omega\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}.$$
No contractibility, connected boundary, or mesh hypothesis is required. The scalar estimate uses the full H(curl) norm; no estimate by curl alone is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron. Then
$$\{u\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):\operatorname{curl}u=0\}=\nabla H_0^1(\Omega).$$
The gradient range is closed in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, and $\|q\|_{H^1}\le C_\Omega\|\nabla q\|_2$ for $q\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. The boundary is connected as a consequence of these stated geometric hypotheses; it is not an extra assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded open set and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is
compactly embedded in $L^p(\Omega)$: the inclusion is bounded, and every
sequence bounded in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging in
$L^p(\Omega)$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is needed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume AC. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be nonempty, bounded, and open. Write $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, $B=
abla H_0^1(\Omega)$, and let $P_B$ denote the $H$-orthogonal projection onto $B$. Let $S_h\subset H_0^1(\Omega)$ and $V_h\subset H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ be finite-dimensional subspaces with $B_h=
abla S_h\subset V_h$. Suppose linear projections $\Pi_h^0:H_0^1	o S_h$ and $\Pi_h^1:H_0(\operatorname{curl})	o V_h$ satisfy $\Pi_h^1
abla=
abla\Pi_h^0$. For $v_h\in V_h\cap B_h^\perp$, put $w_h=(I-P_B)v_h$. Then $w_h\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})\cap B^\perp$, $\operatorname{curl}w_h=\operatorname{curl}v_h$, and
$$\|v_h-w_h\|_2\le\|\Pi_h^1w_h-w_h\|_2.$$
If moreover $\sup_h\|\Pi_h^1\|_{H	o H}\le M$ and $\Pi_h^1f	o f$ in $H$ for each fixed $f\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})$, every $H$-convergent sequence of lifts $w_h$ has $\|v_h-w_h\|_2	o0$. Here the $H$ operator norm means that the graph-space operators possess bounded extensions to $H$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, and let $x\in H$. Then there is exactly one point $p\in C$ with $\|x-p\|=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$, that is, a unique nearest point of $C$ to $x$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be closed and convex with $x\in H$, and let $p\in C$. Then $p$ is the nearest point of $C$ to $x$ if and only if

$$\operatorname{Re}\langle x-p,\ y-p\rangle\le0 \qquad \text{for every } y\in C .$$

In particular, for the nearest point the inequality holds, and conversely any $p\in C$ satisfying the inequality is nearest.

derivations.claim: Put $B=\nabla H_0^1$, closed by [F5]. For a graph-bounded sequence $v_h\in X_h$, choose the decompositions $v_h=z_h+\nabla q_h$ from [F2], using AC on this countable family of nonempty decomposition sets. The sequence $z_h$ is bounded in $H_0^1$. By [F4], extract a subsequence on which all three components converge in $L^2$, using three successive subsequences. On this subsequence the lifts $w_h=(I-P_B)v_h=(I-P_B)z_h$ converge in $L^2$, since $I-P_B$ is a contraction.

The continuous kernel $K$ is closed in $L^2$: if $k_j\in K$ converges in $L^2$, it is Cauchy in the curl graph norm, its graph limit lies in $H_0(\operatorname{curl})$ by the closure definition, and its curl remains zero. Let $P_K$ be its orthogonal projection. A graph-bounded sequence $u_j\in Y:=H_0(\operatorname{curl})\cap K^\perp$ satisfies $u_j=(I-P_K)z_j$ by [F2], since $\nabla q_j\in K$. Therefore the same componentwise Rellich argument proves compactness of $Y\hookrightarrow L^2$. If no continuous curl Poincare constant existed on $Y$, choose $u_j\in Y$ with $\|u_j\|_2=1$ and $\|\operatorname{curl}u_j\|_2<1/j$. Compactness gives $u_j\to u$ in $L^2$ along a subsequence; their curls tend to zero, so graph closure puts $u\in K$, while the closed orthogonality conditions put $u\in K^\perp$ and $\|u\|_2=1$. This contradiction proves $\|u\|_2\le C_\Omega\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_2$ on $Y$.

The gap estimate [F5], using the relative degree-zero commutation in [F1], gives $\|v_h-w_h\|_2\le\|\Pi_h^1w_h-w_h\|_2\to0$. For clarity, this last limit uses both strong convergence on each fixed field and the uniform $L^2$ operator bound; it does not follow from pointwise convergence alone on a moving sequence. The strong limit of $w_h$ need only lie in $L^2$: the bounded extensions converge on all $L^2$ by density, as proved in [F5]. Hence $v_h$ converges strongly along the same subsequence. This proves discrete compactness without any topological exactness assumption.

For $v_h\in Z_h$, set $w=(I-P_K)v_h\in Y$. Its curl equals that of $v_h$. This curl belongs to the next relative graph space: approximate $v_h$ by compactly supported smooth fields in the curl graph norm; their curls converge in $L^2$, have zero divergence, and are compactly supported, hence converge also in the divergence graph norm. Since the finite element spaces form the relative subcomplex, $\operatorname{curl}v_h$ belongs to its discrete degree-two target. Commutation and identity on that discrete next-degree space therefore imply $e=v_h-\Pi_h^1w\in K_h$. Hence $(v_h,e)=0$, and $\|v_h\|_2^2=(v_h,\Pi_h^1w)\le M\|v_h\|_2\|w\|_2\le MC_\Omega\|v_h\|_2\|\operatorname{curl}v_h\|_2$. Division when $v_h\ne0$ proves the mesh-uniform inequality on $Z_h$; the zero case is immediate. No limit in $h$ or finite-coarse-mesh exception is required for this inequality.

On the original contractible domain, [F3] implies $K_h=V_h\cap B$. If $v_h=
abla p\in K_h$ with $p\in H_0^1$, then on every tetrahedron $v_h=a+b	imes x$ has curl $2b=0$, so it is constant. The scalar function $p-a\cdot x$ has zero weak gradient on the connected open tetrahedron; [[thm-zero-weak-gradient-implies-componentwise-constancy]], whose AC hypothesis is included here, makes it constant almost everywhere there, so $p$ is affine on that cell. We establish the face values directly, without using a trace characterization. On an interior face $F$, integration by parts on its two adjacent cells shows that the distributional gradient of the piecewise-affine representative is its piecewise constant gradient plus the jump $[p]n_F$ times surface measure on $F$. A nonzero jump cannot be represented by an $L^2$ function: choose a smooth tangential bump $\eta$ supported in the relative interior of $F$ with $\int_F[p]\eta
e0$, choose a coordinate $i$ with $(n_F)_i
e0$, and test that component with $\eta(x')\chi(s/\delta)e_i$, where $s$ is signed normal distance and $\chi$ is smooth with $\chi(0)=1$. The face pairing is a fixed nonzero number, while the pairing with any $L^2$ function tends to zero as $O(\sqrt\delta)$ because the test support has volume $O(\delta)$. Since $p\in H^1$, its distributional gradient is $L^2$, so $[p]=0$ on $F$. For a boundary face, the closure definition of $H_0^1$ gives compactly supported smooth $p_j	o p$ in $H^1(\Omega)$; their zero extensions are Cauchy in $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ and, by the completeness of $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ under AC ([[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]]), converge to a zero extension $P$ of $p$. Apply the same face argument to $P$, whose exterior value is zero, to conclude $p|_F=0$. These traces are affine polynomials, so their almost-everywhere equalities hold everywhere, including face vertices.  At each mesh vertex, choose a sufficiently small neighborhood meeting only cells incident to that vertex. The matching tetrahedra triangulate this neighborhood in the closure of a Lipschitz three-manifold, whose local model is a ball at an interior vertex and a half-ball at a boundary vertex. Each incident tetrahedron is the cone from the vertex over its opposite face, so the cross-section of the star by a sufficiently small sphere is its simplicial link. The local ball or half-ball model makes that link a connected triangulated sphere or disk. Join interior points of any two link triangles by a path in that link, perturbing the path to avoid the finitely many link vertices and to cross edges transversely. Each successive pair of triangles shares a link edge, hence the corresponding tetrahedra share a face containing the original vertex. This establishes the required face chain. Equality of the affine values therefore propagates to every tetrahedron incident at the vertex. The common nodal values assemble a continuous piecewise affine function on $\overline\Omega$, equal to $p$ almost everywhere, hence in $W_h^0$. The zero boundary-face values just proved imply all boundary nodal values vanish, so the assembled function belongs to $S_h$. Conversely $
abla S_h\subset K_h$. Consequently $K_h=B_h$, $Z_h=X_h$, and step 2.2 is the asserted inequality on $X_h$.

In general topology $B\subset K$ and $B_h\subset K_h$. Closedness of $B$ gives $K=B\oplus\mathcal H$, while finite-dimensional orthogonal decomposition gives $K_h=B_h\oplus\mathcal H_h$ and $Z_h=X_h\cap\mathcal H_h^\perp$. The unit ball of $\mathcal H$ is graph bounded and lies in $B^\perp$; [F2] and [F4] make it relatively compact by the argument in step 1.1. A Hilbert space with compact unit ball is finite dimensional: otherwise choose successive unit vectors orthogonal to their predecessors, obtaining pairwise distance $\sqrt2$ and contradicting compactness. The discrete harmonic space is finite dimensional as a subspace of $V_h$. Nonzero $a_h\in\mathcal H_h$ has $\|a_h\|_2>0$ but curl zero, disproving a curl Poincare bound on all $X_h$ whenever such a mode exists. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 still prove compactness of $X_h$ and step 2.2 proves the quotient inequality. The proof uses AC for selections and imported analytic suppliers, CC for the projection/Poincare interfaces, and CC/DC through the exact Rellich supplier; it asserts no choice-free version.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The covariant affine Piola map for $N_h^1$ and contravariant affine Piola map for $N_h^2$ use the orientation-preserving cell maps and conventions of [[def-covariant-contravariant-piola-maps-and-hdiv-hcurl]]. Their differential and moment identities are those of [[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]]. The edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom are respectively the oriented edge circulation, oriented face-normal flux, and cell integral.

In the two conformity conditions above, each cellwise polynomial restriction has a unique polynomial representative on its closed cell, and those representatives define the displayed edge and face integrals. Thus the global edge and face moments are part of the assembled-space definition; their correspondence with all cochains is proved by the local unisolvence and commuting-moment items, not inferred from rough-field traces.

On an oriented tetrahedron $K$ with vertices $x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3$, let $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$ for $0\le i<j\le3$. Then the six edge circulations $\ell_{rs}(v)=\int_{[x_r,x_s]}v\cdot t_{rs}\,ds$ satisfy $\ell_{rs}(\phi_{ij})=\delta_{(r,s),(i,j)}$. The six functions form a basis of the local space $\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:i<j\}=\{a+b\times x:a,b\in\mathbb R^3\}$, so these edge circulations are unisolvent degrees of freedom.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh. The four face-normal fluxes are unisolvent on each $RT_0(K)$, and matching face fluxes assemble a global $H(\operatorname{div})$ field. For smooth scalar $f$, smooth vector fields $u,v$, and the canonical interpolants determined by vertex values, oriented edge circulations, oriented face-normal fluxes, and cell integrals, the interpolation maps satisfy cellwise
$$
abla I_h^0f=I_h^1
abla f,\qquad \operatorname{curl}I_h^1u=I_h^2\operatorname{curl}u,\qquad \operatorname{div}I_h^2v=I_h^3\operatorname{div}v.$$
Any assignment of one real oriented value to each global mesh edge determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^1$; any assignment of one real oriented flux to each global mesh face determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^2$. These assemblies belong to $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$, respectively, with the global spaces and conventions of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Applying the local moment identities to polynomial cell restrictions also proves that the global finite-element spaces form the subcomplex $W_h^0\xrightarrow{
abla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$. The canonical interpolation identities themselves apply to smooth inputs; they do not extend the canonical edge moments to arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ inputs.

derivations.claim: In the reference coordinates, $\lambda_1=x_1$, $\lambda_0=1-x_1-x_2-x_3$, so $\phi_{01}=(1-x_2-x_3,x_1,x_1)$. Along $[0,1]$, parameterized by $x(t)=(t,0,0)$, this field has tangent component $1$; therefore its oriented circulation is $\int_0^1 1\,dt=1$.

Differentiating the displayed polynomial gives $\operatorname{curl}\phi_{01}=(0,-2,2)$. The oriented face $[0,1,2]$ lies in $x_3=0$ with normal $e_3$ and area $1/2$, so its curl flux is $2\cdot(1/2)=1$. Its oriented boundary is $[1,2]-[0,2]+[0,1]$; by [F2], the first two circulations vanish and the last is one, agreeing with the flux by [F3].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The covariant affine Piola map for $N_h^1$ and contravariant affine Piola map for $N_h^2$ use the orientation-preserving cell maps and conventions of [[def-covariant-contravariant-piola-maps-and-hdiv-hcurl]]. Their differential and moment identities are those of [[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]]. The edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom are respectively the oriented edge circulation, oriented face-normal flux, and cell integral.

In the two conformity conditions above, each cellwise polynomial restriction has a unique polynomial representative on its closed cell, and those representatives define the displayed edge and face integrals. Thus the global edge and face moments are part of the assembled-space definition; their correspondence with all cochains is proved by the local unisolvence and commuting-moment items, not inferred from rough-field traces.

Assume Countable Choice for the graph-space uniqueness and $L^2$ conventions of [[def-na-hcurl-space]]. Let $V_h=N_h^1$ be the lowest-order edge space on a finite tetrahedral mesh, as in [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. It is finite dimensional: restriction to the finitely many cells injects it into the finite product of the local spaces, each spanned by at most six Whitney edge fields. Injectivity holds because the cells cover $\Omega$ up to their measure-zero facets. Use the componentwise real $L^2$ inner product defined in [[def-na-hcurl-space]]. Define its curl kernel and the $L^2$ gauge space by
$$K_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{curl}v_h=0\},\qquad Z_h:=V_h\cap K_h^\perp.$$
The quotient $\dot V_h:=V_h/K_h$ has norm $\|[v_h]\|_{\operatorname{curl}}:=\|\operatorname{curl}v_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$; this is well-defined and positive definite because two representatives differ by an element of $K_h$. The bilinear form induced by curl-curl is $a_h([u_h],[v_h])=(\operatorname{curl}u_h,\operatorname{curl}v_h)_{L^2}$. A representative of a quotient solution is fixed by the gauge condition $u_h\in Z_h$. The mixed gauge system uses a multiplier $p_h\in K_h$:
$$a_h(u_h,v_h)+(p_h,v_h)_{L^2}=f(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h),\qquad (u_h,q_h)_{L^2}=0\quad(q_h\in K_h).$$
The quotient energy norm, rather than the full $H(\operatorname{curl})$ norm, is the norm controlled by this definition.

Assume Countable Choice for the graph spaces and real $L^2$ product as in [[def-na-curl-curl-kernel-quotient-gauge]]. Let $V_h$ be that finite-dimensional real edge space, $K_h=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{V_h})$, and $Z_h=V_h\cap K_h^\perp$. Here $V_h^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(V_h,\mathbb R)$ is the algebraic dual of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. For every $f\in V_h^*$ there is a unique pair $(u_h,p_h)\in Z_h\times K_h$ satisfying
$$ (\operatorname{curl}u_h,\operatorname{curl}v_h)_{L^2}+(p_h,v_h)_{L^2}=f(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h),\qquad (u_h,q_h)_{L^2}=0\quad(q_h\in K_h).$$
The gauge multiplier is the $L^2$ Riesz representative of $f|_{K_h}$. The quotient solution satisfies the exact stability identity
$$\|\operatorname{curl}u_h\|_{L^2}=\|f|_{Z_h}\|_{(Z_h,\|\operatorname{curl}(\cdot)\|_{L^2})^*},\qquad \|p_h\|_{L^2}=\|f|_{K_h}\|_{(K_h,\|\cdot\|_{L^2})^*}.$$
The constraint form $b(v,q)=(v,q)_{L^2}$ has inf-sup constant one when $K_h\ne\{0\}$, $V_h$ has the $H(\operatorname{curl})$ graph norm and $K_h$ has the $L^2$ norm; if $K_h=\{0\}$ the constraint is vacuous. The curl form is coercive with constant one on $Z_h$ in the quotient curl norm. No mesh-uniform estimate in the full graph norm is claimed here.

derivations.claim: The field $v(x)=(x_1,0,0)$ is vector-valued affine, so it belongs to $[P_1(K)]^3$. Its componentwise curl is zero because its only nonzero component depends only on $x_1$. Hence $(\operatorname{curl}v,\operatorname{curl}v)_{L^2(K)}=0$.

By [F1], every $q_h\in W_h^0=P_1(K)$ has constant gradient, while $v$ is nonconstant on the interior of $K$. Thus $v\notin\nabla W_h^0$. The kernel of the naive nodal curl-curl energy is therefore strictly larger than the compatible discrete gradient image, and its representative is not unique without a gauge as in [F2].

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for weak-derivative uniqueness and the real $L^2$ product below, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open. Here $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is the set of triples of real scalar $L^2$ classes from [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Define
$$ (u,v)_{L^2(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=1}^3\int_\Omega u_jv_j\,dx,\qquad \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$
Each scalar pairing is well-defined and induces its quotient norm by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]; the finite sum is therefore a real inner product on the triple space with the displayed norm. A test field $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ means a triple of real-valued members of the test-function space $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. Writing $\varphi=(\varphi_x,\varphi_y,\varphi_z)$, its classical curl is the coordinate expression of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
$$\operatorname{curl}\varphi=(\partial_y\varphi_z-\partial_z\varphi_y,\partial_z\varphi_x-\partial_x\varphi_z,\partial_x\varphi_y-\partial_y\varphi_x).$$
For $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the triple of scalar distributions whose action on a vector test field is the sum of the three component pairings, determined by
$$\langle \operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,dx,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$
The integral is finite because $u$ and the smooth compactly supported field $\operatorname{curl}\varphi$ are componentwise in $L^2$ and scalar Cauchy–Schwarz applies. On tests supported in a fixed compact $K\Subset\Omega$, the same estimate gives $|\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle|\le C_{u,K}\max_{|\alpha|\le1}\sup_K|D^\alpha\varphi|$ with a finite $C_{u,K}$. This proves continuity on each fixed-support test space; the LF universal property of [[lem-test-function-lf-topology-universal-property]], for the test topology of [[def-test-function-topology]], makes the pairing a vector distribution on $\Omega$.
If this vector distribution is represented by an $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ class, that class is unique almost everywhere componentwise by the injection of locally integrable functions into scalar distributions in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], under the stated Countable Choice assumption.
Define
$$H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\text{ is represented by an element of }L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)\}$$
with graph norm $\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. No boundary condition is imposed by this definition. Fields are real-valued; equality is equality of almost-everywhere classes.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Assume Countable Choice for the H(curl), H(div), and real $L^2$ inner-product interfaces used here; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed. Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching tetrahedral mesh with realization $|\mathcal T|=\overline\Omega$. Define $C_k(\mathcal T;\mathbb R)$ by extending the oriented chain groups of [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]] to real coefficients, and put $C^k=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(C_k,\mathbb R)$ with coboundary $\delta^k=\partial_{k+1}^*$. The degrees of freedom give a cochain isomorphism from
$$W_h^0\xrightarrow{\nabla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$$
to $C^0\xrightarrow{\delta^0}C^1\xrightarrow{\delta^1}C^2\xrightarrow{\delta^2}C^3$. Consequently the discrete cohomology in degree $k$ is naturally isomorphic to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(H_k(|\mathcal T|;\mathbb R),\mathbb R)$. If $\overline\Omega$ is nonempty, connected, and contractible, then the sequence is exact at every positive-degree space, $\ker\nabla$ consists of constants, and $\operatorname{div}:N_h^2\to N_h^3$ is onto. For general topology, define
$$\mathcal H_h^1:=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{N_h^1})\cap(\nabla W_h^0)^\perp,\qquad \mathcal H_h^2:=\ker(\operatorname{div}|_{N_h^2})\cap(\operatorname{curl}N_h^1)^\perp$$
using the $L^2$ inner product. Then $\ker\operatorname{curl}=\nabla W_h^0\oplus\mathcal H_h^1$ and $\ker\operatorname{div}=\operatorname{curl}N_h^1\oplus\mathcal H_h^2$, with $\dim\mathcal H_h^k=\dim H_k(|\mathcal T|;\mathbb R)$ for $k=1,2$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

derivations.claim: On $\overline\Omega$, $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\ge R-r>0$, so every component of $u$ and its first derivatives are bounded; hence $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and its classical curl is also in $L^2$. Direct differentiation by [F2] gives $\operatorname{div}u=2xy/(x^2+y^2)^2-2xy/(x^2+y^2)^2=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}u=0$. Thus [F1] places $u$ in H(curl) with zero curl.

Write $e_\theta=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta,0)$. On the torus boundary the normal is a linear combination of the meridional radial vector $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)$ and $e_3$, whereas $u=e_\theta/\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$; hence $u\cdot n=0$. Along the core curve, $u(\gamma(\theta))=e_\theta/R$ and $\gamma'(\theta)=R e_\theta$, so $\int_\gamma u\cdot d\ell=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,d\theta=2\pi$. A single-valued $C^1$ potential would have zero integral around every closed curve by [F4], so this field is not such a gradient and represents a nonzero period. This is the type of harmonic component retained by [F3].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded open set with no boundary regularity assumed, let $1\le p<n$ and
$p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. For every $1\le q<p^{*}$ the space
$W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is compactly embedded in $L^q(\Omega)$: every sequence
bounded in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging in $L^q(\Omega)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge2$, $1\le p<n$ and $p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. There is $C(n,p)$ with
$$\|u\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\Omega)}\le C(n,p)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$$
for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume Countable Choice. For any open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$n\ge1$, any $1\le p\le\infty$ and any
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, extension by zero
$$E_0u(x)=u(x)\ \ (x\in\Omega),\qquad E_0u(x)=0\ \ (x\notin\Omega),$$
acted on representatives, sends $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ linearly into
$W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$. For every $u\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
and every coordinate direction $i$, the class $D_i(E_0u)$ is the zero
extension of the class $D_iu$, and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|D_i(E_0u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom of Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]).** Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and $\mathcal F\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$. Its closure in the supremum metric is compact if and only if $\mathcal F$ is equicontinuous and pointwise bounded.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same field
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in the real case from
[[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]], and suppose $X\subseteq Y$
with **continuous inclusion** $J:X\to Y$: there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|x\|_Y\le C\|x\|_X$ for every $x\in X$.

One says that $X$ is **compactly embedded** in $Y$, written $X\Subset Y$, when
the inclusion operator $J$ is a compact operator in the sense of
[[def-compact-linear-operator]]: the image under $J$ of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]).

**The sequential form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom of Dependent Choice
([[def-dependent-choice]]). Then $X\Subset Y$ if and only if every bounded
sequence $(x_j)$ in $X$ has a subsequence $(x_{j_k})$ converging in $Y$:
Indeed, compact closure gives the sequence conclusion by
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]]. Conversely, fix bounded $B\subseteq X$
and let $K=\overline{J(B)}$. For any sequence $(y_j)$ in $K$, Countable
Choice selects $b_j\in B$ with $\|y_j-b_j\|_Y<1/j$ (start at $j=1$);
a convergent subsequence of $(b_j)$ gives one of $(y_j)$ with the same limit,
which belongs to the closed set $K$. Thus $K$ is sequentially compact and
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] makes it compact. The empty case is
immediate. Both readings
of $X\Subset Y$ are used on this page; the second is the form in which the
compactness theorems below are stated.

Continuity of the inclusion is a separate hypothesis and is never inferred
from compactness: a compact operator is bounded by
[[def-compact-linear-operator]] and [[def-bounded-linear-operator]], but the
definition above fixes the continuity of $J$ in advance. On this page the
continuity of every Sobolev inclusion is verified separately, through the
corresponding Sobolev embedding theorem.

derivations.claim: If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)=L^2(\Omega)=\{0\}$ and the conclusion holds. Assume $\Omega\ne\varnothing$. First consider $d=1$. Choose a bounded open interval $I=(a,b)$ with $\overline\Omega\subset I$ and let $L=b-a$. By [F4] and the closure definition [F8], each $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ has zero extension $E_0v|_I\in W_0^{1,p}(I)$: choose $\varphi_m\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ converging to $v$ in $W^{1,p}$ and extend each by zero into $C_c^\infty(I)$. Countable Choice selects this approximating sequence. For every such smooth extension $\varphi_m$, [F6] gives $|\varphi_m(x)-\varphi_m(y)|\le |x-y|^{1-1/p}\|\varphi_m'\|_{L^p(I)}$ and $\|\varphi_m\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}\le L^{1-1/p}\|\varphi_m'\|_{L^p(I)}$, because it vanishes near both endpoints. Applying the second inequality to differences shows that $(\varphi_m)$ is uniformly Cauchy; its continuous uniform limit $w$ represents $E_0v|_I$ since $\varphi_m\to E_0v$ in $L^p(I)$. For every $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(I)$, uniform convergence and $\varphi_m'\to E_0(v')$ in $L^p(I)$ give $\int_Iw\zeta'=-\int_IE_0(v')\zeta$. Thus $w'=E_0(v')$ weakly and [F4] gives $\|w'\|_{L^p(I)}=\|v'\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$. Passing to the limit in the two displayed inequalities gives the same Hölder and supremum bounds for $w$.

Now let $d\ge2$. Put $s_0=\max(1,2d/(d+2))$ and $s_1=\min(p,d)$. The strict hypothesis gives $s_0<s_1$; set $r=(s_0+s_1)/2$. Then $1<r<p$, $r<d$, and $2<r^*=dr/(d-r)$. By finite-measure Hölder [F3], $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow W_0^{1,r}(\Omega)$ continuously: the function and gradient $L^r$ norms are bounded by their $L^p$ norms, and a $C_c^\infty$ approximating sequence in $W^{1,p}$ also converges in $W^{1,r}$. Therefore [F1] gives compactness of $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)\to L^2(\Omega)$.

For a bounded sequence $(v_j)$ in $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$, the representatives $w_j$ from step 1.1 are uniformly bounded by $L^{1-1/p}\sup_j\|
abla v_j\|_p$ and share the modulus $|w_j(x)-w_j(y)|\le |x-y|^{1-1/p}\sup_j\|
abla v_j\|_p$. Arzelà–Ascoli [F7] gives a uniformly convergent subsequence on the fixed compact interval $[a,b]$. Its restrictions converge in $L^2(\Omega)$ by [F5], proving compactness. For each $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ the same supremum estimate gives $\|v\|_2\le |\Omega|^{1/2}L^{1-1/p}\|
abla v\|_p\le L^{3/2-1/p}\|
abla v\|_p$, proving continuity.

In the $d\ge2$ branch, for $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$, [F2] and [F3] yield the continuous estimate $\|v\|_2\le |\Omega|^{1/2-1/r^*}\|v\|_{r^*}\le C|\Omega|^{1/2-1/r^*+1/r-1/p}\|\nabla v\|_p$, using the Sobolev inequality [F2] with exponent $r$. Thus the inclusion is continuous on the $W_0^{1,p}$ norm. Finally [F5] and the closure definition [F8] give $C_c^\infty(\Omega)\subset W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ dense in $L^2(\Omega)$. The preceding arguments prove the complete $d=1$ and $d\ge2$ branches; [F9] then gives the claimed compact embedding in its continuous/sequential sense.

citations.quote:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then

$$\|\tau_h f-f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(h \to 0).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that

derivations.claim: Let $s(t)=\sum_{j=1}^m x_j\mathbf1_{E_j}(t)$ be a simple function with disjoint measurable $E_j$. Extend it by zero to $\mathbb R$. For an interval partition $\mathcal P$, let $P_\mathcal P f$ be the average of $f$ on each cell $I$. By [F4], $\|\,|I|^{-1}\int_I f\|_X\le |I|^{-1}\int_I\|f\|_X$. For $p>1$, scalar Hölder gives $|I|\|\,|I|^{-1}\int_I f\|_X^p\le\int_I\|f\|_X^p$; for $p=1$ the first inequality gives the same assertion directly. Summing proves contraction on $L^p$. To justify density for arbitrary completed Lebesgue level sets, write $E=B\cup N$ with $B$ Borel and $N$ contained in a Borel null set $Z$ by [F3], after intersecting all sets with $(0,T)$. The Borel set $B\cup Z$ differs from $E$ by a null set. Choose an open superset $O$ with excess less than $\eta$. The bounded open set $O\cap(0,T)$ is the union of the countably many rational-endpoint open intervals contained in it. Enumerate those intervals, and let $J_m$ be their first $m$ unions. By continuity from below [F3], $|(O\cap(0,T))\setminus J_m|\to0$. Thus a finite union of intervals differs from $E$ in measure by less than $2\eta$ for large $m$. Round the finitely many endpoints by continuous linear ramps, whose error is supported in intervals of arbitrarily small total length. It follows that continuous $X$-valued functions are dense in $L^p(0,T;X)$ by applying this construction to the finitely many level sets of a simple approximation [F1]. For continuous $g$, uniform continuity gives $\|P_\mathcal P g-g\|_{L^p}\le T^{1/p}\sup_{|s-t|\le\max|I|}\|g(s)-g(t)\|_X\to0$. Contraction now yields $\|P_\mathcal P f-f\|_{L^p}\le2\|f-g\|_{L^p}+\|P_\mathcal P g-g\|_{L^p}$, proving the averages assertion.

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a simple $s$ with $\|f-s\|_{L^p(0,T;X)}<\varepsilon/3$ by [F1]. Extend both functions by zero outside $(0,T)$. Translation is an isometry of the whole-line Bochner norm because it preserves Lebesgue measure; step 1.1 therefore gives, for all sufficiently small $h$, $\|f(\cdot-h)-f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R;X)}\le2\|f-s\|_{L^p}+\|s(\cdot-h)-s\|_{L^p}<\varepsilon$. Restriction to compact subintervals proves the translation assertion.

Extend $f$ by zero to $\mathbb R$ and use the kernels from [F5]. Replacing the measurable level sets of simple approximants by Borel representatives modulo null sets gives a Borel version by [F3]; composing the simple approximants with $s\mapsto t-s$ shows the Bochner integrand is strongly measurable in $s$. Its $L^p(\mathbb R)$ section norm is at most $2\rho_\delta(s)\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R;X)}$ by translation invariance and Minkowski. Scalar integral Minkowski [F4] makes the $s$-integral of this norm finite in $L^p$, so the convolution is defined for a.e. $t$; by linearity of the defining simple-function limit and $\int\rho_\delta=1$, $\rho_\delta*f(t)-f(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}\rho_\delta(s)(f(t-s)-f(t))\,ds$ there.
