Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

$W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ formula from
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] is independent of the representatives
of its Sobolev and derivative classes and defines a norm: it is finite,
absolutely homogeneous, subadditive, and zero exactly on the zero $L^p$ class.
This holds at $p=1$ and $p=\infty$, and when $k=0$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the only class is zero and the formula is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with
$n\ge1$, and let all functions below be real- or complex-valued classes in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. Weak differentiation is complex-linear wherever
the derivatives exist: if $v_j=D^\alpha u_j$ weakly for $j=1,2$ and

$$av_1+bv_2=D^\alpha(au_1+bu_2)\quad\text{weakly}.$$

$$v=D^\alpha u,\qquad w=D^\beta u$$

   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC, and HB.  A real or complex Banach space $X$
is reflexive if and only if every norm-bounded sequence in $X$ has a
subsequence that converges weakly to a point of $X$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

Let $A$ be at most countable ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then
$B$ is at most countable.

The proof establishes the sharper statement about subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ from
which this follows: **a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is finite if it is
bounded above, and countably infinite if it is not.**

**No choice principle is used.** This is the point of the lemma rather than a
footnote to it. The enumeration of an unbounded $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is built
by always taking the *least* element of $S$ above the previous one, and the least
element of a nonempty set of naturals is canonical
([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): it is determined by $S$, not selected from it.
Replacing "least" by "some" would turn the construction into an appeal to
dependent choice.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

The **ultrafilter extension principle** says that every filter on a set is contained in an ultrafilter on that set ([[def-ultrafilter]]).

It is also called the **ultrafilter lemma** and is equivalent over ZF to the Boolean prime ideal theorem, abbreviated BPI. Items below write **assume UL/BPI** precisely when they use this extension principle; they do not thereby assume the full axiom of choice.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

In ZF, the Axiom of Dependent Choice implies the Axiom of Countable Choice:
every at most countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-choice-function]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Let $D$ be the countable rational box-step dense family in [F4]. Zero extension embeds $L^p(\Omega)$ isometrically in $L^p(\mathbb R^d)$. Given $g\in L^p(\Omega)$, choose $s\in D$ approximating its zero extension $\widetilde g$; then $\|s|_\Omega-g\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le\|s-\widetilde g\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}$. Thus the restrictions of $D$ are countable and dense in $L^p(\Omega)$. Their finite products give a countable dense subset of $Y$; balls centered there with rational radii form a countable base by [F12].

Let $(u_j)$ be Cauchy in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$. By [F1], the coordinate sequences $(u_j)$ and $(\partial_i u_j)$ are Cauchy in $L^p(\Omega)$ for each $i$. Countable Choice is available by [A1], so [F6] gives limits $u,g_i\in L^p(\Omega)$. Fix $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with compact support $K$. By [F10], $K$ has finite measure and $\varphi,\partial_i\varphi$ are bounded there; Hölder [F9] therefore lets both sides of $\int_\Omega u_j\partial_i\varphi=-\int_\Omega(\partial_i u_j)\varphi$ pass to the limits $u$ and $g_i$. Hence $g_i=\partial_i u$ weakly for each $i$, so $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ and $u_j\to u$ in its norm by coordinate convergence. Thus $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is Banach.

Each factor of $Y$ is Banach by [F6], so the finite product is Banach for its maximum norm by [F7]. Let $(y_j)$ be a bounded sequence in $Y$. Its finitely many coordinate sequences are bounded in $L^p(\Omega)$; by [F8] and the bounded-sequence criterion [F11], successive subsequence extractions give one subsequence weakly convergent in every coordinate. Every bounded linear functional on $Y$ is the sum of its restrictions to the coordinate factors, so this subsequence converges weakly in $Y$. Thus [F11] makes $Y$ reflexive. By [F1], $\Phi$ is a bounded linear isomorphism onto its image $S:=\Phi(W^{1,p}(\Omega))$. The image $S$ is closed in $Y$: a convergent sequence in $S$ has Cauchy preimages by the lower norm bound in [F1], and they converge by step 1.2. Hahn–Banach and [F3] make $S$ reflexive. The inverse isomorphism $\Phi^{-1}:S\to W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ preserves weak convergence, so [F11] shows that $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is reflexive.

By [F2], $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is a closed linear subspace of the reflexive Banach space $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ from step 2.1. Hahn–Banach and [F3] therefore make $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ reflexive and Banach with its inherited norm.

Let $S_0=\Phi(W_0^{1,p}(\Omega))\subseteq Y$. The countable base from step 1.1 restricts to a countable base of $S_0$. By [A1], Countable Choice selects one point from each nonempty member of this relative base; the resulting countable set meets every nonempty relatively open set and is dense in $S_0$. Since $\Phi$ is an isomorphism with equivalent norms by [F1], $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is separable by [F5].
Steps 3.1 and 4.1 establish that $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is a separable reflexive real Banach space with its inherited norm, as claimed.

citations.quote:
Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]). Its **partial sums** are the unique sequence $(s_n)$ in $[0,+\infty]$ satisfying

$$s_0=0,\qquad s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n.$$

To apply [[thm-recursion]] with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$. Recursion gives a unique state sequence; induction makes its first coordinate $n$, and its second coordinates are exactly the unique $(s_n)$ satisfying the displayed recurrence. Addition of two nonnegative extended reals is always defined, including when either is $+\infty$. The sequence $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing, and its **nonnegative extended sum** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n\in[0,+\infty],$$

whose existence follows from completeness of the extended real line ([[lem-extended-reals-complete]]). More generally, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$\sum_{k\ge m}a_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{m+j}.$$

Finite sums use the same recursion: $\sum_{k<n}a_k=s_n$, so the empty sum at $n=0$ is $0$. A double sum such as $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}$ means that the inner nonnegative extended sum is formed first and the resulting nonnegative extended sequence is then summed.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The Cauchy sequence has a subsequence $(f_k)$ with $\|f_{k+1}-f_k\|_{L^p(X)}\le2^{-k}$ for $k\ge1$, by recursively taking the least eligible indices. Countable Choice [A1] selects strongly measurable representatives for these classes. Put $g_N(t)=\sum_{k=1}^N\|f_{k+1}(t)-f_k(t)\|_X$. By [F3], $g_N$ is measurable; Minkowski [F4] gives $\|g_N\|_{L^p}\le\sum_{k=1}^N2^{-k}\le1$. Monotone convergence [F5] gives $g(t)=\sum_{k\ge1}\|f_{k+1}(t)-f_k(t)\|_X$ with $\int g^p\le1$. Thus $g<\infty$ almost everywhere: for $A=\{g=\infty\}$, $M^p\mathbf1_A\le g^p$ for every $M>0$, and [F6] gives $M^p\mu(A)\le1$, forcing $\mu(A)=0$.

Outside the null set where $g=\infty$, the sequence $f_k(t)$ is Cauchy in $X$ and converges to $f(t)\in X$ by [F1]; set $f=0$ on that null set. For each $k$, choose a simple sequence $s_{k,m}\to f_k$ almost everywhere, as supplied by [F2] and [A1]. The sets $E_{k,m}=\{t:\|s_{k,m}(t)-f_k(t)\|_X>2^{-k}\}$ are measurable by [F3], and their indicators tend to zero almost everywhere as $m\to\infty$. Dominated convergence [F6] on the finite interval [F8] lets Countable Choice [A1] select $m_k$ with $\mu(E_{k,m_k})\le2^{-k}$. By [F7], the set $N=\bigcap_{j\ge1}\bigcup_{k\ge j}E_{k,m_k}$ has measure at most $\sum_{k\ge j}2^{-k}\le2^{1-j}$ for every $j$, hence is null. Outside $N$ and the previous null set, $s_{k,m_k}(t)\to f(t)$, so $f$ is strongly measurable by [F2]. Also $\|f-f_1\|_X\le g$ almost everywhere; [F6] makes this difference $L^p$, and Minkowski [F4] gives $f\in L^p$. For each $N$, $\|f(t)-f_N(t)\|_X\le\sum_{k\ge N}\|f_{k+1}(t)-f_k(t)\|_X\to0$ and is bounded by $g(t)$. Dominated convergence [F6] gives $\|f-f_N\|_{L^p(X)}\to0$.

The original sequence is Cauchy and has the subsequence $f_N\to f$; given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ with $\|f_N-f\|_{L^p(X)}<\varepsilon/2$ and then take the original index sufficiently far out that its distance to $f_N$ is below $\varepsilon/2$. The triangle inequality [F4] proves convergence of the entire sequence to $f$, so $L^p(0,T;X)$ is complete.

derivations.claim: Suppose, for contradiction, that $F$ has no zero in $\overline B_R(0)$. Then $F(x)\ne0$ there, and $G(x):=-R\,F(x)/|F(x)|$ is a continuous map $\overline B_R(0)\to\overline B_R(0)$ whose values all lie on the sphere. After rescaling the ball to the unit ball, [F1] gives a fixed point $x=G(x)$.

Since $G(x)$ lies on the sphere, $|x|=R$. The fixed-point equation gives $F(x)\cdot x=F(x)\cdot(-R F(x)/|F(x)|)=-R|F(x)|<0$, contradicting the assumed positive boundary pairing. Thus $F$ has a zero in the closed ball.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
$\widehat S_d$ be the reference simplex, let $\widehat P$ be a finite
dimensional $\mathbb K$-space of polynomial functions on it, let
$\widehat F$ be any facet, and let integer $m\ge0$. For $1\le p,q\le\infty$ there is a finite
constant $C$ such that
$$|v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat S_d)}+\|v\|_{L^p(\widehat F)}\le C\|v\|_{L^q(\widehat S_d)}\qquad(v\in\widehat P).$$
For every pair of integers $0\le m\le\ell$, there is also a finite
constant $C$ such that
$$|v|_{W^{\ell,p}(\widehat S_d)} \le C|v|_{W^{m,q}(\widehat S_d)}\qquad(v\in\widehat P).$$
For finitely many facets, one constant works for all of them. In particular,
every linear degree-of-freedom functional on $\widehat P$ is bounded with
respect to the $L^q(\widehat S_d)$ norm.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: On a $d\ge2$ reference simplex with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d$, take the nodes $(\alpha_0/k,\ldots,\alpha_d/k)$ for nonnegative integers $\alpha_j$ with $\sum_j\alpha_j=k$. They are unisolvent for $\mathbb P_k$. Indeed, use induction on $d+k$, with the zero-dimensional constant case and the degree-one vertex case as bases. For $k\ge2$, restriction to the face $\lambda_0=0$ vanishes identically by the dimension induction, so the polynomial is $\lambda_0 R$ with $\deg R\le k-1$. At nodes with $\alpha_0\ge1$, the affine change $\lambda_0=(1+(k-1)\mu_0)/k$ and $\lambda_j=(k-1)\mu_j/k$ for $j\ge1$ identifies the remaining nodes with the degree-$(k-1)$ barycentric lattice. The induction makes $R$ vanish at every node of that lattice, hence $R=0$. The number of barycentric nodes is $\binom{k+d}{d}$ by placing $d$ separators among $k$ stars; this equals the number of degree-at-most-$k$ monomials in $d$ variables, so it is $\dim\mathbb P_k$ and the unisolvent values define a basis. In $d=1$, the equally spaced $k+1$ nodes are unisolvent because a nonzero degree-$k$ polynomial has at most $k$ roots. On a shared face the two cells have the same face nodes; unisolvence of the face restriction makes their polynomial traces agree when the shared nodal values agree. The same face-node unisolvence shows that zero nodal coefficients on a boundary facet give its zero polynomial trace; in $d=1$ the boundary facets are the zero-valued endpoints. Unisolvence also means that local nodal interpolation reproduces every polynomial in $\mathbb P_k$, so the local basis sums to one and reproduces affine polynomials. Thus the constructed nodal functions are conforming and have the declared zero boundary values.

If $\delta_h(i,j)\le m$, a path of $m$ common-cell links gives $|z_i-z_j|\le mh$. Any cell containing such a node lies in $B(z_i,(m+1)h)$. In $d\ge2$, quasi-uniformity and shape regularity give $\rho_K\ge\theta h/\sigma$; each cell therefore contains an axis-parallel open cube of side $2\theta h/(\sigma\sqrt d)$ inside an inscribed ball. These cubes are disjoint and lie in the box $(z_i-(m+2)h,z_i+(m+2)h)^d$. By [F4], each has measure at least $(2\theta h/(\sigma\sqrt d))^d$ and the outer box has measure $(2(m+2)h)^d$, so additivity and monotonicity bound the number of such cells by $C(m+1)^d$. In $d=1$, the intervals lie in an interval of length $2(m+1)h$ and have lengths at least $\theta h$, giving the same cell bound. Each cell contains a fixed number $N(d,k)$ of nodes, hence $$\#\{j:\delta_h(i,j)\le m\}\le C(d,k)(m+1)^d.$$ The same packing bound shows that the number of cells incident to any fixed node is uniformly bounded, since all such cells lie in $B(z_i,h)$.

On each reference cell, [F2] bounds the $L^r$ norm above and below by the $\ell^r$ norm of the finitely many nodal coefficients; it also bounds the reference gradient norm above by that coefficient norm. Affine scaling then gives, for $1\le r<\infty$, $$ \Big\|\sum_{i\in I(K)}c_i\phi_i\Big\|_{L^r(K)}^r\asymp h_K^d\sum_{i\in I(K)}|c_i|^r, \qquad \Big\|\nabla\sum_{i\in I(K)}c_i\phi_i\Big\|_{L^r(K)} \le C h_K^{d/r-1}\|c\|_{\ell^r(I(K))}. $$ For $r=\infty$ replace the first factor $h_K^{d/r}$ by $1$. The same statements follow on an interval from $x=a+h_K t$ and the fixed one-dimensional nodal basis. Since $\theta h\le h_K\le h$, all cell scales are uniform in $h$.

For finite $r$, sum the local $L^r$ equivalence in step 2.1 over all cells. Each cell contains a fixed number $N(d,k)$ of nodes, and each global node is incident to uniformly many cells by the packing bound in step 1.2 (in $d=1$ at most two intervals meet at a node). Thus each global coefficient occurs between one and a uniformly bounded number of times, giving the asserted global lower and upper $\ell^r$ scaling. Taking maxima of local polynomial norm equivalences gives the $r=\infty$ scaling.

The interior-node mass matrix is symmetric positive definite because $c^TMc=\|\sum_i c_i\phi_i\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$, which is positive for every nonzero coefficient vector by the lower scaling in step 3.1. Taking $r=2$ there shows $a\|c\|_2^2\le c^TA_hc\le b\|c\|_2^2$ for positive constants independent of the mesh.

Put $\beta=2b$ and $B=I-A_h/\beta$. By step 4.1 and [F3], $\|B\|_{2\to2}\le q:=1-a/(2b)<1$. The matrix $A_h$ has zero $ij$ entry unless $i=j$ or $i,j$ occur in a common cell. Consequently $(B^n)_{ij}=0$ for $n<\delta_h(i,j)$, since a nonzero product of $n$ entries would give a graph path of length at most $n$. The norm-convergent Neumann series gives $$ A_h^{-1}=\beta^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^\infty B^n, \qquad |(A_h^{-1})_{ij}|\le\beta^{-1}\sum_{n\ge\delta_h(i,j)}q^n =\frac{q^{\delta_h(i,j)}}{\beta(1-q)}. $$ If $\delta_h(i,j)=\infty$, every summand is zero and the inverse entry is zero.

Grouping the entry bound of step 5.1 by graph distance and applying the ball count of step 1.2 gives each absolute row sum at most $C\sum_{m\ge0}(m+1)^d q^m<\infty$; the series converges by the ratio test because its term ratio tends to $q<1$. Symmetry of $A_h^{-1}$ gives the same column bound. These constants do not depend on the number of cells.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $0<T<\infty$, and $1\le p<\infty$. For
$f\in L^p(0,T;X)$, translations are continuous in $L^p$ on every compact
subinterval of $(0,T)$. Convolution with a scalar smooth approximate identity
therefore converges to $f$ in $L^p$ on such subintervals. If $\mathcal P_k$
are interval partitions of $[0,T]$ with maximum cell length tending to zero,
the piecewise-constant interval averages of $f$ converge to $f$ in
$L^p(0,T;X)$.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Fix a compact interval $K\subset(0,T)$ and a smooth unit-mass kernel $\rho_\epsilon$ supported in $(-\epsilon,\epsilon)$, with $\epsilon<\operatorname{dist}(K,\{0,T\})$. Set $g=u'$ and $u_\epsilon(t)=\int_0^T\rho_\epsilon(t-r)u(r)\,dr$. This is smooth in $V$: difference quotients of the kernel and each of its derivatives converge uniformly on the compact integration region, and multiplying their uniform error by $\|u\|_{L^1(V)}<\infty$ bounds the error in the differentiated Bochner integral. For $v\in V$, use the scalar test $r\mapsto\rho_\epsilon(t-r)$ in [F1]; since its derivative is $-\rho_\epsilon'(t-r)$, this gives $$\langle Ji\dot u_\epsilon(t),v\rangle =\int_0^T\rho_\epsilon'(t-r)(iu(r),iv)_H\,dr =\int_0^T\rho_\epsilon(t-r)\langle g(r),v\rangle\,dr.$$ Thus the pivot derivative $u_\epsilon':=Ji\dot u_\epsilon$ equals $\rho_\epsilon*g$ in $V^*$. The ordinary $H$ product rule now yields $$\frac{d}{dt}\frac12\|iu_\epsilon(t)\|_H^2 =\langle u_\epsilon'(t),u_\epsilon(t)\rangle.$$ Applying [F2] separately with $(X,r)=(V,p)$ and $(V^*,p')$ proves $u_\epsilon\to u$ in $L^p(K;V)$ and $u_\epsilon'\to u'$ in $L^{p'}(K;V^*)$. Below, $V$-valued functions in $H$ expressions are identified with their images under $i$.

For two small radii $\epsilon,\delta$, put $w=u_\epsilon-u_\delta$ on a fixed nondegenerate compact interval $K\subset(0,T)$. Continuity gives a time $s\in K$ with $\|w(s)\|_H^p\le |K|^{-1}\|w\|_{L^p(K;H)}^p$: otherwise integration contradicts the definition of that norm. Apply the smooth energy identity of step 1.1 to the difference $w$ and integrate between $s$ and any $t\in K$. Hölder [F4] yields $$\sup_{t\in K}\|w(t)\|_H^2 \le |K|^{-2/p}\|w\|_{L^p(K;H)}^2+2\|w'\|_{L^{p'}(K;V^*)}\|w\|_{L^p(K;V)}\longrightarrow0.$$ Indeed [F2] makes both $w$ and $w'$ tend to zero in their indicated norms, and the continuous inclusion [F3] controls the $H$-valued $L^p$ norm. This holds for every $p>1$ without a prior $L^\infty(H)$ bound. Thus the mollifications are uniformly Cauchy in $H$ on $K$.

Completeness of $H$ gives a uniform limit in $C(K;H)$, which agrees almost everywhere with $u$ because $u_\epsilon\to u$ in $L^p(K;H)$. The limits agree on overlapping compact intervals, so they define $u\in C((0,T);H)$. Integrate step 1.1 between arbitrary $s,t\in K$. Uniform convergence passes the endpoint norms to those of $u$, while $$\|\langle u_\epsilon',u_\epsilon\rangle-\langle u',u\rangle\|_{L^1(K)} \le\|u_\epsilon'-u'\|_{L^{p'}(V^*)}\|u_\epsilon\|_{L^p(V)} +\|u'\|_{L^{p'}(V^*)}\|u_\epsilon-u\|_{L^p(V)}\to0.$$ Hence for all $0<s\le t<T$, $$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle\,dr.$$

By [F4], the energy pairing is in $L^1(0,T)$. The identity in step 3.1 therefore shows that $\|u(t)\|_H^2$ has finite limits as $t\downarrow0$ and $t\uparrow T$. For each fixed $v\in V$, the distributional derivative of $(u(t),iv)_H$ is $\langle u'(t),v\rangle\in L^1(0,T)$, so [F5] gives an absolutely continuous representative on $[0,T]$ agreeing with the interior pairing.

For $0<\delta<T$, choose a good time $s_\delta\in(0,\delta)$ with $u(s_\delta)\in V$ and $$\|u(s_\delta)\|_V^p \le\frac2\delta\int_0^\delta\|u(r)\|_V^p\,dr.$$ Such a time exists by averaging over $(0,\delta)$. For every interior $t\in(0,\delta)$, use step 3.1 for the two norm squares and [F5] for the scalar pairing against the fixed vector $u(s_\delta)\in V$. Subtracting twice that pairing identity gives $$\|u(t)-u(s_\delta)\|_H^2 =2\int_{s_\delta}^t\langle u'(r),u(r)-u(s_\delta)\rangle\,dr.$$ Hölder and the triangle inequality bound its absolute value by $$2\|u'\|_{L^{p'}(0,\delta;V^*)} \left(\|u\|_{L^p(0,\delta;V)} +\delta^{1/p}\|u(s_\delta)\|_V\right),$$ which tends to zero as $\delta\downarrow0$. The bound is uniform in $t\in(0,\delta)$, so $u(t)$ is Cauchy in $H$ as $t\downarrow0$ and has a strong limit there. The same argument on $(T-\delta,T)$ gives a strong limit at $T$. Thus $u$ extends to $C([0,T];H)$.

Let $s\downarrow0$ and $t\uparrow T$ in step 3.1. Strong endpoint continuity and integrability of $\langle u',u\rangle$ pass the identity to all $0\le s\le t\le T$. If two continuous representatives agree almost everywhere, their difference is continuous and vanishes on a dense subset, so it vanishes everywhere. This proves uniqueness and the claimed chain rule.

risk_review.notes: Read Proof 1.1–6.1 and all ten direct supplier interfaces. Convolution of the distributional scalar-test identity commutes with differentiation in V-star on interior intervals; differentiation under the smooth scalar kernel is justified by finite-interval integrability and the Bochner norm bound. Mollification converges both in Lp(V) and Lp-prime(V-star), and the H product rule gives the smooth energy equality. The averaging-time estimate proves uniform Cauchyness in H on compact subintervals for every p>1 without an assumed L-infinity bound. Holder passes the paired integrals. The scalar pairings lie in W11, so the exact scalar AC supplier applies under full AC. A good time s_delta has delta^(1/p)||u(s_delta)||V bounded by 2^(1/p)||u||Lp(0,delta;V); subtracting its scalar pairing identity from the norm identity gives a uniform small H oscillation, proving strong endpoint limits. Uniqueness follows from continuous representatives agreeing a.e. s=t and endpoint/zero cases give zero integrals. The mollification supplier Statement supplies convergence; commutation is the direct convolution-of-distribution identity, not an additional unsupported regularity premise. No current defect.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same field
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in the real case from
[[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]], and suppose $X\subseteq Y$
with **continuous inclusion** $J:X\to Y$: there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|x\|_Y\le C\|x\|_X$ for every $x\in X$.

One says that $X$ is **compactly embedded** in $Y$, written $X\Subset Y$, when
the inclusion operator $J$ is a compact operator in the sense of
[[def-compact-linear-operator]]: the image under $J$ of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]).

**The sequential form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom of Dependent Choice
([[def-dependent-choice]]). Then $X\Subset Y$ if and only if every bounded
sequence $(x_j)$ in $X$ has a subsequence $(x_{j_k})$ converging in $Y$:
Indeed, compact closure gives the sequence conclusion by
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]]. Conversely, fix bounded $B\subseteq X$
and let $K=\overline{J(B)}$. For any sequence $(y_j)$ in $K$, Countable
Choice selects $b_j\in B$ with $\|y_j-b_j\|_Y<1/j$ (start at $j=1$);
a convergent subsequence of $(b_j)$ gives one of $(y_j)$ with the same limit,
which belongs to the closed set $K$. Thus $K$ is sequentially compact and
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] makes it compact. The empty case is
immediate. Both readings
of $X\Subset Y$ are used on this page; the second is the form in which the
compactness theorems below are stated.

Continuity of the inclusion is a separate hypothesis and is never inferred
from compactness: a compact operator is bounded by
[[def-compact-linear-operator]] and [[def-bounded-linear-operator]], but the
definition above fixes the continuity of $J$ in advance. On this page the
continuity of every Sobolev inclusion is verified separately, through the
corresponding Sobolev embedding theorem.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define

This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $0<T<\infty$, and $1\le p<\infty$. Then
$L^p(0,T;X)$, with norm
$\|f\|_{L^p(X)}=(\int_0^T\|f(t)\|_X^pdt)^{1/p}$, is complete under Countable
Choice.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Compactness in [F1] makes the image in $H$ of the $V$ unit ball totally bounded. Take a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net in $H$ for this image; since the range $i(V)$ is dense in $H$ by [F1], approximate each net point within $\varepsilon/2$ by a point of $i(V)$. Let $E\subset i(V)$ be the span of these finitely many points. The $H$-orthogonal projection $P_E$ is the best approximation from $E$, so $$\|(I-P_E)iv\|_H\le\varepsilon\|v\|_V\qquad(v\in V).$$ After orthonormalizing a basis, write $e_\ell=iv_\ell$ with $v_\ell\in V$.

For each $j,\ell$, put $a_{j\ell}(t)=(u_j(t),e_\ell)_H$. Its weak derivative is $\langle u_j'(t),v_\ell\rangle$ by [F2]. The uniform bounds and the continuous $V\to H$ inclusion give uniform $L^p$ bounds on $a_{j\ell}$ and uniform $L^q$ bounds on their derivatives. Since $T<\infty$, each coefficient is in $L^1(0,T)$ and its derivative is in $L^1(0,T)$; hence it is in scalar $W^{1,1}(0,T)$ and [F4] gives an absolutely continuous representative. For any such representative, some $s\in[0,T]$ has $|a_{j\ell}(s)|\le T^{-1/p}\|a_{j\ell}\|_{L^p}$; otherwise its $L^p$ norm would exceed that bound. Its total variation is at most $T^{1-1/q}\|a'_{j\ell}\|_{L^q}$ (with $T^{1-1/q}=T$ for $q=\infty$). Thus all coefficients are uniformly bounded, and Hölder gives the common modulus $$|a_{j\ell}(t)-a_{j\ell}(s)| \le C|t-s|^{1-1/q}$$ for $q<\infty$, with $C|t-s|$ for $q=\infty$.

The finitely many coefficient functions of $P_Eu_j$ are uniformly bounded and share the modulus from step 1.2. Choose a finite time grid so the modulus between adjacent grid points is below $\varepsilon$, and finite $\varepsilon$-nets for their bounded coefficient vectors at each grid point. The piecewise-linear interpolants of the finitely many rounded grid values form a finite family; each coefficient vector is within $2\varepsilon$ of its corresponding interpolant in the uniform norm, by the common modulus and the grid-point rounding error. Hence $\{P_Eu_j\}$ is totally bounded in $L^p(0,T;H)$.

By step 1.1, $$\|u_j-P_Eu_j\|_{L^p(0,T;H)} \le\varepsilon\|u_j\|_{L^p(0,T;V)}.$$ For each desired accuracy, choose $\varepsilon$ small and use step 2.1 to approximate the projected family by a finite net. The displayed remainder then shows that the full family is totally bounded in $L^p(0,T;H)$.

From total boundedness, [A1] selects a Cauchy subsequence; [F5] makes it convergent in $L^p(0,T;H)$. This proves relative compactness. If the $L^\infty(H)$ bound is $M$, pairwise differences have $L^\infty(H)$ norm at most $2M$. For $r<p$, finite-interval Hölder gives convergence in $L^r(H)$; for $r\ge p$, $$\|u_j-u_k\|_{L^r(H)}^r \le(2M)^{r-p}\|u_j-u_k\|_{L^p(H)}^p.$$ Completeness in each $L^r(H)$ then gives convergence for every finite $r$. These limits equal the $L^p(H)$ limit since both convergences imply convergence in measure, whose limit is unique up to almost-everywhere equality.
