citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], is a complete normed space over
$\mathbb K$.

Both endpoints $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, as is $k=0$, where the
assertion reduces to the completeness of $L^p$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the zero space and the assertion is trivial.
The Axiom of Choice is used only to derive Countable Choice for the two
published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative
selection inside the finitely many coordinate classes is finite and
choice-free.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Let $V$ be a Banach space and let $W\subseteq V$ be a closed linear subspace,
equipped with the restricted norm. Then $W$ is a Banach space.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.**  For every
measure space $(S,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and every $1<p<\infty$, both
$L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ and $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)$ are reflexive.

Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC, and HB.  A real or complex Banach space $X$
is reflexive if and only if every norm-bounded sequence in $X$ has a
subsequence that converges weakly to a point of $X$.

Let $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. A [[def-banach-space|Banach space]] $X$ is **reflexive** if its canonical map $J_X:X\to X^{**}$ from [[def-canonical-map-into-the-bidual]] is surjective. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), [[thm-canonical-bidual-map-is-an-isometry]] shows that this map is already an isometric embedding. Surjectivity means that every bounded linear functional on $X^*$ is evaluation at a vector of $X$. Merely specifying some isomorphism between $X$ and $X^{**}$ is not this definition.

**Assume HB.**  If $X$ is a real or complex reflexive Banach space and
$Y\subseteq X$ is a closed linear subspace with the restricted norm, then $Y$
is reflexive.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $0<T<\infty$, and $1\le p<\infty$. Then
$L^p(0,T;X)$, with norm
$\|f\|_{L^p(X)}=(\int_0^T\|f(t)\|_X^pdt)^{1/p}$, is complete under Countable
Choice.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a set and let
$\mathcal{F}_0$ be a filter on $X$ ([[def-filter]]). Then there is an ultrafilter
$\mathcal{U}$ on $X$ ([[def-ultrafilter]]) with $\mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{U}$.

The hypothesis is spent exactly once, through Zorn's lemma at step 4.1; the rest
of the argument is a theorem of ZF.

In particular, every set that carries a filter carries an ultrafilter. The proof
uses Zorn's lemma ([[thm-zorn]]) and therefore the Axiom of Choice. That some
choice principle is unavoidable here, if ZF is consistent, is an external
independence result, not proved in this library; see the remarks below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

The **ultrafilter extension principle** says that every filter on a set is contained in an ultrafilter on that set ([[def-ultrafilter]]).

It is also called the **ultrafilter lemma** and is equivalent over ZF to the Boolean prime ideal theorem, abbreviated BPI. Items below write **assume UL/BPI** precisely when they use this extension principle; they do not thereby assume the full axiom of choice.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

In ZF, the Axiom of Dependent Choice implies the Axiom of Countable Choice:
every at most countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-choice-function]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the closure definition in [F1] gives $V=\{0\}$, so every $u_j$ and its $H$ image is zero. The assumed strong $L^p(0,T;H)$ limit is therefore $u=0$ even when $H$ is nonzero; taking $U=0$ proves all conclusions.

Assume $\Omega\ne\varnothing$, put $Q=(0,T)\times\Omega$, and give $Y_0=(L^p(Q;\mathbb R))^d$ its maximum product norm. Each scalar coordinate space is reflexive Banach by [F2], so $Y_0$ is Banach: a Cauchy sequence converges in each coordinate and therefore in the maximum norm. A bounded sequence in $Y_0$ has bounded coordinates; apply [F3] successively to the $d$ coordinates to obtain one subsequence weakly converging in every coordinate. A bounded functional on $Y_0$ is the sum of its restrictions to the coordinate embeddings, so this is weak convergence in $Y_0$. The reverse implication in [F3] makes $Y_0$ reflexive. The Euclidean-vector norm of $Y=L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$ and the $Y_0$ product norm are equivalent because the Euclidean norm and the finite-dimensional $\ell^p$ norm on $\mathbb R^d$ are equivalent. Equivalent norms have the same continuous dual and weak convergence, so $Y$ is reflexive as well.

The gradient map $\Gamma:V\to L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$, $\Gamma v=\nabla v$, is an isometry for the chosen norm and has closed range: if $\nabla v_n$ converges in $L^p$, then $(v_n)$ is Cauchy in $V$; [F1] gives a limit in $V$ whose gradient is that limit.

For a finite-valued simple $U(t)=\sum_{\ell=1}^q\mathbf1_{E_\ell}(t)v_\ell$ with $v_\ell\in V$ and disjoint measurable $E_\ell$, apply [F6] to $\Gamma U(t)=\sum_\ell\mathbf1_{E_\ell}(t)\nabla v_\ell$. It supplies the space-time representative and equality of the Bochner and product $L^p$ norms. Simple-function density from [F6] and completeness of $Y$ from [F2] extend this map to an isometry $\Gamma_p:L^p(0,T;V)\to Y$. Its range $S$ is closed: if $\Gamma_pU_n$ converges in $Y$, the isometry makes $U_n$ Cauchy in $L^p(0,T;V)$; completeness [F5] gives $U_n\to U$, and then $\Gamma_pU_n\to\Gamma_pU$. Thus [F4] makes $S$ a reflexive Banach space.

The sequence $\Gamma_pu_j$ is bounded in $S$. Reflexivity of $S$ and [F3] give a weakly convergent subsequence with limit $G\in S$. Since $G=\Gamma_pU$ for some $U\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $\Gamma_p$ is an isometry, the same subsequence $u_j$ converges weakly to $U$ in $L^p(0,T;V)$; applying any bounded functional after $\Gamma_p^{-1}$ verifies this assertion.

The bounded inclusion in [F5] sends this weak convergence to weak convergence of the $H$-valued images to the image of $U$. By hypothesis those same images converge strongly, hence weakly, to $u$; Hahn–Banach separates distinct points, so $u$ is the image of $U$. Weak convergence in $S$ also implies weak convergence of gradients in $Y$, by restriction of $Y^*$ functionals to $S$.
The subsequence therefore has the asserted weak $L^p(V)$ limit, that limit has $H$ image $u$, and its space-time gradient is the weak limit $G=\nabla U$. This proves all conclusions.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same field
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in the real case from
[[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]], and suppose $X\subseteq Y$
with **continuous inclusion** $J:X\to Y$: there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|x\|_Y\le C\|x\|_X$ for every $x\in X$.

One says that $X$ is **compactly embedded** in $Y$, written $X\Subset Y$, when
the inclusion operator $J$ is a compact operator in the sense of
[[def-compact-linear-operator]]: the image under $J$ of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]).

**The sequential form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom of Dependent Choice
([[def-dependent-choice]]). Then $X\Subset Y$ if and only if every bounded
sequence $(x_j)$ in $X$ has a subsequence $(x_{j_k})$ converging in $Y$:
Indeed, compact closure gives the sequence conclusion by
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]]. Conversely, fix bounded $B\subseteq X$
and let $K=\overline{J(B)}$. For any sequence $(y_j)$ in $K$, Countable
Choice selects $b_j\in B$ with $\|y_j-b_j\|_Y<1/j$ (start at $j=1$);
a convergent subsequence of $(b_j)$ gives one of $(y_j)$ with the same limit,
which belongs to the closed set $K$. Thus $K$ is sequentially compact and
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] makes it compact. The empty case is
immediate. Both readings
of $X\Subset Y$ are used on this page; the second is the form in which the
compactness theorems below are stated.

Continuity of the inclusion is a separate hypothesis and is never inferred
from compactness: a compact operator is bounded by
[[def-compact-linear-operator]] and [[def-bounded-linear-operator]], but the
definition above fixes the continuity of $J$ in advance. On this page the
continuity of every Sobolev inclusion is verified separately, through the
corresponding Sobolev embedding theorem.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $0<T<\infty$, and $1\le p<\infty$. Then
$L^p(0,T;X)$, with norm
$\|f\|_{L^p(X)}=(\int_0^T\|f(t)\|_X^pdt)^{1/p}$, is complete under Countable
Choice.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: View each node in $V^*$ through the canonical embeddings $V\to H\to V^*$, and let $\widehat U_k$ be their continuous affine interpolation. On $I_n^k$ its derivative equals $D_k$. For $0\le s<T$ and $0<t<T-s$, the fundamental theorem for the affine function gives $\widehat U_k(t+s)-\widehat U_k(t)=\int_t^{t+s}D_k(r)\,dr$. Minkowski [F2] and translation invariance of the time integral yield $\|\widehat U_k(\cdot+s)-\widehat U_k\|_{L^q(0,T-s;V^*)} \le s\|D_k\|_{L^q(V^*)}$.

If $t\in I_n^k$, write $t=t_{n-1}^k+\theta\tau_n^k$ with $0<\theta\le1$. Then $\overline U_k(t)-\widehat U_k(t)=(1-\theta)(U_k^n-U_k^{n-1})$. Consequently, for $1<q<\infty$, $$\|\overline U_k-\widehat U_k\|_{L^q(V^*)}^q \le\sum_n\tau_n^k\|U_k^n-U_k^{n-1}\|_{V^*}^q \le\delta_k^q\|D_k\|_{L^q(V^*)}^q.$$ For $q=\infty$, the same pointwise identity gives $\|\overline U_k(t)-\widehat U_k(t)\|_{V^*}\le\delta_k\|D_k\|_{L^\infty(V^*)}$ and hence $\|\overline U_k-\widehat U_k\|_{L^\infty(V^*)}\le\delta_k\|D_k\|_{L^\infty(V^*)}$. Combining the corresponding estimate at $t$ and $t+s$ with step 1.1 proves the stated $(s+2\delta_k)$ translate bound in both cases.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By [F1], the image in $H$ of the $V$ unit ball has compact closure. Choose finitely many centers from that image forming an $\varepsilon$-net, let $E\subset i(V)$ be their span, and let $P_E$ be the $H$-orthogonal projection. Its best-approximation property gives $\|(I-P_E)iv\|_H\le\varepsilon\|v\|_V$ for every $v\in V$. Choose an $H$-orthonormal basis $e_j=iv_j$ of $E$. The scalar coefficients $a_{k,j}^n=(U_k^n,e_j)_H$ have weighted $L^p$ bounds from the $L^p(V)$ bound, and their total variation satisfies $$\sum_n|a_{k,j}^n-a_{k,j}^{n-1}| \le\|v_j\|_V\sum_n\tau_n^k\|D_k\|_{V^*} \le T^{1-1/q}\|v_j\|_V\|D_k\|_{L^q(V^*)}.$$ At least one node value is no larger than its weighted $L^p$ average, so the total-variation bound gives a uniform bound for every nodal coefficient.

The affine scalar interpolants of these finitely many coefficients are uniformly bounded; their derivatives are the pairings of $D_k$ with $v_j$, so their $L^q$ norms are uniformly bounded. Hölder gives a common modulus $C|t-s|^{1-1/q}$ (or $C|t-s|$ for $q=\infty$). Choose a finite time grid on which the modulus between adjacent points is at most $\varepsilon$, and finite $\varepsilon$-nets for the bounded coefficient vectors at each grid point. The piecewise-linear interpolants of the rounded grid values form a finite family within $2\varepsilon$ uniformly of every coefficient vector, so the projected affine family is totally bounded in $C([0,T];E)$. The maximum nodal jump is at most $\delta_k^{1-1/q}\|D_k\|_{L^q(V^*)}\|v_j\|_V$, so the projected piecewise-constant family differs from it uniformly by a quantity tending to zero. Thus $\{P_E\overline U_k\}$ is relatively compact in $L^p(H)$.

The projection remainder satisfies $\|\overline U_k-P_E\overline U_k\|_{L^p(H)} \le\varepsilon\|\overline U_k\|_{L^p(V)}$. Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, steps 3.1 and 4.1 show the full family is totally bounded in $L^p(H)$; [A1] extracts a Cauchy subsequence, which converges by [F3]. This proves relative compactness.

If the nodal values are uniformly bounded by $M$ in $H$, then $\|\overline U_k-\overline U_\ell\|_{L^\infty(H)}\le2M$. For $r<p$, finite-measure Hölder upgrades the strong $L^p(H)$ convergence to $L^r(H)$. For $r\ge p$, $\|\overline U_k-\overline U_\ell\|_{L^r(H)}^r \le(2M)^{r-p}\|\overline U_k-\overline U_\ell\|_{L^p(H)}^p$, so the same subsequence is Cauchy in every finite $L^r(H)$ and converges there by [F3]. These limits equal the strong $L^p(H)$ limit since both convergences imply convergence in measure, whose limit is unique up to almost-everywhere equality.

Its translate bound is s||D||q, and each endpoint interpolation error is at most delta||D||q, giving (s+2delta)||D||q on common intervals, also for q=infinity. Compact projection into a finite span of i(V) has epsilon||v||V error. Weighted coefficient Lp bounds plus sum tau||D|| and finite-time Holder bound all nodes, including the initial node. The maximum scalar jump <=delta^(1-1/q)||D||q||v_j||V vanishes without a minimum-step or step-ratio hypothesis. Projection remainder yields total boundedness in Lp(H). citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix a degree $k\ge1$. The mesh contract has two
branches. In dimensions $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded
polyhedral open set and let $\mathcal T_h$ be finite matching affine
simplex meshes as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], with
$h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}K$, $h\to0$,
$\operatorname{diam}K\le h$, $\operatorname{diam}K\ge\theta h$, and
$\operatorname{diam}K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for constants $\theta>0$ and
$\sigma<\infty$ independent of $h$. In dimension $d=1$, let $\Omega$ be a
bounded interval or a finite union of bounded intervals with pairwise
disjoint closures, and let $\mathcal T_h$ be finite interval partitions of
the component closures meeting only at whole endpoints, with interval lengths
between $\theta h$ and $h$ and $h\to0$.

For each mesh, place the degree-$k$ barycentric Lagrange nodes on every
$d\ge2$ simplex, or the $k+1$ equally spaced Lagrange nodes on every
$d=1$ interval, identify coincident nodes of matching cells, and impose zero
coefficients at every node on $\partial\Omega$. Let $V_h$ be the resulting
scalar continuous piecewise-$\mathbb P_k$ space. If $z_i$ are its interior
nodes, $\phi_i$ the global nodal basis, and
$$
M_{ij}=\int_\Omega\phi_i\phi_j,\qquad A_h=h^{-d}M,
$$
join distinct nodes when they occur in one cell and write $\delta_h(i,j)$ for
the shortest path length in this graph (with $\delta_h(i,j)=\infty$ when
there is no path, and use $q^\infty=0$). Whenever $V_h\ne\{0\}$, there are
$a,b,C>0$ and
$q\in(0,1)$, independent of the mesh, such that
$$\operatorname{spec}(A_h)\subset[a,b],\qquad |(A_h^{-1})_{ij}|\le Cq^{\delta_h(i,j)},\qquad \sup_i\sum_j|(A_h^{-1})_{ij}|+\sup_j\sum_i|(A_h^{-1})_{ij}|\le C.$$
For every cell $K$ and $1\le r<\infty$, if $c_K$ are its local nodal
coefficients and $w_h=\sum_{i\in I(K)}c_i\phi_i$ on $K$, then
$$c_r h_K^{d/r}\|c_K\|_{\ell^r}\le\|w_h\|_{L^r(K)}\le C_r h_K^{d/r}\|c_K\|_{\ell^r},\qquad \|\nabla w_h\|_{L^r(K)}\le C_rh_K^{d/r-1}\|c_K\|_{\ell^r}.$$
At $r=\infty$, omit $h_K^{d/r}$ in the function estimate and replace the
gradient bound by
$\|\nabla w_h\|_{L^\infty(K)}\le Ch_K^{-1}\|c_K\|_{\ell^\infty}$.
Summing gives, for all global nodal coefficients including zero boundary
coefficients,
$$c_r h^{d/r}\|c\|_{\ell^r}\le\Big\|\sum_i c_i\phi_i\Big\|_{L^r(\Omega)}\le C_r h^{d/r}\|c\|_{\ell^r}.$$
with the factor $h^{d/r}$ omitted at $r=\infty$. The empty interior-node
case is interpreted as $V_h=\{0\}$ and has no mass matrix to invert.

Assume Countable Choice. For any open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$n\ge1$, any $1\le p\le\infty$ and any
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, extension by zero
$$E_0u(x)=u(x)\ \ (x\in\Omega),\qquad E_0u(x)=0\ \ (x\notin\Omega),$$
acted on representatives, sends $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ linearly into
$W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$. For every $u\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
and every coordinate direction $i$, the class $D_i(E_0u)$ is the zero
extension of the class $D_iu$, and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|D_i(E_0u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded polyhedral open set with a finite matching
affine simplicial mesh, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $v$ be a real-valued
conforming piecewise polynomial whose polynomial trace vanishes on every boundary
facet. Then
$$v\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega),\qquad \|v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}.$$
Here $W^{1,p}_0$ is the norm closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$; no C1
trace characterization is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ be nonnegative with
$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$.
For $\varepsilon>0$ put $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$
and
$$\Omega_\varepsilon=\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)>\varepsilon\},\qquad\Omega_\varepsilon=\mathbb R^n\ \text{when }\Omega=\mathbb R^n .$$
Then $\rho_\varepsilon*u$ is defined and smooth on $\Omega_\varepsilon$, and
for every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le k$,
$$D^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*u)=\rho_\varepsilon*(D^\alpha u)\qquad\text{on }\Omega_\varepsilon,$$
as pointwise smooth functions for the constructed representatives and as
almost-everywhere classes. Here $D^\alpha u$ is extended by zero off $\Omega$
in the convolution.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Let $f,g \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$ be represented by Borel functions still
denoted $f,g$. For any complex-valued function $u$ on $\mathbb R^n$, use the
support convention

$$\operatorname{supp}(u):=\overline{\{x\in\mathbb R^n:u(x)\ne0\}},$$

which extends the real-valued definition of
[[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]. Define
$$ h(x) := \begin{cases} \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x-y)g(y)\,dy,& \text{if the integral exists},\\ 0,& \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$
Then

$$ \operatorname{supp}(h) \subseteq \overline{\operatorname{supp}(f) + \operatorname{supp}(g)}. $$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The coefficients define a linear map into the algebraic conforming piecewise-polynomial space: shared-face nodes coincide, so the face polynomials have identical nodal data and hence identical traces; all boundary coefficients are zero, so each boundary-facet polynomial vanishes. For $d\ge2$, [F3] therefore gives $V_h\subset W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$. For $d=1$, write a mesh function as $w$, let $M$ bound its finitely many piecewise derivatives, and extend it by zero. It is continuous at every mesh node and at every component endpoint. Integrating the derivative on each of the finitely many subintervals between two points using the fundamental theorem in [F6] shows $|w(x)-w(y)|\le M|x-y|$ on $\mathbb R$; integration by parts on those subintervals shows that the zero extension has the piecewise derivative as its weak derivative. Thus it is compactly supported in $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R)$.

Let $u=E_0v$. For a cell $K$, choose a cube $C_K$ of side $Rh$ centered at an interior point of $K$, where the fixed $R$ is large enough that $K$, every radius-$h$ ball centered at one of its nodes, and every radius-$2h$ ball centered at a point of $K$ lie in $C_K$. The cubes have bounded overlap: if $x\in C_K$, then $K\subset B(x,C_Rh)$; the cells have disjoint interiors and volume at least $c h^d$, so only uniformly many can meet that ball. For smooth $u$ on a cube $C$, the segment fundamental theorem, Hölder, Jensen's inequality, and a change of variables on the two ranges $t\le1/2$ and $t\ge1/2$ give $$ \|u-u_C\|_{L^p(C)}\le C_d\operatorname{diam}(C)\|
abla u\|_{L^p(C)}, \qquad u_C=|C|^{-1}\int_Cu. $$ Indeed, Jensen's inequality and $u(x)-u(y)=\int_0^1
abla u(tx+(1-t)y)\cdot(x-y)\,dt$ give $$ \|u-u_C\|_{L^p(C)}^p\le rac{\operatorname{diam}(C)^p}{|C|} \int_C\int_C\int_0^1|
abla u(tx+(1-t)y)|^p\,dt\,dy\,dx. $$ For $t\ge1/2$ change the $x$ variable, and for $t\le1/2$ change the $y$ variable; both inverse Jacobians are at most $2^d$ and the images stay in $C$. This proves the displayed Poincaré estimate. Since $u=E_0v$ is compactly supported in $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^d)$, [F6] approximates it by smooth functions in that norm, so the same cube estimate holds for $u$.

In the one-dimensional branch, for $x$ in a component interval choose the nearer endpoint; integrating the derivative from that endpoint by [F6] gives $|w(x)|\le M\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R\setminus\Omega)$. Because there are finitely many distinct endpoints, choose $\varepsilon$ smaller than one quarter of their minimum separation. Translate and rescale the bump from [F9] at each endpoint to obtain $\chi_{a,\varepsilon}$ equal to one within $\varepsilon$ of $a$ and zero outside distance $2\varepsilon$. The endpoint supports are disjoint; the product $\eta_\varepsilon=\prod_{a\in\partial\Omega}(1-\chi_{a,\varepsilon})$ is smooth, vanishes within distance $\varepsilon$ of each endpoint, equals one at distance at least $2\varepsilon$, and satisfies $|\eta_\varepsilon'|\le C/\varepsilon$. Thus $w-\eta_\varepsilon w$ and its weak derivative are supported in a boundary layer of measure $O_\Omega(\varepsilon)$ and bounded there by $C_\Omega M$. On each partition interval $\eta_\varepsilon w$ is smooth times polynomial, is continuous at nodes, and vanishes near component endpoints; integration by parts on the finitely many intervals cancels all interior endpoint terms. Its zero extension therefore belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R)$ with derivative $\eta_\varepsilon'w+ \eta_\varepsilon w'$ on the pieces. Hence $\eta_\varepsilon w\to w$ in $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R)$. Each cutoff product has compact support a positive distance from $\mathbb R\setminus\Omega$; convolving it with a sufficiently small mollifier gives a function in $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by [F4] and [F7], and the convolution converges in $W^{1,p}$ by [F4]. This proves $w\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ by [F8] and completes the range assertion in $d=1$.

If $K$ has no boundary node, put $c_K=u_{C_K}$. If it has a boundary node, put $c_K=0$. In $d\ge2$, compactness of the boundary gives a finite subcover of its Lipschitz graph charts; taking the largest chart Lipschitz constant and the smallest chart radius yields uniform $\eta,r_0>0$ such that each boundary point $z$ and $0<r\le r_0$ have an exterior cone sector in $B(z,r)$ of measure at least $\eta r^d$: in a chart $x_d>g(x')$ with Lipschitz constant $L$, the cone $x_d<g(z')-L|x'-z'|$ is exterior, and a fixed smaller cone has that volume. For sufficiently small $h$, a boundary node $z$ of $K$ therefore gives $|C_K\setminus\Omega|\ge\eta'|C_K|$. In $d=1$, at a boundary endpoint the exterior interval inside $C_K$ has a fixed positive fraction of its length; for finitely many separated components take $h$ smaller than their minimum gap divided by $2R$. In the boundary case $u=0$ on $C_K\setminus\Omega$, so $$ |u_{C_K}|\,|C_K\setminus\Omega|^{1/p} \le\|u-u_{C_K}\|_{L^p(C_K\setminus\Omega)}. $$ The cube estimate of step 1.2 then gives, in either case, $$ \|u-c_K\|_{L^p(C_K)}\le Ch\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(C_K)}. $$

Fix $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and let $\delta=\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{supp}\psi,\partial\Omega)>0$. For $h<\delta/2$, $S_h\psi$ is zero on every cell with a boundary node: every point of such a cell is within distance $h$ of the boundary, while the convolution samples only a radius-$h$ ball. Thus $Q_h\psi=0=S_h\psi$ on those cells. Every other cell has only interior nodes, so $Q_h\psi$ is the ordinary nodal interpolant of $S_h\psi$ there. Since $k\ge1$, this interpolant reproduces affine polynomials. Taylor's formula about a cell vertex and the local coefficient estimates in [F1] give $$ \|Q_h\psi-S_h\psi\|_{L^p(K)}\le Ch^2|K|^{1/p}\|D^2\psi\|_\infty, \qquad \|\nabla(Q_h\psi-S_h\psi)\|_{L^p(K)} \le Ch|K|^{1/p}\|D^2\psi\|_\infty. $$ The nonnegative unit-mass kernel gives $S_h\psi\to\psi$ in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ and $\|D^2S_h\psi\|_\infty\le\|D^2\psi\|_\infty$. Summing cell bounds proves $Q_h\psi\to\psi$ in $W^{1,p}$.

For each interior node $z$ of $K$, Hölder [F5] gives $$ |S_hv(z)-c_K|\le\|ho_h\|_{L^{p'}(\mathbb R^d)} \|u-c_K\|_{L^p(B(z,h))} \le Ch^{-d/p}\|u-c_K\|_{L^p(C_K)}. $$ At a boundary node both the coefficient and $c_K$ are zero in the boundary case. If $K$ has no boundary node, every local node is interior and the local nodal basis reproduces the constant $c_K$. Applying the local coefficient estimate of [F1] to the coefficients of $Q_hv-c_K$, and using step 2.2, gives $$ \|Q_hv-c_K\|_{L^p(K)}\le Ch\|
abla u\|_{L^p(C_K)},\qquad \|
abla Q_hv\|_{L^p(K)}\le C\|
abla u\|_{L^p(C_K)}. $$ The boundary-node case uses $c_K=0$; the no-boundary-node case uses $\sum_{z\in K}\phi_z=1$.

Since $v=u$ on $K$, step 2.2 and the first estimate of step 3.1 imply $$ \|v-Q_hv\|_{L^p(K)}\le Ch\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(C_K)}. $$ Raise this and the gradient estimate of step 3.1 to the $p$th power, sum over cells, and use the bounded overlap from step 1.2 and the norm preservation in [F2]. This proves both global estimates in the Statement. Also $\|Q_hw\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C\|w\|_{W^{1,p}}$ for every $w\in W_0^{1,p}$ and all sufficiently small $h$, by the gradient bound and $\|Q_hw\|_p\le\|w\|_p+Ch\|\nabla w\|_p$.

For arbitrary $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [F8] provides $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $\|v-\psi\|_{W^{1,p}}<\varepsilon$. The uniform bound in step 4.1 and the smooth convergence in step 2.3 imply $$ \limsup_{h\to0}\|Q_hv-v\|_{W^{1,p}} \le(C+1)\|v-\psi\|_{W^{1,p}}<(C+1)\varepsilon. $$ Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves strong convergence for every $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and
let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Put
$V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with norm
$\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$, $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. The Poincaré inequality makes this norm equivalent to the full
$W^{1,p}$ norm. [[lem-pe12-w0p-separable-reflexive]] gives separability and
reflexivity, while [[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] gives the dense
continuous compact inclusion $V\Subset H$; these are the hypotheses of the
evolution triple in [[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. The compact-inclusion result
uses the stated threshold also when $d=1$, where it reduces to $p>1$.

A measurable flux $a:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is an admissible
**coercive monotone diffusion flux of p-growth** if it is Carathéodory (for
each $\xi$, $x\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is measurable, and for almost every $x$,
$\xi\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is continuous), and there are constants $C<\infty$,
$\alpha>0$, nonnegative functions $g\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$ and
$h\in L^1(\Omega)$, and one
null set outside which, for all $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|a(x,\xi)|\le C\bigl(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}\bigr),\qquad a(x,\xi)\cdot\xi\ge\alpha|\xi|^p-h(x),$$
$$\bigl(a(x,\xi)-a(x,\eta)\bigr)\cdot(\xi-\eta)\ge0.$$
The induced operator $A:V\to V^*$ is
$$\langle A(v),w\rangle_{V^*,V} =\int_\Omega a(x,\nabla v(x))\cdot\nabla w(x)\,dx.$$
The growth bound and Hölder's inequality make this pairing finite and give
$\|A(v)\|_{V^*}\le C_1(\|g\|_{p'}+\|v\|_V^{p-1})$ for a constant $C_1$.
The finite-dimensional test-coordinate continuity used in the backward Euler
existence argument follows from the stated Carathéodory and growth conditions
by dominated convergence, as proved in
[[thm-pe12-backward-euler-galerkin-existence-energy]]. No additional global
operator-continuity hypothesis is imposed.

For $f\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, a weak evolution solution is a function
$u\in W_p(0,T;V)\cap L^\infty(0,T;H)$ with a continuous $H$ representative
such that $u'+A(u)=f$ in $L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$ and $u(0)=u_0\in H$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be Lebesgue measurable and let $f:\Omega\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a Caratheodory integrand: for every $(s,\xi)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ the map $x\mapsto f(x,s,\xi)$ is measurable ([[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]]), and for almost every $x\in\Omega$ the map $(s,\xi)\mapsto f(x,s,\xi)$ is continuous. If $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R^n$ are measurable, then $x\mapsto f(x,u(x),w(x))$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: Fix arbitrary $\eta\in L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$. By [F1]–[F3], monotonicity gives the finite nonnegative integrals $$0\le\int_Q(q_n-a(x,\eta))\cdot(\xi_n-\eta).$$ Expanding them and using the two weak convergences for the three terms linear in a weakly convergent factor, the limsup hypothesis yields $$0\le\int_Q(q-a(x,\eta))\cdot(\xi-\eta).$$ Indeed the expanded nonnegative sequence has limsup at most the displayed right-hand side, so that right-hand side cannot be negative.

Let $\zeta\in L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$ and $0<\varepsilon\le1$. Substitute $\eta=\xi+\varepsilon\zeta$ and $\eta=\xi-\varepsilon\zeta$ into step 1.1. After dividing by $\varepsilon$, the two inequalities give $$\int_Q(q-a(x,\xi+\varepsilon\zeta))\cdot\zeta\le0,\qquad \int_Q(q-a(x,\xi-\varepsilon\zeta))\cdot\zeta\ge0.$$ The fixed term $q\cdot\zeta$ is integrable by [F3]. For either sign, the flux term satisfies $$|a(x,\xi\pm\varepsilon\zeta)|\,|\zeta|\le C\bigl(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}+|\zeta|^{p-1}\bigr)|\zeta|,$$ which is integrable by [F3]; here $g(x)$ is viewed as constant in time and $Q$ has finite time length. Carathéodory continuity gives pointwise $a(x,\xi\pm\varepsilon\zeta)\to a(x,\xi)$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Dominated convergence [F4] on the flux term in both inequalities proves $\int_Q(q-a(x,\xi))\cdot\zeta=0$ for every $\zeta\in L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$.

Put $w=q-a(x,\xi)\in L^{p'}(Q;\mathbb R^d)$ and choose $\zeta=|w|^{p'-2}w$, defined as zero where $w=0$. Since $(p'-1)p=p'$, this $\zeta$ belongs to $L^p$, and step 2.1 gives $0=\int_Qw\cdot\zeta=\int_Q|w|^{p'}$. Thus $w=0$ almost everywhere, which is the claimed flux identification.

   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $p,q>1$ satisfy $1/p+1/q=1$. For $u,v\ge0$,
$$uv\le\frac{u^p}{p}+\frac{v^q}{q}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and
let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Put
$V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with norm
$\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$, $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. The Poincaré inequality makes this norm equivalent to the full
$W^{1,p}$ norm. [[lem-pe12-w0p-separable-reflexive]] gives separability and
reflexivity, while [[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] gives the dense
continuous compact inclusion $V\Subset H$; these are the hypotheses of the
evolution triple in [[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. The compact-inclusion result
uses the stated threshold also when $d=1$, where it reduces to $p>1$.

A measurable flux $a:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is an admissible
**coercive monotone diffusion flux of p-growth** if it is Carathéodory (for
each $\xi$, $x\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is measurable, and for almost every $x$,
$\xi\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is continuous), and there are constants $C<\infty$,
$\alpha>0$, nonnegative functions $g\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$ and
$h\in L^1(\Omega)$, and one
null set outside which, for all $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|a(x,\xi)|\le C\bigl(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}\bigr),\qquad a(x,\xi)\cdot\xi\ge\alpha|\xi|^p-h(x),$$
$$\bigl(a(x,\xi)-a(x,\eta)\bigr)\cdot(\xi-\eta)\ge0.$$
The induced operator $A:V\to V^*$ is
$$\langle A(v),w\rangle_{V^*,V} =\int_\Omega a(x,\nabla v(x))\cdot\nabla w(x)\,dx.$$
The growth bound and Hölder's inequality make this pairing finite and give
$\|A(v)\|_{V^*}\le C_1(\|g\|_{p'}+\|v\|_V^{p-1})$ for a constant $C_1$.
The finite-dimensional test-coordinate continuity used in the backward Euler
existence argument follows from the stated Carathéodory and growth conditions
by dominated convergence, as proved in
[[thm-pe12-backward-euler-galerkin-existence-energy]]. No additional global
operator-continuity hypothesis is imposed.

For $f\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, a weak evolution solution is a function
$u\in W_p(0,T;V)\cap L^\infty(0,T;H)$ with a continuous $H$ representative
such that $u'+A(u)=f$ in $L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$ and $u(0)=u_0\in H$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Set $e=u-v$. Subtracting the residual definitions gives $e'+A(u)-A(v)=R$ in $L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$. By [F1], testing this identity against $e\in L^p(0,T;V)$ is integrable by [F2], and for every $t$, $$\frac12\|e(t)\|_H^2-\frac12\|e(0)\|_H^2 +\int_0^t\langle A(u)-A(v),e\rangle =\int_0^t\langle R,e\rangle.$$

Strong monotonicity bounds the left integral below by $\mu\int_0^t\|e\|_V^p$. Young's inequality [F3], applied to $(\mu p/2)^{1/p}a$ and $(\mu p/2)^{-1/p}b$, gives the scaled form $$ab\le\frac\mu2a^p+ \frac1{p'}\left(\frac2{\mu p}\right)^{1/(p-1)}b^{p'}$$ gives $|\langle R,e\rangle|\le\frac\mu2\|e\|_V^p+ C_{\mu,p}\|R\|_{V^*}^{p'}$. Integrating and absorbing the first term yields $$\frac12\|e(t)\|_H^2+\frac\mu2\int_0^t\|e\|_V^p \le\frac12\|e(0)\|_H^2+ C_{\mu,p}\|R\|_{L^{p'}(0,t;V^*)}^{p'}.$$ Multiplying by two proves the estimate. If $e(0)=0$ and $R=0$, the nonnegative left side vanishes for every $t$, hence $e(t)=0$ in $H$ and $e=0$ in $L^p(V)$.
