On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

derivations.claim: The product is a Hilbert space: if a sequence is Cauchy in the finite sum-of-squares norm, each edge coordinate is Cauchy in its $H^1$ norm and converges by [F1]; the finitely many coordinate limits form an element of the product and the sum of the finitely many squared errors tends to zero. The product inner product is the sum of the edge inner products.

For each edge $e$, choose $\epsilon_e=\ell_e/2$, which satisfies the hypothesis of [F2]. For either endpoint, [F2] then gives  $$\max\{|w_e(0)|^2,|w_e(\ell_e)|^2\}\le\frac{4}{\ell_e}\|w_e\|_{L^2(0,\ell_e)}^2+\ell_e\|w'_e\|_{L^2(0,\ell_e)}^2\le C_e\|w_e\|_{H^1(0,\ell_e)}^2,$$  where $C_e:=\max\{4/\ell_e,\ell_e\}<\infty$. Thus each endpoint evaluation is a bounded linear functional on its edge $H^1$ space. For every vertex, the difference of two incident endpoint evaluations is therefore continuous; its kernel is closed. Each anchor endpoint evaluation is also continuous and its zero set is closed. There are finitely many vertices, incidences, and anchors, so the intersection of these kernels, namely the trace-matching space and then $V_D$, is closed in the product.

A Cauchy sequence in either constrained space converges in the product by step 1.1. Continuity of every endpoint functional from step 1.2 passes all matching equalities and zero anchor values to the limit, so the limit remains in the same constrained space. The restricted edge-product inner product is positive definite and complete there. Hence both constrained spaces are Hilbert.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the cited one-dimensional
representative interface. A **finite metric graph**
$\Gamma=(V,E,\partial_-,\partial_+,\ell)$ consists of finite vertex and
edge sets $V,E$, endpoint maps $\partial_-,\partial_+:E\to V$, and edge
lengths $0<\ell_e<\infty$. Distinct edges with the same endpoints are
allowed, as are loop edges with $\partial_-e=\partial_+e$. Every vertex is
an endpoint of at least one edge. The two endpoint incidences $(e,-)$ and
$(e,+)$ remain distinct even for a loop. A graph path is a finite sequence
$z_0,e_1,z_1,\ldots,e_n,z_n$ with $n\ge0$ and
$\{\partial_-e_j,\partial_+e_j\}=
\{z_{j-1},z_j\}$ for every $j$; a loop permits $z_{j-1}=z_j$. Vertices in
the same connected edge component are those joined by such a path. Orient
each edge only to choose its coordinate $x_e\in[0,\ell_e]$, with $0$ at
$\partial_-e$ and $\ell_e$ at $\partial_+e$. For $z\in V$, let
$\mathcal I(z):=\{(e,-):\partial_-e=z\}\cup\{(e,+):\partial_+e=z\}$
be its finite set of endpoint incidences.
The edge-product spaces are

$$H:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}L^2(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R),\qquad \mathcal W:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}H^1(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R).$$

For $w_e\in H^1(0,\ell_e)$, its endpoint values mean the values of the unique
absolutely continuous representative supplied by
[[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].
The **trace-matching graph Sobolev space** is the subspace of $\mathcal W$
whose endpoint-incidence traces all agree at each vertex. For a designated
anchor set $D\subseteq V$, define the **anchored graph energy space**

$$V_D:=\{w\in\mathcal W:\ w_{\iota}=w_{\iota'}\text{ whenever }\iota,\iota'\in\mathcal I(v),\quad w_{\iota}=0\text{ for each }v\in D,\ \iota\in\mathcal I(v)\}.$$

We equip $H$ with the edge-sum $L^2$ inner product and $V_D$ with

$$\|w\|_{V_D}^2=\sum_{e\in E}\int_0^{\ell_e}(|w_e|^2+|w'_e|^2)\,dx_e.$$

No Kirchhoff derivative condition is built into $V_D$; that condition is a
natural boundary condition of the later weak diffusion form. The elliptic
and P1 error results below assume that $D$ meets every connected edge
component.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: If $E=\varnothing$, then $H=\{0\}$ and the inequality is $0\le0$. Otherwise fix an edge $e$ in a component containing an anchor. If $e$ is a loop, deleting its interior leaves the component connected because any path that traverses the loop can omit that closed excursion. If its endpoints are distinct, every original path that uses $e$ reaches one endpoint before traversing it; after deleting $e$, vertices are therefore connected to one of its two endpoints. Thus removing $e$ either leaves the component connected or separates it into two components, one containing each endpoint. In the connected case choose either endpoint; in the separated case choose the endpoint in the component containing an anchor. By [F3] there is a finite path from an anchor to that endpoint avoiding $e$. Deleting the portions between repeated vertices gives a simple path, so no edge is traversed twice. For a loop choose its tail incidence; otherwise use the incidence at the chosen endpoint. For any $x$ on $e$, append the segment from that incidence to $x$. The total length is at most $L_\Gamma$, and the common vertex traces agree along the path by [F1]. Since $w=0$ at the anchor, [F1] and [F2] imply $$|w_e(x)|^2\le L_\Gamma \sum_{a\text{ on the concatenated path}}\int_a|w'_a|^2 \le L_\Gamma\sum_{a\in E}\|w'_a\|_{L^2(a)}^2.$$

Integrate the pointwise bound of step 1.1 over every edge and sum. The total measure of the disjoint edge interiors is $\sum_e\ell_e=L_\Gamma$, so $$\|w\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}^2\le L_\Gamma^2\sum_{e\in E}\|w'_e\|_{L^2(e)}^2.$$ Taking nonnegative square roots proves the statement.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

derivations.claim: If $E=\varnothing$, both sides are empty sums and the identity is $0=0$. Otherwise fix an edge $e$ and first suppose $u_e$ is real-valued. By [F1] and [F4], $u'_e$ and $v_e$ have absolutely continuous representatives on $[0,\ell_e]$. They are bounded there. The product $u'_ev_e$ is absolutely continuous: for any disjoint intervals $[a_j,b_j]$, $$\sum_j|u'_e(b_j)v_e(b_j)-u'_e(a_j)v_e(a_j)| \le \|u'_e\|_\infty\sum_j|v_e(b_j)-v_e(a_j)| +\|v_e\|_\infty\sum_j|u'_e(b_j)-u'_e(a_j)|,$$ so the defining absolute-continuity condition follows from that of the two factors. At almost every point both derivatives exist, and [F3] gives $(u'_ev_e)'=u''_ev_e+u'_ev'_e$. Both terms are integrable because $u''_e,v'_e$ are integrable derivatives of absolutely continuous functions and $u'_e,v_e$ are bounded. Applying [F2] to the product therefore yields $$\int_0^{\ell_e}u'_ev'_e\,dx_e =-\int_0^{\ell_e}u''_ev_e\,dx_e +u'_e(\ell_e)v_e(\ell_e)-u'_e(0)v_e(0).$$ If $u_e$ is complex-valued, write the absolutely continuous representative $u'_e=p+iq$. By [F1], $p,q$ are real absolutely continuous functions with derivatives $\operatorname{Re}u''_e,\operatorname{Im}u''_e$ almost everywhere; these derivatives lie in $L^2$ since their absolute values are bounded by $|u''_e|$. The test function $v_e$ is real by definition of $V_D$. Apply the preceding product-rule and fundamental-theorem calculation separately to $pv_e$ and $qv_e$ and combine the two identities, using componentwise complex integration. This proves the same displayed identity for complex $u_e$. The endpoint terms are the head and tail outward derivatives paired with their traces.

Multiply the identity of step 1.1 by $\kappa_e$ and sum over the finite edge set. At each vertex, all endpoint-incidence values of $v$ equal the common trace $v(z)$ by definition of $V_D$; this includes both incidences of a loop. Regrouping the finite endpoint sum by vertices gives the displayed identity. If $z\in D$, then $v(z)=0$; if $z\notin D$, the stated Kirchhoff sum is zero. Hence the boundary contribution vanishes under those conditions.

$V=\{v_i:i<n\}=\{v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\}$ and ordered edges

incidence matrix** of $G$, where, for $i<n$ and $j<m$,

$$b_{ij}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }v_i\text{ is the head of }e_j,\\-1,&\text{if }v_i\text{ is the tail of }e_j,\\0,&\text{if }v_i\notin e_j.\end{cases}$$

simple graph has exactly two distinct endpoints. Different choices of

Choose an orientation of each edge and let $B\in\mathbb R^{V\times E}$ be

Dirichlet restriction $L_D$ is the principal submatrix $(L_C)_{I,I}$. The
finite weighted network diffusion equation is

$$M u'(t)+L_Du(t)=f(t),$$

where $u(t)\in\mathbb R^I$ and $f(t)\in\mathbb R^I$. If $D=\varnothing$,
this is the closed Neumann network equation. If the boundary values are
instead a nonzero vector $g(t)$, restriction of $L_C(u,g)$ to $I$ gives
$M u'+L_Du=f-(L_C)_{I,D}g$.

Laplacian by
[[thm-laplacian-is-the-oriented-incidence-product]]. Zero conductances are
allowed and remove those edges from the diffusion coupling; they do not remove
the vertices or masses.

derivations.claim: Reversing an edge orientation replaces its incidence column $b_e$ by $-b_e$, but the contribution $c_eb_eb_e^{\mathsf T}$ to $BCB^{\mathsf T}$ does not change. If $L_Dx=0$, step 1.1 gives a sum of nonnegative terms equal to $x^{\mathsf T}L_Dx=0$. For every $e\in E_+$ its endpoint difference must therefore be zero. Along every path in $G_+$, $\bar x$ has equal values at successive vertices, hence is constant on each positive-conductance component; it is zero on any such component meeting $D$ because $\bar x=0$ there. Conversely, if these componentwise conditions hold, every edge with $c_e>0$ has zero endpoint difference, while an edge with $c_e=0$ contributes zero regardless of its difference. At a directed network junction, let $n_{\rm in}$ edges carry nonnegative
incoming **mass fluxes** $q^{\rm in}_i$ into the junction, and let
$n_{\rm out}$ edges carry outgoing mass fluxes. A **conservative nonnegative
routing matrix** is a real matrix
$P\in\mathbb R^{n_{\rm out}\times n_{\rm in}}$ such that

$$P_{ji}\ge0,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^{n_{\rm out}}P_{ji}=1 \quad(1\le i\le n_{\rm in}).$$

It routes the incoming flux vector to
$q^{\rm out}=Pq^{\rm in}$. The column $i$ distributes the mass flux arriving
on incoming edge $i$ among the outgoing edges. The column-sum condition
stipulates no source or sink at the junction. It is a model condition on flux;
it does not assert that the densities on incident edges are equal.

derivations.claim: For every outgoing index $j$, $q^{\rm out}_j=\sum_iP_{ji}q^{\rm in}_i$ is a sum of nonnegative terms by [F1] and the assumption $q^{\rm in}\ge0$. Hence $q^{\rm out}\ge0$.

All sums are finite, so they may be interchanged: $$\sum_jq^{\rm out}_j =\sum_j\sum_iP_{ji}q^{\rm in}_i =\sum_i\left(\sum_jP_{ji}\right)q^{\rm in}_i =\sum_iq^{\rm in}_i,$$ where the final equality uses the unit column sums of [F1].

derivations.claim: Under the grounded condition, suppose $x\in\mathbb R^I$ and $x^{\mathsf T}L_Dx=0$. By [F1], the zero extension of $x$ is constant on each positive-conductance component and zero on each such component meeting $D$. The grounded condition says every component containing a free vertex meets $D$, so every free coordinate is zero. Thus $L_D$ has trivial kernel; it is symmetric positive semidefinite by [F1], hence positive definite.

In the closed case, let $K=\ker L_C$. Symmetry implies $L_C(K^\perp)\subseteq K^\perp$: for $x\in K^\perp$ and $k\in K$, $k^{\mathsf T}L_Cx=(L_Ck)^{\mathsf T}x=0$. If a vector $x\in K^\perp$ has $x^{\mathsf T}L_Cx=0$, [F1] puts $x$ in $K$; hence $x=0$. Therefore the restriction $L_C|_{K^\perp}$ is positive definite. It has trivial kernel and is an endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space $K^\perp$, so [F2] makes it onto. Thus each $b\in K^\perp$ has one gauged solution $u\in K^\perp$. By [F5], an orthonormal basis of $K^\perp$ identifies this restriction with a real symmetric positive definite matrix, including the zero-dimensional case.
For $\tau>0$ and any nonzero $x$, [F1] and [F4] give $x^{\mathsf T}(M+\tau L_D)x=x^{\mathsf T}Mx+\tau x^{\mathsf T}L_Dx \ge\sum_i m_ix_i^2>0$. Thus $M+\tau L_D$ is positive definite.

The grounded matrix from step 1.1, the restricted Neumann matrix in the orthonormal coordinates constructed in the preceding argument, and the shifted mass matrix from step 1.3 are all real symmetric positive definite on their stated spaces. Each therefore has trivial kernel and is onto by [F2] on its finite-dimensional domain, so each right-hand side has a unique solution. Applying [F3] gives the exact-arithmetic CG Krylov Galerkin and energy-minimization conclusions.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume $E\ne\varnothing$. For each edge $e$, choose a finite partition
$$0=x_{e,0}<x_{e,1}<\cdots<x_{e,N_e}=\ell_e,$$
where $N_e\ge1$, and let $\mathcal T_h$ be the union of the resulting
interval cells $K_{e,j}=[x_{e,j-1},x_{e,j}]$. Set
$h=\max_{e,j}(x_{e,j}-x_{e,j-1})$. The conforming **P1 edge space** is
$$V_h=\{w\in V_D:\ w_e\text{ is affine on every }K_{e,j}\}.$$
Thus internal nodal values are single-valued along each edge, while the
original-vertex matching and zero-anchor conditions are inherited from
$V_D$. The maximum step $h$ is positive and finite because the mesh has
finitely many cells of positive length.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix an edge cell $K=[a,b]$ of length $h_K=b-a$. By [F1] and [F2], the continuous representative of $u_e$ has endpoint values and the representative of $u'_e$ is absolutely continuous. Thus the slope of the nodal interpolant on $K$ is $$s_K=\frac{u_e(b)-u_e(a)}{h_K} =\frac1{h_K}\int_a^b u'_e(y)\,dy.$$ The fundamental theorem in [F2] justifies this equality.

For any $x\in K$, [F2] and [F3] give $$|u'_e(x)-s_K| \le\frac1{h_K}\int_a^b|u'_e(x)-u'_e(y)|\,dy \le\frac1{h_K}\int_a^b\sqrt{h_K}\|u''_e\|_{L^2(K)}\,dy =\sqrt{h_K}\|u''_e\|_{L^2(K)}.$$ Squaring and integrating over $x\in K$ yields $$\|(u_e-I_hu_e)'\|_{L^2(K)}^2 =\|u'_e-s_K\|_{L^2(K)}^2 \le h_K^2\|u''_e\|_{L^2(K)}^2.$$ The first equality holds because the derivative of the nodal interpolant is the constant slope $s_K$ on K.

Multiply the cell estimate in step 2.1 by $\kappa_e$, sum over all cells, and use $h_K\le h$. The cells partition the edge interiors and their finitely many endpoints have measure zero. Hence $$\sum_e\kappa_e\|(u_e-I_hu_e)'\|_{L^2(e)}^2 \le h^2\sum_e\kappa_e\|u''_e\|_{L^2(e)}^2.$$ Taking square roots proves the displayed error estimate.

At an original vertex, the endpoint nodal value at every incident endpoint incidence is the common trace of $u$, so all interpolant traces agree, including both ends of a loop. At each anchor the nodal value is zero. The interpolant is real-valued, continuous and piecewise affine on each finite edge partition, so its weak derivative is its piecewise constant slope in $L^2$ (the internal endpoint terms cancel when testing against a smooth compactly supported function). Hence it belongs to the edge-product real $H^1$ space. Thus $I_hu\in V_D$ and it is affine on every cell by construction, which is exactly membership in $V_h$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the cited one-dimensional
representative interface. A **finite metric graph**
$\Gamma=(V,E,\partial_-,\partial_+,\ell)$ consists of finite vertex and
edge sets $V,E$, endpoint maps $\partial_-,\partial_+:E\to V$, and edge
lengths $0<\ell_e<\infty$. Distinct edges with the same endpoints are
allowed, as are loop edges with $\partial_-e=\partial_+e$. Every vertex is
an endpoint of at least one edge. The two endpoint incidences $(e,-)$ and
$(e,+)$ remain distinct even for a loop. A graph path is a finite sequence
$z_0,e_1,z_1,\ldots,e_n,z_n$ with $n\ge0$ and
$\{\partial_-e_j,\partial_+e_j\}=
\{z_{j-1},z_j\}$ for every $j$; a loop permits $z_{j-1}=z_j$. Vertices in
the same connected edge component are those joined by such a path. Orient
each edge only to choose its coordinate $x_e\in[0,\ell_e]$, with $0$ at
$\partial_-e$ and $\ell_e$ at $\partial_+e$. For $z\in V$, let
$\mathcal I(z):=\{(e,-):\partial_-e=z\}\cup\{(e,+):\partial_+e=z\}$
be its finite set of endpoint incidences.
The edge-product spaces are

$$H:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}L^2(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R),\qquad \mathcal W:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}H^1(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R).$$

For $w_e\in H^1(0,\ell_e)$, its endpoint values mean the values of the unique
absolutely continuous representative supplied by
[[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].
The **trace-matching graph Sobolev space** is the subspace of $\mathcal W$
whose endpoint-incidence traces all agree at each vertex. For a designated
anchor set $D\subseteq V$, define the **anchored graph energy space**

$$V_D:=\{w\in\mathcal W:\ w_{\iota}=w_{\iota'}\text{ whenever }\iota,\iota'\in\mathcal I(v),\quad w_{\iota}=0\text{ for each }v\in D,\ \iota\in\mathcal I(v)\}.$$

We equip $H$ with the edge-sum $L^2$ inner product and $V_D$ with

$$\|w\|_{V_D}^2=\sum_{e\in E}\int_0^{\ell_e}(|w_e|^2+|w'_e|^2)\,dx_e.$$

No Kirchhoff derivative condition is built into $V_D$; that condition is a
natural boundary condition of the later weak diffusion form. The elliptic
and P1 error results below assume that $D$ meets every connected edge
component.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and assume every connected edge component of the finite metric graph $\Gamma$
has at least one anchor in $D$. Put
$L_\Gamma=\sum_{e\in E}\ell_e$. Then every $w\in V_D$ satisfies

$$\|w\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}\le L_\Gamma \left(\sum_{e\in E}\|w'_e\|_{L^2(e)}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

Let $V_h$ be a finite-dimensional real subspace of an evolution space $V$,
continuously included in $H$. Let $a(t;\cdot,\cdot)$ be real bilinear,
measurable in $t$, uniformly bounded by $M$ and coercive by $\alpha>0$ on
$V_h$. If $f\in L^2(0,T;V_h^*)$ and $u_h^0\in V_h$, then there is a unique
$u_h\in H^1(0,T;V_h)$ with $u_h(0)=u_h^0$ and
$$((u_h)'(t),v_h)_H+a(t;u_h(t),v_h)=\langle f(t),v_h\rangle$$
for every $v_h\in V_h$ and almost every $t$. It satisfies
$$\|u_h(t)\|_H^2+\alpha\int_0^t\|u_h(s)\|_V^2\,ds \le \|u_h^0\|_H^2+\alpha^{-1}\int_0^t\|f(s)\|_{V_h^*}^2\,ds.$$
Here $H^1(0,T;V_h)$ means absolutely continuous $V_h$-valued coefficient
functions whose value and derivative are square-integrable.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $V$ and $H$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective,
continuous linear map with dense range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real linear
dual of $V$. Identify $H$ with its Hilbert dual by its inner product and embed
$H$ into $V^*$ by
$$h\longmapsto\bigl(v\longmapsto (h,i v)_H\bigr).$$
The resulting dense continuous embeddings are written
$$V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^*\hookrightarrow V^*$$
and $(V,H,V^*)$ is called an **evolution triple**. The pairing between $V^*$
and $V$ is denoted $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$.

For a Hilbert space $X$, $L^2(0,T;X)$ is the space of equivalence classes of
strongly measurable $X$-valued functions $w$ with
$$\int_0^T\|w(t)\|_X^2\,dt<\infty.$$
Strong measurability means being an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of
measurable simple functions. For $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$,
say that $g$ is the **weak time derivative** of $u$ when
$$\int_0^T (i u(t),i v)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. The derivative is
unique up to equality almost everywhere. The **parabolic energy space** is
$$W(0,T;V):=\{u\in L^2(0,T;V):u'\in L^2(0,T;V^*)\},$$
with norm
$$\|u\|_{W(0,T;V)}:=\bigl(\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2+ \|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$
No endpoint values are part of this definition; they are assigned only after
a continuous $H$ trace representative has been proved. Separability is an
additional hypothesis when it is needed by a later result.

Assume $E\ne\varnothing$. For each edge $e$, choose a finite partition
$$0=x_{e,0}<x_{e,1}<\cdots<x_{e,N_e}=\ell_e,$$
where $N_e\ge1$, and let $\mathcal T_h$ be the union of the resulting
interval cells $K_{e,j}=[x_{e,j-1},x_{e,j}]$. Set
$h=\max_{e,j}(x_{e,j}-x_{e,j-1})$. The conforming **P1 edge space** is
$$V_h=\{w\in V_D:\ w_e\text{ is affine on every }K_{e,j}\}.$$
Thus internal nodal values are single-valued along each edge, while the
original-vertex matching and zero-anchor conditions are inherited from

finitely many cells of positive length.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The canonical inclusion $i:V_D\to H$ is continuous because $\|v\|_H\le\|v\|_{V_D}$. It is injective because $V_D$ consists of Sobolev classes included in the edge-product $L^2$ classes. To prove density, fix $g=(g_e)\in H$ and $\epsilon>0$. By [F2] and finite choice, choose for each of the finitely many edges a $\phi_e\in C_c^\infty(0,\ell_e)$ with $\|g_e-\phi_e\|_{L^2(e)}<\epsilon/\sqrt{|E|}$. The edge-product function $\phi=(\phi_e)$ has zero endpoint traces, hence belongs to $V_D$, and $\|g-\phi\|_H^2=\sum_e\|g_e-\phi_e\|_{L^2(e)}^2<\epsilon^2$. Thus the range of i is dense in H.

By [F1] and [F3], H and V_D are real Hilbert spaces with dense continuous inclusion. With V_D^* as its continuous real dual, these spaces form the evolution triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]. The mesh has finitely many cells, and a P1 function is determined by its finite list of nodal values; the vertex matching and anchor conditions are linear. Therefore V_h is a finite-dimensional subspace of V_D by [F8].

By [F4] and [F6], the form a is bounded by M=κmax and coercive by α on V_D, hence also on V_h. The restriction F_h(t):=f(t)|_{V_h} is a bounded functional and its norm is at most \|f(t)\|_{V^*}; restriction is a continuous linear map from V_D^* to V_h^*, so F_h is strongly measurable and square-integrable. Thus all hypotheses of [F5] hold for the evolution triple and finite P1 subspace of step 1.2.
Applying [F5] gives the unique semidiscrete solution and its energy estimate for every t in [0,T]. No spatial approximation rate is part of [F5], so none follows here.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Orient each edge coordinate from $0$ at
$\partial_-e$ to $\ell_e$ at $\partial_+e$. For endpoint incidences
$(e,-)$ and $(e,+)$ define the outward derivatives by
$\partial_{\nu_{(e,-)}}u_e=-u'_e(0)$ and
$\partial_{\nu_{(e,+)}}u_e=+u'_e(\ell_e)$. The two incidences are both
included at a loop vertex. For $\iota=(e,\pm)$ write $e(\iota)=e$.
If $u_e\in H^2(0,\ell_e)$, with $H^2$ as defined by
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]],
$v\in V_D$, and each edge has a constant diffusivity $\kappa_e>0$, then

$$\sum_{e\in E}\kappa_e\int_0^{\ell_e}u'_ev'_e\,dx_e =-\sum_{e\in E}\kappa_e\int_0^{\ell_e}u''_ev_e\,dx_e +\sum_{z\in V}v(z)\sum_{\iota\in\mathcal I(z)}\kappa_{e(\iota)}\partial_{\nu_\iota}u_{e(\iota)}(z).$$

Thus zero test traces remove anchored endpoint terms, and a Kirchhoff
condition
$\sum_{\iota\in\mathcal I(z)}\kappa_{e(\iota)}\partial_{\nu_\iota}u_{e(\iota)}(z)=0$ at each free vertex
cancels the remaining terms.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the cited one-dimensional
representative interface. A **finite metric graph**
$\Gamma=(V,E,\partial_-,\partial_+,\ell)$ consists of finite vertex and
edge sets $V,E$, endpoint maps $\partial_-,\partial_+:E\to V$, and edge
lengths $0<\ell_e<\infty$. Distinct edges with the same endpoints are
allowed, as are loop edges with $\partial_-e=\partial_+e$. Every vertex is
an endpoint of at least one edge. The two endpoint incidences $(e,-)$ and
$(e,+)$ remain distinct even for a loop. A graph path is a finite sequence
$z_0,e_1,z_1,\ldots,e_n,z_n$ with $n\ge0$ and
$\{\partial_-e_j,\partial_+e_j\}=
\{z_{j-1},z_j\}$ for every $j$; a loop permits $z_{j-1}=z_j$. Vertices in
the same connected edge component are those joined by such a path. Orient
each edge only to choose its coordinate $x_e\in[0,\ell_e]$, with $0$ at
$\partial_-e$ and $\ell_e$ at $\partial_+e$. For $z\in V$, let
$\mathcal I(z):=\{(e,-):\partial_-e=z\}\cup\{(e,+):\partial_+e=z\}$
be its finite set of endpoint incidences.
The edge-product spaces are

$$H:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}L^2(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R),\qquad \mathcal W:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}H^1(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R).$$

For $w_e\in H^1(0,\ell_e)$, its endpoint values mean the values of the unique
absolutely continuous representative supplied by
[[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].
The **trace-matching graph Sobolev space** is the subspace of $\mathcal W$
whose endpoint-incidence traces all agree at each vertex. For a designated
anchor set $D\subseteq V$, define the **anchored graph energy space**

$$V_D:=\{w\in\mathcal W:\ w_{\iota}=w_{\iota'}\text{ whenever }\iota,\iota'\in\mathcal I(v),\quad w_{\iota}=0\text{ for each }v\in D,\ \iota\in\mathcal I(v)\}.$$

We equip $H$ with the edge-sum $L^2$ inner product and $V_D$ with

$$\|w\|_{V_D}^2=\sum_{e\in E}\int_0^{\ell_e}(|w_e|^2+|w'_e|^2)\,dx_e.$$

No Kirchhoff derivative condition is built into $V_D$; that condition is a
natural boundary condition of the later weak diffusion form. The elliptic
and P1 error results below assume that $D$ meets every connected edge
component.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The form $a$ is symmetric and bilinear. By Cauchy–Schwarz on the finite edge product, $$|a(w,v)|\le\kappa_{\max}\|w'\|_H\|v'\|_H\le\kappa_{\max}\|w\|_{V_D}\|v\|_{V_D}.$$ Thus it is bounded with constant $M=\kappa_{\max}$.

By [F2], $$\|v\|_{V_D}^2=\|v\|_H^2+\|v'\|_H^2\le(1+L_\Gamma^2)\|v'\|_H^2.$$ Consequently $$a(v,v)\ge\kappa_{\min}\|v'\|_H^2\ge\frac{\kappa_{\min}}{1+L_\Gamma^2}\|v\|_{V_D}^2.$$ The form is coercive with $\alpha=\kappa_{\min}/(1+L_\Gamma^2)>0$.
The load $F(v)=\sum_e\int f_ev_e$ is linear and satisfies $$|F(v)|\le\|f\|_H\|v\|_H\le L_\Gamma\|f\|_H\|v'\|_H\le L_\Gamma\|f\|_H\|v\|_{V_D}$$ by [F5] and [F2]. Hence $F$ is bounded on $V_D$.

Apply [F3] to the real Hilbert space [F1], the bounded coercive form from steps 1.1–1.2, and the bounded functional from step 1.3. It gives exactly one $u\in V_D$ satisfying $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for all $v\in V_D$. If this $u$ is edgewise H2, [F6] and the weak equation give, for every $v\in V_D$, $$\sum_e\int_0^{\ell_e}(-\kappa_eu''_e-f_e)v_e\,dx_e+\sum_{z\notin D}v(z)\sum_{\iota\in\mathcal I(z)}\kappa_{e(\iota)}\partial_{\nu_\iota}u_{e(\iota)}(z)=0.$$

Fix an edge and take $v$ smooth with compact support in its interior and zero on every other edge. The vertex sum vanishes, so the integral of $-\kappa_eu''_e-f_e$ against every such test is zero. This residual is in $L^2(0,\ell_e)$; density from [F7] and continuity of the pairing by [F5] imply $-\kappa_eu''_e=f_e$ almost everywhere on that edge. Now fix a free vertex $z$. Prescribe endpoint-incidence value $1$ at every incidence at $z$ and $0$ at incidences at every other vertex, and interpolate linearly on each edge. Both incidences of a loop at $z$ receive value $1$, so this defines a trace-matching test function in $V_D$. Substitution in step 2.1 and the interior equation just proved leaves only the flux sum at $z$, so it is zero. This proves the stated natural Kirchhoff condition.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph with ordered vertex and edge sets.
Choose an orientation of each edge and let $B\in\mathbb R^{V\times E}$ be
the resulting incidence matrix of
[[def-oriented-incidence-matrix-of-a-graph]]: a column has $-1$ at its tail,
$+1$ at its head, and zero elsewhere. Let $D\subseteq V$ be the vertices with
prescribed Dirichlet values and let $I=V\setminus D$ be the free vertices.
Assign a mass $m_i>0$ to each $i\in I$ and a conductance $c_e\ge0$ to each
$e\in E$. Put

$$M=\operatorname{diag}(m_i)_{i\in I},\qquad C=\operatorname{diag}(c_e)_{e\in E},\qquad L_C=BCB^{\mathsf T}.$$

The matrix $L_C$ is the **conductance-weighted graph stiffness**. Its free
Dirichlet restriction $L_D$ is the principal submatrix $(L_C)_{I,I}$. The
finite weighted network diffusion equation is

$$M u'(t)+L_Du(t)=f(t),$$

where $u(t)\in\mathbb R^I$ and $f(t)\in\mathbb R^I$. If $D=\varnothing$,
this is the closed Neumann network equation. If the boundary values are
instead a nonzero vector $g(t)$, restriction of $L_C(u,g)$ to $I$ gives
$M u'+L_Du=f-(L_C)_{I,D}g$.

When every $c_e=1$, $L_C=BB^{\mathsf T}$ agrees with the ordinary graph
Laplacian by
[[thm-laplacian-is-the-oriented-incidence-product]]. Zero conductances are
allowed and remove those edges from the diffusion coupling; they do not remove
the vertices or masses.

Use the data of [[def-finite-weighted-network-diffusion-data]]. Let
$E_+=\{e\in E:c_e>0\}$ and let $G_+=(V,E_+)$; its connected components are
the **positive-conductance components**. For $x\in\mathbb R^I$, let
$\bar x\in\mathbb R^V$ equal $x$ on $I$ and $0$ on $D$. Then

$$x^{\mathsf T}L_Dx=\sum_{e\in E}c_e (\bar x_{\mathrm{head}(e)}-\bar x_{\mathrm{tail}(e)})^2\ge0.$$

Consequently $L_D$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and $x\in\ker L_D$
exactly when $\bar x$ is constant on each positive-conductance component and
that constant is zero on every such component meeting $D$. In the closed
case $D=\varnothing$, every differentiable solution of
$Mu'+L_Cu=f$ satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu(t)=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}f(t).$$

Thus homogeneous closed diffusion conserves weighted mass
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu$, which need not equal the unweighted sum
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u$.

Let $S=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ with $n\ge1$. Identify its real matrices with $M_n(\mathbb R)$, the finite matrix space with row and column indices in $S$ from [[def-matrix-space]], and use the matrix-product and identity conventions of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. A **finite column generator** on $S$ is a real matrix $Q=(q_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfying

$$q_{ij}\ge0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad \sum_{i<n}q_{ij}=0\quad(j<n).$$

The column index $j$ is the source state and the row index $i$ is the destination state: for $i\ne j$, $q_{ij}$ is the transition rate from $j$ to $i$. The exit rate from $j$ is

$$r_j:=-q_{jj}=\sum_{i\ne j}q_{ij}\ge0.$$

A **column probability vector** is $p\in\mathbb R^n$ with $p_i\ge0$ for each $i$ and $\sum_{i<n}p_i=1$. A **subprobability vector** has the same coordinatewise nonnegativity and has coordinate sum at most one. These conventions are used throughout this page.

Let $Q$ be an $n\times n$ finite column generator, let $p_0$ be a column probability vector, and let $t\ge0$. The unique differentiable solution of

$$p'(t)=Qp(t),\qquad p(0)=p_0,$$

is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$. If $\nu>0$ and $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, put $P=I+Q/\nu$; then

$$p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-\nu t}\frac{(\nu t)^k}{k!}P^kp_0.$$

Each term $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector, and the displayed Poisson mixture is a probability vector. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$ and $p(t)=p_0$.

For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

derivations.claim: If $I=\varnothing$, all free-state assertions are vacuous, so assume $I\ne\varnothing$. Put $Q=-LM^{-1}$. For distinct free vertices $i,j$, $Q_{ij}=-L_{ij}/m_j\ge0$ by [F1]. If $D=\varnothing$, [F1] says that $\mathbf1$ is constant on every positive-conductance component, so $L\mathbf1=0$; symmetry gives $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}L=0$. Thus $Q$ has zero column sums and is a finite column generator by [F2]. If $p_0\ge0$ is nonzero, let $s=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}p_0>0$ and $\pi=p_0/s$. By [F2], $e^{tQ}\pi$ is a probability vector, so it is entrywise nonnegative; multiplying by $s$ proves $e^{tQ}p_0\ge0$. If $p_0=0$, its image is zero.

If $D\ne\varnothing$, then $Q$ has nonnegative off-diagonal entries and diagonal entries $Q_{ii}=-L_{ii}/m_i$. Put $\lambda=\max_{i\in I}L_{ii}/m_i\ge0$. If $\lambda=0$, then $L_{ii}=\sum_{e\text{ incident to }i}c_e=0$ for every free vertex. Since each $c_e\ge0$, every conductance incident to a free vertex is zero; hence each free row of $L_D$ vanishes, $Q=0$, and its exponential is the identity. If $\lambda>0$, every entry of $Q+\lambda I$ is nonnegative. For $t\ge0$, each term of the matrix series $e^{t(Q+\lambda I)}=\sum_{k\ge0}t^k(Q+\lambda I)^k/k!$ is entrywise nonnegative. By [F3], since $-\lambda tI$ commutes with $t(Q+\lambda I)$, $$e^{tQ}=e^{-\lambda tI}e^{t(Q+\lambda I)}=e^{-\lambda t}e^{t(Q+\lambda I)}$$ is entrywise nonnegative.

The diagonal entries of $E_F(\tau)$ are $1-\tau L_{ii}/m_i$, and its off-diagonal entries are $-\tau L_{ij}/m_i\ge0$ by [F1]. Thus all entries are nonnegative exactly when each diagonal is nonnegative, which is exactly $\tau\le m_i/L_{ii}$ for every $i$ with $L_{ii}>0$. If a diagonal is negative, applying the step matrix to the corresponding coordinate vector produces a negative coordinate, so the condition is sharp.

The mass state $p=Mu$ satisfies $p'=Qp$ for the homogeneous network equation. Its solution is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p(0)$. Since $M$ and $M^{-1}$ are entrywise positive diagonal matrices, $$u(t)=M^{-1}e^{tQ}Mu(0)=e^{-tM^{-1}L}u(0),$$ where the second equality follows term by term from the matrix exponential series applied to the similarity $M^{-1}QM=-M^{-1}L$. Steps 1.1–1.2 therefore prove positivity of $S_D(t)$ for both boundary cases.

Let $y\ge0$ and solve $(M+\tau L)x=My$. The matrix is symmetric positive definite because for nonzero $x$, $x^{\mathsf T}(M+\tau L)x\ge\sum_i m_i x_i^2>0$ by [F1]; hence the solve exists uniquely. If $x_k<0$ is a minimum coordinate, extend $x$ by zero on $D$. The edge formula for $(Lx)_k$ is a sum of terms $c_e(x_k-\bar x_{\mathrm{other}(e)})$, each nonpositive because every free neighbor has value at least $x_k$ and every Dirichlet value is zero. Therefore $((M+\tau L)x)_k=m_kx_k+\tau(Lx)_k<0$, contradicting $(My)_k=m_ky_k\ge0$. Thus $x\ge0$ and backward Euler is positivity preserving.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a finite metric graph and anchor set $D$, the trace-matching space and
the anchored space $V_D$ of
[[def-anchored-finite-metric-graph-h1-space]] are closed real Hilbert
subspaces of $\bigoplus_{e\in E}H^1(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R)$ with the
edge-product $H^1$ inner product.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear
in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

derivations.claim: The map sending a P1 graph function to its finite list of nodal values is linear and injective, since an affine function on a cell is determined by its two endpoint values. There are finitely many cells, so $V_h$ is finite-dimensional. Its defining vertex and anchor constraints make it a subspace of $V_D$.

For $w,v\in V_D$, [F7] gives $|a(w,v)|\le\kappa_{\max}\|w'\|_H\|v'\|_H \le M_a\|w\|_{V_D}\|v\|_{V_D}$. By path Poincare, $\|v\|_{V_D}^2\le(1+L_\Gamma^2)\|v'\|_H^2$, so $a(v,v)\ge\kappa_{\min}\|v'\|_H^2 \ge\alpha_a\|v\|_{V_D}^2$. Thus $a$ is bounded and coercive with the stated constants and is symmetric.

Apply [F2] with $V=V_D$, subspace $V_h$, form $a$, and load $F$ from the weak problem. Its Hilbert, finite-dimensional inclusion, boundedness, coercivity and bounded-load hypotheses hold by [F1], step 1.1, and step 1.2. Hence a unique Galerkin solution exists and satisfies the displayed Cea estimate. It agrees with the restriction of the same weak equation because the continuous solution is unique by [F6].

Apply the symmetric best-approximation fact [F3] to $u_h$ and choose $v_h=I_hu$. By [F4], this interpolant is in $V_h$ and its energy error is at most $h(\sum_e\kappa_e\|u''_e\|_{L^2(e)}^2)^{1/2}$. Therefore the Galerkin energy error is bounded by the same quantity, as claimed. The rate is conditional on the stated edgewise H2 regularity; no vertex regularity is inferred. By [F5], the natural free-vertex condition is Kirchhoff flux balance.

At a directed network junction, let $n_{\rm in}$ edges carry nonnegative
incoming **mass fluxes** $q^{\rm in}_i$ into the junction, and let
$n_{\rm out}$ edges carry outgoing mass fluxes. A **conservative nonnegative
routing matrix** is a real matrix
$P\in\mathbb R^{n_{\rm out}\times n_{\rm in}}$ such that

$$P_{ji}\ge0,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^{n_{\rm out}}P_{ji}=1 \quad(1\le i\le n_{\rm in}).$$

It routes the incoming flux vector to
$q^{\rm out}=Pq^{\rm in}$. The column $i$ distributes the mass flux arriving
on incoming edge $i$ among the outgoing edges. The column-sum condition
stipulates no source or sink at the junction. It is a model condition on flux;
it does not assert that the densities on incident edges are equal.

Let $P$ be a conservative nonnegative routing matrix from
[[def-conservative-network-advection-routing]], and let
$q^{\rm in}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\rm in}}$ be entrywise nonnegative. Then
$q^{\rm out}=Pq^{\rm in}$ is entrywise nonnegative and
$$\sum_{j=1}^{n_{\rm out}}q^{\rm out}_j =\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\rm in}}q^{\rm in}_i.$$

derivations.claim: If density is continuous with value $\rho=1$ on all three incident edges, the incoming flux is $v_{\rm in}\rho=1$, while the outgoing total is $v_1\rho+v_2\rho=1+2=3$. These are unequal, so this junction rule fails mass conservation in the stipulated model.

The matrix $P=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}$ is entrywise nonnegative and its sole incoming column sums to $1$. With incoming flux $q^{\rm in}=1$, it produces $q^{\rm out}=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}$, whose total is $1$ by [F1, F2]. The corresponding outgoing densities are $(1,0)$, so this conservative routing does not impose equal densities.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph with ordered vertex and edge sets.
Choose an orientation of each edge and let $B\in\mathbb R^{V\times E}$ be
the resulting incidence matrix of
[[def-oriented-incidence-matrix-of-a-graph]]: a column has $-1$ at its tail,
$+1$ at its head, and zero elsewhere. Let $D\subseteq V$ be the vertices with
prescribed Dirichlet values and let $I=V\setminus D$ be the free vertices.
Assign a mass $m_i>0$ to each $i\in I$ and a conductance $c_e\ge0$ to each
$e\in E$. Put

$$M=\operatorname{diag}(m_i)_{i\in I},\qquad C=\operatorname{diag}(c_e)_{e\in E},\qquad L_C=BCB^{\mathsf T}.$$

The matrix $L_C$ is the **conductance-weighted graph stiffness**. Its free
Dirichlet restriction $L_D$ is the principal submatrix $(L_C)_{I,I}$. The
finite weighted network diffusion equation is

$$M u'(t)+L_Du(t)=f(t),$$

where $u(t)\in\mathbb R^I$ and $f(t)\in\mathbb R^I$. If $D=\varnothing$,
this is the closed Neumann network equation. If the boundary values are
instead a nonzero vector $g(t)$, restriction of $L_C(u,g)$ to $I$ gives
$M u'+L_Du=f-(L_C)_{I,D}g$.

When every $c_e=1$, $L_C=BB^{\mathsf T}$ agrees with the ordinary graph
Laplacian by
[[thm-laplacian-is-the-oriented-incidence-product]]. Zero conductances are
allowed and remove those edges from the diffusion coupling; they do not remove
the vertices or masses.

Use the data of [[def-finite-weighted-network-diffusion-data]]. Let
$E_+=\{e\in E:c_e>0\}$ and let $G_+=(V,E_+)$; its connected components are
the **positive-conductance components**. For $x\in\mathbb R^I$, let
$\bar x\in\mathbb R^V$ equal $x$ on $I$ and $0$ on $D$. Then

$$x^{\mathsf T}L_Dx=\sum_{e\in E}c_e (\bar x_{\mathrm{head}(e)}-\bar x_{\mathrm{tail}(e)})^2\ge0.$$

Consequently $L_D$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and $x\in\ker L_D$
exactly when $\bar x$ is constant on each positive-conductance component and
that constant is zero on every such component meeting $D$. In the closed
case $D=\varnothing$, every differentiable solution of
$Mu'+L_Cu=f$ satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu(t)=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}f(t).$$

Thus homogeneous closed diffusion conserves weighted mass
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu$, which need not equal the unweighted sum
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u$.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $$L_C=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0&0\\-1&1&0&0\\0&0&3&-3\\0&0&-3&3\end{pmatrix}.$$ The two independent component indicator vectors $(1,1,0,0)^{\mathsf T}$ and $(0,0,1,1)^{\mathsf T}$ lie in its kernel by [F1], so the steady matrix is singular.

The vector $(1,0,0,0)^{\mathsf T}$ has dot product $1$ with the first component indicator, while every vector in the image of the symmetric matrix $L_C$ is orthogonal to its kernel: for $z=L_Cx$ and $k\in\ker L_C$, $k^{\mathsf T}z=(L_Ck)^{\mathsf T}x=0$. Thus this load is not in the image and the Neumann steady equation has no solution.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the cited one-dimensional
representative interface. A **finite metric graph**
$\Gamma=(V,E,\partial_-,\partial_+,\ell)$ consists of finite vertex and
edge sets $V,E$, endpoint maps $\partial_-,\partial_+:E\to V$, and edge
lengths $0<\ell_e<\infty$. Distinct edges with the same endpoints are
allowed, as are loop edges with $\partial_-e=\partial_+e$. Every vertex is
an endpoint of at least one edge. The two endpoint incidences $(e,-)$ and
$(e,+)$ remain distinct even for a loop. A graph path is a finite sequence
$z_0,e_1,z_1,\ldots,e_n,z_n$ with $n\ge0$ and
$\{\partial_-e_j,\partial_+e_j\}=
\{z_{j-1},z_j\}$ for every $j$; a loop permits $z_{j-1}=z_j$. Vertices in
the same connected edge component are those joined by such a path. Orient
each edge only to choose its coordinate $x_e\in[0,\ell_e]$, with $0$ at
$\partial_-e$ and $\ell_e$ at $\partial_+e$. For $z\in V$, let
$\mathcal I(z):=\{(e,-):\partial_-e=z\}\cup\{(e,+):\partial_+e=z\}$
be its finite set of endpoint incidences.
The edge-product spaces are

$$H:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}L^2(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R),\qquad \mathcal W:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}H^1(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R).$$

For $w_e\in H^1(0,\ell_e)$, its endpoint values mean the values of the unique
absolutely continuous representative supplied by
[[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].
The **trace-matching graph Sobolev space** is the subspace of $\mathcal W$
whose endpoint-incidence traces all agree at each vertex. For a designated
anchor set $D\subseteq V$, define the **anchored graph energy space**

$$V_D:=\{w\in\mathcal W:\ w_{\iota}=w_{\iota'}\text{ whenever }\iota,\iota'\in\mathcal I(v),\quad w_{\iota}=0\text{ for each }v\in D,\ \iota\in\mathcal I(v)\}.$$

We equip $H$ with the edge-sum $L^2$ inner product and $V_D$ with

$$\|w\|_{V_D}^2=\sum_{e\in E}\int_0^{\ell_e}(|w_e|^2+|w'_e|^2)\,dx_e.$$

No Kirchhoff derivative condition is built into $V_D$; that condition is a
natural boundary condition of the later weak diffusion form. The elliptic
and P1 error results below assume that $D$ meets every connected edge
component.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Orient each edge coordinate from $0$ at
$\partial_-e$ to $\ell_e$ at $\partial_+e$. For endpoint incidences
$(e,-)$ and $(e,+)$ define the outward derivatives by
$\partial_{\nu_{(e,-)}}u_e=-u'_e(0)$ and
$\partial_{\nu_{(e,+)}}u_e=+u'_e(\ell_e)$. The two incidences are both
included at a loop vertex. For $\iota=(e,\pm)$ write $e(\iota)=e$.
If $u_e\in H^2(0,\ell_e)$, with $H^2$ as defined by
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]],
$v\in V_D$, and each edge has a constant diffusivity $\kappa_e>0$, then

$$\sum_{e\in E}\kappa_e\int_0^{\ell_e}u'_ev'_e\,dx_e =-\sum_{e\in E}\kappa_e\int_0^{\ell_e}u''_ev_e\,dx_e +\sum_{z\in V}v(z)\sum_{\iota\in\mathcal I(z)}\kappa_{e(\iota)}\partial_{\nu_\iota}u_{e(\iota)}(z).$$

Thus zero test traces remove anchored endpoint terms, and a Kirchhoff
condition
$\sum_{\iota\in\mathcal I(z)}\kappa_{e(\iota)}\partial_{\nu_\iota}u_{e(\iota)}(z)=0$ at each free vertex
cancels the remaining terms.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph with ordered vertex and edge sets.
Choose an orientation of each edge and let $B\in\mathbb R^{V\times E}$ be
the resulting incidence matrix of
[[def-oriented-incidence-matrix-of-a-graph]]: a column has $-1$ at its tail,
$+1$ at its head, and zero elsewhere. Let $D\subseteq V$ be the vertices with
prescribed Dirichlet values and let $I=V\setminus D$ be the free vertices.
Assign a mass $m_i>0$ to each $i\in I$ and a conductance $c_e\ge0$ to each
$e\in E$. Put

$$M=\operatorname{diag}(m_i)_{i\in I},\qquad C=\operatorname{diag}(c_e)_{e\in E},\qquad L_C=BCB^{\mathsf T}.$$

The matrix $L_C$ is the **conductance-weighted graph stiffness**. Its free
Dirichlet restriction $L_D$ is the principal submatrix $(L_C)_{I,I}$. The
finite weighted network diffusion equation is

$$M u'(t)+L_Du(t)=f(t),$$

where $u(t)\in\mathbb R^I$ and $f(t)\in\mathbb R^I$. If $D=\varnothing$,
this is the closed Neumann network equation. If the boundary values are
instead a nonzero vector $g(t)$, restriction of $L_C(u,g)$ to $I$ gives
$M u'+L_Du=f-(L_C)_{I,D}g$.

When every $c_e=1$, $L_C=BB^{\mathsf T}$ agrees with the ordinary graph
Laplacian by
[[thm-laplacian-is-the-oriented-incidence-product]]. Zero conductances are
allowed and remove those edges from the diffusion coupling; they do not remove
the vertices or masses.

Use the data of [[def-finite-weighted-network-diffusion-data]]. Let
$E_+=\{e\in E:c_e>0\}$ and let $G_+=(V,E_+)$; its connected components are
the **positive-conductance components**. For $x\in\mathbb R^I$, let
$\bar x\in\mathbb R^V$ equal $x$ on $I$ and $0$ on $D$. Then

$$x^{\mathsf T}L_Dx=\sum_{e\in E}c_e (\bar x_{\mathrm{head}(e)}-\bar x_{\mathrm{tail}(e)})^2\ge0.$$

Consequently $L_D$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and $x\in\ker L_D$
exactly when $\bar x$ is constant on each positive-conductance component and
that constant is zero on every such component meeting $D$. In the closed
case $D=\varnothing$, every differentiable solution of
$Mu'+L_Cu=f$ satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu(t)=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}f(t).$$

Thus homogeneous closed diffusion conserves weighted mass
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu$, which need not equal the unweighted sum
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u$.

Use the data of [[def-finite-weighted-network-diffusion-data]] and write
$L=L_D$. For any $t\ge0$, the homogeneous exact semigroup
$$S_D(t)=e^{-tM^{-1}L}$$
maps entrywise nonnegative initial vectors to entrywise nonnegative vectors.
For a forward Euler step of size $\tau\ge0$, the map
$$E_F(\tau)=I-\tau M^{-1}L$$
is entrywise nonnegative, and hence positivity preserving for every
nonnegative input, exactly when
$$0\le\tau\le\tau_F:=\min_{\substack{i\in I\\L_{ii}>0}}\frac{m_i}{L_{ii}},$$
where the minimum of an empty set is $+\infty$. For every $\tau>0$, the
backward Euler map $(M+\tau L)^{-1}M$ exists and is positivity preserving.
The forward Euler threshold is sharp for positivity of the full step matrix.

derivations.claim: With the stated orientation, $$B=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad L_C=BCB^{\mathsf T}= \begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\-1&3&-2\\0&-2&2\end{pmatrix}.$$ The graph is connected and both conductances are positive.
The initial weighted mass is $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu(0)=2+2+12=16$. By [F2] it is constant for all times for which the homogeneous solution is evaluated.

The vector $\mathbf1=(1,1,1)^{\mathsf T}$ has $L_C\mathbf1=0$ by the displayed matrix in step 1.1, and its weighted mass at value $8/3$ is $(8/3)(1+2+3)=16$. Thus the stated constant state is an equilibrium with the same weighted mass.
Since $u(0)\ge0$, [F3] implies the exact semigroup trajectory remains entrywise nonnegative for every $t\ge0$.
