Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, each of
measure zero ([[def-measure-zero-and-content-zero]]). Then

$$\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n \quad \text{has measure zero.}$$

By the padding convention of [[def-measure-zero-and-content-zero]] and
[[def-countable]] the same conclusion covers the union of an at most countable
family of null sets, a finite family being extended by copies of $\varnothing$.

**The hypothesis $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is spent at exactly one step, step 2.1
below**, where one covering sequence is selected for every $A_n$ at once. Each
$A_n$ has many such covers and nullity provides no rule for singling one out.
Nothing else in the proof selects anything: the diagonal enumeration and the
estimate are formulas.

derivations.claim: To justify pointwise time estimates without strengthening Countable Choice, let $X$ be either $H^2(D)^d$ or $H^1(D)\cap Q$, let $w\in W^{1,\infty}(0,T;X)$, and let $g=w'\in L^\infty(0,T;X)$ be its weak Bochner derivative. The separability of $X$ is [F6]. Define $G(t)=\int_0^tg(s)\,ds$. By [F5], $\|G(t)-G(s)\|_X\le\|g\|_{L^\infty X}|t-s|$. For $\xi\in X$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$, scalar Fubini gives $-\int_0^T(G(t),\xi)_X\phi'(t)\,dt=-\int_0^T\int_0^t(g(s),\xi)_X\,ds\,\phi'(t)\,dt=\int_0^T(g(s),\xi)_X\phi(s)\,ds.$ Thus $G'=g$ in scalar distributions and $(w-G,\xi)$ has zero distributional derivative.

For $v\in V$, Cauchy–Schwarz for the matrix trace gives $|\operatorname{div}v|=|\operatorname{tr}\nabla v|\le\sqrt d\,|\nabla v|$ almost everywhere. Integrating and applying Cauchy–Schwarz yields $\|b(v,q)\|\le\sqrt d\,\|v\|_V\|q\|_2=M_b\|v\|_V\|q\|_2$, as used in the Statement.

For $q\in H^1(D)\cap Q$, let $I_hq$ be the face-average P1 interpolant from [F3] and set $r_h^0q=I_hq-|D|^{-1}\int_DI_hq$. This belongs to $Q_h$. Since $q$ has mean zero, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|D|^{1/2}\bigl||D|^{-1}\int_DI_hq\bigr|\le\|I_hq-q\|_2$, hence $\|q-r_h^0q\|_2\le2\|q-I_hq\|_2\le2Ch\|q\|_{H^1(D)}$. Thus some finite uniform best-approximation constant exists, as required by the Statement. Now let $r_h$ be the $L^2$-orthogonal projection onto $Q_h$. The finite-dimensional space $Q_h$ is closed in Hilbert $Q$; [F6] gives its unique orthogonal decomposition. Uniqueness makes $r_h$ linear, and Pythagoras gives $\|r_hq\|_2\le\|q\|_2$, so it is bounded. The Statement's selected best-approximation constant therefore yields $\|q-r_hq\|_2=\inf_{q_h\in Q_h}\|q-q_h\|_2\le C_Ih\|q\|_{H^1(D)}$.

A locally integrable scalar function with zero distributional derivative is constant almost everywhere. Indeed, fix $\rho\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$ with $\int\rho=1$. For any $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$, $\psi=\phi-(\int\phi)\rho$ has integral zero, so $\theta(t)=\int_0^t\psi(s)\,ds$ belongs to $C_c^\infty(0,T)$ and $\theta'=\psi$. The zero-derivative identity gives $\int(w-G,\xi)\psi=0$, hence $\int(w-G,\xi)\phi=c_\xi\int\phi$ with $c_\xi=\int(w-G,\xi)\rho$. Injectivity of the locally integrable embedding into distributions [F6] yields $(w-G,\xi)=c_\xi$ almost everywhere.

Choose a countable dense set $(\xi_k)$ in $X$. By [F6], the scalar identities in step 2.1 hold outside one common null set. Choose $t_0$ outside that set where the Bochner representative of $w$ is defined, and put $c=w(t_0)-G(t_0)$. Density gives $w(t)-G(t)=c$ for almost every $t$. Thus $w^*(t)=G(t)+c$ is the unique continuous representative and is Lipschitz with constant $\|w'\|_{L^\infty X}$. Apply this to $u$ and $p$: for all $s,t$, $\|u(t)-u(s)\|_V\le M|t-s|$ and $\|p(t)-p(s)\|_{H^1}\le M|t-s|$. Continuity and their essential bounds then give $\|u(t)\|_V\le M_u$ and $\|p(t)\|_{H^1}\le M$ for every $t$. Also $M\ge M_u$, since the $H^2$ norm controls the $V$ norm. These representatives are the ones used for the nodal errors in the existing smooth velocity theorem.

Write $u_n=u(t_n)$, $\overline u_n=\tau_n^{-1}\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}u(t)\,dt$, and use bars similarly for exact pressure, forcing and convection. For each vector in a basis of the finite-dimensional $V_h$, [F1] and step 3.1 imply that the full scalar momentum residual is the zero distribution. All residual terms are integrable, so [F6] identifies that residual with zero almost everywhere; integrating over each time cell and using $u(t_n)-u(t_{n-1})=\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}u_t$ from step 3.1 gives the exact interval equation. Subtract the mixed backward Euler equations and sum through $m$. The identical forcing averages cancel and the time derivatives telescope, giving for every $v_h\in V_h$ $b(v_h,P(t_m)-P_h^m)=-(e_m-e_0,v_h)_2-\sum_{n\le m}\tau_na_\nu(\overline u_n-u_h^n,v_h)-\sum_{n\le m}\tau_n\bigl(\overline{c(u;u,v_h)}_n-c(u_h^n;u_h^n,v_h)\bigr).$ No projection onto the discrete kernel is used in this identity.

On each time cell, $P_h'=\overline p_h$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open. If $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, then $\operatorname{div}v\in L^2(D)$ and $\int_D\operatorname{div}v=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz open set, where Lipschitz means that $\partial D$ has a finite rigidly moved graph-chart atlas. Here $H^1_0(D)$ is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(D)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Since $D$ has finite measure, Holder makes every $L^2$ class integrable, so the zero-mean condition is well-defined ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]). Define
$$V:=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q:=L^2_0(D):=\{q\in L^2(D;\mathbb R):\int_Dq=0\}.$$
Equip $V$ with $\|v\|_V:=\|
abla v\|_{L^2(D)}$ and $Q$ with $\|q\|_Q:=\|q\|_{L^2(D)}$. The local Poincare inequality [[lem-na-homogeneous-dirichlet-poincare]] makes the first a norm equivalent to the usual $H^1$ norm. For $v\in V$, define $\varepsilon(v):=(
abla v+
abla v^T)/2$ and $b(v,q):=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v$. For viscosity $
u>0$, set $a_
u(u,v):=2
u\int_D\varepsilon(u):\varepsilon(v)$, where $X:Y=\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}Y_{ij}$. The continuous domain class is all bounded connected Lipschitz $D$; the exact mini-element mesh class is the narrower polygonal/polyhedral conforming affine simplicial class.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(2x)=2\sin x\cos x,\quad \cos(2x)=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2\cos^2x-1=1-2\sin^2x,$$
and
$$\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2,\qquad \cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2.$$
When defined, $\tan(2x)=2\tan x/(1-\tan^2x)$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d=2$ or $3$, be a bounded connected Lipschitz polygonal/polyhedral domain with a conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$. On a simplex $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d$, define the scalar interior bubble $b_K=(d+1)^{d+1}\prod_{i=0}^d\lambda_i$. Let
$$S^1_h=\{w\in C^0(\overline D):w|_K\in P_1(K)\},\quad S^1_{h,0}=S^1_h\cap H^1_0(D).$$
The **mini-element spaces** are
$$V_h=[S^1_{h,0}]^d\oplus\bigoplus_{K\in\mathcal T_h}b_K\mathbb R^d\subset H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q_h=S^1_h\cap L^2_0(D).$$
Each bubble is extended by zero off its cell. The zero-boundary conformity of the piecewise affine part is supplied by [[thm-zero-boundary-piecewise-polynomials-in-w10p]]. The local/global dimensions are proved in the next dimension lemma.

On the mini-element spaces of [[def-na-mini-element-p1-bubble-p1-spaces]], there is a Fortin operator $\Pi_h:V\to V_h$ preserving $b(v,q_h)$ for every $q_h\in Q_h$, with $\|\Pi_hv\|_V\le C_F\|v\|_V$. The constant depends only on $d$ and the mesh shape-regularity bound, not on $h$. Consequently
$$\beta_h\ge (C_FC_{\rm div}(D))^{-1}.$$

derivations.claim: Every small triangle is a right isosceles triangle with legs $1/n$ and diameter $\sqrt2/n$. Two triangles in one square share the full diagonal, and triangles in adjacent squares meet along either a full grid edge or a grid vertex; hence the family is matching and conforming. All cells are scaled copies of the same two reference triangles, so their shape ratios are constant and the family is shape-regular and quasi-uniform.

The unit square is a bounded connected Lipschitz polygon in dimension two. Since $h_n=\sqrt2/n\to0$, each mesh lies in the MINI mesh class and the Fortin stability result [F2] applies uniformly in $n$. The displayed mesh picture fixes the diagonal convention; the stability conclusion follows from the stated geometry and the cited theorem, not from the drawing.

Assume Countable Choice, the mini-element hypotheses of [[def-na-mini-navier-stokes-backward-euler-scheme]], $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$, and an initial value $u_h^0\in Z_h$. On every finite positive time partition there is at least one mixed solution $(u_h^n,p_h^n)_{n=1}^N$ of the backward Euler scheme. Every such solution satisfies, for $0\le m\le N$, the work-form inequality
$$ rac12\|u_h^m\|_2^2+ rac12\sum_{n=1}^m\|u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}\|_2^2+
u\sum_{n=1}^m	au_n\|
abla u_h^n\|_2^2\le rac12\|u_h^0\|_2^2+\sum_{n=1}^m	au_n(f_h^n,u_h^n)_{L^2}.$$
Consequently it satisfies the mesh-independent estimate
$$ rac12\|u_h^m\|_2^2+ rac12\sum_{n=1}^m\|u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}\|_2^2+ rac{
u}{2}\sum_{n=1}^m	au_n\|
abla u_h^n\|_2^2\le rac12\|u_h^0\|_2^2+ rac{C_P(D)^2}{2
u}\|f\|_{L^2(0,T;L^2)}^2.$$
The constant is independent of mesh size and time-step sizes.

derivations.claim: Substitute $f_h^n=0$ in the work-form inequality of [F1]. Its right side is exactly $\frac12\|u_h^0\|_2^2$, while the jump and viscosity sums are nonnegative.

The inequality therefore bounds the kinetic energy at each node by its initial value and accounts separately for the nonnegative time-jump and viscous-dissipation terms. It is uniform in $h$ and in all positive step sizes; it does not assert strict decay when the velocity is stationary.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d=2$ or $3$, be a bounded connected Lipschitz polygonal/polyhedral domain with a conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$. On a simplex $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d$, define the scalar interior bubble $b_K=(d+1)^{d+1}\prod_{i=0}^d\lambda_i$. Let
$$S^1_h=\{w\in C^0(\overline D):w|_K\in P_1(K)\},\quad S^1_{h,0}=S^1_h\cap H^1_0(D).$$
The **mini-element spaces** are
$$V_h=[S^1_{h,0}]^d\oplus\bigoplus_{K\in\mathcal T_h}b_K\mathbb R^d\subset H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q_h=S^1_h\cap L^2_0(D).$$
Each bubble is extended by zero off its cell. The zero-boundary conformity of the piecewise affine part is supplied by [[thm-zero-boundary-piecewise-polynomials-in-w10p]]. The local/global dimensions are proved in the next dimension lemma.

Assume Countable Choice as inherited from the energy-space conventions. Interpret each interval forcing average as a Bochner integral; its existence follows from the stated L2 forcing and the Bochner integrability criterion ([[def-countable-choice]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]). Let $D$ be as in [[def-na-evolutionary-incompressible-ns-weak-solution]], let $\mathcal T_h$ be a conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh of $D$, and let $V_h,Q_h,Z_h$ be the MINI spaces and weak divergence kernel of [[def-na-mini-element-p1-bubble-p1-spaces]] and [[def-na-discrete-weak-and-exact-divergence-free-spaces]]. For a partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, write $\tau_n=t_n-t_{n-1}$ and $f_h^n=\tau_n^{-1}\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}f(t)\,dt$. Given $u_h^0\in Z_h$, a **backward Euler mini-element solution** is a sequence $(u_h^n,p_h^n)\in V_h\times Q_h$ satisfying, for $n=1,\ldots,N$,
$$\left(\frac{u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}}{\tau_n},v_h\right)_{L^2}+a_\nu(u_h^n,v_h)+c(u_h^n;u_h^n,v_h)+b(v_h,p_h^n)=(f_h^n,v_h)_{L^2}\quad(v_h\in V_h),$$
$$b(u_h^n,q_h)=0\quad(q_h\in Q_h).$$
All pressure variables use the zero-mean gauge $Q_h\subset L^2_0(D)$. Restriction to $v_h\in Z_h$ eliminates pressure. The equations are well-defined by [[lem-na-mini-be-scheme-is-well-defined]]; this definition claims no solver termination or error rate.

For the conforming mini-element spaces $V_h,Q_h$, define the **weak discrete divergence kernel** by
$$Z_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:b(v_h,q_h)=0\text{ for every }q_h\in Q_h\},$$
and the **exact discrete divergence kernel** by
$$Z_h^0:=\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{div}v_h=0\text{ almost everywhere on }D\}.$$
Since $b(v_h,q_h)=-\int_Dq_h\operatorname{div}v_h$, one has $Z_h^0\subseteq Z_h$. Equality is not part of either definition; the companion example proves strictness for a concrete mesh.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz open set, where Lipschitz means that $\partial D$ has a finite rigidly moved graph-chart atlas. Here $H^1_0(D)$ is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(D)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Since $D$ has finite measure, Holder makes every $L^2$ class integrable, so the zero-mean condition is well-defined ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]). Define
$$V:=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q:=L^2_0(D):=\{q\in L^2(D;\mathbb R):\int_Dq=0\}.$$
Equip $V$ with $\|v\|_V:=\|
abla v\|_{L^2(D)}$ and $Q$ with $\|q\|_Q:=\|q\|_{L^2(D)}$. The local Poincare inequality [[lem-na-homogeneous-dirichlet-poincare]] makes the first a norm equivalent to the usual $H^1$ norm. For $v\in V$, define $\varepsilon(v):=(
abla v+
abla v^T)/2$ and $b(v,q):=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v$. For viscosity $
u>0$, set $a_
u(u,v):=2
u\int_D\varepsilon(u):\varepsilon(v)$, where $X:Y=\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}Y_{ij}$. The continuous domain class is all bounded connected Lipschitz $D$; the exact mini-element mesh class is the narrower polygonal/polyhedral conforming affine simplicial class.

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz domain with $d\in\{2,3\}$, and let $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ as in [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]]. For $a,b,c\in V$, define the real **skew convective form**
$$c(a;b,c):= rac12\int_D ig((a\cdot
abla)b\cdot c-(a\cdot
abla)c\cdot b ig)\,dx.$$
The middle and last slots are displayed separately to emphasize $c(a;b,c)=-c(a;c,b)$. In particular $c(a;b,b)=0$. The integrals are well-defined on $V$ by [[lem-na-evolutionary-skew-convective-form-bound]]. If additionally $\operatorname{div}a=0$, then $c(a;b,c)=\int_D(a\cdot
abla)b\cdot c$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V_h,Q_h$ be the stable mini-element spaces on a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral domain with a conforming mesh, with viscosity $\nu>0$, and let $Z_h=\{v_h:b(v_h,q_h)=0\ \forall q_h\in Q_h\}$. Choose bases of $V_h,Q_h$, let $M$ be the velocity mass matrix, $A$ the Stokes stiffness matrix, and $B$ the constraint matrix with entries $B_{\ell j}=b(\phi_j,\chi_\ell)$. The mass-orthogonal projector onto $Z_h$ is
$$P_M=I-M^{-1}B^T(BM^{-1}B^T)^{-1}B.$$
On the mean-zero pressure coordinates, both the mass pressure Schur matrix $BM^{-1}B^T$ and stiffness pressure Schur matrix $BA^{-1}B^T$ are positive definite. Before imposing the pressure gauge on the full continuous P1 space, the constant pressure is exactly the one-dimensional nullspace of $B^T$.

On the mini-element spaces of [[def-na-mini-element-p1-bubble-p1-spaces]], there is a Fortin operator $\Pi_h:V\to V_h$ preserving $b(v,q_h)$ for every $q_h\in Q_h$, with $\|\Pi_hv\|_V\le C_F\|v\|_V$. The constant depends only on $d$ and the mesh shape-regularity bound, not on $h$. Consequently
$$\beta_h\ge (C_FC_{\rm div}(D))^{-1}.$$

Assume Countable Choice, the mini-element hypotheses of [[def-na-mini-navier-stokes-backward-euler-scheme]], $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$, and an initial value $u_h^0\in Z_h$. On every finite positive time partition there is at least one mixed solution $(u_h^n,p_h^n)_{n=1}^N$ of the backward Euler scheme. Every such solution satisfies, for $0\le m\le N$, the work-form inequality
$$ rac12\|u_h^m\|_2^2+ rac12\sum_{n=1}^m\|u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}\|_2^2+
u\sum_{n=1}^m	au_n\|
abla u_h^n\|_2^2\le rac12\|u_h^0\|_2^2+\sum_{n=1}^m	au_n(f_h^n,u_h^n)_{L^2}.$$
Consequently it satisfies the mesh-independent estimate
$$ rac12\|u_h^m\|_2^2+ rac12\sum_{n=1}^m\|u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}\|_2^2+ rac{
u}{2}\sum_{n=1}^m	au_n\|
abla u_h^n\|_2^2\le rac12\|u_h^0\|_2^2+ rac{C_P(D)^2}{2
u}\|f\|_{L^2(0,T;L^2)}^2.$$
The constant is independent of mesh size and time-step sizes.

Assume Countable Choice. For $d\in\{2,3\}$ and $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ on a bounded Lipschitz domain, the form in [[def-na-evolutionary-skew-convective-form]] is a continuous real trilinear map $V^3	o\mathbb R$, is skew in its last two slots, and satisfies
$$|c(a;b,w)|\le C_D\|a\|_{L^2}^{1/2}\|
abla a\|_{L^2}^{1/2}\|
abla b\|_{L^2}\|
abla w\|_{L^2}.$$
Consequently, if $u\in L^\infty(0,T;L^2)\cap L^2(0,T;V)$, then $c(u;u,\cdot)\in L^{4/3}(0,T;V^*)$. If $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $d=2$, the sharper estimate
$$|c(u;u,w)|\le C_D\|u\|_{L^2}\|
abla u\|_{L^2}\|
abla w\|_{L^2}$$
holds. If $\operatorname{div}a=0$, the skew form agrees with the advective form $\int_D(a\cdot
abla)b\cdot w$.

Assume Countable Choice. For bounded open $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, put $\varepsilon(v)=(
abla v+
abla v^T)/2$. Then
$$2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2^2=\|
abla v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2,$$
so $\|
abla v\|_2\le\sqrt2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2$.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be closed and convex with $x\in H$, and let $p\in C$. Then $p$ is the nearest point of $C$ to $x$ if and only if

$$\operatorname{Re}\langle x-p,\ y-p\rangle\le0 \qquad \text{for every } y\in C .$$

In particular, for the nearest point the inequality holds, and conversely any $p\in C$ satisfying the inequality is nearest.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $p,q>1$ satisfy $1/p+1/q=1$. For $u,v\ge0$,
$$uv\le\frac{u^p}{p}+\frac{v^q}{q}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the measure-theoretic
interfaces cited below. Let $d\ge1$, $0<s<1$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$ and
its sigma-algebra are those of
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]].

For a Lebesgue measurable $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb K$ put
$$[g]_{s,p}:=\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}|g(x)-g(y)|^p\,|x-y|^{-d-sp}\,dx\,dy\Bigr)^{1/p}\in[0,+\infty].$$
The integrand is read as $0$ on the diagonal $x=y$; the integral is the
nonnegative extended integral of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] over the
completed product measure $dx\,dy$ of
[[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]. The **Gagliardo--
Slobodeckij space** of order $s$ and exponent $p$ is
$$W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb K):=\{g\in L^p(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb K):[g]_{s,p}<\infty\},$$
where $L^p(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb K)$ is the quotient of the measurable functions
by almost-everywhere equality
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]); its elements are classes,
and the space is normed by
$$\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^d)}:=\|g\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}+[g]_{s,p}.$$
Write $[g]_{s,p}$ also for the value on a class, and call $[\cdot]_{s,p}$ the
**Slobodeckij seminorm**.

Three conventions are part of the definition. First, the diagonal
$\{(x,y):x=y\}$ is a Lebesgue-null subset of $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$
(its section at every $x$ is a single point, so Tonelli gives product measure
zero), and on the diagonal the integrand is declared zero; thus the convention
changes the integrand only on a null set and does not affect the integral.
Second, the integral is a nonnegative extended integral, so $[g]_{s,p}=+\infty$
is allowed and $W^{s,p}$ is a set of $L^p$ classes with finite seminorm; the
difference $g(x)-g(y)$ is taken between representatives, and changing
representatives on a null set changes the integrand only on a null subset of
the product. Third, the definition is stated on classes but representative
independence is not assumed here: it is the first clause of
[[lem-slobodeckij-seminorm-is-well-defined]], the item that establishes that
this definition is well posed on $L^p$ classes. That the expression
$\|\cdot\|_{W^{s,p}}$ is a genuine norm, and that $W^{s,p}$ is a vector space,
are likewise proved there, not asserted as part of the definition.

On this page the case used is the trace exponent
$$s=\theta:=1-\frac1p\in(0,1),$$
which is available exactly for $1<p<\infty$. For that exponent the weight
simplifies to $|x-y|^{-d-p\theta}=|x-y|^{-d-(p-1)}$. The endpoint $p=1$ is
treated separately on this page and is never described by a space
$W^{0,1}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $0<\theta<1$,
$1\le p<\infty$ with $p\theta<d$ and $p_\star:=\frac{dp}{d-p\theta}$. There is
$C=C(d,p,\theta)>0$ such that every measurable, compactly supported
$f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ satisfies
$$\|f\|_{L^{p_\star}(\mathbb R^d)}^{p}\ \le\ C\,[f]_{\theta,p}^{p}.$$
Consequently, for every bounded open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and every
$1\le q\le p_\star$ there is $C'=C'(d,p,\theta,U,q)$ with
$\|f\|_{L^q(U)}\le C'\bigl(\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}+[f]_{\theta,p}\bigr)$ for
every compactly supported measurable $f$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$,
$H=\mathbb R^d\times(0,\infty)$, and let $T_+$ be the half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]]. Write
$|Du|^p:=\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}|D_ju|^p$ for the sum of the $p$-th powers of the
weak first derivatives, and $[\cdot]_{\theta,p}$ for the Slobodeckij seminorm
of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]. Then for every
$u\in W^{1,p}(H;\mathbb K)$ with $g=T_+u$,
$$[g]_{\theta,p}^p\le C(d,p)\int_H|Du|^p\,dx=C(d,p)\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\|D_ju\|_{L^p(H)}^p\le C(d,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(H)}^p;$$
equivalently $T_+:W^{1,p}(H;\mathbb K)\to W^{\theta,p}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb K)$
is a bounded operator.

The homogeneous estimate is scale invariant: for $r>0$ and
$u_r(x',t):=u(rx',rt)$ one has $g_{u_r}(x')=g(rx')$ and
$$[g_{u_r}]_{\theta,p}^p=r^{-d+p\theta}[g]_{\theta,p}^p,\qquad \int_H|Du_r|^p\,dx=r^{-d+p\theta}\int_H|Du|^p\,dx,$$
because $p\theta=p-1$; so both sides of the homogeneous estimate scale with
the same exponent $r^{-d+p\theta}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, bounded, convex and nonempty, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(n)\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Here $u_\Omega=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u\,dx$ is the mean of $u$ over $\Omega$,
which is well defined because $\Omega$ is nonempty open and bounded. The proof
below gives the explicit choice
$$C(n)=\frac{2\,(2^n-1)}{n},$$
which depends only on the dimension; no dependence on $p$, on the shape of
$\Omega$, on $|\Omega|$ or on the regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1<p<\infty$ and let $f:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable, with
$Hf(t):=t^{-1}\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$. Then
$$\Bigl(\int_0^\infty\bigl(Hf(t)\bigr)^p\,dt\Bigr)^{1/p}\le\frac{p}{p-1}\Bigl(\int_0^\infty f(s)^p\,ds\Bigr)^{1/p},$$
equivalently
$$\int_0^\infty t^{-p}\Bigl(\int_0^t f(s)\,ds\Bigr)^pdt\le\Bigl(\frac{p}{p-1}\Bigr)^p\int_0^\infty f(s)^p\,ds,$$
where both sides are extended nonnegative integrals and $+\infty$ is allowed on
either side. The constant $p/(p-1)$ is sharp: for every $c<p/(p-1)$ there is a
measurable $f$ with $\|Hf\|_{L^p}>c\|f\|_{L^p}$. If $f$ is supported in
$(0,T)$ for some $0<T<\infty$, then the same inequality holds on $(0,T)$,
$$\int_0^T t^{-p}\Bigl(\int_0^t f(s)\,ds\Bigr)^pdt\le\Bigl(\frac{p}{p-1}\Bigr)^p\int_0^T f(s)^p\,ds,$$
with the same constant.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For all
$f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$,

$$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)} ,$$where both sums are taken in the finite-subset-supremum/finite-subset-net sense of [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. The bilinear series is absolutely convergent,$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\bigl|\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}\bigr|\le \Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat f(k)|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} \Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat g(k)|^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

and the value is also the limit of the canonical symmetric partial sums
$\sum_{|k|\le N}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For every
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ and every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$N\in\mathbb N$ with

$$\Bigl\|f-\sum_{|k|\le N}\widehat f(k)e_k\Bigr\|_2<\varepsilon .$$

Thus the symmetric partial sums of the Fourier series converge to $f$ in the
$L^2$ norm, and the finite-subset net of Fourier partial sums converges to $f$
as well. This is norm convergence only: no pointwise or uniform assertion is
made, and no ordering of $\mathbb Z$ other than the symmetric one is required.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

$$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique
holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $C(a,r)$ be a positively oriented circle, and let $f$ be meromorphic on a
neighbourhood of the closed disc $\overline{D(a,r)}$ with no pole on the circle.
Then

$\int_{C(a,r)}f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\sum_{|b-a|<r}\operatorname{Res}(f,b),$

the sum being over the poles of $f$ inside the circle.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

A conditional estimate in an internal claim is used only after its stated geometric or source premise is proved in a later phase. For bounded Hilbert sequences below, weak subsequences can be obtained without an unstated compactness supplier: work in the closure of the countable union of the finite spaces involved and the fixed data, choose a countable dense set, extract successively convergent scalar pairings by interval bisection, and take the diagonal subsequence. Its bounded limiting functional extends by density and is represented by Riesz; norm lower semicontinuity follows by testing against that representative. For an exterior exhaustion the countable nodal bases and bounded-radius cutoffs give the same separable subspace.

Two elementary inequalities used below have direct local proofs. Fix a scale $r>0$, the rectangle $C=[-4r,4r]\times[0,4r]$, and the lower triangle with vertices $(-4r,0),(0,-4r),(4r,0)$. Their union is the fixed convex pentagon $D$. **Part 2: Finite recursive geometry and all boundary-star budgets.** **1. Scales and the true outer-radius restriction**. Let the parent fan radius be H, aperture a_p, and tooth count N. A straight main tooth side has root distance `D comparable to a_p H/N.` Choose selected attachment centers on its middle thirds at spacing ell comparable to b0 D. The child half-container is, in local tangent/normal coordinates, `C_r=[-4r,4r]x[0,4r],   r comparable to sigma ell.` Choose the already free dyadic strip height with 0<epsilon_strip<=c a_c. Its base contains exactly c_-=(-4r,0), o=(0,0), c_+=(4r,0); its other four boundary nodes are (±4r,epsilon_strip r),(±4r,4r). **3. Keeping every long child edge unrefined**. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded, connected and Lipschitz, with $d\in\{2,3\}$, let $\nu>0$, and use the energy weak-solution definition in [[def-na-evolutionary-incompressible-ns-weak-solution]]. For fixed data $(u_0,f)$, if $d=2$, energy weak solutions are unique. If $d=3$ and one velocity $v$ additionally belongs to $C^1([0,T];V_\sigma)$, has $\nabla v\in L^1(0,T;L^\infty(D))$, and its solenoidal equation holds as an identity in $V_\sigma^*$ almost everywhere in time, then every other energy weak-solution velocity with the same data equals $v$. This three-dimensional conclusion is conditional and asserts no uniqueness between arbitrary energy weak-solution velocities. In both cases the associated zero-mean pressures also agree almost everywhere.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

$$w(t,y)=\int_0^\infty[G_t(y-z)-G_t(y+z)]w_0(z)\,dz.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: The choices in **Given** exist by [F8]: take a bump centered at $1/2$ with inner radius $1/24$ and outer radius $1/12$ for $a$, giving a nonzero function compactly supported in $(1/3,2/3)$. Restrict zero-centered bumps to the positive halfline with radii $(1/32,1/16)$ for $\eta$, $(1/8,1/4)$ for $\kappa$ and $\chi$, and $(1/3,1)$ for $\rho$. They have every stated support, plateau and sign property. Put $a_n=2\int_0^1a(x)\sin(n\pi x)\,dx$ and define $$\theta(x,y)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n\sin(n\pi x)\frac{\sinh(n\pi(1-y))}{\sinh(n\pi)},\qquad \widetilde\phi(x,y)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n\cos(n\pi x)\frac{\cosh(n\pi(1-y))}{\sinh(n\pi)}.$$ Repeated integration by parts makes $|a_n|\le C_Nn^{-N}$ for every $N$, since $a$ vanishes near the endpoints. The hyperbolic factors and their derivatives of order $k$ are bounded by $C_kn^k$ uniformly on $[0,1]$. Thus every differentiated series converges absolutely uniformly, and both functions are smooth on the closed square and harmonic. The sine series equals $a$ at $y=0$: indeed the odd, $2$-periodic smooth extension of $a$ has its Fourier series equal to itself. To verify this last assertion directly, its rapid coefficients define a uniformly convergent Fourier series with the same coefficients; their difference has all Fourier coefficients zero. Convolution with the Fejer kernels, which are nonnegative unit-mass kernels concentrating at zero by their formula $N^{-1}|\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e^{ij\pi x}|^2$, converges uniformly to a continuous periodic function by uniform continuity; it vanishes for a function whose coefficients all vanish. Hence the difference is zero. The other boundary values of $\theta$ are zero. Direct differentiation gives $\widetilde\phi_x=\theta_y$ and $\widetilde\phi_y=-\theta_x$. Let $\phi=\widetilde\phi-\int_D\widetilde\phi$, so $\phi\in Q$, $\nabla\phi=\operatorname{rot}\theta$, and $\|\phi\|_2>0$ because $a\ne0$ makes $\theta$ nonconstant.

Define $b=\theta-a\chi$. This is smooth and zero on all four sides. Its normal derivative equals $\partial_n\theta$ everywhere on the boundary: at the bottom $\chi'=0$, at the top $\chi=\chi'=0$, and near the vertical sides $a=a'=0$. Take the function $R(t)=R_{\sqrt t}$ from [F2] and choose $T$ small enough for that construction, with $\sqrt T<1/16$. Set $$\psi_m=a(x)[\kappa(y)h(t,y)+M_0\chi(y)],\qquad \psi=\psi_m+m(t)\theta-m(t)bR(t),$$ $$u=\operatorname{rot}\psi,\qquad p=-m'(t)\phi,\qquad r=-m(t)\operatorname{rot}(bR(t)).$$ All these fields are smooth for $t>0$. On the bottom $\psi_m=-am$, $\theta=a$, and $b=0$; on the other sides $\psi_m=\theta=b=0$. Thus $\psi=0$ on the boundary. The normal derivative of $\psi_m$ is zero on every side: on the bottom it is, up to its sign, $a w(t,0)=0$, and on all other sides the fixed cutoffs or $a,a'$ vanish. Hence $\partial_n(\psi_m+m\theta)=m\partial_n b$, and [F2] makes $\partial_n\psi=0$. Thus $u(t)\in V_\sigma$ exactly, with no-slip on every edge including compatible corner values.

Write $L(t)=\log(1/t)$. By [F1] and [F2], $$\|r\|_\infty\le C|m|,\quad \|r\|_2\le C|m|t^{1/4},\quad \|\nabla r\|_2\le C|m|t^{-1/4},$$ $$\|r_t\|_2+\|\Delta r\|_2\le C(|m'|t^{1/4}+|m|t^{-3/4})\le Ct^{-1/2}L(t)^{-\alpha}.$$ The last function is square integrable near zero because $2\alpha>1$. In particular $r\in L^\infty_tL^2_x\cap L^2_tH^1_x$ and $r(t)\to0$ strongly in $L^2$. The main stream rotation has a uniform $L^2$ bound from bounded $h$ and bounded $\|w\|_2$. Its gradient uses only bounded $h$, $w$ with fixed coefficients and $w_y$ with fixed coefficients, so the heat energy bound makes it $L^2_{t,x}$. The smooth field $m\operatorname{rot}\theta$ has the same required bounds. We obtain $$u\in L^\infty(0,T;L^2(D)^2)\cap L^2(0,T;V_\sigma).$$

The outer harmonic field cancels the entire rough gradient: $(\partial_t-
u\Delta)(m\operatorname{rot}	heta)+
abla p=m'
abla\phi-m'
abla\phi=0$. The main stream has the explicit residual $$(\partial_t-
u\Delta)\psi_m=-
u[a''\kappa h+2a\kappa'w+a\kappa''h]-
u M_0[a''\chi+a\chi''].$$ Its rotation contains only fixed coefficients times $h,w$, except for terms with $\kappa'w_y$. The latter are supported in $y\ge1/8$, a fixed positive distance from $\operatorname{supp}w_0\subset[0,1/16]$, and are square integrable by the off-support Gaussian bound in [F1]. All other terms are uniformly $L^2$ bounded. Together with step 3.1 this proves $$F_L=(\partial_t-

abla)u\in L^2_{t,x}$. Define $f=F_L+N(u)$. It belongs to $L^2_tL^2_x$, and the pointwise positive-time equation is $u_t-
u\Delta u+N(u)+

On $[\varepsilon,T]$, integrate the smooth equation from step 5.1 against $u$. The convection and pressure integrals vanish by divergence and no slip. Thus $$\tfrac12\|u(t)\|_2^2+\nu\int_\varepsilon^t\|\nabla u\|_2^2=\tfrac12\|u(\varepsilon)\|_2^2+\int_\varepsilon^t(f,u).$$ Let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$: strong initial convergence handles the endpoint and the energy and force bounds handle both integrals. This gives energy equality with initial value $u_0$. Similarly integrate the positive-time equation against a fixed solenoidal $V$ test and a smooth scalar time test, integrate by parts in time, and send $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The pressure term vanishes; all remaining integrals converge by the established bounds. The resulting identity is precisely the solenoidal weak equation with initial value $u_0$. Positive-time smoothness and strong initial convergence give the required weak continuity on $[0,T]$. Thus $u$ is a solenoidal energy weak velocity of [F3].

The pressure has zero spatial mean and is in $L^1_tQ$, since $m'\in L^1$ and $\phi\in Q$. It defines a time-distribution pressure for the full momentum equation: test the pointwise equation on compact positive-time intervals; its time-distribution identity on $(0,T)$ follows directly. Also $\|p(t)\|_2=|m'(t)|\|\phi\|_2$, so [F1] and $\|\phi\|_2>0$ imply $p\notin L^{4/3}_tQ$. If a second mean-zero $Q$-valued pressure distribution $q$ represented this same velocity and force, subtract their momentum equations. Every actual MINI subsequential limit supplied by [F5] is a solenoidal energy weak velocity with these same data, hence equals $u$. Steps 1.1–5.1 give all concrete properties and show that no mean-zero endpoint-integrable pressure exists for that limit. This refutes the universal regular-pressure assertion.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

derivations.claim: If $y_0=y_1$ or $z_0=z_1$, the four parameterized boundary sides consist of zero-length sides and two coincident sides traversed in opposite directions; their integrals sum to zero. The flux over this zero-area parameterized rectangle and the displayed iterated integral are also zero. This proves the degenerate cases, with the boundary integral interpreted as that four-side sum. For the remaining steps assume $y_0<y_1$ and $z_0<z_1$. With the stated orientation, the four boundary contributions are $\int_{y_0}^{y_1}E_y(x_0,y,z_0)\,dy$, $\int_{z_0}^{z_1}E_z(x_0,y_1,z)\,dz$, $-\int_{y_0}^{y_1}E_y(x_0,y,z_1)\,dy$, and $-\int_{z_0}^{z_1}E_z(x_0,y_0,z)\,dz$. Apply [F1] to the two differences to rewrite their sum as $-\int_{y_0}^{y_1}\int_{z_0}^{z_1}\partial_zE_y\,dz\,dy+\int_{z_0}^{z_1}\int_{y_0}^{y_1}\partial_yE_z\,dy\,dz$.

The two integrands $\partial_yE_z$ and $\partial_zE_y$ are continuous on the compact rectangle, so each is Riemann integrable by [F2], as is every one-dimensional section, since it too is continuous. Riemann–Fubini [F3] identifies each double integral with either order of its iterated integral. Thus the $\partial_yE_z$ term in step 1.1 can be written in the same $dy$-then-$dz$ order as the other term.

Combining the two terms from step 1.1 using the ordering justified in step 2.1 gives $\int_{y_0}^{y_1}\int_{z_0}^{z_1}(\partial_yE_z-\partial_zE_y)\,dz\,dy$, exactly the $x$-component of the curl flux. Cyclic relabeling gives the other coordinate faces; reversing the orientation changes the sign of every boundary and flux term.

citations.quote:
Let $K$ be a finite oriented three-dimensional cell complex with vertex, edge, face, and volume cochains. An edge cochain records oriented electric line integrals, a face cochain records oriented magnetic fluxes, and a vertex cochain records electric charge. Write $N_v,N_e,N_f,N_c$ for the retained vertex, edge, face, and cell counts. On a periodic cell, identify opposite cells with orientation preserved and let $G,C,D$ be the full vertex-to-edge gradient, edge-to-face curl, and face-to-cell divergence incidence matrices, each the transpose of its signed oriented boundary matrix. For a PEC closure, “interior” means not in the boundary subcomplex. Keep only interior electric edges as unknowns and only interior vertices as volume-charge locations, but keep all face fluxes, including boundary-normal magnetic fluxes, and all cells. This closure has no separate boundary surface-charge cochain. Define $G$ and $C$ by restricting the absolute vertex-edge and edge-face incidence matrices to those rows and columns. This mixed closure imposes zero tangential electric edge cochains on the boundary while allowing a fixed normal magnetic flux on boundary faces. In both cases, $G\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_v}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_e}$, and $D\in\mathbb R^{N_c\times N_f}$ satisfy $CG=0$ and $DC=0$.

The electric, magnetic, and conductive material matrices are real symmetric matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, $M_b\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_f}$, and $S\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, respectively. The first two are positive definite and represent the discrete weighted inner products induced by $\epsilon$ and $\mu^{-1}$; $S$ is positive semidefinite and represents conductivity. Write $\langle e_1,e_2\rangle_{M_e}=e_1^TM_ee_2$, $\langle b_1,b_2\rangle_{M_b}=b_1^TM_bb_2$, and $\|e\|_{M_e}^2=\langle e,e\rangle_{M_e}$, $\|b\|_{M_b}^2=\langle b,b\rangle_{M_b}$. In a homogeneous isotropic periodic Cartesian grid with spacings $h_x,h_y,h_z$ and cell volume $V=h_xh_yh_z$, the diagonal entries for an $x$-edge and an $x$-normal face are $\epsilon V/h_x^2=\epsilon h_yh_z/h_x$ and $\mu^{-1}h_x/(h_yh_z)$; the $y$ and $z$ entries are obtained by cyclic permutation. These values are dual-volume Hodge weights for line-integral and face-flux cochains. A compatible PEC closure uses the corresponding truncated dual volumes for free electric edges, while the magnetic mass includes boundary faces; the resulting matrices remain positive definite. The discrete constraints are $-G^TM_ee^n=\rho^n$ on interior vertices and $Db^{n-1/2}=0$ on all cells.

The minus sign in the electric constraint is essential: an edge oriented from tail to head has incidence entries $-1,+1$, so $-G^T$ is the outgoing-flux divergence. Thus $\rho$ represents physical electric charge with the sign of $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)$ in [[def-transient-maxwell-system-with-material-interfaces]].

For current cochains $j^{n+1/2}$ and charge rows $\rho^n$, the discrete continuity condition means
$$\rho^{n+1}-\rho^n-\Delta t\,G^T\left(j^{n+1/2}+S\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)=0.$$
For PEC this is the interior-vertex volume-charge relation; this closure has no separate boundary surface-charge/current cochain.

The cochain identities $CG=0$ and $DC=0$ are not imposed as an extra numerical approximation: they follow from oriented boundary-of-boundary cancellation, including the PEC row and column restrictions, as proved in [[lem-maxwell-discrete-incidence-identities]]. No cell geometry picture is used as a proof.

Let $X$ be a CW complex. For $n\geq1$, in the integral cellular chain groups with the chosen cell orientations,
$$d_ne^n_\alpha=\sum_\beta[e^n_\alpha:e^{n-1}_\beta]e^{n-1}_\beta.$$
For every $n\geq1$, $d_{n-1}d_n=0$.

derivations.claim: Let $\partial_k$ be the absolute oriented cellular boundary from degree $k$ to degree $k-1$. By [F2], $\partial_1\partial_2=0$. Since $\bar G=\partial_1^T$ and $\bar C=\partial_2^T$, transposition gives $\bar C\bar G=(\partial_1\partial_2)^T=0$. For a polygonal face this is the telescoping sum of endpoint differences around its boundary, including a triangular or rectangular Yee face.

Similarly [F2] gives $\partial_2\partial_3=0$, hence $\bar D\bar C=(\partial_2\partial_3)^T=0$. For a tetrahedral or cubical volume, each edge in the boundary of its oriented boundary has two occurrences with opposite induced signs. The cellular identity covers arbitrary cell attachments as well, so this argument does not restrict the claim to tetrahedra.

Periodic identification identifies faces with the prescribed orientation, so the quotient cell structure retains oriented boundary-of-boundary cancellation. For PEC, let $\bar G,\bar C,\bar D$ be the absolute incidence matrices and let $P_e$ select interior edges and $P_v$ select interior vertices. The matrices are $G=P_e\bar G P_v$, $C=\bar C P_e^T$, and $D=\bar D$. An interior vertex is incident to no boundary edge, so $P_e^TP_e\bar G P_v=\bar G P_v$. Hence $CG=\bar C\bar G P_v=0$, while $DC=\bar D\bar C P_e^T=0$. This retains boundary-face magnetic cochains although boundary electric edge values are fixed.

derivations.claim: The matrix $M_e+(\Delta t/2)S$ is symmetric because both summands are symmetric. For each nonzero $x$, its quadratic form is $x^TM_ex+(\Delta t/2)x^TSx>0+0=0$, using $\Delta t>0$ and the two definiteness hypotheses. Hence it is positive definite.

A positive definite square matrix has trivial kernel: if $(M_e+(\Delta t/2)S)x=0$, then its quadratic form at $x$ is zero and step 1.1 forces $x=0$. A linear map from a finite-dimensional space to itself with trivial kernel is bijective, so the solve exists uniquely for every right-hand side.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega$ be a bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron with a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T_h$, and use the real lowest-order spaces $W_h^0,N_h^1,N_h^2,N_h^3$ defined in [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. The electric trial field is $E_h(t)\in N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$; the magnetic flux field is $B_h(t)\in N_h^2$, with no imposed zero normal trace on $B_h$. PEC means the closure-defined zero tangential subspace from [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]. Periodic analogues use the periodic cell complex. Countable Choice is inherited from the H(div) and affine Piola space definitions in the suppliers; the finite matrix operations below use no additional choice.

Put $V_h:=N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$. Choose an edge basis $\{\phi_i\}_{i=1}^{N_e}$ of the electric trial space $V_h$ and a face basis $\{\psi_a\}_{a=1}^{N_f}$ of $N_h^2$, so $N_e=\dim V_h$ and $N_f=\dim N_h^2$. Define the symmetric mass matrices
$$ (M_e)_{ij}=\int_\Omega \phi_j^T\epsilon\phi_i\,dx,\qquad (M_b)_{ab}=\int_\Omega \psi_b^T\mu^{-1}\psi_a\,dx.$$
They are positive definite by the coefficient bounds in [[def-transient-maxwell-system-with-material-interfaces]] and linear independence of the finite element bases. Let $C$ and $D$ be the coefficient matrices, in these chosen bases, of the restricted map $\operatorname{curl}:V_h\to N_h^2$ and of $\operatorname{div}:N_h^2\to N_h^3$. The moment-commuting supplier gives $DC=0$ on the full spaces, hence also after restriction to $V_h$. Set $j_i(t)=\int_\Omega J_{\rm src}(t)\cdot\phi_i\,dx$, with $J_{\rm src}\in C([0,T];L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$. The lossless, conductivity-free semidiscretization with this source is
$$M_e\dot e-C^TM_b b=-j,\qquad \dot b+Ce=0.$$
The coefficient ODE is defined for arbitrary initial coefficients. To represent the magnetic constraint of the Maxwell model, require $Db(0)=0$: the Faraday row and $DC=0$ give $D\dot b=-DCe=0$, so $Db(t)=Db(0)$ and compatible data remain divergence-free. An incompatible initial divergence is preserved, not corrected by this ODE. This is a spatial Galerkin system only; no time integrator is included. The cochain convention and weak material-interface formulation come from the declared spaces and [[def-transient-maxwell-system-with-material-interfaces]]. Smooth interpolation and a uniformly bounded commuting projection are separate prerequisites for the later error estimate and are not asserted by this definition.

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. For $n=0$, there is exactly one map $Y:I\to M_0(\mathbb R)$, namely the empty-matrix map, and all entrywise differential identities are vacuous. For $n\ge1$ and $a<b$, the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$, with domain-relative one-sided
derivatives at the endpoints. If $n\ge1$ and $a=b$, then $t_0=a$ and there is exactly
one map $Y:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ with $Y(a)=Y_0$. This singleton map
extends to a solution of $Z'=C(a)Z$, $Z(a)=Y_0$, on an open interval
around $a$; any two such local continuations agree on their common interval
containing $a$. No time derivative or IVP solution on the singleton itself
is asserted.

Let $\Omega$ be a bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron with a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T_h$, and use the real lowest-order spaces $W_h^0,N_h^1,N_h^2,N_h^3$ defined in [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. The electric trial field is $E_h(t)\in N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$; the magnetic flux field is $B_h(t)\in N_h^2$, with no imposed zero normal trace on $B_h$. PEC means the closure-defined zero tangential subspace from [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]. Periodic analogues use the periodic cell complex. Countable Choice is inherited from the H(div) and affine Piola space definitions in the suppliers; the finite matrix operations below use no additional choice.

Put $V_h:=N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$. Choose an edge basis $\{\phi_i\}_{i=1}^{N_e}$ of the electric trial space $V_h$ and a face basis $\{\psi_a\}_{a=1}^{N_f}$ of $N_h^2$, so $N_e=\dim V_h$ and $N_f=\dim N_h^2$. Define the symmetric mass matrices
$$ (M_e)_{ij}=\int_\Omega \phi_j^T\epsilon\phi_i\,dx,\qquad (M_b)_{ab}=\int_\Omega \psi_b^T\mu^{-1}\psi_a\,dx.$$
They are positive definite by the coefficient bounds in [[def-transient-maxwell-system-with-material-interfaces]] and linear independence of the finite element bases. Let $C$ and $D$ be the coefficient matrices, in these chosen bases, of the restricted map $\operatorname{curl}:V_h\to N_h^2$ and of $\operatorname{div}:N_h^2\to N_h^3$. The moment-commuting supplier gives $DC=0$ on the full spaces, hence also after restriction to $V_h$. Set $j_i(t)=\int_\Omega J_{\rm src}(t)\cdot\phi_i\,dx$, with $J_{\rm src}\in C([0,T];L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$. The lossless, conductivity-free semidiscretization with this source is
$$M_e\dot e-C^TM_b b=-j,\qquad \dot b+Ce=0.$$
The coefficient ODE is defined for arbitrary initial coefficients. To represent the magnetic constraint of the Maxwell model, require $Db(0)=0$: the Faraday row and $DC=0$ give $D\dot b=-DCe=0$, so $Db(t)=Db(0)$ and compatible data remain divergence-free. An incompatible initial divergence is preserved, not corrected by this ODE. This is a spatial Galerkin system only; no time integrator is included. The cochain convention and weak material-interface formulation come from the declared spaces and [[def-transient-maxwell-system-with-material-interfaces]]. Smooth interpolation and a uniformly bounded commuting projection are separate prerequisites for the later error estimate and are not asserted by this definition.

derivations.claim: Put $x=(e,b)\in\mathbb R^N$, $N=N_e+N_f$, and $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&M_e^{-1}C^TM_b\\-C&0\end{pmatrix}$, $f(t)=(-M_e^{-1}j(t),0)$. By [F2], $x'=Ax+f(t)$. Form the continuous $(N+1)\times(N+1)$ matrix $\mathcal A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}A&f(t)\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and the initial matrix $Y_0$ whose last column is $(x_0,1)^T$ and whose other columns are zero.

If $T=0$, the prescribed initial coefficients determine the unique singleton map. Hold $j$ constant at $j(0)$ and use the matrix $\mathcal A$ of step 1.1 on $[-1,1]$. By [F1] it has a unique matrix solution there through $Y_0$ at zero. Its last column has last entry one and its top block solves the constant-load coefficient ODE, giving the asserted continuation. Uniqueness on any common interval containing zero follows by applying [F1] to each compact subinterval joining zero to a point of overlap. No singleton derivative is taken.

Now assume $T>0$. By [F1], $Y'=\mathcal A(t)Y$, $Y(0)=Y_0$ has a unique global solution. Its last column $(x(t),s(t))^T$ satisfies $s'(t)=0$ and $s(0)=1$, so $s(t)=1$, while the top block satisfies $x'=Ax+f(t)$ and $x(0)=x_0$. Thus it gives a global solution of the Maxwell coefficient system. Any two such coefficient solutions yield two matrix solutions with the same last-column initial data; uniqueness in [F1] forces their last columns to agree.
