citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The covariant affine Piola map for $N_h^1$ and contravariant affine Piola map for $N_h^2$ use the orientation-preserving cell maps and conventions of [[def-covariant-contravariant-piola-maps-and-hdiv-hcurl]]. Their differential and moment identities are those of [[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]]. The edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom are respectively the oriented edge circulation, oriented face-normal flux, and cell integral.

In the two conformity conditions above, each cellwise polynomial restriction has a unique polynomial representative on its closed cell, and those representatives define the displayed edge and face integrals. Thus the global edge and face moments are part of the assembled-space definition; their correspondence with all cochains is proved by the local unisolvence and commuting-moment items, not inferred from rough-field traces.

On an oriented tetrahedron $K$ with vertices $x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3$, let $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$ for $0\le i<j\le3$. Then the six edge circulations $\ell_{rs}(v)=\int_{[x_r,x_s]}v\cdot t_{rs}\,ds$ satisfy $\ell_{rs}(\phi_{ij})=\delta_{(r,s),(i,j)}$. The six functions form a basis of the local space $\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:i<j\}=\{a+b\times x:a,b\in\mathbb R^3\}$, so these edge circulations are unisolvent degrees of freedom.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh. The four face-normal fluxes are unisolvent on each $RT_0(K)$, and matching face fluxes assemble a global $H(\operatorname{div})$ field. For smooth scalar $f$, smooth vector fields $u,v$, and the canonical interpolants determined by vertex values, oriented edge circulations, oriented face-normal fluxes, and cell integrals, the interpolation maps satisfy cellwise
$$
abla I_h^0f=I_h^1
abla f,\qquad \operatorname{curl}I_h^1u=I_h^2\operatorname{curl}u,\qquad \operatorname{div}I_h^2v=I_h^3\operatorname{div}v.$$
Any assignment of one real oriented value to each global mesh edge determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^1$; any assignment of one real oriented flux to each global mesh face determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^2$. These assemblies belong to $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$, respectively, with the global spaces and conventions of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Applying the local moment identities to polynomial cell restrictions also proves that the global finite-element spaces form the subcomplex $W_h^0\xrightarrow{
abla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$. The canonical interpolation identities themselves apply to smooth inputs; they do not extend the canonical edge moments to arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ inputs.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d=2$ or $3$ and let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ map a reference
simplex to an affine cell with $\det A>0$. The contravariant Piola map
$\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{div}}\widehat v=(\det A)^{-1}A\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$
maps $H(\operatorname{div},\widehat S_d)$ into $H(\operatorname{div},K)$ and
$$\operatorname{div}(\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{div}}\widehat v) =(\det A)^{-1}(\widehat{\operatorname{div}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}.$$
The covariant Piola map
$\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{curl}}\widehat v=A^{-T}\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$
maps $H(\operatorname{curl},\widehat S_d)$ into $H(\operatorname{curl},K)$;
in $d=2$ its scalar curl is
$(\det A)^{-1}(\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}$,
and in $d=3$ its vector curl is
$(\det A)^{-1}A(\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}$.
For every $\widehat u\in W^{1,2}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)$, the scalar
pullback $u=\widehat u\circ F^{-1}$ belongs to $W^{1,2}(K;\mathbb R)$ and
its gradient satisfies
$$\nabla u=\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{curl}}(\widehat\nabla\widehat u).$$
For smooth fields, contravariant normal fluxes satisfy
$v\cdot n\,dS=\widehat v\cdot\widehat n\,d\widehat S$; covariant tangential
pullbacks satisfy $v(F(\widehat x))\cdot A\widehat\tau=
\widehat v(\widehat x)\cdot\widehat\tau$ for every reference tangent
$\widehat\tau$. Thus edge line integrals and normal-flux moments are
preserved, and face tangential moments transform with this pullback and
the induced facet surface Jacobian. These formulas record the chosen
orientation; reversing a facet orientation reverses its signed moment.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

derivations.claim: On a fixed reference tetrahedron, each canonical basis function has finite $L^2$ norm. Under the covariant Piola map, [F4] and [F5] give $\|\phi_{K,e}\|_{L^2(K)}\le C_\sigma h_K^{-1}h_K^{3/2}=C_\sigma h_K^{1/2}$ for each edge basis function. Under the contravariant Piola map they give $\|\psi_{K,F}\|_{L^2(K)}\le C_\sigma h_K^{-3}h_Kh_K^{3/2}=C_\sigma h_K^{-1/2}$ for each unit-face-flux RT0 basis function.

By [F3], $\operatorname{div}I_K^2v=I_K^3\operatorname{div}v$, and $I_K^3$ is the cell average because its defining degree of freedom is the cell integral. Thus $|\operatorname{div}v(x)-I_K^3\operatorname{div}v|\le h_K\|\nabla\operatorname{div}v\|_{L^\infty(K)}$ throughout $K$, and $\|\operatorname{div}(v-I_K^2v)\|_{L^2(K)}\le C h_K^{5/2}\|\nabla\operatorname{div}v\|_{L^\infty(K)}$.

Fix $K$ and $x_K\in K$, and put $u_K=u(x_K)$, a constant vector in the local Nedelec space by [F2]. For each of its six edges, the mean-value bound gives $|\int_e(u-u_K)\cdot t\,ds|\le h_K^2\|
abla u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$. By edge-moment unisolvence [F2], $I_K^1(u-u_K)$ is the sum of these six coefficients times the corresponding basis functions. Step 1.1 and $\|u-u_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le C h_K^{5/2}\|
abla u\|_\infty$ therefore yield $\|u-I_K^1u\|_{L^2(K)}\le C_\sigma h_K^{5/2}\|
abla u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$.

Set $q=\operatorname{curl}u$ and $q_K=q(x_K)$, a constant RT0 field. By the curl commuting identity [F3], $\operatorname{curl}I_K^1u=I_K^2q$. Each face-flux coefficient of $q-q_K$ is at most $C h_K^3\|\nabla q\|_{L^\infty(K)}$; multiplying the four coefficients by the RT0 basis bounds in step 1.1 and adding $\|q-q_K\|_{L^2(K)}$ gives $\|\operatorname{curl}(u-I_K^1u)\|_{L^2(K)}\le C_\sigma h_K^{5/2}\|\nabla\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$.

For $v$, set $v_K=v(x_K)$, again a constant in RT0. Each of the four face-flux coefficients of $v-v_K$ is bounded by $C h_K^3\|
abla v\|_{L^\infty(K)}$. The RT0 basis scaling in step 1.1 and $\|v-v_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le C h_K^{5/2}\|
abla v\|_\infty$ give $\|v-I_K^2v\|_{L^2(K)}\le C_\sigma h_K^{5/2}\|
abla v\|_{L^\infty(K)}$.

Square and sum the four local bounds. By [F5], $h_K^5\le C_\sigma h^2|K|$; the cell interiors are disjoint and sum to $\Omega$. Taking square roots gives the displayed global estimate with the maximum cell derivative bound and the factor $|\Omega|^{1/2}$. The matching traces and the conformity part of [F3] assemble the interpolants globally.

2. Solve the electric row
   $$\left(M_e+\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^{n+1}=\left(M_e-\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^n+\Delta t\,C^TM_b b^{n+1/2}-\Delta t\,j^{n+1/2}.$$

The row is well defined for every input because its matrix is invertible by [[lem-maxwell-yee-step-matrix-is-positive-definite]]. This procedure makes no stability claim; the lossless stability condition is proved separately.

For the incidence matrices $G,C,D$ of [[def-maxwell-discrete-cochain-and-yee-grid]], one has $CG=0$ and $DC=0$. The conclusion holds for the full periodic complex and for the PEC mixed closure defined there.

Let $K$ be a finite oriented three-dimensional cell complex with vertex, edge, face, and volume cochains. An edge cochain records oriented electric line integrals, a face cochain records oriented magnetic fluxes, and a vertex cochain records electric charge. On a periodic cell, identify opposite cells with orientation preserved and let $G,C,D$ be the full vertex-to-edge gradient, edge-to-face curl, and face-to-cell divergence incidence matrices, each the transpose of its signed oriented boundary matrix. For a PEC closure, “interior” means not in the boundary subcomplex. Keep only interior electric edges as unknowns and only interior vertices as volume-charge locations, but keep all face fluxes, including boundary-normal magnetic fluxes, and all cells. This closure has no separate boundary surface-charge cochain. Define $G$ and $C$ by restricting the absolute vertex-edge and edge-face incidence matrices to those rows and columns. This mixed closure imposes zero tangential electric edge cochains on the boundary while allowing a fixed normal magnetic flux on boundary faces. In both cases, $G\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_v}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_e}$, and $D\in\mathbb R^{N_c\times N_f}$ satisfy $CG=0$ and $DC=0$.

The first two are positive definite and represent the discrete weighted inner products induced by $\epsilon$ and $\mu^{-1}$; $S$ is positive semidefinite and represents conductivity. Write $\langle e_1,e_2\rangle_{M_e}=e_1^TM_ee_2$, $\langle b_1,b_2\rangle_{M_b}=b_1^TM_bb_2$, and $\|e\|_{M_e}^2=\langle e,e\rangle_{M_e}$, $\|b\|_{M_b}^2=\langle b,b\rangle_{M_b}$. derivations.claim: If $N_e=0$, the electric cochain is necessarily zero and $C$ is the zero map from the zero space. The Faraday row in [F2] makes $b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}$ at every step, while the electric row is an equality in the zero space. Thus $b_c^n=b^{n+1/2}$ is constant and $\mathcal E^n=\tfrac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2$. With the stated convention $\lambda_{\max}=0$, this proves conservation, the lower bound, and positivity on the remaining magnetic state for every $\Delta t>0$; there is no positive-eigenvalue endpoint case. For the rest of the proof assume $N_e>0$. The quotient defining $\lambda_{\max}$ is continuous on the compact set $\{e:e^TM_ee=1\}$, so the maximum exists and is finite. Also $e^TKe=(Ce)^TM_b(Ce)\ge0$, hence $\lambda_{\max}\ge0$. From the first row of [F2], $b^{n-1/2}=b_c^n+\Delta t Ce^n/2$ and $b^{n+1/2}=b_c^n-\Delta t Ce^n/2$. Expanding their $M_b$ inner product gives $\mathcal E^n=\frac12\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2+\frac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2-\frac{\Delta t^2}{8}\|Ce^n\|_{M_b}^2.$

Using [F2], the electric-energy increment is $\frac12\|e^{n+1}\|_{M_e}^2-\frac12\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2=\left(\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)^TM_e(e^{n+1}-e^n)=\Delta t\left(\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)^TC^TM_bb^{n+1/2}.$ The magnetic cross-energy increment is $\frac12(b^{n+1/2})^TM_b(b^{n+3/2}-b^{n-1/2})=-\Delta t\left(\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)^TC^TM_bb^{n+1/2},$ by applying the Faraday row at times $n$ and $n+1$. The two increments cancel, proving conservation.

By the definition of $\lambda_{\max}$, $\|Ce^n\|_{M_b}^2=(e^n)^TKe^n\le\lambda_{\max}\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2$. Substitution into step 1.1 gives the stated lower bound. When $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}<4$, its electric coefficient is positive. If an admissible staggered state has zero energy, the bound forces $e^n=0$ and $b_c^n=0$; the Faraday row in [F2] then gives $b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}$, so $b_c^n=b^{n-1/2}=b^{n+1/2}=0$. Thus the energy is positive definite on update states.

Subtract the electric row in [F2] at indices $n$ and $n-1$, then use the magnetic row to replace $b^{n+1/2}-b^{n-1/2}$; this gives $M_e(e^{n+1}-2e^n+e^{n-1})+\Delta t^2Ke^n=0$. If $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}=4$, a maximizing vector $v$ satisfies $Kv=\lambda_{\max}M_ev$ by the constrained Rayleigh-quotient maximum. Thus $e^n=q_nv$ obeys $q_{n+1}-2q_n+q_{n-1}+\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}q_n=0$, whose characteristic polynomial is $(r+1)^2$. Hence $q_n=(-1)^n(a+bn)$ is a solution and grows linearly when $b\ne0$. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lipschitz polyhedron, or a periodic rectangular cell. The real electric field is $E(t,x)\in\mathbb R^3$ and the magnetic flux density is $B(t,x)\in\mathbb R^3$; the magnetic intensity is $H=\mu^{-1}B$. Let $\epsilon(x)$ and $\mu(x)$ be measurable, time-independent, symmetric matrix fields for which there are constants $0<\epsilon_0\le\epsilon_1$ and $0<\mu_0\le\mu_1$ with
$$\epsilon_0|v|^2\le v^T\epsilon(x)v\le\epsilon_1|v|^2,\qquad \mu_0|v|^2\le v^T\mu(x)v\le\mu_1|v|^2$$
for almost every $x$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^3$. A conductivity tensor $\sigma(x)$, when present, is measurable, symmetric, and positive semidefinite. The coefficients may jump across finitely many Lipschitz material interfaces. No derivative of a coefficient is part of the model.

In each material region the constitutive fields satisfy
$$\partial_t(\epsilon E)=\operatorname{curl}(\mu^{-1}B)-J_{\rm src}-\sigma E,\qquad \partial_t B+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$
Here $J_{\rm src}$ is the impressed free-current density, while $\sigma E$ is the conductive current. Electric charge $\rho$ is constrained by $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)=\rho$ and the total-current continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E)=0$; the magnetic constraint is $\operatorname{div}B=0$. These equalities are distributional. In the lossless branch set $\sigma=0$.

The boundary choice is one of the following. A **periodic boundary** identifies opposite traces of the rectangular cell. A **perfect electric conductor (PEC) boundary** imposes zero tangential trace $n\times E=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. At a material interface with no singular surface charge or current, the weak equations are understood with the transmission conditions $[n\times E]=0$, $[n\cdot B]=0$, $[n\times(\mu^{-1}B)]=0$, and $[n\cdot(\epsilon E)]=0$, where $[q]$ is the trace from one side minus the trace from the other. The interface conditions are part of the model convention; no smooth Taylor expansion across a coefficient jump is asserted.

For PEC, the weak Ampere equation is $(\epsilon E_t,v)_{L^2}-(\mu^{-1}B,\operatorname{curl}v)_{L^2}=-(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E,v)_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ as defined in [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]; the periodic branch uses periodic $H(\operatorname{curl})$ test fields. Faraday’s equation remains $B_t+\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in distributions. These weak forms define the test-space and boundary convention used by the edge finite element method.

The weighted field norms are $\|E\|_\epsilon^2=\int_\Omega E^T\epsilon E\,dx$ and $\|B\|_{\mu^{-1}}^2=\int_\Omega B^T\mu^{-1}B\,dx$. The uniform coefficient bounds make them equivalent to the ordinary $L^2$ norms. All later smooth-error claims require smoothness separately on each mesh-aligned material region.

Let $F=\{(x_0,y,z):y_0\le y\le y_1,\ z_0\le z\le z_1\}$ be an oriented rectangle with normal $e_x$, and let $E$ be a $C^1$ vector field near $F$. Orient $\partial F$ by the outward-normal-first convention. Then
$$\int_{\partial F}E\cdot t\,ds=\int_F(\operatorname{curl}E)\cdot e_x\,dS=\int_{y_0}^{y_1}\int_{z_0}^{z_1}(\partial_yE_z-\partial_zE_y)(x_0,y,z)\,dz\,dy.$$
The identities for normals $e_y$ and $e_z$ follow by cyclic permutation of coordinates. Reversing a face orientation reverses both integrals.

Taylor’s formula with integral remainder gives $\delta_j^2f=\partial_j^2f+O(h_j^2\|\partial_j^4f\|_\infty)$ and $\delta_i\delta_jf=\partial_i\partial_jf+O((h_i^2+h_j^2)\|D^4f\|_\infty)$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega$ be a bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron with a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T_h$, and use the real lowest-order spaces $W_h^0,N_h^1,N_h^2,N_h^3$ defined in [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. The electric trial field is $E_h(t)\in N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$; the magnetic flux field is $B_h(t)\in N_h^2$, with no imposed zero normal trace on $B_h$. PEC means the closure-defined zero tangential subspace from [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]. Periodic analogues use the periodic cell complex. Countable Choice is inherited from the H(div) and affine Piola space definitions in the suppliers; the finite matrix operations below use no additional choice.

Put $V_h:=N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$. Choose an edge basis $\{\phi_i\}_{i=1}^{N_e}$ of the electric trial space $V_h$ and a face basis $\{\psi_a\}_{a=1}^{N_f}$ of $N_h^2$, so $N_e=\dim V_h$ and $N_f=\dim N_h^2$. Define the symmetric mass matrices
$$ (M_e)_{ij}=\int_\Omega \phi_j^T\epsilon\phi_i\,dx,\qquad (M_b)_{ab}=\int_\Omega \psi_b^T\mu^{-1}\psi_a\,dx.$$
They are positive definite by the coefficient bounds in [[def-transient-maxwell-system-with-material-interfaces]] and linear independence of the finite element bases. Let $C$ and $D$ be the coefficient matrices, in these chosen bases, of the restricted map $\operatorname{curl}:V_h\to N_h^2$ and of $\operatorname{div}:N_h^2\to N_h^3$. The moment-commuting supplier gives $DC=0$ on the full spaces, hence also after restriction to $V_h$. Set $j_i(t)=\int_\Omega J_{\rm src}(t)\cdot\phi_i\,dx$, with $J_{\rm src}\in C([0,T];L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$. The lossless, conductivity-free semidiscretization with this source is
$$M_e\dot e-C^TM_b b=-j,\qquad \dot b+Ce=0.$$
The coefficient ODE is defined for arbitrary initial coefficients. To represent the magnetic constraint of the Maxwell model, require $Db(0)=0$: the Faraday row and $DC=0$ give $D\dot b=-DCe=0$, so $Db(t)=Db(0)$ and compatible data remain divergence-free. An incompatible initial divergence is preserved, not corrected by this ODE. This is a spatial Galerkin system only; no time integrator is included. The cochain convention and weak material-interface formulation come from the declared spaces and [[def-transient-maxwell-system-with-material-interfaces]]. Smooth interpolation and a uniformly bounded commuting projection are separate prerequisites for the later error estimate and are not asserted by this definition.

derivations.claim: On a singleton time interval the energy is constant immediately; assume henceforth that the time interval is nondegenerate. In the declared Countable Choice branch [A1], the FE bases and matrices in [F1] are fixed finite objects; the calculation below makes no selection. Differentiating the electric part gives $\frac{d}{dt}\frac12 e^TM_ee=e^TM_e\dot e=e^TC^TM_bb$.

Differentiating the magnetic part gives $\frac{d}{dt}\frac12 b^TM_bb=b^TM_b\dot b=-b^TM_bCe=-e^TC^TM_bb$, because the scalar transpose equals itself. The two derivatives cancel, so $\mathcal H_h'(t)=0$ throughout the interval of existence.

Let $K$ be a finite oriented three-dimensional cell complex with vertex, edge, face, and volume cochains. An edge cochain records oriented electric line integrals, a face cochain records oriented magnetic fluxes, and a vertex cochain records electric charge. Write $N_v,N_e,N_f,N_c$ for the retained vertex, edge, face, and cell counts. On a periodic cell, identify opposite cells with orientation preserved and let $G,C,D$ be the full vertex-to-edge gradient, edge-to-face curl, and face-to-cell divergence incidence matrices, each the transpose of its signed oriented boundary matrix. For a PEC closure, “interior” means not in the boundary subcomplex. Keep only interior electric edges as unknowns and only interior vertices as volume-charge locations, but keep all face fluxes, including boundary-normal magnetic fluxes, and all cells. This closure has no separate boundary surface-charge cochain. Define $G$ and $C$ by restricting the absolute vertex-edge and edge-face incidence matrices to those rows and columns. This mixed closure imposes zero tangential electric edge cochains on the boundary while allowing a fixed normal magnetic flux on boundary faces. In both cases, $G\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_v}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_e}$, and $D\in\mathbb R^{N_c\times N_f}$ satisfy $CG=0$ and $DC=0$.

The electric, magnetic, and conductive material matrices are real symmetric matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, $M_b\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_f}$, and $S\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, respectively. The first two are positive definite and represent the discrete weighted inner products induced by $\epsilon$ and $\mu^{-1}$; $S$ is positive semidefinite and represents conductivity. Write $\langle e_1,e_2\rangle_{M_e}=e_1^TM_ee_2$, $\langle b_1,b_2\rangle_{M_b}=b_1^TM_bb_2$, and $\|e\|_{M_e}^2=\langle e,e\rangle_{M_e}$, $\|b\|_{M_b}^2=\langle b,b\rangle_{M_b}$. In a homogeneous isotropic periodic Cartesian grid with spacings $h_x,h_y,h_z$ and cell volume $V=h_xh_yh_z$, the diagonal entries for an $x$-edge and an $x$-normal face are $\epsilon V/h_x^2=\epsilon h_yh_z/h_x$ and $\mu^{-1}h_x/(h_yh_z)$; the $y$ and $z$ entries are obtained by cyclic permutation. These values are dual-volume Hodge weights for line-integral and face-flux cochains. A compatible PEC closure uses the corresponding truncated dual volumes for free electric edges, while the magnetic mass includes boundary faces; the resulting matrices remain positive definite. The discrete constraints are $-G^TM_ee^n=\rho^n$ on interior vertices and $Db^{n-1/2}=0$ on all cells.

The minus sign in the electric constraint is essential: an edge oriented from tail to head has incidence entries $-1,+1$, so $-G^T$ is the outgoing-flux divergence. Thus $\rho$ represents physical electric charge with the sign of $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)$ in [[def-transient-maxwell-system-with-material-interfaces]].

For current cochains $j^{n+1/2}$ and charge rows $\rho^n$, the discrete continuity condition means
$$\rho^{n+1}-\rho^n-\Delta t\,G^T\left(j^{n+1/2}+S\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)=0.$$
For PEC this is the interior-vertex volume-charge relation; this closure has no separate boundary surface-charge/current cochain.

The cochain identities $CG=0$ and $DC=0$ are not imposed as an extra numerical approximation: they follow from oriented boundary-of-boundary cancellation, including the PEC row and column restrictions, as proved in [[lem-maxwell-discrete-incidence-identities]]. No cell geometry picture is used as a proof.

Set $K=C^TM_bC$. If the retained electric cochain space is zero-dimensional,
define $\lambda_{\max}:=0$; otherwise set
$$\lambda_{\max}:=\max_{e\ne0}\frac{e^TKe}{e^TM_ee}.$$
For a lossless, source-free update from [[alg-maxwell-yee-leapfrog-update]], define
$$\mathcal E^n:=\frac12(e^n)^TM_ee^n+\frac12(b^{n-1/2})^TM_bb^{n+1/2},\qquad b_c^n:=\frac{b^{n-1/2}+b^{n+1/2}}2.$$
Then $\mathcal E^n$ is independent of $n$, and
$$\mathcal E^n\ge\frac12\left(1-\frac{\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}}4\right)\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2+\frac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2.$$
Consequently, the actual strict spectral condition $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}<4$ makes this modified energy positive on admissible staggered states and controls the electric field and the centered magnetic field. When $\lambda_{\max}>0$, at equality the energy loses coercivity and a maximal mode has a repeated root $-1$; above equality a mode grows exponentially. If $\lambda_{\max}=0$, the strict condition is automatic for every $\Delta t>0$ and neither endpoint case occurs.

Choose a finite complex and boundary closure as in [[def-maxwell-discrete-cochain-and-yee-grid]], step size $\Delta t>0$, initial $e^0\in\mathbb R^{N_e}$ and $b^{-1/2}\in\mathbb R^{N_f}$, and source rows $j^{n+1/2}\in\mathbb R^{N_e}$. The output is a sequence $e^n$ at integer times and $b^{n+1/2}$ at half-integer times. For each $n\ge0$, perform the ordered instructions

1. Update the face flux by
   $$b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}-\Delta t\,C e^n.$$

2. Solve the electric row
   $$\left(M_e+\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^{n+1}=\left(M_e-\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^n+\Delta t\,C^TM_b b^{n+1/2}-\Delta t\,j^{n+1/2}.$$

For $S=0$ this is the lossless Yee leapfrog scheme. For $S\succeq0$, the midpoint term is the specified trapezoidal treatment of conductivity. The row is well defined for every input because its matrix is invertible by [[lem-maxwell-yee-step-matrix-is-positive-definite]]. This procedure makes no stability claim; the lossless stability condition is proved separately.

derivations.claim: On a periodic Fourier mode, a forward edge difference in direction $j$ has multiplier $e^{i\theta_j}-1=2i e^{i\theta_j/2}\sin(\theta_j/2)$. The half-cell phase in the edge and face cochain locations is removed by a unitary diagonal change of Fourier basis, so the scaled directional symbol is $i d_j$ with $d_j=2\sin(\theta_j/2)/h_j$. The Cartesian curl symbol is therefore $i\boldsymbol d\times$.

The cross-product matrix $\boldsymbol d\times$ is real skew-symmetric. The identity $-(\boldsymbol d\times)^2=|\boldsymbol d|^2I-\boldsymbol d\boldsymbol d^T$ follows by expanding the vector triple product. Choose a finite complex and boundary closure as in [[def-maxwell-discrete-cochain-and-yee-grid]], step size $\Delta t>0$, initial $e^0\in\mathbb R^{N_e}$ and $b^{-1/2}\in\mathbb R^{N_f}$, and source rows $j^{n+1/2}\in\mathbb R^{N_e}$. The output is a sequence $e^n$ at integer times and $b^{n+1/2}$ at half-integer times. For each $n\ge0$, perform the ordered instructions

1. Update the face flux by
   $$b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}-\Delta t\,C e^n.$$

2. Solve the electric row
   $$\left(M_e+\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^{n+1}=\left(M_e-\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^n+\Delta t\,C^TM_b b^{n+1/2}-\Delta t\,j^{n+1/2}.$$

For $S=0$ this is the lossless Yee leapfrog scheme. For $S\succeq0$, the midpoint term is the specified trapezoidal treatment of conductivity. The row is well defined for every input because its matrix is invertible by [[lem-maxwell-yee-step-matrix-is-positive-definite]]. This procedure makes no stability claim; the lossless stability condition is proved separately.

Set $K=C^TM_bC$. If the retained electric cochain space is zero-dimensional,
define $\lambda_{\max}:=0$; otherwise set
$$\lambda_{\max}:=\max_{e\ne0}\frac{e^TKe}{e^TM_ee}.$$
For a lossless, source-free update from [[alg-maxwell-yee-leapfrog-update]], define
$$\mathcal E^n:=\frac12(e^n)^TM_ee^n+\frac12(b^{n-1/2})^TM_bb^{n+1/2},\qquad b_c^n:=\frac{b^{n-1/2}+b^{n+1/2}}2.$$
Then $\mathcal E^n$ is independent of $n$, and
$$\mathcal E^n\ge\frac12\left(1-\frac{\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}}4\right)\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2+\frac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2.$$
Consequently, the actual strict spectral condition $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}<4$ makes this modified energy positive on admissible staggered states and controls the electric field and the centered magnetic field. When $\lambda_{\max}>0$, at equality the energy loses coercivity and a maximal mode has a repeated root $-1$; above equality a mode grows exponentially. If $\lambda_{\max}=0$, the strict condition is automatic for every $\Delta t>0$ and neither endpoint case occurs.

Let a periodic rectangular cell be discretized by a uniform Cartesian Yee grid with spacings $h_x,h_y,h_z$, $h=\max_jh_j$, and constant scalar coefficients $\epsilon,\mu>0$. Let $(E,B)$ be a source-free smooth periodic Maxwell solution on $[0,T]$, with the spatial derivatives of $E$ through total order four, $\partial_t^4E$, and $\partial_t^3B$ bounded. Sample $E(t_n)$ by exact oriented edge line integrals $e_*^n$ and $B(t_{n+1/2})$ by exact oriented face fluxes $b_*^{n+1/2}$. Define
$$r_h^n=M_e\frac{e_*^{n+1}-2e_*^n+e_*^{n-1}}{\Delta t^2}+C^TM_bCe_*^n,\qquad s_h^n=b_*^{n+1/2}-b_*^{n-1/2}+\Delta t\,Ce_*^n.$$
With the homogeneous diagonal Hodge weights of [[def-maxwell-discrete-cochain-and-yee-grid]], there is a constant $C_T$ independent of the cell counts such that, whenever $\Delta t\le t_n\le T-\Delta t$,
$$\|r_h^n\|_{M_e^{-1}}\le C_T(h^2+\Delta t^2),\qquad \|s_h^n\|_{M_b}\le C_T\Delta t^3.$$
Here $\|r\|_{M_e^{-1}}^2=r^TM_e^{-1}r$. This is a smooth homogeneous periodic consistency result; it asserts no Taylor estimate across coefficient jumps or a PEC boundary closure.

Let $K$ be a finite oriented three-dimensional cell complex with vertex, edge, face, and volume cochains. An edge cochain records oriented electric line integrals, a face cochain records oriented magnetic fluxes, and a vertex cochain records electric charge. Write $N_v,N_e,N_f,N_c$ for the retained vertex, edge, face, and cell counts. On a periodic cell, identify opposite cells with orientation preserved and let $G,C,D$ be the full vertex-to-edge gradient, edge-to-face curl, and face-to-cell divergence incidence matrices, each the transpose of its signed oriented boundary matrix. For a PEC closure, “interior” means not in the boundary subcomplex. Keep only interior electric edges as unknowns and only interior vertices as volume-charge locations, but keep all face fluxes, including boundary-normal magnetic fluxes, and all cells. This closure has no separate boundary surface-charge cochain. Define $G$ and $C$ by restricting the absolute vertex-edge and edge-face incidence matrices to those rows and columns. This mixed closure imposes zero tangential electric edge cochains on the boundary while allowing a fixed normal magnetic flux on boundary faces. In both cases, $G\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_v}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_e}$, and $D\in\mathbb R^{N_c\times N_f}$ satisfy $CG=0$ and $DC=0$.

The electric, magnetic, and conductive material matrices are real symmetric matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, $M_b\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_f}$, and $S\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, respectively. The first two are positive definite and represent the discrete weighted inner products induced by $\epsilon$ and $\mu^{-1}$; $S$ is positive semidefinite and represents conductivity. Write $\langle e_1,e_2\rangle_{M_e}=e_1^TM_ee_2$, $\langle b_1,b_2\rangle_{M_b}=b_1^TM_bb_2$, and $\|e\|_{M_e}^2=\langle e,e\rangle_{M_e}$, $\|b\|_{M_b}^2=\langle b,b\rangle_{M_b}$. In a homogeneous isotropic periodic Cartesian grid with spacings $h_x,h_y,h_z$ and cell volume $V=h_xh_yh_z$, the diagonal entries for an $x$-edge and an $x$-normal face are $\epsilon V/h_x^2=\epsilon h_yh_z/h_x$ and $\mu^{-1}h_x/(h_yh_z)$; the $y$ and $z$ entries are obtained by cyclic permutation. These values are dual-volume Hodge weights for line-integral and face-flux cochains. A compatible PEC closure uses the corresponding truncated dual volumes for free electric edges, while the magnetic mass includes boundary faces; the resulting matrices remain positive definite. The discrete constraints are $-G^TM_ee^n=\rho^n$ on interior vertices and $Db^{n-1/2}=0$ on all cells.

The minus sign in the electric constraint is essential: an edge oriented from tail to head has incidence entries $-1,+1$, so $-G^T$ is the outgoing-flux divergence. Thus $\rho$ represents physical electric charge with the sign of $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)$ in [[def-transient-maxwell-system-with-material-interfaces]].

For current cochains $j^{n+1/2}$ and charge rows $\rho^n$, the discrete continuity condition means
$$\rho^{n+1}-\rho^n-\Delta t\,G^T\left(j^{n+1/2}+S\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)=0.$$
For PEC this is the interior-vertex volume-charge relation; this closure has no separate boundary surface-charge/current cochain.

The cochain identities $CG=0$ and $DC=0$ are not imposed as an extra numerical approximation: they follow from oriented boundary-of-boundary cancellation, including the PEC row and column restrictions, as proved in [[lem-maxwell-discrete-incidence-identities]]. No cell geometry picture is used as a proof.

derivations.claim: Subtract the exact-sample equations with residuals from the numerical rows. With $K=C^TM_bC$, this gives $M_e\delta_{tt}w^n+Kw^n=-r_h^n,\qquad z^{n+1/2}-z^{n-1/2}=-\Delta t\,Cw^n-s_h^n.$ The sign convention for $s_h^n$ is the one in the consistency statement.

Put $V^n=(w^{n+1}-w^n)/\Delta t$, $\bar w^n=(w^{n+1}+w^n)/2$, and $\mathscr E^{n+1/2}=\tfrac12\|V^n\|_{M_e}^2+\tfrac12\langle Cw^{n+1},Cw^n\rangle_{M_b}.$ Expanding about $C\bar w^n$ gives $\mathscr E^{n+1/2}=\frac12\|V^n\|_{M_e}^2+\frac12\|C\bar w^n\|_{M_b}^2-\frac{\Delta t^2}{8}\|CV^n\|_{M_b}^2$. The generalized Rayleigh bound in [F2] yields $\mathscr E^{n+1/2}\ge\tfrac{\gamma_0}{2}\|V^n\|_{M_e}^2+\tfrac12\|C\bar w^n\|_{M_b}^2.$ The initial assumptions therefore give $\mathscr E^{1/2}\ge0$ and $\sqrt{\mathscr E^{1/2}}\le C(h^2+\Delta t^2)$.

The kinetic-energy increment is $\Delta t\langle(V^n+V^{n-1})/2,M_e\delta_{tt}w^n\rangle$, and the curl-potential increment is $\Delta t\langle(V^n+V^{n-1})/2,Kw^n\rangle$. Substituting step 1.1 gives $\mathscr E^{n+1/2}-\mathscr E^{n-1/2}=-\Delta t\left\langle\frac{V^n+V^{n-1}}2,r_h^n\right\rangle.$ By [F4] and Cauchy–Schwarz, the absolute value is at most $\Delta t\|r_h^n\|_{M_e^{-1}}(\|V^n\|_{M_e}+\|V^{n-1}\|_{M_e})/2$.

Coercivity in step 1.2 bounds both velocities by the square roots of their adjacent energies times $\sqrt{2/\gamma_0}$. Factoring the difference of squares and summing (with the zero-energy case obtained by continuity, or by first replacing each square root by $\sqrt{\mathscr E+\delta}$ and letting $\delta\downarrow0$) gives $\max_n(\|V^n\|_{M_e}+\|C\bar w^n\|_{M_b})\le C\left(\sqrt{\mathscr E^{1/2}}+\sum_n\Delta t\|r_h^n\|_{M_e^{-1}}\right)\le C_T(h^2+\Delta t^2).$ The sum has at most $T/\Delta t$ terms, so [F3] gives the final inequality.

Since $w^n=w^0+\Delta t\sum_{m<n}V^m$, the initial bound and step 3.1 imply $\max_n\|w^n\|_{M_e}\le C_T(h^2+\Delta t^2)$. For $n\ge1$, $Cw^n=C\bar w^{n-1}+\Delta t CV^{n-1}/2$ and $\Delta t\|CV^{n-1}\|_{M_b}\le\Delta t\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}}\|V^{n-1}\|_{M_e}\le2\|V^{n-1}\|_{M_e}$ by the strict CFL condition. Thus the same order holds for $\|Cw^n\|_{M_b}$ for $n\ge1$; the $n=0$ curl bound is part of the initial assumptions.

Summing the second equation in step 1.1 from the controlled start $z^{1/2}$ gives $\|z^{n+1/2}\|_{M_b}\le\|z^{1/2}\|_{M_b}+\Delta t\sum_{m=1}^{n}\|Cw^m\|_{M_b}+\sum_{m=1}^{n}\|s_h^m\|_{M_b}.$ The curl sum is bounded by $T\max_m\|Cw^m\|_{M_b}$, and the residual sum is at most $(T/\Delta t)C_T\Delta t^3=C_TT\Delta t^2$ by [F3]. The initial bound and step 4.1 therefore bound both terms by $C_T(h^2+\Delta t^2)$. Combining the electric, curl and magnetic bounds proves the claim.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron and let $\{\mathcal T_h\}$ be a shape-regular family of matching affine tetrahedral meshes with $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}(K)\to0$. For the full lowest-order spaces $E_h^0=W_h^0,E_h^1=N_h^1,E_h^2=N_h^2,E_h^3=N_h^3$ of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]], there are linear projections $\pi_h^k:L^2\Lambda^k(\Omega)\to E_h^k$ satisfying $\pi_h^k|_{E_h^k}=I$ and $d\pi_h^k=\pi_h^{k+1}d$ on $H\Lambda^k(\Omega)$ for $k=0,1,2$. In degree three the exterior derivative is zero. Their norms are uniformly bounded both in $L^2$ and in $H\Lambda^k$, for $k=0,1,2,3$.

There is also a boundary-corrected family of projections $\pi_{h,0}^k:L^2\Lambda^k(\Omega)\to E_{h,0}^k$, where $E_{h,0}^k=E_h^k\cap H_0\Lambda^k(\Omega)$ and $H_0\Lambda^k$ is the graph closure of compactly supported smooth forms. These have the same uniform bounds, are the identity on $E_{h,0}^k$, and commute in degrees zero through two on the homogeneous complex; the terminal degree-three differential is zero. In particular,
$$\pi_{h,0}^0:H_0^1(\Omega)\to W_h^0\cap H_0^1(\Omega),\qquad \pi_{h,0}^1:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega),\qquad \nabla\pi_{h,0}^0=\pi_{h,0}^1\nabla.$$
Here the zero tangential space uses [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]. Each family converges strongly in $L^2$ on every $L^2$ form, uniformly on compact $L^2$ subsets, and in the graph norm on its corresponding graph domain. The full and homogeneous families are separate operators. These are cochain projections; canonical edge moments are not asserted bounded on $H(\operatorname{curl})$.

Let $\Omega$ be a bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron with a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T_h$, and use the real lowest-order spaces $W_h^0,N_h^1,N_h^2,N_h^3$ defined in [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. The electric trial field is $E_h(t)\in N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$; the magnetic flux field is $B_h(t)\in N_h^2$, with no imposed zero normal trace on $B_h$. PEC means the closure-defined zero tangential subspace from [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]. Periodic analogues use the periodic cell complex. Countable Choice is inherited from the H(div) and affine Piola space definitions in the suppliers; the finite matrix operations below use no additional choice.

Put $V_h:=N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$. Choose an edge basis $\{\phi_i\}_{i=1}^{N_e}$ of the electric trial space $V_h$ and a face basis $\{\psi_a\}_{a=1}^{N_f}$ of $N_h^2$, so $N_e=\dim V_h$ and $N_f=\dim N_h^2$. Define the symmetric mass matrices
$$ (M_e)_{ij}=\int_\Omega \phi_j^T\epsilon\phi_i\,dx,\qquad (M_b)_{ab}=\int_\Omega \psi_b^T\mu^{-1}\psi_a\,dx.$$
They are positive definite by the coefficient bounds in [[def-transient-maxwell-system-with-material-interfaces]] and linear independence of the finite element bases. Let $C$ and $D$ be the coefficient matrices, in these chosen bases, of the restricted map $\operatorname{curl}:V_h\to N_h^2$ and of $\operatorname{div}:N_h^2\to N_h^3$. The moment-commuting supplier gives $DC=0$ on the full spaces, hence also after restriction to $V_h$. Set $j_i(t)=\int_\Omega J_{\rm src}(t)\cdot\phi_i\,dx$, with $J_{\rm src}\in C([0,T];L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$. The lossless, conductivity-free semidiscretization with this source is
$$M_e\dot e-C^TM_b b=-j,\qquad \dot b+Ce=0.$$
The coefficient ODE is defined for arbitrary initial coefficients. To represent the magnetic constraint of the Maxwell model, require $Db(0)=0$: the Faraday row and $DC=0$ give $D\dot b=-DCe=0$, so $Db(t)=Db(0)$ and compatible data remain divergence-free. An incompatible initial divergence is preserved, not corrected by this ODE. This is a spatial Galerkin system only; no time integrator is included. The cochain convention and weak material-interface formulation come from the declared spaces and [[def-transient-maxwell-system-with-material-interfaces]]. Smooth interpolation and a uniformly bounded commuting projection are separate prerequisites for the later error estimate and are not asserted by this definition.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh. The four face-normal fluxes are unisolvent on each $RT_0(K)$, and matching face fluxes assemble a global $H(\operatorname{div})$ field. For smooth scalar $f$, smooth vector fields $u,v$, and the canonical interpolants determined by vertex values, oriented edge circulations, oriented face-normal fluxes, and cell integrals, the interpolation maps satisfy cellwise
$$
abla I_h^0f=I_h^1
abla f,\qquad \operatorname{curl}I_h^1u=I_h^2\operatorname{curl}u,\qquad \operatorname{div}I_h^2v=I_h^3\operatorname{div}v.$$
Any assignment of one real oriented value to each global mesh edge determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^1$; any assignment of one real oriented flux to each global mesh face determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^2$. These assemblies belong to $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$, respectively, with the global spaces and conventions of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Applying the local moment identities to polynomial cell restrictions also proves that the global finite-element spaces form the subcomplex $W_h^0\xrightarrow{
abla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$. The canonical interpolation identities themselves apply to smooth inputs; they do not extend the canonical edge moments to arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ inputs.

Assume Countable Choice only in the H(div)/Piola space branch inherited from the suppliers below. Let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh of a bounded polyhedron, with shape-regularity constant $\sigma$ and $h=\max_K h_K$. Assume material interfaces are mesh-aligned. Let $u,v$ be piecewise $C^1$ on cell closures, with $\operatorname{curl}u$, $\operatorname{div}v$ also piecewise $C^1$, and with matching tangential traces of $u$ and matching normal traces of $v$. The canonical edge and face moment interpolants $I_h^1,I_h^2$ are those in [[lem-na-whitney-moments-commute-with-grad-curl-div]]. Then
$$ egin{aligned} &\|u-I_h^1u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}+\|\operatorname{curl}(u-I_h^1u)\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \quad+\|v-I_h^2v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}+\|\operatorname{div}(v-I_h^2v)\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \le C_\sigma h |\Omega|^{1/2}\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\left(\|
abla u\|_{L^\infty(K)}+\|
abla\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^\infty(K)}+\|
abla v\|_{L^\infty(K)}+\|
abla\operatorname{div}v\|_{L^\infty(K)}ight). \end{aligned}$$
The constant depends only on reference-element basis norms and $\sigma$. This estimate is only for the canonical smooth-input interpolants; it makes no boundedness claim on all of $H(\operatorname{curl})$ or $H(\operatorname{div})$.

derivations.claim: The subspace $X_h$ is finite dimensional. In a basis of $X_h$, its $\mu^{-1}$ Gram matrix is symmetric positive definite, so the normal equations have one solution for each $B_0-\pi_h^2B_0$; this defines $P_{X_h}$. Its value lies in $X_h\subset N_h^2$, and the definition of orthogonal projection gives $B_h^0-B_0=-(I-P_{X_h})(B_0-\pi_h^2B_0)\perp_{\mu^{-1}}X_h$. Orthogonal decomposition yields $\|B_h^0-B_0\|_{\mu^{-1}}\le\|B_0-\pi_h^2B_0\|_{\mu^{-1}}$.

Since $I_h^2B_0\in N_h^2$ and $\pi_h^2$ is a projection, $\pi_h^2 I_h^2B_0=I_h^2B_0$. Thus $B_0-\pi_h^2B_0=(I-\pi_h^2)(B_0-I_h^2B_0)$. Uniform boundedness of $\pi_h^2$ on $H(\operatorname{div})$, norm equivalence from the coefficient bounds, and [F3] imply $\|B_0-\pi_h^2B_0\|_{\mu^{-1}}\le C h M_B$. Combining with step 1.1 gives the asserted approximation estimate.

The projection identity and [F1] give $D\pi_h^2B_0=\pi_h^3(\operatorname{div}B_0)=0$. Every element of $X_h$ is a discrete curl, so [F2] gives $D P_{X_h}(B_0-\pi_h^2B_0)=0$. Adding the two terms proves $D B_h^0=0$.

Assume the Countable Choice branch inherited from [[def-maxwell-edge-fem-semidiscretization]]. Let $T\ge0$. For any finite matching mesh, initial edge and face coefficients $(e_0,b_0)$, and continuous load vector $j:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^{N_e}$, the source-driven semidiscrete Maxwell system
$$M_e\dot e-C^TM_bb=-j(t),\qquad \dot b+Ce=0,\qquad (e(0),b(0))=(e_0,b_0)$$
has one and only one global $C^1$ solution on $[0,T]$ when $T>0$, with domain-relative one-sided endpoint derivatives. When $T=0$, there is exactly one map with the prescribed initial value; it extends locally to the same coefficient ODE with the load held constant at $j(0)$, and any two such continuations agree on their common interval containing zero. No derivative or IVP solution on the singleton itself is asserted. The construction and uniqueness argument use finite-dimensional linear algebra and the matrix-ODE supplier; no choice axiom stronger than the inherited Countable Choice branch is used.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lipschitz polyhedron, or a periodic rectangular cell. The real electric field is $E(t,x)\in\mathbb R^3$ and the magnetic flux density is $B(t,x)\in\mathbb R^3$; the magnetic intensity is $H=\mu^{-1}B$. Let $\epsilon(x)$ and $\mu(x)$ be measurable, time-independent, symmetric matrix fields for which there are constants $0<\epsilon_0\le\epsilon_1$ and $0<\mu_0\le\mu_1$ with
$$\epsilon_0|v|^2\le v^T\epsilon(x)v\le\epsilon_1|v|^2,\qquad \mu_0|v|^2\le v^T\mu(x)v\le\mu_1|v|^2$$
for almost every $x$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^3$. A conductivity tensor $\sigma(x)$, when present, is measurable, symmetric, and positive semidefinite. The coefficients may jump across finitely many Lipschitz material interfaces. No derivative of a coefficient is part of the model.

In each material region the constitutive fields satisfy
$$\partial_t(\epsilon E)=\operatorname{curl}(\mu^{-1}B)-J_{\rm src}-\sigma E,\qquad \partial_t B+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$
Here $J_{\rm src}$ is the impressed free-current density, while $\sigma E$ is the conductive current. Electric charge $\rho$ is constrained by $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)=\rho$ and the total-current continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E)=0$; the magnetic constraint is $\operatorname{div}B=0$. These equalities are distributional. In the lossless branch set $\sigma=0$.

The boundary choice is one of the following. A **periodic boundary** identifies opposite traces of the rectangular cell. A **perfect electric conductor (PEC) boundary** imposes zero tangential trace $n\times E=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. At a material interface with no singular surface charge or current, the weak equations are understood with the transmission conditions $[n\times E]=0$, $[n\cdot B]=0$, $[n\times(\mu^{-1}B)]=0$, and $[n\cdot(\epsilon E)]=0$, where $[q]$ is the trace from one side minus the trace from the other. The interface conditions are part of the model convention; no smooth Taylor expansion across a coefficient jump is asserted.

For PEC, the weak Ampere equation is $(\epsilon E_t,v)_{L^2}-(\mu^{-1}B,\operatorname{curl}v)_{L^2}=-(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E,v)_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ as defined in [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]; the periodic branch uses periodic $H(\operatorname{curl})$ test fields. Faraday’s equation remains $B_t+\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in distributions. These weak forms define the test-space and boundary convention used by the edge finite element method.

The weighted field norms are $\|E\|_\epsilon^2=\int_\Omega E^T\epsilon E\,dx$ and $\|B\|_{\mu^{-1}}^2=\int_\Omega B^T\mu^{-1}B\,dx$. The uniform coefficient bounds make them equivalent to the ordinary $L^2$ norms. All later smooth-error claims require smoothness separately on each mesh-aligned material region.

Assume Countable Choice in the inherited edge/face finite-element space branch. Let $V=H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ with the PEC convention in [[def-maxwell-edge-fem-semidiscretization]], and let $V_h=N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$. Define
$$m(u,v)=\int_\Omega v^T\epsilon u\,dx,\qquad a(u,v)=\int_\Omega (\operatorname{curl}v)^T\mu^{-1}\operatorname{curl}u\,dx,\qquad a_+(u,v)=m(u,v)+a(u,v).$$
For $u\in V$, the **Maxwell curl-energy Ritz projection** $R_hu\in V_h$ is the solution of
$$a_+(R_hu,v_h)=a_+(u,v_h)\qquad(v_h\in V_h).$$
Its finite-dimensional well-definedness, orthogonality, and best-approximation property are supplied by [[lem-maxwell-edge-ritz-projection-well-defined]].

In the Countable Choice branch of [[def-maxwell-edge-ritz-projection]], the equation defining $R_hu$ has a unique solution for each $u\in V$. Moreover, with $\|v\|_{a_+}^2=a_+(v,v)$,
$$\|u-R_hu\|_{a_+}\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_{a_+}.$$

Assume the contractible Lipschitz domain and shape-regular mesh-family hypotheses of [[thm-na-uniformly-bounded-commuting-cochain-projection]], with matching affine tetrahedra and the PEC edge space of [[def-maxwell-edge-fem-semidiscretization]]. Faraday’s equation remains $B_t+\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in distributions. These weak forms define the test-space and boundary convention used by the edge finite element method.

The weighted field norms are $\|E\|_\epsilon^2=\int_\Omega E^T\epsilon E\,dx$ and $\|B\|_{\mu^{-1}}^2=\int_\Omega B^T\mu^{-1}B\,dx$. The uniform coefficient bounds make them equivalent to the ordinary $L^2$ norms. All later smooth-error claims require smoothness separately on each mesh-aligned material region.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Use the preceding mesh-size and boundary-shift lemma. All differential-form notation here is the following finite coefficient notation. A degree-$k$ form in $\mathbb R^3$ is $u=\sum_{I}u_I\,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, where the sum is over increasing $k$-tuples $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$, the wedge is alternating, and $\|u\|_2^2=\sum_I\|u_I\|_2^2$. The empty wedge is one. Put $du=\sum_I\sum_{j=1}^3(\partial_j u_I)dx^j\wedge dx^I$, with derivatives interpreted distributionally through integration by parts against compactly supported scalar tests; repeated differentials are zero. The graph space $H\Lambda^k$ consists of the coefficient vectors with $u,du\in L^2$, with norm squared $\|u\|_2^2+\|du\|_2^2$; in top degree $d=0$. These formulas agree with the proved smooth coordinate exterior derivative. Identify vector fields with forms by $\sum_{i=1}^3u_i dx_i$ in degree one, $v_1dx_2\wedge dx_3+v_2dx_3\wedge dx_1+v_3dx_1\wedge dx_2$ in degree two, and $q\,dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dx_3$ in degree three. Thus expansion of the finite formula for $d$ gives grad, curl, and div with exactly these signs; the degree-two coefficients in increasing order are $(v_3,-v_2,v_1)$, so their Euclidean norm equals that of $v$. For a smooth map $G$ from an open subset of $\mathbb R^q$ to $\mathbb R^3$, define its pullback by the finite tangent-Jacobian-minor formula
$$G^*u=\sum_{J}\left(\sum_I u_I(G)\det\bigl(\partial_{j_b}G^{i_a}\bigr)_{a,b=1}^k\right)\,dt^{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dt^{j_k}.$$
Here $J$ ranges over increasing $k$-tuples in $1,\ldots,q$; in degree zero this is composition. If $a:T_k\to\sigma$ is the oriented affine simplex parametrization, define $\int_\sigma G^*u$ as the integral over $T_k$ of the coefficient of $(G\circ a)^*u$ on its positive top wedge. Orientation reversal changes its sign; in degree zero it is evaluation. For averaged moments of merely $L^2$ coefficients, the joint parameter integral is the definition and the estimates below prove it exists and is representative-independent. No unbounded trace of an $L^2$ form on a fixed lower-dimensional surface is being defined. This is the existing smooth simplex-integration convention, extended only through the displayed integrable averages. Write $E_h^k$ for the four full Whitney spaces and $E_{h,0}^k$ for the subspaces with all boundary $k$-simplex moments zero; $E_{h,0}^3=E_h^3$. Let $H_0\Lambda^k$ be the graph closure of compactly supported smooth $k$-forms; in degrees zero and one these are $H_0^1$ and the defined $H_0(\operatorname{curl})$.

Fix nonnegative $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B_1)$ with integral one. For each oriented mesh $k$-simplex $\sigma$, define
$$m_{\sigma}^{+,k}(u)=\int_{B_1}\rho(y)\int_\sigma(F_{\epsilon,y}^{+})^*u\,dy,\qquad m_{\sigma}^{-,k}(u)=\int_{B_1}\rho(y)\int_\sigma(F_{\epsilon,y}^{-})^*\widetilde u\,dy,$$
where $\widetilde u$ is zero extension and a degree-zero simplex integral is evaluation. Whitney reconstruction from these moments defines $Q_h^{+,k}:L^2\Lambda^k\to E_h^k$ and $Q_h^{-,k}:L^2\Lambda^k\to E_{h,0}^k$. For $0<\epsilon\le\epsilon_0$,
$$\|Q_h^{\pm,k}u\|_2\le C\epsilon^{-3/2}\|u\|_2,\qquad \|(Q_h^{\pm,k}-I)v_h\|_2\le C\epsilon\|v_h\|_2,$$
where the second bound uses respectively $v_h\in E_h^k$ or $v_h\in E_{h,0}^k$. Constants are independent of $h,\epsilon$. For $k=0,1,2$, $dQ_h^{+,k}=Q_h^{+,k+1}d$ on $H\Lambda^k$ and $dQ_h^{-,k}=Q_h^{-,k+1}d$ on $H_0\Lambda^k$. In degree three, both exterior derivatives are zero. The relative Whitney spaces equal $E_h^k\cap H_0\Lambda^k$.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh. The four face-normal fluxes are unisolvent on each $RT_0(K)$, and matching face fluxes assemble a global $H(\operatorname{div})$ field. For smooth scalar $f$, smooth vector fields $u,v$, and the canonical interpolants determined by vertex values, oriented edge circulations, oriented face-normal fluxes, and cell integrals, the interpolation maps satisfy cellwise
$$
abla I_h^0f=I_h^1
abla f,\qquad \operatorname{curl}I_h^1u=I_h^2\operatorname{curl}u,\qquad \operatorname{div}I_h^2v=I_h^3\operatorname{div}v.$$
Any assignment of one real oriented value to each global mesh edge determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^1$; any assignment of one real oriented flux to each global mesh face determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^2$. These assemblies belong to $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$, respectively, with the global spaces and conventions of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Applying the local moment identities to polynomial cell restrictions also proves that the global finite-element spaces form the subcomplex $W_h^0\xrightarrow{
abla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$. The canonical interpolation identities themselves apply to smooth inputs; they do not extend the canonical edge moments to arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ inputs.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

$$H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)}^{\,H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)},$$
where the norm is that of [[def-na-hcurl-space]]. This is the closure-defined zero-tangential subspace used on this page. Identifying this closure with the full kernel of a particular boundary trace map is not part of the definition.

derivations.claim: If $T=0$, [F1] supplies the unique initialized map; Ritz best approximation [F3] and interpolation [F4] give the electric and curl error at zero, and [F5] gives the magnetic error and divergence compatibility. Norm equivalence [F6] proves the stated estimate on the singleton. Hence assume $T>0$. We first justify the closure and time derivatives; $E_t,E_{tt}$ denote the classical time derivatives. For each $u=E(t),E_t(t),E_{tt}(t)$, zero boundary tangential trace makes the boundary edge moments of $I_h^1u$ zero, so [F7] gives $I_h^1u\in V_h$. By [F4], $I_h^1u\to u$ in $H(\operatorname{curl})$ as $h\to0$, and [F9] gives $u\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})$. Uniform bounds on $E_{tt}$ give $L^2$-Lipschitz continuity of $E_t$ by the pointwise mean-value bound [F8]. For a compact smooth vector test $\psi$, dominated differentiation gives $\frac d{dt}(\operatorname{curl}E_t,\psi)=\frac d{dt}(E_t,\operatorname{curl}\psi)=(E_{tt},\operatorname{curl}\psi)=(\operatorname{curl}E_{tt},\psi)$. The uniform bound on $\operatorname{curl}E_{tt}$ and [F8], followed by $L^2$ density, therefore give $\|\operatorname{curl}E_t(t)-\operatorname{curl}E_t(s)\|_2\le K|t-s|$. The same test identities for $E$ show $E$ is graph-norm $C^1$ with derivative $E_t$: subtract the value of $E_t(s)$ from its difference quotient and use the just-proved Lipschitz bound, first in test pairings and then by density. Difference quotients of $E_t$ are uniformly graph bounded; their $L^2$ parts converge to $E_{tt}$ by dominated convergence, and their curls converge distributionally to $\operatorname{curl}E_{tt}$. Density and uniform boundedness upgrade the latter to weak $L^2$ convergence. Consequently every bounded graph-linear functional of $E_t$ is differentiable with derivative its value on $E_{tt}$. In particular the finite Ritz Gram equations give $(R_hE)_t=R_hE_t$ and $(R_hE)_{tt}=R_hE_{tt}$, with a bounded second derivative; continuity of $E_{tt}$ in the graph norm is unnecessary.

The initialization gives $\theta_h(0)=0$. Test the semidiscrete Ampere row at $t=0$ and subtract the exact weak row. By the curl orthogonality in [F5], $(\mu^{-1}(B_h^0-B(0)),\operatorname{curl}v_h)=0$ for every $v_h$, so $\dot E_h(0)$ is the $\epsilon$-orthogonal projection of $E_t(0)$ onto $V_h$. The zero tangential boundary trace gives zero boundary edge moments for $I_h^1E_t(0)$; [F7] therefore places this interpolant in $V_h$. Its best-approximation error is at most $\|E_t(0)-I_h^1E_t(0)\|_\epsilon\le Ch$ by [F4]. Also $\|R_hE_t(0)-E_t(0)\|_\epsilon\le Ch$ by [F3,F4]. Hence $\|\dot\theta_h(0)\|_\epsilon\le Ch$.

Differentiate the exact weak Ampere equation in [F2] and use $B_t=-\operatorname{curl}E$. Since $\mu$ is time-independent, this gives, for every $v\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$, $(\epsilon E_{tt},v)+(\mu^{-1}\operatorname{curl}E,\operatorname{curl}v)=-(\partial_tJ_{\rm src},v).$ Differentiating the finite-dimensional Ampere row and using $\dot b+Ce=0$ gives the identical Galerkin equation for $E_h$: $(\epsilon \ddot E_h,v_h)+(\mu^{-1}\operatorname{curl}E_h,\operatorname{curl}v_h)=-(\partial_tJ_{\rm src},v_h).$ The solution exists by [F1]; the exact time pairings are differentiable by step 1.1, and the discrete differentiation is valid because $J_{\rm src}$ is $C^1$.

Let $R_h$ be fixed in time and put $\theta_h=E_h-R_hE$. Step 1.1 justifies $(R_hE)_{tt}=R_hE_{tt}$ for its time-independent Gram matrix. Subtract the two equations in step 2.1 and use Ritz orthogonality [F3], namely $a(E-R_hE,v_h)=-m(E-R_hE,v_h)$. For every $v_h\in V_h$ this yields $m(\ddot\theta_h,v_h)+a(\theta_h,v_h)=m((I-R_h)(E_{tt}-E),v_h).$ The zero tangential boundary trace gives zero boundary edge moments for $I_h^1(E_{tt}-E)$, so [F7] places this interpolant in $V_h$. Best approximation [F3] and the canonical estimate [F4] then show uniformly in time that $\|(I-R_h)(E_{tt}-E)\|_\epsilon\le C h$.

Define $Q_h(t)=\tfrac12(\|\dot\theta_h(t)\|_\epsilon^2+\|\operatorname{curl}\theta_h(t)\|_{\mu^{-1}}^2)$. Test the equation in step 3.1 with $v_h=\dot\theta_h$. Symmetry gives $Q_h'(t)=m((I-R_h)(E_{tt}-E),\dot\theta_h),\qquad |Q_h'(t)|\le\|(I-R_h)(E_{tt}-E)\|_\epsilon\sqrt{2Q_h(t)}.$ For $\delta>0$, the derivative of $\sqrt{Q_h+\delta}$ has absolute value at most $Ch/\sqrt2$ by step 3.1. The scalar mean-value bound [F8], the initial estimate in step 1.2 and then $\delta\downarrow0$ give $\sqrt{Q_h(t)}\le Ch$ on $[0,T]$. The finite-dimensional mean-value bound and $\theta_h(0)=0$ also give $\sup_t\|\theta_h(t)\|_\epsilon\le T\sup_t\|\dot\theta_h(t)\|_\epsilon\le Ch$.

By step 4.1, $\theta_h$ is $O(h)$ in the electric $L^2$ norm and its curl norm. The Ritz best-approximation estimate [F3] and interpolation estimate [F4] give $\|R_hE-E\|_{L^2}+\|\operatorname{curl}(R_hE-E)\|_{L^2}\le Ch$. The triangle inequality therefore gives the asserted electric and curl error bound.

Subtract the exact Faraday equation from the semidiscrete magnetic row and integrate in time: $B_h(t)-B(t)=B_h^0-B(0)-\int_0^t\operatorname{curl}(E_h(s)-E(s))\,ds.$ The initial difference is $O(h)$ by [F5], and the curl error is $O(h)$ uniformly by step 5.1, so the magnetic $L^2$ error is at most $Ch+TCh$. Also $D B_h(t)=D B_h^0-\int_0^t D C e_h(s)\,ds=0$ by [F5] and the discrete identity $DC=0$ in [F2]. Norm equivalence [F6] completes the result.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lipschitz polyhedron, or a periodic rectangular cell. The real electric field is $E(t,x)\in\mathbb R^3$ and the magnetic flux density is $B(t,x)\in\mathbb R^3$; the magnetic intensity is $H=\mu^{-1}B$. Let $\epsilon(x)$ and $\mu(x)$ be measurable, time-independent, symmetric matrix fields for which there are constants $0<\epsilon_0\le\epsilon_1$ and $0<\mu_0\le\mu_1$ with
$$\epsilon_0|v|^2\le v^T\epsilon(x)v\le\epsilon_1|v|^2,\qquad \mu_0|v|^2\le v^T\mu(x)v\le\mu_1|v|^2$$
for almost every $x$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^3$. A conductivity tensor $\sigma(x)$, when present, is measurable, symmetric, and positive semidefinite. The coefficients may jump across finitely many Lipschitz material interfaces. No derivative of a coefficient is part of the model.

In each material region the constitutive fields satisfy
$$\partial_t(\epsilon E)=\operatorname{curl}(\mu^{-1}B)-J_{\rm src}-\sigma E,\qquad \partial_t B+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$
Here $J_{\rm src}$ is the impressed free-current density, while $\sigma E$ is the conductive current. Electric charge $\rho$ is constrained by $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)=\rho$ and the total-current continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E)=0$; the magnetic constraint is $\operatorname{div}B=0$. These equalities are distributional. In the lossless branch set $\sigma=0$.

The boundary choice is one of the following. A **periodic boundary** identifies opposite traces of the rectangular cell. A **perfect electric conductor (PEC) boundary** imposes zero tangential trace $n\times E=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. At a material interface with no singular surface charge or current, the weak equations are understood with the transmission conditions $[n\times E]=0$, $[n\cdot B]=0$, $[n\times(\mu^{-1}B)]=0$, and $[n\cdot(\epsilon E)]=0$, where $[q]$ is the trace from one side minus the trace from the other. The interface conditions are part of the model convention; no smooth Taylor expansion across a coefficient jump is asserted.

For PEC, the weak Ampere equation is $(\epsilon E_t,v)_{L^2}-(\mu^{-1}B,\operatorname{curl}v)_{L^2}=-(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E,v)_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ as defined in [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]; the periodic branch uses periodic $H(\operatorname{curl})$ test fields. Faraday’s equation remains $B_t+\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in distributions. These weak forms define the test-space and boundary convention used by the edge finite element method.

The weighted field norms are $\|E\|_\epsilon^2=\int_\Omega E^T\epsilon E\,dx$ and $\|B\|_{\mu^{-1}}^2=\int_\Omega B^T\mu^{-1}B\,dx$. The uniform coefficient bounds make them equivalent to the ordinary $L^2$ norms. All later smooth-error claims require smoothness separately on each mesh-aligned material region.

derivations.claim: The tangential electric field vanishes on $x=0,a$ and $y=0,b$ because $\Phi=0$ there; it also vanishes on $z=0,d$ because the only component of $E$ is normal to those faces. Direct differentiation gives $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)=0$. Thus both divergence constraints and the PEC trace hold.

Differentiation gives $B_t=-\operatorname{curl}E$. The $z$ component of $\operatorname{curl}B$ is $-(k_x^2+k_y^2)\Phi\sin(\omega t)/\omega$, with the other two components zero. Since $\epsilon\omega^2=(k_x^2+k_y^2)/\mu$, the expression $-(k_x^2+k_y^2)\Phi\sin(\omega t)/(\mu\omega)$ equals $-\epsilon\omega\Phi\sin(\omega t)=\epsilon E_t$. Hence $\epsilon E_t=\operatorname{curl}(\mu^{-1}B)$. At $t=0$, $x=a/(2m)$ and $y=b/(2n)$, the electric component is $E_z=E_0\ne0$, so this is a nonzero cavity mode. The angular frequency is therefore $\omega=(\epsilon\mu)^{-1/2}\sqrt{(m\pi/a)^2+(n\pi/b)^2}$.

Choose a finite complex and boundary closure as in [[def-maxwell-discrete-cochain-and-yee-grid]], step size $\Delta t>0$, initial $e^0\in\mathbb R^{N_e}$ and $b^{-1/2}\in\mathbb R^{N_f}$, and source rows $j^{n+1/2}\in\mathbb R^{N_e}$. The output is a sequence $e^n$ at integer times and $b^{n+1/2}$ at half-integer times. For each $n\ge0$, perform the ordered instructions

1. Update the face flux by
   $$b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}-\Delta t\,C e^n.$$

2. Solve the electric row
   $$\left(M_e+\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^{n+1}=\left(M_e-\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^n+\Delta t\,C^TM_b b^{n+1/2}-\Delta t\,j^{n+1/2}.$$

For $S=0$ this is the lossless Yee leapfrog scheme. For $S\succeq0$, the midpoint term is the specified trapezoidal treatment of conductivity. The row is well defined for every input because its matrix is invertible by [[lem-maxwell-yee-step-matrix-is-positive-definite]]. This procedure makes no stability claim; the lossless stability condition is proved separately.

For the incidence matrices $G,C,D$ of [[def-maxwell-discrete-cochain-and-yee-grid]], one has $CG=0$ and $DC=0$. The conclusion holds for the full periodic complex and for the PEC mixed closure defined there.

Let $K$ be a finite oriented three-dimensional cell complex with vertex, edge, face, and volume cochains. An edge cochain records oriented electric line integrals, a face cochain records oriented magnetic fluxes, and a vertex cochain records electric charge. Write $N_v,N_e,N_f,N_c$ for the retained vertex, edge, face, and cell counts. On a periodic cell, identify opposite cells with orientation preserved and let $G,C,D$ be the full vertex-to-edge gradient, edge-to-face curl, and face-to-cell divergence incidence matrices, each the transpose of its signed oriented boundary matrix. For a PEC closure, “interior” means not in the boundary subcomplex. Keep only interior electric edges as unknowns and only interior vertices as volume-charge locations, but keep all face fluxes, including boundary-normal magnetic fluxes, and all cells. This closure has no separate boundary surface-charge cochain. Define $G$ and $C$ by restricting the absolute vertex-edge and edge-face incidence matrices to those rows and columns. This mixed closure imposes zero tangential electric edge cochains on the boundary while allowing a fixed normal magnetic flux on boundary faces. In both cases, $G\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_v}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_e}$, and $D\in\mathbb R^{N_c\times N_f}$ satisfy $CG=0$ and $DC=0$.

The electric, magnetic, and conductive material matrices are real symmetric matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, $M_b\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_f}$, and $S\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, respectively. The first two are positive definite and represent the discrete weighted inner products induced by $\epsilon$ and $\mu^{-1}$; $S$ is positive semidefinite and represents conductivity. Write $\langle e_1,e_2\rangle_{M_e}=e_1^TM_ee_2$, $\langle b_1,b_2\rangle_{M_b}=b_1^TM_bb_2$, and $\|e\|_{M_e}^2=\langle e,e\rangle_{M_e}$, $\|b\|_{M_b}^2=\langle b,b\rangle_{M_b}$. In a homogeneous isotropic periodic Cartesian grid with spacings $h_x,h_y,h_z$ and cell volume $V=h_xh_yh_z$, the diagonal entries for an $x$-edge and an $x$-normal face are $\epsilon V/h_x^2=\epsilon h_yh_z/h_x$ and $\mu^{-1}h_x/(h_yh_z)$; the $y$ and $z$ entries are obtained by cyclic permutation. These values are dual-volume Hodge weights for line-integral and face-flux cochains. A compatible PEC closure uses the corresponding truncated dual volumes for free electric edges, while the magnetic mass includes boundary faces; the resulting matrices remain positive definite. The discrete constraints are $-G^TM_ee^n=\rho^n$ on interior vertices and $Db^{n-1/2}=0$ on all cells.

The minus sign in the electric constraint is essential: an edge oriented from tail to head has incidence entries $-1,+1$, so $-G^T$ is the outgoing-flux divergence. Thus $\rho$ represents physical electric charge with the sign of $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)$ in [[def-transient-maxwell-system-with-material-interfaces]].

For current cochains $j^{n+1/2}$ and charge rows $\rho^n$, the discrete continuity condition means
$$\rho^{n+1}-\rho^n-\Delta t\,G^T\left(j^{n+1/2}+S\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)=0.$$
For PEC this is the interior-vertex volume-charge relation; this closure has no separate boundary surface-charge/current cochain.

The cochain identities $CG=0$ and $DC=0$ are not imposed as an extra numerical approximation: they follow from oriented boundary-of-boundary cancellation, including the PEC row and column restrictions, as proved in [[lem-maxwell-discrete-incidence-identities]]. No cell geometry picture is used as a proof.

derivations.claim: Apply $-G^T$ to the electric row in [F1]. Since $G^TC^T=(CG)^T=0$ and the initial Gauss relation holds, this gives $-G^TM_ee^1-\rho^1=\Delta t\,G^Tj^{1/2}=\Delta t J G^T\mathbf e_0.$ By [F2], the residual is $-\Delta t J$ at $v_0$, $+\Delta t J$ at $v_1$, and zero at the other vertices. It is nonzero because $J\ne0$.
If instead the charge were updated by $\rho^1=\rho^0+\Delta t G^Tj^{1/2}$, the same calculation would give $-G^TM_ee^1-\rho^1=0$. The drift is therefore exactly the discrete-continuity defect.

Consider a homogeneous isotropic periodic Yee grid with $\epsilon,\mu>0$, wave speed $c=(\epsilon\mu)^{-1/2}$, spacings $h_x,h_y,h_z$, and $N_x,N_y,N_z$ cells. Its allowed wave angles are $\theta_j=2\pi m_j/N_j$. On a mode with wave vector $k_j=\theta_j/h_j$, the transverse curl-curl eigenvalue is
$$\lambda(\theta)=c^2\sum_{j\in\{x,y,z\}}\frac{4}{h_j^2}\sin^2\left(\frac{\theta_j}{2}\right),$$
and the lossless Yee leapfrog dispersion relation is
$$\sin^2\left(\frac{\omega\Delta t}{2}\right)=c^2\Delta t^2\sum_{j\in\{x,y,z\}}\frac{\sin^2(\theta_j/2)}{h_j^2}.$$
The exact finite-grid strict condition is $\Delta t^2\max_{\theta}\lambda(\theta)<4$, as in [[thm-maxwell-yee-strict-cfl-modified-energy]]. The rectangular sufficient bound is
$$\Delta t<\frac{1}{c\sqrt{h_x^{-2}+h_y^{-2}+h_z^{-2}}};$$
it is exact when every $N_j$ is even. For a cubic grid this bound is $\Delta t<h/(c\sqrt3)$. Odd cell counts may have a smaller finite-grid maximum, so the finite-grid eigenvalue is the exact criterion.

derivations.claim: For $\theta=(\pi,0,0)$, the sine-square sum is $1$, so $\sin^2(\omega_{\rm ax}\Delta t/2)=c^2\Delta t^2/h^2$. Its symbol direction is the $x$-axis, and $p=(0,1,0)$ is orthogonal to it, so this is a transverse mode.

For $\theta=(\pi,\pi,\pi)$, the sum is $3$ and $p=(1,-1,0)/\sqrt2$ is orthogonal to $(1,1,1)$. Thus $\sin^2(\omega_{\rm corner}\Delta t/2)=3c^2\Delta t^2/h^2$. The maximum eigenvalue is $12c^2/h^2$, so strict positivity requires $\Delta t<h/(c\sqrt3)$; equality places the maximal mode at the repeated-root endpoint.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.
