Work in exact real arithmetic. Let $n\ge1$ and $V=\mathbb R^n$, and let
$A=A^{\mathsf T}$ satisfy $x^{\mathsf T}Ax>0$ for every nonzero $x$.
Give $V$ the energy inner product $a(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}Ay$ and norm
$\|x\|_A^2=a(x,x)$ of
[[def-energy-inner-product-and-norm-for-a-hermitian-positive-definite-matrix]].
An operator $S$ is $A$-self-adjoint when $a(Sx,y)=a(x,Sy)$ for all $x,y$;
it is positive when $a(Sx,x)>0$ for every nonzero $x$. An $A$-orthogonal
projection is an idempotent $A$-self-adjoint operator.
Let $\mathcal I$ be a finite ordered nonempty set and, for each
$i\in\mathcal I$, choose a full-column-rank prolongation
$R_i\in\mathbb R^{n\times n_i}$ with $1\le n_i\le n$, and put
$V_i=\operatorname{Ran}(R_i)$.
A one-level method has $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. A two-level method has
$\mathcal I=\{0,1,\ldots,m\}$, where $R_0=P$ and $V_0$ is the designated
coarse space. Restriction of a global residual is $R_i^{\mathsf T}$ and
prolongation of a local coefficient vector is $R_i$. Define the local energy
matrix
$$A_i=R_i^{\mathsf T}AR_i.$$
When the coarse index $0$ is present, $A_0=P^{\mathsf T}AP$ is the Galerkin
coarse matrix of [[def-galerkin-coarse-grid-correction]]. By
[[thm-galerkin-coarse-correction-is-energy-orthogonal-projector]], it is SPD
and the exact coarse solve is well-defined.

For each $i\in\mathcal I$, the exact local correction and additive
preconditioner are
$$ \Pi_i=R_iA_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}A, \qquad B=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}R_iA_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}. $$
When the spaces span $V$, the exact additive Schwarz preconditioned operator
is $BA=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\Pi_i$. For a fixed ordering of $\mathcal I$, a
multiplicative sweep applies its corrections in that order; if $0$ is present,
it is first. For an inexact additive method, replace each exact $A_i^{-1}$ by
the inverse of an SPD matrix $\widetilde A_i$ satisfying, for fixed
$0<\alpha\le\beta$,
$$ \alpha A_i\preceq \widetilde A_i\preceq\beta A_i, \qquad \widetilde B=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}R_i\widetilde A_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}. $$
For symmetric matrices, $X\preceq Y$ means
$z^{\mathsf T}Xz\le z^{\mathsf T}Yz$ for every vector $z$. The order
inequalities define uniform local spectral equivalence in this pair. The
lemma [[lem-schwarz-local-matrices-are-well-defined]] proves the remaining
local inverse and well-definedness claims.

For the data of [[def-overlapping-schwarz-subspace-correction-data]], every
local matrix $A_i=R_i^{\mathsf T}AR_i$ with $i\in\mathcal I$ is symmetric
positive definite and therefore invertible. If the coarse index $0$ is
present, then $A_0=P^{\mathsf T}AP$ is the SPD Galerkin coarse matrix. Hence
every exact local solve in the definition exists uniquely.

Let $A_h\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive definite and let
$P\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}$ have full column rank, where $1\le m\le n$. Put
$A_H=P^{\mathsf T}A_hP$. Then $A_H$ is symmetric positive definite, hence
invertible, and the map $C=I_n-PA_H^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}A_h$ of
[[def-galerkin-coarse-grid-correction]] satisfies

$$C^2=C,\qquad CP=0,\qquad P^{\mathsf T}A_hC=0,\qquad C^{\mathsf T}A_h=A_hC.$$

Consequently $\operatorname{Ran}(C)=\operatorname{Ran}(P)^{\perp_{A_h}}$;
$C$ is the orthogonal projector onto that complement in the energy inner
product $\langle x,y\rangle_{A_h}:=x^{\mathsf T}A_hy$.

For matrices of the appropriate shapes and a scalar $\lambda$,

$$(A+B)^{\mathsf T}=A^{\mathsf T}+B^{\mathsf T},\qquad (\lambda A)^{\mathsf T}=\lambda A^{\mathsf T},\qquad (A^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}=A,$$

and

$$(AB)^{\mathsf T}=B^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}.$$

Thus transpose is linear and involutive and reverses products.

derivations.claim: Fix $i\in\mathcal I$ with $i\ne0$. Multiplication using [F1] gives $\Pi_i^2 =R_iA_i^{-1}(R_i^{\mathsf T}AR_i)A_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}A =\Pi_i.$ By [F2], $A_i^{-1}$ is symmetric; [F4] therefore gives $\Pi_i^{\mathsf T}A=A\Pi_i$. Its range is contained in $\operatorname{Ran}(R_i)$, and $\Pi_iR_i=R_i$, so its range is exactly $V_i$.

If $0\in\mathcal I$, write $\Pi_0=I-C$ with $C$ from [F3]. Since $C^2=C$ and $C$ is $A$-self-adjoint, $I-C$ is also idempotent and $A$-self-adjoint. Moreover, $\operatorname{Ran}(I-C)=\ker C=\operatorname{Ran}(P)$ because $C$ projects onto $\operatorname{Ran}(P)^{\perp_A}$. Thus $\Pi_0$ is the $A$-orthogonal projection onto $V_0$. If $0\notin\mathcal I$, there is no coarse projection to check.

For every present index $i$, idempotence and $A$-self-adjointness give $a(\Pi_i x,(I-\Pi_i)x)=a(x,\Pi_i(I-\Pi_i)x)=0$. Expanding the squared norm of $x=\Pi_i x+(I-\Pi_i)x$ proves the Pythagorean identity. Also $a(\Pi_i x,x)=a(\Pi_i x,\Pi_i x)$ by the same orthogonality.

derivations.claim: The block matrix $\mathcal D$ is SPD by [F2]. The spanning assumption makes the concatenated map $R$ surjective. If $x^{\mathsf T}Bx=0$, then $0=(R^{\mathsf T}x)^{\mathsf T}\mathcal D^{-1}(R^{\mathsf T}x),$ so $R^{\mathsf T}x=0$ because $\mathcal D^{-1}$ is SPD. Surjectivity of $R$ then gives $x=0$. Thus $B$ is SPD and has an inverse.

For fixed $x$, define $z_*=\mathcal D^{-1}R^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}x$. Then $Rz_*=BB^{-1}x=x$, so it is feasible. For any other feasible $z$, write $w=z-z_*$. Then $Rw=0$ and $z_*^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Dw=x^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}Rw=0$. Therefore $z^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Dz=z_*^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Dz_*+w^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Dw\ge z_*^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Dz_*$. Direct multiplication gives $z_*^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Dz_*=x^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}x$. This proves the minimum identity.

Work in exact real arithmetic. Let $n\ge1$ and $V=\mathbb R^n$, and let
$A=A^{\mathsf T}$ satisfy $x^{\mathsf T}Ax>0$ for every nonzero $x$.
Give $V$ the energy inner product $a(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}Ay$ and norm
$\|x\|_A^2=a(x,x)$ of
[[def-energy-inner-product-and-norm-for-a-hermitian-positive-definite-matrix]].
An operator $S$ is $A$-self-adjoint when $a(Sx,y)=a(x,Sy)$ for all $x,y$;
it is positive when $a(Sx,x)>0$ for every nonzero $x$. An $A$-orthogonal
projection is an idempotent $A$-self-adjoint operator.
Let $\mathcal I$ be a finite ordered nonempty set and, for each
$i\in\mathcal I$, choose a full-column-rank prolongation
$R_i\in\mathbb R^{n\times n_i}$ with $1\le n_i\le n$, and put
$V_i=\operatorname{Ran}(R_i)$.
A one-level method has $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. A two-level method has
$\mathcal I=\{0,1,\ldots,m\}$, where $R_0=P$ and $V_0$ is the designated
coarse space. Restriction of a global residual is $R_i^{\mathsf T}$ and
prolongation of a local coefficient vector is $R_i$. Define the local energy
matrix
$$A_i=R_i^{\mathsf T}AR_i.$$
When the coarse index $0$ is present, $A_0=P^{\mathsf T}AP$ is the Galerkin
coarse matrix of [[def-galerkin-coarse-grid-correction]]. By
[[thm-galerkin-coarse-correction-is-energy-orthogonal-projector]], it is SPD
and the exact coarse solve is well-defined.

For each $i\in\mathcal I$, the exact local correction and additive
preconditioner are
$$ \Pi_i=R_iA_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}A, \qquad B=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}R_iA_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}. $$
When the spaces span $V$, the exact additive Schwarz preconditioned operator
is $BA=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\Pi_i$. For a fixed ordering of $\mathcal I$, a
multiplicative sweep applies its corrections in that order; if $0$ is present,
it is first. For an inexact additive method, replace each exact $A_i^{-1}$ by
the inverse of an SPD matrix $\widetilde A_i$ satisfying, for fixed
$0<\alpha\le\beta$,
$$ \alpha A_i\preceq \widetilde A_i\preceq\beta A_i, \qquad \widetilde B=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}R_i\widetilde A_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}. $$
For symmetric matrices, $X\preceq Y$ means
$z^{\mathsf T}Xz\le z^{\mathsf T}Yz$ for every vector $z$. The order
inequalities define uniform local spectral equivalence in this pair. The
lemma [[lem-schwarz-local-matrices-are-well-defined]] proves the remaining
local inverse and well-definedness claims.

For the data of [[def-overlapping-schwarz-subspace-correction-data]], every
$\Pi_i=R_iA_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}A$ is an $A$-orthogonal projection, meaning
an idempotent $A$-self-adjoint operator, with range $V_i$. Consequently, for every
$x\in V$,
$$ \|x\|_A^2=\|\Pi_i x\|_A^2+\|(I-\Pi_i)x\|_A^2, \qquad a(\Pi_i x,x)=\|\Pi_i x\|_A^2. $$

For the data of [[def-overlapping-schwarz-subspace-correction-data]], assume
$\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}V_i=V$. Let
$R=[R_i]_{i\in\mathcal I}$ and
$\mathcal D=\operatorname{diag}(A_i)_{i\in\mathcal I}$, so
$B=R\mathcal D^{-1}R^{\mathsf T}$. Then $B$ is SPD and, for every $x\in V$,
$$ x^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}x = \min_{\substack{z=(z_i)_{i\in\mathcal I}\\Rz=x}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I}z_i^{\mathsf T}A_i z_i. $$

For the data of [[def-overlapping-schwarz-subspace-correction-data]], every
local matrix $A_i=R_i^{\mathsf T}AR_i$ with $i\in\mathcal I$ is symmetric
positive definite and therefore invertible. If the coarse index $0$ is
present, then $A_0=P^{\mathsf T}AP$ is the SPD Galerkin coarse matrix. Hence
every exact local solve in the definition exists uniquely.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: The stable-decomposition hypothesis implies that the local spaces span $V$, so [F3] makes $B$ SPD. Each $\Pi_i$ is $A$-self-adjoint by [F2], hence $T=BA=\sum_i\Pi_i$ is $A$-self-adjoint. Moreover $a(Tx,x)=\sum_i\|\Pi_i x\|_A^2\ge0$; if this is zero, then every $\Pi_i x=0$. For any $v_i\in V_i$, [F2] gives $\Pi_i v_i=v_i$, so $a(x,v_i)=a(\Pi_i x,v_i)=0$. The spaces span $V$, hence $x=0$ and $T$ is positive.

Fix $x\ne0$ and choose the decomposition $x=\sum_iR_i z_i$ from the stable-decomposition hypothesis. Orthogonal projection gives $\|x\|_A^2 =\sum_i a(x,R_i z_i) =\sum_i a(\Pi_i x,R_i z_i) \le \left(\sum_i\|\Pi_i x\|_A^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_i z_i^{\mathsf T}A_i z_i\right)^{1/2}.$ The last inequality is [F5] in the product inner product on the finite tuple space. The assumed bound on the second factor yields $a(Tx,x)=\sum_i\|\Pi_i x\|_A^2\ge C_0^{-1}\|x\|_A^2$, proving the lower Rayleigh bound.

For each $x$, write $\Pi_i x=R_i y_i$ with $y_i=A_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}Ax$. The synthesis hypothesis and [F2] give $\|Tx\|_A^2 =\left\|\sum_iR_i y_i\right\|_A^2 \le C_1\sum_i\|\Pi_i x\|_A^2 =C_1a(Tx,x).$ Set $q=a(Tx,x)/\|x\|_A^2$. [F5] gives $q\|x\|_A\le\|Tx\|_A$, while the displayed inequality gives $\|Tx\|_A^2\le C_1q\|x\|_A^2$. If $q>0$, these imply $q\le C_1$; if $q=0$, the same upper bound is immediate.

By [F4] and the assumed lower order bound, every $\widetilde A_i$ is SPD. For every SPD matrix $M$ and vector $y$, $y^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}y =\max_z\bigl(2y^{\mathsf T}z-z^{\mathsf T}Mz\bigr),$ because completing the square subtracts $(z-M^{-1}y)^{\mathsf T}M(z-M^{-1}y)$. Since $\widetilde A_i\preceq\beta A_i$, this maximum for $\widetilde A_i$ is at least the maximum for $\beta A_i$, namely $\beta^{-1}y^{\mathsf T}A_i^{-1}y$; since $\alpha A_i\preceq\widetilde A_i$, it is at most the maximum for $\alpha A_i$, namely $\alpha^{-1}y^{\mathsf T}A_i^{-1}y$. Thus $\beta^{-1}A_i^{-1}\preceq\widetilde A_i^{-1}\preceq\alpha^{-1}A_i^{-1}$. Summing after congruence by $R_i$ yields $\beta^{-1}B\preceq\widetilde B\preceq\alpha^{-1}B$.

Step 1.4 establishes that each inverse in $\widetilde B$ is SPD. By the stable-decomposition hypothesis, the local spaces span $V$; hence if $x\ne0$ then $R_i^{\mathsf T}x\ne0$ for some $i$, since otherwise $x$ would be Euclidean-orthogonal to their span $V$. Therefore $x^{\mathsf T}\widetilde Bx=\sum_i(R_i^{\mathsf T}x)^{\mathsf T}\widetilde A_i^{-1}(R_i^{\mathsf T}x)>0$, so $\widetilde B$ is symmetric positive definite. It follows that $\widetilde BA$ is $A$-self-adjoint and positive, because $A\widetilde BA$ is symmetric positive definite; the inexact Rayleigh quotient and condition number are therefore defined. The matrix comparison in step 1.4 bounds $a(\widetilde BAx,x)=x^{\mathsf T}A\widetilde BAx$ below by $\beta^{-1}x^{\mathsf T}ABAx$ and above by $\alpha^{-1}x^{\mathsf T}ABAx$. The exact bounds in steps 1.2 and 1.3 therefore give the stated inexact minimum, maximum, and condition-ratio bounds.

derivations.claim: For an arbitrary initial error $x$, set $e_{-1}=x$, $d_0=\Pi_0x$, and $e_0=x-d_0$. For $i=1,\ldots,m$, set $d_i=\Pi_i e_{i-1}$ and $e_i=e_{i-1}-d_i$. By [F2], each correction is orthogonal to its updated error, so telescoping gives $D:=\sum_{i=0}^m\|d_i\|_A^2 =\|x\|_A^2-\|e_m\|_A^2.$ Also $e_{i-1}=x-d_0-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}d_j$.

Fix a local index $i\ge1$ and set $b_i=\|\Pi_i x\|_A$, $c_i=\|d_i\|_A$, and $q_i=\|\Pi_i d_0\|_A$. Since $x=e_{i-1}+d_0+\sum_{j<i}d_j$ and $\Pi_i$ is an orthogonal projection, $a(\Pi_i x,e_{i-1})=a(\Pi_i x,\Pi_i e_{i-1})=a(\Pi_i x,d_i)$ and $a(\Pi_i x,d_0)=a(\Pi_i x,\Pi_i d_0)$. Thus $b_i^2=a(\Pi_i x,d_i)+a(\Pi_i x,\Pi_i d_0)+\sum_{j<i}a(\Pi_i x,d_j)$. The first term has absolute value at most $b_i c_i$ and the second at most $b_i q_i$ by [F4]; the remaining terms are at most $b_i\sum_{j<i}\epsilon_{ij}c_j$ by [A2]. If $b_i=0$ the resulting bound is immediate; otherwise divide by $b_i$ to obtain $b_i\le c_i+q_i+\sum_{j<i}\epsilon_{ij}c_j.$

Let $L$ be the strict lower-triangular part of $G$, and let $b,c,q\in\mathbb R^m$ have entries $b_i,c_i,q_i$. They are nonnegative and $0\le Lc\le Gc$ entrywise. Hence $\|Lc\|_2\le\|Gc\|_2\le\rho\|c\|_2$, and step 2.1 yields $\|b\|_2\le(1+\rho)\|c\|_2+\|q\|_2.$ Furthermore, by [F2], $\|q\|_2^2 =\sum_{i=1}^m a(\Pi_i d_0,d_0) =a\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\Pi_i d_0,d_0\right) \le a(Td_0,d_0) \le C_1\|d_0\|_A^2.$ The first inequality uses that $\Pi_0$ is positive semidefinite; the last is [F3].

By $(r+s)^2\le2r^2+2s^2$, steps 1.1 and 3.1 give $\sum_{i=0}^m\|\Pi_i x\|_A^2 =\|d_0\|_A^2+\|b\|_2^2 \le(1+2C_1)\|d_0\|_A^2 +2(1+\rho)^2\sum_{i=1}^m\|d_i\|_A^2 \le K D.$ The left side is $a(Tx,x)$, which [F3] bounds below by $C_0^{-1}\|x\|_A^2$. Thus $D\ge(C_0K)^{-1}\|x\|_A^2$. Since $D\le\|x\|_A^2$ by step 1.1, $C_0K\ge1$.

Step 1.1 now gives $\|E_{\mathrm{mult}}x\|_A^2 =\|e_m\|_A^2 =\|x\|_A^2-D \le\left(1-\frac1{C_0K}\right)\|x\|_A^2.$ Taking the supremum over nonzero $x$ proves the operator-norm bound; finiteness of $C_0,K$ makes the contraction factor strictly less than one.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$, $\Omega=(0,1)^d$, and let
$M\ge2$ and $n\ge2$ be integers. Write $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ for the standard
coordinate vectors in $\mathbb R^d$. In every cube of side $a=1/M$, for each
coordinate permutation $\pi$ use the simplex whose successive vertices,
with $x$ the cube's lower corner, are
$x$, $x+a e_{\pi(1)}$, $x+a(e_{\pi(1)}+e_{\pi(2)})$, through
$x+a\sum_{r=1}^d e_{\pi(r)}$. Subdivide each cube into $n^d$ uniform fine
cubes and apply the same permutation rule at fine scale; this gives a
matching, shape-regular affine simplicial fine mesh refining the coarse mesh.
Write $H=\sqrt d\,a$ and
$h=\sqrt d\,a/n$. Assume an overlap radius $\delta=q a/n$ with integer
$\lceil\sqrt d\rceil\le q\le n$, so $h\le\delta\le a$. For each
coarse cube $Q_j$, let $\Omega_j$ be its closed $\ell^\infty$-neighborhood of
radius $\delta+h$, intersected with $\overline\Omega$. Let $V_H\subset V_h
\subset H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the continuous zero-boundary P1 spaces on the
coarse and fine meshes, and let
$$ V_j=\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{supp}v_h\subseteq\Omega_j\}. $$
Here $\|x\|_\infty=\max_r|x_r|$,
$\operatorname{dist}_\infty(x,Q)=\inf_{y\in Q}\|x-y\|_\infty$, an
$\ell^\infty$-neighborhood of radius $r$ is
$\{x:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(x,Q)\le r\}$, and $\operatorname{supp}v$ is
the closure in $\overline\Omega$ of $\{x:v(x)\ne0\}$.
For the Poisson energy $a(u,v)=\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,dx$, every
$u_h\in V_h$ has a decomposition $u_h=u_0+\sum_j u_j$ with
$u_0\in V_H$ and $u_j\in V_j$ satisfying
$$ a(u_0,u_0)+\sum_j a(u_j,u_j) \le C_{\rm FE}\left(1+\left(\frac H\delta\right)^2\right)a(u_h,u_h). $$
The constant $C_{\rm FE}$ depends only on $d$, the fixed uniform
shape-regularity bound, the Scott–Zhang constant, and the reference P1 product
interpolation constants; it is independent of $M,n,\delta$.

Use the data of [[def-overlapping-schwarz-subspace-correction-data]] and
assume the local spaces span $V$. Suppose $0<C_0,C_1<\infty$ satisfy:

- for every $x\in V$, there are local vectors $z_i$ such that
  $x=\sum_iR_i z_i$ and $\sum_i z_i^{\mathsf T}A_i z_i\le C_0\|x\|_A^2$;
- for every tuple $(z_i)$,
  $\|\sum_iR_i z_i\|_A^2\le C_1\sum_i z_i^{\mathsf T}A_i z_i$.

For an $A$-self-adjoint positive operator $T$, define
$$ \lambda_{\min}^A(T)=\inf_{x\ne0}\frac{a(Tx,x)}{a(x,x)},\qquad \lambda_{\max}^A(T)=\sup_{x\ne0}\frac{a(Tx,x)}{a(x,x)},\qquad \kappa_A(T)=\frac{\lambda_{\max}^A(T)}{\lambda_{\min}^A(T)}. $$
Then the exact additive Schwarz operator $T=BA$ is $A$-self-adjoint positive and
$$ \lambda_{\min}^A(BA)\ge C_0^{-1},\qquad \lambda_{\max}^A(BA)\le C_1,\qquad \kappa_A(BA)\le C_0C_1. $$
If the inexact local matrices satisfy
$\alpha A_i\preceq\widetilde A_i\preceq\beta A_i$ for
$0<\alpha\le\beta$, then
$$ \lambda_{\min}^A(\widetilde BA)\ge(\beta C_0)^{-1},\qquad \lambda_{\max}^A(\widetilde BA)\le C_1/\alpha,\qquad \kappa_A(\widetilde BA)\le(\beta/\alpha)C_0C_1. $$

Use the exact data of
[[def-overlapping-schwarz-subspace-correction-data]], with one coarse space
$V_0$ and $m\ge1$ local spaces $V_1,\ldots,V_m$. Assume the stable-decomposition
and synthesis hypotheses of
[[thm-additive-schwarz-stable-decomposition-condition-number]] hold with
constants $C_0,C_1$. Suppose a symmetric matrix
$G=(\epsilon_{ij})_{i,j=1}^m$ has nonnegative entries and
$$ |a(v_i,v_j)|\le\epsilon_{ij}\|v_i\|_A\|v_j\|_A \quad(v_i\in V_i,\ v_j\in V_j). $$
For a real matrix $M$, write $\|M\|_2=\sup_{y\ne0}\|My\|_2/\|y\|_2$ for its

citations.quote:
Work in exact real arithmetic. Let $n\ge1$ and $V=\mathbb R^n$, and let
$A=A^{\mathsf T}$ satisfy $x^{\mathsf T}Ax>0$ for every nonzero $x$.
Give $V$ the energy inner product $a(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}Ay$ and norm
$\|x\|_A^2=a(x,x)$ of
[[def-energy-inner-product-and-norm-for-a-hermitian-positive-definite-matrix]].
An operator $S$ is $A$-self-adjoint when $a(Sx,y)=a(x,Sy)$ for all $x,y$;
it is positive when $a(Sx,x)>0$ for every nonzero $x$. An $A$-orthogonal
projection is an idempotent $A$-self-adjoint operator.
Let $\mathcal I$ be a finite ordered nonempty set and, for each
$i\in\mathcal I$, choose a full-column-rank prolongation
$R_i\in\mathbb R^{n\times n_i}$ with $1\le n_i\le n$, and put
$V_i=\operatorname{Ran}(R_i)$.
A one-level method has $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. A two-level method has
$\mathcal I=\{0,1,\ldots,m\}$, where $R_0=P$ and $V_0$ is the designated
coarse space. Restriction of a global residual is $R_i^{\mathsf T}$ and
prolongation of a local coefficient vector is $R_i$. Define the local energy
matrix
$$A_i=R_i^{\mathsf T}AR_i.$$
When the coarse index $0$ is present, $A_0=P^{\mathsf T}AP$ is the Galerkin
coarse matrix of [[def-galerkin-coarse-grid-correction]]. By
[[thm-galerkin-coarse-correction-is-energy-orthogonal-projector]], it is SPD
and the exact coarse solve is well-defined.

For each $i\in\mathcal I$, the exact local correction and additive
preconditioner are
$$ \Pi_i=R_iA_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}A, \qquad B=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}R_iA_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}. $$
When the spaces span $V$, the exact additive Schwarz preconditioned operator
is $BA=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\Pi_i$. For a fixed ordering of $\mathcal I$, a
multiplicative sweep applies its corrections in that order; if $0$ is present,
it is first. For an inexact additive method, replace each exact $A_i^{-1}$ by
the inverse of an SPD matrix $\widetilde A_i$ satisfying, for fixed
$0<\alpha\le\beta$,
$$ \alpha A_i\preceq \widetilde A_i\preceq\beta A_i, \qquad \widetilde B=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}R_i\widetilde A_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}. $$
For symmetric matrices, $X\preceq Y$ means
$z^{\mathsf T}Xz\le z^{\mathsf T}Yz$ for every vector $z$. The order
inequalities define uniform local spectral equivalence in this pair. The
lemma [[lem-schwarz-local-matrices-are-well-defined]] proves the remaining
local inverse and well-definedness claims.

derivations.claim: Direct expansion gives $x^{\mathsf T}A_Nx=h^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N(x_j-x_{j-1})^2$ with $x_0=x_N=0$. It is positive for every nonzero vector because vanishing of all successive differences and $x_0=0$ forces every $x_j=0$. For the point-patch injection $R_i=e_i$, the local matrix is $A_i=e_i^{\mathsf T}A_Ne_i=2/h$. Thus [F1] gives $B_N=\sum_i e_i(h/2)e_i^{\mathsf T}=(h/2)I$. Each corresponding nodal hat is supported on two adjacent mesh intervals, so neighboring local supports overlap and at most three closed supports meet at a point.

For $k=1,\ldots,N-1$, set $v_j^{(k)}=\sin(jk\pi/N)$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The endpoints vanish. With $\theta=k\pi/N$, the identity $v_{j-1}^{(k)}+v_{j+1}^{(k)}=2\cos(\theta)v_j^{(k)}$ gives $A_Nv^{(k)}=\frac{2}{h}(1-\cos\theta)v^{(k)}.$ These eigenvalues are distinct because cosine is strictly decreasing on $(0,\pi)$. Since $A_N$ is symmetric, eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal: for $k\ne l$, $(\lambda_k-\lambda_l)(v^{(k)})^{\mathsf T}v^{(l)}=(A_Nv^{(k)})^{\mathsf T}v^{(l)}-(v^{(k)})^{\mathsf T}A_Nv^{(l)}=0$. The vectors are nonzero, so the $N-1$ orthogonal vectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^{N-1}$. Multiplication by $B_N=(h/2)I$ gives eigenvalues $1-\cos(k\pi/N)$ for $B_NA_N$.

The smallest and largest values occur at $k=1$ and $k=N-1$, respectively. Therefore $\kappa_A(B_NA_N) =\frac{1-\cos((N-1)\pi/N)}{1-\cos(\pi/N)} =\frac{1+\cos(\pi/N)}{1-\cos(\pi/N)}.$ As $N\to\infty$ the numerator tends to $2$ and the positive denominator tends to $0$, so the condition numbers diverge.

derivations.claim: The grounded two-node graph with unit conductance from each node to ground and conductance $\alpha$ between the nodes has matrix $A_\alpha=I_2+\alpha \begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.$ For $x=(x_1,x_2)$, $x^{\mathsf T}A_\alpha x=x_1^2+x_2^2+\alpha(x_1-x_2)^2$, so $A_\alpha$ is SPD. The coarse and local injections are $R_0=e_1$ and $R_1=e_2$, hence $A_0=A_1=1+\alpha$. The additive preconditioner from [F1] is therefore $B_\alpha=(1+\alpha)^{-1}I_2$. There is one local subspace, so its pairwise overlap matrix is the fixed $1\times1$ matrix $[1]$, independent of $\alpha$.

The vectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ are eigenvectors of $A_\alpha$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $1+2\alpha$. Thus $B_\alpha A_\alpha$ has eigenvalues $(1+\alpha)^{-1}$ and $(1+2\alpha)/(1+\alpha)$, so $\kappa_A(B_\alpha A_\alpha)=1+2\alpha\to\infty$. The low-energy channel vector $(1,1)$ is not in the one-node coarse space $V_0$, and the growing condition number disproves the claim.

derivations.claim: Given a fine vector $u$, let $u_H$ be its coarse nodal interpolant: $(u_H)_{2k}=u_{2k}$ and $(u_H)_{2k-1}=(u_{2k-2}+u_{2k})/2$. Define $\eta_k=u_{2k-1}-(u_{2k-2}+u_{2k})/2$ and $u_k=\eta_k\phi_{2k-1}$. Nodal values give $u=u_H+\sum_{k=1}^M u_k$.

On each fine interval, at most one odd nodal hat has nonzero derivative. Thus only the coarse derivative and at most one local derivative can be nonzero there. The elementary inequality $(s+t)^2\le2(s^2+t^2)$, which follows from $(s-t)^2\ge0$, and integration give $\left\|v_0+\sum_kv_k\right\|_A^2 \le2\left(\|v_0\|_A^2+\sum_k\|v_k\|_A^2\right).$ Hence $C_1\le2$.

On each pair of fine intervals set $a_k=u_{2k-1}-u_{2k-2}$ and $b_k=u_{2k}-u_{2k-1}$. The coarse energy on that coarse interval is $(a_k+b_k)^2/(2h)\le(a_k^2+b_k^2)/h$, exactly its fine energy contribution. Summing over $k$ gives $\|u_H\|_A^2\le\|u\|_A^2$.

Since $\eta_k=(a_k-b_k)/2$ and $(a_k-b_k)^2\le2(a_k^2+b_k^2)$, the local energy is $\|u_k\|_A^2=2\eta_k^2/h\le(a_k^2+b_k^2)/h$. Summing gives $\sum_k\|u_k\|_A^2\le\|u\|_A^2$. The decomposition in step 1.1 therefore has total energy at most $2\|u\|_A^2$, so $C_0\le2$.

Apply [F1] to the exact Schwarz data [F2] with $C_0\le2$ and $C_1\le2$ to obtain $\kappa_A(BA)\le4$. This finite one-dimensional split has a global coarse space; higher-dimensional overlap estimates are handled separately on the A page.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

derivations.claim: The spaces $X_i$ and their matrix spaces $\mathcal L(X_i,X_j)$ have finite bases, so [F2] makes them Banach and [F1] applies. Put $G=C\circ S$. The composition rule gives $DG(x)=DC(y)DS(x)$. Composition of bounded linear maps is the bounded bilinear map $(A,B)\mapsto A\circ B$, since $\|A\circ B\|_{\rm op}\le\|A\|_{\rm op}\|B\|_{\rm op}$. Applying its product rule and the composition rule in [F1] to this derivative identity, then evaluating on $k$, gives $D^2G(x)[h,k]=D^2C(y)[DS(x)h,DS(x)k]+DC(y)D^2S(x)[h,k]$.

Since $E=T\circ G$, [F1] gives $DE(x)=DT(G(x))DG(x)$. Differentiate this bounded-operator product in direction $h$ and evaluate on $k$: the derivative of $DT\circ G$ contributes $D^2T(z)[DG(x)h,DG(x)k]$, and the derivative of $DG$ contributes $DT(z)D^2G(x)[h,k]$. Substituting $DG(x)=DC(y)DS(x)$ and step 1.1 yields the stated formula.

Let $U_h\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_h}$ and $U_H\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_H}$ be open,
with $n_h,n_H\ge1$. Let $F_h:U_h\to\mathbb R^{n_h}$ and
$F_H:U_H\to\mathbb R^{n_H}$ be residual maps, and let $f_h\in\mathbb R^{n_h}$.
The equation on the fine level is $F_h(u)=f_h$. Choose linear maps
$I: \mathbb R^{n_h}\to\mathbb R^{n_H}$ (iterate restriction),
$R: \mathbb R^{n_h}\to\mathbb R^{n_H}$ (residual restriction), and
$P: \mathbb R^{n_H}\to\mathbb R^{n_h}$ (prolongation). No equality among
$I$, $R$, and $P$ is imposed by this definition. Choose positive diagonal
matrices $D^{\rm pre}$ and $D^{\rm post}$, damping factors
$0<\omega_{\rm pre},\omega_{\rm post}\le1$, finite sweep counts
$\nu_{\rm pre},\nu_{\rm post}\in\mathbb N_0$, a finite positive coarse-solver
operation budget $B_H$, and a positive integer $\gamma$.

A **coarse-solver call** with target $g\in\mathbb R^{n_H}$ and initial value
$z\in U_H$ must return within $B_H$ declared operations either an exact selected
root $(v,\texttt{exact-root},0)$ with $F_H(v)=g$, an inexact value
$(v,\texttt{inexact-root},\eta)$ with the explicitly computed residual
$\eta=\|F_H(v)-g\|_2>0$, or one of
$\texttt{branch-failure}$, $\texttt{domain-failure}$, and
$\texttt{budget-exhausted}$. The solver contract requires it to return the
initial value unchanged as `exact-root` when $F_H(z)=g$ and $z$ is the selected
root. A direct formula, an exact local branch, or a finite iterative solver may
be supplied; the definition makes no claim that any solver finds a root from an
arbitrary initial value.

For a starting fine iterate $u\in U_h$, do the following in exact real
arithmetic.

1. Perform $\nu_{\rm pre}$ nonlinear damped-Jacobi sweeps. In each sweep,
form the trial value
$$\widetilde u:=u-\omega_{\rm pre}(D^{\rm pre})^{-1}(F_h(u)-f_h).$$
If $\widetilde u\notin U_h$, return the current valid fine iterate $u$ with
status `domain-failure`; otherwise set $u:=\widetilde u$.

2. Set $u_H=Iu$. If $u_H\notin U_H$, return the last valid fine iterate
with status `domain-failure`. Otherwise set $r_h=f_h-F_h(u)$ and
$$g_H=F_H(u_H)+Rr_h=Rf_h+\tau(u),\qquad \tau(u):=F_H(Iu)-RF_h(u).$$

3. Set $z=u_H$ and initialize a finite diagnostic list $\Delta=()$. For
$t=1,\ldots,\gamma$, call the declared coarse solver on $(g_H,z,B_H)$. On
`branch-failure`, `domain-failure`, or `budget-exhausted`, return the last
valid fine iterate with that status and the diagnostics accumulated so far.
On `exact-root` or `inexact-root`, append the returned status and residual to
$\Delta$, replace $z$ by the returned value, and append any nested diagnostics
returned by the coarse call. Reusing $g_H$ while starting at the current $z$
makes repeated coarse calls a bounded V/W-style cycle.

4. Form the trial correction
$$\widetilde u:=u+P(z-Iu).$$
If $\widetilde u\notin U_h$, return the current valid fine iterate $u$ with
status `domain-failure` and $\Delta$; otherwise set $u:=\widetilde u$.

5. Perform $\nu_{\rm post}$ nonlinear damped-Jacobi sweeps. In each sweep,
form the trial value
$$\widetilde u:=u-\omega_{\rm post}(D^{\rm post})^{-1}(F_h(u)-f_h).$$
If $\widetilde u\notin U_h$, return the current valid fine iterate $u$ with
status `domain-failure` and $\Delta$; otherwise set $u:=\widetilde u$.
Compute the final fine residual
$\eta_h:=\|F_h(u)-f_h\|_2$. Return the resulting iterate with status
`exact-root` and residual $0$ if $\eta_h=0$, and with status `inexact-root`
and residual $\eta_h$ if $\eta_h>0$, together with $\Delta$. Thus the status
used when this procedure is called recursively
always certifies the residual for its own level equation; zero residuals
reported by inner coarse calls do not by themselves certify that the returned
fine iterate is a root.

Every loop count and solver budget is finite. `V` and `W` refer to the cases
$\gamma=1$ and $\gamma=2$. A multi-level cycle uses this two-grid procedure at
each level, with the next-level cycle supplied as the coarse solver and a
finite level cap. Fixed-point consistency, linear reduction, local convergence,
and work bounds are separate claims.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For a level-$j$ invocation of [[alg-fas-vw-cycle]], let $u^*$ satisfy
$F_j(u^*)=f_j$. Suppose each selected pre/post smoother leaves every exact
root fixed, every restriction $I_ju^*$ lies in $U_{j-1}$ and is selected as
the exact coarse root at its zero-defect target, and the base solver returns
any initial exact root unchanged. Then the exact-branch FAS V/W cycle leaves
$u^*$ fixed. This holds for arbitrary admissible transfer maps $I_j,R_j,P_j$;
no identity such as $R_j=I_j$ or $I_jP_j=I$ is needed.

Consider one exact-branch two-grid cycle from [[alg-fas-two-grid-cycle]]. Let
$F_h:U_h\to\mathbb R^{n_h}$ and $F_H:U_H\to\mathbb R^{n_H}$ be $C^1$ on
open sets, let $I,R,P$ be linear, and suppose $F_h(u_*)=f_h$ and
$Iu_*\in U_H$. Assume the exact coarse solver selects the local root branch
through $Iu_*$ and $DF_H(Iu_*)$ is invertible. Suppose the pre/post smoothing
maps are $C^1$ and fix $u_*$. The selected coarse root $v(u)$ is locally $C^1$,
and the derivative of the actual FAS cycle $E$ at $u_*$ is
$$DE(u_*)=DS^{\rm post}(u_*)\bigl[I_{n_h}-P\,DF_H(Iu_*)^{-1}R\,DF_h(u_*)\bigr]DS^{\rm pre}(u_*).$$

No identity between $R$ and $I$, or between the coarse operator and a
rediscretized fine operator, is assumed in this derivative formula.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and write $J(x)=DF(x)$ as a matrix in the standard basis. The matrix
of $DF(x)$ agrees with the Jacobian matrix by
[[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For a
matrix $A$ let
$\|A\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$. Let $K\subseteq U$ be convex,
let $x_*,x\in K$, and suppose for some $L\ge0$ that
$$\|J(y)-J(z)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|y-z\|_2\qquad(y,z\in K).$$
Then
$$\|F(x)-F(x_*)-J(x)(x-x_*)\|_2\le\frac{L}{2}\|x-x_*\|_2^2.$$

derivations.claim: In the two-grid case, [F2] identifies $DE(u_*)$ as the derivative of the actual pre-smoother, implicit coarse-branch correction, and post-smoother composition. For a recursive V/W cycle, $q$ in the hypotheses is the derivative norm of that full composed map.

Fix $x\in K$ and put $e=x-u_*$. Apply [F3] with its variables $x=u_*$ and $x_*=x$. Reversing the resulting difference and using $E(u_*)=u_*$ gives $\|E(x)-u_*-DE(u_*)e\|_2\le\frac{L}{2}\|e\|_2^2.$ Thus, since $\|DE(u_*)\|_{\rm op}=q$ and $\|e\|_2\le r$, $\|E(x)-u_*\|_2\le q\|e\|_2+\frac{L}{2}\|e\|_2^2\le\kappa\|e\|_2,\qquad \kappa:=q+Lr/2<1.$
For $x\in K$, step 1.2 gives $\|E(x)-u_*\|_2\le\kappa\|x-u_*\|_2\le\kappa r<r$, so $E(x)\in K$. This proves invariance of the stated ball.

For an iterate starting at $u_0\in K$, invariance keeps every $u_k$ in $K$ and step 1.2 gives $\|u_{k+1}-u_*\|_2\le\kappa\|u_k-u_*\|_2$. Induction yields $\|u_k-u_*\|_2\le\kappa^k\|u_0-u_*\|_2$; because $0\le\kappa<1$, the right side tends to zero.

provide the level-$(j-1)$ cycle as the coarse-solver interface to

immediately with the last valid fine-level iterate. Each recursive call
lowers $j$, and all within-level loops have the finite budgets required by

solves the nonlinear equations, that the cycles converge, or that their work

$A_j\in\mathbb R^{n_j\times n_j}$, $0\le j\le J$, with $n_j\ge1$, and

1. If $j=0$, return the exact solution $A_0^{-1}b$.
2. Starting from $x$, perform $\nu_1$ pre-sweeps

4. Correct $x\leftarrow x+P_je$, then perform $\nu_2$ post-sweeps

Let $A_h\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive definite and let
$P\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}$ have full column rank, where $1\le m\le n$. Put

invertible, and the map $C=I_n-PA_H^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}A_h$ of
[[def-galerkin-coarse-grid-correction]] satisfies

$$C^2=C,\qquad CP=0,\qquad P^{\mathsf T}A_hC=0,\qquad C^{\mathsf T}A_h=A_hC.$$

The FAS coarse target is $g_H=A_{j-1}u_H+P_j^{\mathsf T}r_j,$ so its residual relative to the starting coarse value $u_H$ is exactly $P_j^{\mathsf T}r_j$.

Let $e_t=z_t-u_H$ be the current coarse difference after $t$ recursive coarse calls. By [A1], the next FAS coarse call equals the correction-cycle call with initial iterate $z_t$ and right side $g_H$. Applying [F4] with $a=u_H$, $x=e_t$, and $b=P_j^{\mathsf T}r_j$ gives $\operatorname{Cycle}(j-1,z_t,g_H)=u_H+\operatorname{Cycle}(j-1,e_t,P_j^{\mathsf T}r_j).$ Thus each coarse difference update is exactly the error update in [F2], including repeated W-cycle calls.

After the same number of coarse calls, [F1] prolongs the same error correction as [F2]. Their post-smoothers are identical residual-correction updates, so their returned fine iterates agree. The base case and this induction step prove equality at every level.

Let $U_h\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_h}$ and $U_H\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_H}$ be open,
with $n_h,n_H\ge1$. Let $F_h:U_h\to\mathbb R^{n_h}$ and
$F_H:U_H\to\mathbb R^{n_H}$ be residual maps, and let $f_h\in\mathbb R^{n_h}$.
The equation on the fine level is $F_h(u)=f_h$. Choose linear maps
$I: \mathbb R^{n_h}\to\mathbb R^{n_H}$ (iterate restriction),
$R: \mathbb R^{n_h}\to\mathbb R^{n_H}$ (residual restriction), and
$P: \mathbb R^{n_H}\to\mathbb R^{n_h}$ (prolongation). No equality among
$I$, $R$, and $P$ is imposed by this definition. Choose positive diagonal
matrices $D^{\rm pre}$ and $D^{\rm post}$, damping factors
$0<\omega_{\rm pre},\omega_{\rm post}\le1$, finite sweep counts
$\nu_{\rm pre},\nu_{\rm post}\in\mathbb N_0$, a finite positive coarse-solver
operation budget $B_H$, and a positive integer $\gamma$.

A **coarse-solver call** with target $g\in\mathbb R^{n_H}$ and initial value
$z\in U_H$ must return within $B_H$ declared operations either an exact selected
root $(v,\texttt{exact-root},0)$ with $F_H(v)=g$, an inexact value
$(v,\texttt{inexact-root},\eta)$ with the explicitly computed residual
$\eta=\|F_H(v)-g\|_2>0$, or one of
$\texttt{branch-failure}$, $\texttt{domain-failure}$, and
$\texttt{budget-exhausted}$. The solver contract requires it to return the
initial value unchanged as `exact-root` when $F_H(z)=g$ and $z$ is the selected
root. A direct formula, an exact local branch, or a finite iterative solver may
be supplied; the definition makes no claim that any solver finds a root from an
arbitrary initial value.

For a starting fine iterate $u\in U_h$, do the following in exact real
arithmetic.

1. Perform $\nu_{\rm pre}$ nonlinear damped-Jacobi sweeps. In each sweep,
form the trial value
$$\widetilde u:=u-\omega_{\rm pre}(D^{\rm pre})^{-1}(F_h(u)-f_h).$$
If $\widetilde u\notin U_h$, return the current valid fine iterate $u$ with
status `domain-failure`; otherwise set $u:=\widetilde u$.

2. Set $u_H=Iu$. If $u_H\notin U_H$, return the last valid fine iterate
with status `domain-failure`. Otherwise set $r_h=f_h-F_h(u)$ and
$$g_H=F_H(u_H)+Rr_h=Rf_h+\tau(u),\qquad \tau(u):=F_H(Iu)-RF_h(u).$$

3. Set $z=u_H$ and initialize a finite diagnostic list $\Delta=()$. For
$t=1,\ldots,\gamma$, call the declared coarse solver on $(g_H,z,B_H)$. On
`branch-failure`, `domain-failure`, or `budget-exhausted`, return the last
valid fine iterate with that status and the diagnostics accumulated so far.
On `exact-root` or `inexact-root`, append the returned status and residual to
$\Delta$, replace $z$ by the returned value, and append any nested diagnostics
returned by the coarse call. Reusing $g_H$ while starting at the current $z$
makes repeated coarse calls a bounded V/W-style cycle.

4. Form the trial correction
$$\widetilde u:=u+P(z-Iu).$$
If $\widetilde u\notin U_h$, return the current valid fine iterate $u$ with
status `domain-failure` and $\Delta$; otherwise set $u:=\widetilde u$.

5. Perform $\nu_{\rm post}$ nonlinear damped-Jacobi sweeps. In each sweep,
form the trial value
$$\widetilde u:=u-\omega_{\rm post}(D^{\rm post})^{-1}(F_h(u)-f_h).$$
If $\widetilde u\notin U_h$, return the current valid fine iterate $u$ with
status `domain-failure` and $\Delta$; otherwise set $u:=\widetilde u$.
Compute the final fine residual
$\eta_h:=\|F_h(u)-f_h\|_2$. Return the resulting iterate with status
`exact-root` and residual $0$ if $\eta_h=0$, and with status `inexact-root`
and residual $\eta_h$ if $\eta_h>0$, together with $\Delta$. Thus the status
used when this procedure is called recursively
always certifies the residual for its own level equation; zero residuals
reported by inner coarse calls do not by themselves certify that the returned
fine iterate is a root.

Every loop count and solver budget is finite. `V` and `W` refer to the cases
$\gamma=1$ and $\gamma=2$. A multi-level cycle uses this two-grid procedure at
each level, with the next-level cycle supplied as the coarse solver and a
finite level cap. Fixed-point consistency, linear reduction, local convergence,
and work bounds are separate claims.

Let $E:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be the actual exact-branch error map of one fixed
FAS two-grid or recursive V/W cycle, with $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ open. Let
$u_*\in U$ be a fine root for which the selected smoothers and coarse branches
fix $u_*$, so $E(u_*)=u_*$. Assume $E$ is $C^1$ on a neighborhood of the
closed Euclidean ball $K=\overline B_2(u_*,r)\subset U$. Put
$q=\|DE(u_*)\|_{\rm op}$, where for a linear map $T$ the induced Euclidean
operator norm is $\|T\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Tv\|_2$. Suppose $q<1$ and
$$\|DE(x)-DE(y)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in K)$$
for some $L\ge0$. If $q+Lr/2<1$, then $E(K)\subseteq K$ and every iteration
$u_{k+1}=E(u_k)$ starting in $K$ satisfies
$$\|u_k-u_*\|_2\le(q+Lr/2)^k\|u_0-u_*\|_2.$$
This is a local result for the derivative of the actual cycle; it supplies no
global-start or mesh-independent rate unless $q,L,r$ are verified uniformly.

derivations.claim: Let $z=u_{\rm pre}+P(v(u)-Iu_{\rm pre})$ and $\widehat z=u_{\rm pre}+P(\widehat v-Iu_{\rm pre})$ be the exact and inexact corrected states. By [F1], subtraction cancels $u_{\rm pre}$ and $Iu_{\rm pre}$, so $\widehat z-z=P(\widehat v-v(u))$. Hence [A1] gives $\|\widehat z-z\|_2\le\|P\|_{\rm op}\|\widehat v-v(u)\|_2\le\|P\|_{\rm op}M_H\eta.$

Applying the same post-smoother to the two corrected states and using [A2] yields $\|\widehat E(u)-E(u)\|_2\le L_{\rm post}\|P\|_{\rm op}M_H\eta$. For an iteration, the triangle inequality and [F2] therefore give $\|u_{k+1}-u_*\|_2\le\|\widehat E(u_k)-E(u_k)\|_2+\|E(u_k)-u_*\|_2\le L_{\rm post}\|P\|_{\rm op}M_H\eta_k+\kappa\|u_k-u_*\|_2.$

derivations.claim: The continuous model is $-u''+u^3=0$ on $(0,3)$ with zero endpoint values, and this proof concerns the specified finite-difference residual. The vectors $(1,1)^{\mathsf T}$ and $(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}$ are eigenvectors of $A$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $3$, so $z^{\mathsf T}Az\ge\|z\|_2^2$. For real $s,t$, $(s-t)(s^3-t^3)=(s-t)^2(s^2+st+t^2)\ge0$, since $s^2+st+t^2=((2s+t)^2+3t^2)/4$. Therefore, for $a,b\in\mathbb R^2$, $\langle a-b,F(a)-F(b)\rangle=(a-b)^{\mathsf T}A(a-b)+\sum_{i=1}^2(a_i-b_i)(a_i^3-b_i^3)\ge\|a-b\|_2^2$. Since $F(0)=0$, any other root $a$ would give $0=\langle a,F(a)-F(0)\rangle\ge\|a\|_2^2$, so $u_*=0$ is the unique root. Direct differentiation gives $DF(0)=A$.

Direct multiplication gives $AP=P$, $P^{\mathsf T}AP=2$, and hence $F_H(v)=P^{\mathsf T}F(Pv)=2v+2v^3.$ Writing $m=Iu=(u_1+u_2)/2$, [F1] gives the coarse target $g(u)=F_H(m)-P^{\mathsf T}F(u)=2m^3-u_1^3-u_2^3.$ The scalar map $\phi(v)=2v+2v^3$ has $\phi'(v)=2+6v^2\ge2$ and limits $\pm\infty$ at $v\to\pm\infty$, so for every $g$ it has one exact root. An exact direct solver is $v(g)=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\sinh\!\left(\frac13\operatorname{arsinh}\!\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}g\right)\right),$ because $\sinh(3t)=3\sinh(t)+4\sinh^3(t)$; thus $\phi(v(g))=g$. The displayed formula is a composition of smooth real functions, so the selected branch, correction map $C$, and cycle map $E$ are $C^2$ on an open neighborhood of the ball. At $g=0$ the branch has $v=0$ and $\phi'(0)=2$.

The pre/post map has derivative at zero $B_s=DS(0)=I_2-\tfrac14A=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/4\\1/4&1/2\end{pmatrix}.$ The coarse-branch equation has right side $g(u)$, a cubic with $Dg(0)=0$. Differentiating $\phi(v(u))=g(u)$ at zero gives $2Dv(0)=Dg(0)=0$. The derivative of the coarse correction is $Q=I_2-PI=I_2-\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},$ the orthogonal projection onto $(1,-1)$. The symmetric vector $(1,1)$ is an eigenvector of $B_s$ with eigenvalue $3/4$, and $(1,-1)$ has eigenvalue $1/4$. Thus for $E=S\circ C\circ S$, [F2] gives $DE(0)=B_sQB_s=\tfrac1{16}Q,\qquad q=\|DE(0)\|_2=\tfrac1{16}.$

It remains to bound the derivative variation. Set $r=1/100$ and $m(u)=(u_1+u_2)/2$. On $\|u\|_2\le r$, $|m|\le r/\sqrt2,\quad |g(u)|<2r^3,\quad \|Dg(u)\|_2<6r^2,\quad \|D^2g(u)\|_{\rm op}<11r.$ The first inequality is Cauchy--Schwarz. The second follows from $g=2m^3-u_1^3-u_2^3$ and $|u_1|^3+|u_2|^3\le\|u\|_2^3$. Differentiating gives $Dg=6m^2Dm-3(u_1^2,u_2^2)$ and $D^2g=12m(Dm\otimes Dm)-\operatorname{diag}(6u_1,6u_2)$, which give the last two bounds. If $\phi(v(u))=g(u)$, then $|v|\le|g|/2<r^3$, $\|Dv\|\le\|Dg\|/2<3r^2$, and twice differentiating yields $\|D^2v\|<\tfrac12\bigl(11r+12r^3(3r^2)^2\bigr)=5.5r+54r^7.$ Writing $C(u)=Qu+Pv(u)$, it follows that $\|DC\|<1.001$ and $\|D^2C\|<0.08$ on this ball.

Since $\|B_s\|_2=3/4$, $\|S(u)\|_2\le3r/4+r^3/4<r$ for $u$ in the radius-$r$ ball. Orthogonality of $Q u$ and $P v(u)$ gives $\|C(S(u))\|_2^2\le r^2+2r^6<4r^2$. On the radius-$2r$ ball, $\|DS\|_2<0.751$ and $\|D^2S\|_{\rm op}\le0.03$; on the radius-$r$ ball, $\|D^2S\|_{\rm op}\le0.015$. The formula [F5] for $E=S\circ C\circ S$ therefore gives $\|D^2E(u)\|_{\rm op}\le0.03(1.001\cdot0.751)^2+0.751\bigl(0.08\cdot0.751^2+1.001\cdot0.015\bigr)<0.07<1.$ For each unit $w\in\mathbb R^2$, apply [F4] on the open radius-$r$ ball to the map $u\mapsto DE(u)w$; the Hessian bound gives derivative norm less than $1$. The pre/post map $S$ fixes zero because $F(0)=0$. At $u=0$, [F1] gives restricted value $Iu=0$ and coarse target $F_H(0)=0$; by step 1.2, the exact selected coarse root is $v=0$, so the correction is zero and $E(0)=0$. By steps 1.3 and 2.1, $q=1/16$, $L=1$, and $r=1/100$, hence $q+Lr/2=\tfrac1{16}+\tfrac1{200}=\tfrac{27}{400}<1.$ Applying [F3] proves invariance of the ball and the stated local error rate. Let $E:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be the actual exact-branch error map of one fixed
FAS two-grid or recursive V/W cycle, with $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ open. Let
$u_*\in U$ be a fine root for which the selected smoothers and coarse branches
fix $u_*$, so $E(u_*)=u_*$. Assume $E$ is $C^1$ on a neighborhood of the

$q=\|DE(u_*)\|_{\rm op}$, where for a linear map $T$ the induced Euclidean
operator norm is $\|T\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Tv\|_2$. Suppose $q<1$ and
$$\|DE(x)-DE(y)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in K)$$
for some $L\ge0$. If $q+Lr/2<1$, then $E(K)\subseteq K$ and every iteration

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

$U_i\subseteq X_i$ be open for $i=0,1,2$. Suppose $S:U_0\to U_1$, $C:U_1\to U_2$, and

derivations.claim: Let $P(v)=(0,v)^{\mathsf T}$. For any pre-smoothed $(x,y)$, [F1] gives $g_H=F_H(y)+R(-F_\mu(x,y))=y-y=0.$ The exact coarse solution is $v=0$, so prolonging $v-I(x,y)=-y$ sets the second fine coordinate to zero. The following post-sweep leaves it zero. Hence the actual cycle map is $E_\mu(x,y)=(s_\mu(s_\mu(x)),0).$

Write $a=1-\mu/2$ and $r=r_\mu\le0.1$. For $|x|\le r$, $|s_\mu(x)|\le r+\tfrac12r^3\le1.005r,\quad |s_\mu'(x)|\le1.015,\quad |s_\mu'(s_\mu(x))|\le1.02,$ and $|s_\mu''(x)|\le3r$, $|s_\mu''(s_\mu(x))|\le3.015r$. By [F4], $(s_\mu\circ s_\mu)''=s_\mu''(s_\mu)(s_\mu')^2+s_\mu'(s_\mu)s_\mu''$, so these bounds give $|(s_\mu\circ s_\mu)''(x)|<7r$. The derivative matrix of $E_\mu$ is $\operatorname{diag}((s_\mu\circ s_\mu)'(x),0)$, so [F3] gives $\|DE_\mu(z)-DE_\mu(z')\|_{\rm op}\le7r\|z-z'\|_2$ on the ball.

Since $F_\mu(x,y)=0$ implies $y=0$ and $x(\mu+x^2)=0$, for $\mu>0$ the unique fine root is $(0,0)$. Also $s_\mu'(0)=1-\mu/2$, so differentiating the two sweeps gives $DE_\mu(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}(1-\mu/2)^2&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad q_\mu=(1-\mu/2)^2.$

With $r^2=\mu/100$, $q_\mu+\frac{(7r)r}{2}=(1-\mu/2)^2+\frac{7\mu}{200}=1-\frac{193}{200}\mu+\frac14\mu^2\le1-\frac{143}{200}\mu<1.$ Thus [F2] applies on this ball. Its certified radius $r_\mu=\sqrt{\mu/100}$ tends to zero as $\mu\downarrow0$; at $\mu=0$, $q_0=1$ and the strict derivative hypothesis fails. For $\mu<0$, the scalar equation $\mu x+x^3=0$ has the additional roots $x=\pm\sqrt{-\mu}$, which is the pitchfork bifurcation.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open. Write $B(x,r)$ for the open Euclidean ball from [[def-metric-ball]] with distance induced by [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A family of cells is **locally finite** here when every compact subset of $\Omega$ meets only finitely many cells. A bounded set is **Jordan measurable** when its Jordan inner and outer contents agree ([[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]]). A **cell particle rule** is a nonempty locally finite family of bounded Jordan-measurable cells $C_j\subseteq\Omega$ whose interiors are disjoint and whose union covers $\Omega$ up to their shared boundaries, together with nodes $x_j\in C_j$ and positive volumes $V_j=\int 1_{C_j}$. The cell volume integral is Riemann-defined and equals the Jordan content ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]). Its fill radius is $h=\sup_j\sup_{y\in C_j}|y-x_j|$, using the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; require $0<h<\infty$. Assume finite constants $C_V,C_L>0$ satisfy $V_j\le C_Vh^d$ and the local volume bound

$$\sum_{j:C_j\cap B(x,r)\ne\varnothing}V_j\le C_L(r+h)^d$$

for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and $r>0$. For continuous $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with compact support contained in $\Omega$ (support as in [[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]), define $Q_hg=\sum_jV_jg(x_j)$; local finiteness makes this sum finite. For specified parameters $R>0$ and $\varepsilon>0$, an evaluation point $x\in\mathbb R^d$ is **interior** relative to $(R,\varepsilon)$ when $B(x,R\varepsilon+2h)\subset\Omega$; in a kernel application, $R$ is the chosen support-radius bound for the unscaled kernel. For periodic calculations, use the periodic extensions of the field and particle rule on $\mathbb R^d$, so no kernel support is truncated.

The cell rule is integration-compatible: for every continuous $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with compact support contained in $\Omega$, only finitely many cells meet $\operatorname{supp}(g)$, every cell integral appearing below is Riemann-defined, and
$$\int_\Omega g(y)\,dy=\sum_{j:C_j\cap\operatorname{supp}(g)\ne\varnothing}\int_{C_j}g(y)\,dy.$$
This finite partition identity is part of the quadrature data.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

On a bounding rectangle for each cell, [F3] gives |∫_{C_j}(g−g(x_j))|≤∫_{C_j}|g−g(x_j)|≤V_j osc_{C_j}(g). Summing proves the first inequality.

For y,z∈C_j, [F1] gives |y−x_j|≤h and |z−x_j|≤h; the triangle inequality in [F2] gives |y−z|≤2h. Hence |g(y)−g(z)|≤2hL_g and osc_{C_j}(g)≤2hL_g. Substituting this bound in step 1.1 proves the second inequality.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An **admissible smoothing kernel** is a radial function $W\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^d,[0,\infty))$, supported in the closed Euclidean ball $\overline B(0,R)$ of some radius $R>0$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), with $\int_{\mathbb R^d}W(z)\,dz=1$. Here radial means $W(z)=w(|z|)$ for some function $w:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, and $C_c^2$ means twice continuously differentiable with compact support. All vector norms are the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and $\|D^2W\|_\infty$ uses the induced operator norm. Throughout this pair, $L^\infty$ norms are suprema of Euclidean norms, and norms of multilinear derivatives are the induced operator norms. Compactly supported integrals use [[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]], where $\operatorname{supp}f$ is the closure of the set on which $f$ is nonzero.

For $\varepsilon>0$ define the scaled kernel $W_\varepsilon(z)=\varepsilon^{-d}W(z/\varepsilon)$. Write $M_0=\|W\|_\infty$, $M_1=\|\nabla W\|_\infty$, $M_2=\|D^2W\|_\infty$, $m_2=\int |z|^2W(z)\,dz$, and $m_3=\int |z|^3|\nabla W(z)|\,dz$. The norm functions and moment integrands are continuous with compact support. They are bounded and Riemann integrable on a bounding Jordan box by [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]], so these constants are finite.

For continuous $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, define the full-space smoother and its kernel-gradient operator by
$$S_\varepsilon f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x-z)W_\varepsilon(z)\,dz,\qquad D_\varepsilon f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(y)\nabla W_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy.$$
For each fixed $x$, both scalar integrands and every component of the vector integrand are continuous and compactly supported, hence Riemann integrable on a bounding Jordan box by [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. Thus the displayed integrals exist as compactly supported Riemann integrals; the vector integral defining $D_\varepsilon f$ is taken componentwise.

This page fixes $\varepsilon$ in the finite-particle system. Limits $\varepsilon\to0$ are used only in the stated kernel-bias and joint-refinement results.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

For each k, z_kW_ε(z) is continuous and compactly supported, so [F3] makes it integrable on a bounding box. Apply [F2] to T(u)=εu: ∫z_kW_ε(z)dz=ε∫u_kW(u)du=0 by step 1.1. This holds for every k, so both vector first moments vanish.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $a<b$. Let $F,G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. Suppose $f,g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ are Riemann integrable and agree on $(a,b)$ with $F'$ and $G'$, respectively. Then $Fg$ and $fG$ are Riemann integrable and

$$\int_a^b F(x)g(x)\,dx+\int_a^b f(x)G(x)\,dx=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Equivalently,

$$\int_a^b Fg=[FG]_a^b-\int_a^b fG.$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An **admissible smoothing kernel** is a radial function $W\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^d,[0,\infty))$, supported in the closed Euclidean ball $\overline B(0,R)$ of some radius $R>0$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), with $\int_{\mathbb R^d}W(z)\,dz=1$. Here radial means $W(z)=w(|z|)$ for some function $w:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, and $C_c^2$ means twice continuously differentiable with compact support. All vector norms are the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and $\|D^2W\|_\infty$ uses the induced operator norm. Throughout this pair, $L^\infty$ norms are suprema of Euclidean norms, and norms of multilinear derivatives are the induced operator norms. Compactly supported integrals use [[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]], where $\operatorname{supp}f$ is the closure of the set on which $f$ is nonzero.

For $\varepsilon>0$ define the scaled kernel $W_\varepsilon(z)=\varepsilon^{-d}W(z/\varepsilon)$. Write $M_0=\|W\|_\infty$, $M_1=\|\nabla W\|_\infty$, $M_2=\|D^2W\|_\infty$, $m_2=\int |z|^2W(z)\,dz$, and $m_3=\int |z|^3|\nabla W(z)|\,dz$. The norm functions and moment integrands are continuous with compact support. They are bounded and Riemann integrable on a bounding Jordan box by [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]], so these constants are finite.

For continuous $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, define the full-space smoother and its kernel-gradient operator by
$$S_\varepsilon f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x-z)W_\varepsilon(z)\,dz,\qquad D_\varepsilon f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(y)\nabla W_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy.$$
For each fixed $x$, both scalar integrands and every component of the vector integrand are continuous and compactly supported, hence Riemann integrable on a bounding Jordan box by [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. Thus the displayed integrals exist as compactly supported Riemann integrals; the vector integral defining $D_\varepsilon f$ is taken componentwise.

This page fixes $\varepsilon$ in the finite-particle system. Limits $\varepsilon\to0$ are used only in the stated kernel-bias and joint-refinement results.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open. Write $B(x,r)$ for the open Euclidean ball from [[def-metric-ball]] with distance induced by [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A family of cells is **locally finite** here when every compact subset of $\Omega$ meets only finitely many cells. A bounded set is **Jordan measurable** when its Jordan inner and outer contents agree ([[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]]). A **cell particle rule** is a nonempty locally finite family of bounded Jordan-measurable cells $C_j\subseteq\Omega$ whose interiors are disjoint and whose union covers $\Omega$ up to their shared boundaries, together with nodes $x_j\in C_j$ and positive volumes $V_j=\int 1_{C_j}$. The cell volume integral is Riemann-defined and equals the Jordan content ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]). Its fill radius is $h=\sup_j\sup_{y\in C_j}|y-x_j|$, using the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; require $0<h<\infty$. Assume finite constants $C_V,C_L>0$ satisfy $V_j\le C_Vh^d$ and the local volume bound

$$\sum_{j:C_j\cap B(x,r)\ne\varnothing}V_j\le C_L(r+h)^d$$

for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and $r>0$. For continuous $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with compact support contained in $\Omega$ (support as in [[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]), define $Q_hg=\sum_jV_jg(x_j)$; local finiteness makes this sum finite. For specified parameters $R>0$ and $\varepsilon>0$, an evaluation point $x\in\mathbb R^d$ is **interior** relative to $(R,\varepsilon)$ when $B(x,R\varepsilon+2h)\subset\Omega$; in a kernel application, $R$ is the chosen support-radius bound for the unscaled kernel. For periodic calculations, use the periodic extensions of the field and particle rule on $\mathbb R^d$, so no kernel support is truncated.

The cell rule is integration-compatible: for every continuous $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with compact support contained in $\Omega$, only finitely many cells meet $\operatorname{supp}(g)$, every cell integral appearing below is Riemann-defined, and
$$\int_\Omega g(y)\,dy=\sum_{j:C_j\cap\operatorname{supp}(g)\ne\varnothing}\int_{C_j}g(y)\,dy.$$
This finite partition identity is part of the quadrature data.

For the scaled kernels of [[def-scaled-symmetric-compact-kernel-family]] and every ε>0, supp W_ε⊂\overline B(0,Rε), ∫W_ε=1, ∫zW_ε(z)dz=0, and ∫|z|²W_ε(z)dz=ε²m₂. Pointwise, ∇W_ε(z)=ε^(−d−1)∇W(z/ε) and D²W_ε(z)=ε^(−d−2)D²W(z/ε); consequently their sup norms equal ε^(−d−1)M₁ and ε^(−d−2)M₂.

Let g be compactly supported and Lipschitz with constant L_g, meaning |g(y)−g(x)|≤L_g|y−x|, with supp(g)⊂Ω, and use the cells and nodes of [[def-meshfree-cell-quadrature-and-fill-radius]]. Define osc_C(g)=sup_{y,z∈C}|g(y)−g(z)| and let J_g={j:C_j∩supp(g)≠∅}. Then

$$\left|\int_\Omega g(y)dy-Q_hg\right|\le\sum_{j\in J_g}V_j\operatorname{osc}_{C_j}(g)\le 2hL_g\sum_{j\in J_g}V_j.$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$,
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]). Let
$M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $M \ge 0$ satisfy

$$\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } t \in (a,b).$$

Then

$$\lVert f(b) - f(a)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,(b-a).$$

**No integrability of $f'$ is assumed**, so the theorem applies to every
differentiable $f$; that is why it is proved from the scalar mean value theorem
rather than from
[[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]].
[[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]] records the comparison between the
two routes.

**The equality form is not asserted, and for $m \ge 2$ it is false.** There need
be **no** $\xi \in (a,b)$ with $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)(b-a)$; the companion page
carries a differentiable witness on $[0,1]$. The $\xi$ produced in the proof
below depends on the fixed vector $u = f(b)-f(a)$ and is a mean value point of
the **real** function $t \mapsto \langle u, f(t)\rangle$, not of $f$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

derivations.claim: Put g₀(y)=f(y)W_ε(x−y). On any segment y(t)=y₀+t(y₁−y₀), [F6] gives the chain and product rules, and Cauchy-Schwarz [F7] gives |(g₀∘y)'(t)|≤(ε^(−d)M₀||∇f||∞+ε^(−d−1)M₁||f||∞)|y₁−y₀| by [F3]. Applying [F5] on that segment gives the same Lipschitz constant for g₀. Its support is contained in the closed ball \overline B(x,Rε), hence in B(x,(R+1)ε). By [F2], the total volume of cells meeting that support is at most C_L((R+1)ε+h)^d≤C_L(R+2)^dε^d. Apply [F4] and cancel ε^d; the factor 2 is absorbed into C. This gives the first inequality.

Put g₁(y)=f(y)∇W_ε(x−y). On any segment y(t)=y₀+t(y₁−y₀), [F6] gives componentwise chain and product rules, and Cauchy-Schwarz [F7] gives ||(g₁∘y)'(t)||₂≤(ε^(−d−1)M₁||∇f||∞+ε^(−d−2)M₂||f||∞)|y₁−y₀| by [F3]. Applying the vector mean value inequality [F5] bounds its Lipschitz constant by this expression. Its support is contained in the same closed ball, so [F2] gives the active-volume bound from step 1.1. Apply [F4] to each vector component; taking the Euclidean norm costs at most a factor √d, and [F4] contributes a factor 2; both are absorbed into C. Cancelling ε^d proves the second inequality.

Let f∈C²(R^d) have bounded Hessian and define S_εf(x)=∫f(x−z)W_ε(z)dz. Then for every ε>0 and x∈R^d,

$$|S_\varepsilon f(x)-f(x)|\le \frac{m_2}{2}\varepsilon^2\|D^2f\|_\infty.$$

Let f∈C³(R^d) have bounded third derivative and define D_εf(x)=∫f(y)∇W_ε(x−y)dy. Then for every ε>0 and x∈R^d,

$$|D_\varepsilon f(x)-\nabla f(x)|\le \frac{m_3}{6}\varepsilon^2\|D^3f\|_\infty,$$

where ||D³f||∞ is the supremum of the operator norm of the trilinear derivative.

Assume the cell rule of [[def-meshfree-cell-quadrature-and-fill-radius]], h≤ε≤1, x is interior, and f∈C¹(R^d) is bounded with bounded first derivative. Define

Fix d,N≥1, positive masses m_1,…,m_N, ε>0, the kernel W_ε from [[def-scaled-symmetric-compact-kernel-family]], and a pressure map P∈C¹((0,∞)×R,R). Positions q_i and velocities v_i lie in R^d with the Euclidean inner product from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and specific internal energies e_i lie in R. Define

$$\rho_i(q)=\sum_{j=1}^Nm_jW_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j),\qquad p_i=P(\rho_i,e_i),\qquad A_i=\frac{p_i}{\rho_i^2}.$$

The state domain is U={ (q,v,e): ρ_i(q)>0 for every i }. On U, the fixed-width semidiscrete system is

$$\dot q_i=v_i,\qquad \dot v_i=-\sum_{j=1}^Nm_j(A_i+A_j)\nabla W_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j),\qquad \dot e_i=A_i\sum_{j=1}^Nm_j(v_i-v_j)\cdot\nabla W_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j).$$

A controlled tube is a compact subset of U on which ρ_i≥ρ_*>0 for every i. The system is semidiscrete: time remains continuous while the spatial state is represented by finitely many particles. It has fixed masses and fixed ε, includes the displayed matched internal-energy equation, and contains no artificial viscosity. No continuum Euler convergence is part of this definition.

Let K be a nonempty compact convex subset of the positive-density domain of [[def-regularized-conservative-sph-system]]. Use ||z||#=max_i{|q_i|,|v_i|,|e_i|}, M=Σ_im_i, V=sup_{z∈K}max_i|v_i|, K₁=||∇W_ε||∞, K₂=||D²W_ε||∞, and a(ρ,e)=P(ρ,e)/ρ². Define A₀=max_{z∈K,1≤i≤N}|a(ρ_i(q),e_i)|, A_ρ=max_{z∈K,1≤i≤N}|∂_ρa(ρ_i(q),e_i)|, A_e=max_{z∈K,1≤i≤N}|∂_ea(ρ_i(q),e_i)|, and A_Lip=2MK₁A_ρ+A_e. By [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], these maxima are finite and attained, since K is nonempty compact and the functions involved are continuous. Then the full state vector field F is Lipschitz on K with constant

$$L=\max\{1,\ M(2K_1A_{\mathrm{Lip}}+4A_0K_2),\ 2MVA_{\mathrm{Lip}}K_1+2MA_0K_1+4MA_0VK_2\}.$$

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Fix z₀∈U. Since U is open, choose a nonempty nondegenerate closed box K about z₀ small enough to lie in U. It is convex and compact by [F4]. Each ρ_i is continuous and positive on K, so [F4] gives a positive minimum for each; taking the minimum over finitely many i gives a positive lower density bound on K. [F2] makes F Lipschitz there. Regard F as time-independent on R×U and apply [F3] to obtain a unique local C¹ solution. No choice principle is used.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let K be a nonempty compact convex subset of the positive-density domain of [[def-regularized-conservative-sph-system]]. Use ||z||#=max_i{|q_i|,|v_i|,|e_i|}, M=Σ_im_i, V=sup_{z∈K}max_i|v_i|, K₁=||∇W_ε||∞, K₂=||D²W_ε||∞, and a(ρ,e)=P(ρ,e)/ρ². Define A₀=max_{z∈K,1≤i≤N}|a(ρ_i(q),e_i)|, A_ρ=max_{z∈K,1≤i≤N}|∂_ρa(ρ_i(q),e_i)|, A_e=max_{z∈K,1≤i≤N}|∂_ea(ρ_i(q),e_i)|, and A_Lip=2MK₁A_ρ+A_e. By [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], these maxima are finite and attained, since K is nonempty compact and the functions involved are continuous. Then the full state vector field F is Lipschitz on K with constant

$$L=\max\{1,\ M(2K_1A_{\mathrm{Lip}}+4A_0K_2),\ 2MVA_{\mathrm{Lip}}K_1+2MA_0K_1+4MA_0VK_2\}.$$

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Since z(t)∈K and ||F(w)||#≤B for every w∈K, ||ż(t)||#≤B; applying [F7] to the Volterra formula gives ||z(t+s)−z(t)||#≤Bs. Then [F3] bounds the defect integrand by LBs. A second application of [F7] and integration of LBs give the local defect norm bound LBh²/2.

Suppose Z_k∈K. By convexity of K the segment from Z_k to z(kh) lies in K, so [F3] gives ||Z_k+hF(Z_k)−(z(kh)+hF(z(kh)))||#≤(1+hL)||Z_k−z(kh)||#. The triangle and homogeneity properties in [F6], together with the defect from step 1.1, yield e_{k+1}≤(1+hL)e_k+LBh²/2, where e_k=||Z_k−z(kh)||#.
