Let $X:=C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ be the real continuous functions on $[0,1]$
([[def-continuous-real-functions-on-a-compact-metric-space]]) with the supremum
norm $\|u\|_\infty:=\sup_{0\le x\le1}|u(x)|$. The interval $[0,1]$ is a
nonempty compact metric space by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]. Pointwise addition and real scalar multiplication preserve continuity. The supremum is finite by [[thm-c-k-complete-in-the-sup-metric]]; the pointwise absolute-value inequalities give $\|u+v\|_\infty\le\|u\|_\infty+\|v\|_\infty$ and $\|cu\|_\infty=|c|\|u\|_\infty$, and $\|u\|_\infty=0$ holds exactly when $u=0$. Thus this is a real norm ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). Its induced metric is the complete supremum metric of [[thm-c-k-complete-in-the-sup-metric]], so $X$ is Banach ([[def-banach-space]]). Fix a continuous real kernel
$k:[0,1]^2\to\mathbb R$. The integral $\int_0^1$ below is the ordinary Riemann
integral, equivalently the Riemann–Stieltjes integral with integrator $y\mapsto y$
([[def-riemann-stieltjes-sum-and-integral]]). For $u\in X$, define
$$(Ku)(x):=\int_0^1 k(x,y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad 0\le x\le1.$$
The integrand is continuous in $y$, so this integral exists by
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]].

A finite quadrature rule on $[0,1]$ consists of an integer $m\ge1$, nodes
$y_1,\ldots,y_m\in[0,1]$, and real weights $w_1,\ldots,w_m$. It acts on a
function $g$ defined at the nodes by
$$Q(g):=\sum_{j=1}^m w_jg(y_j).$$
Its Nyström operator is the finite-sum rule
$$(K_Q u)(x):=Q\bigl(k(x,\cdot)u(\cdot)\bigr)        =\sum_{j=1}^m w_jk(x,y_j)u(y_j).$$
In particular, for the composite midpoint rule with $N\ge1$ panels,
$h:=1/N$, $y_j:=(j+\tfrac12)h$ for $0\le j<N$, and $w_j=h$, the operator
is denoted $K_N$. The nodes and weights are those of
[[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]].

For a right-hand side $f\in X$, the Nyström equation is
$$u_Q-K_Qu_Q=f.$$
This definition asserts neither consistency nor convergence of $K_Q$ to $K$.

Let $X:=C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ ([[def-continuous-real-functions-on-a-compact-metric-space]]),
let $m\ge1$, let $y_1,\ldots,y_m\in[0,1]$, and let
$\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_m\in X$. Define the finite-rank linear map
$$ (Fu)(x):=\sum_{j=1}^m\psi_j(x)u(y_j) $$
and, for $f\in X$, define the square matrix and vector
$$ M_{ij}:=\delta_{ij}-\psi_j(y_i),\qquad b_i:=f(y_i),\qquad 1\le i,j\le m. $$
Then the solutions of $(I-F)u=f$ are in bijection with the solutions $c\in\mathbb R^m$
of $Mc=b$, via
$$u(x)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m\psi_j(x)c_j,\qquad c_i=u(y_i).$$
The nullspaces of $I-F$ and $M$ are linearly isomorphic by
$c\mapsto\sum_j\psi_jc_j$. In particular, $I-F$ is bijective if and only if
$M$ is nonsingular.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $X:=C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ with
$\|u\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|u(x)|$
([[def-continuous-real-functions-on-a-compact-metric-space]],
[[thm-c-k-complete-in-the-sup-metric]]) and let
$k:[0,1]^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The map
$$ (Ku)(x):=\int_0^1 k(x,y)u(y)\,dy $$
uses the ordinary Riemann integral of [[def-riemann-stieltjes-sum-and-integral]] and defines a bounded linear operator $K:X\to X$, and it is compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]).

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

Assume AC. Let $k:[0,1]^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and let $K$ be its integral
operator from [[def-nystrom-quadrature-and-finite-rank-operators]]. For each
$N\ge1$, let $K_N$ use the composite midpoint rule with $h=1/N$. Then each
$K_N$ is a bounded linear map $X\to X$, $K$ is compact, the family $(K_N)_{N\ge1}$
is collectively compact (the union of the
images of the unit ball has compact closure in $X$), and
$$\|K_Nu-Ku\|_\infty\longrightarrow0\qquad\text{for every }u\in X.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X\ne\{0\}$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), let $K:X\to X$
be compact, and let $(K_n)_{n\ge1}$ be bounded linear operators such that
$$\overline{\bigcup_{n\ge1}K_n(B_X)}$$
is compact for the closed unit ball $B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le1\}$ and
$K_nx\to Kx$ in norm for every $x\in X$. Suppose $I-K$ is injective. Then
there are $n_0\ge1$ and $C<\infty$ such that $I-K_n$ is boundedly invertible
for every $n\ge n_0$ and
$$\sup_{n\ge n_0}\|(I-K_n)^{-1}\|\le C.$$
For any $f,f_n\in X$, if $u$ and $u_n$ solve $(I-K)u=f$ and
$(I-K_n)u_n=f_n$, then for $n\ge n_0$,
$$\|u_n-u\|\le C\bigl(\|(K_n-K)u\|+\|f_n-f\|\bigr).$$
The theorem does not assert that $\|K_n-K\|\to0$.

Let $a<b$, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and put $h=(b-a)/n$. If
$f\in C^2([a,b])$, define $M_2=\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f''(x)|$. The composite
midpoint value $Q_M(f;a,b,n)$ of [[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]] satisfies

$$\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q_M(f;a,b,n)\right|\le\frac{(b-a)h^2}{24}M_2.$$

The integral is the Riemann integral. This is an exact-arithmetic quadrature
bound; evaluation and summation roundoff are not included.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space. Every member of
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is bounded, so the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(f,g):=\sup_{x\in K}|f(x)-g(x)|$$

is defined on $C(K,\mathbb{R})$. With this metric,
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is complete.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space
([[def-metric-compactness]]). Define

$$C(K,\mathbb{R}):=\{\,f\in\mathbb{R}^{K}:f:(K,d)\to(\mathbb{R},d_{\mathbb{R}})\text{ is continuous}\,\},$$

where $\mathbb{R}^{K}$ is the function space of [[def-function-space]] and
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t)=|s-t|$ is the usual metric
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

This definition introduces the set of continuous functions only. Boundedness
and the supremum metric are assertions to be proved, not clauses of the
definition.

derivations.claim: By [F7] and [F8], the space $X$ satisfies the Banach and nonzero hypotheses of [F5]. By [F3], $K$ is compact; [F4] gives bounded linear $K_N$ with the required collective compactness and pointwise convergence; the Statement assumes $I-K$ injective. Thus [F5] supplies $N_0$ and a common bound $C$ for $(I-K_N)^{-1}$ for all $N\ge N_0$.
For each fixed $x$, apply [F6] to the $C^2$ function $g_x(y)=k(x,y)u(y)$. The common derivative bound gives $|K_Nu(x)-Ku(x)|\le h^2M_2/24$ for every $x$, hence $\|K_Nu-Ku\|_\infty\le h^2M_2/24$.

The function-equation inverse from step 1.1 and [F2] make the finite matrix nonsingular and define its unique reconstruction $u_N$. Subtracting the exact and discrete equations gives $(I-K_N)(u_N-u)=f_N-f+(K_N-K)u.$ Applying the inverse bound $C$ from step 1.1, then the triangle inequality and step 1.2, proves the stated estimate.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

Let $X:=C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ and let $a:[0,1]^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous.
Use $S_x$ from [[lem-half-order-singular-integral-exists]] to define
$$(Ku)(x):=S_x\bigl(y\mapsto a(x,y)u(y)\bigr).$$
For an integer $n\ge1$, set $h:=1/n$ and $y_j:=jh$ for $j=0,\ldots,n$.
Define the nonnegative piecewise-linear hat functions by
$$\phi_{n,0}(y):=\max(1-y/h,0),\qquad   \phi_{n,n}(y):=\max(1-(1-y)/h,0),$$
and, for $1\le j<n$,
$$\phi_{n,j}(y):=\max(1-|y-y_j|/h,0).$$
Their piecewise-linear interpolant is
$$I_ng:=\sum_{j=0}^n g(y_j)\phi_{n,j}.$$
The product weights and product-integration operator are
$$w_{n,j}(x):=S_x(\phi_{n,j}),\qquad   (K_nu)(x):=\sum_{j=0}^n w_{n,j}(x)a(x,y_j)u(y_j)   =S_x\bigl(I_n(y\mapsto a(x,y)u(y))\bigr).$$
The kernel factor $s(x,y)=|x-y|^{-1/2}$ is integrated in the weights; the smooth
factor $a(x,y)u(y)$ is interpolated. This item defines the pointwise formulas;
the subsequent results on this page establish their mapping properties,
stability, and error estimates.

For $x\in[0,1]$, $g\in C([0,1],\mathbb R)$, and $0<\varepsilon<1$, let
$$S_{x,\varepsilon}(g):=\int_{[0,1]\setminus(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)}|x-y|^{-1/2}g(y)\,dy,$$
where the integral is the sum of the ordinary Riemann integrals on the at most
two remaining closed intervals, and an empty interval contributes zero. The
limit
$$S_x(g):=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}S_{x,\varepsilon}(g)$$
exists. The map $S_x:C([0,1],\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R$ is linear and positive, and its
operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]) is
$$\|S_x\|=S_x(1)=2\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{1-x}\le2\sqrt2.$$

Put $s(t):=|t|^{-1/2}$ for $t\in[-1,1]\setminus\{0\}$. For $x,x'\in[0,1]$,
define
$$T(x,x'):=\int_0^1|s(x-y)-s(x'-y)|\,dy$$
as an improper Riemann integral split at the distinct points among $x$ and
$x'$; an endpoint value at a singular point is omitted. If $x=x'$, set
$T(x,x)=0$. These improper integrals exist and are finite. The modulus
$$\tau(d):=\sup\{T(x,x'):x,x'\in[0,1],\ |x-x'|\le d\}$$
is finite and satisfies $\tau(d)\to0$ as $d\downarrow0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom of Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]).** Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and $\mathcal F\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$. Its closure in the supremum metric is compact if and only if $\mathcal F$ is equicontinuous and pointwise bounded.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

Let $a<b$ and let $f$ be $C^2$ on an open interval containing $[a,b]$. Put
$M:=\sup_{t\in[a,b]}|f''(t)|$, which is finite, and let $L$ be the unique affine
function with $L(a)=f(a)$ and $L(b)=f(b)$. Then for every $x\in[a,b]$,
$$|f(x)-L(x)|\le \frac{M}{2}(x-a)(b-x).$$

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space. Every member of
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is bounded, so the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(f,g):=\sup_{x\in K}|f(x)-g(x)|$$

is defined on $C(K,\mathbb{R})$. With this metric,
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is complete.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of

   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of

   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space. Every member of
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is bounded, so the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(f,g):=\sup_{x\in K}|f(x)-g(x)|$$

is defined on $C(K,\mathbb{R})$. With this metric,
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is complete.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order ([[def-nat-order]]); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
([[lem-nat-add-commutative]]) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$. The metric used here is $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, supplied over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]].

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

derivations.claim: By [F8], the square is compact, so [F7] makes $A=\|a\|_\infty$ finite. In the Banach normed space [F9], the hat functions in [F1] are nonnegative and on each panel the two adjacent hats add to $1$, while all other hats vanish. Hence $\sum_{j=0}^n\phi_{n,j}=1$ pointwise. Positivity and linearity in [F2] give $w_{n,j}(x)\ge0$ and $\sum_j|w_{n,j}(x)|=\sum_jw_{n,j}(x)=S_x(1)=2\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{1-x}\le2\sqrt2.$ For every $u\in X$, the same bound shows $\|K_nu\|_\infty\le2\sqrt2 A\|u\|_\infty$.
For $d:=|x-x'|$, [F3] gives an upper bound $\tau(d)$ for the improper kernel translation integral, with $\tau(d)\to0$ as $d\downarrow0$.

For fixed $u$, [F4] makes $(x,y)\mapsto g_x(y)$ uniformly continuous. By step 1.1 the hats are nonnegative and sum to $1$, so on a panel $[y_j,y_{j+1}]$, $I_ng_x(y)$ is a convex combination of the two endpoint values. Hence $\|I_ng_x-g_x\|_\infty\to0$ uniformly in $x$, and the operator bound in [F2] yields $\|K_nu-Ku\|_\infty\le2\sqrt2\|I_ng_x-g_x\|_\infty\to0$.

Write $g_x(y)=a(x,y)u(y)$. The identities in [F1], the translation bound in [F3], and the operator bound in [F2] show $|Ku(x)-Ku(x')|\le A\|u\|_\infty\tau(d)+2\sqrt2\|u\|_\infty\omega_a(d),$ where $\tau(d)$ is the translation bound from step 1.2 and $\omega_a(d):=\sup_{|x-x'|\le d,y}|a(x,y)-a(x',y)|\to0$ by [F4] on the compact square from [F8]. Replacing $g_x$ by $I_ng_x$ gives the same bound for $K_nu$: by step 1.1 the interpolant is a convex combination of nodal values, so $\|I_ng_x\|_\infty\le\|g_x\|_\infty$ and $\|I_n(g_x-g_{x'})\|_\infty\le\|g_x-g_{x'}\|_\infty$. Thus $K$ and all $K_n$ map into $X$ and have a common equicontinuity modulus. The formula [F1] and linearity of $S_x$ in [F2] make $K$ linear; its operator bound follows from [F2]. Each $K_n$ is linear by [F11], and step 1.1 bounds it. By [F9] and [F10], both are bounded linear maps. Their images of the unit ball are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. By [F5] and [A1], $K$ is compact by [F12], and $(K_n)$ is collectively compact.

For each fixed $n,j$, take $a\equiv1$ and $u=\phi_{n,j}$ in the preceding continuity argument; then $K_nu(x)=w_{n,j}(x)$, so each weight function is continuous. Consequently the coefficient functions $x\mapsto w_{n,j}(x)a(x,y_j)$ in the finite-node representation are continuous.
Under the $C^2$ extension hypothesis, [F6] bounds $\|I_ng_x-g_x\|_\infty\le M_2h^2/8$ uniformly in $x$. Applying [F2] gives $\|K_nu-Ku\|_\infty\le2\sqrt2 M_2h^2/8=\sqrt2 M_2h^2/4$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

Let $X:=C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ and let $a:[0,1]^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous.
Use $S_x$ from [[lem-half-order-singular-integral-exists]] to define
$$(Ku)(x):=S_x\bigl(y\mapsto a(x,y)u(y)\bigr).$$
For an integer $n\ge1$, set $h:=1/n$ and $y_j:=jh$ for $j=0,\ldots,n$.
Define the nonnegative piecewise-linear hat functions by
$$\phi_{n,0}(y):=\max(1-y/h,0),\qquad   \phi_{n,n}(y):=\max(1-(1-y)/h,0),$$
and, for $1\le j<n$,
$$\phi_{n,j}(y):=\max(1-|y-y_j|/h,0).$$
Their piecewise-linear interpolant is
$$I_ng:=\sum_{j=0}^n g(y_j)\phi_{n,j}.$$
The product weights and product-integration operator are
$$w_{n,j}(x):=S_x(\phi_{n,j}),\qquad   (K_nu)(x):=\sum_{j=0}^n w_{n,j}(x)a(x,y_j)u(y_j)   =S_x\bigl(I_n(y\mapsto a(x,y)u(y))\bigr).$$
The kernel factor $s(x,y)=|x-y|^{-1/2}$ is integrated in the weights; the smooth
factor $a(x,y)u(y)$ is interpolated. This item defines the pointwise formulas;
the subsequent results on this page establish their mapping properties,
stability, and error estimates.

Assume AC and let $a:[0,1]^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. For $K$ and $K_n$
from [[def-half-order-product-integration]], put $A:=\|a\|_\infty$ and
$h:=1/n$. Then both operators are bounded linear maps from $X=C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ to itself, $K$ is
compact, and $(K_n)$ is collectively compact and converges pointwise in norm to
$K$. Their product weights satisfy
$$w_{n,j}(x)\ge0,\qquad \sum_{j=0}^n|w_{n,j}(x)|  =2\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{1-x}\le2\sqrt2$$
for every $x\in[0,1]$. If each $g_x(y):=a(x,y)u(y)$ extends to a $C^2$
function on a neighborhood of $[0,1]$ and
$M_2:=\sup_{x,y}|\partial_y^2g_x(y)|<\infty$, then
$$\|K_nu-Ku\|_\infty\le\frac{\sqrt2}{4}M_2h^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X\ne\{0\}$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), let $K:X\to X$
be compact, and let $(K_n)_{n\ge1}$ be bounded linear operators such that
$$\overline{\bigcup_{n\ge1}K_n(B_X)}$$
is compact for the closed unit ball $B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le1\}$ and
$K_nx\to Kx$ in norm for every $x\in X$. Suppose $I-K$ is injective. Then
there are $n_0\ge1$ and $C<\infty$ such that $I-K_n$ is boundedly invertible
for every $n\ge n_0$ and
$$\sup_{n\ge n_0}\|(I-K_n)^{-1}\|\le C.$$
For any $f,f_n\in X$, if $u$ and $u_n$ solve $(I-K)u=f$ and
$(I-K_n)u_n=f_n$, then for $n\ge n_0$,
$$\|u_n-u\|\le C\bigl(\|(K_n-K)u\|+\|f_n-f\|\bigr).$$
The theorem does not assert that $\|K_n-K\|\to0$.

Let $X:=C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ ([[def-continuous-real-functions-on-a-compact-metric-space]]),
let $m\ge1$, let $y_1,\ldots,y_m\in[0,1]$, and let
$\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_m\in X$. Define the finite-rank linear map
$$ (Fu)(x):=\sum_{j=1}^m\psi_j(x)u(y_j) $$
and, for $f\in X$, define the square matrix and vector
$$ M_{ij}:=\delta_{ij}-\psi_j(y_i),\qquad b_i:=f(y_i),\qquad 1\le i,j\le m. $$
Then the solutions of $(I-F)u=f$ are in bijection with the solutions $c\in\mathbb R^m$
of $Mc=b$, via
$$u(x)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m\psi_j(x)c_j,\qquad c_i=u(y_i).$$
The nullspaces of $I-F$ and $M$ are linearly isomorphic by
$c\mapsto\sum_j\psi_jc_j$. In particular, $I-F$ is bijective if and only if
$M$ is nonsingular.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space. Every member of
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is bounded, so the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(f,g):=\sup_{x\in K}|f(x)-g(x)|$$

is defined on $C(K,\mathbb{R})$. With this metric,
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is complete.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space
([[def-metric-compactness]]). Define

$$C(K,\mathbb{R}):=\{\,f\in\mathbb{R}^{K}:f:(K,d)\to(\mathbb{R},d_{\mathbb{R}})\text{ is continuous}\,\},$$

where $\mathbb{R}^{K}$ is the function space of [[def-function-space]] and
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t)=|s-t|$ is the usual metric
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

This definition introduces the set of continuous functions only. Boundedness
and the supremum metric are assertions to be proved, not clauses of the
definition.

derivations.claim: By [F5], $X$ is a nonzero Banach space. By [F2], $K$ is compact and $(K_n)$ consists of bounded linear maps that are collectively compact and pointwise norm convergent to $K$. With AC and the assumed injectivity of $I-K$, [F3] gives $n_0$ and $C$ such that $I-K_n$ is invertible and $\|(I-K_n)^{-1}\|\le C$ for all $n\ge n_0$.

The inverse in step 1.1 gives a unique solution to $(I-K_n)u_n=f_n$. By [F2] each coefficient function in [F1] is continuous, so [F4] applies: the finite grid matrix is nonsingular and its solution reconstructs exactly this $u_n$.

Subtracting $(I-K)u=f$ from $(I-K_n)u_n=f_n$ gives $(I-K_n)(u_n-u)=f_n-f+(K_n-K)u.$ Apply the inverse bound in [F3] and then the consistency bound in [F2]: $\|u_n-u\|_\infty\le C\bigl(\|f_n-f\|_\infty+\|K_nu-Ku\|_\infty\bigr) \le C\left(\|f_n-f\|_\infty+\frac{\sqrt2}{4}M_2h^2\right).$ This is the claimed error estimate.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$r\in\{2m-1,2m\}$. A **Gaussian quadrature moment datum of order $r$** is a
finite positive measure $\mu$ on the relative Borel sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B([a,b])$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure-space]],
[[def-measure]], [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) such that
$\mu([a,b])>0$, and whose **relative support**
$$ S_\mu:=\{x\in[a,b]:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open }U\subseteq[a,b]\text{ with }x\in U\} $$
contains at least $m+1$ distinct points. For every integer $0\le k\le r$,
require $x\mapsto |x|^k$ to be integrable with respect to $\mu$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]) and put
$M_k:=\int_{[a,b]}x^k\,d\mu(x)$. Powers use the natural-exponent
recursion of [[def-integer-power]], with $x^0=1$ for every real $x$, including
$x=0$; thus $M_0$ is the integral of the constant function $1$.

The branch $r=2m-1$ supplies all moments used to construct the monic
degree-$m$ orthogonal polynomial and prove rule exactness. The stronger branch
$r=2m$ also defines its squared norm and is used for the remainder formula.
Because $[a,b]$ is bounded and $\mu$ is finite, these absolute-moment
integrability conditions follow from finiteness; they are stated to make the
two moment interfaces explicit.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_m$ be its monic degree-$m$ orthogonal
polynomial and write its ordered roots as
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, as established in
[[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. For
$i=1,\ldots,m$, define the Lagrange cardinal polynomial
$$ \ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j} $$
using the convention of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
the **Gaussian quadrature weights** and the **m-node Gaussian rule** by
$$ w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i) $$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], and let $Q_m$ and $w_i$ be the rule and weights of
[[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. For every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most
$2m-1$,
$$ \int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i). $$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.

Its Nyström operator is the finite-sum rule
$$(K_Q u)(x):=Q\bigl(k(x,\cdot)u(\cdot)\bigr)        =\sum_{j=1}^m w_jk(x,y_j)u(y_j).$$

Let $X:=C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ ([[def-continuous-real-functions-on-a-compact-metric-space]]),
let $m\ge1$, let $y_1,\ldots,y_m\in[0,1]$, and let
$\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_m\in X$. Define the finite-rank linear map
$$ (Fu)(x):=\sum_{j=1}^m\psi_j(x)u(y_j) $$
and, for $f\in X$, define the square matrix and vector
$$ M_{ij}:=\delta_{ij}-\psi_j(y_i),\qquad b_i:=f(y_i),\qquad 1\le i,j\le m. $$
Then the solutions of $(I-F)u=f$ are in bijection with the solutions $c\in\mathbb R^m$
of $Mc=b$, via
$$u(x)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m\psi_j(x)c_j,\qquad c_i=u(y_i).$$

derivations.claim: Since $Ku(x)=\alpha m_0+\beta x m_1$, any solution is affine and has the form $u(x)=1+\alpha m_0+\beta x m_1$. Integrating this identity against $1$ and against $y$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}1-\alpha&-\beta/2\\-\alpha/2&1-\beta/3\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}m_0\\m_1\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}1\\1/2\end{pmatrix}.$ At the specified parameters the determinant is $(3/4)(5/6)-(1/4)(1/8)=19/32\ne0$, and solving gives $m_0=92/57$, $m_1=16/19$, hence $u(x)=(80+24x)/57$.

The function $u$ is affine and $yu(y)$ is quadratic, so [F3] gives $Q_2(u)=m_0$ and $Q_2(yu)=m_1$. Substituting these two exact quadrature moments into the Nyström formula [F4] yields $1+\alpha m_0+\beta x m_1=u(x)$ for every $x$; thus the continuous solution is also a Nyström solution.

Any solution $v$ of the inhomogeneous two-node Nyström equation has the form $v(x)=1+\alpha Q_2(v)+\beta xQ_2(yv)$, hence is affine. Exactness [F3] then makes its two moments satisfy the same nonsingular system in step 1.1, so those moments and the reconstructed function are unique; step 2.1 supplies existence. A nonzero vector in the grid-matrix kernel would, by the nullspace correspondence [F5], give a nonzero homogeneous solution, which could be added to this solution and contradict uniqueness. Thus the grid matrix is nonsingular, and its reconstruction is the displayed solution.

On each midpoint panel, direct integration gives $\int_{jh}^{(j+1)h}y\,dy=h(j+\tfrac12)h$ and $\int_{jh}^{(j+1)h}y^2\,dy-h((j+\tfrac12)h)^2=h^3/12.$ Summing the $N$ panels yields $Q_N(y)=1/2$ and $Q_N(y^2)=1/3-h^2/12$.

Any discrete solution has the form $u_N(x)=1+c_Nx$ because the range of $K_N$ is contained in the span of $x$. Its coefficient satisfies $c_N=\lambda(1/2+c_N(1/3-h^2/12))$, hence $c_N=\lambda/(2(\delta+\lambda h^2/12))$; the denominator is positive, so the discrete solution is unique.

On the direction $x$, $Kx=(\lambda/3)x$, so $I-K$ scales that direction by $\delta$. Also $K_Nx=\lambda(1/3-h^2/12)x$, so $I-K_N$ scales it by $\delta+\lambda h^2/12$. Directly using the exact and discrete coefficients from steps 1.1 and 2.1 gives $\|K_Nu-Ku\|_\infty=\frac{\lambda^2h^2}{24\delta},\qquad \|u_N-u\|_\infty=\frac{\lambda^2h^2}{24\delta(\delta+\lambda h^2/12)}.$ The ratio of solution error to quadrature residual is exactly $(\delta+\lambda h^2/12)^{-1}$, and the stated lower bound follows when $\lambda h^2/12\le\delta$.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$ and an integer resolution $N\ge2$, where
$N\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and put $h=1/N$. Real scalar and
array operations use the field $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-reals-field]]). Let
$J_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}^d$; each coordinate index addition below is reduced
to the unique element of $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ congruent modulo $N$. The unit
torus $\mathbb T^d$ means the unit cube with opposite faces identified, so
fields and arrays are periodic across those faces. Write
$\mathbf 1=(1,\ldots,1)$ and let $e_i$ be the $i$th standard coordinate vector.
Cell $j$ has centre $x_j=h(j+\tfrac12\mathbf 1)$. The pressure value $q_j$ is
stored at that centre. Velocity component $i$ is stored at the right face of
cell $j$, with centre $x_j+\tfrac h2e_i$.

Let $\widetilde Q_h$ be all real scalar cell arrays and let
$Q_h=\{q\in\widetilde Q_h:h^d\sum_jq_j=0\}$. Let $V_h$ be the real vector
face arrays $v=(v_{i,j})_{1\le i\le d,\,j\in J_N}$. Give them the mass inner products
$$ (q,r)_{Q_h}=h^d\sum_{j\in J_N}q_jr_j,\qquad (v,w)_{M_h}=h^d\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{j\in J_N}v_{i,j}w_{i,j}. $$
Define the pressure gradient $G_h:\widetilde Q_h\to V_h$ and velocity
divergence $D_h:V_h\to Q_h$ by
$$ (G_hq)_{i,j}=\frac{q_{j+e_i}-q_j}{h},\qquad (D_hv)_j=\sum_{i=1}^d\frac{v_{i,j}-v_{i,j-e_i}}{h}. $$
The compatible pressure Laplacian is $\Delta_h=D_hG_h$; its restriction to
$Q_h$ is negative semidefinite, and $G_h$ annihilates constants. Define the
componentwise vector Laplacian by
$$ (\Delta_h^Vv)_{i,j}=h^{-2}\sum_{\ell=1}^d (v_{i,j+e_\ell}-2v_{i,j}+v_{i,j-e_\ell}),\qquad A_h=-\Delta_h^V, $$
and the discrete velocity-gradient seminorm by
$$ \|\mathcal G_hv\|_{M_h}^2=h^{d-2}\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{\ell=1}^d\sum_{j\in J_N} |v_{i,j+e_\ell}-v_{i,j}|^2. $$
The fixed cell/face placement is part of the definition; collocated central
differences are a different discretization.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Reindexing the finite periodic sums gives, for every cell array $q$ and face array $v$, $$ (G_hq,v)_{M_h} =h^d\sum_{i,j}\frac{(q_{j+e_i}-q_j)v_{i,j}}h =-h^d\sum_jq_j\sum_i\frac{v_{i,j}-v_{i,j-e_i}}h =-h^d\sum_jq_j(D_hv)_j. $$ In particular, when $q\in Q_h$, this is $(G_hq,v)_{M_h}=-(q,D_hv)_{Q_h}$, the negative-adjoint identity in the stated mass pairings.

Let $q\in Q_h$. Since $q$ has mean zero, $$ q_x=N^{-d}\sum_{y\in J_N}(q_x-q_y), $$ and [F3]–[F4] give the finite-sum Cauchy--Schwarz inequality $$ \|q\|_{Q_h}^2\le N^{-2d}\sum_{x,y\in J_N}|q_x-q_y|^2. $$ For each ordered pair $(x,y)$ choose the path that changes coordinates in the order $1,\ldots,d$, moving forward modulo $N$ in each coordinate. It has at most $dN$ directed edges. Cauchy--Schwarz along the path bounds $|q_x-q_y|^2$ by $dN$ times the sum of squared edge differences on it.

For any cell array $q$, applying the explicit weighted-sum identity of step 1.1 with $v=G_hq$ gives $$ h^d\sum_jq_j(\Delta_hq)_j=-(G_hq,G_hq)_{M_h}\le0. $$ If $\Delta_hq=0$, then $G_hq=0$, so $q_{j+e_i}=q_j$ for every $i,j$. Coordinate steps connect all cells of the periodic grid, hence $q$ is constant. Every constant has zero gradient, so the kernel on all cell arrays is exactly the constants.

For every $v$, summing $D_hv$ over cells cancels each face value once with its opposite occurrence, so $D_hv$ has zero mean. The same is true of $\Delta_hq=D_h(G_hq)$. Therefore $\Delta_h$ restricts to a linear map $Q_h\to Q_h$. Its kernel there is zero by step 2.1, and its domain and codomain are the same finite-dimensional space.

Rank-nullity [F2] now gives $\dim\operatorname{im}\Delta_h=\dim Q_h$; since the image is a subspace of $Q_h$, the restriction is onto as well as one-to-one. Thus each mean-zero right-hand side has a unique mean-zero pressure solution.

Fix one directed edge in coordinate $i$. For each coordinate $r<i$, its value along the path is $y_r$; to use the fixed edge, $y_r$ is fixed and $x_r$ has at most $N$ choices. For each $r>i$, the path still has value $x_r$; then $x_r$ is fixed and $y_r$ has at most $N$ choices. In coordinate $i$ there are at most $N^2$ ordered start/end pairs. Hence this edge occurs in at most $N^{d+1}$ paths. Summing the path bounds and dividing by $N^{2d}$ yields $$ \|q\|_{Q_h}^2\le dN^{2-d}\sum_{i,j}|q_{j+e_i}-q_j|^2 =d\|G_hq\|_{M_h}^2. $$ Taking nonnegative square roots proves the stated inequality.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the closed interval between $c$ and $x$, and define
$P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(c)(t-c)^j/j!$. If $x\ne c$, there is a point
$\xi$ strictly between $c$ and $x$ such that
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}(x-c)^{n+1}.
$$
For $x=c$, the remainder is zero.

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

derivations.claim: For $g\in C^3(\mathbb T^d)$, Taylor's formula with Lagrange remainder at the midpoint and [F3] with $m=2$ give $$ g(x+h e_i/2)-g(x-h e_i/2)=h\,\partial_i g(x)+r, \qquad |r|\le h^3\|\partial_i^3g\|_\infty/24. $$ The same midpoint formula, with the two cell centres surrounding face $x_j+he_i/2$, gives $$ (G_hR_hp)_{i,j}=\partial_i p(x_j+he_i/2)+O(h^2), $$ with the pointwise error bounded by $h^2\|\partial_i^3p\|_\infty/24$.

For $g\in C^4(\mathbb T^d)$, [F3] with $m=3$ at $x$ gives $$ g(x+h e_i)-2g(x)+g(x-h e_i)=h^2\partial_i^2g(x)+r, $$ where the two fourth-order Lagrange remainders have total absolute value at most $h^4\|\partial_i^4g\|_\infty/12$. Apply this in every coordinate to $u_i$ at its face centre. It follows that $(A_hR_hu)_{i,j}=-(\Delta u_i)(x_j+he_i/2)+O(h^2)$, with the error bounded by $h^2\sum_\ell\|\partial_\ell^4u_i\|_\infty/12$.

Applying the midpoint formula to component $u_i$ at cell centre $x_j$ shows, by [F3] with $m=2$, $$ (D_hR_hu)_j=\sum_i\partial_i u_i(x_j)+r_j, \qquad |r_j|\le\frac{h^2}{24}\sum_i\|\partial_i^3u_i\|_\infty. $$ Thus the discrete divergence differs pointwise from the sampled continuous divergence by $O(h^2)$.

Each pointwise error bound in steps 1.1–1.2 is uniform. The weighted mass of the grid contains $h^dN^d=1$ total cell volume and there are $d$ velocity components. Therefore the corresponding mass norms are bounded by the same constants (or their finite $d$-component sum) times $h^2$. Combining the divergence, vector Laplacian and pressure gradient bounds proves the first claim. The scalar mass norm is defined on all cell arrays, so no zero-mean hypothesis on the residual is needed.

On each cell centred at $x_j$, fix $x$ and put $z=x-x_j$ and $\psi(t)=g(x_j+tz)$ for $0\le t\le1$. By [F3] with $m=1$ and [F4], $g(x)=g(x_j)+\nabla g(x_j)\cdot z+r_j(x)$ with $|r_j(x)|\le C_d\|D^2g\|_\infty|z|^2$. The linear term integrates to zero on the centred cell, so the difference between $h^dg(x_j)$ and $\int_{C_j}g$ is at most $C_dh^{d+2}\|D^2g\|_\infty$. Summing the $N^d$ cells yields $$ \left|h^d\sum_jg(x_j)-\int_{\mathbb T^d}g(x)\,dx\right| \le C_dh^2\|D^2g\|_\infty. $$ The face centres for any fixed component likewise centre a translated partition into cells of side $h$, so the same estimate holds for their samples. If the integral vanishes, this gives the stated discrete-mean bound.

citations.quote:
Let $n,m\ge1$, $V=M_{n\times1}(\mathbb R)$, and
$Q=M_{m\times1}(\mathbb R)$. Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric
positive definite, let $B\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb R)$ have full row rank
(meaning $B^Tq=0$ implies $q=0$), and let
$M_Q\in M_m(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric positive definite. The saddle system
and its matrix are
$$ K=\begin{pmatrix}A&B^T\\B&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Au+B^Tp=f,\quad Bu=g. $$
Define the positive pressure Schur matrix
$$ S:=BA^{-1}B^T. $$
In the block-LU convention of [[def-block-lu-factorisation]], the trailing
Schur complement of $A$ in $K$ is $-S$. The exact block solve first solves
$Au_0=f$, then $Sp=Bu_0-g$, and finally $Au=f-B^Tp$; the theorem
[[thm-na-saddle-point-exact-schur-solve]] verifies this procedure and
well-definedness.

For a scaling $\gamma>0$, the pressure-mass block-diagonal preconditioner is
$$ P_\gamma=\operatorname{diag}(A,\gamma M_Q). $$
It is symmetric positive definite. If $P_\gamma=CC^T$ is its Cholesky
factorization with $C$ lower triangular and positive on the diagonal, the
symmetric preconditioned system is $C^{-1}KC^{-T}y=C^{-1}r$, with the usual
change of unknown. This is the symmetric-preconditioning convention of
[[def-left-right-and-symmetric-positive-definite-preconditioning]]. No
spectral bound, Krylov iteration count, complexity estimate, or generic speed
improvement is part of this definition.

Let

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}A_{11}&A_{12}\\A_{21}&A_{22}\end{pmatrix}$$

be a square block matrix over a field, with $A_{11}$ square and invertible, and
let $S:=A_{22}-A_{21}A_{11}^{-1}A_{12}$.

1. One has the exact block factorisation
   $$A=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\A_{21}A_{11}^{-1}&I\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}A_{11}&A_{12}\\0&S\end{pmatrix}.$$
2. If $S=\widetilde L\widetilde U$ is any normalised LU factorisation, then
   $$A=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\A_{21}A_{11}^{-1}&\widetilde L\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}A_{11}&A_{12}\\0&\widetilde U\end{pmatrix}$$
   is a block LU factorisation across the same partition.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

derivations.claim: Positive definiteness of $A$ makes its kernel zero: if $Ax=0$, then $x^TAx=0$, so the positivity hypothesis forces $x=0$. Since $A$ is a square matrix on a finite-dimensional space, [F3] makes its image full-dimensional; thus $A$ is invertible. For nonzero $q\in\mathbb R^m$, full row rank gives $B^Tq\ne0$. Put $y=A^{-1}B^Tq$, which is nonzero. Then $$ q^TSq=(B^Tq)^TA^{-1}(B^Tq)=(Ay)^Ty=y^TAy>0. $$ Therefore $S$ is symmetric positive definite.

Apply [F2] to $K$ with leading block $A$, upper-right block $B^T$, lower-left block $B$, and lower-right block $0$. Its trailing Schur complement is $0-BA^{-1}B^T=-S$. Hence $$ K=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\BA^{-1}&I\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}A&B^T\\0&-S\end{pmatrix}, $$ and both diagonal blocks of the upper factor are invertible by the hypotheses and step 1.1.

Solve the lower-triangular factor against $(f,g)$ first. It gives the intermediate vector $(f,g-BA^{-1}f)$. The second block row of the upper solve is $-Sp=g-BA^{-1}f$, so $p=S^{-1}(BA^{-1}f-g)$. The first row gives $u=A^{-1}(f-B^Tp)$. Substitution verifies $Au+B^Tp=f$ and $Bu=BA^{-1}f-Sp=g$. Invertibility of the diagonal blocks in step 2.1 makes both triangular solves unique, so this is the unique solution.

Let $n,m\ge1$, $V=M_{n\times1}(\mathbb R)$, and
$Q=M_{m\times1}(\mathbb R)$. Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric
positive definite, let $B\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb R)$ have full row rank
(meaning $B^Tq=0$ implies $q=0$), and let
$M_Q\in M_m(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric positive definite. The saddle system
and its matrix are
$$ K=\begin{pmatrix}A&B^T\\B&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Au+B^Tp=f,\quad Bu=g. $$
Define the positive pressure Schur matrix
$$ S:=BA^{-1}B^T. $$
In the block-LU convention of [[def-block-lu-factorisation]], the trailing
Schur complement of $A$ in $K$ is $-S$. The exact block solve first solves
$Au_0=f$, then $Sp=Bu_0-g$, and finally $Au=f-B^Tp$; the theorem
[[thm-na-saddle-point-exact-schur-solve]] verifies this procedure and
well-definedness.

For a scaling $\gamma>0$, the pressure-mass block-diagonal preconditioner is
$$ P_\gamma=\operatorname{diag}(A,\gamma M_Q). $$
It is symmetric positive definite. If $P_\gamma=CC^T$ is its Cholesky
factorization with $C$ lower triangular and positive on the diagonal, the
symmetric preconditioned system is $C^{-1}KC^{-T}y=C^{-1}r$, with the usual
change of unknown. This is the symmetric-preconditioning convention of
[[def-left-right-and-symmetric-positive-definite-preconditioning]]. No
spectral bound, Krylov iteration count, complexity estimate, or generic speed
improvement is part of this definition.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Fix $q\in Q$ and put $w=A^{-1}B^Tq$. By [F1] and symmetry of $A$, $$ b(v,q)=q^TBv=v^TB^Tq=v^TAw=a(v,w) $$ for every $v\in V$. By [F3], $|a(v,w)|\le\|v\|_A\|w\|_A$. If $w\ne0$, equality is attained at $v=w$; if $w=0$, both sides are zero. Hence $$ \sup_{v\ne0}\frac{|b(v,q)|}{\sqrt{a(v,v)}} =\sqrt{a(w,w)}=\sqrt{q^TBA^{-1}B^Tq}. $$

The upper energy inequality in the statement implies $\sqrt{a(v,v)}\le\sqrt\Lambda\|v\|_V$, so the supremum in step 1.1 is at least $\beta\|q\|_Q/\sqrt\Lambda$. The lower energy inequality implies $\sqrt{a(v,v)}\ge\sqrt\alpha\|v\|_V$; continuity of $b$ therefore makes that supremum at most $C_b\|q\|_Q/\sqrt\alpha$. Squaring these inequalities and using step 1.1 proves both displayed Schur bounds.

For nonzero $q$, the lower bound in step 2.1 is positive because $\beta>0$ and $M_Q$ is positive definite. Thus $S$ is positive definite, and the two quadratic-form inequalities are the stated pressure-mass spectral equivalence.

$Q=M_{m\times1}(\mathbb R)$. Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric
positive definite, let $B\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb R)$ have full row rank
(meaning $B^Tq=0$ implies $q=0$), and let
$M_Q\in M_m(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric positive definite. The saddle system
and its matrix are
$$ K=\begin{pmatrix}A&B^T\\B&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Au+B^Tp=f,\quad Bu=g. $$
Define the positive pressure Schur matrix
$$ S:=BA^{-1}B^T. $$
In the block-LU convention of [[def-block-lu-factorisation]], the trailing
Schur complement of $A$ in $K$ is $-S$. The exact block solve first solves
$Au_0=f$, then $Sp=Bu_0-g$, and finally $Au=f-B^Tp$; the theorem
[[thm-na-saddle-point-exact-schur-solve]] verifies this procedure and
well-definedness.

For a scaling $\gamma>0$, the pressure-mass block-diagonal preconditioner is
$$ P_\gamma=\operatorname{diag}(A,\gamma M_Q). $$
It is symmetric positive definite. If $P_\gamma=CC^T$ is its Cholesky
factorization with $C$ lower triangular and positive on the diagonal, the
symmetric preconditioned system is $C^{-1}KC^{-T}y=C^{-1}r$, with the usual
change of unknown. This is the symmetric-preconditioning convention of
[[def-left-right-and-symmetric-positive-definite-preconditioning]]. No
spectral bound, Krylov iteration count, complexity estimate, or generic speed
improvement is part of this definition.

Let $V,Q$ be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces with norms
$\|\cdot\|_V,\|\cdot\|_Q$. Let $a(v,w)=v^TAw$ be symmetric positive
definite, and let $b(v,q)=q^TBv$ be a bilinear constraint form, represented
by the matrices in
[[def-na-symmetric-saddle-point-system-and-block-preconditioners]]. Suppose
that, for constants $\alpha,\Lambda,C_b,\beta>0$,
$$ \alpha\|v\|_V^2\le a(v,v)\le\Lambda\|v\|_V^2, \quad |b(v,q)|\le C_b\|v\|_V\|q\|_Q, \quad \sup_{v\ne0}\frac{|b(v,q)|}{\|v\|_V}\ge\beta\|q\|_Q. $$
If $M_Q$ is the pressure mass matrix for $\|\cdot\|_Q$, then the positive
Schur matrix $S=BA^{-1}B^T$ satisfies, for every $q\in Q$,
$$ \frac{\beta^2}{\Lambda}q^TM_Qq \le q^TSq \le\frac{C_b^2}{\alpha}q^TM_Qq. $$
Thus pressure-mass Schur equivalence is conditional on the actual inf-sup,
continuity, and velocity stiffness scalings shown here.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

derivations.claim: By [F3], the SPD matrices $A$ and $\gamma M_Q$ have symmetric positive square roots and inverse square roots. Put $$ T=(\gamma M_Q)^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2},\qquad X=P_\gamma^{-1/2}KP_\gamma^{-1/2} =\begin{pmatrix}I&T^T\\T&0\end{pmatrix}. $$ Then $TT^T=(\gamma M_Q)^{-1/2}S(\gamma M_Q)^{-1/2}$. Congruencing [F2] by $(\gamma M_Q)^{-1/2}$ shows $a_\gamma I\le TT^T\le b_\gamma I$. Hence $TT^T$ is positive definite and all its eigenvalues $\mu_j$ lie in $[a_\gamma,b_\gamma]$.

By [F3], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $y_1,\ldots,y_m$ of $TT^T$, with eigenvalues $\mu_j>0$. Set $x_j=T^Ty_j/\sqrt{\mu_j}$. Then $Tx_j=\sqrt{\mu_j}y_j$ and $$ x_i^Tx_j=\frac{y_i^TTT^Ty_j}{\sqrt{\mu_i\mu_j}}=\delta_{ij}, $$ so the $x_j$ are orthonormal. On the two-dimensional space spanned by $(x_j,0)$ and $(0,y_j)$, $X$ has matrix $$ \begin{pmatrix}1&\sqrt{\mu_j}\\\sqrt{\mu_j}&0\end{pmatrix}, $$ whose characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2-\lambda-\mu_j$. Its two roots are $\lambda_-(\mu_j)$ and $\lambda_+(\mu_j)$.

The matrix $TT^T$ is positive definite by step 1.1, so for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$, $x=T^T(TT^T)^{-1}y$ satisfies $Tx=y$. Thus $T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is onto, and [F4] gives $\dim\ker T=n-m$. For $x\in\ker T$, $X(x,0)=(x,0)$, giving eigenvalue $1$ on this kernel. The $m$ orthonormal pairs from step 2.1 and this $n-m$ dimensional kernel account for all $n+m$ dimensions and hence for the full spectrum of $X$.

If $C$ is the Cholesky factor in the symmetric-preconditioning definition, then $P_\gamma=CC^T$. Let $O=P_\gamma^{-1/2}C$; step 1.1 gives $OO^T=I$, so $O$ is orthogonal and $$ C^{-1}KC^{-T}=O^T(P_\gamma^{-1/2}KP_\gamma^{-1/2})O. $$ Therefore the published Cholesky-symmetric preconditioning has the same spectrum as $X$. Since $\lambda_-$ decreases and $\lambda_+$ increases on $s>0$, the eigenvalue intervals follow from step 1.1.

Fix $d\ge1$, $N\ge2$, $h=1/N$, viscosity $\nu>0$, and time step $k>0$.
Given $u^n\in V_h$ with $D_hu^n=0$, a mean-zero
pressure $p^n\in Q_h$, and a force $f^{n+1}\in V_h$ whose components each
have zero discrete mean,
$$h^d\sum_{j\in J_N}f_{i,j}^{n+1}=0\qquad(1\le i\le d),$$
define the next step by the following two solves and update:

1. Find $\widetilde u^{n+1}\in V_h$ satisfying
$$ \frac{\widetilde u^{n+1}-u^n}{k}+\nu A_h\widetilde u^{n+1}+G_hp^n=f^{n+1}. $$

2. Find the unique $\phi^{n+1}\in Q_h$ satisfying
$$ \Delta_h\phi^{n+1}=k^{-1}D_h\widetilde u^{n+1}. $$

3. Set
$$ u^{n+1}=\widetilde u^{n+1}-kG_h\phi^{n+1},\qquad p^{n+1}=p^n+\phi^{n+1}. $$

The pressure is kept in $Q_h$ after every solve; the constant pressure mode
is set to zero. The procedure is only asserted for the periodic staggered
grid and the admissible data stated here. The separate well-definedness
theorem [[thm-na-periodic-pressure-correction-solves-well-defined]] verifies
both solves and the preserved constraints.

$p^n\in Q_h$, and $f^{n+1}\in V_h$ whose components each have zero discrete
mean,
$$h^d\sum_{j\in J_N}f_{i,j}^{n+1}=0\qquad(1\le i\le d).$$
