Assume Countable Choice, let $\Omega$ and $\mathcal T_h$ be as in
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-poisson-method]], and let $f\in L^2(\Omega)$. The
exact weak problem has a unique solution $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, and the
discrete problem has a unique solution $u_h\in V_h^{CR,0}$. The exact
existence argument uses Countable Choice through Hilbert-space structure and
Lax–Milgram. The finite-dimensional discrete existence and uniqueness
argument uses no choice principle.

In the Poisson setting of [[def-crouzeix-raviart-poisson-method]],
$\|\cdot\|_{\sharp,h}$ is a norm on $X_h=H^1_0(\Omega)+V_h^{CR,0}$.
Its restriction to $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is the gradient norm, equivalent to the
$H^1$ norm, and its restriction to $V_h^{CR,0}$ is a norm.

Assume Countable Choice and the setup of [[def-crouzeix-raviart-face-average-interpolant]], a
shape-regular affine mesh, and $1/2<r\le1$. The face-average interpolant is
defined for every $u\in H^{1+r}(K)$ by the traces of
[[lem-crouzeix-raviart-simplex-traces-and-green-identity]] and reproduces
$\mathbb P_1(K)$. Uniformly over all cells,
$$\|\nabla(u-I_K^{CR}u)\|_{L^2(K)} \le C h_K^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(K)},\qquad \|u-I_K^{CR}u\|_{L^2(K)} \le C h_K^{1+r}|u|_{H^{1+r}(K)}.$$
For each facet $F\subset\partial K$,
$$h_F^{-1/2}\|\gamma_F(u-I_K^{CR}u)\|_{L^2(F)} \le C h_K^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(K)}.$$
If $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then the global interpolant has matching interior
face means and zero boundary face means, so $I_h^{CR}u\in V_h^{CR,0}$.

Assume Countable Choice. For every matching shape-regular simplicial mesh and
$v_h\in V_h^{CR,0}$,
$$\sum_{F\in\mathcal F^\circ\cup\mathcal F^\partial} h_F^{-1}\|[v_h]_F\|_{L^2(F)}^2 \le C\|\nabla_hv_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.$$
On an interior facet, $[v_h]_F=v_{K^+}-v_{K^-}$; on a boundary facet,
$[v_h]_F=v_K$. The constant depends only on $d$ and the shape-regularity
bound.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1/2<r\le1$, let $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)\cap H^{1+r}(\Omega)$ solve
$-\Delta u=f\in L^2(\Omega)$ distributionally, and let $h$ be the maximum
cell diameter of a finite matching shape-regular mesh. With the method of
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-poisson-method]], define
$$\mathcal R_h(u;v_h):=\widetilde a_h(u,v_h)-F_h(v_h),\qquad v_h\in V_h^{CR,0},$$
where $\widetilde a_h$ is the cellwise extension in [[def-crouzeix-raviart-poisson-method]]. Then
$$|\mathcal R_h(u;v_h)|\le C h^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)} \|\nabla_hv_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
If also $1/2<s\le1$ and $\zeta\in H^1_0(\Omega)\cap H^{1+s}(\Omega)$,
then
$$|\mathcal R_h(u;I_h^{CR}\zeta)|\le C h^{r+s} |u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)}|\zeta|_{H^{1+s}(\Omega)}.$$
The constants depend only on $d$, the shape-regularity bound, $r$, and $s$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded coercive sesquilinear form (bilinear over $\mathbb R$), and $F$ a bounded functional with the test-linearity required by $a$. Let $V_h$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with norm $\|\cdot\|_h$, not necessarily a subspace of $V$. Suppose the algebraic sum $X_h=V+V_h$ is equipped with a norm extending these norms, and $\widetilde a_h:X_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ is a bounded sesquilinear extension of a discrete form $a_h$ with bound $M_h$. Over $\mathbb C$, both forms are linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second; over $\mathbb R$, they are bilinear. Assume $a_h$ is coercive on $V_h$ with constant $\alpha_h>0$, and let $F_h$ be bounded on $V_h$ with the matching test-linearity. The exact and discrete equations have unique solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+M_h/\alpha_h)\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\alpha_h,$$

where $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}|F_h(w_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|/\|w_h\|_h$ when $V_h\ne\{0\}$, and $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u):=0$ when $V_h=\{0\}$. The estimate requires the bounded extension and does not assert that every nonconforming, penalty, or discontinuous Galerkin form has one.

For a family of these problems, suppose $M_h\le\overline M<\infty$ and $\alpha_h\ge\underline\alpha>0$ uniformly. Writing $E_h=\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h$, the uniform bound is
$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+\overline M/\underline\alpha)E_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\underline\alpha.$$
Thus uniform control of $E_h$ and $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)$ gives a uniform error budget; if both tend to zero, the errors tend to zero, and if both are $O(h^p)$ for a fixed $p>0$, the error is $O(h^p)$. No rate is inferred without those approximation, residual, and stability bounds.

For every interior facet $F$, define $\phi_F$ to equal $\phi_{K,F}$ on each
cell $K$ incident to $F$ and zero on all other cells, where
$\phi_{K,F}$ is the local shape polynomial of
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-local-p1-element]]. Then
$\{\phi_F:F\in\mathcal F^\circ\}$ is a basis of the space in
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-global-space]]. The face mean $\bar v_F:=|F|^{-1}\int_F
v_K\,dS$ is single-valued for $v\in V_h^{CR,0}$ and
$\dim V_h^{CR,0}=|\mathcal F^\circ|$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral domain and
$\mathcal T_h$ any finite matching shape-regular simplicial mesh. There is a
constant $C$ depending only on $\Omega$, $d$, and the shape-regularity bound
such that every $v_h\in V_h^{CR,0}$ satisfies
$$\|v_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\|\nabla_hv_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and satisfy
$a<x\cdot e<b$ for a unit vector $e$ and all $x\in\Omega$, with $a<b$.
Then every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ satisfies
$$\|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le(b-a)\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
The argument assumes Countable Choice through the stated Sobolev,
product-measure, and affine change-of-variables interfaces; it does not use the
Axiom of Choice.

For every interior facet $F$, define $\phi_F$ to equal $\phi_{K,F}$ on each
cell $K$ incident to $F$ and zero on all other cells, where
$\phi_{K,F}$ is the local shape polynomial of
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-local-p1-element]]. Then
$\{\phi_F:F\in\mathcal F^\circ\}$ is a basis of the space in
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-global-space]]. The face mean $\bar v_F:=|F|^{-1}\int_F
v_K\,dS$ is single-valued for $v\in V_h^{CR,0}$ and
$\dim V_h^{CR,0}=|\mathcal F^\circ|$.

In the Poisson setting of [[def-crouzeix-raviart-poisson-method]],
$\|\cdot\|_{\sharp,h}$ is a norm on $X_h=H^1_0(\Omega)+V_h^{CR,0}$.
Its restriction to $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is the gradient norm, equivalent to the
$H^1$ norm, and its restriction to $V_h^{CR,0}$ is a norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: The interpolant $I_h^{CR}u$ belongs to $V_h^{CR,0}$. Summing the local gradient estimates in [F3] over cells gives $\sum_K\|\nabla(u-I_K^{CR}u)\|_{L^2(K)}^2\le Ch^{2r}\sum_K|u|_{H^{1+r}(K)}^2 \le Ch^{2r}|u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)}^2,$ since the cell-pair domains $K\times K$ are disjoint subsets of $\Omega\times\Omega$ for each gradient component.

The exact space $V=H^1_0(\Omega)$ is Hilbert in the gradient norm: it is Hilbert in $H^1$ by [F8], and continuous Poincare gives $\|v\|_{H^1}^2\le(1+C_P^2)\|
abla v\|_2^2$, so the equivalent gradient norm is complete. In that norm $a$ is bounded and coercive with constants $M=\alpha=1$. The discrete space $V_h$ has its explicit finite face basis [F7]; the common comparison inner product restricts to its norm by [F2], and [F9] makes $V_h$ Hilbert. Thus the two Hilbert-space hypotheses of [F6] hold. By [F10], the exact load satisfies $|F(v)|\le C_P\|f\|_2\|v\|_{\sharp,h}$, and the discrete load satisfies $|F_h(w_h)|\le C_D\|f\|_2\|
abla_hw_h\|_2\le C_D\|f\|_2\|w_h\|_{\sharp,h}$ using [F7]. Finally, Holder gives $|\widetilde a_h(z,w_h)|\le\|
abla_hz\|_2\|
abla_hw_h\|_2\le\|z\|_{\sharp,h}\|w_h\|_{\sharp,h}$, so the bounded-extension constant is $M_h=1$.

By [F4], choose a constant $C_J$ such that $\|v_h\|_{\sharp,h}^2=\|\nabla_hv_h\|_2^2+\sum_Fh_F^{-1}\|[v_h]_F\|_2^2 \le(1+C_J)\|\nabla_hv_h\|_2^2=(1+C_J)a_h(v_h,v_h).$ Thus $a_h$ is coercive in the comparison norm with $\alpha_h=(1+C_J)^{-1}>0$, uniformly in the mesh.

If $V_h=\{0\}$, [F6] defines $\delta_h^{\rm nc}(u)=0$, which satisfies the required bound. Otherwise, the residual in [F6] is $\delta_h^{\rm nc}(u)=\sup_{w_h\ne0}\frac{|F_h(w_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_{\sharp,h}}\le Ch^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)},$ because [F5] gives the numerator bound and $\|w_h\|_{\sharp,h}\ge\|\nabla_hw_h\|_2$.

On an interior facet, $[u-I_h^{CR}u]=-[I_h^{CR}u]$ because $u$ has a common trace; on a boundary facet its trace is $-I_h^{CR}u$ because $u$ has zero trace. The face terms in [F3], squared and summed over facets with each cell incident to at most $d+1$ facets, give $\sum_F h_F^{-1}\|[u-I_h^{CR}u]_F\|_{L^2(F)}^2 \le Ch^{2r}|u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)}^2.$ Together with step 1.1, this proves $\|u-I_h^{CR}u\|_{\sharp,h}\le Ch^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)}$, hence the same upper bound for the infimum in [F6].

Apply [F6] using steps 2.1, 1.2, 1.3, and 1.4. The constants $M_h=1$ and $\alpha_h=(1+C_J)^{-1}$ are uniform, so its estimate gives $\|u-u_h\|_{\sharp,h}\le Ch^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)}$. The interpolation and consistency constants depend only on $d$, shape regularity, and $r$, and the jump constant $C_J$ has the same dependence. The Poincare constants $C_P,C_D$ in step 1.2 establish Hilbert-space/load hypotheses but do not enter the Strang error bound. Thus this proof yields an error constant depending only on $d$, shape regularity, and $r$ (and is compatible with the weaker dependence stated above). The broken-gradient term is one of the nonnegative terms in the squared comparison norm, yielding the final assertion.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded domain and let $1/2<s\le1$. Say that $\Omega$ has
a **Dirichlet Poisson smoothing index $s$** with constant $C_{\rm reg}$ if,
for every $g\in L^2(\Omega)$, there is a unique $\zeta_g\in H^1_0(\Omega)$
satisfying
$$\int_\Omega\nabla\zeta_g\cdot\nabla v\,dx =\int_\Omega g v\,dx\qquad(v\in H^1_0(\Omega)),$$
and $\zeta_g\in H^{1+s}(\Omega)$ with
$$\|\zeta_g\|_{H^{1+s}(\Omega)}\le C_{\rm reg}\|g\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
This is a hypothesis about the continuous adjoint Poisson problem. It is not
asserted for every bounded domain.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a shape-regular affine $d$-simplex,
$F\subset\partial K$ a facet, and $1/2<r\le1$. Every $q\in H^r(K)$ has a
single-valued $L^2(F)$ trace $\gamma_Fq$. For $1/2<r<1$,
$$\|\gamma_Fq\|_{L^2(F)} \le C\left(h_K^{-1/2}\|q\|_{L^2(K)} +h_K^{r-1/2}[q]_{H^r(K)}\right),$$
and
$$\|\gamma_Fq-\operatorname{avg}_F\gamma_Fq\|_{L^2(F)} \le C h_K^{r-1/2}[q]_{H^r(K)},$$
while for $r=1$,
$$\|\gamma_Fq\|_{L^2(F)} \le C\left(h_K^{-1/2}\|q\|_{L^2(K)} +h_K^{1/2}\|\nabla q\|_{L^2(K)}\right),$$
and the face-mean fluctuation is bounded by
$C h_K^{1/2}\|\nabla q\|_{L^2(K)}$.
The constant depends only on $d$, the shape-regularity bound, and $r$.

If $u\in H^1(K)$, $\nabla u\in H^r(K;\mathbb R^d)$, and
$f=-\Delta u\in L^2(K)$ distributionally, then for every $w\in H^1(K)$,
$$\int_Kfw\,dx=\int_K\nabla u\cdot\nabla w\,dx -\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_F(\gamma_F\nabla u\cdot n_{K,F})\gamma_Fw\,dS.$$
Here $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit normal. The trace threshold $r>1/2$ is
used to make the normal-gradient trace an $L^2$ function.

The two cell traces of a global $H^1(\Omega)$ function agree on a shared
interior facet, and the trace of a global $H^1_0(\Omega)$ function vanishes
on a boundary facet. More generally, if $1/2<r<1$ and $q\in H^r(\Omega)$,
then its two traces on each shared interior facet agree almost everywhere.

Assume Countable Choice and the setup of [[def-crouzeix-raviart-face-average-interpolant]], a
shape-regular affine mesh, and $1/2<r\le1$. The face-average interpolant is
defined for every $u\in H^{1+r}(K)$ by the traces of
[[lem-crouzeix-raviart-simplex-traces-and-green-identity]] and reproduces
$\mathbb P_1(K)$. Uniformly over all cells,
$$\|\nabla(u-I_K^{CR}u)\|_{L^2(K)} \le C h_K^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(K)},\qquad \|u-I_K^{CR}u\|_{L^2(K)} \le C h_K^{1+r}|u|_{H^{1+r}(K)}.$$
For each facet $F\subset\partial K$,
$$h_F^{-1/2}\|\gamma_F(u-I_K^{CR}u)\|_{L^2(F)} \le C h_K^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(K)}.$$
If $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then the global interpolant has matching interior
face means and zero boundary face means, so $I_h^{CR}u\in V_h^{CR,0}$.

Assume Countable Choice. For every matching shape-regular simplicial mesh and
$v_h\in V_h^{CR,0}$,
$$\sum_{F\in\mathcal F^\circ\cup\mathcal F^\partial} h_F^{-1}\|[v_h]_F\|_{L^2(F)}^2 \le C\|\nabla_hv_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.$$
On an interior facet, $[v_h]_F=v_{K^+}-v_{K^-}$; on a boundary facet,
$[v_h]_F=v_K$. The constant depends only on $d$ and the shape-regularity
bound.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1/2<r\le1$, and let $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)\cap
H^{1+r}(\Omega)$ solve $-\Delta u=f\in L^2(\Omega)$ on a bounded connected
Lipschitz polyhedral domain. On any finite matching shape-regular mesh, the
solution $u_h$ of the Crouzeix–Raviart method satisfies
$$\|u-u_h\|_{\sharp,h}\le C h^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)}.$$
In particular, $\|\nabla_h(u-u_h)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$ obeys the same bound.
The constant is independent of the mesh size and may depend on $\Omega$, $d$,
the shape-regularity bound, and $r$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1/2<r\le1$, let $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)\cap H^{1+r}(\Omega)$ solve
$-\Delta u=f\in L^2(\Omega)$ distributionally, and let $h$ be the maximum
cell diameter of a finite matching shape-regular mesh. With the method of
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-poisson-method]], define
$$\mathcal R_h(u;v_h):=\widetilde a_h(u,v_h)-F_h(v_h),\qquad v_h\in V_h^{CR,0},$$
where $\widetilde a_h$ is the cellwise extension in [[def-crouzeix-raviart-poisson-method]]. Then
$$|\mathcal R_h(u;v_h)|\le C h^r|u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)} \|\nabla_hv_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
If also $1/2<s\le1$ and $\zeta\in H^1_0(\Omega)\cap H^{1+s}(\Omega)$,
then
$$|\mathcal R_h(u;I_h^{CR}\zeta)|\le C h^{r+s} |u|_{H^{1+r}(\Omega)}|\zeta|_{H^{1+s}(\Omega)}.$$
The constants depend only on $d$, the shape-regularity bound, $r$, and $s$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ and $\mathcal T$ be as in
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-global-space]], let $V:=H^1_0(\Omega)$, let
$V_h:=V_h^{CR,0}$, and let $f\in L^2(\Omega)$. The exact Poisson form and
load are
$$a(u,v):=\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,dx,\qquad F(v):=\int_\Omega f v\,dx\quad (u,v\in V).$$
An exact solution is a $u\in V$ satisfying $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in V$.
For $v_h,w_h\in V_h$, define the broken form and discrete load by
$$a_h(v_h,w_h):=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}\int_K\nabla v_h\cdot\nabla w_h\,dx, \qquad F_h(w_h):=\int_\Omega f w_h\,dx.$$
The discrete problem is to find $u_h\in V_h$ such that
$a_h(u_h,w_h)=F_h(w_h)$ for every $w_h\in V_h$.

Put $X_h:=V+V_h$. For each cell facet $F\subset\partial K$, let
$\gamma_{F,K}$ denote the trace supplied by
[[lem-crouzeix-raviart-simplex-traces-and-green-identity]].
For $z\in X_h$ and $w_h\in V_h$, define the comparison-space extension
$$\widetilde a_h(z,w_h):=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}\int_K \nabla(z|_K)\cdot\nabla w_h\,dx.$$
Each restriction $z|_K$ belongs to $H^1(K)$, and this extension agrees with
$a_h$ when $z\in V_h$.

On an interior facet
$F=K^+\cap K^-$ choose either ordering and define
$[z]_F:=\gamma_{F,K^+}z-\gamma_{F,K^-}z$; on a boundary facet of $K$ set
$[z]_F:=\gamma_{F,K}z$. The mesh-dependent comparison expression is
$$\|z\|_{\sharp,h}^2:= \sum_{K\in\mathcal T}\|\nabla(z|_K)\|_{L^2(K)}^2+ \sum_{F\in\mathcal F^\circ\cup\mathcal F^\partial} h_F^{-1}\|[z]_F\|_{L^2(F)}^2,\qquad z\in X_h.$$
The next items prove the required definiteness, stability, and consistency
properties; this definition makes no assertion that $V_h\subset V$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: Put $e:=u-u_h$. If $e=0$ in $L^2$, the conclusion holds. Otherwise apply [F1] with $g=e$ to obtain $\zeta\in H^1_0(\Omega)\cap H^{1+s}(\Omega)$ with $\|\zeta\|_{H^{1+s}}\le C_{\rm reg}\|e\|_2$. Testing its weak equation on $C_c^\infty(\Omega)\subset H^1_0(\Omega)$ gives $-\Delta\zeta=e$ distributionally.

Let $I_hu$ be the global interpolant and put $w_h:=I_hu-u_h\in V_h^{CR,0}$. The jump of $e$ decomposes as $[e]=[u-I_hu]+[w_h]$. The local face estimate in [F3], using the common trace of $u$ on interior facets and its zero boundary trace, gives $\sum_Fh_F^{-1}\|[u-I_hu]_F\|_2^2\le Ch^{2r}|u|_{H^{1+r}}^2.$ By [F4] and the triangle inequality (which follows for the finite direct sum of face $L^2$ spaces by expanding squares and applying [F8]), $\left(\sum_Fh_F^{-1}\|[w_h]_F\|_2^2ight)^{1/2} \le C\|
abla_hw_h\|_2 \le C igl(\|
abla_h(I_hu-u)\|_2+\|
abla_he\|_2 igr) \le Ch^r|u|_{H^{1+r}},$ where [F3] bounds the first term and [F5] the second. Combining these estimates yields $\left(\sum_Fh_F^{-1}\|[e]_F\|_2^2ight)^{1/2} \le Ch^r|u|_{H^{1+r}}.$ Each $[e]_F$ has zero face mean: on interior facets the means of $u$ and $u_h$ match, and on boundary facets both are zero.

Apply [F2] on every cell with $w=e|_K$ and sum. Write $[e]_F$ for the difference of its two traces on an interior facet and its trace on a boundary facet. Since $-\Delta\zeta=e$, $\|e\|_2^2=\sum_K\int_K
abla e\cdot
abla\zeta\,dx -\sum_F\int_F(\gamma_F
abla\zeta\cdot n_F)[e]_F\,dS.$ For interior $F$, $n_F$ is the outward normal of either fixed plus cell; for a boundary facet it is the outward cell normal. The global traces of $
abla\zeta$ match across interior facets by [F2].

By the trace fluctuation bound [F2], Holder [F8] on the disjoint union of facets gives $\left|\sum_F\int_F(\gamma_F\nabla\zeta\cdot n_F)[e]_F\,dS\right| \le\left(\sum_Fh_F\|q_F-\operatorname{avg}_Fq_F\|_2^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_Fh_F^{-1}\|[e]_F\|_2^2\right)^{1/2} \le Ch^s|\zeta|_{H^{1+s}}\,h^r|u|_{H^{1+r}},$ where $q_F$ is the corresponding normal trace. The last inequality uses that each cell has $d+1$ facets, $h_F\le h$, and the cell Gagliardo seminorms sum to at most the global seminorm.

Split the volume term in step 2.1 as $\sum_K\int_K
abla e\cdot
abla(\zeta-I_h\zeta) +\widetilde a_h(e,I_h\zeta).$ By [F7], linearity, and the discrete equation $a_h(u_h,I_h\zeta)=F_h(I_h\zeta)$, the second term is $\widetilde a_h(u,I_h\zeta)-F_h(I_h\zeta)$, the consistency residual in [F6]. Holder [F8] on the cells bounds the first term, and [F3] applied with exponent $s$ together with [F5] gives $\|
abla_he\|_2\|
abla_h(\zeta-I_h\zeta)\|_2 \le Ch^r|u|_{H^{1+r}}h^s|\zeta|_{H^{1+s}}.$ Together with [F6], its magnitude is at most $Ch^{r+s}|u|_{H^{1+r}}|\zeta|_{H^{1+s}}$.

Substitute the bounds from steps 2.2 and 3.1 in the identity of step 2.1. This gives $\|e\|_2^2\le Ch^{r+s}|u|_{H^{1+r}}|\zeta|_{H^{1+s}} \le CC_{\rm reg}h^{r+s}|u|_{H^{1+r}}\|e\|_2$ by step 1.1. Since $e\ne0$, divide by $\|e\|_2$ to obtain the stated result.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set,
$0<r<1$, and let $q$ be a measurable real function on $U$. Define
$$[q]_{H^r(U)}^2:=\int_U\int_U\frac{|q(x)-q(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{d+2r}}\,dx\,dy,$$
with the diagonal integrand set to zero, and
$H^r(U):=\{q\in L^2(U):[q]_{H^r(U)}<\infty\}$, using almost-everywhere
classes and norm $\|q\|_{H^r(U)}^2:=\|q\|_{L^2(U)}^2+[q]_{H^r(U)}^2$.
For $u\in H^1(U)$, write $u\in H^{1+r}(U)$ when each weak derivative
$\partial_j u$ belongs to $H^r(U)$, and define

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: On $0<x<1/4$, writing $c(y)=y(1-y)$, one has $\partial_xu=\tfrac34c(y)x^{-1/4},\qquad \partial_yu=(1-2y)x^{3/4}.$ Everywhere else the cutoff and its derivative are bounded. Since $u$ and $\partial_yu$ are square integrable and $|\partial_xu|^2\le C(1+x^{-1/2})$, the weak first derivatives lie in $L^2(\Omega)$; the classical interior derivatives give the distributional derivatives because test functions are compactly supported away from the boundary. Thus $u\in H^1(\Omega)$.

To prove the zero-boundary condition, let $\theta_\epsilon(t):=\sigma((t-\epsilon)/\epsilon)$. By [F1], it is smooth, zero for $t\le\epsilon$, and one for $t\ge2\epsilon$. Since $\sigma'$ is continuous and vanishes outside $[0,1]$, $\|\theta_\epsilon'\|_\infty\le C/\epsilon$. Set $\eta_\epsilon(x,y)=\theta_\epsilon(x)\theta_\epsilon(y)\theta_\epsilon(1-y)$. Each $\eta_\epsilon u$ is smooth and compactly supported in $\Omega$, since the $x$ cutoff removes the only nonsmooth boundary point and $\chi$ vanishes near $x=1$. Write $u-\eta_\epsilon u=(1-\theta_\epsilon(x))u+\theta_\epsilon(x)(1-\theta_\epsilon(y)\theta_\epsilon(1-y))u$. In the first term, all support lies in $x<2\epsilon$; the squared $L^2$ and derivative errors are bounded by $C\epsilon^{2(3/4)-1}=C\epsilon^{1/2}$, including the $\epsilon^{-1}u$ cutoff derivative. In the second term, support lies in the two strips of width $2\epsilon$ near $y=0,1$. There $|u|\le Cx^{3/4}\operatorname{dist}(y,\{0,1\})$ and its first derivatives are bounded by $Cx^{3/4}+Cx^{-1/4}\operatorname{dist}(y,\{0,1\})$; integrating the strips shows the squared errors and cutoff-derivative terms are $O(\epsilon)$. Thus $\eta_\epsilon u\to u$ in $H^1(\Omega)$, so the closure definition gives $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$.

Choose $0<\delta<1/12$ so small that $c(y')/c(y)\le1.05$ whenever $0<x<\delta$, $1/3\le y\le2/5$, and $y\le y'\le y+x$. For the pairs below, $x'\le3x<1/4$, so both points lie where $\chi=1$; also $c(y)$ is bounded below by a positive constant on this $y$ interval. For $2x\le x'\le3x$ and $y\le y'\le y+x$, the values of $\partial_xu(x,y)$ and $\partial_xu(x',y')$ then differ by at least $\tfrac34c(y)x^{-1/4}\bigl(1-1.05\,2^{-1/4}\bigr).$ Thus $|\partial_xu(x,y)-\partial_xu(x',y')|\ge Cx^{-1/4}$. Also $|(x,y)-(x',y')|\le\sqrt5x$. By [F2], restricting the $H^{1/2}$ Gagliardo integral to these pairs gives a lower bound $C\int_0^\delta x^{-1/2}x^{-3}\,x^2\,dx =C\int_0^\delta x^{-3/2}\,dx=\infty,$ where the two factors of $x$ are the lengths of the $x'$ and $y'$ intervals. Thus $\partial_xu\notin H^{1/2}(\Omega)$.

Let $D=\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)=\sqrt2$. For $1/2<r<1$ and $x\ne y$, $|x-y|^{-3}=|x-y|^{2r-1}|x-y|^{-2-2r}\le D^{2r-1}|x-y|^{-2-2r}$. Integrating gives $[q]_{H^{1/2}(\Omega)}^2\le D^{2r-1}[q]_{H^r(\Omega)}^2$ for every $q\in H^r(\Omega)$, so $H^r(\Omega)\subset H^{1/2}(\Omega)$. If $u\in H^{1+r}(\Omega)$ for such an $r$, [F4] would imply $\partial_xu\in H^r(\Omega)$ and hence $H^{1/2}(\Omega)$, contradicting step 2.1. Thus no exponent $r\in(1/2,1)$ satisfies the refuted claim.

It remains to exclude $r=1$. For $0<x<1/4$, the cutoff is one and $-\Delta u=	frac{3}{16}c(y)x^{-5/4}+2x^{3/4}$. On $1/3\le y\le2/5$, $c(y)$ is bounded below by a positive number, so this classical Laplacian is bounded below by $c_0x^{-5/4}$ for some $c_0>0$; its square has divergent integral at $x=0$. Since the distributional Laplacian agrees with this classical function in the open square, it has no $L^2$ representative. By [F5], $u
otin H^2(\Omega)=W^{2,2}(\Omega)$. The example still defines a bounded weak functional on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ by $v\mapsto\int_\Omega
abla u\cdot
abla v$, using Holder [F5]; it does not supply the $L^2$ source assumed by the method. Since the example has no $H^{1+r}$ regularity with $r>1/2$, it does not satisfy the trace hypothesis in [F3], and no normal-gradient trace conclusion is claimed.
Step 3.1 excludes every $r\in(1/2,1)$, and step 3.2 excludes $r=1$. These are all exponents in the asserted range, so the counterexample refutes the Statement.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $1<p<\infty$ and $p'=p/(p-1)$. For each facet $F$ of
$\widehat S_d$, restriction of smooth functions extends uniquely to a
bounded linear trace map
$$\gamma_F:W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)\to L^p(F;\mathbb R).$$
For real-valued $u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)$ and
$G\in W^{1,p'}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R^d)$, the facet traces satisfy
$$\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,\operatorname{div}G+\nabla u\cdot G\,dx =\sum_{F\subset\partial\widehat S_d}\int_F\gamma_Fu\,\gamma_FG\cdot\widehat n_F\,dS.$$
Here $\gamma_FG$ is the componentwise trace and $\widehat n_F$ is the
outward unit normal. The bounded C1-domain trace and Green theorems are not
used for the simplex.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

Assume Countable Choice, as in
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and
[[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]]. For an open set
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, an integer $k\ge0$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, set
$$H^k(\Omega;\mathbb K):=W^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The elements are the same almost-everywhere classes, and their weak
derivatives and norm are exactly those already defined for $W^{k,2}$. When the
scalar field is fixed, write $H^k(\Omega)$.

The notation $H^k_0(\Omega)$ is reserved for the later definition by closure of
compactly supported smooth functions in the Sobolev norm. This item assigns no
boundary values to an equivalence class and asserts no characterization by
pointwise vanishing or by traces.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ be the reference map and let $\widehat w=w\circ F_K$. By [F2], $\widehat w\in W^{1,2}(\widehat S_d)$ and its norm is bounded by a finite constant depending on $A_K$ times $\|w\|_{W^{1,2}(K)}$. The surface Jacobian $J_F$ is positive and constant by [F3]. Define $T_{K,F}w$ by pullback of $\gamma_{\widehat F}\widehat w$; then $$\|T_{K,F}w\|_{L^2(F)}^2=J_F\|\gamma_{\widehat F}\widehat w\|_{L^2(\widehat F)}^2\le J_F C_{\widehat F}^2\|\widehat w\|_{W^{1,2}(\widehat S_d)}^2\le C_{K,F}^2\|w\|_{W^{1,2}(K)}^2.$$ Thus the trace is bounded, and it agrees with ordinary restriction for smooth $w$ by [F1].

Let $w\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. For each $m\ge1$, the closure property [F4] and Countable Choice [F5] give $\phi_m\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with $\|w-\phi_m\|_{W^{1,2}(\Omega)}<1/m$. Restriction to $K$ cannot increase this norm, so step 1.1 gives $$\|T_{K,F}(w|_K)-T_{K,F}(\phi_m|_K)\|_{L^2(F)}\le C_{K,F}/m.$$ The support of each $\phi_m$ is compactly contained in $\Omega$, hence $\phi_m$ vanishes in a neighborhood of the boundary facet $F$ and its trace is zero by step 1.1. Letting $m\to\infty$ proves $T_{K,F}(w|_K)=0$.

If $p$ is polynomial on $K$, then it is smooth and step 1.1 identifies $T_{K,F}(p)$ with its classical restriction. Therefore for a global piecewise-polynomial $p\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, step 2.1 makes that restriction zero on each boundary facet. This proves the final assertion.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix polynomial degree $k\ge0$, $1\le p,q\le\infty$, and integers
$0\le m\le\ell\le k$. Let the shape-regular affine simplex family be as in
[[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. For every cell $K$ in that family,
there is a constant independent of cell size such that, for every
$v\in\mathbb P_k(K)$ and every facet $F\subset\partial K$,
$$|v|_{W^{\ell,p}(K)} \le C h_K^{m-\ell+d(1/p-1/q)}|v|_{W^{m,q}(K)},$$
$$\|v\|_{L^p(F)} \le C h_K^{(d-1)/p-d/q}\|v\|_{L^q(K)}.$$
Use $1/\infty=0$. Constants may depend on $d,k,p,q$ and the family shape
regularity bound, but not on $K$ or $h_K$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to each component $\partial_jv_h$, which has degree at most $k-1$. Summing the $d$ squared inequalities and using [F3] gives $\|\partial_{n_{K,F}}v_h\|_{L^2(F)}^2\le \|\nabla v_h\|_{L^2(F)}^2\le C_0^2h_K^{-1}\|\nabla v_h\|_{L^2(K)}^2$ for a finite $C_0$ depending only on $d,k$ and the shape bound.
Multiply step 1.1 by $h_F$ and use $h_F/h_K\le C$ from [F2]. Choose $C_{\mathrm{tr}}:=\max\{1,C_0\sqrt C\}$; this is positive, finite, uniform over the family, and proves the required bound.

If the family contains a cell, fix one of its facets and test the inequality with the affine polynomial $p(x):=n_{K,F}\cdot x$, which belongs to $\mathbb P_k(K)$ because $k\ge1$. Then $\nabla p=n_{K,F}$ and $\partial_{n_{K,F}}p=1$, so $h_F\|\partial_{n_{K,F}}p\|_F^2=(|K|/|F|)|F|=|K|=\|\nabla p\|_K^2>0$. Thus, for a family containing a cell, every admissible positive constant satisfies $C_{\mathrm{tr}}^2\ge1$. For an empty family the bound is vacuous; in either case step 2.1 selects $C_{\mathrm{tr}}\ge1$.

boundaries.evidence: An empty family has no cells or facets, so the bound is vacuous; step 2.1 still selects Ctr=max{1,C0 sqrt(C)}>=1. Step 3.1 conditions the necessity witness on existence of a cell.
Step 1.1 gives zero on both sides when the cell polynomial is constant, including the zero polynomial.

For a family containing a cell, the affine normal-coordinate polynomial in step 3.1 proves every admissible constant has Ctr^2>=1, including k=1. The chosen constant is at least 1 even for an empty family.

boundaries.reason: The shape-regular affine mesh hypothesis excludes degenerate cells.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 covers k=1 and explicitly selects the positive constant Ctr>=1.
Step 1.1 sums only finitely many cellwise inequalities and makes no selection from an arbitrary family.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For $n\ge1$ and
$s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ to be the normed-space completion
of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ with the positive-definite norm
$q_s(u)=\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\widehat u\|_2$ from
[[def-bessel-potential-pre-hilbert-norm-on-schwartz-space]] and
[[lem-bessel-potential-norm-is-positive-definite]].

Concretely, its elements are equivalence classes $[u_j]$ of norm-Cauchy
sequences $(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ in Schwartz space, where
$(u_j)\sim(v_j)$ exactly when
$\lim_{j\to\infty}q_s(u_j-v_j)=0$. The metric completion carries the unique
compatible Banach-space structure supplied by
[[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]] and
[[thm-metric-completion-carries-a-unique-banach-space-structure]]; its norm
is $\|[u_j]\|_{H^s}=\lim_j q_s(u_j)$. The constant-sequence map
$u\mapsto[(u,u,\ldots)]$ is the canonical dense linear isometry from Schwartz
space. At this definition stage $H^s$ is an abstract completion; no
identification with a subset of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ is implicit.

The only choice assumption is Countable Choice, used by the cited metric
completion theorem in its countable-sequence construction and completeness
argument. No full Axiom of Choice or dependent choice is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, and let
$H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion of
[[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical embedding
$E_s:H^s(\mathbb R^n)\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Write
$\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$ for the Japanese bracket, $\mathcal F$
for the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform, and
$u_g(\phi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}g(\xi)\phi(\xi)\,d\xi$ for the regular tempered
distribution of $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$. Define
$$\mathcal W_s=\bigl\{u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n):\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal Fu=u_g \text{ in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)\text{ for some }g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)\bigr\}.$$
Then:

1. The canonical embedding restricts to a bijection
   $E_s:H^s(\mathbb R^n)\to\mathcal W_s$. Thus, after identifying a completion
   class with its image under $E_s$, $H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ is **exactly** the set
   of tempered distributions whose bracket-weighted Fourier transform is the
   regular distribution of an $L^2$ class, and that class $g$ is unique.
2. The norm identity is exact:
$$\|U\|_{H^s}=\|g\|_2=\bigl\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)\bigr\|_2 \qquad(U\in H^s),$$
   where the last expression means the $L^2$ norm of the unique density $g$ of
   the distributional product $\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)$, and the
   defining completion norm $q_s(\phi)=\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\widehat\phi\|_2$
   of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] is not renormalized.
3. The product $\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal Fu$ is distributional
   multiplication of $\mathcal Fu$ by the smooth polynomially bounded bracket
   weight, not an a priori pointwise product; and $H^s$ elements are completion
   classes, not initially assumed to be functions.

Nothing here replaces the bracket weight by the Laplacian weight
$(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{s/2}$, and no pointwise value of $g$ at an individual
frequency is asserted before $g$ is obtained from the defining condition.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite

u.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim: First consider the hyperplane $\mathbb R^{d-1}\times\{0\}$ and $U\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. Write $G(x')=U(x',0)$. Fourier inversion in the last coordinate and Fubini on the absolutely integrable Schwartz integrands give $\widehat G(\xi')=\int_{\mathbb R}\widehat U(\xi',\eta)\,d\eta$.

Apply Cauchy–Schwarz in $\eta$ with weights $\langle(\xi',\eta)\rangle^{s}$ and its reciprocal; this follows by expanding $0\le\|f-\lambda g\|_2^2$ and minimizing over the complex scalar $\lambda$. Both weighted factors lie in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ for fixed $\xi'$, the reciprocal factor by [A1] and the weighted Fourier transform because $U$ is Schwartz. The reciprocal-square integral is $\int_{\mathbb R}(1+|\xi'|^2+\eta^2)^{-s}\,d\eta=C_s(1+|\xi'|^2)^{1/2-s}\le C_s,$ by the substitution $\eta=(1+|\xi'|^2)^{1/2}t$ and [A1, F5]. Therefore $|\widehat G(\xi')|^2\le C_s\int_{\mathbb R}(1+|\xi'|^2+\eta^2)^s|\widehat U(\xi',\eta)|^2\,d\eta$. Tonelli [F4] and Plancherel [F1] give $\|G\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{d-1})}\le C_s\|U\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}$.

Since Schwartz space is dense in the completion [F2], the estimate of step 2.1 makes the restrictions of every Cauchy representative a Cauchy sequence in $L^2$; completeness [F3] defines a bounded trace on the hyperplane. The same estimate applied to the difference of two representatives proves independence of the representative and linearity.

This trace is local. For Schwartz $W$, let $W_t(x'):=W(x',t)$. Partial Plancherel in the tangential variables, Fubini [F4], and the weighted Cauchy--Schwarz estimate of step 2.1 give $\|W_t-W_0\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{d-1})}^2\le\int_{\mathbb R^{d-1}}J_t(\xi')G(\xi')\,d\xi',$ where $J_t(\xi'):=\int_{\mathbb R}(1+|\xi'|^2+\eta^2)^{-s}|e^{2\pi i\eta t}-1|^2\,d\eta$ and $G(\xi'):=\int_{\mathbb R}(1+|\xi'|^2+\eta^2)^s|\widehat W(\xi',\eta)|^2\,d\eta$. Choose $0<\delta<\min\{1,2s-1\}$. Since $|e^{i\alpha}-1|^2\le C_\delta|\alpha|^\delta$, the substitution $\eta=(1+|\xi'|^2)^{1/2}r$ using [F5] gives $J_t(\xi')\le C_{s,\delta}|t|^\delta(1+|\xi'|^2)^{(1-2s+\delta)/2}\le C_{s,\delta}|t|^\delta$. Also $\int G(\xi')\,d\xi'=\|W\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}^2$ by [F1, F4]. Hence $\|W_t-W_0\|_2^2\le C_{s,\delta}|t|^\delta\|W\|_{H^s}^2$. Applying this estimate to differences of two slice parameters, density of Schwartz space and completeness [F3] give every $W\in H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ a continuous $L^2(\mathbb R^{d-1})$ slice representative whose value at $t=0$ is the trace from step 3.1. It agrees with the ordinary sections for almost every $t$: choose Schwartz approximants with summable squared $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ errors and apply Fubini [F4] to their squared slice errors. If two extensions agree on $K$, their difference vanishes on an interior prism beside every relatively compact patch $E$ of $F$. Fubini [F4] makes almost every interior slice zero on $E$; continuity then makes the trace zero there. A countable exhaustion covers $F$ up to its lower-dimensional boundary, which has surface measure zero, so the trace is independent of the extension. For a translation $b$ and orthogonal map $R$, $\widehat{W(R^{-1}(\cdot-b))}(\xi)=e^{-2\pi i b\cdot\xi}\widehat W(R^{-1}\xi)$ by change of variables [F5]; since $|\det R|=1$ and $\langle R\xi\rangle=\langle\xi\rangle$, the whole-space norm is invariant. Thus the hyperplane estimate from step 2.1 applies to the supporting plane of $F$ and then restricts to $F$.

The reciprocal eta weight is integrable exactly for s>1/2. For delta in (0,min(1,2s-1)), the slice increment estimate is uniform in tangential frequency. Density gives continuous L2 slices; summable squared whole-space errors and Fubini identify a.e. slices, and interior prisms give locality on facet patches. citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For $n\ge1$ and
$s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ to be the normed-space completion
of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ with the positive-definite norm
$q_s(u)=\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\widehat u\|_2$ from
[[def-bessel-potential-pre-hilbert-norm-on-schwartz-space]] and
[[lem-bessel-potential-norm-is-positive-definite]].

Concretely, its elements are equivalence classes $[u_j]$ of norm-Cauchy
sequences $(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ in Schwartz space, where
$(u_j)\sim(v_j)$ exactly when
$\lim_{j\to\infty}q_s(u_j-v_j)=0$. The metric completion carries the unique
compatible Banach-space structure supplied by
[[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]] and
[[thm-metric-completion-carries-a-unique-banach-space-structure]]; its norm
is $\|[u_j]\|_{H^s}=\lim_j q_s(u_j)$. The constant-sequence map
$u\mapsto[(u,u,\ldots)]$ is the canonical dense linear isometry from Schwartz
space. At this definition stage $H^s$ is an abstract completion; no
identification with a subset of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ is implicit.

The only choice assumption is Countable Choice, used by the cited metric
completion theorem in its countable-sequence construction and completeness
argument. No full Axiom of Choice or dependent choice is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, and let
$H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion of
[[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical embedding
$E_s:H^s(\mathbb R^n)\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Write
$\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$ for the Japanese bracket, $\mathcal F$
for the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform, and
$u_g(\phi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}g(\xi)\phi(\xi)\,d\xi$ for the regular tempered
distribution of $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$. Define
$$\mathcal W_s=\bigl\{u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n):\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal Fu=u_g \text{ in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)\text{ for some }g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)\bigr\}.$$
Then:

1. The canonical embedding restricts to a bijection
   $E_s:H^s(\mathbb R^n)\to\mathcal W_s$. Thus, after identifying a completion
   class with its image under $E_s$, $H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ is **exactly** the set
   of tempered distributions whose bracket-weighted Fourier transform is the
   regular distribution of an $L^2$ class, and that class $g$ is unique.
2. The norm identity is exact:
$$\|U\|_{H^s}=\|g\|_2=\bigl\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)\bigr\|_2 \qquad(U\in H^s),$$
   where the last expression means the $L^2$ norm of the unique density $g$ of
   the distributional product $\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)$, and the
   defining completion norm $q_s(\phi)=\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\widehat\phi\|_2$
   of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] is not renormalized.
3. The product $\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal Fu$ is distributional
   multiplication of $\mathcal Fu$ by the smooth polynomially bounded bracket
   weight, not an a priori pointwise product; and $H^s$ elements are completion
   classes, not initially assumed to be functions.

Nothing here replaces the bracket weight by the Laplacian weight
$(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{s/2}$, and no pointwise value of $g$ at an individual
frequency is asserted before $g$ is obtained from the defining condition.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $s\ge0$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty open set. Use $H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ with the Bessel-potential completion convention of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]]. Realize this completion in $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ by the canonical injection
$$\iota_sU:=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\bigl(\langle\xi\rangle^{-s}J_sU\bigr),$$
where $J_s:H^s(\mathbb R^d)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ is the weighted Fourier isometry of [[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]] and $\mathcal F_2$ is the unitary transform of [[thm-plancherel]]. Since $s\ge0$, multiplication by $\langle\xi\rangle^{-s}$ is bounded on $L^2$ with norm at most one and is injective. Hence $\iota_s$ is linear, injective, and satisfies $\|\iota_sU\|_2\le\|U\|_{H^s}$; it sends each canonical Schwartz class to that function's almost-everywhere class. Equivalently, for a Cauchy representative $[u_j]$, $\iota_s[u_j]=\lim_j u_j$ in $L^2$, because $\widehat u_j=\langle\xi\rangle^{-s}J_su_j$ converges in $L^2$ and $\mathcal F_2^{-1}$ is continuous. Identify $U$ with this $L^2$ class, and write $U|_D:=(\iota_sU)|_D$. Define the **restriction space**
$$H^s(D):=\{U|_D:U\in H^s(\mathbb R^d)\},\qquad \|u\|_{H^s(D)}:=\inf\{\|U\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}:U|_D=u\text{ a.e. on }D\}.$$
Two extensions represent the same element exactly when their restrictions agree almost everywhere on $D$. This is the convention for fractional-order spaces on the polyhedral domain and its affine simplex cells used in the Nitsche items on this page. No $C^1$ boundary or trace theorem is part of this definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge2$, be a nondegenerate affine simplex, let $F$ be one of its facets, and let $s>1/2$. Restriction of smooth functions has a unique bounded extension
$$T_F:H^s(K)\longrightarrow L^2(F),\qquad \|T_Fv\|_{L^2(F)}\le C_s\|v\|_{H^s(K)},$$
where $H^s(K)$ is the restriction space of [[def-nitsche-restriction-bessel-potential-sobolev-spaces]]. The constant depends only on $s$ and the Fourier normalization, not on the location or orientation of the supporting hyperplane. If $V\in H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ is an extension of $v$, then $T_Fv$ is the restriction to $F$ of the unique $L^2$ hyperplane trace of $V$; hence it is independent of the chosen extension.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p<\infty$, and let
$\widehat S_d$ be the reference simplex. Then restrictions of functions
smooth on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\widehat S_d}$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)$ in its Sobolev norm. No density assertion for
$p=\infty$ is made.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1<p<\infty$ and $p'=p/(p-1)$. For each facet $F$ of
$\widehat S_d$, restriction of smooth functions extends uniquely to a
bounded linear trace map
$$\gamma_F:W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)\to L^p(F;\mathbb R).$$
For real-valued $u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)$ and
$G\in W^{1,p'}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R^d)$, the facet traces satisfy
$$\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,\operatorname{div}G+\nabla u\cdot G\,dx =\sum_{F\subset\partial\widehat S_d}\int_F\gamma_Fu\,\gamma_FG\cdot\widehat n_F\,dS.$$
Here $\gamma_FG$ is the componentwise trace and $\widehat n_F$ is the
outward unit normal. The bounded C1-domain trace and Green theorems are not
used for the simplex.

Assume Countable Choice. For every $1\le p<\infty$ there is
$C_{d,p}<\infty$ such that for all
$u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)$,
$$\|u-u_{\widehat S_d}\|_{L^p(\widehat S_d)} \le C_{d,p}|u|_{W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)},\qquad u_{\widehat S_d}:=|\widehat S_d|^{-1}\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,dx.$$

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then

$$\|\tau_h f-f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(h \to 0).$$

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y

2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

derivations.claim: For $U\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ and $0<s<1$, the map $(x,y)\mapsto(x,z=y-x)$ is an invertible linear $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^{2d}$ with determinant of absolute value $1$. Apply the change-of-variables formula in [F6] to the nonnegative integrand, then Tonelli and Plancherel in the $x$ variable, to obtain $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\frac{|U(x)-U(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{d+2s}}\,dx\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|\widehat U(\xi)|^2\left(\int_{\mathbb R^d}\frac{|e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot z}-1|^2}{|z|^{d+2s}}\,dz\right)d\xi=c_{d,s}\int_{\mathbb R^d}|\xi|^{2s}|\widehat U(\xi)|^2\,d\xi.$ The inner integral is finite because its numerator is at most $C|z|^2$ near zero and at most $4$ at infinity, giving radial integrals $\int_0^1r^{1-2s}dr$ and $\int_1^\infty r^{-1-2s}dr$; it is positive for $\xi\ne0$. Rotation and dilation, each covered by [F6], give the factor $c_{d,s}|\xi|^{2s}$. The vector-valued version follows by applying this identity to each component and summing. Since $1+|\xi|^{2s}$ is comparable to $\langle\xi\rangle^{2s}$, this identifies the whole-space intrinsic norm with the Bessel norm on Schwartz functions.

We construct finitely many boundary charts. At each boundary point choose an inward direction in the interior cone of the simplex; in a sufficiently small rotated box the active facet inequalities solve for the vertical coordinate and give $t>g(x')$, where $g$ is the maximum of finitely many affine functions. Inactive facets stay away after shrinking the box. If the affine functions are $\ell_j$, then $|g(x')-g(y')|\le L|x'-y'|$ with $L:=\max_j|\nabla\ell_j|$, so $g$ is Lipschitz in this explicit sense. Compactness gives a finite cover of the boundary by smaller such boxes and one interior open set covering the remaining compact subset. Choose nonnegative smooth cutoffs $\eta_j$ supported in the corresponding larger chart sets and positive on the smaller cover. Their sum is positive on a neighborhood of the closed simplex, so $\psi_j:=\eta_j/(\sum_i\eta_i)$ there form a smooth finite partition of unity. Multiplication by each cutoff is bounded in the intrinsic norm: expand $\chi(x)w(x)-\chi(y)w(y)$ into $\chi(x)(w(x)-w(y))+w(y)(\chi(x)-\chi(y))$; the second term is bounded by $C\|w\|_2^2$ because $|\chi(x)-\chi(y)|\le\min(C|x-y|,2\|\chi\|_\infty)$ and the resulting radial kernel is integrable for $0<s<1$.

The identity extends to the completion, and that completion is exactly the $L^2$ functions with finite displayed intrinsic seminorm. For the converse density, choose smooth cutoffs $\chi_R$ equal to one on $B_R$, supported in $B_{2R}$, with $|\nabla\chi_R|\le C/R$. For any such function $W$, the difference quotient of $(1-\chi_R)W$ is the sum of $(1-\chi_R(x))(W(x)-W(y))$ and $W(y)(\chi_R(y)-\chi_R(x))$. Dominated convergence sends the first term to zero in the weighted pair $L^2$ norm; for the second, integration in $x-y$ gives at most $C R^{-2s}\|W\|_2^2$. Thus $\chi_RW\to W$ in the intrinsic norm. For compactly supported $W$, translation is continuous in $L^2$ both for $W$ and for $G_W(x,y):=(W(x)-W(y))/|x-y|^{d/2+s}$ under the simultaneous translation $(x,y)\mapsto(x-a,y-a)$. Choose a nonnegative smooth compactly supported unit-mass mollifier $\rho$. For a scalar function $Z$ and probability density $\rho_\varepsilon$, scalar Jensen gives $|\int \rho_\varepsilon(a)Z(a)\,da|^2\le\int\rho_\varepsilon(a)|Z(a)|^2\,da$. For a finite-dimensional Euclidean-valued $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$, apply this to each real component and sum: $|\int \rho_\varepsilon Z|^2=\sum_{j=1}^m|\int\rho_\varepsilon Z_j|^2\le\sum_{j=1}^m\int\rho_\varepsilon|Z_j|^2=\int\rho_\varepsilon|Z|^2$. Applying this inequality to the scalar or vector differences for $W$ and $G_W$, then Tonelli, gives $\|\rho_\varepsilon*W-W\|_2^2+[\rho_\varepsilon*W-W]_{s,\mathbb R^d}^2\le\int\rho_\varepsilon(a)\bigl(\|W(\cdot-a)-W\|_2^2+\|G_W(\cdot-a,\cdot-a)-G_W\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{2d})}^2\bigr)\,da.$ The right side tends to zero because both translation differences tend to zero as $a\to0$ and the mollifier supports shrink to zero. The convolution is smooth by [F5], so $C_c^\infty$ is dense. Conversely, an intrinsic-Cauchy smooth sequence has an $L^2$ limit and a weighted-pair-$L^2$ limit; an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence identifies the latter with the difference quotient of the former. Completeness and [F1] therefore identify the completion with the intrinsic space.

For a boundary-localized piece, reflect across its graph by $R(x',t)=(x',2g(x')-t)$ and set the extension below the graph to $w(R(x',t))$. The horizontal coordinates are unchanged and the vertical difference is bounded by $|t-u|+2L|x'-y'|$, so $|Rx-Ry|\le C|x-y|$; since $R^2$ is the identity, the reverse bound follows by applying the same estimate to $Rx,Ry$. Thus $R$ is bi-Lipschitz. Because $g$ is a finite maximum of affine functions, partition each integration region into the finitely many open affine pieces; their boundaries lie in finitely many hyperplanes and are null. On each piece $R$ is an affine $C^1$ diffeomorphism with determinant of absolute value $1$. Apply the nonnegative change-of-variables formula in [F6] on each such piece (and in the $y$ variable for the mixed term); Tonelli combines the resulting estimates. Consequently same-side double integrals are bounded by a constant multiple of the upper-side integral. For $x$ above and $y$ below the graph, write their heights above the graph as $a,b\ge0$. Choose chart supports with positive margin to the artificial box edges, so cross pairs for extension by zero contribute at most $C\|w\|_2^2$; the interior piece has positive distance from the simplex boundary and obeys the same bound. Restricting any whole-space extension decreases both the $L^2$ norm and the nonnegative pair integral. Conversely, step 2.2 supplies a bounded extension of every intrinsic reference-simplex function; together with step 2.1 this proves equivalence of the intrinsic and restriction $H^s$ norms for $0<s<1$. Pull back by the shape-regular affine map. The map from the reference open simplex to the cell interior and its product map on the double integral are invertible affine $C^1$ diffeomorphisms. abla_{\widehat x}\widehat w=A_K^T(

abla w\|_{L^2(K)}\le C h_K^{1-d/2}\|
abla w\|_{L^2(K)}$, while $\|\widehat w\|_{L^2(\widehat K)}^2=|\det A_K|^{-1}\|w\|_{L^2(K)}^2$. This gives $\|T_Fw\|_{L^2(F)}^2\le C J_F|\det A_K|^{-1} igl(\|w\|_{L^2(K)}^2+\|A_K\|^2\|

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge2$, a degree $k\ge1$, and a shape-regular matching affine simplicial mesh family as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. There is a selected constant $1\le C_{\mathrm{tr}}<\infty$, depending only on $d,k$ and the shape-regularity bound, such that for every cell $K$, every facet $F\subset\partial K$, and every scalar $v_h|_K\in\mathbb P_k(K)$,
$$h_F\|\partial_{n_{K,F}}v_h\|_{L^2(F)}^2\le C_{\mathrm{tr}}^2\|\nabla v_h\|_{L^2(K)}^2,$$
where $h_F=|K|/|F|$ and $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit normal of $K$ on $F$.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

derivations.claim: Sum [F1] over all boundary facets. Each cell contributes at most $N_\partial$ copies of its squared gradient norm, so $\sum_F h_F\|\partial_n v_h\|_F^2\le N_\partial C_{\mathrm{tr}}^2\sum_K\|\nabla v_h\|_K^2=N_\partial C_{\mathrm{tr}}^2\|\nabla v_h\|_\Omega^2$. Taking square roots proves the first inequality.

Choose a point $x_0$ in the interior of a mesh cell. The finite union of cells is compact and bounded, so the ray $x_0+tv$ has a last point in that union for every unit direction $v$. Choose $v$ outside the finitely many measure-zero sets of directions whose ray meets a cell face of dimension at most $d-2$ or is parallel to a facet plane; the excluded directions are measure zero because each such face has dimension at most $d-2$ and radial projection from $x_0$ has dimension at most $d-2$ on the $(d-1)$-sphere. The last point therefore lies in the relative interior of a facet and the ray crosses it transversally. If two cells meet at a point in the relative interior of a common facet, their interiors lie on opposite sides: if both lay on the same side of its affine hyperplane, a sufficiently small point displaced to that side near the facet point would lie in the interior of both nondegenerate simplices, contradicting their disjoint interiors in [F3]. Thus such a shared-facet point is interior to the union, contrary to its being the last point on the ray. The last point is consequently on a one-cell boundary facet. Since the local result gives $C_{\mathrm{tr}}\ge1$, we obtain $1\le N_\partial$ and $C_\partial=\sqrt{N_\partial}C_{\mathrm{tr}}\ge1$.

Apply [F4] on each facet and then finite-sum Cauchy–Schwarz to obtain $\left|\sum_F\int_F(\partial_n v_h)v_h\right|\le\sum_F(h_F^{1/2}\|\partial_n v_h\|_F)(h_F^{-1/2}\|v_h\|_F)\le\left(\sum_Fh_F\|\partial_n v_h\|_F^2\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_Fh_F^{-1}\|v_h\|_F^2\right)^{1/2}.$ Substitute the first inequality from step 1.1 to get the stated bound.
