Let $X_c$ and $X_f$ be finite-dimensional real vector spaces and set $X=X_c\oplus X_f$; elements are written $(u_c,u_f)$, with $u_c$ the resolved component and $u_f$ the unresolved component. For a real vector space $Y$, let $Y^*$ be its space of real linear functionals. Let $A_{cc}:X_c\to X_c^*$, $A_{cf}:X_f\to X_c^*$, $A_{fc}:X_c\to X_f^*$, and $A_{ff}:X_f\to X_f^*$ be linear maps, with $A_{ff}$ invertible, and let $F_c\in X_c^*$ and $F_f\in X_f^*$. The linear equation on $X$ has block form
$$\begin{pmatrix}A_{cc}&A_{cf}\\A_{fc}&A_{ff}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u_c\\u_f\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}F_c\\F_f\end{pmatrix}.$$
The fine residual for a resolved vector $v_c$ is $r_f(v_c):=F_f-A_{fc}v_c$. Exact elimination gives $u_f=A_{ff}^{-1}r_f(u_c)$ and the Schur equation
$$\left(A_{cc}-A_{cf}A_{ff}^{-1}A_{fc}\right)u_c=F_c-A_{cf}A_{ff}^{-1}F_f.$$

A **residual closure** selects a linear map $T:X_f^*\to X_f$ to approximate the exact inverse $A_{ff}^{-1}:X_f^*\to X_f$. It defines $\widetilde A_{cc}:=A_{cc}-A_{cf}TA_{fc}$, $\widetilde F_c:=F_c-A_{cf}TF_f$, and the modeled fine component $\widetilde u_f:=T r_f(\widetilde u_c)$, where $\widetilde u_c$ solves $\widetilde A_{cc}\widetilde u_c=\widetilde F_c$. This is a finite-dimensional algebraic closure; an application to a PDE requires its own residual, spaces, invertibility, and approximation-defect analysis.

derivations.claim: Write the exact Schur operator and load as $S=A_{cc}-A_{cf}GA_{fc}$ and $g=F_c-A_{cf}GF_f$, so $Su_c=g$. Put $\Delta:=T-G$. The approximate quantities satisfy $\widetilde S=S-A_{cf}\Delta A_{fc}$ and $\widetilde g=g-A_{cf}\Delta F_f$.

Since $\widetilde S\widetilde u_c=\widetilde g$, step 1.1 gives $\widetilde S(\widetilde u_c-u_c)=\widetilde g-\widetilde S u_c=-A_{cf}\Delta(F_f-A_{fc}u_c)=-A_{cf}\Delta r_f$. Apply the induced operator norms and multiply by $\|\widetilde S^{-1}\|$ to prove the coarse bound.

The exact fine component is $u_f=G r_f$. The modeled component is $\widetilde u_f=T(r_f-A_{fc}(\widetilde u_c-u_c))$. Subtracting gives $\widetilde u_f-u_f=(T-G)r_f-TA_{fc}(\widetilde u_c-u_c)$. The triangle inequality and operator norms give the stated fine-scale bound.

Fix an integer $N\ge1$, put $h=1/N$, and let $x_j=jh$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The cells are $K_j=[x_{j-1},x_j]$. For $g_0,g_1\in\mathbb R$, let $S_h(g_0,g_1)$ be the finite-dimensional affine space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ that are affine on each cell and have endpoint values $g_0,g_1$. Write $V_h=S_h(0,0)$ for the homogeneous test and trial vector space; explicitly, $S_h(g_0,g_1)=\ell+V_h$ with $\ell(x)=(1-x)g_0+xg_1$. “P1” means polynomial degree at most one on each interval.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and $f\in C([0,1])$. The stationary boundary-value problem is to find $u\in C^2([0,1])$ such that $-\epsilon u''+b u'=f$ on $(0,1)$, with prescribed endpoint values $u(0)=g_0$ and $u(1)=g_1$. Its dimensionless cell Péclet number is $\mathrm{Pe}=|b|h/(2\epsilon)>0$. The stability theorem on this page uses the homogeneous branch $g_0=g_1=0$; the general endpoint notation also permits the boundary-layer example.

Use the uniform mesh, coefficients, and spaces of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]]. On every cell set
$$\tau=\frac{h}{2|b|}\left(\coth(\mathrm{Pe})-\frac1{\mathrm{Pe}}\right),\qquad \coth s:=\frac{\cosh s}{\sinh s}.$$
For $w\in S_h(g_0,g_1)+C^2([0,1])$ and $v_h\in V_h$, define
$$a_h(w,v_h):=\epsilon\int_0^1w'v_h'\,dx+b\int_0^1w'v_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K(-\epsilon w''+bw')(bv_h')\,dx,$$
$$F_h(v_h):=\int_0^1fv_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K f(bv_h')\,dx.$$
Second derivatives are taken classically on each cell. The strong equation residual is $R_K(w):=-\epsilon w''+bw'-f$. For P1 trial functions, $w_h''=0$ on each cell, so the cell term is $\tau\int_K(bw_h')(bv_h')$. On the smooth consistency extension it retains $-\epsilon w''$; thus the full residual pairing is $\tau\int_K(R_K(w)+f)(bv_h')$, while the load contains the matching $f$ term. The SUPG equation is $a_h(w_h,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$ and adds the same residual-weighted streamline test perturbation to the differential equation and its load.

derivations.claim: Put $q(s)=s\cosh s-\sinh s$. Then $q(0)=0$ and $q'(s)=s\sinh s>0$ for $s>0$, so $q(s)>0$ and $m(s)=q(s)/(s\sinh s)>0$.
The identity $\coth s-1=2/(e^{2s}-1)$ and $e^{2s}-1=\int_0^{2s}e^t\,dt>2s$ give $m(s)<1$.

For $0<s\le1$, $q(s)=\int_0^s t\sinh t\,dt\ge s^3/3$. The function $\sinh s/s$ is increasing because its derivative is $q(s)/s^2>0$, hence $\sinh s\le s\sinh 1$ on this range. Therefore $m(s)\ge s/(3\sinh1)$. For every $s>0$, monotonicity of $\sinh$ also gives $q(s)\le\sinh(s)\int_0^s t\,dt=s^2\sinh(s)/2$, whence $m(s)\le s/2$.

Since $\sinh s>s$ for $s>0$, $m'(s)=s^{-2}-(\sinh s)^{-2}>0$. Thus for $s\ge1$, $m(s)\ge m(1)=\coth1-1$. Together with step 2.2 this proves the two-sided bound. Substituting $s=\mathrm{Pe}$ into [F2] gives the stated lower and first upper bounds on $\tau$, using $h(2|b|)^{-1}\min\{\mathrm{Pe},1\}=\frac12\min\{h^2/(2\epsilon),h/|b|\}$. The last upper bound follows from $m(\mathrm{Pe})\le\mathrm{Pe}/2$.

Fix $d\ge2$ and a bounded connected polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$. Let $\{\mathcal T_h\}$ be a shape-regular family of finite matching affine simplicial meshes in the sense of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]: one finite constant $\sigma$ satisfies $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every cell of every mesh. Put $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}h_K$. Let $V_h$ be the space of continuous functions on $\overline\Omega$ that are affine on every cell and vanish on $\partial\Omega$.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$, $c\in C(\overline\Omega)$, and $f\in C(\overline\Omega)$. Define $B:=\|b\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ and $C:=\|c\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$. Assume a fixed $\omega>0$ satisfies $c-\frac12\nabla\cdot b\ge\omega$ on $\Omega$. The boundary condition for this branch is $u=0$ on the whole boundary, including the inflow part $\{x\in\partial\Omega:b(x)\cdot n(x)<0\}$. A classical exact solution is a function $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ satisfying $-\epsilon\Delta u+b\cdot\nabla u+cu=f$ in $\Omega$ and this boundary condition.

Use the model and notation of [[def-supg-general-convection-diffusion-reaction-model]]. Define $s_b(K)=h_K/\|b\|_{L^\infty(K)}$ when that norm is positive and $s_b(K)=+\infty$ otherwise; define $s_c(K)=\omega/\|c\|_{L^\infty(K)}^2$ when that norm is positive and $s_c(K)=+\infty$ otherwise. For each cell set
$$\delta_K:=\theta\min\left\{\frac{h_K^2}{\epsilon},s_b(K),s_c(K)\right\},\quad 0<\theta\le\frac14.$$
The minimum is finite and positive because its first entry is finite and positive. This scaling gives $\delta_K\|c\|_{L^\infty(K)}^2\le\omega/4$.

For a trial function $w$ that is the sum of a cellwise smooth function and a member of $V_h$, and $v_h\in V_h$, define the element residual $R_K(w):=-\epsilon\Delta_K w+b\cdot\nabla w+cw$, and
$$a_h(w,v_h):=\epsilon(\nabla w,\nabla v_h)_\Omega+(b\cdot\nabla w+cw,v_h)_\Omega+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\delta_K(R_K(w),b\cdot\nabla v_h)_K,$$
$$F_h(v_h):=(f,v_h)_\Omega+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\delta_K(f,b\cdot\nabla v_h)_K.$$
Here $(g_1,g_2)_D:=\int_Dg_1g_2\,dx$ and $\Delta_K$ is the classical Laplacian restricted to the interior of $K$. For $w_h\in V_h$, $\Delta_Kw_h=0$ because $w_h$ is affine on $K$. No stability claim is part of this definition.

Use the fixed dimension $d\ge2$ and the finite shape-regular affine simplicial mesh family from [[def-supg-general-convection-diffusion-reaction-model]] and [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Let $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$, and on each simplex $K$ let $I_Ku=\sum_{i=0}^d u(a_i)\lambda_i$ be its nodal affine interpolant, where $a_i$ are the vertices and $\lambda_i$ the barycentric coordinates. Set $I_hu|_K=I_Ku$ and $M_2:=|\Omega|^{1/2}\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$, using the Euclidean matrix norm for $D^2u$. There is a constant $C_I$ depending only on $d$ and the shape-regularity bound such that
$$\|u-I_hu\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_Ih^2M_2,\qquad \|\nabla(u-I_hu)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_IhM_2.$$
If $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, then $I_hu=0$ on every boundary facet.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Let $s>0$ and define $m(s):=\coth s-1/s$ and $c_*:=\min\{(3\sinh 1)^{-1},\coth 1-1\}>0$. Then
$$c_*\min\{s,1\}\le m(s)<1,\qquad m(s)\le s/2.$$
Consequently, for the parameter in [[def-supg-one-dimensional-residual-form]],

derivations.claim: For $v_h\in V_h$, continuity and piecewise absolute continuity give $\int_0^1bv_h'v_h\,dx=\frac b2\sum_K[v_h^2]_{\partial K}=\frac b2(v_h(1)^2-v_h(0)^2)=0$. The endpoint values vanish by [F1].

Integration by parts, with $v_h(0)=v_h(1)=0$, gives $\epsilon(u',v_h')+(bu',v_h)=(-\epsilon u''+bu',v_h)=(f,v_h)$. The stabilization contribution to $a_h(u,v_h)$ is $\sum_K\tau(-\epsilon u''+bu',bv_h')_K$, which equals $\sum_K\tau(f,bv_h')_K$ by the strong equation. This is exactly the stabilization contribution to $F_h$, so $a_h(u,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$.

Substituting step 1.1 into [F2] with $w_h=v_h$ yields the displayed identity. Its right side is nonnegative by [F3] and $\epsilon>0$. If it is zero, then $v_h'=0$ on every cell; continuity makes $v_h$ constant on $[0,1]$, and its zero endpoints force $v_h=0$. Hence this quadratic form is a norm squared.

In a basis of the finite-dimensional space $V_h$, the discrete form defines a square linear map $V_h\to V_h^*$. Use the uniform mesh, coefficients, and spaces of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]]. On every cell set
$$\tau=\frac{h}{2|b|}\left(\coth(\mathrm{Pe})-\frac1{\mathrm{Pe}}\right),\qquad \coth s:=\frac{\cosh s}{\sinh s}.$$
For $w\in S_h(g_0,g_1)+C^2([0,1])$ and $v_h\in V_h$, define
$$a_h(w,v_h):=\epsilon\int_0^1w'v_h'\,dx+b\int_0^1w'v_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K(-\epsilon w''+bw')(bv_h')\,dx,$$
$$F_h(v_h):=\int_0^1fv_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K f(bv_h')\,dx.$$
Second derivatives are taken classically on each cell. The strong equation residual is $R_K(w):=-\epsilon w''+bw'-f$. For P1 trial functions, $w_h''=0$ on each cell, so the cell term is $\tau\int_K(bw_h')(bv_h')$. On the smooth consistency extension it retains $-\epsilon w''$; thus the full residual pairing is $\tau\int_K(R_K(w)+f)(bv_h')$, while the load contains the matching $f$ term. The SUPG equation is $a_h(w_h,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$ and adds the same residual-weighted streamline test perturbation to the differential equation and its load.

Assume the one-dimensional model of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]] with homogeneous data $g_0=g_1=0$, and the form of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-residual-form]]. Let $u\in C^2([0,1])$ solve $-\epsilon u''+bu'=f$ with $u(0)=u(1)=0$. Then $a_h(u,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$ for every $v_h\in V_h$. For every $v_h\in V_h$,
$$a_h(v_h,v_h)=\epsilon\|v_h'\|_{L^2(0,1)}^2+\tau b^2\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\|v_h'\|_{L^2(K)}^2.$$
The right-hand side is a squared norm on $V_h$. Consequently the finite-dimensional SUPG system has a unique solution.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N=1$ be a finite interval partition, $h:=\max_j(x_{j+1}-x_j)$, and $u\in C^2([0,1])$. Let $I_hu$ be the continuous piecewise-linear function with nodal values $I_hu(x_j)=u(x_j)$. Then

$$\|(u-I_hu)'\|_{L^2(0,1)}\le h\|u''\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}.$$

If $u(0)=u(1)=0$, then $I_hu$ also vanishes at both endpoints.

Let $0=x_0<\cdots<x_N=1$ be a finite interval partition with maximum cell length $h$, and let $u\in C^2([0,1])$. Let $I_hu$ be the continuous piecewise-linear interpolant with the same nodal values as $u$. Then
$$\|u-I_hu\|_{L^2(0,1)}\le h^2\|u''\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}.$$

Let $s>0$ and define $m(s):=\coth s-1/s$ and $c_*:=\min\{(3\sinh 1)^{-1},\coth 1-1\}>0$. Then
$$c_*\min\{s,1\}\le m(s)<1,\qquad m(s)\le s/2.$$
Consequently, for the parameter in [[def-supg-one-dimensional-residual-form]],
$$0<\frac{c_*}{2}\min\left\{\frac{h^2}{2\epsilon},\frac{h}{|b|}\right\}\le\tau<\frac{h}{2|b|},\qquad \tau\le\frac{h^2}{8\epsilon}.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Let $I_hu$ be the nodal interpolant, $\eta:=u-I_hu$, and $e_h:=u_h-I_hu$. The homogeneous endpoint data imply $I_hu\in V_h$, so $e_h\in V_h$. By [F3] and [F4], $\|\eta'\|_2\le hM$ and $\|\eta\|_2\le h^2M$.

By [F2], $a_h(e_h,e_h)=a_h(\eta,e_h)$. The convection term satisfies $(b\eta',e_h)=-(b\eta,e_h')$: cell boundary terms cancel at interior nodes because $\eta$ and $e_h$ are continuous, and the two outer terms vanish. The diffusion and P1 stabilization terms are bounded by $\sqrt{\epsilon}\|\eta'\|_2\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$ and $|b|\sqrt{\tau}\|\eta'\|_2\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$. The additional consistency-extension term involving $-\epsilon\eta''$ is bounded by $\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}\|\eta''\|_2\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$, because $\sqrt{\tau}|b|\|e_h'\|_2\le\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$. The integrated convection term is bounded by $\|\eta\|_2\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}/\sqrt{\tau}$, since $\sqrt{\tau}|b|\|e_h'\|_2\le\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$. Therefore $|a_h(\eta,e_h)|\le\left(\sqrt{\epsilon}\|\eta'\|_2+|b|\sqrt{\tau}\|\eta'\|_2+\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}\|\eta''\|_2+\frac{\|\eta\|_2}{\sqrt{\tau}}\right)\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$.

If $e_h=0$, its norm estimate is immediate. Otherwise, divide step 2.1 by $\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$ and use [F2] to get $\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}\le(\sqrt{\epsilon}+|b|\sqrt{\tau})\|\eta'\|_2+\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}\|\eta''\|_2+\|\eta\|_2/\sqrt{\tau}$.

Since $I_hu$ is affine on each cell, $\eta''=u''$ cellwise and $\|\eta''\|_2\le M$. With $u-u_h=\eta-e_h$, the triangle inequality, [F1], [F3], [F4], and step 3.1 give $\|u-u_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}\le\left[h\sqrt{\epsilon+\tau b^2}+h\sqrt{\epsilon}+h|b|\sqrt{\tau}+\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}+\frac{h^2}{\sqrt{\tau}}\right]M$.

From [F5], $h|b|\sqrt{\tau}\le h^{3/2}\sqrt{|b|/2}$. If $\mathrm{Pe}\le1$, then $\tau\ge c_*h^2/(4\epsilon)$, so $h^2/\sqrt{\tau}\le2c_*^{-1/2}h\sqrt{\epsilon}$, and $\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}\le h\sqrt{\epsilon}/\sqrt8$. If $\mathrm{Pe}\ge1$, then $\tau\ge c_*h/(2|b|)$, so $h^2/\sqrt{\tau}\le(2/c_*)^{1/2}h^{3/2}\sqrt{|b|}$; also $\epsilon\le |b|h/2$ and $\tau<h/(2|b|)$ imply $\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}\le h^{3/2}\sqrt{|b|}/(2\sqrt2)$. Finally $h\sqrt{\epsilon+\tau b^2}\le h\sqrt{\epsilon}+h|b|\sqrt{\tau}$. These inequalities prove the second estimate with a universal constant depending only on $c_*$.

derivations.claim: On a cell $K_{ij}$ with local coordinates $(\xi,\eta)\in[0,1]^2$, the corner values are $\sigma_{ij}(1,-1,-1,1)$ with $\sigma_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}$. Q1 interpolation therefore gives $q_h|_{K_{ij}}=\sigma_{ij}(1-2\xi)(1-2\eta)$. Its integral on every cell is zero, so its global mean is zero, and it is nonzero at every mesh node.

For any Q1 velocity component $v_1$, $\partial_xv_1$ on a cell is affine in $\eta$ and independent of $\xi$. Since $\int_0^1(1-2\xi)\,d\xi=0$, $\int_{K_{ij}}q_h\partial_xv_1=0$. Let $X_c$ and $X_f$ be finite-dimensional real vector spaces and set $X=X_c\oplus X_f$; elements are written $(u_c,u_f)$, with $u_c$ the resolved component and $u_f$ the unresolved component. For a real vector space $Y$, let $Y^*$ be its space of real linear functionals. Let $A_{cc}:X_c\to X_c^*$, $A_{cf}:X_f\to X_c^*$, $A_{fc}:X_c\to X_f^*$, and $A_{ff}:X_f\to X_f^*$ be linear maps, with $A_{ff}$ invertible, and let $F_c\in X_c^*$ and $F_f\in X_f^*$. The linear equation on $X$ has block form
$$\begin{pmatrix}A_{cc}&A_{cf}\\A_{fc}&A_{ff}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u_c\\u_f\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}F_c\\F_f\end{pmatrix}.$$
The fine residual for a resolved vector $v_c$ is $r_f(v_c):=F_f-A_{fc}v_c$. Exact elimination gives $u_f=A_{ff}^{-1}r_f(u_c)$ and the Schur equation
$$\left(A_{cc}-A_{cf}A_{ff}^{-1}A_{fc}\right)u_c=F_c-A_{cf}A_{ff}^{-1}F_f.$$

A **residual closure** selects a linear map $T:X_f^*\to X_f$ to approximate the exact inverse $A_{ff}^{-1}:X_f^*\to X_f$. It defines $\widetilde A_{cc}:=A_{cc}-A_{cf}TA_{fc}$, $\widetilde F_c:=F_c-A_{cf}TF_f$, and the modeled fine component $\widetilde u_f:=T r_f(\widetilde u_c)$, where $\widetilde u_c$ solves $\widetilde A_{cc}\widetilde u_c=\widetilde F_c$. This is a finite-dimensional algebraic closure; an application to a PDE requires its own residual, spaces, invertibility, and approximation-defect analysis.

Use the block operators and residual closure of [[def-supg-variational-multiscale-block-closure]]. Equip $X_c,X_f$ and their duals with norms, and use the corresponding induced operator norms. Let $G:=A_{ff}^{-1}$, assume the exact Schur system has a solution $u_c$, and put $r_f:=F_f-A_{fc}u_c$. Suppose the closure map $T$ has $\widetilde S:=A_{cc}-A_{cf}TA_{fc}$ invertible, and let $\widetilde u_c$ solve the approximate Schur system. Then
$$\|\widetilde u_c-u_c\|\le\|\widetilde S^{-1}\|\,\|A_{cf}\|\,\|T-G\|\,\|r_f\|,$$
and for the modeled fine component $\widetilde u_f=T(F_f-A_{fc}\widetilde u_c)$,
$$\|\widetilde u_f-u_f\|\le\|T-G\|\,\|r_f\|+\|T\|\,\|A_{fc}\|\,\|\widetilde u_c-u_c\|.$$
The exact fine scale is $u_f=G r_f$. These bounds concern finite-dimensional algebraic blocks; they do not certify a universal PDE subgrid model.

derivations.claim: Here $G=1/2$, so the exact Schur coefficient is $2-1/2=3/2$ and the exact coarse solution is $u_c=2/3$. The exact unresolved component is $u_f=G(F_f-A_{fc}u_c)=-1/3$.
Replacing $G$ by $T=1/4$ gives the approximate Schur coefficient $2-1/4=7/4$, hence $\widetilde u_c=4/7$, and $\widetilde u_f=T(F_f-A_{fc}\widetilde u_c)=-1/7$. The coarse error is $|4/7-2/3|=2/21$.

The bound in [F2] equals $(4/7)\cdot1\cdot(1/4)\cdot(2/3)=2/21$, because $\|\widetilde S^{-1}\|=4/7$, $|A_{cf}|=1$, $|T-G|=1/4$, and $|F_f-A_{fc}u_c|=2/3$. Thus the defect bound is attained exactly in this finite example.

Fix an integer $N\ge1$, put $h=1/N$, and let $x_j=jh$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The cells are $K_j=[x_{j-1},x_j]$. For $g_0,g_1\in\mathbb R$, let $S_h(g_0,g_1)$ be the finite-dimensional affine space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ that are affine on each cell and have endpoint values $g_0,g_1$. Write $V_h=S_h(0,0)$ for the homogeneous test and trial vector space; explicitly, $S_h(g_0,g_1)=\ell+V_h$ with $\ell(x)=(1-x)g_0+xg_1$. “P1” means polynomial degree at most one on each interval.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and $f\in C([0,1])$. The stationary boundary-value problem is to find $u\in C^2([0,1])$ such that $-\epsilon u''+b u'=f$ on $(0,1)$, with prescribed endpoint values $u(0)=g_0$ and $u(1)=g_1$. Its dimensionless cell Péclet number is $\mathrm{Pe}=|b|h/(2\epsilon)>0$. The stability theorem on this page uses the homogeneous branch $g_0=g_1=0$; the general endpoint notation also permits the boundary-layer example.

Use the uniform mesh, coefficients, and spaces of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]]. On every cell set
$$\tau=\frac{h}{2|b|}\left(\coth(\mathrm{Pe})-\frac1{\mathrm{Pe}}\right),\qquad \coth s:=\frac{\cosh s}{\sinh s}.$$
For $w\in S_h(g_0,g_1)+C^2([0,1])$ and $v_h\in V_h$, define
$$a_h(w,v_h):=\epsilon\int_0^1w'v_h'\,dx+b\int_0^1w'v_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K(-\epsilon w''+bw')(bv_h')\,dx,$$
$$F_h(v_h):=\int_0^1fv_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K f(bv_h')\,dx.$$
Second derivatives are taken classically on each cell. The strong equation residual is $R_K(w):=-\epsilon w''+bw'-f$. For P1 trial functions, $w_h''=0$ on each cell, so the cell term is $\tau\int_K(bw_h')(bv_h')$. On the smooth consistency extension it retains $-\epsilon w''$; thus the full residual pairing is $\tau\int_K(R_K(w)+f)(bv_h')$, while the load contains the matching $f$ term. The SUPG equation is $a_h(w_h,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$ and adds the same residual-weighted streamline test perturbation to the differential equation and its load.

Let $s>0$ and define $m(s):=\coth s-1/s$ and $c_*:=\min\{(3\sinh 1)^{-1},\coth 1-1\}>0$. Then
$$c_*\min\{s,1\}\le m(s)<1,\qquad m(s)\le s/2.$$
Consequently, for the parameter in [[def-supg-one-dimensional-residual-form]],
$$0<\frac{c_*}{2}\min\left\{\frac{h^2}{2\epsilon},\frac{h}{|b|}\right\}\le\tau<\frac{h}{2|b|},\qquad \tau\le\frac{h^2}{8\epsilon}.$$

derivations.claim: The function $u(x)=x-(e^x-1)/(e-1)$ satisfies the endpoint conditions. Its derivatives are $u'=1-e^x/(e-1)$ and $u''=-e^x/(e-1)$, so $-u''+u'=1$. Hence $u(1/2)=u_*:=1/2-1/(\sqrt e+1)>0$.

Let $\phi$ be the midpoint hat function and $U$ its coefficient. Its derivative is $2$ on the left cell and $-2$ on the right. Thus $\int_0^1|\phi'|^2dx=4$, $\int_0^1\phi'\phi\,dx=\frac12[\phi^2]_0^1=0$, and $\int_0^1\phi\,dx=1/2$. Also $\int_0^1\phi'\,dx=\phi(1)-\phi(0)=0$, so the stabilization load vanishes. The single discrete equation is therefore $4(1+M\tau)U=1/2$, so $U=1/[8(1+M\tau)]$.

Since $\tau>0$ by [F3], $U\to0$ as $M\to\infty$, whereas the exact value $u_*>0$ from step 1.1 is fixed. In particular, every $M$ satisfying $M\tau>1/(4u_*)-1$ gives $U<u_*/2$. Oversizing the parameter can therefore smear this discrete solution.

derivations.claim: Put $r=b/\epsilon$. The function $u(x)=(e^{rx}-1)/(e^r-1)$ has endpoint values $0,1$, and $-\epsilon u''+bu'=(-\epsilon r^2+br)e^{rx}/(e^r-1)=0$. Hence it is the exact solution.

Let $\phi$ be the P1 hat function at $x=h=1/2$, let $\chi_h\in S_h(0,1)$ have nodal values $(0,0,1)$, and write $u_h=U\phi+\chi_h$. Put $D=\epsilon+\tau b^2>0$ by [F3]. Since $\phi'=1/h$ on the left cell and $-1/h$ on the right, $\int_0^1(\phi')^2dx=2/h$ and $\int_0^1\phi'\phi\,dx=\frac12[\phi^2]_0^1=0$, so $a_h(\phi,\phi)=2D/h$. Also $\chi_h'=0$ on the left and $1/h$ on the right, giving $D\int\chi_h'\phi'=-D/h$ and $b\int\chi_h'\phi=b/h\int_h^1\phi=b/2$. Thus $a_h(\chi_h,\phi)=-D/h+b/2$ and the one interior equation is $D(2U-1)/h+b/2=0$. By [F2] and the Péclet formula in [F1], $D=\epsilon+(bh/2)(\coth(\mathrm{Pe})-1/\mathrm{Pe})=(bh/2)\coth(\mathrm{Pe})$, so $U=(1-\tanh(\mathrm{Pe}))/2=1/(e^{2\mathrm{Pe}}+1)$. The exact value $u(h)=(e^{bh/\epsilon}-1)/(e^{2bh/\epsilon}-1)$ is the same number because $2\mathrm{Pe}=bh/\epsilon$.

At $x=0.99$, the piecewise-linear value is $u_h(0.99)=0.98+0.02U$, which tends to $0.98$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. The exact value is $(e^{0.99b/\epsilon}-1)/(e^{b/\epsilon}-1)$, which tends to zero because $b>0$ and $0.99<1$. Therefore the pointwise error tends to $0.98$. The exact midpoint node does not resolve the exponential layer inside the final cell.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and use the negative-sign $2\pi$ normalization.  If
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\widehat f},$$

where $\widehat f$ is the integral Fourier transform.  If
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\mathcal F_2f},$$

where $\mathcal F_2$ is the Plancherel extension.  These equalities are in
$\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and therefore depend only on the corresponding
almost-everywhere classes.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Assume countable choice. For $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $a,b\in\mathbb R^n$, and invertible real $n\times n$ matrix $A$, put $\tau_af(x)=f(x-a)$ and $M_bf(x)=e^{2\pi ib\cdot x}f(x)$. Then, at every frequency,
$$\widehat{\tau_af}(\xi)=e^{-2\pi ia\cdot\xi}\widehat f(\xi),\qquad\widehat{M_bf}(\xi)=\widehat f(\xi-b),\qquad\widehat{f\circ A}(\xi)=|\det A|^{-1}\widehat f(A^{-T}\xi).$$
Also $\widehat{f(-\cdot)}(\xi)=\widehat f(-\xi)$ and $\widehat{\overline f}(\xi)=\overline{\widehat f(-\xi)}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, and let
$H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion of
[[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical embedding
$E_s:H^s(\mathbb R^n)\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Write
$\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$ for the Japanese bracket, $\mathcal F$
for the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform, and
$u_g(\phi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}g(\xi)\phi(\xi)\,d\xi$ for the regular tempered
distribution of $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$. Define
$$\mathcal W_s=\bigl\{u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n):\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal Fu=u_g \text{ in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)\text{ for some }g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)\bigr\}.$$
Then:

1. The canonical embedding restricts to a bijection
   $E_s:H^s(\mathbb R^n)\to\mathcal W_s$. Thus, after identifying a completion
   class with its image under $E_s$, $H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ is **exactly** the set
   of tempered distributions whose bracket-weighted Fourier transform is the
   regular distribution of an $L^2$ class, and that class $g$ is unique.
2. The norm identity is exact:
$$\|U\|_{H^s}=\|g\|_2=\bigl\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)\bigr\|_2 \qquad(U\in H^s),$$
   where the last expression means the $L^2$ norm of the unique density $g$ of
   the distributional product $\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)$, and the
   defining completion norm $q_s(\phi)=\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\widehat\phi\|_2$
   of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] is not renormalized.
3. The product $\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal Fu$ is distributional
   multiplication of $\mathcal Fu$ by the smooth polynomially bounded bracket
   weight, not an a priori pointwise product; and $H^s$ elements are completion
   classes, not initially assumed to be functions.

Nothing here replaces the bracket weight by the Laplacian weight
$(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{s/2}$, and no pointwise value of $g$ at an individual
frequency is asserted before $g$ is obtained from the defining condition.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

derivations.claim: Set $h=x-y$ and use translation invariance in [F2] and Tonelli [F3] on the nonnegative integrand. This gives $[f]_{1/2,2}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\frac{\|f(\cdot+h)-f(\cdot)\|_2^2}{|h|^3}dh.$ For each $h$, Plancherel and the translation formula [F1]–[F2] express the squared norm in the integrand as $\int_{\mathbb R^2}|e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot h}-1|^2|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$.

Tonelli [F3] now yields $[f]_{1/2,2}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2J(\xi)d\xi,\qquad J(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\frac{|e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot h}-1|^2}{|h|^3}dh.$ If $\xi=0$, then $J(\xi)=0$. If $\xi\ne0$, rotate $h$ so that $\xi\cdot h=|\xi|h_1$, then substitute $z=|\xi|h$ using [F5]; the Jacobian is $|\xi|^{-2}$ and $|h|^{-3}=|\xi|^3|z|^{-3}$, so $J(\xi)=c_*|\xi|$ with $c_*=\int_{\mathbb R^2}|e^{2\pi iz_1}-1|^2|z|^{-3}dz$. This constant is finite: for $|z|\le1$, $|e^{2\pi iz_1}-1|\le2\pi|z|$, and for $|z|>1$ it is at most $2$; polar integration gives finite bounds $C\int_0^1dr$ and $C\int_1^\infty r^{-2}dr$. It is positive because the numerator is positive on a nonempty open set.

Substitution of $J(\xi)=c_*|\xi|$ into step 2.1 gives the exact seminorm identity. By [F4], the Bessel norm is the weighted Fourier norm; for every $r\ge0$, $(1+4\pi^2r^2)^{1/2}$ is bounded above and below by positive constants times $1+r$. Hence that norm is equivalent to $\|f\|_2^2+\int |\xi||\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$, and step 2.1 proves the asserted equivalence. Equivalent norms have the same Cauchy sequences and completion classes, proving the final claim.

Assume Countable Choice.  For $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and every
multi-index $\alpha$,

$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha u) =(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu, \qquad \mathcal F(x^\alpha u) =\left(-\frac1{2\pi i}\right)^{|\alpha|} \partial_\xi^\alpha\mathcal Fu.$$

Every operation and equality is in $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: In polar coordinates, $\int_{\mathbb R^2}P_t(z)\,dz=t\int_0^\infty r(r^2+t^2)^{-3/2}dr=1$; the same estimate shows $P_t\in L^1$. Direct differentiation of $t(|z|^2+t^2)^{-3/2}$ gives $(\Delta_z+\partial_t^2)P_t=0$ for $t>0$.

Put $F(t,\xi)=\widehat{P_t}(\xi)$. For $t$ in any compact subinterval of $(0,\infty)$, $P_t$ and its first two $t$-derivatives are dominated by integrable radial functions, so differentiation under the Fourier integral is valid. Fourier transforming the harmonic identity in step 1.1 and using [F1] gives $\partial_t^2F-(2\pi|\xi|)^2F=0$. Also $|F(t,\xi)|\le\|P_t\|_1=1$. For fixed $\xi$, the change $z=tw$ gives $F(t,\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}P_1(w)e^{-2\pi itw\cdot\xi}dw$; dominated convergence yields $F(t,\xi)\to1$ as $t\downarrow0$. The solutions of this constant-coefficient ODE are linear combinations of $e^{2\pi|\xi|t}$ and $e^{-2\pi|\xi|t}$ when $\xi\ne0$; boundedness removes the growing term, and the boundary limit fixes the coefficient to one. When $\xi=0$, the bounded affine solutions are constant and the same limit gives one. Hence $F(t,\xi)=e^{-2\pi|\xi|t}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, define
$$[f]_{1/2,2}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\int_{\mathbb R^2}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|^2}{|x-y|^3}\,dx\,dy.$$
There is a finite constant $c_*>0$ such that
$$[f]_{1/2,2}^2=c_*\int_{\mathbb R^2}|\xi|\,|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi.$$
Consequently, the norm $\|f\|_2^2+[f]_{1/2,2}^2$ is equivalent on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$ to the Bessel-potential norm $\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. The two completions therefore define the same $H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^2)$ space with equivalent norms.

derivations.claim: In a graph chart write $\Phi(p)=(p,\psi(p))$. The map $\Phi$ is bi-Lipschitz: $|p-q|\le|\Phi(p)-\Phi(q)|\le(1+\operatorname{Lip}(\psi)^2)^{1/2}|p-q|$. Its surface Jacobian $J_\Phi=(1+|\nabla\psi|^2)^{1/2}$ is bounded above and below almost everywhere. Therefore the $L^2$ norm and the double-integral seminorm of a function supported a positive distance inside this chart are comparable to those of its pullback; pairs with one point outside the chart contribute at most a constant times the $L^2$ norm because the support is separated from the chart edge. By [F1], each localized chart Bessel norm is thus equivalent to the localized surface chordal norm.

Write $g_j=\chi_jg$, so $g=\sum_{j=1}^Jg_j$. The inequality $|g(x)-g(y)|^2\le J\sum_j|g_j(x)-g_j(y)|^2$ shows that the global chordal norm is bounded by the sum of localized chordal norms from step 1.1. Conversely, $|g_j(x)-g_j(y)|\le |\chi_j(x)|\,|g(x)-g(y)|+|g(y)|\,|\chi_j(x)-\chi_j(y)|.$ Each $\chi_j$ is Lipschitz. The second term contributes at most $C\|g\|_{L^2}^2$ to the squared seminorm, since $\int_\Gamma|x-y|^{-1}ds_x$ is uniformly bounded in $y$: in each chart the surface area of a radius-$r$ disk is at most $Cr^2$, and summing dyadic annuli gives $\int_{|x-y|<1}|x-y|^{-1}ds_x\le C\sum_{m\ge0}2^{-m}<\infty$; the part $|x-y|\ge1$ is bounded by the finite surface area. Hence the sum of localized chordal norms is bounded by the global chordal norm. Combining both comparisons with step 1.1 proves the two-sided equivalence for smooth $g$. Equivalent norms have the same completion, which proves the stated extension.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and use the negative-sign $2\pi$ normalization.  If
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\widehat f},$$

where $\widehat f$ is the integral Fourier transform.  If
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\mathcal F_2f},$$

where $\mathcal F_2$ is the Plancherel extension.  These equalities are in
$\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and therefore depend only on the corresponding
almost-everywhere classes.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<n$ and $p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. There is a constant $C(n,p)$ such that
$$\|u\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\mathbb R^n)}\le C(n,p)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}$$
for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$; here $|Du|$ is the Euclidean norm of the weak gradient.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\psi:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be $L$-Lipschitz, put $\Phi(z,t)=(z,t+\psi(z))$, and let $G=\{(z,s):s>\psi(z)\}$. Pullback by $\Phi$ and by its inverse preserves volume and is bounded on $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$. The localized pullbacks from either side of a Lipschitz graph to flat half-boxes are bounded in $H^1$. A function $u\in H^1$ up to the graph has a bounded local $L^2$ trace $\tau u$, obtained from its flattened one-dimensional endpoint trace. For compactly supported smooth $\eta$ in a graph chart,
$$\int_G\big((\partial_j u)\eta+u\partial_j\eta\big)\,dx=\int_{\partial G}(\tau u)\eta n_j\,dS.$$
Here, with derivatives defined almost everywhere,
$$dS=\sqrt{1+|\nabla\psi(z)|^2}\,dz,\qquad n\,dS=(\partial_1\psi,\partial_2\psi,-1)\,dz.$$
For a domain below the graph the normal sign reverses. These graph surface measures and normals agree on overlapping rigid graph charts, so they define an intrinsic surface measure and almost-everywhere unit outward normal on a compact Lipschitz boundary. Such a boundary satisfies $|\Gamma\cap B(x,r)|\le Cr^2$ for small $r$ and $|\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,\Gamma)<\delta\}|\le C\delta$ for small $\delta$.

Matching local traces on the two sides make piecewise $H^1$ functions glue to $H^1$ with the piecewise weak gradient. A zero-trace $H^1$ function supported inside a boundary chart extends by zero through the graph with no distributional boundary derivative; it can be approximated in $H^1$ by smooth functions supported strictly on its own side. The corresponding assertions hold after finite chart localization on a bounded Lipschitz domain or bounded boundary collar.

Assume Countable Choice. For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, define
$$[f]_{1/2,2}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\int_{\mathbb R^2}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|^2}{|x-y|^3}\,dx\,dy.$$
There is a finite constant $c_*>0$ such that
$$[f]_{1/2,2}^2=c_*\int_{\mathbb R^2}|\xi|\,|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi.$$
Consequently, the norm $\|f\|_2^2+[f]_{1/2,2}^2$ is equivalent on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$ to the Bessel-potential norm $\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. The two completions therefore define the same $H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^2)$ space with equivalent norms.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set whose boundary is locally a Lipschitz graph, with $D$ on one side in each chart. It need not be connected. There is one linear operator $E:H^1(D)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $Ef=f$ almost everywhere on $D$, which maps $H^2(D)$ boundedly into $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Its support can be confined to a fixed bounded neighborhood of $\overline D$. The bounds depend only on a finite choice of boundary charts and cutoffs. In particular no mesh enters them.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

derivations.claim: The flat trace estimate. First take $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and write $\widehat u(\xi,\tau)$ for its full Fourier transform, with $\xi\in\mathbb R^2$ tangential and $\tau\in\mathbb R$ normal. Fourier inversion [F2] in $\tau$ and Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] give $|\widehat{u(\cdot,0)}(\xi)|^2\le C\left(\int_{\mathbb R}(1+|\xi|^2+\tau^2)|\widehat u(\xi,\tau)|^2d\tau\right)(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1/2},$ because $\int_{\mathbb R}(1+|\xi|^2+\tau^2)^{-1}d\tau=\pi(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1/2}$. Multiplying by $(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$, integrating in $\xi$, and applying [F1] proves $\|u(\cdot,0)\|_{H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^2)}\le C\|u\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^3)}$.

A flat right inverse. Given $g\in H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^2)$, put $a(\xi)=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$ and define $\widehat{Eg}(\xi,t)=\widehat g(\xi)e^{-a(\xi)|t|}\chi(t)$, where $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ equals $1$ near $0$. Then $Eg(\cdot,0)=g$. Direct integration uses $\int_0^\infty e^{-2at}dt=(2a)^{-1}$ and $|\xi|^2\le a^2$ to give $\|Eg\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^3)}^2\le C\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}|\widehat g(\xi)|^2d\xi$. Plancherel [F1] therefore gives a bounded right inverse on the flat boundary.

Flattening an arbitrary Lipschitz chart. Extend its graph function to a globally Lipschitz function with the same constant by the infimum extension, and use the shear in [F7]. The whole-space extension and smooth density in [F92], followed by bounded shear pullback, reduce the one-sided trace estimate to step 1.1; the endpoint trace of [F7] identifies the continuous boundary values on the smooth approximants and hence the one-sided trace independently of an extension. For the fixed Lipschitz chart partition, multiplication by a bounded Lipschitz cutoff $\chi$ is bounded on $H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^2)$: split the difference of $\chi g$ into $\chi(x)(g(x)-g(y))+g(y)(\chi(x)-\chi(y))$ and use $|\chi(x)-\chi(y)|\le\min(L_\chi|x-y|,2\|\chi\|_\infty)$. In two dimensions its extra Slobodeckij integral is bounded by $C\|g\|_2^2$, since the radial integrals near zero and infinity are respectively $\int_0^1dr$ and $\int_1^\infty r^{-2}dr$. Thus [F8] gives the required Bessel multiplier bound. On chart overlaps, [F7] supplies the same intrinsic surface measure; graph distances are bi-Lipschitz comparable and its graph area densities are bounded above and below. Consequently the localized surface double integrals, with denominator $|x-y|^3$, compare in both directions with their planar pullbacks using the graph measure in each variable, without any unproved Lipschitz volume substitution. Positive support margins inside each chart bound all zero-extension tail terms by $C\|g\|_2^2$. These observations justify the finite chart norm and the summed trace estimate. To lift $g$, take each zero-extended localized input $(\chi_jg)\circ\Phi_j$ in that Bessel space, use the flat right inverse of step 2.1, and push it through the inverse shear of [F7]. Multiply by a smooth ambient cutoff supported in the chart and equal to one near the support of $\chi_j$ on the surface. Its trace is exactly $\chi_jg$, not $\chi_j^2g$. The finite sum therefore has trace $\sum_j\chi_jg=g$ and bounded whole-space $H^1$ norm. The chart cutoffs give bounded support near $\Gamma$. The same construction on the other side proves the localized exterior-collar assertion.

The bounded extension $E:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with the correct restriction is supplied directly by the already proved general Lipschitz extension construction in [F92]; that construction assumes no boundary trace theorem. Its compact-support cutoff is allowed there. In a flattened collar, the one-dimensional fundamental theorem and Cauchy--Schwarz give $\|f(\cdot,t)-\tau f\|_{L^2(K)}^2\le t\int_0^t\|\partial_s f(\cdot,s)\|_{L^2(K)}^2ds$ for a compact tangential set $K$ and $t>0$, with $t$ measured into the chosen side. The weak-coordinate and endpoint argument of [F7] passes this to $H^1$ functions. Thus the trace just constructed agrees with the boundary restriction for a continuous $H^1$ representative, since continuity gives the same local $L^2$ limit.

The homogeneous energy trace. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, [F3] gives $\|u\|_6\le C\|
abla u\|_2$; hence it continues to every element of $\dot H^1$ by completion. Fix $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ equal to $1$ near $\Gamma$. Hölder's inequality [F5] on the bounded support of $
abla\zeta$ gives $\|\zeta u\|_{H^1}\le C(\|
abla u\|_2+\|u\|_6)\le C\|u\|_{\dot H^1}$. Applying the trace bound of step 3.1 to $\zeta u$ proves $\|\gamma u\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}\le C\|u\|_{\dot H^1}$; the compactly supported right inverse from step 3.1 is also a right inverse into $\dot H^1$.

derivations.claim: Let $\mu$ be any probability measure on $K$ and let $s_\#\mu$ be its pushforward under $y\mapsto sy$. The pushforward map in [F1] is bijective, with inverse dilation by $1/s$. Taking the infimum over all probability measures therefore gives $I(sK)=I(K)-\log s$. Exponentiating the definition yields $\operatorname{cap}(sK)=e^{-I(sK)}=s e^{-I(K)}=s\operatorname{cap}(K)$.

In the curve integral, substitute $Y=sy$. Arclength contributes $ds_Y=s\,ds_y$, while $\lambda_s(sy)=s^{-1}\lambda(y)$, so their product is $\lambda(y)ds_y$. The kernel identity $-\log|sx-sy|=-\log|x-y|-\log s$ then gives $V_{\Gamma_s}\lambda_s(sx)=-\frac1{2\pi}\int_\Gamma\bigl(\log|x-y|+\log s\bigr)\lambda(y)\,ds_y=V_\Gamma\lambda(x)-\frac{\log s}{2\pi}\int_\Gamma\lambda\,ds_y,$ as asserted.

routine_steps.claim: Write $H_k(r)=G_k(r)-G_0(r)$. The identity $H_k(r)=\frac{ik}{4\pi}\int_0^1e^{ikr\theta}d\theta$ follows by integrating the derivative of the exponential from $0$ to $r$; it implies $H_k$ and its first radial derivative are bounded for $0<r\le r_0$. Its Cartesian first derivatives are bounded as well. Therefore the single-layer trace integrals with kernel $H_k$ and their first normal derivatives have identical limits from both sides, and the double-layer trace integral with kernel $\partial_{n_y}H_k$ also has identical limits: the kernels are bounded near the diagonal and the surface measure of a shrinking disk tends to zero. Thus these remainder terms do not change any of the three stated jumps.

Fix $x_0\in\Gamma$ and rotate/translate so $x_0=0$, $n(x_0)=e_3$, and a neighborhood of $\Gamma$ is $y=(z,\psi(z))$ with $\psi(0)=0$, $D\psi(0)=0$, $|\psi(z)|\le C|z|^2$, and $|D\psi(z)|\le C|z|$. For the Laplace kernel, the single-layer trace kernel is locally bounded by $C|z|^{-1}$, which is surface-integrable; dominated convergence gives the same trace from both sides. In the normal derivative, the planar leading term is $-t(4\pi(|z|^2+t^2)^{3/2})^{-1}\lambda(0)$. Its integral over the tangent plane is $-\tfrac12\operatorname{sgn}(t)\lambda(0)$ by polar coordinates. Subtracting this leading term leaves an integrable remainder with a common two-sided limit: the curvature shift $\psi(z)=O(|z|^2)$ changes $s/(|z|^2+s^2)^{3/2}$ by at most $C|z|^{-1}$ because its $s$-derivative is bounded by $C|z|^{-3}$; replacing $\lambda(0)$ by $\lambda(z,\psi(z))J(z)=\lambda(0)+O(|z|)$ contributes at most $C|t||z|/(|z|^2+t^2)^{3/2}$, whose disk integral is $O(|t||\log|t||)$. Hence the interior-minus-exterior conormal jump is $\lambda(0)$.

The double-layer trace has planar leading term $t(4\pi(|z|^2+t^2)^{3/2})^{-1}\phi(0)$, whose tangent-plane integral is $\tfrac12\operatorname{sgn}(t)\phi(0)$. The graph normal and area factor satisfy $n(y)J(y)=(-D\psi(z),1)$, so its numerator is $t+O(|z|^2)$. As in step 2.1, subtracting the planar term leaves an integrable $C|z|^{-1}$ curvature remainder plus a density remainder with disk integral $O(|t||\log|t||)$; both have the same limit from either side. Thus $\gamma^-D_0\phi=-\tfrac12\phi+K_0\phi$ and $\gamma^+D_0\phi=\tfrac12\phi+K_0\phi$ for a common remainder $K_0\phi$, giving jump $-\phi$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **polyhedral boundary** is such a boundary made from finitely many planar polygonal faces meeting along edges and vertices; all surface-discretization claims below use this polyhedral subclass. For the fixed-atlas space conventions below, the boundary data include a compatible Borel surface measure $dS$ and an almost-everywhere unit outward normal $n$, with the following graph realizations and bounded positive graph area densities on every chosen chart. These compatible realizations are supplied data for the Countable-Choice space assertions, not conclusions from bare Lipschitzness under Countable Choice. Under the Axiom of Choice, [[lem-bem-lipschitz-graph-sobolev-and-green-interface]] constructs them for every compact Lipschitz boundary and proves their compatibility; the general analytical trace and layer theorems state that axiom. On polyhedral charts the data are directly the finite face areas and face normals. The normal points from $\Omega^-$ into $\Omega^+$. In a rigid chart with $\Omega^-$ above the graph $x_3=\psi(x_1,x_2)$ it is $n=(\partial_1\psi,\partial_2\psi,-1)/\sqrt{1+|\nabla\psi|^2}$ almost everywhere; reverse the sign when the domain is below the graph. Rigid coordinates transform this vector to physical coordinates. The graph surface measure is $dS=\sqrt{1+|\nabla\psi|^2}\,dx_1dx_2$. Compatibility on overlaps is part of the fixed boundary data; the cited AC graph theorem proves it for arbitrary Lipschitz charts. On a polyhedron these are the face-area measure and outward face normals.

Fix a finite Lipschitz graph atlas $\{(U_j,\psi_j)\}_{j=1}^J$, with surface parametrizations $\Phi_j(z)=(z,\psi_j(z))$ in the rigid chart coordinates, and a subordinate finite Lipschitz partition of unity $\{\chi_j\}_{j=1}^J$ whose chartwise supports have positive distance from the chart edges. On $\mathbb R^2$, use the real subspace of the real-order Bessel-potential completion in [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]]. Its published norm uses the weight $(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$. Fix here the equivalent Hilbert norm
$$q(g)^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}|\widehat g(\xi)|^2d\xi.$$
The inequalities $(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\le(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\le2\pi(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$ identify the same completion and classes under the negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier convention of [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-fractional-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]. $$\|g\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}^2=\sum_{j=1}^J q(g_j)^2.$$
Its inner product is the sum of the real weighted Fourier inner products. This Hilbert norm is equivalent to the finite sum of chart norms: $(\sum_jq(g_j)^2)^{1/2}\le\sum_jq(g_j)\le\sqrt J(\sum_jq(g_j)^2)^{1/2}$. It controls $L^2(\Gamma)$, because graph surface Jacobians are bounded above and below and $g=\sum_j\chi_jg$. It is complete: a chart-norm Cauchy sequence has a global $L^2$ limit by that bound; its localized pullbacks converge in $L^2$ to the pullbacks of this limit, while completeness of each Euclidean weighted space gives convergence in each $q$ norm. The two limits agree, so the limit belongs to the defined chart space and convergence holds in the finite square sum.

Let real $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ be the continuous real dual, with its operator norm and pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_\Gamma$; the dual of this real Hilbert space is Hilbert by [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]. The interior and exterior traces of an $H^1$ function are denoted $\gamma^-u$ and $\gamma^+u$; their common chartwise trace space is $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ once the applicable trace theorem is proved. This fixed-atlas chart-space convention applies to the stated Lipschitz geometry, including its polyhedral and $C^2$ subclasses. It defines the Hilbert and dual norms; no boundary trace or lifting theorem is assumed by that convention.

The complex space is the Hilbert complexification of the real space: $\|g_1+ig_2\|^2=\|g_1\|^2+\|g_2\|^2$. Its $H^{-1/2}$ is the continuous conjugate dual, with pairing linear in the density and conjugate-linear in the trace, extending the real pairing. A complex density is a distribution via the **bilinear** test action $T_\lambda(v)=\langle\lambda,\overline v\rangle_\Gamma$. For either scalar field the continuous realization $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\subset L^2(\Gamma)\subset H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ uses $\langle f,g\rangle_\Gamma=\int_\Gamma f\overline g\,dS$ in the complex case and $\int_\Gamma fg\,dS$ in the real case. These inclusions follow from the just-proved $H^{1/2}\to L^2$ bound and Cauchy–Schwarz.

No smoothness at edges or vertices is included in this definition. The normal is only used almost everywhere. On every Lipschitz boundary use the intrinsic graph surface measure just specified, with the chart partition; on a polyhedral boundary it equals the sum of planar face-area measures. The general Lipschitz class and its $C^2$ subclass therefore use the same measure and orientation conventions.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Write $a(\xi)=(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$. For a compactly supported smooth flat-space function $v$, Fourier inversion in the last coordinate and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|\widehat{v(\cdot,0)}(\xi)|^2\le C a(\xi)^{-1}\int(a(\xi)^2+4\pi^2\tau^2)|\widehat v(\xi,\tau)|^2d\tau$. Integration in $\xi$ proves the flat $H^1\to H^{1/2}$ trace estimate. The lift $\widehat{Lg}(\xi,t)=\widehat g(\xi)e^{-a(\xi)|t|}\chi(t)$, with $\chi=1$ near zero and compactly supported, has trace $g$ and $H^1$ norm bounded by $C\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}$, by integrating $e^{-2a|t|}$. In a $C^2$ graph chart $x=(z,t+\psi(z))$, the change of variables has determinant one and bounded derivative and inverse derivative; the chain rule bounds the two $H^1$ norms. Graph and chart distances and surface Jacobians are uniformly comparable, so the Slobodeckij double integral gives the corresponding $H^{1/2}$ norm comparison. A finite partition of unity and smaller chart cutoffs therefore transport the flat trace and lifts to the surface. For each bounded physical chart piece and flat half-box use [F92]. A $C^2$ graph map has bounded derivative, inverse derivative and Jacobian, so the classical chain rule and change of variables bound composition on smooth approximants; passing their functions and derivatives in $L^2$ gives the weak composition formula and $H^1$ convergence for all inputs. This proves the one-sided trace/extension passage without assuming smoothness of an arbitrary Sobolev representative. For the normal-coordinate identity, smooth approximants from [F92] satisfy the classical one-variable FTC. Their traces converge by the flat trace estimate, and their normal-derivative integrals converge in tangential $L^2$, uniformly over a bounded normal interval, by Cauchy–Schwarz. Taking these limits supplies the $L^2$ slice representative and its integral identity for every normal parameter. A zero-trace $H^1$ function then has zero-extension in $H^1$ (the distributional boundary derivative is its trace times $n$, which vanishes), and the kernel of the trace is $H^1_0$: in a flat half-chart a zero-trace function satisfies $v(z,t)=\int_0^t\partial_tv(z,s)ds$, whence $\epsilon^{-2}\int_{0<t<2\epsilon}|v|^2\le C\int_{0<t<2\epsilon}|\partial_tv|^2\to0$. Cutting it off for $t<\epsilon$ therefore changes its $H^1$ norm by a quantity tending to zero; convolution of each resulting interior-supported function proves the claim. Transport this construction by the graph maps and sum the partition. For the trace interpretation, in a flattened half-collar, first for smooth functions and then by $H^1$ approximation, the fundamental theorem of calculus and Cauchy–Schwarz give $\|v(\cdot,t)-\gamma v\|_{L^2}^2\le t\int_0^t\|\partial_sv(\cdot,s)\|_{L^2}^2ds$. In a $C^2$ graph chart, the map $(z,t)\mapsto\Phi(z)+tn_{\Phi(z)}$ is $C^1$ and at $t=0$ its tangent columns and unit-normal column are linearly independent. The Euclidean inverse-function theorem gives a local normal collar with bounded derivative, inverse derivative and Jacobian after shrinking to a compact subchart; a finite cover provides the required fixed bounds; transporting this estimate proves $L^2$ convergence of the normal slices to the Sobolev trace from either side. These arguments apply to $C^2$ charts directly and do not import any polyhedral trace theorem. To verify density of the declared ambient smooth densities in $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, lift any chart datum by the constructed compactly supported global $H^1$ lift, mollify that lift in $H^1$ as in [F92], and apply the bounded trace estimate: the traces of the smooth approximants converge in the chart norm. They are also dense in $L^2(\Gamma)$ by chart cutoffs and ordinary mollification. Their density in $H^{-1/2}$ follows by Hilbert duality: an annihilator in $H^{1/2}$ would have zero $L^2$ pairing with every such density and hence be zero; Riesz identifies the dual of the negative space with the positive space.

routine_steps.claim: Put $P_k=-\Delta-k^2$ and $G_k(x)=e^{ik|x|}/(4\pi|x|)$. Radial differentiation gives $P_kG_k=0$ for $x\ne0$. On a punctured test-function support, integration by parts gives the inner boundary contribution $\int_{|x|=\epsilon}(G_k\partial_r v-v\partial_rG_k)dS\to v(0)$, since $G_k=O(\epsilon^{-1})$ and $\partial_rG_k=-1/(4\pi\epsilon^2)+O(1)$. Thus $P_kG_k=\delta_0$ distributionally. Choose $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ equal to one on a ball larger than every difference $x-y$ needed for the fixed bounded target and source sets. The function $g=\zeta G_k$ is in $L^1$ and $P_kg=\delta_0+h$ with smooth compactly supported $h$ supported away from zero. Hence $(4\pi^2|\xi|^2-k^2)\widehat g(\xi)=1+\widehat h(\xi)$. For large $|\xi|$ this gives $|\widehat g|\le C(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1}$; for bounded $\xi$ the same estimate follows from $g\in L^1$ with a larger constant. Plancherel now proves $g*:H^{-1}(\mathbb R^3)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ and $g*:L^2\to H^2$. For distributions of bounded support these coincide on the chosen target set with $G_k*$, since the kernels agree on all differences there.

For $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, the distribution $T_\lambda$ defined by $T_\lambda(v)=\lambda(v|_\Gamma)$ (using the complex-bilinear distributional convention) is supported on $\Gamma$ and is in $H^{-1}(\mathbb R^3)$ by step 1.1. Thus $S_k\lambda=G_k*T_\lambda$ is globally $H^1$ near the surface by step 2.1; it has a common trace and solves $P_kS_k\lambda=0$ off $\Gamma$. For smooth $\lambda$, Fubini identifies the convolution with the classical single-layer integral, because $1/|x-y|$ is locally integrable in three dimensions.

Given $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, take a bounded interior lift $F_0$ from step 1.1. On $H^1_0(\Omega^-)$ apply [F2] to $b(v,w)=\int(\nabla v\cdot\overline{\nabla w}+v\bar w)$ and the functional $-b(F_0,w)$. This produces $F=F_0+v$ with trace $\phi$, $(-\Delta+1)F=0$, and $\|F\|_{H^1}\le C\|\phi\|_{H^{1/2}}$. Define $q\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ by $\langle q,g\rangle=b(F,Lg)$ for an interior lift $Lg$. Independence follows since differences of lifts are in $H^1_0$, and boundedness follows from step 1.1. For $f=F1_{\Omega^-}$ and any smooth compactly supported test $v$, two weak integrations by parts give $P_kf(v)=-(1+k^2)\int_{\Omega^-}Fv+q(v|_\Gamma)-\int_\Gamma\phi\partial_nv$. In distributions, the last term is minus the source of the classical double layer. Convolving this equality with $G_k$ is legitimate because $f$ has compact support, and $G_k*P_kf=(P_kG_k)*f=f$. Consequently define $D_k\phi=S_kq-(1+k^2)G_k*f-f.$ For smooth $\phi$, the differentiated fundamental-solution identity and distributional convolution identify this expression away from $\Gamma$ with $\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_k(x-y)\phi(y)dS_y$. The first term is $H^1$ near $\Gamma$, the second is $H^2$ by step 2.1, and $f$ restricts to $F$ and zero on the two sides. This proves the asserted bounded piecewise $H^1$ extension and its uniqueness by density. It also shows its trace jump is $-\phi$.

Away from $\Gamma$, the kernel $G_k(x-y)$ and every target derivative are smooth in the ambient source variable $y$; after restriction to the $C^2$ surface they have uniformly bounded $H^{1/2}$ norms on compact target sets. The source normal in $D_k$ is $C^1$, which suffices for its integral against $\phi\in L^2$. Thus all target derivatives can be passed through these pairings and integrals, proving smoothness in $x$ there. Uniformly for bounded $y$ and $r\to\infty$, $G_k(r\omega-y)=O(r^{-1})$ and $(\partial_r-ik)G_k(r\omega-y)=O(r^{-2})$ together with any fixed finite number of $y$ derivatives; these follow by differentiating $|r\omega-y|=r-\omega\cdot y+O(r^{-1})$. The same estimates hold after one source normal derivative. The $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ norm of the first remainder is $O(r^{-2})$ by its uniform value and first source derivative bounds, so pairing with $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}$ proves the single-layer radiation condition. The double-layer radiation condition follows by integration against $\phi\in L^2(\Gamma)$ and the source normal derivative remainder bound. This proves all assertions.
