citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
nonempty bounded connected extension domain, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then there is
$C=C(\Omega,p)$ such that every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u(x)\,dx.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $\Gamma$ be any compact Lipschitz boundary in the geometry of [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]; no polyhedral restriction is imposed. The interior trace $\gamma^-:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. On every bounded exterior boundary collar $C=\Omega^+\cap U$, where $U$ is a bounded neighborhood of $\Gamma$ with Lipschitz collar boundary, the exterior trace $\gamma^+:H^1(C)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. The corresponding localized assertion holds over each boundary chart. Thus an exterior function has this trace whenever it is $H^1$ up to the boundary on such collars; membership in $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega^+)$ alone does not assert a boundary trace. There is a bounded linear right inverse $L:H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\gamma(Lg)=g$. There is also a bounded extension operator $E:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $(Eu)|_{\Omega^-}=u$.

Let $\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ denote the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ in the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$. Its elements have an $L^6$ representative, the trace $\gamma:\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded, and the right inverse above may be chosen with compact support near $\Gamma$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set whose boundary is locally a Lipschitz graph, with $D$ on one side in each chart. It need not be connected. There is one linear operator $E:H^1(D)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $Ef=f$ almost everywhere on $D$, which maps $H^2(D)$ boundedly into $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Its support can be confined to a fixed bounded neighborhood of $\overline D$. The bounds depend only on a finite choice of boundary charts and cutoffs. In particular no mesh enters them.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used through the cited Countable-Choice and
Dependent-Choice interfaces (completed-product Fubini, approximate identities,
the fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions), for
the countable selections of cutoffs and mollifier scales below, and through the
earlier ACL reconstruction lemma. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be
open, $n\ge1$, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
For an almost-everywhere class $u$ on $\Omega$ the following are equivalent:

1. $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$;
2. $u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $u$ has one measurable ACL representative
   $u^*$ whose classical coordinate derivatives $\partial_i u^*$ exist almost
   everywhere, are measurable, and belong to $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

In that case $\partial_i u^*$ is a representative of $D_i u$ for every
$i$, that is, $D_i u=\partial_i u^*$ almost everywhere.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, there is only the zero class, its representative
$u^*=0$ is ACL, and every displayed assertion holds vacuously.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], is a complete normed space over
$\mathbb K$.

Both endpoints $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, as is $k=0$, where the
assertion reduces to the completeness of $L^p$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the zero space and the assertion is trivial.
The Axiom of Choice is used only to derive Countable Choice for the two
published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative
selection inside the finitely many coordinate classes is finite and
choice-free.

derivations.claim: We justify the Sobolev slices. On each bounded spherical shell $a<|x|<b$ with $R/2<a<R<b$, $u$ belongs to $H^1$: bounded volume and $L^6$ give $L^2$, and its weak gradient is already $L^2$. Use [F4] to approximate it by ambient smooth $u_m$ in $H^1$ on a slightly larger shell. The polar formula [F90] and $a^2\le r^2\le b^2$ bound $\int_{S^2}\|u_m(r\omega)-u_l(r\omega)\|_{H^1(a,b)}^2d\sigma(\omega)$ by $C\|u_m-u_l\|_{H^1}^2$, because the radial derivative of a smooth approximant is $\omega\cdot\nabla u_m$. Take a subsequence with summable successive $H^1$ errors; Cauchy–Schwarz on the finite angular measure and Tonelli show that the successive slice norms are summable for almost every $\omega$. Completeness [F5] gives an $H^1(a,b)$ slice limit, identified by the polar $L^2$ limit with $u(r\omega)$ and derivative $\omega\cdot\nabla u(r\omega)$. Countably many overlapping shells exhaust $r>R/2$, so their representatives agree on overlaps off one angular null set; their values at $R$ define the usual trace, since the one-dimensional $H^1$ endpoint estimate passes smooth approximants to that value. By [F5] the slices are locally absolutely continuous.

For almost every direction $\omega\in S^2$, the radial slice $r\mapsto u(r\omega)$ is locally H1 for $r\ge R$, and $\int_R^\infty|u(r\omega)|^6r^2dr<\infty$. Thus there is a sequence $r_m\to\infty$ with $u(r_m\omega)\to0$. For each such direction the radial derivative is square integrable with weight $r^2$; the one-dimensional fundamental theorem on $[R,r_m]$ and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|u(R\omega)|^2\le\left(\int_R^\infty|\partial_ru(r\omega)|^2r^2dr\right)\left(\int_R^\infty r^{-2}dr\right)=R^{-1}\int_R^\infty|\partial_ru(r\omega)|^2r^2dr.$ Integrating over $S^2$ by [F3,F90] yields $\|u\|_{L^2(\partial B_R)}\le R^{1/2}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\Omega^+\setminus B_R)}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\Gamma$ and the chartwise norm on $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ be as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. For a measurable $g$ define
$$\|g\|_{H^{1/2}_{\mathrm{ch}}(\Gamma)}^2=\|g\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}^2+\int_\Gamma\int_\Gamma\frac{|g(x)-g(y)|^2}{|x-y|^3}\,ds_xds_y.$$
There are constants $c,C>0$ depending only on the fixed finite atlas and partition such that, first for smooth $g$ and then by completion,
$$c\|g\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}\le\|g\|_{H^{1/2}_{\mathrm{ch}}(\Gamma)}\le C\|g\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, bounded, convex and nonempty, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(n)\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Here $u_\Omega=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u\,dx$ is the mean of $u$ over $\Omega$,
which is well defined because $\Omega$ is nonempty open and bounded. The proof
below gives the explicit choice
$$C(n)=\frac{2\,(2^n-1)}{n},$$
which depends only on the dimension; no dependence on $p$, on the shape of
$\Omega$, on $|\Omega|$ or on the regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is used.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\Gamma$ be a polyhedral boundary as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. A **conforming surface triangulation** $\mathcal T_h$ is a finite collection of nondegenerate closed planar triangles covering $\Gamma$, with disjoint relative interiors, such that two distinct triangles meet only in a common full edge, a common vertex, or not at all. For $T\in\mathcal T_h$, write $h_T=\operatorname{diam}(T)$ and let $\rho_T$ be the radius of the largest disk contained in $T$; the family is **shape regular** if $\sup_{h,T}h_T/\rho_T<\infty$, and **quasi-uniform** if $\inf_{h,T}h_T/h>0$ for $h=\max_{T\in\mathcal T_h}h_T$.

The conforming **P0 density space** is $X_h=\{\lambda_h\in L^2(\Gamma):\lambda_h|_T\text{ is constant for every }T\in\mathcal T_h\}$. The continuous inclusion $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Gamma)$ follows because each chart Bessel norm controls its L2 norm and the fixed partition is finite. Hence every $\lambda_h$ defines a bounded functional $v\mapsto\int_\Gamma\lambda_hv$ on $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$; thus $X_h\subset H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$. This inclusion makes the single-layer Galerkin method conforming in its energy space.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, and let
$H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion of
[[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical embedding
$E_s:H^s(\mathbb R^n)\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Write
$\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$ for the Japanese bracket, $\mathcal F$
for the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform, and
$u_g(\phi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}g(\xi)\phi(\xi)\,d\xi$ for the regular tempered
distribution of $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$. Define
$$\mathcal W_s=\bigl\{u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n):\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal Fu=u_g \text{ in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)\text{ for some }g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)\bigr\}.$$
Then:

1. The canonical embedding restricts to a bijection
   $E_s:H^s(\mathbb R^n)\to\mathcal W_s$. Thus, after identifying a completion
   class with its image under $E_s$, $H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ is **exactly** the set
   of tempered distributions whose bracket-weighted Fourier transform is the
   regular distribution of an $L^2$ class, and that class $g$ is unique.
2. The norm identity is exact:
$$\|U\|_{H^s}=\|g\|_2=\bigl\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)\bigr\|_2 \qquad(U\in H^s),$$
   where the last expression means the $L^2$ norm of the unique density $g$ of
   the distributional product $\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)$, and the
   defining completion norm $q_s(\phi)=\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\widehat\phi\|_2$
   of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] is not renormalized.
3. The product $\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal Fu$ is distributional
   multiplication of $\mathcal Fu$ by the smooth polynomially bounded bracket
   weight, not an a priori pointwise product; and $H^s$ elements are completion
   classes, not initially assumed to be functions.

Nothing here replaces the bracket weight by the Laplacian weight
$(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{s/2}$, and no pointwise value of $g$ at an individual
frequency is asserted before $g$ is obtained from the defining condition.

Assume Countable Choice.  For $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and every
multi-index $\alpha$,

$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha u) =(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu, \qquad \mathcal F(x^\alpha u) =\left(-\frac1{2\pi i}\right)^{|\alpha|} \partial_\xi^\alpha\mathcal Fu.$$

Every operation and equality is in $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.

For each zero-extended localized pullback $g_j=(\chi_jv)\circ\Phi_j$ in the chart-space definition, let $g_{j,\epsilon}$ have Fourier transform $1_{\{|\xi|\le\epsilon^{-1}\}}\widehat g_j$. The weighted characterization and differentiation in [F4] give $\|g_j-g_{j,\epsilon}\|_2\le C\epsilon^{1/2}q(g_j)$ and $\|g_{j,\epsilon}\|_{H^1}\le C\epsilon^{-1/2}q(g_j)$ by comparing the weights on the discarded and retained frequencies. Fix Lipschitz chart cutoffs $\beta_j$ equal to one on the fixed chart support of $\chi_j$ and compactly supported inside the charts. Transport $\beta_jg_{j,\epsilon}$ back and sum to obtain $v_\epsilon$. Bounded graph area densities and the finite partition give $\|v-v_\epsilon\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}\le C\epsilon^{1/2}\|v\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}$. Each band-limited function is smooth, and the compactly supported chart products transported to the surface are Lipschitz, including across coplanar face edges. Their restrictions thus belong to $H^1(T)$ on every triangle, even when it crosses such an edge. On each planar face the graph maps are affine with uniformly bounded derivative and inverse derivative; the product and chain rules give $\|\nabla_\Gamma v_\epsilon\|_2\le C\epsilon^{-1/2}\|v\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}$. These constants depend only on the fixed atlas and cutoffs. The averages form an $L^2$ orthogonal projection, so $\|(I-\Pi_h)z\|_2\le\|z\|_2$. Applying the shape-independent convex Poincare inequality [F2] on every triangle gives $\|(I-\Pi_h)v_\epsilon\|_2\le Ch\|\nabla_\Gamma v_\epsilon\|_2$. For $h\le1$, take $\epsilon=h$ and combine these estimates to obtain $\|(I-\Pi_h)v\|_2\le Ch^{1/2}\|v\|_{H^{1/2}}$. For $h>1$, use projection contraction and the fixed $H^{1/2}\to L^2$ inclusion from [F1]. This proves the first estimate with no dependence on any triangle aspect ratio or family shape-regularity bound.

Under the face alignment hypothesis, facewise $C^1$ $\lambda$ with square-integrable derivatives restricts to $H^1(T)$ on each triangle. More generally assume directly that $\lambda|_T\in H^1(T)$. Apply [F2] on the relative interior of each planar triangle, which is convex, to obtain $\|\lambda-\Pi_h\lambda\|_{L^2(T)}\le Ch_T\|\nabla_\Gamma\lambda\|_{L^2(T)}$. Squaring and summing yields $\|\lambda-\Pi_h\lambda\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}\le Ch\|\nabla_\Gamma\lambda\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}$.

For any $\lambda\in L^2(\Gamma)$ put $e=\lambda-\Pi_h\lambda$. For any $w\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, [F3] gives $\int_Te\,ds=0$, hence $\int_\Gamma ew\,ds=\sum_T\int_Te(w-w_T)\,ds.$ Cauchy–Schwarz over the finite element sum and step 1.1 give $|\langle e,w\rangle|\le \|e\|_{L^2}\|w-\Pi_hw\|_{L^2}\le Ch^{1/2}\|e\|_{L^2}\|w\|_{H^{1/2}}.$ Taking the supremum over $\|w\|_{H^{1/2}}\le1$ proves the general negative-norm bound. When the hypotheses of step 1.2 hold, its additional factor $h\|\nabla_\Gamma\lambda\|_{L^2}$ proves the stated $h^{3/2}$ bound.

Let $\mathbb S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ with its usual surface-area measure $dS$, normalized so $\int_{\mathbb S^2}dS=4\pi$. For an integer $\ell\ge0$, let $\mathcal H_\ell$ be the complex vector space of restrictions to $\mathbb S^2$ of homogeneous degree-$\ell$ polynomials $P(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ satisfying $\Delta P=0$. Give $\mathcal H_\ell$ the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb S^2}f\overline g\,dS$, linear in the first argument. An orthonormal basis is not fixed by this definition; the addition-theorem item proves that $\dim\mathcal H_\ell=2\ell+1$ and that such a finite basis exists.

If $Y_{\ell m}\in\mathcal H_\ell$ is later chosen from an orthonormal basis and $v\ne0$, its associated homogeneous harmonic polynomial is $H_{\ell m}(v)=|v|^\ell Y_{\ell m}(v/|v|)$. At $v=0$ use the polynomial value: $H_{00}(0)=Y_{00}$ and $H_{\ell m}(0)=0$ for $\ell>0$. This is the regular-solid-harmonic convention used in the 3D evaluator.

For every integer $\ell\ge0$, the space $\mathcal H_\ell$ of [[def-three-dimensional-spherical-harmonic-space]] has dimension $2\ell+1$. For any orthonormal basis $\{Y_{\ell m}:-\ell\le m\le\ell\}$, there is a basis-independent normalized zonal polynomial $P_\ell$ such that
$$\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}Y_{\ell m}(\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\omega')}=\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}P_\ell(\omega\cdot\omega'),\qquad P_\ell(1)=1.$$
It obeys $|P_\ell(t)|\le1$ for $-1\le t\le1$ and the generating identity
$$\frac1{\sqrt{1-2rt+r^2}}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}r^\ell P_\ell(t),\qquad -1\le t\le1,\quad 0\le r<1.$$
Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $A\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$ be a unital subalgebra which separates points. Then $A$ is dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$ for the supremum metric.
For $n\ge1$, $c\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and $r>0$, the Euclidean closed ball $\overline B_2(c,r)$ and Euclidean sphere $S_2(c,r)$ are compact.

derivations.claim: For a homogeneous polynomial $Q_n$ of degree $n$, direct differentiation and Euler's identity give $\Delta(|x|^{2j}Q_n)=2j(2n+2j+1)|x|^{2j-2}Q_n+|x|^{2j}\Delta Q_n$. For homogeneous $P$ of degree $n$, set $H=P+\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}a_j|x|^{2j}\Delta^jP$, where $a_0=1$ and $a_{j+1}=-a_j/[2(j+1)(2n-2j-1)]$. Substitution into the displayed identity makes the coefficient of each $|x|^{2j}\Delta^{j+1}P$ equal to $a_j+2(j+1)(2n-2j-1)a_{j+1}=0$; the last Laplacian power vanishes by degree. Thus $H$ is homogeneous harmonic and $P-H$ is divisible by $|x|^2$. Induction on degree shows that restrictions of polynomials are finite sums of elements of the spaces $\mathcal H_j$.

The polar-coordinate identity $\Delta=\partial_{rr}+2r^{-1}\partial_r+r^{-2}\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$ applied to $r^\ell Y(\omega)$, whose extension is harmonic by [F1], gives $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y$. On the sphere, integration by parts gives $\langle v,\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}w\rangle=\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}v,w\rangle$: in $(\theta,\phi)$ coordinates integrate the $\phi$ derivative over its period and the $\theta$ term with weight $\sin\theta$; the pole boundary terms vanish because smooth functions and their spherical gradients are bounded while $\sin\theta\to0$. Distinct degrees have distinct eigenvalues, so their spaces are orthogonal.

Choose a finite orthonormal basis from [F2] and write $g=\sum_m c_mY_{\ell m}$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|g(\omega)|^2\le(\sum_m|c_m|^2)(\sum_m|Y_{\ell m}(\omega)|^2)$. Orthonormality identifies the first sum with $\|g\|_2^2$, and [F2] gives the second as $(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$. Taking the supremum proves the evaluation bound.

Real polynomial restrictions contain constants and separate distinct points of $\mathbb S^2$ by a coordinate function. Compactness and [F3] make them dense in real $C(\mathbb S^2)$; applying this separately to real and imaginary parts gives density in complex $C(\mathbb S^2)$. By step 1.1 this is density of the algebraic sum of the $\mathcal H_j$. For continuous $f$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite sum $q$ of harmonic modes with $\|f-q\|_\infty<\varepsilon$. Put $P_{\le N}f=\sum_{\ell=0}^N P_\ell f$ and $V_N=\bigoplus_{\ell=0}^N\mathcal H_\ell$. Orthogonality from step 1.2 makes $f-P_{\le N}f$ orthogonal to $V_N$, so Pythagoras shows $P_{\le N}f$ is a best $L^2$ approximation in $V_N$. For $N$ at least the largest degree in $q$, $\|f-P_{\le N}f\|_2\le\|f-q\|_2\le\sqrt{4\pi}\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, the ordered partial sums converge in $L^2$.

For smooth $f$ and $\ell\ge1$, self-adjointness just proved gives $P_\ell(\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}^m f)=(-\ell(\ell+1))^mP_\ell f$. The finite-dimensional projection is a contraction in $L^2$, hence $\|P_\ell f\|_2\le[\ell(\ell+1)]^{-m}\|\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}^m f\|_2$. Taking $m$ arbitrarily large proves the asserted decay (and degree zero is absorbed into $C_m(f)$).

Let $X_1,X_2,X_3$ be the infinitesimal rotation fields on the sphere about the coordinate axes. Rotations preserve $\mathcal H_\ell$ and surface measure, so $X_j$ preserves $\mathcal H_\ell$ and is skew-adjoint. Expanding these three fields in spherical coordinates gives $X_1^2+X_2^2+X_3^2=\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$. Thus $\sum_j\|X_jg\|_2^2=-\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g,g\rangle=\ell(\ell+1)\|g\|_2^2$, so each $X_j$ has operator norm at most $\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}$ on $\mathcal H_\ell$. Iteration and step 1.3 bound every word of $q$ rotation derivatives pointwise by $\sqrt{(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)}[\ell(\ell+1)]^{q/2}\|g\|_2$. A finite smooth coordinate cover of the compact sphere expresses each coordinate derivative through order $p$ as bounded smooth combinations of words in the $X_j$ of order at most $p$; compactness supplies a finite cover by [F3], and absorbing its chart bounds gives the stated $C_p(1+\ell)^{p+1/2}$ estimate.

For real $z>0$, let $D_z:=z^{-1}\frac{d}{dz}$ and define, for integers $\ell\ge0$,
$$j_\ell(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(\frac{\sin z}{z}\right),\qquad h_\ell^{(1)}(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(-i\frac{e^{iz}}{z}\right).$$
The definition fixes the outgoing $e^{iz}$ convention. The functions solve the radial Helmholtz equation and have the recurrence, origin, Wronskian, and infinity behavior by [[lem-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-radial-solutions]].

These symbolic definitions assert no stable or certified numerical evaluation algorithm for large $\ell$ or $z$.

For the functions of [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]], define
$$L_\ell y:=y''+\frac2z y'+\left(1-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{z^2}\right)y\qquad(z>0).$$
Then $L_\ell j_\ell=L_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}=0$, and for $y=j,h^{(1)}$,
$$y_{\ell+1}(z)=\frac{\ell}{z}y_\ell(z)-y_\ell'(z),\qquad y_\ell'(z)=y_{\ell-1}(z)-\frac{\ell+1}{z}y_\ell(z)\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
The regular-origin and outgoing-infinity normalizations are
$$j_\ell(z)=\frac{z^\ell}{(2\ell+1)!!}+O(z^{\ell+2}),\quad h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=-i(2\ell-1)!!z^{-\ell-1}(1+O(z))\quad(z\downarrow0),$$
$$j_\ell(z)=\frac{\sin(z-\ell\pi/2)}z+O(z^{-2}),\quad h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=(-i)^{\ell+1}\frac{e^{iz}}z+O(z^{-2})\quad(z\to\infty),$$
where $(-1)!!:=1$. Their Wronskian is
$$j_\ell(z)(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z)-j_\ell'(z)h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=\frac{i}{z^2}.$$

derivations.claim: Conjugating the definition in [F1] commutes with its real differential operator; applying that operator to $ie^{-iz}/z$ defines $h_\ell^{(2)}=\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}}$, which solves the same real-coefficient radial equation as its conjugate. The sine identity gives $j_\ell=(h_\ell^{(1)}+h_\ell^{(2)})/2$.

Put $h=h_\ell^{(1)}$. Substitution of $j=(h+\bar h)/2$ into [F2] yields $(\bar h h'-\bar h' h)/2=i/z^2$. The left side is $i\operatorname{Im}(\bar h h')$, giving the stated identity. If $h(z)=0$, its left side is zero, contradicting $z^{-2}>0$; conjugation gives the same nonvanishing for $h_\ell^{(2)}$. The nonzero Wronskian also proves linear independence.
By the chain rule, $\partial_r h(kr)=k h'(kr)$. Multiplying the identity in step 2.1 by $kr^2$ gives $r^2\operatorname{Im}(\bar h(kr)\partial_r h(kr))=r^2 k/(k^2r^2)=1/k$.

Assume Countable Choice and use the negative-sign $2\pi$ normalization.  If
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\widehat f},$$

where $\widehat f$ is the integral Fourier transform.  If
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\mathcal F_2f},$$

where $\mathcal F_2$ is the Plancherel extension.  These equalities are in

Assume Countable Choice. For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, define
$$[f]_{1/2,2}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\int_{\mathbb R^2}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|^2}{|x-y|^3}\,dx\,dy.$$
There is a finite constant $c_*>0$ such that
$$[f]_{1/2,2}^2=c_*\int_{\mathbb R^2}|\xi|\,|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi.$$
Consequently, the norm $\|f\|_2^2+[f]_{1/2,2}^2$ is equivalent on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$ to the Bessel-potential norm $\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. The two completions therefore define the same $H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^2)$ space with equivalent norms.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

routine_steps.claim: In surface coordinates put $r=|x-y|$. The $C^2$ graph bounds give $|n_y\cdot(x-y)|\le Cr^2$ and $|n_y-n_x|\le Cr$. Therefore both kernels $L_V=G_k(x-y)$ and $L_K=\partial_{n_y}G_k(x-y)$ satisfy $|L(x,y)|\le C/r$. Their first target-coordinate derivatives satisfy $|\partial_xL|\le C/r^2$: for $K$, differentiating the numerator tangentially gives $n_y\cdot t_x=(n_y-n_x)\cdot t_x=O(r)$, and differentiating the radial factors gives at worst $O(r^2)O(r^{-4})$. Fixed $k$ only changes the constants. Localize targets and sources by chart cutoffs; for near-diagonal pieces use a common graph chart and absorb its bounded surface Jacobian into the source kernel. Off-diagonal pieces have bounded first target derivatives. Each resulting chart kernel $l(z,w)$, extended with cutoffs by zero, thus has size $C/|z-w|$ and target derivative size $C/|z-w|^2$.

For a target translation $h$, $\delta=|h|<1/4$, consider $l(z+h,w)-l(z,w)$. Where $|z-w|\le2\delta$, integrate each size bound separately (including the ball around $z+h$), obtaining $C\delta$. On the complement the segment from $z$ to $z+h$ stays at distance at least $|z-w|/2$, so the derivative bound and polar integration give $C\delta\int_{2\delta}^{C}r^{-1}dr\le C\delta(1+|\log\delta|)$. This bounds both the supremum over $z$ of its absolute integral in $w$ and the supremum over $w$ of its absolute integral in $z$. Cauchy–Schwarz in the weighted kernel integral then proves the Schur estimate $\|Tf\|_2\le C\|f\|_2$ and $\|(Tf)(\cdot+h)-Tf\|_2\le C\delta(1+|\log\delta|)\|f\|_2.$ Indeed $|\int lf|^2\le(\int|l|)(\int|l||f|^2)$ and integration uses the two bounds. The cutoff support is fixed and bounded.

For any $0<s<1$, integrate the square of the last translation bound against $|h|^{-2-2s}dh$ for $|h|<1$; polar coordinates give the finite integral $C\int_0^1r^{1-2s}(1+|\log r|)^2dr$. The $|h|\ge1$ part is bounded by the $L^2$ estimate. Hence each localized $T$ maps $L^2$ boundedly to $H^s$ in the difference norm, in particular for $s=3/4$. To check the equivalent Fourier norm directly, apply Plancherel to differences and Tonelli: the inner integral $\int|e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot h}-1|^2|h|^{-2-2s}dh$ equals $c_s|\xi|^{2s}$ by scaling and rotation, with $0<c_s<\infty$ since near zero the numerator is $O(|h|^2)$ and at infinity it is bounded. This also identifies the half-order norm in [F3].

A bounded family of functions supported in a fixed compact chart and bounded in $H^{3/4}$ is precompact in $H^{1/2}$. Here is a direct verification. For a smooth compactly supported mollifier $\rho_\epsilon$, $|1-\widehat\rho(\epsilon\xi)|\le C\min(\epsilon|\xi|,1)$ and thus $\|f-\rho_\epsilon*f\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\epsilon^{1/4}\|f\|_{H^{3/4}}$ by the Fourier weights. For fixed $\epsilon$, the convolutions and their first two derivatives are uniformly bounded and have one fixed bounded support, by Cauchy–Schwarz with the fixed derivatives of $\rho_\epsilon$. They are precompact in $C^1$ on a containing rectangle: choose increasingly fine finite grids, take convergent subsequences of the finitely many value and first-derivative samples, and use the uniform first/second derivative bounds to extend sample convergence uniformly. A diagonal subsequence gives convergence of both values and first derivatives. Uniform $C^1$ convergence on a fixed compact support implies $H^{1/2}$ convergence, since the difference-norm integrand near the diagonal is bounded by $\|\nabla f\|_\infty^2|z-w|^{-1}$ and away from the diagonal by a constant times $\|f\|_\infty^2|z-w|^{-3}$. The uniform mollification error now gives finite nets for the original family in $H^{1/2}$, hence compact closure in its complete Hilbert norm.

Since $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ embeds boundedly in $L^2(\Gamma)$, steps 1.1–4.1 and the finite chart partition make both boundary integrals compact on $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$. The single-layer integral agrees on smooth densities with $V_k$ of [F1]. For smooth densities, the normal-slice limits computed in [F2] are the Sobolev traces of [F1]: the planar half-Poisson terms have uniformly bounded mass, and the integrable $C/r$ curvature remainders and smooth-density remainders have uniform integral bounds on the compact surface, so the pointwise slice limits also converge in $L^2$ by dominated convergence. The normal-slice estimate proved in [F1] identifies this $L^2$ limit with the weak trace. Consequently [F2] identifies the double-layer exterior trace with $\tfrac12I+K_k$. Boundedness and density extend both identities to every $H^{1/2}$ density. Therefore $A_{k,\eta}=\tfrac12I+K_k-i\eta V_k$, and its displayed compact perturbation follows by addition and scalar multiplication of the compact maps just proved.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume [[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]].

Let $\Omega^-$ be a nonempty bounded connected open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ whose boundary $\Gamma=\partial\Omega^-$ is a compact connected orientable Lipschitz surface. A **Lipschitz graph chart** is a rigid coordinate change in which $\Gamma$ is the graph $x_3=\psi(x_1,x_2)$ of a Lipschitz function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$, with $\Omega^-$ on one side of that graph. A **polyhedral boundary** is such a boundary made from finitely many planar polygonal faces meeting along edges and vertices; all surface-discretization claims below use this polyhedral subclass. Put $\Omega^+=\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline{\Omega^-}$ and assume $\Omega^+$ is connected. For the fixed-atlas space conventions below, the boundary data include a compatible Borel surface measure $dS$ and an almost-everywhere unit outward normal $n$, with the following graph realizations and bounded positive graph area densities on every chosen chart. These compatible realizations are supplied data for the Countable-Choice space assertions, not conclusions from bare Lipschitzness under Countable Choice. Under the Axiom of Choice, [[lem-bem-lipschitz-graph-sobolev-and-green-interface]] constructs them for every compact Lipschitz boundary and proves their compatibility; the general analytical trace and layer theorems state that axiom. On polyhedral charts the data are directly the finite face areas and face normals. The normal points from $\Omega^-$ into $\Omega^+$. In a rigid chart with $\Omega^-$ above the graph $x_3=\psi(x_1,x_2)$ it is $n=(\partial_1\psi,\partial_2\psi,-1)/\sqrt{1+|\nabla\psi|^2}$ almost everywhere; reverse the sign when the domain is below the graph. Rigid coordinates transform this vector to physical coordinates. The graph surface measure is $dS=\sqrt{1+|\nabla\psi|^2}\,dx_1dx_2$. Compatibility on overlaps is part of the fixed boundary data; the cited AC graph theorem proves it for arbitrary Lipschitz charts. On a polyhedron these are the face-area measure and outward face normals.

Fix a finite Lipschitz graph atlas $\{(U_j,\psi_j)\}_{j=1}^J$, with surface parametrizations $\Phi_j(z)=(z,\psi_j(z))$ in the rigid chart coordinates, and a subordinate finite Lipschitz partition of unity $\{\chi_j\}_{j=1}^J$ whose chartwise supports have positive distance from the chart edges. On $\mathbb R^2$, use the real subspace of the real-order Bessel-potential completion in [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]]. Its published norm uses the weight $(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$. Fix here the equivalent Hilbert norm
$$q(g)^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}|\widehat g(\xi)|^2d\xi.$$
The inequalities $(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\le(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\le2\pi(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$ identify the same completion and classes under the negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier convention of [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-fractional-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the

4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Fix $a>0$, $k>0$, and $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb S^2;\mathbb C)$. Write $S_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=a\}$. The sound-soft exterior Helmholtz problem is to find a complex-valued $u\in C^2(\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>a\})$ that extends continuously to $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|\ge a\}$ and satisfies $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ for $|x|>a$, with boundary restriction $u|_{S_a}(a\omega)=f(\omega)$, and
$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\sup_{\omega\in\mathbb S^2}\left|r\bigl(\partial_r u(r\omega)-ik u(r\omega)\bigr)\right|=0.$$
The time factor is $e^{-i\omega t}$, so this is the outgoing convention. The obstacle is the closed ball $\{|x|\le a\}$; its boundary is smooth and its exterior is connected. This definition makes no claim for nonspherical obstacles or nonsmooth data.

Let $\mathcal H_\ell$ be the degree-$\ell$ spaces on $\mathbb S^2$ from [[def-three-dimensional-spherical-harmonic-space]], with surface measure of total mass $4\pi$, and let $P_\ell$ be orthogonal projection in $L^2(\mathbb S^2)$. Define $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$ by the polar-coordinate identity $\Delta=\partial_{rr}+2r^{-1}\partial_r+r^{-2}\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$. Then $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g=-\ell(\ell+1)g$ for $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$; for all smooth $v,w$ on the sphere, $\langle v,\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}w\rangle=\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}v,w\rangle$; the spaces are mutually orthogonal and their algebraic sum is uniformly dense in $C(\mathbb S^2;\mathbb C)$. For smooth $f$, for every integer $m\ge1$ there is a constant $C_m(f)$ such that $\|P_\ell f\|_2\le C_m(f)(1+\ell)^{-m}$. For $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$,
$$\|g\|_\infty\le\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}}\,\|g\|_2.$$
For each integer $p\ge0$ there is $C_p$ independent of $\ell,g$ such that $\|g\|_{C^p(\mathbb S^2)}\le C_p(1+\ell)^{p+1/2}\|g\|_2$.
The angular Dirichlet form satisfies $-\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g,g\rangle=\ell(\ell+1)\|g\|_2^2$ for $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$.
For every continuous $f$, the ordered partial sums $\sum_{\ell=0}^N P_\ell f$ converge to $f$ in $L^2(\mathbb S^2)$.

For real $z>0$, let $D_z:=z^{-1}\frac{d}{dz}$ and define, for integers $\ell\ge0$,
$$j_\ell(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(\frac{\sin z}{z}\right),\qquad h_\ell^{(1)}(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(-i\frac{e^{iz}}{z}\right).$$
The definition fixes the outgoing $e^{iz}$ convention. The functions solve the radial Helmholtz equation and have the recurrence, origin, Wronskian, and infinity behavior by [[lem-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-radial-solutions]].

These symbolic definitions assert no stable or certified numerical evaluation algorithm for large $\ell$ or $z$.

For the functions of [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]], define
$$L_\ell y:=y''+\frac2z y'+\left(1-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{z^2}\right)y\qquad(z>0).$$
Then $L_\ell j_\ell=L_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}=0$, and for $y=j,h^{(1)}$,
$$y_{\ell+1}(z)=\frac{\ell}{z}y_\ell(z)-y_\ell'(z),\qquad y_\ell'(z)=y_{\ell-1}(z)-\frac{\ell+1}{z}y_\ell(z)\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
The regular-origin and outgoing-infinity normalizations are
$$j_\ell(z)=\frac{z^\ell}{(2\ell+1)!!}+O(z^{\ell+2}),\quad h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=-i(2\ell-1)!!z^{-\ell-1}(1+O(z))\quad(z\downarrow0),$$
$$j_\ell(z)=\frac{\sin(z-\ell\pi/2)}z+O(z^{-2}),\quad h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=(-i)^{\ell+1}\frac{e^{iz}}z+O(z^{-2})\quad(z\to\infty),$$
where $(-1)!!:=1$. Their Wronskian is
$$j_\ell(z)(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z)-j_\ell'(z)h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=\frac{i}{z^2}.$$

For real $z>0$, let $h_\ell^{(1)}$ be defined in [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]] and set $h_\ell^{(2)}(z)=\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(z)}$. Then both solve the degree-$\ell$ spherical radial Helmholtz equation, are linearly independent, and
$$\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(z)}(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z)\bigr)=z^{-2}.$$
In particular, neither vanishes for $z>0$, and for $k>0$, $r>0$,
$$r^2\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)}\,\partial_r h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)\bigr)=1/k.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $\ell$ and any $v\in\mathcal H_\ell$. Define $w_v(r)=\langle u(r,\cdot),v\rangle_{L^2(\mathbb S^2)}$. Integrating the polar-coordinate Helmholtz equation against $v$, using $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}v=-\ell(\ell+1)v$ and the angular integration-by-parts identity from [F2], gives $w_v''+2r^{-1}w_v'+(k^2-\ell(\ell+1)r^{-2})w_v=0$. Since this holds for every vector in the finite-dimensional space, the projected vector $u_\ell(r,\cdot)$ solves the same scalar radial equation componentwise.

The two functions $h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ and $h_\ell^{(2)}(kr)$ solve this equation and have nonzero Wronskian by [F3]–[F4]; hence at any fixed $r_0>a$ their value-derivative vectors form an invertible $2\times2$ matrix. Solve this matrix equation to match a coefficient and its derivative at $r_0$. The difference then solves a first-order system $Y'=M(r)Y$ with continuous $M$ and zero initial data. On each compact interval where $\|M\|\le C$, integration gives $|Y(r)|\le C\int_{r_0}^r|Y(s)|ds$ (or the reversed integral for $r<r_0$); Grönwall's inequality gives $Y=0$. Extending across compact intervals proves every coefficient is a linear combination of the two modes.

Apply the uniform radiation condition [F1] to any $v\in\mathcal H_\ell$ and integrate it against $\bar v$; its coefficient tends to zero because its magnitude is bounded by the uniform supremum times $\|v\|_{L^1}$. At $\ell=0$, direct differentiation of $h_0^{(1)}(z)=-ie^{iz}/z$ gives $(h_0^{(1)})'=(i-z^{-1})h_0^{(1)}$, and conjugation gives the corresponding incoming formula. For $\ell\ge1$ use the derivative recurrence in [F3]. In both cases the asymptotic gives $r(\partial_r-ik)h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)\to0$. For the incoming conjugate, the same recurrence gives $r(\partial_r-ik)h_\ell^{(2)}(kr)=-2i\,\overline{(-i)^{\ell+1}}e^{-ikr}+o(1)$, whose magnitude tends to $2$. Thus its coefficient in the mode combination from step 1.2 must vanish. Since this holds for every $v$, the projected vector is $c_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ for a fixed $c_\ell\in\mathcal H_\ell$. The argument treats each degree separately and uses no interchange of the degree sum with the limit $r\to\infty$.

The weak definition fixes the normalization at infinity through $u\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$; arbitrary additive constants are excluded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<n$ and $p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. There is a constant $C(n,p)$ such that
$$\|u\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\mathbb R^n)}\le C(n,p)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}$$
for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$; here $|Du|$ is the Euclidean norm of the weak gradient.

For every $y\in\mathbb R^3$, the locally integrable kernel $G_3(x,y)=(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}$ of [[def-bem-newtonian-kernel-in-three-dimensions]] satisfies $-\Delta_xG_3(x,y)=\delta_y$ in the sense of distributions: for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}G_3(x,y)(-\Delta\varphi(x))\,dx=\varphi(y).$$

For $x\ne y$ in $\mathbb R^3$, the Newton kernel is $G_3(x,y)=(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}$. Its distributional fundamental-solution property $-\Delta_xG_3(x,y)=\delta_y$ is proved in [[lem-bem-newtonian-kernel-is-fundamental-solution]]. The kernel fixes the sign and $4\pi$ normalization for every three-dimensional layer operator on this page.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

For $t>0$ and $z\in\mathbb R^2$, let
$$P_t(z)=\frac{t}{2\pi(|z|^2+t^2)^{3/2}}.$$
Then $P_t\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ has integral one and, under the negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier convention,
$$\widehat{P_t}(\xi)=e^{-2\pi|\xi|t}\qquad(\xi\in\mathbb R^2).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set whose boundary is locally a Lipschitz graph, with $D$ on one side in each chart. It need not be connected. There is one linear operator $E:H^1(D)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $Ef=f$ almost everywhere on $D$, which maps $H^2(D)$ boundedly into $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Its support can be confined to a fixed bounded neighborhood of $\overline D$. The bounds depend only on a finite choice of boundary charts and cutoffs. In particular no mesh enters them.

derivations.claim: By [F1], extension and a bounded-support cutoff put $u^-$ in $L^6(\Omega^-)$; $u^+\in L^6(\Omega^+)$ by definition. Thus $U\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$. Both pieces are $H^1$ in bounded boundary collars: on such a collar Holder gives local $L^2$ from $L^6$, and their gradients are already $L^2$. The fixed finite atlas also gives $\phi\in L^2(\Gamma)\subset L^1(\Gamma)$.

For a compactly supported smooth $\eta$, integration by parts for one weak derivative gives $\langle\partial_j U,\eta\rangle=\int_{\Omega^-}(\partial_j u^-)\eta+\int_{\Omega^+}(\partial_j u^+)\eta+\int_\Gamma\phi n_j\eta\,dS.$ Here is a polyhedral justification that introduces no hidden edge flux. In a graph chart integrate the vertical derivative by the one-dimensional fundamental theorem; for tangential derivatives use the graph change $x_3=t+\psi(x')$ and its piecewise affine chain rule. The graph boundary contribution is $(u^+-u^-)n_j\,dS$. A chart partition sums these formulas; derivatives of the partition cancel. For the approximation, extend each collar restriction across the boundary using [F6], apply a bounded-support cutoff, and mollify. The derivative commutation and $L^2$ approximate-identity convergence in [F4], applied to the function and each weak first derivative, give $H^1$ convergence; the bounded trace in [F1] gives trace convergence. Thus the displayed identity passes from smooth restrictions to the given pieces. Internal planar-sector boundaries cancel because the restrictions of one $H^1$ function have the same interface trace. Only first derivatives are integrated and edges have surface measure zero; no derivative of the discontinuous face normal is taken. The imposed jump makes $u^+-u^-=\phi$. Taking the divergence of the displayed distributional identity, and using stationarity for the smooth global test $\eta$, gives $\langle-\Delta U,\eta\rangle=\int_\Gamma\phi\,\partial_n\eta\,dS.$

Put $P(x)=\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_3(x,y)\phi(y)dS_y$ off $\Gamma$. Since $|\partial_{n_y}G_3|\le(4\pi)^{-1}|x-y|^{-2}$ and $\int_{B_R(a)}|x-y|^{-2}dx\le CR$ uniformly in $a,y$, [F3] defines $P\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R^3)$ and gives $\int_{B_R(a)}|P|\le CR\|\phi\|_{L^1(\Gamma)}.$ For the uniform ball estimate, if $|a-y|\le2R$ enclose the ball in $B_{3R}(y)$ and integrate radially; otherwise $|x-y|\ge|a-y|/2>R/2$, giving the same bound. Off $\Gamma$ all kernel derivatives are uniformly bounded on compact sets, so differentiation under the surface integral proves smoothness and harmonicity. Differentiating [F2] with respect to the source variable gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\partial_{n_y}G_3(x,y)(-\Delta\eta(x))dx=\partial_n\eta(y).$ This differentiation is valid distributionally: $|x-y|^{-2}$ is locally volume integrable, and integration by parts outside a ball of radius $\epsilon$ leaves a boundary term $O(\epsilon)$ for the first derivative of $G_3$. Fubini using that same local integrability therefore yields $\langle-\Delta P,\eta\rangle=\int_\Gamma\phi\partial_n\eta\,dS$.

Set $w=U-P$. Steps 2.1 and 2.2 show $\Delta w=0$ distributionally on the whole space. Choose a nonnegative unit-mass smooth bump $\rho$ supported in $B_1$ and let $w_\epsilon=w*\rho_\epsilon$. By [F4], $w_\epsilon$ is smooth and harmonic everywhere: $\Delta w_\epsilon(x)=\langle w,\Delta\rho_\epsilon(x-\cdot)\rangle=0$. Holder and step 2.2 give, for fixed $\epsilon$, $\int_{B_R(a)}|w_\epsilon|\le C(R+\epsilon)^{5/2}\|U\|_6+C(R+\epsilon)\|\phi\|_1.$ For a smooth harmonic $h$, differentiation of its spherical average gives $\frac{d}{dr}[(4\pi)^{-1}\int_{S^2}h(a+r\omega)d\omega]=(4\pi r^2)^{-1}\int_{B_r(a)}\Delta h=0$ by [F5]. Its limit at zero is $h(a)$, and radial integration gives the ball mean-value formula. Apply this to $h=w_\epsilon$ to obtain $|w_\epsilon(a)|\le |B_R|^{-1}\int_{B_R(a)}|w_\epsilon|\to0$ as $R\to\infty$. Thus $w_\epsilon=0$. Localizing $w$ to a slightly larger bounded set and applying the $L^1$ approximate-identity convergence of [F4] gives $w_\epsilon\to w$ in $L^1$ on every compact set. Hence $U=P$ almost everywhere. The smooth harmonic $P$ supplies the asserted representatives.

Fix a face-interior point $x$ and select a planar smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in that face and equal to one in a neighborhood of $x$. Split $\phi=\chi\phi+(1-\chi)\phi$. The second density is supported a positive distance from $x$, so its potential extends smoothly through a neighborhood of $x$ and has boundary value its kernel integral. For the first density, choose planar coordinates with outward normal $e_3$. Direct differentiation gives the potential $\frac12P_t*(\chi\phi)$ for $t>0$ and $-\frac12P_{|t|}*(\chi\phi)$ for $t<0$, where $P_t(z)=t/(2\pi(|z|^2+t^2)^{3/2})$. Its mass is one by [F5], while its mass outside each fixed disk tends to zero by direct radial integration. Uniform continuity of the compactly supported $C^1$ density therefore gives the two limits $\pm\phi(x)/2$, locally uniformly in the face interior. The same-face boundary kernel is identically zero, and the complementary integral is nonsingular near $x$, proving the claimed $K_{\rm ker}$ formula. Local uniform convergence also implies local $L^2$ convergence. On a compact tangential set $K$, parametrize either side by its nonnegative normal distance $t$. For $t>0$ the $H^1$ slice identity $\|f(\cdot,t)-\gamma f\|_{L^2(K)}^2\le t\int_0^t\|\partial_s f(\cdot,s)\|_{L^2(K)}^2ds$ follows from the fundamental theorem and the $H^1$ approximation constructed in step 2.1; hence those same local $L^2$ limits are the Sobolev traces. Exhaust each open face by compact subsets; the finite edge and vertex set has area zero. This proves the almost-everywhere trace-average assertion.

Finally, facewise $C^1$ functions agreeing on shared edges are continuous piecewise $C^1$ in each piecewise affine graph chart. Their weak first derivatives are the bounded sectorwise derivatives: integration by parts on the planar sectors cancels all shared-edge boundary terms. After the chart cutoffs they belong to $H^1$ on $\mathbb R^2$, hence to its $H^{1/2}$ Bessel space by the Fourier weight inequality. Thus such densities satisfy the stated $H^{1/2}$ hypothesis even when nonzero at edges and vertices. No face-interior-core density assertion at the critical exponent is needed.

boundaries.reason: The boundary is nonempty by the polyhedral-domain hypotheses.

boundaries.evidence: The representation is linear in phi, so zero density gives the zero kernel potential; the identity in step 4.1 applies to this input.

boundaries.reason: No cardinality-one or unit-parameter endpoint is asserted.
The boundary is a Lipschitz polyhedron and the theorem excludes degenerate domain geometry.

The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are explicit hypotheses; the proof uses the stated trace and mollifier suppliers in steps 1.1–4.1.

The kernel representation is not a biconditional.

Restated F1 accurately and supplied step 2.1 approximation using the bounded Lipschitz extension supplier, now explicitly cited as F6 for both interior and exterior collars, followed by derivative commutation and L2 approximate-identity convergence in F4. Bounded trace convergence passes the first-order identity with no edge flux. Step 4.1 cites the actual approximation for the normal-slice identity, preserving the full Sobolev-density representation and face-interior half-jumps. This is the repairer's check, not independent review.

prior_risk_reviews.notes: All six steps checked. Piecewise weak first derivative adds phi n surface term, giving -Delta U source integral phi partial_n eta with no edge-normal differentiation. Kernel derivative is locally volume integrable, and ball integral O(R)||phi||1 plus U in L6 makes harmonic mollified difference vanish by ball means as R grows. Planar Poisson localization gives face-interior half jumps and H1 slices identify weak traces; no pointwise edge assertion or false face-interior core density used.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<n$ and $p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. There is a constant $C(n,p)$ such that
$$\|u\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\mathbb R^n)}\le C(n,p)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}$$
for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$; here $|Du|$ is the Euclidean norm of the weak gradient.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $\Gamma$ be any compact Lipschitz boundary in the geometry of [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]; no polyhedral restriction is imposed. The interior trace $\gamma^-:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. On every bounded exterior boundary collar $C=\Omega^+\cap U$, where $U$ is a bounded neighborhood of $\Gamma$ with Lipschitz collar boundary, the exterior trace $\gamma^+:H^1(C)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. The corresponding localized assertion holds over each boundary chart. Thus an exterior function has this trace whenever it is $H^1$ up to the boundary on such collars; membership in $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega^+)$ alone does not assert a boundary trace. There is a bounded linear right inverse $L:H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\gamma(Lg)=g$. There is also a bounded extension operator $E:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $(Eu)|_{\Omega^-}=u$.

Let $\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ denote the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ in the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$. Its elements have an $L^6$ representative, the trace $\gamma:\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded, and the right inverse above may be chosen with compact support near $\Gamma$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For the connected exterior domain $\Omega^+$ of [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]], let
$$E^+(\Omega^+)=\{u\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega^+):u\in L^6(\Omega^+),\ \nabla u\in L^2(\Omega^+)\}.$$
There is a constant $C$ depending only on $\Omega^-$ and its fixed trace atlas such that every $u\in E^+(\Omega^+)$ has $\gamma^+u\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and
$$\|\gamma^+u\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}\le C\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\Omega^+)}.$$

For $x\ne y$ in $\mathbb R^3$, the Newton kernel is $G_3(x,y)=(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}$. Its distributional fundamental-solution property $-\Delta_xG_3(x,y)=\delta_y$ is proved in [[lem-bem-newtonian-kernel-is-fundamental-solution]]. The kernel fixes the sign and $4\pi$ normalization for every three-dimensional layer operator on this page.

Write $G_3$ for the Newton kernel of [[def-bem-newtonian-kernel-in-three-dimensions]]. For a smooth density $\lambda$ on $\Gamma$, the classical single-layer potential is
$$S\lambda(x)=\int_\Gamma G_3(x,y)\lambda(y)\,dS_y,\qquad x\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\Gamma.$$

Let $\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ in the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|
abla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$, using its $L^6$ representative and the trace from [[lem-bem-lipschitz-trace-and-lifting]]. For $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, consider the equation for $u\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}
abla u\cdot
abla v\,dx=\langle\lambda,\gamma vangle_\Gamma\qquad(v\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)).$$
Call such a function a weak single-layer potential and write $S\lambda=u$ when it exists. Define the exterior energy space $E^+(\Omega^+)=\{u\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega^+):u\in L^6(\Omega^+),\ 
abla u\in L^2(\Omega^+)\}$. For a weakly harmonic function $u^-\in H^1(\Omega^-)$, define its weak outward conormal by $\langle\partial_n^-u^-,gangle=\int_{\Omega^-}
abla u^-\cdot
abla L^-g$, where $L^-g$ is any $H^1$ trace lift. For a harmonic $u^+\in E^+(\Omega^+)$, use the same fixed normal $n$ by $\langle\partial_n^+u^+,gangle=-\int_{\Omega^+}
abla u^+\cdot
abla L^+g$ for a compactly supported local lift. In either case the value is independent of the lift: the difference of two lifts has zero trace, and weak harmonicity makes its gradient pairing zero. The exterior formula also gives $\int_{\Omega^+}
abla u^+\cdot
abla v^+=-\langle\partial_n^+u^+,\gamma^+v^+angle$ for every $v^+\in E^+(\Omega^+)$. Indeed, subtract a compactly supported lift of $\gamma^+v^+$; the remaining zero-trace finite-energy function is approximated in gradient norm by compactly supported zero-trace functions using radial cutoffs: $\|v^+
abla\chi_R\|_2\le C\|v^+\|_{L^6(\{R<|x|<2R\})}	o0$. Boundary-chart flattening, zero extension, inward translation, and convolution approximate each zero-trace cutoff by interior smooth tests, so weak harmonicity makes its gradient pairing zero. This proves the energy identity without a flux assumption at infinity. Existence, uniqueness, agreement with the displayed kernel for smooth densities, and the conormal jump are proved in [[thm-bem-single-layer-transmission-mapping-and-coercivity]]. The weak definition fixes the normalization at infinity through $u\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$; arbitrary additive constants are excluded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, and the compact Lipschitz geometry and normal $n$ of [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. Let $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and let $(u^-,u^+)\in H^1(\Omega^-)\times E^+(\Omega^+)$ satisfy
$$\gamma^-u^- -\gamma^+u^+=-\phi,$$
$$\int_{\Omega^-}\nabla u^-\cdot\nabla v+\int_{\Omega^+}\nabla u^+\cdot\nabla v=0\qquad(v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)).$$
Then, with smooth representatives off $\Gamma$,
$$u^\pm(x)=\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_3(x,y)\phi(y)\,dS_y,\qquad x\in\Omega^\pm.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent for each $x\notin\Gamma$, and equality holds without any vanishing condition at edges or vertices.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, and the polyhedral geometry and normal $n$ of [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. Let $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and let $(u^-,u^+)\in H^1(\Omega^-)\times E^+(\Omega^+)$ satisfy
$$\gamma^-u^- -\gamma^+u^+=-\phi,$$
$$\int_{\Omega^-}\nabla u^-\cdot\nabla v+\int_{\Omega^+}\nabla u^+\cdot\nabla v=0\qquad(v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)).$$
Then, with smooth representatives off $\Gamma$,
$$u^\pm(x)=\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_3(x,y)\phi(y)\,dS_y,\qquad x\in\Omega^\pm.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent for each $x\notin\Gamma$, and equality holds without any vanishing condition at edges or vertices.

If additionally the restriction of $\phi$ to each closed face extends to a $C^1$ function on a planar neighborhood of that face, define, at a face-interior point $x$,
$$K_{\rm ker}\phi(x)=\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_3(x,y)\phi(y)\,dS_y.$$
This integral is absolutely convergent (the same-face integrand is zero away from $y=x$), and the interior/exterior normal limits are $K_{\rm ker}\phi(x)\mp\phi(x)/2$. Thus their Sobolev trace average agrees almost everywhere with $K_{\rm ker}\phi$; equivalently this is its principal-value realization. All assertions about values at edges and vertices themselves remain Sobolev trace assertions, not a pointwise half-jump formula there. In particular the statement includes facewise smooth densities agreeing across shared edges and taking nonzero values there.

routine_steps.claim: The affine class is nonempty: choose a bounded interior trace lift $L\phi$ from [F1] and take $(u_0^-,u_0^+)=(-L\phi,0)$. Its trace jump is $-\phi$ and its energy is at most $C\|\phi\|_{H^{1/2}}^2$. Let $Z=\mathcal A_0$, the linear space of matching-trace pairs.

Equip $Z$ with $a_Z(v,w)=\int_{\Omega^-}
abla v^-\cdot
abla w^-+\int_{\Omega^+}
abla v^+\cdot
abla w^+$. A matching pair glues to a function $v$ on $\mathbb R^3$. In each Lipschitz graph chart, integration by parts for smooth approximants gives the distributional derivative of the glued function as the two piecewise derivatives plus the interface term $(\gamma^+v^+ -\gamma^-v^-)n_j$; trace continuity from [F1] passes this identity to $H^1$ functions, and the interface term vanishes. The glued function is in $L^6$: the exterior part is by definition in $L^6$, and the bounded interior part has a bounded $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ extension from [F1], to which [A1] applies after a bounded-support cutoff. Its global weak gradient is the two piecewise gradients. First show that any such $L^6$ function with global gradient in $L^2$ belongs to $\dot H^1$: take cutoffs $\chi_R=1$ on $B_R$, supported in $B_{2R}$, with $|
abla\chi_R|\le C/R$. The gradient tail tends to zero, and Hölder gives $R^{-1}\|v\|_{L^2(B_{2R}\setminus B_R)}\le C\|v\|_{L^6(B_{2R}\setminus B_R)}	o0$. Thus $\chi_Rv	o v$ in gradient norm; each compactly supported H1 cutoff is approximated in H1 by smooth compactly supported functions. Hence $v\in\dot H^1$, and [A1] gives $\|v\|_6\le C\|
abla v\|_2$. A Cauchy sequence in $Z$ now glues to a Cauchy sequence in $\dot H^1$; its limit restricts to an interior H1 function and an exterior $E^+$ function, and bounded traces preserve the matching condition. Hence $Z$ is complete in $a_Z$. Also $a_Z(v,v)=0$ forces the glued $L^6$ function to be a constant and therefore zero, so $a_Z$ is a Hilbert inner product.

The trace jump is the affine constraint. For any $g\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, restrict the bounded global lift $Lg$ of [F1] to both sides; the resulting matching pair lies in $Z$. Stationarity in step 3.1 and the weak conormal conventions [F4] give $\langle\partial_n^-u^- -\partial_n^+u^+,gangle=0$. Thus the conormals agree. The exterior energy trace bound [F2] and energy bound in step 3.1 bound $\gamma^+u^+$; the identity $\gamma^-u^-=\gamma^+u^+-\phi$ then bounds the interior trace and their average. For the common conormal use the interior lift alone: $|\langle q_\phi,gangle|=|\int_{\Omega^-}
abla u^-\cdot
abla L^-g|\le C\|
