The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For every $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, with $\Gamma$ as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]], there is a unique $u=S\lambda\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfying the weak single-layer equation of [[def-bem-laplace-layer-potentials-and-energy-spaces]]. It is harmonic on $\Omega^-$ and $\Omega^+$, its two traces agree, and its weak conormal traces satisfy
$$\partial_n^-u-\partial_n^+u=\lambda\quad\hbox{in }H^{-1/2}(\Gamma).$$
The trace operator $V\lambda:=\gamma u$ maps $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ boundedly into $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, and there are constants $C,c>0$ depending on $\Gamma$ such that
$$\|u\|_{\dot H^1}+\|V\lambda\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}},\qquad \langle\lambda,V\lambda\rangle_\Gamma\ge c\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2.$$
If $\lambda\in L^\infty(\Gamma)$ (in particular for facewise smooth densities reaching edges or discontinuous P0 densities), this weak potential agrees away from $\Gamma$ with $\int_\Gamma(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}\lambda(y)dS_y$.

Write $G_3$ for the Newton kernel of [[def-bem-newtonian-kernel-in-three-dimensions]]. For a smooth density $\lambda$ on $\Gamma$, the classical single-layer potential is
$$S\lambda(x)=\int_\Gamma G_3(x,y)\lambda(y)\,dS_y,\qquad x\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\Gamma.$$

Let $\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ in the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|
abla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$, using its $L^6$ representative and the trace from [[lem-bem-lipschitz-trace-and-lifting]]. For $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, consider the equation for $u\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}
abla u\cdot
abla v\,dx=\langle\lambda,\gamma vangle_\Gamma\qquad(v\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)).$$
Call such a function a weak single-layer potential and write $S\lambda=u$ when it exists. Define the exterior energy space $E^+(\Omega^+)=\{u\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega^+):u\in L^6(\Omega^+),\ 
abla u\in L^2(\Omega^+)\}$. For a weakly harmonic function $u^-\in H^1(\Omega^-)$, define its weak outward conormal by $\langle\partial_n^-u^-,gangle=\int_{\Omega^-}
abla u^-\cdot
abla L^-g$, where $L^-g$ is any $H^1$ trace lift. For a harmonic $u^+\in E^+(\Omega^+)$, use the same fixed normal $n$ by $\langle\partial_n^+u^+,gangle=-\int_{\Omega^+}
abla u^+\cdot
abla L^+g$ for a compactly supported local lift. In either case the value is independent of the lift: the difference of two lifts has zero trace, and weak harmonicity makes its gradient pairing zero. The exterior formula also gives $\int_{\Omega^+}
abla u^+\cdot
abla v^+=-\langle\partial_n^+u^+,\gamma^+v^+angle$ for every $v^+\in E^+(\Omega^+)$. Indeed, subtract a compactly supported lift of $\gamma^+v^+$; the remaining zero-trace finite-energy function is approximated in gradient norm by compactly supported zero-trace functions using radial cutoffs: $\|v^+
abla\chi_R\|_2\le C\|v^+\|_{L^6(\{R<|x|<2R\})}	o0$. Boundary-chart flattening, zero extension, inward translation, and convolution approximate each zero-trace cutoff by interior smooth tests, so weak harmonicity makes its gradient pairing zero. This proves the energy identity without a flux assumption at infinity. Existence, uniqueness, agreement with the displayed kernel for smooth densities, and the conormal jump are proved in [[thm-bem-single-layer-transmission-mapping-and-coercivity]]. The weak definition fixes the normalization at infinity through $u\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$; arbitrary additive constants are excluded.

Let $\Gamma$ be a polyhedral boundary as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. A **conforming surface triangulation** $\mathcal T_h$ is a finite collection of nondegenerate closed planar triangles covering $\Gamma$, with disjoint relative interiors, such that two distinct triangles meet only in a common full edge, a common vertex, or not at all. For $T\in\mathcal T_h$, write $h_T=\operatorname{diam}(T)$ and let $\rho_T$ be the radius of the largest disk contained in $T$; the family is **shape regular** if $\sup_{h,T}h_T/\rho_T<\infty$, and **quasi-uniform** if $\inf_{h,T}h_T/h>0$ for $h=\max_{T\in\mathcal T_h}h_T$.

The conforming **P0 density space** is $X_h=\{\lambda_h\in L^2(\Gamma):\lambda_h|_T\text{ is constant for every }T\in\mathcal T_h\}$. The continuous inclusion $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Gamma)$ follows because each chart Bessel norm controls its L2 norm and the fixed partition is finite. Hence every $\lambda_h$ defines a bounded functional $v\mapsto\int_\Gamma\lambda_hv$ on $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$; thus $X_h\subset H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$. This inclusion makes the single-layer Galerkin method conforming in its energy space.

Assume [[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]].

Let $\Omega^-$ be a nonempty bounded connected open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ whose boundary $\Gamma=\partial\Omega^-$ is a compact connected orientable Lipschitz surface. A **Lipschitz graph chart** is a rigid coordinate change in which $\Gamma$ is the graph $x_3=\psi(x_1,x_2)$ of a Lipschitz function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$, with $\Omega^-$ on one side of that graph. A **polyhedral boundary** is such a boundary made from finitely many planar polygonal faces meeting along edges and vertices; all surface-discretization claims below use this polyhedral subclass. Put $\Omega^+=\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline{\Omega^-}$ and assume $\Omega^+$ is connected. For the fixed-atlas space conventions below, the boundary data include a compatible Borel surface measure $dS$ and an almost-everywhere unit outward normal $n$, with the following graph realizations and bounded positive graph area densities on every chosen chart. These compatible realizations are supplied data for the Countable-Choice space assertions, not conclusions from bare Lipschitzness under Countable Choice. Under the Axiom of Choice, [[lem-bem-lipschitz-graph-sobolev-and-green-interface]] constructs them for every compact Lipschitz boundary and proves their compatibility; the general analytical trace and layer theorems state that axiom. On polyhedral charts the data are directly the finite face areas and face normals. The normal points from $\Omega^-$ into $\Omega^+$. In a rigid chart with $\Omega^-$ above the graph $x_3=\psi(x_1,x_2)$ it is $n=(\partial_1\psi,\partial_2\psi,-1)/\sqrt{1+|\nabla\psi|^2}$ almost everywhere; reverse the sign when the domain is below the graph. Rigid coordinates transform this vector to physical coordinates. The graph surface measure is $dS=\sqrt{1+|\nabla\psi|^2}\,dx_1dx_2$. Compatibility on overlaps is part of the fixed boundary data; the cited AC graph theorem proves it for arbitrary Lipschitz charts. On a polyhedron these are the face-area measure and outward face normals.

Fix a finite Lipschitz graph atlas $\{(U_j,\psi_j)\}_{j=1}^J$, with surface parametrizations $\Phi_j(z)=(z,\psi_j(z))$ in the rigid chart coordinates, and a subordinate finite Lipschitz partition of unity $\{\chi_j\}_{j=1}^J$ whose chartwise supports have positive distance from the chart edges. On $\mathbb R^2$, use the real subspace of the real-order Bessel-potential completion in [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]]. Its published norm uses the weight $(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$. Fix here the equivalent Hilbert norm
$$q(g)^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}|\widehat g(\xi)|^2d\xi.$$
The inequalities $(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\le(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\le2\pi(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$ identify the same completion and classes under the negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier convention of [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-fractional-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]. Define the real space $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ by requiring every localized chart pullback $g_j=(\chi_jg)\circ\Phi_j$, extended by zero outside its chart, to belong to that Euclidean space, and fix the **square-sum chart norm**
$$\|g\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}^2=\sum_{j=1}^J q(g_j)^2.$$
Its inner product is the sum of the real weighted Fourier inner products. The following fixed-data norm and completeness assertions use only Countable Choice and the supplied compatible measure with bounded positive chart densities; they make no geometry-existence or atlas-compatibility assertion under that weaker axiom. This Hilbert norm is equivalent to the finite sum of chart norms: $(\sum_jq(g_j)^2)^{1/2}\le\sum_jq(g_j)\le\sqrt J(\sum_jq(g_j)^2)^{1/2}$. It controls $L^2(\Gamma)$, because graph surface Jacobians are bounded above and below and $g=\sum_j\chi_jg$. It is complete: a chart-norm Cauchy sequence has a global $L^2$ limit by that bound; its localized pullbacks converge in $L^2$ to the pullbacks of this limit, while completeness of each Euclidean weighted space gives convergence in each $q$ norm. The two limits agree, so the limit belongs to the defined chart space and convergence holds in the finite square sum.

Let real $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ be the continuous real dual, with its operator norm and pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_\Gamma$; the dual of this real Hilbert space is Hilbert by [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]. The interior and exterior traces of an $H^1$ function are denoted $\gamma^-u$ and $\gamma^+u$; their common chartwise trace space is $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ once the applicable trace theorem is proved. This fixed-atlas chart-space convention applies to the stated Lipschitz geometry, including its polyhedral and $C^2$ subclasses. It defines the Hilbert and dual norms; no boundary trace or lifting theorem is assumed by that convention.

The complex space is the Hilbert complexification of the real space: $\|g_1+ig_2\|^2=\|g_1\|^2+\|g_2\|^2$. Its $H^{-1/2}$ is the continuous conjugate dual, with pairing linear in the density and conjugate-linear in the trace, extending the real pairing. A complex density is a distribution via the **bilinear** test action $T_\lambda(v)=\langle\lambda,\overline v\rangle_\Gamma$. For either scalar field the continuous realization $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\subset L^2(\Gamma)\subset H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ uses $\langle f,g\rangle_\Gamma=\int_\Gamma f\overline g\,dS$ in the complex case and $\int_\Gamma fg\,dS$ in the real case. These inclusions follow from the just-proved $H^{1/2}\to L^2$ bound and Cauchy–Schwarz.

No smoothness at edges or vertices is included in this definition. The normal is only used almost everywhere. On every Lipschitz boundary use the intrinsic graph surface measure just specified, with the chart partition; on a polyhedral boundary it equals the sum of planar face-area measures. The general Lipschitz class and its $C^2$ subclass therefore use the same measure and orientation conventions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded coercive sesquilinear form (bilinear over $\mathbb R$), and $F$ a bounded functional with the test-linearity required by $a$. Let $V_h$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with norm $\|\cdot\|_h$, not necessarily a subspace of $V$. Suppose the algebraic sum $X_h=V+V_h$ is equipped with a norm extending these norms, and $\widetilde a_h:X_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ is a bounded sesquilinear extension of a discrete form $a_h$ with bound $M_h$. Over $\mathbb C$, both forms are linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second; over $\mathbb R$, they are bilinear. Assume $a_h$ is coercive on $V_h$ with constant $\alpha_h>0$, and let $F_h$ be bounded on $V_h$ with the matching test-linearity. The exact and discrete equations have unique solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+M_h/\alpha_h)\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\alpha_h,$$

where $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}|F_h(w_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|/\|w_h\|_h$ when $V_h\ne\{0\}$, and $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u):=0$ when $V_h=\{0\}$. The estimate requires the bounded extension and does not assert that every nonconforming, penalty, or discontinuous Galerkin form has one.

For a family of these problems, suppose $M_h\le\overline M<\infty$ and $\alpha_h\ge\underline\alpha>0$ uniformly. Writing $E_h=\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h$, the uniform bound is
$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+\overline M/\underline\alpha)E_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\underline\alpha.$$
Thus uniform control of $E_h$ and $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)$ gives a uniform error budget; if both tend to zero, the errors tend to zero, and if both are $O(h^p)$ for a fixed $p>0$, the error is $O(h^p)$. No rate is inferred without those approximation, residual, and stability bounds.

derivations.claim: The fixed square-sum chart norm makes $H^{1/2}$ a real Hilbert space, hence its continuous dual $H^{-1/2}$ is Hilbert under the fixed dual norm by the trace-space convention in [F3]. Apply Lax–Milgram using [A1] to obtain the unique exact solution $\lambda$. By [F3], the restriction of $a$ to $X_h$ remains bounded and coercive and the restricted load is bounded, so Lax–Milgram on the finite-dimensional real Hilbert space $X_h$ gives the unique $\lambda_h$.

routine_steps.claim: Define $a(\lambda,\mu)=\langle\mu,V\lambda\rangle$. Boundedness follows from [F1] and the dual norm. For $u=S\lambda$ and $v=S\mu$, the weak equations [F2] give $a(\lambda,\mu)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v=a(\mu,\lambda)$, so $a$ is symmetric; with [F1] it is coercive. The load $F_f(\mu)=\langle\mu,f\rangle$ is bounded by duality.

Apply [F4] with $V=H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, $V_h=X_h$, common norm $\|\cdot\|_{H^{-1/2}}$, extension $\widetilde a_h=a$, and $F_h=F_f|_{X_h}$. The bounded-form constant is at most $C$ and the coercivity constant is at least $c$ by [F1]; the consistency defect is zero because both discrete objects are restrictions of the exact form and load. Its estimate is therefore $\|\lambda-\lambda_h\|\le(1+C/c)\inf_{\mu_h\in X_h}\|\lambda-\mu_h\|$, as stated.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For the $C^2$ boundary and orientation of [[def-bem-smooth-helmholtz-combined-field-operator]], there are bounded traces from either side of a bounded collar into $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, bounded trace lifts into $H^1(\Omega^-)$ and into compactly supported $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$, and bounded extensions of the classical layers
$$S_k:H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)\longrightarrow H^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R^3),\qquad D_k:H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\longrightarrow H^1(\Omega^-)\oplus H^1_{\rm loc}(\overline{\Omega^+}).$$
Here the exterior local space means $H^1$ on each bounded exterior collar/domain truncation, including its boundary. Both restrictions solve $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ weakly and have bounded weak conormals in $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$. With the fixed normal $n$, they obey Green's identity, with duality linear in the conormal and conjugate-linear in the trace. Their exterior restrictions are smooth away from $\Gamma$ and satisfy the uniform Sommerfeld condition $\sup_\omega|r(\partial_r-ik)u(r\omega)|\to0$. Bounds are at fixed $k$ and fixed bounded neighborhoods. The single layer has one trace across $\Gamma$.

$$\|g\|_\infty\le\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}}\,\|g\|_2.$$
For each integer $p\ge0$ there is $C_p$ independent of $\ell,g$ such that $\|g\|_{C^p(\mathbb S^2)}\le C_p(1+\ell)^{p+1/2}\|g\|_2$.
The angular Dirichlet form satisfies $-\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g,g\rangle=\ell(\ell+1)\|g\|_2^2$ for $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$.

Choose $a$ so large that $\overline{\Omega^-}\subset B_a$, and fix $r>a$. The annular domain $B_r\setminus\overline{\Omega^-}$ has inner boundary $\Gamma$ and outer sphere. We derive the Green formula for this arbitrary weak solution from the trace/lift part of [F1]. A zero-trace $H^1$ function supported in a boundary chart is approximable by smooth functions supported on its own side: flatten the chart and use $v(z,t)=\int_0^t\partial_sv(z,s)ds$, which gives $\epsilon^{-2}\int_{0<t<2\epsilon}|v|^2\le C\int_{0<t<2\epsilon}|\partial_tv|^2	o0$. A cutoff removing $t<\epsilon$ therefore converges in $H^1$, and subsequent interior mollification, followed by the finite chart partition, proves the claim. Hence the weak PDE applies to every $H^1$ test with zero trace on both boundaries. For a compact inner trace lift $Lg$, define $\langle q^+,gangle=-\int(
abla u\cdot\overline{
abla Lg}-k^2u\overline{Lg})$. The preceding approximation makes this independent of the lift, and [F1] bounds it in $H^{-1/2}$. For any test subtract its inner trace lift and an outer-sphere lift supported away from $\Gamma$; the remaining test has zero trace on both boundaries. The weak PDE kills that remainder, and classical integration by parts near the outer sphere is valid by step 1.1. Testing the resulting identity with $u$ gives $\int_{B_r\setminus\overline{\Omega^-}}(|
abla u|^2-k^2|u|^2)dx=\int_{|x|=r}\partial_ru ar u\,dS-\langle q^+,\gamma^+uangle.$ The last term is zero by the zero trace. The left side is real, hence $J(r)=r^2\operatorname{Im}\int_{\mathbb S^2}\partial_ru(r\omega)\overline{u(r\omega)}d\omega=0$. Only the original obstacle boundary has zero trace; no zero trace is assumed on the enclosing sphere.

At this fixed $r$, both $u(r,\cdot)$ and $\partial_ru(r,\cdot)$ are smooth, so their ordered harmonic projections converge in $L^2$ by [F2]. Cauchy–Schwarz passes the inner product to the limit of finite orthogonal sums. By [F2]–[F3], this gives $J(r)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{\ell=0}^N\|c_\ell\|_2^2/k.$ Every summand is nonnegative and step 2.1 gives zero, so all $c_\ell=0$. Completeness in [F2] now makes $u(r,\cdot)=0$ in $L^2$, hence pointwise by smoothness. This holds for every $r>a$, so $u=0$ on $|x|>a$. No degree sum was interchanged with the radiation limit at infinity.

The harmonic lift $w$ of step 1.1 vanishes on $(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline{B_a})\times\mathbb R$, a nonempty open subset of $\Omega^+\times\mathbb R$. The latter is connected because $\Omega^+$ is connected by hypothesis. [F4] gives $w=0$ everywhere there, hence $u=w(\cdot,0)=0$ on $\Omega^+$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(D,\varphi)$ be a regular surface patch and let $q$ be a continuous real-valued function on $\varphi[D]$. For a continuous scalar field $q$ on the patch image, $\int_Sq\,dS:=\int_D(q\circ\varphi)J_\varphi$, and $\operatorname{Area}(S):=\int_DJ_\varphi$.

Here $S$ denotes the patch with its chosen parametrization. Both integrands are bounded and Riemann integrable on the compact Jordan region $D$ by continuity ([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]). Boundary values are included in the parameter integral but may be changed on the content-zero boundary without changing its value.

Let $\Gamma$ be a polyhedral boundary as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. A **conforming surface triangulation** $\mathcal T_h$ is a finite collection of nondegenerate closed planar triangles covering $\Gamma$, with disjoint relative interiors, such that two distinct triangles meet only in a common full edge, a common vertex, or not at all. For $T\in\mathcal T_h$, write $h_T=\operatorname{diam}(T)$ and let $\rho_T$ be the radius of the largest disk contained in $T$; the family is **shape regular** if $\sup_{h,T}h_T/\rho_T<\infty$, and **quasi-uniform** if $\inf_{h,T}h_T/h>0$ for $h=\max_{T\in\mathcal T_h}h_T$.

The conforming **P0 density space** is $X_h=\{\lambda_h\in L^2(\Gamma):\lambda_h|_T\text{ is constant for every }T\in\mathcal T_h\}$. The continuous inclusion $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Gamma)$ follows because each chart Bessel norm controls its L2 norm and the fixed partition is finite. Hence every $\lambda_h$ defines a bounded functional $v\mapsto\int_\Gamma\lambda_hv$ on $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$; thus $X_h\subset H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$. This inclusion makes the single-layer Galerkin method conforming in its energy space.

For $x\ne y$ in $\mathbb R^3$, the Newton kernel is $G_3(x,y)=(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}$. Its distributional fundamental-solution property $-\Delta_xG_3(x,y)=\delta_y$ is proved in [[lem-bem-newtonian-kernel-is-fundamental-solution]]. The kernel fixes the sign and $4\pi$ normalization for every three-dimensional layer operator on this page.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

Fix an integer $p\ge0$, a finite set of source labels $J$ with positions $y_j\in\mathbb R^3$ and charges $q_j\in\mathbb C$, a center $c$, and a radius $a\ge0$ with $|y_j-c|\le a$. For each $0\le\ell\le p$, supply an orthonormal basis $\{Y_{\ell m}:-\ell\le m\le\ell\}$ of $\mathcal H_\ell$ from [[def-three-dimensional-spherical-harmonic-space]]; its existence and dimension are given by [[lem-three-dimensional-laplace-spherical-harmonic-addition-theorem]]. Form moments
$$M_{\ell m}=\sum_{j\in J}q_j\overline{H_{\ell m}(y_j-c)}.$$
For every target $x$ with $r=|x-c|>a$, evaluate the truncated single-cluster multipole field
$$\widetilde U_p(x)=4\pi\sum_{\ell=0}^p\frac{1}{2\ell+1}\frac{1}{r^{\ell+1}}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}M_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m}\!\left(\frac{x-c}{r}\right).$$
The output is an approximation to $U(x)=\sum_{j\in J}q_j/|x-y_j|$. This is the source-cluster-to-target evaluator only; it makes no 3D tree-translation or global all-target complexity claim.

For the arithmetic count, store each basis polynomial by its monomial coefficient array. Basis setup is done once for the chosen $p$. To evaluate the displayed formula directly, evaluate every basis polynomial by summing its monomials at each source and target point, then accumulate the moments and target sums. This convention makes the basis-evaluation work explicit rather than treating each special-function evaluation as free.

For the single-cluster evaluator of [[alg-three-dimensional-laplace-cluster-expansion]], let $Q=\sum_{j\in J}|q_j|$. If a target satisfies $r=|x-c|>a$, then its potential error obeys
$$|U(x)-\widetilde U_p(x)|\le\frac{Q}{r}\frac{(a/r)^{p+1}}{1-a/r}.$$
If a target region is contained in a ball of radius $b$ centered at $d$, with $R=|d-c|>a+b$, then every target in the region has error at most
$$\frac{Q}{R-b}\frac{\bigl(a/(R-b)\bigr)^{p+1}}{1-a/(R-b)}.$$
Let $S=|J|$ and let $T_0$ be the number of targets. Under the monomial-coefficient evaluation convention of the algorithm, forming moments and evaluating the truncated field costs $O((S+T_0)(p+1)^4)$ arithmetic operations after the basis coefficient arrays have been prepared. If all basis values at sources and targets are supplied, the coefficient accumulation and expansion evaluation alone cost $O((S+T_0)(p+1)^2)$. This is a single-cluster estimate; it is not a 3D multilevel FMM tree complexity theorem.

derivations.claim:
Fix a target node $x_i$, source node $y_j$, and points $x\in T_i$, $y\in S_j$ in their subtriangles. The paths $x(t)=x_i+t(x-x_i)$ and $y(t)=y_j+t(y-y_j)$ stay in $T$ and $S$ by convexity. Every pair on either path with the other variable fixed has distance at least $d$. Apply [F3] to $t\mapsto G_3(x(t),y)$ and then to $t\mapsto G_3(x_i,y(t))$; using [F2] and $|x-x_i|\le h_T$, $|y-y_j|\le h_S$ gives
$$|G_3(x,y)-G_3(x_i,y_j)|\le\frac{h_T+h_S}{4\pi d^2}.$$

One midpoint refinement divides a triangle into four triangles with half-length sides; the determinant of each affine map is $1/4$, so each new area is one quarter of the old area. Induction gives $\sum_iw_i=|T|$ and $\sum_jv_j=|S|$. Integrate the pointwise bound of step 1.1 over each $T_i\times S_j$ and sum; the area sums give $|A_{TS}-B_{TS}|\le |T||S|(h_T+h_S)/(4\pi d^2)$.

After $m$ midpoint refinements every subtriangle diameter is at most $2^{-m}$ times its initial diameter. Since $d>0$ and the right side of step 2.1 is proportional to $h_T+h_S$, it tends to zero; for every prescribed positive quadrature tolerance a finite $m$ suffices. With exact algebraic coordinates, finite arithmetic and a certified strict lower bound for $d$ can be enclosed outward to any requested positive radius. If the geometry or arithmetic certificate is absent, no certified numerical result follows from this lemma.

For each target node the hypotheses in [F4] give the displayed uniform single-cluster error. Multiplication by its positive weight and summation bounds the target sum error by $W_T$ times that tail. The source charges must be $q_j=v_j/(4\pi)$ because the evaluator sums $q_j/|x-y_j|$ while the physical kernel is $1/(4\pi|x-y|)$. Adding the centroid residual from step 2.1 and the separately certified node-evaluation and outward-arithmetic radii by the triangle inequality proves the stated total entry bound. No cluster conclusion is asserted when $R\le a+b$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the $C^2$ geometry of [[def-bem-smooth-helmholtz-combined-field-operator]]. For each fixed $k>0$ and real $\eta\ne0$, its operator extends boundedly to complex $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and
$$A_{k,\eta}=\tfrac12I+K_k-i\eta V_k,\qquad V_k=\gamma S_k,$$
where both $K_k$ and the restriction $V_k:H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ are compact. Thus $2A_{k,\eta}=I-\mathcal K_{k,\eta}$ with compact $\mathcal K_{k,\eta}=-2K_k+2i\eta V_k$. No uniform estimate in $k$ is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For the $C^2$ boundary and orientation of [[def-bem-smooth-helmholtz-combined-field-operator]], there are bounded traces from either side of a bounded collar into $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, bounded trace lifts into $H^1(\Omega^-)$ and into compactly supported $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$, and bounded extensions of the classical layers
$$S_k:H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)\longrightarrow H^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R^3),\qquad D_k:H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\longrightarrow H^1(\Omega^-)\oplus H^1_{\rm loc}(\overline{\Omega^+}).$$
Here the exterior local space means $H^1$ on each bounded exterior collar/domain truncation, including its boundary. Both restrictions solve $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ weakly and have bounded weak conormals in $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$. With the fixed normal $n$, they obey Green's identity, with duality linear in the conormal and conjugate-linear in the trace. Their exterior restrictions are smooth away from $\Gamma$ and satisfy the uniform Sommerfeld condition $\sup_\omega|r(\partial_r-ik)u(r\omega)|\to0$. Bounds are at fixed $k$ and fixed bounded neighborhoods. The single layer has one trace across $\Gamma$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On the $C^2$ surface of [[def-bem-smooth-helmholtz-combined-field-operator]], the extensions of [[lem-bem-smooth-trace-and-helmholtz-layer-extension]] satisfy, for $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$,
$$\gamma^-D_k\phi-\gamma^+D_k\phi=-\phi,\qquad \partial_n^-D_k\phi-\partial_n^+D_k\phi=0,$$
$$\gamma^-S_k\lambda-\gamma^+S_k\lambda=0,\qquad \partial_n^-S_k\lambda-\partial_n^+S_k\lambda=\lambda.$$
Trace and conormal equalities hold in $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, respectively; both conormals use the same normal $n$ pointing out of $\Omega^-$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega^-,\Gamma,\Omega^+$ have the $C^2$ geometry of [[def-bem-smooth-helmholtz-combined-field-operator]]. If $u\in H^1(\Omega^+\cap B_R)$ for every ball containing $\overline{\Omega^-}$ solves $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ weakly for a real $k>0$, has zero trace on $\Gamma$, and satisfies
$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\sup_{\omega\in\mathbb S^2}|r(\partial_r-ik)u(r\omega)|=0,$$
then $u=0$ on $\Omega^+$. The radiation condition refers to the smooth representative away from the boundary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a Banach space
over a fixed field $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $K:X\to X$ be a compact operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) and put $A:=I-K$. Then:

1. $A$ is injective if and only if it is surjective, and in that case $A$ is
   boundedly invertible;
2. for every $y\in X$ the equation $Ax=y$ has a solution if and only if
   $\varphi(y)=0$ for every $\varphi\in\ker A^*$, the transpose
   $A^*=I-K^*$ acting on $X^*$
   ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]);
3. $\ker A$ and the cokernel $X/\operatorname{ran}A$
   ([[def-quotient-vector-space-coset-notation]]) are finite dimensional with
   equal dimensions over $F$ ([[def-dimension]]).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

routine_steps.claim: Suppose $A_{k,\eta}\phi=0$ and set $u=D_k\phi-i\eta S_k\phi$. Here $\phi\in H^{1/2}$ is a valid single-layer density by the continuous inclusions $H^{1/2}\subset L^2\subset H^{-1/2}$, the last inclusion following from Cauchy–Schwarz and the continuous $H^{1/2}\to L^2$ embedding. By [F2], $u^+$ is outgoing, weak Helmholtz and has zero exterior trace. [F3] gives $u^+=0$, so also $\partial_n^+u=0$.

By [F2], $\gamma^-u-\gamma^+u=-\phi$, so $\gamma^-u=-\phi$. The conormal jump is $\partial_n^-u-\partial_n^+u=-i\eta\phi$, whence $\partial_n^-u=-i\eta\phi=i\eta\gamma^-u$. The products here use the $L^2$ realization of $H^{1/2}$ as an element of its dual $H^{-1/2}$.

The interior weak Green identity [F2] tested with $u^-$ gives $\int_{\Omega^-}(|\nabla u^-|^2-k^2|u^-|^2)dx=\langle\partial_n^-u,\gamma^-u\rangle=i\eta\|\gamma^-u\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}^2.$ The left side is real. Taking imaginary parts and using real $\eta\ne0$ gives $\gamma^-u=0$, and step 2.1 gives $\phi=0$. Thus $A_{k,\eta}$ is injective.

By [F1], $2A_{k,\eta}=I-\mathcal K_{k,\eta}$ with compact $\mathcal K_{k,\eta}$. Injectivity and [F4] make $I-\mathcal K_{k,\eta}$ boundedly invertible, hence so is $A_{k,\eta}$. Its finite inverse norm gives the estimate. For a prescribed $f$, use $\phi=A_{k,\eta}^{-1}f$; [F2] gives the outgoing solution and the operator identity gives its trace $f$. The difference of any two such solutions satisfies [F3], proving uniqueness.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For every $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, with $\Gamma$ as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]], there is a unique $u=S\lambda\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfying the weak single-layer equation of [[def-bem-laplace-layer-potentials-and-energy-spaces]]. It is harmonic on $\Omega^-$ and $\Omega^+$, its two traces agree, and its weak conormal traces satisfy
$$\partial_n^-u-\partial_n^+u=\lambda\quad\hbox{in }H^{-1/2}(\Gamma).$$
The trace operator $V\lambda:=\gamma u$ maps $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ boundedly into $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, and there are constants $C,c>0$ depending on $\Gamma$ such that
$$\|u\|_{\dot H^1}+\|V\lambda\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}},\qquad \langle\lambda,V\lambda\rangle_\Gamma\ge c\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2.$$
If $\lambda\in L^\infty(\Gamma)$ (in particular for facewise smooth densities reaching edges or discontinuous P0 densities), this weak potential agrees away from $\Gamma$ with $\int_\Gamma(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}\lambda(y)dS_y$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For every $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, the affine class $\mathcal A_\phi$ in [[def-bem-double-layer-transmission-space]] has a unique minimum-energy pair $D\phi=(u^-,u^+)$. It is harmonic on both sides, satisfies
$$\gamma^-D\phi-\gamma^+D\phi=-\phi,\qquad \partial_n^-D\phi=\partial_n^+D\phi,$$
and obeys
$$\|\nabla u^-\|_{L^2(\Omega^-)}+\|\nabla u^+\|_{L^2(\Omega^+)}\le C\|\phi\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}.$$
Consequently the average trace $K\phi=(\gamma^-D\phi+\gamma^+D\phi)/2$ is in $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and the common conormal $q_\phi=\partial_n^-D\phi=\partial_n^+D\phi$ is in $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, with both maps bounded. For every $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, the weak potential agrees away from $\Gamma$, with smooth representatives, with the absolutely convergent integral $\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_3(x,y)\phi(y)dS_y$. No vanishing condition at polyhedral edges or vertices is required.

For $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ and $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ define the Laplace Calderon boundary operators by
$$V\lambda=\gamma S\lambda,\qquad K\phi=\tfrac12(\gamma^-D\phi+\gamma^+D\phi),$$
$$K'\lambda=\tfrac12(\partial_n^-S\lambda+\partial_n^+S\lambda),\qquad W\phi=-\partial_n^-D\phi=-\partial_n^+D\phi.$$
Here $\gamma S\lambda$ is the common trace, conormal traces use the orientation of [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]], and the last equality is meaningful because the weak double layer has a common conormal derivative. This page uses the real duality pairing between $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ and $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$. The well-definedness and bounded mapping properties of $V,K,K',W$ are proved in [[thm-bem-calderon-mapping-and-jump-identities]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $\Gamma$ be any compact Lipschitz boundary in the geometry of [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]; no polyhedral restriction is imposed. The interior trace $\gamma^-:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. On every bounded exterior boundary collar $C=\Omega^+\cap U$, where $U$ is a bounded neighborhood of $\Gamma$ with Lipschitz collar boundary, the exterior trace $\gamma^+:H^1(C)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. The corresponding localized assertion holds over each boundary chart. Thus an exterior function has this trace whenever it is $H^1$ up to the boundary on such collars; membership in $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega^+)$ alone does not assert a boundary trace. There is a bounded linear right inverse $L:H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\gamma(Lg)=g$. There is also a bounded extension operator $E:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $(Eu)|_{\Omega^-}=u$.

Let $\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ denote the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ in the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$. Its elements have an $L^6$ representative, the trace $\gamma:\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded, and the right inverse above may be chosen with compact support near $\Gamma$.

routine_steps.claim: The bounds for $V$ and $K$ are respectively the trace bound in [F1] and the average-trace bound in [F2]. The bound for $W$ is the common-conormal bound in [F2] and the definition in [F3]. For $K'$, harmonicity of $S\lambda$ and the weak conormal definition give, for every $g\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, $|\langle\partial_n^-S\lambda,g\rangle|\le\|\nabla S\lambda\|_{L^2(\Omega^-)}\|\nabla L^-g\|_{L^2(\Omega^-)}\le C\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}}\|g\|_{H^{1/2}},$ and the exterior estimate is identical with an exterior local lift. Thus both conormals, and their average $K'\lambda$, lie in $H^{-1/2}$ with the claimed bound.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Gamma$ be as above, let $\mathcal T_h$ be any finite conforming surface triangulation, and let $X_h$ be its P0 space. For every $f\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ there are unique $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ and $\lambda_h\in X_h$ satisfying
$$\langle\mu,V\lambda\rangle_\Gamma=\langle\mu,f\rangle_\Gamma\quad(\mu\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)),\qquad \langle\mu_h,V\lambda_h\rangle_\Gamma=\langle\mu_h,f\rangle_\Gamma\quad(\mu_h\in X_h).$$
For constants $c,C>0$ from [[thm-bem-single-layer-transmission-mapping-and-coercivity]],
$$\|\lambda-\lambda_h\|_{H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)}\le(1+C/c)\inf_{\mu_h\in X_h}\|\lambda-\mu_h\|_{H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)}.$$
The method is conforming because $X_h\subset H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$; this is an exact Galerkin estimate and contains no quadrature or geometry error.

Let $\{\mathcal T_h\}$ be a shape-regular family of conforming surface triangulations of $\Gamma$ from [[def-bem-surface-mesh-and-piecewise-constant-density-space]], and let $h=\max_{T\in\mathcal T_h}h_T$. For $v\in L^1(\Gamma)$ define the element-average projection
$$\Pi_hv|_T=|T|^{-1}\int_Tv\,ds.$$
There is a family-independent constant $C$ such that
$$\|v-\Pi_hv\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}\le Ch^{1/2}\|v\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}\qquad(v\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)).$$
For every $\lambda\in L^2(\Gamma)$, without any alignment condition on the mesh,
$$\|\lambda-\Pi_h\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)}\le Ch^{1/2}\|\lambda-\Pi_h\lambda\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}.$$
If, in addition, every triangle $T$ is contained in a single face of the given planar face decomposition and $\lambda$ is continuously differentiable on each face (with facewise derivatives square integrable), then
$$\|\lambda-\Pi_h\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)}\le Ch^{3/2}\|\nabla_\Gamma\lambda\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}.$$
Here $\nabla_\Gamma\lambda$ is the ordinary two-dimensional gradient on each planar face; neither the density nor its derivatives need agree across face edges. More generally, the same $h^{3/2}$ bound holds whenever $\lambda|_T\in H^1(T)$ for every triangle, with the gradient norm taken elementwise. Facewise regularity alone does not ensure this condition when a triangle crosses an edge between coplanar faces.

$$\gamma^-D\phi-\gamma^+D\phi=-\phi,\qquad \partial_n^-D\phi=\partial_n^+D\phi,$$
and obeys
$$\|\nabla u^-\|_{L^2(\Omega^-)}+\|\nabla u^+\|_{L^2(\Omega^+)}\le C\|\phi\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}.$$
Consequently the average trace $K\phi=(\gamma^-D\phi+\gamma^+D\phi)/2$ is in $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and the common conormal $q_\phi=\partial_n^-D\phi=\partial_n^+D\phi$ is in $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, with both maps bounded. For every $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, the weak potential agrees away from $\Gamma$, with smooth representatives, with the absolutely convergent integral $\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_3(x,y)\phi(y)dS_y$. No vanishing condition at polyhedral edges or vertices is required.

For $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ and $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ define the Laplace Calderon boundary operators by
$$V\lambda=\gamma S\lambda,\qquad K\phi=\tfrac12(\gamma^-D\phi+\gamma^+D\phi),$$
$$K'\lambda=\tfrac12(\partial_n^-S\lambda+\partial_n^+S\lambda),\qquad W\phi=-\partial_n^-D\phi=-\partial_n^+D\phi.$$
Here $\gamma S\lambda$ is the common trace, conormal traces use the orientation of [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]], and the last equality is meaningful because the weak double layer has a common conormal derivative. This page uses the real duality pairing between $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ and $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$. The well-definedness and bounded mapping properties of $V,K,K',W$ are proved in [[thm-bem-calderon-mapping-and-jump-identities]].

$$V:H^{-1/2}\to H^{1/2},\quad K:H^{1/2}\to H^{1/2},\quad K':H^{-1/2}\to H^{-1/2},\quad W:H^{1/2}\to H^{-1/2}.$$
Their weak traces satisfy
$$\gamma^-S\lambda=\gamma^+S\lambda=V\lambda,\qquad \partial_n^-S\lambda=K'\lambda+\tfrac12\lambda,\quad \partial_n^+S\lambda=K'\lambda-\tfrac12\lambda,$$
$$\gamma^-D\phi=K\phi-\tfrac12\phi,\qquad \gamma^+D\phi=K\phi+\tfrac12\phi,\qquad \partial_n^-D\phi=\partial_n^+D\phi=-W\phi.$$
All equalities are in the stated Sobolev trace or dual spaces and use the outward normal orientation fixed on the A page.

nonempty bounded connected extension domain, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then there is
$C=C(\Omega,p)$ such that every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u(x)\,dx.$$

The interior trace $\gamma^-:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. Its elements have an $L^6$ representative, the trace $\gamma:\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded, and the right inverse above may be chosen with compact support near $\Gamma$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For the connected exterior domain $\Omega^+$ of [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]], let

$$r_j=(1+z_j)/2,\quad a_j=2^{-(\rho+1)}w_j,\qquad s_i=(1+\zeta_i)/2,\quad b_i=v_i/2.$$

$$Q_{n,\alpha}^{D}(G)=\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{i=1}^n a_jb_iG(r_j,s_i).$$
It approximates $\int_0^1\int_0^1r^{1-\alpha}G(r,s)\,ds\,dr$. When $G(r,s)=(1+s^2)^{-\alpha/2}q(r,rs)$ for a continuous $q:T\to\mathbb R$, this target is the triangle integral identified in [[thm-duffy-weak-singularity-transform]]. The finite nodes and weights are well-defined by the supplied Gauss–Jacobi rule; the error estimate for such transformed amplitudes is [[cor-duffy-weighted-product-gauss-error]].

Then the rule of [[alg-duffy-weighted-product-gauss-quadrature]] satisfies
$$\left|\int_T\|(x,y)\|_2^{-\alpha}q(x,y)\,dx\,dy-Q_{n,\alpha}^{D}(G)\right| \le K_\rho\|\partial_r^{2n}G\|_\infty+M_\rho K_0\|\partial_s^{2n}G\|_\infty,$$
where $G$ is the transformed amplitude from [[thm-duffy-weak-singularity-transform]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $(D,\varphi)$ be a regular surface patch and let $q$ be a continuous real-valued function on $\varphi[D]$. For a continuous scalar field $q$ on the patch image, $\int_Sq\,dS:=\int_D(q\circ\varphi)J_\varphi$, and $\operatorname{Area}(S):=\int_DJ_\varphi$.

Here $S$ denotes the patch with its chosen parametrization. Both integrands are bounded and Riemann integrable on the compact Jordan region $D$ by continuity ([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]). Boundary values are included in the parameter integral but may be changed on the content-zero boundary without changing its value.

derivations.claim: Parametrize $T$ and $S$ by affine maps $t(u)$ and $s(v)$ from $\Delta_2=\{(u_1,u_2):u_i\ge0,\ u_1+u_2\le1\}$. Their constant surface Jacobians are $J_T=|(t_1-t_0)\times(t_2-t_0)|$ and $J_S=|(s_1-s_0)\times(s_2-s_0)|$. With $L(u,v)=t(u)-s(v)$ on $P=\Delta_2\times\Delta_2$, the nonnegative change of variables in [F8] gives $\mathcal I_{TS}=(J_TJ_S/(4\pi))\int_P|L(z)|^{-1}dz$, initially allowing an infinite value. The zero set $Z=P\cap L^{-1}(0)$ is the parameterized diagonal of $T\cap S$ and has dimension $2$, $1$, or $0$ for coincident, edge-sharing, or vertex-sharing panels.

Cut $P$ by each non-identically-zero coordinate hyperplane $L_i=0$. Enumerate each cell’s finitely many vertices by active boundary-hyperplane sets, discarding infeasible intersections. The at most eight resulting full-dimensional sign cells cover $P$ up to their boundaries; those boundaries are contained in finitely many hyperplanes and have four-dimensional measure zero by Fubini in [F8]. For any $z_0\in Z$ and interior point $z$ of a sign cell, $L((1-t)z_0+tz)=tL(z)$ for $0<t\le1$, so every $z_0$ belongs to that cell's closure. The simultaneous zero set of its signed nonnegative affine coordinates is therefore a nonempty face.

Triangulate each cell by pulling from a global vertex ordering that lists all vertices in $Z$ first and uses the same induced order on shared faces. The pulling induction is complete: for any point other than the first vertex, extend the segment from that vertex through the point to its last point in the cell; the exit point lies on a facet not containing the first vertex, so cones over those facets cover the cell, and overlaps occur only on their boundaries. Induction triangulates those facets and the common induced ordering makes adjacent cell triangulations agree. Every full-dimensional cell has a vertex in its nonempty face $Z$, hence its first vertex is in $Z$; each resulting four-simplex therefore has a zero vertex. In a simplex with signed affine coordinates nonnegative, their common zero set is exactly the convex hull of the zero vertices, so the zero face has dimension $j\in\{0,1,2\}$, covering all three contact types including coincident panels.

In a resulting four-simplex $\Sigma=[v_0,\ldots,v_4]$, order the vertices so exactly $v_0,\ldots,v_j$ lie in $Z$, put $d=3-j$ and $D=|\det(v_1-v_0,\ldots,v_4-v_0)|$, and define $B(b)=\sum_{m=j+1}^4b_mL(v_m)$ on the opposite face $\Delta_d$. That face contains no zero of $L$, so compactness gives $c=\min_{\Delta_d}|B|>0$. The join coordinates $z=(1-r)\sum_{i=0}^ja_iv_i+r\sum_{m=j+1}^4b_mv_m$, with $a\in\Delta_j$, $b\in\Delta_d$, and $0\le r\le1$, are one-to-one in the interiors and have absolute Jacobian $D r^{3-j}(1-r)^j$: the $j$ independent $a$ directions scale by $1-r$, the $d$ independent $b$ directions by $r$, and the radial column supplies $D$. Also $L(z)=rB(b)$.

The kernel times this Jacobian has radial factor $r^{2-j}(1-r)^j$. For $j=0,1,2$, $\int_0^1r^{2-j}(1-r)^jdr=(2-j)!j!/3!$ and $|\Delta_j|=1/j!$, so $\int_\Sigma|L(z)|^{-1}dz=D(2-j)!/6\int_{\Delta_d}|B(b)|^{-1}db$. This is finite because $|B|\ge c$. For $d=1$, split the unit square into its two triangles and swap coordinates on one to get $\int_0^1g(t)dt=\int_R(g(x)+g(y))dxdy$ with $g=|B|^{-1}$. For $d=2$, $(u,v)=(1-x,y)$ maps $R=\{0\le y\le x\le1\}$ onto $\Delta_2$ with determinant one. For $d=3$, set $u=1-x$, $v=y$, $w=(x-y)t$ on $R\times[0,1]$; the remaining barycentric coordinate is $(x-y)(1-t)$ and the Jacobian is $x-y$. Thus each case is a finite sum of reference-triangle integrals, including all zero-face dimensions, and each transformed amplitude is smooth near $R$ because its denominator is bounded below by $c$. The coefficients $c_m$ include the positive factor $J_TJ_S/(4\pi)$ from step 1.1 and the positive simplex determinants and radial factors above.

The positive bound $c$ is effectively certifiable from the finitely many vectors $L(v_m)$. Enumerate every nonempty face of their convex hull and solve the finite affine normal equations for the point nearest zero on its affine span, retaining feasible barycentric coordinates; a global minimizer lies in the relative interior of a smallest face and has zero tangential derivative there, so this enumeration finds the minimum. Row-reduce degenerate systems and include their lower-dimensional faces. Positivity follows from the zero-face characterization in step 4.1. For algebraic panel coordinates, exact algebraic comparisons and interval refinement yield a rational $0<\underline c<c$. For each polynomial parameterization $B(\xi)$ whose admissible domain lies in a unit cube and whose image lies in the image under $L$ of the opposite face, set $h=|B|^2\ge c^2$ on that admissible domain, $P_{0,0}=1$, out-of-range $P_{\beta,j}=0$, and $P_{\beta+e_i,j}=\partial_iP_{\beta,j}-(j-\tfrac12)P_{\beta,j-1}\partial_i h$. The product and chain rules inductively give $\partial^\beta h^{-1/2}=\sum_{j=0}^{|\beta|}P_{\beta,j}h^{-1/2-j}$; hence $M_\beta=\sum_j\operatorname{coefabs}(P_{\beta,j})\underline c^{-1-2j}$ bounds each required derivative there, since the absolute coefficient sum bounds a polynomial on the containing unit cube. Compose the triangle coordinates with the Duffy map before using a full square as the admissible domain; no positive denominator bound is asserted on an extension outside that image. Apply the finite Leibniz rule to polynomial prefactors such as $x-y$ and add the bounds for finite amplitude sums before using these estimates for $q_m$. Differentiation under the finite $t$ integral in the $d=3$ map is justified by these uniform bounds and the fundamental theorem of calculus.

For each smooth reference amplitude $q_m$ in step 5.1, the Duffy map $D(r,s)=(r,rs)$ from [F5] gives $\int_Rq_m=\int_0^1\int_0^1rG_m(r,s)\,ds\,dr$, $G_m(r,s)=q_m(r,rs)$. With $n\ge1$, the positive product rule in [F6] has error at most $K_1\|\partial_r^{2n}G_m\|_\infty+\tfrac12K_0\|\partial_s^{2n}G_m\|_\infty$, since $\int_0^1r\,dr=1/2$. The derivative bounds are computed in step 6.1; add the separately certified node-value, fiber, and outward-arithmetic radii with the coefficients $c_m$.

This bound gives effective termination. Fix $n=1$ and subdivide $R$ into similar triangles of maximum diameter $h$; after affine pullback the second pure derivatives of $q_m(A(r,rs))$ are bounded by $C h^2\|D^2q_m\|_\infty$, so the positive-rule errors sum to $O(h^2)$ after multiplying by the affine Jacobians, whose sum is one. Indeed, $D(r,s)=(r,rs)$ has $\partial_r^2D=\partial_s^2D=0$, so the pure second-derivative chain rules contain only the Hessian of $q_m$ and two factors from the affine map, each of size $O(h)$. Its nonzero mixed derivative is not part of the Gaussian remainder used here. In the $d=3$ fiber, composite midpoint quadrature on $M$ equal subintervals has error at most $B_{tt}/(24M^2)$ by the one-variable Gaussian remainder [F7]. Choose $h,M$ so these bounds consume less than half the requested tolerance, then refine outward interval enclosures for the remaining half. Exact algebraic input makes incidence, determinant, and strict-positive denominator decisions finite; every refinement terminates because the certified lower bounds are positive. With other coordinate formats, require supplied certified incidence, nondegeneracy, separation, and arithmetic bounds; absent or failed certificates return uncertified.

If $T,S$ are disjoint, $d_0=\operatorname{dist}(T,S)>0$. The parameter kernel $g(u,v)=|L(u,v)|^{-1}$ is smooth on $\Delta_2\times\Delta_2$ with denominator at least $d_0$. Compose $L$ with the Duffy parameterizations of both triangles; it is polynomial on a product of unit squares and still has norm at least $d_0$, so the recurrence of step 6.1 with a rational lower bound below $d_0$ supplies explicit uniform derivatives. Integrating over $v$ defines $q(u)=\int_{\Delta_2}g(u,v)dv$; differentiation under this finite integral is justified by those uniform bounds, and the simplex mass is $1/2$. The affine map $(u_1,u_2)=(1-x,y)$ sends the outer triangle to $R$. Evaluate each inner $v$ integral by the positive composite $\alpha=0$ Duffy rule; its error bound is uniform in $u$. Apply the outer rule of step 7.1 to $q$. Subdividing both reference triangles and using their computed second-derivative bounds makes the inner errors $O(h^2)$ uniformly in $u$ and the outer error $O(h^2)$; positivity and bounded total weight let these errors add. Thus the disjoint smooth fallback terminates at every positive tolerance, with its two numerical radii charged separately.

To identify the double integral with the weak matrix entry, use barycentric coordinates $(u_1,u_2,1-u_1-u_2)$ and cutoffs $\chi_n=\prod_{i=1}^3\min(1,nu_i)$ on each panel. They are bounded by one and converge almost everywhere and in $L^2$ to the panel indicator. By [F1], each cutoff is an $L^2$ density and the fixed $H^{1/2}$ chart norm controls $L^2$, so these cutoffs converge in $H^{-1/2}$ by duality; boundedness of $V$ in [F3] gives $\langle\chi_n1_T,V(\chi_n1_S)\rangle\to\langle1_T,V1_S\rangle$. For the trace identification, a finite union of planar faces satisfies $|\Gamma\cap B(x,r)|\le Cr^2$; dyadic annuli imply $\int_{\Gamma\cap B(x,\delta)}|x-y|^{-1}dS_y\le C\delta$. Splitting at distance $2\delta$ and using $|\nabla_xG_3|=(4\pi|x-y|^2)^{-1}$ gives continuity modulus $C\delta(1+|\log\delta|)$ for each bounded cutoff potential throughout a bounded neighborhood of $\Gamma$: the area and near-integral bounds are uniform for ambient target points, and the same near/far split applies there. By [F3] the off-surface kernel integral represents its weak potential; by [F4] its continuous restriction is its Sobolev trace, and Fubini [F8] identifies the pairing with the cutoff double integral. Absolute integrability from the touching-panel calculation in step 5.1 and the disjoint case in step 8.2 dominates these integrands, so dominated convergence gives $\langle1_T,V1_S\rangle=\mathcal I_{TS}$ for coincident, edge-sharing, vertex-sharing, and disjoint panels.
