The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, an open set
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

**Restriction.** Let $F\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ with $|\alpha|\le k$. By the restriction and locality
clause of
[[lem-weak-derivative-linearity-locality-and-commutation]], applied with
$V=\Omega$, the class $F|_\Omega$ lies in $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$D^\alpha(F|_\Omega)=(D^\alpha F)|_\Omega$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$;
by [[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere|the uniqueness of weak
derivatives]] the derivative class of the restriction is determined by the
class of $F$ alone. So restriction is a well-defined operation on Sobolev
classes, and the norm formula of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] gives
$\|F|_\Omega\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\le\|F\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}$, since each
restricted derivative has no larger $L^p$ norm.

**Extension domain.** For fixed $k,p,\Omega$ and scalar field $\mathbb K$, call
$\Omega$ a **$W^{k,p}$-extension domain** if there is a bounded linear operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$$
such that, for every $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$,
$$(Eu)|_\Omega=u\qquad\text{as an almost-everywhere class on }\Omega.$$
Equivalently, the restriction map in the first paragraph possesses a bounded
linear right inverse. Boundedness of $E$ is the finiteness of the operator
norm
$$\|E\|=\sup\{\|Eu\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}:u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\le1\};$$
the displayed right-inverse identity is an identity of $L^p(\Omega)$ classes,
not of pointwise values.

The operator, and the numerical bound $\|E\|$, may depend on $k$, $p$,
$\Omega$ and $\mathbb K$. This definition asserts no common operator for all
indices at once, no linearity of some canonically selected extension, and no
control of pointwise values on $\partial\Omega$; in particular it does not
define a trace operator. No claim is made here that zero extension is an
extension operator for a general open set, and none that any particular open
set fails to be an extension domain; both assertions belong to later items of
this page and to its companion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], is a complete normed space over
$\mathbb K$.

Both endpoints $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, as is $k=0$, where the
assertion reduces to the completeness of $L^p$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the zero space and the assertion is trivial.
The Axiom of Choice is used only to derive Countable Choice for the two
published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative
selection inside the finitely many coordinate classes is finite and
choice-free.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $A \subseteq X$
carry the subspace metric $d_A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]). Then:

1. **Under countable choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]),
   if $(A,d_A)$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]), then $A$ is closed
   in $(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-topology]]). No completeness hypothesis on $X$ is needed.
2. **In ZF, without a choice axiom**, if $(X,d)$ is complete and $A$ is closed
   in $(X,d)$, then $(A,d_A)$ is complete.

Consequently, under countable choice, a subspace of a complete metric space is
complete if and only if it is closed.

The following form of the first direction is also choice-free: a complete
subspace contains the ambient limit of every convergent sequence of its
points. Hence it is closed whenever every point of its ambient closure is
already known to be the limit of a sequence from that subspace. This last
condition is pointwise existence, not a chosen family of sequences.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the geometry and trace conventions of [[def-signorini-partial-trace-space]]. Then the maps $T_D,T_C:H^1(Ω;\mathbb R^2)\to L^2(Γ_D;\mathbb R^2),L^2(Γ_C;\mathbb R^2)$ are bounded and linear, and $V=\ker T_D$ is a Hilbert space with the inherited $H^1$ inner product.

Assume the geometry and trace conventions of [[def-signorini-partial-trace-space]]. Then the maps $T_D,T_C:H^1(Ω;\mathbb R^2)\to L^2(Γ_D;\mathbb R^2),L^2(Γ_C;\mathbb R^2)$ are bounded and linear, and $V=\ker T_D$ is a Hilbert space with the inherited $H^1$ inner product.

Let $\psi\in C(\Gamma_C;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\psi\le0$. Define the unilateral frictionless **contact set**
$$K:=\{v\in V:T_Cv\cdot n\ge\psi\quad\text{for arclength-almost every point of }\Gamma_C\}.$$
Given the elasticity form $a$ and bounded load $F$ of [[def-signorini-elasticity-contact-model]], the **contact variational inequality** is to find $u\in K$ such that
$$a(u,v-u)\ge F(v-u)\qquad\text{for every }v\in K.$$
The set $K$ is nonempty, closed and convex by [[lem-signorini-contact-set-closed-convex-nonempty]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. A **bounded connected Lipschitz polygon** $Ω\subset\mathbb R^2$ is a bounded connected open set whose boundary is a simple closed polygonal curve and, near every boundary point after a rigid coordinate change, is the graph of a Lipschitz function with $Ω$ on one side. Assume $Ω$ is a $W^{1,2}$-extension domain in the sense of [[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]. Fix two disjoint closed straight segments $Γ_D,Γ_C\subset\partialΩ$, each of positive length and each lying strictly inside a straight side of $∂Ω$.

As part of the geometry data, fix bounded $C^1$ subdomains $U_D,U_C\subsetΩ$ (in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]) whose boundaries have relatively open flat patches containing $Γ_D,Γ_C$, respectively. Such collars can be chosen as sufficiently thin stadium-shaped domains along slightly longer segments of the same polygon sides, with their rounded ends outside the prescribed segments. Let $T_D,T_C$ be the restrictions to these segments of the bounded trace operators on $U_D,U_C$ supplied by [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], applied componentwise to the restrictions of functions in $H^1(Ω;\mathbb R^2)$. For $j\in\{D,C\}$, if $v\in H^1(Ω;\mathbb R^2)$ has a representative on $U_j$ extending continuously to $\overline{U_j}$, then $T_jv$ agrees in $L^2(Γ_j;\mathbb R^2)$ with that extension's restriction to $Γ_j$, by the trace theorem's agreement clause. In particular, this holds for $v\in H^1(Ω;\mathbb R^2)\cap C(\overlineΩ;\mathbb R^2)$.

Define
$$V:=\{v\in H^1(Ω;\mathbb R^2):T_Dv=0\text{ in }L^2(Γ_D;\mathbb R^2)\},\qquad \|v\|_V:=\|v\|_{H^1(Ω)}.$$
The contact normal $n\in\mathbb R^2$ is a fixed unit vector on $Γ_C$, oriented so that a positive value of $T_Cv\cdot n$ opens the contact gap. No pointwise value of a general $H^1$ class is used in this definition.

Let $\psi\in C(\Gamma_C;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\psi\le0$. Define the unilateral frictionless **contact set**
$$K:=\{v\in V:T_Cv\cdot n\ge\psi\quad\text{for arclength-almost every point of }\Gamma_C\}.$$
Given the elasticity form $a$ and bounded load $F$ of [[def-signorini-elasticity-contact-model]], the **contact variational inequality** is to find $u\in K$ such that
$$a(u,v-u)\ge F(v-u)\qquad\text{for every }v\in K.$$
The set $K$ is nonempty, closed and convex by [[lem-signorini-contact-set-closed-convex-nonempty]].

derivations.claim: The zero field belongs to $V$, and $T_C0\cdot n=0\ge\psi$ almost everywhere, so $0\in K$. If $v,w\in K$ and $0\le t\le1$, linearity of $T_C$ gives $T_C(tv+(1-t)w)\cdot n-\psi=t(T_Cv\cdot n-\psi)+(1-t)(T_Cw\cdot n-\psi)\ge0$ almost everywhere, so $tv+(1-t)w\in K$.

If $g_m\in L^2_+(\Gamma_C)$ and $g_m\to g$ in $L^2$, then $g^-:=\max\{-g,0\}\le|g-g_m|$ almost everywhere for each $m$, hence $\|g^-\|_2\le\|g-g_m\|_2\to0$ and $g\ge0$ almost everywhere. Thus the cone is closed; it is convex by pointwise convexity. By [F1] and [F3], the affine map $v\mapsto T_Cv\cdot n-\psi$ is continuous into $L^2(\Gamma_C)$, so its preimage of that closed convex cone is closed in $V$. This proves the claim.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
nonempty bounded connected extension domain, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then there is
$C=C(\Omega,p)$ such that every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u(x)\,dx.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and Lipschitz, with $d\in\{2,3\}$. Under Countable Choice there is a bounded linear map $B_D:L^2_0(D)\to H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ such that
$$\operatorname{div}B_Dq=q,\qquad \|\nabla B_Dq\|_2\le C_{\rm div}(D)\|q\|_2.$$
For a chosen finite cover and tree decomposition from [[lem-na-lipschitz-domain-finite-star-shaped-cover]] and [[lem-na-finite-cover-zero-mean-data-decomposition]], one valid bound is $C_{\rm div}(D)=\sum_i C_{U_i}D_i$; it is finite and independent of any finite-element mesh.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
nonempty bounded connected extension domain, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then there is
$C=C(\Omega,p)$ such that every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u(x)\,dx.$$

A **bounded connected Lipschitz polygon** $Ω\subset\mathbb R^2$ is a bounded connected open set whose boundary is a simple closed polygonal curve and, near every boundary point after a rigid coordinate change, is the graph of a Lipschitz function with $Ω$ on one side. Fix two disjoint closed straight segments $Γ_D,Γ_C\subset\partialΩ$, each of positive length and each lying strictly inside a straight side of $∂Ω$.

As part of the geometry data, fix bounded $C^1$ subdomains $U_D,U_C\subsetΩ$ (in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]) whose boundaries have relatively open flat patches containing $Γ_D,Γ_C$, respectively. For $j\in\{D,C\}$, if $v\in H^1(Ω;\mathbb R^2)$ has a representative on $U_j$ extending continuously to $\overline{U_j}$, then $T_jv$ agrees in $L^2(Γ_j;\mathbb R^2)$ with that extension's restriction to $Γ_j$, by the trace theorem's agreement clause. In particular, this holds for $v\in H^1(Ω;\mathbb R^2)\cap C(\overlineΩ;\mathbb R^2)$.

Define
$$V:=\{v\in H^1(Ω;\mathbb R^2):T_Dv=0\text{ in }L^2(Γ_D;\mathbb R^2)\},\qquad \|v\|_V:=\|v\|_{H^1(Ω)}.$$
The contact normal $n\in\mathbb R^2$ is a fixed unit vector on $Γ_C$, oriented so that a positive value of $T_Cv\cdot n$ opens the contact gap. No pointwise value of a general $H^1$ class is used in this definition.

Assume the geometry and trace conventions of [[def-signorini-partial-trace-space]]. Then the maps $T_D,T_C:H^1(Ω;\mathbb R^2)\to L^2(Γ_D;\mathbb R^2),L^2(Γ_C;\mathbb R^2)$ are bounded and linear, and $V=\ker T_D$ is a Hilbert space with the inherited $H^1$ inner product.

Let $\Gamma_D$ be a fixed straight segment of length $L>0$ in the geometry of [[def-signorini-partial-trace-space]]. For every planar infinitesimal rigid motion $r(x)=a+\omega Jx$, where $a\in\mathbb R^2$, $\omega\in\mathbb R$, and $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, there is a constant $C=C(\Omega,\Gamma_D)$ such that
$$\|r\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C\|T_Dr\|_{L^2(\Gamma_D)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Use the polygon, displacement space and oriented contact normal from [[def-signorini-partial-trace-space]]. Let the constant shear modulus satisfy $\mu>0$, let the finite Lam\'e parameter satisfy $\lambda\ge0$, and let $F:V\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded linear functional. For $v\in V$, define the weak symmetric gradient
$$\varepsilon(v):=\frac{\nabla v+(\nabla v)^T}{2}.$$
For $u,v\in V$, define the isotropic small-strain elasticity form
$$a(u,v):=\int_\Omega 2\mu\,\varepsilon(u):\varepsilon(v)+\lambda\,\operatorname{div}u\,\operatorname{div}v\,dx.$$
The strain and form conventions are the algebraic formulas in [[def-linear-elasticity-displacement-formulation-and-data]]. The present domain is the partial-trace space $V$; all coercivity and well-posedness claims for it are proved locally below.

Let $\Gamma_D$ be a fixed straight segment of length $L>0$ in the geometry of [[def-signorini-partial-trace-space]]. For every planar infinitesimal rigid motion $r(x)=a+\omega Jx$, where $a\in\mathbb R^2$, $\omega\in\mathbb R$, and $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, there is a constant $C=C(\Omega,\Gamma_D)$ such that
$$\|r\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C\|T_Dr\|_{L^2(\Gamma_D)}.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Set $G=

abla z,G)=\|

$$f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).$$

derivations.claim: The set $V_h$ is finite dimensional. By [F3], $K_h$ is the intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces in $V_h$, so it is closed and convex. The zero field is in $V_h$, and $0\ge I_h\psi(a)=\psi(a)$ at every contact vertex since $\psi\le0$; hence $0\in K_h$ and $K_h$ is nonempty.

Fix a contact edge $e=[a,b]$. For $v_h\in K_h$, the function $q_h:=v_h\cdot n-I_h\psi$ is affine on $e$ and is nonnegative at $a,b$ by [F3]. Thus $q_h((1-t)a+tb)=(1-t)q_h(a)+tq_h(b)\ge0$ throughout $e$. Convexity [F5] gives $I_h\psi((1-t)a+tb)\ge\psi((1-t)a+tb)$, so $v_h\cdot n\ge\psi$ on every contact edge. Since $v_h\in C(\overline\Omega)$, [F4] identifies its contact trace with this restriction. Therefore $v_h\in K$ and $K_h\subseteq K$.

Let $v\in K\cap H^2\cap C(\overline\Omega)$. Its continuous gap $T_Cv\cdot n-\psi$ is nonnegative almost everywhere by [F1], hence everywhere: if it were negative at one point, continuity would make it negative on a subsegment of positive length. Define $I_hv$ cell by cell as the affine polynomial matching $v$ at the three vertices. On a shared edge the two affine traces agree at both endpoints, so they agree along the whole edge. For every test function compactly supported in $\Omega$, integration by parts on each triangle cancels the internal-edge boundary terms because these traces agree; the remaining piecewise constant gradients are in $L^2(\Omega)$. Hence $I_hv\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$ and is globally continuous. Its boundary values on $\Gamma_D$ are zero: $v\in V$ means $T_Dv=0$ almost everywhere, and [F4] identifies this trace with the continuous boundary restriction, which therefore vanishes everywhere on the segment. Since the mesh resolves $\Gamma_D$, the affine boundary traces of $I_hv$ vanish there, so $I_hv\in V_h$. At every contact node, $I_hv(a)=v(a)$ and [F4] identifies the contact trace with the continuous restriction; the continuous gap is nonnegative, so the nodal constraints hold and $I_hv\in K_h$.

On an edge, the consistent P1 mass matrix is $h_k\begin{pmatrix}1/3&1/6\\1/6&1/3\end{pmatrix}$, whose eigenvalues are $h_k/6,h_k/2$. Let $d\ge1$, let $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded open
reference cell, let $q\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **reference finite element** is a
triple $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ where $\widehat P$ is an
$N$-dimensional subspace of $[C(\overline{\widehat K};\mathbb K)]^q$ for
$N\in\mathbb N_0$ and
$\widehat\Sigma=(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N)$ is a list of
linear functionals on $\widehat P$ for which
$$J_{\widehat\Sigma}:\widehat P\to\mathbb K^N,\qquad J_{\widehat\Sigma}(p):=(\widehat\sigma_1(p),\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N(p)),$$

is **unisolvent**. Its **shape functions** are the unique dual basis
$\widehat\phi_1,\ldots,\widehat\phi_N\in\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}$.

$\widehat P$, fix for each $i$ a bounded linear extension of

chosen extensions is
$$\widehat I:X\to\widehat P,\qquad \widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i.$$

zero spaces, and the shape-function list is empty. The corresponding
interpolation formula is the empty sum, hence the zero map into $\{0\}$.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels

derivations.claim: By [F2]–[F4], the discrete VI on $V_h$ has a unique solution $u_h$. Fix any $v_h\in K_h$. Since $K_h\subseteq K$, [F1] applies at $z=u_h$ and gives $a(u,u_h-u)\ge F(u_h-u)$; equivalently $a(u,e)\le F(e)$ for $e:=u-u_h$. The discrete inequality tested at $v_h$ gives $a(u_h,e-\delta)\ge F(e-\delta)$ for $\delta:=u-v_h$. Rearranging these two inequalities yields $a(e,e)\le F(\delta)-a(u_h,\delta)=\eta_{\rm feas}(v_h)+a(e,\delta)$; [F1] also gives $\eta_{\rm feas}(v_h)\ge0$.

For the convergence clause, let $v_h=I_hu$. By [F2] the nodal interpolant belongs to $K_h$. Apply [F5] on each cell for $m=0,1$. The cell interiors partition $\Omega$ up to the finite edge union [F6]; summing the squared local estimates gives $\|u-I_hu\|_V\le C(h+h^2)|u|_{H^2(\Omega)}\to0$.

By [F3], $\alpha\|e\|_V^2\le a(e,e)$ and $|a(e,\delta)|\le M\|e\|_V\|\delta\|_V$. The inequality of step 1.1 and $M\|e\|\|\delta\|\le(\alpha/2)\|e\|^2+(M^2/(2\alpha))\|\delta\|^2$ imply $\|e\|_V^2\le(2/\alpha)\eta_{\rm feas}(v_h)+(M^2/\alpha^2)\|u-v_h\|_V^2$. Since $v_h$ was arbitrary, take the infimum to obtain the displayed Falk bound.

The functional $R(v):=a(u,v)-F(v)$ is bounded on $V$, with $\|R\|_{V^*}\le M\|u\|_V+\|F\|_{V^*}$ by [F3]. Thus $0\le\eta_{\rm feas}(I_hu)=R(I_hu-u)\le(M\|u\|+\|F\|)\|I_hu-u\|_V\to0$. Substitute $v_h=I_hu$ in step 2.1 and use step 1.2 to conclude $\|u-u_h\|_V\to0$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(\mathcal T_h)$ be a family of matching, boundary-conforming, shape-regular affine triangular meshes of the polygon from [[def-signorini-partial-trace-space]], with $h:=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}(K)$. Assume both $\Gamma_D$ and $\Gamma_C$ are unions of boundary edges of each mesh, and let $\mathcal N_h^C$ be the vertices on $\Gamma_C$. The conforming continuous P1 displacement space is
$$V_h:=\{v_h\in V\cap C(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^2):v_h|_K\in\mathbb P_1(K;\mathbb R^2)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T_h\}.$$
For continuous $\psi$ on $\Gamma_C$, let $I_h\psi$ be its continuous piecewise-affine nodal interpolant on the contact edges. Under the additional obstacle hypotheses $\psi\le0$ and convexity of $\psi$ in arclength on $\Gamma_C$, define
$$K_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:v_h(a)\cdot n\ge I_h\psi(a)\text{ for every }a\in\mathcal N_h^C\}.$$
The nodal inequalities are exactly the plan's vertex constraints. The well-definedness and conformity claims are proved in [[lem-signorini-nodal-contact-set-conforming]].

Under [[def-signorini-nodal-p1-contact-scheme]], $K_h$ is a nonempty closed convex subset of the finite-dimensional space $V_h$ and $K_h\subseteq K$. If $v\in K\cap H^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)\cap C(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$, its global P1 nodal interpolant $I_hv$ is well defined, belongs to $V_h$, and lies in $K_h$.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

In the setting of [[def-signorini-elasticity-contact-model]], the form $a$ is well defined, symmetric, and satisfies
$$|a(u,v)|\le(2\mu+2\lambda)\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\|v\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\qquad(u,v\in V).$$

Assume the geometry of [[def-signorini-partial-trace-space]] and let $V=\{v\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^2):T_Dv=0\}$. Then there is $c_K>0$, depending on $\Omega$ and $\Gamma_D$, such that
$$\|v\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le c_K\|\varepsilon(v)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\qquad(v\in V).$$

For the spaces and basis of [[def-signorini-dual-mortar-contact-pair]], put $d_i:=\sum_{e_k\ni a_i}h_k$. Then
$$\int_{\Gamma_C}\chi_i\phi_j\,ds=d_i\delta_{ij}\qquad(0\le i,j\le N).$$
The pair $(\Lambda_h,W_h)$ satisfies the mesh-independent trace-space inf-sup bound
$$\inf_{0\ne\lambda_h\in\Lambda_h}\sup_{0\ne g_h\in W_h}\frac{\int_{\Gamma_C}\lambda_hg_h\,ds}{\|\lambda_h\|_{L^2(\Gamma_C)}\|g_h\|_{L^2(\Gamma_C)}}\ge\frac1{\sqrt3}.$$
Moreover, $\lambda_h\in\Lambda_h^+$ defines a nonnegative functional on the cone of nonnegative functions in $W_h$, and $\langle\lambda_h,g_h\rangle=\sum_i d_i\lambda_i g_h(a_i)$.

Let $(\mathcal T_h)$ be a family of matching, boundary-conforming, shape-regular affine triangular meshes of the polygon from [[def-signorini-partial-trace-space]], with $h:=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}(K)$. Assume both $\Gamma_D$ and $\Gamma_C$ are unions of boundary edges of each mesh, and let $\mathcal N_h^C$ be the vertices on $\Gamma_C$. The conforming continuous P1 displacement space is
$$V_h:=\{v_h\in V\cap C(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^2):v_h|_K\in\mathbb P_1(K;\mathbb R^2)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T_h\}.$$
For continuous $\psi$ on $\Gamma_C$, let $I_h\psi$ be its continuous piecewise-affine nodal interpolant on the contact edges. Under the additional obstacle hypotheses $\psi\le0$ and convexity of $\psi$ in arclength on $\Gamma_C$, define
$$K_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:v_h(a)\cdot n\ge I_h\psi(a)\text{ for every }a\in\mathcal N_h^C\}.$$
The nodal inequalities are exactly the plan's vertex constraints. The well-definedness and conformity claims are proved in [[lem-signorini-nodal-contact-set-conforming]].

Under [[def-signorini-nodal-p1-contact-scheme]], $K_h$ is a nonempty closed convex subset of the finite-dimensional space $V_h$ and $K_h\subseteq K$. If $v\in K\cap H^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)\cap C(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$, its global P1 nodal interpolant $I_hv$ is well defined, belongs to $V_h$, and lies in $K_h$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $K\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded coercive bilinear form with constants $M,\alpha>0$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]; no symmetry is assumed), and let $F:H\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded linear functional. Then there is exactly one $u\in K$ with
$$a(u,\,v-u)\ge F(v-u)\qquad\text{for every }v\in K .$$

Under [[def-signorini-nodal-p1-contact-scheme]], let the contact vertices be $a_0,\ldots,a_N$ and define $B:V_h\to\mathbb R^{N+1}$ by $B_i(v_h)=v_h(a_i)\cdot n$. Then $B$ is onto. In particular, for each $i$ there is $w_i\in V_h$ with $B_j(w_i)=\delta_{ij}$ for every contact vertex $a_j$.

derivations.claim: By [F1]–[F2], the restricted form and load meet the hypotheses of [F5], so the discrete VI has exactly one solution $u_h\in K_h$. By [F6], the contact-coordinate map $B:V_h\to\mathbb R^{N+1}$ is onto; fix test functions $w_i$ with $B_j(w_i)=\delta_{ij}$.

Define the residual $r_h(v_h):=a(u_h,v_h)-F(v_h)$. If $k\in\ker B$, then $u_h\pm tk\in K_h$ for every real $t$, so the VI tested with both signs gives $r_h(k)=0$. If $g_i>0$, then $u_h\pm tw_i\in K_h$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$, so $r_h(w_i)=0$; if $g_i=0$, the feasible variation $u_h+tw_i$ for $t>0$ gives $r_h(w_i)\ge0$. Set $\lambda_i:=r_h(w_i)/d_i$. Then $\lambda_i\ge0$ and $\lambda_i g_i=0$.

For arbitrary $v_h\in V_h$, write $v_h=\sum_i B_i(v_h)w_i+k$ with $k:=v_h-\sum_iB_i(v_h)w_i\in\ker B$. Step 2.1 gives $r_h(v_h)=\sum_iB_i(v_h)r_h(w_i)=\sum_i d_i\lambda_iB_i(v_h)=b_h(v_h,\lambda_h)$ by [F3], with $\lambda_h:=\sum_i\lambda_i\chi_i\in\Lambda_h^+$. Thus the saddle stationarity equation holds. If another multiplier gives the same stationarity, surjectivity of $B$ and $d_i>0$ force each coefficient to equal $\lambda_i$, proving multiplier uniqueness.

Conversely, suppose a feasible displacement and nonnegative coefficients satisfy stationarity and $\lambda_i g_i=0$. For $w_h\in V_h$, define its nodal gap $g_i(w_h):=B_i(w_h)-I_h\psi(a_i)$, so $g_i=g_i(u_h)$. For any feasible $v_h$, biorthogonality [F3] gives $a(u_h,v_h-u_h)-F(v_h-u_h)=\sum_i d_i\lambda_i(B_i(v_h)-B_i(u_h))=\sum_i d_i\lambda_i(g_i(v_h)-g_i(u_h))=\sum_i d_i\lambda_i g_i(v_h)\ge0$, since $g_i(u_h)=0$ whenever $\lambda_i>0$ and $g_i(v_h)\ge0$ by [F4]. Hence the saddle system is equivalent to the VI, and $\mathcal R_h=\sum_i d_i\lambda_i g_i=0$ exactly.

By [F4], $\psi\le0$ and the nodal interpolant satisfies $I_h\psi(a_i)=\psi(a_i)$, so the zero displacement satisfies every defining inequality of $K_h$ and $0\in K_h$. Taking $v_h=0$ in the discrete VI gives $a(u_h,u_h)\le F(u_h)\le\|F\|_{V^*}\|u_h\|_V$. Coercivity [F2] yields $\alpha\|u_h\|_V^2\le\|F\|_{V^*}\|u_h\|_V$, so either $u_h=0$ or division gives $\|u_h\|_V\le\|F\|_{V^*}/\alpha$. The trace inf-sup bound in [F3] and exact edge-integral definition of $b_h$ establish the stated discrete stability and consistency.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 obtains a displacement from the nonempty closed-convex discrete set.
Step 5.1 explicitly treats the u_h=0 branch before division.
Step 1.1 and Step 3.1 show the KKT construction applies with a single contact edge and its two nodal coordinates.

boundaries.reason: The theorem assumes a valid fixed mesh with positive edge lengths and coercivity alpha>0.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 3.1 and 4.1 use positive endpoint weights d_i and nodal complementarity.
Step 1.1 uses the Countable Choice branch of finite-dimensional Stampacchia.
Steps 1.1–3.1 derive KKT multipliers and stationarity from the VI.
Step 4.1 proves KKT feasibility and complementarity imply the discrete VI.

risk_review.notes: Checked all five steps and ten actual dependencies, including the independently derived diagonal pairing and onto contact-coordinate hats. Every h_k>0 gives d_i>0. ker B variations annihilate residual; inactive coordinates admit both signs and active coordinates positive variations, giving nonnegative lambda_i=r(w_i)/d_i and lambda_i*g_i=0. Decomposing an arbitrary field by hats proves stationarity and onto B proves uniqueness; reversing stationarity/complementarity proves the VI. The exact edge pairing yields zero integrated gap residual. psi<=0 ensures 0 in K_h for the displacement bound; u_h=0 is handled before division. The independent local mass-matrix eigenvalue bounds give 1/sqrt(3) only on the L2 trace pair, without claiming H1-multiplier inf-sup or nonmatching stability. Krause–Wohlmuth §2 pp.2–3 is dual-basis context, not a contact theorem. No reader/refuter finding or defect.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded open set of one of the following two kinds ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]).

**Trace conventions.** If $n=1$, then $\Omega=(a,b)$ is a bounded interval and $T$ is the endpoint-pair trace of [[lem-one-dimensional-trace-truncation-compatibility]], ordered componentwise. If $n\ge2$, then $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain and $T$ is the trace operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. An **obstacle** is a real function $\psi$ with $\psi\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ ([[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) such that $T\psi\le0$ — componentwise at the two endpoints when $n=1$, and almost everywhere on $\partial\Omega$ when $n\ge2$. By [[lem-one-dimensional-trace-truncation-compatibility]] for $n=1$ and [[lem-positive-part-of-a-zero-trace-function-has-zero-trace]] for $n\ge2$, this boundary order condition is equivalent to $\psi^+\in H^1_0(\Omega)$.

**The obstacle admissible set** is
$$K:=\{\,v\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R):v\ge\psi\text{ a.e. on }\Omega\,\},$$
where the inequality $v\ge\psi$ is imposed on almost-everywhere classes and is therefore independent of the chosen representatives ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

**Data.** Let $a:H^1_0(\Omega)\times H^1_0(\Omega)\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded coercive bilinear form with constants $M,\alpha>0$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]) and let $F\in H^{-1}(\Omega)$ ([[def-h-minus-one-as-the-dual-of-h-one-zero]]).

**The obstacle variational inequality** is the problem: find $u\in K$ with
$$a(u,\,v-u)\ge F(v-u)\qquad\text{for every }v\in K .$$

**Energy and reaction.** In the symmetric case the associated **energy** is $J(v):=\tfrac12a(v,v)-F(v)$ for $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$; the **reaction distribution** of a solution $u$ is the distribution on $\Omega$ defined by
$$\Lambda_u(\varphi):=a(u,\varphi)-F(\varphi)\qquad(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)),$$
the right-hand side being well defined on real test functions because $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)\subseteq H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]). It is linear and continuous: boundedness gives $|\Lambda_u(\varphi)|\le(M\|u\|_{H^1}+\|F\|_{H^{-1}})\|\varphi\|_{H^1}$, and for tests supported in a compact $S\subseteq\Omega$, $\|\varphi\|_{H^1}\le\sqrt{(n+1)|S|}\max_{|\alpha|\le1}\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_\infty$. Thus $|\Lambda_u|$ is a seminorm continuous on every fixed-support test space and hence continuous for [[def-test-function-topology]]. Its complex-linear extension is $\Lambda_u(\varphi_1+i\varphi_2)=\Lambda_u(\varphi_1)+i\Lambda_u(\varphi_2)$ for real tests $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$, giving a distribution in the convention of [[def-distribution]]; nonnegativity is tested on real nonnegative tests.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $I=(a,b)$ with $-\infty<a<b<\infty$, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb R)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Let $u^*$ be its unique absolutely continuous representative on $[a,b]$ ([[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]]) and put $Tu:=(u^*(a),u^*(b))\in\mathbb R^2$, ordered componentwise. Then:

1. $T$ is well defined, linear and bounded, and $\ker T=W_0^{1,p}(I)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).
2. For every $k\in\mathbb R$ the function $(u-k)^+$ belongs to $W^{1,p}(I)$, and $T\bigl((u-k)^+\bigr)=(Tu-k)^+$ componentwise; moreover $(u-k)^+\in W_0^{1,p}(I)$ if and only if $Tu\le(k,k)$ componentwise. In particular $T(u^+)=(Tu)^+$, $T(u^-)=(Tu)^-$ and $T|u|=|Tu|$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

derivations.claim: The function $\psi$ is continuous and piecewise affine, hence belongs to $H^1(0,1)$; its endpoint values are $0$ and $-1/2$, so [F1] applies. The displayed $u$ is continuous at $a_0$, has derivative $0$ from both sides there, and has endpoint values $u(0)=u(1)=0$. By [F2], its endpoint trace is zero and therefore $u\in H^1_0(0,1)$. On $[0,a_0]$, $u=\psi=0$; on $(a_0,1]$, $u\ge0>\psi$. Thus $u\in K$, and equality $u=\psi$ holds exactly on $[0,a_0]$.

On $(a_0,1)$, direct differentiation gives $u''(x)=4-6x$; on $(0,a_0)$, $u''=0$. The derivative $u'$ is continuous at $a_0$, so its distributional derivative is the piecewise function just computed, with no point mass at $a_0$. For $z=v-u\in H^1_0(0,1)$, [F6] supplies a sequence $z_m\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$ converging in $H^1$. Piecewise integration by parts for each $z_m$ has cancelling interface terms because $u'$ is continuous; passing to the limit in the $L^2$ pairings gives $\int_0^1u'z'=-\int_0^1u''z$. Since $f=-1$ on the first interval and $f=-u''$ on the second, this yields $a(u,v-u)-F(v-u)=\int_0^{a_0}(v-u)\,dx=\int_0^{a_0}v\,dx\ge0$, where the last inequality uses $v\ge\psi=0$ almost everywhere on $(0,a_0)$. Hence $u$ solves the variational inequality. The same integration by parts against compactly supported tests gives reaction density $-u''-f=1$ on $(0,a_0)$ and $0$ on $(a_0,1)$; no point mass occurs at $a_0$ because $u'$ is continuous.

The function $f$ is bounded on both subintervals, hence belongs to $L^2(0,1)$. The form is symmetric and bounded since $|a(w,z)|\le\|w'\|_2\|z'\|_2\le\|w\|_{H^1}\|z\|_{H^1}$ by [F4]. By [F3], $a(w,w)=\|w'\|_2^2\ge c_P^{-2}\|w\|_{H^1}^2$ for some $c_P>0$. Thus the form is bounded, symmetric and coercive in the sense of [F5]. The load is bounded because $|F(z)|\le\|f\|_2\|z\|_2\le c_P\|f\|_2\|z\|_{H^1}$ by [F3]–[F4]. If $\widetilde u\in K$ is another solution, test its inequality with $u$ and the one for $u$ with $\widetilde u$, then add; symmetry gives $a(u-\widetilde u,u-\widetilde u)\le0$. Coercivity forces $u=\widetilde u$.

$$V_h:=\{v_h\in V\cap C(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^2):v_h|_K\in\mathbb P_1(K;\mathbb R^2)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T_h\}.$$
For continuous $\psi$ on $\Gamma_C$, let $I_h\psi$ be its continuous piecewise-affine nodal interpolant on the contact edges. Under the additional obstacle hypotheses $\psi\le0$ and convexity of $\psi$ in arclength on $\Gamma_C$, define
$$K_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:v_h(a)\cdot n\ge I_h\psi(a)\text{ for every }a\in\mathcal N_h^C\}.$$
The nodal inequalities are exactly the plan's vertex constraints. The well-definedness and conformity claims are proved in [[lem-signorini-nodal-contact-set-conforming]].

Let $\psi\in C(\Gamma_C;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\psi\le0$. Define the unilateral frictionless **contact set**
$$K:=\{v\in V:T_Cv\cdot n\ge\psi\quad\text{for arclength-almost every point of }\Gamma_C\}.$$
Given the elasticity form $a$ and bounded load $F$ of [[def-signorini-elasticity-contact-model]], the **contact variational inequality** is to find $u\in K$ such that
$$a(u,v-u)\ge F(v-u)\qquad\text{for every }v\in K.$$
The set $K$ is nonempty, closed and convex by [[lem-signorini-contact-set-closed-convex-nonempty]].

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$. For $x,y\in I$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$, the point $\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y$ belongs to $I$. The function $f$ is **convex** when the convex-combination inequality holds for every weight in $[0,1]$:

$$f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).$$

It is **strictly convex** when this inequality is strict whenever $x\ne y$ and $0<\lambda<1$. It is **concave** (respectively **strictly concave**) when $-f$ is convex (respectively strictly convex). It is **midpoint convex** when the displayed inequality is required only at $\lambda=1/2$.

derivations.claim: The polynomial $\psi(s)=-1+4s(1-s)$ has endpoint values $-1$ and midpoint value $0$, and $\psi(s)=-(2s-1)^2$ shows its maximum is $0$. For $s_0,s_1\in[0,1]$ and $t\in[0,1]$, direct expansion gives $\psi((1-t)s_0+ts_1)-[(1-t)\psi(s_0)+t\psi(s_1)]=4t(1-t)(s_1-s_0)^2\ge0$, with strict inequality when $0<t<1$ and $s_0\ne s_1$. Thus [F2] says $\psi$ is strictly concave, not convex, and the convex-obstacle premise is absent.

The vector field $v_h(x,y)=(-x,0)$ is affine on each triangle and is zero on $\Gamma_D$, hence belongs to $V_h$. On the two contact vertices its normal value is $-1$, equal to the endpoint obstacle values, so both nodal inequalities hold. Along all of $\Gamma_C$, $v_h\cdot n=-1$, while at $s=1/2$ the obstacle equals $0$; continuity gives an interval around that midpoint on which $-1<\psi(s)$. Therefore the continuum contact inequality fails on a set of positive arclength and $v_h\notin K$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the setting of [[def-signorini-contact-variational-inequality]], including the Axiom of Choice for the trace/Poincare interfaces and Countable Choice. For every bounded linear load $F:V\to\mathbb R$, there is exactly one $u\in K$ satisfying the contact variational inequality. With $\alpha:=2\mu/c_K^2$, where $c_K$ is from [[lem-signorini-partial-dirichlet-korn-coercivity]], solutions for two loads $F_1,F_2$ satisfy
$$\alpha\|u_1-u_2\|_V\le\|F_1-F_2\|_{V^*}.$$

Use the polygon, displacement space and oriented contact normal from [[def-signorini-partial-trace-space]]. Let the constant shear modulus satisfy $\mu>0$, let the finite Lam\'e parameter satisfy $\lambda\ge0$, and let $F:V\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded linear functional. For $v\in V$, define the weak symmetric gradient
$$\varepsilon(v):=\frac{\nabla v+(\nabla v)^T}{2}.$$
For $u,v\in V$, define the isotropic small-strain elasticity form
$$a(u,v):=\int_\Omega 2\mu\,\varepsilon(u):\varepsilon(v)+\lambda\,\operatorname{div}u\,\operatorname{div}v\,dx.$$
The strain and form conventions are the algebraic formulas in [[def-linear-elasticity-displacement-formulation-and-data]]. The present domain is the partial-trace space $V$; all coercivity and well-posedness claims for it are proved locally below.

$$K:=\{v\in V:T_Cv\cdot n\ge\psi\quad\text{for arclength-almost every point of }\Gamma_C\}.$$
Given the elasticity form $a$ and bounded load $F$ of [[def-signorini-elasticity-contact-model]], the **contact variational inequality** is to find $u\in K$ such that
$$a(u,v-u)\ge F(v-u)\qquad\text{for every }v\in K.$$
The set $K$ is nonempty, closed and convex by [[lem-signorini-contact-set-closed-convex-nonempty]].

Assume both $\Gamma_D$ and $\Gamma_C$ are unions of boundary edges of each mesh, and let $\mathcal N_h^C$ be the vertices on $\Gamma_C$. The conforming continuous P1 displacement space is
$$V_h:=\{v_h\in V\cap C(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^2):v_h|_K\in\mathbb P_1(K;\mathbb R^2)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T_h\}.$$
For continuous $\psi$ on $\Gamma_C$, let $I_h\psi$ be its continuous piecewise-affine nodal interpolant on the contact edges. Under the additional obstacle hypotheses $\psi\le0$ and convexity of $\psi$ in arclength on $\Gamma_C$, define
$$K_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:v_h(a)\cdot n\ge I_h\psi(a)\text{ for every }a\in\mathcal N_h^C\}.$$
The nodal inequalities are exactly the plan's vertex constraints. The well-definedness and conformity claims are proved in [[lem-signorini-nodal-contact-set-conforming]].

Let $\mathcal T$ be a matching affine simplicial mesh of $\Omega$ as defined
in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Fix $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and an integer $q\ge1$. On each
cell let $\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q)$ denote the
restrictions to $K$ of $\mathbb K^q$-valued polynomials of total degree at
most $k$. The **broken polynomial space** is the finite product
$$V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:=\prod_{K\in\mathcal T}\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q),$$
viewed as functions defined almost everywhere cell by cell. For an interior
facet $F=K\cap K'$, the **jump** is the difference of the two polynomial
traces, with either fixed ordering of $K,K'$; its vanishing is independent of
that ordering. The **conforming polynomial space** is
$$V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}:=\{v\in V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:v|_{F,K}=v|_{F,K'}\text{ on every interior facet }F\}.$$
The **zero-boundary subspace** consists of those $v\in V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}$
whose polynomial trace is zero on every boundary facet. These are algebraic
definitions. The Sobolev inclusions and the zero-boundary closure conclusion
are proved separately in the corresponding local theorems on matching
piecewise polynomials and zero-boundary values. If $\mathcal T=\varnothing$,
then $\Omega=\varnothing$ by the mesh definition; the empty product is the
zero vector space consisting of the unique empty function, and the trace
conditions are vacuous.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Under [[def-signorini-nodal-p1-contact-scheme]], $K_h$ is a nonempty closed convex subset of the finite-dimensional space $V_h$ and $K_h\subseteq K$. If $v\in K\cap H^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)\cap C(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$, its global P1 nodal interpolant $I_hv$ is well defined, belongs to $V_h$, and lies in $K_h$.

In the setting of [[def-signorini-elasticity-contact-model]], the form $a$ is well defined, symmetric, and satisfies
$$|a(u,v)|\le(2\mu+2\lambda)\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\|v\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\qquad(u,v\in V).$$

Assume the geometry of [[def-signorini-partial-trace-space]] and let $V=\{v\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^2):T_Dv=0\}$. Then there is $c_K>0$, depending on $\Omega$ and $\Gamma_D$, such that
$$\|v\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le c_K\|\varepsilon(v)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\qquad(v\in V).$$

Assume the setting of [[def-signorini-contact-variational-inequality]], including the Axiom of Choice for the trace/Poincare interfaces and Countable Choice. For every bounded linear load $F:V\to\mathbb R$, there is exactly one $u\in K$ satisfying the contact variational inequality. With $\alpha:=2\mu/c_K^2$, where $c_K$ is from [[lem-signorini-partial-dirichlet-korn-coercivity]], solutions for two loads $F_1,F_2$ satisfy
$$\alpha\|u_1-u_2\|_V\le\|F_1-F_2\|_{V^*}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $K\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded coercive bilinear form with constants $M,\alpha>0$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]; no symmetry is assumed), and let $F:H\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded linear functional. Then there is exactly one $u\in K$ with
$$a(u,\,v-u)\ge F(v-u)\qquad\text{for every }v\in K .$$

On each fixed contact mesh in [[def-signorini-dual-mortar-contact-pair]], assume $K_h\subseteq K$, the elasticity form is bounded and coercive on $V_h$ with constants $M,\alpha>0$, and $F$ is bounded. Then the nodal contact variational inequality has a unique displacement $u_h$ and a unique multiplier $\lambda_h=\sum_i\lambda_i\chi_i\in\Lambda_h^+$ satisfying
$$a(u_h,v_h)-F(v_h)=b_h(v_h,\lambda_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h),$$
$$g_i:=u_h(a_i)\cdot n-I_h\psi(a_i)\ge0,\quad \lambda_i\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i=0\quad(0\le i\le N).$$
These saddle equations are equivalent to the discrete VI, and the integrated complementarity residual is exactly $\mathcal R_h:=\int_{\Gamma_C}\lambda_h(T_Cu_h\cdot n-I_h\psi)\,ds=\sum_i d_i\lambda_i g_i=0$. The trace-pair inf-sup bound is at least $1/\sqrt3$ in the stated $L^2$ norms by [[lem-signorini-dual-mortar-biorthogonality-and-infsup]], and the displacement satisfies $\|u_h\|_V\le\|F\|_{V^*}/\alpha$. The coupling uses exact edge integrals and has no contact quadrature defect.

derivations.claim: The vectors $(1,1)^T$ and $(1,-1)^T$ are eigenvectors of $A$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $3$, so $A$ is symmetric positive definite. Also $A^{-1}=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. For $f^{(1)}=(1,1/5)^T$, the unconstrained solution is $g=A^{-1}f^{(1)}=(11/15,7/15)^T$, which has positive entries, and $Ag-f^{(1)}=0$. Thus every VI test has zero residual and the complementarity equations hold with $\rho=0$. The scaling between $\rho_i$ and the mortar coefficient $\lambda_i$ agrees with [F1].

For $f^{(2)}=(1,-1)^T$, take $g=(1/2,0)^T$ and compute $Ag=(1,-1/2)^T$, so $Ag-f^{(2)}=(0,1/2)^T=\rho$. Both vectors are componentwise nonnegative and $\rho_1g_1=0=\rho_2g_2$. For every $z\in\mathbb R_+^2$, $\rho\cdot(z-g)=\rho_2z_2\ge0$, so this is the VI solution with exactly the second gap active.

Let $e_1,e_2$ be the standard coordinate vectors and write $r:=Ag-f$. If $g\ge0$, $r\ge0$, and $r_i g_i=0$, then for every $z\ge0$, $r\cdot(z-g)=\sum_i r_i z_i-\sum_i r_i g_i=\sum_i r_i z_i\ge0$, so the complementarity equations imply the VI. Conversely, suppose $g$ solves the VI. If $g_i>0$, choose $0<t<g_i$ and test with $z=g+te_i$ and $z=g-te_i$; the two inequalities give $r_i\ge0$ and $r_i\le0$, hence $r_i=0$. If $g_i=0$, test with $z=g+te_i$ for any $t>0$ to get $r_i\ge0$. Thus $r\ge0$ and $r_i g_i=0$ for both coordinates, proving equivalence. If $g,\widetilde g$ both solve the VI for the same load, testing with each other and adding gives $-(g-\widetilde g)^TA(g-\widetilde g)\ge0$. The eigenvalues computed in step 1.1 are positive, so $A$ is positive definite and this forces $g=\widetilde g$; then $\rho=Ag-f$ is also unique. Thus the displayed complementarity solutions are the unique ones for their respective loads.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a gas constant $R>0$, an adiabatic exponent $\gamma>1$, a constant reference entropy $s_0\in\mathbb R$, shear viscosity $\mu>0$, bulk viscosity $\zeta\ge0$, and heat conductivity $\kappa>0$. Put $c_v=R/(\gamma-1)$. A conservative state is $U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$. Its **admissible state set** is

$$\mathcal G=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\ E>\frac{|m|^2}{2\rho}\right\}.$$

For $U\in\mathcal G$, define the velocity $u=m/\rho$, internal-energy density $\varepsilon=E-|m|^2/(2\rho)$, pressure $p=(\gamma-1)\varepsilon$, temperature $T=p/(R\rho)$, specific entropy $s(U)=c_v\log(p/\rho^\gamma)+s_0$, and mathematical entropy $\eta(U)=-\rho s(U)$. The Euler flux in coordinate direction $j$ is

$$F_j(U)=\bigl(\rho u_j,\ m u_j+p e_j,\ (E+p)u_j\bigr),\qquad j=1,\ldots,d,$$

where $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^d$. The mathematical entropy flux is $q_j(U)=\eta(U)u_j$.

For a differentiable velocity field, write $D=\operatorname{sym}\nabla u$ with $D_{ab}=(\partial_bu_a+\partial_au_b)/2$, and $D^0=D-(\operatorname{tr}D/d)I$. The Newtonian stress and Fourier viscous flux are

$$\tau=2\mu D^0+\zeta(\operatorname{tr}D)I, \qquad F_j^{\mathrm{visc}}=\bigl(0,\tau_{j1},\ldots,\tau_{jd},\ u\cdot\tau_{j\cdot}+\kappa\partial_jT\bigr).$$

The **compressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier balance law** is the conservative system

$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jF_j(U) =\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jF_j^{\mathrm{visc}}(U,\nabla u,\nabla T).$$

Unless a boundary is specified separately, a periodic solution means that all fields and fluxes are periodic in each spatial coordinate. The positive parameters and the inequalities defining $\mathcal G$ imply $p>0$ and $T>0$.

derivations.claim: On the convex half-space $\rho>0$, set $g(\rho,m)=|m|^2/(2\rho)$. For any direction $(a,b)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$, differentiating twice along $(\rho+ta,m+tb)$ gives $\frac{d^2}{dt^2}g(\rho+ta,m+tb)|_{t=0}=|b-(m/\rho)a|^2/\rho\ge0$. Thus $g$ is convex on that half-space.

Let $U_0=(\rho_0,m_0,E_0)$ and $U_1=(\rho_1,m_1,E_1)$ lie in $\mathcal G$, and let $0\le t\le1$. Then $\rho_t=(1-t)\rho_0+t\rho_1>0$ and convexity from step 1.1 gives $g(\rho_t,m_t)\le(1-t)g(\rho_0,m_0)+tg(\rho_1,m_1)$. The strict endpoint inequalities $E_i>g(\rho_i,m_i)$ imply $E_t>g(\rho_t,m_t)$, so $U_t\in\mathcal G$.

The function $g$ is continuous where $\rho>0$, so the strict inequalities $\rho>0$ and $E-g(\rho,m)>0$ define an open set there. Step 2.1 proves convexity, and choosing $t=1/2$ proves the arithmetic-mean assertion.

derivations.claim: Set $\varepsilon=E-|m|^2/(2\rho)$ and $u=m/\rho$. Rewriting the entropy gives $\eta=-c_v\rho\log((\gamma-1)\varepsilon)+c_v\gamma\rho\log\rho-s_0\rho$. For an increment $\delta U=(a,b,c)$, its first internal-energy variation is $\delta\varepsilon=c-u\cdot b+|u|^2a/2$, and its second directional variation is $D^2\varepsilon[\delta U,\delta U]=-|b-ua|^2/\rho$. The chain rule therefore yields $D^2\eta[\delta U,\delta U]=c_v\left(\frac{\gamma}{\rho}a^2-\frac{2}{\varepsilon}a\,\delta\varepsilon+\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon^2}(\delta\varepsilon)^2+\frac1{\varepsilon}|b-ua|^2\right)$. The first three terms have matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\gamma/\rho&-1/\varepsilon\\-1/\varepsilon&\rho/\varepsilon^2\end{pmatrix}$, whose leading diagonal entry is positive and determinant is $(\gamma-1)/\varepsilon^2>0$. The last term is nonnegative. If the full quadratic form is zero, then $a=\delta\varepsilon=0$ and $b=0$; the formula for $\delta\varepsilon$ then gives $c=0$. Thus the Hessian is positive definite.

Differentiating the same expression for $\eta$ gives $\beta=c_v\rho/\varepsilon=1/T$ and $v=(c_v\gamma-s-\beta|u|^2/2,\beta u,-\beta)$. Positive definiteness from step 1.1 makes $D_Uv=D_U^2\eta$ invertible, so the inverse function theorem gives a smooth local inverse near each state. Since $\mathcal G$ is convex by [F2], integrating the positive Hessian along the segment between any two distinct states also gives strict convexity of $\eta$ on $\mathcal G$.

Fix $j$ and an arbitrary variation $dU=(d\rho,dm,dE)$, and write $du_j=(dm_j-u_j\,d\rho)/\rho$. Differentiating the flux in [F1] gives $dF_j=(u_jd\rho+\rho du_j,\ u_jdm+m\,du_j+e_jdp,\ u_j(dE+dp)+(E+p)du_j)$. With $v_m=\beta u$ and $v_E=-\beta$ from step 2.1, the $dp$ terms in $v^TdF_j-u_jv^TdU$ cancel, and the coefficient of $du_j$ is $\rho v_\rho+\beta\rho|u|^2-\beta(E+p)=-\rho s=\eta$, using $E=\varepsilon+\rho|u|^2/2$, $p=(\gamma-1)\varepsilon$, and $\beta\varepsilon=c_v\rho$. Thus $v^TdF_j=u_jv^TdU+\eta\,du_j=dq_j$ for every variation, proving $\nabla_Uq_j=v^TDF_j$ directly.

Direct substitution of $v$, $F_j$, and $q_j$ gives $v^TF_j-q_j=\bigl(\rho(c_v\gamma-s-\beta|u|^2/2)+\beta\rho|u|^2-\beta E+\rho s\bigr)u_j$. Using $E=\varepsilon+\rho|u|^2/2$ and $\beta\varepsilon=c_v\rho$, the coefficient simplifies to $c_v(\gamma-1)\rho=R\rho$. This proves $\psi_j=\rho R u_j$ and completes the stated entropy-pair and potential identities.

$$F_j^{\mathrm{ec}}(U_L,U_R)= \begin{cases} F_j(U_L),&\Delta v=0,\\[2mm] F_j(\bar U)+\dfrac{\Delta\psi_j-\Delta v^TF_j(\bar U)}{\|\Delta v\|^2}\,\Delta v,&\Delta v\ne0. \end{cases}$$

The norm is Euclidean in the $d+2$ conservative-state coordinates. The convexity result [[lem-compressible-admissible-state-set-open-convex]] ensures $\bar U\in\mathcal G$.

For the ideal-gas model in [[def-compressible-navier-stokes-fourier-model]], the mathematical entropy $\eta=-\rho s$ has positive-definite Hessian on $\mathcal G$. Its entropy variables are

$$v(U)=\nabla_U\eta(U)=\left(c_v\gamma-s-\frac{\beta|u|^2}{2},\ \beta u,\ -\beta\right),\qquad \beta=\frac{c_v\rho}{\varepsilon}=\frac1T.$$

The Euler entropy flux $q_j(U)=\eta(U)u_j$ is compatible with $F_j$, meaning $\nabla_Uq_j=(\nabla_U\eta)^TDF_j$, and its entropy potential is $\psi_j(U)=v(U)^TF_j(U)-q_j(U)=\rho R u_j$. Consequently $U\mapsto v(U)$ is a local diffeomorphism at every $U\in\mathcal G$ and $\eta$ is strictly convex on $\mathcal G$.

The set $\mathcal G$ in [[def-compressible-navier-stokes-fourier-model]] is open and convex in $\mathbb R^{d+2}$. In particular, the arithmetic mean of any two admissible conservative states is admissible.

derivations.claim: If $U_L=U_R$, then $\Delta v=0$ and [F1] gives $F_j^{\mathrm{ec}}(U_L,U_R)=F_j(U_L)$. If $U_L\ne U_R$, convexity [F3] keeps the segment $U(t)=U_L+t(U_R-U_L)$ in $\mathcal G$, and $\Delta v^T(U_R-U_L)=\int_0^1 (U_R-U_L)^TD_U^2\eta(U(t))(U_R-U_L)\,dt>0$ by [F2]. Hence $\Delta v\ne0$, so the denominator in [F1] is nonzero; also $\bar U\in\mathcal G$. This proves well-definedness and consistency.

Exchanging $U_L$ and $U_R$ leaves $\bar U$ fixed and changes the signs of both $\Delta v$ and $\Delta\psi_j$. Thus the scalar correction coefficient in [F1] changes sign while its vector factor changes sign, leaving the flux unchanged. The diagonal branch is also symmetric.

Fix a state $X\in\mathcal G$ and write $U_R=X+h/2$, $U_L=X-h/2$ for small $h$. The entropy compatibility in [F2] implies $D_U\psi_j(X)=F_j(X)^TD_Uv(X)$. Symmetric Taylor expansions therefore give $\Delta v=D_Uv(X)h+O(|h|^3)$ and $\Delta\psi_j=F_j(X)^TD_Uv(X)h+O(|h|^3)$, so $N:=\Delta\psi_j-\Delta v^TF_j(X)=O(|h|^3)$. Positive definiteness of $D_Uv(X)$ implies $|\Delta v|\ge c|h|$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $h=0$.

When $\Delta v\ne0$, dotting [F1] with $\Delta v$ cancels its denominator and gives $\Delta v^TF_j(\bar U)+\Delta\psi_j-\Delta v^TF_j(\bar U)=\Delta\psi_j$. When $\Delta v=0$, step 1.1 gives $U_L=U_R$, so both sides are zero.

On that neighborhood, the correction $N\Delta v/|\Delta v|^2$ is $O(|h|^2)$ and tends to zero on the diagonal. Differentiating the symmetric Taylor remainders gives $\partial_hN=O(|h|^2)$, $\partial_XN=O(|h|^3)$, $\partial_h\Delta v=O(1)$, and $\partial_X\Delta v=O(|h|)$. The quotient rule then shows that the correction derivatives are bounded and tend to zero as $h\to0$; its diagonal extension is $C^1$. Away from the diagonal the denominator is nonzero by step 1.1 and the formula is smooth. Thus the flux is locally Lipschitz everywhere on $\mathcal G\times\mathcal G$.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a gas constant $R>0$, an adiabatic exponent $\gamma>1$, a constant reference entropy $s_0\in\mathbb R$, shear viscosity $\mu>0$, bulk viscosity $\zeta\ge0$, and heat conductivity $\kappa>0$. Put $c_v=R/(\gamma-1)$. A conservative state is $U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$. Its **admissible state set** is

$$\mathcal G=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\ E>\frac{|m|^2}{2\rho}\right\}.$$

For $U\in\mathcal G$, define the velocity $u=m/\rho$, internal-energy density $\varepsilon=E-|m|^2/(2\rho)$, pressure $p=(\gamma-1)\varepsilon$, temperature $T=p/(R\rho)$, specific entropy $s(U)=c_v\log(p/\rho^\gamma)+s_0$, and mathematical entropy $\eta(U)=-\rho s(U)$. The Euler flux in coordinate direction $j$ is

$$F_j(U)=\bigl(\rho u_j,\ m u_j+p e_j,\ (E+p)u_j\bigr),\qquad j=1,\ldots,d,$$

where $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^d$. The mathematical entropy flux is $q_j(U)=\eta(U)u_j$.

For a differentiable velocity field, write $D=\operatorname{sym}\nabla u$ with $D_{ab}=(\partial_bu_a+\partial_au_b)/2$, and $D^0=D-(\operatorname{tr}D/d)I$. The Newtonian stress and Fourier viscous flux are

$$\tau=2\mu D^0+\zeta(\operatorname{tr}D)I, \qquad F_j^{\mathrm{visc}}=\bigl(0,\tau_{j1},\ldots,\tau_{jd},\ u\cdot\tau_{j\cdot}+\kappa\partial_jT\bigr).$$

The **compressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier balance law** is the conservative system

$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jF_j(U) =\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jF_j^{\mathrm{visc}}(U,\nabla u,\nabla T).$$

Unless a boundary is specified separately, a periodic solution means that all fields and fluxes are periodic in each spatial coordinate. The positive parameters and the inequalities defining $\mathcal G$ imply $p>0$ and $T>0$.

For the ideal-gas model in [[def-compressible-navier-stokes-fourier-model]], the mathematical entropy $\eta=-\rho s$ has positive-definite Hessian on $\mathcal G$. Its entropy variables are

$$v(U)=\nabla_U\eta(U)=\left(c_v\gamma-s-\frac{\beta|u|^2}{2},\ \beta u,\ -\beta\right),\qquad \beta=\frac{c_v\rho}{\varepsilon}=\frac1T.$$

The Euler entropy flux $q_j(U)=\eta(U)u_j$ is compatible with $F_j$, meaning $\nabla_Uq_j=(\nabla_U\eta)^TDF_j$, and its entropy potential is $\psi_j(U)=v(U)^TF_j(U)-q_j(U)=\rho R u_j$. Consequently $U\mapsto v(U)$ is a local diffeomorphism at every $U\in\mathcal G$ and $\eta$ is strictly convex on $\mathcal G$.

For $U\in\mathcal G$, let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)$ and $W=(W_1,\ldots,W_d)$ be arrays of entropy-variable gradients, with $Z_k,W_k\in\mathbb R^{d+2}$. Write $Z_{k,m_\ell}$ for the momentum-variable component and $Z_{k,E}$ for the energy-variable component. Define

$$G_{k\ell}(Z)=Z_{k,m_\ell}+u_\ell Z_{k,E},\qquad c_k(Z)=Z_{k,E},$$

and $G^0(Z)=\operatorname{sym}G(Z)-(\operatorname{tr}G(Z)/d)I$. Define the linear map

$$\mathcal R_U Z=\bigl(\sqrt{2\mu T}\,G^0(Z),\ \sqrt{\zeta T}\,\operatorname{tr}G(Z),\ \sqrt{\kappa}\,T c(Z)\bigr).$$

The bilinear form

$$\mathcal B_U(Z,W)=2\mu T\,G^0(Z):G^0(W)+\zeta T\,\operatorname{tr}G(Z)\operatorname{tr}G(W)+\kappa T^2\sum_{k=1}^d c_k(Z)c_k(W)$$

has the factorization $\mathcal B_U(Z,W)=(\mathcal R_UZ)\cdot(\mathcal R_UW)=\sum_{j,k}Z_j^TK_{jk}(U)W_k$, so $K(U)=\mathcal R_U^*\mathcal R_U$ is a symmetric positive-semidefinite block matrix. For $Z_k=\partial_kv(U)$, its blocks give exactly the model viscous flux $F_j^{\mathrm{visc}}=\sum_kK_{jk}(U)\partial_kv$, and

$$\sum_{j,k}(\partial_jv)^TK_{jk}(U)(\partial_kv)=\frac{\tau:\nabla u}{T}+\frac{\kappa|\nabla T|^2}{T^2}\ge0.$$

derivations.claim: By [F2] and the balance law [F1], $\partial_t\eta+\sum_j\partial_jq_j=v^T\sum_j\partial_jF_j^{\mathrm{visc}}=\sum_j\partial_j(v^TF_j^{\mathrm{visc}})-\sum_j(\partial_jv)^TF_j^{\mathrm{visc}}$. The second equality is the product rule applied componentwise to each finite-dimensional flux vector.

From the explicit entropy variables in [F2] and viscous flux in [F1], the momentum and stress-work terms cancel pointwise: $v^TF_j^{\mathrm{visc}}=(T^{-1}u)\cdot\tau_{j\cdot}-T^{-1}(u\cdot\tau_{j\cdot}+\kappa\partial_jT)=-\kappa\frac{\partial_jT}{T}$. Substitution into step 1.1 and the factorization identity [F3] gives the displayed local balance and its nonpositive right-hand side.

Let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,M\}$ be a nonempty finite periodic node set. Let $H\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ be diagonal with strictly positive entries, and for each direction $j=1,\ldots,d$ let $D_j\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ satisfy the periodic diagonal-norm SBP identities

$$HD_j+D_j^TH=0,\qquad D_j\mathbf1=0.$$

For a nodal array $w=(w_i)_{i\in\mathcal I}$, $D_jw$ means componentwise matrix multiplication, $(D_jw)_i=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal I}(D_j)_{i\ell}w_\ell$. Given admissible nodal states $U_i\in\mathcal G$, write $v_i=v(U_i)$. Define the semidiscrete system

$$\dot U_i+2\sum_{j=1}^d\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal I}(D_j)_{i\ell}F_j^{\mathrm{ec}}(U_i,U_\ell) =\sum_{j,k=1}^d\left[D_j\left(\bigl(K_{jk}(U_i)(D_kv)_i\bigr)_{i\in\mathcal I}\right)\right]_i, \qquad i\in\mathcal I,$$

where $F_j^{\mathrm{ec}}$ is the two-point flux in [[def-ideal-gas-entropy-conservative-pair-flux]] and $K_{jk}$ is the viscous block matrix in [[lem-compressible-viscous-flux-entropy-variable-factorization]]. This definition specifies a periodic semidiscrete operator on $\mathcal G^M$; it does not include a time discretization or a positivity limiter.

The flux in [[def-ideal-gas-entropy-conservative-pair-flux]] is well-defined for every pair in $\mathcal G\times\mathcal G$, symmetric in its two states, and consistent in the sense that $F_j^{\mathrm{ec}}(U,U)=F_j(U)$. It satisfies

$$(v(U_R)-v(U_L))^TF_j^{\mathrm{ec}}(U_L,U_R)=\psi_j(U_R)-\psi_j(U_L).$$

The flux is locally Lipschitz on $\mathcal G\times\mathcal G$.

For $U\in\mathcal G$, let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)$ and $W=(W_1,\ldots,W_d)$ be arrays of entropy-variable gradients, with $Z_k,W_k\in\mathbb R^{d+2}$. Write $Z_{k,m_\ell}$ for the momentum-variable component and $Z_{k,E}$ for the energy-variable component. Define

$$G_{k\ell}(Z)=Z_{k,m_\ell}+u_\ell Z_{k,E},\qquad c_k(Z)=Z_{k,E},$$

and $G^0(Z)=\operatorname{sym}G(Z)-(\operatorname{tr}G(Z)/d)I$. Define the linear map

$$\mathcal R_U Z=\bigl(\sqrt{2\mu T}\,G^0(Z),\ \sqrt{\zeta T}\,\operatorname{tr}G(Z),\ \sqrt{\kappa}\,T c(Z)\bigr).$$

The bilinear form

$$\mathcal B_U(Z,W)=2\mu T\,G^0(Z):G^0(W)+\zeta T\,\operatorname{tr}G(Z)\operatorname{tr}G(W)+\kappa T^2\sum_{k=1}^d c_k(Z)c_k(W)$$

has the factorization $\mathcal B_U(Z,W)=(\mathcal R_UZ)\cdot(\mathcal R_UW)=\sum_{j,k}Z_j^TK_{jk}(U)W_k$, so $K(U)=\mathcal R_U^*\mathcal R_U$ is a symmetric positive-semidefinite block matrix. For $Z_k=\partial_kv(U)$, its blocks give exactly the model viscous flux $F_j^{\mathrm{visc}}=\sum_kK_{jk}(U)\partial_kv$, and

$$\sum_{j,k}(\partial_jv)^TK_{jk}(U)(\partial_kv)=\frac{\tau:\nabla u}{T}+\frac{\kappa|\nabla T|^2}{T^2}\ge0.$$

derivations.claim: For each direction set $Q_j=HD_j$. Then [F1] gives $Q_j^T=-Q_j$ and $Q_j\mathbf1=HD_j\mathbf1=0$. Skew-symmetry also gives $\mathbf1^TQ_j=-(Q_j\mathbf1)^T=0$.

Multiply the semidiscrete equation by $H_{ii}$ and sum in $i$. For the Euler term, each component of $\sum_{i,\ell}(Q_j)_{i\ell}F_j^{\mathrm{ec}}(U_i,U_\ell)$ is zero: swapping $i$ and $\ell$ changes the sign of $Q_j$ by step 1.1 and leaves the flux unchanged by [F2]. The viscous term sums to $\mathbf1^THD_jW=\mathbf1^TQ_jW=0$ for each nodal flux array $W$. Thus the weighted sum of each conservative component has derivative zero.

By the chain rule, the Euler contribution to the entropy derivative is $-2\sum_{j,i,\ell}(Q_j)_{i\ell}v_i^TF_j^{\mathrm{ec}}(U_i,U_\ell)$. Skew-symmetry and flux symmetry [F2], after swapping the two indices in one copy of the sum, rewrite this as $-\sum_{j,i,\ell}(Q_j)_{i\ell}(v_i-v_\ell)^TF_j^{\mathrm{ec}}(U_i,U_\ell)$. The entropy-potential identity [F2] changes the summand to $(Q_j)_{i\ell}(\psi_j(U_i)-\psi_j(U_\ell))$. Both its row sum and column sum vanish by step 1.1, so the total Euler contribution is zero.

For each viscous direction, $v^THD_jW=-(D_jv)^THW$ by $D_j^TH=-HD_j$. Applying this to $W_i=\sum_kK_{jk}(U_i)(D_kv)_i$ shows that the remaining entropy derivative is exactly the negative sum in the Statement. Each nodal quadratic form is nonnegative by [F3], and each weight $H_{ii}$ is positive; hence the derivative is nonpositive.
