Let $m\ge1$, let $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_m)$ with $d_i\ge0$, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be as in [[def-reaction-vector-field-and-quasipositivity]]. A **semilinear vector reaction-diffusion system** is
$$
u_t=D\Delta u+F(u),\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x),
$$
on either a flat periodic torus $\mathbb T_L^d$ or a bounded connected polyhedral domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with homogeneous no-flux conditions $d_i\partial_nu_i=0$ on each boundary face. Equivalently, $\partial_nu_i=0$ is required for components with $d_i>0$; components with $d_i=0$ require no boundary condition. The diffusion matrix is diagonal and independent of $u$; this definition does not include cross-diffusion.

A classical solution is **bounded in the rectangle $R$** on $[0,T]$ if $u(x,t)\in R$ at every point and time in its stated solution class, with $R$ as in [[def-reaction-invariant-rectangle]]. This item fixes the continuous PDE convention; the finite-volume and periodic discrete operators are defined separately.

Fix $d\ge1$, side lengths $L_j>0$, and integers $N_j\ge3$. Put $h_j=L_j/N_j$, $\mathbb T_L^d=\prod_{j=1}^d(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z)$, and $G_h=\prod_{j=1}^d(\mathbb Z/N_j\mathbb Z)$. Grid nodes are $x_i=((i_j+\tfrac12)h_j)_{j=1}^d$ modulo the side lengths, grid indices wrap modulo $N_j$, and $P_hu=(u(x_i))_{i\in G_h}$ denotes sampling. The cell volume is $m_h=\prod_jh_j$. The positive periodic heat stencil is the unit-diffusivity specialization of the periodic operator in [[def-parabolic-theta-finite-difference-scheme]]:
$$
(A_h^{\rm per}v)_i=\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{2v_i-v_{i+e_j}-v_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.
$$
For $s$ species with diffusivities $d_r\ge0$, the reaction-diffusion grid generator acts on species $r$ by $-d_rA_h^{\rm per}$. Each grid node has weight $m_h=\prod_jh_j$; the stencil has zero row and column sums, so each species' weighted sum is conserved by diffusion. Its matrix representation satisfies $L_h=m_hA_h^{\rm per}$, with symmetric $L_h$, nonpositive off-diagonal entries and $L_h\mathbf1=0$.

The sign convention is that $A_h^{\rm per}$ is nonnegative and $-d_rA_h^{\rm per}$ generates diffusion. The exact eigenvalues of the positive stencil are supplied by [[lem-periodic-heat-difference-amplification-symbol]]. This grid is the only spatial discretization used in the periodic error theorem; no mesh-uniform claim for general finite-volume meshes is made there.

On the finite periodic rectangular $d$-grid of [[def-parabolic-theta-finite-difference-scheme]], let $\ell_j\in\{0,\ldots,N_j-1\}$ and
$$
\phi_\ell(i)=\exp\left(2\pi\mathrm i\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{\ell_ji_j}{N_j}\right).
$$
Then $\phi_\ell$ is an eigenvector of $A_h^{\rm per}$ with eigenvalue
$$
\lambda_\ell=4\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{\kappa_j}{h_j^2}\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi\ell_j}{N_j}\right)\ge0.
$$
For zero source, the $\theta$ update multiplies this mode at each step by
$$
g_\theta(\ell)=\frac{1-(1-\theta)\Delta t\lambda_\ell}{1+\theta\Delta t\lambda_\ell}.
$$
The displayed modes form a basis of the complexified grid space, so this factor describes the full periodic update.

derivations.claim: Write $u=y_*+\varepsilon w$. Differentiability of $F$ gives $F(y_*+\varepsilon w)=F(y_*)+\varepsilon Jw+o(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon Jw+o(\varepsilon)$, so the linearized equation is $w_t=D\Delta w+Jw$. For a continuous torus mode $w(t,x)=a(t)e^{2\pi i\sum_jk_jx_j/L_j}$, direct differentiation gives $\Delta w=-\lambda_kw$ and hence $a'=(J-\lambda_kD)a$.

For every $\lambda\ge0$, $\operatorname{tr}(J-\lambda D)=\operatorname{tr}J-\lambda(d_1+d_2)<0$. Expanding the $2\times2$ determinant gives $\det(J-\lambda D)=(J_{11}-\lambda d_1)(J_{22}-\lambda d_2)-J_{12}J_{21}=d_1d_2\lambda^2-\beta_T\lambda+\det J=q(\lambda)$.

For the grid, insert a Fourier vector from [F3] into the linearized finite system. By [F2] its diffusion part multiplies that mode by $-D\lambda_{h,\ell}$; the reaction Jacobian acts on the species coordinate by $J$. Therefore the mode coefficient satisfies $a'=(J-\lambda_{h,\ell}D)a$. The basis assertion in [F3] ensures these are the actual grid mode matrices.

The characteristic polynomial of a real $2\times2$ matrix $A$ is $\mu^2-\operatorname{tr}(A)\mu+\det(A)$. If $\operatorname{tr}(A)<0$ and $\det(A)<0$, its discriminant $\operatorname{tr}(A)^2-4\det(A)$ is positive and the real roots have negative product, so one is positive. If $\operatorname{tr}(A)<0$ and $\det(A)>0$, real roots have negative sum and positive product, so both are negative; nonreal roots are conjugate with real part $\operatorname{tr}(A)/2<0$. If the determinant is zero, one eigenvalue is zero and the other is the trace, which is negative. Applying these alternatives to $A=J-\lambda D$ proves the mode tests in the Statement.

Since $d_1d_2>0$ and $\det J>0$, the upward-opening quadratic $q$ is negative at some $\lambda\ge0$ exactly when its minimum occurs at a positive point and its discriminant is strictly positive. Its minimizer is $\beta_T/(2d_1d_2)$, so the first condition is $\beta_T>0$; its discriminant is $\beta_T^2-4d_1d_2\det J$, so the second condition is the strict inequality in the Statement. Under these conditions both roots are positive because their sum is $\beta_T/(d_1d_2)>0$ and product is $\det J/(d_1d_2)>0$, and factorization gives $q<0$ precisely between them. The mode tests from step 2.2 then prove the continuous-spectrum and finite-grid criteria without replacing either actual spectrum by all real wavenumbers.

Let $\mathcal T=(\mathcal K,\mathcal F)$ be a finite TPFA-admissible cell-face mesh from [[def-fv-admissible-cell-face-mesh]] and [[def-tpfa-harmonic-face-scheme]]. Impose homogeneous no-flux boundary conditions: boundary faces contribute zero flux and therefore no conductance. For adjacent cells $K,L$, set
$$
c_{KL}=\sum_{F=K|L}T_F,
$$
where the sum is over their common interior faces and is zero when they are not adjacent. Set $c_{KL}=c_{LK}$ and $m_K=|K|$. If more than one face separates a cell pair, summing their conductances gives the same cell-balance flux as retaining the faces separately. Define the symmetric matrix $L_h$ by $(L_h)_{KK}=\sum_{L\ne K}c_{KL}$ and $(L_h)_{KL}=-c_{KL}$ for $K\ne L$.

For species diffusivities $d_r\ge0$, the no-flux finite-volume diffusion equation is $M U_r'+d_r L_h U_r=0$ for each species $r$, where $M=\operatorname{diag}(|K|)$. Its component equation is
$$
|K|(U_{K,r})'=d_r\sum_{L:c_{KL}>0}c_{KL}(U_{L,r}-U_{K,r}).
$$
The equality is the usual shared-face TPFA balance with outward flux $T_F(U_{K,r}-U_{L,r})$ and no boundary flux. The matrix $L_h$ is symmetric, has zero row sums and nonpositive off-diagonal entries, and obeys $v^{\mathsf T}L_hv=\sum_{\{K,L\}}c_{KL}(v_K-v_L)^2\ge0$, where the sum is over unordered adjacent cell pairs. With $M=\operatorname{diag}(|K|)$, the generator $-M^{-1}L_h$ is self-adjoint in the weighted pairing $\langle v,w\rangle_M=v^{\mathsf T}Mw$. This definition makes no accuracy claim for arbitrary admissible meshes.

The positive periodic heat stencil is the unit-diffusivity specialization of the periodic operator in [[def-parabolic-theta-finite-difference-scheme]]:
$$
(A_h^{\rm per}v)_i=\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{2v_i-v_{i+e_j}-v_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.
$$
For $s$ species with diffusivities $d_r\ge0$, the reaction-diffusion grid generator acts on species $r$ by $-d_rA_h^{\rm per}$. Each grid node has weight $m_h=\prod_jh_j$; the stencil has zero row and column sums, so each species' weighted sum is conserved by diffusion. Its matrix representation satisfies $L_h=m_hA_h^{\rm per}$, with symmetric $L_h$, nonpositive off-diagonal entries and $L_h\mathbf1=0$.

The sign convention is that $A_h^{\rm per}$ is nonnegative and $-d_rA_h^{\rm per}$ generates diffusion. The exact eigenvalues of the positive stencil are supplied by [[lem-periodic-heat-difference-amplification-symbol]]. For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be the reaction vector field of [[def-reaction-vector-field-and-quasipositivity]], and let $R\subset U$ be a state set. A vector $c\in[0,\infty)^m$ is a **stoichiometric conservation vector on $R$** if $c^TF(z)=0$ for every $z\in R$. It is a **stoichiometric dissipation vector on $R$** if $c^TF(z)\le0$ for every $z\in R$. The corresponding pointwise mass is $c^Tz$.

For a Lebesgue measurable domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and a measurable field $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ such that $\int_\Omega|c^Tu(x)|\,dx<\infty$, the continuous total mass is $\mathcal M_c(u)=\int_\Omega c^Tu(x)\,dx$, with Lebesgue integration. In particular, this is defined for bounded measurable fields on finite-volume domains. For any finite index set $I$ with assigned positive weights $m_i$, the discrete total mass of states $U_i\in\mathbb R^m$ is $\mathcal M_{c,h}(U)=\sum_{i\in I}m_ic^TU_i$. The weights and index set are part of the discrete model. Conservation and dissipation always refer to these stated functionals and the stated state set; no claim is made for a different weight vector or for reactions outside $R$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Fix a species $r$ and put $A_r=-d_rM^{-1}L$. If $d_r=0$, the solution is constant. If $d_r>0$, then $(A_r)_{ij}=d_rc_{ij}/m_i\ge0$ for $i
e j$, every row sums to zero, and $(A_r)_{ii}=-d_r\sum_{j
e i}c_{ij}/m_i$. Choose $\alpha>0$ at least as large as every exit rate $d_r\sum_{j
e i}c_{ij}/m_i$, and set $P=I+A_r/\alpha$. Then $P$ is entrywise nonnegative with row sums one. Matrix multiplication shows inductively that every $P^k$ has these same properties.

Symmetry of $L$ and $L\mathbf1=0$ give $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}L=0$. Hence $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}MA_r=-d_r\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}L=0$, and multiplication by every power of $A_r$ gives $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}MA_r^k=0$ for $k\ge1$. The exponential series therefore yields $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Me^{tA_r}=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}M$, so the weighted sum of species $r$ is conserved.

If $d_r=0$, $e^{tA_r}=I$ has nonnegative entries and row sums one. Otherwise use the $\alpha$ and $P$ of step 1.1. Since $A_r=\alpha(P-I)$, [F3] gives $e^{tA_r}=e^{\alpha tP}e^{-\alpha tI}$. By [F3], this exponential has derivative $A_re^{tA_r}$ and initial value $I$, so it solves the finite ODE; [F6] gives uniqueness.

The initial inequalities are $u_r(0)-a_r\mathbf1\ge0$ and $b_r\mathbf1-u_r(0)\ge0$. Applying the nonnegative matrix $e^{tA_r}$ and using $e^{tA_r}\mathbf1=\mathbf1$ from step 2.1 proves $a_r\mathbf1\le e^{tA_r}u_r(0)\le b_r\mathbf1$. **Input:** Either the no-flux TPFA discretization of [[def-fv-tpfa-no-flux-diffusion-specialization]] or the periodic-grid discretization of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]; a reaction field $F$; a reaction-inward rectangle $R$ such that $F$ is $C^1$ on an open neighborhood of $R$ and $DF$ is bounded on some closed neighborhood of $R$; a state $U^n$ with each cell/node state in $R$; and a time step $\tau\ge0$.

**Procedure:**

1. At every cell/node $i$, solve the exact reaction IVP $\dot z=F(z)$ from $z(0)=U_i^n$ to time $\tau$, and set $V_i=\Phi_F^\tau(U_i^n)$.
2. For each species $r$, apply the exact diffusion map $e^{-\tau d_rM^{-1}L_h}$ in the TPFA case or $e^{-\tau d_rA_h^{\rm per}}$ in the periodic-grid case to the vector $(V_{i,r})_i$; call the output $U^{n+1}_{\cdot,r}$.
3. Return $U^{n+1}$.

This order is the **reaction-then-diffusion Lie composition**. The maps in both substeps are exact flows. The algorithm makes no claim about an approximate ODE or matrix-exponential solver; any such solver error requires a separate bound. Under the hypotheses of [[thm-quasipositive-reaction-flow-preserves-invariant-rectangle-and-mass]] and [[thm-fv-and-periodic-diffusion-flow-preserves-rectangles-and-mass]], each substep is well-defined for all finite $\tau$ on $R$.

Let $R=\prod_{i=1}^m[a_i,b_i]$ be the reaction-inward rectangle of [[def-reaction-invariant-rectangle]]. Fix $d\ge1$, side lengths $L_j>0$, and integers $N_j\ge3$. Put $h_j=L_j/N_j$, $\mathbb T_L^d=\prod_{j=1}^d(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z)$, and $G_h=\prod_{j=1}^d(\mathbb Z/N_j\mathbb Z)$. Grid nodes are $x_i=((i_j+\tfrac12)h_j)_{j=1}^d$ modulo the side lengths, grid indices wrap modulo $N_j$, and $P_hu=(u(x_i))_{i\in G_h}$ denotes sampling. The cell volume is $m_h=\prod_jh_j$. The positive periodic heat stencil is the unit-diffusivity specialization of the periodic operator in [[def-parabolic-theta-finite-difference-scheme]]:
$$
(A_h^{\rm per}v)_i=\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{2v_i-v_{i+e_j}-v_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.
$$
For $s$ species with diffusivities $d_r\ge0$, the reaction-diffusion grid generator acts on species $r$ by $-d_rA_h^{\rm per}$. Each grid node has weight $m_h=\prod_jh_j$; the stencil has zero row and column sums, so each species' weighted sum is conserved by diffusion. Its matrix representation satisfies $L_h=m_hA_h^{\rm per}$, with symmetric $L_h$, nonpositive off-diagonal entries and $L_h\mathbf1=0$.

The sign convention is that $A_h^{\rm per}$ is nonnegative and $-d_rA_h^{\rm per}$ generates diffusion. The exact eigenvalues of the positive stencil are supplied by [[lem-periodic-heat-difference-amplification-symbol]]. This grid is the only spatial discretization used in the periodic error theorem; no mesh-uniform claim for general finite-volume meshes is made there.

Let $m\ge1$, let $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_m)$ with $d_i\ge0$, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be as in [[def-reaction-vector-field-and-quasipositivity]]. A **semilinear vector reaction-diffusion system** is
$$
u_t=D\Delta u+F(u),\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x),
$$
on either a flat periodic torus $\mathbb T_L^d$ or a bounded connected polyhedral domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with homogeneous no-flux conditions $d_i\partial_nu_i=0$ on each boundary face. Equivalently, $\partial_nu_i=0$ is required for components with $d_i>0$; components with $d_i=0$ require no boundary condition. The diffusion matrix is diagonal and independent of $u$; this definition does not include cross-diffusion.

A classical solution is **bounded in the rectangle $R$** on $[0,T]$ if $u(x,t)\in R$ at every point and time in its stated solution class, with $R$ as in [[def-reaction-invariant-rectangle]]. This item fixes the continuous PDE convention; the finite-volume and periodic discrete operators are defined separately.

Let $u_r\in C^4(\mathbb T_L^d)$, and let $P_hu_r$ denote its samples on the periodic rectangular grid of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]. For every grid node $i$,
$$
\left|(A_h^{\rm per}P_hu_r)_i+P_h(\Delta u_r)_i\right|\le\frac1{12}\sum_{j=1}^dh_j^2\|\partial_{jjjj}u_r\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d)}.
$$
For $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_m)$, define the sampled spatial residual $r_h=D(P_h\Delta u-\Delta_hP_hu)$, where $\Delta_h=-A_h^{\rm per}$ acts componentwise. If the indicated fourth derivatives are uniformly bounded for $0\le t\le T$, then $\|r_h(t)\|_\infty\le C_{\rm sp}h_{\max}^2$ with $C_{\rm sp}=\frac{d_{\max}}{12}\sum_j\|\partial_{jjjj}u\|_{L^\infty}$ componentwise, uniformly in the mesh.

Let $u:[0,T]\times\mathbb T_L^d\to R$ have bounded spatial derivatives through order two, with $R$ a compact rectangle. Let $F\in C^2$ on a neighborhood of $R$, and let $\mathcal A_h=-D A_h^{\rm per}$ be the periodic-grid diffusion generator from [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]. Define $F_h(P_hu)=P_h(F(u))$ pointwise. Then, uniformly over all periodic grids with $h_j=L_j/N_j$ and $N_j\ge3$,
$$\sup_{\substack{N_j\ge3\ (1\le j\le d),\ 0\le t\le T}}\left\|\mathcal A_hF_h(P_hu(t))-DF(P_hu(t))\mathcal A_hP_hu(t)\right\|_\infty\le C_{\rm com}<\infty,$$
where $C_{\rm com}$ depends only on the dimension, $D$, the suprema of $D^2u$, $DF$, $D^2F$, and the compact state rectangle, not on the mesh widths. This is the finite-grid commutator used in the first-order split-error proof; it is not a claim for arbitrary meshes or unbounded operators.

Consider either the no-flux TPFA cell system of [[def-fv-tpfa-no-flux-diffusion-specialization]] or the periodic grid system of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]. Write its finite index set as $I$, its positive diagonal mass matrix as $M=\operatorname{diag}(m_i)$, and its stiffness matrix as $L$. In both cases $L=L^{\mathsf T}$, $L\mathbf1=0$, and $L_{ij}=-c_{ij}$ for $i\ne j$, where $c_{ij}=c_{ji}\ge0$. For each species $r$, let $d_r\ge0$ and solve $M u_r'+d_rLu_r=0$. Assume $a_r\le b_r$ for every species. If initially $u_{i,r}\in[a_r,b_r]$ for all $i,r$, then the solution exists for all $t\ge0$ and remains in those intervals. More precisely, each species evolution matrix has nonnegative entries and row sums one, so it is a contraction in the maximum norm. The flow also preserves each weighted species sum $\sum_i m_i u_{i,r}$ and therefore every finite linear combination of species sums, including $\mathcal M_{c,h}$ of [[def-stoichiometric-mass-invariant]].

Choose either the no-flux TPFA system of [[def-fv-tpfa-no-flux-diffusion-specialization]] or the periodic grid system of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]], and use the exact reaction-then-diffusion step of [[alg-exact-lie-reaction-diffusion-step]]. Let $R=\prod_{r=1}^m[a_r,b_r]$ be reaction-inward, and suppose $F$ is $C^1$ on a neighborhood of $R$ with derivative bounded on a closed neighborhood. If every cell/node state of $U^n$ lies in $R$, then every cell/node state of $U^{n+1}$ lies in $R$ for every finite $\tau\ge0$. If $c^TF=0$ throughout $R$, then $\mathcal M_{c,h}(U^{n+1})=\mathcal M_{c,h}(U^n)$; if $c^TF\le0$ throughout $R$, then $\mathcal M_{c,h}(U^{n+1})\le\mathcal M_{c,h}(U^n)$. Here $\mathcal M_{c,h}(U)=\sum_i m_i c^TU_i$ uses the cell/node weights of the chosen discretization.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

**Input:** Either the no-flux TPFA discretization of [[def-fv-tpfa-no-flux-diffusion-specialization]] or the periodic-grid discretization of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]; a reaction field $F$; a reaction-inward rectangle $R$ such that $F$ is $C^1$ on an open neighborhood of $R$ and $DF$ is bounded on some closed neighborhood of $R$; a state $U^n$ with each cell/node state in $R$; and a time step $\tau\ge0$.

**Procedure:**

1. At every cell/node $i$, solve the exact reaction IVP $\dot z=F(z)$ from $z(0)=U_i^n$ to time $\tau$, and set $V_i=\Phi_F^\tau(U_i^n)$.
2. For each species $r$, apply the exact diffusion map $e^{-\tau d_rM^{-1}L_h}$ in the TPFA case or $e^{-\tau d_rA_h^{\rm per}}$ in the periodic-grid case to the vector $(V_{i,r})_i$; call the output $U^{n+1}_{\cdot,r}$.
3. Return $U^{n+1}$.

This order is the **reaction-then-diffusion Lie composition**. The maps in both substeps are exact flows. The algorithm makes no claim about an approximate ODE or matrix-exponential solver; any such solver error requires a separate bound. Under the hypotheses of [[thm-quasipositive-reaction-flow-preserves-invariant-rectangle-and-mass]] and [[thm-fv-and-periodic-diffusion-flow-preserves-rectangles-and-mass]], each substep is well-defined for all finite $\tau$ on $R$.

For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $R=\prod_{i=1}^m[a_i,b_i]$ be the reaction-inward rectangle of [[def-reaction-invariant-rectangle]]. Assume $F$ from [[def-reaction-vector-field-and-quasipositivity]] is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of $R$, and its derivative is bounded on some closed neighborhood of $R$. For any $z_0\in R$, the IVP $z'=F(z)$ has a unique solution for every $t\ge0$, and $z(t)\in R$. If $c$ is a conservation vector on $R$, then $c^Tz(t)=c^Tz_0$; if it is a dissipation vector, then $c^Tz(t)$ is nonincreasing. When every $a_i=0$, quasi-positivity implies the lower-face condition on $R$; upper-face inwardness remains a separate hypothesis.

derivations.claim: Let $Y_h(t)=P_hu(t)$ and $E_h(s)=e^{s\mathcal A_h}$. By [F1]–[F3], the sampled equation is $Y_h'=\mathcal A_hY_h+F_h(Y_h)+r_h$, where $F_h$ applies $F$ at each node and $\|r_h(t)\|_\infty\le C_{\rm sp}h_{\max}^2$. Differentiate $E_h(\tau-s)Y_h(t+s)$ using [F9], then integrate from $s=0$ to $s=\tau$ using [F10]; this gives $ Y_h(t+\tau)=E_h(\tau)Y_h(t)+\int_0^\tau E_h(\tau-s)\bigl(F_h(Y_h(t+s))+r_h(t+s)\bigr)\,ds. $ By [F5], $\|E_h(s)\|_{\infty\to\infty}\le1$.

For any two grid states $X,Z$ nodewise in $R$, the reaction flows satisfy $\|\Phi_{F_h}^\tau(X)-\Phi_{F_h}^\tau(Z)\|_\infty\le e^{L_F\tau}\|X-Z\|_\infty$, where $L_F=\sup_R\|DF\|$; this follows by subtracting their nodewise integral equations and applying [F7]. Composing with the diffusion contraction [F5] gives $\|S_{h,\tau}(X)-S_{h,\tau}(Z)\|_\infty\le e^{L_F\tau}\|X-Z\|_\infty$ for the exact Lie map $S_{h,\tau}$.

Write $V_h(s)=\Phi_{F_h}^s(Y_h(t))$ for the nodewise exact reaction flow. By [F8], [F11], and integration of its reaction ODE using [F10], the exact Lie step from $Y_h(t)$ equals $E_h(\tau)Y_h(t)+\int_0^\tau E_h(\tau)F_h(V_h(s))\,ds$. Subtract the identity in step 1.1 and add and subtract $E_h(\tau)F_h(Y_h(t+s))$ inside the integrand. The defect is therefore the sum of $ \int_0^\tau [E_h(\tau)-E_h(\tau-s)]F_h(Y_h(t+s))\,ds, \quad \int_0^\tau E_h(\tau)[F_h(V_h(s))-F_h(Y_h(t+s))]\,ds, \quad -\int_0^\tau E_h(\tau-s)r_h(t+s)\,ds. $

For a scalar $C^2$ component $g$, two integrations of $g''$ give $g(x+h)-2g(x)+g(x-h)=\int_0^h(h-s)(g''(x+s)+g''(x-s))\,ds$, so the absolute centered second difference divided by $h^2$ is at most $\|g''\|_\infty$. Applying this in each coordinate to $u$ and using [A1] gives $\|\mathcal A_hY_h(t)\|_\infty\le C_u$ independently of the mesh. By [F4], $\mathcal A_hF_h(Y_h)-DF(Y_h)\mathcal A_hY_h$ is uniformly bounded; [A1] bounds $DF$, so $\|\mathcal A_hF_h(Y_h(t+s))\|_\infty\le C_A$ for all $s$ and grids. Since $E_h'(r)=E_h(r)\mathcal A_h$ by [F9] and $E_h$ contracts by [F5], $ \|[E_h(\tau)-E_h(\tau-s)]F_h(Y_h(t+s))\|_\infty \le \int_{\tau-s}^{\tau}\|E_h(r)\mathcal A_hF_h(Y_h(t+s))\|_\infty\,dr \le C_As. $ Thus the first integral in step 2.1 has norm at most $C_A\tau^2/2$.

The reaction path $V_h(s)$ stays in $R$ by [F11], so its time derivative is uniformly bounded by $\sup_R\|F\|$. Also $\|Y_h(t+s)-Y_h(t)\|_\infty\le s\sup\|u_t\|_\infty$. Hence, integrating both time derivatives by [F10], $\|V_h(s)-Y_h(t+s)\|_\infty\le C s$. The mean-value bound for $F$ on the convex rectangle $R$ and contraction of $E_h$ show that the second integral in step 2.1 has norm at most $C\tau^2/2$. The residual term has norm at most $C_{\rm sp}\tau h_{\max}^2$ by [F3] and [F5]. Consequently the one-step defect is at most $C(\tau^2+\tau h_{\max}^2)$ with $C$ independent of grid and step.

Set $e_n=\|U^n-Y_h(t_n)\|_\infty$. By [F6] and the assumed PDE range, both inputs in step 1.2 lie in $R$. Applying that stability estimate and the defect bound of step 3.2 gives $e_{n+1}\le e^{L_F\tau}e_n+C\tau(\tau+h_{\max}^2)$, with $e_0=0$. Iterating, $e_n\le C\tau(\tau+h_{\max}^2)\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}e^{L_Fk\tau}\le CT e^{L_FT}(\tau+h_{\max}^2)$ for $n\tau\le T$. This proves the stated estimate after enlarging $C_T$.

Let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^d(0,L_j)$, where $L_j>0$, and let integers $N_j\ge2$ define $h_j=L_j/N_j$. The finite cell set is $I_h=\prod_{j=1}^d\{0,\ldots,N_j-1\}$, cell centers are $x_i=((i_j+\tfrac12)h_j)_{j=1}^d$, and every cell has volume $m_h=\prod_jh_j$. This is the uniform orthogonal Cartesian mesh; adjacent center segments are perpendicular to their shared faces. Take the scalar cellwise coefficient to be $\lambda_K=1$ and give boundary faces homogeneous no-flux data, so they contribute no flux.

For a grid vector $v=(v_i)_{i\in I_h}$, define the positive cell-centered stencil
$$
(A_h^Nv)_i=\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{2v_i-v_{i+e_j}-v_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2},
$$
where an unavailable neighbor at a boundary is assigned the value of the boundary cell itself. Indeed a face normal to direction $j$ has area $|F|=m_h/h_j$ and adjacent centers are distance $h_j$ apart, so its TPFA transmissibility is $|F|/h_j=m_h/h_j^2$; dividing the cell balance by $m_h$ gives the displayed coefficient. Boundary faces contribute zero flux. Thus $M_h=m_hI$ and $L_h^N=m_hA_h^N$ are the mass and stiffness matrices of the no-flux specialization in [[def-fv-tpfa-no-flux-diffusion-specialization]]. For species diffusivities $d_r\ge0$, the finite-volume diffusion equation is $U_r'=-d_rA_h^NU_r$.

Define the doubled periodic grid with $2N_j$ cells per direction on side lengths $2L_j$, using the same widths $h_j$, as in [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]. The reflection map $E_h$ extends $U$ evenly across every boundary face: in one coordinate, its extended index is $i$ for $0\le i<N_j$ and $2N_j-1-i$ for $N_j\le i<2N_j$; apply this coordinatewise. This finite reflection convention is used in the error theorem below.

Fix $d\ge1$, side lengths $L_j>0$, and integers $N_j\ge3$. Put $h_j=L_j/N_j$, $\mathbb T_L^d=\prod_{j=1}^d(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z)$, and $G_h=\prod_{j=1}^d(\mathbb Z/N_j\mathbb Z)$. Grid nodes are $x_i=((i_j+\tfrac12)h_j)_{j=1}^d$ modulo the side lengths, grid indices wrap modulo $N_j$, and $P_hu=(u(x_i))_{i\in G_h}$ denotes sampling. The cell volume is $m_h=\prod_jh_j$. The positive periodic heat stencil is the unit-diffusivity specialization of the periodic operator in [[def-parabolic-theta-finite-difference-scheme]]:
$$
(A_h^{\rm per}v)_i=\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{2v_i-v_{i+e_j}-v_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.
$$
For $s$ species with diffusivities $d_r\ge0$, the reaction-diffusion grid generator acts on species $r$ by $-d_rA_h^{\rm per}$. Each grid node has weight $m_h=\prod_jh_j$; the stencil has zero row and column sums, so each species' weighted sum is conserved by diffusion. Its matrix representation satisfies $L_h=m_hA_h^{\rm per}$, with symmetric $L_h$, nonpositive off-diagonal entries and $L_h\mathbf1=0$.

The sign convention is that $A_h^{\rm per}$ is nonnegative and $-d_rA_h^{\rm per}$ generates diffusion. The exact eigenvalues of the positive stencil are supplied by [[lem-periodic-heat-difference-amplification-symbol]]. This grid is the only spatial discretization used in the periodic error theorem; no mesh-uniform claim for general finite-volume meshes is made there.

Fix $T>0$, a rectangular torus $\mathbb T_L^d$, and $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_m)$ with $d_r\ge0$. Let $F\in C^2(U,\mathbb R^m)$ on an open neighborhood $U$ of a compact reaction-inward rectangle $R$, and let $u\in C^1([0,T];C^4(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^m))$ solve $u_t=D\Delta u+F(u)$ with $u(x,t)\in R$. For each periodic grid of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]], let $P_hu(t)$ be the samples, and start the exact Lie algorithm [[alg-exact-lie-reaction-diffusion-step]] from $U^0=P_hu(0)$, using the periodic branch and uniform steps $\tau=T/N$. There is a constant $C_T$, depending on $u,F,D,R,T,L,d,m$ but not on the grid widths or $N$, such that
$$
\max_{0\le n\le N}\|U^n-P_hu(t_n)\|_\infty\le C_T(\tau+h_{\max}^2),\qquad t_n=n\tau.
$$
The estimate is for exact reaction and diffusion subflows, a fixed smooth solution, and the periodic centered grid. It gives no error claim for a general finite-volume mesh, nonsmooth solutions, approximate subsolvers, or nonlinear cross-diffusion.

**Input:** Either the no-flux TPFA discretization of [[def-fv-tpfa-no-flux-diffusion-specialization]] or the periodic-grid discretization of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]; a reaction field $F$; a reaction-inward rectangle $R$ such that $F$ is $C^1$ on an open neighborhood of $R$ and $DF$ is bounded on some closed neighborhood of $R$; a state $U^n$ with each cell/node state in $R$; and a time step $\tau\ge0$.

**Procedure:**

1. At every cell/node $i$, solve the exact reaction IVP $\dot z=F(z)$ from $z(0)=U_i^n$ to time $\tau$, and set $V_i=\Phi_F^\tau(U_i^n)$.
2. For each species $r$, apply the exact diffusion map $e^{-\tau d_rM^{-1}L_h}$ in the TPFA case or $e^{-\tau d_rA_h^{\rm per}}$ in the periodic-grid case to the vector $(V_{i,r})_i$; call the output $U^{n+1}_{\cdot,r}$.
3. Return $U^{n+1}$.

This order is the **reaction-then-diffusion Lie composition**. The maps in both substeps are exact flows. The algorithm makes no claim about an approximate ODE or matrix-exponential solver; any such solver error requires a separate bound. Under the hypotheses of [[thm-quasipositive-reaction-flow-preserves-invariant-rectangle-and-mass]] and [[thm-fv-and-periodic-diffusion-flow-preserves-rectangles-and-mass]], each substep is well-defined for all finite $\tau$ on $R$.

Let $R=\prod_{i=1}^m[a_i,b_i]$ be the reaction-inward rectangle of [[def-reaction-invariant-rectangle]]. Assume $F$ from [[def-reaction-vector-field-and-quasipositivity]] is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of $R$, and its derivative is bounded on some closed neighborhood of $R$. For any $z_0\in R$, the IVP $z'=F(z)$ has a unique solution for every $t\ge0$, and $z(t)\in R$. If $c$ is a conservation vector on $R$, then $c^Tz(t)=c^Tz_0$; if it is a dissipation vector, then $c^Tz(t)$ is nonincreasing. When every $a_i=0$, quasi-positivity implies the lower-face condition on $R$; upper-face inwardness remains a separate hypothesis.

For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

derivations.claim: For each coordinate define $r_j(k_j)=k_j$ if $0\le k_j<N_j$ and $r_j(k_j)=2N_j-1-k_j$ if $N_j\le k_j<2N_j$. Then $(E_hU)_k=U_{(r_j(k_j))_j}$. At an interior original index, the doubled periodic stencil uses the same two neighbors as $A_h^N$. At the left boundary, the doubled neighbor $k_j=-1$ is represented by $2N_j-1$, whose reflected index is $0$, so its value is $U_i$; the right-boundary ghost similarly equals the last cell value. Therefore $ A_{2h}^{\rm per}E_hU=E_hA_h^NU $ for every array $U$.

From step 1.1, $(A_{2h}^{\rm per})^kE_h=E_h(A_h^N)^k$ for every integer $k\ge0$, by induction. The exponential power series [F6] then gives $e^{-\tau d_rA_{2h}^{\rm per}}E_h=E_he^{-\tau d_rA_h^N}$ for each species. The nodewise reaction flow also commutes with $E_h$: reflected copies start from identical values and solve the same IVP, so uniqueness [F5] keeps them identical.

At time zero, $E_hP_hu(0)$ is exactly the sample of the even-reflected continuous initial data on the doubled torus. Step 2.1 shows that the periodic split update of this array is the even extension of the no-flux TPFA split update. Induction over $n$ therefore identifies the periodic numerical iterates with $E_hU^n$.

The even-reflected function is $C^1_tC^4_x$ by [A1]. On every reflected open subrectangle, reflection preserves the Laplacian and acts only by coordinate sign changes on first derivatives; since the PDE has constant diagonal diffusion and pointwise reaction, the reflected function satisfies the same equation there. The equality extends across each interface by continuity of the function and its time and second spatial derivatives. Thus the doubled function solves the periodic problem covered by [F3]. Its samples are $E_hP_hu(t_n)$, and step 3.1 plus reflection gives $ \|E_hU^n-E_hP_hu(t_n)\|_\infty=\|U^n-P_hu(t_n)\|_\infty. $ Apply [F3] on the doubled grid, whose counts $2N_j$ are at least four, to obtain the bound.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

derivations.claim: On an element $[0,h]$, the two affine basis functions are $\phi_1(x)=1-x/h$ and $\phi_2(x)=x/h$. Direct integration gives $ \int_0^h\phi_1^2\,dx=\int_0^h\phi_2^2\,dx=h/3,\quad \int_0^h\phi_1\phi_2\,dx=h/6, $ and their derivatives are $-1/h$ and $1/h$, so the element stiffness entries are $1/h,-1/h,-1/h,1/h$. Assembling the two elements yields the displayed matrices: $ M=\frac h6\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&4&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad K=\frac1h\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}. $ The Neumann condition is natural in this stiffness form and adds no boundary matrix.

Write $M=(h/6)B$ and $K=C/h$ for the displayed integer matrices. Direct multiplication verifies $ B^{-1}=\frac1{12}\begin{pmatrix}7&-2&1\\-2&4&-2\\1&-2&7\end{pmatrix},\qquad B^{-1}C=\frac1{12}\begin{pmatrix}9&-12&3\\-6&12&-6\\3&-12&9\end{pmatrix}. $ Thus $M^{-1}K=6B^{-1}C/h^2$, so in particular $(M^{-1}K)_{13}=3/(2h^2)$. With $e_3=(0,0,1)^T$, the ODE gives $u'(0)=-\nu M^{-1}Ke_3$, whose first component is $-3\nu/(2h^2)<0$.

The linear field $u\mapsto-\nu M^{-1}Ku$ is globally Lipschitz. By [F1], $e^{-t\nu M^{-1}K}e_3$ solves the IVP, and [F2] makes it the unique solution. Since $u_1(0)=0$ and $u_1'(0)<0$ by step 2.1, the right difference quotient $u_1(t)/t$ is negative for all sufficiently small $t>0$. Hence the consistent-mass P1 semidiscrete diffusion is not positivity preserving, despite the nonnegative initial nodal vector.

Let $F\in C^1$ and let $y_*\in\mathbb R^2$ be a homogeneous equilibrium, $F(y_*)=0$. Set $J=DF(y_*)=(J_{ij})$, assume $\operatorname{tr}J<0$ and $\det J>0$, and let $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,d_2)$ with $d_1,d_2>0$. For any spatial eigenfunction of $-\Delta$ with eigenvalue $\lambda\ge0$, the linearized reaction-diffusion mode has matrix $J-\lambda D$. For the continuous rectangular torus, $\lambda=\lambda_k=\sum_j(2\pi k_j/L_j)^2$ with $k\in\mathbb Z^d$. For the periodic grid of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]], the mode indexed by $\ell$ has $\lambda=\lambda_{h,\ell}=4\sum_jh_j^{-2}\sin^2(\pi\ell_j/N_j)$, with $0\le\ell_j<N_j$.

Define
$$
\beta_T=d_2J_{11}+d_1J_{22},\qquad q(\lambda)=\det(J-\lambda D)=d_1d_2\lambda^2-\beta_T\lambda+\det J.
$$
For either domain or grid and each actual mode, $J-\lambda D$ has a positive-real-part eigenvalue exactly when $q(\lambda)<0$; it is Hurwitz exactly when $q(\lambda)>0$, and has a zero eigenvalue when $q(\lambda)=0$. Thus the continuous or discrete linear instability criterion tests the actual corresponding spectrum. If all nonnegative $\lambda$ are regarded as continuously available, then a diffusion-driven unstable band exists exactly when $\beta_T>0$ and $\beta_T^2>4d_1d_2\det J$; its endpoints are
$$
\lambda_\pm=\frac{\beta_T\pm\sqrt{\beta_T^2-4d_1d_2\det J}}{2d_1d_2}.
$$
On a bounded torus or a finite grid, the band criterion alone is not enough: at least one actual Laplacian eigenvalue must lie strictly between $\lambda_-$ and $\lambda_+$.

The coefficient in the dispersion polynomial is $\beta_T=d_2J_{11}+d_1J_{22}=9/10$ and $d_1d_2=1/5$. Therefore $ q(\lambda)=\tfrac15\lambda^2-\tfrac9{10}\lambda+1 =\tfrac15(\lambda-2)(\lambda-\tfrac52). $

For the continuous torus mode $k=1$, $\lambda=(2\pi/L)^2=9/4$. This lies strictly between $2$ and $5/2$, so step 2.1 gives $q(9/4)<0$. By [F1], the mode matrix has one positive eigenvalue and one negative eigenvalue. This example proves a linear mode instability only; it does not assert nonlinear pattern existence or stability.

F(u,v)=\bigl(1-\tfrac52u+u^2v,\ \tfrac32u-u^2v\bigr)
$$
with diagonal diffusivity $D=\operatorname{diag}(1/10,2)$. Its homogeneous equilibrium is $(u_*,v_*)=(1,3/2)$. On the one-dimensional torus of length $L=4\pi/3$, the continuous reaction-diffusion linearization has an unstable Fourier mode with wave number $k=1$.

Let $F\in C^1$ and let $y_*\in\mathbb R^2$ be a homogeneous equilibrium, $F(y_*)=0$. Set $J=DF(y_*)=(J_{ij})$, assume $\operatorname{tr}J<0$ and $\det J>0$, and let $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,d_2)$ with $d_1,d_2>0$. For any spatial eigenfunction of $-\Delta$ with eigenvalue $\lambda\ge0$, the linearized reaction-diffusion mode has matrix $J-\lambda D$. For the continuous rectangular torus, $\lambda=\lambda_k=\sum_j(2\pi k_j/L_j)^2$ with $k\in\mathbb Z^d$. For the periodic grid of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]], the mode indexed by $\ell$ has $\lambda=\lambda_{h,\ell}=4\sum_jh_j^{-2}\sin^2(\pi\ell_j/N_j)$, with $0\le\ell_j<N_j$.

Define
$$
\beta_T=d_2J_{11}+d_1J_{22},\qquad q(\lambda)=\det(J-\lambda D)=d_1d_2\lambda^2-\beta_T\lambda+\det J.
$$
For either domain or grid and each actual mode, $J-\lambda D$ has a positive-real-part eigenvalue exactly when $q(\lambda)<0$; it is Hurwitz exactly when $q(\lambda)>0$, and has a zero eigenvalue when $q(\lambda)=0$. Thus the continuous or discrete linear instability criterion tests the actual corresponding spectrum. If all nonnegative $\lambda$ are regarded as continuously available, then a diffusion-driven unstable band exists exactly when $\beta_T>0$ and $\beta_T^2>4d_1d_2\det J$; its endpoints are
$$
\lambda_\pm=\frac{\beta_T\pm\sqrt{\beta_T^2-4d_1d_2\det J}}{2d_1d_2}.
$$
On a bounded torus or a finite grid, the band criterion alone is not enough: at least one actual Laplacian eigenvalue must lie strictly between $\lambda_-$ and $\lambda_+$.

Let $\mathcal T=(\mathcal K,\mathcal F)$ be a finite TPFA-admissible cell-face mesh from [[def-fv-admissible-cell-face-mesh]] and [[def-tpfa-harmonic-face-scheme]]. Impose homogeneous no-flux boundary conditions: boundary faces contribute zero flux and therefore no conductance. For adjacent cells $K,L$, set
$$
c_{KL}=\sum_{F=K|L}T_F,
$$
where the sum is over their common interior faces and is zero when they are not adjacent. Set $c_{KL}=c_{LK}$ and $m_K=|K|$. If more than one face separates a cell pair, summing their conductances gives the same cell-balance flux as retaining the faces separately. Define the symmetric matrix $L_h$ by $(L_h)_{KK}=\sum_{L\ne K}c_{KL}$ and $(L_h)_{KL}=-c_{KL}$ for $K\ne L$.

For species diffusivities $d_r\ge0$, the no-flux finite-volume diffusion equation is $M U_r'+d_r L_h U_r=0$ for each species $r$, where $M=\operatorname{diag}(|K|)$. Its component equation is
$$
|K|(U_{K,r})'=d_r\sum_{L:c_{KL}>0}c_{KL}(U_{L,r}-U_{K,r}).
$$
The equality is the usual shared-face TPFA balance with outward flux $T_F(U_{K,r}-U_{L,r})$ and no boundary flux. The matrix $L_h$ is symmetric, has zero row sums and nonpositive off-diagonal entries, and obeys $v^{\mathsf T}L_hv=\sum_{\{K,L\}}c_{KL}(v_K-v_L)^2\ge0$, where the sum is over unordered adjacent cell pairs. With $M=\operatorname{diag}(|K|)$, the generator $-M^{-1}L_h$ is self-adjoint in the weighted pairing $\langle v,w\rangle_M=v^{\mathsf T}Mw$. This definition makes no accuracy claim for arbitrary admissible meshes.

**Input:** Either the no-flux TPFA discretization of [[def-fv-tpfa-no-flux-diffusion-specialization]] or the periodic-grid discretization of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]; a reaction field $F$; a reaction-inward rectangle $R$; coordinate constants $L_i\ge0$ such that $|F_i(z)-F_i(w)|\le L_i|z_i-w_i|$ whenever $z,w\in R$ differ only in coordinate $i$, as required in [[lem-forward-euler-reaction-step-preserves-invariant-rectangle-and-mass]]; $\tau_R=\min_{i:L_i>0}L_i^{-1}$, with $\tau_R=+\infty$ if every $L_i=0$; a state $U^n$ with every cell/node state in $R$; and $0\le\tau\le\tau_R$.

**Procedure:**

1. At every cell/node, compute the forward-Euler reaction value $V_i=U_i^n+\tau F(U_i^n)$.
2. For each species $r$, apply the exact diffusion map $e^{-\tau d_rM^{-1}L_h}$ in the TPFA case or $e^{-\tau d_rA_h^{\rm per}}$ in the periodic-grid case to $(V_{i,r})_i$.
3. Return the resulting state $U^{n+1}$.

This is an approximate reaction substep followed by exact diffusion. The bound $\tau\le\tau_R$ is part of the input contract and is needed for the stated rectangle guarantee; no diffusion CFL restriction is needed because the diffusion map is exact. The procedure makes no claim about finite-precision evaluation of either step.

Choose either the no-flux TPFA system of [[def-fv-tpfa-no-flux-diffusion-specialization]] or the periodic grid system of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]. Use [[alg-euler-reaction-lie-diffusion-step]] with a reaction-inward rectangle $R$, an initial state in $R$, and $0\le\tau\le\tau_R$ from [[lem-forward-euler-reaction-step-preserves-invariant-rectangle-and-mass]]. Then every component of the output state lies in $R$. The functional $\mathcal M_{c,h}$ is unchanged when $c^TF=0$ throughout $R$, and is nonincreasing when $c^TF\le0$ throughout $R$. The diffusion substep here is exact; no positivity assertion for a forward-Euler diffusion substep is made.

derivations.claim: On $[0,1]$, $F(0)=F(1)=0$, so the field points inward at both endpoints. Also $|F'(u)|=|r(1-2u)|\le r$, giving the coordinate Lipschitz constant $L=r$ and Euler restriction $\tau\le1/r$.

For $u\in[0,1]$, set $\alpha=\tau r\in[0,1]$. The Euler value is $u^+=u+\alpha u(1-u)\ge0$, while $ 1-u^+=(1-u)(1-\alpha u)\ge0 $ because both factors are nonnegative. Thus the reaction step preserves $[0,1]$.

If $\alpha=\tau r>1$, choose $u$ with $1/\alpha<u<1$. Then $1-u^+=(1-u)(1-\alpha u)<0$, so the Euler map leaves $[0,1]$. Together with step 2.1 this proves the stated necessary-and-sufficient bound for the reaction map.

The reaction map satisfies the hypothesis of [F3] by step 2.1; applying [F2] and then [F3] proves that the full TPFA Lie update also remains in $[0,1]$. For a grid state $U=(u_i)_i$ with positive weights $m_i$, its Euler reaction mass increment is $\sum_i m_i\tau r u_i(1-u_i)$. This is strictly positive for $\tau>0$ exactly when some $u_i\in(0,1)$, and is zero when every $u_i\in\{0,1\}$; for $\tau=0$ it is zero for every state. Thus the mass claim in the Statement holds, and no mass-conservation claim is made.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge2$. For every integer $k\ge0$ and
$1\le p\le\infty$, there is a bounded linear operator
$$E_{k,p}:W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^d)$$
whose restriction to $\widehat S_d$ is the input class. Consequently
$\widehat S_d$ is a $W^{k,p}$-extension domain in the sense of
[[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]. The operator may
be chosen with support in one fixed bounded set.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume Countable Choice. For any open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$n\ge1$, any $1\le p\le\infty$ and any
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, extension by zero
$$E_0u(x)=u(x)\ \ (x\in\Omega),\qquad E_0u(x)=0\ \ (x\notin\Omega),$$
acted on representatives, sends $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ linearly into
$W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$. For every $u\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
and every coordinate direction $i$, the class $D_i(E_0u)$ is the zero
extension of the class $D_iu$, and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|D_i(E_0u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $d=n-1$, $1\le p<\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$H=\{x=(x',x_n)\in\mathbb R^n:x_n>0\}$ with
$\partial H=\mathbb R^d\times\{0\}$. Write $\partial_n$ for the last
coordinate derivative.

(i) For every $u\in C(\overline H)\cap W^{1,p}(H;\mathbb K)$ with compact
support, the classical boundary function $g=u(\cdot,0)$ satisfies
$$|g(x')|^p\le p\int_0^\infty|u(x',t)|^{p-1}\,|\partial_nu(x',t)|\,dt$$
for a.e. $x'\in\mathbb R^d$, hence
$\|g\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}^p\le p\,\|u\|_{L^p(H)}^{p-1}\|\partial_nu\|_{L^p(H)}\le p\,\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(H)}^p$.
For every $h>0$ the strip form
$$h\,|g(x')|^p\le C_p\Bigl(\int_0^h|u(x',t)|^pdt+h^p\int_0^h|\partial_nu(x',t)|^pdt\Bigr)$$
holds for a.e. $x'$, with $C_p=2^{p-1}$ for $1<p<\infty$ and $C_1=1$.

(ii) There is a unique bounded linear operator
$T_+:W^{1,p}(H;\mathbb K)\to L^p(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb K)$ with
$T_+u=u(\cdot,0)$ for every compactly supported
$u\in C(\overline H)\cap W^{1,p}(H)$, and
$\|T_+u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}\le C(n,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(H)}$; it is the unique
bounded extension of classical restriction, and $T_+u$ depends only on the
a.e. class of $u$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$
If $F:M\to N$ and $G:N\to P$ are smooth, then $d(G\circ F)_p=dG_{F(p)}\circ dF_p$ for every $p\in M$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded polyhedral open set with a finite matching
affine simplicial mesh, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $v$ be a real-valued
conforming piecewise polynomial whose polynomial trace vanishes on every boundary
facet. Then
$$v\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega),\qquad \|v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}.$$
Here $W^{1,p}_0$ is the norm closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$; no C1
trace characterization is used.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For each mesh triangle $K$, apply [F1] to pull $u|_K$ back to the reference triangle, and then apply [F2]. This gives a continuous representative on $\overline K$. It is unique: if two continuous representatives differed at one point, continuity would make them differ on a nonempty open subset of $K$, contradicting [F6]. Thus each cellwise nodal value is individually well-defined.

Put $z=E_0u$, the zero extension from [F3]. On either side of any straight line, the half-space trace is obtained from the positive-half-space trace in [F4] by a translation and, when needed, a reflection; [F5] verifies that these changes preserve the Sobolev class and norm. The two traces of a global $H^1(\mathbb R^2)$ class across such a line agree: choose $z_m\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ converging to $z$ by [F4]; the two traces of each $z_m$ are its same classical restriction, and boundedness of the two trace maps passes this equality to the limit. On the exterior half-space of each side of $\Omega$, $z=0$, so both its exterior trace and its interior trace are zero.

If $K_+$ and $K_-$ share an interior edge, every point $x$ in the relative interior of that edge has a ball $B\subset\Omega$ meeting only those two cells. By [F2], $u|_B$ has a continuous representative. On each of the two open half-balls $B\cap K_\pm$, this representative and the corresponding representative from step 1.1 agree almost everywhere, hence everywhere by [F6]. Taking limits to $x$ shows the two cell values agree at $x$; continuity along the closed edge gives agreement at its endpoints as well. For an interior mesh vertex, take a ball about the vertex contained in $\Omega$ and repeat this argument for every incident cell.

Let $x$ lie in the relative interior of a boundary mesh edge $E$. Choose a ball $B$ centered at $x$ small enough that its interior half-ball lies in the unique incident triangle $K$ and its other boundary is disjoint from all mesh edges. By [F9] choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B)$ equal to one near $x$. On the interior half-space define $v=\chi u_K$ inside $B$ and zero outside, where $u_K$ is the continuous cell representative from step 1.1. The cutoff vanishes near the circular part of $\partial B$, so the weak test identity shows $v\in H^1$ of that half-space; it is compactly supported and continuous on the closed half-space. Its class is $\chi z$ there. By linearity and boundedness of the trace, and by approximation with the smooth functions in step 1.2, $T(\chi z)=\chi Tz=0$ on the side. The classical-restriction clause of [F4] gives $T v=\chi u_K|_E$, so $u_K=0$ almost everywhere near $x$ on $E$. Continuity from step 1.1 makes this value zero at every point of that edge, including its endpoints.

Interior edge values agree by step 2.1. At a boundary vertex, the incident triangles form a connected fan because the square is convex; the fan is a chain under adjacency across edges containing that vertex, and at least one end cell has a boundary edge. Step 2.2 gives zero at the vertex in that end cell, and step 2.1 propagates that value through the fan. Thus all cell values at every shared vertex agree and boundary vertex values are zero. The affine traces of adjacent P1 interpolants agree because they agree at both edge endpoints, so $I_hu$ is continuous; on each boundary edge it is affine with both endpoint values zero, hence its trace is zero. Apply [F8] to conclude $I_hu\in H^1_0(\Omega)$.

$(\widehat S_d,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ be a reference finite element
whose polynomial space contains $\mathbb P_k$. Assume its degrees of
freedom are bounded on $W^{\ell,p}(\widehat S_d)$ for an integer
$\ell\ge1$, let $r,m\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $\widehat I$ be its
interpolant. Thus
$\widehat Iq=q$ for $q\in\mathbb P_k$. On a shape-regular affine mesh
as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], for each cell $K$ with its
orientation-preserving reference map $F_K$ define
$$I_Kv=(\widehat I(v\circ F_K))\circ F_K^{-1}.$$
For every such cell, if $\ell\le r\le k+1$ and $0\le m\le r$, then for
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$,
$$|v-I_Kv|_{W^{m,p}(K)}\le C h_K^{r-m}|v|_{W^{r,p}(K)}.$$
If $\ell>k+1$ and $0\le m\le k+1$, then for $v\in W^{\ell,p}(K)$,
$$|v-I_Kv|_{W^{m,p}(K)} \le C\sum_{n=k+1}^{\ell}h_K^{n-m}|v|_{W^{n,p}(K)}.$$
The constants are uniform over the mesh family and depend on the stated
reference element, exponents and shape-regularity bound. For Lagrange
elements in the existing mesh dimension range $d\ge2$, assume additionally
the Axiom of Choice for the automatic nodal-boundedness application. Then
[[thm-lagrange-point-evaluation-threshold-on-reference-simplex]] supplies
the boundedness hypothesis when $\ell>d/p$; unisolvence of a particular
node set remains a separate hypothesis.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open
and let $\Phi:U\to V$ be a $C^k$ diffeomorphism with inverse
$\Psi:=\Phi^{-1}:V\to U$. Fix open sets $U_0\subset\subset U$ and
$V_0\subset\subset V$ with $\Phi(U_0)\subseteq V_0$, and suppose that on
$\overline{U_0}$ the derivatives of $\Phi$ through order $k$ are bounded and
that on $\overline{V_0}$ the derivatives of $\Psi$ through order $k$ are
bounded; in the situation of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] these are exactly the compact
patches on which the flattening chart and its inverse have bounded derivatives
through order $k$. Then:

1. for every $u\in W^{k,p}(V_0;\mathbb K)$ the composition
$u\circ\Phi$ belongs to $W^{k,p}(U_0;\mathbb K)$, and for every
$1\le|\alpha|\le k$ its weak derivatives satisfy, almost everywhere on
$U_0$,
$$D^\alpha(u\circ\Phi)=\sum_{1\le|\beta|\le|\alpha|}\bigl((D^\beta u)\circ\Phi\bigr)\,P_{\alpha\beta}\bigl(D\Phi,\dots,D^k\Phi\bigr),$$
where $P_{\alpha\beta}$ is a universal polynomial with integer coefficients,
whose values on $\overline{U_0}$ are bounded by a constant depending only on
$n,k$ and the stated bounds for $\Phi$;

2. there is a constant $C$, depending only on $n$, $k$, $p$ and the two sets of
chart bounds, with
$$\|u\circ\Phi\|_{W^{k,p}(U_0)}\le C\,\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(V_0)}\qquad\text{for all }u\in W^{k,p}(V_0;\mathbb K).$$
If in addition $\Psi(V_0)\subseteq U_0$ (equivalently, under the stated
$\Phi(U_0)\subseteq V_0$, $\Phi(U_0)=V_0$), the same assertion holds for
composition with $\Psi$ from $W^{k,p}(U_0)$ to $W^{k,p}(V_0)$.

For $k=1$ only the first derivatives of $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ enter, so bounded
$C^1$ chart and inverse data suffice; no $C^1$-only claim is made for $k>1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $N\in\mathbb N_0$, choose
$x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\overline{\widehat S_d}$, and let
$\ell\ge1$ be an integer. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $\ell>d/p$, then each
point evaluation has a unique continuous-representative value and
$$|u(x_j)|\le C\|u\|_{W^{\ell,p}(\widehat S_d)}.$$
If $p=\infty$, the same conclusion holds for every $\ell\ge1$.
Consequently any finite set of Lagrange nodal evaluations is bounded on
the stated Sobolev space and defines a well-defined degree-of-freedom
functional there. No boundedness at $\ell=d/p$ is asserted.

derivations.claim: First apply [F4] to $w=v\circ\Psi$ on the interiors of the reference and curved cells. The maps extend to a $C^2$ diffeomorphism on neighborhoods of the compact cell closures, and the stated derivative, inverse-derivative, and Jacobian bounds give $w\in H^2(\widetilde K)$ with $\|w\|_{H^2(\widetilde K)}\le C\|v\|_{H^2(K)}$. Now [F5] supplies the unique continuous representative $\widetilde v$ of $w$ on $\overline{\widetilde K}$, so its three reference-vertex values are defined. The function $\widetilde v\circ\Psi^{-1}$ is continuous on $\overline K$ and represents $v$, by the inverse-composition part of [F4]. If $g$ is any other continuous representative of $v$ on $\overline K$, then $g\circ\Psi$ is a continuous representative of $w$ and equals $\widetilde v$ by [F5]; hence the representative on $K$ is unique. Its values at the curved-cell vertices are exactly the pulled-back nodal values. Applying [F4] to the inverse map also gives the uniform $L^2$ and $H^1$ norm bounds needed when the interpolation error is pushed back to $K$.

Apply [F1] to $w$ on the affine triangle $\widetilde K$. The mapped interpolant is exactly $(I_{\widetilde K}w)\circ\Psi^{-1}$ because its three nodal values are those of $v$ at the three image vertices. The affine estimates give $\|w-I_{\widetilde K}w\|_{L^2(\widetilde K)}\le C h_K^2\|w\|_{H^2(\widetilde K)}$ and $|w-I_{\widetilde K}w|_{H^1(\widetilde K)}\le Ch_K\|w\|_{H^2(\widetilde K)}$, using the assumed diameter comparability.

Push the error through $\Psi^{-1}$ using step 1.1. The resulting uniform norm bounds are the two claimed estimates. AC is used in [F5] for the continuous representative and nodal evaluations, including the automatic nodal-boundedness application in [F1]; Countable Choice is used through [F1] and [F4].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: By [F4], Lebesgue measure is countably additive and hence finitely additive. The partition hypotheses therefore give $\sum_iw_{ji}=|T_j|$ for every target cell and $\sum_jw_{ji}=|S_i|$ for every source cell; omitted partition boundaries are null and do not change these measures. The same finite additivity gives $\int_{T_j}v=\sum_iw_{ji}v_i$.
For any target cellwise-constant $z$, sum over target cells: $\int_\Omega(v-Rv)z=\sum_j z_j(\sum_iw_{ji}v_i-|T_j|(Rv)_j)=0$ by [F1] and step 1.1. Thus $v-Rv$ is orthogonal to the target subspace.

Orthogonality with $z=Rv$ gives $\|v\|_2^2=\|Rv\|_2^2+\|v-Rv\|_2^2$, so $\|Rv\|_2\le\|v\|_2$. All terms are finite because the partitions are finite, cells have finite volume, and $v$ is piecewise constant.

By the column-sum identity in step 1.1, $\int Rv=\sum_j|T_j|(Rv)_j=\sum_i|S_i|v_i=\int v$. If each $v_i\ge0$, every overlap weight is nonnegative, so the defining finite weighted average is nonnegative.

The exact and approximate domains are $\Omega=\Phi(\widehat\Omega)$ and $\Omega_h=\Phi_h(\widehat\Omega)$. Define $e_0=\|\Phi-\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega)}$ and $e_1=\|D\Phi-D\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega;op)}$. A geometry approximation claim must separately state bounds on $e_0,e_1$, both Jacobian lower bounds, and boundary-trace compatibility; none follows from the word “isoparametric.”

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be an elementary set
([[def-elementary-set-in-rn]]). If

$$A \;=\; \bigcup_{j<m} B_j \;=\; \bigcup_{l<p} C_l$$

for finite lists of pairwise disjoint half-open boxes ([[def-half-open-box]]),
then

$$\sum_{j<m}\operatorname{vol}(B_j) \;=\; \sum_{l<p}\operatorname{vol}(C_l)$$

in $[0,+\infty]$. Consequently there is exactly one function
$\mu_0 : \mathcal{E}_n \to [0,+\infty]$, the **elementary volume**, whose value
at $A$ is the sum of the volumes of the members of any presentation of $A$ by a
finite list of pairwise disjoint half-open boxes. It satisfies
$\mu_0(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\mu_0(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every
half-open box $B$.

Fix $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of
functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, writing $x_i := x(i)$ for $i < n$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). A **parameter** is a function $n \to
\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, where $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup
\{-\infty, +\infty\}$ carries the total order of [[def-extended-reals]]. For a
pair $(a,b)$ of parameters set

$$B(a,b) \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n \;:\; a_i < x_i \le b_i \ \text{ for every } i < n \,\},$$

both comparisons taken in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$. A **half-open box** is a set
of this form. For a single $u \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ write $\mathbf{u}$ for
the constant parameter with value $u$, and abbreviate
$(u,v]^n := B(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$; thus $\mathbb{R}^n = (-\infty,+\infty]^n$
and $(0,1]^n$ is the **unit cube**. At $n = 1$, and for real $a_0 < b_0$, the box
$B(a,b)$ is the half-open interval $(a_0,b_0]$ of [[def-interval]].

**A box is nonempty exactly when $a_i < b_i$ for every $i < n$.** If some
$a_i \ge b_i$ then no real $x_i$ satisfies both $a_i < x_i$ and $x_i \le b_i$, by
transitivity of the order, so $B(a,b) = \varnothing$. Conversely suppose
$a_i < b_i$ for every $i$. Then in each coordinate some real $t$ satisfies
$a_i < t \le b_i$: if $b_i \in \mathbb{R}$ take $t := b_i$, which is $> a_i$; if
$b_i = +\infty$ then $a_i \ne +\infty$, so take $t := a_i + 1$ when $a_i$ is real
and $t := 0$ when $a_i = -\infty$. Assembling one such $t$ in each coordinate
gives a point of $B(a,b)$; the assembly is a definition by cases on finitely many
coordinates and selects nothing.

**The parameters of a nonempty box are determined by the set.** Let
$B := B(a,b) \ne \varnothing$, fix $i < n$ and put
$S_i := \{\, x_i : x \in B \,\}$. Then $S_i = \{\, t \in \mathbb{R} : a_i < t \le b_i \,\}$:
the inclusion $\subseteq$ is the defining condition, and for $\supseteq$ take any
$y \in B$ and replace its $i$-th coordinate by $t$, which leaves every other
defining inequality untouched. Now $b_i = +\infty$ exactly when $S_i$ has no
upper bound in $\mathbb{R}$, and otherwise $b_i$ is the greatest element of
$S_i$; likewise $a_i = -\infty$ exactly when $S_i$ has no lower bound in
$\mathbb{R}$, and otherwise $a_i$ is the greatest lower bound of $S_i$ in
$\mathbb{R}$. So $B$ determines $a_i$ and $b_i$ for every $i$, and hence
determines $(a,b)$.

**Volume.** For a half-open box $B$ define $\operatorname{vol}(B) \in
[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ by

- $\operatorname{vol}(\varnothing) := 0$;
- if $B \ne \varnothing$, with its unique parameter pair $(a,b)$, then
  $\operatorname{vol}(B) := +\infty$ when $a_i = -\infty$ or $b_i = +\infty$ for
  some $i < n$, and
  $$\operatorname{vol}(B) := \prod_{i<n}(b_i - a_i)$$
  when every $a_i$ and every $b_i$ is real.

The product is the finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. In the last clause every
factor $b_i - a_i$ is a strictly positive real, since $a_i < b_i$ in
$\mathbb{R}$, so the product is a strictly positive real ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]],
claim 6) and in particular no factor is $0$ and no product of the form
$0 \cdot (\pm\infty)$ is ever formed. That is what the case split buys: a box
with a degenerate side is **empty**, not a box of volume $0$ with an infinite
side. So $\operatorname{vol}$ is a total function on the half-open boxes with
values in $[0,+\infty]$, and $\operatorname{vol}(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$,
$\operatorname{vol}\big((0,1]^n\big) = 1$.

**Agreement with the published rectangle volume.** For real parameters with
$a_i < b_i$ for every $i < n$, the closed rectangle $[a,b]$ of
[[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]] has
$\operatorname{vol}[a,b] = \prod_{j<n}(b_j-a_j)$, which is the value assigned
above to $B(a,b)$. The two notions of volume therefore agree wherever both are
written, and no second notion of volume is introduced.

Fix $n \ge 1$. A subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is an **elementary set** when
there are a natural number $m$ and a list $B_0, \dots, B_{m-1}$ of half-open
boxes ([[def-half-open-box]]), that is a function $j \mapsto B_j$ on
$\{\, j \in \mathbb{N} : j < m \,\}$ whose values are half-open boxes, with

$$E \;=\; \bigcup_{j<m} B_j .$$

Write $\mathcal{E}_n$ for the family of all elementary subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

The list is part of the data of the presentation and not of the set: one
elementary set has many presentations, and nothing below reads a presentation
off a set. At $m = 0$ the union is empty, so $\varnothing \in \mathcal{E}_n$; at
$m = 1$ every half-open box is elementary, $\mathbb{R}^n = (-\infty,+\infty]^n$
included. The boxes of a presentation are not required to be disjoint or
nonempty.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

Orient every top-dimensional cell of a matching simplicial mesh by the
ambient orientation of $\mathbb R^d$, and orient each facet by the induced
boundary convention of [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. In the sum
of the oriented boundaries of all top-dimensional cells, every interior
facet occurs twice with opposite signs; every boundary facet occurs once.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Each entry of $\operatorname{cof}(A)$ is a signed $(d-1)$-minor, hence a polynomial of degree $d-1$ in the entries of $A$. On the bounded matrix ball $\|A\|_{op},\|A_h\|_{op}\le M$, its derivative is bounded by a constant depending only on $d,M$. The mean-value inequality therefore gives $\|\operatorname{cof}(A)-\operatorname{cof}(A_h)\|_{op}\le C(d,M)\|A-A_h\|_{op}=C(d,M)e_1$.

Let $T$ have orthonormal columns spanning the reference facet tangent space, so $Q=[T,\widehat n]$ is orthogonal. The squared Gram-metric surface factor is $\det(T^TA^TAT)$. The identity $\operatorname{cof}(A)^T\operatorname{cof}(A)=\operatorname{cof}(A^TA)$ and orthogonal covariance of cofactors show $\widehat n^T\operatorname{cof}(A^TA)\widehat n$ is the bottom-right cofactor of $Q^TA^TAQ$, which is exactly $\det(T^TA^TAT)$. Therefore $\|\operatorname{cof}(A)\widehat n\|^2=\det(T^TA^TAT)$. For a regular chart write $D\widehat f=TR$, where $R$ is an invertible $(d-1)\times(d-1)$ matrix. Then $\det(D\widehat f^TA^TAD\widehat f)=\det(R)^2\det(T^TA^TAT)$ and $\det(D\widehat f^TD\widehat f)=\det(R)^2$. Taking positive square roots gives the stated chart-factor relation, also for $A_h$.

If $\sigma_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_d(A)>0$ are the singular values, the smallest singular value of $\operatorname{cof}(A)$ is $\prod_{i=2}^d\sigma_i(A)=\det(A)/\sigma_1(A)\ge j_*/M$.
