citations.quote:
Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Let $\widehat\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded reference domain and let $\Phi,\Phi_h:\overline{\widehat\Omega}\to\mathbb R^d$ be cellwise $C^2$ admissible maps with matching traces, positive Jacobians, and common image topology. The exact and approximate domains are $\Omega=\Phi(\widehat\Omega)$ and $\Omega_h=\Phi_h(\widehat\Omega)$. Define $e_0=\|\Phi-\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega)}$ and $e_1=\|D\Phi-D\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega;op)}$. A geometry approximation claim must separately state bounds on $e_0,e_1$, both Jacobian lower bounds, and boundary-trace compatibility; none follows from the word “isoparametric.”

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Direct differentiation gives $D\Phi=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\x/2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and determinant $1$; the stated inverse is verified by substitution. On a triangle with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_i$ and vertex first-coordinates $x_i$, exact quadratic expansion gives $I_h(x^2/4)-x^2/4=\frac14\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i\lambda_j(x_i-x_j)^2$. Since $|x_i-x_j|\le h_K$ and $0\le\lambda_i\le1$, this is bounded by $Ch_K^2$.

Differentiating the barycentric expression in step 1.1, only the factors $\lambda_i\lambda_j$ vary; their derivatives are bounded by $C h_K^{-1}$ using [F2], while $|x_i-x_j|^2\le h_K^2$. The product rule therefore gives a derivative bound $Ch_K$. Thus $\|D(I_h(x^2/4)-x^2/4)\|_{L^\infty(K)}\le Ch_K$, yielding the global $Ch$ derivative estimate and the $Ch^2$ value estimate. By [F3] these are the geometry errors $e_1$ and $e_0$.

The first coordinate of $\Phi_h$ is $x$, and on each vertical segment its second coordinate is the continuous piecewise-affine function $y+I_h(x^2/4)(x,y)$. Its slope on every subsegment is $1+\partial_y I_h(x^2/4)\ge1-Ch$. Choose $h$ with $Ch\le1/2$. Integration over the finitely many subsegments makes this coordinate strictly increasing with increment at least half the vertical increment. Equal images must therefore have equal first coordinates and then equal second-coordinate inputs; hence $\Phi_h$ is injective. The same derivative estimate gives $\det D\Phi_h=1+\partial_yI_h(x^2/4)\ge1/2$.

The same averaging identity gives $q-P_Tq$ orthogonal to every target-cellwise constant, so $P_T$ is the orthogonal projection.

By [F2], $Rv_S=P_Tv_S$. Thus $u-Rv_S=(u-P_Tu)+P_T(u-v_S)$; the two terms are orthogonal and $P_T$ is contractive by step 1.2. The first term has norm $\eta_T$ and the second is at most $\eta_S$, whence $\|u-Rv_S\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}\le\eta_T+\eta_S$.

Fix a compatible labeled initial mesh. Recursive reference-edge closure of any finite marked set terminates, produces a matching conforming NVB descendant, and preserves the shape bound of [[lem-afem-nvb-shape-regularity-and-three-generation-properties]]. For any sequence of finite request sets $Q_k$, with three uniform generations requested on each cell of $Q_k$, there is a constant $C_{\rm gen}$ depending only on the initial mesh such that
$$\#\mathcal T_n-\#\mathcal T_0\le C_{\rm gen}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\#Q_k.$$
For the algorithm [[alg-dorfler-marking-and-conforming-nvb-refinement]], keep $M_k=M_{E,k}\cup M_{O,k}$ as the bulk-marked set and use its original edge-neighbor request set $Q_k$. Then $\#Q_k\le4\#M_k$, so with $C_{\rm cl}=4C_{\rm gen}$,
$$\#\mathcal T_n-\#\mathcal T_0\le C_{\rm cl}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\#M_k.$$
The constant is for the cumulative sequence; no uniform bound on the added cells in one single refinement call is asserted.

Fix a reference matching affine simplicial mesh as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. An admissible curved cell is the image of a closed reference simplex $\widehat K$ under a map $F_K\in C^2(\widehat K;\mathbb R^d)$ that extends to a diffeomorphism on a neighborhood, is orientation preserving, and satisfies $0<j_0\le J_K:=\det DF_K\le j_1$ and $\|DF_K\|+\|(DF_K)^{-1}\|+\|D^2F_K\|\le C_F$. The physical cells have disjoint interiors, cover the domain up to their shared facets, and maps agree on each common reference facet under the prescribed affine facet identification. Define the volume metric $G_K=DF_K^TDF_K$, volume factor $J_K=\sqrt{\det G_K}$, and for a reference facet parametrization $\widehat f$ the surface metric $G_{K,\widehat f}=D(F_K\circ\widehat f)^TD(F_K\circ\widehat f)$ and surface factor $\sqrt{\det G_{K,\widehat f}}$. The positive-Jacobian lower bound is the admissibility certificate; it is not inferred from a drawing or from Delaunay quality.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to the finite request. Its output is a conforming affine triangulation, so each interior edge is represented by the same complete reference segment from both incident cells; no hanging edge subdivision remains.

On a common edge, the assumed geometry map has one trace from the shared reference segment. By [F2] the two incident curved-cell parametrizations use that same trace, and injectivity prevents distinct reference interfaces from being identified as overlapping physical interiors. Thus the physical curved interface matches.

Assume Countable Choice, as in
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and
[[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]]. For an open set
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, an integer $k\ge0$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, set
$$H^k(\Omega;\mathbb K):=W^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The elements are the same almost-everywhere classes, and their weak
derivatives and norm are exactly those already defined for $W^{k,2}$. When the
scalar field is fixed, write $H^k(\Omega)$.

The notation $H^k_0(\Omega)$ is reserved for the later definition by closure of
compactly supported smooth functions in the Sobolev norm. This item assigns no
boundary values to an equivalence class and asserts no characterization by
pointwise vanishing or by traces.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Let $\widehat\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded reference domain and let $\Phi,\Phi_h:\overline{\widehat\Omega}\to\mathbb R^d$ be cellwise $C^2$ admissible maps with matching traces, positive Jacobians, and common image topology. The exact and approximate domains are $\Omega=\Phi(\widehat\Omega)$ and $\Omega_h=\Phi_h(\widehat\Omega)$. Define $e_0=\|\Phi-\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega)}$ and $e_1=\|D\Phi-D\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega;op)}$. A geometry approximation claim must separately state bounds on $e_0,e_1$, both Jacobian lower bounds, and boundary-trace compatibility; none follows from the word “isoparametric.”

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\widehat\Omega=[-1,1]^2$, let $\mathcal T_h$ be a matching shape-regular affine triangulation, and put $\Phi(x,y)=(x,y+x^2/4)$. Let $I_h$ be the vertexwise P1 interpolant and $\Phi_h(x,y)=(x,y+I_h(x^2/4))$. In the notation of [[def-curved-domain-geometry-approximation]], there is a constant $C$ depending only on the shape-regularity bound such that $e_0\le Ch^2$ and $e_1\le Ch$. For sufficiently small $h$, $\det D\Phi_h\ge1/2$, and $\Phi_h$ is globally one-to-one on the square. The exact map has $\det D\Phi=1$ and a global inverse $(X,Y)\mapsto(X,Y-X^2/4)$.

Let $\Phi,\Phi_h$ be the orientation-preserving maps of [[def-curved-domain-geometry-approximation]], with $J,J_h\ge j_*>0$ and $\|D\Phi\|_\infty+\|D\Phi_h\|_\infty\le M$. Set $B=J D\Phi^{-1}D\Phi^{-T}$ and $B_h=J_hD\Phi_h^{-1}D\Phi_h^{-T}$. Then $\|B-B_h\|_\infty\le C e_1$, where $C$ depends only on $d,j_*,M$. Consequently $|\int_{\widehat\Omega}
abla v^T(B-B_h)
abla w|\le C e_1\|
abla v\|_2\|
abla w\|_2$ for $v,w\in H^1(\widehat\Omega)$.

Assume AC and Countable Choice. In dimension two let $K=\Psi(\widetilde K)$, where $\widetilde K$ is a shape-regular affine triangle of diameter comparable to $h_K$, and $\Psi$ extends to a $C^2$ diffeomorphism on a neighborhood of $\overline{\widetilde K}$. Assume $\|D\Psi\|_\infty+\|D\Psi^{-1}\|_\infty+\|D^2\Psi\|_\infty+\|J_\Psi^{-1}\|_\infty$ are uniformly bounded. Let $v$ denote its continuous representative and set $I_Kv=(I_{\widetilde K}(v\circ\Psi))\circ\Psi^{-1}$, the mapped nodal P1 interpolant. For $v\in H^2(K)$, $\|v-I_Kv\|_{L^2(K)}\le C h_K^2\|v\|_{H^2(K)}$ and $|v-I_Kv|_{H^1(K)}\le C h_K\|v\|_{H^2(K)}$, with $C$ uniform over the family.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let
$\Omega=(-1,1)^2$ have a finite matching affine triangular mesh, and let
$u\in H^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)\cap H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. On each triangle
take the unique continuous representative of the restriction of $u$. These
representatives give one well-defined value at every mesh vertex. The global
nodal P1 interpolant $I_hu$, affine on each triangle and equal to these values
at its vertices, is continuous, has zero trace on every boundary edge, and
belongs to $H^1_0(\Omega)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded coercive form with boundedness constant $M$ and coercivity constant $\alpha>0$, and $F:V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded functional linear in the real case and conjugate-linear in the complex test argument. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be finite-dimensional, and let $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ be bounded, with $F_h$ having the same test-linearity as $F$, and $a_h$ coercive with constant $\alpha_h>0$ in the inherited norm. Both $a$ and $a_h$ are sesquilinear (bilinear over $\mathbb R$), linear in their first argument and conjugate-linear in their second over $\mathbb C$. There are unique exact and discrete solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\left((1+M/\alpha_h)\|u-v_h\|_V+\frac{\delta_{a,h}(v_h)+\delta_{F,h}}{\alpha_h}\right),$$

where the defects are those of [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]. For a family of meshes this is a uniform estimate whenever $\inf_h\alpha_h>0$ and the displayed approximation and defect terms are uniformly controlled. The term $\delta_{F,h}$ retains source approximation and data oscillation.

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. In the **exact variational problem**, $V$ is a Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ is a bounded coercive sesquilinear form (bilinear when $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$), linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second when $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$, and $F:V\to\mathbb K$ is bounded and has the same linearity in its test argument as the second argument of $a$. Exact solutions satisfy $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in V$. Boundedness and coercivity have the meanings in [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]].

For a **conforming perturbed Galerkin problem**, $V_h\subseteq V$ is a finite-dimensional subspace, $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ are the discrete form and load, and $u_h\in V_h$ solves $a_h(u_h,w_h)=F_h(w_h)$. Its discrete coercivity constant is any $\alpha_h>0$ such that $\operatorname{Re}a_h(w_h,w_h)\ge\alpha_h\|w_h\|_V^2$ for every $w_h\in V_h$. For $v_h\in V_h$, define

$$\delta_{a,h}(v_h):=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|a(v_h,w_h)-a_h(v_h,w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_V},\qquad \delta_{F,h}:=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|F(w_h)-F_h(w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_V}.$$

If $V_h=\{0\}$, both defects are defined to be zero. The load defect $\delta_{F,h}$ includes any source approximation or data oscillation; it is not assumed small or zero without a separate bound.

For a **nonconforming problem**, the exact space $V$ and finite-dimensional trial space $V_h$ need not satisfy $V_h\subseteq V$. Put $X_h:=V+V_h$ and equip it with a norm $\|\cdot\|_h$ whose restrictions to $V$ and $V_h$ are norms. The discrete form $a_h$ is defined on $V_h\times V_h$, and a bounded extension $\widetilde a_h:X_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ means $\widetilde a_h=a_h$ on $V_h\times V_h$ and $|\widetilde a_h(z,w_h)|\le M_h\|z\|_h\|w_h\|_h$. For an exact solution $u\in V$, define the nonconforming consistency defect

$$\delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_h(u):=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|F_h(w_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_h},$$

with value zero if $V_h=\{0\}$. This residual need not vanish: the exact weak equation is only asserted for tests in $V$.

Geometry and quadrature defects are components of the appropriate form defect when the implemented form is compared with the pulled-back exact form. No exact Galerkin orthogonality is asserted after replacing the form or test space.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\widehat\Omega=(-1,1)^2$ carry a finite matching affine triangular mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Let $\Phi,\Phi_h:\overline{\widehat\Omega}	o\mathbb R^2$ be continuous and $C^1$ on each closed triangle, with matching traces on shared edges, and suppose $\|D\Phi\|_\infty+\|D\Phi_h\|_\infty\le M$, $e_0=\|\Phi-\Phi_h\|_\infty$, and $e_1=\|D\Phi-D\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty;op}$. Let $G$ be a scalar physical boundary lift on an open convex neighborhood containing both images and every segment joining corresponding image points, with $\|DG\|_\infty\le L_1$ and $\|D^2G\|_\infty\le L_2$. Define the piecewise pullback gradients by $
abla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi)=D\Phi^T

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Input two cyclic vertex lists for positive-area convex polygons in $\mathbb R^2$, with rational coordinates. The closing edge is implicit; if the last listed vertex repeats the first, delete that final copy. Delete consecutive duplicate vertices, including across the cyclic endpoint, then return unresolved if a list has fewer than three vertices, any remaining repeated vertex, a zero-length edge, or zero signed shoelace area. Reverse a negatively oriented list so both polygons are counterclockwise. For each list, certify convexity as follows: for every directed edge, evaluate the orientation of that edge with every listed vertex and require every sign to be nonnegative; if three consecutive vertices are collinear, require the middle one to lie between the other two; and for every pair of nonadjacent closed edges, certify that they do not intersect. Test the latter exactly using the four orientation signs: two segments $AB,CD$ intersect if the signs for $C,D$ against $AB$ are strictly opposite and the signs for $A,B$ against $CD$ are strictly opposite, or if one of these signs is zero and its point lies in the closed coordinatewise bounding rectangle of the corresponding segment. Return unresolved if any certificate check fails. These finite checks certify that each normalized list is the simple counterclockwise boundary of its convex hull, allowing redundant collinear vertices.

For every rational orientation test, clear one common positive denominator from the coordinates of its three points and call [[alg-certified-dyadic-geometric-predicate]] on the resulting integer (hence dyadic) points. Propagate any result other than an exact positive, zero, or negative sign as unresolved. For each directed edge of $Q$, clip the current cyclic list of $P$ to that edge's closed left half-plane, treating a point $X$ as inside exactly when $s(X)\ge0$, where $s(X)$ is its signed edge determinant. Traverse cyclically by setting $S$ to the last current vertex and then taking each current vertex in list order as $E$. Apply exactly one of these branches:

- If $s(S)\ge0$ and $s(E)\ge0$, append $E$.
- If $s(S)\ge0>s(E)$, append $S+t(E-S)$.
- If $s(S)<0\le s(E)$, append $S+t(E-S)$ and then $E$.
- If $s(S)<0$ and $s(E)<0$, append nothing.

In either crossing branch set $t=s(S)/(s(S)-s(E))$. The strict sign inequalities make this denominator nonzero and give $t\in[0,1]$; when an endpoint sign is zero the intersection is that endpoint. No division is performed in either noncrossing branch. Remove consecutive duplicate output vertices after each pass, including a duplicate across the cyclic endpoint, and continue with the next edge of $Q$. If the current list is empty, it remains empty. Return the final rational cyclic list and area zero when it has fewer than three noncollinear vertices; otherwise return its exact shoelace area. No floating tolerance is used.

The algorithm's finite certificate accepts only a simple counterclockwise cycle whose vertices lie in the closed left half-plane of every directed edge, with any collinear consecutive triple ordered monotonically. Each edge is therefore a supporting boundary segment of the convex hull of the listed vertices; the simple closed cycle with positive area traverses that hull boundary once, so the certified input is the stated convex polygon. Now fix one directed edge of $Q$ and write $s(X)$ for its signed edge determinant. If $s(S),s(E)\ge0$, the whole segment remains and the traversal appends $E$. If $s(S)\ge0>s(E)$, it appends the crossing point; if $s(S)<0\le s(E)$, it appends the crossing point and $E$; and if both signs are negative, it appends nothing. In either crossing case, $s(S)-s(E)$ has the strict sign of the crossing and is nonzero, and $t=s(S)/(s(S)-s(E))$ lies in $[0,1]$. If an endpoint lies on the clipping line, the formula gives that endpoint exactly. Thus each pass returns the cyclic boundary of the preceding convex intersection with this closed half-plane, preserving isolated boundary vertices and degenerate point or segment outputs.

Induction over the finite edge list of $Q$ shows the final polygon is $P$ intersected with every defining half-plane of $Q$, hence is exactly $P\cap Q$. Each pass processes a finite list and adds at most two crossings per clip edge, so the finitely many passes terminate.

The final vertices are rational because every crossing uses rational operations with a nonzero exact denominator. For a nondegenerate simple polygon the shoelace sum equals its signed area; the output is counterclockwise, so this is its nonnegative Lebesgue area. A convex intersection with fewer than three noncollinear vertices is empty or lies in an affine line. By [F4], the line and all its subsets are Lebesgue null, so the returned area is zero in these degenerate cases.

In the affine-dimension-two branch, after each insertion the augmented triangles are exactly the $d=2$ lower simplices of the inserted sites together with the three synthetic vertices, as defined in [[lem-lower-lifted-facets-cover-the-convex-hull]], using the restriction of the common fixed-universe formal heights to that prefix. Uninserted sites are excluded from the prefix support tests; the universe and ranks remain fixed throughout. After removing synthetic vertices, the output triangulates the input convex hull with weakly empty original circumdisks and coherent lexicographic ties. In dimensions zero and one, the algorithm returns the defined single site or consecutive chain.

A compatible labeled initial mesh is a finite matching affine simplicial triangulation $\mathcal T_0$ of a polygon in $\mathbb R^2$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], equipped with labels on its edges such that each triangle has one edge labeled $0$ and two labeled $1$, and every shared edge has the same label from both incident triangles. Matching means that distinct cell interiors are disjoint and any nonempty cell intersection is a whole common face: in two dimensions it may be a vertex or an edge. For a descendant triangle of generation $g(K)$, its three edge labels, in any order, are $(g(K)+1,g(K)+1,g(K))$. The unique edge labeled $g(K)$ is its reference edge.

To bisect $K$, join the midpoint of its reference edge to the opposite vertex. The two resulting triangles have generation $g(K)+1$. In each child, the two new half-edges and the bisector receive label $g(K)+2$; the one inherited nonreference edge retains label $g(K)+1$ and is the child's reference edge. A finite bisection forest is the collection of the initial triangles and all descendants reached by finitely many such bisections; its leaves form a triangulation when all shared-edge subdivisions agree. The admissible family $\mathbb T(\mathcal T_0)$ consists of the matching conforming leaf triangulations generated by these compatible bisections. A refinement $\mathcal T\le\mathcal T_*$ means every cell of $\mathcal T_*$ lies in a cell of $\mathcal T$.

For deterministic operational ordering, fix a finite starting mesh in this family and a total order of its cells. Enumerate those operational roots as $K_1,\ldots,K_N$ in that order; this starting mesh may already be a geometric descendant of $\mathcal T_0$, and operational numbering does not reset its generations or edge labels. Give root $K_r$ identifier $(r,\varnothing)$ and order its three vertices lexicographically by their two real coordinates. If a parent has identifier $(r,w)$, with $w$ a finite binary word, let $A$ be the earlier endpoint of its labeled reference edge in its stored vertex list, let $B$ be the other endpoint, let $C$ be the opposite vertex, and let $M=(A+B)/2$. Its children with vertex sets $\{A,M,C\}$ and $\{B,M,C\}$ receive identifiers $(r,w0)$ and $(r,w1)$, respectively. Each child's stored vertex list is the parent list restricted to its two retained vertices, in their previous order, followed by $M$. These lists are bookkeeping orders, independent of the orientation convention for affine reference maps. Compare identifiers first by root rank, then lexicographically by binary word, with $0<1$ and a proper prefix before its extensions. This is a total order, so every finite nonempty pending set has a unique least identifier. Distinct roots or distinct binary paths have distinct identifiers, and a retained cell keeps its identifier and vertex list through all subsequent calls. This operational decoration changes no geometric bisection, reference edge, admissible triangulation or finite-element space.

The compatible initial labeling is a hypothesis, not a consequence of an arbitrary initial triangulation. This definition is two-dimensional and makes no claim about three-dimensional closure or complexity.

For any compatible 2D initial labeling from [[def-afem-nvb-labelled-triangulation-family]], every conforming NVB descendant has shape regularity bounded by a constant depending only on the initial mesh. Three complete generations of uniform bisection of a triangle split each original edge at its midpoint, create a new interior midpoint on the median from the opposite vertex, and give child diameters at most half the parent diameter.

Let a compatible labeled reference triangulation be refined by recursive reference-edge closure as in [[alg-dorfler-marking-and-conforming-nvb-refinement]]. The closure terminates in a matching conforming affine descendant. If every cell is mapped through one common injective geometry map whose traces agree on common reference facets, the resulting curved cells also have matching interfaces.

Input: a finite labeled conforming mesh $\mathcal T$, exact nonnegative arrays $(\eta_K^2)_{K\in\mathcal T}$ and $(o_K^2)_{K\in\mathcal T}$, where $\eta_K^2$ is the cell estimator contribution and $o_K^2$ the cell data-oscillation contribution, bulk-fraction parameters $\theta_E,\theta_O\in(0,1]$, a per-call total bisection budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$, and a stable total order of mesh identifiers. On the first call on a mesh not yet carrying operational forest identifiers, rank its cells by the supplied order and initialize the operational roots and vertex lists of [[def-afem-nvb-labelled-triangulation-family]]. This initialization preserves the supplied order on those cells and does not change their geometric generations or labels. On subsequent calls retain that forest decoration and use its identifier order. Thus each current input leaf, including every generated descendant, has a specified identifier. For an array $q_K\ge0$ and $\theta\in(0,1]$, sort by decreasing $q_K$ and then increasing identifier. If $\sum_Kq_K=0$, return the empty set. Otherwise return the shortest initial segment whose sum is at least $\theta\sum_Kq_K$. Thus these parameters are fractions of the squared contributions (the square-root convention for the usual estimator-norm parameter). Call the resulting sets $M_E,M_O$ and set $M=M_E\cup M_O$.

Before modifying the mesh, form the original edge-neighbor request set
$$Q=\{L\in\mathcal T:L=K\text{ or }L\text{ shares an edge with some }K\in M\}.$$
Thus $M_E,M_O$ and their union $M$ remain the bulk marks; $Q$ is the larger refinement request, with $M\subseteq Q$ and $\#Q\le4\#M$ because a triangle has at most three edge neighbors. For $M=\varnothing$, also $Q=\varnothing$. Set a remaining-generation flag $q_K=3$ on each cell in $Q$ and $q_K=0$ on every other cell. Repeatedly take the pending leaf with least stable identifier and process its reference edge. If the reference edge is on the polygon boundary, bisect that leaf. If its interior reference neighbor has the same generation, bisect the compatible pair simultaneously. If the neighbor has generation one lower, recursively process that neighbor first and then re-inspect the original leaf; this follows the finite reference-edge chain until the edge can be split conformingly. Every split leaf $T$ is replaced by its two children with the binary-path identifiers and stored vertex lists prescribed by [[def-afem-nvb-labelled-triangulation-family]], each inheriting $q_T-1$ when $q_T>0$ and otherwise $0$. Thus conformity splits may propagate without scheduling extra uniform generations, while every originally requested cell in $Q$ and its descendants complete all three requested generations. Process simultaneous pairs in the same transaction and use the fixed identifier order for all pending leaves. Stop when all remaining-generation flags vanish. Count every bisection against $B$. If closure or a pending request would exceed the remaining budget, discard the tentative splits and their new identifiers, retaining the original identifiers and vertex lists, and return the original mesh with status budget-exhausted; otherwise return the refined matching mesh with status complete. Invalid arrays, nonfinite or negative entries, invalid parameters, or incompatible labels return invalid-input without changing the mesh. All arithmetic and comparisons in this mathematical algorithm are exact; implementation error, linear algebra, and quadrature are outside its scope.

Input the exact dyadic square $[-1,1]^2$, a tolerance $0<\tau\le1/4$, and the exact shear $\Phi(x,y)=(x,y+x^2/4)$. Use the unweighted indexed corner list $S=((1,(-1,-1)),(2,(1,-1)),(3,(1,1)),(4,(-1,1)))$ with all weights absent, and call [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]] in its ordinary $g=0$ branch with no prescribed insertion permutation, so sites are inserted in increasing identifier order. If the call does not return a triangulation, return unresolved. Verify that the output consists of two triangles covering the square and sharing one diagonal; otherwise return unresolved. The boundary features are the four closed edges and four vertices; features are incident when their sets intersect, and separation is the minimum Euclidean distance between nonincident feature sets. Record the interior boundary-angle certificate $\alpha=\pi/2$ and the nonincident-feature separation certificate $\sigma=1$. Label the shared diagonal reference on both triangles and label the boundary edges nonreference. For each seed triangle, sort its three input site identifiers increasingly and use the resulting triple as its seed key. Sort the two distinct keys lexicographically and assign operational root ranks $1,2$ in that order. Initialize their identifiers $(1,\varnothing),(2,\varnothing)$ and stored vertex lists by [[def-afem-nvb-labelled-triangulation-family]], retaining the just-assigned compatible reference-edge labels. All subsequent calls use the resulting persistent root-and-binary-path order, including on generated children; the site-key order is bookkeeping and does not relabel an edge. Set $k=0$. While $(3/2)2^{-k}(2\sqrt2)>\tau$, set $\eta_K^2=1$, $o_K^2=0$ on every current cell and call [[alg-dorfler-marking-and-conforming-nvb-refinement]] with $\theta_E=1$, $\theta_O=1$. Start the cycle budget at $B=1$; if the call returns `budget-exhausted`, retry from the unchanged mesh with $B$ doubled until it returns `complete`. A complete call requests three generations on every cell and uses recursive conformity closure; then set $k\leftarrow k+1$ and test the diameter bound again. Map every output reference triangle by the common shear $\Phi$ and return the mapped cells, feature certificates, and $k$. If a predicate is unresolved, the Delaunay seed does not have the stated two-triangle form, or closure returns invalid input, return `unresolved`.

Fix a reference matching affine simplicial mesh as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. An admissible curved cell is the image of a closed reference simplex $\widehat K$ under a map $F_K\in C^2(\widehat K;\mathbb R^d)$ that extends to a diffeomorphism on a neighborhood, is orientation preserving, and satisfies $0<j_0\le J_K:=\det DF_K\le j_1$ and $\|DF_K\|+\|(DF_K)^{-1}\|+\|D^2F_K\|\le C_F$. The physical cells have disjoint interiors, cover the domain up to their shared facets, and maps agree on each common reference facet under the prescribed affine facet identification. Define the volume metric $G_K=DF_K^TDF_K$, volume factor $J_K=\sqrt{\det G_K}$, and for a reference facet parametrization $\widehat f$ the surface metric $G_{K,\widehat f}=D(F_K\circ\widehat f)^TD(F_K\circ\widehat f)$ and surface factor $\sqrt{\det G_{K,\widehat f}}$. The positive-Jacobian lower bound is the admissibility certificate; it is not inferred from a drawing or from Delaunay quality.

Let $\widehat\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded reference domain and let $\Phi,\Phi_h:\overline{\widehat\Omega}\to\mathbb R^d$ be cellwise $C^2$ admissible maps with matching traces, positive Jacobians, and common image topology. The exact and approximate domains are $\Omega=\Phi(\widehat\Omega)$ and $\Omega_h=\Phi_h(\widehat\Omega)$. Define $e_0=\|\Phi-\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega)}$ and $e_1=\|D\Phi-D\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega;op)}$. A geometry approximation claim must separately state bounds on $e_0,e_1$, both Jacobian lower bounds, and boundary-trace compatibility; none follows from the word “isoparametric.”

derivations.claim: Directly from the square coordinates, each interior angle is $\pi/2$, opposite edges and nonincident vertices/edges are separated by distance $2$, so $\sigma=1$ is a valid lower certificate [A1]. The four corners are distinct dyadic sites in convex position. By [F1] the returned Delaunay triangulation covers the square; with four extreme vertices it has exactly two triangles sharing one diagonal. Each is right isosceles. Labeling the shared diagonal as reference on both sides gives compatible initial labels. The two seed triangles have different vertex-site sets, hence distinct sorted site-index triples; their lexicographic ranks initialize two distinct operational roots without changing those edge labels.

In each call the squared estimator array is constantly one and the oscillation array is zero. With $\theta_E=1$, the shortest initial segment whose sum reaches the total contains every cell, so every current cell is requested for three generations. The persistent root-and-binary-path identifiers in [F2] assign a unique order to every generated pending leaf; child identifiers are determined by the stored parent vertex list before it is replaced. At every stage the pending set is finite, so its least identifier exists. The recursive closure theorem [F4] says this finite request terminates, so some finite number $N$ of bisections suffices. By [F6], failed budget calls discard tentative splits and their identifiers, leaving the same ordered input mesh for retry; repeated doubling eventually reaches $B\ge N$ and a complete call.

The shear extends to the global $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\Phi(x,y)=(x,y+x^2/4)$ of $\mathbb R^2$, with explicit inverse $\Phi^{-1}(X,Y)=(X,Y-X^2/4)$ and determinant $\det D\Phi=1$. On the square, $D\Phi=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\x/2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and both $\|D\Phi\|_{op}$ and $\|D\Phi^{-1}\|_{op}$ are at most $3/2$ by the Frobenius bound. The second derivatives of the map and its inverse have operator norm $1/2$. Thus the shear satisfies the positive-Jacobian, derivative, inverse-derivative and $C^2$ bounds of [F5]; its cell traces agree because every cell uses the same global map, and its injectivity verifies the common-map hypothesis of [F4].

Each right-isosceles triangle has its hypotenuse as reference edge. Bisection at the hypotenuse midpoint joins that point to the right-angle vertex; the two resulting triangles have equal legs of half the parent hypotenuse and hence are right isosceles, with their inherited leg as hypotenuse/reference. Thus every bisection in the closure process preserves the $45^\circ$ minimum angle; [F3] supplies the uniform shape bound and three-generation diameter reduction.

By [F3], each complete three-generation request reduces every requested parent diameter by at least one half; closure only adds bisections, which cannot increase diameter. The initial reference diameter is $2\sqrt2$. Since $\|D\Phi\|_{op}\le\|D\Phi\|_F\le3/2$ on the square, the mean-value inequality gives mapped diameter at most $(3/2)2^{-k}2\sqrt2$. A finite integer $k$ satisfies the stopping inequality for every $\tau>0$.

Let $A_K=Da_K$. The bounds in step 1.3 imply $\kappa_2(D\Phi)\le\|D\Phi\|_{op}\|D\Phi^{-1}\|_{op}\le9/4$. Since $D(\Phi\circ a_K)=D\Phi(a_K)A_K$, submultiplicativity gives $\kappa_2(D(\Phi\circ a_K))\le(9/4)\kappa_2(A_K)$. The spectral condition number of $D(\Phi\circ a_K)^TD(\Phi\circ a_K)$ is the square of that derivative condition number, and $\kappa_2(A_K^TA_K)=\kappa_2(A_K)^2$, proving the stated $81/16$ metric bound. The reference triangles have disjoint interiors in a square of area $4$. Any right-isosceles reference triangle of diameter at least $\tau/(3/2)$ has area at least $\tau^2/9$; disjoint interiors therefore allow at most $36/\tau^2$ such cells. This packing bound is consistent with the finite uniform refinement and the stated positive feature and angle certificates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: $g'(t)=a(\pi/4)\sec^2(\pi t/4)>0$, so $H$ maps $[-1,1]^2$ bijectively onto $[-a,a]^2$, since $g(-1)=-a$ and $g(1)=a$. Its Gram determinant gives the same volume factor by [F2]. On the top sector, $\theta'=-\pi/4$ and $r_s=1-a/\sin\theta\ge1-a\sqrt2>0$ because $\sin\theta\ge\sqrt2/2$. Polar-coordinate differentiation gives $\det DF=r r_s(-\theta')>0$; the Gram determinant satisfies $\sqrt{\det(DF^TDF)}=\det DF$. Rotations preserve these determinants.

At $s=0$, $F(t,0)=(a\cot\theta(t),a)=(g(t),a)$, which is exactly the trace of $H$ on its top edge; at $s=1$, $r=1$, so the outer trace is the unit-circle arc from angle $3\pi/4$ to $\pi/4$. The two radial side traces match those of adjacent rotated sectors. Hence all ten pieces meet only along identical mapped edges.

For each angle $\theta\in[\pi/4,3\pi/4]$, the square boundary on that ray has radius $a/\sin\theta$ and the unit-circle boundary has radius $1$. The sector map covers exactly the radii between them. Four rotated angular ranges cover the annulus outside the central square, with shared corner rays only; $H$ covers the central square. Therefore the ten mapped triangles cover the unit disk without interior overlap.

The central area is $4a^2=1$. By [F3], the sector area is the polar integral $\frac12\int_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4}(1-a^2\csc^2\theta)d\theta$. Since $[-\cot\theta]_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4}=2$, this equals $\pi/4-a^2=(\pi-1)/4$. Four rotated sectors have total area $\pi-1$, so the union area is $\pi$, consistent with the unit disk.

citations.quote: Let $\widehat\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded reference domain and let $\Phi,\Phi_h:\overline{\widehat\Omega}\to\mathbb R^d$ be cellwise $C^2$ admissible maps with matching traces, positive Jacobians, and common image topology. The exact and approximate domains are $\Omega=\Phi(\widehat\Omega)$ and $\Omega_h=\Phi_h(\widehat\Omega)$. Define $e_0=\|\Phi-\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega)}$ and $e_1=\|D\Phi-D\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega;op)}$. A geometry approximation claim must separately state bounds on $e_0,e_1$, both Jacobian lower bounds, and boundary-trace compatibility; none follows from the word “isoparametric.”

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable domain of finite positive measure. Let $\mathcal S=(S_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $\mathcal T=(T_j)_{j=1}^n$ be finite measurable partitions of $\Omega$ up to null sets, with disjoint interiors modulo null sets and positive cell volumes. Define exact overlap weights $w_{ji}=|T_j\cap S_i|$. For source constants $v_i$, the intersection-volume remap is the target piecewise-constant field $Rv$ whose value on $T_j$ is $ (Rv)_j=|T_j|^{-1}\sum_i w_{ji}v_i$. All weights are exact measures; an approximate clipping weight is not silently substituted.

Assume Countable Choice. Under the finite partition hypotheses of [[def-intersection-volume-conservative-remapping]], let $P_0(\mathcal T)$ be the target cellwise-constant subspace of $L^2(\Omega)$. For every source piecewise-constant $v$, $Rv$ is the $L^2$ orthogonal projection of $v$ onto $P_0(\mathcal T)$, hence $\|Rv\|_2\le\|v\|_2$. It preserves total mass, $\int_\Omega Rv=\int_\Omega v$, and if all $v_i\ge0$ then every target value $(Rv)_j\ge0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The shear is a global $C^1$ diffeomorphism with inverse $(X,Y)\mapsto(X,Y-X^2/4)$ and derivative $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\x/2&1\end{pmatrix}$ of determinant $1$. Apply [F4] to each overlap to see that its physical area equals the reference overlap area. In the reference square, the two diagonals meet at the center; the two diagonals divide the square into four corner triangles, each with base $2$ along a side and altitude $1$ to the center, so each nonempty source-target overlap has area $1$.
Each target triangle has area $2$ and receives source mass $2(1)+0(1)=2$, so its target average is $1$. The source mass is $2\cdot2+0\cdot2=4$, and target mass is $2(1)+2(1)=4$.
The exact remap therefore has source values $(2,0)$, four nonempty overlaps of area $1$, target cell areas $2$, and target averages $(1,1)$. This explicitly verifies the remap formula.

derivations.claim: Differentiate $\Phi$ to obtain $D\Phi=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\x/2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\det D\Phi=1$. The quadratic term makes the image of a nonvertical straight edge a parabolic arc, while vertical edges remain vertical.
Apply [F2] on the shape-regular mesh to get the stated value error, derivative error, and positive-Jacobian certificate.

On each shared reference edge, the two affine traces of $I_h(x^2/4)$ agree at its endpoints and therefore agree everywhere on that edge. Thus $\Phi_h$ has matching traces; the exact map is globally smooth and has matching traces as well. On each boundary edge, $\Phi_h$ is the straight segment joining the exact images of its vertices. The vertical boundary traces agree exactly with $\Phi$; on each horizontal boundary segment, $\Phi_h(x,\pm1)=(x,\pm1+I_h(x^2/4))$, so the boundary discrepancy is bounded by $Ch^2$ from step 1.2. Compatibility here does not assert equality of the exact parabolic arcs and their straight approximations. By [F2], $\Phi_h$ is continuous and injective on the compact square, hence by [F4] is a homeomorphism onto its image, as is $\Phi$. Its cell restrictions are invertible affine maps extending to neighborhood diffeomorphisms; the exact restrictions extend by the global shear. These facts verify matching and boundary-trace compatibility and common image topology in [F1].

Step 1.1 bounds $D\Phi$ uniformly, and step 1.2 gives $\|D\Phi_h\|_\infty\le\|D\Phi\|_\infty+Ch$ and determinant lower bounds $J=1$, $J_h\ge1/2$. Apply [F3] cellwise, with the compatible maps from step 2.1, and substitute $e_1\le Ch$ from step 1.2. This yields $\|B-B_h\|_\infty\le Ch$ with constants uniform over the mesh family.

For a weighted site $(p,w)$, define its power distance from $x\in\mathbb R^3$ by
$$\pi_{(p,w)}(x)=\|x-p\|^2-w.$$
Its lifted point is $\widehat p=(p,\|p\|^2-w)\in\mathbb R^4$. A lower face of the lifted convex hull is a face supported by a nonvertical hyperplane $z=\ell(x)$ with every lifted site on or above that hyperplane. The projection of the union of lower faces is the **regular subdivision** of the projected sites; a simplex in that subdivision has an empty power sphere, meaning its common power distance is no larger than that of any input site.

The lex-refined lift is interpreted over the ordered rational-function field of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]], using one fixed finite universe of all input sites. When every weight is zero, the regular subdivision is the ordinary 3D Delaunay subdivision and power spheres are circumspheres. A weighted site is **original-hidden** if its unperturbed lift is not a vertex of any lower face of the original lifted convex hull, and **formal-hidden** if its lex-refined lift is not a vertex of any lower face of the fixed formal lifted convex hull. These notions can differ; the algorithm's `hidden` report means formal-hidden. A nonsimplicial lower face is refined with the same fixed-universe lexicographic lift convention. For projected affine dimension below three, the algorithm reports `lower-dimensional` with that dimension and the exact deduplicated site list, and makes no tetrahedralization claim. A tetrahedral output is claimed only on the full-dimensional branch with nondegenerate projected bases.

derivations.claim: For every $n\ge1$, $\varepsilon_n\in\mathbb D$ and the four sites therefore satisfy the dyadic-coordinate input condition of [F1]. The first three points are noncollinear in $z=0$ and $p_4$ has positive height, so the four points are affinely independent and form a nondegenerate tetrahedron. Its volume is one third of base area $1/2$ times height $\varepsilon_n$, namely $V_n=\varepsilon_n/6$. With only these four sites, its circumsphere contains no other site in its interior, so [F1] makes it an empty-sphere Delaunay tetrahedron.

The total face area $S_n$ is at least the base area $1/2$ and is bounded above uniformly in $n$, since every edge length is at most $2$ and each of the four face areas is at most half the product of two such edge lengths; in particular $S_n\le8$. The inradius is $r_n=3V_n/S_n=\varepsilon_n/(2S_n)$, so $\varepsilon_n/16\le r_n\le\varepsilon_n$ and $r_n\to0$. The diameter is at least $|p_1-p_2|=1$. Thus empty-sphere Delaunay membership imposes no positive uniform inradius-to-diameter bound in three dimensions.

Let $k>0$, $x\in\mathbb R$ be the Cartesian normal coordinate, and $y\in\mathbb R^2$ the tangential coordinate. Let $\sigma$ be nonnegative, continuous, piecewise $C^1$, and zero for $x\le0$. Define
$$S(x)=\int_0^x\sigma(t)\,dt,\qquad X(x)=x+iS(x),\qquad s(x)=X'(x)=1+i\sigma(x).$$
The pulled-back constant-coefficient Helmholtz operator in the layer is
$$\frac1{s(x)}\partial_x\left(\frac1{s(x)}\partial_x\right)+\Delta_y+k^2.$$
This definition concerns the homogeneous Cartesian branch only; it makes no claim for heterogeneous media, curved stretches, grazing or evanescent uniform attenuation, discretizations, or finite-element convergence.

derivations.claim: For the stated mode, $\partial_xu=iqs(x)u$, so $s^{-1}\partial_xu=iqu$ and $s^{-1}\partial_x(s^{-1}\partial_xu)=s^{-1}\partial_x(iqu)=-q^2u$. Also $\Delta_yu=-|\eta|^2u$. Since $q^2+|\eta|^2=k^2$, substitution into [F1] gives zero.

At $x=0$, $S(0)=0$ and $\sigma(0)=0$ by continuity and the definition, so $X(0)=0$, $s(0)=1$, and the stretched mode and its normal flux equal $e^{i\eta\cdot y}$ and $iqe^{i\eta\cdot y}$, respectively, exactly as in the physical outgoing mode. Since $|e^{iq(x+iS)+i\eta\cdot y}|=e^{-qS}$, the bounds follow from $q\ge q_0$ and, when assumed, $S(x)\ge\sigma_0x$. As $q\downarrow0$, the attenuation bound tends to one, so this proof gives no uniform grazing decay.

For real $z>0$, let $D_z:=z^{-1}\frac{d}{dz}$ and define, for integers $\ell\ge0$,
$$j_\ell(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(\frac{\sin z}{z}\right),\qquad h_\ell^{(1)}(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(-i\frac{e^{iz}}{z}\right).$$
The definition fixes the outgoing $e^{iz}$ convention. The functions solve the radial Helmholtz equation and have the recurrence, origin, Wronskian, and infinity behavior by [[lem-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-radial-solutions]].

These symbolic definitions assert no stable or certified numerical evaluation algorithm for large $\ell$ or $z$.

For the functions of [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]], define
$$L_\ell y:=y''+\frac2z y'+\left(1-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{z^2}\right)y\qquad(z>0).$$
Then $L_\ell j_\ell=L_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}=0$, and for $y=j,h^{(1)}$,
$$y_{\ell+1}(z)=\frac{\ell}{z}y_\ell(z)-y_\ell'(z),\qquad y_\ell'(z)=y_{\ell-1}(z)-\frac{\ell+1}{z}y_\ell(z)\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
The regular-origin and outgoing-infinity normalizations are
$$j_\ell(z)=\frac{z^\ell}{(2\ell+1)!!}+O(z^{\ell+2}),\quad h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=-i(2\ell-1)!!z^{-\ell-1}(1+O(z))\quad(z\downarrow0),$$
$$j_\ell(z)=\frac{\sin(z-\ell\pi/2)}z+O(z^{-2}),\quad h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=(-i)^{\ell+1}\frac{e^{iz}}z+O(z^{-2})\quad(z\to\infty),$$
where $(-1)!!:=1$. Their Wronskian is
$$j_\ell(z)(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z)-j_\ell'(z)h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=\frac{i}{z^2}.$$

derivations.claim: Direct differentiation of $h_0=-ie^{iz}/z$ gives the finite expression $h_\ell(z)=(-i)^{\ell+1}e^{iz}\sum_{m=0}^{\ell}i^m A_{\ell m}z^{-m-1},\qquad A_{\ell m}=\frac{(\ell+m)!}{m!(\ell-m)!2^m}.$ Indeed it holds at $\ell=0$; substituting this expression in $h_{\ell+1}=\ell h_\ell/z-h_\ell'$ gives $A_{\ell+1,m}=A_{\ell m}+(\ell+m)A_{\ell,m-1}$ (out-of-range coefficients are zero), and the displayed factorial formula satisfies that recurrence and the $m=0$ base.

Let $F_\ell=|h_\ell|^2$. The radial recurrence gives $h_{\ell+1}=(2\ell+1)h_\ell/z-h_{\ell-1}$. Also $F_\ell'=2\operatorname{Re}(\bar h_\ell h_{\ell-1})-2(\ell+1)F_\ell/z$ by [F2]. Expanding the squared modulus and eliminating the real cross term yields $F_{\ell+1}=F_{\ell-1}-(2\ell+1)F_\ell'/z-(2\ell+1)F_\ell/z^2.$ From $F_0=z^{-2}$ and $F_1=z^{-2}+z^{-4}$, coefficient comparison yields $S_{\ell+1,0}=S_{\ell-1,0}=1$ and, for $1\le q\le\ell$, $S_{\ell+1,q}=S_{\ell-1,q}+(2\ell+1)(2q-1)S_{\ell,q-1}$. The displayed factorial coefficients satisfy this: the ratios are $S_{\ell-1,q}/S_{\ell+1,q}=(\ell-q)(\ell-q+1)/[(\ell+q)(\ell+q+1)]$ and $S_{\ell+1,q}/S_{\ell,q-1}=(2q-1)(\ell+q)(\ell+q+1)/(2q)$, whose difference gives the recurrence. At the top index $q=\ell+1$, $S_{\ell+1,\ell+1}=(2\ell+1)^2S_{\ell,\ell}$; thus induction proves the stated sum at every degree.

Every $S_{\ell m}$ is positive, so differentiating the finite sum gives $F_\ell'(z)<0$. For $0\le m\le\ell-1$, $S_{\ell m}/S_{\ell-1,m}=(\ell+m)/(\ell-m)\ge1$, and the degree-$\ell$ sum has one additional positive term. Hence $|h_\ell|$ decreases with $z$ and $|h_{\ell-1}|\le|h_\ell|$. For $\ell\ge1$, [F2] now implies $|h_\ell'|\le|h_{\ell-1}|+(\ell+1)|h_\ell|/z\le(1+(\ell+1)/z)|h_\ell|$; for $\ell=0$ the same bound follows by differentiating $h_0=-ie^{iz}/z$.

Differentiating the finite sum in step 1.1 cancels its $ie^{iz}$ derivative in $h_\ell'-ih_\ell$, so $|z(h_\ell'-ih_\ell)|\le\sum_{m=0}^{\ell}(m+1)A_{\ell m}z^{-m-1}$. The lowest-power term of the positive modulus sum gives $|h_\ell(z_0)|\ge A_{\ell\ell}z_0^{-\ell-1}$. For $j=\ell-m$, factorial cancellation gives $\frac{A_{\ell,\ell-j}}{A_{\ell\ell}}=\frac{2^j}{j!}\prod_{s=0}^{j-1}\frac{\ell-s}{2\ell-s}\le\frac{2^j}{j!}.$ Using $z\ge z_0$ and $m+1\le\ell+1$, the quotient in the claim is at most $(\ell+1)\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}(2z_0)^j/j!\le(\ell+1)e^{2z_0}$.

Fix $a>0$, $k>0$, and $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb S^2;\mathbb C)$. Write $S_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=a\}$. The sound-soft exterior Helmholtz problem is to find a complex-valued $u\in C^2(\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>a\})$ that extends continuously to $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|\ge a\}$ and satisfies $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ for $|x|>a$, with boundary restriction $u|_{S_a}(a\omega)=f(\omega)$, and
$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\sup_{\omega\in\mathbb S^2}\left|r\bigl(\partial_r u(r\omega)-ik u(r\omega)\bigr)\right|=0.$$
The time factor is $e^{-i\omega t}$, so this is the outgoing convention. The obstacle is the closed ball $\{|x|\le a\}$; its boundary is smooth and its exterior is connected. This definition makes no claim for nonspherical obstacles or nonsmooth data.

Let $\mathcal H_\ell$ be the degree-$\ell$ spaces on $\mathbb S^2$ from [[def-three-dimensional-spherical-harmonic-space]], with surface measure of total mass $4\pi$, and let $P_\ell$ be orthogonal projection in $L^2(\mathbb S^2)$. Define $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$ by the polar-coordinate identity $\Delta=\partial_{rr}+2r^{-1}\partial_r+r^{-2}\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$. Then $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g=-\ell(\ell+1)g$ for $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$; for all smooth $v,w$ on the sphere, $\langle v,\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}w\rangle=\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}v,w\rangle$; the spaces are mutually orthogonal and their algebraic sum is uniformly dense in $C(\mathbb S^2;\mathbb C)$. For smooth $f$, for every integer $m\ge1$ there is a constant $C_m(f)$ such that $\|P_\ell f\|_2\le C_m(f)(1+\ell)^{-m}$. For $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$,
$$\|g\|_\infty\le\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}}\,\|g\|_2.$$
For each integer $p\ge0$ there is $C_p$ independent of $\ell,g$ such that $\|g\|_{C^p(\mathbb S^2)}\le C_p(1+\ell)^{p+1/2}\|g\|_2$.
The angular Dirichlet form satisfies $-\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g,g\rangle=\ell(\ell+1)\|g\|_2^2$ for $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$.
For every continuous $f$, the ordered partial sums $\sum_{\ell=0}^N P_\ell f$ converge to $f$ in $L^2(\mathbb S^2)$.

For real $z>0$, let $h_\ell^{(1)}$ be defined in [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]] and set $h_\ell^{(2)}(z)=\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(z)}$. Then both solve the degree-$\ell$ spherical radial Helmholtz equation, are linearly independent, and
$$\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(z)}(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z)\bigr)=z^{-2}.$$
In particular, neither vanishes for $z>0$, and for $k>0$, $r>0$,
$$r^2\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)}\,\partial_r h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)\bigr)=1/k.$$

Let $u$ be a classical solution of $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ for $r>a$, where $k>0$, and satisfy the outgoing condition in [[def-pe18-exterior-helmholtz-problem]]. For each $\ell$, its orthogonal projection $u_\ell(r,\cdot)$ onto $\mathcal H_\ell$ has the form $u_\ell(r,\cdot)=c_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ with a fixed vector $c_\ell\in\mathcal H_\ell$. Before imposing outgoingness, every degree-$\ell$ coefficient is a linear combination of $h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ and $h_\ell^{(2)}(kr)=\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)}$. This statement is modewise; it does not assert convergence of the partial-wave series as $r\to\infty$.

derivations.claim: By [F4], for every degree $\ell$ the projection of $u$ has the form $u_\ell(r,\cdot)=c_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ with $c_\ell$ independent of $r$. $$\tau_\ell(k,R)=k\frac{(h_\ell^{(1)})'(kR)}{h_\ell^{(1)}(kR)},\qquad T_{k,R}g=\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\tau_\ell(k,R)g_\ell.$$
The associated outgoing extension for $r\ge R$ is
$$v(r,\omega)=\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\frac{h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)}{h_\ell^{(1)}(kR)}g_\ell(\omega).$$
The denominator is nonzero by [[lem-pe18-spherical-hankel-radial-identities]]. The convergence, smoothness, PDE, and radiation properties are asserted in [[thm-pe18-exact-spherical-dtn-map-on-smooth-data]].

Let $\mathcal H_\ell$ be the degree-$\ell$ spaces on $\mathbb S^2$ from [[def-three-dimensional-spherical-harmonic-space]], with surface measure of total mass $4\pi$, and let $P_\ell$ be orthogonal projection in $L^2(\mathbb S^2)$. Define $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$ by the polar-coordinate identity $\Delta=\partial_{rr}+2r^{-1}\partial_r+r^{-2}\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$. Then $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g=-\ell(\ell+1)g$ for $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$; for all smooth $v,w$ on the sphere, $\langle v,\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}w\rangle=\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}v,w\rangle$; the spaces are mutually orthogonal and their algebraic sum is uniformly dense in $C(\mathbb S^2;\mathbb C)$. For smooth $f$, for every integer $m\ge1$ there is a constant $C_m(f)$ such that $\|P_\ell f\|_2\le C_m(f)(1+\ell)^{-m}$. For $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$,
$$\|g\|_\infty\le\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}}\,\|g\|_2.$$
For each integer $p\ge0$ there is $C_p$ independent of $\ell,g$ such that $\|g\|_{C^p(\mathbb S^2)}\le C_p(1+\ell)^{p+1/2}\|g\|_2$.
The angular Dirichlet form satisfies $-\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g,g\rangle=\ell(\ell+1)\|g\|_2^2$ for $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$.
For every continuous $f$, the ordered partial sums $\sum_{\ell=0}^N P_\ell f$ converge to $f$ in $L^2(\mathbb S^2)$.

For real $z>0$, let $h_\ell^{(1)}$ be defined in [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]] and set $h_\ell^{(2)}(z)=\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(z)}$. Then both solve the degree-$\ell$ spherical radial Helmholtz equation, are linearly independent, and
$$\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(z)}(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z)\bigr)=z^{-2}.$$
In particular, neither vanishes for $z>0$, and for $k>0$, $r>0$,
$$r^2\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)}\,\partial_r h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)\bigr)=1/k.$$

$$|h_\ell(z)|^2=\sum_{m=0}^{\ell}S_{\ell m}z^{-2m-2},\qquad S_{\ell m}=\frac{(2m)!(\ell+m)!}{4^m(m!)^2(\ell-m)!}.$$

derivations.claim: By [F3], $|\tau_\ell|\le k+(\ell+1)/R$. The $C^p$ estimate in [F5] and the super-polynomial decay in [F2] show that for every $p$, $\sum_\ell\|\tau_\ell g_\ell\|_{C^p}<\infty$. Thus the defining series converges in every smooth norm to a smooth function $T_{k,R}g$.

For $r\ge R$, the positive coefficient formula for $|h_\ell(z)|^2$ in [F3] makes $|h_\ell(kr)/h_\ell(kR)|\le1$. The derivative estimate in [F3] bounds one radial derivative of the ratio by $k+(\ell+1)/r$ times this ratio; repeated radial derivatives are bounded by polynomials in $1+\ell$ on each compact annulus by differentiating the radial ODE in [F5]. Angular derivatives likewise contribute only polynomial factors. Thus [F2] and the evaluation bound make the extension series and its derivatives through order two uniformly convergent on $R\le r\le R_1$. Termwise differentiation is valid; each summand solves the Helmholtz equation by [F5], its trace is $g_\ell$, and its radial derivative at $R$ is $\tau_\ell g_\ell$. Summing proves the trace, derivative, and PDE claims.

For each fixed $\ell$, the finite formula in [F3] gives $r(\partial_r-ik)\bigl(h_\ell(kr)/h_\ell(kR)\bigr)\to0$. The last bound in [F3], multiplied by $\|g_\ell\|_\infty$, dominates the absolute value of this degree's radiation residual by $(\ell+1)e^{2kR}\sqrt{(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)}\|g_\ell\|_2$, a summable sequence by [F2]. Dominated convergence for this series proves uniform convergence of the full radiation residual to zero.

Let $w$ be any other classical outgoing extension of $g$. By [F4], its degree-$\ell$ projection is $d_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ for a fixed $d_\ell\in\mathcal H_\ell$. Its trace at $R$ is $g_\ell$, so $d_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kR)=g_\ell$. Nonvanishing in [F3] forces $d_\ell=g_\ell/h_\ell^{(1)}(kR)$, the same coefficient as the constructed extension in [F1]. Their difference has every harmonic projection zero and is continuous; density in [F2] implies the difference vanishes. This proves uniqueness and the well-definedness claimed in [F1].

Fix $0<a<R$ and $k>0$. The coefficient energy space $\mathcal V_{a,R}$ consists of sequences $u=(u_\ell)_{\ell\ge0}$ with $u_\ell\in H^1((a,R);\mathcal H_\ell)$ and
$$\|u\|_{\mathcal V}^2=\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\int_a^R\left(r^2\|u_\ell'(r)\|_2^2+(1+\ell(\ell+1))\|u_\ell(r)\|_2^2\right)dr<\infty.$$
For smooth inner data $f$ on $\mathbb S^2$, let $f_\ell$ be its projection onto $\mathcal H_\ell$ and define the affine trial space $\mathcal V_f=\{u\in\mathcal V_{a,R}:u_\ell(a)=f_\ell\text{ for every }\ell\}$ and test space $\mathcal V_0=\{v\in\mathcal V_{a,R}:v_\ell(a)=0\text{ for every }\ell\}$. Traces and continuity of the following form are established in [[lem-pe18-modal-trace-and-form-continuity]]. With the inner product linear in its first argument, set
$$\mathfrak a_{k,a,R}(u,v)=\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\int_a^R\left(r^2\langle u_\ell',v_\ell'\rangle+(\ell(\ell+1)-k^2r^2)\langle u_\ell,v_\ell\rangle\right)dr-R^2\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\tau_\ell(k,R)\langle u_\ell(R),v_\ell(R)\rangle.$$
The exact-DtN variational problem is to find $u\in\mathcal V_f$ such that $\mathfrak a_{k,a,R}(u,v)=0$ for every $v\in\mathcal V_0$. The assigned theorem on this page proves existence and uniqueness.

For every $k,R>0$ and smooth $g$ on $\mathbb S^2$, the series in [[def-pe18-exact-spherical-dtn-map]] converges in $C^\infty(\mathbb S^2)$ to $T_{k,R}g$, and $|\tau_\ell(k,R)|\le k+(\ell+1)/R$. Its outgoing extension converges in $C^2$ on each compact annulus $R\le r\le R_1$, solves $(\Delta+k^2)v=0$, has trace $v(R,\cdot)=g$ and radial derivative $\partial_rv(R,\cdot)=T_{k,R}g$, and satisfies the uniform outgoing Sommerfeld condition as $r\to\infty$. It is the unique classical outgoing extension of $g$.

derivations.claim: Each $H^1((a,R);\mathcal H_\ell)$ is complete because $\mathcal H_\ell$ is finite dimensional. A Cauchy sequence in the weighted square-sum norm is Cauchy in each coordinate; take its coordinatewise $H^1$ limits. For every finite number of coordinates the squared norm of the limit is bounded by the liminf of the sequence norms, so the coordinatewise limit has finite total norm; applying the same argument to differences shows convergence in the sum norm. Tails of the defining convergent nonnegative series tend to zero, so finite-degree truncations are dense. For any scalar or finite-dimensional Hilbert-valued $w\in H^1(a,R)$, set $A=\|w\|_{L^2(a,R)}$ and $B=\|w'\|_{L^2(a,R)}$. Absolute continuity and $|w(R)|^2-|w(t)|^2=2\operatorname{Re}\int_t^R\langle w'(s),w(s)\rangle ds$ give, after averaging $t$ over $[a,R]$ and applying Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|w(R)\|^2\le(R-a)^{-1}A^2+2AB$. Multiplying by $1+\ell$ and using $2(1+\ell)AB\le(1+\ell)^2A^2+B^2$, $(1+\ell)^2\le2(1+\ell(\ell+1))$, and $B^2\le a^{-2}\int_a^Rr^2\|w'\|^2dr$ gives $(1+\ell)\|w(R)\|^2\le C_{a,R}\int_a^R\left(r^2\|w'\|^2+(1+\ell(\ell+1))\|w\|^2\right)dr$. Replacing $r$ by $a+R-r$ proves the same inequality at the inner endpoint. Summing with $w=u_\ell$ proves the weighted trace estimate.

The volume terms of $\mathfrak a$ are bounded by a constant times $\|u\|_{\mathcal V}\|v\|_{\mathcal V}$ because $r$ lies in $[a,R]$ and $k$ is fixed. By [F2], $|\tau_\ell|\le C_{k,R}(1+\ell)$. Cauchy–Schwarz over degrees and the trace estimate from step 1.1 give $\sum_\ell |\tau_\ell\langle u_\ell(R),v_\ell(R)\rangle|\le C\left(\sum_\ell(1+\ell)\|u_\ell(R)\|_2^2\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_\ell(1+\ell)\|v_\ell(R)\|_2^2\right)^{1/2}\le C\|u\|_{\mathcal V}\|v\|_{\mathcal V}.$ Thus the boundary series is absolutely convergent and the whole form is continuous.

The angular Dirichlet form satisfies $-\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g,g\rangle=\ell(\ell+1)\|g\|_2^2$ for $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$.
For every continuous $f$, the ordered partial sums $\sum_{\ell=0}^N P_\ell f$ converge to $f$ in $L^2(\mathbb S^2)$.

$$\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(z)}(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z)\bigr)=z^{-2}.$$
In particular, neither vanishes for $z>0$, and for $k>0$, $r>0$,

The angular energy of degree $\ell$ is $\ell(\ell+1)$ times its squared $L^2$ norm. Consequently its total $\mathcal V$ energy is at most $C_{a,R,k}\sum_\ell(1+\ell)^2\|f_\ell\|_2^2$, which is finite by [F4]. Thus it belongs to $\mathcal V_f$.

Let $w\in\mathcal V_0$ solve the homogeneous variational equation. Testing against functions supported in a single degree and compactly supported in $(a,R)$ shows distributionally that $(r^2w_\ell')'+(k^2r^2-\ell(\ell+1))w_\ell=0$. Since the coefficients are smooth and $r>0$, this one-dimensional equation implies $w_\ell\in C^2([a,R];\mathcal H_\ell)$. Integrating by parts and allowing arbitrary outer test trace yields $w_\ell'(R)=\tau_\ell w_\ell(R)$; the inner trace is $w_\ell(a)=0$.

Each modal coefficient satisfies $(r^2u_\ell')'+(k^2r^2-\ell(\ell+1))u_\ell=0$ and $u_\ell'(R)=\tau_\ell u_\ell(R)$ by [F3]. Integration by parts against a finite-degree test with zero inner trace makes its modal volume term equal $R^2u_\ell'(R)\overline{v_\ell(R)}$; the outer term in [F1] subtracts exactly $R^2\tau_\ell u_\ell(R)\overline{v_\ell(R)}$. Hence the form vanishes for every finite-degree test. Finite-degree truncations converge in $\mathcal V$, and [F2] extends the identity to every test in $\mathcal V_0$. This proves existence.

The radial ODE solution is $w_\ell(r)=A_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)+B_\ell h_\ell^{(2)}(kr)$: the two solutions have nonzero Wronskian by [F5], and matching value and derivative at one radius followed by uniqueness of the linear initial-value equation spans all solutions. The parenthesized factor is the nonzero Wronskian divided by $h_\ell^{(1)}(kR)$, so $B_\ell=0$. The inner condition and [F5] then give $A_\ell=0$. Let $k>0$, $x\in\mathbb R$ be the Cartesian normal coordinate, and $y\in\mathbb R^2$ the tangential coordinate. Let $\sigma$ be nonnegative, continuous, piecewise $C^1$, and zero for $x\le0$. Define
$$S(x)=\int_0^x\sigma(t)\,dt,\qquad X(x)=x+iS(x),\qquad s(x)=X'(x)=1+i\sigma(x).$$
The pulled-back constant-coefficient Helmholtz operator in the layer is
$$\frac1{s(x)}\partial_x\left(\frac1{s(x)}\partial_x\right)+\Delta_y+k^2.$$
This definition concerns the homogeneous Cartesian branch only; it makes no claim for heterogeneous media, curved stretches, grazing or evanescent uniform attenuation, discretizations, or finite-element convergence.

Let $k>0$, $\eta\in\mathbb R^2$ satisfy $|\eta|<k$, and let $q=\sqrt{k^2-|\eta|^2}>0$ be the outgoing normal branch. In the stretch of [[def-pe18-cartesian-complex-stretch-pml]],
$$u(x,y)=e^{iqX(x)+i\eta\cdot y}$$
solves the pulled-back Helmholtz equation. At $x=0$, its value and normal flux $(1/s)\partial_xu$ agree with those of the physical mode $e^{iqx+i\eta\cdot y}$. Its modulus is $e^{-qS(x)}$. If a family of modes satisfies $q\ge q_0>0$, then $|u(x,y)|\le e^{-q_0S(x)}$ uniformly; whenever $S(x)\ge\sigma_0x$ for some $\sigma_0>0$, this is at most $e^{-q_0\sigma_0x}$. No uniform bound is asserted as $q\downarrow0$.

derivations.claim: Parameterize the stretched contour by the real physical coordinate $x\in[0,L]$. For a source at $x'$, set $x_<=\min(x,x')$, $x_>=\max(x,x')$, and $X_<=X(x_<)$, $X_>=X(x_>)$. The functions $y_1(X)=\sin(kX)$ and $y_2(X)=\sin(k(X_L-X))$ solve the homogeneous equation and vanish at the respective endpoints; their Wronskian in the order $y_1y_2'-y_1'y_2$ is the constant $-k\sin(kX_L)$. The real parameter orders the two sides of the contour, and the one-sided derivatives in the contour coordinate satisfy $\left.\partial_XG\right|_{x\to x'^+}-\left.\partial_XG\right|_{x\to x'^-}=-1$, as required by [A1].

Fix $a>0$, $k>0$, and $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb S^2;\mathbb C)$. Write $S_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=a\}$. The sound-soft exterior Helmholtz problem is to find a complex-valued $u\in C^2(\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>a\})$ that extends continuously to $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|\ge a\}$ and satisfies $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ for $|x|>a$, with boundary restriction $u|_{S_a}(a\omega)=f(\omega)$, and
$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\sup_{\omega\in\mathbb S^2}\left|r\bigl(\partial_r u(r\omega)-ik u(r\omega)\bigr)\right|=0.$$
The time factor is $e^{-i\omega t}$, so this is the outgoing convention. The obstacle is the closed ball $\{|x|\le a\}$; its boundary is smooth and its exterior is connected. This definition makes no claim for nonspherical obstacles or nonsmooth data.

For real $z>0$, let $D_z:=z^{-1}\frac{d}{dz}$ and define, for integers $\ell\ge0$,
$$j_\ell(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(\frac{\sin z}{z}\right),\qquad h_\ell^{(1)}(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(-i\frac{e^{iz}}{z}\right).$$
The definition fixes the outgoing $e^{iz}$ convention. The functions solve the radial Helmholtz equation and have the recurrence, origin, Wronskian, and infinity behavior by [[lem-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-radial-solutions]].

These symbolic definitions assert no stable or certified numerical evaluation algorithm for large $\ell$ or $z$.

For the functions of [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]], define
$$L_\ell y:=y''+\frac2z y'+\left(1-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{z^2}\right)y\qquad(z>0).$$
Then $L_\ell j_\ell=L_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}=0$, and for $y=j,h^{(1)}$,
$$y_{\ell+1}(z)=\frac{\ell}{z}y_\ell(z)-y_\ell'(z),\qquad y_\ell'(z)=y_{\ell-1}(z)-\frac{\ell+1}{z}y_\ell(z)\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
The regular-origin and outgoing-infinity normalizations are
$$j_\ell(z)=\frac{z^\ell}{(2\ell+1)!!}+O(z^{\ell+2}),\quad h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=-i(2\ell-1)!!z^{-\ell-1}(1+O(z))\quad(z\downarrow0),$$
$$j_\ell(z)=\frac{\sin(z-\ell\pi/2)}z+O(z^{-2}),\quad h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=(-i)^{\ell+1}\frac{e^{iz}}z+O(z^{-2})\quad(z\to\infty),$$
where $(-1)!!:=1$. Their Wronskian is
$$j_\ell(z)(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z)-j_\ell'(z)h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=\frac{i}{z^2}.$$

For $a>0$, $k>0$, and the convention in [[def-pe18-exterior-helmholtz-problem]], every classical outgoing solution of $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ on $r>a$ with zero Dirichlet trace at $r=a$ is identically zero.

derivations.claim: Substituting [F2] into the Hankel ratio cancels the factor $-i/k$ and gives $u(r)=(a/r)e^{ik(r-a)}$, so $u(a)=1$. Direct differentiation yields $u'=(ik-r^{-1})u$ and $u''=(-k^2-2ik/r+2/r^2)u$. In three dimensions a radial function satisfies $\Delta u=u''+2u'/r$; hence $u''+2u'/r+k^2u=0$ by cancellation of each coefficient, in agreement with [F3] after setting $z=kr$.
The same derivative identity gives $r(u'-iku)=-u(r)$ and $|u(r)|=a/r\to0$. Thus the outgoing condition holds, and the displayed mode is an outgoing monopole solution.

If $w$ is any other classical outgoing solution with boundary value $1$, then $w-u$ is a classical outgoing solution with zero Dirichlet trace on $r=a$. By [F4], $w-u=0$. Hence the displayed field is the unique outgoing monopole solution.
