Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

derivations.claim: Let $v\in C_c^\infty(Q)$ and write $x=(t,x')$ with first library coordinate $t=x_0$ and $x'=(x_1,\ldots,x_{d-1})$ (the empty tuple when $d=1$). For fixed $x'$ and $0<t<1$, the one-dimensional fundamental theorem gives $v(t,x')=\int_0^t\partial_0v(s,x')\,ds$. Cauchy--Schwarz and $t\le1$ imply $|v(t,x')|^2\le\int_0^1|\partial_0v(s,x')|^2\,ds$. Integrating first in $t$ and then in $x'$ gives $\|v\|_2^2\le\|\partial_0v\|_2^2$. By [F1], approximating any $v\in H^1_0(Q)$ in $H^1$ and passing to the limit proves the displayed Poincaré bound.

The map $J:H^1(Q)\to L^2(Q)^{d+1}$, $J(v)=(v,\partial_0v,\ldots,\partial_{d-1}v)$, is an isometry for the Sobolev norm by [F1]. The target is separable: extend each coordinate by zero to $\mathbb R^d$ and restrict the countable dense rational-box family [F3]. The image $J(H^1(Q))$ and its subset $J(H^1_0(Q))$ are separable subspaces of a second-countable metric space: intersect a countable base with the subspace and choose one point from each nonempty basic set, a countable selection allowed by Countable Choice. Thus $H^1_0(Q)$ is separable.

For $v\in C_c^\infty(Q)$, extend it by zero to $D=(-1,2)^d$ and identify opposite faces of $D$ to obtain a smooth function on the torus of side length $3$. The extension preserves the $H^1$ norms. By [F1], for every $v\in H^1_0(Q)$ choose test functions converging to $v$ in $H^1$; their periodic zero extensions are Cauchy in $H^1$ on this torus, so the extension is in periodic $H^1(D)$ and the same norm bound holds.

Rescale $D$ affinely to the unit torus using [F7]; the characters on the side-length-$3$ torus are $e^{2\pi i k\cdot x/3}$. For a periodic $H^1(D)$ function $V$, integration by parts on smooth periodic approximants and passage in $H^1$ give $\widehat{\partial_jV}(k)=(2\pi i k_j/3)\widehat V(k)$ for $0\le j<d$. The zero extension in step 1.3 is supported away from the identified faces, so its weak derivatives on the torus are exactly its zero-extended weak derivatives on $Q$. Parseval [F4] therefore yields $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+|k|^2)|\widehat V(k)|^2\le C_d\|V\|_{H^1(D)}^2$, with a fixed constant accounting for the side length $3$. Hence for every integer $N\ge1$, $\sum_{|k|>N}|\widehat V(k)|^2\le C_dN^{-2}\|V\|_{H^1(D)}^2$.

Let $(v_n)$ be bounded in $H^1_0(Q)$, and write $V_n$ for the periodic zero extensions from step 1.3. For each fixed Fourier mode $k$, the complex coefficients are bounded, so their real and imaginary parts are bounded real sequences. Use the following fixed extraction rule for any bounded real sequence $(b_n)$: let $m$ be the least positive integer bounding all $|b_n|$, start with $[-m,m]$, and bisect repeatedly, keeping the left closed half if it contains infinitely many terms and otherwise the right closed half. At stage $r$ take the least index larger than the previous index whose term lies in the retained interval. Each such index exists, and the selected terms are Cauchy because the intervals are nested with lengths tending to zero; [F5] then implies they converge. This defines a unique subsequence from the input sequence, without choice. Enumerate the real and imaginary parts of the Fourier modes, recursively apply this fixed rule to the current subsequence for the next coordinate, and let $n_r$ be the $r$th index of the $r$th nested subsequence. These diagonal indices increase strictly and form a tail subsequence of every fixed earlier extraction, so every coefficient converges; this recursion uses a specified function, not Dependent Choice. If its terms are $V_{n_r},V_{n_s}$, then for fixed $N$ the sum of squared coefficient differences over $|k|\le N$ tends to zero as $r,s\to\infty$, while by step 2.1 the sum over $|k|>N$ is at most $C N^{-2}$ uniformly in $r,s$. First choose $N$ large, then $r,s$ large; Parseval shows $(V_{n_r})$ is Cauchy in $L^2(D)$. Completeness gives an $L^2(D)$ limit, and restriction to $Q$ gives the required $L^2(Q)$ convergence.

Fix $d\ge1$, $Y=(0,1)^d$, and Countable Choice for the Sobolev conventions of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $C^\infty_\#(Y)$ be the restrictions to $Y$ of smooth $\mathbb Z^d$-periodic real functions on $\mathbb R^d$. Define
$$H^1_\#(Y):=\overline{C^\infty_\#(Y)}^{\,H^1(Y)},\qquad V_\#:=\left\{v\in H^1_\#(Y):\int_Yv\,dy=0\right\}.$$
The integral is the normalized cell mean because $|Y|=1$. Derivatives are weak derivatives on $Y$ and the periodic condition is the closure convention in this definition; no pointwise boundary trace is being imposed. Equip $V_\#$ with the inherited $H^1$ norm.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

derivations.claim: For smooth periodic $v$ and each coordinate $0\le i<d$, opposite-face values agree, so integrating that coordinate derivative over $Y$ and applying the one-dimensional FTC [F2] gives $\int_Y\partial_i v=0$. Approximate an arbitrary $v\in H^1_\#(Y)$ in $H^1$ by smooth periodic functions using [F1]; convergence of the derivatives in $L^2(Y)$ implies convergence of their integrals by [F3] and $|Y|=1$. Thus every component of $\int_Y\nabla v$ is zero.

For smooth periodic $v$, write $m=\int_Yv(y)\,dy$. For $x,y\in Y$, telescope from $y$ to $x$ one coordinate at a time, in order $0,\ldots,d-1$. The $i$th difference is the integral of $\partial_i v$ along a segment of length at most one, with the earlier coordinates fixed at $x$ and later coordinates fixed at $y$. Cauchy--Schwarz [F3] bounds its square by the integral of $|\partial_i v|^2$ along the full unit coordinate interval. The inequality $|\sum_{i<d} b_i|^2\le d\sum_{i<d}|b_i|^2$ and Tonelli [F4], integrating in $x$ and $y$, then give $\int_Y\int_Y|v(x)-v(y)|^2\,dy\,dx\le d\sum_{i<d}\|\partial_i v\|_2^2.$ For each $x$, Jensen's inequality gives $|v(x)-m|^2=|\int_Y(v(x)-v(y))dy|^2\le\int_Y|v(x)-v(y)|^2dy$. Integrating in $x$ proves the stated inequality for smooth periodic mean-zero $v$.

Approximate any $v\in V_\#$ in $H^1$ by smooth periodic $v_n$ using Countable Choice [F5]. Their means converge to zero by Cauchy--Schwarz, so $v_n-\int_Yv_n$ are smooth periodic mean-zero functions converging to $v$ in $H^1$. Passing to the limit in step 1.2 proves the inequality on $V_\#$. By [F7], $H^1(Y)$ is complete. Its closure-defined subspace $H^1_\#(Y)$ is closed, and the mean is continuous by $|\int_Yv|\le\|v\|_2\le\|v\|_{H^1}$, so $V_\#$ is closed in $H^1(Y)$. Every $H^1$-Cauchy sequence in $V_\#$ therefore has an ambient limit in $V_\#$, proving completeness of its inherited norm. The inequality shows the gradient norm and $H^1$ norm are equivalent, hence the gradient norm is complete too.

derivations.claim:
Tile $\mathbb R^d$ by cells $C_k^\epsilon=\epsilon(k+Y)$. Only $O_d(\epsilon^{-d})$ cells meet the fixed compact support of $\varphi$. On each such cell choose its lower corner $x_k=\epsilon k$. The mean-value bound gives $|\varphi(x)-\varphi(x_k)|\le\sqrt d\epsilon\|
abla\varphi\|_\infty$. By [F3], $\int_{C_k^\epsilon}|g(x/\epsilon)|dx=\epsilon^d\|g\|_{L^1(Y)}$. Therefore replacing $\varphi$ by $\varphi(x_k)$ on every intersecting cell changes the integral by at most $C\epsilon\|g\|_1\|
abla\varphi\|_\infty$; for sufficiently small $\epsilon$, every such cell is contained in $Q$ because the support is compact in $Q$. Extend $\varphi$ by zero to a compactly supported $C^1$ function on $\mathbb R^d$. For all sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the grid sum has only cells in a fixed bounded box, and $$\left|\epsilon^d\sum_k\varphi(\epsilon k)-\int_{\mathbb R^d}\varphi(x)\,dxight|\le\sum_k\int_{C_k^\epsilon}|\varphi(\epsilon k)-\varphi(x)|\,dx\le C\epsilon\|
abla\varphi\|_\infty,$$ since the total volume of those cells is uniformly bounded. Thus the grid Riemann sums converge. By [F3], the change-of-variables identity first holds for $g^+$ and $g^-$ separately; subtracting their finite integrals gives $\int_{C_k^\epsilon}g(x/\epsilon)\,dx=\epsilon^d\int_Yg$ for signed $g$. The cell-corner sum is therefore $\epsilon^d\sum_k\varphi(\epsilon k)\int_Yg$, which converges to the stated mean times integral.

The same tiling bounds the $L^2$ rescaling: each cell has $\int_{C_k^\epsilon}|g(x/\epsilon)|^2dx=\epsilon^d\|g\|_2^2$ by [F3], and at most $C_d\epsilon^{-d}$ cells meet $Q$ when $\epsilon\le1$. Summing gives the asserted uniform bound.

The averaging result applied to every $C_c^\infty(Q)$ test gives convergence of pairings against that dense class. The uniform $L^2$ bound in step 1.2, together with $|\int_Yg|\le\|g\|_2$, lets one approximate an arbitrary $L^2(Q)$ test by [F2] and pass the pairing limit. This proves weak $L^2$ convergence.

For coefficient $a$, cell $Y$, and zero-mean periodic space $V_\#$ from [[def-periodic-scalar-diffusion-data]] and [[def-periodic-zero-mean-cell-space]], and for $p\in\mathbb R^d$, the **weak periodic cell equation** asks for $\chi_p\in V_\#$ such that
$$\int_Y a(y)(p+
abla_y\chi_p(y))\cdot
abla_yv(y)\,dy=0\qquad(v\in V_\#).$$
The sign convention is $p+
abla_y\chi_p$; the zero-mean condition fixes the additive constant. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Let $Y=(0,1)^d$ and $V_\#$ be the mean-zero periodic $H^1$ space of [[def-periodic-zero-mean-cell-space]]. Then every $v\in V_\#$ satisfies
$$\|v\|_{L^2(Y)}\le\sqrt d\,\|
abla v\|_{L^2(Y)},$$
and every $v\in H^1_\#(Y)$ satisfies $\int_Y
abla v=0$. Consequently $\|
abla v\|_2$ is a complete norm on $V_\#$ equivalent to its inherited $H^1$ norm.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and the unit cell $Y=(0,1)^d$ with Lebesgue measure $|Y|=1$. Assume Countable Choice for the $L^2$ conventions of [[def-countable-choice]]. A **uniformly elliptic periodic scalar diffusion coefficient** is a measurable real function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ such that $a(y+k)=a(y)$ for almost every $y$ and every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and there are constants $0<\lambda\le\Lambda<\infty$ with $\lambda\le a(y)\le\Lambda$ almost everywhere on $Y$. Coefficients are identified when they agree almost everywhere.

For $\epsilon>0$, the physical scalar coefficient is $a_\epsilon(x)=a(x/\epsilon)$ and the associated matrix is $a_\epsilon(x)I_d$. The bounded-domain branch used on this page is $\Omega=(0,1)^d$ with homogeneous zero boundary values. Its weak equation for datum $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is
$$\int_\Omega a(x/\epsilon)\nabla u_\epsilon\cdot\nabla v\,dx=\int_\Omega fv\,dx\qquad(v\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)).$$
No coefficient regularity beyond measurability and the displayed bounds is part of this definition.

For every $\epsilon>0$, the map $x\mapsto x/\epsilon$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^d$. By [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]], its pullback preserves Lebesgue measurability and takes null-set changes to null-set changes (apply the theorem also to the inverse map). Thus $a_\epsilon$ is a well-defined almost-everywhere class independent of the representative of $a$. The same result applies to every affine translation and positive dilation used in periodic sampling below, so almost-everywhere coefficient bounds are preserved under those pullbacks.

The ellipticity bounds hold almost everywhere on all of $\mathbb R^d$, not just on $Y$: periodicity transfers the exceptional null set from $Y$ to each lattice translate, translations preserve null sets by the same change-of-variables theorem, and the countably many translates cover $\mathbb R^d$ up to their null boundaries.

On $V_\#$ with gradient inner product, define $b(u,v)=\int_Ya
abla u\cdot
abla v$ and $F_p(v)=-\int_Ya p\cdot
abla v$. By [F5] and Cauchy--Schwarz, $|b(u,v)|\le\Lambda\|
abla u\|_2\|
abla v\|_2$, $b(v,v)\ge\lambda\|
abla v\|_2^2$, and $|F_p(v)|\le\Lambda|p|\|
abla v\|_2$. Thus [F2]–[F4] apply and give a unique $\chi_p$ with $b(\chi_p,v)=F_p(v)$ for every $v$. Rearranging is exactly [F1].

Test the equation with $v=\chi_p$. Then $\lambda\|
abla\chi_p\|_2^2\le\int_Ya|
abla\chi_p|^2=-\int_Ya p\cdot
abla\chi_p\le\Lambda|p|\|
abla\chi_p\|_2$. If the gradient norm is zero the estimate is immediate; otherwise divide by it. The $L^2$ bound follows from [F2].

For $p,q\in\mathbb R^d$ and scalars $s,t$, the function $s\chi_p+t\chi_q$ satisfies the cell equation with datum $sp+tq$, by linearity of the integral in both $p$ and the corrector. Uniqueness in step 1.1 therefore gives $\chi_{sp+tq}=s\chi_p+t\chi_q$.

Let $Q=Y=(0,1)^d$, let $\epsilon_n>0$ tend to zero, and let $(u_n)$ be bounded in $L^2(Q)$. We say $u_n$ **two-scale converges weakly** to $u\in L^2(Q\times Y)$ along $(\epsilon_n)$ if for every finite sum
$$\Phi(x,y)=\sum_{r=1}^m\phi_r(x)\psi_r(y),\quad \phi_r\in C_c^\infty(Q),\quad\psi_r\in C_\#^\infty(Y),$$
one has
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_Qu_n(x)\Phi(x,x/\epsilon_n)\,dx=\int_Q\int_Yu(x,y)\Phi(x,y)\,dy\,dx.$$
Here $C_\#^\infty(Y)$ is the smooth $\mathbb Z^d$-periodic class from [[def-periodic-zero-mean-cell-space]]. The test definition is independent of how a finite sum is represented because both sides are linear in $\Phi$.

Let $Y=(0,1)^d$, $Q=(0,1)^d$, $g\in L^1(Y)$ be extended $\mathbb Z^d$-periodically, and $\varphi\in C_c^1(Q)$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$,
$$\int_Q\varphi(x)g(x/\epsilon)\,dx\longrightarrow\left(\int_Yg\right)\left(\int_Q\varphi\right).$$
If $g\in L^2(Y)$ and $0<\epsilon\le1$, then $\|g(\cdot/\epsilon)\|_{L^2(Q)}\le C_d\|g\|_{L^2(Y)}$. In particular, for $g\in L^2(Y)$, $g(\cdot/\epsilon)\rightharpoonup\int_Yg$ weakly in $L^2(Q)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]), let $\mu\times\nu$ be the
product measure on the product sigma-algebra
$\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]), and
let $\overline{\mu\times\nu}$ be its completion
([[def-completed-product-measure]]). Write $\mathbf 1_A(x)\mathbf 1_B(y)$ for
the **rectangle kernel** of a measurable rectangle $A\times B$
([[def-measurable-rectangle]]) with $\mu(A)<+\infty$ and $\nu(B)<+\infty$. Then
the set of finite complex linear combinations of such rectangle kernels is
dense both

1. in $L^2(\mu\times\nu;\mathbb C)$, and
2. in $L^2(\overline{\mu\times\nu};\mathbb C)$
   ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

derivations.claim: Let $M=\sup_n\|u_n\|_2$. By [F7], extend functions by zero to see that $L^2(Q\times Y)$ is separable; [F3] says the allowed test subspace is dense there. Intersect a countable base of its metric topology with that subspace and, using [F4], choose one point from every nonempty intersection. The rational span of these points is a countable dense family $D$. For each fixed $\Phi\in D$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\left|\int_Qu_n(x)\Phi(x,x/\epsilon_n)dx\right|\le M\|\Phi(\cdot,\cdot/\epsilon_n)\|_2,$ which is bounded by [F2]. For a bounded real sequence $(b_n)$ fix this extraction rule: let $m$ be the least positive integer bounding every $|b_n|$, start with $[-m,m]$, bisect repeatedly, and retain the left closed half when it contains infinitely many terms, otherwise the right closed half. From the $r$th retained interval take the term with least index larger than the previously selected index. Such indices exist; nestedness and vanishing interval lengths make the selected sequence Cauchy, and [F5] makes it convergent. This uniquely specified extraction map requires no choice. Enumerate $D$, recursively apply this map to each scalar pairing on the current subsequence, and take as $n_r$ the $r$th index of the $r$th nested subsequence. The indices increase strictly and their tail lies in every fixed earlier subsequence, so all pairings with $D$ converge. Recursion of the specified map does not use Dependent Choice.

Denote the limit on $D$ by $L_0$. For each $\Phi\in D$, step 1.1 and [F2] give $|L_0(\Phi)|\le M\|\Phi\|_{L^2(Q\times Y)}$. Limits preserve rational linearity; the bound makes $L_0$ uniformly continuous, so it has a unique continuous extension $L$ to all of the real Hilbert space $L^2(Q\times Y)$, with $\|L\|\le M$. To verify real homogeneity, first fix $\Phi\in D$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, and choose rationals $q_m\to t$. Since $q_m\Phi\in D$, $L(q_m\Phi)=q_mL_0(\Phi)$; continuity and $q_m\Phi\to t\Phi$ give $L(t\Phi)=tL(\Phi)$. For arbitrary $h\in L^2(Q\times Y)$, choose $\Phi_j\in D$ with $\Phi_j\to h$; then $t\Phi_j\to th$, and continuity gives $L(th)=tL(h)$. Additivity also passes from $D$ by continuity, so $L$ is bounded and real-linear.

By [F6], choose $u\in L^2(Q\times Y)$ such that $L(\Phi)=\int_{Q\times Y}u\Phi$. Fix any allowed smooth product test $\Psi$ and choose $\Phi_j\in D$ with $\Phi_j\to\Psi$ in product $L^2$. Along the extracted subsequence, [F2] applied to $\Psi-\Phi_j$ gives $\limsup_n\left|\int_Qu_n(\Psi-\Phi_j)(x,x/\epsilon_n)dx\right|\le M\|\Psi-\Phi_j\|_2.$ Also $|L(\Psi-\Phi_j)|\le M\|\Psi-\Phi_j\|_2$. Since the pairings for $\Phi_j$ converge to $L(\Phi_j)$, letting $j\to\infty$ proves convergence for $\Psi$ to $L(\Psi)=\int u\Psi$. This is precisely the two-scale convergence in [F1].

Assume Countable Choice and let $Q=(0,1)^d$, $d\ge1$. Then $H^1_0(Q;\mathbb R)$ is a separable real Hilbert space. It satisfies
$$\|v\|_{L^2(Q)}\le\|\partial_0v\|_{L^2(Q)}\le\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(Q)}\qquad(v\in H^1_0(Q)).$$
Moreover, every sequence bounded in $H^1_0(Q)$ has a subsequence converging in $L^2(Q)$. These conclusions use Countable Choice only; no Axiom of Choice or Dependent Choice is needed in the proof below.

Let $Q=Y=(0,1)^d$, let $\epsilon_n\downarrow0$ (monotonicity may be dropped; only $\epsilon_n\to0$ is used), and suppose $(u_n)$ is bounded in $L^2(Q)$. Then some subsequence two-scale converges in the sense of [[def-periodic-two-scale-convergence]] to a function $u\in L^2(Q\times Y)$.

Here $C_\#^\infty(Y)$ is the smooth $\mathbb Z^d$-periodic class from [[def-periodic-zero-mean-cell-space]]. The test definition is independent of how a finite sum is represented because both sides are linear in $\Phi$.

Let $Y=(0,1)^d$, $Q=(0,1)^d$, $g\in L^1(Y)$ be extended $\mathbb Z^d$-periodically, and $\varphi\in C_c^1(Q)$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$,
$$\int_Q\varphi(x)g(x/\epsilon)\,dx\longrightarrow\left(\int_Yg\right)\left(\int_Q\varphi\right).$$
If $g\in L^2(Y)$ and $0<\epsilon\le1$, then $\|g(\cdot/\epsilon)\|_{L^2(Q)}\le C_d\|g\|_{L^2(Y)}$. In particular, for $g\in L^2(Y)$, $g(\cdot/\epsilon)\rightharpoonup\int_Yg$ weakly in $L^2(Q)$.

Fix $d\ge1$, $Y=(0,1)^d$, and Countable Choice for the Sobolev conventions of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $C^\infty_\#(Y)$ be the restrictions to $Y$ of smooth $\mathbb Z^d$-periodic real functions on $\mathbb R^d$. Define
$$H^1_\#(Y):=\overline{C^\infty_\#(Y)}^{\,H^1(Y)},\qquad V_\#:=\left\{v\in H^1_\#(Y):\int_Yv\,dy=0\right\}.$$
The integral is the normalized cell mean because $|Y|=1$. Derivatives are weak derivatives on $Y$ and the periodic condition is the closure convention in this definition; no pointwise boundary trace is being imposed. Equip $V_\#$ with the inherited $H^1$ norm.

Let $Y=(0,1)^d$ and $V_\#$ be the mean-zero periodic $H^1$ space of [[def-periodic-zero-mean-cell-space]]. Then every $v\in V_\#$ satisfies
$$\|v\|_{L^2(Y)}\le\sqrt d\,\|
abla v\|_{L^2(Y)},$$
and every $v\in H^1_\#(Y)$ satisfies $\int_Y
abla v=0$. Consequently $\|
abla v\|_2$ is a complete norm on $V_\#$ equivalent to its inherited $H^1$ norm.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: By [F1]–[F2], first extract a subsequence converging weakly in $H^1_0(Q)$ to some $u\in H^1_0(Q)$, and then a further subsequence converging strongly in $L^2(Q)$ to the same $u$. By [F3], extract successive further subsequences on which each of the $d$ components of $\nabla u_n$ two-scale converges; since there are finitely many components, one subsequence works for all. Write its vector limit as $G(x,y)$.

For every allowed product test $\phi(x)\psi(y)$, strong $L^2$ convergence and the uniform sampled-test bound in [F4] show that replacing $u_n$ by $u$ in its pairing changes the limit by zero. Weak $L^2$ averaging in [F4], applied to $\psi(x/\epsilon_n)$ against $u\phi\in L^2(Q)$, then gives limit $\int_Q u\phi\int_Y\psi$. Thus the two-scale limit of $u_n$ is the $y$-independent function $u(x)$.

Set $H(x,y):=G(x,y)-\nabla_xu(x)$. For a smooth compactly supported $\phi(x)$ and constant vector $c$, test gradient convergence componentwise with $\phi c$. Ordinary weak $H^1$ convergence gives $\int_{Q\times Y}G\cdot\phi c=\int_Q\nabla u\cdot\phi c$. By Cauchy--Schwarz and Tonelli [F8], $x\mapsto\int_YH(x,y)\,dy$ lies in $L^2(Q)$ and pairs to zero with every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(Q)$; [F9] makes it zero almost everywhere.

Let $\Phi(x,y)=\sum_r\phi_r(x)\Psi_r(y)$ be a smooth periodic vector field, compactly supported in $x$, with $\operatorname{div}_y\Phi=0$, and put $\Phi_n(x)=\Phi(x,x/\epsilon_n)$. By [F10], $\operatorname{div}\Phi_n=(\operatorname{div}_x\Phi)(x,x/\epsilon_n)+\epsilon_n^{-1}(\operatorname{div}_y\Phi)(x,x/\epsilon_n)=(\operatorname{div}_x\Phi)(x,x/\epsilon_n)$. The field $\Phi_n$ is a valid compactly supported smooth test in the weak-derivative identity [F7], so $\int_Q\nabla u_n\cdot\Phi_n=-\int_Qu_n\operatorname{div}\Phi_n$. Taking limits by componentwise two-scale convergence for the two allowed tests $\Phi$ and $\operatorname{div}_x\Phi$ gives $\int_{Q\times Y}G\cdot\Phi=-\int_{Q\times Y}u\,\operatorname{div}_x\Phi=\int_{Q\times Y}\nabla_xu\cdot\Phi$, where the last equality is weak integration by parts. Thus $H$ is orthogonal to every such divergence-free field.

For every nonzero $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ and every real $c\perp k$, use slow tests $\phi(x)c\cos(2\pi k\cdot y)$ and $\phi(x)c\sin(2\pi k\cdot y)$ in step 3.1. They are divergence-free in $y$. The resulting pairings show that each real and imaginary component of $\widehat H(x,k)\cdot c$ pairs to zero with every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(Q)$, so [F9] makes it zero almost everywhere. There are countably many $k$ and a finite basis of each $k^\perp$, so [A1] permits one null set outside which $\widehat H(x,k)$ is parallel to $k$ for all $k$; the zero coefficient is zero by step 2.2.

For $k\ne0$ define $\widehat u_1(x,k)=(\widehat H(x,k)\cdot k)/(2\pi i|k|^2)$ and set $\widehat u_1(x,0)=0$. The parallel property from step 4.1 gives $2\pi i k\widehat u_1(x,k)=\widehat H(x,k)$. Moreover $|\widehat u_1(x,k)|\le |\widehat H(x,k)|/(2\pi|k|)$, so Parseval [F6] and Tonelli [F8] give $\int_Q\sum_k(1+|k|^2)|\widehat u_1(x,k)|^2dx\le C_d\|H\|_{L^2(Q\times Y)}^2$. The zero coefficient makes this limit mean-zero. Define $u_1$ as the product-space $L^2(Q\times Y)$ limit of these partial sums. Their $y$-gradients converge there, and the coefficient identity identifies the gradient limit with $H$. Conjugate symmetry makes the limit real, and the integrated estimate gives the stated square-integrable $H^1(Y)$ slice norm. Hence $u_1\in L^2(Q;V_\#)$ with $\nabla_yu_1=H$, completing the decomposition.

For the usual PDE coordinate labels $i=1,\ldots,d$, write $x_i:=x(i-1)$, set $e_i:=\widetilde e_{i-1}$, write $p_i:=p(i-1)$, and set $\partial_i:=\partial_{i-1}$ in the multi-index convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. The same shift applies to vector and tensor components, so component label $i$ means library index $i-1$. By [[lem-periodic-cell-corrector-wellposedness]], let $\chi_i:=\chi_{e_i}$ be the unique mean-zero solution of the periodic cell equation. Define $\chi_p=\sum_{i=1}^d p_i\chi_i$ and define the constant matrix $A^*$ by its columns:
$$A^*e_i:=\int_Ya(y)(e_i+
abla\chi_i(y))\,dy\qquad(1\le i\le d).$$
Equivalently, $A^*p=\int_Ya(y)(p+
abla\chi_p(y))dy$. All integrals are finite because $a\in L^\infty(Y)$ and $
abla\chi_i\in L^2(Y)$. This definition does not itself assert symmetry or ellipticity.

Assume $a,\lambda,\Lambda,Y,V_\#$ are as in [[def-periodic-scalar-diffusion-data]] and [[def-periodic-zero-mean-cell-space]]. For each $p\in\mathbb R^d$, the equation in [[def-periodic-cell-problem]] has a unique solution $\chi_p\in V_\#$. The map $p\mapsto\chi_p$ is linear, and
$$\|\nabla\chi_p\|_{L^2(Y)}\le(\Lambda/\lambda)|p|,\qquad \|\chi_p\|_{L^2(Y)}\le\sqrt d(\Lambda/\lambda)|p|.$$

Let $Y=(0,1)^d$ and $V_\#$ be the mean-zero periodic $H^1$ space of [[def-periodic-zero-mean-cell-space]]. Then every $v\in V_\#$ satisfies
$$\|v\|_{L^2(Y)}\le\sqrt d\,\|
abla v\|_{L^2(Y)},$$
and every $v\in H^1_\#(Y)$ satisfies $\int_Y
abla v=0$. Consequently $\|
abla v\|_2$ is a complete norm on $V_\#$ equivalent to its inherited $H^1$ norm.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and the unit cell $Y=(0,1)^d$ with Lebesgue measure $|Y|=1$. Assume Countable Choice for the $L^2$ conventions of [[def-countable-choice]]. A **uniformly elliptic periodic scalar diffusion coefficient** is a measurable real function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ such that $a(y+k)=a(y)$ for almost every $y$ and every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and there are constants $0<\lambda\le\Lambda<\infty$ with $\lambda\le a(y)\le\Lambda$ almost everywhere on $Y$. Coefficients are identified when they agree almost everywhere.

For $\epsilon>0$, the physical scalar coefficient is $a_\epsilon(x)=a(x/\epsilon)$ and the associated matrix is $a_\epsilon(x)I_d$. The bounded-domain branch used on this page is $\Omega=(0,1)^d$ with homogeneous zero boundary values. Its weak equation for datum $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is
$$\int_\Omega a(x/\epsilon)\nabla u_\epsilon\cdot\nabla v\,dx=\int_\Omega fv\,dx\qquad(v\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)).$$
No coefficient regularity beyond measurability and the displayed bounds is part of this definition.

For every $\epsilon>0$, the map $x\mapsto x/\epsilon$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^d$. By [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]], its pullback preserves Lebesgue measurability and takes null-set changes to null-set changes (apply the theorem also to the inverse map). Thus $a_\epsilon$ is a well-defined almost-everywhere class independent of the representative of $a$. The same result applies to every affine translation and positive dilation used in periodic sampling below, so almost-everywhere coefficient bounds are preserved under those pullbacks.

The ellipticity bounds hold almost everywhere on all of $\mathbb R^d$, not just on $Y$: periodicity transfers the exceptional null set from $Y$ to each lattice translate, translations preserve null sets by the same change-of-variables theorem, and the countably many translates cover $\mathbb R^d$ up to their null boundaries.

Test the corrector equation for $\chi_p$ with $\chi_q$. It gives $\int_Ya(p+
abla\chi_p)\cdot
abla\chi_q=0$. Interchanging $p,q$ gives $\int_Ya(q+
abla\chi_q)\cdot
abla\chi_p=0$. Thus $p\cdot A^*q=\int_Ya(p+
abla\chi_p)\cdot(q+
abla\chi_q)=q\cdot A^*p,$ where the first equality follows from [F1] after adding the zero term with $
abla\chi_p$, and the last integral is symmetric in $p,q$. Hence $A^*$ is symmetric.

Taking $q=p$ in the same identity yields $p\cdot A^*p=\int_Ya|p+
abla\chi_p|^2$. Since the mean of $p+
abla\chi_p$ is $p$ by [F3], Cauchy--Schwarz on the unit-measure cell gives $\int_Y|p+
abla\chi_p|^2\ge|p|^2$. The lower coefficient bound in [F4] proves $p\cdot A^*p\ge\lambda|p|^2$.

The cell equation makes $\chi_p$ the minimizer of $J_p(v)=\int_Ya|p+
abla v|^2$ over $v\in V_\#$. Indeed, for $v=\chi_p+w$, expansion gives $J_p(v)=J_p(\chi_p)+2\int_Ya(p+
abla\chi_p)\cdot
abla w+\int_Ya|
abla w|^2$, whose middle term is zero and last term is nonnegative. Taking the competitor $v=0$ gives $p\cdot A^*p=J_p(\chi_p)\le J_p(0)=\int_Ya|p|^2\le\Lambda|p|^2$.

Bounds are preserved by the same affine pullback [F1]. Hence the generic cell-corrector result [F2] applies to $b$ and gives its unique mean-zero cell solution; energy expansion around that solution shows it is the unique minimizer in the Statement. Set $v_m(y)=m^{-1}\chi_p(	heta+my)-c$, where $c$ is its mean on $Y$. Periodic smooth approximants to $\chi_p$ converge on every bounded union of cells, and affine pullback [F5] shows $v_m\in V_\#$ with $
abla_yv_m=
abla\chi_p(	heta+my)$. The flux $q(z)=a(z)(p+
abla\chi_p(z))$ is periodic and divergence-free by the cell equation. Test the cell equation with the mean-zero real and imaginary parts of $e^{-2\pi i k\cdot z}$ for $k
e0$. Their gradients are the corresponding parts of $-2\pi i k e^{-2\pi i k\cdot z}$, so combining the two zero identities gives $k\cdot\widehat q(k)=0$ (and the identity is automatic at $k=0$). For a Fourier polynomial, $q(	heta+my)$ has only frequencies $mk$, with coefficients multiplied by phases, and each remains perpendicular to $mk$; hence it is divergence-free. For any periodic $h\in L^2(Y)$, affine change of variables [F6] gives $\int_Y|h(	heta+my)|^2dy=m^{-d}\int_{	heta+mY}|h(z)|^2dz$. The latter box meets at most $(m+2)^d$ unit lattice cells, so periodicity bounds this by $m^{-d}(m+2)^d\|h\|_{L^2(Y)}^2$. Thus composition with $y\mapsto	heta+my$ is bounded on periodic $L^2$, and the divergence-free identity passes from Fourier polynomials to $q$ in $L^2$. Therefore $\int_Yb(y)(p+
abla v_m)\cdot
abla z=0$ for every smooth periodic $z$, and by density for every $z\in V_\#$. Uniqueness of the cell solution for $b$ identifies it with $v_m$.

The sampled tensor flux is $\int_Yq(\theta+my)dy$. By [F6], applied to the positive and negative parts of each component, this equals $m^{-d}\int_{\theta+mY}q(z)dz$. The box $\theta+mY$ is a union, up to null boundaries, of $m^d$ cells $\theta+k+Y$ with integer $k$, so periodicity makes each cell integral equal to $\int_{\theta+Y}q$. A translated unit cell has the same integral as $Y$: partition it at the integer coordinate faces and translate each resulting piece by an integer lattice vector into $Y$; applying [F6] to positive and negative parts and using periodicity gives equality componentwise. Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and the unit cell $Y=(0,1)^d$ with Lebesgue measure $|Y|=1$. Assume Countable Choice for the $L^2$ conventions of [[def-countable-choice]]. A **uniformly elliptic periodic scalar diffusion coefficient** is a measurable real function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ such that $a(y+k)=a(y)$ for almost every $y$ and every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and there are constants $0<\lambda\le\Lambda<\infty$ with $\lambda\le a(y)\le\Lambda$ almost everywhere on $Y$. Coefficients are identified when they agree almost everywhere.

For $\epsilon>0$, the physical scalar coefficient is $a_\epsilon(x)=a(x/\epsilon)$ and the associated matrix is $a_\epsilon(x)I_d$. The bounded-domain branch used on this page is $\Omega=(0,1)^d$ with homogeneous zero boundary values. Its weak equation for datum $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is
$$\int_\Omega a(x/\epsilon)\nabla u_\epsilon\cdot\nabla v\,dx=\int_\Omega fv\,dx\qquad(v\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)).$$
No coefficient regularity beyond measurability and the displayed bounds is part of this definition.

For every $\epsilon>0$, the map $x\mapsto x/\epsilon$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^d$. By [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]], its pullback preserves Lebesgue measurability and takes null-set changes to null-set changes (apply the theorem also to the inverse map). Thus $a_\epsilon$ is a well-defined almost-everywhere class independent of the representative of $a$. The same result applies to every affine translation and positive dilation used in periodic sampling below, so almost-everywhere coefficient bounds are preserved under those pullbacks.

The ellipticity bounds hold almost everywhere on all of $\mathbb R^d$, not just on $Y$: periodicity transfers the exceptional null set from $Y$ to each lattice translate, translations preserve null sets by the same change-of-variables theorem, and the countably many translates cover $\mathbb R^d$ up to their null boundaries.

derivations.claim: For either $b=a$ or $b(y)=a(\theta+ry)$, define $c_b=(\int_0^1b^{-1})^{-1}$ and $h_b=c_b/b-1$. The ellipticity bounds make $h_b\in L^\infty(0,1)$, and $\int_0^1h_b=0$. Put $\chi_b(t)=\int_0^th_b(s)ds$. For every smooth periodic $\varphi$, Fubini [F5] gives $\int_0^1\chi_b(t)\varphi'(t)dt=\int_0^1h_b(s)(\varphi(1)-\varphi(s))ds=-\int_0^1h_b(s)\varphi(s)ds$, so $h_b$ is its periodic weak derivative. By [F4], the symmetric Fourier partial sums of $\chi_b$ are real trigonometric polynomials and converge in $H^1(0,1)$, since both $\chi_b$ and $h_b$ are in $L^2$ and their Fourier coefficients satisfy the weak-derivative relation; after subtracting its mean, the limit belongs to $V_\#$ by the closure definition. Since $b(1+h_b)=c_b$ almost everywhere, for every $v\in V_\#$ we have $\int_0^1b(1+\chi_b')v'=c_b\int_0^1v'=0$ by [F6]. Thus it solves the cell equation. If two mean-zero solutions existed, testing their difference equation by the difference would give $\int b|\chi'-\widetilde\chi'|^2=0$; the periodic Poincare inequality [F6] then makes their difference zero. This proves both harmonic-mean formulas, including the nonperiodic-in-$y$ sampled coefficient under periodic coupling.

Put $g=1/a$ and $I=\int_0^1g$. Write $r=N+s$ with integer $N\ge1$ and $0\le s<1$. Periodicity gives $\int_0^r g(\theta+t)dt=NI+R,\qquad R=\int_\theta^{\theta+s}g(t)dt,$ so $\int_0^1g(\theta+ry)dy=I+(R-sI)/r$. Since $0<g\le1/\lambda$, both $R$ and $sI$ lie in $[0,s/\lambda]$, hence $|R-sI|\le s/\lambda\le1/\lambda$. In particular the weaker bound $|I_r-I|\le2/(\lambda r)$ holds. Also $I,I_r\ge1/\Lambda$. Therefore $|A_r-A^*|=\frac{|I_r-I|}{I_rI}\le\frac{2}{\lambda r}\Lambda^2,$ as claimed.

Assume Countable Choice and let $Q=(0,1)^d$, $d\ge1$. Then $H^1_0(Q;\mathbb R)$ is a separable real Hilbert space. It satisfies
$$\|v\|_{L^2(Q)}\le\|\partial_0v\|_{L^2(Q)}\le\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(Q)}\qquad(v\in H^1_0(Q)).$$
Moreover, every sequence bounded in $H^1_0(Q)$ has a subsequence converging in $L^2(Q)$. These conclusions use Countable Choice only; no Axiom of Choice or Dependent Choice is needed in the proof below.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

abla u_n\overset{2}{ightharpoonup}

Here vector-valued two-scale convergence means componentwise convergence as in [[def-periodic-two-scale-convergence]], and $L^2(Q;V_\#)$ denotes product-measurable functions whose $y$-slices lie in $V_\#$ almost everywhere and whose squared $H^1(Y)$ slice norms are integrable over $Q$.

Let $Y=(0,1)^d$, $Q=(0,1)^d$, $g\in L^1(Y)$ be extended $\mathbb Z^d$-periodically, and $\varphi\in C_c^1(Q)$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$,
$$\int_Q\varphi(x)g(x/\epsilon)\,dx\longrightarrow\left(\int_Yg\right)\left(\int_Q\varphi\right).$$
If $g\in L^2(Y)$ and $0<\epsilon\le1$, then $\|g(\cdot/\epsilon)\|_{L^2(Q)}\le C_d\|g\|_{L^2(Y)}$. In particular, for $g\in L^2(Y)$, $g(\cdot/\epsilon)\rightharpoonup\int_Yg$ weakly in $L^2(Q)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let $X^*$ be its bounded $\mathbb K$-linear dual, with the operator norm, as in [[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]. The **weak topology** $\sigma(X,X^*)$ is the initial topology induced by all maps $f:X\to\mathbb K$, $f\in X^*$, where the scalars have their usual topology. Explicitly it is generated by the subbasis

$$\{f^{-1}(V):f\in X^*,\ V\subseteq\mathbb K\text{ open}\}.$$

The initial-topology construction in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]] establishes existence and says that finite intersections of these sets form a basis. The empty intersection is $X$. This is the coarsest topology making every bounded scalar-linear functional continuous, and it is contained in the norm topology. This definition uses no choice principle and does not assert separation of points without a norming hypothesis. For $X=\{0\}$ it is the unique topology on that singleton.

Fix $d\ge1$, $Y=(0,1)^d$, and Countable Choice for the Sobolev conventions of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $C^\infty_\#(Y)$ be the restrictions to $Y$ of smooth $\mathbb Z^d$-periodic real functions on $\mathbb R^d$. Define
$$H^1_\#(Y):=\overline{C^\infty_\#(Y)}^{\,H^1(Y)},\qquad V_\#:=\left\{v\in H^1_\#(Y):\int_Yv\,dy=0\right\}.$$
The integral is the normalized cell mean because $|Y|=1$. Derivatives are weak derivatives on $Y$ and the periodic condition is the closure convention in this definition; no pointwise boundary trace is being imposed. Equip $V_\#$ with the inherited $H^1$ norm.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Equip $H^1_0(Q)$ with gradient norm, equivalent to its Sobolev norm by [F4]. The form $b_\epsilon(u,v)=\int_Qa(x/\epsilon)
abla u\cdot
abla v$ is bounded by $\Lambda\|
abla u\|_2\|
abla v\|_2$ and coercive with constant $\lambda$; $F(v)=\int_Qfv$ is bounded by $\|f\|_2\|
abla v\|_2$. Thus [F5] gives a unique $u_\epsilon$. The same argument using [F3] gives a unique $u_0$. Testing with $u_\epsilon$ gives $\|
abla u_\epsilon\|_2\le\lambda^{-1}\|f\|_2$ (with the zero-gradient case immediate).

For smooth periodic mean-zero $w$, let $\widehat w(k)$ be its Fourier coefficients and $P_Nw=\sum_{|k|\le N}\widehat w(k)e^{2\pi i k\cdot y}$. Periodic integration by parts gives $\widehat{\partial_jw}(k)=2\pi i k_j\widehat w(k)$. Parseval [F10], applied to $w$ and all its first derivatives, yields $$\|w-P_Nw\|_{H^1(Y)}^2=\sum_{|k|>N}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat w(k)|^2\longrightarrow0.$$ The zero coefficient vanishes, and the symmetric truncation preserves reality. For each finite truncation, approximate its finitely many coefficients by rational real and imaginary parts while imposing $c_{-k}=\overline{c_k}$; this gives a countable family of rational-coefficient, real, mean-zero trigonometric polynomials dense in the smooth periodic mean-zero functions in $H^1(Y)$. If $v\in V_\#$, choose a smooth periodic $w$ arbitrarily close to $v$ in $H^1$ by [F10], then replace $w$ by $w-\int_Yw$; since $\int_Yv=0$, this subtraction still approximates $v$. The rational polynomials are therefore dense in all of $V_\#$.

The library represents $\mathbb R^d$ as functions on $d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$, with standard basis $\widetilde e_j$ for $j<d$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). For the usual PDE coordinate labels $i=1,\ldots,d$, write $x_i:=x(i-1)$, set $e_i:=\widetilde e_{i-1}$, write $p_i:=p(i-1)$, and set $\partial_i:=\partial_{i-1}$ in the multi-index convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. The same shift applies to vector and tensor components, so component label $i$ means library index $i-1$. By [[lem-periodic-cell-corrector-wellposedness]], let $\chi_i:=\chi_{e_i}$ be the unique mean-zero solution of the periodic cell equation. Define $\chi_p=\sum_{i=1}^d p_i\chi_i$ and define the constant matrix $A^*$ by its columns:
$$A^*e_i:=\int_Ya(y)(e_i+
abla\chi_i(y))\,dy\qquad(1\le i\le d).$$
Equivalently, $A^*p=\int_Ya(y)(p+
abla\chi_p(y))dy$. All integrals are finite because $a\in L^\infty(Y)$ and $
abla\chi_i\in L^2(Y)$. This definition does not itself assert symmetry or ellipticity.

$$\|\nabla\chi_p\|_{L^2(Y)}\le(\Lambda/\lambda)|p|,\qquad \|\chi_p\|_{L^2(Y)}\le\sqrt d(\Lambda/\lambda)|p|.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For each smooth periodic scalar $v$, [F2] gives $\int_Ya(e_j+\nabla\chi_j)\cdot\nabla v=0$, so $\operatorname{div}_y q^j=0$ distributionally. Its mean is zero by the definition of $A^*$ in [F1]. Testing with the real and imaginary parts of $e^{-2\pi i m\cdot y}$ therefore gives, for every nonzero Fourier mode $m\in\mathbb Z^d$, $m\cdot\widehat q^j(m)=0$, and $\widehat q^j(0)=0$.

For $m\ne0$ define $\widehat\sigma^j_{ik}(m)=\frac{m_k\widehat q_i^j(m)-m_i\widehat q_k^j(m)}{2\pi i|m|^2},\qquad \widehat\sigma^j_{ik}(0)=0.$ Then $\widehat\sigma^j_{ik}=-\widehat\sigma^j_{ki}$ and $\sum_k2\pi im_k\widehat\sigma^j_{ik}(m)=\widehat q_i^j(m)-\frac{m_i}{|m|^2}\sum_km_k\widehat q_k^j(m)=\widehat q_i^j(m)$ by step 1.1. Also $|\widehat\sigma^j(m)|\le C_d|m|^{-1}|\widehat q^j(m)|$, so $\sum_m(1+|m|^2)|\widehat\sigma^j(m)|^2\le C_d\sum_m|\widehat q^j(m)|^2$. By [F3], the symmetric Fourier partial sums and each of their first derivatives are Cauchy in $L^2$, since differentiation multiplies the coefficients by $2\pi i m_k$. Their $L^2$ limits satisfy the weak-derivative identity by passing to the limit in integration by parts against smooth tests. Thus the partial sums converge in $H^1$ to a tensor in the periodic $H^1$ closure, with zero mean and the asserted norm bound. The coefficient identity and completeness [F3] give its divergence $q^j$; conjugate symmetry makes it real.

This procedure defines a real-arithmetic finite-dimensional FE-HMM discretization. Its output is $U_H$ unless an `ExactSolve` call returns `singular-system`, in which case that token is returned; [[lem-fehmm-micro-cell-solves-wellposedness]] proves the exceptional branch is unreachable for the stated inputs. It makes no bit-complexity claim, no coefficient-oracle claim, and no claim about numerically computing its exact integral entries; those entries are the mathematical values of the displayed integrals. Fix $Q=(0,1)^2$ and coefficient $a$ from [[def-periodic-scalar-diffusion-data]]. Use the diagonal of the square from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$ as a two-triangle initial matching macro mesh. Label that shared diagonal $0$ in both triangles and each exterior edge $1$. It is a compatible labeled mesh in the sense of [[def-afem-nvb-labelled-triangulation-family]]. The macro input is any finite admissible descendant triangulation $\mathcal T$ of this mesh. Its cells are closed affine triangles as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]].

Choose $\epsilon>0$, a micro side length $\delta>0$, $f\in L^2(Q)$, and a finite matching triangulation $\mathcal M$ of the unit square whose opposite boundary edges and vertices match under translation by the PDE coordinate vectors $e_1,e_2$ of [[def-periodic-cell-correctors-and-effective-tensor]]. The periodic micro space is
$$W_{\mathcal M}:=\{z\in V_\#:z\text{ is continuous and affine on every triangle of }\mathcal M\}.$$
Here $z$ means an $H^1_\#(Y)$ class with a continuous periodic piecewise-affine representative; the periodic closure condition identifies opposite traces. Thus $W_{\mathcal M}$ is the finite-dimensional mean-zero subspace of the periodic P1 space, as proved in [[lem-fehmm-micro-cell-solves-wellposedness]]. Let $V_H$ be the conforming zero-boundary continuous piecewise-affine macro space on $\mathcal T$, using [[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]]. Its inclusion in $H^1_0(Q)$ is supplied by [[thm-matching-continuous-piecewise-polynomials-are-wkp]] and [[thm-zero-boundary-piecewise-polynomials-in-w10p]].

Identify vertices of $\mathcal M$ that match under the opposite-edge translations, and order the resulting periodic vertex classes by the lexicographically least representative of each class. Let $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_N$ be the continuous periodic P1 nodal functions for these classes, with $\phi_i=1$ at class $i$ and $0$ at the other classes. Set $m_i=\int_Y\phi_i\,dy$. If $N=1$, use the empty basis of $W_{\mathcal M}$; otherwise use
$$\psi_i:=\phi_i-\frac{m_i}{m_1}\phi_1\qquad(2\le i\le N)$$
as the ordered basis of $W_{\mathcal M}$. The nodal basis spans the full periodic P1 space, and these functions form a basis of its mean-zero subspace.

Use the following exact solver on the systems assembled below. Given a real matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, `ExactSolve(A,b)` returns the empty vector if $n=0$. Otherwise use temporary solver labels $1,\ldots,n$, with solver coordinate $i$ corresponding to library coordinate $i-1$ of $\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-function-space]]), and form the augmented matrix $[A\mid b]$. For $k=1,\ldots,n$, choose the least row index $p\ge k$ whose current entry in column $k$ is nonzero; if there is no such row, return `singular-system`. Swap the entire augmented rows $p$ and $k$. For each $i=k+1,\ldots,n$, set $r=A_{ik}/A_{kk}$, replace the entire augmented row $i$ by row $i-r\,\mathrm{row}_k$, and set its column-$k$ entry to zero. After this loop, compute in order $k=n,n-1,\ldots,1$ by
$$x_k=\frac{b_k-\sum_{j=k+1}^n A_{kj}x_j}{A_{kk}},$$
using entries of the resulting upper-triangular augmented matrix. Return the vector $x\in\mathbb R^n$ whose library coordinate $x(k-1)$ equals $x_k$. All arithmetic and zero tests are exact over $\mathbb R$; the systems assembled below are positive definite.

Order macro triangles by lexicographic order of their barycenters. For each such $K$, use its barycenter $x_K$ as the single quadrature point with positive weight $|K|$, and set
$$b_K(y):=a\!\left(\frac{x_K}{\epsilon}+\frac{\delta}{\epsilon}y\right)\quad(y\in Y).$$
The affine change-of-variables theorem [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]] makes this a measurable coefficient class independent of the representative of $a$, with $\lambda\le b_K\le\Lambda$ almost everywhere. For each PDE coordinate vector $e_j$ of [[def-periodic-cell-correctors-and-effective-tensor]], in order $j=1,2$, assemble
$$G^K_{i\ell}:=\int_Yb_K\nabla\psi_\ell\cdot\nabla\psi_i\,dy,\qquad r^K_{i,j}:=-\int_Yb_K e_j\cdot\nabla\psi_i\,dy$$
over the micro-basis indices $2\le i,\ell\le N$. If that basis is empty, set $w^h_{K,j}=0$; otherwise call `ExactSolve(G^K,r^K_{\cdot,j})`, index its returned coordinates by $2,\ldots,N$, and set $w^h_{K,j}=\sum_{\ell=2}^N x_\ell\psi_\ell$. Then set
$$A^h_Ke_j:=\int_Yb_K(y)(e_j+\nabla_yw^h_{K,j}(y))\,dy.$$
If the micro call returns `singular-system`, propagate that output; [[lem-fehmm-micro-cell-solves-wellposedness]] proves this branch is not reached. Otherwise identify solver index $i-1$ with micro-basis index $i$ for $2\le i\le N$ and use the returned coefficient as $x_i$ in the displayed sum. The `singular-system` branch is included to make the solver instruction total.

Order the interior vertices of $\mathcal T$ lexicographically and let $\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_M$ be the corresponding nodal basis of $V_H$. If $M=0$, set $U_H=0$. Otherwise assemble
$$H_{rs}:=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}|K|\,\nabla\varphi_s|_K\cdot A^h_K\nabla\varphi_r|_K,\qquad F_r:=\int_Qf\varphi_r\,dx,$$
call `ExactSolve(H,F)`. If it returns `singular-system`, propagate that output; the well-posedness lemma proves this branch is not reached. Otherwise set $U_H:=\sum_{s=1}^M x_s\varphi_s$, with solver index $s$ identified with macro-basis index $s$. This basis system is exactly the variational system
$$B_H(U,V)=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}|K|\,\nabla U|_K\cdot A^h_K\nabla V|_K=\int_QfV\qquad(V\in V_H).$$
The macro matrix is positive definite and its `singular-system` branch is unreachable by [[lem-fehmm-micro-cell-solves-wellposedness]]. Output $U_H$. The centroid quadrature is positive and exact for constants, which is the only quadrature property used in the error theorem.

Fix $d\ge1$, $Y=(0,1)^d$, and Countable Choice for the Sobolev conventions of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $C^\infty_\#(Y)$ be the restrictions to $Y$ of smooth $\mathbb Z^d$-periodic real functions on $\mathbb R^d$. Define
$$H^1_\#(Y):=\overline{C^\infty_\#(Y)}^{\,H^1(Y)},\qquad V_\#:=\left\{v\in H^1_\#(Y):\int_Yv\,dy=0\right\}.$$
The integral is the normalized cell mean because $|Y|=1$. Derivatives are weak derivatives on $Y$ and the periodic condition is the closure convention in this definition; no pointwise boundary trace is being imposed. Equip $V_\#$ with the inherited $H^1$ norm.

Let $Y=(0,1)^d$ and $V_\#$ be the mean-zero periodic $H^1$ space of [[def-periodic-zero-mean-cell-space]]. Then every $v\in V_\#$ satisfies
$$\|v\|_{L^2(Y)}\le\sqrt d\,\|
abla v\|_{L^2(Y)},$$
and every $v\in H^1_\#(Y)$ satisfies $\int_Y
abla v=0$. Consequently $\|
abla v\|_2$ is a complete norm on $V_\#$ equivalent to its inherited $H^1$ norm.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and the unit cell $Y=(0,1)^d$ with Lebesgue measure $|Y|=1$. Assume Countable Choice for the $L^2$ conventions of [[def-countable-choice]]. A **uniformly elliptic periodic scalar diffusion coefficient** is a measurable real function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ such that $a(y+k)=a(y)$ for almost every $y$ and every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and there are constants $0<\lambda\le\Lambda<\infty$ with $\lambda\le a(y)\le\Lambda$ almost everywhere on $Y$. Coefficients are identified when they agree almost everywhere.

For $\epsilon>0$, the physical scalar coefficient is $a_\epsilon(x)=a(x/\epsilon)$ and the associated matrix is $a_\epsilon(x)I_d$. The bounded-domain branch used on this page is $\Omega=(0,1)^d$ with homogeneous zero boundary values. Its weak equation for datum $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is
$$\int_\Omega a(x/\epsilon)\nabla u_\epsilon\cdot\nabla v\,dx=\int_\Omega fv\,dx\qquad(v\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)).$$
No coefficient regularity beyond measurability and the displayed bounds is part of this definition.

For every $\epsilon>0$, the map $x\mapsto x/\epsilon$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^d$. By [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]], its pullback preserves Lebesgue measurability and takes null-set changes to null-set changes (apply the theorem also to the inverse map). Thus $a_\epsilon$ is a well-defined almost-everywhere class independent of the representative of $a$. The same result applies to every affine translation and positive dilation used in periodic sampling below, so almost-everywhere coefficient bounds are preserved under those pullbacks.

The ellipticity bounds hold almost everywhere on all of $\mathbb R^d$, not just on $Y$: periodicity transfers the exceptional null set from $Y$ to each lattice translate, translations preserve null sets by the same change-of-variables theorem, and the countably many translates cover $\mathbb R^d$ up to their null boundaries.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh of a bounded
polyhedral open set $\Omega$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let $v$ be a
real-valued scalar member of the conforming piecewise-polynomial space in
[[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]]. Then $v\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$.
Its weak gradient agrees almost everywhere on each cell with the ordinary
cellwise polynomial gradient.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded polyhedral open set with a finite matching
affine simplicial mesh, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $v$ be a real-valued
conforming piecewise polynomial whose polynomial trace vanishes on every boundary
facet. Then
$$v\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega),\qquad \|v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}.$$
Here $W^{1,p}_0$ is the norm closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$; no C1
