This procedure defines a real-arithmetic finite-dimensional FE-HMM discretization. Its output is $U_H$ unless an `ExactSolve` call returns `singular-system`, in which case that token is returned; [[lem-fehmm-micro-cell-solves-wellposedness]] proves the exceptional branch is unreachable for the stated inputs. It makes no bit-complexity claim, no coefficient-oracle claim, and no claim about numerically computing its exact integral entries; those entries are the mathematical values of the displayed integrals. Fix $Q=(0,1)^2$ and coefficient $a$ from [[def-periodic-scalar-diffusion-data]]. Use the diagonal of the square from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$ as a two-triangle initial matching macro mesh. Label that shared diagonal $0$ in both triangles and each exterior edge $1$. It is a compatible labeled mesh in the sense of [[def-afem-nvb-labelled-triangulation-family]]. The macro input is any finite admissible descendant triangulation $\mathcal T$ of this mesh. Its cells are closed affine triangles as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]].

Choose $\epsilon>0$, a micro side length $\delta>0$, $f\in L^2(Q)$, and a finite matching triangulation $\mathcal M$ of the unit square whose opposite boundary edges and vertices match under translation by the PDE coordinate vectors $e_1,e_2$ of [[def-periodic-cell-correctors-and-effective-tensor]]. The periodic micro space is
$$W_{\mathcal M}:=\{z\in V_\#:z\text{ is continuous and affine on every triangle of }\mathcal M\}.$$
Here $z$ means an $H^1_\#(Y)$ class with a continuous periodic piecewise-affine representative; the periodic closure condition identifies opposite traces. Thus $W_{\mathcal M}$ is the finite-dimensional mean-zero subspace of the periodic P1 space, as proved in [[lem-fehmm-micro-cell-solves-wellposedness]]. Let $V_H$ be the conforming zero-boundary continuous piecewise-affine macro space on $\mathcal T$, using [[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]]. Its inclusion in $H^1_0(Q)$ is supplied by [[thm-matching-continuous-piecewise-polynomials-are-wkp]] and [[thm-zero-boundary-piecewise-polynomials-in-w10p]].

Identify vertices of $\mathcal M$ that match under the opposite-edge translations, and order the resulting periodic vertex classes by the lexicographically least representative of each class. Let $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_N$ be the continuous periodic P1 nodal functions for these classes, with $\phi_i=1$ at class $i$ and $0$ at the other classes. Set $m_i=\int_Y\phi_i\,dy$. If $N=1$, use the empty basis of $W_{\mathcal M}$; otherwise use
$$\psi_i:=\phi_i-\frac{m_i}{m_1}\phi_1\qquad(2\le i\le N)$$
as the ordered basis of $W_{\mathcal M}$. The nodal basis spans the full periodic P1 space, and these functions form a basis of its mean-zero subspace.

Use the following exact solver on the systems assembled below. Given a real matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, `ExactSolve(A,b)` returns the empty vector if $n=0$. Otherwise use temporary solver labels $1,\ldots,n$, with solver coordinate $i$ corresponding to library coordinate $i-1$ of $\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-function-space]]), and form the augmented matrix $[A\mid b]$. For $k=1,\ldots,n$, choose the least row index $p\ge k$ whose current entry in column $k$ is nonzero; if there is no such row, return `singular-system`. Swap the entire augmented rows $p$ and $k$. For each $i=k+1,\ldots,n$, set $r=A_{ik}/A_{kk}$, replace the entire augmented row $i$ by row $i-r\,\mathrm{row}_k$, and set its column-$k$ entry to zero. After this loop, compute in order $k=n,n-1,\ldots,1$ by
$$x_k=\frac{b_k-\sum_{j=k+1}^n A_{kj}x_j}{A_{kk}},$$
using entries of the resulting upper-triangular augmented matrix. Return the vector $x\in\mathbb R^n$ whose library coordinate $x(k-1)$ equals $x_k$. All arithmetic and zero tests are exact over $\mathbb R$; the systems assembled below are positive definite.

Order macro triangles by lexicographic order of their barycenters. For each such $K$, use its barycenter $x_K$ as the single quadrature point with positive weight $|K|$, and set
$$b_K(y):=a\!\left(\frac{x_K}{\epsilon}+\frac{\delta}{\epsilon}y\right)\quad(y\in Y).$$
The affine change-of-variables theorem [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]] makes this a measurable coefficient class independent of the representative of $a$, with $\lambda\le b_K\le\Lambda$ almost everywhere. For each PDE coordinate vector $e_j$ of [[def-periodic-cell-correctors-and-effective-tensor]], in order $j=1,2$, assemble
$$G^K_{i\ell}:=\int_Yb_K\nabla\psi_\ell\cdot\nabla\psi_i\,dy,\qquad r^K_{i,j}:=-\int_Yb_K e_j\cdot\nabla\psi_i\,dy$$
over the micro-basis indices $2\le i,\ell\le N$. If that basis is empty, set $w^h_{K,j}=0$; otherwise call `ExactSolve(G^K,r^K_{\cdot,j})`, index its returned coordinates by $2,\ldots,N$, and set $w^h_{K,j}=\sum_{\ell=2}^N x_\ell\psi_\ell$. Then set
$$A^h_Ke_j:=\int_Yb_K(y)(e_j+\nabla_yw^h_{K,j}(y))\,dy.$$
If the micro call returns `singular-system`, propagate that output; [[lem-fehmm-micro-cell-solves-wellposedness]] proves this branch is not reached. Otherwise identify solver index $i-1$ with micro-basis index $i$ for $2\le i\le N$ and use the returned coefficient as $x_i$ in the displayed sum. The `singular-system` branch is included to make the solver instruction total.

Order the interior vertices of $\mathcal T$ lexicographically and let $\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_M$ be the corresponding nodal basis of $V_H$. If $M=0$, set $U_H=0$. Otherwise assemble
$$H_{rs}:=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}|K|\,\nabla\varphi_s|_K\cdot A^h_K\nabla\varphi_r|_K,\qquad F_r:=\int_Qf\varphi_r\,dx,$$
call `ExactSolve(H,F)`. If it returns `singular-system`, propagate that output; the well-posedness lemma proves this branch is not reached. Otherwise set $U_H:=\sum_{s=1}^M x_s\varphi_s$, with solver index $s$ identified with macro-basis index $s$. This basis system is exactly the variational system
$$B_H(U,V)=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}|K|\,\nabla U|_K\cdot A^h_K\nabla V|_K=\int_QfV\qquad(V\in V_H).$$
The macro matrix is positive definite and its `singular-system` branch is unreachable by [[lem-fehmm-micro-cell-solves-wellposedness]]. Output $U_H$. The centroid quadrature is positive and exact for constants, which is the only quadrature property used in the error theorem.

For every macro cell $K$ in [[alg-fehmm-periodic-cell-micro-macro]], the coefficient $b_K$ satisfies $\lambda\le b_K\le\Lambda$. For each $p\in\mathbb R^2$, both the full cell problem on $V_\#$ and its restriction to $W_{\mathcal M}$ have unique solutions $w_{K,p}$ and $w^h_{K,p}$. The tensors
$$A_K^{\rm ex}p=\int_Yb_K(p+\nabla w_{K,p}),\qquad A_K^hp=\int_Yb_K(p+\nabla w^h_{K,p})$$
are symmetric and satisfy $\lambda I\le A_K^{\rm ex},A_K^h\le\Lambda I$. Consequently the macro FE-HMM system in the algorithm has a unique solution. The exact Gaussian-elimination calls specified there terminate without the `singular-system` branch and return the unique solutions of the assembled micro and macro variational systems.

Assume $a,\lambda,\Lambda,Y,V_\#$ are as in [[def-periodic-scalar-diffusion-data]] and [[def-periodic-zero-mean-cell-space]]. For each $p\in\mathbb R^d$, the equation in [[def-periodic-cell-problem]] has a unique solution $\chi_p\in V_\#$. The map $p\mapsto\chi_p$ is linear, and
$$\|\nabla\chi_p\|_{L^2(Y)}\le(\Lambda/\lambda)|p|,\qquad \|\chi_p\|_{L^2(Y)}\le\sqrt d(\Lambda/\lambda)|p|.$$

Write $e_p=w^h_{K,p}-w_{K,p}$. Subtracting the two variational equations gives $\int_Yb_K
abla e_p\cdot
abla z_h=0$ for every $z_h\in W_{\mathcal M}$. Thus $e_p$ is orthogonal in the $b_K$ gradient inner product to the whole micro space. For any $z_h$, $\|
abla(w_{K,p}-z_h)\|_{b_K}^2=\|
abla e_p\|_{b_K}^2+\|
abla(w^h_{K,p}-z_h)\|_{b_K}^2,$ which proves the best-approximation inequality.

For $p,q\in\mathbb R^2$, the symmetric energy representation in [F2] and the full/discrete equations imply $p\cdot(A_K^h-A_K^{m ex})q=\int_Yb_K
abla e_p\cdot
abla e_q.$ Indeed, expanding the two energy bilinear forms leaves this term; each cross term vanishes by testing the full equation with the difference in $V_\#$ or the discrete equation with a micro function in $W_{\mathcal M}$. Taking $q=p$ proves the identity. For unit $p,q$, Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the right side by $\|
abla e_p\|_{b_K}\|
abla e_q\|_{b_K}\le\eta_K^2$ by step 1.1. The supremum over unit vectors is the operator norm, giving the final bound.

A compatible labeled initial mesh is a finite matching affine simplicial triangulation $\mathcal T_0$ of a polygon in $\mathbb R^2$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], equipped with labels on its edges such that each triangle has one edge labeled $0$ and two labeled $1$, and every shared edge has the same label from both incident triangles. Matching means that distinct cell interiors are disjoint and any nonempty cell intersection is a whole common face: in two dimensions it may be a vertex or an edge. For a descendant triangle of generation $g(K)$, its three edge labels, in any order, are $(g(K)+1,g(K)+1,g(K))$. The unique edge labeled $g(K)$ is its reference edge.

To bisect $K$, join the midpoint of its reference edge to the opposite vertex. The two resulting triangles have generation $g(K)+1$. In each child, the two new half-edges and the bisector receive label $g(K)+2$; the one inherited nonreference edge retains label $g(K)+1$ and is the child's reference edge. A finite bisection forest is the collection of the initial triangles and all descendants reached by finitely many such bisections; its leaves form a triangulation when all shared-edge subdivisions agree. The admissible family $\mathbb T(\mathcal T_0)$ consists of the matching conforming leaf triangulations generated by these compatible bisections. A refinement $\mathcal T\le\mathcal T_*$ means every cell of $\mathcal T_*$ lies in a cell of $\mathcal T$.

For deterministic operational ordering, fix a finite starting mesh in this family and a total order of its cells. Enumerate those operational roots as $K_1,\ldots,K_N$ in that order; this starting mesh may already be a geometric descendant of $\mathcal T_0$, and operational numbering does not reset its generations or edge labels. Give root $K_r$ identifier $(r,\varnothing)$ and order its three vertices lexicographically by their two real coordinates. If a parent has identifier $(r,w)$, with $w$ a finite binary word, let $A$ be the earlier endpoint of its labeled reference edge in its stored vertex list, let $B$ be the other endpoint, let $C$ be the opposite vertex, and let $M=(A+B)/2$. Its children with vertex sets $\{A,M,C\}$ and $\{B,M,C\}$ receive identifiers $(r,w0)$ and $(r,w1)$, respectively. Each child's stored vertex list is the parent list restricted to its two retained vertices, in their previous order, followed by $M$. These lists are bookkeeping orders, independent of the orientation convention for affine reference maps. Compare identifiers first by root rank, then lexicographically by binary word, with $0<1$ and a proper prefix before its extensions. This is a total order, so every finite nonempty pending set has a unique least identifier. Distinct roots or distinct binary paths have distinct identifiers, and a retained cell keeps its identifier and vertex list through all subsequent calls. This operational decoration changes no geometric bisection, reference edge, admissible triangulation or finite-element space.

The compatible initial labeling is a hypothesis, not a consequence of an arbitrary initial triangulation. This definition is two-dimensional and makes no claim about three-dimensional closure or complexity.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general

Its mean flux is $\int_0^1a_\kappa=(1+\kappa)/2$. These correctors yield the stated diagonal entries.

Since $0<\kappa\le1$, the tangential eigenvalue is at least the normal one: $(1+\kappa)^2-4\kappa=(1-\kappa)^2\ge0$. The spectral condition number is therefore their ratio, $(1+\kappa)^2/(4\kappa)$, which diverges as $\kappa\downarrow0$. Every fixed $\kappa$ remains positive and satisfies [F1]; only a uniform-in-contrast condition number fails.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

derivations.claim: The displayed bilinear form in [F1] is symmetric, so $A_h$ is self-adjoint. Its quadratic form is a sum of positive transmissibility-weighted squared jumps in the cell branch and is $\int_0^L|u_h'|^2$ in the interval branch, so it is nonnegative. If it is zero, every interior jump vanishes in the cell branch, and connectedness makes all cell values equal; in the interval branch the derivative is zero on every segment, and continuity makes the function constant. Conversely, constants have zero quadratic form. Thus $\ker A_h=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}$.

Self-adjointness implies $\operatorname{ran}A_h\subseteq(\ker A_h)^\perp$: for $z=A_hx$ and $c\in\ker A_h$, $\langle z,c\rangle_h=\langle x,A_hc\rangle_h=0$. Rank-nullity gives $\dim\operatorname{ran}A_h=\dim X_h-\dim\ker A_h=\dim(\ker A_h)^\perp$, so equality holds. The orthogonal complement of the constants is exactly $X_{h,0}$.

The restriction of $A_h$ to $X_{h,0}$ maps into $X_{h,0}$ and has trivial kernel by step 1.1. It is therefore bijective on this finite-dimensional space. Hence each mean-zero source has a unique mean-zero inverse, and projecting an arbitrary source onto $X_{h,0}$ defines $A_h^\dagger$.

On $X_{h,0}$ the restriction of $A_h$ is self-adjoint positive definite by step 1.1. If $x,y\in X_{h,0}$, write $x=A_hs$ and $y=A_ht$ with $s,t\in X_{h,0}$; then $\langle A_h^\dagger x,y\rangle_h=\langle s,A_ht\rangle_h=\langle A_hs,t\rangle_h=\langle x,A_h^\dagger y\rangle_h$, so its inverse is self-adjoint. Also, for nonzero $x=A_hs$, $\langle A_h^\dagger x,x\rangle_h=\langle s,A_hs\rangle_h>0$.

If $X_{h,0}=\{0\}$ the claimed inequality is immediate. Otherwise its unit sphere is compact and nonempty. The continuous quadratic form $u_h\mapsto\langle A_hu_h,u_h\rangle_h$ attains a minimum there by [F2]. The minimum is positive, since a zero value would put a unit mean-zero vector in the constant kernel from step 1.1. Calling the minimum $\lambda_h>0$, homogeneity gives $\|u_h-\bar u_h\mathbf1\|_h^2\le\lambda_h^{-1}\langle A_hu_h,u_h\rangle_h$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open,
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ have real
and imaginary parts of class $C^k$. For each multi-index
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ with $|\alpha|\le k$, the componentwise classical
derivative $\partial^\alpha u$ is locally integrable and is the weak
derivative $D^\alpha u$. By the uniqueness lemma, it represents the unique
locally integrable weak-derivative class. For $\alpha=0$, this says
$D^0u=u$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion is vacuous: there is only the zero
class and every displayed test identity is zero.

derivations.claim: On every segment between adjacent centers, $I_hv$ has slope $h^{-1}\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}}v'(s)\,ds$, so Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its squared derivative integral by $\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}}|v'|^2$. It is constant on the boundary half-cells. Summing proves $\|(I_hv)'\|_2\le\|v'\|_2$. The fundamental-theorem identity in [F2] gives $|v(x)-I_hv(x)|\le 2\sqrt h\|v'\|_{L^2(K)}$ on each center interval $K$ and the same bound on each boundary half-cell. Squaring and summing proves $\|v-I_hv\|_2\le Ch\|v'\|_2$; then $\|I_hv\|_2\le\|v\|_2+Ch\|v'\|_2$.

For an affine function $w_h$ on an interval $J$ of length $h$ with endpoint values $a,b$, direct integration gives $\|w_h'\|_{L^2(J)}^2=(b-a)^2/h$ and $\|w_h\|_{L^2(J)}^2=h(a^2+ab+b^2)/3\ge h(a^2+b^2)/6$. Hence $\|w_h'\|_{L^2(J)}\le\sqrt{12}h^{-1}\|w_h\|_{L^2(J)}$. Summing this inequality over the affine segments proves the inverse estimate $\|w_h'\|_2\le\sqrt{12}h^{-1}\|w_h\|_2$ on $V_h$; the constant boundary segments add no derivative.

Since $P_hI_hv=I_hv$ and $P_h$ is an $L^2$ contraction, $\|P_hv-I_hv\|_2=\|P_h(v-I_hv)\|_2\le Ch\|v'\|_2$ by step 1.1. The triangle inequality with step 1.1 gives $\|P_hv-v\|_2\le Ch\|v'\|_2$. Apply step 1.2 to $P_hv-I_hv\in V_h$, and then step 1.1, to obtain $\|(P_hv)'\|_2\le\|(I_hv)'\|_2+Ch^{-1}\|P_hv-I_hv\|_2\le C\|v'\|_2$. The $L^2$ contraction gives the full $H^1$ stability.

If $v\in C^2([0,L])$, linear interpolation on each interior segment has $H^1$ error tending to zero, while on a boundary half-cell the derivative error is bounded by $\sqrt h\|v'\|_\infty$. Thus $\|I_hv-v\|_{H^1}\to0$. Step 2.1 applied to $v-I_hv$ gives $\|P_hv-I_hv\|_{H^1}\le C\|v-I_hv\|_{H^1}\to0$, so $P_hv\to v$ in $H^1$.

For arbitrary $v\in H^1(0,L)$, let $v'$ be its $L^2$ weak derivative and use [F3] to choose $q_j\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$ with $q_j\to v'$ in $L^2$. Define $v_j(x)=v(0)+\int_0^xq_j(s)\,ds$ using the representative in [F2]. Then $v_j\in C^\infty([0,L])$ and $\|v_j'-v'\|_2=\|q_j-v'\|_2\to0$, while Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\|v_j-v\|_2\le L\|q_j-v'\|_2$. Hence $v_j\to v$ in $H^1$. Uniform stability from step 2.1 and smooth convergence from step 3.1 yield $$\|P_hv-v\|_{H^1}\le C\|v-v_j\|_{H^1}+\|P_hv_j-v_j\|_{H^1}+\|v_j-v\|_{H^1};$$ first let $h\to0$ with $j$ fixed and then let $j\to\infty$. Thus $P_hv\to v$ in $H^1$ for every $v\in H^1(0,L)$.

For $g\in L^2(0,L)$ and $\delta>0$, [F3] gives $q\in C_c^\infty(0,L)\subset H^1(0,L)$ with $\|g-q\|_2<\delta$. The orthogonal projector is an $L^2$ contraction by [F1], and step 2.1 gives $P_hq\to q$ in $L^2$. Therefore $$\|P_hg-g\|_2\le2\|g-q\|_2+\|P_hq-q\|_2,$$ so $\limsup_{h\to0}\|P_hg-g\|_2\le2\delta$. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ proves strong $L^2$ convergence for every $g\in L^2(0,L)$.

finite_smoke.asserts:
Under the finite-dimensional hypotheses of [[alg-phase-field-sav-cahn-hilliard-step]], the displayed SAV linear system has a unique solution at every step. Every solution conserves the discrete mean and obeys
$$\widetilde E_h(u^{n+1},r^{n+1})+\frac\kappa2\langle A_h\delta u,\delta u\rangle_h+(\delta r)^2+M\tau\langle A_h\mu^{n+1},\mu^{n+1}\rangle_h=\widetilde E_h(u^n,r^n),$$
where $\delta u=u^{n+1}-u^n$, $\delta r=r^{n+1}-r^n$, and
$$\widetilde E_h(u,r)=\frac\kappa2\langle A_hu,u\rangle_h+r^2.$$
Thus $\widetilde E_h$ is nonincreasing. This conclusion is about the modified energy; it does not assert monotonicity of the original physical energy $\mathcal E_h(u)=\frac\kappa2\langle A_hu,u\rangle_h+E_{1,h}(u)$.

Let $X_h$ be either finite-dimensional realization in [[def-phase-field-discrete-realizations]], with real inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_h$, constant vector $\mathbf1$, self-adjoint nonnegative $A_h$ with kernel $\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}$, and $A_h^\dagger$ from [[lem-phase-field-neumann-laplacian-kernel-and-gauge]]. Let $P_{c,h},P_{e,h}:X_h\to\mathbb R$ be the differentiable convex energy components specified there; $\nabla_hP$ denotes the Riesz gradient relative to $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_h$. Put
$$\mathcal E_h(u)=\frac\kappa2\langle A_hu,u\rangle_h+P_{c,h}(u)-P_{e,h}(u),\qquad \mu_h(u,v)=\kappa A_hu+\nabla_hP_{c,h}(u)-\nabla_hP_{e,h}(v).$$
Given $u^n\in X_h$, $\tau>0$, and $M>0$, the backward-Euler convex-splitting step is:

1. **Allen–Cahn branch.** Return the minimizer over $v\in X_h$ of
$$J_{AC}(v)=\frac{1}{2M\tau}\|v-u^n\|_h^2+\frac\kappa2\langle A_hv,v\rangle_h+P_{c,h}(v)-\langle\nabla_hP_{e,h}(u^n),v\rangle_h,$$
and set $\mu^{n+1}=\mu_h(u^{n+1},u^n)$.

2. **Cahn–Hilliard branch.** Restrict to the affine set $\langle v,\mathbf1\rangle_h=\langle u^n,\mathbf1\rangle_h$ and return the minimizer of
$$J_{CH}(v)=\frac{1}{2M\tau}\langle A_h^\dagger(v-u^n),v-u^n\rangle_h+\frac\kappa2\langle A_hv,v\rangle_h+P_{c,h}(v)-\langle\nabla_hP_{e,h}(u^n),v\rangle_h,$$
then set $\mu^{n+1}=\mu_h(u^{n+1},u^n)$.

For the finite-volume realization, $P_{c,h}(u)=\sum_K|K|F_c(u_K)$ and $P_{e,h}(u)=\sum_K|K|F_e(u_K)$. For the conforming interval realization, these are the exact integrals of $F_c$ and $F_e$ over the reconstructed piecewise-affine state. The recurrence, minimizer equivalence, uniqueness, conservation, and energy bounds are proved in [[thm-phase-field-convex-splitting-step-existence-and-energy]]. This is the selected backward-Euler branch; it asserts no ARS(2,2,2), Lie, or Strang property.

Use either connected no-flux realization in [[def-phase-field-discrete-realizations]]. In its finite-volume branch, assume the interior cell graph is connected; in its interval conforming branch, assume $N\ge1$. Write $\bar u_h=\langle u_h,\mathbf1\rangle_h/\langle\mathbf1,\mathbf1\rangle_h$ and $X_{h,0}=\{u_h:\bar u_h=0\}$. Then $A_h$ is self-adjoint and nonnegative, $\ker A_h=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}$, and $\operatorname{ran}A_h=X_{h,0}$. The restriction $A_h:X_{h,0}\to X_{h,0}$ is positive definite and invertible. Define $A_h^\dagger u_h$ by first projecting $u_h$ onto $X_{h,0}$ and then applying this self-adjoint positive inverse. For each fixed finite mesh there is $C_h<\infty$ such that
$$\|u_h-\bar u_h\mathbf1\|_h^2\le C_h\langle A_hu_h,u_h\rangle_h.$$
For a one-cell mesh, $X_{h,0}=\{0\}$ and the inequality is vacuous.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

derivations.claim: In either realization, the quartic leading part $Q_{4,h}$ of $P_{c,h}$ is continuous and strictly positive on the unit sphere of any fixed norm on $X_h$: it is a positive weighted sum of $u_K^4$ in the finite-volume branch and $\int_0^L v^4$ in the conforming branch, which is positive for every nonzero state. The sphere is compact, so [F3] gives $c_h:=\min_{\|u\|=1}Q_{4,h}(u)>0$. Homogeneity gives $Q_{4,h}(u)\ge c_h\|u\|^4$. The formulas in [F4] show that the remaining quadratic term in $P_{c,h}$ is nonnegative, so $P_{c,h}$ is coercive. The second directional derivatives of the two potential functionals are the corresponding weighted sum or integral of $F_c''(u)w^2$ and $F_e''(u)w^2$; [F4] makes them nonnegative, so both are convex. Thus both quartic realizations satisfy the coercivity and convexity assumptions.

The Allen–Cahn objective is continuous and coercive: its positive quadratic term is nonnegative, $P_{c,h}$ is coercive, and the remaining term is linear. For any fixed trial value, a nonempty sublevel set is closed and bounded, hence compact in the finite-dimensional space; [F3] gives a minimizer. The quadratic term $\frac1{2M\tau}\|v-u^n\|_h^2$ is strictly convex, while the remaining nonlinear and quadratic terms are convex by [F2] and the hypotheses, so the minimizer is unique.

Let $a=u^{n+1}$, $b=u^n$, and $\delta=a-b$. Convexity gives $P_{c,h}(a)-P_{c,h}(b)\le\langle\nabla_hP_{c,h}(a),\delta\rangle_h$ and $-P_{e,h}(a)+P_{e,h}(b)\le-\langle\nabla_hP_{e,h}(b),\delta\rangle_h$. Also $\frac\kappa2(\langle A_ha,a\rangle_h-\langle A_hb,b\rangle_h)=\kappa\langle A_ha,\delta\rangle_h-\frac\kappa2\langle A_h\delta,\delta\rangle_h\le\kappa\langle A_ha,\delta\rangle_h$ by nonnegativity in [F2]. Adding these inequalities gives $\mathcal E_h(a)-\mathcal E_h(b)\le\langle\mu^{n+1},\delta\rangle_h$.

Differentiating $J_{AC}$ in an arbitrary direction $w$ gives $\langle (u^{n+1}-u^n)/(M\tau)+\kappa A_hu^{n+1}+\nabla_hP_{c,h}(u^{n+1})-\nabla_hP_{e,h}(u^n),w\rangle_h=0$. Since this holds for every $w$, the vector inside the pairing is zero; multiplying by $-M$ gives the stated Allen–Cahn recurrence.

The Cahn–Hilliard affine set is nonempty because it contains $u^n$. Its objective is continuous and coercive on that affine set by coercivity of $P_{c,h}$ and nonnegativity of the $A_h$ quadratic term. The inverse quadratic term is strictly positive on every nonzero mean-zero direction by [F2], so $J_{CH}$ is strictly convex on the affine set. The compact-sublevel argument of step 1.2 and [F3] therefore gives a unique minimizer.

At the Cahn–Hilliard minimizer, the directional derivative vanishes for every mean-zero direction $w$. Thus $\mu^{n+1}+(M\tau)^{-1}A_h^\dagger(u^{n+1}-u^n)$ is orthogonal to the mean-zero subspace and is therefore constant. Applying $A_h$ and using [F2] gives $(u^{n+1}-u^n)/\tau=-MA_h\mu^{n+1}$. The affine constraint itself gives $\langle u^{n+1},\mathbf1\rangle_h=\langle u^n,\mathbf1\rangle_h$.

In the Allen–Cahn branch, step 1.2 gives $\delta=-M\tau\mu^{n+1}$, so step 1.3 yields $\mathcal E_h(a)-\mathcal E_h(b)\le-M\tau\|\mu^{n+1}\|_h^2$. In the Cahn–Hilliard branch, step 3.1 gives $\delta=-M\tau A_h\mu^{n+1}$, so $\langle\mu^{n+1},\delta\rangle_h=-M\tau\langle A_h\mu^{n+1},\mu^{n+1}\rangle_h\le0$. These are the two asserted energy inequalities.

Use the finite-dimensional realization and the hypotheses of [[alg-phase-field-convex-splitting-backward-euler]]. Assume $P_{c,h}$ is convex and coercive on $X_h$, and $P_{e,h}$ is differentiable and convex. For every $u^n$, $M>0$, and $\tau>0$, both branches have a unique minimizer. Their first-order conditions are exactly
$$\frac{u^{n+1}-u^n}{\tau}=-M\mu^{n+1}\quad\text{(Allen–Cahn)},$$
$$\frac{u^{n+1}-u^n}{\tau}=-M A_h\mu^{n+1}\quad\text{(Cahn–Hilliard)}.$$
The Cahn–Hilliard branch conserves $\langle u^n,\mathbf1\rangle_h$. With $\mathcal E_h$ as in the algorithm,
$$\mathcal E_h(u^{n+1})+M\tau\|\mu^{n+1}\|_h^2\le\mathcal E_h(u^n)\quad\text{(Allen–Cahn)},$$
$$\mathcal E_h(u^{n+1})+M\tau\langle A_h\mu^{n+1},\mu^{n+1}\rangle_h\le\mathcal E_h(u^n)\quad\text{(Cahn–Hilliard)}.$$
For the quartic split in [[def-phase-field-gradient-flow-and-double-well]], the required convexity and coercivity hold for both realizations.

Use either connected no-flux realization in [[def-phase-field-discrete-realizations]]. In its finite-volume branch, assume the interior cell graph is connected; in its interval conforming branch, assume $N\ge1$. Write $\bar u_h=\langle u_h,\mathbf1\rangle_h/\langle\mathbf1,\mathbf1\rangle_h$ and $X_{h,0}=\{u_h:\bar u_h=0\}$. Then $A_h$ is self-adjoint and nonnegative, $\ker A_h=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}$, and $\operatorname{ran}A_h=X_{h,0}$. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz domain, let $d\ge1$, and fix constants $\varepsilon>0$, $M>0$, and $\kappa>0$. Put
$$F_\varepsilon(s)=\frac{(s^2-1)^2}{4\varepsilon^2},\qquad f_\varepsilon(s)=F_\varepsilon'(s)=\frac{s^3-s}{\varepsilon^2},$$
and define the free energy on $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)\cap L^4(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ by
$$\mathcal E_\varepsilon(u)=\int_\Omega\left(\frac{\kappa}{2}|\nabla u|^2+F_\varepsilon(u)\right)\,dx.$$
Here $H^1=W^{1,2}$ and weak derivatives have the meaning in [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The finite-energy initial class consists of $u_0\in H^1(\Omega)\cap L^4(\Omega)$.

The **Allen–Cahn gradient flow** is
$$u_t=-M\mu,\qquad \mu=-\kappa\Delta u+f_\varepsilon(u),\qquad \partial_nu=0,\qquad u(0)=u_0.$$
The **Cahn–Hilliard gradient flow** is
$$u_t=M\Delta\mu,\qquad \mu=-\kappa\Delta u+f_\varepsilon(u),\qquad \partial_nu=\partial_n\mu=0,\qquad u(0)=u_0.$$
For weak solutions, the no-flux conditions are encoded by the natural weak formulations with all $H^1(\Omega)$ test functions. In dimensions $d\ge5$, the finite-energy class $H^1\cap L^4$ alone does not in general make $f_\varepsilon(u)$ a continuous functional on $H^1(\Omega)$: it gives only $f_\varepsilon(u)\in L^{4/3}$, while $H^1(\Omega)$ need not embed into $L^4(\Omega)$. Thus any weak solution tested against all $H^1$ functions must have the additional integrability needed to make the nonlinear pairing continuous. The chemical potential $\mu$ is the variational derivative of $\mathcal E_\varepsilon$, and the mobilities select the $L^2$ metric for Allen–Cahn and the mean-zero $H^{-1}$ metric for Cahn–Hilliard. In the Cahn–Hilliard flow, the no-flux equation conserves $\int_\Omega u$; the Allen–Cahn flow has no such conservation law in general. No maximum-principle property is part of these definitions.

The convergence theorem on this page is restricted to one space dimension. Assuming the Axiom of Choice for the following standard embedding consequences, if $d=2$ and $\Omega$ is a bounded $W^{1,p}$ extension domain for every $1<p<2$ as defined in [[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]], then [[thm-critical-sobolev-embedding-into-every-finite-lq]] gives $H^1(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^4(\Omega)$. If $d=3$ and $\Omega$ is a bounded $W^{1,2}$ extension domain, then [[thm-sobolev-embedding-on-bounded-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n]] gives $H^1(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^4(\Omega)$. These are the exact extra extension hypotheses for the quartic-energy claim. In dimensions $d\ge4$ no assertion that every $H^1$ state has finite quartic energy is made; the explicit initial class above remains $H^1\cap L^4$. No sharp-interface limit as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ is part of either definition.

derivations.claim: Substitute the exact trajectory into the backward-Euler split. For Allen–Cahn define $R_n^{AC}:=y(t_{n+1})-y(t_n)+M\tau(G_{c,h}(y(t_{n+1}))-G_{e,h}(y(t_n)))$. For Cahn–Hilliard define $R_n^{CH}:=y(t_{n+1})-y(t_n)+M\tau A_h(G_{c,h}(y(t_{n+1}))-G_{e,h}(y(t_n)))$. The exact integral equations express these residuals as $M$ times the quadrature difference $\tau G_{c,h}(y(t_{n+1}))-\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}G_{c,h}(y(s))ds+\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}G_{e,h}(y(s))ds-\tau G_{e,h}(y(t_n))$, with an additional $A_h$ in the Cahn–Hilliard branch. The bounded derivatives on the compact exact trajectory and $\|y(t)-y(s)\|\le C|t-s|$ imply $\|R_n^{AC}\|_h\le C\tau^2$ and $\|R_n^{CH}\|_{-1,h}\le C\tau^2$; in the latter case $R_n^{CH}$ lies in the mean-zero range of $A_h$ by [F3].

Convexity of $P_{c,h}$ and nonnegativity of $A_h$ make $G_{c,h}$ monotone. By [F4], $G_{e,h}$ is globally Lipschitz with constant $L_e=2/\varepsilon^2$. In the quartic realizations, the lower bound $F_\varepsilon(s)\ge s^4/(8\varepsilon^2)-1/(4\varepsilon^2)$ and the energy inequality in [F2] also bound every numerical state on the fixed finite-dimensional space.

In the Allen–Cahn branch put $e_n=u^n-y(t_n)$. Subtract the exact residual equation from the numerical recurrence and pair with $e_{n+1}$. The identity $2\langle e_{n+1}-e_n,e_{n+1}\rangle_h=\|e_{n+1}\|_h^2-\|e_n\|_h^2+\|e_{n+1}-e_n\|_h^2$ and monotonicity from step 2.1 leave only the explicit term and residual on the right. In the Cahn–Hilliard branch both errors have mean zero. Pair the original difference equation with $A_h^\dagger e_{n+1}$. Self-adjointness and $A_hA_h^\dagger e_{n+1}=e_{n+1}$ give $2\langle e_{n+1}-e_n,A_h^\dagger e_{n+1}\rangle_h=\|e_{n+1}\|_{-1,h}^2-\|e_n\|_{-1,h}^2+\|e_{n+1}-e_n\|_{-1,h}^2$. The explicit term obeys $|\langle G_{e,h}(u^n)-G_{e,h}(y_n),e_{n+1}\rangle_h|\le L_e\|e_n\|_{-1,h}\|e_{n+1}\|_{1,h}$, where $\|v\|_{1,h}^2=\langle A_hv,v\rangle_h$. Cauchy–Schwarz in this inner product gives the bound. Young's inequality absorbs half of the positive $M\tau\kappa\|e_{n+1}\|_{1,h}^2$ term and leaves $C\tau\|e_n\|_{-1,h}^2$. The residual from step 1.1 satisfies $|\langle R_n^{CH},A_h^\dagger e_{n+1}\rangle_h|=|\langle R_n^{CH},e_{n+1}\rangle_{-1,h}|\le C\tau^2\|e_{n+1}\|_{-1,h}\le\frac\tau8\|e_{n+1}\|_{-1,h}^2+C'\tau^3$. Hence, for small $\tau$, $\|e_{n+1}\|_{-1,h}^2\le(1+C\tau)\|e_n\|_{-1,h}^2+C\tau^3$.

In either recurrence, $e_0=0$. Iterating $z_{n+1}\le(1+C\tau)z_n+C\tau^3$ for $n\tau\le T$ gives $z_n\le C\tau^3\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(1+C\tau)^j\le C_T\tau^2$, since $(1+C\tau)^n\le e^{CT}$. Taking square roots gives the two asserted $O(\tau)$ bounds. The constants include the fixed-mesh operator norms, the fixed parameters $M,\kappa,\varepsilon$, and the trajectory bounds.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz domain, let $d\ge1$, and fix constants $\varepsilon>0$, $M>0$, and $\kappa>0$. Put
$$F_\varepsilon(s)=\frac{(s^2-1)^2}{4\varepsilon^2},\qquad f_\varepsilon(s)=F_\varepsilon'(s)=\frac{s^3-s}{\varepsilon^2},$$
and define the free energy on $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)\cap L^4(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ by
$$\mathcal E_\varepsilon(u)=\int_\Omega\left(\frac{\kappa}{2}|\nabla u|^2+F_\varepsilon(u)\right)\,dx.$$
Here $H^1=W^{1,2}$ and weak derivatives have the meaning in [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The finite-energy initial class consists of $u_0\in H^1(\Omega)\cap L^4(\Omega)$.

The **Allen–Cahn gradient flow** is
$$u_t=-M\mu,\qquad \mu=-\kappa\Delta u+f_\varepsilon(u),\qquad \partial_nu=0,\qquad u(0)=u_0.$$
The **Cahn–Hilliard gradient flow** is
$$u_t=M\Delta\mu,\qquad \mu=-\kappa\Delta u+f_\varepsilon(u),\qquad \partial_nu=\partial_n\mu=0,\qquad u(0)=u_0.$$
For weak solutions, the no-flux conditions are encoded by the natural weak formulations with all $H^1(\Omega)$ test functions. In dimensions $d\ge5$, the finite-energy class $H^1\cap L^4$ alone does not in general make $f_\varepsilon(u)$ a continuous functional on $H^1(\Omega)$: it gives only $f_\varepsilon(u)\in L^{4/3}$, while $H^1(\Omega)$ need not embed into $L^4(\Omega)$. Thus any weak solution tested against all $H^1$ functions must have the additional integrability needed to make the nonlinear pairing continuous. The chemical potential $\mu$ is the variational derivative of $\mathcal E_\varepsilon$, and the mobilities select the $L^2$ metric for Allen–Cahn and the mean-zero $H^{-1}$ metric for Cahn–Hilliard. In the Cahn–Hilliard flow, the no-flux equation conserves $\int_\Omega u$; the Allen–Cahn flow has no such conservation law in general. No maximum-principle property is part of these definitions.

The convergence theorem on this page is restricted to one space dimension. Assuming the Axiom of Choice for the following standard embedding consequences, if $d=2$ and $\Omega$ is a bounded $W^{1,p}$ extension domain for every $1<p<2$ as defined in [[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]], then [[thm-critical-sobolev-embedding-into-every-finite-lq]] gives $H^1(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^4(\Omega)$. If $d=3$ and $\Omega$ is a bounded $W^{1,2}$ extension domain, then [[thm-sobolev-embedding-on-bounded-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n]] gives $H^1(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^4(\Omega)$. These are the exact extra extension hypotheses for the quartic-energy claim. In dimensions $d\ge4$ no assertion that every $H^1$ state has finite quartic energy is made; the explicit initial class above remains $H^1\cap L^4$. No sharp-interface limit as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ is part of either definition.

Let $\Omega=(0,L)$ and let $V_h$ be the conforming interval space in [[def-phase-field-discrete-realizations]], with center spacing $h$. Let $I_hv$ interpolate the absolutely-continuous representative of $v\in H^1(0,L)$ at the centers and extend it constantly to the two boundary half-cells. Let $P_h$ be the exact $L^2$-orthogonal projection onto $V_h$. There is a constant $C$ independent of $h$ such that
$$\|I_hv\|_{H^1}\le C\|v\|_{H^1},\qquad \|v-I_hv\|_{L^2}\le Ch\|v'\|_{L^2},\qquad \|P_hv\|_{H^1}\le C\|v\|_{H^1}.$$
In addition, $\|P_hv-v\|_{L^2}\le Ch\|v'\|_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H^1(0,L)$, $P_hv\to v$ in $H^1(0,L)$ for every $v\in H^1(0,L)$, and $P_hg\to g$ in $L^2(0,L)$ for every $g\in L^2(0,L)$ as $h\to0$.

Use the finite-dimensional realization and the hypotheses of [[alg-phase-field-convex-splitting-backward-euler]]. Assume $P_{c,h}$ is convex and coercive on $X_h$, and $P_{e,h}$ is differentiable and convex. For every $u^n$, $M>0$, and $\tau>0$, both branches have a unique minimizer. Their first-order conditions are exactly
$$\frac{u^{n+1}-u^n}{\tau}=-M\mu^{n+1}\quad\text{(Allen–Cahn)},$$
$$\frac{u^{n+1}-u^n}{\tau}=-M A_h\mu^{n+1}\quad\text{(Cahn–Hilliard)}.$$
The Cahn–Hilliard branch conserves $\langle u^n,\mathbf1\rangle_h$. With $\mathcal E_h$ as in the algorithm,
$$\mathcal E_h(u^{n+1})+M\tau\|\mu^{n+1}\|_h^2\le\mathcal E_h(u^n)\quad\text{(Allen–Cahn)},$$
$$\mathcal E_h(u^{n+1})+M\tau\langle A_h\mu^{n+1},\mu^{n+1}\rangle_h\le\mathcal E_h(u^n)\quad\text{(Cahn–Hilliard)}.$$
For the quartic split in [[def-phase-field-gradient-flow-and-double-well]], the required convexity and coercivity hold for both realizations.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $W^{1,p}$-extension domain
([[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]) and let
$1\le p<\infty$. Then $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is compactly embedded in
$L^p(\Omega)$: every sequence bounded in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ has a subsequence
converging in $L^p(\Omega)$. Every bounded $C^1$ domain is an example.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $V\Subset H\hookrightarrow V^*$ be a Banach evolution triple. For each
$k$, let $0=t_0^k<\cdots<t_{N_k}^k=T$ be a partition with maximum step
$\delta_k\to0$, let $U_k^n\in V$, and define $\overline U_k(t)=U_k^n$ on
$I_n^k=(t_{n-1}^k,t_n^k]$ and
$D_k(t)=(U_k^n-U_k^{n-1})/\tau_n^k$ there. Suppose, for some
$1<p<\infty$ and $1<q\le\infty$,
$$\sup_k\|\overline U_k\|_{L^p(0,T;V)} +\sup_k\|D_k\|_{L^q(0,T;V^*)}<\infty.$$
Then the time translates satisfy, on their common intervals,
$$\|\overline U_k(\cdot+s)-\overline U_k\|_{L^q(V^*)} \le (s+2\delta_k)\|D_k\|_{L^q(V^*)},$$
and $(\overline U_k)$ is relatively compact in $L^p(0,T;H)$. If also
$\sup_{k,n}\|U_k^n\|_H<\infty$, every convergent subsequence converges in
every $L^r(0,T;H)$ with $1\le r<\infty$.

Assume Countable Choice. Every bounded sequence in a separable real Hilbert
space $X$ has a weakly convergent subsequence. If $V$ is a separable real
Hilbert space, then $L^2(0,T;V)$ and $L^2(0,T;V^*)$ are separable real Hilbert
spaces, their product is a separable Hilbert space, and the graph of the weak
time-derivative operator is closed there. Consequently $W(0,T;V)$ is a closed
Hilbert subspace of that product and every bounded sequence in $W(0,T;V)$ has
a weakly convergent subsequence.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $X_h$ be either finite-dimensional realization in [[def-phase-field-discrete-realizations]], with real inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_h$, constant vector $\mathbf1$, self-adjoint nonnegative $A_h$ with kernel $\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}$, and $A_h^\dagger$ from [[lem-phase-field-neumann-laplacian-kernel-and-gauge]]. Let $P_{c,h},P_{e,h}:X_h\to\mathbb R$ be the differentiable convex energy components specified there; $\nabla_hP$ denotes the Riesz gradient relative to $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_h$. Put
$$\mathcal E_h(u)=\frac\kappa2\langle A_hu,u\rangle_h+P_{c,h}(u)-P_{e,h}(u),\qquad \mu_h(u,v)=\kappa A_hu+\nabla_hP_{c,h}(u)-\nabla_hP_{e,h}(v).$$
Given $u^n\in X_h$, $\tau>0$, and $M>0$, the backward-Euler convex-splitting step is:

1. **Allen–Cahn branch.** Return the minimizer over $v\in X_h$ of
$$J_{AC}(v)=\frac{1}{2M\tau}\|v-u^n\|_h^2+\frac\kappa2\langle A_hv,v\rangle_h+P_{c,h}(v)-\langle\nabla_hP_{e,h}(u^n),v\rangle_h,$$
and set $\mu^{n+1}=\mu_h(u^{n+1},u^n)$.

2. **Cahn–Hilliard branch.** Restrict to the affine set $\langle v,\mathbf1\rangle_h=\langle u^n,\mathbf1\rangle_h$ and return the minimizer of
$$J_{CH}(v)=\frac{1}{2M\tau}\langle A_h^\dagger(v-u^n),v-u^n\rangle_h+\frac\kappa2\langle A_hv,v\rangle_h+P_{c,h}(v)-\langle\nabla_hP_{e,h}(u^n),v\rangle_h,$$
then set $\mu^{n+1}=\mu_h(u^{n+1},u^n)$.

For the finite-volume realization, $P_{c,h}(u)=\sum_K|K|F_c(u_K)$ and $P_{e,h}(u)=\sum_K|K|F_e(u_K)$. For the conforming interval realization, these are the exact integrals of $F_c$ and $F_e$ over the reconstructed piecewise-affine state. The recurrence, minimizer equivalence, uniqueness, conservation, and energy bounds are proved in [[thm-phase-field-convex-splitting-step-existence-and-energy]]. This is the selected backward-Euler branch; it asserts no ARS(2,2,2), Lie, or Strang property.

derivations.claim: For $v\in H^1(0,L)$, choose a point $y$ with $|v(y)|\le L^{-1/2}\|v\|_2$; such a point exists since $v$ has a continuous representative. For every $x$, [F8] and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|v(x)|\le |v(y)|+\int_0^L|v'|\le L^{-1/2}\|v\|_2+\sqrt L\|v'\|_2$. Thus $H^1(0,L)$ embeds continuously in $L^\infty(0,L)$.

By [F2], $u_h^0=P_hu_0$ is uniformly bounded in $H^1$; step 1.1 bounds it in $L^\infty$, so its gradient and quartic terms in [F1] give a uniform initial-energy bound. The energy inequalities in [F3] then give $\sup_{h,\tau,n}\|u_h^n\|_{H^1}<\infty$: the gradient term controls $\|u_h'\|_2$, and the algebraic identity $$F_\varepsilon(s)-\left(\frac{s^4}{8\varepsilon^2}-\frac1{4\varepsilon^2}\right)=\frac{(s^2-2)^2}{8\varepsilon^2}\ge0$$ controls $\|u_h\|_4$ and, by [F8], $\|u_h\|_2$. Step 1.1 gives $\sup_{h,\tau,n}\|u_h^n\|_\infty<\infty$. For Allen–Cahn, the update in [F9] gives $D_\tau u_h^n=-M\mu_h^{n+1}$; hence the summed dissipation in [F3] and $\|w\|_{V^*}\le\|w\|_2$ give $\|D_\tau u_{h,\tau}\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}\le C$. For Cahn–Hilliard, summing [F3] bounds $\partial_x\mu_{h,\tau}$ in $L^2$. Its mean is $$\overline\mu_h^{n+1}=L^{-1}\int_0^L\bigl(F_c'(u_h^{n+1})-F_e'(u_h^n)\bigr)\,dx,$$ because $\int_0^L A_hu_h^{n+1}\,dx=0$ and the Riesz gradients in [F9] pair with $1$ as derivatives of the integral potentials in [F1]; this mean is uniformly bounded by the $L^\infty$ bound. For $g=\mu_h^{n+1}-\overline\mu_h^{n+1}$, [F8] and Cauchy--Schwarz give $|g(x)|=|L^{-1}\int_0^L(g(x)-g(y))\,dy|\le\int_0^L|g'|\le\sqrt L\|g'\|_2$, so $\|g\|_2\le L\|\partial_x\mu_h^{n+1}\|_2$. Thus $\mu_{h,\tau}$ is bounded in $L^2(0,T;H^1)$. For each $v\in V$, the CH update in [F9] gives $D_\tau u_h^n=-MA_h\mu_h^{n+1}\in V_h$ and orthogonality gives $(D_\tau u_h^n,v)_{L^2}=(D_\tau u_h^n,P_hv)_{L^2}=-M\int_0^L(\mu_h^{n+1})_x(P_hv)_x\,dx$. The uniform H1 stability of $P_h$ in [F2] therefore bounds the discrete derivative in $L^2(0,T;V^*)$.

The piecewise-constant reconstructions take values in $V=H^1(0,L)$ and have uniformly bounded $L^2(0,T;V)$ norms by step 2.1. The interval embedding in [F5] supplies $V\Subset H$, and [F4] supplies the evolution triple. The time steps tend to zero and step 2.1 supplies the discrete-derivative bound, so [F6] gives a subsequence converging strongly in $L^2(0,T;L^2)$. Applying [F7] to the same bounded $L^2(0,T;H^1)$ sequence and taking a further subsequence gives weak $L^2(H^1)$ convergence to the same $u$, since the strong $L^2$ limit is unique. The Cahn–Hilliard chemical potentials are bounded in $L^2(H^1)$ by step 2.1, so [F7] also gives a weak limit $\mu$.

Let $w_{h,\tau}(t)=u_h^{n+1}-u_h^n$ on $t\in(t_n,t_{n+1})$. Then $w_{h,\tau}=\tau D_\tau u_{h,\tau}$, so step 2.1 gives $\|w_{h,\tau}\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}\le C\tau$; the uniform H1 bound gives $\|w_{h,\tau}\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}\le C$. For every $w\in V$, the evolution-triple pairing and Cauchy--Schwarz give $\|w\|_H^2=\langle w,w\rangle_{V^*,V}\le\|w\|_{V^*}\|w\|_V$. Integrating and applying Cauchy--Schwarz in time shows $\|w_{h,\tau}\|_{L^2(0,T;H)}^2\le C\tau$, so adjacent time-level reconstructions differ by a term tending to zero in $L^2((0,T)\times(0,L))$. By step 1.1 both adjacent states are uniformly bounded in $L^\infty$; the polynomial split derivatives $F_c'$ and $F_e'$ are Lipschitz on this common bounded range. Therefore their values at adjacent levels differ by a term tending to zero in $L^2$, and strong convergence from step 3.1 implies convergence of each split term, and hence $f_\varepsilon$, strongly in $L^2$ to its value at $u$.

Let $\phi\in C^1([0,T]\times[0,L])$ vanish at $T$. The sets $\{\phi(t):0\le t\le T\}$ and $\{\partial_t\phi(t):0\le t\le T\}$ are compact in $H^1$ and $L^2$, respectively, by continuity in those norms. Uniform operator bounds and strong convergence of $P_h$ in [F2] imply uniform projector convergence on each compact set: cover the set by finitely many balls of radius $\delta$, use convergence at their centers, and bound the errors inside each ball by the uniform operator norm plus $1$. Uniform continuity of $\partial_t\phi$ then shows the projected time difference quotients converge in $L^2$ to $\partial_t\phi$. Use $P_h\phi(t_{n+1})$ as the spatial test in the discrete equation [F9] and sum by parts in time. The terminal term vanishes exactly because $\phi(T)=0$; the initial term is $(P_hu_0,P_h\phi(t_1))=(u_0,P_h\phi(t_1))\to(u_0,\phi(0))$. Strong convergence of the tests, weak convergence of $u_{h,\tau}$ in $L^2(H^1)$ from step 3.1, and strong convergence of the nonlinear terms from step 4.1 permit passage in every sum, yielding the Allen–Cahn identity in the Statement.

In the Cahn–Hilliard branch, apply the same test passage to the first mixed equation [F9]. The weak $L^2(H^1)$ convergence of $\mu_{h,\tau}$ from step 3.1 and strong convergence of the tests give $-\int u\phi_t+M\int\mu_x\phi_x=\int u_0\phi(0)$. For any $\psi\in H^1(0,L)$ and $\eta\in L^2(0,T)$, test the second mixed equation [F9] with $P_h\psi$, multiply by $\eta(t)$, and integrate in time. By [F2], $P_h\psi\to\psi$ in $H^1$; weak convergence of $\mu_{h,\tau}$ and $u_{h,\tau}$ in $L^2(H^1)$ and strong convergence of the split potential in $L^2$ from step 4.1 pass the identity to the integrated form in the Statement. Finally, the discrete mean is constant by [F3]. Strong convergence in $L^2((0,T)\times(0,L))$ makes the mean functions converge in $L^2(0,T)$ by Cauchy–Schwarz in space, so the limit has that mean for almost every time.

and define the free energy on $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)\cap L^4(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ by
$$\mathcal E_\varepsilon(u)=\int_\Omega\left(\frac{\kappa}{2}|\nabla u|^2+F_\varepsilon(u)\right)\,dx.$$

The **Allen–Cahn gradient flow** is
$$u_t=-M\mu,\qquad \mu=-\kappa\Delta u+f_\varepsilon(u),\qquad \partial_nu=0,\qquad u(0)=u_0.$$
The **Cahn–Hilliard gradient flow** is
$$u_t=M\Delta\mu,\qquad \mu=-\kappa\Delta u+f_\varepsilon(u),\qquad \partial_nu=\partial_n\mu=0,\qquad u(0)=u_0.$$
For weak solutions, the no-flux conditions are encoded by the natural weak formulations with all $H^1(\Omega)$ test functions. The chemical potential $\mu$ is the variational derivative of $\mathcal E_\varepsilon$, and the mobilities select the $L^2$ metric for Allen–Cahn and the mean-zero $H^{-1}$ metric for Cahn–Hilliard. In the Cahn–Hilliard flow, the no-flux equation conserves $\int_\Omega u$; the Allen–Cahn flow has no such conservation law in general. No maximum-principle property is part of these definitions.

The convergence theorem on this page is restricted to one space dimension. Assuming the Axiom of Choice for the following standard embedding consequences, if $d=2$ and $\Omega$ is a bounded $W^{1,p}$ extension domain for every $1<p<2$ as defined in [[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]], then [[thm-critical-sobolev-embedding-into-every-finite-lq]] gives $H^1(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^4(\Omega)$. If $d=3$ and $\Omega$ is a bounded $W^{1,2}$ extension domain, then [[thm-sobolev-embedding-on-bounded-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n]] gives $H^1(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^4(\Omega)$. Assume $P_{c,h}$ is convex and coercive on $X_h$, and $P_{e,h}$ is differentiable and convex. For every $u^n$, $M>0$, and $\tau>0$, both branches have a unique minimizer. Their first-order conditions are exactly
$$\frac{u^{n+1}-u^n}{\tau}=-M\mu^{n+1}\quad\text{(Allen–Cahn)},$$
$$\frac{u^{n+1}-u^n}{\tau}=-M A_h\mu^{n+1}\quad\text{(Cahn–Hilliard)}.$$
The Cahn–Hilliard branch conserves $\langle u^n,\mathbf1\rangle_h$. With $\mathcal E_h$ as in the algorithm,
$$\mathcal E_h(u^{n+1})+M\tau\|\mu^{n+1}\|_h^2\le\mathcal E_h(u^n)\quad\text{(Allen–Cahn)},$$
$$\mathcal E_h(u^{n+1})+M\tau\langle A_h\mu^{n+1},\mu^{n+1}\rangle_h\le\mathcal E_h(u^n)\quad\text{(Cahn–Hilliard)}.$$
For the quartic split in [[def-phase-field-gradient-flow-and-double-well]], the required convexity and coercivity hold for both realizations.

The first state equation gives $a-1=-2\mu_1$, hence $2a^3+7a-5=0$. The polynomial is strictly increasing because its derivative is $6a^2+7>0$, and its values at $0$ and $1$ are $-5$ and $4$; therefore it has exactly one root $a\in(0,1)$.

The initial gradient energy is $\frac12\langle A_hu^0,u^0\rangle_h=2$ and both potential terms vanish, so $E_h(u^0)=2$. For $u^1=(a,-a)$ the gradient energy is $2a^2$ and the potential energy is $\frac12(1-a^2)^2$. Since $0<a<1$, $(1-a^2)^2<1-a^2$, hence $E_h(u^1)<2=E_h(u^0)$. Let $d\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $a,b:U\to\mathbb R^d$. The **additive autonomous ODE partition** with components $a$ and $b$ is the initial-value problem
$$y'(t)=a(y(t))+b(y(t)),\qquad y(t_0)=y_0\in U,$$
in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. The term *autonomous* means that neither component has a separate time argument. A numerical method may evaluate $a$ explicitly and solve an equation involving $b$ implicitly; this naming convention does not assert that either exact subflow exists or that an implicit stage has a solution.

Let $a,b:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^3$ fields on an open set, and restrict attention to points and time intervals for which the unique local solutions of $x'=a(x)$ and $x'=b(x)$ remain in $U$. Denote their exact solution maps by $\Phi_a^t$ and $\Phi_b^t$. The **Lie split map** applies $a$ and then $b$:
$$L_h:=\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^h.$$
The **Strang split map** applies half of $a$, then $b$, then half of $a$:
$$S_h:=\Phi_a^{h/2}\circ\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^{h/2}.$$
Define the vector-field Lie bracket convention
$$[a,b](y):=Db(y)a(y)-Da(y)b(y).$$
This definition is finite-dimensional. It asserts neither that an unbounded operator has a common invariant domain nor that its commutators are bounded.

Let $a,b\in C^3(U,\mathbb R^d)$ define the additive IVP of [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]] and have exact subflows on a common compact convex tube over $[0,T]$. Assume $a,b$ are Lipschitz there with constants $L_a,L_b$, and the exact solution, all split stages, and all numerical states remain in that tube with positive margin. For all sufficiently small $h=T/N$ and exact initial data, the exact Lie and Strang split maps of [[def-exact-split-flows-lie-strang-and-bracket]] satisfy
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n^{\rm Lie}-y(t_n)\|_2\le C_1h,\qquad \max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n^{\rm Strang}-y(t_n)\|_2\le C_2h^2.$$
The constants may depend on the tube, the fields, and $T$. For approximate subflows, suppose $\|\widehat\Phi_c^s(u)-\Phi_c^s(u)\|_2\le\epsilon_c(s)$ for $c\in\{a,b\}$ and every admitted starting state $u$. If all approximate compositions stay in the tube, their composed one-step maps are Lipschitz with constant $1+\widehat Lh$ for some $\widehat L\ge0$, and
$$\epsilon_b(h)+\exp(L_bh)\epsilon_a(h)=O(h^2)$$
for Lie and
$$\epsilon_a(h/2)+\exp(L_ah/2)\epsilon_b(h)+\exp((L_a/2+L_b)h)\epsilon_a(h/2)=O(h^3)$$
for Strang, then the same respective global orders hold. These additional conditions keep subflow-solver errors separate from splitting errors.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a time interval $[0,T]$ with $T>0$, and a nonempty bounded open reference domain $\widehat\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with compact Jordan closure; Jordan measurability means equality of finite-rectangle inner and outer contents ([[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]]). In dimension $d=1$, require $\widehat\Omega$ to be a finite union of bounded open intervals with pairwise disjoint closures. In dimensions $d\ge2$, require a finite piecewise-$C^1$ boundary presentation: a finite family of compact boundary faces $S_1,\ldots,S_q$ and a compact edge set $E$ such that the faces cover $\partial\widehat\Omega$, each face lies in a regular $C^1$ hypersurface patch, $S_i\cap E$ is surface-null, all face overlaps lie in $E$, and off $E$ the boundary is locally one $C^1$ graph with $\widehat\Omega$ on one side. The faces carry that side's outward unit normal.

An **ALE moving-domain map** is a map $A:[0,T]\times\overline{\widehat\Omega}\to\mathbb R^d$ whose space-time restriction extends to a $C^2$ map on a neighborhood of this set, and for each $t$ the map $A_t(\xi):=A(t,\xi)$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism on neighborhoods of the closures. Write $\Omega(t):=A_t(\widehat\Omega)$ and $J(\xi,t):=\det D_\xi A_t(\xi)>0$. Define the **mesh velocity** in physical coordinates by $w_m(x,t):=\partial_t A_t(A_t^{-1}(x))$. In $d=1$ the moving boundary consists of the transported interval endpoints. In $d\ge2$, require the transported faces under $A_t$ to satisfy the same finite piecewise-$C^1$ boundary-presentation conditions; the diffeomorphism carries the reference faces and edge set to that presentation, with the transported outward normal.

This definition fixes the regularity and sign conventions for the continuous ALE identities. It does not assert a discrete approximation property, a nonintersection theorem for a computed mesh, or well-posedness of a coupled PDE.

derivations.claim: Fix $(\xi,t)$ and write $H=\partial_tF(\xi,t)$. Differentiability gives $F(\xi,t+h)=F+hH+o(h)$. Since $F$ is invertible, factor this as $F[I+hF^{-1}H+o(h)]$. The permutation expansion of the determinant gives $\det(I+hK+o(h))=1+h\operatorname{tr}K+o(h)$: the identity permutation contributes $1+h\sum_jK_{jj}+o(h)$, while every nonidentity permutation contains at least two off-diagonal factors of order $h$. Hence $\partial_tJ=J\operatorname{tr}(F^{-1}H)$.

Differentiate $w_m(A_t(\xi),t)=\partial_tA_t(\xi)$ in $\xi$. The chain rule and equality of the mixed derivatives of the $C^2$ map give $H=(D_xw_m)(A_t(\xi),t)F$. Therefore $\operatorname{tr}(F^{-1}H)=\operatorname{tr}(F^{-1}(D_xw_m)F)=\operatorname{tr}(D_xw_m)=\operatorname{div}_xw_m$, using cyclic invariance of trace. Substitution into step 1.1 proves the identity.

Let $I_1,I_2$ and the common trace space $\Lambda$ be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, with $\dim\Lambda\ge1$, and set $X_i:=I_i\oplus\Lambda$. The trace map is $\gamma_i(x_i,\lambda_i)=\lambda_i$. Let $M_i$ and $A_i$ be self-adjoint positive-definite operators on $X_i$, let $\Delta t>0$, and define the local backward-Euler block $B_i:=\Delta t^{-1}M_i+A_i$. In coordinates $I_i\oplus\Lambda$, write

$$B_i=\begin{pmatrix}B_{i,00}&B_{i,0\Gamma}\\B_{i,\Gamma0}&B_{i,\Gamma\Gamma}\end{pmatrix},\qquad g_i=(g_{i,0},g_{i,\Gamma}).$$

For a prescribed local trace $\lambda_i$, solve the interior equation $B_{i,00}x_i+B_{i,0\Gamma}\lambda_i=g_{i,0}$ and define the outward algebraic interface flux $q_i:=B_{i,\Gamma0}x_i+B_{i,\Gamma\Gamma}\lambda_i-g_{i,\Gamma}$. Eliminating $x_i$ gives $q_i=S_i\lambda_i-f_i$, where $S_i:=B_{i,\Gamma\Gamma}-B_{i,\Gamma0}B_{i,00}^{-1}B_{i,0\Gamma}$ and $f_i:=g_{i,\Gamma}-B_{i,\Gamma0}B_{i,00}^{-1}g_{i,0}$. The sign convention is outward flux on each subdomain.

The monolithic interface equations are trace continuity $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\lambda$ and flux balance $q_1+q_2=0$, equivalently $(S_1+S_2)\lambda=f_1+f_2$. These finite-dimensional matrices represent a linear diffusion-transmission step; no nonlinear fluid-structure well-posedness is asserted.

derivations.claim: For $x\ne0$, $\langle Kx,x\rangle=\langle B(x,0),(x,0)\rangle>0$. Thus $K$ has zero kernel and is invertible because it is an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional space.

For fixed $z$, put $x_*=-K^{-1}Cz$. Expanding the quadratic form and completing the square gives $\langle B(x,z),(x,z)\rangle=\langle K(x-x_*),x-x_*\rangle+\langle(D-C^*K^{-1}C)z,z\rangle$. The first term is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at $x=x_*$, proving the minimum formula.

If $z\ne0$, then $(x_*,z)\ne0$, so positive definiteness of $B$ gives $\langle Sz,z\rangle=\langle B(x_*,z),(x_*,z)\rangle>0$. Hence $S$ is positive definite; applying this to each $B_i$ in [F1] proves the final claim.

derivations.claim: The interior rows of the two local blocks give their backward-Euler subdomain equations; after eliminating those rows, the common trace row is $q_1+q_2=0$ by the definition in [F1]. For a common trace $\lambda$, the paired interface work is therefore $\langle q_1,\lambda\rangle+\langle q_2,\lambda\rangle=\langle q_1+q_2,\lambda\rangle=0$; this cancellation uses the shared trace and outward-flux sign convention.

On $V$, the assembled bilinear form associated with $\Delta t^{-1}M_i+A_i$ is positive definite: for $v\in V\setminus\{0\}$, at least one $v_i\ne0$, and every corresponding summand $\Delta t^{-1}\langle M_iv_i,v_i\rangle+\langle A_iv_i,v_i\rangle$ is positive. Hence the finite-dimensional restricted operator has zero kernel and is invertible, so the variational step has a unique solution. Test the monolithic equation with $v=u^{n+1}$ and multiply by $\Delta t$. For each $i$, self-adjointness gives $2\langle M_i(u_i^{n+1}-u_i^n),u_i^{n+1}\rangle=\|u_i^{n+1}\|_{M_i}^2-\|u_i^n\|_{M_i}^2+\|u_i^{n+1}-u_i^n\|_{M_i}^2$. Summing this identity and retaining $\Delta t\sum_i\langle A_i u_i^{n+1},u_i^{n+1}\rangle$ yields the stated equality.
If $F_i^{n+1}=0$ for both subdomains, the right-hand side is zero and both the time-jump term and diffusion term on the left are nonnegative. Therefore $\|u^{n+1}\|_M^2\le\|u^n\|_M^2$.

$$\partial_t J(\xi,t)=J(\xi,t)\,\operatorname{div}_x w_m(A_t(\xi),t).$$

This is the continuous geometric conservation identity. It makes no discrete or time-integration claim.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, and suppose $Dg(x)$ is invertible for every $x\in U$. Let $K\subseteq U$ be compact and Jordan measurable. For a bounded function $f:g(K)\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is Riemann integrable on $g(K)$;
2. $x\mapsto f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|$ is Riemann integrable on $K$.

When either condition holds,
$$\int_{g(K)}f(y)\,dy=\int_K f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|\,dx.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

if its indicator $1_E$ is Riemann integrable on a fixed nondegenerate bounding
rectangle $Q$. In that case

$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its boundary $\partial E$ is null, equivalently has content zero.
A bounded real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable if and only if its discontinuity set is null.

derivations.claim: Put $\widehat K=\overline{\widehat\Omega}$, $K_t=A_t(\widehat K)=\overline{\Omega(t)}$, and let $B_t=\partial\Omega(t)$ and $\widehat B=\partial\widehat\Omega$. These boundaries are finite endpoint sets, hence compact. Covering each point by intervals of arbitrarily small total length shows that both have Jordan content zero and are compact Jordan sets. By [F10] the boundaries are null and the two open domains are Jordan measurable.

For any continuous $h$ on $K_t$, its zero extensions from $\Omega(t)$ and $K_t$ to a nondegenerate closed interval containing $K_t$ in its interior are bounded and can be discontinuous only at $B_t$. By [F11] they are integrable. Their difference is supported on $B_t$ and bounded in absolute value by a constant times $1_{B_t}$; [F8] gives $\int 1_{B_t}=0$, so [F7] shows their integrals agree. The same argument applies on $\widehat K$ and $\widehat\Omega$. The map image in [F3] is compact Jordan, and [F5] makes $g(\cdot,t)$ and $G(\cdot,t)$ integrable on the compact closures. Change of variables on those closures, followed by the open/closed equalities just proved, gives $I(t)=\int_{\widehat K}G(\xi,t)\,d\xi=\int_{\widehat\Omega}G(\xi,t)\,d\xi$, where $G(\xi,t):=g(A_t(\xi),t)J(\xi,t)$.

For small nonzero $h$, apply [F6] to $s\mapsto G(\xi,s)$ between $t$ and $t+h$. The difference quotient equals $\partial_tG(\xi,\theta_\xi)$ at an intermediate time. By [F9], $\partial_tG$ is uniformly continuous on $\widehat K$ times a compact time neighborhood of $t$, so these quotients converge uniformly in $\xi$ to $\partial_tG(\xi,t)$. The latter and each quotient are integrable on $\widehat K$ by [F5]; [F7] and [F8] bound the integral of their difference by its uniform norm times $\operatorname{cont}(\widehat K)$. Since $I(t)=\int_{\widehat K}G(\xi,t)\,d\xi$ by step 2.1, it follows that $I'(t)=\int_{\widehat K}\partial_tG(\xi,t)\,d\xi$.

The chain and product rules together with [F2] give $I'(t)=\int_{\widehat K}J(\partial_tg+\partial_xg\,w_m+g\,\partial_xw_m)(A_t(\xi),t)\,d\xi$. This integrand is continuous on the compact reference closure; [F3] changes variables on the compact closures, and step 2.1 converts the resulting physical-domain integrals to open-domain integrals. Thus $I'(t)=\int_{\Omega(t)}[\partial_tg+\partial_x(gw_m)](x,t)\,dx$.

The function $x\mapsto g(x,t)w_m(x,t)$ is differentiable on each compact image interval and its derivative is continuous, hence integrable there by [F5]. Apply [F4] to obtain $\int_{\alpha_j}^{\beta_j}\partial_x(gw_m)\,dx=g(\beta_j,t)w_m(\beta_j,t)-g(\alpha_j,t)w_m(\alpha_j,t)$. Summing right endpoints with normal $+1$ and left endpoints with normal $-1$ proves the boundary term. No choice axiom is used.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a time interval $[0,T]$ with $T>0$, and a nonempty bounded open reference domain $\widehat\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with compact Jordan closure; Jordan measurability means equality of finite-rectangle inner and outer contents ([[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]]). In dimension $d=1$, require $\widehat\Omega$ to be a finite union of bounded open intervals with pairwise disjoint closures. In dimensions $d\ge2$, require a finite piecewise-$C^1$ boundary presentation: a finite family of compact boundary faces $S_1,\ldots,S_q$ and a compact edge set $E$ such that the faces cover $\partial\widehat\Omega$, each face lies in a regular $C^1$ hypersurface patch, $S_i\cap E$ is surface-null, all face overlaps lie in $E$, and off $E$ the boundary is locally one $C^1$ graph with $\widehat\Omega$ on one side. The faces carry that side's outward unit normal.

An **ALE moving-domain map** is a map $A:[0,T]\times\overline{\widehat\Omega}\to\mathbb R^d$ whose space-time restriction extends to a $C^2$ map on a neighborhood of this set, and for each $t$ the map $A_t(\xi):=A(t,\xi)$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism on neighborhoods of the closures. Write $\Omega(t):=A_t(\widehat\Omega)$ and $J(\xi,t):=\det D_\xi A_t(\xi)>0$. Define the **mesh velocity** in physical coordinates by $w_m(x,t):=\partial_t A_t(A_t^{-1}(x))$. In $d=1$ the moving boundary consists of the transported interval endpoints. In $d\ge2$, require the transported faces under $A_t$ to satisfy the same finite piecewise-$C^1$ boundary-presentation conditions; the diffeomorphism carries the reference faces and edge set to that presentation, with the transported outward normal.

This definition fixes the regularity and sign conventions for the continuous ALE identities. It does not assert a discrete approximation property, a nonintersection theorem for a computed mesh, or well-posedness of a coupled PDE.

For the ALE moving-domain map $A_t$ of [[def-ale-moving-domain-map]], let $F(\xi,t):=D_\xi A_t(\xi)$ and $J(\xi,t):=\det F(\xi,t)$. Then

$$\partial_t J(\xi,t)=J(\xi,t)\,\operatorname{div}_x w_m(A_t(\xi),t).$$

This is the continuous geometric conservation identity. It makes no discrete or time-integration claim.

Under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of a nonempty bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, consists of compact faces $S_1,\ldots,S_q$ covering its boundary, each a compact Borel subset of a regular $C^1$ hypersurface patch, and a compact edge set $E\subset\partial\Omega$. Require $S_j\cap E$ to have surface measure zero in each face, using [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. E contains the boundaries of the faces relative to their patches and every overlap $S_i\cap S_j$, i different from j. At every point outside E the domain boundary is locally a single $C^1$ graph with Omega on one side. Each face carries this actual outward unit normal off E. Values assigned to the normal on E do not affect its integral.

For a specified finite gluing also list the open pieces with disjoint interiors, the shared faces, and their opposite outward normals. Require the pieces to cover the final domain up to their boundary faces, and the exposed faces to give its specified presentation. Internal faces are counted twice before cancellation, once from each side. The phrase piecewise smooth by itself supplies none of this data.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, and suppose $Dg(x)$ is invertible for every $x\in U$. Let $K\subseteq U$ be compact and Jordan measurable. For a bounded function $f:g(K)\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is Riemann integrable on $g(K)$;
2. $x\mapsto f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|$ is Riemann integrable on $K$.

When either condition holds,
$$\int_{g(K)}f(y)\,dy=\int_K f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|\,dx.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at

which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
