The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its indicator $1_E$ is Riemann integrable on a fixed nondegenerate bounding
rectangle $Q$. In that case
$$\int_Q1_E=\operatorname{cont}(E).$$

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its boundary $\partial E$ is null, equivalently has content zero.
A bounded real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable if and only if its discontinuity set is null.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $n\ge1$, let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]$ with $a_j<b_j$, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and Borel. If $f$ is Riemann integrable, then $f\in L^1(\lambda_n|_Q)$ and its Lebesgue and Riemann integrals agree.

derivations.claim: Put $\widehat K=\overline{\widehat\Omega}$, $K_t=A_t(\widehat K)=\overline{\Omega(t)}$, and let $B_t=\partial\Omega(t)$ and $\widehat B=\partial\widehat\Omega$. Cover each compact face in either finite boundary presentation by finitely many smaller regular $C^1$ graph charts with bounded base and bounded graph derivative. For a base grid of side $\delta$, each chart needs at most $C\delta^{-(d-1)}$ base cubes; the Lipschitz bound places each graph portion in an axis-parallel $d$-cube of side $C'\delta$. The total covering volume is at most $C''\delta$, which tends to zero. Since there are finitely many faces, both boundaries are compact Jordan sets of content zero. By [F11] they are null and the open domains are Jordan measurable; by the compact-image conclusion in [F4], $K_t$ is compact Jordan.

For any continuous $h$ on $K_t$, its zero extensions from $\Omega(t)$ and $K_t$ to a nondegenerate closed rectangle containing $K_t$ in its interior are bounded and have discontinuities only on $B_t$, a null set, so [F12] makes them integrable. Their difference is supported on $B_t$ and bounded in absolute value by a constant times $1_{B_t}$. By [F8], $\int 1_{B_t}=0$, and [F7] shows the two integrals agree. The same argument applies to $\widehat K$ and $\widehat\Omega$. By [F10], continuous integrands on the compact closures are integrable, so [F4] applies to the compact closures. Consequently, for $G(\xi,t):=g(A_t(\xi),t)J(\xi,t)$, $I(t):=\int_{\Omega(t)}g\,dx=\int_{\widehat K}G(\xi,t)\,d\xi=\int_{\widehat\Omega}G(\xi,t)\,d\xi$.

For small nonzero $h$, apply [F6] to $s\mapsto G(\xi,s)$ between $t$ and $t+h$. The difference quotient equals $\partial_tG(\xi,\theta_\xi)$ at an intermediate time. By [F9], $\partial_tG$ is uniformly continuous on $\widehat K$ times a compact time neighborhood of $t$, so these quotients converge uniformly in $\xi$ to $\partial_tG(\xi,t)$. The derivative and difference quotients are continuous on the compact Jordan set $\widehat K$, hence integrable by [F10]. [F7] and [F8] bound the integral of their difference by its uniform norm times $\operatorname{cont}(\widehat K)$. Since $I(t)=\int_{\widehat K}G(\xi,t)\,d\xi$ by step 2.1, $I'(t)=\int_{\widehat K}\partial_tG(\xi,t)\,d\xi$. The chain and product rules then give $I'(t)=\int_{\widehat K}J(\partial_tg+\nabla_xg\cdot w_m)+g\partial_tJ\,d\xi$.

Substitute [F2] into step 3.1 and use $\nabla_xg\cdot w_m+g\operatorname{div}_xw_m=\operatorname{div}_x(gw_m)$. The resulting integrand is continuous on the moving closure. Apply [F4] to the compact closures and use the open/closed integral equality from step 2.1 to obtain $I'(t)=\int_{\Omega(t)}(\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}_x(gw_m))\,dx$.

Set $f=\operatorname{div}_x(gw_m)$ and choose a nondegenerate closed box $Q$ containing $K_t$ in its interior. The field $gw_m$ is $C^1$ on the moving closure, so $f$ is continuous and bounded there. Its zero extension $\widetilde f$ from the open set $\Omega(t)$ to $Q$ is Borel: each strict superlevel is a relatively open subset of $\Omega(t)$, together with $Q\setminus\Omega(t)$ when the level is negative. Step 2.1 gives its Riemann integrability. By [A1] and [F13], its Riemann integral over $Q$ equals its Lebesgue integral, which is the Lebesgue integral of $f$ over $\Omega(t)$. Thus the Jordan volume integral in step 4.1 is exactly the volume integral used by [F5]. Apply [F5] to $gw_m$ on the finite piecewise-$C^1$ presentation [F3] to obtain $\int_{\Omega(t)}\operatorname{div}_x(gw_m)\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega(t)}gw_m\cdot n\,dS$. Substitution into step 4.1 proves the asserted identity. Countable Choice is used through [F5] and [F13].

Fix $N\ge1$, a reference cell width $\Delta\xi>0$, a time step $\Delta t>0$, and a physical period length $L>0$. Let $I_1,I_2$ and the common trace space $\Lambda$ be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, with $\dim\Lambda\ge1$, and set $X_i:=I_i\oplus\Lambda$. The trace map is $\gamma_i(x_i,\lambda_i)=\lambda_i$. Let $M_i$ and $A_i$ be self-adjoint positive-definite operators on $X_i$, let $\Delta t>0$, and define the local backward-Euler block $B_i:=\Delta t^{-1}M_i+A_i$. In coordinates $I_i\oplus\Lambda$, write

$$B_i=\begin{pmatrix}B_{i,00}&B_{i,0\Gamma}\\B_{i,\Gamma0}&B_{i,\Gamma\Gamma}\end{pmatrix},\qquad g_i=(g_{i,0},g_{i,\Gamma}).$$

For a prescribed local trace $\lambda_i$, solve the interior equation $B_{i,00}x_i+B_{i,0\Gamma}\lambda_i=g_{i,0}$ and define the outward algebraic interface flux $q_i:=B_{i,\Gamma0}x_i+B_{i,\Gamma\Gamma}\lambda_i-g_{i,\Gamma}$. Eliminating $x_i$ gives $q_i=S_i\lambda_i-f_i$, where $S_i:=B_{i,\Gamma\Gamma}-B_{i,\Gamma0}B_{i,00}^{-1}B_{i,0\Gamma}$ and $f_i:=g_{i,\Gamma}-B_{i,\Gamma0}B_{i,00}^{-1}g_{i,0}$. The sign convention is outward flux on each subdomain.

The monolithic interface equations are trace continuity $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\lambda$ and flux balance $q_1+q_2=0$, equivalently $(S_1+S_2)\lambda=f_1+f_2$. These finite-dimensional matrices represent a linear diffusion-transmission step; no nonlinear fluid-structure well-posedness is asserted.

Let $B=\begin{pmatrix}K&C\\C^*&D\end{pmatrix}$ be a self-adjoint positive-definite operator on a finite-dimensional real inner-product direct sum $I\oplus\Lambda$. Then $K$ is positive definite, $S:=D-C^*K^{-1}C$ is positive definite on $\Lambda$, and for every $z\in\Lambda$,

$$\langle Sz,z\rangle=\min_{x\in I}\langle B(x,z),(x,z)\rangle.$$

In particular, the local Schur operators $S_i$ in [[def-ale-linear-diffusion-transmission-model]] are positive definite.

**Inputs:** Positive-definite real Schur operators $S_1,S_2$ on the nonzero finite-dimensional trace space $\Lambda$, loads $f_1,f_2\in\Lambda$, a parameter $\alpha>0$, initial incoming datum $r_1^0\in\Lambda$, tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, and integer pass budget $M\ge1$.

All vector norms on $\Lambda$ and operator norms on its endomorphisms are induced by its specified real inner product. Set $R_i:=(\alpha I-S_i)(\alpha I+S_i)^{-1}$, $q_i:=\|R_i\|$, and $q:=q_1q_2$. For each pass $m=0,\ldots,M-1$, perform in order

$$ (S_1+\alpha I)\lambda_1^{m+1}=r_1^m+f_1,\quad r_2^{m+1}=(\alpha I-S_1)\lambda_1^{m+1}+f_1;\quad (S_2+\alpha I)\lambda_2^{m+1}=r_2^{m+1}+f_2,\quad r_1^{m+1}=(\alpha I-S_2)\lambda_2^{m+1}+f_2. $$

If $\|r_1^{m+1}-r_1^m\|\le (1-q)\varepsilon/\|(\alpha I+S_1)^{-1}\|$, return `converged` with trace $\lambda_1^{m+1}$ and pass count $m+1$. If all $M$ passes are used without this test succeeding, return `budget_exhausted` with the last trace $\lambda_1^M$ and pass count $M$. This procedure states the finite stop predicate but makes no claim about its error certificate.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

derivations.claim: For each $i$, $S_i+\alpha I$ is self-adjoint positive definite because $\langle(S_i+\alpha I)z,z\rangle=\langle S_i z,z\rangle+\alpha\|z\|^2>0$ for every $z\ne0$. It is therefore invertible on the finite-dimensional space $\Lambda$; its inverse and the operators $R_i$ have finite norms, and $\|(\alpha I+S_1)^{-1}\|>0$ because $\Lambda\ne\{0\}$. Each first solve uniquely determines $\lambda_1^{m+1}$, the first exchange uniquely determines $r_2^{m+1}$, the second solve uniquely determines $\lambda_2^{m+1}$, and the last exchange uniquely determines $r_1^{m+1}$. Since $M$ is finite, these operations define all passes up to $M$; the tests either return `converged` at the first pass that satisfies them or, if none does, return `budget_exhausted` with the last trace. Thus the algorithm is well-defined and terminates within its stated budget.

By [F1] and [F2], $S:=S_1+S_2$ is positive definite, so the monolithic trace $\lambda_*=S^{-1}(f_1+f_2)$ exists uniquely. Set $p_i^*:=S_i\lambda_*-f_i$; then $p_1^*+p_2^*=0$. Define $r_1^*:=\alpha\lambda_*+p_1^*$ and $r_2^*:=\alpha\lambda_*+p_2^*$.

The first Robin equation in [F3] is equivalent to $r_1=\alpha\lambda_1+p_1$, and its exchange is $r_2=\alpha\lambda_1-p_1$; the second equation and exchange have the same forms with indices 1 and 2 reversed. Since $p_2^*=-p_1^*$, the pair $(r_1^*,r_2^*)$ is unchanged by both exchanges, so $\lambda_*$ gives a fixed point.

Conversely, at any fixed point the two exchange equalities give $r_2=\alpha\lambda_1-p_1=\alpha\lambda_2+p_2$ and $r_1=\alpha\lambda_1+p_1=\alpha\lambda_2-p_2$. Adding the equalities for $r_2$ and $r_1$ yields $2\alpha(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)=0$, hence $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$; subtracting yields $p_1+p_2=0$. Thus the common trace solves the unique monolithic equation from step 1.2, proving the fixed point is unique.

By [F2] and [F4], in an orthonormal eigenbasis of $S_i$, $R_i$ has eigenvalues $(\alpha-\sigma)/(\alpha+\sigma)$ with $\sigma>0$. Each has absolute value strictly below $1$, so $q_i<1$. Subtracting the fixed-point equations from the iteration equations in [F3] gives $r_2^{m+1}-r_2^*=R_1(r_1^m-r_1^*)$ and then $r_1^{m+1}-r_1^*=R_2(r_2^{m+1}-r_2^*)$. Therefore the displayed error map holds and $q=q_1q_2<1$.

Put $e_m=r_1^m-r_1^*$ and $d_m=r_1^{m+1}-r_1^m$. The error map in step 3.1 gives $d_m=(R_2R_1-I)e_m$. Since $\|R_2R_1\|\le q<1$, the reverse triangle inequality yields $\|d_m\|\ge(1-q)\|e_m\|$. The first solve in [F3] gives $\lambda_1^{m+1}-\lambda_*=(\alpha I+S_1)^{-1}e_m$. Therefore the stop test in [F3] implies $\|\lambda_1^{m+1}-\lambda_*\|\le\|(\alpha I+S_1)^{-1}\|\,\|d_m\|/(1-q)\le\varepsilon$. If the finite pass budget is exhausted without this test, no trace certificate has been issued.

Expanding the flux difference in [F2] gives $J_i^{n+1}U_i'=\mu(c_{i-1/2}^n)^+U_{i-1}+[J_i^n-\mu((c_{i+1/2}^n)^+-(c_{i-1/2}^n)^-)]U_i-\mu(c_{i+1/2}^n)^-U_{i+1}$. Let $I_1,I_2$ and the common trace space $\Lambda$ be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, with $\dim\Lambda\ge1$, and set $X_i:=I_i\oplus\Lambda$. The trace map is $\gamma_i(x_i,\lambda_i)=\lambda_i$. Let $M_i$ and $A_i$ be self-adjoint positive-definite operators on $X_i$, let $\Delta t>0$, and define the local backward-Euler block $B_i:=\Delta t^{-1}M_i+A_i$. In coordinates $I_i\oplus\Lambda$, write

$$B_i=\begin{pmatrix}B_{i,00}&B_{i,0\Gamma}\\B_{i,\Gamma0}&B_{i,\Gamma\Gamma}\end{pmatrix},\qquad g_i=(g_{i,0},g_{i,\Gamma}).$$

For a prescribed local trace $\lambda_i$, solve the interior equation $B_{i,00}x_i+B_{i,0\Gamma}\lambda_i=g_{i,0}$ and define the outward algebraic interface flux $q_i:=B_{i,\Gamma0}x_i+B_{i,\Gamma\Gamma}\lambda_i-g_{i,\Gamma}$. Eliminating $x_i$ gives $q_i=S_i\lambda_i-f_i$, where $S_i:=B_{i,\Gamma\Gamma}-B_{i,\Gamma0}B_{i,00}^{-1}B_{i,0\Gamma}$ and $f_i:=g_{i,\Gamma}-B_{i,\Gamma0}B_{i,00}^{-1}g_{i,0}$. The sign convention is outward flux on each subdomain.

The monolithic interface equations are trace continuity $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\lambda$ and flux balance $q_1+q_2=0$, equivalently $(S_1+S_2)\lambda=f_1+f_2$. These finite-dimensional matrices represent a linear diffusion-transmission step; no nonlinear fluid-structure well-posedness is asserted.

Let $B=\begin{pmatrix}K&C\\C^*&D\end{pmatrix}$ be a self-adjoint positive-definite operator on a finite-dimensional real inner-product direct sum $I\oplus\Lambda$. Then $K$ is positive definite, $S:=D-C^*K^{-1}C$ is positive definite on $\Lambda$, and for every $z\in\Lambda$,

$$\langle Sz,z\rangle=\min_{x\in I}\langle B(x,z),(x,z)\rangle.$$

In particular, the local Schur operators $S_i$ in [[def-ale-linear-diffusion-transmission-model]] are positive definite.

Assume the finite-dimensional diffusion-transmission model of [[def-ale-linear-diffusion-transmission-model]]. Let $V:=\{(v_1,v_2)\in X_1\oplus X_2:\gamma_1v_1=\gamma_2v_2\}$ be the common-trace space, take $u^n\in V$, and let $F_i^{n+1}\in X_i$. In the block notation of the definition, set the local right-hand side to $g_i:=\Delta t^{-1}M_i u_i^n+F_i^{n+1}$; assemble the local equations with common trace and the outward algebraic fluxes $q_i$ from that definition. There is a unique $u^{n+1}\in V$ satisfying

$$\sum_{i=1}^2\left(\left\langle M_i\frac{u_i^{n+1}-u_i^n}{\Delta t},v_i\right\rangle+\langle A_i u_i^{n+1},v_i\rangle\right)=\sum_{i=1}^2\langle F_i^{n+1},v_i\rangle\qquad(v\in V).$$

It obeys the exact identity

$$\frac12\left(\|u^{n+1}\|_M^2-\|u^n\|_M^2+\|u^{n+1}-u^n\|_M^2\right)+\Delta t\|u^{n+1}\|_A^2=\Delta t\sum_{i=1}^2\langle F_i^{n+1},u_i^{n+1}\rangle,$$

where $\|v\|_M^2:=\sum_i\langle M_iv_i,v_i\rangle$ and $\|v\|_A^2:=\sum_i\langle A_iv_i,v_i\rangle$. In the unforced case the monolithic backward-Euler energy is nonincreasing.

**Inputs:** Positive-definite real Schur operators $S_1,S_2$ on the nonzero finite-dimensional trace space $\Lambda$, loads $f_1,f_2\in\Lambda$, a parameter $\alpha>0$, initial incoming datum $r_1^0\in\Lambda$, tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, and integer pass budget $M\ge1$.

All vector norms on $\Lambda$ and operator norms on its endomorphisms are induced by its specified real inner product. Set $R_i:=(\alpha I-S_i)(\alpha I+S_i)^{-1}$, $q_i:=\|R_i\|$, and $q:=q_1q_2$. For each pass $m=0,\ldots,M-1$, perform in order

$$ (S_1+\alpha I)\lambda_1^{m+1}=r_1^m+f_1,\quad r_2^{m+1}=(\alpha I-S_1)\lambda_1^{m+1}+f_1;\quad (S_2+\alpha I)\lambda_2^{m+1}=r_2^{m+1}+f_2,\quad r_1^{m+1}=(\alpha I-S_2)\lambda_2^{m+1}+f_2. $$

If $\|r_1^{m+1}-r_1^m\|\le (1-q)\varepsilon/\|(\alpha I+S_1)^{-1}\|$, return `converged` with trace $\lambda_1^{m+1}$ and pass count $m+1$. If all $M$ passes are used without this test succeeding, return `budget_exhausted` with the last trace $\lambda_1^M$ and pass count $M$. This procedure states the finite stop predicate but makes no claim about its error certificate.

Assume the model, positive Schur operators, and algorithm of [[def-ale-linear-diffusion-transmission-model]], [[lem-ale-schur-complement-positive-and-minimizes-energy]], and [[alg-ale-robin-robin-partitioned-iteration]], with $\alpha>0$. Every Robin solve in the algorithm exists uniquely, and for every admitted input it returns `converged` with the current first-subdomain trace on the first passing test, or returns `budget_exhausted` with $\lambda_1^M$ after at most $M$ passes. Let $\lambda_*$ be the unique monolithic trace solving $(S_1+S_2)\lambda_*=f_1+f_2$, and put $R_i=(\alpha I-S_i)(\alpha I+S_i)^{-1}$ and $q_i=\|R_i\|$, $q=q_1q_2$. Then $q<1$, the unique fixed point of the iteration corresponds exactly to $\lambda_*$, and the incoming-data error satisfies

$$r_1^{m+1}-r_1^*=R_2R_1(r_1^m-r_1^*),\qquad\|r_1^{m+1}-r_1^*\|\le q\|r_1^m-r_1^*\|.$$

If the algorithm's stop test succeeds at pass $m+1$, its returned trace satisfies $\|\lambda_1^{m+1}-\lambda_*\|\le\varepsilon$. A `budget_exhausted` return carries no such certificate.

derivations.claim: The local backward-Euler blocks are $B_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)$ and $B_2=\operatorname{diag}(1,1)$, which are positive definite. With zero off-diagonal blocks between the interior and trace coordinates, their Schur operators are $S_1=2$ and $S_2=1$, so [F2] applies.

On pass one, $\lambda_1^1=(2+1)/3=1$, $r_2^1=(1-2)1+1=0$, $\lambda_2^1=(0+5)/2=2.5$, and $r_1^1=(1-1)2.5+5=5$. Here $q_1=|(1-2)/(1+2)|=1/3$, $q_2=0$, and the stop threshold is $0.1/(1/3)=0.3$; the incoming-data change is $|5-2|=3$, so the algorithm does not stop.

The monolithic scalar equation is $3\lambda=6$, hence $\lambda_*=2$. Its fluxes are $q_1=2(2)-1=3$ and $q_2=1(2)-5=-3$, so they balance and the interface work $\lambda_*(q_1+q_2)$ vanishes as in [F3].

On pass two, $\lambda_1^2=(5+1)/3=2$, $r_2^2=(1-2)2+1=-1$, $\lambda_2^2=(-1+5)/2=2$, and $r_1^2=(1-1)2+5=5$. The incoming-data change is $0\le0.3$, so [F4] returns `converged` with trace $2$; [F5] certifies its error is at most $0.1$ relative to $\lambda_*=2$ from step 2.1.

For each integer $n\ge0$, define the Legendre polynomial
$$
P_n(x):=\frac{1}{2^n n!}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(x^2-1)^n,
$$
with $n!$ as in [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]] and repeated derivatives as in [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]]. Define the unweighted pairing of real polynomials by
$$
\langle p,q\rangle_L:=\int_{-1}^1p(x)q(x)\,dx,\qquad \|p\|_L^2:=\langle p,p\rangle_L.
$$
The integral is the ordinary integral of a continuous function; polynomial products are continuous and hence integrable by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]] and [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. The normalization and all polynomial identities needed for the orthogonal Galerkin scale are proved in [[lem-legendre-weighted-derivative-orthogonality-and-norm]].

For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn}, \qquad \int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]), and suppose

$$f(a) \;=\; f(b) .$$

Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with $f'(c) = 0$.

**Three hypotheses, three different jobs.** Continuity on the **closed**
interval is what the extreme value theorem consumes; differentiability on the
**open** interval is what Fermat's theorem consumes, and it is asked for
nowhere else; and $f(a) = f(b)$ is what forces the extremum inside when neither
extremum is attained in the interior. Continuity at the two endpoints cannot be
dropped, and a false statement later on this page records a witness for that.

**Differentiability is meant with respect to the domain $[a,b]$.** For $c$ in
the open interval that is the same condition as differentiability of any
restriction of $f$ to a subinterval around $c$, since only points near $c$
enter, but the phrase is fixed here so that the citation of
[[thm-fermat-interior-extremum]], whose hypothesis is interiority in the
domain, is exact.

derivations.claim: Suppose $P_p$ has only $m<p$ sign-changing roots $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ in $(-1,1)$ and set $q(x)=\prod_{j=1}^m(x-r_j)$, with $q=1$ if $m=0$. At each sign-changing root both $P_p$ and $q$ change sign, while at every other real root $P_p$ does not change sign; therefore $P_pq$ has one constant sign on $(-1,1)$ and is not identically zero. It is continuous and nonzero on some open interval, so its integral is nonzero. But $\deg q=m<p$, and [F2] gives $\int_{-1}^1P_pq=0$, a contradiction. Thus $P_p$ has at least $p$ sign-changing roots in the open interval.

A degree-$p$ polynomial cannot have more than $p$ distinct roots. The $p$ roots obtained in step 1.1 therefore exhaust its degree; each has multiplicity one and there are no other roots. Rolle's theorem [F3] between consecutive roots gives $p-1$ distinct roots of $P_p'$ in $(-1,1)$. Since $P_p'$ has degree $p-1$, these are all its roots and each is simple. None equals an endpoint, so adjoining $-1$ and $1$ gives $p+1$ distinct nodes, including the case $p=1$ where there are no interior critical points.

derivations.claim: Apply Leibniz's rule to the $n$th derivative in the definition. Every term differentiates $(1-t)^{n+d-1}$ at most $n$ times, so it contains a factor $(1-t)^{d-1}$. After division the result is a polynomial. The original factor has degree $2n+d-1$ and leading coefficient $(-1)^{n+d-1}$; differentiating $n$ times and dividing by the leading term $(-1)^{d-1}t^{d-1}$ of $(1-t)^{d-1}$ shows that $\phi_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $\binom{2n+d-1}{n}$. The coefficient of $t^n$ in $t^n(1-t)^{n+d-1}$ is $1$, so its $n$th derivative at zero is $n!$ and $\phi_n(0)=(-1)^n$.

If $r$ has degree below $n$, multiply the Rodrigues formula by $w_dr$ and integrate. Integrating by parts $n$ times is allowed by [A1] and gives $\int_0^1w_d(t)\phi_n(t)r(t)\,dt=\frac1{n!}\int_0^1t^n(1-t)^{n+d-1}r^{(n)}(t)\,dt=0$, because $r^{(n)}=0$. Thus $\phi_n$ is orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial, and the degree conclusion in step 1.1 makes the family an orthogonal basis of each polynomial space.

For nonnegative integers $a,b$, let $B(a,b)=\int_0^1t^a(1-t)^b\,dt$. The case $a=0$ gives $B(0,b)=1/(b+1)$; for $a\ge1$, integration by parts with $u=t^a$ and $dv=(1-t)^b\,dt$ gives $B(a,b)=aB(a-1,b+1)/(b+1)$. Iterating yields $B(a,b)=a!b!/(a+b+1)!$. Applying $n$ integrations by parts to the Rodrigues formula with $r(t)=t^n$ gives $\int_0^1w_d\phi_nt^n\,dt=B(n,n+d-1)=n!(n+d-1)!/(2n+d)!$. Since $t^n=\phi_n/\kappa_n+r$ for some $r$ of degree below $n$, where $\kappa_n=\binom{2n+d-1}{n}$, orthogonality gives $\|\phi_n\|_{L^2(w_d)}^2=\kappa_n B(n,n+d-1)=1/(2n+d)$.

Write $q=\sum_{n=0}^pc_n\phi_n$. By the endpoint and norm identities, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|q(0)|^2=\left|\sum_{n=0}^pc_n(-1)^n\right|^2\le\left(\sum_{n=0}^p(2n+d)\right)\left(\sum_{n=0}^p\frac{|c_n|^2}{2n+d}\right)=(p+1)(p+d)\|q\|_{L^2(w_d)}^2$. Equality is attained by the polynomial $K_p(t,0)=\sum_{n=0}^p(2n+d)(-1)^n\phi_n(t)$: its endpoint value and squared norm both equal $\sum_{n=0}^p(2n+d)=(p+1)(p+d)$. Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

For a finite sum $u=\sum u_n$, orthogonality gives $\|u-P_pu\|_{\mathcal H_\alpha^\ell}^2=\sum_{n>p}(1+\mu_n)^\ell\|u_n\|_\alpha^2\le(1+\mu_{p+1})^{\ell-m}\sum_{n>p}(1+\mu_n)^m\|u_n\|_\alpha^2$, because $\mu_n=n(n+d+|\alpha|)$ is increasing for $n\ge0$. Truncation is contractive in every coefficient norm $\mathcal H_\alpha^s$, and finite sums are dense by the definition of the completion. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn}, \qquad \int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.
For $a\le b$, every continuous real function on $[a,b]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

derivations.claim: Fix $k\ge1$ and put $w_k(x)=(1-x^2)^k$. For $n\ge k$, the polynomial $Q_{n,k}:=D^k(w_kD^kP_n)$ has degree $n$. Integrating by parts $k$ times moves the outer derivative block onto a polynomial $q$ and gives $\int Q_{n,k}q=(-1)^k\int w_kD^kP_nD^kq=\int P_nD^k(w_kD^kq)$; all boundary terms vanish because derivatives of $w_k$ of orders below $k$ vanish at both endpoints. The final polynomial paired with $P_n$ has degree at most $\deg q<n$, so [F1] makes the integral zero. The leading coefficient of $Q_{n,k}$ is $(-1)^k(n+k)!/(n-k)!$ times the leading coefficient of $P_n$. Orthogonality and the degree statement in [F1] therefore give $Q_{n,k}=(-1)^k\lambda_{n,k}P_n$, where $\lambda_{n,k}=(n+k)!/(n-k)!$.

For $n,m\ge k$, integrate by parts $k$ times and use step 1.1 to obtain $\int_{-1}^1w_kP_n^{(k)}P_m^{(k)}=(-1)^k\int_{-1}^1P_nD^k(w_kP_m^{(k)})=\lambda_{m,k}\int_{-1}^1P_nP_m.$ The first identity in [F1] makes this zero for $n\ne m$ and equal to $\lambda_{n,k}2/(2n+1)$ for $n=m$, proving the repeated derivative orthogonality formula.

Write $c_n=(f,P_n)_{L^2}/\|P_n\|_2^2$. The absolutely continuous representatives in [F3] justify $k$ integrations by parts; all boundary terms vanish because $w_k$ has endpoint zeros of order $k$. Step 1.1 then gives $\int_{-1}^1w_kf^{(k)}P_n^{(k)}=\lambda_{n,k}c_n\|P_n\|_2^2\qquad(n\ge k).$ The functions $w_k^{1/2}P_n^{(k)}$ are mutually orthogonal by step 2.1 and have squared norms $\lambda_{n,k}\|P_n\|_2^2$. Applying finite Bessel inequalities to $w_k^{1/2}f^{(k)}$ and then increasing the finite index set yields $\sum_{n\ge k}\lambda_{n,k}|c_n|^2\|P_n\|_2^2\le\int_{-1}^1w_k|f^{(k)}|^2\le\|f^{(k)}\|_2^2.$

Density [F2] and the best-approximation property of finite orthogonal projections imply $\Pi_Mf\to f$ in $L^2$: first approximate $f$ by a polynomial and then take $M$ at least its degree. Orthogonality [F1] and Pythagoras give $\|f-\Pi_Nf\|_2^2=\sum_{n>N}|c_n|^2\|P_n\|_2^2$. Since $\lambda_{n,k}$ increases for $n\ge k$, step 3.1 bounds this tail by $\lambda_{N+1,k}^{-1}\|f^{(k)}\|_2^2$, which is the stated factorial estimate. When $k=0$, the same finite Pythagoras identity directly gives contraction.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: For $0<\tau<1$ and integer $n\ge1$ define $B_{n,\tau}(t)=\sum_{j=\lceil n\tau\rceil}^n\binom njt^j(1-t)^{n-j}$. Then $0\le B\le1$, $\deg B\le n$, and $|B'|\le n$. If $t\le\tau-\delta$ for fixed $\delta>0$, Chernoff's bound follows directly from $1_{j\ge n\tau}\le e^{z(j-n\tau)}$ for $z>0$: $B_{n,\tau}(t)\le e^{-zn\tau}(1-t+te^z)^n.$ For sufficiently small fixed $z$, the exponent per $n$ is negative uniformly because its derivative at $z=0$ is $t-\tau\le-\delta$. Applying the same argument to the complementary lower tail gives exponential smallness of $1-B$ on $t\ge\tau+\delta$. Differentiation telescopes to one binomial atom times $n$; away from the threshold its probability is bounded by the same tail estimate with gap $\delta/2$ for all sufficiently large $n$, and increasing the constant covers the finitely many smaller $n$. Thus $B$ and $1-B$ switch from exponentially small to $1+O(e^{-cn})$ across a strip of fixed width, and their derivatives outside that strip are $O(ne^{-cn})$.

Choose $0<\rho<1/(32A)$ and a finite coordinate-grid cover of $S$ by boxes of radius $\rho$ with centers $a_i\in S$, $1\le i\le m$. In each coordinate form a left increasing binomial factor with threshold $a_{i,j}-3\rho/2$ and a right decreasing factor with threshold $a_{i,j}+3\rho/2$; omit the left factor when its threshold is at most zero and the right factor when its threshold is at least one. Their product $b_i$ has degree at most $4n$, lies in $[0,1]$, equals $1+O(e^{-cn})$ on the inner box of radius $\rho$ and its first derivatives there are $O(ne^{-cn})$; outside the outer box of radius $2\rho$ its value and first derivatives are $O(ne^{-cn})$. The omitted boundary factors require no suppression on a side where the outer box does not meet $S$.

Let $T_{i,s}$ be the total-degree-$s$ Taylor polynomial at $a_i$. When $a_i$ is on the boundary, take limits of interior centers; all derivatives extend continuously to $S$. On the intersection of the outer box and $S$, convexity keeps the Taylor segment inside the triangle, so [F1] and the multinomial formula give $|f-T_{i,s}|+|\nabla(f-T_{i,s})|\le CM(s+1)(4A\rho)^s\le CM2^{-s}$ after enlarging $C$ for small $s$. On all of $S$, the coefficient formula for $T_{i,s}$ gives $|T_{i,s}|+|\nabla T_{i,s}|\le CM(s+1)^2D^s$ for a fixed $D>1$ depending only on $A$.

Set $w_i=b_i\prod_{j<i}(1-b_j)$ and $w_0=\prod_{j\le m}(1-b_j)$. Then $\sum_{i=0}^m w_i=1$ and $0\le w_i\le1$. At every point of $S$ some inner box applies, so one factor $1-b_i$, together with its first derivatives, is exponentially small there; the product rule and $|b_j'|\le Cn$ give $\|w_0\|_{W^{1,\infty}(S)}\le Cne^{-cn}$. Outside the outer box for a fixed $i$, the same product rule gives $|w_i|+|\nabla w_i|\le Cne^{-cn}$.

Put $q=\sum_{i=1}^m w_iT_{i,s}$. Since $f-q=w_0f+\sum_iw_i(f-T_{i,s})$, the near-box and far-box bounds of steps 3.1 and 3.2 give $\|f-q\|_{W^{1,\infty}(S)}\le CM\{n2^{-s}+n(s+1)^2D^se^{-cn}\}.$ Choose fixed $\varepsilon>0$ with $\varepsilon\le1$ and $\varepsilon\log D<c/2$, and let $s=\lfloor\varepsilon n\rfloor$. Then the right side is at most $CM e^{-b_0n}$. Each $w_i$ has degree at most $4mn$, so $q$ has total degree at most $4mn+s\le(4m+1)n$. Choose $n=\lfloor p/(4m+1)\rfloor$; for the finitely many $p$ with $n=0$, the zero polynomial and an enlarged constant handle the claim. This proves the exponential estimate for every $p\ge1$.

On the interval let $P$ be the $L^2$ orthogonal projection of $f'$ onto $\mathbb P_{p-1}$ and put $J_pf(t)=f(0)+\int_0^tP(s)ds$. The positive-definite finite polynomial Gram matrix gives a unique projection; Pythagoras gives $\|P\|_2\le\|f'\|_2$ and $\|f'-P\|_2\le\|f'-r\|_2$ for every $r\in\mathbb P_{p-1}$. Orthogonality to constants gives $\int_0^1P=\int_0^1f'$, and [F4] evaluates the latter as $f(1)-f(0)$. Thus $J_pf(1)=f(0)+\int_0^1P=f(1)$, while $J_pf(0)=f(0)$ by construction. The derivatives of $f'$ satisfy a factorial bound with fixed constants $M'=MA$ and $A'=2A$, since $(j+1)!\le2^j j!$ for $j\ge1$. For $p\ge2$, apply step 4.1 to $f'$ with degree $p-1$; best approximation of the $L^2$ projection then gives $\|f'-P\|_2\le CMe^{-b(p-1)}$, which is at most $C'Me^{-b'p}$ after changing constants. For $p=1$, the derivative contraction and the bound $\|f'\|_2\le MA$ give the same asserted estimate after enlarging $C'$. Finally $f-J_pf=\int_0^t(f'-P)$ and [F2] bounds its $L^2$ norm by $\|f'-P\|_2$. The derivative and value bounds prove the stated interval estimate.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

An **$L^1$ approximate identity** on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a family
$(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of functions in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where

$$\|K_\varepsilon\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx,$$

such that:

1. $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} K_\varepsilon(x)\,dx = 1$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$;
2. there is $M < \infty$ with $\|K_\varepsilon\|_1 \le M$ for every
   $\varepsilon > 0$;
3. for every $\delta > 0$,
   $$ \int_{|x|>\delta} |K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

This is the general notion used later for both compactly supported mollifiers
and the Gaussian family.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

derivations.claim: On the unit square, for smooth $v$ the one-dimensional identity $|g(t)|\le\int_0^1|g(s)|ds+\int_0^1|g'(s)|ds$ applied first in $x$ and then in $y$ gives $\|v\|_\infty\le\|v\|_{L^1}+\|v_x\|_{L^1}+\|v_y\|_{L^1}+\|v_{xy}\|_{L^1}\le\sum_{i,j=0}^1\|\partial_x^i\partial_y^jv\|_{L^2}$ by [F2]. For $v\in H^2((0,1)^2)$ extend across $x=0$ by $Ev(x,y)=3v(-x,y)-2v(-2x,y)$ for small $x<0$, and across $x=1$ by $Ev(x,y)=3v(2-x,y)-2v(3-2x,y)$ for small $x>1$; use the same two formulas in $y$. The coefficients satisfy $3-2=1$ for values and $-3+4=1$ for first normal derivatives. For a smooth test $\phi$ across $x=0$, changing variables in the zeroth-order pairing gives $\psi_0(t)=\phi(t)-3\phi(-t)+2\phi(-t/2)$, so $\psi_0(0)=0$. For the first normal derivative, the corresponding test combination is $\psi_1(t)=\phi(t)+3\phi(-t)-4\phi(-t/2)$, also with $\psi_1(0)=0$. These formulas follow by rewriting the reflected integrals over $t>0$ and applying the chain rule. Multiply each combined test by a cutoff that is zero on $(0,\varepsilon)$ and one on $(2\varepsilon,\infty)$ before using the weak derivative identity on the original open square. If $|\chi_\varepsilon\prime|\le C/\varepsilon$, then $|\psi_j\chi_\varepsilon\prime|\le C$ on the strip because $\psi_j(t)=O(t)$; for any relevant $g\in L^2$, Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the cutoff error by $C\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\|g\|_{L^2(0,2\varepsilon)}\le C\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\|g\|_{L^2(0,1)}\to0$. Thus the reflected piecewise formulas are the weak derivatives through order two, including mixed derivatives. Changes of variables bound each derivative norm by a fixed multiple of $\|v\|_{H^2}$. Reflect successively across the four sides, cut off in the enlarged square, and mollify. For every weak derivative through order two, inserting a translated compactly supported kernel into its weak derivative identity gives $D^\alpha(v*\varphi_\varepsilon)=(D^\alpha v)*\varphi_\varepsilon$ on the original square: the sign from integration by parts cancels the sign from differentiating the kernel in its integration variable. Thus [F3] gives smooth approximants converging in $H^2$. The smooth inequality makes them uniformly Cauchy, yielding a continuous representative and the same bound for every $H^2$ class. Scaling gives $\|v\|_{L^\infty(Q)}\le C(r^{-1}\|v\|_2+\|Dv\|_2+r\|D^2v\|_2)$ on a rectangle of side comparable to $r$; a parallelogram with fixed aspect ratio has the same estimate after an affine change of variables.

Let $d\ge2$ and let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh of a bounded polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ in the sense of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. A **degree map** is a function $p:\mathcal T\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite values. The broken simplex space associated with $(\mathcal T,p)$ is
$$
V^{\mathrm{br}}(\mathcal T,p):=\{v\in L^2(\Omega):v|_K\in\mathbb P_{p_K}(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\},
$$
where $p_K:=p(K)$ and $\mathbb P_m(K)$ denotes restrictions of real polynomials of total degree at most $m$. Its **conforming hp space** is the subspace of functions whose two polynomial traces agree on every interior facet. The zero-boundary hp space further requires the polynomial trace to vanish on every boundary facet. For an interior facet $F=K\cap K'$, its trace degree is $p_F:=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$; equality of the two traces means that their common polynomial belongs to $\mathbb P_{p_F}(F)$.

A **matching affine tensor-box mesh** is a finite face-to-face partition of a bounded polytope into affine images of $[-1,1]^d$, with pairwise disjoint interiors. For a scalar degree $p_K$ on each box, the local tensor space is $\mathbb Q_{p_K}(K)$, the pullback of polynomials of degree at most $p_K$ in each reference coordinate. The conforming box hp space is defined by equality of polynomial traces across every shared face, and its zero-boundary subspace by zero traces on the exterior faces. For a shared face $F=K\cap K'$, set $p_F=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$; its common trace lies in $\mathbb Q_{p_F}(F)$ in tangential reference coordinates. This definition of tensor boxes does not include curved or non-affine cells.

On either mesh, **h-refinement** replaces one cell by a finite matching partition of that cell and assigns degrees to the children; **p-refinement** raises at least one cell degree while leaving the mesh fixed; **hp-refinement** performs both operations. A local polynomial basis is **hierarchical** if its ordered degree layers span the nested spaces $\mathbb P_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb P_p$ (or $\mathbb Q_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb Q_p$), with each new layer extending the preceding span. For example, pullbacks of reference monomials $\widehat x^\nu$ ordered by $|\nu|$ give such a basis for $\mathbb P_p$, and tensor monomials $\xi^\nu$ ordered by $\max_i\nu_i$ give one for $\mathbb Q_p$. This basis convention does not assert stability of a particular basis or projector.

derivations.claim: On a triangle, monomials $x^iy^j$ with $i,j\ge0$ and $i+j\le p_k$ form a basis of $\mathbb P_{p_k}$. Counting by total degree gives $\dim\mathbb P_{p_k}=\sum_{r=0}^{p_k}(r+1)=(p_k+1)(p_k+2)/2$.

The broken product over $\mathcal T_k$ therefore has dimension $\#\mathcal T_k(p_k+1)(p_k+2)/2$. By [F1], trace matching and any zero-boundary conditions define a linear subspace, whose dimension cannot exceed the broken dimension. Using $\#\mathcal T_k\le C_0k$ and $p_k\le C_1k$, and $k\ge1$, gives $N_k\le C_0k(C_1k+1)(C_1k+2)/2\le C_2k^3$ for an explicit finite $C_2$ depending only on $C_0,C_1$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh of a bounded
polyhedral open set $\Omega$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let $v$ be a
real-valued scalar member of the conforming piecewise-polynomial space in
[[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]]. Then $v\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$.
Its weak gradient agrees almost everywhere on each cell with the ordinary
cellwise polynomial gradient.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

derivations.claim: If the mesh is empty, its domain is empty by the mesh convention and the assertion is immediate. Otherwise, because the mesh and every local degree are finite, $v$ and each cellwise first derivative $g_i:=\partial_i(v|_K)$ are bounded on each closed cell; a finite union then puts $v,g_i$ in $L^2(\Omega)$. If the mesh is simplicial, set $p_*=\max_{K\in\mathcal T}p_K$. Every restriction lies in $\mathbb P_{p_*}(K)$, and the trace-matching condition is unchanged. Applying [F2] at the single degree $p_*$ proves the claim on this branch.

Suppose the cells are affine tensor boxes. Fix a coordinate $i$. On each cell, apply [F3] to the smooth field $v\varphi e_i$; its divergence is $v\,\partial_i\varphi+g_i\varphi$. Sum the finitely many resulting identities. At an interior face the two outward normals are opposite, because the adjacent cell interiors lie on opposite sides of its supporting hyperplane; the common trace in [F1] therefore makes the two fluxes cancel. The boundary-face terms vanish since $\varphi$ has compact support in $\Omega$. Thus $\int_\Omega v\,\partial_i\varphi=-\int_\Omega g_i\varphi$.

By [F4], step 1.2 says that $g_i$ is the weak $i$th derivative of $v$. This holds for every coordinate $i$, and step 1.1 supplies $v,g_i\in L^2$; hence $v\in H^1(\Omega)$ with the stated cellwise weak gradient. Together with the simplex branch of step 1.1 this proves the assertion for both mesh types.

Let $d\ge2$ and let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh of a bounded polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ in the sense of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. A **degree map** is a function $p:\mathcal T\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite values. The broken simplex space associated with $(\mathcal T,p)$ is
$$
V^{\mathrm{br}}(\mathcal T,p):=\{v\in L^2(\Omega):v|_K\in\mathbb P_{p_K}(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\},
$$
where $p_K:=p(K)$ and $\mathbb P_m(K)$ denotes restrictions of real polynomials of total degree at most $m$. Its **conforming hp space** is the subspace of functions whose two polynomial traces agree on every interior facet. The zero-boundary hp space further requires the polynomial trace to vanish on every boundary facet. For an interior facet $F=K\cap K'$, its trace degree is $p_F:=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$; equality of the two traces means that their common polynomial belongs to $\mathbb P_{p_F}(F)$.

A **matching affine tensor-box mesh** is a finite face-to-face partition of a bounded polytope into affine images of $[-1,1]^d$, with pairwise disjoint interiors. For a scalar degree $p_K$ on each box, the local tensor space is $\mathbb Q_{p_K}(K)$, the pullback of polynomials of degree at most $p_K$ in each reference coordinate. The conforming box hp space is defined by equality of polynomial traces across every shared face, and its zero-boundary subspace by zero traces on the exterior faces. For a shared face $F=K\cap K'$, set $p_F=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$; its common trace lies in $\mathbb Q_{p_F}(F)$ in tangential reference coordinates. This definition of tensor boxes does not include curved or non-affine cells.

On either mesh, **h-refinement** replaces one cell by a finite matching partition of that cell and assigns degrees to the children; **p-refinement** raises at least one cell degree while leaving the mesh fixed; **hp-refinement** performs both operations. A local polynomial basis is **hierarchical** if its ordered degree layers span the nested spaces $\mathbb P_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb P_p$ (or $\mathbb Q_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb Q_p$), with each new layer extending the preceding span. For example, pullbacks of reference monomials $\widehat x^\nu$ ordered by $|\nu|$ give such a basis for $\mathbb P_p$, and tensor monomials $\xi^\nu$ ordered by $\max_i\nu_i$ give one for $\mathbb Q_p$. This basis convention does not assert stability of a particular basis or projector.

For $p\ge1$ and $g\in L^2(-1,1)$, define the degree-$(p-1)$ Legendre orthogonal projection
$$
\Pi_{p-1}g:=\sum_{n=0}^{p-1}\frac{2n+1}{2}\left(\int_{-1}^1g(t)P_n(t)\,dt\right)P_n.
$$
For $c\in\mathbb R$, define the endpoint-anchored integrated projector
$$
\mathcal I_p(c,g)(x):=c+\int_{-1}^x\Pi_{p-1}g(t)\,dt,\qquad -1\le x\le1.
$$
If an absolutely continuous function $f$ is represented as $f(x)=f(-1)+\int_{-1}^xf'(t)\,dt$ with $f'\in L^2$, write $I_pf:=\mathcal I_p(f(-1),f')$. The finite sum and integral are defined for every such input; no choice axiom is used in this definition.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the closed interval between $c$ and $x$, and define
$P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(c)(t-c)^j/j!$. If $x\ne c$, there is a point
$\xi$ strictly between $c$ and $x$ such that
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}(x-c)^{n+1}.
$$
For $x=c$, the remainder is zero.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn}, \qquad \int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Assume Countable Choice. On a finite matching affine simplicial mesh or a finite face-to-face affine tensor-box mesh, a piecewise polynomial scalar function whose two traces agree on every interior facet belongs to $H^1(\Omega)$, and its weak gradient equals its ordinary cellwise polynomial gradient almost everywhere. The simplex degrees may vary by cell; the box degrees may also vary.

derivations.claim: On the reference cube define $I_p^{(j)}$ by applying [F2] in coordinate $j$, holding all other coordinates fixed, and put $\mathcal I_p=I_p^{(1)}\cdots I_p^{(d)}$. Each factor maps degree-at-most-$p$ polynomials in its coordinate to the same degree space, so $\mathcal I_p\widehat u_K\in\mathbb Q_p$. Fix a smooth one-dimensional section $f$ and write $g=f'$. By [F6], $f(x)-f(-1)$ is the Riemann integral of $g$ from $-1$ to $x$; [F7] identifies it with the Lebesgue integral used in [F2] and the coefficient formula [F2] (applied to the continuous products $gP_n$). Orthogonality [F5] makes the constant coefficient exact, so $I_pf$ preserves both endpoints. The bound $|f(-1)|\le2^{-1/2}\|f\|_{L^2}+\sqrt2\|f'\|_{L^2}$ follows by averaging $f(x)=f(-1)+\int_{-1}^xf'$ over $x$ and applying Cauchy–Schwarz [F4, F7]; together with $\|\Pi_{p-1}f'\|_2\le\|f'\|_2$ this gives $\|I_pf\|_{L^2}+\|(I_pf)'\|_{L^2}\le C\|f\|_{H^1}$ uniformly in $p$. Also, if an absolutely continuous $w$ vanishes at $-1$, then $w(x)=\int_{-1}^xw'$ and Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] gives $\|w\|_{L^2}\le2\|w'\|_{L^2}$.

Fix $j$ and a subset $S$ of the coordinate indices. If $j\in S$, then $\partial_S(I_p^{(j)}-I)\widehat u_K=(\Pi_{p-1}^{(j)}-I)\partial_j\partial_{S\setminus\{j\}}\widehat u_K$. If $j\notin S$, then $\partial_S(I_p^{(j)}-I)\widehat u_K=(I_p^{(j)}-I)\partial_S\widehat u_K$, whose $j$ derivative is $(\Pi_{p-1}^{(j)}-I)\partial_j\partial_S\widehat u_K$ and whose value at $-1$ is zero. Thus in either case the error is controlled by the Legendre projection tail of $g=\partial_j\partial_T\widehat u_K$, where $T=S\setminus\{j\}$ in the first case and $T=S$ in the second. Write $r=|T|\le d-1$ and let $T_{p-1}$ be its Taylor polynomial at zero through degree $p-1$. Taylor's Lagrange remainder [F3] bounds $|g-T_{p-1}|$ on $[-1,1]$ by $M(p+r+1)!R^{-p-r-1}/p!$. Orthogonality of $\Pi_{p-1}^{(j)}$ gives $\|g-T_{p-1}\|_2^2=\|g-\Pi_{p-1}^{(j)}g\|_2^2+\|\Pi_{p-1}^{(j)}g-T_{p-1}\|_2^2$, so the projection error is at most $\sqrt2 M(p+r+1)!R^{-p-r-1}/p!$. For fixed $d,R,q$ this is at most $C_{d,R,q}M q^p$: the factorial ratio is bounded by a fixed-degree polynomial in $p$, while $(Rq)^{-p}$ decays geometrically. Anchoring at $-1$ and the one-dimensional Poincare estimate from step 1.1 use [F6, F7] for the continuous error derivative and give the same bound for each mixed derivative of $(I_p^{(j)}-I)\widehat u_K$.

The estimate in step 1.1 is stable in every mixed derivative: if a mixed derivative includes coordinate $j$, differentiating $I_p^{(j)}$ there gives the contractive projection $\Pi_{p-1}^{(j)}$; if it omits $j$, the one-dimensional $H^1$ bound in step 1.1 controls the application of $I_p^{(j)}$ using that derivative and its additional $j$ derivative. Summing over the finitely many subsets $S$ gives $\|I_p^{(j)}f\|_{\mathrm{mix}}\le C_d\|f\|_{\mathrm{mix}}$ uniformly in $p$. The telescoping identity $\mathcal I_p-I=\sum_{j=1}^d I_p^{(1)}\cdots I_p^{(j-1)}(I_p^{(j)}-I)$ and step 2.1 now imply $\|\widehat u_K-\mathcal I_p\widehat u_K\|_{H^1([-1,1]^d)}\le C_{d,R,q}M q^p$.

The one-dimensional projector preserves both endpoints. It commutes with reflection: both the reflected polynomial and the projection of the reflected function have the same derivative, since reflection preserves the polynomial subspace and the $L^2$ inner product, and they have the same value at the left endpoint by preservation of the right endpoint. Coordinate projectors commute under coordinate permutations. On a shared box face the relative affine parameter map is an affine automorphism of the reference cube face: it permutes the supporting facet hyperplanes and preserves their vertices, so its linear part is a signed coordinate permutation. Thus the restrictions of the transported tensor projectors are the same tangential projector applied to the common trace of $u$, and the resulting cell traces match. The conformity result [F8] gives $u_p\in H^1(\Omega)$; since $u\in H^1(\Omega)$, the local estimates sum to the stated global $H^1$ estimate. Scaling from each reference cell to its physical affine box multiplies the local estimate by a fixed cell-dependent factor; the mesh has finitely many cells, so taking the largest factor gives the global constant $C_{\mathcal T,d,R,q}$.

For $p\ge1$ and $g\in L^2(-1,1)$, define the degree-$(p-1)$ Legendre orthogonal projection
$$
\Pi_{p-1}g:=\sum_{n=0}^{p-1}\frac{2n+1}{2}\left(\int_{-1}^1g(t)P_n(t)\,dt\right)P_n.
$$
For $c\in\mathbb R$, define the endpoint-anchored integrated projector
$$
\mathcal I_p(c,g)(x):=c+\int_{-1}^x\Pi_{p-1}g(t)\,dt,\qquad -1\le x\le1.
$$
If an absolutely continuous function $f$ is represented as $f(x)=f(-1)+\int_{-1}^xf'(t)\,dt$ with $f'\in L^2$, write $I_pf:=\mathcal I_p(f(-1),f')$. The finite sum and integral are defined for every such input; no choice axiom is used in this definition.

For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn}, \qquad \int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.

For $s\ge0$, define $H_L^s$ as the completion of finite Legendre sums $p=\sum_{n=0}^Mc_nP_n$ in the coefficient norm
$$
\|p\|_{H_L^s}^2=\sum_{n=0}^M(1+n(n+1))^s\frac{2}{2n+1}|c_n|^2.
$$
The coefficients are unique because the polynomials have distinct degrees by [[lem-legendre-weighted-derivative-orthogonality-and-norm]]. At $s=0$ this norm is exactly the unweighted $L^2([-1,1])$ norm on finite sums, by the same lemma; its completion is denoted $L_L^2$. Define the degree-$N$ orthogonal projection on finite sums by
$$
\Pi_Nu=\sum_{n=0}^Nc_nP_n.
$$
It extends to the coefficient completion by truncation. This explicitly coefficient-defined scale uses the Legendre weight $1$ on $[-1,1]$; no equivalence with an unweighted derivative-based Sobolev norm is asserted here.

For fixed $s\ge0$, $x\mapsto x^s$ is nondecreasing on $(0,\infty)$: its derivative is $s x^{s-1}\ge0$ by [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]] and real powers are positive by [[def-real-power]] and [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], so the mean-value theorem [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] applies. Thus the spectral factors $(1+n(n+1))^s$ are positive and nondecreasing with $n$; the full weights $w_n$ below need not be nondecreasing.

For $w_n=(1+n(n+1))^s\frac{2}{2n+1}>0$, the coefficient map $(c_n)\mapsto(\sqrt{w_n}c_n)$ is an isometry onto real $\ell^2$. Thus the coefficient model of $H_L^s$ is exactly
$$\left\{(c_n)_{n\ge0}:\sum_{n\ge0}(1+n(n+1))^s\frac{2}{2n+1}|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
Finite-support sequences are dense by truncation, and completeness of $\ell^2$ from [[lem-square-summable-sequences-form-a-hilbert-space]] makes this the completion.

Let $s\ge0$, $N\ge0$, and $u=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nP_n\in H_L^s$ from [[def-legendre-weighted-sobolev-scale]]. Then
$$
\|u-\Pi_Nu\|_{L_L^2}\le(1+(N+1)(N+2))^{-s/2}\|u\|_{H_L^s}.
$$
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.
For $a\le b$, every continuous real function on $[a,b]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

derivations.claim: By [F2], finite Legendre sums span all polynomials. The density facts [F8] and [F9] imply that polynomials are dense in $L^2(-1,1)$: first approximate an $L^2$ class by a compactly supported smooth function, then approximate that function uniformly on $[-1,1]$ by a polynomial. The coefficient norm at $s=0$ is the ordinary $L^2$ norm on finite Legendre sums by [F2]–[F3], and [F10] makes $L^2(-1,1)$ complete. Hence the identity on finite sums extends to an isometry from $H_L^0$ onto $L^2(-1,1)$. Since each spectral weight for $s\ge0$ is at least its $s=0$ weight, [F3] gives a continuous embedding $H_L^s\to H_L^0$. Thus $g$ has the canonical $L^2$ class in the Statement, and Cauchy–Schwarz [F7] on the interval of length two gives $g\in L^1$. Then [F5] makes $u$ absolutely continuous. The definition [F1] makes $I_pu$ the integral of a polynomial of degree at most $p-1$, hence a degree-at-most-$p$ polynomial. By the finite projection formula in [F1] and Legendre orthogonality [F2], $g-\Pi_{p-1}g$ is orthogonal to constants, so $\int\Pi_{p-1}g=\int g$ and the endpoint values agree. The primitive defining $I_pu$ is absolutely continuous by [F5].

Apply [F6] to the two primitives in step 1.1; their a.e. derivatives are $g$ and $\Pi_{p-1}g$, so $e=u-I_pu$ has derivative $e'=g-\Pi_{p-1}g$. By [F3] the finite projection is the truncation in [F1]; the tail estimate [F4] with $N=p-1$ gives $\|e'\|_{L^2}\le(1+p(p+1))^{-s/2}\|g\|_{H_L^s}$. Since $e(-1)=0$, $e(x)=\int_{-1}^xe'(t)\,dt$; Cauchy–Schwarz [F7] and integration over an interval of length two give $\|e\|_{L^2}\le2\|e'\|_{L^2}$. Therefore $\|e\|_{H^1}^2=\|e\|_{L^2}^2+\|e'\|_{L^2}^2\le5\|e'\|_{L^2}^2$, proving the estimate.

For an integer $d\ge1$, put $w_d(t)=(1-t)^{d-1}$ on $[0,1]$ and, for $n\ge0$, define
$$\phi_n(t):=\frac{(-1)^n}{n!}(1-t)^{-(d-1)}\frac{d^n}{dt^n}\bigl(t^n(1-t)^{n+d-1}\bigr).$$
The quotient extends to a polynomial of degree $n$. These polynomials are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2(w_d\,dt)$, with
$$\phi_n(0)=(-1)^n,\qquad \operatorname{lc}(\phi_n)=\binom{2n+d-1}{n},\qquad \int_0^1w_d\phi_n^2\,dt=\frac1{2n+d}.$$
Consequently, for every $p\ge0$ the squared norm of endpoint evaluation $q\mapsto q(0)$ on $\mathbb P_p([0,1])$ with this weighted $L^2$ norm is exactly $(p+1)(p+d)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $d\ge2$ and let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh of a bounded polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ in the sense of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. A **degree map** is a function $p:\mathcal T\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite values. The broken simplex space associated with $(\mathcal T,p)$ is
$$
V^{\mathrm{br}}(\mathcal T,p):=\{v\in L^2(\Omega):v|_K\in\mathbb P_{p_K}(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\},
$$
where $p_K:=p(K)$ and $\mathbb P_m(K)$ denotes restrictions of real polynomials of total degree at most $m$. Its **conforming hp space** is the subspace of functions whose two polynomial traces agree on every interior facet. The zero-boundary hp space further requires the polynomial trace to vanish on every boundary facet. For an interior facet $F=K\cap K'$, its trace degree is $p_F:=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$; equality of the two traces means that their common polynomial belongs to $\mathbb P_{p_F}(F)$.

A **matching affine tensor-box mesh** is a finite face-to-face partition of a bounded polytope into affine images of $[-1,1]^d$, with pairwise disjoint interiors. For a scalar degree $p_K$ on each box, the local tensor space is $\mathbb Q_{p_K}(K)$, the pullback of polynomials of degree at most $p_K$ in each reference coordinate. The conforming box hp space is defined by equality of polynomial traces across every shared face, and its zero-boundary subspace by zero traces on the exterior faces. For a shared face $F=K\cap K'$, set $p_F=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$; its common trace lies in $\mathbb Q_{p_F}(F)$ in tangential reference coordinates. This definition of tensor boxes does not include curved or non-affine cells.

On either mesh, **h-refinement** replaces one cell by a finite matching partition of that cell and assigns degrees to the children; **p-refinement** raises at least one cell degree while leaving the mesh fixed; **hp-refinement** performs both operations. A local polynomial basis is **hierarchical** if its ordered degree layers span the nested spaces $\mathbb P_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb P_p$ (or $\mathbb Q_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb Q_p$), with each new layer extending the preceding span. For example, pullbacks of reference monomials $\widehat x^\nu$ ordered by $|\nu|$ give such a basis for $\mathbb P_p$, and tensor monomials $\xi^\nu$ ordered by $\max_i\nu_i$ give one for $\mathbb Q_p$. This basis convention does not assert stability of a particular basis or projector.

derivations.claim: Fix $y\in F$ and let $q_y(t)=v((1-t)y+ta)$. This is a polynomial of degree at most $p$ in $t$, and $q_y(0)=v(y)$. In the map $(y,t)\mapsto(1-t)y+ta$, each tangent direction in $F$ is scaled by $1-t$, while the remaining component is the altitude $H_F$; hence the absolute volume Jacobian is $H_F(1-t)^{d-1}$, as stated in [F2]. The cellwise normal derivative $\partial_n v=n_F\cdot\nabla v$ is a polynomial of degree at most $p-1$. If $p=0$ it is zero. If $p\ge1$, repeat step 1.1 with degree $m=p-1$; the endpoint factor becomes $p(p+d-1)$.
