derivations.claim: Fix a component $q\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, a test function $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and a coordinate $j$. The finite physical partition and face-equality convention are those of [F1]. On each cell $K$, the vector field $G_K:=v_q\phi e_j$ is $C^1$ up to the cell boundary. By [F3], $\int_K v_q\,\partial_j\phi+\partial_jv_q\,\phi=\int_{\partial K}v_q\phi\,n_{K,j}\,dS.$ Summing this identity over the finitely many cells is legitimate because both volume terms are integrable by the hypotheses and [F4]. On a shared face the two normal fluxes add to $(v_{q,K}-v_{q,K'})\phi n_{K,j}$, which is zero by the matching-trace assumption; edge overlaps have surface measure zero by [F2]. The exterior boundary term is zero because $\phi$ is compactly supported in $\Omega$. Therefore $\int_\Omega v_q\,\partial_j\phi=-\sum_K\int_K\partial_jv_q\,\phi.$

For every component $q$ and coordinate $j$, define $g_{qj}$ to equal the classical $\partial_jv_q$ on each open cell and arbitrarily on the cell faces. The faces have $d$-dimensional measure zero under the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation, and the finite sum of cellwise $L^2$ norms is finite, so $g_{qj}\in L^2(\Omega)$. Step 1.1 gives the weak-derivative identity for every test function, hence $D_jv_q=g_{qj}$ weakly. Each component of $v$ is also square integrable on the finite bounded cell partition; [F4] therefore gives $v\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$ with the asserted componentwise gradient.

citations.quote: Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.

$$N_\alpha(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d):=\prod_{r=1}^d B^{(r)}_{i_r,p_r,\Xi_r}(\xi_r).$$

Choose finitely many control points $P_\alpha\in\mathbb R^d$ and positive weights $w_\alpha$, and write $0<w_-:=\min_\alpha w_\alpha\le\max_\alpha w_\alpha=:w_+<\infty$. The weight denominator, rational basis, and associated rational spline space are
$$W(\xi):=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}w_\alpha N_\alpha(\xi),\qquad R_\alpha(\xi):=\frac{w_\alpha N_\alpha(\xi)}{W(\xi)},\qquad \mathcal N_h:=\operatorname{span}\{R_\alpha:\alpha\in\mathcal I\}.$$
The corresponding NURBS geometry map is
$$F(\xi):=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}R_\alpha(\xi)P_\alpha.$$
Equivalently, let $\widetilde F(\xi):=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}(w_\alpha P_\alpha,w_\alpha)N_\alpha(\xi)\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ and let $\Pi(y,z):=y/z$ for $z>0$. Then $F=\Pi\circ\widetilde F$ wherever $W>0$.

An admissible NURBS patch map is a continuous, globally injective, bi-Lipschitz map $F:\overline{\widehat\Omega}\to\overline\Omega$ whose restriction to every nonempty knot cell is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto its image. There are constants $0<j_-\le j_+<\infty$ and $1\le L<\infty$ such that, almost everywhere on every cell,
$$j_-\le J_F:=\det DF\le j_+,\qquad \|DF\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L,\qquad \|DF^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L.$$
The physical image $\Omega$ is required to be a bounded Lipschitz domain. The images of the finite knot cells form a face-to-face partition with the piecewise $C^1$ boundary presentation of [[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]; the map agrees on each shared cell face.

A finite multipatch geometry consists of finitely many such patch maps with disjoint physical interiors, a connected bounded Lipschitz union, and matching full physical faces wherever two patches meet. Positive weights only define a positive denominator and a convex rational basis; they do not assert global injectivity, positive Jacobian, or interface matching. Exact NURBS representation means exact representation of the specified CAD map and does not assert that this map is the exact geometry of a target physical domain.

derivations.claim: Each tensor product $N_\alpha$ is nonnegative by [F1]. On any open tensor knot cell, each coordinate lies in one nonempty knot interval, so finite distributivity and [F1] give $\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}N_\alpha(\xi)=\prod_{r=1}^d\left(\sum_{i_r}B^{(r)}_{i_r,p_r,\Xi_r}(\xi_r)\right)=1.$ Hence $0\le N_\alpha\le1$ on the cell. The endpoint values follow by the one-sided endpoint convention in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]].

Since every coefficient $w_\alpha$ is between $w_-$ and $w_+$, the identity in step 1.1 yields $w_-\sum_\alpha N_\alpha\le W=\sum_\alpha w_\alpha N_\alpha\le w_+\sum_\alpha N_\alpha,$ so $w_-\le W\le w_+$. Thus each $R_\alpha$ is well-defined and nonnegative, and $\sum_\alpha R_\alpha=\frac{\sum_\alpha w_\alpha N_\alpha}{W}=1.$ For any coefficients $c_\alpha$, $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha R_\alpha=(1/W)\sum_\alpha(c_\alpha w_\alpha)N_\alpha$. Multiplication of each coefficient by the nonzero $w_\alpha$ is a bijection on the finite coefficient space, so the span equals $S_h/W$.

On the open knot cell all $N_\alpha$ and $W$ are polynomial and $W\ge w_->0$ by step 2.1. The ordinary quotient rule gives the displayed gradient formula. Also $\|\nabla W\|_\infty\le\sum_\alpha w_\alpha\|\nabla N_\alpha\|_\infty\le G_W$ and $N_\alpha\le1$ by step 1.1. Applying these bounds to the quotient rule proves the stated derivative estimate. The finite number of polynomial pieces makes each $G_N$ finite.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

If independent, Gram--Schmidt replaces each $c_i$ by $q_i=c_i-\sum_{k<i}\operatorname{proj}_{q_k}c_i$; subtracting combinations of earlier columns preserves the determinant, the $q_i$ are orthogonal, and $\|q_i\|\le\|c_i\|$ by the Pythagorean identity. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For the finite tensor-product basis and weights of [[def-nurbs-patch-map-and-rational-spline-space]], the denominator satisfies $w_-\le W(\xi)\le w_+$, the rational basis is nonnegative and sums to one, and
$$\mathcal N_h=\{s/W:s\in S_h\},\qquad S_h:=\operatorname{span}\{N_\alpha:\alpha\in\mathcal I\}.$$
On each open knot cell, the rational basis functions are differentiable and
$$\nabla R_\alpha=\frac{w_\alpha}{W}\nabla N_\alpha-\frac{w_\alpha N_\alpha}{W^2}\nabla W.$$
In particular, if $G_N:=\max_\alpha\|\nabla N_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells})}$ and $G_W:=w_+\sum_\alpha\|\nabla N_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells})}$, then
$$\|\nabla R_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells})}\le \frac{w_+G_N}{w_-}+\frac{w_+G_W}{w_-^2}.$$
These derivative bounds depend on the fixed degrees and knot cells; no degree-independent bound is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice and the admissible piecewise $C^1$ NURBS map $F:\widehat\Omega\to\Omega$ of [[def-nurbs-patch-map-and-rational-spline-space]]. Write $J_F=\det DF$, and assume $j_-\le J_F\le j_+$ and $\|DF\|_{\mathrm{op}},\|DF^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L$ almost everywhere on the cells. For every $u\in H^1(\Omega)$, its pullback $\widehat u=u\circ F$ lies in $H^1(\widehat\Omega)$, with cellwise weak gradient
$$\nabla_\xi\widehat u=DF^\mathsf T(\nabla_xu)\circ F.$$
The inverse pullback also preserves $H^1$, and
$$\|\widehat u\|_{H^1(\widehat\Omega)}\le j_-^{-1/2}\sqrt{1+L^2}\,\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)},\qquad \|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le j_+^{1/2}\sqrt{1+L^2}\,\|\widehat u\|_{H^1(\widehat\Omega)}.$$
Pullback maps $H^1_0(\Omega)$ onto $H^1_0(\widehat\Omega)$. For a vector field $\widehat v=v\circ F$, the physical gradient is $(\nabla_\xi\widehat v)DF^{-1}$, so the scalar diffusion and finite-Lamé elasticity forms are transformed by the same Jacobian and inverse-map factors.

Assume Countable Choice. Let a bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\in\{2,3\}$, be the union of finitely many bounded knot-cell images with disjoint interiors and a face-to-face finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation. Let $m\ge1$ and let $v: \Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$ on the closure of each cell, with each component's cell gradient square integrable. Suppose the two one-sided vector values agree on every shared face. Then $v\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$; its weak gradient is the piecewise classical componentwise gradient. This is the interface condition used to form conforming multipatch isogeometric spaces. Boundary conditions remain an additional restriction such as membership in $H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$.

derivations.claim: Work on the finite common refinement and set $e:=g-s$. The continuous positive denominator is polynomial on each geometry cell, so $g$, $s$, $e$, $s/W$ and $e/W$ are continuous and C1 up to each refined cell boundary. Their classical cell gradients are square integrable on this finite partition; [F3] therefore puts them in H1 with these weak gradients. On each cell, $u-v_h=(\widehat u-s/W)\circ F^{-1}=(e/W)\circ F^{-1}$. Since $W\ge w_->0$, the cellwise quotient rule gives $\left|\frac eW\right|\le \frac{|e|}{w_-},\qquad \left|\nabla\!\left(\frac eW\right)\right|\le\frac{|\nabla e|}{w_-}+\frac{G_W|e|}{w_-^2}.$ Taking the $H^1$ norm and using the triangle inequality yields $\|e/W\|_{H^1(\widehat\Omega)}\le C_W\|e\|_{H^1(\widehat\Omega)}$.

The traces of $e/W$ match because the traces of $\widehat u$, $s$, and $W$ match and $W$ is positive. Its cell gradients are square integrable by step 1.1, so [F3] gives $e/W\in H^1(\widehat\Omega)$. By [A1], [F2] maps $s/W\in H^1(\widehat\Omega)$ to $v_h\in H^1(\Omega)$. Applying its inverse-map estimate to $(e/W)\circ F^{-1}$ gives $\|u-v_h\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C_F\|e/W\|_{H^1(\widehat\Omega)}\le C_FC_W\|g-s\|_{H^1(\widehat\Omega)}.$ This is the claimed estimate, with all constants retaining the map and weight dependence.

For a multi-index $\alpha=(i_1,\ldots,i_d)$ in the finite product index set $\mathcal I$, define the tensor-product basis function
$$N_\alpha(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d):=\prod_{r=1}^d B^{(r)}_{i_r,p_r,\Xi_r}(\xi_r).$$

Choose finitely many control points $P_\alpha\in\mathbb R^d$ and positive weights $w_\alpha$, and write $0<w_-:=\min_\alpha w_\alpha\le\max_\alpha w_\alpha=:w_+<\infty$. The weight denominator, rational basis, and associated rational spline space are
$$W(\xi):=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}w_\alpha N_\alpha(\xi),\qquad R_\alpha(\xi):=\frac{w_\alpha N_\alpha(\xi)}{W(\xi)},\qquad \mathcal N_h:=\operatorname{span}\{R_\alpha:\alpha\in\mathcal I\}.$$
The corresponding NURBS geometry map is
$$F(\xi):=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}R_\alpha(\xi)P_\alpha.$$
Equivalently, let $\widetilde F(\xi):=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}(w_\alpha P_\alpha,w_\alpha)N_\alpha(\xi)\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ and let $\Pi(y,z):=y/z$ for $z>0$. Then $F=\Pi\circ\widetilde F$ wherever $W>0$.
The basis properties in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]] give nonnegative tensor factors summing to one. Consequently the weights' convex combination satisfies $W\ge w_->0$; the later item `lem-positive-nurbs-basis-and-quotient-derivative` records the full rational-basis consequences.

An admissible NURBS patch map is a continuous, globally injective, bi-Lipschitz map $F:\overline{\widehat\Omega}\to\overline\Omega$ whose restriction to every nonempty knot cell is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto its image. There are constants $0<j_-\le j_+<\infty$ and $1\le L<\infty$ such that, almost everywhere on every cell,
$$j_-\le J_F:=\det DF\le j_+,\qquad \|DF\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L,\qquad \|DF^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L.$$
The physical image $\Omega$ is required to be a bounded Lipschitz domain. The images of the finite knot cells form a face-to-face partition with the piecewise $C^1$ boundary presentation of [[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]; the map agrees on each shared cell face.

A finite multipatch geometry consists of finitely many such patch maps with disjoint physical interiors, a connected bounded Lipschitz union, and matching full physical faces wherever two patches meet. Positive weights only define a positive denominator and a convex rational basis; they do not assert global injectivity, positive Jacobian, or interface matching. Exact NURBS representation means exact representation of the specified CAD map and does not assert that this map is the exact geometry of a target physical domain.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Fix a reference matching affine simplicial mesh as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. An admissible curved cell is the image of a closed reference simplex $\widehat K$ under a map $F_K\in C^2(\widehat K;\mathbb R^d)$ that extends to a diffeomorphism on a neighborhood, is orientation preserving, and satisfies $0<j_0\le J_K:=\det DF_K\le j_1$ and $\|DF_K\|+\|(DF_K)^{-1}\|+\|D^2F_K\|\le C_F$. The physical cells have disjoint interiors, cover the domain up to their shared facets, and maps agree on each common reference facet under the prescribed affine facet identification. Define the volume metric $G_K=DF_K^TDF_K$, volume factor $J_K=\sqrt{\det G_K}$, and for a reference facet parametrization $\widehat f$ the surface metric $G_{K,\widehat f}=D(F_K\circ\widehat f)^TD(F_K\circ\widehat f)$ and surface factor $\sqrt{\det G_{K,\widehat f}}$. The positive-Jacobian lower bound is the admissibility certificate; it is not inferred from a drawing or from Delaunay quality.

Let $\widehat\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded reference domain and let $\Phi,\Phi_h:\overline{\widehat\Omega}\to\mathbb R^d$ be cellwise $C^2$ admissible maps with matching traces, positive Jacobians, and common image topology. The exact and approximate domains are $\Omega=\Phi(\widehat\Omega)$ and $\Omega_h=\Phi_h(\widehat\Omega)$. Define $e_0=\|\Phi-\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega)}$ and $e_1=\|D\Phi-D\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega;op)}$. A geometry approximation claim must separately state bounds on $e_0,e_1$, both Jacobian lower bounds, and boundary-trace compatibility; none follows from the word “isoparametric.”

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $P^m$ and $N^n$ be smooth manifolds with $m<n$, and let $F:P\to N$ be a
$C^1$ map. Then $F(P)\subseteq N$ is a null subset of $N$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: In the normalized cube every point has some ordering of its $d$ coordinates, hence belongs to at least one displayed simplex; strict order specifies exactly one interior. For a permutation $\pi$, the closed ordered region is the convex hull of the chain vertices $0,e_{\pi(d)},e_{\pi(d)}+e_{\pi(d-1)},\ldots,\sum_{r=1}^de_{\pi(r)}$: the barycentric coefficients are $1-t_{\pi(d)}$, $t_{\pi(d)}-t_{\pi(d-1)},\ldots,t_{\pi(2)}-t_{\pi(1)},t_{\pi(1)}$. Thus a tie between consecutive coordinates sets exactly the corresponding barycentric coefficient to zero. For two permutations, the common weak order groups precisely the coordinates whose order is reversed into equal blocks; their intersection is the convex hull of the common chain vertices at the block boundaries, hence is a whole face of each simplex. This proves the subdivision is a simplicial complex with disjoint interiors. On a rectangular face one coordinate is $0$ or $1$; the remaining subdivision orders the remaining normalized coordinates. Adjacent rectangles have the same intervals in those coordinates and the same increasing-axis convention, so their induced face subdivisions coincide. The affine diagonal maps preserve these face identities. Therefore the finite subdivision is a matching affine simplicial mesh as required in [F2].

On a closed rectangle each map is a quotient of finite polynomials with denominator bounded below by a positive number. Its cell expression therefore extends smoothly across the rectangle into a neighborhood. Its derivatives, including second derivatives, are bounded there after shrinking the neighborhood. The determinant extends continuously with a positive lower bound on the closed cell. Its restriction to each closed simplex is injective by global injectivity of the map on $\overline Q$. This restriction actually extends injectively to some neighborhood of that simplex: otherwise there exist distinct pairs of points at distance at most $1/n$ from the simplex with equal images. Compactness [F3] gives convergent subsequences with limits in the simplex; equality of images and injectivity force the same limit, contradicting local injectivity [F3] near that limit. A smaller neighborhood retains positive determinant, so the restriction is a neighborhood diffeomorphism. These arguments apply separately to $F$ and $G$.

Continuity of the original maps makes the restricted traces agree on shared simplex facets, including those lying on original knot planes. Global injectivity preserves disjoint interiors and makes intersections of physical cells precisely the images of the corresponding reference intersections. Their union is the original image. The map, inverse, determinant and finite second-derivative bounds from step 1.2 give all curved-cell requirements [F2]. The reference simplices here are actual parameter simplices; if one instead precomposes with a map from a unit simplex, its Jacobian scaling factors must be retained.

The cell restrictions do not alter the global maps, their physical images, or their value and almost-everywhere derivative differences. Every introduced reference-simplex facet lies in an affine hyperplane, the image of an affine $C^1$ map from $\mathbb R^{d-1}$ into $\mathbb R^d$. By [F4] and [A1] each such hyperplane is null, and the finite union of introduced facets is null. Thus taking essential suprema over the refined interiors gives the same $e_1$; continuity gives the same $e_0$. To state separate finite error bounds as required by [F2], write $P^F_\alpha,P^G_\beta$ for the two finite control-point lists and $L_F,L_G$ for their admissibility derivative bounds. The nonnegative rational coefficients in [F1] sum to one, so $e_0\le\max_\alpha|P^F_\alpha|+\max_\beta|P^G_\beta|$; the operator-norm triangle inequality gives $e_1\le L_F+L_G$. The two positive determinant lower bounds are their respective admissibility constants $j_-^F,j_-^G$. These coarse bounds establish the finite geometry interface; no smallness or mesh-dependent convergence follows from admissibility alone. Since both maps are bi-Lipschitz bijections of the closed box, $G\circ F^{-1}$ is the required homeomorphism between the closed image domains. The within-mesh trace matching in step 2.1 supplies boundary-trace compatibility in [F2]; no exterior trace equality between distinct maps has been proved.

Each normalized ordered-coordinate simplex belongs to a finite set depending only on $d$. Under diagonal scaling, diameter increases by at most $\max_r\ell_r$ and inradius decreases by at most the factor $\min_r\ell_r$ relative to the normalized simplex. Hence the diameter/inradius ratio is at most $\kappa$ times the largest ratio in that fixed finite set. This proves the stated reference shape bound. The remaining uniform curved-map bounds are exactly the additional displayed family assumptions; finite-grid smoothness in step 1.2 supplies only finite-grid constants. No analysis-space change was made in the subdivision.

risk_review.notes: Checked all five steps against the exact matching simplicial mesh, curved-cell and common-reference geometry definitions, Euclidean inverse function theorem, Heine–Borel, Bolzano–Weierstrass and lower-dimensional null-image Statement. Coordinate ordering gives chain-vertex simplices with common whole faces; neighboring rectangles induce identical facet subdivisions. The closed rational expressions extend smoothly with positive determinant. A hypothetical sequence of collisions near a compact injective simplex converges to one point, contradicting local injectivity, so a neighborhood diffeomorphism exists. Facet nullity preserves essential suprema; G composed with F inverse supplies topology. Uniform shape and second-derivative bounds remain explicit extra family conditions.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

For each degree $d\in\{0,\ldots,p\}$, the functions $B_{j,d,\xi}$ are indexed by $1\le j\le n+p-d$. Set
$$B_{j,0,\xi}(x)=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}(x),\qquad 1\le j\le n+p.$$
For $1\le d\le p$ and $1\le j\le n+p-d$, define recursively
$$B_{j,d,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}B_{j,d-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+d+1}-x}{\xi_{j+d+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,d-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. For every degree $d$ and every allowed index $j$, set $B_{j,d,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. In particular, the degree-$p$ family has indices $1\le j\le n$. Its basis and regularity properties are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Assume Countable Choice. Let a bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\in\{2,3\}$, be the union of finitely many bounded knot-cell images with disjoint interiors and a face-to-face finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation. Let $m\ge1$ and let $v: \Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$ on the closure of each cell, with each component's cell gradient square integrable. Suppose the two one-sided vector values agree on every shared face. Then $v\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$; its weak gradient is the piecewise classical componentwise gradient. This is the interface condition used to form conforming multipatch isogeometric spaces. Boundary conditions remain an additional restriction such as membership in $H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

derivations.claim: The $k=1$ polynomial coefficient formula in [F1] is $x=\sum_i t_iB_i(x)$, while $\sum_iB_i=1$, so $S_rf:=\sum_if(t_i)B_i$ reproduces every affine function. On a cell $(\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, all active Greville points lie in $J_m=[\xi_{m-p},\xi_{m+p+1}]\cap[0,1]$, made from at most $2p+1$ nonempty adjacent spans. Nonnegativity and partition of unity give $|S_rf(x)|\le\|f\|_{L^\infty(J_m)}$ for $x$ in that cell. For a $C^1$ section $f$ with $M_g$-Lipschitz derivative, set $T(x)=f(c)+f'(c)(x-c)$ at the left endpoint $c$ of $J_m$. If $y=c$, then $(f-T)(y)=0$; if $y\ne c$, apply [F2] to $f-T$ on the interval with endpoints $c,y$. At the resulting interior point $\zeta$, $|(f-T)(y)|=|f'(\zeta)-f'(c)|\,|y-c|\le M_g|J_m|^2$. At $x\in(\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, nonnegativity and partition of unity give $|S_r(f-T)(x)|\le M_g|J_m|^2$. Since $S_rT=T$, $|f(x)-S_rf(x)|\le2M_g|J_m|^2\le2(2p_r+3)^2h_r^2M_g$. Thus each coordinate operator is a sup-norm contraction; the finite operators commute, so the telescoping identity for $I-S_d\cdots S_1$, commutation of different-coordinate operators, and contraction of each $S_r$ let us sum these bounds on the original $g$ and prove the function estimate with $E$.

For one coordinate write $c_i$ for its coefficient, keeping all other Greville samples fixed. Summation of the derivative formula from [F1] gives, on open cells,
$$\left(\sum_ic_iB_{i,p}\right)'=\sum_{\substack{2\le i\le n\\\xi_{i+p}>\xi_i}}\frac{p(c_i-c_{i-1})}{\xi_{i+p}-\xi_i}B_{i,p-1}.$$
Here the nonempty-support lower-degree functions $B_{i,p-1}$, $2\le i\le n$, form a nonnegative partition on each open cell; the two omitted boundary functions vanish there. Terms with $\xi_{i+p}=\xi_i$ are omitted because their lower-degree splines have empty support, so no undefined $0/0$ coefficient is used. Put $\Delta_i=t_i-t_{i-1}=(\xi_{i+p}-\xi_i)/p$. For every included term $\Delta_i>0$, apply [F2] to the coordinate section of $g$ on $[t_{i-1},t_i]$: its derivative quotient $(c_i-c_{i-1})/\Delta_i$ equals $\partial_rg$ at some point between the two Greville samples, with all other coordinates fixed at their samples. If $\Delta_i=0$, then $c_i=c_{i-1}$ and the corresponding lower-degree spline has empty support, so its contribution to the derivative is absent. At a cell point $x$ in the support of an included lower-degree factor, both Greville endpoints lie in $[\xi_i,\xi_{i+p}]$, within $p_rh_r$ of $x_r$; the intermediate point lies there as well. In every other active coordinate, the sample and $x_s$ lie in a common degree-$p_s$ support of length at most $(p_s+1)h_s$. Therefore each gradient value in the nonnegative partition sum is evaluated within distance $R$ of $x$. The $M_g$-Lipschitz gradient yields $|\partial_r\mathcal Sg(x)-\partial_rg(x)|\le M_gR$. Summing squared component bounds proves the gradient estimate.

At an interior knot of multiplicity at most $p$, continuity follows from [F1]. At a knot of multiplicity $p+1$, the left and right pieces are clamped there; the only nonzero endpoint coefficient from each side has Greville point equal to that knot. Their face restrictions are therefore the same tangential sampled sum, so they agree; repeating this argument in each coordinate also gives agreement at intersections of repeated-knot faces. Thus the tensor construction is continuous on the closed box. Its piecewise polynomial gradients are bounded on the finite Cartesian grid, whose rectangular cells form a matching cell partition under the identity map. Under [A1], applying [F3] proves H1 membership and identifies the cell gradients as weak derivatives. The unit box has volume one, so the $L^2$ errors are bounded by the displayed sup bounds. By [F4], $\|g-\mathcal Sg\|_{H^1}=\sqrt{\|g-\mathcal Sg\|_2^2+\|\nabla(g-\mathcal Sg)\|_2^2}\le M_g\sqrt{E^2+dR^2}\le M_g(E+\sqrt d R)$.

At an exterior endpoint of a clamped vector, only its first, respectively last, basis function has value one; the rest are zero. The corresponding Greville point is that endpoint. Substitution into the tensor formula gives exactly the asserted tangential face formula and zero-face preservation. Reflection reverses the knot list and sends each Greville point to $1-t_i$. On open knot cells it reverses the indexed basis functions by the Cox–de Boor recurrence in [F1], starting with the interval indicators. At a fully repeated knot the individual right-cell conventions need not commute with reflection, but the constructed sampled sum is continuous by step 2.1, so equality of the reflected sums on open cells extends to every knot and endpoint. Permuting coordinates merely permutes finite product factors. Consequently aligned face formulas agree under all declared identifications. Constant multiplication commutes with their finite linear sums.

Use the zero-based reindexing $t_i=\xi_{i+1}$ of the clamped knot vector
in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]], so $t_0\le\cdots\le t_{n+p}$ with
$n\ge p+1$. Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $d\in\mathbb N$, and let the controls
be $P_0,\ldots,P_{n-1}\in\mathbb R^d$. Let $k$ be a
nonempty span index with $t_k<u<t_{k+1}$, where $u$ is not already a knot.
Insert $u$ between $t_k$ and $t_{k+1}$ to obtain $t'$. The output controls
$Q_0,\ldots,Q_n$ are defined by

$$Q_i=\begin{cases}P_i,&0\le i\le k-p,\\\alpha_iP_i+(1-\alpha_i)P_{i-1},&k-p+1\le i\le k,\\P_{i-1},&k+1\le i\le n,\end{cases}\qquad\alpha_i=\frac{u-t_i}{t_{i+p}-t_i}.$$

The middle range is empty when $p=0$. The curve uses the same degree and
the B-spline basis for the new knot vector. Each denominator in the middle
range is positive and each $\alpha_i$ lies in $[0,1]$, so the update is an
exact affine blend. This procedure inserts one knot that is new to the
vector; repeated insertion at an existing knot is not part of this
algorithm's input contract.

Let $t_0\le\cdots\le t_{n+p}$ be a clamped knot vector of degree $p$ as
in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]], with $a=t_0$ and $b=t_{n+p}$, and
let $\xi(v)_j=v_{j-1}$ be the one-based version of any zero-based knot
vector $v$. Write $B_{i,q,v}=B_{i+1,q,\xi(v)}$ for the basis in
[[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. Let a B-spline curve be
$C(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}P_iB_{i,p,t}(x)$ with $d\in\mathbb N$ and
$P_i\in\mathbb R^d$. Insert
one new knot $u$ strictly inside a nonempty span by
[[alg-single-new-b-spline-knot-insertion]], obtaining knots $t'$ and
controls $Q_i$. Write $B'_{i,q}=B_{i,q,t'}$. Then, for every $x\in[a,b]$,
$$C(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}Q_iB_{i,p,t'}(x).$$

Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let the reference patch be $\widehat\Omega=(0,1)^d$. For each coordinate $r$, fix a degree $p_r\in\mathbb N_0$, a finite clamped knot vector $\Xi_r$ on $[0,1]$, and its one-dimensional B-spline basis $B^{(r)}_{i_r,p_r,\Xi_r}$ from [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. For a multi-index $\alpha=(i_1,\ldots,i_d)$ in the finite product index set $\mathcal I$, define the tensor-product basis function
$$N_\alpha(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d):=\prod_{r=1}^d B^{(r)}_{i_r,p_r,\Xi_r}(\xi_r).$$

Choose finitely many control points $P_\alpha\in\mathbb R^d$ and positive weights $w_\alpha$, and write $0<w_-:=\min_\alpha w_\alpha\le\max_\alpha w_\alpha=:w_+<\infty$. The weight denominator, rational basis, and associated rational spline space are
$$W(\xi):=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}w_\alpha N_\alpha(\xi),\qquad R_\alpha(\xi):=\frac{w_\alpha N_\alpha(\xi)}{W(\xi)},\qquad \mathcal N_h:=\operatorname{span}\{R_\alpha:\alpha\in\mathcal I\}.$$
The corresponding NURBS geometry map is
$$F(\xi):=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}R_\alpha(\xi)P_\alpha.$$
Equivalently, let $\widetilde F(\xi):=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}(w_\alpha P_\alpha,w_\alpha)N_\alpha(\xi)\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ and let $\Pi(y,z):=y/z$ for $z>0$. Then $F=\Pi\circ\widetilde F$ wherever $W>0$.
The basis properties in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]] give nonnegative tensor factors summing to one. Consequently the weights' convex combination satisfies $W\ge w_->0$; the later item `lem-positive-nurbs-basis-and-quotient-derivative` records the full rational-basis consequences.

An admissible NURBS patch map is a continuous, globally injective, bi-Lipschitz map $F:\overline{\widehat\Omega}\to\overline\Omega$ whose restriction to every nonempty knot cell is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto its image. There are constants $0<j_-\le j_+<\infty$ and $1\le L<\infty$ such that, almost everywhere on every cell,
$$j_-\le J_F:=\det DF\le j_+,\qquad \|DF\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L,\qquad \|DF^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L.$$
The physical image $\Omega$ is required to be a bounded Lipschitz domain. The images of the finite knot cells form a face-to-face partition with the piecewise $C^1$ boundary presentation of [[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]; the map agrees on each shared cell face.

A finite multipatch geometry consists of finitely many such patch maps with disjoint physical interiors, a connected bounded Lipschitz union, and matching full physical faces wherever two patches meet. Positive weights only define a positive denominator and a convex rational basis; they do not assert global injectivity, positive Jacobian, or interface matching. Exact NURBS representation means exact representation of the specified CAD map and does not assert that this map is the exact geometry of a target physical domain.

For the finite tensor-product basis and weights of [[def-nurbs-patch-map-and-rational-spline-space]], the denominator satisfies $w_-\le W(\xi)\le w_+$, the rational basis is nonnegative and sums to one, and
$$\mathcal N_h=\{s/W:s\in S_h\},\qquad S_h:=\operatorname{span}\{N_\alpha:\alpha\in\mathcal I\}.$$
On each open knot cell, the rational basis functions are differentiable and
$$\nabla R_\alpha=\frac{w_\alpha}{W}\nabla N_\alpha-\frac{w_\alpha N_\alpha}{W^2}\nabla W.$$
In particular, if $G_N:=\max_\alpha\|\nabla N_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells})}$ and $G_W:=w_+\sum_\alpha\|\nabla N_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells})}$, then
$$\|\nabla R_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells})}\le \frac{w_+G_N}{w_-}+\frac{w_+G_W}{w_-^2}.$$
These derivative bounds depend on the fixed degrees and knot cells; no degree-independent bound is asserted.

derivations.claim: Write the homogeneous control array as $\widetilde P_\alpha=(w_\alpha P_\alpha,w_\alpha)$. The tensor spline $\widetilde F(\xi)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}\widetilde P_\alpha N_\alpha(\xi)$ has first $d$ components $W(\xi)F(\xi)$ and last component $W(\xi)$ by [F3]. Fix the coordinate direction in which $u$ is inserted and fix a multi-index of all other coordinates. Grouping the finite sum over the remaining index writes the corresponding slice as a B-spline curve with controls in $\mathbb R^{d+1}$. By [F2], knot insertion leaves that slice unchanged for every value of the insertion coordinate. Multiplication by the fixed transverse tensor basis function and summation over all transverse indices show that the entire updated homogeneous spline $\widetilde F'$ equals $\widetilde F$ pointwise.

In the active range, each updated last coordinate is $\alpha_iw_i+(1-\alpha_i)w_{i-1}$ by [F1]; it is positive because both old weights are positive and $0<\alpha_i<1$. Copied weights are positive as well. Thus all updated weights are positive and [F4] gives $W'(\xi)>0$ on the closed patch. Since $\widetilde F'=\widetilde F$, their first $d$ components and last components agree, and division by this positive common last component gives $F'(\xi)=F(\xi)$ for every $\xi\in\overline{\widehat\Omega}$.

Let $d\in\{2,3\}$, let $F,G:(0,1)^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be admissible piecewise $C^1$ maps on a common finite refinement of their knot partitions, and suppose almost everywhere that both maps have positive Jacobian determinants and
$$\|DF\|_{\rm op},\|DG\|_{\rm op},\|DF^{-1}\|_{\rm op},\|DG^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\le M,\qquad M\ge1.$$
Set $\delta=\|DF-DG\|_{L^\infty({\rm op})}$, the essential supremum of the operator-norm difference on that common refinement, and define the unit-diffusion pullback tensors
$$K_F=(\det DF)DF^{-1}DF^{-\mathsf T},\qquad K_G=(\det DG)DG^{-1}DG^{-\mathsf T}.$$
Then, almost everywhere,
$$\|K_F-K_G\|_{\rm op}\le(dM^{d+1}+2M^{d+3})\delta.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

Identify $\mathbb{Z}$ with its canonical copy inside $\mathbb{R}$, along the
embeddings $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]],
[[def-integers]]). Then for every real $x$ there is **exactly one** integer $m$
with

$$m \;\le\; x \;<\; m + 1 .$$

It is written $\lfloor x \rfloor$ and called the **integer part**, or **floor**,
of $x$.

**Two independent ingredients are needed and neither may be dropped.** Existence
is the Archimedean property ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) together with the
well-ordering of $\mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): the first says
that $x$ is caught between two integers at all, the second picks the *least*
integer above $x$. Uniqueness is the discreteness of $\mathbb{Z}$: no integer
lies strictly between $m$ and $m+1$.

This lemma is stated once here and reused. It is what turns "the nearest integer
to $x$" from a picture into an object, and the companion page's oscillator
$\psi(x) = \inf_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |x - n|$ is computed from it in one line.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Put $E=A'-A$ and $e=W'-W$. By [F1], $|E|\le\epsilon_A$, $|e|\le\epsilon_W$, $W'\ge m$ and $|F|\le R$. Direct differentiation of the finite polynomial pieces gives $\|DE\|\le H\epsilon_A$, $|De|\le H\epsilon_W$ and $|DW'|\le(w_++\epsilon_W)H$. These inequalities use $\|z\otimes q\|=|z||q|$ for each numerator term. Interior multiplicity at most degree makes every $N_\alpha$ continuous; thus $F,G,E,e$ have matching traces. Positive denominator makes each rational cell piece smooth through that cell's closure.

The exact identity $G-F=(E-Fe)/W'$ yields $|G-F|\le T/m=E_0$. Differentiating on a cell yields
$$DG-DF=\frac{DE-eDF-F\otimes De}{W'}-\frac{(E-Fe)\otimes DW'}{(W')^2}.$$
Using step 1.1 and $\|DF\|\le L$ proves $\|DG-DF\|\le E_1$. No derivative error is assumed in this argument.

The continuous piecewise smooth function $q=G-F$ is $E_1$-Lipschitz on the convex box. The finitely many knot hyperplanes have dense complement in $Q$; by [A1], approximate any $x,y\in\overline Q$ by sequences $x_n,y_n\in Q$ whose coordinates avoid all knot values. The segment $[x_n,y_n]$ is not contained in any knot hyperplane and meets each such hyperplane in at most one point, so it splits into finitely many subsegments, each in one closed cell. For endpoints $a,b$ of one subsegment, if $q(a)=q(b)$ the desired bound is immediate; otherwise set $e=(q(b)-q(a))/|q(b)-q(a)|$ and apply [F6] to $t\mapsto e\cdot q(a+t(b-a))$. This function is continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable on $(0,1)$ using the cell expression, so $|q(b)-q(a)|=|e\cdot(Dq(\zeta)(b-a))|\le E_1|b-a|$ for some $\zeta$ in the subsegment. Summing subsegment lengths proves $|q(x_n)-q(y_n)|\le E_1|x_n-y_n|$. Continuity of $q$ gives $|q(x)-q(y)|\le E_1|x-y|$ in the limit. Applying the same scalar mean-value argument to $F$, whose cell derivative norm is at most $L$, gives $|F(x)-F(y)|\le L|x-y|$ on $\overline Q$. Consequently $|G(x)-G(y)|\ge(c-E_1)|x-y|$ and $|G(x)-G(y)|\le(L+E_1)|x-y|$. The first inequality proves global injectivity and the inverse Lipschitz bound.

At every cell point, $DG=DF(I+(DF)^{-1}(DG-DF))$ and the second term in parentheses has norm at most $LE_1<1$. Its smallest singular value is at least $1-LE_1$, so the inverse bound is $L/(1-LE_1)$. Along the straight matrix homotopy from $DF$ to $DG$, the same bound prevents a singular matrix; the determinant therefore keeps its positive sign. The determinant's absolute value is the product of singular values, giving $\det DG\ge j_-(1-LE_1)^d$. The derivative upper bound is the triangle inequality. These inequalities extend to each closed cell by continuity of that cell's polynomial-rational expression.

Openness needs no topological or choice assumption. On the original open image $\Omega=F(Q)$ define $r=q\circ F^{-1}$; step 2.1 and the global lower bound give $\operatorname{Lip}(r)\le E_1/c=:t<1$. Fix $z_0\in\Omega$ and a closed ball of radius $\rho$ centered there contained in $\Omega$. For $y$ within $(1-t)\rho/2$ of $z_0+r(z_0)$, $T_y(z)=y-r(z)$ maps this closed ball into itself and contracts by $t$: indeed $|T_y(z)-z_0|\le(1-t)\rho/2+t\rho<\rho$. [F3] supplies a unique fixed point, and its equation $z+r(z)=y$ puts this neighborhood inside $G(Q)$. Hence $G(Q)$ is open.

The explicitly assumed Lipschitz boundary presentation, step 2.1, step 2.2 and the cellwise smooth local inverse [F4] give exactly admissibility [F1]. For the sufficient $C^1$ extension alternative, local inverses [F4] map boundary coordinate halfspaces near a box point to finitely many $C^1$ inequalities with independent inward gradients. Choose the image of the sum of the active inward coordinate vectors as vertical direction; every active inequality has positive vertical derivative. The one-variable inverse furnished by [F4] expresses each as $t>g_i(y)$, with $g_i$ locally $C^1$. Their intersection is $t>\max_i g_i(y)$, a Lipschitz graph. Shrink this neighborhood so local coordinates describe the image of a neighborhood of the chosen preimage. If remote preimages still entered every such shrinking image neighborhood, choose points $y_n$ in those neighborhoods with preimages $x_n$ outside that fixed preimage neighborhood. Compactness [F4] gives a convergent subsequence with limit $x\in\overline Q$ and continuity gives $G(x)=G(x_0)$, contradicting injectivity from step 2.1. Thus no remote image component changes the local graph. The finitely many smooth rational faces give the required boundary presentation. If all interior multiplicities are at most $p_r-1$, the polynomial pieces match through first derivatives, hence the rational pieces give a $C^1$ extension across internal faces. At exterior box faces extend the outermost polynomial pieces with the same matching identities. Positive denominator and nonsingular derivatives persist in a sufficiently small neighborhood of the compact box by continuity, establishing the alternative.

Step 2.2 gives the map bounds $M$, and step 1.2 gives $e_1\le E_1$. Apply [F2] without repeating its determinant/inverse calculation to obtain the tensor and form bounds. In a family with the specified uniform constants, $E_1=O(h^s)$, so the smallness holds eventually, $M$ remains bounded and the geometry form defect is $O(h^s)$. This statement does not bound a changed load or quadrature rule.

By [F5], bracket $2^b x$ between adjacent integers, select the closer endpoint with the prescribed tie rule, and rescale. A real scalar therefore differs from its specified nearest grid multiple by at most $\eta_b$. Componentwise rounding therefore gives the stated $\sqrt d\,\eta_b$ homogeneous numerator error and $\eta_b$ weight error. Since $\eta_b<w_-/2$, $m\ge w_-/2$, $T\le(\sqrt d+R)\eta_b$, and $w_++\epsilon_W\le w_++w_-/2$. Substitute these bounds in $E_0,E_1$ to obtain $E_0\le2(\sqrt d+R)\eta_b/w_-$ and $E_1\le D\eta_b<\min(c/2,1/(2L))$. The denominator, value, derivative, determinant, injectivity and openness conclusions follow from steps 1.1–3.1. A sufficiently large integer $b$ exists because $2^{-b}$ tends to zero; this is a specified integer rounding construction, with no arbitrary choice. The $C^1$ knot branch of step 4.1 gives its boundary admissibility. Step 5.1 then gives the geometry form rate when $D\eta_b\le h^s$.

For one admissible patch map $F:\widehat\Omega\to\Omega$, let $S_h$ be a finite tensor-product B-spline space on a knot grid refining the geometry grid, and let $W$ be the positive denominator of the geometry representation. The parametric rational analysis space is
$$\widehat V_h:=\{s/W:s\in S_h\}.$$
Its physical push-forward is $\{\,\widehat v\circ F^{-1}:\widehat v\in\widehat V_h\,\}$. The homogeneous-Dirichlet conforming space is the subspace of these functions that belongs to $H^1_0(\Omega)$; the unconstrained conforming version is the subspace belonging to $H^1(\Omega)$. These spaces are finite dimensional because the tensor B-spline coefficient set is finite.

For vector-valued elasticity in $\mathbb R^d$, use the componentwise product $\widehat V_h^{\,d}:=(\widehat V_h)^d$, push it forward component by component, and intersect with $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ or $H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ as appropriate. This remains finite dimensional because it is a subspace of the finite product of scalar coefficient spaces. Trace equality is required componentwise on each shared full face.

For finitely many matching patches, use one such local rational space on each patch. A global trial function is a piecewise physical function whose traces agree pointwise on every shared full face and which belongs to the chosen global $H^1$ or $H^1_0$ space. Under [[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]], the vector-valued trace-matching lemma [[lem-matching-nurbs-patch-traces-give-h1-conformity]] proves the H1 part of this interface rule componentwise, including the Cartesian product used for elasticity. Nonmatching interfaces are excluded; a mortar or Nitsche method requires a separate stability and consistency result.

The refinement labels have the following meanings.

- **h-refinement** inserts a new knot into a nonempty span at fixed degree and updates homogeneous control data by [[alg-single-new-b-spline-knot-insertion]]. Theorem [[thm-homogeneous-nurbs-knot-insertion-preserves-patch-geometry]] proves exact map preservation for this operation.
- **p-refinement** raises a coordinate degree and replaces the homogeneous representation only when an exact representation with positive new weights is supplied. A degree label alone does not certify geometry preservation or an approximation rate.
- **k-refinement** raises degree and chooses knot multiplicities to obtain a declared continuity, commonly the maximal $C^{p_r-1}$ continuity at simple interior knots. Exact geometry preservation requires the same positive homogeneous representation check as p-refinement.

On each cell, the pullback of scalar gradients and of the linear-elasticity strain is computed using [[lem-isogeometric-pullback-energy-norm-equivalence]]. Exact geometry does not assert exact quadrature. A discretization using an approximate map or quadrature must retain its separate form and load defects.

Assume Countable Choice. Let a bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\in\{2,3\}$, be the union of finitely many bounded knot-cell images with disjoint interiors and a face-to-face finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation. Let $m\ge1$ and let $v: \Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$ on the closure of each cell, with each component's cell gradient square integrable. Suppose the two one-sided vector values agree on every shared face. Then $v\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$; its weak gradient is the piecewise classical componentwise gradient. This is the interface condition used to form conforming multipatch isogeometric spaces. Boundary conditions remain an additional restriction such as membership in $H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, open, bounded, connected, and Lipschitz. Use the real spaces $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ and $Q=L^2_0(D)$, norms $\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}$ and $\|q\|_Q=\|q\|_{L^2(D)}$, and $b(v,q)=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v$ as in [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]]. For a real normed space $X$, write $X'$ for its continuous real dual with operator norm $\|F\|_{X'}=\sup_{\|x\|_X\le1}|F(x)|$. Let $\mu\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $0<\mu_0\le\mu(x)\le\mu_1<\infty$ almost everywhere, let $\lambda\ge0$ be a scalar, and let $f\in V'$. For any $w,z\in H^1(D;\mathbb R^d)$ define $\varepsilon(w)=(\nabla w+\nabla w^T)/2$ and
$$a_\mu(w,z)=2\int_D\mu\,\varepsilon(w):\varepsilon(z),\qquad \mathcal E_\lambda(w,z)=a_\mu(w,z)+\lambda\int_D\operatorname{div}w\,\operatorname{div}z,$$
and $\sigma_\lambda(w)=2\mu\varepsilon(w)+\lambda(\operatorname{div}w)I_d$. The homogeneous-Dirichlet model restricts these forms to $V$, with displacement zero on the full boundary; an example may prescribe a different boundary partition but gains no well-posedness claim from this definition. This is a linear small-strain model; no nonlinear, injectivity, or contrast-independent estimate is asserted.

Countable Choice is inherited through the imported Sobolev and Stokes-space conventions; this definition makes no arbitrary-index selection.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of [[def-linear-elasticity-displacement-formulation-and-data]]. For every finite $\lambda\ge0$ there is a unique $u\in V$ such that $\mathcal E_\lambda(u,v)=f(v)$ for every $v\in V$. It satisfies
$$
\|u\|_V\le\mu_0^{-1}\|f\|_{V'},\qquad \sqrt{\mathcal E_\lambda(u,u)}\le\mu_0^{-1/2}\|f\|_{V'}.
$$
For every finite-dimensional conforming subspace $V_h\subset V$, the Galerkin solution $u_h$ is unique and
$$
\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac{2\mu_1+d\lambda}{\mu_0}\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.
$$

derivations.claim: A single-patch analysis space is finite dimensional because its tensor coefficient set is finite. A finite multipatch space is a subspace of the finite product of these local spaces and is therefore finite dimensional. Its definition imposes global $H^1_0$ membership, so conformity follows directly from [F1] and the hypothesis $V_h\subset V$. When conformity is instead checked from cell traces, [F2] applies only after its specified finite cell presentation, closed-cell regularity, integrability and face equalities have all been verified; trace equality alone is not that verification. Thus the stipulated $V_h$ is a finite-dimensional conforming subspace of $V$.

The typed domain, real displacement space, coefficient, load, strain and form in the Statement are exactly those fixed in [F3]. By step 1.1 the isogeometric space is a finite-dimensional conforming subspace. Thus the actual PE19 estimate [F4] applies and gives existence, uniqueness and the displayed constant. Since $\lambda$ appears in the numerator, this application supplies no bound uniform in $\lambda$.
