$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let a bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\in\{2,3\}$, be the union of finitely many bounded knot-cell images with disjoint interiors and a face-to-face finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation. Let $m\ge1$ and let $v: \Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$ on the closure of each cell, with each component's cell gradient square integrable. Suppose the two one-sided vector values agree on every shared face. Then $v\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$; its weak gradient is the piecewise classical componentwise gradient. This is the interface condition used to form conforming multipatch isogeometric spaces. Boundary conditions remain an additional restriction such as membership in $H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$.

derivations.claim: The two constants are square integrable on their bounded rectangles, hence $v\in L^2(D)$. Choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty((0,1))$ with $\int_0^1\eta(y)\,dy\ne0$, and choose $\psi\in C_c^\infty((-1,1))$ with $\psi(0)=1$. For $0<\varepsilon<1$, set $\phi_\varepsilon(x,y)=\psi((x-1)/\varepsilon)\eta(y)\in C_c^\infty(D)$.

Since $v$ vanishes for $x<1$ and equals one for $x>1$, a change of variable $t=(x-1)/\varepsilon$ gives $\int_Dv\,\partial_x\phi_\varepsilon\,dxdy=\left(\int_0^1\eta\right)\int_1^2\varepsilon^{-1}\psi'((x-1)/\varepsilon)dx=-\psi(0)\int_0^1\eta,$ which is a fixed nonzero number. If an $L^2$ weak derivative $g=\partial_xv$ existed, [F2] and Cauchy--Schwarz would make the absolute value at most $\|g\|_2\|\phi_\varepsilon\|_2$. But $\|\phi_\varepsilon\|_2=\sqrt\varepsilon\|\psi\|_2\|\eta\|_2\to0$, contradiction. Therefore $v\notin H^1(D)$. Its two constant traces across $x=1$ are 0 and 1, violating [F1] even though the geometry is matching; the sufficient condition of [F3] does not apply.

For one admissible patch map $F:\widehat\Omega\to\Omega$, let $S_h$ be a finite tensor-product B-spline space on a knot grid refining the geometry grid, and let $W$ be the positive denominator of the geometry representation. The parametric rational analysis space is
$$\widehat V_h:=\{s/W:s\in S_h\}.$$
Its physical push-forward is $\{\,\widehat v\circ F^{-1}:\widehat v\in\widehat V_h\,\}$. The homogeneous-Dirichlet conforming space is the subspace of these functions that belongs to $H^1_0(\Omega)$; the unconstrained conforming version is the subspace belonging to $H^1(\Omega)$. These spaces are finite dimensional because the tensor B-spline coefficient set is finite.

For vector-valued elasticity in $\mathbb R^d$, use the componentwise product $\widehat V_h^{\,d}:=(\widehat V_h)^d$, push it forward component by component, and intersect with $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ or $H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ as appropriate. This remains finite dimensional because it is a subspace of the finite product of scalar coefficient spaces. Trace equality is required componentwise on each shared full face.

For finitely many matching patches, use one such local rational space on each patch. A global trial function is a piecewise physical function whose traces agree pointwise on every shared full face and which belongs to the chosen global $H^1$ or $H^1_0$ space. Under [[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]], the vector-valued trace-matching lemma [[lem-matching-nurbs-patch-traces-give-h1-conformity]] proves the H1 part of this interface rule componentwise, including the Cartesian product used for elasticity. Nonmatching interfaces are excluded; a mortar or Nitsche method requires a separate stability and consistency result.

The refinement labels have the following meanings.

- **h-refinement** inserts a new knot into a nonempty span at fixed degree and updates homogeneous control data by [[alg-single-new-b-spline-knot-insertion]]. Theorem [[thm-homogeneous-nurbs-knot-insertion-preserves-patch-geometry]] proves exact map preservation for this operation.
- **p-refinement** raises a coordinate degree and replaces the homogeneous representation only when an exact representation with positive new weights is supplied. A degree label alone does not certify geometry preservation or an approximation rate.
- **k-refinement** raises degree and chooses knot multiplicities to obtain a declared continuity, commonly the maximal $C^{p_r-1}$ continuity at simple interior knots. Exact geometry preservation requires the same positive homogeneous representation check as p-refinement.

On each cell, the pullback of scalar gradients and of the linear-elasticity strain is computed using [[lem-isogeometric-pullback-energy-norm-equivalence]]. Exact geometry does not assert exact quadrature. A discretization using an approximate map or quadrature must retain its separate form and load defects.

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.

Let $F$ be the tensor-product NURBS patch of [[def-nurbs-patch-map-and-rational-spline-space]]. Insert a knot $u$ that is new and strictly inside a nonempty span in one coordinate direction. Apply [[alg-single-new-b-spline-knot-insertion]] to every control-net slice in that direction, using homogeneous controls $(w_\alpha P_\alpha,w_\alpha)\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$. Then the updated homogeneous tensor spline is pointwise unchanged, every updated weight is positive, and the rational patch map remains exactly $F$ on $\overline{\widehat\Omega}$.

derivations.claim: The degree-two Bernstein functions are $B_0^2(t)=(1-t)^2$, $B_1^2(t)=2t(1-t)$, and $B_2^2(t)=t^2$. Thus $\sum_{i=0}^2B_i^2(t)=1$ and $\sum_{i=0}^2(i/2)B_i^2(t)=t$. For $P_{ij}=(i/2,j/2)$, unit weights make the tensor denominator one; summing the first and second control coordinates yields $\xi$ and $\eta$. Hence the elevated representation is still exactly the identity map, with positive weights.

The midpoint $1/2$ is new and lies strictly inside the single nonempty span of the clamped degree-two Bernstein knot vector. Apply [F3] to each fixed-coordinate control-net slice first in $\xi$, then in $\eta$. Each insertion preserves the entire homogeneous geometry and positive weights, so the final patch is exactly $F(\xi,\eta)=(\xi,\eta)$. The resulting degree-two univariate knot vectors have a simple interior knot; [F2] gives $C^1$ continuity in both coordinate directions. This is the stated k-refinement, and no general p/k geometry-preservation claim is needed.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R$ be open and let
$a:\Omega\to\mathbb R^n$, $c:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$.
The scalar first-order equation

$$u_t(x,t)+a(x,t)\cdot\nabla_x u(x,t)+c(x,t)u(x,t)=f(x,t)$$

is a **linear transport equation**.

Fix $(x_0,t_0)\in\Omega$. A **characteristic through $(x_0,t_0)$** is a
solution $X(\cdot)$ of the ODE

$$X'(s)=a(X(s),s),\qquad X(t_0)=x_0,$$

on an interval containing $t_0$. The corresponding space-time curve is
$s\mapsto (X(s),s)$. If these initial-value problems have unique solutions for
varying initial data, write $X(s;t_0,x_0)$ for the solution through
$(x_0,t_0)$. The resulting maps $x_0\mapsto X(s;t_0,x_0)$, on the domains
where they are defined, form the **characteristic flow** of the transport
field. Without uniqueness there are characteristics, but no single-valued
characteristic flow.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

derivations.claim: Periodicity and continuity on the compact cylinder $K\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]$ give finite bounds $M_K:=\sup\|b\|_2$ and $L:=\sup\|D_xb\|$ there. The same bounds hold on all spatial translates. By [F5] each time slice is globally $L$-Lipschitz in $x$. Since $[0,T]\subset\operatorname{int}K$, choose $\delta>0$ small enough that every radius-$\delta$ time interval centered in $[0,T]$ lies in $K$, $\delta(M_K+1)\le1$, and $\delta(L+1)<1$. On each corresponding unit-radius state cylinder, [F2] therefore gives a unique local solution through its center.

Partition the finite interval between $s$ and any $t\in[0,T]$ into finitely many subintervals of length at most $\delta$. Apply [F2] successively at each endpoint, using the preceding endpoint value as the next initial state. The resulting curves agree on their shared endpoints and have the same derivative $b(r,X(r))$ there, so they concatenate to a solution on $[0,T]$. Repeated local uniqueness from [F2] proves uniqueness on the concatenated interval. This is a finite construction and selects no family of local solutions over an infinite index set.

For the constructed solution on $[0,T]$, [F3] and [F4] give $\|X(t;s,x)-x\|_2\le\int_{\min(s,t)}^{\max(s,t)}\|b(r,X(r))\|_2\,dr\le M_T|t-s|$. Thus its graph lies in the stated compact tube. For a period vector $\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell$, the curve $X(t;s,x+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell)-\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell$ solves the same IVP as $X(t;s,x)$ by periodicity of $b$; uniqueness gives periodic equivariance.

A **smooth hybrid ODE system** on a finite horizon $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$ and positive integer state dimension $d\ge1$, consists of a finite mode set $M$, an open state-time domain $D_m\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ and a $C^1$ vector field $f_m:D_m\to\mathbb R^d$ for each $m\in M$, a finite set of directed transitions $(m,n)$, and for each transition a $C^1$ scalar guard $g_{mn}:D_m\to\mathbb R$, a declared crossing orientation $\sigma_{mn}\in\{-1,+1\}$, and a $C^1$ reset map $R_{mn}:U_{mn}\to\mathbb R^d$ on an open neighborhood $U_{mn}\subseteq D_m$ of the guard zero set, satisfying $(t,R_{mn}(t,x))\in D_n$ for every $(t,x)\in U_{mn}$. Here $C^1$ has the meaning in [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. In mode $m$, a trajectory is a solution of the first-order initial-value problem $y'=f_m(t,y)$ in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. It follows that mode only until the selected event time.

An **event time** for transition $(m,n)$ is a time $\tau$ at which $g_{mn}(\tau,y(\tau))=0$ and the guard crosses in its declared direction, meaning $\sigma_{mn}\frac{d}{dt}g_{mn}(t,y(t))|_{t=\tau}>0$. It is **transverse** with margin $\nu>0$ on a bracket when $\sigma_{mn}\frac{d}{dt}g_{mn}(t,y(t))\ge\nu$ throughout that bracket. At an event, the state changes from $y(\tau^-)$ to $R_{mn}(\tau,y(\tau^-))$ and the mode changes from $m$ to $n$. A **deterministic event-priority rule** is a fixed total order on the finite outgoing transition set of each mode; if several enabled guards vanish at exactly the same first time, the least transition in that order is selected.

A hybrid trajectory has a **finite separated event list** on $[0,T]$ when it has finitely many event times $0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_N<T$ and some $\delta>0$ with $\tau_{j+1}-\tau_j\ge\delta$ for each adjacent pair. The definition does not assert that a solution exists, that an event is detected, or that the event list is finite. Those are separate hypotheses or conclusions.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is

Let $d\ge1$, let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_d>0$, and let $N_1,\ldots,N_d\ge1$ be integers. The periodic rectangular box is
$$\mathbb T^d_{\ell}:=\mathbb R^d/(\ell_1\mathbb Z\times\cdots\times\ell_d\mathbb Z).$$
Set $h_j:=\ell_j/N_j$. Its uniform tensor grid has nodes $x_{\boldsymbol i}=(i_1h_1,\ldots,i_dh_d)$, indexed by $0\le i_j<N_j$, with indices understood modulo $N_j$.

For node data $V_{\boldsymbol i}$ and a lift $x\in\mathbb R^d$ of a point on the torus, define
$$q_j:=\left\lfloor x_j/h_j\right\rfloor,\qquad \theta_j:=x_j/h_j-q_j\in[0,1),$$
and for $\boldsymbol\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d$ define
$$w_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}(x):=\prod_{j=1}^d\theta_j^{\epsilon_j}(1-\theta_j)^{1-\epsilon_j}.$$
The tensor-product multilinear interpolant is
$$\mathcal I_hV(x):=\sum_{\boldsymbol\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d}w_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}(x)V_{([q_1+\epsilon_1]_{N_1},\ldots,[q_d+\epsilon_d]_{N_d})},$$
where $[k]_N$ is the residue in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. The formula is unchanged when a period $\ell_j$ is added to $x_j$, so it defines an interpolant on $\mathbb T^d_{\ell}$. If $N_j=1$, the two corner indices in that coordinate coincide; the formula still gives the same node value.

For a continuous periodic function $v$, $\mathcal I_hv$ means the interpolant of its grid samples. Put $h:=\max_jh_j$.

derivations.claim: Each factor $\theta_j$ and $1-\theta_j$ is nonnegative, so every $w_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}(x)\ge0$. Summing over all binary vectors factorizes as $\sum_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}w_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}(x)=\prod_{j=1}^d((1-\theta_j)+\theta_j)=1$. Thus $\mathcal I_hV(x)$ is a convex combination of its corner data, even when wrapping makes two corner indices coincide.

If $V_{\boldsymbol i}\ge0$ at every node, each summand in the interpolant is nonnegative, so its value is nonnegative; the same convex-combination identity bounds it by the minimum and maximum corner data.

At each $x$, [F1] and the triangle inequality give $|\mathcal I_hV(x)-\mathcal I_hW(x)|\le\sum_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}w_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}(x)|V_{\boldsymbol i(\boldsymbol\epsilon)}-W_{\boldsymbol i(\boldsymbol\epsilon)}|\le\|V-W\|_{\ell^\infty}\sum_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}w_{\boldsymbol\epsilon}(x)=\|V-W\|_{\ell^\infty}$. Taking the supremum over $x$ proves the stated contraction; no estimate in this argument uses the displacement size.

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\ell_j>0$, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$. Suppose $b:J\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is $C^1$ and periodic in $x_j$ with period $\ell_j$ for every $j$. Choose a compact interval $K\subset J$ with $[0,T]\subset\operatorname{int}K$, and put $M_K:=\sup_{K\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$. For every $s\in[0,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, there is a unique solution $X(\cdot;s,x)$ of
$$X'(t)=b(t,X(t)),\qquad X(s;s,x)=x,$$
on the whole interval $[0,T]$. The lifted flow is periodic-equivariant:
$$X(t;s,x+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell)=X(t;s,x)+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell\qquad(\boldsymbol k\in\mathbb Z^d),$$
where $\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell=(k_1\ell_1,\ldots,k_d\ell_d)$. If $M_T:=\sup_{[0,T]\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$, then
$$\|X(t;s,x)-x\|_2\le M_T|t-s|\qquad(t\in[0,T]).$$
Thus each characteristic stays in a compact tube $[0,T]\times\overline B(x,M_TT+1)$.

Let $a$ be $C^1$ on an open neighborhood of the graph of a characteristic
$X(\cdot;\xi_0)$ solving

$$X'(t)=a(X(t),t),\qquad X(t_0;\xi_0)=\xi_0,$$

on a compact interval $I$ containing $t_0$. Then, after shrinking to a
neighborhood $U_0$ of $\xi_0$, every initial point $\xi\in U_0$ determines a
characteristic $X(\cdot;\xi)$ on the same interval $I$, the map
$(t,\xi)\mapsto X(t;\xi)$ is continuous on $I\times U_0$, and for each
$t\in I$ the map $\xi\mapsto X(t;\xi)$ is $C^1$. Its Jacobian matrix
$Y(t,\xi)=D_\xi X(t;\xi)$ satisfies

$$Y'(t,\xi)=D_xa(X(t,\xi),t)\,Y(t,\xi),\qquad Y(t_0,\xi)=I_n.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For every $n\ge1$ and every real matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$,
$$A\text{ is invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\det(A)\ne0.$$

For each fixed $n\ge1$, the function $\det:M_n(\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R$ is evaluation of the polynomial
$$P_n:=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}x_{\sigma(i),i}$$
in the $n^2$ commuting variables $x_{ri}$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

derivations.claim: By [F1], both the forward flow $\Phi_{t,s}$ and the reverse-time flow $\Phi_{s,t}$ are defined. Uniqueness of the ODE implies that following the same characteristic first from $s$ to $t$ and then backward to $s$ returns the initial point; likewise in the opposite order. Thus $\Phi_{s,t}\circ\Phi_{t,s}=\mathrm{id}$ and $\Phi_{t,s}\circ\Phi_{s,t}=\mathrm{id}$. By [F2] both maps are $C^1$, so $\Phi_{t,s}$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism.
Applying [F3] to $\Phi_{s,t}\circ\Phi_{t,s}=\mathrm{id}$ gives $D\Phi_{s,t}(\Phi_{t,s}(x))D\Phi_{t,s}(x)=I_d$. Hence $D\Phi_{t,s}(x)$ is invertible, and [F4] gives $\det D\Phi_{t,s}(x)\ne0$.

For fixed $s,x$, the function $r\mapsto\det D\Phi_{r,s}(x)$ is continuous by [F2] and [F5], and equals $1$ at $r=s$. It never vanishes by step 2.1. If it were negative at some $r$, [F6] on the interval between $s$ and $r$ would force a zero, a contradiction. Therefore it is positive at every $r$, including the chosen $t$.

1. If $B<M$, return `budget-exhausted` before changing the input data.
2. For $n=0,\ldots,M-1$ and each arrival node $x_{\boldsymbol i}$, compute the explicit backward Euler foot lift

   Reduce each coordinate modulo its period when evaluating the periodic interpolant.

Suppose $b:J\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is $C^1$ and periodic in $x_j$ with period $\ell_j$ for every $j$. Choose a compact interval $K\subset J$ with $[0,T]\subset\operatorname{int}K$, and put $M_K:=\sup_{K\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$. For every $s\in[0,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, there is a unique solution $X(\cdot;s,x)$ of
$$X'(t)=b(t,X(t)),\qquad X(s;s,x)=x,$$
on the whole interval $[0,T]$. The lifted flow is periodic-equivariant:
$$X(t;s,x+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell)=X(t;s,x)+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell\qquad(\boldsymbol k\in\mathbb Z^d),$$
where $\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell=(k_1\ell_1,\ldots,k_d\ell_d)$. If $M_T:=\sup_{[0,T]\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$, then
$$\|X(t;s,x)-x\|_2\le M_T|t-s|\qquad(t\in[0,T]).$$
Thus each characteristic stays in a compact tube $[0,T]\times\overline B(x,M_TT+1)$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-periodic-c1-velocity-has-global-characteristic-flow]], fix $s,t\in[0,T]$ and let $\Phi_{t,s}(x):=X(t;s,x)$ on the periodic lift $\mathbb R^d$. Then $\Phi_{t,s}$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with inverse $\Phi_{s,t}$, and
$$\det D_x\Phi_{t,s}(x)>0\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\ell_j>0$, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$. Suppose $b:J\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is $C^1$ and periodic in $x_j$ with period $\ell_j$ for every $j$. Choose a compact interval $K\subset J$ with $[0,T]\subset\operatorname{int}K$, and put $M_K:=\sup_{K\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$. For every $s\in[0,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, there is a unique solution $X(\cdot;s,x)$ of
$$X'(t)=b(t,X(t)),\qquad X(s;s,x)=x,$$
on the whole interval $[0,T]$. The lifted flow is periodic-equivariant:
$$X(t;s,x+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell)=X(t;s,x)+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell\qquad(\boldsymbol k\in\mathbb Z^d),$$
where $\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell=(k_1\ell_1,\ldots,k_d\ell_d)$. If $M_T:=\sup_{[0,T]\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$, then

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $E \subseteq U$ is Lebesgue measurable, then $T(E)$ is
Lebesgue measurable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $N \subseteq U$ is Lebesgue null, then $T(N)$ is
Lebesgue null.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Put $\Lambda=\prod_j\ell_j\mathbb Z$ and $\widehat A_i=\bigcup_{k\in\Lambda}(A_i+k)$. By [F2] and [F4] this countable periodic lift is measurable, and $E_i:=\Phi^{-1}(\widehat A_i)$ is measurable by [F1] and [F2]. Hence $D_i=E_i\cap\Omega$ is measurable. Equivariance makes $E_i$ periodic and makes the torus preimage independent of representatives.

If $|D_i|=0$, [F3] and [F4] make $\bigcup_{k\in\Lambda}(D_i+k)$ null. Every point of $E_i$ outside $H$ lies in one open tile, so periodicity gives $E_i\subseteq H\cup\bigcup_{k\in\Lambda}(D_i+k)$. By [F4] and [F5], $E_i$ is null; [F3] then makes $\Phi(E_i)=\widehat A_i$ null. This contradicts $A_i\cap\Omega\subseteq\widehat A_i$ and $|A_i|>0$ by [F6]. Thus $|D_i|>0$. Also $D_i\subseteq\Omega$, so [F5] and [F6] give $|D_i|\le\prod_j\ell_j<\infty$.

Bijectivity on the torus preserves exact unions and disjointness. For a partition only up to null sets, lift its omitted set and pairwise overlaps periodically; these are null by [F3]–[F5]. Their inverse images are null by [F1] and [F3], so restricting to $\Omega$ gives a departure partition up to null sets. Finally, a half-open tensor cell with nonempty interior is measurable with positive volume by [F5], so it is included in the result.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R$ be open and let
$a:\Omega\to\mathbb R^n$, $c:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$.
The scalar first-order equation

$$u_t(x,t)+a(x,t)\cdot\nabla_x u(x,t)+c(x,t)u(x,t)=f(x,t)$$

is a **linear transport equation**.

Fix $(x_0,t_0)\in\Omega$. A **characteristic through $(x_0,t_0)$** is a
solution $X(\cdot)$ of the ODE

$$X'(s)=a(X(s),s),\qquad X(t_0)=x_0,$$

on an interval containing $t_0$. The corresponding space-time curve is
$s\mapsto (X(s),s)$. If these initial-value problems have unique solutions for
varying initial data, write $X(s;t_0,x_0)$ for the solution through
$(x_0,t_0)$. The resulting maps $x_0\mapsto X(s;t_0,x_0)$, on the domains
where they are defined, form the **characteristic flow** of the transport
field. Without uniqueness there are characteristics, but no single-valued
characteristic flow.

Inputs are a periodic grid from [[def-semilagrangian-periodic-grid-and-interpolant]], a finite horizon $T>0$, a positive integer $M$ of time steps, a periodic $C^1$ velocity $b$, periodic initial data $u_0$, node values $U^0_{\boldsymbol i}=u_0(x_{\boldsymbol i})$, and a nonnegative integer step budget $B$. Write $\Delta t=T/M$ and $t_n=n\Delta t$. The output is either `success` with $U^0,\ldots,U^M$, or `budget-exhausted` with no partial final state.

1. If $B<M$, return `budget-exhausted` before changing the input data.
2. For $n=0,\ldots,M-1$ and each arrival node $x_{\boldsymbol i}$, compute the explicit backward Euler foot lift
   $$\widetilde x_{\boldsymbol i}^{\,n}:=x_{\boldsymbol i}-\Delta t\,b(t_{n+1},x_{\boldsymbol i}).$$
   Reduce each coordinate modulo its period when evaluating the periodic interpolant.
3. Set
   $$U_{\boldsymbol i}^{n+1}:=\mathcal I_h U^n(\widetilde x_{\boldsymbol i}^{\,n}).$$
4. After the $M$ finite updates, return `success` with all node arrays.

The finite step budget counts time updates. Every update evaluates one foot per grid node and a finite sum of $2^d$ interpolation terms. The procedure imposes no bound on $\|b\|\Delta t/h$; the floor-and-fraction convention in the interpolation definition applies even when a foot crosses many grid cells.

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\ell_j>0$, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$. Suppose $b:J\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is $C^1$ and periodic in $x_j$ with period $\ell_j$ for every $j$. Choose a compact interval $K\subset J$ with $[0,T]\subset\operatorname{int}K$, and put $M_K:=\sup_{K\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$. For every $s\in[0,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, there is a unique solution $X(\cdot;s,x)$ of
$$X'(t)=b(t,X(t)),\qquad X(s;s,x)=x,$$
on the whole interval $[0,T]$. The lifted flow is periodic-equivariant:
$$X(t;s,x+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell)=X(t;s,x)+\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell\qquad(\boldsymbol k\in\mathbb Z^d),$$
where $\boldsymbol k\boldsymbol\ell=(k_1\ell_1,\ldots,k_d\ell_d)$. If $M_T:=\sup_{[0,T]\times[0,\ell_1]\times\cdots\times[0,\ell_d]}\|b\|_2$, then
$$\|X(t;s,x)-x\|_2\le M_T|t-s|\qquad(t\in[0,T]).$$
Thus each characteristic stays in a compact tube $[0,T]\times\overline B(x,M_TT+1)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $b\in C^1([0,T]\times\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$ be periodic in space, and set
$$M:=\sup\|b\|_2,\qquad L_x:=\sup\|D_xb\|,\qquad L_t:=\sup\|\partial_tb\|_2,$$
where the suprema are over one full periodic time-space cylinder. For $0\le t_n<t_{n+1}\le T$, $\Delta t=t_{n+1}-t_n$, and an arrival lift $x$, let $X(t_n;t_{n+1},x)$ be the exact backward characteristic foot. The explicit Euler foot $x-\Delta t\,b(t_{n+1},x)$ satisfies
$$\bigl\|X(t_n;t_{n+1},x)-(x-\Delta t\,b(t_{n+1},x))\bigr\|_2\le\frac12(L_xM+L_t)(\Delta t)^2.$$
The estimate is local for every positive $\Delta t$; it requires no relation between displacement and grid width.

For the periodic tensor interpolant of [[def-semilagrangian-periodic-grid-and-interpolant]], every value is a convex combination of the $2^d$ corner data. Consequently nonnegative data remain nonnegative, the interpolant lies between the minimum and maximum corner values, and for any node arrays $V,W$,
$$\|\mathcal I_hV-\mathcal I_hW\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb T^d_\ell)}\le\|V-W\|_{\ell^\infty}.$$
These conclusions hold at every foot, with no displacement-to-cell-size restriction.

Let $u\in C^2(\mathbb T^d_\ell)$ and let $h_j$ be the coordinate mesh widths in [[def-semilagrangian-periodic-grid-and-interpolant]]. Then
$$\|\mathcal I_hu-u\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb T^d_\ell)}\le\frac18\sum_{j=1}^dh_j^2\|\partial_{jj}u\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb T^d_\ell)}.$$
The estimate includes grid nodes and periodic cell endpoints.

derivations.claim: Along the exact characteristic $X(\cdot;t_{n+1},x_{\boldsymbol i})$, [F1] gives $X'=b(t,X)$. The chain rule [F4] therefore gives $\frac{d}{dt}u(X(t),t)=u_t+b\cdot\nabla u=0$. Hence $u(x_{\boldsymbol i},t_{n+1})=u(X(t_n;t_{n+1},x_{\boldsymbol i}),t_n)$.

Add and subtract $(\mathcal J_hu^n)(\widetilde x_{\boldsymbol i}^{\,n})$ and $u(\widetilde x_{\boldsymbol i}^{\,n},t_n)$. The operator bound gives a first difference at most $\Lambda E_n$; the interpolation defect contributes at most $C_Ih^{r+1}$; and the spatial Lipschitz bound for $u$ plus the foot error contributes at most $L_uC_F(\Delta t)^{q+1}$. Since $\Lambda\ge1$, this is at most $\delta_h+\Lambda E_n$. Taking the maximum over nodes yields $E_{n+1}\le\Lambda E_n+\delta_h$.

Induction on $n$ in the recurrence gives $E_n\le\Lambda^nE_0+\delta_h\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\Lambda^k$: at $n=0$ the sum is empty, and the recurrence multiplies the preceding finite sum by $\Lambda$ and adds its next term. Taking $n=N$ proves the first bound.

If $\Lambda=1$, the sum in step 3.1 is $N=T/\Delta t$, so substituting the definition of $\delta_h$ gives the second bound. The default Euler and tensor multilinear branch has the stated local constants by [F5]–[F7]. Therefore the displayed sufficient refinement conditions make both error terms and the initial error tend to zero. No step uses $\|b\|\Delta t/h\le1$; consistency follows from the two explicit defect terms rather than a classical advective CFL condition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be convex. Then $f$ is locally Lipschitz on $U$: every $a\in U$ has a neighbourhood on which one finite constant bounds $|f(x)-f(y)|$ by $\|x-y\|_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

derivations.claim: If $U$ is empty, all assertions are vacuous. If $n=0$ and $U$ is nonempty, then $U=\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$, $\partial f(0)=\{0\}$, and $f$ is differentiable with derivative zero. Every localization ball is $\{0\}$; set $H(0)=f(0)$. Then $F^*(0)=-f(0)$ and $g(0)=0$, so the remaining assertions hold directly. Henceforth assume $n\ge1$. At $x\in U$, the directional slope $d(v)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}[f(x+tv)-f(x)]/t$ exists and is finite: convexity makes these quotients monotone in $t$, while local Lipschitz continuity bounds them. Positive homogeneity follows by rescaling $t$. Convexity applied at the midpoint of $x+2tv$ and $x+2tw$ gives $d(v+w)\le d(v)+d(w)$. By [A1] and [F2], Hahn-Banach extends zero on $\{0\}$ to a linear functional $p\cdot v\le d(v)$. The chord inequality gives $d(y-x)\le f(y)-f(x)$, so $p\in\partial f(x)$.

If $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz on a ball and $x$ lies in its concentric half ball, testing the support inequality at $x\pm te$ for every unit vector $e$ and sufficiently small $t>0$ gives $|p\cdot e|\le L$. Thus all its subgradients have norm at most $L$. On compact subsets this follows by a finite cover. If $x_j\to x$, $p_j\to p$, and $p_j\in\partial f(x_j)$, pass to the limit in every support inequality using continuity of $f$; hence $p\in\partial f(x)$. Differentiability gives $\partial f(x)=\{Df(x)\}$ by testing both signs of small increments. Conversely, if $\partial f(x)=\{p\}$, the local bound and [F3] imply that every choice $q_y\in\partial f(y)$ converges to $p$ as $y\to x$: otherwise [A1] selects a contrary sequence with a convergent subsequence whose limit is a different limiting subgradient. The inequalities $p\cdot h\le f(x+h)-f(x)\le q_{x+h}\cdot h$ then prove differentiability with derivative $p$.

Set $H(z)=\sup\{f(x)+p\cdot(z-x):x\in K,\ p\in\partial f(x)\}$. The local bounds from step 2.1 make slopes and intercepts uniformly bounded. Thus this supremum is finite, convex and globally Lipschitz; support inequalities give $H\le f$ on $U$, and the terms at $z=x\in K$ give equality on $K$. This definition uses all supports, without choosing one for each point.

Since $H$ is globally Lipschitz, $F(z)-p\cdot z\to+\infty$ as $|z|\to\infty$. Continuity and compact extreme values give a minimizer. The identity that $F-|\cdot|^2/2$ is convex implies strict convexity of $F$ and uniqueness of this minimizer, denoted $g(p)$. Its minimizing property is exactly $p\in\partial F(g(p))$. More precisely, $p\in\partial F(x)$ iff $p-x\in\partial H(x)$. One direction is immediate. For the other, test the support inequality for $F$ at $x+t(y-x)$, divide by $t>0$, and let $t\downarrow0$; convexity makes the directional slope of $H$ at $x$ no larger than the full chord slope $H(y)-H(x)$, yielding $H(y)-H(x)\ge(p-x)\cdot(y-x)$. Monotonicity of supports of $H$, obtained by adding their two defining inequalities, therefore gives $(p-q)\cdot(g(p)-g(q))\ge |g(p)-g(q)|^2$. Hence $g$ is one-Lipschitz.

The supremum defining $F^*(p)$ is finite and attained uniquely at $g(p)$. Evaluating the two suprema at each other's maximizers gives $0\le F^*(p+k)-F^*(p)-g(p)\cdot k\le (g(p+k)-g(p))\cdot k\le |k|^2$. This proves $DF^*=g$, whose continuity follows from its Lipschitz bound. It also proves the asserted subgradient inverse relation.

A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.
If $T:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m$ is Lipschitz and $E$ is null, then $T[E]$ is null.

every $i<n$ write $[u,v]$ for the closed rectangle and
$V(u,v) := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : u_i<x_i<v_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$ for

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]); a **closed cube** of side

$$\lambda^{\mathrm{cl}}(E) := \inf\Big\{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\operatorname{vol}[u^k,v^k] \;:\; E \subseteq \bigcup_{k}[u^k,v^k]\Big\},\qquad \lambda^{\mathrm{op}}(E) := \inf\Big\{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\prod_{i<n}(v^k_i-u^k_i) \;:\; E \subseteq \bigcup_{k}V(u^k,v^k)\Big\},$$

$$\lambda^{\mathrm{cb}}(E) := \inf\Big\{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\ell_k^{\,n} \;:\; E \subseteq \bigcup_{k}\prod_{i<n}[c^k_i,\,c^k_i+\ell_k]\Big\},$$

$\prod_i[-k,-k+2k]$. Then

$$\lambda^{\mathrm{cl}}(E) \;=\; \lambda^{\mathrm{op}}(E) \;=\; \lambda^{\mathrm{cb}}(E) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(E).$$

derivations.claim: Shrink to a ball $\overline B_R\subseteq U$ on which $g(x)=f(x)+\lambda|x|^2/2$ is convex and $f(0)>f(x)$ for $0<|x|\le R$. By [F1], $f$ is continuous. Given $0<r<R/4$, the compact annulus $r\le|x|\le R$ has a strictly positive gap $c=f(0)-\max f$. Fix $0<\eta\le\delta$ with $\eta R<c/2$. For every $|q|\le\eta$, all global maximizers of $f(x)+q\cdot x$ on $\overline B_R$ lie in $B_r$, since their value at zero is $f(0)$ and annulus values are at most $f(0)-c+\eta R$. Their maximizing pairs form a closed subset of the compact product $\overline B_R\times\overline B_\eta$, so their set $K$ is compact and lies in $B_r$.

At a maximizing pair $(x,q)$, $f(z)\le f(x)-q\cdot(z-x)$ on $\overline B_R$. Put $v=-q+\lambda x$. Expanding the quadratic gives $g(x+h)\le g(x)+v\cdot h+\lambda|h|^2/2$. Convexity gives the reverse support $g(z)\ge g(x)+v\cdot(z-x)$: for $h=z-x$ and small $t>0$, convexity on the segment from $x-th$ to $z$ yields $g(z)-g(x)\ge(g(x)-g(x-th))/t\ge v\cdot h-\lambda t|h|^2/2$, and let $t\downarrow0$. Thus $f$ is differentiable at $x$, $p_x=Df(x)=-q$, and $f(x)+p_x\cdot(z-x)-\lambda|z-x|^2/2\le f(z)\le f(x)+p_x\cdot(z-x)$ for $z\in\overline B_R$; in particular the slope at each $x\in K$ is unique.

For distinct $x,y\in K$, set $d=y-x$. The support bounds in step 2.1 and $f(y)\le f(x)+p_x\cdot d$ give $(p_x-p_y)\cdot h\le\lambda|d+h|^2/2$ whenever $y+h\in B_R$. If $p_x\ne p_y$, take $h=|d|(p_x-p_y)/|p_x-p_y|$, which is admissible since $|y+h|<3r<R$. Then $|p_x-p_y||d|\le2\lambda|d|^2$. Equal slopes need no estimate, so $x\mapsto p_x$ is $2\lambda$-Lipschitz on $K$.

For each coordinate set $P_j(z)=\inf_{x\in K}(p_x^j+2\lambda|z-x|)$. Compactness makes this finite; the triangle inequality makes it $2\lambda$-Lipschitz, and step 3.1 gives $P_j(x)=p_x^j$ on $K$. Hence $P=(P_1,\ldots,P_m)$ is $2\lambda\sqrt m$-Lipschitz and, since each $|q|\le\eta$ has a maximizer in $K$ with $P(x)=-q$, $P(K)\supseteq\overline B_\eta$. If $K$ were null, [F2] would make $P(K)$ null, contradicting the positive outer measure of $B_\eta$; thus $K$ has positive outer measure. If $\lambda=0$, this same construction makes $P$ constant while its image contains $\overline B_\eta$, a contradiction, so no strict-maximum case is missed. Countable Choice required by [F2] follows from [A1].

Since $K$ has positive outer measure, it cannot be contained in the given null set $N$. Choose $x\in K\setminus N$ and its maximizing slope $q$; then $|x|<r$ and $|q|\le\eta\le\delta$. This proves both conclusions.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.
Every subset of a null subset of $\mathbb R^m$ is null. Assuming countable choice, every countable union of null subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ is null.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(P, \le)$ be a
nonempty poset in which **every chain has an upper bound**. Then $P$ has a
maximal element ([[def-maximal-element]]).

Note the hypothesis asks only for an upper bound, not a least upper bound, and
the conclusion asserts only that a maximal element exists, never that a greatest
one does.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), let $c$ be a nonzero real and write
$cE := \{\, cx : x \in E \,\}$ for $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, where
$(cx)_i := cx_i$. Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\,\lambda_n^*(E)$ for every subset $E$, the
   product being defined in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|c|^{\,n} > 0$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $cE$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

At $c = -1$ the map is reflection in the origin and $|c|^{\,n} = 1$, so it
preserves outer measure, measurability and measure. The value $c = 0$ is
excluded because $0E$ is $\{0\}$ or $\varnothing$ and carries no information
about $E$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the
plane of pairs of naturals is countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

The bijection is exhibited, not merely asserted to exist. Define $2^m$ by
recursion on $m$ ([[thm-recursion]]) by $2^0 = 1$ and $2^{\sigma(m)} = 2^m + 2^m$,
and set

$$J(m,n) = 2^m \cdot \sigma(n + n), \qquad \text{that is} \qquad J(m,n) = 2^m(2n+1).$$

Then $J$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ onto
$\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, and $\sigma$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ onto
$\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, so $\sigma^{-1} \circ J$ is a bijection
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. What makes $J$ bijective is the
decomposition of a nonzero natural into a power of two times an odd number,
existence and uniqueness both.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order ([[def-nat-order]]); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
([[lem-nat-add-commutative]]) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]). Its **partial sums** are the unique sequence $(s_n)$ in $[0,+\infty]$ satisfying

$$s_0=0,\qquad s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n.$$

To apply [[thm-recursion]] with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$. Recursion gives a unique state sequence; induction makes its first coordinate $n$, and its second coordinates are exactly the unique $(s_n)$ satisfying the displayed recurrence. Addition of two nonnegative extended reals is always defined, including when either is $+\infty$. The sequence $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing, and its **nonnegative extended sum** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n\in[0,+\infty],$$

whose existence follows from completeness of the extended real line ([[lem-extended-reals-complete]]). More generally, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$\sum_{k\ge m}a_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{m+j}.$$

Finite sums use the same recursion: $\sum_{k<n}a_k=s_n$, so the empty sum at $n=0$ is $0$. A double sum such as $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}$ means that the inner nonnegative extended sum is formed first and the resulting nonnegative extended sequence is then summed.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ be its partial sums and let
$S = \{\, s_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ be the range of $(s_n)$ ([[def-series]]).
Then:

1. $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $s_n \ge 0$ for every
   $n$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** $S$ is bounded above
   ([[def-bounded-set]]), and in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; \sup S ,$$
   so in particular $s_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ for every $n$;
3. if $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]) and $\sum a_k$ diverges.

This is the theorem that makes the nonnegative theory work: for terms of one
sign, convergence is a boundedness question and no candidate limit is ever
needed. Every comparison test on this page is an application of it.

derivations.claim: Fix $R\ge1$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$. For each $p\in C\cap B(0,R)$, differentiability gives a nonempty set of radii $0<r_p<1$ such that $|g(p+h)-g(p)-Dg(p)h|\le\varepsilon|h|$ whenever $|h|\le5r_p$. By [A1], choose one such radius for each $p$. Divide this ball family into dyadic radius classes $[2^{-j-1},2^{-j})$, largest first. In each class use [F3] on the set of subfamilies disjoint from all previously selected balls; the union of any chain is an upper bound, so a maximal disjoint subfamily exists. The union of selected subfamilies is disjoint. It is countable by [F8]: enumerate $\mathbb Q^n$ and assign to each ball the first rational point it contains; disjoint balls get distinct points. If a rejected ball has radius $r$ and meets a selected ball of radius $R_s>r/2$, then $r<2R_s$ and every point of the rejected ball is within $2r+R_s<5R_s$ of the selected center. Thus the fivefold dilates of a countable disjoint subfamily $B(p_i,r_i)$ cover $C\cap B(0,R)$.

Put $v_n=\lambda(B(0,1))$. For any selected ball $B(p_i,r_i)$, the image $g(B(p_i,5r_i))$ lies within distance $5\varepsilon r_i$ of $g(p_i)+Dg(p_i)B(0,5r_i)$. This affine image lies in a disk of radius $5Lr_i$ centered at $g(p_i)$ in an affine subspace of dimension $q\le n-1$. In orthonormal coordinates centered at $g(p_i)$ and adapted to that subspace, the tube lies in a box with $q$ side lengths at most $10Lr_i+10\varepsilon r_i$ and $n-q$ side lengths $10\varepsilon r_i$. Subdivide each side into intervals of length at most $\varepsilon r_i$. The number of resulting boxes is at most $c_n(1+L/\varepsilon)^q$; each is contained in an axis-parallel cube of side at most $c_n\varepsilon r_i$. Since $q\le n-1$ and $\varepsilon<1$, their total cube volume is at most $C_n\varepsilon(L+1)^{n-1}r_i^n$ for a finite constant $C_n\ge1$ depending only on $n$. This constructs actual null covers without a rotation-invariance theorem or an area formula.

The selected balls lie in $B(0,R+1)$ and are pairwise disjoint. By [F5], each has measure $v_n r_i^n$, and the containing ball has measure $v_n(R+1)^n$. Countable additivity and monotonicity [F6] give $\sum_i r_i^n\le(R+1)^n$, using $v_n>0$. The Countable Choice hypotheses of [F5] and [F6] follow from [A1].

The fivefold balls in step 1.1 cover $C\cap B(0,R)$, and step 1.2 supplies a finite cube cover of each corresponding image with total volume at most $C_n\varepsilon(L+1)^{n-1}r_i^n$. By [A1], choose one such finite cover for each selected ball. Index these cubes by $(i,j)$; [F7] enumerates the resulting subset of $\mathbb N^2$. Every finite partial sum is at most $C_n\varepsilon(L+1)^{n-1}\sum_i r_i^n\le C_n\varepsilon(L+1)^{n-1}(R+1)^n$ by [F9] and step 2.1. For any cover budget $\delta>0$, take $\varepsilon=\min\{1/2,\delta/[C_n(L+1)^{n-1}(R+1)^n]\}>0$; the bound is then at most $\delta$. By [F1], $g(C\cap B(0,R))$ is null.

The set $C$ is the union of $C\cap B(0,R)$ over integers $R\ge1$. Each image in this countable union is null by step 3.1; [F2] therefore gives that $g(C)$ is null. Its Countable Choice hypothesis follows from [A1].
